# Patrologia Latina, volume 108 — English translation

# Patrologia Latina, vol. 108

## Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal Library

A complete, uniform, comprehensive, economical library of all the holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reissue of all the surviving monuments of Catholic tradition from the first twelve centuries of the Church, based on the most accurate editions, compared with one another and with several manuscript codices, and corrected with the utmost care; continuously illustrated with dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged with all works discovered after the extensive editions produced during the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume and each author of importance; embellished with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of every page and indicating the subject matter below; augmented with works both doubtful and apocryphal, and with others possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; and enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, by which it may readily be learned which Fathers commented on the individual texts of the biblical books, and in what places in their works they did so.

An exceptionally accurate edition, easily to be preferred to all others if one considers the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the reprinted works, the extremely convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the entire work, the low price, and above all this collection—single, methodical, and chronological—which for the first time in our library has gathered together six hundred fragments and little works previously scattered here and there, drawn from works relating to every age, place, language, and form.

## Second Series

In which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III, edited by J.-P. Migne, editor of the universal library of the clergy, or of the complete courses in each branch of ecclesiastical learning.

The Patrology has been printed in two editions: one Latin, the other Greek-Latin. The Latin edition is sold in 1,200 French francs; the Greek-Latin in 1,300. The purely Latin edition embraces all authors, both Western and Eastern; the latter, however, are presented in it only in Latin translation.

[Col. 0009C]

## (Year 834.) Four Books of Commentaries on Exodus by Blessed Rabanus Maurus, Abbot of Fulda and Archbishop of Mainz

### Preface to Freculphus, Bishop of Lisieux

[Col. 0009A] Among the other Scriptures contained in the Pentateuch of the Law, the Book of Exodus deservedly stands out. In it, nearly all the sacraments by which the present Church is instituted, nourished, and governed are expressed figuratively. For there, through the bodily departure of the children of Israel from earthly Egypt, our departure from spiritual Egypt is signified; there, through the crossing of the Red Sea and the drowning of Pharaoh and the Egyptians, the mystery of baptism and the destruction of spiritual enemies are prefigured. There, the sacrifice of the typological lamb and the celebration of Passover disclose the Passion of the true Lamb and our redemption. There, manna from heaven and drink from the rock are given to the needy people, so that it may teach us to desire heavenly bread and the drink of life. There, commandments and judgments are delivered to the people of God on the mountain, so that we may learn to submit to heavenly disciplines. There, the construction of the tabernacle and its vessels, together with worship and sacrifices, is commanded, so that the marvelous adornment of the holy Church and the rite of spiritual sacrifices may be intimated. There, the ingredients of spiritual anointing and fragrant incense are prepared, so that the sanctification of the Holy Spirit and the mystery of sacred prayers may be commended to us.

We find all these things explained in this way not only in the sayings of the Fathers who preceded us, but also most certainly through the tradition and writings of the apostles themselves. For Paul, writing to the Corinthians, says:

> I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, that all our fathers were under the cloud, and all passed through the sea; and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea; and all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink. For they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them; but the rock was Christ. (1 Corinthians 10)

Thus also the evangelist John, when describing the Lord’s Passion in his Gospel, reached the place where the legs of those hanging on the cross were to be broken. Drawing his testimony from this, he says:

> When they came to Jesus, and saw that he was already dead, they did not break his legs; but one of the soldiers opened his side with a lance, and immediately blood and water came out.

And shortly afterward:

> These things happened, he says, so that Scripture might be fulfilled: “You shall not break a bone of him,” and so forth.

Therefore, dearest Freculphus, chief among bishops, it seems to me that meditation on this book is necessary, since it contains such great force of heavenly sacraments and mysteries that we are instructed fully in the worship of Christ not only by evangelical traditions but also by those of the Law.

I have done what you ordered me in your letter: I have gathered into one volume, from the sayings of the holy Fathers everywhere, explanations of the individual sentences; and wherever I was less able to find explanations among the ancients, I inserted my own expositions according to the likeness of their meanings, insofar as divine grace granted me the ability.

I therefore beg you, if you judge the completed work worthy, to apply it to your own benefit and that of others; and, in accordance with the rule of charity, to share with your neighbors the good which you recognize as having been divinely bestowed upon you. For the rest, I also ask you to assist my weakness with your prayers, beseeching the heavenly Majesty that in the storm of this present sea he may govern me by his grace in such a way that, in this present life, he may grant me to be useful in his service and, in the life to come, blessed through the aid of his generosity.

# The Commentaries on Exodus Begin

## Book One

### Chapter One  
#### On Israel’s Entry into Egypt and the Oppression with Which the Egyptians Afflicted the Israelites

“These are the names of the sons of Israel who entered Egypt with Jacob. Each entered with his household: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Zebulun and Benjamin, Dan and Naphtali, Gad and Asher” (Exodus 1).

What, then, do these eleven sons of Jacob who entered Egypt with him—or rather twelve, when Joseph is added—signify, except the order of the apostles? Concerning them the Savior himself says:

> As the Father sent me, so I also sent you into the world. (John 6)

That Egypt here figuratively signifies the world is confirmed by many prophetic utterances. Moreover, the seventy-five persons who are described as having entered Egypt together with the patriarch mentioned above typologically designate the order of preachers, because the Savior had sent seventy disciples to preach the word of God throughout the whole world, so that they might teach the Law’s Pentateuch to be observed spiritually.

Alternatively, these seventy persons who entered Egypt are mystically understood according to the number of remission: namely, so that remission of sins might be granted to this age, which was represented by Egypt, after so many sins and sacrileges.

Joseph, however, was in Egypt. Concerning our Redeemer John wrote:

> He was in the world, and the world was made through him, and the world did not know him. (John 1)

After Joseph had died, together with all his brothers and that entire generation, the children of Israel increased, and, as though sprouting, multiplied; they became exceedingly strong and filled the land. (From Isidore.)

After Joseph and his brothers died, the children of Israel increased and became exceedingly strong. So also our true Joseph, after tasting death for all, through which he destroyed the devil who held the power of death, caused the people of the faithful to multiply. For unless, as he himself says, the grain of wheat had fallen into the earth and died, it would certainly not have produced such abundant fruit throughout the whole earth (John 12).

Morally, likewise, if Joseph dies in you—that is, if you receive the mortification of Christ in your body and put your member to death with respect to sin—then the children of Israel, that is, good and spiritual thoughts, multiply in you. For each day that vices die in you, the number of virtues increases; and you will multiply in the land, namely in your own flesh, through which virtues are exercised.

Meanwhile a new king arose over Egypt who did not know Joseph, and he said to his people:

> Behold, the people of the children of Israel are numerous and stronger than we are. Come, let us wisely oppress them, lest they multiply.

In the Chronicles of Eusebius and Jerome we read that after Jacob’s entry into Egypt, Amosis was the first to reign, for twenty-five years; after him Nebron, for thirteen years; then Amenophis, for twenty-one years; after him Mephres, for twelve years; after him Mispharmuthosis, for twenty-six years; after him Tithimoris, for nine years; then Amonaphis, for thirty-one years. Under him Amram fathered Moses when he was seventy years old.

So he appointed taskmasters over them, to afflict them with burdens; and they built the store-cities of Pharaoh, Pithom and Raamses. But the more they oppressed them, the more they multiplied and grew. The Egyptians hated the children of Israel and afflicted them, mocking and envying them, and making their lives bitter with hard labor in clay and bricks, and with every kind of service by which they were burdened in the work of the land.

Mystically, however, we must first see who this king is who knew Joseph, and who he is who did not know him.

As long, then, as our king—that is, the spirit of our mind—retains the memory of Joseph, namely Christ—for this king in Egypt is remembered, that is, our spirit in our flesh, which is not improperly called Egypt—the children of Israel, namely rational thoughts or virtues, are not afflicted. They are not consumed by clay and bricks, that is, by earthly cares; nor is straw, that is, frivolous and irrational activity, mixed with them; nor are the males killed, that is, works already brought to perfection.

But if our mind does not know Christ, then the wisdom of the flesh, which is hostile to God, succeeds to the kingdom. It addresses its own people, namely bodily desires; and, summoning the leaders of vices, it takes counsel against Israel about how it may be oppressed by the evils mentioned above.

You, therefore, who hear these things: if, after the gift of baptism, you perform the works of this world, know that another king has arisen in you who does not know Joseph.

The king of Egypt who does not know Joseph may also be understood as the devil, who said in his heart, “There is no God.” He speaks, in a manner of speaking, to his own nation, namely the apostate angels:

> Behold, the men of Israel have increased and become exceedingly strong against us.

These are those who can see God with the mind. And how did the devil learn that the nation of Israel is strong, unless because he has often engaged it in combat and has often been defeated? But what he fears—that war may at some time arise against them, that they may join with their adversaries, and that, after defeating them, they may depart from their land—shows that he had foreknowledge of the things predicted by the patriarchs and prophets concerning the coming of Christ. He therefore knows that war threatens him, since he perceived that the one was coming who would confidently triumph over him and his satellites.

Pharaoh therefore teaches the Israelites to build cities for him: Pithom, which is interpreted as “mouth of defection” or “mouth of the abyss,” and Raamses, which is interpreted as “holding malice” or “the agitation of the moth.”

See what sort of cities Pharaoh commanded to be built for him. Pharaoh is interpreted as “the destroyer” and is the true enemy of the people of God. He commands the building of a city called “the contempt of the mouth” or “the mouth of the abyss,” when he persuades people to speak falsehood and prepares a pit of destruction for those who obey him and act deceitfully with their tongues.

The other city, called “the agitation of the moth” or “holding malice,” is built wherever the malicious one himself injects malice into a perverse mind and introduces the plague of greed. For who are those who follow him except those who gather riches through fraud and store up their treasures on earth, where moth destroys and thieves break in and steal?

If, therefore, we give thanks for our substance to the giver of all good things, show mercy from it to our needy neighbors, and join ourselves in obedience to the preachers of truth, the spiritual Pharaoh will say of us:

> The children of Israel have greatly prevailed against us, and they are joining themselves to our enemies.

For we will prevail over him and, against his will, depart from his land. We will put off the old person with his deeds, and, leaving behind the image of our earthly parent, we will put on the image of the heavenly Redeemer.

For this is what chiefly troubles the devil, and through his teachers and officials—namely heretics, philosophers, and false Christians—he strives to afflict us with burdens of crimes, lest we depart free from the slavery of sins and vices.

What is said—“The more they oppressed them, the more they multiplied and grew”—signifies that the more fiercely the devil persecutes Christians and increases temptations and torments, the more the elect grow in the increase of their merits and multiply in the recompense of rewards.

The text continues:

### Chapter Two  
#### On the Hebrew Midwives and Pharaoh’s Command Concerning the Killing of the Males

The king of Egypt said to the Hebrew midwives, one of whom was called Shiphrah and the other Puah, commanding them:

> When you act as midwives for the Hebrew women, and the time of delivery has come, if it is a male, kill him; if it is a female, preserve her. (Exodus 1)

Some have said that these midwives—Puah, which may be rendered among us as “reddish” or “modest,” and Shiphrah, which is interpreted as “her bird,” “beauty,” or “pleasing”—represent the form of rational education, which is subtle, beautiful, and modest, and suitable and useful for both spiritual and bodily disciplines.

Midwives are in a certain sense intermediaries, and they foster both males and females. Thus this common education in rational knowledge reaches almost all faculties: it instructs all and nurtures all. Whether one wishes to contemplate heavenly things or to administer worldly affairs, it is readily available to its possessors.

If someone possesses a manly spirit in this education and wishes to seek heavenly things, through such instruction he will approach the understanding of divine matters more readily. But if someone wishes to conduct secular business through it, he will find it exceedingly useful for that purpose. (From Isidore.)

Pharaoh also orders the males to be killed and the females to live. So too the devil, lest the strength of faith prevail, strives to ensure that, once the virtues have been killed, the vices remain. He hastens to kill in a person the strongest and manliest thoughts of the soul, by which we seize heavenly and divine things—that is, reason, prudence, innocence, and faith—and to bring to life in him what appears feminine, weak, fragile, and prone to vices: ambition, drunkenness, lust, anger, cruelty, fury, and other things like them, which are represented under the figure of females.

The midwives, however, feared God and did not act according to the command of the king of Egypt; rather, they preserved the males. Having summoned them to himself, the king said:

> Why did you intend to do this, preserving the boys?

They replied:

> The Hebrew women are not like the Egyptian women. They themselves possess the skill of midwifery, and before we come to them, they give birth.

Therefore God dealt well with the midwives, and the people increased and became exceedingly strong. And because the midwives feared God, he built houses for them.

(From Augustine.)

It is commonly asked whether such lies were approved by divine authority, since it is written that God dealt well with the midwives; but whether he forgave the lie on account of their mercy, or whether he judged the lie itself worthy of reward, is uncertain.

The midwives were doing one thing when they gave life to the infants and another when they lied to Pharaoh. In giving life to them, they performed an act of mercy; but by that lie they acted for their own sake, so that Pharaoh might not harm them. This may pertain not to praise but to pardon.

Nor does it seem to me that authority for lying is thereby offered. Rather, it is made clear by the recompense what the guilt of lying deserves. The reward for their kindness, which is in eternal life, could be granted, while for the guilt of the lie an earthly recompense was assigned instead: in the life which they sought to preserve by lying, they received the good things they had done, but they did not possess the further reward of their merit which they might have expected.

Pharaoh then commanded all his people, saying:

> Whatever male is born, throw it into the river; whatever is female, preserve it.

See what the prince of this world commanded his people: namely, that they seize our infants and throw them into the river. Consider, therefore, O human being, what awaits you after you have been born—or rather, reborn.

It is precisely what is read in the Gospel, where the baptism of the Lord is mentioned:

> Jesus, it says, when he had come up from baptism, was led by the Spirit into the wilderness, to be tempted by the devil. (Matthew 4)

This, then, awaits you: that, cleansed by saving waters and made a new person, you endure the snares and temptations of the devil and his ministers. Their desire is to submerge in the waters whatever male and distinguished work you produce.

Of these waters the Prophet says:

> For the waters have come up to my soul. (Psalm 68)

What counsel, then, shall we give you except that, like a Levite, you hide for three months the handsome male infant when he is born, lest the enemy seize and kill him?

For example, if you give alms, since this is a work of God, you beget a male child. But if you do it in such a way that you become known to human beings, your almsgiving is seized by the Egyptians and submerged in spiritual waters.

See, therefore, that you do not forget the Lord’s command, which instructs you:

> When you give alms, let your left hand not know what your right hand is doing, so that your almsgiving may be in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you. (Matthew 6)

The same must be done with fasting, prayer, and the other spiritual practices, lest we lose the fruit of our labor and the Lord say of us:

> Truly, truly, I say to you, they have received their reward. (Matthew 6)

### Chapter Three  
#### On the Birth of Moses and His Exposure in the River

After these things a man from the house of Levi went out and took a wife from his own lineage. She conceived and bore a son; and seeing that he was beautiful, she hid him for three months.

When she could no longer conceal him, she took a basket of reeds, smeared it with bitumen and pitch, placed the infant inside it, and set him among the rushes on the bank of the river. His sister stood at a distance, watching what would happen.

Then the daughter of Pharaoh came down to bathe in the river, and her maidens walked along the bank of the channel. When she saw the basket among the papyrus, she sent one of her attendants. The attendant brought it and opened it; and, seeing the little child crying inside, she took pity on him and said:

> He is one of the infants of the Hebrews.

The child’s sister said to her:

> Do you want me to go and call a Hebrew woman who can nurse the infant for you?

She answered:

> Go.

The girl went and called the child’s mother. Pharaoh’s daughter said to her:

> Take this child and nurse him for me; I will give you your wages.

The woman took him and nursed the child. When he had grown, she brought him to Pharaoh’s daughter, who adopted him as a son and called his name Moses, saying:

> Because I drew him out of the water. (Exodus 2)

Josephus records the matter as follows.

Fearing that Amram might be seized and perish in the king’s anger together with the child, and that he might thwart God’s providence, he decided instead to provide for the child’s safety in this way and revealed this plan for concealing him.

They prepared a round vessel woven from willow, about the size of a small boat, large enough for the infant to lie in comfortably; then they smeared it with bitumen. The nature of bitumen is such that, when applied to willow vessels, it prevents water from entering.

They therefore placed the infant inside it, set it beside the river, and entrusted his safety to God.

Thermothe was the king’s daughter. While she was playing near the bank of the river, she saw the vessel being carried along by the current and ordered that the little boat be brought to her.

When those assigned to this task came with the boat, she saw the infant and was exceedingly delighted because of his size and appearance. God had shown such care for Moses that he caused him to be considered worthy of food and care even by those who, because of his birth, had decreed the destruction of the entire Hebrew race.

Thermothe, the king’s daughter, ordered a woman to be brought who would give the infant the breast. But the infant did not approach her breasts; rather, he avoided them, and he did the same with many women.

Mary, attending what was happening—not, it seems, as someone merely standing among the others [wording uncertain]—said:

> In vain, O queen, do you call these women to nourish the infant, since none of them is related to him. But if you order one of the Hebrew women to be brought, I think that, as one of his own people, he will be able to accept her breast.

Since she was thought to have spoken well, the queen ordered her to go and bring someone who could nurse him.

Having received this authority, she returned, bringing the mother, whom no one recognized. The infant, in a certain sense gladly, approached her breast; and, at the queen’s request, the child’s nourishment was entrusted to her with every care.

In accordance with what happened, the child was given his name because he had been saved from the river. For the Egyptians call water [term absent or uncertain in the supplied text], and a person saved [term absent or uncertain in the supplied text]; combining these two, they gave him the name Moses, that is, “saved from the water.”

The parents of Moses, whose faith and works were adorned by the natural law, are the patriarchs, from whom Moses himself and those who received the Law in its written form were born.

Moses is therefore hidden for three months, born in his parents’ house, since the old Law lay hidden for three periods among the Jewish people before the coming of Christ: under the judges, under the kings, and under the priests. Then he came who gave the Law and entrusted it to the nations to be observed spiritually throughout the breadth of the world.

Pharaoh’s daughter is the Church gathered from the nations. Although she now rejoices in a true parent, namely God the Father, previously, when she served idols, she followed another father. Of this the divine voice in the psalm says to her:

> Hear, O daughter, and see; incline your ear, forget your people and your father’s house. (Psalm 44)

She therefore left her father’s house and came to be baptized, to be washed from the sins she had contracted in her father’s house. Coming to baptism, she received the Law. At that time the Law was within a little basket of reeds, woven from many branches or from papyrus and smeared with pitch and bitumen, because it was enclosed in the cheap and earthly traditions of the Jews and was, so to speak, fouled by them. Then the Church tore it away from the marshy and muddy places of carnal understanding and brought it within the halls of true wisdom and the royal chambers.

It spent its infancy among its own people, namely among those who did not know how to understand it spiritually, so that it became the food of little children and nursing infants. But when it came to the Church and was rightly understood through her, it became stronger. (From Isidore.)

What, then, does it mean that the woman who nursed the child received payment from Pharaoh’s daughter? It means that the Synagogue, among whom the Law was born and nourished, received this payment from the Church: seeing that those who had believed from the nations had turned so completely toward the Lord that they utterly rejected and no longer worshiped idols, the Synagogue itself was thereby taught to be ashamed of worshiping idols.

Alternatively, Moses is found exposed on the bank of the river when the Lord, whose type Moses bore, is found by believers at the river of the laver and the water of baptism.

The infant cried because Christ mourned the sins of the old person whom he had assumed. For this reason also, when he raised Lazarus, he wept, lamenting the unbelief of the Jews.

Pharaoh’s daughter, descending to the river’s laver, gathered up the infant. The Church from the nations, desiring the sanctification of the saving laver, receives Christ, expelled by the Synagogue, his carnal mother, like an infant, because he then appeared small when he was seen in human form.

She found Moses enclosed in a little vessel made from many wild branches. The Church finds Christ hidden in the hearts of the saints, who, woven together into his unity and into the members of many brothers, have all become one body in Christ; receiving him with religious observance, they protect him.

### Chapter Four  
#### How Moses Killed the Egyptian Who Was Quarreling with an Israelite, and His Flight into the Land of Midian

In those days, after Moses had grown up, he went out to his brothers and saw their affliction. He saw an Egyptian striking one of his Hebrew brothers.

When he had looked around this way and that and saw that no one was present, he struck down the Egyptian and hid him in the sand.

Going out the next day, he saw two Hebrews quarreling. He said to the one who was doing the wrong:

> Why are you striking your neighbor?

He replied:

> Who appointed you ruler and judge over us? Do you intend to kill me as you killed the Egyptian yesterday?

Moses was afraid and said:

> How has this matter become known? (Exodus 2)

(From Augustine.)

It is asked whether this revealed a praiseworthy disposition in him, because he committed this sin, just as the earth is sometimes praised for its fertility in producing even useless plants before it produces useful seeds; or whether the deed itself should be justified altogether.

The latter does not seem so, because he did not yet possess any legitimate authority, whether divinely granted or established by human society. Nevertheless, as Stephen says in the Acts of the Apostles, he thought that his brothers would understand that God was granting them salvation through him (Acts 7). By this testimony Moses appears to have been already divinely admonished, so that he could dare what Scripture leaves unmentioned at that point.

(From Isidore.)

Moses therefore freed his foreign brother from the Egyptian who was inflicting injury. Unable to tolerate the brother’s being left unavenged, he defended him and killed the Egyptian.

The obvious meaning of this figure is that the devil, who injures us in this pilgrimage, is killed by the Lord Christ, who defends us.

As for the fact that he buried the slain man in the sand, it clearly shows that the presence of his corpse already lies hidden in those who possess no stable foundation. For this reason the Lord builds the Church upon a rock, and compares those who hear his word and do it to a prudent man who builds his house upon rock, lest it fall and collapse under temptations.

But those who hear and do not act he compares to a foolish man building upon sand; when his house is tested, it produces a great ruin.

In the fact that Moses wished to reconcile the two Hebrews who were quarreling, he bears, as some think, a type of Christ. Desiring to reconcile the discord of the two peoples in himself, Christ joined and united them in himself, as the cornerstone.

But the one who inflicted injury on his neighbor and dishonorably rejected the reconciler represents the Jewish people, who received Christ’s preaching—the word of reconciliation—with ingratitude.

He was always the true enemy of the believing people, as it is read in the Gospel: when the man born blind had been enlightened by Christ, they cursed him, saying:

> You are his disciple; but we are disciples of Moses. (John 9)

And elsewhere:

> We do not want this man to reign over us. (Matthew 27)

### Chapter Five  
#### On Moses and His Wife, and How the Lord Appeared to Him in a Flame of Fire in the Middle of a Bush While He Was Feeding the Sheep
Pharaoh heard this speech and sought to kill Moses. But Moses, fleeing from his presence, stayed in the land of Midian and sat beside a well. Now the priest of Midian had seven daughters, who came to draw water; and when they had filled the troughs, they wanted to water their father’s flocks. Shepherds came up and drove them away. Moses rose, defended the girls, and watered their sheep. When they returned to Raguel their father, he said to them, “Why have you come back more quickly than usual?” They replied, “An Egyptian rescued us from the shepherds’ hands; moreover, he drew water for us and gave the sheep drink.” But he said, “Where is he? [Col. 0018A] Why did you leave the man? Call him, so that he may eat bread.” Moses therefore swore that he would dwell with him, and so forth.

Moses’ flight, by which he departed from Egypt and migrated to the land of Midian, signifies that our Redeemer, leaving the city of the Jewish people, migrated among the apostles in order to summon the Gentiles. There he first encountered opposition, and afterward devoted obedience—a meaning well expressed by the names themselves. For Egypt, which is interpreted as “darkness,” signifies the darkness of unbelieving minds. Midian, however, means “contradiction” or “answer,” indicating the Gentiles who at first contradicted the preaching of the Gospel. Hence Simeon is read in the Gospel to have said to Mary concerning Christ: “This one,” he says, “is destined for the fall and resurrection of many in Israel, and for a sign that will be contradicted” [Col. 0018B] (Luke 2). Later they answered him with pious devotion and good works.

Moses therefore sat beside the well to which the seven daughters of the priest of Midian had come to draw water, so that they might water their father’s flocks. Shepherds opposed them, but Moses, defending the girls, watered their sheep. Thus our Redeemer, presiding over knowledge of the law or worldly wisdom, bestows spiritual teaching upon the seven churches coming to him from the house of the devil, by which they can refresh the perceptions of their hearts and give the drink of life to those obedient to him. He also restrained false shepherds—that is, philosophers or priests of idols—from harming them.

The fact that Raguel was astonished that his daughters had returned more quickly than usual signifies the devil’s amazement at the swift conversion of the Gentiles to faith in Christ [Col. 0018C], because they were more ready for obedience to the Gospel, for which they were even prepared to die, than they had ever been to persist in his worship or in idolatry.

Moses therefore took one of Raguel’s seven daughters—Raguel is interpreted as “the pasture of God” or “God is his friend”—whose name was Sephora, interpreted as “beauty” or “pleasing.” She bore him a son whom he named Gersan, interpreted as “stranger.” She also bore another, who was called Eliezer, interpreted as “my God is my helper.” This occurred when our Redeemer joined to himself, in a spiritual marriage, the sevenfold Church from the Gentile people. Although she is sevenfold through the gift of the Holy Spirit, she is nevertheless one in the Catholic faith. Of her he says in the Song of Songs: “My dove is one, chosen of her mother” (Song 6).

She bore one son [Col. 0018D] who is called “stranger,” and another who is called “God’s help.” These names aptly suit the Christian people, summoned from both circumcision and uncircumcision. For those are strangers who, while dwelling in this world, now journey as exiles from their heavenly homeland; nevertheless, they will never lack God’s help.

After a long time the king of Egypt died, and the children of Israel, groaning because of their labors, cried out. Their cry arising from their labors ascended to God, and he heard their groaning and remembered the covenant he had made with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. The Lord therefore looked upon the children of Israel and took notice of them.

After Moses had taken a wife in the land of Midian, the king of Egypt died, because after Christ had summoned the Gentiles throughout the whole world to faith through the Gospel, the dominion of the devil—which had previously held the world captive through idolatry—was destroyed and diminished [Col. 0019A].

And the children of Israel, groaning because of their labors, cried out, when believers grieve over the corruption of the flesh and send tears of repentance from the contagion of sin to the pious ears of the Creator. Of them it is rightly said that their cry arising from their labors ascended to God, and that he heard their groaning and remembered the covenant he had made with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob: for “the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are open to their prayers,” and he delivered them from all their tribulations.

Now Moses was pasturing the sheep of Jethro, his kinsman, the priest of Midian. When he had driven the flock into the interior of the desert, he came to the mountain of God, Horeb [Col. 0019B]. The Lord appeared to him in a flame of fire from the midst of a bush, and he saw that the bush was burning yet was not consumed (Exodus 3).

Moses, mingling with the Egyptians, was, as it were, awake; therefore, while he was situated in Egypt, he did not hear the voice of the Lord. But after he had killed the Egyptian and fled into the desert, there, while he spent forty years, he fell asleep, as it were, away from the tumult of restless earthly desires. For this reason he was deemed worthy to perceive the divine voice: through heavenly grace, the more he grew sluggish toward external things that might be desired, the more truly he kept watch for understanding things within.

For when the mind is lulled by external activities, then it penetrates the words of God more truthfully, when it takes care to admit him and flees the tumult of worldly affairs. A person is poorly awake, however, when the heat of worldly business disturbs him with excessive agitation [Col. 0019C].

Indeed, while the multitude of earthly thoughts roars, it closes the ears of the heart; and in the secret chamber of the mind, the less the noise of agitated cares is restrained, the less the voice of the presiding Judge is heard. A person cannot adequately attend to both things while divided between them. While he desires to be instructed inwardly yet remains entangled outwardly, from the very source where he desires outward hearing, he becomes inwardly deaf.

The Lord appeared to Moses in the bush, sending him to a people whom he knew would become wicked. There was a flame in the bush—that is, among the thorns—and the bush was not burned. The thorns are the sins of the Jews; the flame in the bush is the word of God. The fact, therefore, that the law was given to them was a flame in the bush; and the fact that their sins were not consumed when the law was given is shown by the bush not being burned beneath the fire [Col. 0019D]. (From Isidore.)

Others understand the burning but unconsumed bush to mean that the Church is inflamed by persecutions, yet does not perish because the Lord speaks within her. The fact that the Lord is read to have appeared to Moses in that same bush shows that he appears with believers nowhere but in the Church, because no one can be worthy to stand or see God except one who has laid aside all earthly and mortal vices. This was signified by the sandals removed from Moses.

Hence what follows: “When the Lord saw that he was proceeding to look, he called him from the midst of the bush and said, ‘Moses, Moses.’ He answered, ‘Here I am.’ And he said, ‘Do not come nearer. Remove the sandal from your feet’ [Col. 0020A], ‘for the place on which you stand is holy ground.’”

What Moses is ordered to do by removing his sandals also has another figurative meaning. It was the custom of the ancients that, if a bride wished to repudiate her bridegroom, his sandal was removed, and this was a sign of repudiation. Therefore Moses is ordered to remove his sandals, lest he approach as a bridegroom wearing sandals to the Church signified by the bush. This was reserved for Christ, who was the true bridegroom, concerning whom John says: “I am not worthy to loosen the strap of his sandal” (Matthew 3)—just as was said of Joshua and Moses.

The Hebrews, however, say that God appeared to Moses in a bush and not in another kind of tree so that the Jews might not perhaps carve an idol in that same tree. For God has always removed the opportunity for idolatry.

The text continues: “I am,” he said, “the God of your father, [Col. 0020B] the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.” From this it is shown that the preceding deeds of good parents often assist the merits of their children, because the love they earned from God through faith and good works overflows upon their children.

Thus the Israelites often deserved to be delivered from hardships because of the merits of their fathers. In the Book of Kings, or Chronicles, it is written that the Lord said to Solomon when he sinned: “Because you have had this in your heart and have not kept my covenant and my statutes, which I commanded you, but have broken them, I will tear your kingdom apart and give it to your servant. Nevertheless, I will not do this in your days, for the sake of David your father. I will tear it from the hand of your son; yet I will not take away the whole kingdom, but will give one tribe to your son, for the sake of David my servant, and Jerusalem, which I chose” (2 Chronicles 9) [Col. 0020C].

Likewise, to Hezekiah, the leader of my people: “Thus says the Lord, the God of your father David: I have heard your prayer and seen your tear; behold, I have healed you,” and so forth (2 Kings 20).

## CHAPTER VI. Concerning the Lord’s command that Moses descend into Egypt to Pharaoh, so that he might release the Israelites from the land of Egypt; and concerning the sign of the staff changed into a serpent and of the leprous hand

Moses hid his face. For he did not dare to look directly at God. The Lord said to him: “I have seen the affliction of my people in Egypt and have heard its cry, because of the harshness of those who are set over the work. And knowing its suffering, I have come down to free it from the hands of the Egyptians and to lead it out of that land [Col. 0020D] into a good and spacious land, into a land flowing with milk and honey, to the regions of the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites. The cry of the children of Israel has therefore come to me, and I have seen their affliction by which they are oppressed by the Egyptians. But come, I will send you to Pharaoh, so that you may lead my people, the children of Israel, out of Egypt” (Exodus 3).

When the land of Canaan is promised to the Israelite people, we must consider that the prosperity of the present life is sometimes given in order to summon people to a better life, and sometimes in order to condemn them more fully forever. This is why the land of Canaan is promised to the Israelite people: so that they might one day be summoned to hope for eternal things.

For that inexperienced people would not have believed the promises of God concerning something distant if they had not also received something nearby from the one who made the promise. Therefore, so that they might be strengthened more certainly in faith concerning eternal things, they are drawn not only by hope toward realities, but also by realities toward hope, as the Psalmist clearly testifies, saying: “He gave them the regions of the nations, and they possessed the labor of peoples, so that they might keep his statutes and seek his law” (Psalm 104) [Col. 0021A].

For something concerning the present life also had to be promised to an inexperienced people, so that they might be established more firmly in the future. If the carnal people had not received small things, they would not have believed great ones. Therefore almighty God, by granting earthly things, urges them toward heavenly things, so that, receiving what they could see, they might learn to hope for what they could not see; and so that they might become more steadfast concerning invisible things, insofar as visible promises supported them toward certainty of hope. (From Augustine.)

As for the statement that he would bring them into a land flowing with milk and honey, the question is whether we should understand spiritually a land flowing with milk and honey, since literally this was not the land given to the people of Israel; or whether this is simply a manner of speaking, referring to the praise of its abundance and sweetness.

Moses said to God: “Behold, I shall go to the children of Israel and say to them, ‘The God of your fathers has sent me to you.’ If they say to me, ‘What is his name?’ what shall I say to them?” God said to Moses: “‘I am who I am.’ Thus you shall say to the children of Israel: ‘The Lord God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has sent me to you.’ This is my name forever.”

Blessed Jerome, writing to Marcella about the names of God, places the name *Escher eheie*—which is read in Exodus as “He who is has sent me”—in sixth place [Col. 0021C]. For God alone, who has no beginning, truly possesses the name of essence, and this name was conveyed to holy Moses through an angel. When Moses asked what the name of the one who commanded him to go to the people and free them from Egypt was, he answered: “I am who I am,” and, “You shall say to the children of Israel: ‘He who is has sent me to you.’”

In comparison with the one who truly is, because he is immutable, those things that have been made and are changeable are, as it were, nonexistent. For what is said to have been is no longer; and what is said to be is not yet. God alone simply is: he does not know having been, and he does not know being about to be. The Father alone, with the Son and the Holy Spirit, truly is. [Col. 0021D] Compared with his essence, our being is nonbeing. Hence in conversation we say: “God lives”—he who lives by the life of essence, which death does not possess.

“You shall go, then, you and the elders of Israel, to the king of Egypt, and you shall say to him: ‘The Lord God of the Hebrews has called us. We shall go a three days’ journey into the wilderness, so that we may sacrifice to the Lord our God.’ But I know that the king of Egypt will not let you go unless compelled by a mighty hand. For I will stretch out my hand and strike Egypt with all my wonders that I shall perform in its midst, and after this he will let you go.”

The fact that the Lord sent Moses to Pharaoh to chastise his obstinacy and finally to bring about his death signifies that the Lord would send the law to destroy the devil’s dominion [Col. 0022A] and to draw the human race away from his worship. And just as it was not Moses but the Lord who freed the people from the servitude of the Egyptians, so it was not the law but Christ, through his passion and resurrection, who freed the world from the snare of death. (From Gregory.)

Moses was sent to summon them when Pharaoh had already been trained to oppress them through harsh labors. Thus, while one called to the minds of the Israelites shamefully clinging to Egypt, as it were, another dragged them while calling, and another drove them while raging; and the people, fixed shamefully in servitude, were moved either by the attraction of good things or by the pressure of evil ones.

This occurs daily, when the wicked are permitted to rage against the elect because of the heavenly rewards that are preached, so that if we neglect to leave when summoned to the land of promise, we may at least be driven out by the pressures of persecution [Col. 0022B]. Thus Egypt—that is, the present life—which has oppressed us while flattering us, may assist us by pressing us; and while crushing the yoke of servitude by its soothing, may show us the way of freedom by tormenting us.

This, then, is why the righteous are permitted to be afflicted by the unjust: so that, while they hear of future goods that they desire, they may also suffer present evils that they dread; and so that, while love summons them, suffering may drive them toward an easier departure.

[Col. 0022C] “I will give this people favor in the sight of the Egyptians; and when you go out, you shall not go out empty-handed. But every woman shall ask her neighbor and her houseguest for silver and gold vessels and clothing. You shall place these upon your sons and daughters, and you shall strip Egypt.” (From Augustine.)

The command by which the Lord ordered the Hebrews through Moses to receive from the Egyptians gold and silver vessels and clothing, adding, “and you shall plunder them,” cannot be judged unjust. It was God’s command, concerning which one ought not to pass judgment but to obey it. For he knows how justly he gave the command; it belongs to a servant to carry out obediently what he commanded.

Moses answered: “They will not believe me or listen to my voice, but will say, ‘The Lord did not appear to you.’” He therefore said to him: “What is that which you hold in your hand?” He answered, “A staff.” He said, “Throw it on the ground.” He threw it down, and it became a serpent, so that Moses fled from it. The Lord said, “Stretch out your hand and seize it by the tail.” He stretched out his hand and held it, and it became a staff again (Exodus 4).

Who is signified by Moses except the Jewish people, and what by the staff except the power of divinity? [Col. 0022D] What is signified by the serpent except the mortality of our Redeemer? Since death comes through the serpent, mortality is rightly signified in the serpent. Or certainly, since it is written, “Be wise as serpents” (Matthew 10), and since that supreme wisdom itself—that is, the wisdom of God—deigned to become incarnate, his mortality is rightly figured in the serpent.

Hence in the Gospel he speaks of his passion, saying: “As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up” (John 3). Moses therefore held the staff because, before the Redeemer’s coming, the Jewish people were fixed upon divine power. But he threw the staff onto the ground because that same people, through the patriarchs and prophets, announced that God would become incarnate [Col. 0023A].

The staff is changed into a serpent because our Redeemer, remaining God in himself, became mortal among human beings. But when Moses saw the serpent, he was terrified and fled, because the Jewish people, when they saw the Redeemer of the human race as mortal, were afraid to believe that he was God.

He is ordered to seize the serpent by the tail because that faithless people, which now refuses to believe, will gather itself to faith in the final part of the Lord’s body—that is, at a later time in the holy Church, namely at the end of the world—so that it will seize the serpent by the tail. For the one whom it had previously despised as mortal, it will confess as its Redeemer in the final period of the Church.

But the serpent immediately returns to a staff, because as soon as the Jewish people believes in our Redeemer, our same Redeemer will appear for judgment in the power of his divinity [Col. 0023B], so that the serpent too may be a staff. For the one who was despised on earth as a human being will be seen, coming from heaven, as God above the angels.

(From Isidore.) Alternatively: the staff is Christ in death, and yet Moses was terrified and fled. What does Moses’ fleeing from that serpent mean except what is read as having occurred in the Gospel: Christ died, the apostles were terrified, and they withdrew from the hope in which they had stood?

But what does the command, “Seize it by the tail,” mean except “the things that come afterward”? “You shall see my back,” this signified. First the serpent was made; but when its tail was seized, it became a staff, because first he was killed, and afterward, when everything had been accomplished, he returned by rising to what he had been. Once death had been destroyed through the restoration of life, nothing serpentine appeared in him [Col. 0023C].

There is also in the serpent’s tail the end of the age, because the mortality of the Church, which is his body, rolls onward through slippery times: some depart and others come through death. Death was sown, as it were, through the serpent; but at the final end, like the tail of the age, we return to the hand of God. Once seized, we will be separated, and when the last enemy, death, has been destroyed, we who rise again will be the staff of the kingdom in God’s right hand.

Again the Lord said: “Put your hand into your bosom.” When he had put it into his bosom, he brought it out leprous, like snow. “Put your hand back into your bosom,” he said. He put it back and brought it out again, and it was like the rest of his flesh. “If they do not believe you,” he said, “or listen to the message of the first sign, they will believe the message of the second sign. But if they do not believe even these two signs, nor listen to your voice [Col. 0023D], take water from the river and pour it on the dry ground; and whatever you draw from the river will become blood.”

The whiteness of the skin in leprosy is disease, not brightness. For God’s own inheritance—that is, his people—sent away from him became unclean, as is written concerning it: “Why do you turn your face away, and your right hand from the midst of your bosom?” (Psalm 73). But what else does he say? “Bring it back into your bosom.” He brought it back, and it returned to its former color.

So now the Jewish people is alienated from the bosom of God and remains unclean outside; but he brings it back, and it returns to its former color, when it recognizes the Lord Savior. For now partial blindness has happened to Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles enters, and thus all Israel will be saved [Col. 0024A].

Then the waters poured by Moses onto the earth are changed into blood—that is, the peoples into the blood and faith of Christ. For, as the Apocalypse says, “The waters that you saw are peoples and nations” (Revelation 17).

## CHAPTER VII. Concerning Moses’ return to Egypt and the angel’s encounter with him on the way

[Col. 0024A] Moses said: “I beg you, Lord, I am not eloquent from yesterday or the day before yesterday; and ever since you spoke to your servant, I have been slower and more hesitant of tongue” (Exodus 4).

(From Augustine.) What Moses said to the Lord—“I beg you, Lord, I am not eloquent from yesterday, nor from the day before yesterday, nor since you began to speak to your servant”—can be understood [Col. 0024B] as expressing his belief that, by God’s will, he could suddenly become eloquent, when he says, “nor since you began to speak to your servant.” It is as though he were showing that it could have happened that, although he had not been eloquent before yesterday or the day before yesterday, he suddenly became so from the moment the Lord began to speak with him.

The Lord said to him: “Who made the human mouth? Or who made the mute and the deaf, the seeing and the blind? Is it not I?” There are people who bring accusations against God—or rather against the Scripture of the Old Testament—because God said that he himself had made the blind and the mute. What, then, do they say about the Lord Christ, who plainly says in the Gospel: “I came so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John 9)?

Who except foolish people would believe that anything could happen to a human being in bodily defects that God did not will? Yet no one doubts that he wills everything justly.

“Go, therefore, and I will be with your mouth, and I will teach you what you shall speak.” In what the Lord says to Moses—“But now go: I will open your mouth and instruct you in what you are to say” [Col. 0024C]—it is sufficiently clear that not only the instruction of the mouth, but the opening itself, pertains to God’s will and grace. For he does not say, “Open your mouth, and I will instruct you,” but assigns both to himself: “I will open and I will instruct.”

Elsewhere he says in the psalm: “Open your mouth wide, and I will fill it” (Psalm 80). There he signifies that in a human being there is a willingness to receive what God gives to one who wills it: “Open your mouth wide” pertains to the will, and “I will fill it” to God’s grace. Here, however, he says, “I will open your mouth and instruct you.”

But Moses said: “I beg you, Lord, send whom you will send.”

The Lord was angry with Moses and said: “Is there not Aaron your brother, the Levite? I know that he is eloquent [Col. 0024D]. Behold, he himself will come out to meet you. When he sees you, he will rejoice in his heart. Speak to him and put my words in his mouth. I will be with your mouth and with his mouth, and I will show you what you must do. He himself will speak for you to the people; he will be your mouth, while you will be to him in matters pertaining to God. Take this staff also in your hand, with which you will perform the signs.”

(From Augustine.) How is God’s anger to be understood? Since he does not become angry like a human being, through irrational disturbance, this must always be retained wherever Scripture says something of this kind, so that the same things need not be said repeatedly.

Nevertheless, it is reasonably asked why, when angry, he spoke here about Moses’ brother, saying that he himself would speak to the people for Moses. It seems as though, because Moses distrusted him, he did not give him the full ability he had been going to give him, and wished to accomplish through two what could have been accomplished through one if Moses had believed [Col. 0025A].

Yet, when all the same words are considered more carefully, they do not signify that the Lord, as an act of vengeance, gave Aaron to him in anger. For he says: “Is there not Aaron your brother, the Levite? I know that he is eloquent; he himself will speak.” These words show that God was rather rebuking the one who was afraid to go, because Moses himself was less capable, even though he had a brother through whom he could say to the people whatever he wished—since Moses was weak of voice and slower of tongue, although he ought to have hoped for everything from God.

Moreover, the very things that he had promised a little earlier he repeats after becoming angry. For he had said: “I will be with your mouth, and I will teach you what you shall speak”; or, as other copies have it, “I will open your mouth and instruct you.” [Col. 0025B] Now, however, he says: “I will be with your mouth and with his mouth”; or, “I will open your mouth and his mouth and instruct you in what you must do.”

But when he added, “He himself will speak to you for the people,” it seems that the opening of the mouth was granted because Moses had said that he was slow of tongue. As for weakness of voice, the Lord did not wish to provide him with anything, but for this reason added the assistance of his brother, who could use a voice sufficient for teaching the people.

When he says, “You shall put my words in his mouth,” he shows that Moses would give them to him by speaking. For if Aaron were merely to hear them, as the people did, Moses would have put them in his ears. Further, when he says shortly afterward, “He himself will speak to you for the people,” and, “He himself will be your mouth,” “for the people” is also understood here. When he says, “He will speak to you for the people,” he sufficiently indicates primacy in Moses and ministry in Aaron [Col. 0025C].

When he says, “You will be to him in matters pertaining to God,” there is perhaps a great mystery to investigate: in these matters Moses represented the figure of an intermediary between God and Aaron, while Aaron was an intermediary between Moses and the people.

Therefore, when Moses says that he has not been eloquent from yesterday or the day before yesterday, since the Lord spoke to him, but is slow and hesitant of tongue, he shows that all human beings, in comparison with the divine word, must be considered not only ineloquent but also mute.

As long as Moses was in Egypt, he did not confess himself slow of tongue. For among the Egyptians his eloquence was incomparable. When he began to hear the voice of God, he then perceived that he was slow of tongue. But because he was progressing toward recognizing himself, he rightly heard from the Lord: “I will be with your mouth” [Col. 0025D].

## CHAPTER VIII. Concerning Moses’ return to Egypt and the angel’s encounter with him on the way

[Col. 0025D] Moses took his wife and sons and set them upon a donkey. He returned to Egypt, carrying the staff of God in his hand. The Lord said to him as he returned to Egypt: “See that you perform before Pharaoh all the wonders that I have placed in your hand. I will harden his heart, and he will not let the people go” (Exodus 4).

How, then, does the Lord say here, “I will harden his heart, and he will not let the people go,” when the Apostle speaks of him in this way: “He desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (1 Timothy 2)? The Lord is said to harden Pharaoh, not because he himself makes him hard and disobedient, but because, finding him hardened, he justly abandons him so that he may not be corrected [Col. 0026A].

“You shall say to him: ‘Thus says the Lord: Israel is my firstborn son. I said to you, “Let my son go, so that he may serve me”; but you refused to let him go. Behold, I will kill your firstborn son.’”

He calls Israel his firstborn son because, in the patriarchs, Israel was chosen first for faith in and knowledge of the one God and for receiving the law in written form. Afterward, through the Gospel, the Gentiles were to be summoned to faith in Christ.

When they were on the journey at an inn, the Lord encountered him and wanted to kill him. Immediately Sephora took a very sharp stone, circumcised the foreskin of her son, touched his feet, and said: “You are a bridegroom of blood to me.” [Col. 0026B] And he released him after she had said, “You are a bridegroom of blood to me,” because of the circumcision.

The Lord said to Aaron: “Go to meet Moses in the desert.” He went to meet him at the mountain of God and kissed him.

(From Augustine.) First it is asked whom the angel wanted to kill: Moses, because it is said, “The angel encountered him and sought to kill him.” For whom would he be understood to have encountered except the one who presented himself to the whole company of his followers, and from whom the others were led? Or did he seek to kill the child, whom his mother helped by circumcising him? On this interpretation, he would have wanted to kill the infant because he was uncircumcised, and thus to enforce the command of circumcision through the severity of punishment.

If this is so, it is initially uncertain of whom he had said, “He sought to kill him,” [Col. 0026C] because it was not known whom he meant, unless the answer is found in what follows. It is certainly a remarkable and unusual way of speaking to say first, “He encountered him and sought to kill him,” when nothing had previously been said about him.

Yet there is a similar instance in the psalm: “Its foundations are in the holy mountains; the Lord loves the gates of Zion” (Psalm 86). The psalm begins there, and nothing had been said about the one—whether male or female—whose foundations he intended by saying, “Its foundations are in the holy mountains.” But because it follows, “The Lord loves the gates of Zion,” the foundations must be understood either as the Lord’s or Zion’s; and for easier comprehension, more likely Zion’s, so that they are understood as the foundations of the city.

So here, before the infant has been named, it is said: “He encountered him and sought to kill him,” so that from what follows we may recognize of whom he had spoken. Nevertheless, if anyone wishes to understand this of Moses, there is no need to resist strongly [Col. 0026D].

Rather, if possible, let us understand what the following means: that the angel withdrew from killing either of them because the woman said, “You are a bridegroom of blood to me,” or, according to other copies, “The blood of the circumcision of the infant stood.” For it does not say that he withdrew from him because she circumcised the infant, but because the blood of the circumcision stood—not because it flowed, but because it stood, as I believe, in a great mystery.

[Col. 0027A] According to the historical sense, a Gentile mother, astonished at the novelty of the event and ignorant of the command given to Abraham concerning circumcision, could have said to Moses, “You are a bridegroom of blood to me,” as though she were saying: “The custom of your people compels me to shed the blood of my son because of circumcision, something that other peoples do not customarily do.”

According to the mystery, Sephora represents the Church from the Gentiles. With the sharpest stone—that is, the teaching of the Holy Spirit, or that rock of which the Apostle says, “The rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10)—she teaches the stripping away of the old person with his deeds, so that the Gentile people may cleanse themselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God.

The blood of circumcision then stands when what is mortal is swallowed up by life and this corruptible thing has put on incorruption. The sacrament of circumcision is then truly completed, when it is no longer permitted to sin or to endure the struggle of resisting flesh [Col. 0027B].

(From Augustine.) It was said above that Moses placed his wife and children on vehicles so that he might go with them into Egypt. Later, however, his father-in-law Jethro came to meet him with them, apparently after the people had been led out of Egypt. It may therefore be asked how both statements can be true.

It must be understood that, after the killing of Moses or the child that was to be carried out by the angel, Moses returned with the little ones. Some have thought that the angel caused this terror for the reason that the female sex should not accompany Moses as an impediment to the mystery divinely entrusted to him.

## CHAPTER IX. Concerning Moses and Aaron’s approach to Pharaoh

After this Moses and Aaron entered and said to Pharaoh [Col. 0027C]: “Thus says the Lord God of Israel: ‘Let my people go, so that they may sacrifice to me in the wilderness.’”

But he replied: “Who is the Lord, that I should listen to his voice and let Israel go? I do not know the Lord, and I will not let Israel go” (Exodus 5).

Pharaoh expresses in his speech the proud defiance of the devil, who refused to submit to God but declared himself equal to the Most High. For unless compelled by torments, he does not wish to render service to God. Hence in the Gospel, when he tempted God, he said, as though doubting his divinity: “If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become loaves of bread” (Matthew 4).

But afterward, as though beaten by him, he emits a voice of supplication, which he would never have uttered unless compelled. For it is written: “The demons cried out and said to Jesus, ‘Why have you come to torment us before the time? We know that you are the Son of God’” (Matthew 8).

When they felt the torments, they recognized the Lord whom they had refused to recognize before the blows. Pharaoh likewise said before the scourges that he did not know the Lord; but after the scourges he asks the Lord to plead for him.

The text continues: “The God of the Hebrews has called us, so that we may go a three days’ journey into the wilderness and sacrifice to the Lord our God, lest pestilence or the sword overtake us.”

It is asked how the people are told that God commanded he would lead them out of Egypt into the land of Canaan, while Pharaoh is told that they wished, by his command, to leave on a three days’ journey into the wilderness to sacrifice to their God.

It must be understood that, although God knew what he would do and foresaw that Pharaoh would not consent to release the people, what would first be said was also what would first take place if Pharaoh released them. For the fact that everything happened as the subsequent Scripture testifies was merited by the obstinacy of Pharaoh and his people [Col. 0028A].

(From Isidore.) God does not command something deceitfully when he knows that the one commanded will not do it, so that he may receive a just judgment.

Mystically, what is the three days’ journey that we must travel so that, leaving Egypt, we may reach the place where we ought to sacrifice? This way is Christ, who said: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14). We must travel this way for three days.

For whoever confesses the Lord Jesus with his mouth and believes in his heart that God raised him from the dead on the third day will be saved [Col. 0028B]. This, then, is the three-day way by which one reaches the place where sacrifice is offered to the Lord and a sacrifice of praise is rendered, as is said later.

“We will sacrifice,” they say, “the abominations of the Egyptians to the Lord our God.” For the Egyptians disdain eating sheep. But what the Egyptians abominate, the Israelites offer to God. They sacrifice to God the simplicity of conscience that the wise people of this age—that is, the citizens of Egypt—regard as foolishness. They seek to please God by that which they consider rejected and contemptible by the age and by the world, according to the Apostle who says: “God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise” (1 Corinthians 1).

## CHAPTER X. [Col. 0028C] Where Pharaoh forbids straw to be given to the Israelites; and concerning the Israelites’ complaint about the burden of their labor
The king of Egypt said to them: “Why are you, Moses and Aaron, distracting the people from their work? Go to your burdens.” And Pharaoh said: “The people of the land are numerous. You see that the multitude has increased; how much more, then, if we give them rest from their work?” On that day, therefore, he commanded the overseers of the work and the taskmasters of the people, saying: “You shall no longer give straw to the people for making bricks, as before. Let them go and gather stubble for themselves. Yet you shall impose upon them the same quota of bricks that they previously made, and you shall reduce nothing. They are idle, and for that reason they cry out, saying, ‘Let us go and sacrifice to our God.’ Let them be oppressed with work and complete it, so that they may not heed deceitful words,” and so forth.

*(From Isidore.)* From the moment Moses began to speak to Pharaoh, the people of God were afflicted more severely. So also, once the word of God has been brought into a human soul, the crafty enemy rises up more fiercely and inflicts greater vices by which the soul may be overcome. Before the word that would reprove vices had come, they remained at peace; but when the word of God began to distinguish one person from another, then great disturbance arose.

The overseers of the Israelites saw themselves in an evil situation because it was said to them, “Nothing shall be reduced from the number of bricks required each day.” They met Moses and Aaron, who were standing opposite them as they came out from Pharaoh, and said to them: “May the Lord look upon this and judge: you have made our odor offensive before Pharaoh and his servants, and you have placed a sword in their hand to kill us.”

*(From Augustine.)* When light sent by God deigns to illumine the human heart, temptations immediately increase from the hidden adversary against the mind that has begun to shine. For the crafty enemy strives to inflame with unlawful desires the minds of those whom he sees gleaming with the light of righteousness, so that they often feel themselves pressed more heavily by temptations than when they did not see the rays of the inner light.

Thus the Israelites, after they had been called, complained against Moses about the increase of their labor, saying: “May the Lord look upon this and judge: you have made our odor offensive before Pharaoh and his servants.” For when they wished to depart from Egypt, Pharaoh had taken away their straw, yet he still demanded work of the same measure. The mind therefore murmurs, as it were, against the law; after receiving its knowledge, it bears sharper goads of temptation. When it sees its labors increasing, it grieves that, in doing what displeases the adversary, it has become offensive in Pharaoh’s eyes.

Moses returned to the Lord and said: “Lord, why have you afflicted this people? Why did you send me? For from the time I entered in to Pharaoh to speak in your name, you have afflicted your people, and you have not delivered them.” The Lord said to Moses: “Now you shall see what I will do to Pharaoh. For by a strong hand he will let them go, and by a mighty hand he will drive them out of his land” (Exod. VI).

*(From Augustine.)* The words Moses says to the Lord—“Why have you afflicted this people, and for what purpose have you sent me? From the time I entered in to Pharaoh to speak in your name concerning this people, he has afflicted them still more, and you have not delivered your people”—are not words of defiance or indignation, but of inquiry and prayer. This is clear from what the Lord answered him. He did not rebuke his unbelief, but disclosed what he was going to do.

## CHAPTER XI. On the fact that the Lord Adonai revealed his name to Moses, and on the command given to Israel

The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “I am the Lord, who appeared to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob as God Almighty; but I did not reveal my name, Adonai, to them,” and so forth (Exod. VI).

Adonai is the seventh in the sequence of the names of God. It is generally interpreted as “Lord,” either because he rules over all creation or because every creature serves his lordship. He is therefore called both Lord and God because he rules over all or because he is feared by all.

How, then, is it now said that the Lord did not reveal his name to Abraham, concerning whom it is written: “The Lord appeared to Abraham and said to him: ‘I am the Lord Almighty; walk before me and be perfect. I will establish my covenant between me and you, and I will multiply you exceedingly’” (Gen. XVII)? Or how was his name not revealed to Isaac, to whom the Lord himself said: “I will be with you and bless you; for to you and to your seed I will give all these regions, and in your seed all the nations of the earth shall be blessed”? Or how was the Lord’s name hidden from Jacob, who said: “I saw the Lord face to face, and my life was preserved” (Gen. XXXII)?

But if we examine Scripture according to the truth, we shall recognize that something was revealed to Moses that had not been made known to the earlier Fathers. For the nearer the coming of Truth in the flesh approached, the more clearly the mysteries were revealed to the Fathers, since by being born and dying they themselves anticipated the times of the Lord’s incarnation. Hence it is now said to Moses: “I am the Lord, who appeared to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob as God Almighty, but I did not reveal my name, Adonai, to them.”

Therefore David also says: “I have understood more than all my teachers, and I have understood more than the elders” (Ps. CXVIII). And the Lord says to the apostles in the Gospel: “Blessed are the eyes that see what you see. For I say to you that many prophets and righteous people desired to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear and did not hear it” (Matt. XIII).

“Therefore say to the children of Israel: ‘I am the Lord, who will lead you out from the prison of the Egyptians, and will rescue you from slavery, and redeem you with an outstretched arm and with great judgments. I will take you to myself as a people, and I will be your God. You shall know that I am the Lord your God, who brought you out from the prison of the Egyptians and brought you into the land over which I raised my hand, to give it to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. I will give it to you as a possession. I am the Lord.’”

Moses therefore reported everything to the children of Israel, but they did not heed him because of their anguish of spirit and their most oppressive labor.

Mystically, the prison of the Egyptians signifies the temptations of this world by which the saints are afflicted. For the Lord delivers the children of Israel with an outstretched arm—that is, with great power and might, or in the Son through whom he made all things. Because of the effect of his mighty works, the Son is called the arm of God when he rescues his saints from the power of the devil and from slavery to sins, and brings them into the spiritual land of the heavenly homeland, concerning which he swore—that is, firmly promised—to our fathers, the patriarchs, prophets, and apostles, that he would give it to them and to their seed as a possession. The seed means all who have faithfully followed their faith and works, so that they may possess it forever.

The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “Enter and speak to Pharaoh, king of Egypt, that he may let the children of Israel go from his land.” Moses answered before the Lord: “Behold, the children of Israel do not listen to me; how, then, will Pharaoh listen, since I am uncircumcised of lips?”

*(From Augustine.)* When Moses says, “Behold, I have a weak voice; how, then, would Pharaoh listen to me?” he does not appear to excuse himself on account of the weakness of his voice because of the multitude of the people, but even because of one man. It is surprising if his voice was so weak that he could not be heard by a single person. Or perhaps, because he was a king, Pharaoh did not permit them to speak to him at close range?

## CHAPTER XII. On the numbering of Levi’s descendants, the command given to Pharaoh, and the manifestation of the signs

These are the heads of their households according to their families: the sons of Reuben, Israel’s firstborn, were Enoch, Phallu, Esrom, and Charmi. These are the clans of Reuben. The sons of Simeon were Jamuel, Jamin, Abad, Jachin, Soher, and Saul, the son of the Canaanite woman. These are the descendants of Simeon. And these are the names of the sons of Levi according to their clans: Gerson, Laath, and Merari (Exod. VI).

There is no doubt that this passage contains a sacramental meaning. Scripture, wishing to demonstrate Moses’ origin, since his work was now being demanded, began with Jacob’s firstborn, Reuben; then it proceeded to Simeon; then to Levi; and it went no farther, because Moses was descended from Levi. These are the men who had already been mentioned among the seventy-five with whom Israel entered Egypt.

God did not wish the first or second tribe, but the third—that is, the Levitical tribe—to be priestly. Aaron took as his wife Elisabeth, the daughter of Aminadab and sister of Naasson; she bore him Nadab and Abihu, Eleazar and Ithamar. Aminadab was the son of Esrom, the son of Phares, the son of Judah.

From this it is evident that the royal and priestly lineages were joined together at the very beginning of the law. Therefore there is no doubt that, according to the faith of the Gospel, our Redeemer was descended both from the royal and from the priestly line.

The Lord said to Moses: “Behold, I have appointed you as God to Pharaoh, and your brother Aaron shall be your prophet. You shall speak everything that I command you; he shall speak to Pharaoh, so that he may let the children of Israel go from his land” (Exod. VII).

*(From Augustine.)* In Sacred Scripture, God is sometimes spoken of by designation, and sometimes according to his essence. He is called God by designation, as when it is now said to Moses: “Behold, I have appointed you as God to Pharaoh”; and as Moses says again: “If anyone does this or that, bring him before the gods” (Exod. XXII), meaning the priests. The Psalmist likewise says: “God has stood in the assembly of gods; in the midst he judges gods” (Ps. LXXXI).

God is called according to his essence when he says to Moses: “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.” Therefore the apostle Paul, wishing to distinguish the designated name of God from his essence, says: “Their fathers are theirs, and from them, according to the flesh, is Christ, who is God over all, blessed forever” (Rom. IX).

The designated God is God among all; the essential God is God over all. Thus, in order to affirm that Christ is God by nature, Paul declared not merely that he is God, but that he is God over all. For any righteous person is also called god, but only among all, because he is God by designation. Christ, however, is God over all, because he is God by nature.

*(From Augustine.)* It should be noted that when Moses was sent to the people, he was not told, “Behold, I have made you God to the people, and your brother shall be your prophet”; rather, he says, “Your brother shall speak to you concerning the people.” It is also said to the people: “He shall be your mouth, and you shall be to him in the things concerning God”; it is not said, “You shall be God to him.”

To Pharaoh, however, Moses is said to have been given as God, and Aaron was given as Moses’ prophet—but in relation to Pharaoh. This makes clear to us that a prophet of God is one who speaks to us what he has heard from God, and that a prophet of God is nothing other than a proclaimer of God’s words to human beings, who either cannot or do not deserve to hear God directly.

It follows: “But I will harden his heart, and I will multiply my signs and wonders in the land of Egypt, and he will not listen to you.
