I will stretch out my hand over Egypt and lead out my army and my people, the children of Israel, from the land of Egypt, by very great judgments. And the Egyptians shall know that I am the Lord.”

God repeatedly says, “I will harden Pharaoh’s heart,” and seems to give this as the reason why he does so.

*(From Augustine.)* “I will harden,” he says, “Pharaoh’s heart, and I will fulfill my signs and wonders in Egypt,” as though it were necessary for Pharaoh’s heart to be hardened so that God’s signs might be multiplied or fulfilled in Egypt.

God therefore makes use of evil hearts for what he wishes to reveal to the good, or by which he will make people good. Although the quality of each heart in evil—that is, the kind of heart it has toward evil—comes about through the fault that has grown from the choice of the will, nevertheless the fact that this evil quality is moved in one direction or another, whether toward this or toward that, occurs through the causes by which the mind is driven. Whether these causes arise or do not arise is not in human power; rather, they come from the hidden providence of God, which is entirely just and wise and orders and governs the whole universe he created.

For Pharaoh to have such a heart that God’s patience would not move him toward piety but rather toward impiety was the result of his own vice. But the fact that circumstances arose by which his heart, already so malicious through its own vice, resisted God’s commands—that is what is called “hardened,” because it did not consent flexibly but resisted inflexibly—was the work of divine ordering. For such a heart, not merely a just hardening but an evidently just punishment was being prepared, by which those who fear God would be corrected.

Suppose, for example, that profit is proposed as the reason for committing murder. The miser is moved one way, the person who despises money another: the former toward committing the crime, the latter toward avoiding it. Yet the proposal of profit itself was not within the power of either of them. In the same way, causes arise for evil people that are not indeed in their power, but these causes make them what they find them already to be through their own vices, formed by their earlier will.

It should also be considered whether “I will harden” can be understood as though he were saying, “I will demonstrate how hard he is.”

Moses was eighty years old, and Aaron eighty-three, when they spoke to Pharaoh. What does this number of years in the life of the lawgiver and the first priest according to the law signify, if not the mystery of the law and the priesthood? When Moses and Aaron spoke to Pharaoh, Moses was eighty years old and Aaron eighty-three, because when the law was offered to the nations for salvation through holy teachers, it taught spiritual circumcision perfectly. The holy preachers themselves also devoted themselves perfectly to keeping themselves pure from every defilement of flesh and spirit, and thus to preaching the faith of the Holy Trinity perfectly to others.

The Lord said to Moses and Aaron: “When Pharaoh says to you, ‘Show signs,’ say to Aaron: ‘Take your staff and throw it down before Pharaoh, and let it become a serpent.’”

*(From Augustine.)* In this case there was certainly no need for the ministry of speech, for which Aaron seemed to have been appointed because of the weakness of Moses’ voice. A staff had to be thrown down so that it might become a dragon. Why, then, did Moses himself not do this, unless Aaron’s mediation between Moses and Pharaoh represents some great reality?

Moses and Aaron went in to Pharaoh and did as the Lord had commanded. Aaron took his staff before Pharaoh and his servants, and it became a serpent.

*(From Augustine.)* It should also be noted that when this sign was to be performed before Pharaoh, the Septuagint reads: “And Aaron threw down his staff.” If it had said simply, “He threw down the staff,” there would have been no question. But since it adds “his,” although Moses had given it to him, perhaps this was not said without reason. Or was the staff common to both of them, so that whichever of them it was called, it would rightly be called his?

Pharaoh summoned the wise men and the sorcerers, and they too performed similar acts by their Egyptian enchantments and certain secret arts. Each threw down his staff, and they became dragons. But Aaron’s staff devoured their staffs—or, according to the Septuagint, “Aaron’s staff swallowed their staff.”

If it had been said, “Aaron’s dragon swallowed their staffs,” it would be understood that the true dragon of Aaron did not swallow those imaginary creations but the staffs. For it could swallow what they were, not what they appeared to be but were not. But since it says, “Aaron’s staff swallowed their staffs,” a dragon could certainly swallow staffs, but a staff could not swallow a dragon. Yet the object is called by the name of that from which it was changed, not of that into which it was changed. Because it also returned to what it had been, it ought to be called by the name of what it principally was.

What, then, should we say about the staffs of the magicians? Were they also made into real dragons? Were they called staffs for the same reason as Aaron’s staff, or did they only appear to be what they were not through magical deception? Why, then, are they called both staffs and dragons on both sides?

Thus, in those imaginary forms, there is no difference in the manner of speaking. But it is difficult to explain how, even if real dragons were made from the magicians’ staffs, neither the magicians nor the evil angels by whose ministry those things were performed were nevertheless creators of the dragons.

For throughout the corporeal things of the world, in all the elements, there are certain hidden seminal principles. When a temporal and causal opportunity is supplied, they burst forth into the forms appropriate to them, according to their own modes and limits. Thus the angels who bring about these things are not called creators of animals, just as farmers are not to be called creators of crops, trees, or any of the things that grow from the earth, although they know how to provide certain visible opportunities and causes by which those things may be born.

What these beings do visibly, the angels do invisibly. God alone is the one Creator, who inserted the causes themselves and the seminal principles into created things.

The matter has been stated briefly. If it were explained by examples and extended discussion so that it might be more easily understood, a lengthy treatment would be required; the reason for our haste excuses us from that.

*(From Isidore.)* Mystically, Moses threw his staff before Pharaoh, and it became a serpent and devoured the serpents of the Egyptians. This signifies that the Word would become flesh, who would empty the venom of the dreadful serpent through the forgiveness and remission of sins.

The staff is the direct, royal word, full of power and bearing the insignia of sovereignty. The staff became a serpent in the same way that he who was the Son of God, born from God the Father, became the son of man, born from a virgin. Raised up like a serpent on the cross, he poured medicine upon the wounds of humanity. Hence the Lord himself says: “Just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the desert, so the Son of Man must be lifted up” (John III).

Moses’ staff, changed into a dragon, swallowed the staffs of the magicians. Likewise Christ, after the dignity of his glory, became obedient to the Father unto death, and through that death of the flesh destroyed the sting of death, as the prophet testifies: “I shall be your death, O death; I shall be your sting, O hell” (Hos. XIII).

Alternatively: Moses, coming to Egypt and carrying the staff with which he chastises Egypt, signifies the law, which strikes the world with the ten plagues of its commandments. Therefore the staff by which Egypt is corrupted and Pharaoh overcome is the cross of Christ, by which the world is conquered and the prince of this world is triumphed over.

The fact that the staff, once thrown down, becomes a serpent signifies what Wisdom says: “Be wise,” it says, “as serpents” (Matt. X). The fact that the staff devoured the serpents of the magicians signifies that the cross of Christ, whose preaching appeared to be foolishness, overcame all worldly wisdom.

That Moses’ staff contains the mystery of the cross is indicated by the Lord when he says concerning Moses: “For he wrote about me” (John V). When the staff was thrown upon the ground, it was then changed into a serpent, because when the cross came to human belief, through the mystery of Christ’s Passion it made the wisdom of this world foolish.

“They also,” it says, “performed similar acts by their enchantments, and Pharaoh’s heart was hardened, and he did not listen to them, as the Lord had said.” When this is said, Pharaoh’s heart appears to have been hardened because the Egyptian magicians also performed similar acts. But what follows will show how great that hardening was, even after the magicians had failed.

*(From Isidore.)* Spiritually, the Lord hardened Pharaoh’s heart—namely, he hardened the devil after sin in such a way that he would never be softened by contrition for repentance, as it is written of him in Job: “His heart will be hardened like a stone” (Job XLI).

After this, the plagues are brought upon Egypt. Although those events took place bodily in Egypt, they are nevertheless now enacted spiritually in us; for Egypt is a figure of the world.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the changing of water into blood

The Lord God also said to Moses: “Say to Aaron: ‘Take your staff and stretch out your hand over the waters of Egypt, over their rivers, streams, marshes, and all their pools of water, so that they may be changed into blood; and there shall be blood throughout all the land of Egypt, both in wooden vessels and in vessels of stone.’” Moses and Aaron did so, as the Lord had commanded, and so forth (Exod. VII).

The fact that the river waters were changed into blood is very appropriately understood as repayment: the river to which the Egyptians had cruelly handed over the Hebrew infants to be killed returned to the perpetrators of the crime a draught of blood.

*(From Isidore.)* Mystically, the Egyptian waters are the wandering and slippery doctrines of the philosophers. They are rightly changed into blood because, in considering the causes of things, they think according to the flesh.

But when the cross of Christ displayed the light of truth to this world, it rebuked it with such corrections that, from the nature of their punishments, the philosophers might recognize their own errors.

All the Egyptians dug around the river for water to drink, for they could not drink the water of the river.

What does it signify that, after the river water had been changed into blood, the Egyptians dug around the river seeking water to drink, except that the Gentile world, confounded by its contemplation of secular philosophy, when it sees that philosophy offers it nothing vital or wholesome, seeks everywhere, by investigation and salutary reflection, a draught of wisdom? Yet it will not truly find it at that time unless it reaches the fountain of life, who says: “Let whoever thirsts come to me and drink, and from his belly shall flow living waters” (John VII).

## CHAPTER XIV. On the production of frogs

The Lord said to Moses: “Say to Aaron: ‘Stretch out your hand over the rivers, streams, and marshes, and bring frogs up over the land of Egypt.’” Aaron stretched out his hand over the waters of Egypt, and the frogs came up and covered the land of Egypt (Exod. VIII).

*(From Isidore.)* In the second plague frogs are produced. They are thought figuratively to signify the poems of the poets, who, with a kind of empty and inflated modulation, like the sounds and croakings of frogs, brought tales of deception into this world.

A frog is exceedingly talkative vanity. This animal is useful for nothing else except that it produces the sound of its voice through disgraceful and importunate cries.

The magicians also performed similar acts by their enchantments and brought frogs up over the land of Egypt.

Pharaoh summoned Moses and Aaron and said to them: “Pray to the Lord to take the frogs away from me and from my people, and I will let the people go to sacrifice to the Lord.”

*(From Augustine.)* “The Egyptian magicians also performed similar acts by their enchantments and brought frogs up over the land of Egypt.” It is asked how they did this, if it had already been done everywhere. The same question arises concerning how they changed water into blood, if all the water of Egypt had already been changed into blood.

It must therefore be understood that the region where the children of Israel lived had not been struck by such plagues. From there the magicians could either draw water that they would change into blood, or bring frogs out of the water merely to display their magical power. They could also have done this after those events had been brought to an end; but Scripture, narrating rapidly, joined together what could have happened later.

Moses and Aaron went out from Pharaoh, and Moses cried to the Lord concerning the appointed time for the frogs that he had arranged with Pharaoh. The Lord did according to Moses’ word, and the frogs died in the houses, villages, and fields. They gathered them into enormous heaps, and the land stank.

When Pharaoh saw that relief had been granted, he hardened his heart and did not listen to them, as the Lord had said.

*(From Augustine.)* “Pharaoh saw,” it says, “that relief had come, and his heart was hardened, and he did not listen to them, as the Lord had said.” Here it is evident that the hardening of Pharaoh’s heart was caused not only by the fact that his magicians performed similar acts, but also by God’s very patience, through which he spared him.

God’s patience, in relation to human hearts, is useful to some for repentance and useless to others, who resist God and persevere in evil. Yet it is not useless in itself; it is useless according to the evil heart, as we have already said.

The Apostle also says this: “Do you not know that God’s patience leads you to repentance? But according to your hardness and impenitent heart, you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and the revelation of the just judgment of God, who will repay each person according to his works” (Rom. II).

Elsewhere, when he said, “We are the good odor of Christ in every place,” he added: “both among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing” (II Cor. II). He did not say that he was the good odor of Christ to those who are being saved but a bad odor to those who are perishing; he simply said that he was a good odor.

Yet those people are such that they perish even through a good odor, according to the quality of their hearts, as has often been said. That quality must be changed by a good will through the grace of God, so that the judgments of God—which harm evil hearts—may begin to benefit them.

Therefore, when his heart had been changed for the better, he sang: “My soul shall live and shall praise you, and your judgments shall help me” (Ps. CXVIII). He did not say, “Your gifts and rewards,” but “Your judgments.”

It is a great thing to be able to say with sincere confidence: “Test me, Lord, and try me; burn my kidneys and my heart” (Ps. XXV). And lest he seem to attribute anything to his own powers, he immediately added: “For your mercy is before my eyes, and I have been pleasing in your truth” (ibid.).

He recalls the mercy shown toward him, so that he may be pleasing in the truth, just as all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth.

## CHAPTER XV. On the gnats

The Lord said to Moses: “Speak to Aaron: ‘Stretch out your staff and strike the dust of the earth, and let there be gnats throughout all the land of Egypt.’” They did so. Aaron stretched out his hand, holding the staff, and struck the dust of the earth, and gnats came upon human beings and animals. All the dust of the earth became gnats throughout the whole land of Egypt (Exod. VIII).

*(From Isidore.)* After this, gnats are produced. This creature is suspended by wings as it flies through the air, but it is so delicate and tiny that it escapes the sight of the eye unless it is observed with great sharpness. It pierces the body on which it settles with a most painful sting, so that although no one can see it flying, he immediately feels its arrival.

This kind of creature is compared with heretical subtlety, which pierces souls with subtle verbal stings and ensnares them with such cunning that the deceived person neither sees nor understands by what means he is deceived.

The magicians also acted similarly by their enchantments, attempting to bring forth gnats, but they could not. Gnats were upon human beings and animals.

The magicians said to Pharaoh: “This is the finger of God.” Pharaoh’s heart was hardened, and he did not listen to them, as the Lord had commanded.

*(From Augustine.)* The magicians said to Pharaoh, “This is the finger of God.” How could they not bring forth gnats? Since they knew the power of their wicked arts, they certainly perceived that their efforts had not been frustrated by arts like theirs, as though Moses were more powerful in such arts, but by the finger of God, who works through Moses.

The finger of God, as the Gospel plainly states, is understood to be the Holy Spirit. For one Evangelist, narrating the Lord’s words, says: “If I cast out demons by the finger of God” (Luke XI); another Evangelist, narrating the same event, wished to explain what the finger of God is and said: “If I cast out demons by the Spirit of God” (Matt. XII).

Although the magicians—whose power Pharaoh trusted—therefore confessed that the finger of God was present in Moses, through whom they had been overcome and their enchantments frustrated, nevertheless Pharaoh’s heart was hardened, now with an utterly astonishing hardness.

Why the magicians failed in this third plague—for the plagues began when the water was changed into blood—is difficult both to perceive and to explain. They could also have failed at the first sign, when the staff was changed into a serpent, or at the first plague, when the water was changed into blood, or at the second, concerning the frogs, if this had been the finger of God, that is, the Spirit of God.

For what utterly foolish person would say that the finger of God could hinder the magicians’ efforts in this sign but could not do so in the earlier ones? There is therefore certainly a reason why they were permitted to perform those things up to this point.

Perhaps the Trinity is being commended. In any case, it is true that the greatest philosophers among the Gentiles, so far as can be discovered in their writings, philosophized without the Holy Spirit, although they did not remain silent about the Father and the Son. Didymus also recalls this in the book he wrote concerning the Holy Spirit.

*(From Isidore.)* Mystically, just as the Holy Spirit, reconciled and appeased, grants rest to the meek and humble of heart, so the hostile and adverse spirit harasses the harsh and proud with agitation. Those very small flies signified this agitation, under which Pharaoh’s magicians failed, saying: “This is the finger of God.”

## CHAPTER XVI. On the bringing forth of flies

The Lord also said to Moses: “Rise at dawn and stand before Pharaoh. For he will go out to the waters, and you shall say to him: ‘Thus says the Lord: Let my people go, so that they may sacrifice to me. But if you do not let them go, behold, I will send upon you, your servants, your people, and your houses every kind of fly. All the houses of the Egyptians shall be filled with flies of every kind, and likewise the whole land in which they are. On that day I will make the land of Goshen, where my people is, marvelous, so that there will be no flies there. You shall know that I am the Lord in the midst of the land, and I will set a division between my people and your people’” (Exod. VIII).

*(From Augustine.)* What Scripture has made explicit here must not be understood as though it happened only wherever it is mentioned. Rather, it should be understood that the same thing occurred in the earlier and later signs: the land in which God’s people lived was not afflicted by such plagues.

It was appropriate for this to be stated explicitly at this point, from which begin signs that the magicians did not even attempt to imitate. For clearly, since gnats had been everywhere in Pharaoh’s kingdom but had not been in the land of Goshen, where the Israelites lived, the magicians attempted to perform a similar act and were completely unable to do so.

Until they failed, nothing had been said about the separation of that land. But once events began to occur which they no longer dared even to attempt to imitate, the separation was mentioned.

*(From Isidore.)* In the fourth place Egypt is struck by flies. The fly is an excessively insolent and restless creature. What else does it signify but the insolent anxieties of carnal desires? Egypt is therefore struck by flies because the hearts of those who love this world are assailed by the restlessness of their desires.

The Septuagint translators, moreover, rendered the word as *kynomyia*, that is, “dog-fly.” Through it, dog-like behavior is signified, in which the will of the human mind and the lust of the flesh are reproved. In this passage the dog-fly may also signify the forensic eloquence of human beings, by which they tear one another apart like dogs.

Pharaoh summoned Moses and Aaron and said to them: “Go, sacrifice to your God in this land.” For he did not want them to go where they said they would go; he wanted them to sacrifice there, in Egypt.

This is shown by Moses’ words that follow, where he says that it could not be done because of the abominations of the Egyptians. For it is written:

“Moses said: ‘It cannot be done in this way. We shall sacrifice to the Lord our God the abominations of the Egyptians.’”

As though he were saying: “We cannot sacrifice to the Lord our God, in their presence, those animals that the Egyptians abominate.” The Egyptians disdain eating sheep. Hence it is also written in Genesis: “All shepherds of sheep are detestable to the Egyptians” (Gen. XLVI).

When he added, “If we sacrifice before them what the Egyptians worship, they will stone us,” he taunted the Gentiles themselves, because they worshiped the forms of animals as the supreme God, impressed upon wood and stone. They worshiped Jupiter-Ammon in the form of a ram, Anubis in the form of a dog, and Apis in the form of a bull, along with other portents rather than divinities, which Egypt itself believed it was venerating with divine worship. Therefore Moses and Aaron said that they wished to go where the Egyptians would not see their abominations being sacrificed.

*(From Augustine.)* This should be understood mystically in the way stated above: sheep and their shepherds were abominable to the Egyptians, and therefore the Israelites received a land set apart when they came into Egypt. Likewise, the sacrifices of the Israelites are abominations to the Egyptians, just as the life of the righteous is an abomination to the wicked.

*(From Gregory.)* Holy men offer sheep to the Lord because they present their simplicity as a sacrifice to almighty God. But the Egyptians abominate sheep because the citizens of this world reject and despise the simplicity of the good.

Just as there are evil deeds that the good detest, so the causes of good deeds are abominations to the reprobate. Hence it is written: “The righteous abhor an ungodly man, and the ungodly abhor those who are in the right way” (Prov. XLIX).

## CHAPTER XVII. On the severe pestilence sent upon the animals of Egypt
And the Lord said to Moses: “Go in to Pharaoh and speak to him: Thus says the Lord, the God of the Hebrews: Let my people go, that they may sacrifice to me. But if you still refuse and retain them, behold, my hand will be upon your fields, upon your horses and asses, camels, oxen, and sheep—a very grievous pestilence” [Col. 0039B] (Exod. IX).

But the fact that Egypt is struck fifth among the animals, by the death of livestock, rebukes here the senselessness or stupidity of mortal human beings, who, like irrational cattle, imposed the worship and name of God upon images—not only of human beings but also of animals—impressed in wood, metals, and stones; and in those things which they themselves believed to be honored with divine worship, they saw lamentable punishments being inflicted.

“And all the animals of the Egyptians died. But of the animals of the children of Israel nothing at all perished. And Pharaoh sent to see, and there was nothing dead of what Israel possessed. And the heart of Pharaoh was hardened, and he did not let the people go.”

(From Augustine.) How was this hardening of Pharaoh’s heart produced from contrary causes? For if the livestock of the Israelites too had died [Col. 0039C], then there would seem to have been a suitable reason why his heart was hardened to despise God—as though his magicians too had caused the Israelites’ livestock to die. But now, seeing that not one animal among the Hebrews’ herds had died, how could he have been moved to fear or believe? “For this reason it was hardened”—that is, the hardening proceeded even to this point.

And the Lord said to Moses and Aaron: “Take full handfuls of ashes from the furnace, and let Moses scatter them toward heaven before Pharaoh. Let them become dust over the land of Egypt. For there shall be boils and swelling blisters upon human beings and animals throughout the whole land of Egypt.”

(From Augustine.) What does God mean when he says to Aaron and Moses, “Take for yourselves full handfuls of ashes from the furnace, and let Moses scatter them toward heaven before Pharaoh and [Col. 0039D] before his servants, and let dust be made throughout the whole land of Egypt”? The earlier signs were performed with a rod, which Aaron—not Moses—extended over the water or used to strike the ground. But now, after two signs have intervened, concerning the dog-fly and the death of the livestock, in which neither Aaron nor Moses performed anything with his hand, Moses is commanded to scatter ashes from the furnace toward heaven. Both are ordered to take them, but he is to scatter them not upon the earth but toward heaven. This is as though Aaron, who was given for the people, ought to strike the earth or extend his hand over the earth or the water; but Moses, of whom it was said, “He will be to you in matters pertaining to God,” is commanded to scatter ashes toward heaven.

What do those two earlier signs mean, in which neither Moses nor Aaron performs anything with his hand? What does this difference signify? Surely it is not meaningless.

“And they took ashes from the furnace and stood before Pharaoh. And Moses scattered them toward heaven, and there arose boils—swelling blisters—upon human beings and animals. The magicians could not stand before Moses because of the boils that were upon them and throughout the whole land of Egypt.”

(From Isidore.) In the boils, the deceitful and festering wickedness of this age is rebuked; in the blisters, swelling and inflated pride; in the inflammations, the anger of rage and madness. Up to this point, punishments of this kind temper the world through the figures of its errors. After this, however, blows come from above: namely, voices, thunder, hail, and fire running about, as will be shown in what follows.

And the Lord said to Moses: “Rise early in the morning and stand before Pharaoh, and say to him: Thus says the Lord, the God of the Hebrews: Let my people go, that they may sacrifice to me. For this time I will send all my plagues upon your heart, upon your servants, and upon your people, so that you may know that there is none like me in all the earth. For now, if I stretch out my hand, I will strike you and your people with pestilence, and you will perish from the earth. But for this reason I have appointed you, that I may show my strength in you and that my name may be proclaimed throughout all the earth.”

The Apostle also set forth these words of Scripture when he was dealing with that same exceedingly difficult passage. There he said also: “But if God, wishing to show his wrath and to make his power known, endured with great patience the vessels of wrath, sparing those whom he had foreknown would become evil—vessels which he says were prepared for destruction—and in order,” he says, “to make known the riches of his glory upon the vessels of mercy” (Rom. IX).

Hence the voice of the vessels of mercy is found in the Psalms: “My God, his mercy will go before me. My God has shown me good things in the presence of my enemies” (Ps. LVIII).

God therefore knows how to make good use of the wicked. Yet in them he does not create human nature for wickedness; rather, he brings them forth patiently for as long as he knows is necessary—not without purpose, but using them for the admonition and encouragement of the good. Behold, the proclamation of God’s name throughout the whole earth benefits the vessels of mercy. Pharaoh was therefore preserved for their benefit, as Scripture testifies and the outcome demonstrates.

“Send, therefore, now, and gather your animals and everything that you have in the field. For human beings and animals, and everything that is found outside and has not been gathered from the fields, shall be struck by the hail and shall die.”

(From Augustine.) What does God command Pharaoh when he threatens that he will make a great hailstorm—that he should hasten to gather his animals and whatever he had in the field, lest they perish in the hail? He seems to give this warning not so much in anger as in mercy. But this does not present a difficulty, since God tempers punishment even when he is angry.

What rightly causes concern is this: for what animals is he now providing, if all had died in the preceding plague, where it is written that God distinguished between the livestock of the Hebrews and that of the Egyptians, so that none of the former died while all the livestock of the Egyptians died?

Is the difficulty resolved by the fact that he had foretold the death of those animals that were in the field, so that these are understood to be all of them, while those that were in the houses are understood to have escaped? They could have been gathered even by people who doubted, and kept in the house, lest what Moses had foretold the Lord would do prove true. From these, some could again have been in the fields, and he now warns that they should be gathered into houses lest they perish in the hail.

This is especially supported by what Scripture next says: “Whoever feared the word of the Lord among Pharaoh’s servants gathered his livestock into the houses. But whoever did not set his mind upon the word of the Lord left his livestock in the field.” This could therefore have occurred when God also threatened the death of the livestock, although Scripture had been silent about it.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Concerning the Sending of the Hail

And the Lord said to Moses: “Extend your hand toward heaven, and there shall be hail throughout the whole land of Egypt” (Exod. IX).

Behold, again he is commanded to extend his hand not toward the earth but toward heaven, as earlier with the ashes.

“And Moses extended his rod toward heaven, and the Lord gave thunder and hail, and lightning running across the earth,” and the rest.

(From Isidore.) In the seventh place, blows come upon Egypt from above: namely, voices and thunder, hail, and running fire. In the thunder, rebukes and divine corrections are understood, because he does not strike in silence but gives forth voices; and he sends teaching from heaven, by which the world, chastised from heaven, may recognize its guilt.

He also gives hail, by which the still-tender beginnings of vices are laid waste. He also gives fire, knowing that there are thorns and thistles which that fire must consume. Concerning this the Lord says, “I have come to cast fire upon the earth” (Luke XII). By this fire the incitements of pleasure and lust are consumed.

And Pharaoh sent and summoned Moses and Aaron, saying to them: “I have sinned even now. The Lord is righteous; I and my people are wicked. Pray to the Lord, so that God’s thunder and the hail may cease, and I will let you go, and you shall remain here no longer.”

Moses said: “When I have gone out of the city, I will spread my palms toward the Lord, and the thunder shall cease, and there shall be no hail, so that you may know that the earth belongs to the Lord. But I know that neither you nor your servants yet fear the Lord God,” and the rest (Luke XII).

(From Augustine.) Amid the crash of heaven, which was violent in the hail, Pharaoh for the third time asked Moses to pray [Col. 0041D] for him, confessing his own iniquity and that of his people. Moses said to him: “I know that neither you nor your servants yet fear the Lord.”

What kind of fear was he seeking from one for whom this fear was not yet the fear of the Lord? It is easy to fear punishment, but this is not fear of God—the fear of devotion, namely, which Jacob recalls when he says: “Unless the God of my father Abraham, and the Fear of Isaac, had been with me, you would now have sent me away empty.”

And the Lord said to Moses: “Go in to Pharaoh. For I have hardened his heart and the hearts of his servants, so that I may perform these signs of mine among them, and so that you may recount in the hearing of your son and your grandsons how often I have crushed the Egyptians and performed my signs among them, and you may know that I am the Lord God” (Gen. XXXI), and the rest.

What the Lord says to Moses—“Go in to Pharaoh. For I have hardened his heart and the hearts of his servants, so that these signs of mine may come upon them in due order” (Exod. X)—is not to be understood as though God had need of anyone’s wickedness. Rather, it should be understood as if he were saying: “I was patient with him and his servants, so that I would not remove them, so that my signs might come upon them in due order.” For by the patience of God the evil mind became more obstinate; and because that patience was exercised toward him, his heart is said to have been hardened.

## CHAPTER XIX. Concerning the Locusts

And the Lord said to Moses: “Extend your hand over the land of Egypt for the locusts, so that they may come up upon it and devour every plant that was left over from the hail.” And Moses extended his rod over the land of Egypt (Exod. XVIII).

(From Isidore.) The locusts are mentioned in the eighth place. Some think that through this kind of plague the instability of the human race—divided and at variance with itself—is refuted. In another sense, locusts are to be understood as representing the mobility of frivolity, like wandering and leaping souls directed toward the pleasures of the world.

“And the Lord brought in a scorching wind throughout that entire day and night; and when morning came, the scorching wind lifted the locusts, which came up over the whole land of Egypt and settled throughout all the borders of Egypt, innumerable—such as had never been before that time, nor would ever be afterward. They covered the entire surface of the earth, laying everything waste. Thus the vegetation of the land was devoured, and every fruit on the trees that the hail had left; nothing green at all remained on the trees or on the plants of the land throughout all Egypt.”

(From Gregory.) “The scorching wind,” he says, “lifted the locusts, which came up over the whole land of Egypt and covered the entire face of the earth, laying everything waste. Thus the vegetation of the land was devoured, and every fruit that was on the trees.”

The plagues inflicted upon Egypt from heaven, which were once physically imposed in accordance with the deserts of the Egyptians, signified spiritually the evils that strike perverse minds every day. Egypt was afflicted by those plagues in such a way that, shaken by an external blow and suffering, it might perceive what losses of devastation it had inwardly endured through its negligence. Thus, while the least things perished outwardly, they might recognize their greater sins through the likeness of those things and feel the heavier burdens they bore within.

What, then, do the locusts signify by their symbolism? They do more harm to human crops than all other small animals, and therefore signify the tongues of those who fly about—tongues that corrupt the minds of earthly people when they see them produce something good and spoil it by praising it without measure.

The fruit of the Egyptians is the work of the lovers of empty glory, which the locusts destroy when the flattering tongue inclines the worker’s heart to seek transitory praise. Locusts eat the plants when flatterers exalt the words of speakers with popular approval. They devour the fruits of trees when they weaken through vain praises the works of those who are already regarded as strong.

“Moses went out from Pharaoh’s presence and prayed to the Lord, who caused a most violent west wind to blow. It seized the locusts and cast them into the Red Sea. Not one remained throughout all the borders of Egypt. And the Lord hardened Pharaoh’s heart, and he did not let the children of Israel go.”

(From Augustine.) Scripture certainly recalled the benefit of God, that he removed the locusts, and afterward said that God hardened Pharaoh’s heart. By his benefit and his patience—through which that obstinacy arose, while Pharaoh was being spared—as with all evil human hearts, they grow hard by misusing God’s patience.

## CHAPTER XX. Concerning the Sending of the Darkness

And the Lord said to Moses: “Extend your hand toward heaven, and let there be darkness over the land of Egypt, so dense that it may be felt.” Moses extended his hand toward heaven [Col. 0043B], and dreadful darkness arose throughout the whole land of Egypt. For three days no one saw his brother, nor did anyone move from the place where he was (Exod. X).

(From Isidore.) The ninth plague was darkness. This occurred either so that the blindness of their minds might be rebuked, or so that they might understand that the reasons of divine dispensation and providence are exceedingly obscure. “He made darkness his hiding place.” Those who rashly and presumptuously desire to investigate these things, asserting one claim after another, fall into thick and tangible darkness of ignorance.

## CHAPTER XXI. Concerning the Last of the Ten Plagues, That Is, the Destruction of the Firstborn, and the Mystical Interpretation of the Ten Plagues

And the Lord said to Moses: “I will yet bring one plague upon Pharaoh and Egypt; and after this he will let you go and compel you to depart” (Exod. XI).

(From Isidore.) At the end, the firstborn are destroyed. The firstborn of Egypt are wiped out—whether this means their principalities and powers and the rulers of this world, or the authors and inventors of the false religions that existed in this world, which the truth of Christ extinguished and destroyed together with their authors.

This has been said with reference to the mystical sense. But if we must also treat the moral interpretation, we shall say that every soul, while it lives in errors and ignorance of the truth in this world, is situated in Egypt.

When the law of God begins to draw near to it, it turns its waters into blood—that is, it turns the fluid and slippery life of youth toward the blood of the Old or New Testament. Then it draws out from it vain and empty talk, and a complaint like the croaking of frogs against the providence of God. It also cleanses its evil thoughts and scatters the stings of cunning, like the bite of gnats. It drives away the bites of lust, like the darts of the dog-fly. It destroys within it stupidity and an understanding like that of beasts, through which a human being, though honored, did not understand, but was compared with foolish animals and became like them.

It also rebukes its boils, and extinguishes within it the swelling and fever of sins and arrogance, together with the heat of rage. After this it applies the voices of the sons of thunder—that is, evangelical and apostolic teachings. It also brings the chastisement of hail, so as to restrain luxury and pleasures. At the same time it applies the fire of repentance, so that one may say: “Was not our heart burning within us?” (Luke XXIV).

Nor does it withhold from the soul the examples of locusts, by which all its restless and turbulent movements may be bitten and consumed. Thus it too may say what the Apostle teaches, that “all things should be done in order” (II Cor. XII).

When it has been sufficiently chastised in accordance with its ways and restrained for the correction of a more reformed life; when it has perceived the author of its blows and has begun to confess that “it is the finger of God,” and has received a small measure of understanding, then especially it sees the darkness of its deeds; then it senses the gloom of its errors.

When it has reached this point, it will deserve that the firstborn of Egypt be extinguished within it. I think that something like the following may be understood by this.

When every soul has reached the fullness of its age, and a kind of natural law within it begins to defend its rights, it undoubtedly produces its first movements according to the desire of the flesh—movements stirred up by the fuel of concupiscence or anger.

Therefore, as something especially significant and not common to other human beings, the Prophet says of Christ alone: “He shall eat butter and honey” (Ps. VII). “Before he knows how to reject evil, he will choose the good”; or, as another reading has it, “Before the child knows good or evil, he will resist wickedness so as to choose what is good.”

Another Prophet, speaking as though about himself, said: “Remember not the sins of my youth and my ignorance” (Ps. XXIV).

Because these first movements of the soul, produced according to the flesh, rush into sin, the Egyptian firstborn are rightly consigned to death; they are extinguished only if the conduct of the rest of life directs its course toward greater amendment.

Thus, in the soul which the divine law takes up from errors, chastises, and corrects, the firstborn of the Egyptians are also understood to have been destroyed—unless, after all this, it persists in unbelief and refuses to join the Israelite people, to come out from the deep and depart safely, but remains in iniquity and sinks like lead into exceedingly deep water.

For iniquity, according to the vision of the prophet Zechariah, sits upon a talent of lead (Zech. V). Therefore the one who remains in iniquity is said to be submerged in the deep like lead.

Indeed, as we observed above, some prodigies were administered through Aaron, some through Moses, and some through the Lord himself. These may be understood to the extent that we recognize that in certain matters people are not to be cleansed through the sacrifices of priests and the observances of bishops, which is represented by the person of Aaron; in others they are to be corrected through knowledge of the divine law, which is represented by Moses’ office; while in still others—those which are more difficult—they are corrected only with difficulty by the power of the Lord himself.

Nor should we regard as pointless the observation that at first Moses did not enter to Pharaoh but met him as he was going out to the waters; afterward he entered to him. After this, he did not enter at all but approached when summoned—and in this, as I think, something may be understood.

Whether our struggle in the word of God and in religion is against Pharaoh, or whether we are trying to rescue souls possessed by him from his power, and there is a contest for us in disputation, we ought not at once, on the first assault, to enter into the deepest places of the questions. Rather, we must meet the adversary, and meet him at his waters.

His waters are the authorities of the pagan philosophers. There, then, we who wish to dispute must first meet him, so that we may refute them and show them that they are in error. Afterward we must enter into the interior of the conflict.

For the Lord says: “Unless someone first binds the strong man, he cannot enter his house and plunder his goods” (Matt. XII). Therefore the strong man must first be bound for us and constrained by the bonds of argument; then we must enter to plunder his goods and liberate the souls whom he had possessed through the fraud of deception.

When we have done this repeatedly and stood against him—stood in the manner in which the Apostle says, “Stand therefore, with your loins girded in truth” (Eph. VI), and again, “Stand in the Lord and act manfully” (Phil. IV)—when we have stood against him in this way, that ancient and crafty artificer will even pretend to be defeated and to yield, in case he may thereby make us more negligent in the contest.

He will also pretend to repent and will beg us to depart, but not to depart far. For he wants us to remain close to him in some measure; he wants us not to withdraw far from his borders. But unless we withdraw farther from him and cross the sea, and say, “As far as the east is from the west, so far has he removed our iniquities from us,” we cannot be saved.

Moreover, these ten plagues with which Egypt was struck may be compared with the times of the Roman Empire, because these events were made as a figure of our own. Both peoples—the Israelite and the Christian—belong to one God; the cause of both peoples is one.

The synagogue of the Israelites was subjected to the Egyptians; the Church of the Christians was subjected to the Romans. The Egyptians persecuted; the Romans also persecuted. There were ten acts of opposition against Moses; here there were ten inflicted against Christ. The plagues of the Egyptians were diverse; here there were diverse calamities of the Romans.

For, to compare the plagues with one another insofar as a figure may be compared with its form:

There the first punishment involved blood, either flowing from wells or running together in rivers. Here the first plague under Nero required that blood be everywhere: whether through those dying from diseases in the city or through blood poured out in wars throughout the world.

There the next plague appeared through frogs making noise and leaping about in the inner chambers. They were almost the cause of famine and death for the inhabitants. Here the next punishment, under Domitian, similarly drove nearly all Roman citizens to want and scattered them into exile through the wicked and unrestrained movements of his guards and soldiers, who carried out the bloody commands of their savage prince.

There the third affliction involved gnats—very small and very fierce flies—which, often in the midst of the summer heat, gather densely in barren places, darting about in flight and settling upon the hair of human beings and the bristles of animals with a burning bite [the final wording is materially uncertain in the supplied text].

Here likewise, under Trajan, the plague stirred up the Jews. Although they had been scattered everywhere and had by that time ceased to be at rest, they were suddenly inflamed and raged throughout the world against those among whom they lived, while many cities also suffered terrible ruin from frequent earthquakes that overthrew them at the same time.

There, in the fourth plague, there were dog-flies, fierce fosterers of decay and mothers of worms. Here likewise the fourth plague, under Marcus Antoninus, was a pestilence spread through many provinces. It infected all Italy, including the city of Rome, and the Roman army, dispersed across distant frontiers into various winter quarters, was destroyed by death and handed over at once to decay and worms.

There the fifth punishment was completed by the sudden death of the livestock and animals. Here likewise the fifth vengeance, under Severus the persecutor, through the frequent civil wars, shattered the very organs and supports of the commonwealth: that is, the populations of the provinces and the religious institutions of the soldiers.

There the sixth affliction brought swelling blisters and oozing boils. Here likewise the sixth punishment, which followed the persecution of Maximus, who had ordered bishops and clergy in particular—while leaving the common populace aside, that is, the leading persons of the churches—to be tortured, was raised up by swelling anger and envy, not through the slaughter of the common people but through the wounds and deaths of princes and powerful men.

There the seventh plague is counted as the hail that was driven down in abundance and brought death to human beings and animals. Here likewise there was a seventh plague under Gallus and Volusianus, who succeeded Decius, the persecutor, after he had been killed. For then pestilence was spread through all the territories of the Roman Empire, from east to west, and destroyed almost every class of human beings. At that time it also corrupted the side and poured nourishment into decay.

There, to bring about the eighth destruction of Egypt, locusts were stirred up everywhere and laid everything waste. Here likewise, for the eighth destruction of the Roman city, peoples were stirred up from every direction and brought devastation; through slaughter and fires they destroyed all the provinces.

There the ninth disturbance consisted of prolonged, thick, and tangible darkness, threatening altogether more danger than it inflicted. Here the same punishment occurred when, under Aurelian as he decreed persecution, a terrible and mournful thunderbolt amid dreadful storms fell at his very feet, showing what a mighty avenger could do when such vengeance was demanded—unless he were also merciful and patient. Nevertheless, within six months three emperors were killed: Aurelian, Tacitus, and Florianus, each slain for different reasons.

There finally the tenth plague, which was the last of all, was the killing of the children whom each man had first begotten. Here likewise the tenth—that is, the final—punishment is the destruction of all the idols, which they had loved above all because they were the first things they had made.

There the king felt, tested, and believed in the power of God, and therefore allowed God’s people to depart. Here too he felt, tested, and believed in the power of God, and therefore allowed God’s people to depart freely.

There God’s people were never afterward returned to slavery. Here God’s people were never afterward compelled to idolatry.

There the precious vessels of the Egyptians were handed over to the Hebrews [Col. 0047A]. Here the principal pagan temples yielded to the churches of the Christians.

Indeed, as I said, I think this must be proclaimed: just as Egypt, after these ten plagues, rushed upon the Hebrews whom it had released, intending to pursue them, and eternal destruction overwhelmed it through the sea that flowed over it, so persecution by the nations will remain for us, who travel freely as pilgrims, until we cross the Red Sea—that is, the fire of judgment—with the Lord himself as leader and judge.

But those into whom the form of the Egyptians is transferred, raging through the power permitted them for a time, persecute Christians with the gravest torments by God’s permission. Nevertheless, all these enemies of Christ, together with their king the Antichrist, will receive the lake of eternal fire. Entering it through the great darkness that prevents it from being seen, they will suffer everlasting destruction, burning in immortal punishments.

## CHAPTER XXII. The Lord’s Command Given through Moses to the Children of Israel, That They Should Ask Their Neighbors and Friends for Vessels of Gold and Silver

The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “Say, therefore, to all the people: Let every man ask from his friend, and every woman from her neighbor, vessels of gold and silver. And the Lord will give grace to his people in the sight of the Egyptians” (Exod. XI).

No one should think that an example is thereby being given for despoiling one’s neighbor in this way.

(From Augustine.) God commanded this, because he knew what each person ought to suffer. The Israelites did not commit theft; they rendered service to God who commanded it. In the same way, when a judge’s minister kills someone whom the judge ordered to be killed, he is certainly a murderer if he does so willingly, even if he kills someone whom he knows ought to have been killed by the judge.

There is also another difficulty. If the Hebrews lived separately in the land of Goshen, where the plagues by which Pharaoh’s kingdom was afflicted did not occur, how could each one ask his neighbor or neighbor-woman for gold, silver, and clothing? This is especially difficult because when the command is first given through Moses, it is written this way: “and a woman from her neighbor,” and *concellaria* or *concellania*, if that is the proper word, or “her cohabitant.”

It must therefore be understood that not Hebrews alone lived in the land of Goshen, but that some Egyptians also lived there with them as fellow inhabitants. Through the merit of the Hebrews, those benefits too could reach these Egyptians, so that the Egyptian inhabitants would love them and readily grant what they requested. Yet God did not judge these people to have been so alien to the injuries and opposition endured by God’s people that they should not also be struck by this loss, although they had not been struck by the plagues because the land was being spared.

(From Gregory.) Here too we must carefully consider that minds attached to the practice of carnal life cannot be torn away from low things unless they advance gradually through a progressively led preaching.

For this reason, those situated in Egypt are approached with pious and righteous moderation while their hidden desire is accommodated; after taking away the golden and silver vessels of their neighbors, they are commanded to depart.

When they have been led to Mount Sinai and received the law, they are commanded to exact “an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth” (Exod. XXI). Yet later, when grace has been revealed, one struck on one cheek is commanded to offer the other also (Matt. V).

Because anger always demands more in revenge than an injury has received, they first learn not to return evils in greater measure; later they learn to endure evils willingly even when they have been multiplied.

For this reason he prohibited certain things to the same unformed people, while preserving certain others for their former use; nevertheless, he arranged these very things in the pattern of a better life.

In Egypt, brute animals were sacrificed to idols, and afterward the sacrifice of animals became part of their practice, so that, while they admitted something from their former custom, the weak might be consoled by having something of their former practice.

Yet, by a wondrous dispensation of counsel, what the Lord retained for them from their carnal custom, he turned more powerfully into a figure of the spirit. For what do the sacrifices of those animals signify except the death of the Only-Begotten? What do the sacrifices of those animals signify except the extinction of our carnal life?

Thus, by accommodating himself to the weakness of the unformed people, he is said to have condescended to them; and from the same source, through the shadowed forms of allegories, a greater strength of the spirit is announced to them.

## CHAPTER XXIII. Concerning the Institution of Passover in the Land of Egypt
The Lord also said to Moses and Aaron in the land of Egypt: “This month shall be for you the beginning of months; it shall be the first among the months of the year. Speak to the whole assembly of the children of Israel and say to them: On the tenth day of this month, each man shall take a lamb for his family and household. But if the number is too small to be sufficient for eating the lamb, he shall take his neighbor who is joined to his household, according to the number of persons who are sufficient for eating the lamb. The lamb shall be without blemish, male, and a year old. According to the same rite you shall also take a kid, and you shall keep it until the fourteenth day of this month; and the entire multitude of the children of Israel shall sacrifice it toward evening” (Exod. XII).

“For this month shall be for you the beginning of months; it shall be the first among the months of the year.” Among the Hebrews, he calls the first month Nisan, in which heaven and earth were created and the beginning of the world came into being. One must always observe in it the full moon occurring after the spring equinox. In this month the Israelite people were liberated from Egyptian servitude, and the human race was rescued and transferred from the power of the devil through the blood of Christ.

The lamb is commanded to be taken on the tenth day of the month and kept until the fourteenth day of that same month, toward evening, and then sacrificed. Likewise, our Redeemer, coming to Jerusalem on the tenth day—that is, five days before Passover—taught the word of God in the temple and among the assembly of the Jews who were plotting against him. He awaited the fourteenth day, on which, celebrating the mystical Passover with his disciples, he was handed over by Judas the betrayer into the hands of the Jews, and on the following day he was sacrificed upon the cross for our redemption.

But the fact that the lamb is taken on the tenth day of the month but is not sacrificed until the fourteenth signifies that Christ’s passion was indeed prefigured through the Law, yet was completed only when the grace of the Gospel shone forth. The number ten belongs to the Law because of the Decalogue, while the number four expresses the New Testament because of the four Gospels.

The command, therefore, that each person take a lamb for his family and household, and that, if the number of those eating is too small to consume the lamb, he take his neighbor who is joined to his household so that there may be a sufficient number to eat the lamb, signifies typologically that not only Jews but also Gentiles were to be summoned to faith in Christ and to the sacrifice of the true Lamb. The Jewish nation alone was not sufficient to celebrate the spiritual Passover; the Gentiles, too, who were neighbors to the household of Judah, had to be brought in, so that the house of God might be filled with the number of its banqueters, and the lamb’s flesh, worthily eaten, might be transformed for the faithful into nourishment for eternal life.

The fact that the same lamb was commanded to be eaten in the evening signifies that Christ’s passion was to be completed in the final age of the world. Finally, the command that a kid likewise be taken and kept until the fourteenth day is rightly understood as referring to the mystery of Christ’s incarnation. For what need was there to instruct that a sheep or lamb be taken from sheep and a kid from goats, unless he were being prefigured whose flesh was propagated not only from the righteous but also from sinners? Nevertheless, the Jews attempt to understand this as requiring a kid to be taken for the celebration of Passover. They think the statement, “Take it from the sheep and the goats,” means that either a lamb should be taken from lambs or a kid from kids, if the former is unavailable.

[Col. 0048C]

Yet when the realities have been fulfilled, it is evident in Christ what was prefigured by that command:

“And they shall take some of its blood and put it on the two doorposts and on the lintels of the houses in which they will eat it. They shall eat its flesh roasted by fire that night, and unleavened bread with wild lettuces.” You shall not eat anything from it raw, nor boiled in water, but only roasted by fire. You shall eat its head with its feet and its entrails, and nothing of it shall remain until morning. If anything remains, you shall burn it with fire. Whatever is left of it in the morning,” he says, “you shall burn with fire” (Exod. XII).

(From Augustine.) One may ask how anything could remain, since they had been warned that, if a household did not have a sufficient number to consume the animal, neighbors were to be brought in. But since it is said, “You shall not break any of its bones,” it is understood that bones would necessarily remain to be burned with fire.

“You shall eat it in this manner: you shall gird your loins, put your sandals on your feet, and hold staffs in your hands; and you shall eat it in haste. For it is the Passover—that is, the Lord’s passing-over. And I will pass through the land of Egypt that night, and I will strike every firstborn in the land of Egypt, from man to beast; and against all the gods of Egypt I will execute judgments: I am the Lord” (Exod. XII).

(From Gregory.) All these things plainly provide us with great edification if they are examined through mystical interpretation. For who the lamb’s blood is, we have learned not by hearing but by drinking. His blood is placed on the two doorposts when it is imbibed not only with the mouth of the body but also with the mouth of the heart.

The lamb’s blood is placed on both doorposts when the sacrament of his passion is received with the mouth for redemption and also contemplated with an attentive mind for imitation. Whoever receives the blood of our Redeemer in such a way that he is not yet willing to imitate his passion has placed the blood on one doorpost.

It must also be placed on the lintels of the houses. What do we understand spiritually by houses except our minds, in which we dwell through thought? The lintel of a house is its intention itself, which rises above its action. Therefore, whoever directs the intention of his thought toward imitation of the Lord’s passion places the lamb’s blood on the lintel of the house.

Or certainly the houses themselves are our bodies, in which we dwell for as long as we live; and we place the lamb’s blood on the lintel of the house because we carry the cross of his passion on our foreheads.

Of this lamb it is further said: “And they shall eat the flesh roasted by fire that night.” We eat the lamb at night when, in the sacrament, we now receive the Lord’s body, while we do not yet see one another’s consciences. Yet the lamb’s flesh must be roasted, because water dissolves flesh that has been boiled, whereas fire without water cooks and strengthens it. Thus the fire cooked the flesh of our Lamb, because the force of his passion made him stronger for resurrection and strengthened him for incorruption. For his flesh, which gained strength through death, was hardened by fire.

Therefore, through the Psalmist also he says: “My strength has dried up like a potsherd” (Ps. XXI).

[Col. 0050C]

For what is a potsherd before fire except soft clay? But fire makes it solid. Thus the strength of his humanity dried up like a potsherd, because through the fire of his passion it grew toward the strength of incorruption.

Yet merely receiving the sacraments of our Redeemer is not sufficient for the mind’s true solemnity unless good works are joined to them as well. For what benefit is it to receive his body and blood with the mouth while opposing him through wicked conduct? Hence it is further said concerning the eating:

“And unleavened bread with bitter herbs.”

He eats bread without leaven who performs right actions without the corruption of vainglory; who carries out the commands of mercy without mixing in sin, lest he wickedly seize what he appears to distribute rightly.

Those who mixed the leaven of sin into their good action are addressed by the Lord through the prophet’s voice in rebuke:

“Come to Bethel and act impiously.”

And shortly afterward:

“And sacrifice praise from leaven” (Amos IV).

He offers praise from leaven who prepares a sacrifice to God from plunder.

Wild lettuce is exceedingly bitter. The lamb’s flesh is therefore to be eaten with wild lettuce so that, when we receive the body of our Redeemer, we may afflict ourselves in tears for our sins, so that the very bitterness of repentance may wipe from the stomach of the mind the perverse love of this life.

Here it is also added:

“You shall not eat anything from it raw, nor boiled in water.”

Now the very words of the historical account no longer repel historical understanding. Did that Israelite people, while in Egypt, ordinarily eat a lamb raw, so that the Law had to say to them, “You shall not eat anything from it raw”? It adds, “nor boiled in water.”

But what does water signify except human knowledge? In accordance with what is said through Solomon in the voice of heretics: “Stolen waters are sweeter” (Prov. IX).

What does the raw flesh of the lamb signify except his humanity, thoughtlessly and irreverently rejected? For everything that we contemplate carefully, we cook in the mind. But the lamb’s flesh must be eaten neither raw nor boiled in water, because our Redeemer must neither be regarded as merely a man nor be considered, through human wisdom, in terms of how God could have become incarnate.

Whoever believes our Redeemer to be merely a man eats nothing other than the lamb’s raw flesh, since he has been unwilling to cook it through an understanding of his divinity. Whoever attempts to examine the mysteries of his incarnation according to human wisdom wishes to cook the lamb’s flesh in water; that is, he wishes to penetrate the mystery of the divine dispensation through a disordered form of knowledge.

Therefore, whoever desires to celebrate the solemnity of paschal joy must neither cook the lamb in water nor eat it raw. He must neither seek to penetrate the depth of his incarnation through human wisdom nor believe in him as though he were merely a man. Rather, he must eat the flesh roasted by fire, so that he may know that all things are ordered through the power of the Holy Spirit.

Of this it is rightly added:

“You shall eat its head with its feet and its entrails.”

Why is our Redeemer Alpha and Omega (Rev. I)? He is God before the ages and man at the end of the ages. To eat the head of the lamb is to receive his divinity through faith. To eat the feet of the lamb is to pursue the traces of his humanity with love and imitation.

But what are the entrails except his hidden and mystical commandments? We eat them when we receive the words of life eagerly. In this word “devouring,” what else is condemned than the sluggishness of our laziness? We neither seek his words and mysteries for ourselves nor listen willingly when they are spoken by others.

“Nothing of it shall remain until morning,” because his words must be examined with great diligence, so that before the day of resurrection appears, all his commandments may be penetrated through understanding and practice during the calling of this present life.

But since it is exceedingly difficult for all the Lamb’s discourse to be understood and all his mystery to be penetrated, it is rightly added:

“If anything remains, you shall burn it with fire.”

We burn with fire what remains of the lamb when we humbly reserve for the power of the Holy Spirit whatever we cannot understand and penetrate concerning the mystery of his incarnation. No one should presumptuously dare either to despise or to denounce what he does not understand; rather, he hands it over to the fire when he reserves it for the Holy Spirit.

Since, then, we have learned how the Passover is to be eaten, let us now recognize how it ought to be eaten. It follows:

“You shall eat it in this manner: you shall gird your loins.”

What is understood by the kidneys except the pleasure of the flesh? Hence the Psalmist also petitions, saying: “That our kidneys…” (Ps. XXVI). For if he had not known that the pleasure of lust resides in the kidneys, he would not have asked that they be burned.

Because the devil’s power has prevailed especially through lust over the human race, the Lord’s voice says of him: “His strength is in his loins” (Job XXXVIII).

Whoever therefore eats the Passover ought to have his loins girded, so that one who celebrates the solemnity of resurrection and incorruption may no longer be subject to corruption through vices, but may subdue pleasures and restrain the flesh from lust. For whoever is still subject through lack of self-control to the corruption of the flesh has not understood the solemnity of incorruption.

These things are harsh to some, but the gate that leads to life is narrow, and we already have many examples of those who practiced self-restraint.

“You shall have sandals on your feet.”

For what are our feet except our works? And what are sandals except the skins of dead animals? Sandals protect the feet. What are the dead animals from whose skins our feet are protected except the ancient Fathers who preceded us to the heavenly homeland? When we behold their examples, we protect the feet of our own works.

To have sandals on one’s feet is therefore to contemplate the life of the dead and to guard one’s footsteps from the wound of sin.

“Hold staffs in your hands.”

What does the Law signify by a staff except pastoral guardianship? It should be noted that we are first commanded to gird our loins and afterward to hold staffs, because those should undertake pastoral care who already know how to subdue the fluids of lust in their own bodies. Thus, when they preach strength to others, they themselves do not collapse weakly before soft desires.

It is rightly added:

“And you shall eat in haste.”

The word “in haste” admonishes us to learn with haste the commandments of God, the mysteries of the Redeemer, and the joys of the heavenly Father, and to strive with haste to fulfill the precepts of life. For although we know that today we are still permitted to act well, we do not know whether we shall be permitted to do so tomorrow.

Let us therefore eat the Passover in haste—that is, let us yearn eagerly for the solemnity of the heavenly homeland. Let no one grow sluggish on the journey of this life, lest he lose his place in the homeland.

For Christ is our Passover, as Paul testifies when he says: “For Christ our Passover has been sacrificed” (1 Cor. V).

As for what follows, “He executed judgment against their gods,” the Hebrews assert that on the night when the people departed, all the temples in Egypt were destroyed, either by an earthquake or by flashes of lightning.

Spiritually, however, we say that, when those departing from Egypt go forth, the idols of error fall and every form of worship belonging to perverse doctrines is shaken.

“The blood shall be for you as a sign in the houses in which you are. I shall see the blood and pass over you, and there shall be no plague among you to destroy you when I strike the land of Egypt.”

The blood of Christ is a sign for believers, so that the destroyer may not harm them, because for Christians the memory of Christ’s passion is the greatest protection against enemies.

The command that this same blood, applied with a bundle of hyssop, be sprinkled on the lintel and on both doorposts signifies that we must celebrate the sacrament of Christ’s passion according to the Catholic faith.

Hyssop is a plant with humble roots, clinging to rock and suitable for cleansing the lungs. So too the faith of Christ—which the Lord himself compares in the Gospel to a mustard seed (Matt. XIII)—when received with humble devotion and firmly retained in the heart, purifies and cleanses all the inward affections of the soul and makes a person fit for the heavenly sacraments.

“You shall keep this day as a memorial and celebrate it as a solemn feast to the Lord throughout your generations, as an everlasting observance.”

(From Augustine.) What is written, “And you shall make this day a fixed observance for your generations, everlasting”—or “eternal,” which in Greek is called αἰώνιον—must not be understood as though any of these passing days could itself be eternal. Rather, that is eternal which this day signifies, just as when we call God himself eternal, we do not thereby call these two syllables “eternal,” but what they signify.

Nevertheless, one must carefully investigate how Scripture customarily calls something eternal, lest perhaps it has called it solemnly eternal because they would consider it impious to omit it or change it of their own accord.

One thing is commanded to continue until it has been performed as prescribed, as when the ark was commanded to circle the walls of Jericho seven times. Another thing is commanded to be observed in such a way that no limit is set for the observance—whether solemnly every day, every month, or every year, or at fixed intervals of many or of certain years.

Either, therefore, it called it eternal because they should not dare to cease celebrating it of their own accord; or, as I have said, the signs themselves are not to be understood as eternal, but rather the realities signified by them.

“You shall eat unleavened bread for seven days. On the first day there shall be no leaven in your houses. Whoever eats anything leavened, that person shall perish from Israel, from the first day to the seventh day.”

What does the command that those who are going to celebrate Passover eat unleavened bread for seven days signify except that all who celebrate in true faith the mysteries of Christ’s passion and resurrection ought to lead the whole of the present life—which unfolds under the number seven days—without the leaven of malice and wickedness, entirely undefiled?

Hence it follows:

“The first day,” he says, “shall be holy and solemn, and the seventh day shall be honored with the same festival. You shall do no work on them, except what pertains to eating, and you shall observe the unleavened bread.”

He calls the first day the beginning of faith and the seventh day the end of the present life. The whole period of the present life ought to be kept as a festival by true Israelites—that is, honored in the mystery of Christ’s passion and resurrection. They are to do no work in it except what pertains to eating, because they are not permitted to labor in the desire for the world or in the work of sins, but must continually toil in meditation on the Holy Scriptures and in good works by which they prepare eternal nourishment in heaven for the saints.

Hence it follows:

“From the first month, from the fourteenth day of the month toward evening, you shall eat unleavened bread until the twenty-first day of the same month toward evening.”

What does the evening of the fourteenth day of the first month, on which Passover was celebrated and the sacrifice of the lamb completed, signify except the laying aside of the old man and the beginning of a new way of life, which begins in baptism, where Christ’s death is represented?

Hence the Apostle also says:

“All of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death. We were buried with him through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life” (Rom. VI).

Therefore, from the evening of the fourteenth day of the first month, for a complete week—that is, throughout the whole week—we are commanded to eat unleavened bread, because from the reception of holy baptism until the end of life we ought to live simply and without deceit.

Hence Peter also says:

“Having put aside all malice and all deceit, hypocrisy, envy, and every kind of slander, like newborn infants, desire the rational milk without deceit, so that by it you may grow toward salvation.”

It follows:

“Whoever eats anything leavened, his soul shall perish from Israel, both the stranger and the native of the land.”

For plainly everyone who lives deceitfully, and who, polluted by erroneous teaching, brings the present life to its end, will then be separated from the assembly of the saints and punished with everlasting torments without end; he will perish eternally.

And the people, bowing down, worshiped. The children of Israel departed and did as the Lord had commanded Moses and Aaron.

The Passover takes place in the slaughter of the lamb; Christ is killed, of whom it is said in the Gospel: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John II).

The lamb is sacrificed in the evening; at the evening of the world, Christ suffered.

Those who celebrate Passover are forbidden to break the bones; the Lord’s bones are not broken on the cross, as the evangelist testifies when he says: “You shall not break any of his bones.”

The doorposts of the Israelites are smeared with the lamb’s blood so that the destroying angel may not dare to bring ruin. The faithful people are marked on their foreheads with the sign of the Lord’s passion for the protection of salvation, so that only those who have been marked in heart and on forehead with the blood of the Lord’s passion may be freed from destruction. They also proclaim through their deeds: “The light of your countenance has been marked upon us, O Lord” (Ps. IV).

Hence this solemnity is called *phase*, which we may call “passing-over,” because, as we proceed from worse things to better, we abandon the darkness of Egypt.

## CHAPTER XXIV. The Lord’s Passing-Over through the Land of Egypt at Midnight, and the Slaughter of the Firstborn

It happened at midnight that the Lord struck every firstborn in the land of Egypt, from the firstborn of Pharaoh who sat upon his throne to the firstborn of the captive woman who was in prison, and every firstborn of the beasts. Pharaoh rose during the night, together with all his servants and all Egypt; and a great cry arose in Egypt, for there was no house in which someone dead did not lie (Exod. XII).

“It says that a great cry arose in the land of Egypt, for there had not been a house in which someone dead did not lie. Could there not have been some house that had no firstborn?”

(From Augustine.) Since only the firstborn were dying, how was there no house that did not have a dead person? Or had God’s foreknowledge also arranged this, so that absolutely every house would have firstborn children who could be struck among the Egyptians?

Certainly, the Egyptians living in the land of Goshen should not be thought to have been exempt from this plague. The plague concerned people or animals, not the land: human beings and animals who were firstborn died through a hidden, angelic stroke. Nothing had happened in heaven or on earth, as with the frogs, locusts, or darkness, by which those who lived there would be afflicted. Since the land of Goshen had been free from such plagues, the benefit would undoubtedly have extended to those Egyptians who lived in that same land with the Hebrews. But in the case of the firstborn, all were struck.

The children of Israel did as Moses had commanded them, and they asked the Egyptians for vessels of gold and silver and clothing. The Lord granted his people favor in the sight of the Egyptians; they lent them these things, and the Israelites despoiled the Egyptians.

This had already happened before the deaths of the Egyptians’ firstborn, but it is now repeated by recapitulation. The narrative already recorded when it happened. For how could this now have occurred, so that amid such mourning over the deaths of their own people the Egyptians would lend these things to the children of Israel?
