Unless someone should perhaps say that the Egyptians who lived in the land of Goshen with the Hebrews were not struck by this plague either.

(From Isidore.) What did these things prefigure except that in the gold, silver, and clothing of the Egyptians certain forms of learning are signified—forms of learning acquired from the customs of the nations through useful study?

Or perhaps they signify this: precious souls from the nations themselves, like vessels of gold and silver, together with their own bodies, which the clothing signifies, join themselves to the people of God, so that together they may be liberated from this world as from Egypt.

Then the people took the kneaded dough before it was leavened, tied it up in their cloaks, and placed it upon their shoulders.

The statement that the children of Israel departed from Egypt with the leaven removed signifies that we too must strive with all our strength, if possible, to leave behind the allurements of this world and not walk in the leaven of the old malice and wickedness, but in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth, which is the conduct of the new man, having left behind the old man with his vices.

Since, from the beginning of the Book of Exodus, we have described the growth of the Israelite people in Egypt and the plagues inflicted upon the Egyptians because of their disobedience, and have brought the first book as far as the celebration of the typological Passover, we rightly judge that the beginning of the following book should commence with the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt.

# BOOK TWO

## PREFACE

All Scripture established by divine inspiration, according to the Apostle’s statement (2 Tim. III), is useful for teaching, for refutation, for correction, and for instruction in righteousness.

Therefore, whoever diligently meditates upon it and examines it inwardly finds in its wording a pleasing lesson, in its meaning a wholesome counsel, and in its mystery a venerable sacrament.

For the historical meaning of the divine books alone is not sufficient for readers. They must also carefully consider what the prophetic discourse wishes to suggest to them through allegory.

Thus, in the present book, when through the historical account we hear that the Egyptians deserved just punishment because of the cruelty they exercised against the children of Israel and because of the disobedience by which they opposed the divine command, we ought to reflect upon the liberation of those Israelites from spiritual Egypt and their entry into the land of promise, where each of the faithful receives spiritual milk and honey in sufficient measure.

We ought also to reflect upon the powerful slaughter of spiritual enemies in the waters of baptism, accomplished by the hand of almighty God, so that, instructed by all these things, we may at the same time be prepared for every good work.

After the commemoration of Passover, there follows a discourse on the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt, introduced as follows.

## CHAPTER ONE. The Departure of the Children of Israel from Egypt, from Rameses to Succoth, Their First Encampment; and the Rite of Passover Explained There by Moses
The children of Israel set out from Ramesse for Succoth, about six hundred thousand foot soldiers, apart from children and women; and a mixed multitude of innumerable people also went up with them (Exod. XII).

*(From Ambrose. [Col. 0056B])* It is clear that human beings are signified, whether among the male servants, the women, or those ages that were not fit for military service, so that we should understand the six hundred thousand foot soldiers as referring only to those who could be armed for a military march.

It is commonly asked whether the Hebrews could have reached so large a number during those years in Egypt. For the text says later:

“Now the dwelling of the children of Israel, during which they dwelt in Egypt, was four hundred and thirty years. And when these were completed, on that very day the whole army of the Lord went out from the land of Egypt.”

For anyone who examines the sacred Scriptures carefully will not find so many years between Jacob’s entry into Egypt and the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt. Accordingly, the calculation followed by Eusebius in the *Chronicle* of his history is plainly founded upon the truth. He calculates the four hundred and thirty years from that promise by which God called Abraham to leave his own land and go to the land of Canaan. For the Apostle too, when he praised and commended Abraham’s faith, referred to that promise in which he wishes Christ to be understood as the one foretold by the prophets—that is, the promise in which God promised Abraham that all the tribes of the earth would be blessed in him.

“This I say,” he writes, “because the law, which was made four hundred and thirty years afterward, does not annul the covenant confirmed by God, so as to abolish the promises” (Gal. III).

Thus the Apostle says that the law was made four hundred and thirty years after the promise by which Abraham was called and believed God, not from the time when Jacob entered Egypt. Moreover, the very text of Exodus sufficiently indicates this. It does not say, “The sojourning of the children of Israel, during which they sojourned in the land of Egypt, was four hundred and thirty years,” but says plainly: “during which they sojourned in the land of Egypt and Canaan, they and their fathers” [Col. 0056C–0057A].

It is therefore clear that the time of the patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob must also be included in the calculation, from the time when Abraham began to sojourn in the land of Canaan—that is, from the promise in which the Apostle praises his faith—up to the time when Israel entered Egypt. Throughout all this period the fathers sojourned in the land of Canaan, and afterward Israel’s descendants in Egypt; thus the four hundred and thirty years were completed, from the promise until Israel’s departure from Egypt, when the law was given on Mount Sinai, a law that does not annul the covenant so as to abolish the promises.

In the seventy-fifth year of his life, as Scripture says (Acts VII), Abraham went out into the land of Canaan, and he fathered Isaac when he was one hundred years old [Col. 0057B]. Thus twenty-five years elapsed from the promise until Isaac’s birth. To these are added all the years of Abraham’s life, namely, one hundred and eighty, making two hundred and five; at that time Jacob was one hundred and twenty years old. For the twins, Jacob and Esau, were born when their father was sixty. Ten years later Jacob entered Egypt, when he was one hundred and thirty years old, while Joseph was thirty-nine.

Thus, from the promise until Jacob’s entry into Egypt, there were two hundred and fifteen years. Joseph then lived seventy-one years from that thirty-ninth year of his life, in which his father found him in Egypt, since the total length of his life was one hundred and ten years. When these seventy-one years are added to the two hundred and fifteen, the total is two hundred and eighty-six years [Col. 0057C].

There remain one hundred and forty-four or forty-five years, during which the people of Israel are understood to have served in Egypt after Joseph’s death. If one considers how greatly they could have multiplied during these years through human fertility, with the assistance of him who wished them to multiply exceedingly, it is found not to be surprising that the people departed from Egypt as six hundred thousand foot soldiers, apart from the accompanying household, which included servants, women, and the weak in age.

Therefore, when God said to Abraham, “Know for certain that your seed will be a sojourner in a land not its own; and they will reduce them to slavery and afflict them for four hundred years” (Gen. XV), this must not be understood as though God’s people were subjected to that harsh slavery for four hundred years. Rather, since it is written, “In Isaac shall your seed be called” (Gen. XXI), four hundred and five years are counted from the year of Isaac’s birth until the year of the departure from Egypt [Col. 0057D].

When, then, one subtracts the twenty-five years from the four hundred and thirty—the period from the promise until Isaac’s birth—it is not surprising that Scripture wished to call the four hundred and five years, in round terms, four hundred years, since it commonly names periods in such a way that what slightly exceeds or falls short of a more complete number is not counted.

Thus the statement, “They will reduce them to slavery and afflict them for four hundred years,” should not be referred to the idea that they were held in slavery for that entire period. Rather, the four hundred years should be referred to the statement, “Your seed will be a sojourner in a land not its own.” For whether in the land of Canaan or in Egypt, that seed was a sojourner before it received as an inheritance what had been promised by God, which happened after they had been freed from Egypt.

A hyperbaton should therefore be understood here, and the order of the words should be: “Know for certain that your seed will be a sojourner in a land not its own for four hundred years.” The intervening words—“And they will reduce them to slavery and afflict them”—should be understood as an insertion, so that this insertion does not belong to the four hundred years. For it was at the end of this total period of years, that is, after Joseph’s death, that the people of God underwent harsh slavery in Egypt.

And the Lord said to Moses and Aaron:

“This is the ordinance of the Passover: No foreigner shall eat of it. But every purchased servant shall be circumcised, and then he may eat. The sojourner and the hired worker shall not eat of it” [Col. 0058A–B].

By “foreigner” he means a Gentile who has not yet been reborn through holy baptism. To such a person the Lord’s body and blood must in no way be given, because just as he is outside the religious observance, so he must also be outside the communion.

But he commands that the purchased servant be circumcised, so that he may be permitted to eat the Passover. What is a purchased servant except one who has been bought at the price of Christ’s blood? Such a person must first be circumcised—not with the circumcision of the flesh, but of the heart—and then eat the body of the spotless Lamb.

For the Apostle Peter says to such people:

“Gird up the loins of your mind; be sober; hope perfectly in the grace that is being offered to you in the revelation of Jesus Christ” (1 Pet. I).

And shortly afterward:

“Knowing that you were not redeemed from your futile way of life inherited from your fathers with perishable things, with gold or silver, but with the precious blood, as of a spotless and undefiled lamb, Christ. He was foreknown before the foundation of the world, but was manifested in the last times for your sake, who through him are faithful in God, who raised him from the dead and gave him glory, so that your faith and hope might be in God. Purifying your souls in obedience to charity, in brotherly love, love one another more earnestly from a simple heart, having been born again not from perishable seed but imperishable, through the word of the living and abiding God” (ibid.).

The sojourner and the hired worker likewise cannot eat the Passover. Who is the sojourner except one who has recently come to the faith and is not yet firm in the Catholic religion? The hired worker, however, is one who labors only for earthly profits and seeks no future reward [Col. 0058C].

Such people are certainly not worthy to receive Christ’s body, because either they do not firmly believe in him or truly love him; and for that reason they are unworthy to share in him.

The text continues:

“It shall be eaten in one house. You shall not carry any of its flesh outside, and you shall not break any of its bones.”

The flesh of the lamb is commanded to be eaten in one house because the mystery of his passion is rightly celebrated in the one Catholic Church. Nor is it permitted to carry any of its flesh outside, because neither pagans, Jews, heretics, nor anyone at all who is outside the Church is admitted to this communion; their faith, teaching, and manner of life are foreign to the rule of ecclesiastical discipline.

“Nor,” he says, “shall you break any of its bones.”

The Evangelist John shows what this signifies when he recounts the Lord’s passion in his Gospel:

“Since it was the Preparation, so that the bodies might not remain upon the cross on the Sabbath—for that Sabbath was a great day—the Jews asked Pilate that their legs might be broken and they might be taken away. So the soldiers came and broke the legs of the first man who had been crucified with him, and of the other. But when they came to Jesus and saw that he was already dead, they did not break his legs; instead, one of the soldiers pierced his side with a spear, and immediately blood and water came out. He who saw it has borne witness, and his testimony is true; and he knows that he speaks the truth, so that you also may believe. For these things happened so that the Scripture might be fulfilled: ‘You shall not break a bone of him.’ And again another Scripture says: ‘They will look upon him whom they pierced’” (John XIX; Zech. XII) [Col. 0058D–0059B].

Alternatively: not breaking the bones of the lamb means, in the dispensation of Christ’s incarnation, not corrupting the strength of his divinity through blasphemy, because Christ is one, both God and man. Whoever says that Christ was born from the Virgin Mary as a mere man, and not as the true Christ, has broken the bones of the lamb.

“The whole assembly of the children of Israel shall do this. But if any foreigner wishes to join your settlement and to celebrate the Lord’s Passover, every male of his must first be circumcised, and then he shall celebrate it properly; and he shall be like a native of the land.”

This plainly means the following to true Israelites and to the ecclesiastical people who celebrate the true Passover: If any unbeliever, an outsider to Christian worship, wishes to join this communion, he must first strip off the old man with his deeds and put on the new man, who has been created according to God in righteousness and the holiness of truth [Col. 0059C].

Thus he will worthily be joined to the heavenly guests and will properly partake of spiritual banquets.

“There shall be one law for the native and for the settler who sojourns among you.”

For God is not a respecter of persons, but in every nation whoever fears God and practices righteousness is acceptable to him. There is no distinction between Jew and Gentile, slave and free, but Christ is all and in all (Acts X).

And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying:

“Sanctify to me every firstborn that opens the womb among the children of Israel, both of human beings and of animals; for all are mine” (Exod. XIII), and so forth [Col. 0059D].

Through Moses, the Lord commends to the people the remembrance of their deliverance and of the slaughter of the Egyptians, so that they might know themselves obligated to offer to the Lord their firstborn and the firstborn of their animals. In delivering them, he had destroyed all the firstborn of the Egyptians.

Accordingly, the people themselves will say later:

“The Lord killed every firstborn in the land of Egypt, from the firstborn of man to the firstborn of animals. Therefore I sacrifice to the Lord everything that opens the womb of the male sex, and I redeem all the firstborn of my sons at a price” (Exod. XV).

Mystically, however, we offer our firstborn to the Lord when we sanctify to him the beginnings of our works. Whatever proceeds from the womb of good will and good thought into the open expression of sound speech [Col. 0060A] and good action rightly belongs to the Lord, who himself has given the will and the ability to accomplish according to his good pleasure.

“Whatever you have that is male, you shall consecrate to the Lord. You shall exchange the firstborn of a donkey for a sheep. But if you do not redeem it, you shall kill it.”

Every male firstborn—that is, every manly and perfect work—we ought to apply to divine grace, not to ourselves. Whatever is feminine, soft, and weak in our conduct, we ought to attribute to our weakness, not to the Lord.

*(From Gregory.)* What is signified by a donkey except impurity, and what by a sheep except innocence? To exchange the firstborn of a donkey for a sheep is to convert the beginnings of an impure life to the simplicity of innocence, so that after the sinner has done those things that are impure and rejected by the Lord, he may now bring forth by his actions those things that can be placed upon God’s altar [Col. 0060B].

For all human beings are born in sins, conceived through the pleasure of the flesh, and have drawn the origin of guilt along with them. Hence it comes about that we become entangled in sins even through our own will.

But whoever converts the malice of the flesh to innocence of heart exchanges the firstborn of a donkey for a sheep, because he converts the impurity of his former life to innocence. Whoever ceases to be what he formerly was and, having taken hold of purity of the flesh, preserves innocence has exchanged the firstborn of a donkey for a sheep in God’s offering.

“It shall therefore be like a sign in your hand and like something hanging before your eyes as a reminder, because the Lord brought you out of Egypt with a strong hand.”

*(From Augustine.)* What does the statement mean, when he was giving the commandment concerning the Passover, “It shall be for you like a sign in your hand”—or, according to other copies, “upon your hand”? Is it to be understood as referring to your works, that is, as something you should place above your works?

The Passover, because of the slaughter of the sheep, pertains to the faith of Christ and to the blood by which we were redeemed. This faith must be placed above works, so that it may be, as it were, upon the hand, in opposition to those who gloried in the works of the law.

The Apostle speaks about this matter and works hard to place faith before works, so that good works may depend upon it and be preceded by it, rather than faith itself appearing to be repaid as though it were merited by good works. Faith belongs to grace.

“But if it is by grace, it is no longer from works; otherwise grace is no longer grace” (Rom. XI).

When Pharaoh had sent out the people, the Lord did not lead them by the road through the land of the Philistines, which was nearby, thinking that they might perhaps regret their departure if they saw war rising against them and return to Egypt. Instead, he led them around by the road of the wilderness, which is beside the Red Sea.

*(From Gregory.)* This shows that everything that can rightly be done by prudent counsel ought to be done in order to avoid what is adverse, even when God is most openly our helper.

Often converts, who at the very entrance and beginning of their conversion receive either the most peaceful tranquility of the flesh, or gifts of prophecy, or teachings of doctrine, or miracles of signs, or the grace of healing, are afterward wearied by severe trials of temptation. When they were beginning, they believed themselves entirely free from such temptations. This is done by divine providential arrangement, so that they are not touched by the harshness of temptation at the beginning of their conversion. For if the bitterness of temptation met them at the outset, they might easily return to what they had left behind; and they had not yet gone far from those things, since, when first tempted by vices lying close at hand, they are drawn back.

Hence it is written:

“When Pharaoh had sent out the people, the Lord did not lead them by the road through the land of the Philistines, which was nearby, thinking that he might perhaps regret it if he saw war rising against him and return to Egypt.”

Therefore, when those who are leaving Egypt first set out, nearby wars are taken away from them, because those who are abandoning the world are initially shown a certain tranquility, lest, disturbed in their tenderness and at the beginning of their journey, they become frightened and return to what they escaped.

First they experience the sweetness of security; first they are nourished by peace. After they have come to know that sweetness, they endure the contests of temptation all the more readily, the more deeply they have come to know God.

“And the children of Israel went up armed from the land of Egypt.”

*(From Jerome.)* Aquila, who interprets the word word-for-word—not, as some think, contentiously, but more carefully—translated the passage where the Septuagint reads, “In the fifth generation the children of Israel went up from the land of Egypt,” as follows: “And the children of Israel went up armed from the land of Egypt.”

Although, because of the ambiguity of the Greek expression, what we have rendered “armed” may be understood as “equipped” or “provided,” on account of the possessions with which they had despoiled the Egyptians, nevertheless, where the Septuagint has “in the fifth generation,” those who have carefully examined the books of the Hebrews assert that the text says not “in the fifth generation” but simply “fifth.” The sense would therefore be something like: “Fifth, the children of Israel went up from the land of Egypt.” Because this seemed difficult to understand, the word “generation” was added.

All Judea loudly proclaims that Aquila translated accurately both elsewhere and especially in this passage, and all the benches of the synagogues resound with the same testimony.

But if someone wishes to know, according to the Septuagint, how the children of Israel went up from Egypt “in the fifth generation,” this must be calculated through their generations: that is, from Jacob himself, who entered Egypt, to Moses, who went out with the people, five generations are counted, as some maintain. Jacob is found to be the first, Levi the second, Kohath the third, Amram the fourth, and Moses the fifth [Col. 0061C–D].

The Latin translator calls these descendants *progenies*, which the Greeks call γενεὰς (*geneas*), and which are called “generations” in the Gospel. They are counted only through the succession of persons, not by the number of years.

Others, however, count not from Jacob through Levi to Moses, but through the tribe of Judah, which was the royal tribe. Thus, from Perez, the son of Judah, who entered Egypt with his father Judah, to Salmon, who entered the promised land as leader of that tribe, there are five generations:

Perez fathered Hezron; Hezron fathered Aram; Aram fathered Amminadab; Amminadab fathered Nahshon; and Nahshon fathered Salmon.

## CHAPTER II

Concerning the second encampment, namely from Succoth to Etham, and concerning the pillar of cloud and fire [Col. 0062A].

Having departed from Succoth, they encamped at Etham, at the farthest boundaries of the wilderness. The Lord went before them by day in a pillar of cloud to show them the way, and by night in a pillar of fire, so that he might be their guide on the journey at both times. The pillar of cloud by day and the pillar of fire by night never failed to remain before the people.

And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying:

“Speak to the children of Israel: Let them turn back and encamp opposite Pi-hahiroth, which is between Migdol and the sea, opposite Baal-zephon. You shall encamp in its sight beside the sea” (Exod. XIII).

From Ramesse, which is interpreted as “the movement of the moth” or “of thunder,” they came, he says, to Succoth [Col. 0062B]. The interpreters of names report that among the Hebrews Succoth means “tents.”

*(From Origen.)* When, therefore, warned by the voice of the Gospel, you abandon Egypt, shake off from yourself the moths of every corruption, and reject the impulses of vices, you will dwell in tents. You will dwell in tents from which we do not wish to be stripped, but rather clothed upon. Dwelling in tents indicates that the one who hastens toward God is unencumbered and free from every impediment.

Yet one must not remain even there. The journey must be pressed forward; the camp must be moved from Succoth as well, and one must hasten to reach Etham.

Etham, or Othon, is said to be translated into our language as “strength” or “his signs.” And rightly so. Here you hear that God went before them by day in a pillar of cloud and by night in a pillar of fire. You do not find this happening at Ramesse, nor at Succoth, which is called the second encampment of those setting out. Rather, this is the third encampment, where divine signs occur.

Recall what was read above, when Moses said to Pharaoh:

“We shall go three days’ journey into the wilderness, and sacrifice to the Lord our God.”

This, then, was the three-day period toward which Moses was hastening, while Pharaoh opposed him. For Pharaoh said to them: “Do not go farther.” Pharaoh did not permit the children of Israel to reach the place of signs; he did not permit them to proceed far enough to enjoy the mysteries of the third day.

Listen to what the prophet says:

“He will revive us after two days; on the third day he will raise us up, and we shall live in his presence” (Hos. III) [Col. 0062C–D].

The first day for us is the Savior’s passion; the second is when he descended into the underworld; the third is the day of resurrection. Therefore, on the third day, God went before them by faith in a pillar of cloud, and by night in a pillar of fire.

If, in accordance with what we said above, the Apostle rightly teaches us that the mysteries of baptism are contained in these words, it is necessary that those who are baptized into Christ be baptized into his death, be buried with him, and rise with him from the dead on the third day. According to what the Apostle says, he also raised them together with himself and made them sit together in the heavenly places.

When, therefore, the mystery of the third day has been received by you, God will begin to lead you, and thereafter he himself will show you the way of salvation.

But let us see what is said next to Moses and what road is commanded to be chosen:

“Let them turn back,” he says, “and encamp opposite Pi-hahiroth,” and so forth.

At the Lord’s command, the children of Israel turned back from Etham and encamped opposite Pi-hahiroth, which is between Migdol and the sea, opposite Baal-zephon; they set up camp beside the sea.

Pi-hahiroth means “the mouth of nobles”; Migdol means “tower”; Baal-zephon means “Lord of the north” [Col. 0063A]. It is fitting that, instructed by the mouth of teachers, you ascend the tower of virtues and remember that you must always fight against the Lord of the north—that is, the devil, prince of the unbelieving.

According to another edition, the passage is read as follows:

“From Othon,” he says, “turn back and travel between Epauleum and Migdol, which is opposite Baal-zephon.”

These names are interpreted as follows: Epauleum means “a winding ascent”; Migdol means “tower”; Baal-zephon means “an ascent of a watchtower” or “having a watchtower” [Col. 0063B].

Perhaps you believed that the road shown by the Lord would be level and smooth, with no difficulty or labor at all. It is an ascent, and a winding ascent. The road by which one travels toward virtue is not a downhill path but an ascent.

Hear also the Lord saying in the Gospel:

“How narrow and constricted is the way that leads to life” (Matt. VII).

There is therefore a road on which they travel: a winding ascent, and an ascent of a watchtower, or one having a watchtower. The ascent pertains to actions, the watchtower to faith. He shows, therefore, that there is much difficulty and much labor both in actions and in faith. For many temptations confront us, and many stumbling blocks confront those wishing to undertake certain actions. Then, in faith, you will find many winding paths, very many questions, many objections of heretics, and many contradictions of unbelievers. This road must be travelled by those who follow God; but there is also a tower on this road. What is this tower? Surely the one of which he spoke in the Gospel. For he says:

“Which of you, wishing to build a tower, will not first sit down and calculate the cost, whether he has enough to complete it?” (Luke XIV).

*(From Isidore.)* This, then, is the tower: the lofty and elevated seat of virtues.

Already the Lord is seen at night in a pillar of fire and by day in a pillar of cloud, going before the people and becoming their guide on the journey. This cloud going before them is Christ. He is also the pillar, because he is upright and firm and supports our weakness; shining by night and not shining by day, so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind [Col. 0063C].

The sacrament of Christ may also appropriately be understood as present in the terror of night, because at that time there will be a great tribulation of the world, like fire: it will shine for the righteous and burn the unrighteous.

Again, a careful examination of this pillar of fire and cloud permits another interpretation. What does it mean that the pillar of cloud, which went before the people in the wilderness, shone with the brilliance of fire not by day but by night, except that our Redeemer, offering guidance to those who follow him through the example of his conduct, shone with no light for those who trusted in their own righteousness, but kindled the fires of his love in those who acknowledged the darkness of their sins?

The text continues:

“And Pharaoh will say concerning the children of Israel: ‘They are confined in the land; the wilderness has shut them in.’ And I will harden his heart, and he will pursue you,” and so forth.

The journey of life is not undertaken without the waves of temptations, as the Apostle says:

“All who wish to live piously in Christ suffer persecution” (2 Tim. III).

When Pharaoh brings persecutions and confines a Christian through tribulations, he thinks that he can quickly overthrow him from the faith. But if, following Moses—that is, the law of God—you undertake this journey, the Egyptian will indeed pursue and harass you.

But see what happens:

“The angel of the Lord, who went before the camp of Israel, lifted himself up and went behind them; and together with him the pillar of cloud, leaving its former position, stood behind them between the camp of the Egyptians and that of the Israelites.”

This pillar of cloud becomes a wall for the people of God, but imposes darkness and gloom upon the Egyptians. The pillar of fire is not transferred to the Egyptians so that they may see the light. They remain in darkness because they loved darkness more than light.

You too, therefore, if you withdraw from the Egyptians and flee the power of demons, see how many divine aids are prepared for you; see how many helpers you employ. Only remain strong in faith. Do not let the Egyptian cavalry and chariots frighten you, and do not complain against Moses—that is, against the law of God—and say as some of them said:

“Were there no graves in Egypt, that you brought us out to die in this wilderness? It would have been better for us to serve the Egyptians than to die in this wilderness.”

These are the words of a spirit growing weary in temptation. But who is so blessed that he can pass through the weight of temptations in such a way that no thought of uncertainty steals into his mind?

Consider what the Lord says to that great foundation of the Church and most solid rock upon which Christ founded the Church:

“O you of little faith, why did you doubt?” (Matt. XIV).

Nevertheless, since they say, “It would have been better for us to serve the Egyptians than to die in the wilderness,” these words are expressions of temptation and weakness. Otherwise the statement is false, for it is far better to die in the wilderness than to serve the Egyptians.

Whoever dies in the wilderness, by the very fact that he has been separated from the Egyptians, departed from the rulers of darkness, and escaped from Satan’s power, has made some progress, even if he was unable to reach perfection.

For whoever seeks the perfect life is better off dying on the journey [Col. 0064D] than never setting out at all to seek perfection.

Hence the opinion of those who, while describing the road of virtue as excessively arduous and enumerating its many difficulties, dangers, and falls, conclude that it should not even be undertaken or begun, appears to be mistaken.

It is far better, even if necessary, to die on this journey than to remain among the Egyptians, be killed, and be overwhelmed by false and bitter waves.

## CHAPTER III

Concerning the passage of the children of Israel to the Red Sea and the drowning of the Egyptians in the waters [Col. 0065A].

And Moses said to the people:

“Do not be afraid. Stand firm and see the great deeds of the Lord that he will accomplish today. For the Egyptians whom you see now, you will never see again forever,” and so forth (Exod. XIV).

*(From Augustine.)* How should these words be understood, since the Israelites later saw the Egyptians? Is it because those who saw them at that time did not see them again, since both those who were pursuing them died and all these Israelites died, each on the day of his own death? Their descendants, however, saw the descendants of the Egyptians.

Or should “you will not see them as you see them today” be understood to mean: not as you see them today, pursuing you and coming after you in such a great multitude that there is no question at all? Nor is there any difficulty concerning the eternal time mentioned here, since even if they will see one another at the time of the resurrection, they will certainly not see one another as they do today.

*(From Origen.)* Meanwhile Moses cries out to the Lord. How does he cry out? No sound of his cry is heard, and yet God says to him, “Why are you crying out to me?” I would like to know how the saints cry out to the Lord without a voice.

The Apostle teaches (Gal. IV) that “God sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, ‘Abba, Father.’” And he adds: “The Spirit himself intercedes for us with inexpressible groanings.” Again he says (Rom. VIII): “He who searches hearts knows what the Spirit desires, because he intercedes for the saints according to God.”

Thus, when the Holy Spirit intercedes with God, the cry of the saints is heard through their silence [Col. 0065B].

And what follows? Moses is commanded to strike the sea with his staff, so that it may split open and give way to the people of God as they enter, and the elements may obey the divine will and serve it. The waters that had been feared become a wall on the right and left for God’s servants; they not only do no harm but also provide protection.

The text continues:

“When Moses had stretched out his hand over the sea, the Lord drove it back with a strong and burning wind throughout the whole night and turned it into dry land,” and so forth.

What is Moses stretching out his hand over the sea except the law alone, revealed through Scripture, showing that divine power has acted in the waters?

The Lord drove the sea back with a strong and burning wind—that wind of which it is said in the Psalms:

“With a mighty wind you will shatter the ships of Tarshish” (Ps. XLVII).

And it is written in the Acts of the Apostles that, while the disciples were reclining in the upper room on Zion on the day of Pentecost, “suddenly there came from heaven a sound as of a mighty wind, and it filled the whole house where they were sitting; and divided tongues appeared to them as of fire, and one rested upon each of them,” and so forth (Acts II) [Col. 0065C–D].

The Lord therefore drove back the sea with a strong and burning wind throughout the whole night and turned it into dry land, since throughout the whole period of this life, which is signified by night, the grace of the Holy Spirit makes the waters of baptism passable for believers. Through these waters they pass from spiritual Egypt into the promised land, while the army of their pursuing enemies is drowned in the same element.

The hour of the night at which this passage took place also fittingly corresponds to the divine mystery. For the text continues:

“The morning watch had come; and behold, the Lord, looking upon the camp of the Egyptians through the pillar of fire and cloud, killed their army and overturned the wheels of their chariots, and they were carried into the depths,” and so forth.

It was said above that the pillar of fire and cloud signified the Mediator himself between God and human beings: gentle toward the righteous, terrifying to sinners, supporting the godly and killing the ungodly.

Therefore, the morning watch, when our Savior, victorious over death, rose from the underworld and was resurrected in glory, is rightly the time at which it is said that the Lord, looking upon the camp of the Egyptians through the pillar of fire and cloud, killed their army.

He killed the army of the spiritual Egyptians together with the true Pharaoh when he submerged the devil and his satellites, together with all spiritual wickedness and the multitude of sinners, in the spiritual waters where believers, baptized in the likeness of his death, rise from the death of sins; and he condemned them to eternal destruction [Col. 0066A–B].

Nor will they be permitted thereafter to keep under their power the true Israelites who have been predestined to eternal life, because those whom divine foreknowledge predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified.

When the Egyptians were fleeing, the waters came against them, and the Lord overwhelmed them amid the waves. The waters returned and covered the chariots and all the horsemen of Pharaoh’s army, who had entered the sea in pursuit. Not even one of them survived. (From Origen.) For the wave is forced into a heap, and the water, driven back upon itself, bends; the liquid receives solidity, and the floor of the sea dries into dust. Understand the goodness of God the Creator: if you obey his will, if you follow his law, he compels even the elements to serve you against their own nature.

But the children of Israel went through the midst of the dry sea, and the waters were like a wall for them on their right and on their left. I have heard from the elders that, in this passage through the sea, separate divisions of water were made for each of the tribes of Israel, and that a distinct path was opened in the sea for every tribe. They demonstrated this from what is written in the Psalms: “He divided the Red Sea into divisions” (Psalm 135), by which several divisions are taught to have been made, not one only. Likewise, from the words, “There was Benjamin, the youngest, in ecstasy; the princes of Judah, their leaders; the princes of Zebulun, the princes of Naphtali” (Psalm 67), the separate entrance of each tribe also seems to be enumerated. I have considered it religiously appropriate not to remain silent about these things, as they were preserved by the elders in the divine Scriptures.

What, then, are we taught by these things that we have already discussed above? What is the Apostle’s meaning in them? He calls this baptism “completed in Moses in the cloud and in the sea,” so that you also, who are baptized in Christ in water and the Holy Spirit, may know that the Egyptians will afterward pursue you and try to bring you back into their service: namely, the rulers of this world and the spiritual forces of wickedness, whom you formerly served. They indeed try to pursue you, but you descend into the water and escape unharmed; after your sins have been washed away, you rise as a new person, ready to sing a new song.

But the Egyptians, pursuing you afterward, will be drowned in the abyss, even if they seem to ask Jesus not to send them into the abyss. Yet we can also derive another understanding from these things. If you flee Egypt, if you leave behind the darkness of ignorance and follow the law of God through Moses, but the sea confronts you and the waves of those who oppose you come against you, strike the resisting waves with the rod of Moses—that is, with the word of the law and the vigilance of the Scriptures. By disputing, open a path for yourself through your adversaries; immediately the waves will yield, and the defeated waters will give way to the victors, while those who shortly before opposed them will wonder, be astonished, and stand fixed in amazement.

With the legitimate lines of your arguments you will cut a straight path of faith, and you will advance so far by the word of teaching that your hearers, whom you have instructed with the rod of the law, will themselves now rise against the Egyptians like the waves of the sea. They will not merely attack them, but overcome and extinguish them.

They extinguish Egypt who do not perform the works of darkness. They extinguish Egypt who live not carnally but spiritually. They extinguish Egypt who either drive filthy and impure thoughts from their hearts or do not admit them at all, just as the Apostle says: “Taking up the shield of faith, so that you may be able to extinguish all the flaming arrows of the evil one” (Ephesians 6). In this way, even today we can see the Egyptians dead and lying on the shore, and their chariots and horses submerged. We can also see Pharaoh himself submerged, if we live with such faith that God swiftly crushes Satan beneath our feet, through Jesus Christ our Lord.

## CHAPTER IV. On the song that Moses and the children of Israel sang to the Lord after the crossing of the Red Sea

Then Moses and the children of Israel sang this song to the Lord and said:

> “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously exalted;  
> he has cast horse and rider into the sea” (Exodus 15).

(From Origen.) We read of many songs being found in the divine Scriptures. Yet this is the first of them all: after the Egyptians and Pharaoh had been drowned, the people of God sang it after their victory. It is indeed the custom of the saints, whenever the adversary is defeated, to offer God a hymn of thanksgiving, since they know that victory has been prepared not by their own strength but by God’s grace. As they sing the hymn, they also take up timbrels in their hands, as is reported concerning Mary, the sister of Moses and Aaron.

Therefore, if you too have crossed the Red Sea, if you have seen the Egyptians drowned and Pharaoh destroyed and cast into the depths of the abyss, you can sing a hymn to God; you can utter a voice of thanksgiving and say:

> “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously honored;  
> he has cast horse and rider into the sea.”

You say this better and more worthily if you have a timbrel in your hand—that is, if you have crucified your flesh with its vices and desires, and if you have put to death your members that are upon the earth. Yet let us see what he says: “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously glorified.”

As far as we are able to conjecture—for it seems to me that to be glorified is one thing and to be glorified gloriously another—it appears that there is a distinction. For when the Lord Jesus Christ assumed flesh from the Virgin for our salvation, he was indeed glorified, because he came to seek what had perished; yet he was not glorified gloriously. For it is said of him: “We saw him, and he had neither form nor beauty, and his appearance was dishonored among the sons of men” (Isaiah 23). He was glorified also when he came to the cross and endured death, but, so to speak, he was glorified humbly, not gloriously.

But since Christ had to suffer these things and thus enter into his glory, when he comes in the glory of the Father and of the holy angels, when he comes in his majesty to judge the earth, and when he will also destroy the true Pharaoh—that is, the devil—by the breath of his mouth; when he shines in the majesty of his Father, and after the coming of his humility reveals to us a second coming of glory, then the Lord is not merely glorified but glorified gloriously, when all glorify the Son just as they honor the Father.

> “He has cast horse and rider into the sea.  
> The Lord is my strength and my praise,  
> and he has become my salvation.”

The human beings who pursue us are horses; and, so to speak, all who have been born in the flesh are figuratively horses. But they have their riders. There are horses whom the Lord mounts, and they go throughout the whole earth. Concerning them it is said: “Your riding is salvation.” There are also horses who have the devil and his angels as riders.

Judas was a horse; but as long as he had the Lord as his rider, he belonged to the riding of salvation. Sent with the other apostles, he granted salvation to the sick and healing to the infirm. But when he submitted himself to the devil—for after the morsel Satan entered into him—Satan became his rider. Led by Satan’s reins, he began to ride against the Lord and our Savior.

All who persecute the saints are neighing horses; but they have riders who drive them—evil angels—and therefore they are fierce. Thus the Lord cast horse and rider into the sea, and he became my salvation.

> “This is my God, and I will honor him;  
> the God of my father, and I will exalt him.”

He is therefore both my God and the God of my father. Christ is our Father, who made and begot us; and he himself says: “I am going to my Father and your Father, my God and your God” (John 16). If I recognize that God is my God, I will glorify him. But if I also recognize how Christ is the God of my Father, I will exalt him.

> “The Lord who crushes wars—the Lord is his name.”

Do not think that the Lord crushes only visible battles. He also crushes those battles that are fought not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers and against the rulers of the darkness of this world. The Lord is his name, and there is no creature over which he is not Lord.

> “He cast Pharaoh’s chariots and his army into the sea;  
> his chosen riders, his threefold sentries, he drowned in the Red Sea.””

Pharaoh, as though more powerful in wickedness and holding the kingdom of evil, drives chariots. It is not enough for him to mount one horse; he drives many at once and forces many at once by the blows of a twisted whip. Whoever you see more shameful in lust, fiercer in unbelief, more sordid in greed, and more criminal in impiety—know that such people belong to Pharaoh’s chariots. He sits upon them, yokes them to his chariot, is carried and whirled along by them, and drives them with loosened reins across the open fields of crime.

There are other chosen riders, certainly chosen for wickedness. But we have already spoken above about the riders; now let us see who the threefold sentries are. It seems to me that the threefold sentries are mentioned because the way in which human beings sin is threefold. Sin is committed either in deed, in speech, or in thought. Therefore, in each person, three sentries are said to besiege these three ways of sinning in us, always watching and setting ambushes, so that one may draw an evil word from the miserable human being, another may extort an unrighteous deed, and another may seize a wicked thought.

Finally, the seed of the word of God is also described as falling and perishing in three places: one beside the road, where it is trampled by people; another among thorns; and another on rocky ground. Conversely, the good earth is said to bear a threefold harvest: a hundredfold, sixtyfold, or thirtyfold (Matthew 4).

These threefold sentries, then, are wicked angels from Pharaoh’s army. They stand in such paths, watching each of us, so that through these things they may lead us into sin. The Lord will drown them in the Red Sea and, on the day of judgment, hand them over to the fiery waves and cover them with a sea of punishments.

> “The abysses covered them.”

These are surely the abysses of which it is written in Job, where Leviathan is described: “He considered the abyss as though it were growing old.” And in the Gospel the demons begged Jesus not to command them to go into the abyss.

> “They descended into the depths like a stone.”

(From Augustine.) Why did they fall into the depths like a stone? Because they were not stones of the kind from which children could be raised up for Abraham, but stones of the kind that loved the depths and cherished the liquid element—that is, they desired the bitter and fleeting pleasure of present things.

> “Your right hand, Lord, has been magnified in strength;  
> your right hand, Lord, has struck down the enemy.”

What is this right hand except the one of which it is written in the Psalm:

> “The right hand of the Lord has shown strength;  
> the right hand of the Lord has exalted me” (Psalm 117)?

Through the mystery of the cross, it killed the true and ancient enemy and, through death, destroyed him who held the power of death—that is, the devil—binding the strong man and plundering his goods, and casting the dragon, namely the ancient serpent, whose tail dragged down a third of the stars, into the lake of burning fire prepared for him and his angels.

Hence it follows:

> “In the multitude of your glory you cast down my adversaries.”

The glory of the Lord’s resurrection was the devil’s disgrace, since he had plotted Christ’s death with the Jews.

> “You sent forth your wrath, which devoured them like stubble.”

The final vengeance inflicted upon the devil and his angels seems to those who suffer it already to be wrath. Yet it is justly imposed upon sinners by the one who judges all things with tranquility, without disturbance of mind. It devours them like stubble because it devastates them powerfully and tortures them on every side.

> “By the breath of your anger the waters were gathered together.”

A lake of sulfur, corresponding to their merits, is assigned to them; submerged beneath it, they groan forever. But because this punishment will be paid in full at the final judgment, and the hour of vengeance is still delayed, the enemies seem to be given an opportunity to persecute. They abuse God’s patience, storing up wrath for themselves on the day of wrath and of the revelation of God’s just judgment, although he will most certainly come to give his saints the rewards of eternal blessedness and to inflict vengeance on his adversaries in a flame of fire.

Hence it follows:

> “The flowing wave stood still;  
> the abysses were gathered in the midst of the sea.  
> The enemy said: ‘I will pursue and overtake;  
> I will divide the spoils; my soul shall be filled.  
> I will draw my sword; my hand shall destroy them.’  
> You blew with your breath, and the sea covered them;  
> they sank like lead in the mighty waters.”

(From Augustine.) “You sent your breath, and the sea covered them.” Here the Spirit of God has already been mentioned for the fifth time, so that in this number we may understand the saying: “This is the finger of God” (Exodus 8).

First, where it is written: “The Spirit of God was borne over the waters” (Genesis 1). Second, where it is said: “My Spirit will not remain in these men, for they are flesh.” Third, where Pharaoh says to Joseph: “The Spirit of God is in you” (Genesis 6). Fourth, where the Egyptian magicians say: “This is the finger of God.” Fifth, in this song: “You sent your Spirit, and the sea covered them.”

Remember, however, that the Spirit of God is mentioned not only in relation to benefits but also in relation to vengeance. For what else did he say above? “By the breath of your anger the water was divided.” Thus this Spirit of God was, for the Egyptians, the Spirit of his anger: the division of the waters harmed them, so that when they entered, they could be overwhelmed by the returning waters. But for the children of Israel, whom the division of the water benefited, it was not the Spirit of God’s anger.

This signifies that, on account of different operations and effects, the Spirit of God is named in different ways, although it is one and the same Spirit, who is also understood as the Holy Spirit in the unity of the Trinity. Accordingly, I do not think that anyone other than this same Spirit is signified when the Apostle says:

> “You did not receive the spirit of slavery again in fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption, in whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father’” (Romans 8).

For by the same Spirit of God—that is, by the finger of God—with which the law was written on tablets of stone, fear was instilled in those who did not yet understand grace, so that through the law they might be convicted of their weakness and sins, and the law might become their pedagogue, leading them to the grace that is in the faith of Jesus Christ.

Concerning this Spirit of adoption and grace—that is, concerning this work of the Spirit of God by which grace and rebirth into eternal life are imparted—it is said: “The Spirit gives life,” whereas it had previously been said: “The letter kills” (2 Corinthians 3), meaning the letter that merely commands in writing, without the assistance of grace.

(From Origen.) “They sank,” he says, “like lead into extremely powerful water.” Sinners are heavy. Indeed, iniquity is shown sitting upon a talent of lead, as the prophet Zechariah says:

> “I saw a woman sitting upon a talent of lead, and I said, ‘What is this?’ And he answered, ‘Iniquity’” (Zechariah 5).

Hence the wicked sank into the depths like lead in extremely powerful water. But the saints do not sink; they walk upon the waters, because they are light and are not weighed down by the burden of sin. Thus the Lord and Savior walked upon the waters, for he is the one who truly knew no sin. His disciple Peter also walked upon them, although he was briefly afraid. He was not yet so great and such a one that he had no admixture at all of the nature of lead.

Let the fire refine and dissolve, so that all may become good gold, since the gold of that land which the saints will possess is said to be good. Just as a furnace tests gold, so temptation tests righteous people. Everyone must therefore come to the fire; everyone must come to the smelting furnace. The Lord both smelts and purifies the children of Judah.

But when someone comes there, if he has brought many good works and only a little iniquity, that little, like lead, is dissolved and purified in the fire, and the whole remains pure gold. If someone brings more lead there, more of him is burned, so that he may be refined more thoroughly, and so that, even if only a little gold remains, it may nevertheless be purified. But if someone comes there entirely made of lead, what is written will happen to him:

> “He sinks into the depths like lead in extremely powerful water.”

> “Who is like you among the gods, Lord?  
> Who is like you, glorious among the holy ones,  
> wondrous in majesty, performing miracles?”

When it says, “Who is like you among the gods,” it does not compare God with the idols of the nations, nor with the demons that falsely assume for themselves the name of gods. Rather, it calls those gods who are named gods through grace and participation in God. Concerning them Scripture says elsewhere:

> “I said, ‘You are gods’” (Psalm 13).

And again:

> “God stood in the assembly of gods” (ibid.).

Yet although they are capable of God and seem to receive this name by grace, no one is found to be like God either in power or in nature. And although the Apostle John says:

> “Little children, we do not yet know what we shall be. But when it is revealed to us”—that is, concerning the Lord—“we shall be like him” (1 John 3),

this likeness is nevertheless referred not to nature but to grace. For example, if we say that a painting is like the person whose image is expressed in the painting, it is called similar insofar as grace is concerned—that is, in appearance—but insofar as substance is concerned, it is utterly dissimilar. One is the appearance of flesh and a living body; the other is a coloring applied upon lifeless boards, and so forth.

Therefore, no one among the gods is like the Lord. No one is invisible, no one incorporeal, no one immutable, no one without beginning and without end, and no one the creator of all things, except the Father with the Son and the Holy Spirit.

> “You stretched out your right hand,  
> and the earth devoured them.”

(From Augustine.) Earth has plainly been put in place of water. For this whole final or weaker part of the world is designated by the name “earth,” according to what is often said:

> “God, who made heaven and earth” (Psalm 148).

And in the distribution of that Psalm, after the heavenly things have been mentioned, it says:

> “Praise the Lord from the earth,”

and then it goes through those things in praise that also pertain to the waters.

(From Origen.) Even today the earth devours the impious. Does it not seem to you that the one who is always thinking about earth is devoured by earth; the one who always performs earthly deeds, speaks about earth, quarrels about earth, desires earth, and places all his hope in earth; the one who does not look toward heaven, does not think about the future, has not attained the judgment of God, and does not desire his blessed promises, but always thinks about present things and sighs after earthly things?

When you see such a person, say that the earth has devoured him. And if you see someone devoted to the lust of the flesh and bodily pleasures, in whom the mind has no strength because the desire of the flesh has gained possession of everything, say of him also that the earth has devoured him.

What he says still troubles me: “You stretched out your right hand, and the earth devoured them,” as though the reason they were devoured by the earth were that the Lord stretched out his right hand. If you consider how the Lord, exalted upon the cross, stretched out his hands all day toward the unbelieving and disobedient people, and how death from the crime they had committed overwhelmed the unbelieving people who cried, “Crucify him, crucify him” (Matthew 27), you will clearly understand how he stretched out his right hand and the earth devoured them. Nevertheless, we must not despair completely. For it is possible that, if the one who has been devoured should perhaps repent, he may again be vomited out, as Jonah was.

> “You led your people in your righteousness,  
> this people whom you redeemed.  
> You comforted them by your strength  
> and in your holy resting-place.”

The Lord leads his people, whom he redeemed through the washing of regeneration, in righteousness. He also comforts them by the consolation of the Holy Spirit, in his strength and in his resting-place. For hope of future things produces rest for those who labor, just as the hope of a crown, for those engaged in combat, eases the pain of wounds.

> “The nations heard and were angry;  
> pains seized the inhabitants of Philistia.  
> Then the leaders of Edom hastened,  
> and the princes of Moab;  
> trembling seized them,  
> and all the inhabitants of Canaan melted away.”

As far as history is concerned, it is clear that none of these nations was present at the miracles that took place. How, then, do they appear to have been terrified by trembling, or to have hastened, as it says, or for the Philistines, Moabites, Edomites, and the remaining nations it lists to have been angry?

But if we return to the spiritual understanding, you will find that the Philistines—that is, “those who beware of the cup”—and Edom, which is interpreted as “earthly,” tremble. All their leaders run about and are terrified, constricted by pains, when they see their kingdoms, which are in hell, invaded by the one who descended into the lower regions of the earth to rescue those who were held by death.

Fear and trembling seized them because they sensed the greatness of his arm. Hence also all the inhabitants of Canaan melted away—those whose name is interpreted as “changeable” and “mobile”—when they saw their kingdoms shaken, the strong man bound, and his goods plundered.

> “Let fear and trembling therefore come upon them  
> because of the greatness of your arm.”

What do the demons fear? What do they tremble at? Without doubt, the cross of Christ, on which they were triumphed over and on which their principalities and powers were stripped away.

Fear and trembling will therefore fall upon them when they see the sign of the cross faithfully fixed in us, and the greatness of that arm which the Lord stretched out upon the cross, as he says:

> “All day long I stretched out my hands toward a people that did not believe and contradicted me” (Romans 10).

They will not fear you in any other way, nor will your trembling come upon them in any other way, unless they see the cross of Christ in you, unless you too are able to say:

> “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of my Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Galatians 6).

> “Let them become like a stone until your people pass over, Lord,  
> until this people of yours pass over, whom you acquired.”

To become like a stone is not to be stone by nature. For something that was not a stone would not become one. We say this against those who claim that Pharaoh or the Egyptians were of an evil nature and that they were brought into these things not by freedom of choice, and also against those who accuse God the Creator as cruel because he turns human beings into stones.

Before they blaspheme, let such people consider what is written with the utmost care. It does not say merely, “Let them become like a stone,” and then remain silent; rather, it establishes a time and determines the measure of condemnation. For it says:

> “Until your people pass over.”

This implies that, once the people have passed over, they will no longer be like stones. In this, it seems to me, something prophetic is concealed. I see that the earlier people, who existed before us, became like a hard and unbelieving stone, but not to such an extent that they would remain in the nature of stone. They remain so “until this people passes over, this people whom you acquired.”

For “a partial blindness has happened in Israel according to the flesh, until the fullness of the nations should enter” (Romans 11). When the fullness of the nations has entered, then all Israel also, which through the hardness of unbelief had become like a stone, will be saved.

And do you wish to see how it will be saved? “God,” he says, “is able to raise up children for Abraham from stones.” The stones therefore remain for now, until your people pass over, Lord—your people whom you acquired.

But if the Lord himself is the creator of all things, we must see how he is said here to have acquired what unquestionably belongs to him. It is also said in another song, in Deuteronomy:

> “Is he not himself your God, who made you, created you, and acquired you?” (Deuteronomy 32).

It seems that each person acquires what was not his. Hence, finally, the heretics also say concerning the Savior that those whom he acquired were not his. He purchased human beings by paying a price, they say, although the Creator had made them; and it is certain, they argue, that each person buys what is not his own. For the Apostle says:

> “You were bought with a price” (1 Corinthians 5).

But hear what the prophet says:

> “You were sold because of your sins, and because of your iniquities I dismissed your mother” (Isaiah 50).

You see, therefore, that we are all indeed God’s creatures; yet each person is sold by his own sins and, because of his iniquities, departs from his own Creator. We belong to God insofar as we were created by him; but we have become servants of the devil insofar as we were sold by our sins.

When Christ came, he redeemed us while we were serving the master to whom we had sold ourselves by sinning. Thus he appears to have received as his own those whom he had created, but to have acquired as strangers those who, by sinning, had sought a master who was a stranger to him.

Perhaps it is rightly said that Christ redeemed us, since he gave his own blood as our price. But what did the devil give in order to purchase us? Therefore, if this seems obscure, listen: murder is the devil’s money. For he was a murderer from the beginning. You committed murder: you received the devil’s money. Adultery is the devil’s money, for the devil’s image and inscription are upon it. You committed adultery: you received a coin from the devil. Theft, false testimony, rapacity, violence—all these are the devil’s revenue and the devil’s treasure. Such money proceeds from his mint.

With this money, therefore, he purchases those whom he purchases and makes his slaves all who receive even the smallest amount from such revenue.

> “You will bring them in and plant them on the mountain of your inheritance.”

God does not wish to plant us in Egypt, nor in fallen and lowly places; he wishes to plant those whom he plants on the mountain of his inheritance. The prophet says:

> “You brought a vine out of Egypt;  
> you expelled the nations and planted it.  
> You made a path before it;  
> you planted its roots, and it filled the earth.  
> Its shadow covered the mountains,  
> and its branches were like the cedars of God” (Psalm 79).

Do you now perceive how and where God plants? He does not plant in valleys but on mountains, in lofty and elevated places. Those whom he leads out of Egypt—that is, whom he brings from the world to faith—he does not wish to place again in lowly conditions, but wishes their way of life to be exalted.

He wishes us to dwell on mountains; yet even on the mountains he does not wish us to creep along the ground. Nor does he wish his vine to have its fruit lying low upon the earth. Rather, he wishes its branches to be led upward, placed on high, and trained—not on just any lowly trees, but on the lofty and highest cedars of God.

I think that the cedars of God are the prophets and apostles. We are to be joined to them as branches to the vine that God brought out of Egypt; our shoots are to spread through their branches, and, leaning upon them, we are to become trained branches, bound together by the ties of mutual love, and undoubtedly bearing abundant fruit. For every tree that does not bear fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire (Matthew 3).

> “In the dwelling-place that you prepared,  
> which you prepared, Lord.”

See the goodness of the merciful Lord: he does not wish to lead you into labor, nor does he wish you yourself to make a dwelling for yourself. He leads you already to a dwelling that has been prepared. Hear the Lord saying in the Gospel:

> “Others have labored, and you have entered into their labor” (John 4).

> “The sanctuary, Lord,  
> which your hands have prepared.”

The Lord’s sanctuary is the tabernacle of God, like a temple by which those who approach are sanctified. He does not say that it was made by human hands, but by the hand of God. What, then? For your sake God both plants and builds; he becomes a farmer and a builder, so that nothing may be lacking for you. Hear Paul also saying:

> “You are God’s agriculture, God’s building” (1 Corinthians 3).

What, then, is this sanctuary, which was not made by human hand but prepared by God’s hands? Hear Wisdom saying:

> “He who built himself a house” (Proverbs 9).

I think, however, that this is more rightly understood of the Lord’s incarnation. The temple of flesh is not built in the Virgin by human hand—that is, not by human work—but, as Daniel says above, the stone cut out without hands grows and becomes a great mountain. This is the sanctuary of the assumed flesh, cut without hands—that is, without human work—from the mountain of human nature and the substance of flesh.

> “Lord, who reign forever and ever,  
> and forever, and still further.”

Whenever “forever” is said, a length of time is indeed indicated, but some end is also implied. And if it is said “into another age,” some longer duration is certainly meant, but an end is nevertheless posited. Whenever “ages of ages” are named, perhaps—although unknown to us—a certain limit established by God is nevertheless indicated.

But when he adds here, “and still further,” he leaves no sense of any limit or end. Whatever you may imagine as the point at which an end could exist, the prophetic word always says to you, “and still further.” It is as though it were speaking to you and saying: “Do you think that the Lord will reign into the age of the age? And still further. Do you think he will reign into the ages of ages? And still further.” Whatever you may say about the duration of his reign, the Prophet always says to you, “and still further.”

> “Pharaoh’s cavalry entered the sea with his chariots and riders,  
> and the Lord brought the waters of the sea upon them.  
> But the children of Israel walked on dry ground  
> in the midst of the sea.”

If you are a child of Israel, you too can walk on dry ground in the midst of the sea. If you are in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation, it can happen that, like the light of the sun, holding fast the word of life unto glory, you walk in the midst of sinners without being drenched by the moisture of sin.

It can happen that, as you pass through this world, no wave of lust sprinkles you and no surge of desire strikes you. Whoever is an Egyptian and follows Pharaoh is submerged in the waves of vices. But whoever follows Christ, and walks as he walked, has a wall formed for him on the right and on the left.

He himself walks along the middle path on dry ground; he does not turn to the right or to the left, until he comes out into freedom and sings a hymn of victory to the Lord, saying:

> “I will sing to the Lord,  
> for he has been gloriously honored.”

## CHAPTER V. On the journey of the children of Israel from the Red Sea to Marah, where Moses, at the Lord’s command, sweetened the bitter waters with wood, and where the Lord also established commandments and judgments for them

Now Moses brought Israel away from the Red Sea, and they went out into the desert of Shur. They traveled for three days through the wilderness and found no water. Then they came to Marah, but they could not drink the waters of Marah because they were bitter. Therefore he gave the place an appropriate name, calling it Marah, that is, “bitterness.”

The people murmured against Moses, saying, “What shall we drink?” But he cried out to the Lord, who showed him a piece of wood. When he had put it into the waters, they were changed into sweetness (Exodus, chapter 45 [sic]).

(From Isidore.) When the peoples had gone out from the Red Sea, the desert confronted them. Entering it for three days, they had no water, and they came to the spring of Marah, which received its name from its bitterness. The people murmured when they saw the waters and could not endure drinking them. Moses put wood into the waters, and they became sweet.

Understand that the bitter waters signify the letter that kills and the law. If confession of the cross is introduced into them and the mystery of the Lord’s Passion is joined to them, then the bitter water becomes sweet, and the bitterness of the letter is turned into the sweetness of spiritual understanding.

Hence it is also written:

> “The Lord established a law and judgments for his people,  
> and he tested them” (Leviticus 20).

In another sense also, the fact that the bitter waters become sweet when they receive wood was an indication that the bitterness of the nations would one day be changed, through the wood of Christ’s cross, into a use of sweetness.

There he established commandments and judgments for them, and there he tested them, saying:

> “If you listen to the voice of the Lord your God, and do what is right before him, and obey his commandments, and keep all his precepts, I will not bring upon you any of the sicknesses that I brought upon Egypt. For I am the Lord your Savior,” and so forth.

(From Origen.) It seems to say that if someone keeps the commandments, he will suffer no illness—that is, he will experience neither fever nor any other bodily pain. I do not think that these are the things promised to those who keep the divine commandments. Otherwise, the case of Job would refute us: Job was most righteous and most observant of all piety, yet he was covered from head to foot with a most grievous ulcer.

Those who keep the commandments are therefore not said to be free from illnesses of this kind. Rather, they will not have the illnesses that the Egyptians have. Egypt is figuratively called the world. To love the world and the things that are in the world is an Egyptian illness. To observe days, months, and seasons, to seek signs, and to cling to the courses of the stars is an Egyptian illness. To serve the lust of the flesh, devote oneself to pleasures, and give oneself over to delights is an Egyptian illness.

The person who keeps the commandments is free from these illnesses and diseases.

## CHAPTER VI. On the fact that, journeying from Marah, the children of Israel came to Elim, and from Elim to the desert of Sin, which is between Elim and Sinai; where the Lord gave them quail in the evening and rained manna in the morning
After this he says that they came to Elim: “and there were there twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees” (Exod. ch. 15). Do you suppose that it is without significance that the people are not led to Elim first, where there were twelve springs of water, in which they had found no bitterness—indeed, where there was great pleasantness because of the abundance of palm trees? Rather, they are first led to false and bitter waters, which, after they have been made sweet through the wood shown by the Lord, are followed by the arrival at the springs.

If we follow only the historical account, it does not greatly edify us to know to which place they came first and to which second. But if we search out the hidden mystery in these things, we discover the order of faith. First the people are led to the literal meaning of the Law; as long as it remains in its bitterness, they cannot withdraw from it. But when it has been made sweet through the wood of life, and the Law has begun to be understood spiritually, then one passes from the Old Testament to the New and comes to the twelve apostolic springs. There also seventy palm trees are found. For it was not only the twelve apostles who preached the faith of Christ; the other seventy, sent to preach the word of God, are also mentioned. Through them the world would recognize the palm of Christ’s victory.

They set out from Elim, and the whole multitude of the children of Israel came into the desert of Sin, which is between Elim and Sinai, on the fifteenth day of the second month, after they had gone out from the land of Egypt. And the whole congregation of the children of Israel murmured against Moses and against Aaron in the wilderness. The children of Israel said to them: “Would that we had died by the hand of the Lord in the land of Egypt, when we sat over pots of meat and ate bread to the full. Why have you brought us out into this wilderness, to kill this whole multitude with hunger?” (Exod. ch. 16).

[From Origen.] Suppose that, for the correction of the readers, the people’s sin is indicated: that they murmured and were ungrateful for the divine benefits, even while they were receiving the heavenly manna. Why, moreover, is the day on which the people murmured recorded? “In the second month,” he says, “on the fifteenth day of the month.” This certainly has not been written without reason. Recall the laws concerning Passover that were stated, and you will find that this is the time appointed for a second Passover to be made by those who were unclean in soul or occupied with foreign business. Those, therefore, who were not unclean in soul and were not traveling far made Passover on the fourteenth day of the first month. But those who were traveling and were unclean celebrated the second Passover at this time—the same time at which the manna descended from heaven. On the day when the first Passover is celebrated, manna does not descend; rather, it descends on the day when the second Passover is celebrated.

Let us see, then, what order of mystery is contained in these events. The first Passover belongs to the first people; the second Passover belongs to us. For we were unclean in soul, worshiping wood and stone, and, in ignorance of God, serving those who by nature were not gods. We were also the ones who were traveling far away. Concerning them the Apostle says: “We were strangers and sojourners, having no hope of the covenants of God, and without God in this world.” Yet manna is not given from heaven on the day when the first Passover is celebrated, but on the day when the second is celebrated. For the bread that descended from heaven did not come to those who celebrated the first solemnity, but to us who received the second. Our Passover is Christ sacrificed, who descended from heaven as the true bread for us.

Meanwhile, let us see what is shown to have happened on this day. On the fifteenth day of the second month the people murmured and said: “It would have been better for us to die in Egypt, when we ate over pots of meat.” O ungrateful people, desiring Egypt although they had seen the Egyptians destroyed! They seek the meats of Egypt, though they had seen the flesh of the Egyptians given to the fish of the sea and the birds of heaven. They murmur against Moses—or rather, they were crying out against God. At first this is forgiven, and perhaps a second and third time as well. But if they do not cease and persist, hear what follows after the people’s murmuring.

In the Book of Numbers it is reported, and the Apostle repeats it in his writings, saying: “Neither murmur, as some of them murmured and perished by serpents” (1 Cor. 10). The people who murmured were consumed in the wilderness by the poisonous bite of serpents. Let us see what this means for us who hear these things—yes, for us, for whom they were written. Those events happened for their correction, but they were written for us, upon whom the ends of the ages have come. Such things are forgiven those who are making a beginning; but upon those who do not cease, punishment is severely inflicted. Serpents are sent against them—that is, they are handed over to unclean spirits and poisonous demons, who destroy them with hidden and concealed bites and consume them with thoughts shut up within, in the innermost chambers of the heart.

For God, who heard the murmuring of the children of Israel, says: You see that our murmuring is not hidden from the Lord. He hears everything; and because he does not punish immediately, he awaits our repentance and conversion. But what is recounted after this? The Lord said to Moses: “Behold, I will rain down bread for you from heaven. Let the people go out and gather enough for each day, so that I may test him [Col. 0078C] whether he will walk in my law or not.”

[From Augustine.] This testing is a proving, not a seduction into sin. Nor is it a proving so that God may know, but so that he may show people to themselves, that they may become humbler in asking for help and acknowledging God’s grace.

“On the sixth day let them prepare what they are to bring in, and let it be double what they were accustomed to gather each day.” I ask, then, on what day manna began to be given from heaven, and I wish to compare our Sunday with the Sabbath of the Jews.
