For it is evident from the divine Scriptures that manna was first given on earth on Sunday. As Scripture says, it was gathered for six successive days, but on the seventh day, which is the Sabbath, it ceased; without doubt, therefore, its beginning was on the first day, which is Sunday.

If it is established from the divine Scriptures that God rained manna on Sunday and did not rain it on the Sabbath, let the Jews understand that even then our Sunday was placed before the Jewish Sabbath. It was already then indicated that on their Sabbath no grace of God descended to them from heaven, and that no heavenly bread, which is the word of God, came to them. For the prophet says elsewhere: “For many days the children of Israel shall sit without king, without prince, without prophet, without sacrifice, without offering, without priest” (Hos. 3).

But on our Sunday the Lord always rains manna from heaven. Even today, I say, the Lord rains manna from heaven. These heavenly utterances are what have been read to us; the words recited to us have descended from God. Therefore, because we receive such manna, manna is always given to us from heaven.

Those unhappy people grieve and sigh and call themselves wretched, because they do not deserve to receive manna as their fathers received it. They never eat manna. For they cannot eat what is fine like coriander seed and white like frost. They perceive nothing fine, subtle, or spiritual in the word of God, but everything fat and coarse. The heart of that people has indeed become fat.

The interpretation of the name also expresses the same thing. For manna is interpreted as “What is this?” See whether the very force of the name does not summon you to learning, so that when you hear the law of God being recited, you may always inquire and ask the teachers, “What is this?” For this is what manna indicates.

But if you wish to eat manna—that is, if you desire to receive the words—know that it is fine and exceedingly subtle, like coriander seed. It has within it something of a vegetable, by which it can nourish and refresh the weak, because “the one who is weak should eat vegetables” (Rom. 14). It also has something of hardness, and therefore it is like frost. But it possesses great whiteness and sweetness. What is whiter or more radiant than divine instruction? What is sweeter or more pleasant than the utterances of the Lord, which are “sweeter than honey and the honeycomb”?

But what does it mean that on the sixth day twice as much is gathered and stored—enough even for the Sabbath? According to our understanding, we must not pass over this lazily or carelessly. This is the sixth day, the life in which we now are. For in six days God made this world. Therefore, in this life we must store up and lay away as much as will be sufficient for the future day. If you acquire any good work here, if you store up any justice, mercy, or piety, this will be food for you in the age to come.

In another way, the soul receives the heavenly manna when, lifted up by a voice of compunction, it is astonished by a new form of inner nourishment, so that, filled with divine sweetness, it rightly answers, “What is this?” For when it is lifted above lowly thought and beholds things above, it marvels at them as at something unfamiliar; and when, with this utterance, the filth of our sluggishness is broken, the habit of our former life is immediately changed. Thus the soul, breathed upon by the heavenly Spirit, desires above what it had despised and despises below what it had desired.

Moses and Aaron said to all the children of Israel: “In the evening you shall know that the Lord brought you out of the land of Egypt, and in the morning you shall see the glory of the Lord.” Among other things Moses and Aaron say to the people: “For the Lord has heard your murmuring, with which you murmur against us.” But what are we? Your murmuring is not against us, but against God. They did not wish to claim for themselves a power equal to God’s; therefore they said: “What are we?”—so that the people might know that they had murmured against the one who had sent them and who was working through them.

Moses said to Aaron: “Say to the whole congregation of the children of Israel: Draw near before the Lord, for he has heard your murmuring.” And when Aaron spoke to the whole assembly of the children of Israel, they looked toward the wilderness, and behold, the glory of the Lord appeared in the cloud.

The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “I have heard the murmuring of the children of Israel. Speak to them: In the evening you shall eat meat, and in the morning you shall be filled with bread, and you shall know that I am the Lord your God.”

God commands the people through Moses: “In the evening you shall eat meat, and in the morning you shall be filled with bread.”

[From Augustine.] Behold, bread is named for every kind of nourishment. For by this name meat is also included, since meat too is nourishment; yet he does not call only those things bread that are made from grain. We customarily call those things bread in the proper sense. But he calls manna by the name of bread.

Nor is it without significance that he says he will give meat in the evening and bread in the morning. Something similar was also signified in Elijah, when a raven brought him food. Or does the meat in the evening and the bread in the morning signify the one who was handed over because of our sins and rose again for our justification? In the evening he died from weakness and was buried; in the morning he appeared to the disciples, having risen in power.

It happened in the evening, and a quail came up and covered the camp. In the morning dew also lay around the camp. When it had covered the surface of the earth, there appeared in the wilderness something fine, as if pounded with a pestle, resembling frost upon the ground. When the children of Israel saw it, they said to one another, “Manhu”—which means, “What is this?” For they did not know what it was. Moses said to them: “This is the bread that the Lord has given you to eat. This is the word that the Lord has commanded: Let each one gather from it as much as is sufficient for eating, an omer for each person. According to the number of your souls who dwell in the tent, so shall you take.”

The children of Israel did so. They gathered, one more and another less, and measured it by the measure of an omer. The one who had gathered more had nothing extra, nor did the one who had prepared less find that he had too little; each gathered according to what he was able to eat.

Moses said to them: “Let no one leave any of it until morning.” But they did not listen to him; some left part of it until morning, and it began to breed worms and became rotten, and Moses was angry with them. They gathered it each morning, each as much as could suffice for eating. When the sun grew hot, it melted.

On the sixth day they gathered twice as much food, that is, two omers for each person, and so forth.

[From Isidore.] What are we to understand by the food of birds except preachers sent by God, who pass through sounding words like winged creatures through the air? By faith these are food for those who strive to reach the homeland of the heavenly kingdom.

The food of birds can also signify the utterances of the Old Law, which fed the carnal people as if with meat through words sent by God, like winged creatures. Hence they are given in the evening, because everything granted to them in a carnal manner was destined to have an end.

When the light of faith was revealed, manna was given to the people—manna, that is, Christ, who descended from heaven like living bread. He is rained upon the whole world through the evangelical clouds, no longer upon the murmuring and testing Synagogue, but upon the believing Church that places its hope in him.

This is the unfailing manna. This is the true bread and the heavenly food of angels, by which the Word of God feeds corruptible beings incorruptibly. In order that a human being might eat it, he became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1); those who feed on him live spiritually. For those who received the ancient figure in a carnal manner died.

It is not inappropriate that heavenly utterances are also signified by manna; hence the interpretation of the name has this meaning. Manna, or manhu, is interpreted as “What is this?” When we hear the law of God recited in church, we ask the teachers, saying, “What is this?”

Morally, manna, which was given to the people from above, signifies the wonder of heavenly sweetness. The sweet food received from above is called manhu; for manhu, as stated above, means “What is this?” We say, “What is this?” when, not knowing what we behold, we marvel at it.

The soul therefore receives heavenly manna when, lifted up by a voice of compunction, it is astonished by a new form of inner nourishment, so that, filled with divine sweetness, it rightly answers, “What is this?” When it is lifted above lowly thought, it marvels in an unfamiliar way at what it beholds above; and when, with this utterance, the filth of our sluggishness is broken, the habit of our former life is immediately changed. Thus the soul, breathed upon by the heavenly Spirit, desires above what it had despised and despises below what it had desired.

[From Isidore.] This manna was fine like coriander seed, white and sweet. What is finer than the word of God, what more subtle, or what sweeter and more pleasant than the utterances of God, which are “sweeter than honey and the honeycomb”?

But what does it mean that on the sixth day twice as much is ordered to be gathered, enough also for the Sabbath? This sixth day is the sixth age of the world, in which we now live. In this age the person gathers twice as much who, because of the hope of eternal life, both hears and performs the word of God. In this age the person stores up twice as much who both lives well and shows mercy to others.

What was stored up for the Sabbath did not become rotten. For good works performed for the sake of future rest remain in the age to come. But those who were unbelieving and kept manna apart from the purpose of the Sabbath saw worms boil out of it, and it became rotten. So also, for those who store up treasure for the sake of the present life and love of the world, that worm which will not die boils out.

These are the worms generated by avarice and the blind desire for wealth. These are those who possess money and, seeing their brothers in need, close their hearts against them. But for the person who sins after receiving the word of God, that very word of God becomes a worm—a worm that continually gnaws his conscience and eats away at the secrets of his heart.

Nevertheless, Christ too is a worm, as he himself says: “But I am a worm and not a man” (Ps. 21). For just as he is for some a cause of ruin and for others of resurrection, so in the manna itself he becomes, for the faithful, the sweetness of honey, but for the unfaithful, a worm.

Moses said to Aaron: “Take one vessel and put in it as much manna as an omer can contain, and place it before the Lord, to be kept for your generations, as the Lord commanded Moses.” Aaron placed it in the tabernacle to be preserved, and so forth.

[From Augustine.] It may be asked where Aaron was to place it before God, when there was neither any image nor had the ark of the covenant yet been established. Or did he perhaps speak of the future when he said, “You shall store it away,” so that it would be understood that it could be placed before God when the ark was to exist? Or was “before God” said of what is done through the very devotion of offering, wherever it might be placed? For where is God not present?

But the addition, “And Aaron placed it before the testimony to be preserved,” more clearly reveals the former meaning. In this way Scripture spoke by anticipation of what happened later, when the tabernacle of the testimony came into being.

The children of Israel ate manna for forty years, until they came to an inhabited land. They were nourished by this food until they touched the borders of the land of Canaan. “The children of Israel,” it says, “ate manna for forty years, until they came to an inhabited land.” They ate manna until they came to the land of Canaan.

Scripture has indicated by anticipation—that is, by mentioning here what happened later—that the children of Israel ate nothing but manna in the wilderness. For when it says “until the inhabited land,” it means a land that is no longer wilderness. This does not mean that as soon as they came to the inhabited land they ceased to eat manna, but that they had not ceased before then. After crossing the Jordan, the cessation of manna is signified, when they ate the bread of the land.

Therefore, once they had entered the inhabited land but before they crossed the Jordan, they could have eaten either manna alone or both kinds of food. For it can be understood that manna did not cease until the Jordan had been crossed.

But why, amid the scarcity of that wilderness, did they desire meat when they had gone out from Egypt with their many flocks? This is a difficult question, unless perhaps one says that, since there were not enough pastures throughout the wilderness and the fertility of the flocks seemed destined to diminish, they spared their animals so that, when everything failed, they would not also lack what was necessary for sacrifices—or unless some other explanation can be given by which the question may be resolved.

It is more fitting, however, to believe that they did not desire meat that they could have obtained from their flocks, but the meat that was lacking from the waters. For they did not find such meat in that wilderness, and therefore ortygometra was given to them—that is, birds, which many Latins have translated as “quails,” although ortygometra is a different kind of bird, even if it is not entirely unlike quails. God knew what they desired and with what kind of meat to satisfy their desire. But because Scripture had said that they desired meat without specifying what kind of meat, the question arose.

It should be noted that, according to another edition, this passage of Scripture reads as follows: “The children of Israel ate manna until they came into the land of Phoenice.” It had already said, “until they came into the inhabited land.” But because it had not expressly stated which land it meant, it seems to have expressed a certain specificity by repeating the statement and saying, “into the land of Phoenice.”

At that time, however, that land must be believed to have been called by this name. For today it is not called by that name. There is another region called Phoenice, belonging to Tyre and Sidon, and it is not recorded that they crossed through it. Nevertheless, Scripture may perhaps have called that land the land of Phoenice because palm trees had begun to grow there after the desolation of the wilderness, since “palm” is called φοῖνιξ in Greek.

At the beginning of their journey they had found a place where there were seventy palm trees and twelve springs. But afterward they were met by the great extent of the wilderness, where there was nothing of this kind, until they came to cultivated regions.

The more probable interpretation, however, is that we should believe that the land was then called by this name. For the names of many lands and places, as well as of rivers and cities, have changed through the passage of time for definite reasons.

It follows: “An omer is one-tenth of an ephah.” An ephah, therefore, is a measure of three modii, as is shown in the Book of Ruth; and an omer is the measure of three Attic choinices. Hence, both in Leviticus and in the Book of Numbers, whenever one-tenth of an ephah is ordered to be offered in sacrifice, the measure of an omer is understood to be intended.

## CHAPTER VII. The departure of the children of Israel from the desert of Sin to Rephidim, where the people murmured because of the lack of water

The whole multitude of the children of Israel therefore set out from the desert of Sin by their stages, according to the word of the Lord, and encamped at Rephidim, where there was no water for the people to drink. They quarreled with Moses and said: “Give us water, so that we may drink.” Moses replied to them: “Why do you quarrel with me? Why do you test the Lord?” The people thirsted there because of the lack of water, and murmured against Moses, saying: “Why have you brought us out of Egypt, to kill us, our children, and our cattle with thirst?” (Exod. 17).

Rephidim is a place in the wilderness near Mount Horeb. It should be understood that the whole wilderness as far as Mount Sinai is called Sin, and that a place containing a single encampment received its name from the whole province, just as Moab is the name both of a city and of a province.

In this wilderness there are five encampments: Suph, the wilderness of Sin, Daphca, Alush, and Rephidim. Hence Exodus briefly records that the whole multitude of the children of Israel set out from the wilderness of Sin by their stages, according to the command of the Lord, and came to Rephidim (Exod. 14). From this it is clear that several encampments are designated by the name of a single region.

Moses cried out to the Lord, saying: “What shall I do with this people? A little more, and they will stone me.” The Lord said to Moses: “Go before the people, and take with you some of the elders of Israel. Take in your hand the staff with which you struck the river, and go. Behold, I will stand before you there upon the rock at Horeb. You shall strike the rock, and water will come out of it, so that the people may drink.”

It is recorded that Aaron, not Moses, struck the river with the staff. For Moses divided the sea with that same staff, not the river. [From Augustine.] What, then, is meant by, “Take the staff with which you struck the river”? Did he perhaps call the sea a river? If so, an example of this manner of speaking must be sought. Or is what Aaron did rather attributed to Moses because God commanded through Moses what Aaron was to do? For in his first words God said this to him concerning his brother: “He shall be to you for the people; you shall be to him in the things pertaining to God.”

Moses did so before the elders of Israel. And because they had tested the Lord, saying, “Is the Lord among us or not?”

[From Isidore.] After the manna, the people complained because of the burning heat of thirst, and a spring burst forth from the rock. That same rock, when struck, stirred the waters and was a figure of Christ, when opened, from whom all things flowed. The wood of the passion approached him like a staff, so that grace might flow forth for believers.

When it was struck, the spring flowed; when Christ was struck on the cross, he poured out upon the thirsty the grace of the laver and the gift of the Holy Spirit. The Apostle proves that this rock bore the figure of Christ when he says: “They drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10).

But what does it mean that the thirsty people murmured against Moses because of the water, and that God therefore commanded him to show them the rock from which they were to drink? What else does this signify except that if someone, while reading Moses, murmurs against him and is displeased with the Law written according to the letter, Moses shows him the rock, which is Christ, and leads him to Christ himself, so that he may drink from him and relieve his thirst?

## CHAPTER VIII. The battle of Amalek against Israel

Amalek came and fought against Israel at Rephidim. Moses said to Joshua: “Choose men, and go out and fight against Amalek. Tomorrow I shall stand on the summit of the hill, with the staff of God in my hand.”

Joshua did as Moses had told him, and fought against Amalek. Moses, Aaron, and Hur went up to the summit of the hill. When Moses raised his hands, Israel prevailed; but when he lowered them for a little while, Amalek overcame them. Moses’ hands were heavy. Therefore they took a stone and placed it beneath him, and he sat upon it. Aaron and Hur supported his hands on either side, and his hands did not grow weary until sunset. Joshua put Amalek and his people to flight by the edge of the sword.

[From Augustine.] “Behold, I shall stand on the summit of the hill, and the staff of God will be in my hand.” Moses says this to Joshua when he orders him to fight against Amalek. The staff of God is now called the staff that was first called Aaron’s staff and afterward Moses’ staff.

It is like the “Spirit of Elijah,” which is the Spirit of God, of whom Elijah became a participant. In the same way, that staff can be called the justice of God, which is ours but is granted by God. Speaking of this, the Apostle rebukes the Jews, saying: “Being ignorant of God’s justice and seeking to establish their own justice” (Rom. 10)—that is, as though they had prepared it for themselves. Against such people he says: “What do you have that you did not receive?”

Mystically, Moses ascends the mountain; Jesus wages war against Amalek; Moses holds the staff and stretches out his arms in the form of a cross. Thus the enemy—that is, the devil—who wishes to block the way to the heavenly homeland, is overcome by the sign of the Lord’s cross.

While Moses raised his hands, Israel prevailed. Again, while he lowered them, Amalek overcame. For when we raise our deeds toward heaven, the rulers of darkness are subjected. But when we pray with lowered hands—that is, when we pursue an earthly way of life—the victorious enemy follows after us.

Moses sits upon the stone of which Zechariah spoke (ch. 5), which had seven eyes, and which in the Book of Samuel is called the stone of help. Aaron and Hur, as if the two peoples or the two Testaments, support both his hands.

Alternatively: Moses sat upon the stone when the Law came to rest in the Church. But this same Law had heavy hands, because it did not bear sinners with mercy but struck them with strict severity.

Aaron means “mountain of strength,” while Hur means “fire.” Whom, then, does this mountain of strength signify except our Redeemer? Concerning him the prophet says: “In the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared at the top of the mountains” (Isa. 2). Or who is signified by fire except the Holy Spirit, concerning whom the same Redeemer says: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth”?

Aaron and Hur therefore support Moses’ heavy hands and, by supporting them, make them lighter, because the Mediator of God and human beings, coming with the fire of the Holy Spirit, shows us through spiritual understanding that the commandments of the Law, which could not be carried when they were held carnally, are more bearable.

He made Moses’ hands lighter, as it were, because he turned the burden of the commandments of the Law toward the virtue of confession. He suggests to us the promise of the mercy that follows when the prophet says: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live” (Ezek. 18).

Again, under the figure of Judah, it is said to every sinful soul: “If a man puts away his wife, and she, departing from him, takes another husband, will he return to her again? Will not that woman be polluted and defiled? Yet you have committed fornication with many lovers. Nevertheless, return to me, says the Lord” (Jer. 3).

Behold, he gives the example of a shameful woman. He shows that after disgrace she cannot be received; but he overcomes that very example through mercy, saying that a woman who has committed fornication cannot be received, and yet he himself waits to receive the fornication-loving soul.

Let us consider the weight of such great compassion. He says that something cannot be done, and demonstrates that he himself can do it even contrary to custom. Behold, he calls the defiled and declares them polluted; he seeks to embrace even those by whom he complains that he has been abandoned.

He therefore bent the harshness of the Law toward mercy, because those whom the Law justly condemns, he mercifully sets free.

The Lord said to Moses: “Write this as a memorial in a book, and deliver it to the ears of Joshua. For I will utterly destroy the memory of Amalek from under heaven.” Moses built an altar and called its name, “The Lord is my exaltation.”

The Lord commands that the war begun against Amalek be written in a book and delivered to the ears of Joshua, and he foretells that he will destroy the memory of Amalek. What does this signify except that almighty God, through the Law represented by Moses, foretells concerning our Savior that he himself will destroy the memory of spiritual enemies and, restraining their assault upon the holy Church, will plunge them into the depth of the abyss—those enemies of whom the prophet says: “Their memory has perished with a sound, but the Lord remains forever” (Ps. 9)?

And to show the soldiers of Christ that at no time should they grow sluggish through the inactivity of laziness, but should always be ready for battle, he added shortly afterward: “For the hand of the Lord alone, and the war of God, shall be against Amalek from generation to generation.”

“The hand of the Lord alone and the war of God against Amalek” means against evil spirits, who continually thirst for bloody and corruptible works. For Amalek is interpreted as “the people of the locust,” or “the people that licks blood.”

When Christ, in his members—that is, in the saints—fights courageously and without ceasing in the present age against spiritual wickedness, this is “from generation to generation,” that is, until the end of the world. Then, when the victory has been perfectly accomplished, the saints will enter the heavenly kingdom in triumph, accompanying their king Christ, and will themselves receive an everlasting kingdom. Then that saying of the Apostle will truly be fulfilled: “Death has been swallowed up in victory.” And elsewhere it is written: “Death shall be no more, neither shall there be mourning nor crying, for the former things have passed away” (Rev. 21).

## CHAPTER IX. The coming of Jethro, the kinsman of Moses, into the wilderness with Moses’ wife and sons, and the advice he gave Moses for lightening the burden of disputes
[Cols. 0086C–0096D] And when Jethro the priest of Midian, Moses’ kinsman, had heard all that the Lord had done for Moses and for his people Israel—how the Lord had brought Israel out of Egypt—he took Zipporah, Moses’ wife, whom Moses had sent back, and her two sons. One of them was named Gershom, his father saying, “I have been a sojourner in a foreign land.” The other was Eliezer, “for,” he said, “the God of my father is my helper and delivered me from Pharaoh’s sword.” Jethro, Moses’ kinsman, therefore came, together with Moses’ sons and wife, to Moses in the wilderness, where he was encamped beside the mountain of God. Aaron and all the elders of Israel also came to eat bread with him before the Lord (Exod. XVIII).

*[From Augustine.]* It is asked: where were they before God, when there was neither a tabernacle nor the ark of the covenant, which were instituted later? For we cannot understand this as referring to the future, as in the case of the manna that was placed in a golden vessel. Therefore, we must understand “before God” as referring to what had already been done. For where is God not present?

On the following day Moses sat to judge the people, and the people stood before Moses from morning until evening. When his kinsman saw everything that he was doing for the people, he said: “What is this that you are doing among the people? Why do you sit alone, while all the people wait from morning until evening?” Moses answered him: “The people come to me to seek God’s judgment. Whenever some dispute arises among them, they come to me, so that I may judge between them and make known to them God’s precepts and his laws.”

*[From Augustine.]* It may be asked how Moses could have said these things, since no law of God had yet been written down—unless it is because the law of God is eternal, and all devout minds consult it, so that whatever they find in it they either do, command, or forbid, according to what that unchangeable truth has prescribed. For must we believe that Moses, although God spoke with him, was accustomed to consult God about every individual matter whenever some dispute arose among the great multitude that kept him occupied in this judicial business from morning until evening? Yet unless he consulted the Lord who presided over his mind, and wisely attended to his law, he would not have discovered what was most just to judge between those in dispute.

But Jethro said: “You are not doing a good thing. You and this people who are with you are exhausting yourselves with fruitless labor. The task is beyond your strength; you alone cannot sustain it. But hear my words and my counsel, and God will be with you.”

When Jethro gives this counsel to his son-in-law Moses, so that neither he nor the people might be worn out by the intolerable burden of judging the people, the first question is why God allowed his servant—God himself spoke so many and such great things with him—to be admonished by a foreigner. In this, Scripture admonishes us that counsel of truth, whoever gives it, must not be despised.

We must also consider whether perhaps God wished Moses to be admonished by a foreigner precisely where pride might have tempted him. For he was seated in judicial eminence. This meaning is indicated when Jethro himself ordered him to choose for judging the people those who hated pride.

Furthermore, how carefully one must observe what Scripture says elsewhere—“My son, do not let your affairs be many” (Eccl. XI)—is sufficiently apparent here also.

Next, Jethro’s words in giving counsel to Moses must be considered. For he says: “Now therefore listen to me, and I will give you counsel, and God will be with you.” Here he seems to me to signify that a mind too intensely occupied with human affairs is, in a certain sense, emptied of God; whereas it becomes fuller of him the more freely it extends itself toward heavenly and eternal things.

He continues: “You shall represent the people before God in matters that concern God, and you shall bring their words to him. You shall show the people the ceremonies and the manner of worship, the way in which they must walk, and the work they must do. But choose from all the people capable men who fear God, in whom there is truth, and who hate greed. Appoint them as tribunes, hundreds’ commanders, fifties’ commanders, and tens’ commanders, to judge the people at all times. Whatever matter is greater, let them refer to you; let them judge only the smaller matters. Thus the burden, divided among others, will be lighter for you. If you do this, you will fulfill the Lord’s command, and you will be able to bear his precepts; and all this people will return peacefully to their homes.”

When he adds, “You shall represent the people before God in matters that concern God; you shall bring their words to God; you shall testify to them God’s precepts and his law; and you shall show them the ways in which they must walk and the works they must do,” he makes clear that these things are to be done for the whole people. For he does not say that he should bring each individual’s words to God, but “their words,” although above he had said, “You shall represent the people in matters that concern God.”

After this, he warns that the individual matters they have among themselves must not be neglected. Accordingly, capable men were to be chosen—men who worshiped God, were just, and hated pride—and appointed over thousands, others over hundreds, others over fifties, and others over tens. Thus he removed from Moses heavy and dangerous occupations, without overburdening the others, since each thousand would have one appointed over it, and under him ten others, and under those twenty more, and under these a hundred more; so that, as is suggested, scarcely any matter requiring judgment would reach each individual officer.

Here too there is an example of humility: Moses, with whom God spoke, did not disdain or despise the counsel of his foreign father-in-law. Although Jethro himself was not an Israelite, it is rightly asked whether he should be regarded among men who worshiped the true God and possessed religious wisdom, like Job, who likewise did not belong to that people. Indeed, this is considered more credible.

The words are ambiguously expressed: whether Jethro sacrificed to the true God among his people when he saw his son-in-law, or whether Moses himself worshiped him. Yet even if worship had been explicitly mentioned, it would seem that honor was being paid to his father-in-law in the manner ordinarily shown to human beings as an expression of respect, as by the patriarchs—for it is written of Abraham that he worshiped the sons of Heth (Gen. XXVII).

What he means by *grammatoisagogues* after the decurions cannot easily be determined, since we have no ordinary use of this name either for offices or for teaching positions. Some learned interpreters have explained it as referring to teachers of letters, who introduce people into literacy, as the Greek word itself suggests. Here it is certainly indicated that, before the law was given, the Hebrews possessed letters; but whether it is possible to investigate from whom these letters began, I do not know.

Some think that they began with the first human beings, were transmitted as far as Noah, and from there to Abraham’s ancestors, and from them to the people of Israel. But how this can be proved, I do not know.

*[From Isidore.]* It is a matter of great wonder, as we have said, that Moses the prophet, filled with God, who spoke with the Lord face to face, accepted counsel from a gentile, so that he might do everything that the man advised. This occurred so that he might provide an example of humility to rulers of peoples and signify an image of the future sacrament.

For he knew that at some time a people gathered from the nations would, at that people’s prompting, supply what was lacking in the law and bring a good and spiritual understanding to the law of God; and he knew that the law would hear that same people and do everything that it said, and that the deficiency of the law would be completed through the Gospel’s prompting.

## CHAPTER X. The arrival of the children of Israel at Mount Sinai, where he commanded the people through Moses to be ready for the third day

In the third month after Israel’s departure from the land of Egypt, on this day, they came into the wilderness of Sinai. For, having set out from Rephidim and reached the wilderness of Sinai, they encamped in that same place; and there Israel pitched its tents facing the mountain.

Moses went up to God, and the Lord called to him from the mountain and said: “These are the things you shall say to the house of Jacob and announce to the children of Israel,” and so forth (Exod. XIX).

*[From Isidore.]* After these events, on the forty-seventh day after Israel’s departure from Egypt, the people came to Mount Sinai. There Moses went up to God, and the Lord descended to him.

What is the moral meaning of Moses’ ascending the mountain and the Lord’s descending upon the mountain? The mountain is the height of our contemplation, to which we ascend so that we may be lifted up to behold those things that exceed our weakness. Yet the Lord descends into it because, when many holy people are making progress, he reveals a little of himself to their understanding.

“You yourselves have seen what I did to the Egyptians, how I carried you on eagles’ wings and took you to myself.” Mystically, he calls the teachings of the two Testaments “eagles’ wings.” Holy Scripture is therefore rightly compared to the feathers of eagles: by its exhortations it raises us from lowly things; by its consolations it carries us; and by its instructions it continually urges us toward the difficult works of the virtues and toward heavenly rewards.

“If, therefore, you will hear my voice and keep my covenant, you shall be my treasured possession among all peoples. For the whole earth is mine; and you shall be for me a kingdom and a holy nation.”

This testimony of praise was once given through Moses to the ancient people of God. Later the apostle Peter rightly gives it to the nations, saying: “But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people of possession” (I Pet. II), because they believed in Christ, who, like a cornerstone, united the nations to the salvation that Israel had in itself.

He calls them a chosen race because of their faith, distinguishing them from those who, by rejecting the living stone, themselves became rejected. He calls them a royal priesthood because they have been united to his body, and he is the supreme King and true Priest, granting them a kingdom as King and cleansing their sin by the sacrifice of his blood as High Priest.

He calls them a royal priesthood so that they may remember to prepare an everlasting kingdom for themselves and always offer to God the sacrifices of an unstained life.

They are also called a holy nation and a people of possession, according to what the apostle Paul says when explaining the prophet’s statement, “But my righteous one lives by faith” (Hab. II): “And if he withdraws, my soul shall have no pleasure in him. But we,” he says, “are not children of withdrawal unto destruction, but of faith unto the acquisition of the soul.”

And in the Acts of the Apostles: “The Holy Spirit has appointed you bishops to govern the Church of the Lord, which he acquired with his own blood” (Acts XX). We have therefore become a people of possession through the blood of our Redeemer, just as Israel was once a people redeemed from Egypt by the blood of the lamb.

Moses came and, having summoned the elders of the people, explained all the words that the Lord had commanded. All the people answered together: “Everything that the Lord has spoken, we will do.” When Moses had reported the words of the people to the Lord, the Lord said to him: “Now I will come to you in the darkness of a cloud, so that the people may hear me speaking with you and believe you forever.”

The darkness and everything that was obscure in God’s coming signify the letter of the law; the mountain, however, and everything that was radiant there signify the spiritual meaning. Everything light and luminous belongs to the faithful; all earth and darkness are intended to terrify unbelievers. The law is therefore given with terror, so that the carnal people might fear God and preserve his law with reverence.

Moses therefore announced the words of the people to the Lord, who said to him: “Go to the people and sanctify them today and tomorrow. Let them wash their garments and be ready for the third day. For on the third day the Lord will descend before all the people upon Mount Sinai.”

It is on this day, as the subsequent events show, that the law written on stone tablets by the finger of God is found to have been given. This third day appears to be the third day of the third month after the departure from Egypt.

From the day on which they celebrated the Passover—that is, sacrificed and ate the lamb—which was the fourteenth day of the first month, until the day on which the law was given, fifty days are counted: seventeen days of the first month, counting the days remaining after the fourteenth; then all thirty days of the second month, making forty-seven; and then the third day of the third month, which is the fiftieth day from the solemnity of the slain lamb.

Thus, in this shadow of the future, corresponding to the festival of the immaculate Lamb, just as the law written by the finger of God was given on the fiftieth day, so in the very truth of the New Testament fifty days are counted from the festival of Christ Jesus, the immaculate Lamb, until the Holy Spirit was given from on high.

We have already said, with the testimony of the Gospel, that the finger of God is the Holy Spirit. What the Lord commanded Moses—to sanctify the people today and tomorrow, to have them wash their garments, and to be ready for the third day—mystically signifies that everyone who desires to come into God’s presence must sanctify himself, that is, prepare himself with sound faith and worthy conduct; and must wash his garments, that is, cleanse his works, in the present and future age, signified by today and tomorrow, so that he may attain the glory of the Lord’s resurrection and immortality.

The third day also indicates this, because Christ rose from the dead on the third day.

“You shall establish boundaries around the people and say: Beware of ascending the mountain or touching its boundaries. Whoever touches the mountain shall surely die. No hand shall touch him; rather, he shall be stoned or pierced with arrows. Whether it is beast or man, it shall not live.”

Why does the Lord, when he is about to give the law, descend in fire and smoke? Is it not because he illuminates the humble by the brightness of his manifestation, while he darkens the eyes of the proud through the obscurity of error?

The mind must first be cleansed of the desire for temporal glory and of every pleasure of carnal lust; then it must be raised to the edge of contemplation. Thus, when the law is received, the people are forbidden to approach the mountain, so that those whose minds are still weak and who desire earthly things may not presume to contemplate sublime realities.

It is rightly said: “If a beast touches the mountain, it shall be stoned.” A beast touches the mountain when a mind subject to irrational desires raises itself to the heights of contemplation. It is struck by stones because, unable to bear the highest things, it is killed by the blows of the heavenly weight.

Therefore, those who strive to grasp the summit of perfection and desire to hold the citadel of contemplation should first test themselves in the field of action through practice. They should carefully determine whether they no longer inflict any evil upon their neighbors; whether they bear patiently the wrongs inflicted by their neighbors; whether temporal goods placed before them do not loosen them through joy; whether, when such goods are taken away, they are not wounded by excessive sorrow.

Then they should consider whether, when they return inwardly to themselves and investigate spiritual things, they drag along with them no shadows of bodily matters—or whether, if they do drag them along, they drive them away by the hand of discernment; and whether, desiring to see the unbounded light, they suppress all the images of their own limitation. In aspiring to touch what is above them, they overcome what they are.

“When the trumpet begins to sound, then they shall ascend the mountain.”

Why does he first forbid the people to ascend the mountain or touch its boundaries, threatening transgressors with death, but now command them to ascend the mountain when the trumpet begins to sound? Is it not because, restraining human boldness, he presses it down, and raises the mind to obey the divine command?

They must therefore ascend the mountain at the sound of the trumpet, because at the voice of sacred preaching the minds of hearers must raise themselves toward heavenly things. The stubborn mind must not rush disorderly into the investigation of heavenly mysteries, driven by the irrational movement of its own presumption; rather, it must follow promptly and devoutly at the divine call, wherever the grace of the giver summons it.

When they had washed their garments, he said to them: “Be ready for the third day, and do not approach your wives.”

Why does he forbid intercourse with their wives after the washing of their garments? Is it not to show us that cleansing one’s works through penitential lamentation is insufficient for the virtue of contemplation without chastity both of body and of soul?

We must therefore cleanse our past actions through the compunction of tears and preserve the complete purity of our hearts, because otherwise we are not sufficient for the contemplation of God and the reception of true wisdom. Hence Truth himself says: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. V). And it is written in Solomon: “The Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit, and wisdom will not enter a soul intent on evil” (Wis. I).

## CHAPTER XI. That on the third day thunder began to be heard, lightning to flash, and clouds to cover the mountain, while the sound of the trumpet resounded more powerfully when the Lord had descended upon the mountain

The third day had now arrived, and morning had dawned. Thunder began to be heard, lightning flashed, and a very dense cloud covered the mountain; and the sound of the trumpet resounded with increasing force (Exod. XIX).

*[From Isidore.]* On the fiftieth day after the Passover had been celebrated, the law was given to Moses. Likewise, on the fiftieth day after the Lord’s Passion, which that Passover prefigured, the promised Holy Spirit, the Paraclete, descended upon the apostles and those who were with them.

When they had reached the number one hundred and twenty of the Mosaic age, and the tongues of believers had been divided, the whole world was filled through the preaching of the Gospel. There the law is said to have been written by the finger of God, and the Lord says of the Holy Spirit: “By the finger of God I cast out demons” (Luke XI).

There the whole people looked upon voices, lamps, and the smoking mountain, together with thunder, lightning, and the resounding blast of the trumpet. In the voices and thunder, the cry of preaching is understood; in the lamps, the brightness of miracles; in the sound of the trumpet, the powerful preaching of the saints. All these things were fulfilled at the coming of Christ and of the Holy Spirit, when all Christ’s disciples thundered forth commandments and signs in a variety of languages.

*Sinai* is interpreted as “bush,” signifying the Church, in which the Lord also speaks to Moses. The fact that the Lord, when about to give the law, descended in fire and smoke signifies that he illuminates the faithful by the brightness of his manifestation and darkens the eyes of unbelievers through the smoke of error.

What is seen in darkness signifies that the ungodly, who set their minds on earthly things, did not recognize him descending—that is, being born in humility—amid the darkness of wickedness. Elsewhere he gave the law in darkness because, to unbelievers who would not follow the truth of his law, he spoke, as it were, through darkness, so that they might see and yet not see.

The people who were in the camp were afraid. When Moses had brought them out from the camp to meet God, they stood at the foot of the mountain.

It is worth observing how the sacred writings, at the beginnings of their narratives, express qualities and indicate the limits of events. Sometimes they signify what is to follow by the position of a place; sometimes by the position of the body; sometimes by the condition of the air; and sometimes by the quality of the time.

Through the position of places, divine Scripture expresses the merits that follow and the boundaries of events. Thus it says of Israel that it could not hear God’s words on the mountain but received the commandments on the plains. It thereby indicates the people’s subsequent weakness: they were unable to ascend to the heights but abandoned themselves to lowly things by living carelessly.

Through the position of the body, it announces what is to come. Thus, in the Acts of the Apostles, Stephen declares that he saw Jesus standing at the right hand of God’s power (Acts VII). Standing is characteristic of one who fights or gives assistance. He is therefore rightly seen standing who offers help in the battle of conflict.

The condition of the air likewise demonstrates what follows. Thus, when the evangelist said that no one from Judea would believe while the Lord was preaching, he first remarked: “It was winter” (John X). For it is written: “Iniquity will abound, and the love of many will grow cold” (Matt. XIV). He therefore took care to mention the season of winter in order to indicate the coldness of wickedness present in the hearts of his hearers.

This is also why, before Peter’s denial, it is mentioned that it was cold and that he stood warming himself by the coals. Within, he had already grown numb from the warmth of charity, and by the coals of the persecutors he was, as it were, warming himself again to a more ardent love of the present life, in burning steadfastness.

The quality of time also expresses the outcome of an action. Thus Judas, who would not return to forgiveness but to the treachery of betrayal, is said to have gone out at night; and as he went out, the evangelist says: “It was night” (John XIII). Hence it is also said to the wicked rich man: “This night they will demand your soul from you” (Luke XII). The soul that is led to darkness is said to be demanded not in the day but in the night.

This is why Solomon, who received wisdom without persevering in it, is described as having received it in a dream and at night. This is why the angels came to Abraham at midday, but, when they were about to punish Sodom, they are remembered as having come to it in the evening.

The whole of Mount Sinai was smoking because the Lord had descended upon it in fire; smoke rose from it as from a furnace. The whole mountain was terrifying, and the sound of the trumpet gradually grew stronger and extended farther and farther.

What is signified by the mountain if not our very contemplation? We ascend it so that we may be lifted up to see those things that exceed our weakness. Yet the Lord descends into it because, when we make much progress, he reveals a little of himself to our understanding.

If one may say that there is anything little or anything at all in him, for he is one and always the same and cannot be understood in parts, yet he is said to be shared by his faithful, although no division whatsoever is admitted into his substance.

But because we cannot express him in perfect speech, hindered by the measure of our humanity, as by the weakness of infancy, we echo him to some extent with a stammer.

He says: “The sound of the trumpet gradually grew stronger and extended farther.” The sound of the trumpet is the speech of preachers, which must be formed according to the understanding of the hearers, as seems appropriate to each person. The inexperience of beginners must not be instructed in the same manner as the capacity of the learned.

Thus Paul said to certain of his hearers: “I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal, as infants in Christ. I gave you milk, not food,” and so forth (I Cor. III). And elsewhere he says: “We speak wisdom among the perfect, which none of the rulers of this age has known” (I Cor. II).

The Lord descended upon Mount Sinai, upon the summit of the mountain, and called Moses to its peak.

Behold, the Lord is said to descend to the summit of the mountain and to call Moses to its peak. This shows that the Lord always summons the progress of his saints to higher and more perfect things. He himself is their supreme perfection, because his perpetual vision is the consummation of every virtue.

When Moses had gone up, the Lord said to him: “Descend and testify to the people, lest perhaps they wish to cross the boundaries in order to see the Lord, and a very great multitude of them perish.”

The Lord warns the people not to cross the appointed boundaries in order to see the Lord, because great discernment is necessary, lest anyone attempt to search into and discuss the divine nature beyond what he ought or is able to understand.

Hence Scripture says: “Whoever searches out majesty will be overwhelmed by glory” (Prov. XXV). And elsewhere Wisdom herself says: “You have found honey; eat what is sufficient for you, lest, when you are filled, you vomit it up and swear falsely by the name of your God” (ibid.).

The Lord spoke all these words to Moses: “I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, from the house of slavery” (Exod. XX).

*[From Origen.]* Everyone who says that he despises the present age—which is figuratively called Egypt—and, to use the words of Scripture, has been translated by the word of God and is not found because he hastens and strives toward the future age: concerning such a soul God says, “I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt.”

These words are not spoken only to those who departed from Egypt, but much more to you who now hear them—provided that you depart from Egypt and no longer serve the Egyptians. God says: “I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, from the house of slavery.”

Consider whether the affairs of this world and the works of the flesh are not a house of slavery; and, conversely, whether abandoning worldly things and living according to God is not a house of freedom, as the Lord says in the Gospels: “If you remain in my word, you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free” (John VIII).

Egypt, therefore, is the house of slavery, while Judea and Jerusalem are the house of freedom. Hear also the apostle proclaiming this according to the wisdom given to him in the mystery: “But the Jerusalem above,” he says, “is free, and she is the mother of us all” (Gal. IV).

Just as this earthly province of Egypt is called the house of slavery for the children of Israel in comparison with Judea and Jerusalem, which became for them the house of freedom, so, in comparison with the heavenly Jerusalem—which, so to speak, is the mother of freedom—this whole world and everything in the world is a house of slavery.

And because, as punishment for sin, humanity had come from the paradise of freedom into the slavery of this world, the first statement of the Decalogue, that is, the first voice of God’s commandments, speaks of freedom, saying: “I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, from the house of slavery.”

While you were in Egypt, you could not hear this voice, even if you were commanded to celebrate the Passover; even if you girded your loins and put sandals on your feet; even if you held a staff in your hand and ate unleavened bread with bitterness.

And what do I mean by saying that, while you were in Egypt, you could not hear these things? Even after you had departed from there, you could not hear them immediately at the first stopping-place, nor at the second, nor at the third; not even when you had crossed the Red Sea, even if you came to Marah and your bitterness had been turned into sweetness; even if you came to Elim, to the twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees; even if you had passed Rephidim and gone farther through the remaining stages—you were not yet judged fit for such words, but only when you came to Mount Sinai.

After many labors had therefore been completed, after many hardships and temptations had been overcome, you would scarcely at last deserve to receive the commandments of freedom and hear from the Lord: “I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, from the house of slavery.”

Yet this statement is not itself still a commandment; it shows who it is that commands. Let us now see what the beginning of the Ten Commandments of the law is, and, if we do not encounter all the beginnings, let us at least explain them as the Lord grants us ability.

## CHAPTER XII. The word of God to the people, setting forth the Decalogue of the law

The first commandment is therefore: “You shall have no other gods besides me.” After this follows: “You shall not make for yourself a carved image, nor any likeness of what is in heaven above, or on the earth below, or in the waters beneath the earth. You shall not worship them or serve them” (Exod. XX).

*[From Origen.]* I think that the apostle Paul also took from this the statement that he writes to the Corinthians: “Indeed, there are those who are called gods, whether in heaven or on earth” (I Cor. VIII). And he added: “Just as there are many gods and many lords; yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things and we from him; and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and we through him.”

What he says amounts to this: Although there are many lords who rule over other nations, and many gods who are worshiped by others, for us there is one God and one Lord.

“You shall not make an idol for yourself, nor any likeness of those things that are in heaven or on earth,” and so forth. To make an idol is therefore one thing, and to make a likeness is another.

If the Lord deigns to enlighten us concerning what must be said, I think the distinction should be understood as follows. Suppose that someone makes, out of some metal—gold or silver—or out of wood or stone, the form of some quadruped, serpent, or bird, and sets up that statue to be worshiped: he has made not an idol but a likeness. Likewise, if he sets up a painting for the same purpose, he must still be said to have made a likeness.

An idol, however, is made by the person who, in accordance with the apostle’s statement that “an idol is nothing,” makes what does not exist. What is this that does not exist? It is a form that the eye has not seen but that the mind itself imagines.

For example, if someone forms a dog’s or ram’s head with human limbs, or again invents two faces in a single human body, or attaches the hindquarters of a horse and a fish to a human chest: whoever makes these and similar things makes not a likeness but an idol. He makes what does not exist and has nothing like itself. For this reason the apostle, knowing these things, says that “an idol is nothing in the world.”

No form is taken from things that exist; rather, it is something that an idle and curious mind invents for itself. A likeness, however, is formed from things that exist in heaven, on earth, or in the waters, as we said above.

Nevertheless, just as it is easy to speak about likenesses of things on earth or in the sea, so it is not equally easy to pronounce upon heavenly things, unless someone says that this may be understood of the sun, moon, and stars; for the pagans also commonly represent the forms of these. But because Moses had been educated in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, he wished to prohibit even those things that they kept hidden and concealed.

“For I am the Lord your God, a jealous Lord.”

Observe God’s kindness: in order to teach us and make us perfect, he does not refuse to assume the language of human emotions. For who, hearing that God is jealous, would not immediately be astonished and think that this was a defect of human weakness? Yet God both does and suffers everything for our sake; and, so that we may be instructed, he speaks to us through emotions familiar and customary to us.

Let us therefore see what he means by saying, “I am a jealous Lord.” To make divine things more readily understood through human realities, according to what we discussed above, let us explain by examples.

Every woman is either under a husband and subject to her husband’s laws, or she is a prostitute and uses the freedom to sin. A man who goes to a prostitute knows that he has gone to a woman who has been prostituted and is open to everyone who desires her; therefore, he cannot be angry if he sees other lovers with her.

But the man who lives in a lawful marriage does not allow his wife the power to sin; rather, he is inflamed with jealousy to preserve the chastity of the marriage, so that he may become her lawful father.

By this example, then, let us understand every soul as either prostituted to demons and possessing many lovers—so that the spirit of fornication enters it for a time, then, when that spirit departs, the spirit of greed enters; after that comes the spirit of pride, then anger, then envy, and afterward vainglory, along with many others—or as joined to a lawful husband.

All these spirits commit fornication with the unbelieving soul in such a way that none envies another or is moved by jealousy against the others. And why do I say that one does not exclude another? Rather, they invite and summon one another willingly, just as we said earlier concerning the spirit that went out from a person and, returning, brought with it seven other spirits more wicked than itself (Luke XI), so that they might dwell together in one soul.

Thus the soul prostituted to demons suffers no jealousy among its lovers. But if it has been lawfully joined to a husband—to that husband whose marriage Paul uses to join and unite souls, as he himself says, “For I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ” (I Cor. XI)—and of whom it is written in the Gospels that “a certain king made a wedding feast for his son” (Matt. XXII), then, when the soul has given itself to this husband’s wedding and entered into a lawful marriage with him, even if it was once sinful and even if it had prostituted itself, nevertheless, if it has surrendered itself to this husband, he no longer permits it to sin.

He cannot endure that the soul which has obtained a husband should again amuse itself with adulterers. His jealousy is aroused against it, and he defends the chastity of the marriage.

God is therefore called jealous because he does not allow the soul devoted to him to mingle with demons. Otherwise, if he sees it violating the laws of marriage and seeking opportunities for sin, then, as it is written, he gives it a bill of divorce and sends it away, saying: “Where is the bill of divorce of your mother, with which I dismissed her?” (Deut. XIV). He also adds: “Behold, you were sold because of your sins, and because of your iniquities I dismissed your mother” (Jer. III).

Visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon their children to the third and fourth generation of those who hate me; and showing mercy to thousands of those who love me [Col. 0097A] and keep my commandments, and so forth.

Now, therefore, let us see, according to the lineage we have described, how God returns the sins of the fathers upon the children to the third and fourth generation, while he does not return them upon the fathers themselves. For he said nothing about the fathers. The devil, therefore, because he has already exceeded every limit in sinning, as the prophet says, “like a garment thickened with blood, he will not be clean,” so he too will not be clean in this age; nor is he corrected on account of sin, nor scourged. For everything is reserved for him for the future. Hence, knowing that the appointed time of punishment was reserved for him, he said to the Savior: “Why have you come to torment us before the time?” (Matt. VIII).

While this world therefore remains, the devil, who is the father of sinners, does not receive his sins. They are returned upon the children [Col. 0097B], that is, upon those whom he has begotten through sin. For human beings, placed in the flesh, are corrected by the Lord, beaten, and scourged. The Lord does not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn back and live. Therefore the kind and merciful Lord returns the sins of the fathers upon the children, so that, just as the fathers—that is, the devil and his angels, and the other rulers of the world and governors of this darkness—are unworthy to be corrected in the present age (for they too become fathers of sin, just as the devil does), and receive in the future what they deserve, so their children—that is, those whom they have persuaded to sin and who have nevertheless been summoned through them to participation and fellowship in sin—receive what they have done, so that they may proceed into the future age more purified [Col. 0097C] and may no longer become the devil’s companions in punishment.

Because the Lord is merciful and desires all human beings to be saved, he therefore says: “I will visit their crimes with a rod, and their sins with scourges. But I will not remove my mercy from them” (Ps. LXXXVIII). The Lord therefore visits souls and seeks out those whom that most wicked father has begotten by persuading them to sin, and he says to each one of them: “Hear, O daughter, and see, and incline your ear, and forget your people and your father’s house” (Ps. XVI).

The Lord therefore visits the time of sin and admonishes you; with scourge and rod he visits you on account of the sin that the devil, your father, has subjected you to, so that he may return it to you as a sign—that is, while you dwell in the body. Thus is fulfilled the statement that the sins of the fathers are returned into the bosoms of the children to the third and fourth [Col. 0097D] generation.

For the Lord is jealous, and he does not wish the soul that he has betrothed to himself in faith to remain in the pollution of sin. Rather, he wishes it to be purified quickly and speedily to cast off all its uncleannesses, even if some uncleanness has perhaps stealthily entered. But if it persists in sins and says, “We will not hear the voice of the Lord; instead, we will do our own will, and we will burn incense to the queen of heaven,” as the prophet reproaches them, then they too are reserved for that sentence of Wisdom which says: “Because I called and you did not listen, but mocked my words, I also will mock your destruction” (Jer. XLIV). Or for that sentence pronounced against them in the Gospel, when the Lord says: “Depart from me into the eternal fire, which God prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. XXV).

We can also understand this statement in another way, since God says that he visits the iniquity of the fathers upon the children to the third and fourth generation, so that among those who follow the sins of their fathers the condemnation of a just sentence may remain. For it would seem almost unjust that one should sin and another pay the penalty for the sins. But the words that follow—“of those who hate me”—remove the difficulty of the threat or command. They are not punished in the third and fourth generation merely because their fathers sinned, when rather the fathers who were sinners ought to have been punished; they are punished because they became imitators of their fathers and hated God. Through inherited evil and impiety they perished, as the branches too grow from the root.

There are some who explain what is now written in Exodus—“returning the iniquities of the fathers upon the children to the third and fourth generation”—by referring the sentence to the human soul. They say that the father in us is the slight movement of the senses and the incitements of vices; the son, if thought has conceived sin; the grandson, if what you have thought and conceived you have carried out in deed; and the great-grandson, that is, the fourth generation, if you have not merely done what is evil and wicked but have gloried in your crimes, according to what is written: “When the impious has come into the depth of evils, he despises” (Prov. XVIII).

But when, according to Ezekiel, the Lord says: “What is this proverb that you turn into a saying among yourselves in the land of Israel, saying, ‘The fathers ate a sour grape, and the children’s teeth were set on edge’? As I live, says the Lord God, this proverb shall no longer be a proverb for you in Israel. Behold, all souls are mine: as the soul of the father is mine, so also the soul of the son is mine. The soul that sins shall itself die” (Ezek. XVIII), he makes clear that the just Judge will repay each person according to his own merits.

For just as the sins of children do not harm fathers who did not provide their children with a wicked example of sin, so the sins of wicked fathers do not pass over upon their children if they do not become imitators of their evil; but “the soul that sins shall itself die.” This is not, of course, through the abolition of its substance, but through deprivation of fellowship with him who says, “I am life” (John XIV). Elsewhere he says: “Everyone who lives and believes in me shall never die. Amen, amen, I say to you: whoever has kept my word shall never see death” (John V).

“For your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Col. III), because we shall live when Christ, our life, appears in glory. And what is written will be fulfilled: “Amen, amen, I say to you: whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life and does not come into judgment, but passes from death into life” (John VIII).

[From Isidore.]

The first commandment of the Decalogue pertains to God the Father, when it says:

“Your Lord God is one God.” Hearing this, you should worship one God the Father, and not pour out your fornication upon many fabricated gods.

The second commandment pertains to the Son, when it says:

[Col. 0099A] “You shall not take the name of your God in vain.” That is, do not think that the Son of God is a creature, since every creature is subject to vanity; rather, believe that he is equal to the Father, God of gods, the Word with God, through whom all things were made (John I).

The third commandment, concerning the sabbath, pertains to the Holy Spirit, by whose gift eternal rest is promised to us. Since the Holy Spirit is so called, God therefore sanctified the seventh day. On the other days of creation no sanctification is mentioned, except on the sabbath, where it says: “God rested” (Gen. I). Accordingly, this commandment pertains to the Holy Spirit both because of the name of sanctification and because of the eternal rest that belongs to the gift of the Holy Spirit. For it says there:

[Col. 0099B] “Remember to sanctify the sabbath day. Six days you shall labor and do all your work. But the seventh day is the sabbath of the Lord your God: you shall do no work.”

In the work of the six days is contained the activity of the six ages. In the seventh, rest is shown: the time of that blessed kingdom, which the Jews sin by celebrating in a carnal manner. To prevent us from adapting ourselves to a faith in falsehood, the prophet cries out, saying: “My soul has hated your new moons and your sabbaths” (Isa. I). How, then, were those sabbaths sanctified which God hated?

That sabbath is sanctified in which, after the good works of this life, eternal rest is promised to us. Therefore, whatever we do, if we do it for the sake of the rest of the future age, we truly observe the sabbath.

After these commandments, the number seven of the commandments follows, pertaining to love of one’s neighbor. It begins with the honor due to parents, although this is fourth in order:

“Honor your father and your mother.”

From their parents human beings first open their eyes, and this life takes its beginning from love of them. Hence this is the first commandment among the seven, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “Honor your father and your mother,” which is “the first commandment” (Matt. XV). But how is it first if it is fourth, unless, as has been said, it is first in the sevenfold number that pertains to love of neighbor, in the second table? For this reason two tables of the law were given.

In this commandment, therefore, children are ordered to honor their parents and not to be insulting toward them, but to show them the reverence owed by filial duty. For whoever does not know how to honor his parents, whom can he spare, since he hates his own?

The fifth:

“You shall not commit adultery,” that is, no one shall mingle with other women outside the bond of marriage in order to satisfy his lust. For the man who approaches another woman in addition to his own wife commits adultery in the strict sense.

The sixth:

“You shall not kill.” For not only does the person who commits murder by deed become a murderer; the person who encounters someone hungry or naked, who might die unless he helps him by providing clothing and food, is likewise held to be a murderer.

The seventh:

[Col. 0100A] “You shall not steal.” This is the vice of rapacity.

The eighth:

“You shall not bear false witness.” This is the crime of lying and falsity.

The ninth:

“You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife.” In this commandment he forbids the intention of adulterous thought. For it is one thing to do such a thing with someone other than one’s wife, and another to desire another man’s wife. Therefore there are two commandments: “You shall not commit adultery,” and “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife.”

The tenth:

“You shall not covet anything belonging to your neighbor.” In this commandment he condemns worldly ambition and restrains the desire for possessions.

Thus the first of these commandments forbids deceit, the second error, the third destroys love of the world, the fourth impiety, the fifth crushes fornication, the sixth cruelty, the seventh rapacity, the eighth kills falsehood, the ninth adulterous thought, and the tenth desire for the world.

[From Augustine.]

It should be noted that just as the Egyptians are struck by ten plagues, so the tablets are inscribed with ten commandments, by which the people of God are ruled and demons are killed. But the first event, performed as a sign—that the rod might be changed into a serpent—does not belong among the ten plagues. It was the entrance itself before Pharaoh, by which Moses, who was about to lead the people of God out of Egypt, was commended. The rebellious were not yet being struck; they were already being terrified by a divine sign.

The rod signified the kingdom of God, and likewise the people of God, since they are the kingdom of God. The serpent, however, signified the time of this mortality; for death was introduced through the serpent. Thus, as though falling from the hand of the Lord onto the earth, they became mortal: hence, when the rod was thrown from the hand, it became a serpent.

Pharaoh’s magicians did the same. When their rods were thrown down, they became serpents; but Moses’ serpent—that is, Moses’ rod—first devoured all the serpents of the magicians. Then, when its tail was grasped, it again became a rod, and the kingdom returned to the hand.

The rods of the magicians are therefore the peoples of the impious, conquered by the name of Christ. When they are transferred into his body, they are devoured, as it were, by Moses’ serpent, until the kingdom of God returns to the hand of God. But at the end of the mortal age, signified by the serpent’s tail, a great sign will occur.

You have heard what you ought to desire; hear what you ought to avoid.

## CHAPTER XIII. Comparison of the Decalogue with the Ten Plagues of Egypt.

The first commandment in the law concerns worship of the one God: “You shall have no other gods,” he says, “besides me.”

Compare the first commandment with the first plague. The first plague of the Egyptians was water changed into blood. Understand the one God, from whom all things exist, in the likeness of water, from which all things are generated. To what does blood pertain except to mortal flesh? What, then, is the changing of water into blood except that “their foolish heart was darkened”? For, claiming to be wise, they became fools, “and they exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of the image of corruptible man” (Rom. I).

The glory of the incorruptible God is like water; the likeness of the image of corruptible man is like blood. This indeed takes place in the heart of the impious, for God remains unchangeable. Since the Apostle said, “They exchanged,” it does not follow that God was changed.

The second commandment is: “You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain.” Whoever takes the name of the Lord his God in vain will not be cleansed. The name of our Lord Jesus Christ is truth. For he himself said: “I am the truth” (John XIV).

Truth therefore commands; vanity defiles. And since whoever speaks truth speaks of God—for whoever speaks a lie speaks from his own nature—speaking truth is speaking rationally. Speaking vanity is making noise rather than speaking. And rightly so, because the second commandment is love of truth, to which love of vanity is opposed.

Truth speaks; vanity makes a din. Consider the second plague, which is opposed to this second commandment. What is that second plague? An abundance of frogs. You have an explicit representation of vanity if you attend to the loquacity of frogs.

Observe the lovers of truth, who do not take the name of the Lord their God in vain, speaking wisdom among the perfect. Even to speak among the perfect what they themselves cannot understand is not to depart from truth and proceed into vanity. For although the imperfect do not grasp something somewhat more elevated that has been discussed concerning the Word of God, through whom all things were made, and although they may grasp what Paul speaks among them as among the little ones of Christ—“Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (I Cor. II)—the former is not thereby truth and the latter vanity.

It would be vanity, however, if we said that Christ had not truly undergone death but had only pretended to do so; if we said that those wounds were only apparitions; if the blood flowing from his wounds were not real but feigned; if he displayed false scars as though they followed false wounds. But when we say that all these things truly happened, we affirm and proclaim them as certain, manifest, and fulfilled.

Although we do not speak of the sublime and unchangeable truth of that God, we nevertheless do not go into vanity. Those who say that all these things in Christ were false and simulated are frogs crying in a swamp. They may possess the din of a voice, but they cannot convey the teaching of wisdom.

Finally, in the Church they speak while clinging to the truth—the truth through which all things were made; the truth, the Word made flesh and dwelling among us; the truth, Christ born from God; one from one, only-begotten and coeternal; the truth who, having taken the form of a servant, was born from the Virgin Mary, suffered, was crucified, rose again, ascended, and is truth everywhere.

And what the little one cannot grasp is nevertheless truth, both in bread and in milk: in the bread of the mature, in the milk of the little ones. For the same bread is made into milk by passing through the flesh.

Those who contradict this truth, deceived by their own vanity and deceiving others, are frogs bringing weariness to the ears rather than nourishment to minds.

Hear, finally, people speaking rationally: “There are neither speeches nor words whose voices are not heard” (Ps. XVIII). But these are not empty voices, because “their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world.”

But if you wish to understand frogs in the opposite sense, recall that verse of the psalm: “Each one spoke vain things to his neighbor” (Ps. XI).

The third commandment is: “Remember to sanctify the sabbath day.” In this third commandment a certain indication of vocation is conveyed: tranquility of heart and mind, which conscience produces. There is sanctification there, because there is the Spirit of God.

Finally, to see vocation is to see rest. “Upon whom,” he says, “shall my spirit rest, except upon the humble and quiet one who trembles at my words?” (Isa. LXVI).

The restless therefore recoil from the Holy Spirit: provocateurs of quarrels, lovers of accusations, sowers of contention, whose inmost thoughts are more desirous of vanity than of truth. Consequently, through their restlessness they do not admit into themselves the rest of the spiritual sabbath.
