Against their restlessness it is said, as though so that they may have the sabbath in their hearts, through the sanctification of the Spirit of God: “Be gentle in hearing the word, so that you may understand.”

“What shall I understand?”

God saying: “Cease from your restlessness; let there be no tumult in your heart through corruption, with fantasies flying about and pricking you. Let it not be so.” For you are going to understand God saying to you: “Be still and see that I am the Lord” (Ps. XLV).

You do not wish to let your restlessness cease, blinded by the corruption of your contentions; you demand to see what you cannot see.

Consider, then, the third plague, which is opposed to this third commandment. Gnats were produced in the land of Egypt from the mud. They are certain very small and extremely restless flies, flying about disorderly, rushing into the eyes, and not allowing a person to rest. When they are driven away, they rush back; when cast off, they return again. Such altogether are the vain fantasies of contentious hearts.

Hold fast to the commandment; beware of the plague.

The fourth commandment is: “Honor your father and your mother.” The fourth plague of the Egyptians is opposed to this. What is cynomia? Cynomia is a dog-fly; it is a Greek word. It is canine not to recognize one’s parents. Nothing is so canine as failing to acknowledge those who have begotten one.

Therefore, deservedly, they are born blind like puppies.

The fifth commandment is: “You shall not commit adultery.” The fifth plague is the death of the Egyptians’ livestock.

Let us compare these things. Consider a man contemplating adultery, not content with his own marriage, unwilling to restrain within himself a certain appetite of the flesh, which we share with animals. To lie together and beget offspring belong also to beasts; to reason and understand is human.

Therefore reason, which presides in the mind, must restrain the lower movements of the flesh as a reigning and ruling power, not release them without measure, unlawfully, indiscriminately, and at random.

For this reason nature, under the Creator’s direction, has given even to animals that they are not moved toward females and intercourse except at fixed times. The animal does not restrain itself by reason at other times; rather, when the movement itself grows cold, it becomes altogether sluggish.

A human being, however, can always be moved because he can also restrain the movement. The Creator has given you the dominion of reason; he has granted you the commands of continence as reins, as though over lower beasts.

You possess what the animal cannot possess. You labor somewhat in restraining yourself; the animal does not labor. But you will rejoice forever in eternity, to which the animal does not attain. If the work brings weariness, let the reward console you.

For patience itself consists in restraining the inner movement. What you share with the animal, you must not release in every respect as an animal would.

But if you despise yourself and neglect the image of God in which he made you, overcome by the desire for conspicuous things, you will be an animal, as though you had lost your humanity—not as though you had been transformed into the nature of an animal, but as one who, while retaining human form, bears the likeness of an animal. You do not heed the saying: “Do not be like the horse and the mule, which have no understanding” (Ps. XXXI).

Perhaps you choose to be an animal for yourself, to wander freely in lust, with no law restraining the appetite of the flesh toward continence. Consider the plague: if you are an animal, you do not fear—but at least fear death.

The sixth commandment is: “You shall not kill.” The sixth plague is boils on the body, bubbling and festering blisters, burning wounds, and furnace ashes.

Such are murderous souls. They burn with anger, because through anger the brotherhood of human beings is destroyed. People burn with anger; they burn also with grace. But one is the heat of health, another the heat of an ulcer.

Burning eruptions throughout the body, conceived murders, fester; this is not health. It seethes, but not from the Spirit of God. For the person who wishes to help also burns: one burns in obedience to a commandment, the other through disease; one with good works, the other with the pus of ulcers.

If we could see the souls of murderers, we would grieve more than over the rotting bodies of the ulcerated.

It follows:

[Col. 0103C] “You shall not steal.” The seventh commandment and the seventh plague are hail upon the crops. Whatever you take away contrary to the commandment, you lose from heaven. For no one has unjust gain without just loss.

For example, the person who steals acquires a garment but loses faith through heavenly judgment. Where there is gain, there is loss: visible gain, invisible loss. Gain from his own blindness; loss from the Lord’s cloud.

For nothing happens without providence, beloved. Do you really think that the things human beings suffer happen while God sleeps? These things seem to happen randomly: clouds gather, rains pour down, hail is hurled, the earth is shaken by thunder, and people are terrified by lightning. They are thought to happen randomly, as though they did not belong to divine providence.

Against such thoughts that psalm remains vigilant: “Praise the Lord from the earth.” After praises had been spoken of heaven, it names “dragons and all abysses, fire, hail, snow, ice, stormy wind, which fulfill his word” (Ps. CXLVIII).

Therefore those who steal outwardly through their evil desire are inwardly pelted with hail by God’s judgment.

O, if they could look into the field of their heart, they would certainly mourn when they found there nothing to place in the mouth of the mind; and if, in their theft, they found something to place in the greed of the belly, the hunger of the inner human being would be greater—a greater hunger, a more dangerous plague, and a heavier death.

Many dead people walk about, and many criminals rejoice in vain riches. Finally, Scripture says that the servant of God is rich inwardly: “The hidden person of your heart, who is before God, is rich,” not rich before human beings (I Pet. III). Where God sees, there is wealth.

What, then, does it profit you? Where human beings do not see, you steal; and where God sees, you are pelted with hail.

The eighth commandment is: “You shall not bear false witness.” The eighth plague is the locust, an animal harmful with its teeth.

What does a false witness desire except to harm by biting and consume by lying? Therefore, warning the people of God not to attack one another with false accusations, the Apostle says: “If you bite and devour one another, see that you are not consumed by one another” (Gal. V).

The ninth commandment is: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife.” The ninth plague is dense darkness.

There is a certain adultery against which the commandment mentioned above was given: one must not even desire another man’s wife in thought. For the man who is moved toward another’s wife is an adulterer simply because he is not content with his own.

But when he not only sins after his own wife but also attempts another’s, there is truly dense darkness. Nothing pains the heart of the sufferer so much, and the person who does this to another wishes to suffer nothing so much himself. Every human being is more ready for what belongs to another.

I do not know whether anyone can bear tolerably the hatred of these darknesses in those who do and desire such things; they are truly blinded by a horrible fury. For it is an untamed fury to trample upon another man’s wife.

The tenth commandment is: “You shall not covet anything belonging to your neighbor”: neither his livestock, nor his property, nor his servant, nor anything at all belonging to your neighbor shall you covet.

The tenth plague, the death of the firstborn, is opposed to this evil plague. When I seek some comparison here, nothing occurs to me for the moment. Perhaps something better may occur to those who inquire more carefully, unless it is because he is reproved for wishing to preserve all the possessions he has for his heirs.

Here, however, the person who covets his neighbor’s property cries out; and the person who takes it away by theft, and the person who steals something from his neighbor, can steal nothing except his neighbor’s property. But theft has already been treated above, where you should understand robbery as well.

For Scripture would not give a commandment concerning theft and remain silent about robbery unless it wished you to understand that, if taking something secretly is punishable, taking it away violently is punishable by a much greater penalty.

Whoever wishes to take something away, whether secretly or openly, has his own commandment; to covet one’s neighbor’s property—which God marks in the heart—is not permitted, even if you seek a lawful succession there.

Finally, those who wish to possess the property of others as though lawfully seek to become heirs of the dying.

For what seems as just as possessing what has been left to oneself and holding it by common right? “What does it matter to you? It was left to me; I obtained an inheritance; I am reading the will.” Nothing seems more just than this language of avarice.

You praise the person as though he possessed the property lawfully; God condemns him as coveting it unjustly. See what kind of person you are when you wish to become someone’s heir. You do not wish him to have heirs.

Among heirs, however, nothing is dearer than the firstborn. Therefore you are punished in your firstborn, when, by coveting another’s property, you seek what was not owed to you by right, as though pursuing it under the shadow of legality.

It is easy enough to lose bodily firstborn brothers. Human beings die, whether they die before their parents or after their parents; they die. What is grievous is that through this hidden and unjust covetousness you may lose the firstborn child of your heart.

For the firstborn in us bears the image of God’s grace. Among all the offspring born within our hearts, faith is the firstborn: no one does good works unless faith has preceded them.

All your good works are your spiritual children. But among them faith is your firstborn. Whoever secretly covets another’s property loses faith inwardly. For you will certainly first become a false and compliant pretender, not out of love but out of fraud, as though loving the person from whom you desire to become heir. While loving him, you seek his death; and so that you may see yourself possessing his property, you begrudge him a successor.

## CHAPTER XIV. Concerning the people’s terror, because they could not endure the greatness of the vision.

Now the whole people saw the voices and the lamps, the sound of the trumpet, and the mountain smoking (Exod. XX).

It is usually asked how the people saw a voice, since a voice seems to belong not to sight but rather to hearing. But it can be understood in a certain way, as I might say: “Let it be seen concerning all the things I have said.” Thus “to see” is customarily used for a general sense, not only of the body but also of the mind.

Hence there is the statement: “When Jacob saw that there was food in Egypt” (Gen. XLI), although he was absent from Egypt. Some, however, have thought that “to see a voice” means nothing other than to understand, since understanding is the sight of the mind.

But since it had to be said briefly here that the people saw the voice and the lamps, and the voice of the trumpet and the smoking mountain, a greater question would arise: how did they hear the lamps and the smoking mountain, which belong to the sense of sight? Unless one says that it should not have been stated so briefly, but rather everything should have been said in full: they heard the voice and saw the lamps, heard the voice of the trumpet, and saw the smoking mountain.

For there were two kinds of voice from the clouds, like thunder and the trumpet. If he called the sound produced by the clouds itself “the voice,” then the general sense—namely, seeing—has been placed in those matters that pertain to hearing, because Scripture wished to include everything briefly, rather than implying hearing in those things that pertain to the sense of sight, as we do not ordinarily speak.

For we ordinarily say, “See what makes a sound”; we do not ordinarily say, “Hear what shines.”

[Col. 0105D] And terrified and shaken by fear, they stood far away, saying to Moses: “Speak to us, and we will hear; let God not speak to us, lest perhaps we die.”

This very clearly signifies that fear pertains rather to the Old Testament, just as love pertains to the New—although the New lies hidden in the Old, and the Old is revealed in the New. But how it can be attributed to such a people that they saw the voice of God, if this is to be understood as meaning “understood,” when they fear God speaking to them lest they die, is not sufficiently clear.

## CHAPTER XV. Moses’ answer to the children of Israel.

And Moses said to the people: “Do not be afraid. For God has come in order to test you, and so that his terror might be in you and you might not sin.” And the people stood far away, but Moses approached the darkness in which God was (Exod. XX).

They had to be restrained from sins by fear—namely, fear that they might suffer bodily punishments—because they were not yet able to love righteousness. In this was their testing by the Lord, by which they were proved, so that what sort of people they were might become apparent: not so that they might become known to God, who was not ignorant of what they were like, but so that they might become known among themselves and to themselves.

The difference belonging to the terrors of the Old Testament is nevertheless greatly emphasized; this is also most appropriately stated in the Epistle to the Hebrews.

Moses, however, entered the cloud where God was—that is, where the clearer signs by which God is known were taking place. For how could there be a cloud for him whom the heaven of heavens cannot contain, unless in the sense that he is nowhere absent, since he is in no place?

In sacred Scripture there is great discernment in understanding. Often, in certain passages, both the history and the allegory must be preserved; often, in certain passages, only the allegory must be sought; and sometimes only the history must necessarily be retained.

For in some passages, as we have said, history and allegory must be held together, so that the slower may be nourished through history and those quicker in intellect through allegory.

Thus, when the people saw the lamps, the sound of the trumpet, and the smoking mountain while God was speaking, they were terrified and asked that the Lord speak to them through Moses. It is written: “The people stood far away; Moses approached the darkness in which God was.”

The crowd of the people is unable to penetrate the darkness of allegories, because it belongs to very few to search out spiritual understanding. Since carnal minds are often nourished by history alone, when God was speaking the people stood far away.

But because all who are spiritual penetrate the cloud of allegories in order to know the words of God spiritually, Moses approached the darkness in which God was.

# BOOK THREE

[Col. 0105]

## PREFACE

[Col. 0105D]

In the preceding book, which we began with the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt, the giving of the law on Mount Sinai was recalled near the end. But, in order to avoid wearying the reader, we judged that the aforesaid book should end there. We have therefore decided that the present book should be composed from what remains of the commandments and judgments given by the Lord through Moses to the people of Israel, so that, just as commandments are joined to commandments, so the books of their exposition may continue one another [Col. 0106D].

## CHAPTER ONE. The legal commandments established by the Lord on Mount Sinai, when he spoke to Moses.

Moreover, the Lord said to Moses: “Thus you shall say to the children of Israel: You have seen that I have spoken to you from heaven. You shall not make gods of silver for yourselves, nor shall you make gods of gold for yourselves. You shall make an altar of earth for me, [Col. 0107A] and upon it you shall offer your burnt offerings and your peace offerings, your sheep and your oxen. In every place where the memory of my name shall be, I will come to you and bless you,” and so on. (Exod. XXII.)

What is said here—“You shall not make gods of silver for yourselves, nor shall you make gods of gold for yourselves”—repeats what was inculcated in the first commandment. By gods of silver and gold, all images are plainly understood, as in the Psalm: “The images of the nations are silver and gold” (Ps. CXIII).

What is added—“You shall make an altar of earth for me”—shows that, in contrast to the forbidden images, an altar was permitted to be made of earthly material solely so that offerings and sacrifices might be presented upon it to the one God. Mystically, to make an altar of earth for God is to hope in the incarnation of the Mediator. For our gift is then accepted by God when, upon this altar, our humility—that is, whatever good it works—has placed it upon faith in the Lord’s incarnation [Col. 0107B]. Thus we receive the offering of our gifts upon an altar of earth if we establish our actions firmly upon faith in the Lord’s incarnation.

Then he added: “But if you make a stone altar for me, you shall not build it of hewn stones. For if you raise a knife over them, it will be defiled.” Hewn stones are those who split unity and separate themselves from fraternal fellowship through hatred or schisms. Christ does not receive such people into his body, whose figure the construction of that altar foreshadows. The unhewn stones, however, from which the altar is commanded to be built, are those made firm by unity of faith and conduct. Of such stones the Apostle says: “You are living stones, [Col. 0107C] built together into a spiritual house” (1 Pet. II). No iron has been applied to these, because they are incorrupt; they have not received the flaming darts of the Evil One, and together they form one altar through unity of faith and harmony of love.

“You shall not go up by steps to my altar”—that is, you shall not come to me by preferring one person step by step over another; nor shall you distinguish between an earlier and a later person in time, because you will not have the divided and separated person as one who is propitious. This is what the Arians do: they divide the indivisible substance of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

“These are the judgments that you shall set before them: If you buy a Hebrew servant, he shall serve you for six years; in the seventh he shall go out free without payment. With whatever garment he entered, with the same he shall go out. If he entered with a wife, his wife shall also go out with him,” and so on. (Exod. XXI.)

The commands concerning the Hebrew servant [Col. 0107D]—that he should serve for six years and then be released freely—were not given so that Christian servants might demand this from their masters. Rather, apostolic authority commands servants to be subject to their masters, lest the name of God and the teaching be blasphemed (1 Tim. VI).

The mystery signified by this command is sufficiently clear: God also commanded that the ear of the man who refused that freedom should be pierced with an awl against the doorpost. It is commanded that, if a Hebrew boy should happen to fall into slavery, he serve for six years, but in the seventh year be released. If he does not wish to leave slavery because of his wife and children, his ear shall be pierced, and he shall be a servant forever.

This is not spoken of the present age but of the age to come, because, after serving through the six ages of this world, [Col. 0108A] we are freed on the seventh day, the eternal Sabbath—provided that we wish to be free while we are still serving sin in this world. But if we do not wish it, our ear will be pierced as a testimony to our disobedience, and with our wife and children, whom we have preferred to freedom—that is, with the flesh and its works—we shall remain perpetually servants of sin forever.

This may also be understood in another way. We should know that both the active and the contemplative life come from God’s grace, but that one is necessary for us whereas the other depends upon our will. For who, having come to know God, enters his kingdom without first doing good? Those who neglect the good they are able to do cannot enter the heavenly homeland without the contemplative life. Nor can they enter without the active life if they neglect to do the good they can do. The former, then, is necessary; the latter depends upon the will.

Therefore it is said to Moses: “If you buy a Hebrew servant, he shall serve you for six years. [Col. 0108B] In the seventh he shall go out free without payment” (Exod. XXI). “Hebrew” is interpreted as “one who passes over.” A Hebrew servant is bought when someone who has already passed in mind from this world is subjected to the service of almighty God. For the person who has learned to pass in mind from this world truly desires to serve God.

Thus Moses passed over in order to see the vision. Likewise David, when he saw the wicked exalted and raised up like the cedars of Lebanon, “passed over, and he was no more” (Ps. XXXVI), because we perhaps believe the power of the wicked to be something great unless we pass over in mind to the enduring age.

The purchased Hebrew servant is commanded to serve for six years, so that in the seventh he may go out free [Col. 0108C] without payment. What does the number six signify if not the perfection of the active life? What does the number seven signify if not the contemplative life? He serves for six years and goes out free in the seventh who, through the active life he has perfectly fulfilled, passes into the freedom of the contemplative life.

It should be noted that he goes out free without payment because those who, after doing everything, say that they are unprofitable servants will doubtless receive the contemplative life by grace, just as the active life itself was a gift.

“With whatever garment he entered, with the same he shall go out”: for it is entirely necessary that each of us persevere in what he begins and continue to the end of his work in the intention with which he began. For the person who does not change the garment of his intention in the active life [Col. 0108D] passes rightly into the contemplative life.

There are some who, even before they are joined to the service of almighty God, already love to do good. There are others who learn good works after they have entered the service of almighty God. Thus, the person who took care to possess good works even before entering God’s service is a Hebrew servant bought with a wife. Often such a person can pass into the contemplative life without abandoning the active life. Hence it is also added there: “If he has a wife, his wife shall also go out with him.”

The wife goes out with him into freedom when the person who has reached contemplation does not abandon outward activity in good works through which he can benefit others.

“But if the master gives him a wife, and she bears him sons and daughters, the woman and her children shall belong to her master; he himself shall go out with his garment” [Col. 0109A]. The master gives a wife to the purchased servant when a preacher joins to good action the person whom he has lawfully devoted to almighty God. Preachers are also called masters, as it is said to the prophet Elisha concerning his preacher: “Do you know that the Lord your master is going to be taken away from you?” (2 Kings II).

The wife of the purchased servant bears sons and daughters when good action produces for him strong or tender fruits. But the woman given by the master remains with that master together with her children. The servant himself goes out with his garment because good action, or the fruits of that good action, is reckoned as the preacher’s reward. He himself, persevering in the intention of his desire, goes out free into contemplation through heavenly grace.

“But if the servant says, ‘I love my master, my wife, and my children; I will not go out free’” [Col. 0109B] (Rom. VIII), the servant loves his master when he carefully keeps the preacher’s words in his mind. He refuses to go out free because he loves his wife and children when, loving the active life and its fruits, he does not wish to pass into contemplation. Considering that he possesses good works in the service of his ministry, he refuses to pass into the repose of freedom.

“But let the master bring him to the gods, and let him be brought to the door and the doorposts; and let him pierce his ear with an awl, so that he may be his servant forever.” The person who has resolved to persevere in the active life is brought by the Lord to the gods when he is instructed by his preacher in the sayings of the ancient Fathers, who were priests for us on the way of almighty God. He is led to the door and doorposts of the tabernacle [Col. 0109C] so that he may hear something about entering the eternal tabernacle and carefully recognize the day of the dreadful judgment, lest through the good works he performs he seek to please human beings.

Thus his ear is pierced with an awl when his mind is struck by the subtle fear of God. Pierced through by the sharpness of the word, he should learn, in everything he does, always to attend to entering the kingdom. Like one whose ear has been pierced at the door and doorpost of the tabernacle, he should carry it with him; he will be a servant forever so that he may be free after this age.

For he is a servant forever who has resolved through the active life to serve human beings, so that after the present age he may be able to attain true freedom. Concerning this Paul says: “For creation itself will be freed from the slavery of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God.” [Col. 0109D] True freedom will then exist in us, when our adoption reaches the glory of the children of God. But now not only is the active life in slavery; even contemplation, by which we are carried above ourselves, does not possess freedom of mind but imitates it, because that innermost repose is seen only in an enigma.

“If anyone sells his daughter as a maidservant, she shall not go out as maidservants customarily go out. If she displeases the eyes of the master to whom she was handed over, he shall release her; but he shall not have the power to sell her to a foreign people if he rejects her. But if he betroths her to his son, he shall treat her according to the custom of daughters. But if he takes another wife for him, he shall provide the girl with marriage, clothing, and the price of her virginity; he shall not deny her these. If he does not do these three things [Col. 0110A], she shall go out freely without payment,” and so on.

“But if anyone,” he says, “sells his daughter as a maidservant”—that is, so that she may be a maidservant, whom the Greeks call οἰκετίαν, “a household servant”—“she shall not go out” in the manner in which maidservants go out. This must be understood as referring to the law given concerning a Hebrew woman, which is observed in the case of males. Why, then, should this woman go out in this manner, unless it is understood that she was humiliated in that service because the master had intercourse with her? This becomes somewhat clearer in what follows.

For it continues: “But if she does not please her master, because he has not named her”—that is, because he did not make her his wife—“he shall compensate her.” This is what was said above: “She shall not go out in the manner in which maidservants go out.” She is ordered to receive something [Col. 0110B] because she was humiliated, since he did not have intercourse with her in such a way as to make her his wife, that is, to name her as his own.

“But if he names her for his son, he shall treat her according to the law of daughters.” Here it begins to become clear how he said above that he had not named her. For what else does “if he names her for his son” mean except that he has joined her to his son as a wife, since he says, “he shall treat her according to the law of daughters”—that is, he shall give her over as a daughter, providing her with a dowry?

Then he adds: “But if he takes another for him”—that is, if he did not regard this woman as a wife for his son but takes another for him—“he shall not defraud her of what is necessary, nor of clothing appropriate to her way of life.” Under the same law, he shall provide what is fitting for her, just as she remained the wife of his son; he should have given it to her even if he had not named her as his wife, [Col. 0110C] though he had humiliated her by having intercourse with her.

“But if he does not do these three things for her, she shall go out freely.” This is understood to mean that, if he has not humiliated her through intercourse, joined her to his son, or, after giving another woman to his son, expelled this one, she shall go away freely—that is, it is enough that she not be held in slavery. She will go away receiving nothing, like the Hebrew servant.

For it is not permitted to her master to join her to a non-Hebrew man, since she may not be handed over to a foreign people. But if he joins her to a Hebrew servant, this is understood to mean that she will go out freely with him, never separated from her husband.

Mystically, if someone entrusts to any teacher for obedience the devoted submission produced by a good disposition, it is not right for that person to be rejected or disgraced and cast away by the teacher. Rather, the teacher should either join the person to himself or to a proven disciple for participation [Col. 0110D] in discipline, if he chooses this, or commend the person to another teacher in whose fellowship he may make progress. He should himself continue to accompany that person with a kindly mind and not allow the person to believe that he has been sent away without the consolation of love.

He has no power to hand the person over to a heretical or schismatic man, who is alien to the people of God. But if he himself is unwilling to undertake the labor required for that person, he should allow the person to depart freely and choose whatever teacher he wishes.

“If anyone strikes someone and he dies, let him be put to death. But if he did not intend it, and God delivered him into his hands, I will appoint for you a place to which he may flee.”

Here it is asked how it was said, “But if he did not intend it, and God delivered him into his hands,” as though, if he killed unintentionally, he could not have killed unless God had delivered the victim into his [Col. 0111A] hands.

It is therefore understood that God alone acted when someone is killed by a person who did not intend it, and it is only for this reason that it was said: “But God delivered him into his hand.” When someone kills intentionally, both he himself kills and God delivers the victim into his hand.

The difference, then, is that in the former case God alone acted; in the latter, both God and the human being acted because of the killer’s will—but not in the same manner, God and the human being. God acts only justly, whereas the human being is deserving of punishment: not because he killed someone whom God did not wish to be killed, but because he acted through iniquity. For he did not provide service to God’s command; he served his own evil desire.

Thus, in one and the same deed, God is praised for his hidden justice, while the human being is punished for his own iniquity. The fact that God did not spare his own Son but delivered him up for all of us [Col. 0111B] does not excuse Judas, who likewise handed Christ over to death.

But he who did not lie in wait, he says, but God delivered him into his hand, I shall appoint for you a place to which he must flee. How this was done is made clear by the book called Jesus Nave [Joshua], when it records that Joshua, at the Lord’s command, designated six cities of refuge for homicides who had committed murder unintentionally: namely, Cades in Galilee, in the mountain-country of Naphtali; Sichem on Mount Ephraim; Cariath Arbe—that is Hebron—in the mountain-country of Judah; and beyond the Jordan, opposite the western region of Jericho, the city of Bosor, situated in the plain wilderness of the tribe of Reuben; and Ramoth in Gilead, of the tribe of Gad; and Gaulon in Basan, of the tribe of Manasseh. These cities were established [Col. 0111C] for all the children of Israel and for the resident aliens dwelling among them, so that anyone who unintentionally struck and killed a person might flee to them and not die at the hand of the one who wished to avenge the shedding of blood, until he stood before the people to present his case.

Mystically, however, if someone, through envy or hatred, strikes another with the sword of malice and brings him into the death of the soul, he himself will be liable to eternal death. Hence Truth itself says: “If anyone causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it is better for him that a millstone be hung around his neck and that he be plunged into the depths” (Matt. XVIII). And John says: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer. And you know that no murderer has eternal life abiding in him” (I John III). Such a person is ordered to be removed from the Lord’s altar, because, unworthy of the Lord’s sacraments, he is rightly excluded [Col. 0111D] from participation in the sacred altar. But he who harms someone not through a deliberate intention of malice, but through carelessness or ignorance, has cities of refuge—namely, the catholic Church—where, constraining himself through the hardship of repentance, he may remain throughout the whole period of the present life, devoting himself to good works; and if he places his hope in the death of the supreme Pontiff, that is, his Redeemer, he will undoubtedly be saved forever.

“Whoever strikes his father or his mother shall surely be put to death.” And a little later: “Whoever curses his father or his mother,” he says, “shall surely be put to death.” What is it to strike one’s father and mother, and to curse one’s father or mother, except to have become impious and opposed to the law [Col. 0112A] that commands parents to be honored, and therefore to be accursed and worthy of death? Spiritually, however, whoever curses the Father—that is, utters blasphemy against God, who is the Father of all—or introduces schisms against the Church, the mother of unity, will be punished with eternal punishment.

“Whoever steals a person and sells him, when convicted of the offense, shall surely be put to death.” By this sentence he strikes heretics: those who by deceit lead a Christian away from the truth of the catholic faith and, through error, hand him over as one subject to evil spirits. He shows that they are to be condemned to eternal punishment.

“If men quarrel and one strikes his neighbor with a stone or with his fist, and he does not die but lies in bed, then, if he rises and walks about outside upon his staff, the one who struck him shall be innocent [Col. 0112B]—provided that he repays for his loss of work and his expenses for physicians,” and so forth. Allegorically: if someone quarrels with his neighbor in anger and strikes him either with a stone or with his fist—that is, if he exasperates him through hardness of mind or stinginess of heart, by despising him or by failing to show him mercy—and the other, weakened by sorrow, languishes in the warmth of love, the guilty party must, through confession, pay the cost of penitential works and the expense of promised amendment to the physicians—that is, to teachers—who may raise up the sick man with the staff of their consolation and, healing him with the applications of their preaching, restore him to his former state of love. For we can attain true innocence if we strive to wash away evil deeds with worthy fruits of repentance.

“Whoever strikes his male or female slave with a rod, and they die at his hand, shall be guilty of the crime,” [Col. 0112C] and so forth. Just as discipline is necessary in the education of those subject to us, so discernment is especially necessary in the administration of correction. For whoever constrains the flock entrusted to him beyond the proper measure of discipline, where he ought to have fostered life, will be found there to have inflicted death. Hence it is also said through Wisdom: “Whoever presses the breasts forcefully produces butter, and whoever squeezes too violently draws blood” (Prov. XXX). A measure must therefore always be maintained in discipline, so that severity may contain gentleness and gentleness severity, so that faith and love may flourish in the one being disciplined and he may not perish utterly through despair or hatred.

“If men quarrel and someone strikes a pregnant woman [Col. 0112D] and causes a miscarriage, but she herself remains alive, he shall be subject to a fine, as much as the woman’s husband demands and the judges determine,” and so forth. Here, as it seems to me, the meaning is this: if someone strikes a woman after conception has taken place and thereby causes a miscarriage, while she herself remains alive, then the striker may compensate for the injury with money, according to what is demanded and what the judges decree. But if her death follows, then the striker, now guilty of homicide, must be punished.

Mystically, however, if someone harms a soul after the seed of the word has been conceived, through carelessness or deceit, so that it cannot bring forth the living shoot of a good work in soundness, even if that soul still remains alive in faith [Col. 0113A], the striker must nevertheless restore the damage inflicted through repentance, according to the teaching of the Gospel. But if that soul, having been slain through error after producing a miscarriage—that is, a deadly work—perseveres in unbelief, without doubt its seducer, like a true murderer, will be liable to eternal death.

**(August.)** It should be noted, however, that another edition reads as follows: “If two men quarrel and one strikes a woman who has a child in her womb, and her child comes out not deformed, he shall suffer a penalty as much as the woman’s husband imposes; and he shall pay according to the demand.” Here the question of the soul is commonly debated: whether what has not been formed can even be understood to possess a soul, and therefore whether this is not homicide, since something without a soul cannot be called disanimated if it did not yet have a soul [Col. 0113B]. For it follows and says: “But if it is formed, he shall give soul for soul.” What else is understood here except that he himself is to die? For this is also prescribed in the other cases arising from this occasion: “Eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot, burning for burning, wound for wound, bruise for bruise”—namely, by the equity of talion (Exod. XXI). The law established this in order to show what vengeance is owed. For unless the law made known what vengeance was owed, how would it be known what pardon should release, so that one could say: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. VI)? The law therefore points out debts, so that when forgiveness is granted it may be apparent what is being forgiven. For we would not forgive debts unless, by the law as our indicator, we had learned what was owed to us. Therefore the law did not wish an unformed miscarriage to pertain to homicide, because a living soul cannot yet be said to exist in a body that lacks sensation, if it is still in flesh not yet formed and therefore not yet endowed with the senses.

**(Orig.)** These two men who quarrel are two disputants concerning doctrines or questions of the law. Since those who quarrel in controversies act against the Apostle’s saying, “Do not quarrel about words; for it is useful for nothing except the subversion of those who hear” (II Tim. II), they therefore strike the pregnant woman and cast out her child, whether already formed or not yet formed. The pregnant woman signifies the soul that has recently conceived the word—for example, a catechumen, who is still inexperienced in the faith [Col. 0113D]. When this soul is scandalized through the contention of certain people, so that it casts away and loses the word of faith that it had conceived only faintly, before it was formed, the one who caused the scandal is said to suffer a penalty. “He shall pay,” it says, “according to what her husband shall impose or assess.” This husband, then, is either Christ, who is the teacher of all, or the one who presides over the Church in Christ’s place, the teacher of souls. Let the one who quarrels with words for the subversion of those who hear suffer a penalty for the soul that casts away the unformed child—that is, let him do penance—and let the one who caused the harm strive again to instruct, restore, and return to the soul what it lost. Let him do this with honor, modesty, and [Col. 0114A] patience, as the Apostle says: “Correcting with gentleness those who resist” (II Tim. II), not with quarrelsomeness, as when he previously caused the scandal.

“But if the child is already formed, he shall give soul for soul.” The formed child may be understood as the word of God in the heart of a soul that has received the grace of baptism, or, more clearly, as the word of faith that it has conceived. If this soul, struck by the contention of teachers, casts away the word and is found to belong to those of whom the Apostle said, “For some have already turned back after Satan” (I Tim. V), it shall give soul for soul. This may be understood as referring to the day of judgment, before that Judge who can destroy soul and body in Gehenna. Or perhaps it can also be applied in this way: whoever is conscious of having caused so great a scandal [Col. 0114B] should place his own soul in the place of the soul of the one whom he scandalized, and labor even unto death to return, to be restored, and to be brought back to the faith.

“Let him give eye for eye.” If he injured the eye of the soul—that is, disturbed its understanding—let his own eye be removed by the one who presides over the Church; and let his understanding, turbulent and fierce, which generates scandal, be cut away. But if he injured the hearer’s tooth, by which the hearer was accustomed to receive the food of God’s word, to break it up and grind it with the molars, and to transmit from it a subtle sense to the soul’s stomach; if he troubled and pulled out this tooth, so that because of his quarrelsomeness the soul could no longer receive God’s word subtly, let the tooth of the one who does not properly grind and divide the foods of Scripture be taken away [Col. 0114C]. Perhaps for this reason it is also said elsewhere: “You have broken the teeth of sinners” (Ps. III). And elsewhere it is likewise written: “Whoever eats a sour grape, his teeth will be set on edge” (Eccli. XXX). And elsewhere: “The Lord will break the molars of lions” (Ps. LVII).

If, therefore, the soul is said to be injured and struck through its members, then hand is also demanded for hand and foot for foot. The hand of the soul is its power, by which it can hold and constrain something—its deeds and strength, so to speak—and the foot is that with which it proceeds toward good or evil. Therefore, if the soul suffers scandal not only in faith but also in its actions, which are signified by hands and feet, the hands of the one who supplied the stumbling-block are removed, because he does not work well, and his feet are removed, because he does not walk well [Col. 0114D]. It will also receive the burning with which he burned and delivered the soul to Gehenna. Through each of these things it is shown that this striker, with all his members mutilated, is to be cut off from the body of the Church, “so that the others,” he says, “seeing it, may have fear and not do likewise” (I Cor. V).

“If anyone strikes the eye of his male or female slave and makes them one-eyed, he shall let them go free for the eye that he removed. And if he knocks out a tooth of his male or female slave, he shall likewise let them go free.” If someone makes his hearer weak with regard to the perception of a sound understanding, or through his insolence knocks out the tooth of discernment by which he could subtly grind the meanings of Scripture and bring them into the soul’s covenant, it is good for him to grant that person [Col. 0115A] the freedom to enter another’s discipleship, lest, on account of the destruction of that soul, while demanding unjust obedience from him, he himself be compelled to pay the penalties of Gehenna.

“If an ox gores a man or woman and they die, it shall be stoned, and its flesh shall not be eaten; but the owner of the ox shall be innocent. But if the ox was accustomed to gore yesterday and the day before, and they warned its owner, yet he did not confine it, and it killed a man or woman, the ox shall be stoned and its owner shall be killed,” and so forth.

**(August.)** It belongs to justice that an animal harmful to human beings should be killed; and what is stated about the bull is to be understood as a part standing for the whole: whatever among domesticated animals is subject to human use yet hostile to human beings. But if it must be killed, must it be stoned? [Col. 0115B] For what difference does it make by what death an animal that must be removed is removed? Moreover, why did he add that its flesh was not to be eaten, unless all these things signify something else, which Scripture is especially accustomed to consider?

The bull, therefore, may signify a stubborn disciple who, through the arrogance of pride, tears at and harms the other sheep of the Lord’s flock. If such a one, without the teacher’s knowledge, gores some man or woman—that is, any strong or weak person—with the horn of his insolence and inflicts the death of the soul upon them, let him be overwhelmed by stones of a severe sentence; and let his flesh not be eaten—that is, let his actions not be imitated. The bull’s owner, however, will be shown to be innocent if he supported its action neither by consent nor by counsel, because the Lord says: “The soul that sins, it shall die [Col. 0115C]; and the righteousness of the righteous shall be upon him, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon him” (Ezek. XVIII).

But if the master and teacher knew the character of such a disciple and, though often warned by the sacred Scriptures, neglected to care for the dangerous animal, he has now become a participant in its action and will rightly be a participant in its punishment, because, according to the Apostle, not only those who do evil but also those who consent to evildoers are worthy of death.

“But if a price is imposed upon him, he shall pay for his life whatever is demanded of him.” By almsgiving and worthy fruits of repentance, let him hasten to free himself from eternal death.

“If it gores a son or daughter, he shall likewise be subject to the same sentence.” In the name of son or daughter, whom can we more appropriately understand than a good hearer, because he diligently strives to learn the things of God [Col. 0115D], to practice them in works, and does so out of desire for eternal life? Whoever strikes such a person will likewise be punished by the judgment imposed on a murderer.

But what follows says: “If it attacks a male slave or a female slave, he shall give thirty shekels of silver to their master, but the ox shall be stoned.” Who can better be understood as a male or female slave than one who, existing in the house of the Church, loves only present things and devotes all his labor to acquiring them; who has not yet deserved to be enrolled among the sons because he has neglected to seek the inheritance of the heavenly homeland? If that proud, horned one inflicts some harm upon him in the things he loves and thereby grieves him, his guardian must repair the damage inflicted by a just amendment [Col. 0116A] according to the commands of the law, through faith, hope, and charity. He must also correct the author of the crime with severe disciplines, since he has acted insolently against what is written: “Do not extort anyone; harm no one” (John I); and again: “What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another.”

This sentence can also be understood in another way: by the sign of the horned ox, let us understand a proud movement of the mind. If its master—that is, the spirit that ought rightly to rule in a human being—does not restrain it, and if, because of its own course, it brings spiritual destruction upon souls or inflicts harm upon bodies, guilt for the crime rebounds both upon its author and upon its guardian, who ought to have prohibited it but did not. Hence Scripture says: “Guard your heart with all vigilance, for [Col. 0116B] from it proceed life or death” (Prov. IV). And again: “The heart of a man directs his way” (Prov. XVI). And again: “The heart of the wise instructs his mouth, and adds grace to his lips” (ibid.). And elsewhere: “From the fruit of his mouth,” he says, “a man’s belly will be filled, and the produce of his lips will satisfy him.”

“If anyone opens a cistern, or digs one, and does not cover it, and an ox or an ass falls into it, the owner of the cistern shall repay the price of the animals,” and so forth (Prov. XVIII). What is it to open a cistern except to penetrate the secrets of sacred Scripture with a vigorous understanding? And what is signified by the ox and the ass—that is, the clean and unclean animal—except a believer or an unbeliever?

Whoever therefore digs a cistern and covers it so that an ox or an ass does not fall into it—that is, whoever already understands deep things in sacred discourse—should cover [Col. 0116C] lofty meanings before those unable to receive them, by silence, lest through a scandal of the mind he destroy either a faithful little one or an unbeliever who might have been able to believe. A price must be paid for the death of the animals, because he is evidently convicted of having admitted that by which he is held guilty and compelled to do penance. For whoever reaches the lofty streams of knowledge but does not conceal these things from the dull hearts of his hearers is condemned as liable to punishment if, through his words, either a clean or an unclean person is ensnared by scandal.

The cistern must therefore be covered, because profound knowledge must be concealed before childish minds, lest from the very place where the heart of the teachers is lifted to the heights, the weakness of the hearers fall into the depths.

“If one man’s ox wounds another man’s ox and it dies, they shall sell the living ox and divide the price; but they shall divide the [Col. 0116D] dead carcass between them,” and so forth.

**(August.)** Is this legal ruling to be observed only in the case of a bull, and not in a similar case involving all cattle? Accordingly, this is to be understood as a part standing for the whole. But this cannot be done with the flesh of the slain animal, since it is not eaten.

Typically, however, if someone placed under the yoke of discipline fatally wounds a companion likewise laboring in the cultivation of the Lord’s field, so that the companion also dies in soul, the guardian of the offender should sell the living ox—that is, reduce the criminal to repentance—according to the Apostle’s instruction to hand such a person over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that his spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord. The guardians of both animals shall divide the price—that is, let them satisfy themselves through the repentance of the offender [Col. 0117A]. They shall likewise divide the dead carcass among themselves, when, on account of the crime committed, each of them grieves with the repentant person, in accordance with Paul’s words: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I do not burn?” (I Cor. XI).

Whoever knew that the disciple was injurious and did not take care to restrain him as far as he could has converted the crime committed into guilt of his own.

“If anyone steals a sheep or an ox and kills or sells it, he shall restore five oxen for one ox and four sheep for one sheep,” and so forth (Exod. XXII).

**(August.)** What justice is it that five are restored for one calf but four for one sheep, unless this is understood to signify something? We can make this distinction between the ox and the sheep: in the ox we may understand [Col. 0117B] a teacher laboring well in the Lord’s field, who cuts the soil of carnal hearts with the evangelical plowshare so that it may be able to bring forth the fruits of virtues. In the sheep, a simple hearer who is content merely with his simplicity. For the greater the usefulness of something, the greater the damage in its destruction; and the lesser the advantage of possessing something, the less the grief at its loss. This is signified by the greater number in the restoration of the ox and the smaller number in that of the sheep.

Whoever fraudulently tears any teacher away from the Lord’s people harms many; for this reason he must subdue all the senses of his body through the practice of repentance, since according to the Lord’s law he must make full payment. But whoever maliciously overturns a simple hearer from his state must chastise his body, [Col. 0117C] which is manifestly composed of four elements, through fasts and vigils, until he deserves to receive complete forgiveness from the Lord.

Again, in another way: the ox is a beast accustomed to the yoke, and it signifies the former people, established under the law of Moses and seeking the judgment of the law, as the Apostle bears witness when he says: “For all who have sinned under the law will be judged by the law” (Rom. II). Therefore a stolen and killed or sold ox is rightly valued at five oxen, when a Jewish person injured against the law is avenged according to the law. Hence it is also written in that same law: “Whoever kills a man shall surely be put to death.” And again: “Eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand,” and so forth.

The sheep, because it is a simple animal, signifies the evangelical person established under the grace of God [Col. 0117D]—a member, that is, of that sheep of whom the Prophet says: “Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter, and he did not open his mouth” (Isa. LIII). As his imitator, he keeps what is written in the Gospel: “If anyone strikes you on the right cheek, offer him the other also” (Matt. V). And again: “Love your enemies, and do good to those who hate you.”

But lest the injury of this simple animal seem to pass without vengeance, the Lawgiver commands that four sheep be restored for one sheep. Therefore the lost sheep demands a fourfold restoration, because whoever fraudulently injures Christian simplicity must hasten to restore it through worthy repentance, according to the teaching of the Gospel.

“If a thief is found [Col. 0118A] breaking into or digging through a house, and, after receiving a wound, dies, the one who struck him shall not be guilty of blood. But if this is done after the sun has risen, the striker has committed murder and shall die,” and so forth.

It is therefore understood that it does not pertain to homicide when a thief is killed at night, but that it does pertain to it when he is killed by day. For this is what he says: “If the sun rises over him.” It could be discerned that he had come to steal, not to kill, and therefore ought not to be killed. This is also found in the ancient secular laws, although this law is older: a nocturnal thief could be killed with impunity in any manner, but a daytime thief only if he defended himself with a weapon; for he is already more than a thief.

Mystically, however, we can understand heretics as thieves. Hence Truth itself says: “All who came before me are thieves and robbers” (John X). And again [Col. 0118B]: “The thief,” he says, “comes only to steal, slaughter, and destroy. But I have come so that they may have life, and have it more abundantly” (ibid.).

Therefore, if a thief—that is, a heretic—attempts to break into or dig through the house of the Church, that is, to invade it through contention or deceit, and, after receiving the wound of just correction, perishes by persevering in the error he conceived, the teacher who deprived him of communion so that he might do penance has not incurred guilt by destroying him.

But if, he says, “he did this after the sun had risen,” he committed murder. The rising sun expresses the light of right knowledge. If a heretic, admonished by a preacher, attempts to abandon the darkness of his error and draw near to the light of truth, it is not right that he should be pierced by the weapon of anathema; rather, bound by the bond of charity, he should be preserved for [Col. 0118C] eternal life, according to the Savior’s saying: “If your brother sins against you, go and correct him between you and him alone. And if he does penance, you have gained your brother,” and so forth (Matt. XVIII).

It follows: “If he does not have anything with which to repay for the theft, he shall be sold.” This means that if he does not have a teachable heart from which he can produce worthy fruits of repentance, he should be excommunicated and, according to the sentence of Truth, regarded as a pagan and a publican.

“If what he stole is found alive with him, whether an ox, an ass, or a sheep, he shall restore double.” The ox and sheep, which divide the hoof and chew the cud, are clean animals; the ass is unclean. If, therefore, a Jewish person believing in Christ from the law, or any simple Christian, or even a pagan not yet reborn in Christ, is found living with a heretic—that is, possessing a right intention in the search for truth—he must be restored twofold: separated from the heretic in whom there is no truth both in soul and in body, and restored in the Church through catholic faith and confession to Christ, the rightful possessor, who is the way, the truth, and the life [Col. 0118D]. Thus he may find there in its entirety what he was seeking in vain elsewhere.

Here Wisdom also exhorts us, saying: “I am the mother of beautiful love, and of fear, and of knowledge, and of holy hope. In me is all grace of the way and of truth; in me is all hope of life and of virtue. Come over to me, all you who desire me, and be filled with my generations. Whoever hears me shall not be confounded, and whoever works in me shall not sin. Those who make me shine shall have eternal life [Col. 0119A]” (Eccli. XXIV). And in the Gospel the Lord himself says: “Whoever thirsts, let him come to me and drink; and from his belly shall flow living waters.”

“If anyone damages his neighbor’s field or vineyard and lets his animal loose to graze on another’s property, he shall restore, as compensation for the damage, whatever is best in his own field or vineyard” (John VII). By this sentence human greed is restrained, and it applies especially against bishops and priests who seek to invade other men’s parishes.

Therefore, whoever releases the carnal appetite, signified by the irrational animal, so that for the sake of greed he may solicit a people not belonging to him and turn their services or payments to his own profit, must, as compensation for the damage, chastise the field of his body or the vineyard of his heart, [Col. 0119B] so that he who has abused what belongs to others through pleasure may learn through fasting and almsgiving to expend what belongs to him.

“If fire breaks out and finds thorns and catches heaps of grain or standing crops in the fields, he who kindled the fire shall repay the damage.” Sacred Scripture teaches us, with great care, how everything that must be done is to be done. We kindle a fire when we prepare correction for those subject to us, so that we may consume the thorns of vices in them. But care must be taken lest, while pursuing vices, we injure virtues, and lest we harm through injustice those who have begun to bring forth in themselves the fruits of good works before bringing them to maturity.

Therefore whoever has committed such damage among the people of God must perform worthy repentance for it and strive through diligent goodness to restore what he previously harmed through negligence [Col. 0119C].

“If anyone entrusts money or a vessel to his neighbor for safekeeping, and it is stolen from the one who received it, then, if the thief is found, he shall restore double; but if the thief is not found, the master of the house shall be brought before the gods, and he shall swear that he did not extend his hand to his neighbor’s property to commit fraud—whether it concerns an ox, an ass, a sheep, a garment, or anything else that can cause damage. The matter of both parties shall come before the gods, and if they judge him guilty, he shall restore double to his neighbor.”

Money or a vessel is entrusted to a friend for safekeeping when, through any preacher, the treasure of God’s word and the vessels of sacred Scripture are entrusted to a simple hearer to preserve in right faith and good works. But if the entrusted money—that is, right faith—is taken away through the confused understanding of some perverse teacher and heretic, the one who maliciously caused the damage through deceit, if he is revealed, must be subjected to repentance as the guardian of the Lord’s money [Col. 0119D], so that, afflicted both in heart and body, he may suffer the worthy penalties of the crime he committed.

But if the author of the error remains hidden, the master of the house shall be brought before the gods. That is, the one who received the Lord’s money in order to guard it faithfully must be presented before an assembly of catholic teachers. By them he must be carefully examined and must make appropriate satisfaction, demonstrating that he did not injure anyone through his own fraud or wickedness, but that he preserved the deposit simply, insofar as he understood it, and did not stain or overthrow through that teaching anyone belonging to the Lord’s flock [Col. 0120A], thereby making himself liable to guilt.

Thus, by the judgment of the holy priests, he shall restore double to his neighbor when he fully renders catholic faith and confession to his preacher, so that the one who previously wandered through insufficient understanding may, fully instructed, show himself truly faithful in all things.

“If anyone entrusts to his neighbor an ass, a sheep, an ox, or any animal for safekeeping, and it dies, or is disabled, or is captured by enemies, with no one seeing it, an oath shall be made between them that he did not extend his hand to his neighbor’s property. The Lord shall accept the oath, and he shall not be compelled to make restitution. But if it was taken away by theft, he shall restore the loss to the owner. If it was devoured by a wild beast, he shall bring to him what was killed, and he shall not make restitution.”

Here we can understand our Redeemer as the neighbor [Col. 0120B]: “Who, though he was in the form of God, did not regard equality with God as something to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men and found in appearance as a man.” This neighbor of ours entrusts an ass, a sheep, an ox, or every kind of animal for safekeeping when he entrusts his animals—that is, human beings—to any preacher to govern: some gifted with intelligence, others simple and innocent, others brutish and dull.

If, therefore, the guardian of the Lord’s flock devotes every concern to these animals and watches over them with vigilant care, it will not harm him if one of them is led astray by evil spirits or dies through its own fault. A pure conscience and an unfeigned faith will suffice for the shepherd, since, [Col. 0120C] working through love, it was devoutly laboring for that person’s salvation. The Lord will therefore accept his good devotion and cause his good effort to redound to his eternal life.

Hence the Apostle says: “Thanks be to God, who always triumphs over us in Christ Jesus and manifests through us the fragrance of his knowledge in every place. For we are the good fragrance of Christ to God among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing: to some, an odor of death unto death; to others, an odor of life unto life” (II Cor. II), and so forth.

But if the master of the household sleeps and does not watch for the thief who is coming, and through his negligence any of these animals perishes, he shall restore the loss to its owner, because through his negligence he failed to guard the Lord’s flock. Hence the Lord says to the prophet: “If, when I say to the wicked, ‘You shall surely die,’ you do not speak so that the wicked may guard himself [Col. 0120D] from his way, that wicked person shall die in his iniquity, but I will require his blood from your hand. But if, when you announce to the wicked that he should turn from his ways, he does not turn from his way, he himself shall die in his iniquity, but you have delivered your soul” (Ezek. XVIII).

The shepherd must always be cautious and continually vigilant in his guardianship. If he sees one of his own torn apart by a demonic beast, he must immediately pour out prayers to the Lord for him, admonish him, and hasten to heal him, lest that person’s destruction become the ruin of his own soul.

If anyone asks his neighbor for anything of these things as a loan, and it has been weakened or has died while the owner is absent, he shall be compelled to make restitution. But if the owner is present, he shall not make restitution—especially if the animal had been hired for payment for its work. We ask a loan from our neighbor, therefore, when, in expectation of eternal recompense, we undertake the care of the Lord’s flock. But if we always place the fear of God before the eyes of our heart, and fear his coming as though he were demanding the money entrusted to us, we are always, as it were, in his presence. Hence Jacob also said to Laban: “Unless the God of my father Abraham, and the fear of Isaac, had been with me, perhaps now you would have sent me away naked” (Gen. XXXI). And the Apostle says: “Knowing the fear of the Lord, we persuade human beings; but to God we are manifest” (II Cor. V). And again he says concerning God: “We speak as before God in Christ.”

Therefore, the loss of weakened or dead livestock is not charged against the shepherd if he has diligently cared for it and, as though God were present, has labored with the greatest devotion, knowing that he would have to render an account. But if some loss occurs while the owner is absent, he shall be compelled to make restitution, because whoever is negligent in pastoral care, and, in accordance with that saying concerning the wicked servant, says in his heart, “My master is delaying his coming,” and begins to beat the boys and the maidservants, and to eat and drink and become drunk, “the master of that servant will come on a day when he does not expect him and at an hour he does not know, and will divide him and appoint his portion with the unbelievers”; and, having been cast into prison, he will not come out from there until he pays the last farthing.

“If anyone seduces a virgin who is not yet betrothed and sleeps with her, he shall endow her and take her as his wife.” To seduce a virgin who is not yet betrothed is to expound, on one’s own authority, any canonical text not yet expounded by another, according to the understanding of the Fathers. But he must give her a dowry and thus take her as his wife, because unless he acquires her through the Catholic faith, he will not be permitted to enjoy her union.

It follows: “If the virgin’s father refuses to give her to him, he shall pay money according to the amount of the dowry that virgins customarily receive.” The father of the virgin—that is, the historical sense of the text—is the meaning from which the discourse arises. Therefore, if the historical sense is found in any passage and is capable of suitably building up the kingdom of charity and sufficiently destroying the kingdom of desire, it does not seem necessary to explain it by an allegorical interpretation. Nevertheless, the reader ought to honor it with the dowry of right faith and thus leave it untouched by his exposition.

“You shall not permit sorcerers to live.” He calls sorcerers those who conduct affairs through the tricks of magical art and demonic fabrications, and who strive to turn people away from the one God, who is the true author of every good thing. The law does not permit them to continue to the harm of human beings, but rather commands that they be destroyed. Figuratively, however, we may understand sorcerers as heretics, who, prompted not by the Spirit of God but by an evil spirit, introduce perverse sects for the deception of human beings. The law of the Lord commands that they be killed—that is, that they be completely separated by anathema from the fellowship of the faithful who live for God with true life—until the sorcery, that is, the error which seemed to live harmfully in them, has been extinguished, lest their communion become a defilement of their simple brothers.

“Whoever lies with an animal shall be put to death.” He forbids human beings to mingle with brute animals, contrary to the natural order, through the impulse of fornication. He also prohibits the company of foolish people, whose association causes a person to fall into the worst fornication—that is, causes the soul, through error, to be separated from God and joined to the devil through wickedness. Hence Scripture says: “The companion of fools will become like them” (Prov. XIII).

## CHAPTER II. Concerning the prohibition of the worship of idols, and the instruction concerning charity and the other ordinances of the law that follow here in the volume

“Whoever sacrifices to gods shall be killed, except to the Lord alone” (Exod. XXII). That is, whoever gives to any creature the divine honor that belongs to God alone is punished in his soul by spiritual death; indeed, because of his impiety, he will be cast into Tartarus, the gehenna of fire, to be punished eternally without any remedy.

“You shall not grieve or oppress the stranger. For you yourselves were strangers in the land of Egypt. You shall not harm the widow or the orphan. If you injure them, they will cry out to me, and I will hear their cry; my anger will be kindled, and I will strike you with the sword. Your wives will be widows, and your children orphans.”

He commends love of neighbor through compassionate mercy, lest people, moved by the fury of anger or driven on by the spur of greed, neglect to preserve the law of nature; rather, they should always remember that saying of the truth which declares: “Everything that you wish people to do to you, do the same to them” (Matt. VII). And as it is written elsewhere: “What one does not wish to have done to oneself, let one not do to another.” Therefore, each person should assist his needy neighbor in his necessity, never harm him, but support him according to his strength.

Alternatively, the widow may be understood as the Church, and the orphan as the Christian people. He forbids the Church to be grieved through persecution or worldly arrogance, lest such harassment reach the spiritual destruction of those who trouble them uselessly with hatred and insults.

“If you lend money to my poor people who live with you, you shall not press him as an exactor, nor oppress him with interest. If you take a garment as a pledge from your neighbor, return it to him before sunset. For it is the only thing with which he covers his body; he has nothing else in which to sleep.”

In his customary manner, the Lord stirs the hearts of his hearers toward mercy and beneficence: they are to preserve love by assisting needy neighbors from the abundance of their possessions, a love that will gain them an eternal reward in heaven.

Alternatively: to lend money to a poor people is to bestow knowledge of the law upon the Gentile people, who are poor in spirit. Yet he forbids pressing or oppressing them with interest—that is, with some excess—because, after receiving grace, he does not wish them to be driven back to observe the ceremonies of the old law, since “Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes.” (From Gregory.)

Likewise, tropologically, he admonishes preachers of the Gospel not to desire an excess of possessions in the present, but, having food and clothing, to be content with these and to remember more earnestly that saying of the Lord in which he declares: “Freely you have received; freely give,” and “your reward will be great in heaven” (Matt. X).

Likewise, according to the allegory, what is understood here by the name of a pledge except the confession of sin? Our brother becomes our debtor when someone near us is shown to have sinned against us. We call sins debts. Hence it is said to the sinful servant: “I forgave you all that debt” (Matt. XVIII). And in the Lord’s Prayer we ask every day: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. VI).

We receive a pledge from our debtor when we retain the confession of his sin from one who is known to have sinned against us; through that confession we are asked to release the sin committed against us. For whoever confesses the sin he has committed and asks forgiveness has already given, as it were, a pledge for the debt.

This pledge is commanded to be returned before sunset, because, before the sun of righteousness sets within us through the grief of the heart, we ought also to return forgiveness to the one from whom we received the confession of guilt, so that the person who remembers having sinned against us may also feel that, by us, what he did has been released.

“You shall not speak abusively of gods.” It is asked which gods are meant: whether the rulers who judge the people, as it was said to Moses that he had been appointed a god to Pharaoh—so that the following words may be understood by way of explanation, as though showing whom he called gods, when he says, “You shall not curse the ruler of your people,” which the Greek has: “You shall not speak evil.” Or should it be understood according to what the Apostle says: “For although there are those who are called gods, whether in heaven or on earth, just as there are many gods and many lords”? By adding “just as there are,” he wished those to be understood as gods who are rightly so called.

Yet it must be understood in this way: what is called *latria* in Greek, and translated into Latin as *servitus*, “service”—that service which is understood to belong to religion—is owed to no one except the one true God, who is our God. Those who are called gods, even if there are some who are rightly so called, are forbidden, not commanded, to be cursed; nevertheless, they are not to be honored with sacrifices or any services of *latria*.

“You shall not delay to offer your tithes and firstfruits. You shall give me the firstborn of your sons. You shall do the same with oxen and sheep,” and so forth. (From Isidore.)

Among these commands, Israel is also ordered to offer to God tithes of all crops and the firstfruits of all things. Spiritually, the firstfruits of crops or of the firstborn signify the beginnings of good works, or the good will itself, which precedes the work—something the Pelagians offend against by attributing it to themselves. But when God commands these to be offered to him, he indicates that they belong to his own grace.

In offering tithes to God, the number ten signifies perfection, because counting increases up to it. Therefore, just as in the firstfruits we are commanded to refer to God the firstfruits of our intentions, so in the tithes we are commanded to refer to God the completion of our works, since from him both the beginning of a good work and the gift of its perfection are granted.

As for the command that the firstborn of animals remain with their mother for seven days and be given to the Lord on the eighth day, this mystically signifies that, in the present time, which is designated by the number seven because it proceeds through the cycle of seven days, each person ought to preserve the firstborn of good works within the unity of the Church and labor to accomplish whatever good he can in the Catholic faith, until the eighth day arrives—that is, the time of resurrection. Then, having been presented before the tribunal of Christ the Judge, he will receive from him the reward of his good works.

Hence the Apostle says: “Do not judge before the time, until the Lord comes, who will both bring to light the hidden things of darkness and reveal the counsels of hearts; and then each person will receive praise from God” (I Cor. IV). And again: “We shall all stand before the tribunal of Christ, so that each person may receive according to what he has done in the body, whether good or evil” (Rom. XIV).

“You shall be holy men for me. You shall not eat flesh that has been tasted by beasts, but shall throw it to the dogs” (Rom. XIV).

Although, according to the historical sense, it is not lawful for a person subject to the divine law to eat flesh polluted and torn by the teeth of beasts, contrary to the law, but rather he must regard it as unclean, nevertheless, in the allegorical sense we may understand flesh as human conduct or animal doctrine, and the beast as a heretic or the devil.

Flesh—that is, conduct—which is torn by the poisonous activity of heretics or deceived by diabolical suggestion, it is not lawful for a Christian to imitate. Rather, he should throw it away as unclean, that is, regard it as suitable and similar to dogs, meaning evil spirits or pagans, according to that word of the Truth which commands that one who does not listen to the Church be regarded “as a pagan and a tax collector” (Matt. XVIII). And the Apostle commands that the sinner be handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord (I Cor. V).

Likewise, through the prohibition of flesh from animals that have died or have been captured by beasts, we may understand that those who are nourished by heavenly bread must not share the table of demons, according to the Apostle’s saying: “You cannot partake of the table of the Lord and of the table of demons” (I Cor. X).

For in these there are truly the dead and those captured by beasts. Since the aforesaid bread is at once holy and also the nourisher of our substance—that is, intelligible bread—he commands that those who are polluted not partake of it, and he does not wish those who have truly been cleansed to be prohibited. Paul plainly commands both things: “Whoever eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord unworthily will be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord” (I Cor. XI). Behold, this person is polluted and unclean: understand him as one who eats unworthily in every respect and is forbidden participation with the saints.
