But what does he add to this? “Let a person examine himself, and so eat of that bread and drink of that cup.” Whoever examines himself, if he is conscious of sin and feels that he has pollution of soul, undoubtedly repents; and after repentance he can again eat of the bread and drink from the holy and undefiled cup.

“You shall not receive a lying report, nor shall you join your hand to say false testimony on behalf of the wicked” (Exod. XXIII). Hence it is also written: “Do not believe every word.” And elsewhere: “A false witness will not go unpunished.” “You shall not follow the crowd to do evil; nor, in judgment, shall you deviate from the truth by agreeing with the opinion of the majority” (Prov. XIX), and so forth.

These things were said so that no one might defend himself by saying that he acted with many others, or think for that reason that it was not a sin.

It follows: “You shall not have pity on the poor in judgment.” If he had not added “in judgment,” there would be a great question. Yet it would have to be understood even if it had not been written. For above he had said: “You shall not join the multitude with the many, so as to pervert judgment,” and consequently “you shall not have pity on the poor” could be understood as referring to judgment.

But since the words “in judgment” have been added, there is no question that this is the command: lest, when we judge, we see that justice is on the side of the rich against the poor and think that we are acting rightly if, out of mercy, we favor the poor against justice. Mercy is good, therefore, but it must not be contrary to judgment. Scripture calls that judgment which is just.

Yet lest anyone think on account of this saying that God forbids mercy, what follows is most appropriately added: “If you meet your enemy’s ox or his ass wandering, lead it back and return it to him.” So that you may know that you have not been forbidden to show mercy, show it even toward your enemies when you are free from the authority of judging. For when you lead back and return your enemy’s wandering ox, you are not sitting as a judge among litigants.

“You shall flee falsehood. You shall not kill the innocent and the just, because I reject the wicked.” The Lord loves truth and judgment, and through the law, the prophets, and the Gospel he exhorts his people to pursue them, because he is not a respecter of persons but repays each according to his works.

“You shall not accept gifts, which blind even the wise and overturn the words of the righteous.” Hence Wisdom says: “Nothing is more wicked than the greedy person; nothing is more unjust than loving money. Such a person has sold his soul, because in his lifetime he cast away his inmost self” (Eccl. X).

“You shall not be troublesome to the stranger, for you know the souls of strangers, since you yourselves were strangers in the land of Egypt” (Eccl. X). Each person ought to consider from his own condition how it is fitting for him to show mercy to others. Hence the Lord also says in the Gospel: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven; give, and it will be given to you” (Luke VI). “With the measure with which you measure, it will be measured back to you.”

“For six years you shall sow your land and gather its produce; but in the seventh year you shall let it go and allow it to rest, so that the poor of your people may eat, and whatever remains the beasts of the field may eat. You shall do the same with your vineyard and your olive grove” (Augustine).

It may be asked what the poor are to gather if, in the seventh year, the land is spared in such a way that it is not even sown. For what was said—“The poor of your people shall eat”—does not pertain to the vineyard and the olive grove, since they cannot take anything from unsown land where crops cannot grow.

Concerning the vineyard and olive grove, he later says that the same must be done; consequently, the earlier command is understood of the fields devoted to grain. It should therefore be taken in this way: “For six years you shall sow your land and gather its fruit,” that is, for six years you shall sow and gather; “but in the seventh you shall not gather,” with the sense understood—“you shall sow,” even though it is not stated—that sowing and gathering pertain to the six years, while in the seventh the thing sown is to be left.

For what will the poor have from it, when even what remains is given to wild beasts? These are animals able to feed on those crops, such as boars and deer and anything of that kind. Yet this would not be said except for the sake of some significance.

For, insofar as the commandments given to human beings are concerned, God is not concerned about oxen. This is not understood as though he himself does not feed those creatures that neither sow nor reap nor gather into a barn, but because he is not concerned to instruct human beings by commandment how to care for their ox. How much less is he concerned to command them how wild beasts should be cared for by human beings, when he himself feeds them with the riches of nature, fruitful everywhere—he who also feeds them during the other six years, when what is sown is gathered.

But if anyone asks what, according to the allegory, the present command concerning leaving the produce of the seventh year for the poor of the people and for the beasts of the earth signifies, let him know that the number six signifies the perfection of works. In the number seven, the rest of souls is expressed.

And rightly we are commanded to sow our land for six years and gather its produce, because in the present life, which consists of six ages, we ought to cultivate the soil of our flesh and sow in it the seeds of virtues, so that the increase of good works and the abundance of reward growing from it may cause us to receive, in the future, the rest of our souls without any further labor of action.

As for the command that the poor of the people or the beasts of the field eat what grows in the seventh year from our former labor, it signifies that, through the services of almsgiving and charity, a reward is prepared for us in the future. Finally, the same vineyard and olive grove indicate works of grace and mercy that prepare future goods.

Therefore, if we are benevolent not only toward our needy friends but also toward our enemies, who are designated by the name of foes, without doubt in the future life—where there is no longer time for working—we shall receive eternal rewards for our good deeds.

Hence the Savior also admonishes us in the Gospel, saying: “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of unrighteousness, so that when you fail, they may receive you into the eternal dwellings” (Luke XVI). Hence also the teacher of the nations says: “Whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly; whoever sows in blessings will reap from blessings eternal life.”

What follows—“For six days you shall labor; on the seventh day you shall cease, so that your ox and your ass may rest, and the son of your maidservant and the stranger may be refreshed”—belongs to the same understanding. That is, in the present time, by laboring well, each person should strive—whether disciplined or dull, slave or free, rich or poor—not to be deprived of eternal rest, but rather, through the merit of right faith and good works, to become a participant in eternal joy.

“Observe everything that I have said to you, and you shall not swear by the name of foreign gods; nor shall it be heard from your mouth.” Here it becomes evident how much the truth of the Gospel surpasses the shadow of the Old Law. There they are merely forbidden to swear by the name of foreign gods; but they are not forbidden to swear by the name of the Lord.

Here, however, people are forbidden to swear altogether—not by heaven, nor by earth, nor by Jerusalem, nor by anything else—so that our speech may be simply “Yes, yes; No, no.” The evangelical truth does not accept an oath, since every truthful statement serves in place of an oath. For just as one who does not speak cannot speak falsely, so one who does not swear cannot commit perjury.

Therefore, lest the practice of swearing should lead to the worship of idols, the ancients, as little children under the law, are warned not to swear by the name of foreign gods; rather, if they wished, they were permitted to swear by the name of God, to whom they were commanded to offer the worship due in every respect. In the same way, the offering of animal sacrifices was granted to them so that they might offer them in the temple of the Lord to the one God, lest they offer to idols what they were unwilling entirely to abandon.

## CHAPTER III. Concerning the three principal solemnities at which the law commanded every male to be presented before the Lord

“Three times each year you shall celebrate feasts” (Exod. XXIII). Here he especially commends three principal festivals to be observed above the other festivals: Passover, Pentecost, and the Feast of Booths.

He then enumerates them: “You shall keep the solemnity of unleavened bread. For seven days you shall eat unleavened bread, as I commanded you, at the time of the month of new produce, when you came out of Egypt. You shall not appear before me empty-handed.”

Among the Hebrews this month is called Nisan; among the Greeks, Xanthicus; among the Latins, April. It is called the month of new produce because new crops were first harvested in that month. (From Josephus.)

Concerning this, we think it appropriate to recall what Josephus reports in the third book of the *Antiquities*: “On the second day of the unleavened-bread festival, which is the sixteenth, they offer to God the firstfruits of the crops that they harvest, before eating from them. Judging God to be justly honored with the firstfruits, through which they have been filled with such abundance, they offer them in this manner: they dry a sheaf of ears, crush them, and make clean barley suitable for cooking; they offer an assarion of it on the altar of God, and, having cast one drachma from it, leave the remainder for the use of the priests. Then everyone may harvest according to his own desire. From the firstfruits of the crops they sacrifice a lamb as a burnt offering to the Lord.”

“And you shall observe the solemnity of the month of firstfruits, of whatever you sow in the field.” (From Josephus.)

Here the same Josephus says: “When the seventh week has passed after this sacrifice—the days of the seven weeks being forty-nine—Pentecost is celebrated. The Hebrews call it Asartha, which signifies Pentecost, that is, the fiftieth day. At it they offer to God loaves made from dried flour, with leaven, two assarions, and two lambs for slaughter.”

“You shall also celebrate a solemnity at the end of the year, when you have gathered all your crops from the field.”

These words also show that the offering is made from crops that are already ripe, since it is then the season of harvest. He calls the end of the year the end of summer, when the fruits of the whole year have already been collected.

This same festival occurs in the seventh month, which the Hebrews call Tishri, the Macedonians *hyperberetaion*, and the Latins October. At its beginning the Jews celebrated a solemnity, blowing trumpets more extensively and offering more sacrifices than during the individual months. In that month were the days of expiation, and on the fifteenth day the days of the Feast of Booths were celebrated—the solemnity of tabernacles—in which many different sacrifices were offered.

This is according to the historical sense.

Spiritually also, we celebrate feasts three times each year when, throughout the whole period of our present life, in the confession of the Holy Trinity through faith, hope, and charity, we joyfully offer our spiritual service of good works to God our Creator.

For we celebrate Passover in the month of new produce when, having been freed from Egyptian slavery through the blood of the spotless Lamb, we pass through spiritual waters from the old person into the new, walking not in the oldness of the letter but in the newness of the Spirit, so that through the grace of Christ, our Lord and Redeemer, we may be able to reach the land of promise.

We celebrate the solemnity of the month of firstfruits when we consecrate to the Lord the firstfruits of all our works, intentions, and words. We also truly celebrate the solemnity at the end of the year, when the Feast of Booths is observed after the fruits have been gathered, when, having gathered the fruits of virtue, we strive to reach the end of life and the entrance into the heavenly kingdom.

We dwell in tabernacles for seven days, because throughout the whole period of our present life we acknowledge that we are strangers in the world and seek rest not here but in the life to come. What is then done worthily, if we diligently consider these things, we strive to fulfill.

What was said above—“You shall not appear before me empty-handed.” (From Gregory.)

A person appears empty before the Lord if he carries nothing with him from the fruit of his labor. One person sweats in the pursuit of honors, another burns with desire to multiply his possessions, another pants after praise. But because, when dying, each person leaves all these things here, he appears empty before the Lord, since he has brought nothing with him before the Judge.

Therefore, through the law, we are salutarily admonished when it says: “You shall not appear empty before the Lord.” Whoever does not provide, by acting well, for obtaining the reward of life appears empty before the Lord.

Hence the Psalmist says concerning the righteous: “They come, they come with rejoicing, carrying their sheaves” (Ps. CXXV). They come to the examination of judgment carrying sheaves who show in themselves the right works by which they may deserve life.

It follows: “Three times a year every male of yours shall appear before the Lord God.” What does it mean that, while women are passed over, the law commands males to be presented before the Lord? It means that our Creator, rejecting whatever is soft, fragile, and weak in our conduct, demands from us strong works of virtue.

For if, in faith in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, we devote ourselves to good works during the time of our present life in order to obtain eternal reward, we undoubtedly establish our male character worthily before the presence of the Lord.

“You shall not sacrifice the blood of my victim over leaven.” Leaven, whose offering in the Lord’s sacrifice is forbidden, signifies, as we have often said, the bitterness of malice and wickedness.

“You shall not sacrifice,” he says, “the blood of my victim over leaven.” It is as though he said: Take care lest, in the offering by which you desire to appease the Lord, you mingle anything deceitful or wicked, because the sincerity of righteousness is especially pleasing to God.

Likewise, let us understand this saying as an admonition that, in the sacrifice of the body and blood of the Lord, we should strive to possess purity of heart and conduct, lest, in offering the drink of life, we appear before the Lord foul and ungrateful.

It follows: “Nor shall the fat of my solemnity remain until morning.” Through this saying he instructs us not to postpone until the morning of the future resurrection the work of mercy or the abundance of other virtues, because there will then be no time for action; that day will be the day of recompense, when each person will receive according to what he did in the time of his flesh, when it was permitted to work.

“You shall bring the firstfruits of the produce of your land into the house of your God.” As you live worthily in the Church of the Lord, gladly present to your Creator the beginnings of all your works, because this is the one house in which the paschal lamb is commanded to be eaten, and it is also the most suitable place for offering every gift.

“You shall not boil a kid in its mother’s milk.” Or, according to another edition: “You shall not boil a lamb in its mother’s milk.”

How this is to be understood according to the literal meaning of the words, I do not know whether it can be discovered. If we take the prohibition of boiling a lamb in milk as given for the sake of some signification, there is no ordinary practice of boiling it in this way. But if it refers to the days when it is being suckled, has any Jew ever observed this by boiling a lamb while it was still nursing, rather than after it had ceased to suck?

What, moreover, does “in its mother’s milk” mean? For even if this were understood literally, could it not be boiled without violating the command if, after it was born, its mother had died and it were suckled by another ewe?

Since commandments are certainly given to signify something, no one doubts that even those commands which can be carried out in observance were not given without reason. They signify something. But how this particular command is to be observed according to the literal meaning of the words is either impossible or unclear.

Nevertheless, I approve the reading concerning Christ: that by this prophecy it was foretold that the infant would not be killed by the Jews when Herod sought him in order to kill him but did not find him. Let “you shall boil” refer to the fire of the Passion, that is, tribulation. Hence it is said: “The furnace tests the vessels of the potter, and temptation through tribulation tests righteous people” (Eccl. XXVII).

Because the infant did not then suffer when, as Herod sought him, such danger appeared imminent, it was foretold in these words: “You shall not boil a lamb in its mother’s milk.”

It is perhaps not absurd, moreover, that others say this command was given prophetically so that good Israelites would not join themselves to evil Jews, by whom Christ suffered, like a lamb in its mother’s milk—that is, at the time when he was conceived. For women are said to begin gathering milk from the time they conceive.

That Christ suffered in that month is shown both by the observance of Passover and by the day of his nativity known to the churches. He who was born in the ninth month, on the eighth day before the Kalends of January, was certainly conceived in the first month, around the eighth day before the Kalends of April. That was also the time of his Passion, in his mother’s milk—that is, in the days of his mother.

Likewise, tropologically: “You shall not boil a kid in its mother’s milk.” Here the kid is introduced under the figure of the sinner. Therefore, one who sins is not to be boiled in his mother’s milk—that is, he is not to be cleansed by the moderate and tender disciplines of the Church. Rather, the sins of one whose crimes are great must be boiled away through more severe commandments, so that the person who ruined himself through the allurements of wantonness may redeem himself through stronger discipline.

## CHAPTER IV. Where he foretells that he will drive the nations away from before the children of Israel by the hand of an angel, provided that they listen to the Lord’s commandments and do them
Behold, I am sending my angel before you, to guard you on the way and to bring you into the place that I have prepared. Pay attention to him and heed his voice; do not think him contemptible, for he will not forgive when you sin, and my name is in him (Exod. XXIII).

According to the historical sense, this sentence signifies Joshua, leader of the Israelite people. He is called an angel because he was sent to carry out the Lord’s commission. For in Greek we call angels *angeloi*, that is, messengers. Joshua may rightly be called a messenger, since among the Israelites he made the Lord’s commands known [Col. 0130C] and proclaimed to the nations the power and terror of God. The Lord commands his people to obey his voice. Hence that same people is reported to have said to him: “As we obeyed Moses,” they say, “so will we obey you. Only may the Lord your God be with you, as he was with Moses. Whoever contradicts your mouth and does not obey all your words that you command him, let him die” (Josh. I).

And he says, “My name is in him.” The name of the Lord was present in Joshua in two ways, since he was also an Israelite. For *Israel* is interpreted as “a man seeing God,” or “a prince with God.” He also bore within himself the name of Jesus, that is, of the Savior, whom he prefigured both in office and in name. For, according to the allegorical sense, that angel himself may be understood as the Lord and our Redeemer. Through the prophet, on account of the dispensation of his humanity, he is called “the angel of great counsel,” because he announces his own will and the will of the Father. Whoever does not heed him will be destroyed from his people. The name of God is truly in him, because although he is true man, he is recognized as true God.

The text continues: “But if you hear his voice and do all that I speak, I will be an enemy to your enemies, and I will afflict those who afflict you. My angel will go before you and bring you to the Amorite, the Hittite, the Perizzite, the Canaanite, the Hivite, and the Jebusite, and so forth.”

Historically, Joshua brought the Israelite people into the promised land, driving out from before them the nations named above, shattering their idols and destroying their altars. Spiritually, however, our Redeemer expels from us these seven nations together with their idols when he drives out the seven principal vices and banishes every deception of the enemy far from our hearts, so that we may possess fully and perfectly the land of our nature.

The root of every evil is pride, concerning which Scripture bears witness: “Pride is the beginning of every sin” (Eccl. X). Its first offspring—namely, the seven principal vices—spring from this poisonous root: vainglory, envy, anger, sadness, avarice, gluttony, and lust. Because our Redeemer grieved that we were held captive by these seven vices of pride, he came to the spiritual battle of liberation filled with the sevenfold Spirit of grace.

The command that we should healthfully possess the territories of these destructive nations is understood as follows. Each vice has its own station in our heart. Taking possession of it, the vice expels Israel—that is, contemplation of the highest and holiest things—from the recesses of our soul, and never ceases to oppose it. For “what partnership is there between righteousness and iniquity? Or what fellowship does light have with darkness?” But when the vices have been overcome by the people of Israel—that is, by the virtues fighting against them—the place that the spirit of lust or fornication had held in our heart will thereafter be occupied by chastity. The place anger had seized will be claimed by strength. The place sadness, which produces death, had occupied will be possessed by salutary and joy-filled sadness. The place acedia had devastated will begin to be cultivated by fortitude. The place pride had trampled down will be adorned by humility. Thus, after each vice has been expelled, the virtues opposed to them will possess their places—that is, their effects.

These virtues are rightly called the children of Israel, that is, souls who see God. When they have expelled all the passions of the heart, they should be regarded not so much as having invaded foreign possessions as having recovered their own.

Indeed, according to ancient tradition, these same lands of the Canaanites, into which the children of Israel were brought, had once been assigned by lot to the sons of Shem in the division of the world. Later the descendants of Ham possessed them through the injustice of invasion. In this, God’s utterly righteous judgment is also confirmed: he expelled the former from places that they had wickedly occupied, and restored these holy people to what had been allotted as their ancestral possession through the division of the world among their lineage.

This figure is also known to apply to us with complete reason. The Lord naturally assigned possession of our heart not to vices but to virtues. After Adam’s transgression, when the vices—like the Canaanite peoples—rose up and drove the virtues from their proper territory, if those virtues are restored to them again through God’s grace and our diligence and labor, they should be believed to have recovered not foreign lands but their own.

These eight vices are also signified in the Gospel: “You shall not worship their gods, nor serve them. You shall not do their works, but you shall destroy them and shatter their statues. You shall serve the Lord your God, and I will bless your bread and your waters and remove sickness from your midst. There shall be neither barren nor sterile person in your land. I will fulfill the number of your days” (Augustine). [Col. 0131A]

Although these promises can also be understood spiritually, when they are understood according to the temporal happiness of human beings they belong to the Old Testament. For although in it there are commandments—apart from those which signify something in the sacramental sense—that pertain to good conduct, its promises are nevertheless carnal and earthly.

Accordingly, in Psalm 72, a man says that his steps had almost slipped and been poured out when he became jealous of sinners, observing the peace of sinners. He saw the wicked enjoying those things that he himself, in accordance with the Old Testament, was expecting from the Lord God, whom he served in return for that reward. When an impious thought began to steal upon him from this—since he supposed that God did not care about human affairs—he says that he was corrected when he did not dare to reject the authority of the saints. He began to understand and said: “This is labor before me, until I enter the sanctuary and understand the final things.”

There the rewards belonging to the New Testament will be given, which the wicked will not receive; and then the punishments of the wicked will take place, which none of the godly will experience.

Nevertheless, the saints receive some blessing in the present life, when the Lord grants them the fruitfulness of good works and an abundance of virtues, so that, as they advance in holy actions, they may complete in practice the observance of the Lord’s law given to them, and thus deserve to attain the rewards of eternal blessedness. Hence the prophet says: “For he who gave the law will give blessing; they will go from virtue to virtue; the God of gods will be seen in Zion” (Ps. LXXXIII). There the number of their days will be fulfilled, where supreme perfection will be bestowed and the permanence of eternity granted.

“I will turn the backs of all your enemies before you, sending hornets ahead of you, which will drive out the Hivite, the Canaanite, and the Hittite before you enter.” The question arises what should be understood by these creatures. God promises this, and the Book of Wisdom also says, where it declares that it was fulfilled: “He sent wasps as forerunners of his army” (Wis. XII). Yet we do not read that this happened—neither in the time of Moses, nor under Joshua son of Nun, nor under the judges, nor under the kings.

Therefore these hornets are to be understood as the stings of fear, perhaps by which the nations mentioned were driven to yield to the children of Israel. For God is speaking, and when something figurative is said in his speech that was not fulfilled literally, this does not undermine the reliability of the historical account, in which the truthfulness of the narrator is evident. Nor does the narrative of the evangelists, understood literally, become defective if something is said figuratively by Christ.

### CHAPTER V  
### In which he explains that he will send hornets before Israel to drive out the foreigners before them, and concerning the blessing of the land to be possessed

“I will not drive them out from before you in a single year, lest the land become desolate and the wild beasts multiply against you. Little by little I will drive them out from your sight, until you have increased and possess the land” (Exod. XXIII).

The Lord clearly indicates why he did not wish to drive out all at once the nations whose land he promised to give to the Israelite people: namely, so that he might test and instruct Israel through them, so that there would be people to rebuke those who sinned and compel the wicked to fear God.

Mystically, however, after many crowds of vices have been expelled from the corruptibility of the flesh, the Lord permits his chosen people to be attacked by certain vices, so that they may always have something against which to exercise themselves and may not, through idleness, fall into an even greater ruin of sins. Hence, when the teacher of the nations asked that the Lord remove from him the angel of Satan who was striking him, he received the answer: “My grace is sufficient for you” (II Cor. XII). “For power is made perfect in weakness.”

“I will set your boundaries from the Red Sea to the sea of the Philistines, and from the desert to the river. I will deliver the inhabitants of the land into your hands, and I will drive them out from your sight. You shall not make a covenant with them or with their gods. They shall not dwell in your land, lest they make you sin against me if you serve their gods; for that would certainly be a snare to you. If you serve their gods, they will be an offense to you.”

Here the Greek text has δουλεύσεις (*douleuseis*), “you will serve,” not λατρεύσεις (*latreuseis*), “you will worship.” Hence it is understood that *dulia* is owed to God as Lord, whereas *latria* is owed only to God as God.

Moses was also told: “Go up to the Lord—you and Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, and seventy elders of Israel—and you shall worship from afar. Moses alone shall go up to the Lord; they shall not approach, and the people shall not go up with him” (Exod. XXIV).

What does it mean that the Lord first commands Moses and Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, and seventy elders of Israel to go up to the Lord, and immediately afterward adds that Moses alone should go up to the Lord, while the others should not approach but worship from afar? Surely it teaches us morally that each person should discern carefully his own strength and the vigor of his spirit, so that he does not presume to raise himself toward the citadel of virtue or the summit of contemplation beyond what he sees himself capable of attaining. Rather, he should advance as far as divine mercy urges him and sacred Scripture teaches him.

As someone has said: “He places his foot on the precipice who does not carefully observe the limit of his own measure.”

The text continues: “But the people shall not go up with him.” By “the people” he means weak hearers, or those who are still entangled in earthly desires. He forbids them to go up with Moses because those whom earthly love holds below will not be able to reach the citadel of knowledge of the divine law.

Moses therefore came and recounted to the people all the words and judgments of the Lord. And the whole people answered with one voice: “All the words that the Lord has spoken we will do and we will hear” (From Augustine).

Up to this point in Scripture, the “justifications” are understood as those statutes given to the people for observance. They begin, as the very words of Scripture indicate, at the passage from which this name “justifications” takes its beginning: the passage concerning the Hebrew slave whose ear is pierced at the doorpost. In all these justifications, one must consider what can be applied to the conduct of life and the practice of good morals. For many things in them signify mysteries rather than instructing our life.

The Latin translators called these statutes *justificationes*, which the Greeks call δικαιώματα (*dikaiōmata*).

It should be noted that the people again answer: “All the words that the Lord has spoken we will do and we will hear,” although the order would seem to require, “We will hear and we will do.” Surely some meaning is hidden here. For if “we will hear” has been put in place of “we will understand,” then it would first have been necessary to render obedience in action to the words of God, so that he might lead them, by the merit of a devotion that neither despises nor fails to perform what has been commanded, to understanding those things that are done at his command.

But we must see whether this people is found to resemble that son who said to his father when commanded, “I will go into the vineyard,” but did not go (Matt. XXI). For the nations that had utterly despised God were later justified through the obedience of one person; though they had not pursued righteousness, they grasped it. [Col. 0134B]

### CHAPTER VI  
### Concerning Moses’ building an altar at the foot of the mountain and the offering of holocausts upon it

“Moses wrote all the words of the Lord. Rising early, he built an altar at the foot of the mountain and twelve pillars for the twelve tribes of Israel” (Exod. XXIV).

It should be noted that Moses built an altar beneath the mountain and twelve stones for the twelve tribes of Israel. The altar, built from twelve stones, is understood to signify that the people themselves are God’s altar, just as they are God’s temple.

Alternatively: Moses builds an altar at the foot of the mountain and sets up twelve pillars for the twelve tribes of Israel when the divine law commands us, before ascending the heights of virtue, to establish the altar of faith in our hearts and to shape our religious practice according to the teaching of the twelve apostles.

“He sent young men from the children of Israel, and they offered holocausts and sacrificed calves as peace offerings to the Lord.”

One who dedicates himself to God offers a holocaust to the Lord. The text rightly says that young men from the children of Israel offered holocausts, because only the strong aspire to the perfection of life. But one who is still a child—that is, inexperienced in faith—or one whom old age weakens, that is, whom a carnal habit burdens, is not fit to offer holocausts to the Lord. Such a person should keep the lower commandments of the law, through which he may be saved.

Hence Truth himself first answered in the Gospel one who asked about salvation: “If you wish to enter life,” he said, “keep the commandments.” Shortly afterward he teaches concerning perfection: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come and follow me” (Matt. XIX).

He offers calves as peace offerings to the Lord who, having restrained the impulses of the vices, presents to God the joy of good works with a peaceful mind.

(From Augustine.) It should be noted, however, that according to another edition the text reads: “And they sacrificed a saving offering to God.” It does not say “a salvific offering,” but “an offering of salvation”; the Greek has σωτηρίου (*sōtēriou*). Hence in the psalm: “I will take the cup of salvation” (Ps. CXV). It does not say “the saving cup.”

Here we must consider whether perhaps the one is signified of whom Simeon said: “For my eyes have seen your salvation” (Luke II). The psalm also commends him where it says: “Announce his salvation from day to day” (Ps. XCV). For what else, if we attend more carefully, does “from day to day” mean than “light from light”—that is, God from God, who is the only-begotten Son?

“Moses took half of the blood and poured it into bowls, and he poured the other half of the blood upon the altar. Then he took the book of the covenant and read it aloud in the hearing of the people.”

It should now be noted that Moses is said to have sacrificed for the first time, as Scripture appears to say, since the people were led out of Egypt. Earlier it had been said of Jethro, his father-in-law, though with some ambiguity, that he had offered sacrifice to God.

It should also be observed that the book of the covenant was read together with the blood of the sacrifice. In this book we should understand those justifications to have been written. For it is made clear later that the Decalogue of the law was written on stone tablets.

“And they said: ‘All that the Lord has spoken we will do and we will hear.’” They do not answer differently—behold, already for the third time.

Then he took the blood and sprinkled it upon the people, saying: “This is the blood of the covenant that the Lord has made with you concerning all these words.”

The apostle Paul, in his Epistle to the Hebrews, explains most clearly how this signifies the blood of the Lord’s passion: “Almost everything is cleansed by blood according to the law, and without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness” (Heb. IX).

For that blood with which Moses sprinkled the people and purified the book of the law, the tabernacle of the covenant, and everything that was in it, saying, “This is the blood of the covenant,” is shown wonderfully to proclaim the blood of the Lord Jesus. By that blood the hearts of all believers are cleansed, by it the faith of the Church is sealed, and by it everything—that is, the whole body of the tabernacle—is sanctified. The Lord said to his disciples: “This is my blood of the New Testament, which will be poured out for many” (Matt. XXVI). What had been shown figuratively through Moses was fulfilled in truth.

Moses and Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, and seventy of the elders of Israel went up, and they saw the God of Israel. Beneath his feet there was something like a work of sapphire stone, and like the sky when it is clear. He did not stretch out his hand against those of the children of Israel who had withdrawn some distance. They saw God, and they ate and drank.

(From Augustine.) Among those who understand correctly, it is established that God is contained by no place, nor does he possess bodily members in some bodily position, as our body does when it sits, lies, or stands, or in any similar condition. Such things belong only to bodies; God, however, is spirit.

Therefore, when he displays himself in bodily form or through signs expressed bodily, it is not his substance that appears—that substance which is identical with what he is—but the assumption of visible forms, which is subject to his omnipotence.

Not one of the elect of Israel disagreed, and they appeared in the place of God and ate and drank. Who could doubt that those whom the text names explicitly, and who are now called the seventy elders, represent the elect of Israel? They undoubtedly represented those who are chosen among God’s people. “For faith does not belong to all,” and “the Lord knows those who are his” (Rom. IX). “In a great house there are vessels not only for honor but also for dishonor.” For “those whom he foreknew, he also predestined; those whom he predestined, he also called; those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified” (Rom. VIII).

Certainly, not one of the elect of Israel disagreed.

The number four is signified in Moses and Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, on account of the four Gospels and the promise of the whole world, which is divided into four parts. Then there were seventy of the elders of Israel—namely, the number seven multiplied by ten—which pertains to signifying the Holy Spirit.

The sapphire signifies heavenly life, especially since it is said to have appeared “like the aspect of the firmament.” Who does not know that the firmament is called heaven? The form of a brick in that sapphire signifies its squareness or stability, or the mystery of that same number four.

That they ate and drank in the place of God signifies sweetness and satisfaction in that kingdom of eternity. “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied” (Matt. V).

Hence the Lord also says that many will come. Who else could they be but the elect—foreknown, predestined, called, justified, and glorified—who will recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven? Elsewhere he himself promises this to his faithful: that he will make them recline, pass by, and serve them (Luke XII).

What does it mean that Joshua son of Nun is not mentioned among those four, yet suddenly appears with Moses and goes up with him onto the mountain to receive the tablets of the law, and then suddenly Joshua is hidden again—that is, no longer mentioned—and Moses receives the law on the two tablets, after which Joshua appears again with him?

Perhaps it signifies the New Testament under the name of Jesus: that it was hidden in the law and at times appears to those who understand.

The fact that Joshua is already called Jesus, although Scripture testifies in the Book of Numbers that he received this name when they were already near entering the promised land, is an instance of *prolepsis*, that is, anticipation: Scripture anticipates what happened later. For all these things were written after they had happened. Therefore, when the event now being mentioned occurred, he was not yet called Jesus; but when it was written down, he was already called by that name.

As the Apostle says, “All these things happened to them as a figure,” but “they were written for our sake” (I Cor. X)—not only the events and words contained in the sacred writings, but also the locations, regions, and seasons, as well as the circumstances of the things in which these events occurred or words were spoken.

### CHAPTER VII  
### Concerning Moses’ ascent of the mountain to receive from the Lord the law written on tablets, which he did

The Lord said to Moses: “Go up to me on the mountain and remain there. I will give you stone tablets, together with the law and commandments that I have written, so that you may teach the children of Israel” (Exod. XXIV).

(From Bede.) Since the Lord was about to give the law to Moses, he first calls him to the summit of the mountain, so that, dwelling there with him on high, he may hear more freely what he is to teach the people when he returns below.

So also in the Gospel the Lord, calling the new heralds of grace to the mountain, instructs them in saving commandments, so that even the position of the place might make clear that he was giving them lofty commands for living and promises of reward. Thus the Lord gave the commandments both of the law and of the Gospel on a mountain, in order thereby to commend the sublimity of both Testaments.

Yet because the law of Scripture was then to be entrusted to one people, Israel, while the grace of the Gospel was to reach all the nations throughout the world through the preaching of the apostles, Moses alone rightly ascended the mountain to learn and receive the law. But the apostles, all together with the Lord on the mountain, heard the teaching of the Gospel while the crowds also listened.

They heard it through the grace of the Holy Spirit, by whom this same grace and truth of the Gospel was given more manifestly to the Church—not only to the apostles, but also to a very large multitude of believers gathered together in the upper room on Mount Zion, when they received it through the division of various languages. By such a miracle the Church of all the nations throughout the world was signified as destined to praise God together in many tongues.

“I will give you stone tablets, together with the law and commandments that I have written, so that you may teach them.”

This resembles the Gospel passage quoted above: “Teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you” (Matt. ult.). Therefore neither Moses, nor the apostles, nor any teacher ought to teach God’s people anything other than what the Lord himself taught and prescribed for us to observe by the decree of his counsel, in the observance of which he wished us to have eternal life.

He wrote these things on stone tablets because he established them, to be guarded with fixed intention, in the hearts of the elect, who are strong through faith. When he presents their examples to us for imitation, he displays the statutes of his law as though they had been written and fixed in stone.

For Daniel saw the Lord, in the figure of a stone cut from the mountains without hands, shatter the splendor of worldly kingdoms, so that his kingdom alone might remain without end (Dan. II). Peter also admonishes the faithful, saying: “You yourselves, like living stones, are being built into a spiritual house” (I Pet. II).

Moses arose, and Joshua his minister.

Joshua, Moses’ minister, signifies the Lord the Savior both by his name and by his action. He is rightly called Moses’ minister because, appearing in the flesh, he deigned to assume in himself the ceremonies of the Mosaic law. He did not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it.

He follows Moses’ footsteps in everything, because in all that Moses speaks or writes, Christ is found—whether typologically or openly designated—as an inseparable companion, if he is sought properly. Hence he says to the Jews: “If you believed Moses, you would perhaps believe me also, for he wrote about me” (John V).

Moses went up the mountain of God and said to the elders: “Wait here until we return to you. You have Aaron and Hur with you. If any matter of dispute arises, refer it to them.”

Aaron is interpreted as “mountain of strength”; Hur as “fire” or “light.” Hence Aaron designates the Lord the Savior, while Hur designates the Holy Spirit.

When Moses therefore went up to the Lord, he left Aaron and Hur—that is, the mountain of strength and the light of fire—in the plains to govern the people.

And if we cannot follow our teachers to the heights of divine contemplation, let us take care, in our concern, that no temptation draw us away from the vicinity of God’s mountain. Rather, according to the measure allotted to us, let us devote ourselves to works of virtue, clinging with steadfast heart to the mysteries of our Redeemer in which we have been instructed, and taking care to preserve undefiled within us the grace of his Spirit with which we have been marked.

If any difficulty arising from adversity assails us, let us immediately invoke the help of that same Redeemer of ours, who is accustomed, through the gift of the Holy Spirit, to protect his faithful from every evil and deliver them.

When Moses had gone up, a cloud covered the mountain.

Just as the mountain on which Moses received the law signifies the height of perfection that was to be written in that same law, so the cloud with which the mountain was covered signifies the grace of divine protection. Each person enjoys this protection all the more abundantly the higher he ascends, with the eyes of his heart opened, to investigate the wonders of God’s law.

The cloud covered not only the mountain on which Moses ascended but also the people walking through the wilderness, who could not in any way ascend to higher places. Nevertheless, the cloud sent from heaven overshadowed them. Hence it is written: “He spread out a cloud as their protection” (Ps. CXIV). For the Lord truly protects all who fear him, the little together with the great, with heavenly blessing.

“And the glory of the Lord dwelt upon Sinai, covering it with a cloud for six days. On the seventh day he called him from the midst of the darkness.”

Not only the elevation but also the name of the mountain on which the law was given figuratively announces the perfection of that law. For Sinai is interpreted as “my measure” or “my jar.” It was therefore divinely arranged that the mountain on which the law was given should be called “my jar,” as though the Lord himself were signifying through this name that his law promulgates a perfect rule of life for all.

It is rightly said that, as Moses ascended, the cloud and the glory of the Lord covered the mountain for six days, but on the seventh day he called him to the higher parts of the mountain. For six days we are commanded to work in the law and to rest on the seventh.

As Moses ascended the mountain, he was covered for six days by the cloud and glory of the Lord, to signify mystically that whoever carries out the Lord’s commandments through righteous works is worthy of divine protection.

But on the seventh day the Lord calls Moses to higher places, because after the perfection of works the law promises us eternal rest. Thus those who have taken care to stand before the Lord in the height of right action may now deserve to ascend to his vision and conversation.

The “midst of the darkness” from which he is said to have been called does not signify that any darkness exists in God, but that he dwells in inaccessible light. As the Apostle likewise says: “No human being has seen him, nor is able to see him” (I Tim. VI).

That darkness is the obscurity of heavenly mysteries, inaccessible to earthly hearts, but penetrable to Moses and to the other blessed who are pure in heart, when divine grace opens the way.

The appearance of the glory of the Lord was like a burning fire upon the summit of the mountain, in the sight of the children of Israel.

The glory of the Lord appeared like a burning fire because it both illuminates the hearts of the elect with the gift of heavenly knowledge and inflames them with the ardor of his love.

The glory of the Lord was therefore seen in cloud, darkness, and fire: in the cloud, because he protects us from the heat of temptations; in the darkness, because the power of his majesty cannot be fully comprehended by any creature—for “the peace of God surpasses all understanding”; and in the burning fire, because he enlightens the minds of the faithful with knowledge of heavenly goods and kindles them with hope and love.

The children of Israel see this glory of the Lord from far away and from below, but Moses penetrates farther by ascending higher. For those who are perfect and exalted see the hidden things of the divine mysteries. Or, remembering our own frailty and sluggishness, if we cannot enter into these things by comprehending them, let us at least take care to remain nearby and gaze upon them through faith, hope, and love.

Moses entered into the midst of the cloud, ascended the mountain, and remained there forty days and forty nights.

Moses entered into the midst of the cloud and ascended the mountain when the preachers of the divine law—among whom Moses was preeminent—penetrate, at the Lord’s invitation and guidance, to contemplate from on high the uncertain and hidden things of divine wisdom.

Moses remained with the Lord for forty days and forty nights so that, through this number of days, he might learn that only those whom the grace of evangelical truth—which was to be written in four books—would assist could fulfill the Decalogue of the law that he had received with his people.

### CHAPTER VIII  
### Concerning what the Lord said to Moses about the offering of firstfruits

The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “Speak to the children of Israel, that they may take firstfruits for me. From every person who offers willingly, you shall receive firstfruits for me” (Exod. XXV).

We too offer the firstfruits of our goods to the Lord when, whenever we do anything good, we attribute the whole of it to divine grace, truly and from the depths of our heart confessing that we cannot have even the beginning of a good action or thought except from the Lord. As for our evils, we confess that they are always begun and completed by us, at the devil’s instigation, and that they can be released only when the Lord grants it.

It is rightly commanded that Moses receive the firstfruits from one who offers willingly, for “God loves a cheerful giver.” The Apostle also commands us to do good not from sadness or necessity but according to the purpose of the heart (II Cor. IX). Knowing that he did this, the prophet gloried in the Lord, saying: “I will sacrifice to you willingly” (Ps. LIII).

“These are the things that you shall receive: gold, silver, bronze, violet-purple, twice-dyed scarlet, fine linen, goats’ hair, rams’ skins dyed red, violet skins, acacia wood, oil for preparing the lamps, spices for the anointing oil, fragrant incense, onyx stones, and gems for adorning the ephod and the breastpiece.”

“They shall make me a sanctuary, and I will dwell in their midst.”

All these things that the Lord commanded the former people materially to offer for the construction of a sanctuary, we too, who desire to be spiritual children of Israel and imitators of the people who see the Lord, must offer through spiritual understanding.

We offer him gold when we shine with the splendor of true wisdom, which consists in right faith; silver when confession of our error becomes salvation; bronze when we rejoice in proclaiming that same faith publicly; violet-purple when we raise our hearts upward; purple when we subject the body to suffering; twice-dyed scarlet when we burn with the twofold love of God and neighbor; fine linen when we practice purity of the flesh; goats’ hair when we put on the garment of repentance and mourning; rams’ skins dyed red when we behold the leaders of the Lord’s flock baptized in their own blood; violet skins when we hope that after death we shall have spiritual bodies in heaven; acacia wood when, having purged away the thorns of sins, we serve the Lord alone with clean flesh and soul; oil for preparing the lamps when we shine with the fruits of charity and mercy; spices for the anointing oil and fragrant incense when we spread the reputation of our good works far and wide, greatly encouraging others by our example to live well; and onyx stones and gems for adorning the ephod and breastpiece when we proclaim, worthy of praise, the miracles of the saints through which their thoughts devoted to God and their virtuous deeds are made known, and when we take these things up for the assistance of our faith wherever necessary.

Because we usually carry burdens on our shoulders, the works of the righteous and their devout labors for the Lord are rightly signified by the ephod, that is, the shoulder garment. Since the seat of thoughts is in the breast, the clean thoughts of the elect are rightly expressed in the breastpiece, which is the priestly garment worn upon the chest. The onyx stones and gems adorn the ephod and breastpiece when the insignia of miracles are joined to the outstanding deeds and thoughts of the highest Fathers.

### CHAPTER IX  
### Concerning the commandment about how the sanctuary is to be constructed
“They shall make me a sanctuary,” he says, “and I shall dwell in their midst, according to every likeness of the tabernacle that I shall show you, and of all its vessels for its worship” [Col. 0140D]. The Lord showed Moses the tabernacle on the mountain and the vessels consecrated for its worship, because, while Moses remained there with him for so long, he openly demonstrated how greatly the angelic virtues—who are his perfect tabernacle in all things—rejoice to obey their Creator with devotion, humility, and purity. From the time they were created, he has never ceased to remain and dwell in them.

The tabernacle, then, which was shown to Moses on the mountain is that heavenly city and homeland which at that time was believed to consist solely of the holy angels. After the passion, resurrection, and ascension into heaven of the mediator between God and human beings, it also received a distinguished and abundant multitude of holy souls. The vessels [Col. 0141A] of that tabernacle are each and every person of the blessed spirits; from all of them Jerusalem itself, which is the mother of us all, consists in true peace and unity.

It should be noted more carefully that the children of Israel are commanded to make a sanctuary for the Lord, not merely somewhat like it, but according to every likeness of the tabernacle that he showed Moses, and of all its vessels for his worship. If, perhaps, you ask how you, earthly human being, may imitate this heavenly tabernacle spiritually, imitate it by loving God and your neighbors; imitate it by helping the wretched—and, if not the angels, who are all blessed, then certainly human beings. They are humble and gentle, reconciled with one another, and obedient to divine commands: imitate this insofar as you are able. They neither speak, do, nor think anything evil, idle, or unjust; tireless in divine praises, they attend upon God in word and mind. Imitate this as much as you can, and you will have built a sanctuary for the Lord according to the example shown to Moses on the mountain.

Then our Lord and Savior, coming with the Father, makes his dwelling with you; indeed, after this life he will introduce you, eternally blessed, into that tabernacle which you imitate. The text continues:

## CHAPTER X. Description of how the ark was to be made: the mercy seat, the cherubim, and also the poles

“And thus you shall make it: construct the ark from acacia wood.” The ark, which is commanded to be made first of all in the tabernacle, appropriately signifies the incarnation itself of our Lord and Savior, in whom [Col. 0141C] all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden. This ark is rightly commanded to be constructed from acacia wood. Acacia wood is said to be of a light and incorruptible nature, not far removed from the quality of white thorn. The ark, therefore, was made from acacia wood because the Lord’s body consisted of members free from every stain of vices. These same woods are very similar to thorns because, although he did not come in sinful flesh, he came in the likeness of sinful flesh, as the Apostle says (Rom. V).

The text continues: “Its length shall be two and a half cubits; its width, one and a half cubits; and its height likewise one and a half cubits.” Josephus clearly indicates the size of that cubit in his *Antiquities*, saying: “The ark was made five palms in length and three in width.” Hence it is plainly evident that he designates the cubit completed by two palms.

Mystically, however, the length of the ark indicates the long-suffering patience of our Lord and Redeemer, with which he lived among human beings. Its width signifies the breadth of the charity by which he wished to come to us and dwell among us. Its height signifies the hope of future exaltation, by which he foresaw either that he himself would be glorified after his passion or that he would glorify others.

Thus it was fitting that the length of the ark was two cubits, on account of the teaching and works by which he shone in the world. But the fact that, beyond the two cubits, the ark also had an additional half-cubit in length may be referred to the slowness of human frailty, which was not yet able to grasp the sublime sayings or deeds of the Savior as it ought. Hence it is openly said concerning certain of his mystical acts: “His disciples did not understand these things at first, but when Jesus was glorified” (John XII). The same is said concerning his more exalted sayings: “This saying was hidden from them, and they did not understand what was said” (Luke II).

The ark had two cubits of length because the Lord appeared glorious in the flesh, in word and deed. It also had a half-cubit because he bore patiently the slowness of the disciples, who, not yet perfect, could not grasp his sayings or deeds. The width of the ark was one cubit, on account of the dispensation of the Lord’s own charity, by which he took care to unite his chosen ones in God.

Thus the ark has one and a half cubits because the Lord, in his single act of compassion, loves us so as to associate us with himself and the Father, and in his equally gracious kindness embraces the capacity for love that can exist in us, whatever its measure in this life, until we may enter into his vision, where we shall love him with all our heart, all our soul, and all our strength. The height of the ark was likewise most fittingly one and a half cubits, signifying the one hope by which the Lord himself, while he was with us in the flesh, awaited the outcome of the future resurrection and later glory, or by which he continually exhorts us, amid the adversities of the world, to rejoice because of the rewards of future goods.

“And you shall overlay it with purest gold, inside and out. Moreover, you shall make a golden crown around it.” The ark is overlaid inside and out with pure gold because the human nature assumed by the Son of God was full of the virtue of the Holy Spirit within and openly manifested the works of the Holy Spirit to human beings outwardly. A golden crown is rightly commanded to be placed around the top of this ark because the Son of God, appearing in the flesh and coming for the redemption of the human race, awaited the appointed time and hour when he would overcome, together with the author of death himself, the death he had accepted for us, and ascend victoriously to the Father in heaven.

“And four golden rings, which you shall place at the four corners of the ark. Let two rings be on one side and two on the other.” The four golden rings are the four books of the Gospels. They are rightly golden because of the brilliance of the wisdom with which they shine. They are rightly compared to rings because the wisdom of God that they proclaim is eternal: the eternal divinity neither began in time nor ceases to exist, and this is the divinity which the human being Christ received.

Therefore, as the hour of his passion approached, he prayed to the Father, saying: “And now glorify me, Father, with yourself, with the glory which I had with you before the world existed” (John XVII).

The ark has four corners because it never ceases to celebrate the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation throughout all the regions of the world in which the holy Church is spread. Four rings are placed at these four corners because the Gospel of Christ is preached in every corner of the world for the salvation of the hearts of the faithful.

There are two rings on one side and two on the other either because two evangelists adhered to the Savior’s discipleship while he preached in the flesh and performed miracles, whereas the other two came to faith in him after his resurrection and ascension into heaven; or because, in the figure of the four living creatures, the two represented by the man and the calf bore signs of his passion and death, while the two represented by the lion and the eagle displayed the insignia of the victory that destroyed death.

The ark had, as it were, two rings on its left side when two evangelists represented the Lord’s incarnation and passion. Likewise, there were two rings on its right side because two evangelists figuratively expressed his resurrection and ascension, which pertain to the glory of the future life.

“You shall also make poles of acacia wood and overlay them with gold. You shall insert them through the rings that are on the sides, so that the ark may be carried by them. They shall always remain in the rings and shall never be removed from them.” The poles by which the ark is carried are the holy teachers who, by preaching the Lord, bring him into the hearts of their hearers. These poles are rightly commanded always to remain in the rings, since all who preach the heavenly mysteries to others must never withdraw their minds from remembrance of sacred Scripture, nor their hands from observing the divine commandments.

The text rightly continues: “And you shall place in the ark the testimony that I shall give you.” For we ought to speak and believe concerning the incarnation of the Son of God only what the Lord himself has deigned to reveal to us through the authors of sacred Scripture.

If you wish to know what that testimony is which Moses received from the Lord to place in the ark, listen to the Apostle: “Behind the veil was the second tabernacle, which is called the Holy of Holies, having a golden censer and the ark of the covenant, covered on every side with gold; in it were a golden urn containing manna, Aaron’s rod that had blossomed, and the tablets of the covenant” (Hebr. IX).

The golden urn containing manna in the ark is the holy soul in Christ, possessing in itself the entire fullness of divinity. Aaron’s rod, which had been cut off and blossomed, is the unconquered power of that priesthood, of which the Prophet says: “The rod of equity is the rod of your kingdom” (Ps. XLIV). After it appeared for a time to have been cut off through death, when the morning of the resurrection grew strong it was found to have blossomed again with greater vitality, and it became known that it would remain forever inviolable and unfading. For Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more; death will no longer rule over him.

The tablets of the covenant in the ark signify in Christ both all knowledge of the Father’s secrets and the power of judgment. On the tablets of the covenant were inscribed the faith in the eternal divinity that created and governs the world, the commandments by which God ought to be served, and the discernment of judgment by which he himself would truly condemn those who disobeyed him and reward those who loved him with mercy.

“You shall also make a mercy seat of pure gold; its length shall be two and a half cubits and its width one and a half cubits.” It is often asked what the mercy seat is, with which the ark was to be covered. But since he commands that it be made of gold and have the same length and width as the ark, there is no doubt that he wished a golden panel to be made large enough to cover the ark.

This mercy seat signifies none other than the Lord Savior, and more particularly the depths of compassion within him. Of him the Apostle says: “God set him forth as an expiation through faith, in his blood” (1 John IV). It is placed above because “mercy triumphs over judgment.” Hence the Psalmist says: “The Lord is gracious to all, and his mercies are over all his works” (Ps. CXLIV).

“You shall also make two golden cherubim, fashioned by hammering, on the two sides of the inner sanctuary. Let one cherub be on one side and the other on the other. Let them cover both sides of the mercy seat, spreading their wings and covering the inner sanctuary. Let them look toward one another, their faces turned toward the mercy seat with which the ark is to be covered, in which you shall place the testimony [Col. 0144B] that I shall give you.”

The prophet Ezekiel clearly declares that *cherub* is the name of angelic virtues. He also indicates that he saw them appear together with others according to the example prescribed here, saying: “And the sound of the wings was heard as far as the outer court, like the sound of the Lord speaking.”

In the singular it is *cherub*, but in the plural *cherubim*, and it is a masculine noun. Greek usage, however, placed *cherubin* in the neuter gender, changing the letter *m* into *n*. Our translator, following the Hebrew idiom, used the masculine gender: “You shall make two golden and fashioned cherubim,” not “two golden and fashioned cherubin.” I believe that through the carelessness of scribes the translation was corrupted, so that *cherubin* was written according to the custom of earlier writers in place of *cherubim*.

*Cherubim*, or *cherubin*, is interpreted as “a multitude of knowledge” or “understanding of knowledge.” This name more rightly suits the angelic powers insofar as they, being perfectly removed from every impulse of impure thought, cleave to the vision of their Creator.

For this reason Moses is commanded to make wings in the figure of the cherubim, or the prophet testifies that he saw them in their actual form. Painters also commonly imitate this, indicating that angels have their seat on high and can move everywhere as though in light flight. They have no sluggishness, but are immediately present wherever they wish, and, as though gazing upon the mercy seat, they overshadow it—that is, they honor it by veiling it—because they attribute the whole state of perpetual blessedness that they possess to the grace of the one from whom they received the ability to do no evil.

There are two cherubim to signify the fellowship of angelic peace, since charity cannot exist between fewer than two. Hence they are commanded to look toward one another and to direct their faces toward the mercy seat, because in the glorification of the divine vision they resound in harmony with one another.

The two cherubim may also signify the two Testaments, one of which proclaims the future incarnation of the Lord and the other the incarnation that has taken place. They look toward one another because, in their testimony to the truth that they preach, they differ from one another in nothing. They turn their faces toward the mercy seat because they strongly commend the Lord’s mercy, in which alone the world has hope. For this reason they are on the two sides of the inner sanctuary: by the preaching of spiritual knowledge, they fill both the times preceding the Lord’s incarnation and those that follow it.

The name “multitude of knowledge,” or “multiplication of knowledge,” also suits them because sacred Scripture is full of spiritual and divine knowledge, and this same knowledge, from the time Scripture itself began to be composed, never ceases to grow and multiply.

The cherubim are rightly said to overshadow the mercy seat of glory because, as the Testament grows through time and knowledge is multiplied, they preach to us the mercy of the Lord Savior and never cease to honor it freely and continually with voices, as though with wings spread for flight. Since the words of speakers, carried through the air as they fly from the mouth of those who speak to the heart of those who hear, can rightly be represented by cherubim with wings spread and prepared for flight.

“From there I shall command and speak with you, above the mercy seat, namely from between the two cherubim that are above the ark of the testimony, concerning everything that I shall command you for the children of Israel” [Col. 0145B].

It was through the grace of God’s mercy that he deigned to appear to human beings after the guilt of transgression and to show them the way of truth after their error. He speaks from between the cherubim because God appeared through angelic vision and not in his own substance. He spoke to Moses, as the Apostle testifies: “The law was established because of transgressions, until the offspring should come to whom he had made the promise, ordained through angels by the hand of a mediator” (Gal. III).

The Lord also speaks from between the two cherubim because, through the words of both Testaments, he instructs us with a harmonious voice in the faith of the truth. Or certainly he speaks from between the cherubim because, through his only-begotten Son, who appeared in the flesh between the two Testaments, God the Father deigned to reveal his will to the human race.

The ark may also figuratively be understood as the holy Church. It is built from incorruptible wood—that is, from holy souls—and, stretched throughout the four regions of the world in the faith of the holy Gospel, it awaits from God the eternal crown of life. It contains within itself the tablets of the covenant through continual meditation on God’s law. It contains the golden urn with manna through faith in the Lord’s incarnation. It contains Aaron’s rod that had blossomed through participation in the Lord’s kingdom and priesthood, as the Apostle Peter says: “But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood” (1 Pet. II). It has the mercy seat above it, so that it may remember that everything good it possesses it has received through the generosity of divine grace.

It also has the cherubim of glory upon the mercy seat: either the angelic protections by which it is always helped by the merciful God, or the Testaments by which it is instructed how to live and how rightly to seek from divine mercy the help needed for right living.

The cherubim are placed above the mercy seat in the same way that the city of Christ—that is, the holy Church—is said to be established upon a mountain, that is, upon Christ himself. This does not mean that his city can be higher than he is, but that, sustained by his support, it may advance. The ark has cherubim above the mercy seat because either angelic ministries or divine utterances help the Church all the more truly insofar as it itself stands established upon the foundation of supreme truth.

## CHAPTER XI. The making of the table, its vessels, and the bread of the Presence to be offered upon it [Col. 0146A]

“You shall also make a table of acacia wood, two cubits long, one cubit wide, and one and a half cubits high” (Exod. XXV).

The table made from acacia wood is sacred Scripture, joined together from the strong words and deeds of the holy Fathers. By showing us what the joys of eternal blessedness are and how they may be attained, it supplies us with food for salvation and life.

It has length when it signifies perseverance in the religion once begun; width when it signifies the breadth of charity; and height when it signifies hope of perpetual reward.

Its length is rightly two cubits because our conduct in this life consists chiefly in two virtues, namely mercy and innocence, as the Apostle James says: “Religion pure and undefiled before God and the Father is this: to visit orphans and widows in their tribulation and to keep oneself unstained by the world” (James I).

The fact that the table has one cubit in width figuratively announces the unity of love commended to us throughout the entire sequence of the Old and New Testaments. Charity is one: that is, a simple and pure devotion of mind by which we are commanded to love God, our neighbors, and even our enemies. Yet with a very great and entirely proper distinction within this love, we must love God first and our enemies afterward. Among our neighbors also, the measure of love to be given should differ according to their merits.

Moreover, the fact that its height was one and a half cubits signifies, as does its width, the unity of our heavenly hope. We await our Lord, when he will return from heaven to reward the servants whom he finds watchful, with their loins girded and the lamps of good works burning. For although there are many dwellings in the Father’s house according to the diversity of merits, there is nevertheless one kingdom of heaven in which all the elect are received.

The remaining half-cubit indicates the beginning of the contemplative life, which some of the saints, while still placed in the flesh, were also granted to enjoy. They were given not only to hope for heavenly rewards but also, by living in part according to them, to taste them in advance.

“And you shall overlay it with purest gold.” The table of the tabernacle is overlaid with gold [Col. 0146D] because sacred Scripture shines brightly with the clarity of heavenly wisdom, and the prophets who composed it were distinguished in life and speech.

“You shall make for it a golden rim around it, and for the rim a crown of embossed work, four fingers high.” A golden rim is made around the table because the teaching of sacred discourse is ministered to us through the most pure mouths of faithful preachers. The speech of those who have handed down the divine mysteries to us does not permit itself to be in any way contaminated by the language of human chatter. Rather, they took care to endure and rebuke not only harmful but also idle human words.

Or certainly a golden rim is made around the table because, when rightly understood in every part of its expression, sacred Scripture sounds forth to us the brilliance of heavenly wisdom.

A crown is added to this rim because the tongue of preachers promises their hearers the reward of eternal life. This crown is rightly commanded to be four fingers high because the height of the everlasting crown is shown to us through the four books of the holy Gospel; or because we must reach the crown of life through guarding evangelical faith and practice.

It is beautifully appropriate that the books are signified by fingers, since the tablets of the law are said to have been written by the finger of God, and in the Gospel the Lord, intending to temper the interpretation of the law, wrote with his finger on the ground (John VIII).

The same crown is rightly commanded to be made of embossed work because the reward of the eternal kingdom is not given indiscriminately to everyone, but is distributed to each person according to the quality of the recipients, by a divinely discriminating judgment.

The golden crown of the Lord’s table would be pure and without embossing if the brilliance of the future reward of the righteous were disclosed as equal for all—like the sun, whose brightness God causes to rise indiscriminately upon the good and the wicked. But just as one star differs from another in glory, so also will be the resurrection of the dead. The crown of the Lord’s table has therefore been furnished with various but suitably ordered carvings.

One future life is promised to all the righteous, but within it each person’s glory is manifold according to the diversity of merits. The fact that, after the one crown previously described, another little golden crown is added may rightly be understood of the reward of those who, by freely choosing perfection of life, surpass the general commandments of sacred Scripture and therefore await, beyond other faithful people, a special reward for their voluntary offering.

Or certainly a golden crown is added to the rim of the Lord’s table when we learn from the words of sacred Scripture that souls departing from the flesh are received into eternal rewards in heaven. Another little crown is added above that crown when the same Scripture reveals that a more exalted glory is reserved for them at the end of the world, when they receive immortal bodies.

“You shall also prepare four golden rings and place them at the four corners of the same table, one at each foot.” What we explained above concerning the ark must also be understood here. The four golden rings are the four books of the Gospels, through whose faith it has come about that all sacred Scripture is read throughout the world and understood in its entirety.

The table has four feet because the entire sequence of divine utterances is distinguished according to a fourfold manner. In all the holy books we must observe what is intimated there as eternal, what is narrated as having happened, what is proclaimed as going to happen, and what is commanded or urged as needing to be done.

Likewise, the table of the tabernacle has four feet because the words of the heavenly oracle are usually understood historically, allegorically, tropologically—that is, morally—or anagogically.

History is present when something is reported in plain speech according to how it was literally done or said, as when it is narrated that the people of Israel, saved from Egypt, made a tabernacle for the Lord in the wilderness.

Allegory is present when the mysteries of Christ and the Church in the present are signified by mystical words or events. In words, as Isaiah says: “A shoot shall go forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root” (Isa. XI). This is to say plainly: The Virgin Mary will be born from David’s stock, and Christ will arise from her stock.

In events, the people saved from slavery in Egypt through the blood of the lamb signify the Church, which has been freed from demonic domination through the passion of Christ.

Tropological, that is, moral, speech concerns the instruction and correction of behavior, whether it is expressed in plain or figurative language. In plain language, as John exhorts us, saying: “My little children, let us not love in word or tongue, but in deed and truth” (1 John III).
