In figurative language, as Solomon says: “Let your garments be white at all times, and let oil never be lacking from your head” (Eccles. IX). This is to say plainly: Let your works be pure at all times, and let charity never be lacking from your heart.

Anagoge—that is, speech leading upward—is speech that discusses future rewards and the future life in heaven, whether in mystical or plain language. In plain language: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. V). In mystical language: “Blessed are those who wash their robes, so that they may have authority over the tree of life and enter the city through the gates.” This is to say openly: Blessed are those who cleanse their thoughts and deeds, so that they may have the power to see the Lord Christ, who said: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” [Col. 0148C] (John XIV), and through the teaching and examples of the Fathers who went before them may enter the kingdom of heaven.

“Under the crown there shall be golden rings, through which the poles may be inserted, so that the table can be carried. You shall also make the poles from acacia wood and cover them with gold, to carry the table.”

The rings are appropriately under the crown because in this life we use the books of the holy Gospel, while we hope for the crown of heavenly life in the future. The poles are inserted through these rings to carry the table because, when the holy teachers refresh the hearts of their hearers with the words of sacred discourse, they must themselves keep their minds fixed in every respect upon evangelical reading, so that they direct the whole purpose of their interpretation and teaching toward its faith and meaning.

“You shall also prepare dishes, bowls, censers, and cups, in which libations are to be offered, from purest gold.” The various vessels made for offering libations are the various distinctions of divine speech, corresponding to the differing capacities of hearers.

For the same teaching cannot suit everyone. The wise must be taught one way, the foolish another; the rich one way, the poor another; the healthy one way, the sick another; the old one way, the young another; men one way, women another; the unmarried one way, the married another; those in authority one way, those subject to authority another.

Nevertheless, all these vessels belong to the table of the tabernacle, and all are intended for offering libations, because whatever a prudent teacher says in various ways according to the diversity of his hearers is found in its entirety within the rule of sacred Scripture and arouses the hearts of the hearers to offer vows of good works to the Lord.

“And you shall place upon the table the bread of the Presence before me always.” The bread of the Presence placed continually upon the table signifies the spiritual teachers who, meditating day and night on the law of the Lord, offer nourishment from the heavenly word to all who enter the Church.

They are rightly called the bread of the Presence because the word of salvation must always be openly available to all the faithful, and the word of consolation ought never to be absent from the pious hearers in the Church.

More fully, Leviticus reports how many and what kind of loaves were to be made and how they were to be placed. The Lord says to Moses: “You shall also take fine flour and bake twelve loaves from it, each containing two-tenths. You shall set them in two rows, six in each row, upon the purest table before the Lord. You shall place upon them the clearest frankincense, so that the bread may be a memorial of the offering of the Lord. On every Sabbath they shall be changed before the Lord, received from the children of Israel as an everlasting covenant. They shall belong to Aaron and his sons, who shall eat them in a holy place” (Lev. XXIV).

The twelve loaves on the table of the tabernacle are the twelve apostles and all their followers in the Church. Since they never cease to nourish the people of God with the food of the word until the consummation of the age, the twelve loaves of the Presence never depart from the Lord’s table.

These loaves are rightly commanded to be made not from just any flour but from fine flour, because whoever ministers the word of life to others must first devote himself to the fruits of virtue, so that what he urges others to do by preaching he may commend also by doing.

The same loaves are also rightly commanded to be placed six on each side of the table, on account of the harmony of charity and fellowship. The Lord is also said to have sent his disciples to preach two by two, figuratively indicating that holy teachers never differ from one another either in their affirmation of the truth or in the affection of love.

Frankincense is placed upon the loaves as a memorial of the Lord’s offering when pure prayer is added to the pious action and teaching of the saints. Through the proper joining of these two, the memory of the sacred offering may always appear before the sight of the supreme Judge.

The loaves are rightly commanded to be changed before the Lord on every Sabbath. The loaves that had been placed on the Lord’s table for seven working days are changed for new ones on the Sabbath when the teachers of the holy Church, having completed the period of their holy labor, are rewarded with eternal rest in heaven and leave others behind them to labor at the same work of preaching the word, under the same hope of reward.

Josephus writes that the loaves were baked before the Sabbath, two and two separately. On the morning of the Sabbath they were offered upon the sacred table and placed six on each side, facing one another, with two golden dishes filled with frankincense set above them; they remained there until the following Sabbath. Then other loaves were brought in their place, while the former ones were presented to the priests. After the frankincense had been burned in the sacred fire in which all the burnt offerings were made, more frankincense was added over the other loaves.

The loaves were therefore placed upon the Lord’s table on the Sabbath with the intention that, once the Sabbath had passed, they should remain there for seven working days. When those seven days had passed, on the arrival of another Sabbath they were consumed as food by the high priest and his sons. For at the beginning of a life devoted to God, rest and eternal life are promised to us, but on the condition that we must attain to them through the labors and good works of temporal life.

## CHAPTER XII. The lampstand
You shall also make a lampstand of pure beaten gold [Col. 0150B] (Exod. XXV). The lampstand of the tabernacle, like the table, signifies the universal Church of the present age. For this reason they are before the veil behind which the ark of the covenant has been placed, because she has not yet been granted entrance into the vision of her Redeemer in heaven. But it is a table because it daily supplies heavenly food to those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, so that they may not fail in temptations. It is a lampstand because it shows the way of light to those who wander. It is both table and lampstand because, instructed in the sacred Scriptures, it has learned both to satisfy the hungry soul with good things and to supply the lamp of the word to those sitting in darkness and the shadow of death.

“Its shaft, its branches, its cups, its spherical ornaments, and its lilies proceeding from it.” The shaft of the lampstand is to be understood as the one who is the head of the Church, the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus [Col. 0150C]. Concerning his body, which we are, the Apostle says, as though of branches proceeding from the shaft: “From whom the whole body, supplied and joined together through its connections and bonds, grows with the increase of God” (Col. II). The branches proceeding from the shaft are therefore preachers who, established by the Lord, have produced a sweet sound in the world, namely, a new song. All the sons of the Church are branches, as the Prophet says to her: “Sing to the Lord a new song; his praise is from the ends of the earth” (Ps. CXLIX).

Since cups are customarily filled with wine, minds of hearers are suitably signified by them, for at the voice of the preachers they are filled with the wine of knowledge. And since the hearts of the faithful, made drunk with this same wine of inner love, strive toward God with tireless desire, it is rightly arranged that on the lampstand [Col. 0150D], after the cups, there are spherical ornaments. For a sphere rolls on every side, because the minds of the elect can neither be held back by any adversities of the world nor corrupted by prosperity, but advance toward God through holy desires in all that befalls them.

And rightly, after the branches, cups, and spherical ornaments, lilies are fashioned on the lampstand, because after the grace of preaching, after the inebriation of spiritual drink, and after the unceasing progress of holy action, there follows that verdant homeland which blossoms for holy souls, that is, for eternal flowers.

“Six branches shall come out from its sides, three from one side and three from the other.” It is indeed established that the number six, in which the world was made, signifies perfection of works. But [Col. 0151A] since it is placed in the description of the branches in such a way that it is divided twice into three, more should be said about the number three. For three branches proceed from one side of the shaft and three from the other, because before the Lord’s coming in the flesh there were teachers who, by mystical speech, indicated the faith of the holy Trinity and preached it insofar as the still inexperienced could grasp it. Hence the Psalmist says: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established, and by the breath of his mouth all their host” (Ps. XXXII).

There are now teachers who openly proclaim this same faith in the holy Trinity, so that all who belong to Christ must be consecrated by this same faith, as the Lord says to the apostles: “Go therefore, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. ult.).

Likewise, three branches come from one side [Col. 0151B] of the lampstand and three emerge from the other, because both before and after the Lord’s incarnation there were three classes of those who faithfully served the Lord in the Church: married people, the continent, and rulers. The prophet Ezekiel mystically describes their distinction when, as the time of the plagues approached, he foretold that only three men—namely Noah, Daniel, and Job—would be delivered.

In Noah, who guided the ark upon the waters, he showed the leaders of the Church; in Daniel, who strove to live continently in the royal court, the continent or virgins; and in Job, who, placed in married life, offered to all a wonderful example of patience, he showed the life of good married people.

Likewise, in the New Testament the Lord indicates the distinction among them under the figure of those who will be found in bed, in the field, and at the mill on the day of judgment: of each pair, he says that one will be taken and the other left (Matt. XXIV). Rest in bed signifies the life of the continent, activity in farming the labor of preachers, and work at the mill the labor of married people.

And because among all these classes some are to be chosen and others rejected, it is rightly said of each that “one of two will be taken and the other will be left.” Since the merit of preachers is higher among the elect than that of those who devote themselves solely to continence and not also to the work of teaching, and since the manner of life of the continent is higher than that of married people, the highest branches proceeding from the shaft on either side rightly signify those who in both Testaments, among their other virtues, devoted themselves to the study of teaching [Col. 0151C].

The lower branches proceeding from both sides of the shaft rightly signify the life of the continent devoted to God. The lowest branches, also arising from the same single stem of the one lampstand, typologically demonstrate the life of good married people, who in the time of both Testaments faithfully serve one and the same Lord.

Thus branches proceed from the shaft at various points; yet all, each bent upward in its own place and order, reach one summit, so that they may preserve an equal position for the lamps above them. For although the elect differ in degrees of merit, they are imbued with one faith in the truth and will arrive at one light of eternal truth in heaven.

And the more diligently someone clings to Christ in this life, the nearer he will be to enjoying his vision in that life [Col. 0152A].

“Three cups shaped like nuts on each branch, together with spherical ornaments and lilies; and likewise three cups shaped like a nut on the other branch, together with spherical ornaments and lilies. This shall be the work of the six branches that are to be produced from the shaft.”

That the nut is customarily used as a figure of the present Church is attested by Solomon, who speaks in the person of faithful teachers: “I went down,” he says in the Song of Songs, “to the garden of nuts, to see the fruits of the valleys” (Song VI). For just as a nut has a sweet fruit within, but cannot display it outwardly unless the hardness of its shell has been broken, so the present life of the righteous preserves the sweetness of spiritual grace in the depths of the heart. Its greatness cannot be perceived at all by those nearby until, when the dwelling of the body has been dissolved, their souls freely behold one another in heavenly light; then it will be hidden from no one how greatly each shines with the grace of the Holy Spirit and how much each is loved by the other [Col. 0152B].

Cups are fashioned on the lampstand in the form of nuts when the elect, desiring to be filled with the wine of wisdom, strive to shape themselves after the example of the righteous who came before them, whom they know to be filled with the great sweetness and love of invisible goods.

That there were three cups, spherical ornaments, and lilies on each branch signifies the three divisions of time in which the elect lived devoted to God, both before the Lord’s incarnation and afterward. There were righteous people before the Law, under the Law, and in the time of the prophets. Likewise, after the Lord’s ascension, the primitive Church was gathered from Israel. Now the Church is being gathered from the Gentiles; at the end of the world it is to be gathered from the remnant of Israel.

The first branch therefore had on one side three cups, spherical ornaments, and lilies, because among the teachers before the Lord’s incarnation there were three orders of those who thirsted for a draught of heavenly grace as for cups, ran most eagerly in the Lord’s way as spherical ornaments, and joyfully awaited the gift of future reward as the whiteness and fragrance of lilies: namely, those before the Law, under the Law, and under the prophets.

The second branch likewise had three cups, spherical ornaments, and lilies, because the continent of that period likewise had three orders of saints according to the aforesaid divisions of time: desiring spiritual drink, running in the way of the Lord’s commandments, and awaiting heavenly rewards [Col. 0152C].

The third branch similarly had three cups and spherical ornaments and three lilies, because there were many married people before the Law, many under the Law, and many in the days of the prophets who rejoiced to hear the word of the Lord, to run in his way, and to await from him the rewards of good works.

Likewise, on the other side of the shaft, the first, second, and third branches each had three cups and spherical ornaments, and also three lilies, because in the New Testament as well, among teachers, the continent, and married people devoted to God, there were three orders distinguished by time: in the primitive Church from Israel, in our gathering from the Gentiles [Col. 0153A], and in the final gathering of the remnant of Israel. All of these, each in its own time, were bound by the word of life to hasten toward the way of peace and desired to see the whiteness of perpetual light.

“But on the lampstand itself there shall be four cups shaped like nuts, together with spherical ornaments and lilies for each one: spherical ornaments beneath the two branches at three points, making six in all, proceeding from the one shaft.”

We have said that the lampstand itself—that is, the central stem of the lampstand from which the branches proceeded—signifies the Lord the Savior, from whose grace the righteous have received whatever good they possess.

Thus, when he said to his disciples in the Gospel, “I am the vine, you are the branches,” he immediately added: “As a branch cannot bear fruit by itself unless it remains in the vine, so neither can you unless you remain in me” (John XV).

Four cups are made on this lampstand because in the four books of the holy Gospel written concerning the Lord we find a taste of new wine, that is, heavenly teaching. It is not old wineskins—that is, minds still clinging to earthly desires—but only hearts renewed by the Spirit of grace that can contain it [Col. 0153B].

Spherical ornaments and lilies are fashioned together beneath each cup, because the same Lord who offered us the cup of spiritual wisdom also showed us the course of devoted action, unhindered and ready, which we ought to possess, and himself granted that we might possess it. And, so that we would not run in vain, he promised us the brightness of the heavenly homeland toward which we should strive, and by his grace opened its entrance to us.

Or, since cups, spherical ornaments, and lilies are commanded to be made beneath the two branches at three points, we may interpret this mystically as follows: among the three classes of the faithful of whom we have often spoken—namely, married people, the continent, and virgins—the Lord both opened the teaching of truth, commanded the course of good works, and promised and granted the blessing of an inheritance that is forever unfading and incorruptible.

And cups, spherical ornaments, and lilies are appropriately commanded to be beneath the branches of the lampstand, not above them, because the hearts of preachers—indeed, of all the elect—are supported by the Lord’s gifts, commandments, and promises so that they cannot fall to lower things, and are lifted up to love and seek heavenly things [Col. 0153C].

The cups, spherical ornaments, and lilies are appropriately beneath the two branches because in both Testaments, although the ceremonies differ, the same devotion to serving the Lord has been commanded to the faithful, and the same glory of the heavenly kingdom has been preserved for them.

But the fourth cup, spherical ornament, and lily, which were above all the branches near the summit of the lampstand itself, properly pertain to the Lord the Savior. He not only grants his elect knowledge of virtues, the practice of them, and their reward, but in himself, the man Christ, also displays the figure of a cup when he declared himself full of the Holy Spirit.

He presented the form of a spherical ornament when, appearing in the world, he rejoiced, without any obstacle from the surrounding circumstances, like a giant to run his course. He displayed the likeness of a lily when, rising from the dead and ascending into heaven, he was glorified with the glory that he had with the Father before the world existed [Col. 0154A].

And rightly this cup, spherical ornament, and lily rose higher than the branches, because the gifts that God the Father bestowed upon the mediator between God and human beings, the man Jesus Christ, transcend every measure of human capacity.

“For to each of us grace was given according to the measure of Christ’s gift” (Eph. IV). But in Christ himself, as the Apostle says, “all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Col. II).

It follows: “Its spherical ornaments and branches shall be from it: all of it beaten from pure gold.”

For the entire work of the lampstand—that is, both the central stem and the branches proceeding from it, with all their ornamentation—is made of gold, because the Lord himself, uniquely free from sin and in every respect distinguished by works of righteousness, appeared in the world [Col. 0154B]. His members likewise imitate that same innocence and righteousness in this present life as far as they are able, and in the future advance by clinging truly to him.

And appropriately this same gold was beaten. For beaten gold is produced by striking, because the Redeemer, who from conception and birth was perfect God and perfect man, endured the pains of suffering and thus reached the glory of the resurrection. All who wish to live devoutly in him suffer persecution; they too, as though enlarged by the beating of metal, advance through the insults of suffering and the grace of immortality.

“You shall make seven lamps and place them on the lampstand, so that they may shine opposite it” (II Tim. III).

The seven lamps are the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. They always remained in the Lord and our Redeemer, and in his members—that is, in all the elect—they have been distributed according to his will [Col. 0154C].

Thus the seven lamps are placed upon the lampstand because upon our Redeemer, the firstborn from the root of Jesse, rested “the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety”; and “the spirit of the fear of the Lord filled him” (Isa. XI). And, as he himself likewise speaks through the same prophet: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me” (Isa. LXI).

What is said, “so that they may shine opposite it,” is explained by what the prophet subsequently added: “He sent me to announce good news to the meek, to heal the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to captives and release to those in prison; to proclaim an acceptable year of the Lord and the day of vengeance of our God” (ibid.).

The snuffers also, and the vessels in which what has been snuffed is extinguished, shall be made of pure gold [Col. 0154D].

There are certain commands in the divine Scriptures that must always be observed by perpetual right, both in this life and in the future, such as: “You shall have no other gods before me” (Exod. XX), and: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your strength; and you shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Deut. VI).

There are others that are commanded to be observed throughout the whole period of this life, but whose reward is received eternally in the future life, such as the Gospel saying: “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity, so that they may receive you into eternal dwellings” (Luke XVI). Here almsgiving is to be practiced for a time; there the fruit of almsgiving is to be received forever [Col. 0155A].

There are also commands that, although carefully observed at the Lord’s command during the time of the Old Testament, are now, with the Gospel shining throughout the world, commanded to be observed in the Church not according to the letter but according to their mystical meaning. Such are the observance of the Sabbath, the rites of sacrifices, the blood of the paschal lamb, and other things of this kind. In their own time these were diligently kept by the people of God, and by them the wicks of the lampstand burned, filled with the oil of devoted faith and kindled with the fire of heavenly speech.

But when the apostles and apostolic men preached that the Lord had brought an end to these and similar observances, and that everything was to be observed more spiritually in the Church than according to the letter, then the wicks of the lampstand were trimmed [Col. 0155B], so that, restored, they might shine more brightly, since, understood more sublimely through the Spirit, they offered the light of saving doctrine to the holy Church.

The snuffers, therefore, and the vessels in which what has been snuffed is extinguished, are made of pure gold, because the divine words by which the cessation of the legal ceremonies is proclaimed, and the hearts of those in whom the figurative shadow of the Law reaches its end, have been illumined by the grace of God, so that the succeeding truth of the Gospel might shine more clearly upon the world.

Likewise, when mortal life has ended and immortal life has taken its place, most of the works or gifts of light that we now use will cease, so that the rewards of eternal light may follow in the presence of the divine vision. Those testimonies of Scripture that affirm that these things will come are therefore golden snuffers, because they are themselves outstanding signs of future glory [Col. 0155C].

The vessels in which what has been snuffed is extinguished are bodies and hearts, surely, of all the righteous, which are immortal. They are therefore most appropriately compared with gold, for in them this eagerly desired transformation will take place, so that after temporal benefits from God they may arrive at eternal ones.

“The entire weight of the lampstand with all its vessels shall be one talent of purest gold.”

The entire weight of the lampstand with all its vessels is the whole body of Christ, with our head, the mediator between God and human beings, together with all his elect, from the greatest to the least—from him “than whom no one is greater among those born of women” to those of whom he says: “See that you do not despise one of these little ones who believe in me.”

All of these, although differing in degrees, ages, sexes, conditions, abilities, and times, cling in their proper time and place to the one author and giver of perpetual light, fixed by the root of their minds to the golden lampstand, so that they may become participants in that same light [Col. 0155D].

This lampstand is rightly said to have one talent of purest gold. For a talent is a full and perfect weight, because “the Lord is just in all his ways.” He who grants his grace to the faithful in this life so that they may act well himself returns in the future life the crown of righteousness for their good works.

In contrast, the prophet Zechariah describes iniquity sitting upon a talent of lead (Zech. V), because to the wicked also, in the same just judgment, he restores according to their deeds: “For you will repay each one according to his works,” he says (Ps. LXI).

Both lead and gold, however, have the measure of a talent, because both in condemning the wicked and in saving and crowning the elect, the judgment of our Creator is just.

“Look and make it according to the pattern that was shown to you on the mountain.”

The mystery of this command is readily apparent from what has been explained above. The pattern of the lampstand that he was to make was shown to Moses on the mountain because, in the height of inner contemplation, he learned openly the manifold mysteries of Christ and the Church. Yet he could not set them forth openly to the people whom he was instructing; rather, he signified them figuratively through the form and work of the lampstand and its vessels, until the Lord and our Redeemer himself came in the flesh and, through the grace of the Holy Spirit given to his Church, disclosed the inner meaning of that figure [Col. 0156B].

The tabernacle that Moses made for the Lord in the wilderness, like the temple that Solomon made in Jerusalem, signifies the state of the holy universal Church, part of which already reigns with the Lord in heaven, while part still journeys away from the Lord in the present life, as its members depart and are succeeded by others.

In the construction of both houses there is normally this principal difference in their figures: the tabernacle signifies the present building of the Church, in which it is daily exercised through labors; the temple signifies the rest of the future life, which is completed by the daily reception of souls departing from this world after their labors.

For Moses established the tabernacle while he and the people of God were still on the journey by which they were proceeding toward the promised land [Col. 0156C]; but Solomon built the temple after he had already obtained the promised land and possessed the kingdom there.

Moses built the tabernacle in the wilderness; Solomon built the temple in Jerusalem, which is interpreted as “vision of peace.” For here the Church is built amid the labor and hardship of a passing life, in thirst and hunger for the everlasting kingdom; there it is brought to completion in the vision and possession of true peace.

Hence it is rightly said in the construction of the temple that “the hammer and the axe and every iron tool were not heard in it while it was being built.” All the stones and timbers had been prepared outside Jerusalem and suitably fitted for their ordered placement; there each was readily and certainly set in its proper place, either joined with mortar or fastened with nails.

For in the peace of heavenly blessedness our faith is not to be tested by tribulations nor our life proved by trials; rather, what in the present age had been disciplined and regularly fitted for the heavenly dwelling is there to be joined together before the sight of its Creator and King by the bond and ties of mutual love, so that it may never be dissolved [Col. 0156D].

The figure of the two sanctuaries may also be distinguished generally in this way: the work of the tabernacle signifies the time of the synagogue, that is, of the ancient people of God; the work of the temple signifies the Church, that is, the multitude of the elect who came to faith after the Lord’s incarnation.

Thus Moses completed the tabernacle with only the Hebrew people, whereas Solomon completed the temple with the gathered multitude of proselytes, aided by the king of Tyre and his craftsmen, who were neither Jews by birth nor by profession [Col. 0157A].

For it is certain that among the earlier people of God, teachers came only from their own nation. But the first leaders of the Church were indeed Hebrews; soon, however, as she grew and spread throughout the world, builders of her structure also arose from the Gentiles. Thus the evangelist Luke himself, and Timothy and Titus, apostolic men, reached her episcopal office through the calling of the Gentiles.

But if we examine the building of both houses more carefully, it mystically describes the state of the entire present Church. From the beginning of the world’s creation until the last elect person who will be born at the end of the age, she never ceases to be built; and with a marvelous variety of figures it portrays also the glory of the future life, which she now enjoys in part but will enjoy eternally in all her members after the end of this age [Col. 0157B].

Therefore, with the Lord’s help, we are about to say something about the tabernacle. First invoking him, we humbly ask him to open the eyes of our hearts, so that we may be able to contemplate “wondrous things from his law,” and understand that in the beauty of precious metals and garments an adornment of manners shining with faith and devotion has been commended to us.

For otherwise that apostolic saying could not apply to us in which he says: “You are the temple of the living God, as God says: ‘I will dwell in them and walk among them’” (I Cor. VI). And John heard “a loud voice from the throne saying: ‘Behold, the tabernacle of God is with human beings, and he will dwell with them’” (Rev. XXI) [Col. 0157C].

Let us imitate the material adornment of either tabernacle or temple by the cultivation of a devout and pure heart and body. But let us also speak more precisely about its spiritual meaning. First, let us briefly examine the material wording of the text.

The tabernacle was a house consecrated to the Lord, thirty cubits long, ten cubits wide, and likewise ten cubits high, with a roof equal throughout, in the manner in which houses are customarily built in Egypt and Palestine.

Its three walls—the southern, northern, and western—were joined together from wooden boards, gilded on both sides. On the eastern side there was a single bar, where the entrance was; it extended through the middle of the boards from corner to corner, that is, from the uppermost point of this wall to the summit of the other wall. The curtains of the tabernacle and its roof rested upon it, and the covering was suspended from five columns [Col. 0157D].

The house was covered above and on every side with curtains woven with marvelous variety; this was properly called the tabernacle. It was also covered on every side with goats’ hair cloths reaching to the ground. There was also another covering for the roof made of red-dyed rams’ skins, and above this again another covering of blue skins.

There was also a veil decorated with embroidered work and hung upon four columns, separating the sanctuary from the Holy of Holies. Inside it was placed the ark of the covenant, and opposite the ark, outside the veil, the altar of incense [Col. 0158A].

In the middle of the sanctuary itself was the lampstand on the southern side; the table stood on the northern side. The altar of burnt offerings was outside, before the entrance to the sanctuary, and the bronze basin stood between this altar and the tabernacle. Around everything was the court of the tabernacle, one hundred cubits long and fifty cubits wide.

Having briefly set these matters forth for purposes of clarification, let us examine the actual words of the historical account, so that through them we may reach more deeply and clearly the allegorical meaning. When the Lord, with Moses staying with him on Mount Sinai for forty days and nights, was giving him the ceremonies of the Law and the rule of life, he said among other things:

## CHAPTER XIII. On the construction of the tabernacle: that is, the ten curtains, the eleven goats’ hair cloths, and the third and fourth coverings of skins [Col. 0158B]

“But you shall make the tabernacle as follows: You shall make ten curtains of twisted linen, and of blue, purple, and twice-dyed scarlet, varied with embroidered work” (Exod. XXVI).

The Lord’s tabernacle is made from curtains varied by a diversity of colors because the holy universal Church is built from many persons of the elect, from many churches throughout the world, and from various flowers of virtues.

All its perfection is contained in the number ten, because although the Church is spread throughout the world among various nations, tribes, peoples, and languages, she subsists wholly in the love of God and neighbor, which is included in the Decalogue of the Law.

Nor can anyone truly reach membership in the Church unless he has learned, with an undivided heart, to love both the one through whom the Church is built and those in whom it is built—that is, God and his elect [Col. 0158C].

The varied beauty of the colors by which these curtains are distinguished is the grace of the various virtues, through which the holy Church, composed by a marvelous and wholly heavenly art, shines before the sight of her Creator.

Thus linen, which indeed grows from the earth but, once extracted from the earth, customarily loses its grassy color through long labor of drying, beating, cleansing, boiling, and spinning, and takes on a white color, signifies bodies shining with the beauty of chastity.

These bodies are born amid the allurements of the flesh, but through the great labor of continence they sweat out, as it were, their natural moisture and attain the beauty of purity worthy of God through diligent perseverance in fasts and vigils, prayers and reading, patience and humility [Col. 0158D].

Of such people the apostolic saying may rightly be spoken: “Do you not know that your bodies are a temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you?” (I Cor. VI).

This linen is twisted into the curtains of the tabernacle because we gird not only the loins of the flesh but, as Peter admonishes, “the loins of our mind in sobriety” (I Pet. I). Thus we restrain both the flesh from wanton movements and the heart from seductive thoughts.

Blue, since it imitates the appearance of air and sky, signifies the minds of the elect, seeking heavenly things with every hope and desire. Commending to us the mystery of this color, the Apostle says: “If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God” (Col. III) [Col. 0159A].

Purple, because it displays the color of blood—and true purple is also dyed with the blood of shellfish—signifies the devoted hearts of those who can say with the Apostle: “I am ready not only to be bound but also to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus” (Acts XXI). And with the Prophet to the Lord: “For your sake we are put to death all day long; we are regarded as sheep for slaughter” (Ps. XLIII).

Scarlet, because it has the appearance of fire, is rightly compared with the most ardent love of the saints. Hence some of them, having conceived this love in the presence of and accompanied by the Lord, said: “Was not our heart burning within us when he spoke to us on the way and opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke ult.).

In contrast, concerning the wicked it is said: “Because iniquity has abounded, the love of many will grow cold” (Matt. XXIV) [Col. 0159B].

This scarlet is as though dyed twice when it flames with love of God and neighbor: when we love him with all our heart, all our soul, and all our strength, and love the other as ourselves.

Thus, in these four colors of the curtains, four forms of the elect’s righteousness are expressed:

- In twisted linen, the flesh shining through chastity.
- In blue, the mind desiring heavenly things.
- In purple, the flesh subjected to sufferings.
- In twice-dyed scarlet, the mind resplendent with love of God and neighbor amid sufferings.

The length of each curtain shall be twenty-eight cubits, and its width shall be four cubits. In the length of the curtains is expressed the holy Church’s patience, long-suffering over time; in their width, the breadth of charity. This width was appropriately four cubits, because there are four books of the Gospels, in which we are taught by the examples and words of our Lord and Redeemer how that same charity is to be maintained. There are also four virtues in the exercise of which this same charity must be practiced: temperance, fortitude, justice, and prudence. That is: charity toward God is to be kept incorrupt and whole, which belongs to temperance; it must not be broken by any misfortune, which belongs to fortitude; it must serve no other, which belongs to justice; and it must remain watchful in discerning matters, lest deceit or fraud gradually creep in, which belongs to prudence.

The length of the curtains was twenty-eight cubits, which is the number four multiplied by seven. By the number seven, because of the Sabbath day, the eternal rest of the saints is usually signified. Thus the length of the curtains extends to four times seven cubits, because through faith and the keeping of evangelical teaching—through which the exercises of the spiritual virtues we have mentioned are practiced—the long-suffering power of the holy Church advances toward eternal rest. There is also another mystery in the number twenty-eight, likewise pertaining to the number seven. For if you wish to count in full order all the numbers from one through seven, you will complete twenty-eight: one, two, three, four, five, six, and seven make twenty-eight. Since, therefore, the twenty-eighth is found among the parts of the number seven, the length of the curtains is rightly contained in it, because the faith and patience of the saints, distinguished by a variety of virtues, in everything they do and suffer await not human glory or favor but the blessedness of heavenly rest.

For this reason the psalm bearing this number is entitled “On the completion of the tabernacle,” and it is clear that the whole of it was sung concerning the perfection of the holy Church—especially because it says: “Worship the Lord in his holy court.” And again: “And in his temple all shall say, ‘Glory’” (Psalm 28). It is fitting, therefore, that Psalm 28 should be inscribed “On the completion of the tabernacle,” because the perfection of the Church journeying through this world consists in advancing through faith and good works toward the rest of the world to come.

Well, then, it follows: “All the tents shall be made of one measure.” Although the curtains differed from one another in their varied decoration, all were nevertheless regulated by one measure of length and width. For although the elect possess different gifts according to the grace given them, there is only one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all.

“Five curtains shall be joined to one another, and another five shall be joined together in a similar manner.” We can also discuss the number of curtains—twice five—in relation to this statement, understanding them as signifying the followers of God in both Testaments. The first five, which protected or formed the front and foremost part of the tabernacle, represented the ancient people of God, who fulfilled the decrees of the Law according to its literal sense in the sacrament of circumcision and sacrifices, and in the observance of its various ceremonies. The following five curtains, which covered or formed the rear of the tabernacle, represent us, who were born after the Lord’s coming in the flesh and, with him revealing and granting them, keep the books and sacraments of the Law spiritually.

Nevertheless, at the time when the tabernacle was erected, all the curtains were joined together, because when the whole beauty of the Catholic Church is considered from the beginning to the end of the age, it certainly adorns God’s tabernacle like one interconnection of ten curtains.

“You shall make loops of blue on the sides and upper edges of the curtains, so that they may be joined to one another.” We said that blue, being the color of the air or sky, is appropriate to signify heavenly goods. Thus the curtains are joined to one another by blue loops when the single hope of heavenly blessedness unites all the hearts of the elect throughout the world in one and the same devotion.

These loops are appropriately so called because they were to be made not only on the sides of the curtains but also on their upper edges—that is, at the extreme ends of their corners. For not only do the life and activity of the saints advance toward perfection along the common path of right intention; even the beginning of good conduct, which is undertaken through the confession of faith and the reception of the heavenly sacraments, is in no way different among them, but is joined by the grace of all truth in equal and undivided fellowship. We also share the end of temporal life with the assurance of one and the same hope, when we close our eyes in death confident that, having first received the viaticum of the heavenly mystery, we shall soon be found in the true life and shall remain there forever.

“Each curtain shall have fifty loops inserted on both sides, so that loop may meet loop and one may be fitted to the other.” We read that the fiftieth year in the Law was called the Jubilee—that is, the year of release, or the year of initiation—during which the whole people rested from all labor on the land and all debts were to be discharged. In the New Testament we know that the grace of the Holy Spirit came upon the apostles on the day of Pentecost, that is, the fiftieth day after the Lord’s resurrection, and consecrated by its coming the beginnings of the nascent Church. Hence it is evident that this number can rightly signify either the grace of the Holy Spirit or the future joy of blessedness, to which one arrives through the gift of that same Spirit and in the possession of which alone one truly rests and rejoices.

The curtains appropriately had fifty loops by which they were joined to one another, because it is only through the gift of the Holy Spirit that the elect are brought to unite with one another in the fellowship of peace, which is the bond of perfection. Nothing other than the hope and remembrance of the future fellowship and peace makes the servants of Christ, separated in this life by times or places, concordant in one devotion.

It is also rightly said that the curtains had loops on both sides, so that each curtain might embrace, as though with arms extended on either side, the curtains nearest to it on both sides. All the faithful must likewise embrace with the outstretched arms of sincere devotion both those who preceded us in Christ and those who followed us; both those who instructed us in Christ and those whom, by Christ’s gift, we instruct. We must honor them all with one affection in Christ.

For each curtain extended upward by means of the supports of the boards, and, with its ornamentation varied in the flowers of its design, shone within at the heights, so that it did not abandon the curtains that were carried upward with it or that shone when placed on high. In their likeness, we are taught both to assist the faithful who are progressing with us in God’s service by admonitions and examples, and to treat with due reverence those who have become our companions in whatever virtue we have been able to advance.

Thus “loop shall meet loop, so that one may be fitted to the other,” when the righteous are bound to one another by harmonious and equal excellence of virtue.

“You shall make fifty golden rings, by which the curtains are to be joined, so that they may become one tabernacle.” This passage is explained more fully below, where it says: “He cast fifty golden rings, which clasp the loops of the curtains, so that one tabernacle might be made.” The number fifty therefore signifies true rest in the Holy Spirit. And because a circle appears to have neither beginning nor end, while gold, on account of its brightness, is more precious than other metals, what is expressed by the fifty golden rings except perpetual brightness and bright perpetuity, the fullness of rest?

The rings clasp the loops of the curtains so that one tabernacle may be made from all of them, when the glory of the heavenly kingdom graciously pours itself into the pure minds of the faithful, so that by such a bond of saving inspiration the Church of Christ may be perfected as one people from both peoples—or rather, from all the elect.

“You shall also make eleven coverings of goats’ hair, to cover the roof of the tabernacle.” This passage is repeated later in the following form: “He also made eleven coverings of goats’ hair, to cover the roof of the tabernacle.”

The coverings, then, by which the tabernacle is covered, are the rulers of the holy Church, by whose industry and labor the beauty of that same Church is protected and guarded with unceasing care: so that the life and faith of the elect may not be corrupted by heretical seduction, disgraced by the wickedness of false Catholics, defiled by the filth of tempting vices, or driven into sorrow by lack of temporal support. The more attentively they gird themselves to endure or repel the violence of the temptations that rush upon them, the greater the freedom they grant their subjects to serve the Lord. They are like coverings that allow the curtains to shine within, while they themselves endure outside the affliction of the storm.

These same coverings are rightly reported to be made of goats’ hair and to number eleven, because the higher the holy preachers are in merit, the humbler they ought to be in spirit, according to the saying of the wise man: “The greater you are, humble yourself in all things” (Ecclesiasticus 3). The eleven, since they go beyond ten but do not reach twelve, the apostolic number, signify transgression of the Law’s Decalogue. Haircloth is also the garment of penitents, as the Psalmist testifies when he says: “But when they troubled me, I clothed myself in sackcloth” (Psalm 35)—that is, I assumed the garment of penitence and humility, by which I might either endure the fury of my persecutors more lightly and calmly, or even appease it.

For if goats, or the hair or skins of goats, always signified the stench of sinners and never at times the humility of penitents, the animal would certainly not be counted among the clean, nor would it be said in praise of the bride: “Your hair is like a flock of goats” (Song of Songs 4). The coverings, therefore, which signify the holy preachers, are both of goats’ hair and eleven in number, because the more diligently they purify their hearts by faith, the more things they find in themselves for which to reproach themselves. Hence they humbly confess: “We all offend in many things.” And: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1).

Yet the perfection of their hearts is mystically declared by the words that follow: “The length of one covering shall be thirty cubits, and its width four.” Here you have, for the length, not the number eleven but ten, multiplied by three. This plainly signifies the virtue of those who perfect the Decalogue of the Law in faith in the Holy Trinity, which works through love. In this perfection, at least in the present life, nothing higher can exist.

You also have four cubits for the width, by which we said that the breadth of sincere charity is signified—that charity which is commended and given to us in the Gospel through Jesus Christ. Thus eleven coverings cover the roof of the tabernacle, made of goats’ hair, thirty cubits in length and four in width, because those supreme preachers who protect the life of the faithful by their exhortations and intercessions, by daily solicitude, vigils, fasts, and their own self-denial, humbly contemplating themselves, confess that they are sinners in view of the excellence of heavenly purity. Yet, so far as the measure of human perfection is concerned, they appear clean and exalted among human beings.

“There shall be one measure for all the coverings. Of these you shall join five separately, and six shall be joined to one another, so that you shall double the sixth covering at the front of the roof.” There shall be one measure for all the coverings because there is one faith in which the whole Church is saved, and one and the same life toward which it hastens—eternal life. Hence those who entered the Lord’s vineyard to labor at different times are all rewarded with the same denarius (Matthew 20).

The division of the coverings into five and six can therefore be understood in accordance with what we explained above concerning the division of the curtains into five and five, since they signify the teachers of both Testaments. The five coverings are aptly compared with the teachers of the ancient people of God, either because they preached the mysteries of the Mosaic Law while also proclaiming the secrets of the Gospel, or because they lived their life in the five ages of the world.

In the six coverings, the teachers of the New Testament can suitably be understood, because they take up spiritually, for the assistance and example of their preaching, everything that divine Scripture reports as done or said in the six ages of the world. They openly declare to their hearers that the Lord’s Passion, through which the world was redeemed on the sixth day of the week, must be believed and confessed, and they affirm that people can be saved only through its mystery. Hence it is rightly commanded that the sixth covering be doubled at the front of the roof, in reference to the confession and imitation of that same Passion of the Lord.

According to the literal sense, the front of the roof means the entrance to the tabernacle, where, as we briefly said above, not boards but pillars were placed, with a bar stretched from one corner of the boards to the other. Therefore, in the actual construction, a double protection of coverings was more necessary there, where the solid strength of the wall was lacking.

Mystically, however, the sixth covering is doubled at the front of the roof when all who enter the holy Church are initiated into the faith and sacraments of the Lord’s Passion in such a way that they understand they must always live in imitation of it as well.

“You shall make fifty loops on the edge of one covering, so that it may be joined to another; and fifty loops on the edge of the other covering, so that it may be joined to the other; and fifty golden clasps, by which the loops shall be joined, so that one covering may be made from all.”

These things may also be understood here as we explained them above concerning the curtains: namely, that remembrance of heavenly rest, which is usually expressed by the number fifty, unites the hearts of the saints in the bond of peace.

Or, if you prefer to hear something new, the coverings signify the humility of exalted men, because they prefer to remember their sins rather than proclaim their virtues; they are more deeply pierced with remorse over virtues they have not yet attained than eager to boast about those they have already attained. The humility of their remorse may therefore be signified by the number fifty, whether of the loops or of the clasps. For the fiftieth is the psalm of penitence, and rightly so: the gift of penitence is granted only by the Holy Spirit’s generosity, and the gift of forgiveness is bestowed upon penitents only through the administration of that same grace of the Holy Spirit.

It is also fitting that fifty loops or clasps join the coverings to one another, because no virtue binds the faithful into one bond of charity more than humility. For the more fully someone recognizes that he is weak, the more earnestly he seeks the help of his neighbor by which he may be strengthened.

The clasps are rightly bronze, because bronze is known to be a highly resonant metal: the humble conscience of the righteous has, as it were, a great voice before God. Hence that poor man David, when he was distressed—not crying out in the ears of human beings but pouring out his prayer before the Lord—said: “Lord, hear my prayer, and let my cry come to you” (Psalm 102).

“But what remains over from the coverings prepared for the roof—that is, the one covering which is extra—with half of it you shall cover the rear of the tabernacle; and one cubit shall hang down on one side and another on the other side, from what is extra in the length of the coverings, protecting both sides of the tabernacle.”

For this to be understood more fully, it is necessary to discuss at somewhat greater length the entire arrangement of the tabernacle itself. We said that the walls of the tabernacle, which consisted of boards and pillars, were thirty cubits long, ten cubits wide, and likewise ten cubits high.

If, then, someone wished to encircle a house across its width with a cord—for example, from the base of one board on the southern side to the base of the board opposite it on the northern side—it is clear that the cord would have to be thirty cubits long: ten cubits for its ascent along the southern wall, another ten cubits for the level stretch across the top between the walls, and a third ten cubits for its descent along the northern wall.

Likewise, if you wished to extend a cord along the length of the house—that is, upward from the bases of the pillars, along the entire length of the house to the western wall, and then downward to its bases—that cord would be fifty cubits long: ten cubits of ascent beside the pillars, thirty cubits of level stretch along the length of the house, and ten cubits again of descent beside the boards of the western wall.

Having considered these things, let us examine the measurements of the curtains with which the house was to be covered, and how they could correspond to the measurements just mentioned. There were ten curtains, each twenty-eight cubits long and four cubits wide. Joined together and made into one, they filled the tabernacle across its width to forty cubits.

Suspend, then, curtains each twenty-eight cubits long, and place them in a house whose measurement across is thirty cubits. You will see that the curtains have ten cubits of level stretch between the walls, while the ascent or descent beside the walls measures nine cubits. Thus the upper edge of the curtains cannot touch the ground; it remains one cubit above it.

You will also see that along the length of the house the curtains have thirty cubits of level stretch, while the ascent or descent on the eastern and western sides of the house measures five cubits. Therefore this lateral upper edge of the curtains does not reach all the way to the ground but remains five cubits above it. It is consequently necessary that the five cubits of curtain remaining after the walls end be brought together on both the eastern and western sides and joined to one another, so that the curtains cover the house on every side except for one cubit above the ground.

So much for the curtains. The coverings, however, had thirty cubits in length and four in width. Since eleven were joined to one another along their sides, they filled forty-four cubits. Place these in the house as well. Since the length of the coverings corresponds to the cord with which you measured the house across, their upper edge reaches all the way to the ground. They have ten cubits of level stretch between the walls and likewise ten cubits of ascent or descent on either side.

This is what Scripture means when it says that one cubit would hang down on one side and another on the other side, from what was extra in the length of the coverings, protecting both sides of the tabernacle. For it properly calls “tabernacle” the actual construction or joining of the curtains, which the coverings exceeded by one cubit on the southern side of the house and by another on the northern side. Thus the coverings reached the ground, because they were thirty cubits long, while the curtains had two cubits less.

Along the length of the house, the measurement of the coverings extended to forty-four cubits: thirty cubits of level stretch from the front of the house to the upper edge of the boards on the western side, with seven cubits hanging down at the front of the house and likewise seven hanging down on the western side. Thus, on the western side, the measurement of the coverings exceeded that of the curtains by two cubits. The curtains, coming from above, as we mentioned earlier, covered five cubits of that western wall and left three untouched.

This is what is now meant by the words: “What remains over from the coverings prepared for the roof—that is, the one covering which is extra—you shall cover half of it over the rear of the tabernacle.” Half of a covering’s width is two cubits, and by this half the rear of the tabernacle was covered—that is, the curtains properly called the tabernacle—because the last covering, extending downward, passed beyond them by two cubits, as we have said.

Likewise, the coverings coming from above covered only seven cubits of the western wall. Yet the remaining three cubits, which were left exposed down to the ground, were not laid open to the violence of the weather. Rather, when the coverings of seven cubits on each side, which remained after the walls ended, were drawn together, the rear of the house was firmly covered down to the ground.

Nor could these coverings merely reach one another and touch in the middle of the wall like the curtains. Since they were seven cubits wide, they exceeded the middle of the wall by two cubits on each side, and were joined by being placed over one another. We think that the same should be understood in every respect of the eastern side of the house. Hence it was commanded above that the sixth covering be doubled at the front of the roof.

We have briefly explained this exceedingly difficult matter as we seemed to understand it, ready to learn a more accurate account if anyone should wish to teach us better. In all these things, however, the clear meaning of your allegory is evident.

The coverings protected the curtains above and below and on every side; and, so that the curtains might shine within with the free display of their beauty, the coverings made them immune outside from every assault of storms, rains, and scorching heat. For the perfect overseers of the holy Church customarily watch over the life of the faithful entrusted to them with such diligent care that they lack neither bodily support nor the aids of spiritual life.

The coverings repel the rains, withstand the storms, keep away the heat of the sun, and strongly encircle everything that attacks from outside, so that the beauty of the curtains may remain undefiled within. This occurs when Augustine dispels the poisons of heretics, whatever might disturb the faith; when Gregory explains the temptations of the ancient enemy that assail good morals; when Cyprian strengthens the weak with pious exhortations, lest they fall in martyrdom; and when other venerable bishops and teachers drive far away whatever temptations might disturb the Church and carefully investigate what may be beneficial for its salvation.

In this way, the religious conduct of the faithful is made secure on every side, so that with a free heart they may pursue virtue, shine brightly in action before their Creator, and direct the eye of the mind toward contemplation of him.

But because among the holy preachers those are most worthy of honor who, besides serving the ministry of preaching and the governance of peoples, also pour out their blood for Christ, it is rightly added: “You shall make another covering for the roof, of skins of rams dyed red.”

Under the name “rams,” holy teachers are sometimes understood, because they are leaders of those who follow the Lord’s flock. Hence the Psalmist beautifully says: “Bring to the Lord, O sons of God; bring to the Lord the sons of rams” (Psalm 28). This plainly means: Bring to the Lord, all angels of God to whom the care of this office has been entrusted; bring to the Lord in the heavens the spirits of the faithful who, by imitation of life and faith, have deserved to become sons of the blessed apostles.

The dyed skins of rams cover the Lord’s tabernacle and defend it from the violence of the weather when holy preachers, by the example of their passion and endurance, strengthen the hearts of the weak, so that they may not fail under the pressures of tribulation.

And because sacred virginity holds an eminent place among the principal members of Christ and the Church, after the varied beauty of the curtains, after the protections of the saints’ haircloth, and after the dyed skins of the rams, there is appropriately added: “And above this, another covering of blue skins.”

Blue is the color of heaven, while a skin is a part and sign of a dead animal. What, then, is signified by blue skins except the virtue of those who, having thoroughly mortified all the enticements of carnal desire, lead, in a certain manner, a heavenly life on earth? Placed among human beings, they imitate rather the purity of angels, and while still held in mortal flesh they strive to anticipate what is promised at the time of future immortality to all the elect who “neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are equal to the angels of God” (Luke 20).

Hence a very great reward rightly remains for so great a virtue, because, as the prophet testifies:

> “Thus says the Lord to the eunuchs who have kept my Sabbaths, chosen the things I willed, and held fast my covenant: I will give them in my house and within my walls a place and a name better than sons and daughters; I will give them an everlasting name that shall not be taken away” (Isaiah 56).

The blue skins therefore rightly occupy the highest place in the house of God; and the heavenly color has received a dwelling near heaven, so that the virginal choirs, who will follow the Lamb in a special nearness of both mind and body, are signified as destined to sing his praises in hymns.

It is rightly said concerning the curtains and coverings that, although they were placed above, they hung down toward the ground, even though the curtains could not reach all the way to the ground. The pillars and boards of the tabernacle, although they were erected upward, nevertheless had bases set upon the ground on which they stood. But of the dyed and blue skins it is said that they covered the roof above. That they were bent down toward the ground is not added, because the other forms of virtue seem to have something in common with those who are still held upon the earth. The contest of martyrdom and the beauty of virginity dedicated to God, however, suspended as it were above the lowest and earthly things, are especially joined to the citizens of heaven.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the boards of the tabernacle, their placement, their bars, and their rings

“You shall also make the boards of the tabernacle standing upright, of sethim wood, each ten cubits long and one and a half cubits wide.”

The sethim wood of which the tabernacle was made is naturally imperishable, exceptionally white and light. It differs from the white thorn chiefly in size, though otherwise it is not greatly different. Hence Jerome sometimes interpreted *sethim* simply as “thorns” in the *Book of Hebrew Names* and in his other works. For example, *Abel sethim* means “mourning of thorns.”

This kind of wood is not easily found except in the deserts of Arabia, where the tabernacle was built. Therefore the Greek or Latin translators could not give it another name besides the Hebrew, since it was unknown among them, although some, wishing to express its natural quality, translated it as “imperishable wood.”

The boards of the tabernacle therefore signify the apostles and their successors, through whose preaching the Church has been spread throughout the world. The width of the boards is the expansion of faith and of the sacraments, which were previously hidden within one Israelite people but, through the ministry of these men, reached the fullness of the whole world.

The width of the boards can also rightly be understood as the expansion of the hearts of the saints, by which they habitually despise the world and are sublimely kindled to desire heavenly things; by which they rejoice in loving not only their friends in God but also their enemies for God’s sake.

According to the Savior’s teaching, thorns are the cares of this age and its deceptive riches and pleasures; the stings of sins are also not inappropriately likened to thorns. Hence it is written: “Thorns grow in the hands of the drunkard” (Proverbs 26)—that is, sins in the works of the foolish.

Because the holy preachers have therefore striven both to cleanse themselves from the stings of vices and to strip themselves of all worldly cares and pleasures, so that with a free mind they might expand in the love of God and neighbor and travel far and wide to preach the word, it is rightly said that the boards of the tabernacle were made of thornwood.

The length of the boards is their height, which was ten cubits, because the holy teachers advance toward perfection through observance of the Decalogue of the Law. They labor in Christ’s vineyard in expectation of the daily denarius—that is, they devote themselves to the word of teaching with the intention of restoring in themselves, by the Creator’s gift, the image of their Creator and King, which they lost through Adam’s sin, and of recovering by right living what they had lost through sin.

The king’s name and image are customarily contained in a denarius. This too is fittingly related to the state of our future blessedness, which is perfected in true love of God and neighbor, since the denarius receives its name from the fact that it is completed by ten coins.

God is often signified by the number three, because of the Trinity that he is; the human being by the number seven, because the body consists of the four well-known elements, while the soul—that is, the substance of the inner person—is usually comprehended in Scripture by a threefold distinction. Hence we are commanded to love God “with all our heart, with all our soul, and with all our strength” (Deuteronomy 6).

The boards, then, by which the whole tabernacle is held together when they are erected and standing, appropriately have a height of ten cubits, because the teachers and rulers of the holy Church serve God with the intention of deserving to see him forever, immortal and blessed, in both soul and body.

That the boards had a width of one and a half cubits shows, by the full cubit, the perfection of good works, and by the remaining half-cubit, the beginning of divine knowledge. For meanwhile we know God through faith, but we hope for full knowledge of him in the future, as our God and Lord Jesus Christ himself says: “If you remain in my word, you will truly be my disciples, and you will know the truth” (John 8). Again, to the Father he says: “This is eternal life: that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent.”

The elect therefore possess in this life a full cubit of good works. But they possess only part of the cubit of blessed reward, insofar as they can anticipate by heavenly desires the joys of the everlasting kingdom and the presence of their Creator. They are made blessed by the completion of this cubit when the promise is fulfilled that he made to the whole people of the elect at the end, saying: “I will deliver him and glorify him; I will fill him with length of days, and I will show him my salvation” (Psalm 90).

On the sides of the boards there shall be joints, by which one board may be connected to another; and in this manner all the boards shall be prepared. The joints on the sides of the boards signify the virtue of humility in the minds of the righteous, by which they are joined to one another most especially in fraternal charity. For when each of them, with a contrite and humbled heart, prepares within himself a dwelling-place for love of his neighbors, and presents himself, by the merit of piety and devotion, to his brethren as one to be loved, then, as it were, all the boards of the tabernacle are joined to one another through the bond of their joints.

When the tabernacle has been erected and regularly arranged beforehand, the framework of the boards in the form of joints cannot be seen; yet how great a strength has united the boards to one another is shown by the firm stability of the unshaken wall. For the humility of the hearts of the saints, by which they are bound together with one another, cannot be seen by people outwardly; but what it accomplishes within is openly evident to all from the most peaceful condition of the holy Church.

That he commands two joints to be made in each board—that is, on both sides of them—can figuratively be understood in two ways: namely, that in prosperity as well as in adversity we should preserve inviolate the rights of charity toward our brethren.

There shall be twenty on the southern side, which faces south; and you shall cast forty silver bases for them, so that two bases may be placed beneath each board, one at each of its two corners.

The length of the tabernacle is not expressly stated, but it is indicated by the fact that its walls were composed of twenty boards, each of which is said to have had a width of one and a half cubits. For twenty cubits and twenty half-cubits together make a total of thirty cubits, which Josephus likewise writes to have been the length of the tabernacle.

And this number suitably encompasses the length of the tabernacle, because there are three virtues in which the whole perfection of the holy Church principally consists—faith, hope, and charity. These are multiplied by ten so that the number thirty may be completed, when good works of the mind are joined to the virtues contained in the Decalogue of the Law. Thus no one should think that faith, hope, and love of God can suffice for him without the performance of works.

But the number of the boards, twenty, also contains a mystery of the great perfection of the saints. For four times five makes twenty; and since the Mosaic Law is contained in five books, while the grace and truth of the New Testament are contained in the four volumes of the holy Gospels, the holy teachers are appropriately expressed by the number twenty. For, with wondrous agreement concerning the truth, they both reveal in the Gospel the mysteries of the Law that had been disclosed and completed, and declare that the sacraments of the Gospel had been prefigured in the Law.

The bases, moreover, on which the boards were supported are the words and books of the Law and the prophets, by which the apostles and Evangelists proved that what they wrote and preached was true and divine. Hence the statement so often repeated in the Gospel: “Then was fulfilled what was spoken through the prophet”; and: “All this happened so that the Scriptures of the prophets might be fulfilled.” The Apostle Peter also, bearing witness concerning the Lord, added: “And we have the prophetic word made more certain, to which you do well to attend” (II Peter 1).

Two bases are properly placed beneath each board, so that the agreement of prophetic testimony may be shown in everything the apostles said. Or, more precisely, two fixed bases are placed beneath each board at its two corners, so that, with its corners well supported, the whole board may stand upright and without deviation. For in the prophetic writings both the beginning and the end of every evangelical and apostolic word are found to have been foreshadowed.

The same bases were rightly made of silver, because of the brightness of the heavenly word. “The sayings of the Lord are pure sayings, silver tested by fire on the earth.”

On the second side of the tabernacle, which faces north, there shall likewise be twenty boards, having forty silver bases. Two bases shall be placed beneath each board.

The southern side of the tabernacle, which faced south, signifies that ancient people of God who, having long before received the light of legal knowledge, used to burn with love for its Creator. The second side, however, which faced north, represents the multitude of the nations, which did not cease to languish in the darkness and cold of unbelief until the time of the Lord’s incarnation.

Concerning its calling, the Lord beautifully says through the prophet: “I will say to the north: Give; and to the south: Do not withhold” (Isaiah 43). This means plainly: “I will say to the people of the nations, long frozen without faith: Give from your sons those who may come together to the faith and confession of my love. I will also say to the Israelite people, which was already enjoying the light of my knowledge: Do not prevent the nations from being received into the lot of election. I will say to Cornelius and his household: Receive the faith and baptism of Christ. I will say to the Jews: Do not compel believers from the nations to be circumcised; once consecrated in the baptismal font, faith and confession of the truth suffice for their salvation.”

The boards on both sides had one and the same number, measurements, and construction. For one and the same faith, hope, and charity are preached to both peoples by the apostles, and both are called to the same promises of the heavenly kingdom.

On the western side of the tabernacle you shall set six boards, and again two others at the corners; and they shall be erected at the rear of the tabernacle.

Josephus writes that the tabernacle had a width of ten cubits. He also writes that its boards were suspended four fingers above the ground; from this he appears to intend it to be understood that the bases of the boards were made of that height.

Again, concerning the chapter now before us and concerning the bars of the boards, he says:

> The rear wall was made of six boards, which formed nine cubits; joined to these were two other boards, each of half a cubit, which they placed at the corners, in the manner of the other boards. Each board had golden rings projecting from its outer faces, fixed as though by certain roots, facing one another in order around the circuit; through them gilded bars were inserted, each having a length of five cubits. They were placed at the joints of the boards, and the end of each bar entered into the end of another bar, like a screw. Behind the walls set lengthwise there was a row running through all the boards, by which the sides of both walls were held together by hooks, with the joints made and inserted into one another. This was devised so carefully so that the tabernacle would not be moved by winds or disturbed by any other cause, but would remain immovable in secure quiet.

This is what Josephus says concerning the literal text.

In accordance with the meanings of the allegory, however, the western side—which receives both walls into itself and completes the structure of the tabernacle—properly signifies the completion of the whole universal holy Church, which is perfected with the end of this world. To this point the faith and right conduct of both peoples will persevere; it reaches as though in the double length of the wall. For it is not credible either that before the time of the Lord’s incarnation there were ever none among the nations who believed, or that now, although the Jewish people is gravely condemned for its faithlessness, there are not some among them—however few—who, rejoicing among Christians, reach salvation each day by believing.

If anyone should presume to deny this, let us say what can in no way be denied: namely, that the spiritual teachers and interpreters of both Testaments, who, in accordance with the Lord’s word, bring forth from their treasure “things new and old” (Matthew 13), will remain in the holy Church until the end of the age.

The tabernacle is appropriately completed on the western side, where the sun is accustomed to close the day and all the stars to set, signifying either the death of each of the elect or the universal end of the whole age.

Concerning this side of the tabernacle it is subsequently said that it faced the sea. It signifies the Red Sea, in which Pharaoh was drowned with his army, and from which Israel, saved by the Lord, went up to Mount Sinai, where he would make the tabernacle. The western side of the tabernacle therefore faces the sea when the holy Church, crowned after the perfection of good works in Christ, will behold with free vision the vices or punishments of the impious, from which, with his help, she was enabled to keep away. Isaiah bears witness to this when he says: “For just as the new heavens and the new earth that I am making shall stand before me, says the Lord, so shall your offspring and your name stand.” And shortly afterward: “They shall go out and see the corpses of the men who transgressed against me. Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched” (Isaiah 66).
