The western side of the tabernacle, then, which is said to face the sea, properly consisted of six boards: either because perfection of good work is customarily expressed by the number six, since on the sixth day the Lord completed the adornment of the world, on the sixth day created humanity in the beginning, and on the sixth day restored the human race through his passion; or because there are six ages of this present world, in which we must be perfected through good works so that in the future we may reach eternal rest and the glory of the resurrection.

But when two other boards, apart from the first six, are commanded to be erected at the corners behind the tabernacle, so that they may receive the walls coming from the eastern side and be joined to the wall of the western side, this pertains to the recompense of the future life, which will follow after the labors and ages of this world.

This recompense is divided in two ways: namely, into the sabbath-rest, that is, the rest of holy souls after the release of their bodies, and into the glory of the resurrection, when incorruptible bodies are received. Both portions of the recompense, common to both peoples, are never brought to an end.

It is appropriately added concerning these same boards: “They shall be joined together from below to above, and one framework shall hold them all together.” For the whole life of the elect, directed toward heavenly things by the same faith and charity, reaches one and the same end of the divine vision; and the preaching of all the saints agrees in one and the same voice of sound doctrine.

The framework of the boards would split apart from one another if what one prophet or apostle had said were denied by another. But because the speech of the divine utterances, which shares in the construction of the Church, raises up the structure, all the boards of the tabernacle are perfectly joined together by one bond and does not permit them to be separated from one another.

A similar joint shall also be maintained for the two boards that are to be placed at the corners; and there shall be eight boards in all, with sixteen silver bases beneath them, two bases being reckoned for each board.

The corner boards are joined in every respect to the boards of the walls, because the glory of the future rest and immortality is most firmly connected with our present manner of life through faith, hope, and charity. Indeed, our present manner of life endures firm and unshaken for this reason: because it believes, hopes for, and loves the gifts of the future recompense.

These boards, whether by their actions they signify the perfection of good natural activity or the future rewards for good works, are each supported by two bases, because the holy prophets also foretold with harmonious voice that all these things would come to pass for the confirmation of evangelical and apostolic preaching.

You shall make bars of acacia wood to hold the boards on one side of the tabernacle, five, and five others on the other side. And bars of the same number shall be made for the western side, passing through the middle of the boards from end to end.

The five bars that hold together the boards of the tabernacle are the five books of the Mosaic Law. By their protection the holy Church is wonderfully guarded against every assault of tempting sins and wicked spirits.

This applies to both sides, because not only did the letter of the Law instruct the former people of God in faith and good works, but also, in the time of the New Testament, the same letter, spiritually understood, instructs us—who serve God—in faith and the practice of the virtues through the greater sweetness of grace in the present, and kindles us in the future toward hope of everlasting recompense.

Bars of the same number are also made for the western side, because the Law, rightly understood, likewise proclaims the completion of good work, when we depart from the flesh for future rewards. Hence, when someone asked, “Good Teacher, what good shall I do, that I may have eternal life?”, the same good Teacher replied: “If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments” (Matthew 19); and he gave him no commandments other than those of the Law.

You shall gild the boards themselves and cast golden rings for them, through which the bars may hold the boards together.

The gilded boards of the tabernacle shine brightly when the whole life and every utterance of the holy preachers display beforehand the light of heavenly wisdom, and nothing other than the beauty of the virtues is seen in them.

The golden rings through which the bars held the boards together signify the blessedness of heavenly life itself, which, because of the glory of its brightness, is rightly compared with gold, and, because of its eternity, rightly with a circle. Hence the Apostle says of it: “A crown of righteousness is laid up for me” (II Timothy 4).

Each board had five circles, not because the heavenly homeland is divided into five parts, but because the same everlasting brightness and bright perpetuity of that kingdom are contained in what is written in Genesis, the same in Exodus, the same in Leviticus, the same in the Book of Numbers, and the same in Deuteronomy.

Five golden rings were fixed into each board of the tabernacle because the hearts of the righteous, greatly expanded through love, read in all the books of the Mosaic Law not only the correction of their works but also the light of everlasting heavenly recompense.

“And you shall cast for them,” he says, “golden rings, through which the bars may hold the boards together.” The bars hold the boards together through the golden rings when the words of sacred speech confirm the stability of the holy Church through the promise of the heavenly kingdom, so that she fears the disturbances of the world less, the more certainly she has learned the stability of everlasting recompense.

It is appropriately added concerning these same bars: “You shall cover them with golden plates.” The bars are covered with golden plates when the superior understanding—namely, one made radiant by evangelical charity—is shown to be present in the words of the divine Law, which appear strong according to the literal sense and most suitable for confirming the life of the faithful.

To give one example: when we read the history of holy Noah, how he wonderfully escaped the flood that destroyed the impious and was preserved in the ark with his own people, it is evident to all that God, loving righteousness and hating iniquity, knows how to rescue the godly from temptation but to punish the impious with just severity. Such a reading, like bars of incorruptible wood, holds together the Lord’s tabernacle, because it fortifies the minds of the faithful, fixed upon the words of unfailing truth, against the assault of temptations.

But just as wooden bars are clothed with golden plates, so the same reading is shown, through spiritual understanding, to be filled with more sacred mysteries: when the ark is recognized as signifying the catholic Church; the water of the flood, baptism; the clean and unclean animals, the spiritual and carnal within the Church; and the smoothed and bitumen-coated wood of the ark, teachers strengthened by the grace of faith.

The raven that went out from the ark and did not return signifies those who, after baptism, fall into apostasy. The olive branch brought into the ark by the dove signifies those who were baptized outside—that is, among heretics—but, because they possess the richness of chastity, deserve through the grace of the Holy Spirit to be brought into the unity of the catholic Church.

The dove that went out from the ark and did not return thereafter signifies those who, released from the flesh, fly away into the free light of the heavenly homeland and will never again return to the labors of earthly pilgrimage.

The bars of acacia wood are therefore surrounded with gold when the firmest testimonies of sacred Scripture, through mystical interpretation, prove them to be transparent with these and similar heavenly and spiritual meanings.

And you shall erect the tabernacle according to the model that was shown to you on the mountain.

The model of the tabernacle was shown to Moses on the mountain because he remained in secret with the Lord and saw the sublime life of angelic purity and immortality. In imitation of it, he appeared to establish human conduct on earth, insofar as mortals were able to imitate it.

The tabernacle is erected according to the model shown to him on the mountain when each of the elect, in imitation of the angelic purity that Moses himself was worthy to contemplate in secret, orders both his work and his mind.

Thus far, as the Lord has granted, we have explained the southern, northern, and western walls of the temple. In what follows, the manner in which the eastern side is arranged is also shown. But first Scripture judged that it should speak of the central wall, which divided the Holy of Holies from the former tabernacle. It follows:

## CHAPTER XV. Concerning the veil that divided the sanctuary and the Holy of Holies, and its pillars; concerning the mercy-seat to be placed over the ark; and also concerning the curtain to be hung at the entrance of the tabernacle, with its pillars and its bars, which extended from corner to corner

“You shall make a veil of violet, purple, twice-dyed scarlet, and twisted linen, woven in embroidered work and beautiful variety, and you shall hang it before four pillars of acacia wood” (Exodus 26).

Josephus, however, reports that the tabernacle was divided in the middle in such a way that twenty cubits of its length belonged to the first chamber, while ten belonged to the second. This corresponds in every respect to the measurements of the temple that was later built by Solomon. Since that temple was sixty cubits long and twenty cubits wide, one third of its length—namely, twenty cubits—was separated for the inner chamber, that is, the Holy of Holies, so that the length and width of that inner chamber were equal.

Thus the inner part of the tabernacle had equal length and width, namely, ten cubits.

What this same veil expresses figuratively, the Apostle clearly declares in the Letter to the Hebrews. There he also explains allegorically why priests continually entered the first tabernacle, completing the duties of sacrifice, but into the second the high priest entered alone once a year, not without blood, which he offered for his own ignorance and that of the people (Hebrews 9).

This veil is interpreted as heaven. The fact that priests entered the first tabernacle throughout the year each day with sacrifices explains the condition of this present life, in which the saints, serving the Lord without interruption, atone for the daily errors of their weakness—errors without which they cannot exist in this life—by daily sacrifices of good works and daily libations of their tears, as true priests of God and of his Christ.

The high priest, however, who entered the Holy of Holies once a year with the blood of victims, is understood to be the great High Priest to whom it was said: “You are a priest forever, according to the order of Melchizedek.” Once offered for our sins, he himself, both priest and victim, entered heaven itself through his own blood, “so that he might now appear before the face of God on our behalf.”

Since this same veil was woven with beautiful variety from violet, purple, twice-dyed scarlet, and twisted linen, who would not see that, even according to the literal sense, it corresponds to the beauty of the heavenly vision? If you consider the beauty and flames of the stars, the manifold appearance of the clouds, or the rainbow itself drawing out a thousand colors opposite the sun, do you not seem to see in the heavens paintings of color, far more numerous and beautiful than those woven into the veil of the tabernacle?

The four pillars before which this veil was hung are the heavenly powers of the angelic ranks, distinguished by four outstanding virtues, about which we spoke above: fortitude, temperance, prudence, and justice.

These virtues are maintained by us in one way amid the labors and hardships of this life, and by angels and holy souls in another way in heaven. There, indeed, in what rules, that which is subject to justice seems to be present. This too belongs to wholly immortal justice: to prefer or equate no good with God; to prudence: to cleave to God most firmly; of fortitude: “to delight in that harmful defect”; the final reference to temperance is syntactically incomplete and uncertain in the supplied text.

Here, however, what justice does in assisting the miserable, what prudence does in avoiding ambushes, what fortitude does in enduring troubles, and what temperance does in restraining evil pleasures will not exist there, where there will be no evil at all.

These pillars are appropriately made of acacia wood, either because angelic spirits were created incorruptible by nature and immortal, or because, having been created without sin, they always preserve the unstained purity of their condition.

Concerning them it is suitably added: “They shall themselves be gilded, and shall have golden capitals, but also silver bases.”

The pillars before which the veil was hung are gilded because the angelic powers placed within the veil of heaven are clothed with the grace of supreme brightness. They have golden capitals because the mind by which they are governed is illumined by the presence of divine knowledge and vision. They also have silver bases because their whole nature rests especially upon this foundation, as upon a base: that they should sing hymns of praise to their Creator and proclaim his will to us, their fellow citizens, who are still pilgrims on earth and are placed, as it were, outside the veil.

The veil shall be inserted through rings, and within it you shall place the ark of the testimony; and the veil shall divide the sanctuary from the Holy of Holies.

Rings, which seem to have neither beginning nor end, are sometimes used in Sacred Scripture to signify eternity. The veil by which heaven is figured is therefore appropriately said to be suspended by rings: either because it was in the eternal counsel of the Divinity when the world was created, in which the heavenly nature has the first and pre-eminent place; or because the firmament of heaven was made in such a way that its structure will never be dissolved.

For since the Lord says, “Heaven and earth will pass away” (Matthew 24), this must be understood of the ethereal heaven.

The ark of the testimony was placed within this veil because Christ Jesus, the mediator between God and humanity, who alone knows the Father’s hidden mysteries, after his passion and resurrection from the dead ascended above the heavens of heavens and sits at the right hand of the Father.

By this veil the sanctuary and the Holy of Holies are divided, because the Church, composed of holy angels and human beings, partly still wanders below as a pilgrim and partly reigns above in the eternal homeland; and, while the veil of heaven separates her citizens from one another, she still possesses them.

You shall also place the mercy-seat over the ark of the testimony in the Holy of Holies.

The mercy-seat is appropriately said to be placed over the ark because it was specially granted by God the Father to the mediator between God and humanity that he should be the propitiation for our sins. Hence Paul also says: “Jesus Christ, who died—indeed, who was raised—who is at the right hand of God, who also intercedes for us” (Romans 8).

The table shall be outside the veil, and the lampstand opposite the table on the southern side of the tabernacle. The table shall stand on the northern side.

The table and lampstand of the tabernacle signify the temporal benefits of God, by which we are refreshed and enlightened in the present, so that, strengthened and assisted by them for a time, and with the grace of our merits increasing, we may be able to enter heaven to eat the bread of angels and to behold the true light of the world.

Both are outside the veil, because only in this life do we need either the Holy Scriptures and teachers or the other sacraments of our redemption. In the future age, when the Lord will proclaim the Father openly to us—that is, will openly show the Father to us—we will no longer need them.

We said above that the southern side of the tabernacle signified the ancient people of God, who first received the light of divine knowledge and first received the fervor of divine love. The northern part of the same tabernacle, however, signified the Church gathered from the nations, which had remained longer in darkness and in the shadow of death.

Accordingly, by a fitting distinction, the lampstand placed in the southern part can signify the grace given to the former people, while the table that stood in the northern part can signify the benefits of God granted to us.

The lampstand is rightly said to have been placed opposite the table because the Scripture of the Law and the prophets looks entirely toward the grace of the Gospel, bearing witness to it and signifying that through it Scripture is to be revealed in its spiritual meaning.

You shall also make a curtain at the entrance of the tabernacle, of violet, purple, twice-dyed scarlet, and twisted linen, in embroidered work.

After completing his account of the veil that divided the sanctuary from the Holy of Holies, he returns to explain the eastern side of the sanctuary, which he had seemed to interrupt for a time when he described its other sides, namely, the southern, northern, and western.

The curtain at the entrance of the tabernacle, woven with a beautiful variety of colors, is therefore the glory of the primitive Church, glorious in the different flowers of its virtues. Concerning it Luke writes: “The multitude of those who believed was of one heart and one soul; there was no division at all among them; and none of them claimed that any of the things he possessed was his own,” and so forth (Acts 4).

There was violet in it, because the Church was accustomed to think about heavenly things and to lead a heavenly life on earth. There was purple, because it was prepared to die for Christ. There was twice-dyed scarlet, because it burned with love of God and neighbor. There was twisted linen, because it rejoiced in restraint of the flesh and chastity.

You shall gild five pillars of acacia wood, before which the curtain shall be hung.

The pillars from which the curtain was suspended are the holy teachers, concerning whom Luke adds immediately afterward: “And with great power the apostles gave testimony to the resurrection of Jesus Christ our Lord” (ibid.).

The more robustly their minds are raised toward heavenly things, the more firmly they are able, by teaching, to lift others toward love of heavenly things.

For just as the apostles and apostolic men may rightly be represented by boards because of their breadth, or because of their teaching, by which, going into all the world, they preach the Gospel to every creature; or because of their brightness, since they extend their love not only to friends but even to enemies, whom they pursue with prayers and acts of kindness; so, because of the unconquerable strength of their hearts and their minds always directed toward heavenly things, they are also figuratively represented, not inappropriately, by the form of pillars.

The Apostle bears witness to this when he says: “James, Cephas, and John, who were considered to be pillars” (Galatians 2).

These pillars are properly made five in number because of the five books of the Law, which the holy teachers must support by the word of their preaching. This was especially necessary for those who established the primitive Church, which was gathered from the Hebrew people and knew itself to be founded solely upon the authority of the Mosaic Law, while the evangelical and apostolic Scriptures had not yet shone throughout the world.

The same pillars are rightly commanded to be made of acacia wood and covered with gold, so that it may be shown that holy preachers must be inwardly sound in strength of heart, failing in nothing, and outwardly conspicuous in the brightness of their works.

Or certainly, the pillars of acacia wood are gilded when those same teachers teach that the strength of their action must always be protected by divine assistance; when, in everything they do, they seek the glory of the Father who is in heaven; and when, in all that they say, they rejoice to make Christ resound, saying: “For we do not preach ourselves, but Jesus Christ as Lord” (II Corinthians 4).

Concerning them it is suitably added: “Their capitals shall be golden, and their bases bronze.”

The golden capitals signify him of whom the Apostle says: “And all things hold together in him; and he is the head of the body, the Church, who is the beginning and the firstborn from the dead” (Ephesians 5).

Nor should it seem incongruous that the one head of the Church, Christ, is represented by the five capitals of the pillars. For there were as many capitals as pillars. The same Lord Christ, head of all the saints, remains in himself always equal and indivisible, yet divides the grace of his Spirit among each of the elect according to the capacity of those who receive it.

Hence not only may the whole Church in general, but also each of its members individually, confidently proclaim that prophetic word: “But now he has exalted my head above my enemies.”

The significance of this head is fittingly represented by the fact that the capitals of these pillars are commanded to be made not gilded, like the pillars and boards, but golden. For all the saints have become partakers of the Holy Spirit and heavenly grace; but he himself was full of grace and truth.

As his forerunner said of him: “For God does not give him the Spirit by measure. The Father loves the Son and has given all things into his hand” (John 1).

The bronze bases are the prophets, by whose testimony the word of the apostles is confirmed. They are appropriately made of bronze either because of the unconquerable confidence of the prophetic mind, or because their word, as the world grows old or passes away, can never be consumed by any antiquity.

For he did not come to abolish the Law or the prophets, but to fulfill them (Matthew 5).

Since we are speaking of the eastern side, it seems appropriate to recall something concerning the interpretation of that singular bar which, as we have already said, was extended from the corner of the boards to the corner of the opposite wall and held together the stability of the entire walls, so that they could not be shaken by the force and assault of storms or bent this way and that.

It is written in the continuation of the sacred history, where Moses is said to have completed everything that the Lord had commanded: “He also made another bar, which passed through the middle of the boards from corner to corner.”

This bar must therefore be understood to have been stretched from the top of the boards on one side to the top of the other side, across the ten cubits of the tabernacle’s width, with both ends firmly placed upon the boards. Thus the side of the tabernacle that consisted not of boards but of pillars would remain no less fixed than the others, even when driven by the wind.

If you also wish to know the mystery of this bar, it plainly and without any ambiguity figuratively proclaims our Redeemer. He reaches, as it were, from corner to corner because, having first chosen the Jewish people, he graciously extended himself also to save the multitude of the nations.

Therefore, just as in the prophets he is rightly called the cornerstone, so in the Law the corner-bar may also rightly be called the angular bar: the cornerstone because of the temple built for God from living stones; the corner-bar because of the tabernacle built for him from incorruptible wood—that is, from the souls of the elect, free from the stain of corruption.

## CHAPTER XVI. Concerning the altar of burnt offering and its vessels
You shall also make the altar of setim wood, five cubits long and the same in width—that is, square—and three cubits high (Exod. XXVII). This altar, properly called the altar of burnt offering, signifies the hearts of the elect, which have been consecrated by his gift for offering sacrifices of good works to God. It is fittingly commanded to be made of setim wood, because the hearts and bodies in which the Spirit of God dwells ought to be pure and incorruptible.

It has five cubits in length and the same in width when each of the faithful strives to exercise all the senses of his body in the length of patience and the breadth of charity, so that, through his sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch, he may always remember that he has been devoted to divine service, according to the Apostle’s statement: “Whether you eat or drink, or whatever else you do, do everything for the glory of God” (I Cor. X). It has three cubits in height when those same hearts of the elect strive toward heavenly things through faith, hope, and charity.

“Its horns shall project from its four corners, and you shall cover it with bronze.” The altar of burnt offering has four corners because the holy Church is spread through the four regions of the world; and because the entire multitude of believers is one in heart and soul, it is rightly represented by a single altar. Four horns proceed from this altar when the hearts of the righteous are fortified by the four virtues so often mentioned. Concerning these it is said in praise of wisdom: “For she teaches sobriety and prudence, justice and virtue, than which nothing is more useful for human beings in life.”

[Col. 0179C] These horns proceed from the altar itself when the faithful do not merely display the defenses of virtue outwardly and before human eyes, but bring them forth from the innermost root of their hearts, with that root as witness. There are four horns at the four corners of the altar when, throughout all the boundaries of the world, the Church remains invulnerable to every ambush of its enemies through the spiritual power of virtue—indeed, it becomes stronger through all who attack it.

That altar is covered with bronze when the virtue begun by the faithful is held firm perseveringly to the end. Since bronze as a metal is accustomed to endure incorruptibly for a long time, it can rightly signify the virtue of perseverance.

[Col. 0179D] If anyone is troubled, on the literal level, by the question of how the wood of the altar could have remained unburned so near such a great fire, let him receive the answer of blessed Jerome on this matter. “The wood of the altar,” he says, “which is from the wood of paradise, is not consumed by the neighboring fire, but is made purer. Nor is it surprising to believe this of the sanctuary, the inner parts of the temple, and the altar of incense, since amianton is also a kind of wood—or a substance resembling wood—which, the more it is burned, is found to be all the cleaner.”

You shall also make for its use pots for receiving the ashes, as well as tongs, forks, and fire pans; you shall make all its vessels of bronze.

[Col. 0180A] We should understand the various vessels of the altar either as different persons among the faithful or, certainly, as the many kinds of their actions or thoughts arranged for the service of their Creator. First, indeed, the pots for receiving the ashes are commanded to be made. That the ashes of the sacrifices are to be understood as a great mystery is attested by the ashes of the red heifer sprinkled for purification, which, as the Apostle also bears witness, sanctified the defiled for the cleansing of the flesh. In this he himself understands the sacrament of the Lord’s Passion to have been prefigured, and he recognizes the event of Christ’s Passion as signified.

[Col. 0180B] Since, therefore, all the sacrifices and victims that were burned on the altar figuratively proclaim either the Lord’s Passion or the devotion of his saints burning with the flame of charity, the ashes of the burnt offerings rightly express either the consummation of the Lord’s Passion or, certainly, the perfection of the virtue of the righteous. This is so when, having been wholly offered to God through the fire of the Holy Spirit, they have deserved to bring their good works to an end and to be carried away into eternal life to receive the rewards of their works.

To make this clearer, let us see what Moses says about the ashes of the burnt offering:

“This is the law of the burnt offering: It shall be burned on the altar throughout the whole night until morning. The fire shall be from the same altar. The priest shall put on his tunic and linen undergarments; and, taking up the ashes which the devouring fire has burned, he shall place them beside the altar. Then he shall remove his former garments, put on others, carry the ashes outside the camp, and have them consumed to the very embers in a most clean place. But the fire on the altar shall always burn.”

[Col. 0180C] The burnt offering is burned on the altar when, in the heart of any elect person who has vowed himself wholly to God, both in flesh and in heart, a good work is performed through the fervent fire of charity. It occurs throughout the whole night until morning when someone persists without ceasing in good works throughout the entire time of this life, until, snatched from the body, he deserves to see the morning of the age to come.

“The fire shall be from the same altar,” because we ought to burn only with that charity which the Lord grants to his Church through the Holy Spirit. Thus the sons of Aaron, because they wished to offer the Lord strange fire rather than the fire once given from heaven, were immediately destroyed by heavenly fire. For whoever performs heavenly works not with the intention of a heavenly reward, but with a view to temporal praise or advantage, is struck by the sentence of heavenly wrath.

[Col. 0180D] “The priest shall put on his tunic and linen undergarments.” The priest who offers the burnt offering is the Lord, because he himself is accustomed to kindle in us the fire of his charity and, through it, to make the offerings of our good actions acceptable to himself. In doing this he is clothed in linen garments, because, in order to stir us to works of virtue, he sets before us examples of his incarnation, purity, and death—realities which, as has often been said, can be signified by wood.

[Col. 0181A] That same priest takes up the ashes which the devouring fire has burned and places them beside the altar when the Lord brings an end to laborious works. He does not command the righteous, once snatched from this life, to struggle further for eternal life, but commands them to receive the crown of righteousness in eternal life.

For when he places the ashes beside the altar, he removes his former garments, bringing before the righteous the memory of the good things they have done; he no longer shows them the clothing of his Passion to imitate, but puts on other garments—those, namely, of which he himself says in the Gospel: “Amen, I say to you, he will gird himself and make them recline” (Luke XII). That is, he will prepare himself for eternal recompense and cause them to rest in eternal repose.

[Col. 0181B] “Having put on other garments, he shall carry the ashes outside the camp,” when the Lord, prepared to reward the labor of his elect, causes whatever good they have done to be seen as already removed from this present life.

Nor is it inappropriate that entry into everlasting life should be signified by a place situated outside the camp, since the Lord also says: “If anyone enters through me, he will be saved, and he will enter and go out and find pasture.” And the Psalmist says: “The Lord will guard your coming in and your going out” (Psalm CXX). The coming in is into the life of the Church in this world; the going out is into that place where the pastures of eternal satisfaction are found.

[Col. 0181C] Therefore, it is not unfitting to understand the place situated outside the camp as that other life, especially since it is said to be a most clean place—a condition which plainly cannot be realized in this life. The most clean place outside the camp is therefore the very spirit of the righteous who have been taken from this life and are rejoicing in the other. In that place the ashes of the burnt offering are consumed to the very embers when the reward of good works is rendered there in such a way that all labor is brought to complete fulfillment.

And because, when the labor of good works has ceased, the charity through which they worked will never cease—but will burn more intensely when the one whom we love is seen eternally—it is rightly added: “But the fire on the altar shall always burn.” And shortly afterward: “This perpetual fire shall never fail from the altar.”

[Col. 0181D] When, therefore, the burnt offering has been consumed entirely to the embers, the fire will never fail from the altar, because, once every kind of labor has been perfectly consumed, charity alone will burn perpetually and never be extinguished.

We have discussed the law of the burnt offering at greater length because of the pots of the altar, which were commanded to be made for receiving the ashes of the sacrifices. The pots therefore receive the holy ashes when all the faithful recall with devout minds either the examples and sacraments of the Lord’s Passion for their own preservation, or, certainly, carefully contemplate the departure of the righteous who preceded them. Having labored for the Lord through great struggles, they now rejoice without end in the prize they have received, their course completed.

[Col. 0182A] After the pots, tongs, forks, and fire pans were commanded to be made. The tongs, it must be understood, were made for tending the fire of the altar. Accordingly, they rightly signify the holy preachers who are accustomed, through their exhortations, to kindle in us the fire of charity as upon God’s altar.

[Col. 0182B] For, like the two teeth of a pair of tongs, they arrange logs upon the altar for kindling this fire when they instruct us through the concordant pages of both Testaments and place in our hearts the words of truth by which we may be more greatly inflamed with desire for eternal things.

Or, alternatively, priests tend the fire of the altar with the tongs—that is, with a double instrument—when, in everything that holy preachers teach, they pour into us the virtue of the twofold love and command us, for its sake, both to burn and to shine.

[Col. 0182C] The forks, which in Greek are called *creagrae*, were kept for this service of the altar so that the cooked flesh of the victims might be brought out from the cauldrons by them and carried to those who were to be refreshed by it. Their use likewise corresponds to the figure of the holy preachers, whose ministry is to refresh the souls of the faithful with the word of faith and, according to the rule of apostolic discernment, to provide those still immature in instruction with the rational and guileless milk of simple teaching, while ministering solid food of loftier doctrine to the more perfect.

[Col. 0182D] Moses rightly commands priests to make forks with which they may arrange the flesh of the sacrifices as required, offering some portions to human beings as clean food, while leaving others to be consumed by the fires of the altar. For there are certain things in the words of God which he has deigned to reveal to our humility and grant for the nourishment of our refreshment. There are also others of such great profundity that they are disclosed only to the knowledge of the Holy Spirit and utterly exceed the measure of our capacity.

Furthermore, the fire pans were appointed for this purpose: by them the holy fire was to be carried from the altar of burnt offering to the altar of incense, morning and evening, so that incense might be placed upon it. These too plainly bear the figure of teachers, who carry fire from the altar of burnt offerings to the altar of incense when they teach their hearers to advance from virtue to virtue and, as their merits increase, gradually to penetrate into the higher and more inward mysteries of the divine vision.

[Col. 0183A] All who, seeing the fervent piety of their neighbors, hasten to imitate them likewise become, as it were, fire pans, because they strive to kindle in their own minds the flame of the heavenly sacrifice which they see in their brethren.

All these vessels are indeed made of bronze when the devotion of the faithful takes care perseveringly to obey the divine commandments, or when it proclaims in the clear voice of diligent exhortation that what it itself does rightly ought also to be done by its neighbors.

You shall also make a bronze grating in the form of a net; at its four corners there shall be four bronze rings, which you shall place beneath the altar’s ledge; for the grating shall extend to the middle of the altar.

The whole altar was commanded to be made hollow, as is taught more clearly below; but it had in its middle a grating, fashioned throughout like a net, upon which the flesh of the victims to be burned was laid, and beneath it a ledge, upon which, when wood had been arranged, the fire always burned, ready to consume the burnt offerings laid above it. Opposite the ledge there was an opening in the eastern wall of the altar, through which wood could be put in to feed the fire, and coals and ashes taken out. We have seen this depicted in the drawing of Cassiodorus the senator, which he himself mentions in his exposition of the Psalms. In it he also gave four feet to each altar, that of burnt offering and that of incense; we think that he learned both this and the arrangement of the tabernacle and temple from Jewish teachers.

[Col. 0183B] Thus God’s altar has in its middle a grating prepared to receive burnt offerings, because the elect prepare a place for the Lord in the inward affection of their heart, where they may place devout thoughts before him. It has beneath the grating a ledge to receive the wood and fire of the burnt offerings, because these same hearts of the elect prepare within themselves a receptacle for hearing heavenly words; warmed—or rather kindled—by them through the gift of the Holy Spirit, they render to God welcome vows of devout thoughts. For the priest lays wood upon the altar’s ledge when any teacher supplies to the minds of faithful people who desire and eagerly seek them the testimonies of the holy Scriptures, by which they may be strengthened further in faith and love. He adds fire to the wood when he teaches that the understanding of the word and the efficacy of devout action are to be sought from God. And the wood burns on the altar when the love of God is poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us. The burnt offering placed upon this fire is consumed when everything which we have resolved to do well is, through the gift of the grace of the Holy Spirit, made acceptable to God by the power of love.

[Col. 0183C] Accordingly, the grating which bears the burnt offerings is rightly commanded to be made like a net, so that through its frequent openings the fire placed beneath may freely penetrate in order to consume every part of the victims. For so, indeed, must everything be done: we must not harden our hearts or, like the Pelagians, shut them against God’s grace; rather, we must diligently open them and, as though many doors had at once been thrown open, earnestly pray that in everything good which we begin or desire to do, he may deign, by his mercy, to enlighten us through each piece of his victim and kindle us in his own love.

The four bronze rings commanded to be made at the same number of corners of the altar are the four books of the Gospels. They are aptly compared with rings because they promise their hearers the everlasting crown of life; aptly bronze, because “their sound has gone forth into all the earth” (Psalm XVIII); aptly placed at the four corners of the altar, that they may strengthen by the word of faith and truth the Church of the faithful spread through every region of the world; and aptly fixed beneath the altar’s ledge, that they may raise the minds of the humble by the defense of their consolation.

[Col. 0183D] You shall also make two poles for the altar of setim wood, and cover them with bronze plates. The poles by which the altar was carried are teachers, who are accustomed, as it were, to carry the holy Church while they strengthen its faith and the sacraments of truth, either by preaching them to those who did not know them or by confirming them in those who already knew and had received them. Since they preach not themselves but what belongs to Jesus Christ, and follow not learned fables but make known to the world the power of our Lord which has been made known by a heavenly oracle, the poles are fittingly put through the rings so that they may carry the altar.

[Col. 0184A] For to carry the Lord’s altar through the rings by poles is for holy teachers, by exhortation, to raise the hearts of the faithful through the words of the Gospel, which will not pass away even when heaven and earth pass away.

There are two poles, so that the word may be preached to each people, Jewish and Gentile. This is also affirmed by the words which follow: “They shall be on both sides of the altar for carrying it.” There shall be teachers who call both Judaism and the Gentile world, by harmonious word and deed, to the one and same grace of faith.

Or, again, poles shall be on both sides of the altar for carrying it when holy preachers teach the minds of the faithful to maintain an unshaken constancy of virtues both in prosperity and adversity, lest the former flatteringly exalt them or the latter frighteningly disturb them.

[Col. 0184B] You shall make it not solid, but empty and hollow within. The altar was commanded to be made not solid but empty and hollow so that it might have abundant room to receive the most holy fire, wood for the fire, and the burnt offerings to be consumed by the fire. Following this example, if you wish to be God’s altar, empty yourself and make yourself void of every thought of worldly things, so that the wood of life, the heavenly words, and the sacrifices of virtues may have sufficient room; and receive the flame of the Holy Spirit, by which these same sacrifices may be consecrated to the Lord and brought steadily to the end of perfection.

Hence it is suitably added in conclusion: “As it was shown to you on the mountain.” Thus the altar is commanded to be hollow and empty as it was shown to Moses on the mountain, because, just as angels and the spirits of the righteous in heaven are empty of sins and full of piety and righteousness, so we on earth, according to our measure, ought to turn from evil and do good.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the court of the tabernacle, its columns, and its bars

You shall also make the court of the tabernacle, on whose south side there shall be curtains of twisted fine linen (Exod. XXVII). Just as the Holy of Holies signifies that part of the holy Church which is in heaven, and the first tabernacle typologically declares the perfect life of the faithful who dwell only in this present age, so the court of the tabernacle, which was on the right, shows the first rudiments of beginners.

Its curtains were therefore rightly made of twisted fine linen, because beginners must take care to restrain the allurements both of flesh and spirit, according to the Apostle’s saying, who, speaking of children of adoption, added: “Therefore, having these promises, beloved, let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit” (II Cor. VII). Fine linen is twisted so that it cannot easily be unravelled, when not only the lust of the flesh is restrained, but even every memory of it is torn out by the roots from the inmost heart.

[Col. 0184D] One side shall extend a hundred cubits in length, with twenty columns and an equal number of bronze bases; their capitals, with their ornaments, shall be silver, and so forth. It is evident that the number one hundred, which in counting on the fingers is transferred from the left hand to the right, sometimes has in Scripture the figure of heavenly life, which is deservedly preferred to the present life just as the right hand is preferred to the left. The mystery of this number is frequently found in the divine writings.

Thus the side of the tabernacle is a hundred cubits long because all who belong to the members of the Church must undertake within themselves the labor of temporal patience and continence for the sake of eternal life in heaven. The columns from which these curtains are suspended on high are holy teachers, who raise the hearts of their hearers, drawn away from earthly contagions, toward the desire for heavenly things. They carefully stretch these hearts out like the Lord’s garment, lest any duplicity be in them, but so that they may shine before the Lord like linen curtains with a simple and pure intention.

[Col. 0185A] These columns were bronze but covered with silver, as is said more clearly below: bronze because of perseverance in virtue, or because of the sound of their preaching; covered with silver because they speak nothing but the word of God, whose brightness is often signified by silver, and because in their actions they display nothing but observance of the divine sayings.

They were not only silvered; their capitals too were wholly silver, for it belongs especially to teachers to subject themselves wholly to the words of holy Scripture and to devote mind and body to them in meditation, preaching, and action.

[Col. 0185B] What could we more fittingly understand by the bronze bases of the columns than the fear of the Lord, the beginning of wisdom? Of it the son of Sirach also says: “The root of wisdom is to fear God” (Ecclus. I). He aptly adds there: “For its branches are long-lived,” because the manifold shoots of virtues which spring from the fear of God as the work and ornaments of columns spring from their bases will never lack the fruit of their reward.

Why there were twenty columns on one side of the court has already been explained above, where the boards of the same number were commanded to be made on one side of the tabernacle.

Likewise, on the north side in length there shall be curtains of one hundred cubits, twenty columns and bronze bases of the same number, and their capitals, with their ornaments, silver. The same things are repeated of the north side which had already been set forth concerning the south, because the heralds of both Testaments raise us with one voice to heavenly things, although they had ceremonies of sacraments differing according to the circumstances of the times.

[Col. 0185C] But in the width of the court that faces west there shall be curtains for fifty cubits, ten columns, and as many bases, and so forth. The breadth of the court which faces the setting of the sun, where, when the labor of day is ended, the sleep-bringing grace of night succeeds, rightly signifies that time when, after death and the cessation of active life, the rest of the elect and eternal reward follow.

Thus those who worked in the vineyard of the highest householder received the rewards of their labor when evening had come. The western side of the court rightly had curtains for fifty cubits and ten columns.

[Col. 0185D] For the number fifty customarily signifies in the Law the fiftieth year, wholly devoted to liberty, rest, and remission, and therefore commanded to be called Jubilee. *Jobel* means “releasing” or “changed.” The number ten likewise undoubtedly signifies these same heavenly rewards, where human nature, raised immortally in each of its two substances, rejoices in the presence of the divine vision.

For God is Trinity, and our body consists of four elements. Our inner person is comprehended by the number three when we are commanded to love God with all our heart, all our soul, and all our strength.

[Col. 0186A] In that breadth of the court which faces east there shall likewise be fifty cubits. The breadth of the court facing east signifies the beginning of our good manner of life, which begins from faith; because of the first reception of heavenly grace it is rightly said to face east, according to blessed Zechariah: “The Dayspring from on high has visited us, to give light to those who sit in darkness and the shadow of death” (Luke II).

On this side there shall be fifty cubits, because, at the very entrance upon their way of life, all who are catechized are taught to hope for remission of sins and eternal rest. Yet another particular division immediately follows, which, rightly considered, has one and the same end.

[Col. 0186B] It follows: “On one side curtains of fifteen cubits shall be assigned, with three columns and as many bases; and on the other side there shall be curtains extending fifteen cubits, three columns, and as many bases.” The number fifteen, consisting of seven and eight, rightly signifies the joys of eternal life, which begin with the sabbath-rest of souls and are perfected in the resurrection of bodies.

At the entrance of the court there shall be a curtain of twenty cubits, of blue, purple, twice-dyed scarlet, and twisted fine linen, the work of an embroiderer. It shall have four columns with as many bases.

[Col. 0186C] At the entrance of the court there are four columns because no one can enter into the unity of the holy Church except through the faith and sacrament of the Gospel, contained in four books. Hence the ancient custom fittingly arose in the Church that the beginnings of the four Gospels should be recited to those who are to be catechized and initiated into Christian sacraments, and that they should be carefully instructed about their figures and order at the opening of their ears, so that they may thereafter know and remember which and how many are the books by whose words they ought especially to be instructed in the faith of truth.

A curtain of twenty cubits is also commanded to be made at this entrance; this number is four multiplied five times. The well-known senses of our body are five: sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch.

[Col. 0186D] The twenty-cubit curtain is therefore suitably suspended on four columns at the entrance of the court, because all who enter the holy Church ought to regulate both their faith and their actions by the rule of the Gospels, so that, restraining every sense of their body from carnal allurements, they may subject them to the divine commands.

For this curtain is not merely raised by four columns, but in its own length has the number five multiplied by four, when humble and devout hearers coming to the faith desire not only to be instructed by the words of the Gospel but also themselves to live an evangelical life, and devote every sense of their body to the obedience of love.

This curtain at the entrance of the court is rightly made not, as in the rest of the court, of twisted fine linen alone, but of the four most noble colors—blue, purple, twice-dyed scarlet, and twisted fine linen—worked by an embroiderer.

[Col. 0187A] For the outward appearance of the Church indeed shines beautifully to catechumens, but its dignity and virtue will appear much more splendid to those who deserve to enter it through the sacrament of baptism.

These colors are interwoven by the embroiderer’s work when every virtue of the faithful shines more brightly by association with neighboring virtues and, as it were, by a certain kinship; although each of these colors may also suit individual persons of the elect.

For one person, because he deserves to contemplate heavenly things more highly, is blue; another, because he suffers more for righteousness, is purple; this one, because he burns with more ardent love for God and neighbor, is twice-dyed scarlet; that one, because he is especially white in the integrity of virginal flesh, is twisted fine linen.

[Col. 0187B] All the columns of the court round about shall be covered with silver plates, with silver capitals and bronze bases. He impresses more carefully what he had said, so as diligently to warn the reader that no one can be counted among the teachers of truth—the columns, that is, of the heavenly court—who has not learned to have, like bronze, unconquerable patience amid adversity; who has not taken care to fortify and adorn himself on every side, as with silver plates, both by observing and proclaiming heavenly words; who has not striven to subject himself wholly to the divine commands, as beneath a silver capital; and who has not been accustomed to establish himself in the fear of God, as on a bronze base.

[Col. 0187C] The court shall occupy one hundred cubits in length and fifty in width; its height shall be five cubits. The Church has one hundred cubits of length because it raises its hands to good works for eternal life; fifty of breadth because it hopes for everlasting rest in the grace of the Holy Spirit, which he willed to signify by the number fifty when he deigned by his coming to consecrate Pentecost, that is, the fiftieth day of the Paschal feast; and five cubits of height according to the number of our bodily senses, because then each shall receive in his own body according to what he has done, whether good or evil.

[Col. 0187D] You shall make all the vessels of the tabernacle for all its uses and ceremonies, both its pegs and those of the court, of bronze. The vessels of the tabernacle prepared for all its uses and ceremonies are the people of the Church serving the Lord in diverse merits and ranks.

All these vessels are commanded to be made of bronze, according to the figure of the mystery often mentioned: that whoever is struck by adversities may persevere to the end, lest through sloth he lose the salvation promised him; or that he may not fear openly to confess, even when enemies resist, the faith which he has learned, and may remember diligently to proclaim to friends as well the gifts he has received. For bronze is sonorous and by nature long-lasting.

[Col. 0188A] The pegs of the tabernacle or court were made for this purpose: fixed at the tops of the columns, they projected outward, and, with the ropes of the veils or curtains placed upon them, they lifted them from the ground and suspended them. Their form and arrangement can not improperly signify the very tongue of teachers, which touches the hearts of its hearers through preaching and, by touching them, raises them up.

Scripture sometimes signifies the sacred writings by ropes. Thus it is written: “A threefold cord is not easily broken” (Eccl. IV), because Scripture, which is customarily interpreted in the historical, allegorical, and moral senses, cannot be corrupted by any perversity of heretics or pagans.

Those curtains or veils themselves must have loops or rings at their upper edges so that they could receive the ropes and allow them to be inserted. If you too wish to become God’s curtain, prepare in your heart a receptacle for his words, by which you may be suspended toward heavenly things.

[Col. 0188B] Let the ropes of the curtains be placed upon the pegs of the columns, so that, spread out and raised aloft, they may complete the beauty of the tabernacle. Let holy preachers entrust the divine words to the hearts of the faithful and, through them, admonish them to be raised from earthly things after the example of the preachers themselves. Let the veils or curtains, spread out and lifted by ropes, display far and wide to all the wondrous beauty of their work, which, when folded up, they could not display.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the oil to be offered from olive trees for preparing the lamps on the tabernacle’s lampstand.

Command the children of Israel to bring you oil from olive trees, pure oil of beaten olives, so that the lamp may burn continually in the tent of testimony, outside the veil that hangs before the testimony; and Aaron and his sons shall set it in place.

Once the adornment of the tabernacle has been arranged, provision is also made for the lamp’s light, so that its admirable beauty may be illuminated by lamp-flames at night just as by the sunlight during the day; [Col. 0188C] nor should any place of darkness, any hour of shadow, ever be found in the house of God.

As for the mystical meaning of the lamp’s light, the Lord declares it in the Gospel. After saying in a parable, “Nor do they light a lamp and put it under a bushel, but on a lampstand, so that it may give light to all who are in the house of God” (Matthew 5), he immediately added plainly: “So let your light shine before people, so that they may see your good works.” The lamp of light in the house of God is therefore the works of the righteous, which illuminate the minds of those who look upon them through their example.

But it must be observed more carefully that, for the lamp to be able to burn continually in God’s tabernacle, the children of Israel are commanded to offer the oil, while Aaron and his sons are commanded to set the lamp itself [Col. 0188D] in place. What is this distinction—that the people should offer oil to nourish the light in the Lord’s house, while the priests should prepare the lamp—unless it is figuratively commanded that faithful and devout hearers bring hearts ready to obey in faith, while teachers, by preaching, minister to them the fire of the heavenly word, by which they may both be enlightened to know and inflamed to love God?

It should also be noted that the children of Israel are not indiscriminately to offer oil, but are commanded to offer oil from olive trees; and, in addition, it is specified that it must be pure and beaten with the pestle. Likewise, no other fire than that which descended from heaven may burn in the holy lamps or be kindled on God’s altar. For “the holy spirit of discipline will flee deceit.”

Let the children of Israel therefore offer [Col. 0189A] oil for God’s lamp, not just any oil, but oil from olive wood, and this pure and beaten with the pestle. Let good hearers offer to spiritual teachers a pure conscience and a fruitful grace of charity, cleansed by the pestle of diligent testing from every mixture of wickedness, so that it may delight to hear his words with the sole intention of pleasing and serving the Lord.

Let Aaron and his sons offer fire not foreign but sent from above, both for kindling the lamp and for consuming the burnt offerings and making the incense fragrant. Let teachers preach not their own word but the Lord’s, declaring confidently: “For we are not like the many, adulterating the word, but from sincerity, but from God, as before God in Christ we speak.”

Let them use this fire to illumine the hearts of their hearers with knowledge of the faith; this fire to perfect and consecrate to God the burnt offerings of their good works; this fire to kindle the incense of holy prayers.

It is rightly said: “So that the lamp may burn continually in the tent of testimony,” because never in the holy Church should the light of preaching be absent, nor the pure humility of hearers who willingly receive it—or rather, diligently seek it. It is rightly added: “Outside the veil that hangs before the testimony.” For we have no need of the lamp of the Scriptures within the veil of heaven, where the ark of the Lord is and the cherubim of glory overshadow the mercy seat—that is, where the ranks of the heavenly host proclaim with harmonious voice the glory of the incarnate Son of God, whom God appointed as a propitiation for our sins.

It rightly follows: “And Aaron and his sons shall set it in place.” For it is not given to everyone to preach the mysteries of the faith among the people, but only to those who are shown to belong to the sons of the high priest—namely, to our Lord and Savior—both by the chastity of faith and by the practice of good works.

It is also rightly added: “And it shall give light before the Lord until morning.” When the night of this age has passed and the morning of the future age has dawned, of which the Prophet says, “In the morning I shall stand before you and see” (Psalm 5), we will no longer need the lamp of books, when the true light of the world appears and illuminates us. Of this the Prophet also says: “But for you who fear my name, the sun of righteousness shall rise” (Malachi 4).

“The worship shall be perpetual through the successive generations of the children of Israel.” For how, in the literal sense, could the worship of the priestly office be perpetual [Col. 0190B], when the priesthood itself, the tabernacle in which it was administered, and the people for whom it was administered ceased to exist long ago?

Hence it is clear that this word is to be fulfilled in the holy Church, where, as teachers and hearers of the truth succeed one another in order, there will never be lacking spiritual children of Israel to offer gifts of devotion in the house of the Lord, nor sons of Aaron—that is, of our true priest—who will minister to them the light of the word. This will continue until, when the state of this age has been completed and the entire tabernacle of God—that is, the whole multitude of the elect—has been transferred to the heavenly kingdom, there will no longer be human beings to be taught by human beings, since God will be all in all.

# BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0189]

## CHAPTER ONE. The establishment of Aaron and his sons for the priesthood

“Bring to yourself Aaron your brother, with his sons, from among the children of Israel, so that they may serve me as priests: Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, Eleazar and Ithamar” (Exodus 28).

Having described the construction of the tabernacle, the priests who are to minister in it are next appointed [Col. 0189D]. Their appointment and attire properly correspond to the priests of the Church, so that everything that shone outwardly in the adornment of those garments may, when spiritually understood, stand forth inwardly and profoundly in the minds of our priests, and shine gloriously in their actions above the merits of the other faithful.

Thus Moses is appropriately commanded to bring Aaron his brother, together with his sons, from among the children of Israel, to serve as priests before the Lord. For it is necessary that all who are to be promoted to a higher rank in the holy Church apply themselves to the law of God with greater diligence—that is, that they unite themselves to the observance of the divine commandments with a more attentive mind than the rest.

This is what it means for those who are to serve as priests to be brought from among the children of Israel to Moses: the rulers and teachers of the holy Church must rise above the common life of the elect by the singular height of their minds, and by familiar examination attend to what the law says generally to all the elect and what it says particularly to the few who are more perfect, so that by the higher excellence of their merits they may attain higher rewards.

For when Moses is commanded to ordain his brother with his sons to the priesthood, what else is mystically commended to us [Col. 0190D] except that all who receive the office of teacher ought to cling to meditation on the divine law with such devotion and love that they may appear to be joined to it as if by a twofold kinship?

Nor is the fact that Aaron’s first sons, after their ordination, perished before the Lord when they offered foreign fire unrelated to the meaning of our miserable age. In it, certain men who have obtained the place of priests and teachers—an exceedingly grave and lamentable thing—are consumed by the fire of heavenly vengeance because they prefer the fire of desire to the fire of heavenly love. Their perpetual condemnation was prefigured by the temporal death of Aaron’s sons.

Yet, in the still more excellent mystery of the figure, just as the tabernacle with its ornaments and vessels signifies the holy Church, distinguished by the most beautiful variety of virtues and faithful persons [Col. 0191A], so too the high priest of that same tabernacle represents the true Pontiff, Jesus Christ, who offered himself as an offering and sacrifice to God for us, as a fragrant aroma, and who may rightly be called Moses’ brother. For who is more closely joined to another by a bond of brotherhood than Christ to Moses, grace to the law, and the New Testament to the Old?

## CHAPTER TWO. The priestly garment of Aaron and his sons

“You shall make a holy garment for your brother, for glory and adornment, and you shall speak to all the wise of heart whom I have filled with the spirit of wisdom, so that they may make Aaron’s garments, in which he may be sanctified and minister to me” (Exodus 28).

The holy garments of Aaron that Moses made for him are works of righteousness and holiness, which Scripture of the sacred law commends to the rulers as things they must possess; and in those who preceded us in Christ it shows examples for them to imitate [Col. 0191B].

The wise of heart, whom God filled with the spirit of wisdom to make these garments, are the prophets and apostles and the other teachers of the truth. They show us most clearly how priests and ministers of the altar ought to live and how they ought to teach, whether by the example of their conduct or by the word of their exhortation.

To them belongs the Apostle’s teaching to Titus: “For a bishop must be blameless, as God’s steward—not arrogant, not quick-tempered, not given to wine, not violent, not greedy for shameful gain, but hospitable, kind, sober, just, holy, self-controlled, holding fast to the faithful word that accords with the teaching” (Titus 1).

## CHAPTER THREE. The making of the shoulder garment

“These are the garments that they shall make: the breastpiece and the shoulder garment, the tunic and the close-fitting linen garment, the turban and the sash. They shall also make holy garments for your brother Aaron and his sons, so that they may serve me as priests. They shall receive gold, violet, purple, scarlet twice-dyed wool, and twisted linen” (Exodus 28).

How each of these was made is explained more fully below. The breastpiece is the garment of the chest; the shoulder garment is the garment of the shoulders; the tunic and the close-fitting linen garment—that is, the shirt—cover the whole body. The turban adorns the head, and the sash binds both the tunic and the shoulder garment more tightly to the body.

To these six kinds of clothing, a seventh and an eighth are added below: namely, the linen undergarments, to cover the flesh of nakedness, and the golden plate above the turban, which stood out above all the others, bearing the inscription of the Lord’s name. The close-fitting linen garment is so called because it clung to the body and was so tightly fastened at the sleeves that it had no wrinkle at all. It descended to the legs; hence in Greek it was called *poderis*, that is, “ankle-length.”

The high priest ordinarily wore these eight kinds of garments at the time of sacrifice. Four of them were also granted to priests of lesser rank: the undergarments, the linen tunic, the sash, and the turban. This was because the more distinguished someone was by rank, the more he ought to shine, and to be admired, by the works of virtue.

Everything was made of gold and precious colors, because nothing base or filthy should appear in the priest’s speech or work. Rather, everything he does, everything he says, and everything he thinks ought to be splendid before human beings and glorious in the sight of the inner Judge.

When it is said, “You shall place them on both sides of the shoulder garment as a memorial for the children of Israel,” the high priest even now bears the patriarchs’ names on the shoulder garment when a teacher or ruler of the Church considers the deeds of his predecessors in everything he does, strives to direct his life according to their example, and endeavors to bear the burden of evangelical perfection.

These names were rightly commanded to be engraved on precious stones. Precious stones are works of spiritual virtues. The priest has precious stones on his shoulders, with the names of the fathers inscribed on them, when he himself becomes admirable to all through the splendor of his good works and teaches that this same splendor was not newly invented by him but handed down to him through the ancient authority of the fathers.

He bears them on his shoulders for a twofold reason: both that he himself may walk humbly subject to the Lord’s commands and that he may always set before his hearers heavenly examples—whether his own or those of the fathers—for them to follow.

The same stones are also rightly commanded to be enclosed and surrounded with gold. Gold signifies either understanding, as stated above, or certainly charity, because just as gold surpasses other metals, so charity surpasses the other virtues. The precious stones are enclosed and surrounded with gold when the practice of virtue is examined on every side with such pure understanding that no vice is allowed to lie hidden in them, nor any impurity remain; and when the virtues themselves are held together by the bond of charity, so that no change in circumstances can make them fall from their state, nor can they slip from the priest’s character through the torpor of the mind’s vigilance.

It rightly follows: “Aaron shall bear their names before the Lord on both shoulders, as a memorial.” The priest bears the fathers’ names on both shoulders as a memorial when, carefully weighing the life of the preceding saints at every moment, he is always armed with the adornment of virtue in adversity and prosperity alike. Thus, in accordance with Paul’s saying, he walks with the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left; and while striving only toward higher things, he is bent toward neither side by any attraction to what is low.

“You shall make hooks of gold and two chains of pure gold, linked to one another, and you shall insert them into the hooks.”

The hooks mentioned here were skillfully fastened at the upper corners of the shoulder garment. The chains that follow seem to have been attached not to the shoulder garment itself but rather to the breastpiece, at its upper corners, by means of golden rings. Thus, when the high priest was clothed, the chains hanging from the breastpiece could be joined to the hooks of the shoulder garment, so that the two garments might adhere firmly to one another. For it is written more explicitly later:

“They made on the breastpiece chains linked to one another, of pure gold, and two hooks, together with the same number of golden rings.” [Col. 0193A] “They placed the rings on both sides of the breastpiece, from which the two chains hung, and they inserted them into the hooks that projected from the corners of the shoulder garment.”

The figure of these things will be treated more fully in the exposition of the breastpiece.

## CHAPTER FOUR. The making of the breastpiece

“You shall make the breastpiece of judgment by skilled workmanship, like the workmanship of the shoulder garment, of gold, violet, purple, twice-dyed scarlet wool, and twisted linen. It shall be square and doubled. It shall be a span in length and a span in width” (Exodus 28).

“By skilled workmanship” means by work of varied design. Just as the perfection of works is expressed in the shoulder garment, so in the breastpiece of judgment, by which the priest’s chest was both covered [Col. 0193B] and adorned, the purity of his heart and thoughts is expressed.

The breastpiece of judgment appropriately follows the shoulder garment, so that when someone has appeared innocent in his actions before human beings, he may strive all the more to stand pure of heart in the sight of the supreme Judge, applying every effort so that whatever he does or judges outwardly toward his neighbors may be approved by the rule of his inner reason and shine as pleasing to his Creator.

The priest is likewise commanded to wear the breastpiece of judgment on his chest because a ruler must always distinguish good from evil by careful examination and diligently consider what is appropriate, for whom, when, and in what manner.

The breastpiece was made double so that it might more easily support the weight of the stones. But this doubling of the breastpiece symbolically admonishes us that the judgment of our examination must be approved by the invisible Judge within and may never deservedly be despised by human estimation outwardly.

The fact that it was square and measured a span displays the tireless and perpetual effort of devout intention. For someone who measures anything by a span extends his hand with the utmost exertion, spreading his fingers so that he may grasp fully and without any uncertainty the measure he seeks. Thus, just as work is expressed by the hand, so by the span is expressed the unbending striving of good action, when each person endeavors to extend his right hand toward all the marks of virtue within his power.

“You shall place in it four rows of stones. In the first row shall be a sardius, a topaz, and an emerald. In the second, a carbuncle, a sapphire, and a jasper. In the third, a ligure, an agate, and an amethyst. In the fourth, a chrysolite, an onyx, and a beryl. They shall be set in gold according to their rows, and they shall bear the names of the twelve children of Israel. Each stone shall bear the name of one of the twelve tribes.”

This arrangement of different gems in the breastpiece signifies the manifold grace of diverse virtues, which in harmonious order …

## CHAPTER FIVE. The tunic of the shoulder garment

“They shall make the shoulder garment of gold, violet, purple, twice-dyed scarlet wool, and twisted linen, by skilled workmanship” (Exodus 28).

Since we ordinarily carry burdens on our shoulders, what does the high priest’s shoulder garment signify except the labors of good works that he must continually bear before the Lord [Col. 0194A]? It is fitting that the command to make the shoulder garment comes first, because whoever is to be promoted to the priesthood and the teaching of God’s people must first have his works examined. When what is outwardly visible to all has appeared blameless, then the integrity of his heart and the sincerity of his faith may appropriately be investigated.

The same shoulder garment is made of gold, violet, purple, twice-dyed scarlet wool, and twisted linen. It is made of gold so that, above all, the understanding of wisdom may shine foremost in the priest’s character.

Then violet, which gleams with an airy color, is added, so that through everything he penetrates by understanding he may rise not toward lowly favor but toward love of heavenly things. Otherwise, while he heedlessly feeds upon his own praises, he may be emptied of the very understanding of truth.

Purple is mixed with gold and violet so that the priestly heart, while hoping in the highest things it preaches, may also restrain within itself the suggestions of vices and oppose them with royal authority. Thus it may always contemplate the nobility of its inner rebirth and defend in its conduct the character of the heavenly kingdom, although, as stated above, the purple color may also signify the shedding of blood for Christ or the endurance of various afflictions.

For this is the cross that we are commanded to bear daily as we follow the Lord. Hence this color rightly shines among the others on the priest’s shoulder, so that it may always teach him to be ready to suffer adversity.

Twice-dyed scarlet wool is added to the gold, violet, and purple so that, before the eyes of the inner Judge, all the good works of the virtues may be adorned by charity, and so that whatever shines before human beings may be kindled in the sight of the hidden Judge by the flame of inward love.

Since charity loves God and neighbor, it shines as though from a double dye. But when the mind strives toward the commandments of charity, it undoubtedly remains that the flesh must be disciplined through abstinence. Therefore twisted linen is added to the twice-dyed scarlet.

Linen arises from the earth with a shining appearance. What else is signified by linen except bodily chastity, glowing with the beauty of purity? This twisted linen is joined to the beauty of the shoulder garment because chastity is brought to the perfect brightness of purity when the flesh is wearied through abstinence.

It may also, and not inappropriately, be said of the scarlet wool, which gleams like fire, that it was perhaps commanded to be twice-dyed because fire ordinarily has a twofold power: burning and giving light. A ruler should imitate its nature in the word of saving instruction, so that he may both open the light of knowledge to those who desire it and, by rebuking, burn away the rust of sins in those who despise it.

“It shall have two edges joined together on both sides of its upper ends, so that they may become one.”

Regarding this, it is later said: “He therefore made the shoulder garment of gold, violet, and purple.” Shortly afterward: “Two edges joined to one another, on both sides of the upper ends.”

From this it seems likely that, when the garments were put on, the edges of both parts were joined to one another on both sides, from top to bottom, so that half of the garment appeared outwardly to the eyes while the other half was hidden inside. The edges of both parts, however, descended to the lower extremities, joined together.

What else is to be understood typologically in this except that, when we show good works outwardly to our neighbors, we should preserve those same works inwardly intact before the Lord? Neither should the purity of chaste thought ever be followed by a lesser perfection of devout action, nor should the outward appearance of good work leave behind, in part, an intention of the mind that is less perfect.

Rather, the two edges of the shoulder garment should be joined to each other, when everything good that we display outwardly we perform inwardly with a pure and simple intention of pleasing God. This is to be so on both sides of the shoulder garment, so that amid adversity and prosperity alike we may always serve our Creator with harmonious action and thought.

The very weave and all the variety of the work were to be of gold, violet, purple, twice-dyed scarlet wool, and twisted linen. Gold was not placed in the lower part of the shoulder garment, violet in another, and other colors in other parts. Rather, all the colors were woven throughout together with the gold itself, because in priestly action no great virtue should ever be interrupted, even for an hour.

The priest or teacher of the faithful should always be bright with the gold of wisdom, always raised toward heavenly things by the violet of hope, always courageous against the battles of vice through the purple of the heavenly kingdom, always aflame with the twice-dyed scarlet of the twofold love, and always radiant with the twisted linen of disciplined flesh.

“You shall take two onyx stones and engrave on them the names of the children of Israel: six names on one stone and the remaining six on the other, according to the order of their birth. By the work of an engraver and the engraving of a jeweler you shall engrave them with the names of the children of Israel, set in gold and surrounded by it. You shall place them on both sides of the shoulder garment as a memorial for the children of Israel.”
