For three reasons Aaron always bore the names of the patriarchs on his shoulders, as well as on his breast, during sacrifices: so that he himself might remember and imitate the faith and life of the patriarchs; so that he might be mindful in prayers and sacrifices of the twelve tribes descended from them; and so that the same people, seeing the names of their fathers written on the ruler’s garment, might take diligent care not to depart from their merits and turn toward the contagion of error.

For this reason, as though arranged for the purpose, it ought always to appear in the priest’s heart. Each stone is inscribed with the name of one of the fathers when the ruler, looking attentively into the lives of the saints, carefully investigates the virtues in which each especially flourished and strives to gather all these things by meditation in the hidden recesses of his breast and bring them forth in action.

Nor was it without a definite sacramental reason that both garments were adorned with precious stones and marked with the names of the fathers. The names are inscribed on the shoulder garment on two stones of one and the same kind, but on the breastpiece on twelve stones of different kinds.

The fact that the fathers were carved on precious stones of one undifferentiated kind clearly signifies that one faith in God, the same charity, and the common hope of heavenly life filled the hearts of all the fathers. The fact that the same names were inscribed on stones of different kinds figuratively declares that there is a manifold variety and grace of good works, by which the faith, hope, and charity of those saints were confirmed and shone forth.

The breastpiece had four rows, each containing three stones. What is figuratively conveyed to us by this except that, in the virtues distinguished as four principal ones, we should hold an unfalsified faith in the Holy Trinity?

We may indeed understand in the varied beauty of the stones not only the manifold splendor of priestly action and thought but also the spiritual gifts of virtues and miracles of healing. Concerning these the Lord himself said to the apostles: “Heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse lepers, cast out demons” (Matthew 10). And again: “These signs will accompany those who believe: in my name they will cast out demons; they will speak in new tongues; they will pick up serpents; and if they drink anything deadly, it will not harm them.”

Whether this or that is intended, both are signified. The two onyx stones on the shoulder garment were also rightly engraved with the same number twelve of the fathers, to signify that the teaching and faith of the apostles would benefit both peoples, namely, the Jews and the Gentiles.

Accordingly, the Lord plainly promised the same intellectual Jerusalem—that is, his Church—through the prophet, saying: “For you shall break through to the right and to the left, and your offspring shall inherit the nations.”

Since onyx is said to be red in color, with each stone having white bands encircling it, who would not see that it signifies either the ardor of charity or the light of knowledge, accompanied by the band of chastity?

The priest bears the names of the fathers inscribed on such stones when he devotes continual effort to following the charity, humility, instruction, and other works of virtue of the righteous who preceded him. He bears them on both shoulders so that, whether a Jew or someone from the nations is present, he may always look upon the splendor in the teacher of truth and devotion by which he himself has advanced toward better things.

“You shall make on the breastpiece chains linked to one another, of pure gold, and two golden rings, which you shall place at the two upper ends of the breastpiece. You shall join the golden chains to the rings that are on its edges, and the ends of the chains shall be joined to the two hooks on both sides of the shoulder garment facing the breastpiece.”

As far as we can understand, the order of the work was as follows. Two hooks were placed above, on the two corners of the shoulder garment, and opposite them two rings were placed above on the two upper corners of the breastpiece. From these hung two golden chains, which, when the garments were put on, were inserted into the hooks projecting from the corners of the shoulder garment, so that the breastpiece and the shoulder garment might be fastened together, as is more clearly written below.

The upper connection between them has been described thus far. The text next speaks of the lower connection, which was beneath the armpits, adding:

“You shall also make two golden rings, which you shall place at the upper ends of the breastpiece and at the edges that face the shoulder garment and look toward its back.”

When it says, “at the edges that face the shoulder garment,” it does not mean at the edges of the shoulder garment, but at those edges that face the shoulder garment—that is, at the edges of the breastpiece, whose own edges are opposite the shoulder garment.

Those rings, which were at the outermost and lowest corners of the breastpiece, had corresponding rings opposite them on both sides of the shoulder garment. These were joined to the first by binding ribbons. The text then adds:

“And also two other golden rings, which are to be placed on both sides of the lower part of the shoulder garment, facing the front of the lower joining, so that it may be fitted to the shoulder garment.”

It says “facing the front of the lower joining” because it had previously spoken of the upper joining, which was above the shoulders. The difference between these two joinings was that the upper one was made with chains, while the lower one was made with binding ribbons [Col. 0197B].

Hence it appropriately continues:

“And the breastpiece shall be fastened by its rings to the rings of the shoulder garment with a violet ribbon, so that the skillfully made joining may remain, and the breastpiece and shoulder garment may not be separated from one another.”

It should not be thought that the two garments ended at the same point. The breastpiece, which was a span high as well as a span wide, was sufficient to cover little more than the chest. The shoulder garment, however, reached down to the sash, as is shown most clearly later, where it is written:

“These parts, front and back, fitted together in such a way that the shoulder garment and the breastpiece were joined to one another, tightened at the sash and more firmly fastened by rings joined by a violet ribbon, so that they would not hang loose or shift apart from each other.”

These things have been said according to the literal sense concerning the connection of the shoulder garment and the breastpiece. But since, as has often been said, the shoulder garment signifies the completion of good works, while the breastpiece signifies the purity of thoughts, the connection that joins them to each other rightly figuratively declares that diligence of mind by which the understanding and faith of faithful teachers are joined to action.

The joining remains skillfully made so that the breastpiece and the shoulder garment cannot be separated from each other when the ruler so excels in learning and in the whole effort of his works that he leaves nothing undone of what he has recognized ought to be done, and through negligence of heart deprives none of the things he sees to be rightly done of the virtue of uprightness.

The high priest’s garments hang loose and shift apart from one another if either the beauty of good works is stained by lesser watchfulness of heart, or the integrity of perfect action does not follow the purity of chaste thought.

But so that these things may not be dissolved from each other, the priest should have on the breastpiece two chains of pure gold—that is, the continuity of chaste and sincere love—firmly attached to his heart. This love should never allow his hand and tongue to disagree with the equity of a pure mind.

And rightly there are two chains: so that he may proceed properly adorned both in those matters that concern the worship of divine service and in those that concern assistance in fraternal need.

Indeed, charity is expressed by golden chains before it is expressed in action, because just as a chain is connected into one from many little rods of gold, so charity is perfected through the manifold practice of the virtues.

Explaining these rods, the Apostle says:

“Love is patient; love is kind. Love is not jealous; it does not act improperly; it is not puffed up; it is not ambitious; it does not seek its own interests; it is not provoked; it does not think evil; it does not rejoice over iniquity, but rejoices with the truth. It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things.”

Let him also have golden rings from which these same chains may hang—that is, the continual remembrance of perpetual and never-ending love in the heavenly homeland, from which alone it is customary for remembrance to be made, so that the bonds of love may remain continuous for us.

Let him have two hooks projecting from the corners of the shoulder-piece, into which the chains may be inserted. This means that at the very beginning of every good action he should have a firm intention of pleasing God, one suitable in every respect for receiving and retaining within itself love of God and of neighbor, so that, whether favorable or adverse circumstances arise, he may never loosen the most salutary restraints of holy devotion. This, then, is what it means for the priest to have on each shoulder hooks that receive the little chains of the breastpiece: in both prosperous and difficult circumstances he should maintain a fixed desire to please God, and through this intention he should be firmly established in love both of God and of his neighbor.

The hooks of the shoulder-piece therefore insert themselves into the golden chains that extend from the upper parts of the breastpiece, when what the mind had rationally tasted of the inner light of love is immediately and gladly embraced by an eagerness to do good; lest the most beautiful form of the breastpiece quickly slip from the priest’s breast, if the neighboring support that should contain it does not grasp it as it hastens toward good action.

As an aid to these same chains, violet ribbons are added, by which the two priestly garments are joined to one another: these are the exceedingly strong bonds of heavenly desire which, inserted into the golden rings, fasten the shoulder-piece to the breastpiece. This occurs when, having recognized the light of the eternal homeland, we sigh for that ineffable glory, and, so that we may deserve to enter it, strive always to serve the Lord in the tabernacle of the present Church with concordant faith and life, conduct and profession.

That the shoulder-piece was fastened by a girdle is more clearly indicated in what follows, where the high priest is clothed: “And he put on the shoulder-piece, and fastening it with the girdle, fitted it to the breastpiece.” Who does not see that the most faithful virtue guarding good works is self-restraint? Concerning this the Lord says in the Gospel: “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning” (Luke 12). The girded loins signify self-restraint; the burning lamps, the practice of the virtues.

“And Aaron shall bear the names of the sons of Israel on the breastpiece of judgment over his heart, when he enters the sanctuary, as a memorial before the Lord forever.” The priest ought always to bear the memory of the fathers in his heart, but especially when, about to minister before the Lord, he ascends to the altar. The more sacred the ministry, the more diligently he should continually cleanse himself through complete devotion and adorn both mind and body with every effort, looking to the examples of the saints and, as their diligent imitator, taking care to present himself fit for the divine sight.

Again, Aaron bears the names of the sons of Israel on his breast as a memorial before the Lord forever when every faithful bishop never ceases to care for those placed under his authority. Rather, he diligently strengthens their lives by exhorting, reproving, and consoling them, and commends them to the Lord in frequent prayers, so that they may be guarded and strengthened.

“But you shall place in the breastpiece of judgment doctrine and truth, and they shall be over Aaron’s heart when he enters before the Lord.” Therefore, doctrine and truth are in the breastpiece of judgment, whether impressed in letters or by being clothed in that same garment, so that he might remember the pursuits of teaching; likewise, he would have the assigned number of the seventy-two disciples around the feet. [The Latin construction is defective.]

For it is clear that just as the twelvefold number of the apostles inaugurated the rank of episcopal dignity, so the seventy-two disciples, who were themselves sent by the Lord to preach the word, marked by their election the lower rank of the priesthood, which is now called the presbyterate.

He also bore seventy-two golden bells, together with an equal number of pomegranates, to show mystically that faith and the practice of righteousness would lead the whole world from the darkness of errors into the true light. For three days and nights contain seventy-two hours; and because the visible Sun of righteousness, illuminating all the regions of the world above and below, makes its circuit three times in seventy-two hours, this number of bells, together with the various colors of the high priest’s tunic, is fittingly employed to teach figuratively that Christ, the Sun of righteousness, would illuminate the whole world and grant it the gift of true faith, which consists in the recognition and confession of the Holy Trinity and in good works.

## CHAPTER VI. On the golden plate to be made to adorn the high priest’s forehead

“You shall also make a plate of pure gold, on which you shall engrave, by the work of an engraver, ‘Holy to the Lord.’ You shall fasten it with a violet ribbon, and it shall be above the tiara, projecting over the forehead of the high priest” (Exodus 28).

This golden plate on the high priest’s forehead, on which “Holy to the Lord”—or “the Holy of the Lord,” as it is called below—was engraved, was more sacred than the other garments, and rightly so. For just as divine power rises above all that it has created, so it was proper that his name, transcending the high priest’s remaining attire and adornment, should project above it and, as though sanctifying everything, occupy an eminent place among them.

It signifies the confidence of our profession, which we carry on our forehead, each of us saying with the Apostle: “But far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Galatians 6).

And rightly this one item in the entire high priest’s attire was made solely of gold, so that it might signify the purity of heart or body in which we ought to conceal or carry the mysteries of our redemption. Or certainly the priest bears upon his forehead “Holy to the Lord,” inscribed in gold, to indicate mystically that we must venerate and embrace the passion of our Lord and Savior, through which we have been redeemed, in such a way that we also recognize that the splendor of his divine majesty, through which we were created, must be confessed. We must confess the death of the humanity he assumed in such a way that we immediately acknowledge that this same humanity rose from death into eternal glory.

The “Holy of the Lord” commanded to be engraved on the plate signifies his holy and venerable name, which among the Hebrews is customarily written with four vowel letters. Its interpretation in their language sounds ineffable—not because it cannot be spoken, but because it cannot be circumscribed by the sense and understanding of any creature.

And rightly the same name of the Lord was written in four letters on the high priest’s forehead, on account of the significance of the four parts of the Lord’s cross, which we were to carry on our forehead: the upper, right, left, and lower parts.

The plate bearing “Holy to the Lord” is fastened to the high priest’s tiara with a violet ribbon when, strengthened in faith by the hope of heavenly rewards, which the violet color signifies, we strive all the more firmly to preserve either the sacraments of our redemption or the image and likeness of our Creator undefiled, because we recognize that there is no other way of salvation.

“And Aaron shall bear the iniquities of the things which the children of Israel offer and sanctify, in all their gifts and offerings.” The high priest bears the iniquities of those under his authority—that is, he carries them away and removes them—when either by teaching he urges them to repentance for their sins, or by pleading for those who repent he wins for them the favor of the just Judge.

He does this with respect to the gifts and offerings that they themselves have offered and sanctified to the Lord when, on account of the worthy fruits of repentance—that is, almsgiving and the other works of righteousness that they have performed—he absolves the penitents from the guilt of the crimes they formerly committed.

“And the plate shall always be on his forehead, that the Lord may be favorable toward them.” For if the plate inscribed with the Lord’s name is always on Aaron’s forehead, the Lord will be favorable toward the children of Israel. When the teacher himself has faithfully subjected himself to divine service with a pure mind, those under his authority, inflamed by his example and admonitions, will likewise strive to live rightly and to earn the favor of the inward examiner.

“And you shall bind the tunic with fine linen.” This is the inner tunic, which above he calls the close-fitting linen garment. Why it is called close-fitting, or why it is commanded to be bound with fine linen, has already been explained above.

It should now be added that soldiers commonly have linen garments, which they call *camisiae*, fitted and close to their bodies so that they may move freely, whether when directing a missile against an enemy, holding a shield, wielding a sword, or doing whatever necessity requires. Joab is also said to have worn such a garment when he killed Amasa—a close-fitting garment measured to his body.

Thus priests, prepared for the ministry of God, also use this tunic, so that, possessing the beauty of garments, they may move with the speed of the unclothed. This linen garment is not only close-fitting; it also signifies that the priesthood has been consecrated to seeking what is true, rather than to caring for and investigating secular affairs.

“And he shall bear the judgment of the children of Israel on his heart, before the Lord always.” The priest bears the judgment of the children of Israel on his heart before the Lord when he examines the cases of those under his authority solely with a view to the inward Judge, so that no human consideration may intrude upon what he administers as one placed in the divine stead.

## CHAPTER VII. On the linen tunic and fine-linen tiara, and the girdle made by embroidered work

“You shall also make the tunic of the shoulder-piece entirely violet” (Exodus 28).

The tunic is called that of the shoulder-piece because no small part of it was covered by the shoulder-piece, distinguishing it from the tunic that was underneath and made of linen. Both are mentioned above in these words: “These are the garments that they shall make: the breastpiece and the shoulder-piece, the tunic and the close-fitting linen garment.”

The inner garment was linen, or fine linen, which is known to be the most noble kind of linen. The outer tunic, however, was entirely violet, admitting no other color at all. By its uniform appearance the text clearly teaches what the priest’s life ought to be: intent continually upon heavenly desires alone, having, according to the Apostle, his manner of life in heaven, and awaiting without weariness the coming of his Savior.

This tunic, like the fine-linen garment, reached all the way to the feet; hence both are called in Greek *poderis*. This was to show that nothing low or sordid should remain in the priestly life, but that everything he did ought to be covered throughout all his members, from head to feet, with the grace of the virtues, as though with the most beautiful heavenly color.

Again, the priest is clothed in a full-length tunic entirely violet, so that all who wish to be saved may be reminded that heavenly work must not merely be begun but persevered in to the end.

“In its upper middle part there shall be an opening, and a woven edge around it, as is customarily made at the edges of garments, so that they may not easily be torn.” The opening of the violet tunic has an exceedingly strong border, woven into it so that it will not easily tear. This occurs when the beginning of our good action, supported by the strong root of divine fear, is shown to be fortified against every ambush of the ancient enemy.

Such an opening clothes and adorns the priest’s neck all around when it grants the ruler confidence to speak and provides him with the greatest authority to preach heavenly things. This means that he has not only lived rightly throughout the course of his life, but that its very beginning also started from righteousness.

The priest’s violet tunic therefore has a woven border at its opening, as is customary at the edges of garments, when each distinguished teacher begins the work of the virtues from a degree of perfection to which anyone laboring earnestly and for a long time scarcely ever arrives. He walks with God his Lord every hour, according to the word of the Prophet, with as much fear of his ministry as another person can scarcely possess when dying or about to enter the final judgment of his Lord.

“Below, toward the feet of the same tunic, make around it something resembling pomegranates, of violet, purple, and twice-dyed scarlet, with bells interspersed among them.”

At the bottom, toward the feet of the tunic, pomegranates and bells are made all around it when the priest has reached such excellence of a life devoted to God that nothing else appears in him except splendor, grace, and, so to speak, the varied flower of good works; and when he opens his mouth, nothing else is heard from him but their most pleasing sound.

Because many seeds are contained within a pomegranate and covered on the outside by a single rind, pomegranates rightly signify the manifold practice of the virtues, covered everywhere by the single protection of love.

Bells are interspersed among them when the priest’s work never differs from the sound of the word he speaks, nor, frightened by adversity, does the sound of his tongue depart from the rectitude of his conduct.

The text beautifully adds: “So that there is a golden bell and a pomegranate; again, another golden bell and a pomegranate.” Golden bells are inserted into the high priest’s violet tunic and surrounded on every side when every word he speaks resounds with the brightness of the heavenly light; and when that same sound, firmly fixed as it were in the violet tunic, is commended to the minds of his hearers also by the sublimity of his works.

“There shall be two pomegranates for each bell, and two bells for each pomegranate,” when everything he says is confirmed by good works and fixed more firmly in the hearts of his hearers, while everything he does is shown to be rational through the discerning sound of his speech.

The text rightly continues:

## CHAPTER VIII. On the fact that Aaron and his sons were clothed in holy garments

“And Aaron shall wear them in the ministry of his office, so that the sound may be heard when he enters and leaves the sanctuary before the Lord, and he may not die” (Exodus 28).

The priest entering or leaving dies if no sound is heard from him, because he provokes the wrath of the hidden Judge against himself if he proceeds without the sound of preaching.

If we wish to attend to the words of Josephus (*Antiquities*), in which he says that there were seventy-two pomegranates on the high priest’s tunic and an equal number of bells, this agrees with the figures of the mysteries: just as he was commanded to bear the apostolic number on his shoulder and the [corresponding number] on his breast, so also the number seventy-two extends down to the feet. This signifies that self-restraint is not imposed violently upon any single member, but is delightfully perfected throughout the entire body.

This linen garment ought to bind the priest’s hands and arms, so that he does nothing except what is useful; his breast, so that he thinks nothing empty; his belly, so that, desiring pleasures beyond measure, he does not presume through gluttony to make it his god. The members below the belly are covered so that, by wantonness, they do not corrupt the entire beauty of the priestly garment. His knees are bound so that they do not grow sluggish in persistent prayer; his shins and feet, so that they do not run toward evil.

Let the priest first put on the close-fitting linen garment, so that he may restrain both his body from wicked works and his mind from depraved thoughts. Then let him receive the violet garment, so that, after the discipline of salutary self-restraint, he may adorn body and soul equally with the garment of spiritual virtues.

“And you shall make a fine-linen tiara.” The tiara, which was also called a *cidaris* and a *mitra*, covered and adorned the high priest’s head. By this garment he was admonished to keep every sense of his head consecrated to God: so that his eyes might not see vanity; his ears, by willingly listening, might not receive reproach against his neighbor; his mouth might not overflow with wickedness; his tongue might not contrive deceit; his heart might not be weighed down by gluttony and drunkenness; and his sense of smell might not embrace a prostitute’s bed sprinkled with myrrh, aloe, and cinnamon.

Josephus explains how this tiara was made (*Book III, chapter 11*), saying:

“Upon his head he wears a cap fashioned like a small reed-cap or helmet, extending over the crown of the head and rising somewhat above the middle of the vertex. It is made, apparently, from woven linen, with ribbons that are repeatedly wrapped and joined together so that it may not easily come apart.”

Josephus further relates that another, larger covering was placed over this cap, suitably made to conceal the entire surface of the head, so that it might not fall while the priest was occupied with the sacrifices. He does not, however, indicate what color it was.

This is what he says about the lesser priest’s tiara. Concerning the high priest’s tiara he testifies as follows:

“The high priest likewise wears a cap fashioned like those of the other priests, and another sewn garment of variegated violet. Around it is also placed a golden crown made three times around. Above this rises, in the middle of the forehead, something like a small golden cup, resembling the plant that we call *acharos* and the Greeks call *hyoscyamus*.”

A little later, after describing its marvelous variety, he adds:

“It has a flower resembling plantain, and the entire crown is engraved all around with these flowers, from the back of the head to both temples. On the forehead, however, it does not have this; rather, there is a golden plate on which the name of God is inscribed in sacred letters.”

The Holy Scripture seems to pass over this second covering and the golden crowns of the high priests in silence. It does, however, briefly mention crowns later, saying: “They made woven tunics for Aaron and his sons, and tiaras with their little crowns, of fine linen.” But it does not say of what material the crowns were made.

When it says, “and tiaras with their little crowns, of fine linen,” it could be understood that both were made of fine linen, if Josephus did not identify the crowns as golden. Since the Temple was still standing and the legal observance was being celebrated, and since Josephus belonged to the priestly lineage, he could very easily have known the entire form of the priestly clothing, not merely by reading about it but by seeing it.

Whether, then, the little crowns were of fine linen or gold, since it is certain that they were made together with the tiaras, let us briefly discuss their significance.

Priests have tiaras with little crowns of fine linen when they guard their sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch in the beauty of chastity in such a way that, for this very guardianship, they hope to receive the crown of life which God promised to those who love him.

“And a girdle made by embroidered work.” Its construction is described more explicitly later: “They made the belt of twisted fine linen, violet, purple, and twice-dyed scarlet, by embroidered work.”

According to Jerome, writing from Josephus, this belt was woven round like the skin of a serpent shed in old age, so that you might think it a long purse. It was woven with a weft of scarlet, purple, and violet, and with a warp of fine linen, for beauty and strength; and it was worked in such a varied design that one might think the different flowers and gems had not been woven by an artisan’s hand but added afterward.

It was four fingers wide. The high priest used this belt specifically, and by it the violet tunic and the shoulder-piece were fastened together. For later it is explicitly said concerning the joining of the shoulder-piece and the breastpiece:

“These things, front and back, fitted together in such a way that the shoulder-piece and the breastpiece were mutually joined, fastened to the belt and more firmly connected by rings, which he inserted; the violet ribbon kept them from hanging loose and moving apart from one another.”

No one, however, doubts that the belt or girdle to which the shoulder-piece was fastened also encircled the violet tunic, which was called the tunic of the shoulder-piece.

Everything said up to this point concerns the high priest’s attire. From here onward the belts and other garments of his sons are explained, when it is said: “For Aaron’s sons you shall prepare linen tunics, belts, and tiaras, for glory and beauty.”

Nothing is determined concerning their belts—whether they too were to be made by embroidered work or of a single color. We must therefore speak first of the high priest’s belt, which was made of those four most noble colors worthy of God. It was fitting that the high priest should have such a belt, since he was always required to be girded with the singular beauty of the virtues. It was fitting that the high priest should walk girded with the changing bloom of shining colors, because, just as every other person must be girded by the discipline of self-restraint lest rebellious flesh disturb the inner peace of the spirit, so the high priest and teacher of the faithful, having subdued every movement of desire in soul and body, ought to be surrounded by the very glory of the virtues.

Thus, in accordance with the example of the flower that came forth from the root of Jesse—that is, the Lord Savior—“righteousness shall be the belt of his loins, and faith the girdle of his reins.”

The linen tunics, belts, and tiaras commanded to be made for Aaron’s sons for glory and beauty can very easily be understood as commending to us inner beauty and glory from what has already been explained.

Priests have linen tunics when they dedicate their entire bodies to the whiteness of chastity. They gird their tunics with belts when they surround that same chastity with vigilant custody of the mind, lest their conscience remain negligent in the practice of good works, or lest through boasting of chastity they diminish even the merit of chastity itself.

“You shall clothe your brother Aaron and his sons with all these things, and you shall consecrate the hands of all of them, sanctify them, so that they may serve as priests for me.”

Aaron and his sons were indeed to be clothed with all these garments, but with this distinction: Aaron himself was to use all of them, while his sons were to use the final three, which are specifically assigned to them when it is said: “For Aaron’s sons you shall prepare linen tunics, belts, and tiaras, for glory and beauty.”

What follows—“You shall also make linen undergarments, to cover the flesh of their nakedness, from the loins to the thighs; and Aaron and his sons shall use them when they enter the tabernacle of testimony or approach the altar to minister in the sanctuary, lest they die as guilty of iniquity”—pertains to both Aaron and his sons, as the words themselves plainly show.

Thus Aaron himself is clothed in all eight of the garments mentioned: the linen undergarments, the linen tunic, the violet tunic, the shoulder-piece, the breastpiece, the belt, the tiara, and the golden plate. His sons, however, use only four of them: the undergarments, the close-fitting linen garment, the belt, and the tiara.

Since the other garments have been discussed above, these undergarments, which are commanded to be made to cover the flesh of their nakedness, specifically signify that portion of chastity which restrains the desire for conjugal intercourse. Without it no one can receive the priesthood or be consecrated to the ministry of the altar—that is, unless he either remains a virgin or, alternatively, has dissolved the bonds of marital union.

This virtue is not imposed as a necessity upon anyone by the law of God; rather, it is to be offered to the Lord by voluntary devotion. Concerning it he himself says: “Not everyone can accept this word” (Matthew 19). Yet he immediately invites those who are able with kind exhortation, saying: “Let the one who is able to accept it accept it.”

A little later he promises a hundredfold reward in this life and eternal life in the age to come to those who have left a wife, other relatives, or the entanglements of this world for his sake.

Hence, to make the distinction clear, Moses is not commanded to clothe Aaron and his sons with this garment, as he says concerning the earlier ones, “You shall clothe your brother Aaron and his sons with all these things.” Rather, he says, “You shall make linen undergarments to cover the flesh.” “They,” he says, “shall cover the flesh of their nakedness.”

You shall make undergarments for the high priest and his sons; you shall teach the rule of chastity; you shall instruct those who serve as priests to abstain from marital embrace. Yet you shall impose no such yoke of continence by force. Whoever wishes to become a priest and serve in the ministry of the altar must voluntarily cease to be the servant of his wife.

Once they have done this, and once they have accepted the commitment to continence and agreed to be ministers of the sanctuary and altar, the divine law will be present, imposing upon them, as it were, the rest of the proper priestly attire and abundantly teaching how they ought to live and teach in righteousness.

“When you have washed the father with his sons in water, you shall clothe Aaron in his garments—that is, the linen garment, the tunic, the shoulder-piece, and the breastpiece, which you shall fasten with the belt. You shall place the tiara on his head, and the holy plate upon the tiara. You shall pour the anointing oil upon his head, and by this rite he shall be consecrated. You shall also bring his sons near, clothe them in linen tunics, gird Aaron and his sons with belts, and place tiaras on them; and they shall be my priests by an everlasting ordinance” (Exodus 29).

Here too Moses does not command that the undergarments be received. Thus it is clear that Aaron and his sons had already clothed themselves in this kind of garment and entered into Moses’ presence in order to be washed, clothed, anointed, and consecrated.

Here we should also note that when Moses was about to consecrate them, he first washed them with water and then placed upon them the attire of the sacred rank. It is plainly necessary that one who is to be promoted to the office of the altar should, at the time of dedication, wash himself with a greater than usual outpouring of tears or compunction, so that the more cleanly he approaches to receive the rank, the more perfectly he may fulfill what he has received.

Once clothed in the sacred garments, the high priest is immediately drenched with the oil of anointing, so that the consecration may be completed through the grace of the Holy Spirit. This does not mean that we can possess the virtues represented by the garments mentioned above without the grace of God; rather, it means that a greater assistance of grace must be supplied by the Lord when someone ascends to a higher rank or is placed over the government of many.

Meanwhile, it should be noted that although in this book of Exodus Aaron is said to be clothed in eight garments, in Leviticus another item appears to have been added: namely, the belt with which the linen tunic was girded before the violet tunic was put on. For it is written:

“When he had washed them, he clothed the high priest in the linen undergarment, girding him with the belt, and putting the violet tunic on him; then he placed the shoulder-piece over it, and fastening it with the girdle, fitted it to the breastpiece.”

However this may have been done, the figure of intellectual clothing is plainly evident from what has been explained.

Since, following the statements of the Fathers, we have touched briefly on the priestly attire, we thought it worth noting also how the four eminent colors from which it was made correspond by an appropriate comparison to the four elements: fine linen or linen to earth, because things grow from it; purple to water, because it is dyed from marine shellfish; violet and scarlet to air and fire, on account of their resemblance in color. Scarlet was dyed twice because fire possesses a twofold power: namely, to give light and to burn.

The Hebrews say that the high priest bore the likeness of all the elements in his attire because, offering sacrifice and praying not only for Israel but for the whole world, he ought to intercede for it. We may perhaps add, not inappropriately, that in each human being the likeness of all the elements is contained: fire in heat, air in breath, water in moisture, and earth in the very solidity of the limbs. Hence physiologists call a human being in Greek *mikros kosmos*, that is, “a small world.”

If you ask what the gold in this same attire signifies according to this interpretation, understand it as the rational virtue within the human being. Hence “Holy to the Lord” is specifically written upon it, because no one ascends to knowledge of his Creator except through this virtue.

For the Apostle says: “That Christ may dwell through faith in our hearts in the inner person” (Ephesians 3).

Therefore Scripture presents the high priest of the Old Testament clothed in this manner so that the high priest of our time may know that he ought to intercede for the entire human race, especially for those who have recognized the truth and carry the sign of that faith upon their forehead. The Apostle admonishes us, saying:

“I urge, then, first of all, that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgivings be made for all people, for kings and all who are in positions of authority” (1 Timothy 2).

If in the high priest whom Moses consecrates we understand the Lord Savior, then rightly he bears in his attire both the figure of the whole world and that of the human being. For he is, as the Apostle says, “the brightness of glory and the figure of God’s substance,” and he bears all things by the word of his truth (Hebrews 1; John 1; Psalm 109).

He is the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world. He is the eternal priest, splendid with every adornment of holiness—not one who earned these things by the exercise of labor after being born in the flesh, but one who, having become incarnate in the Virgin’s womb, received them all at once through the grace of the Holy Spirit coming beforehand.

Beautifully commending his priesthood and intercession for us, the Apostle says:

“But because he remains forever, he has an everlasting priesthood; hence he is able to save forever those who draw near to God through him, since he always lives to intercede for them” (Hebrews 7).

Commending equally the garments and adornments of his virtues, he adds:

“For it was fitting that we should have such a high priest: holy, innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners, and exalted above the heavens.”

He truly had a golden plate on his head on which “Holy to the Lord” was engraved, because he came in the name of the Father, saying: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me; and whoever sees me sees the Father” (John 14).

Thus far the heavenly oracle has indicated what the attire of Aaron and his sons ought to be. It now follows that the manner of their consecration should also be described: how they themselves, and the tabernacle with all its equipment, ought to be dedicated by the offering to the Lord of a calf and two rams, as well as wheat loaves—not only unleavened but also mixed with oil—and, in addition, the oil of anointing.

All these things, indeed, the priests figuratively represent as either the devotion of good works and purity of faith, or the grace of divine illumination; the following words, *sola consecrari oportet* (‘… alone must be consecrated’), are syntactically corrupt or uncertain in the supplied text.

For who does not know that the sacrifice and blood of those animals signify the death and sprinkling of the blood of our Lord, through which we are both absolved from sins and strengthened in good works?

The Apostle teaches what saving mystery is contained in the unleavened loaves, saying:

“Let us therefore celebrate the feast, not with the old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” (1 Corinthians 5).

The cakes and wafers are mixed with, or spread with, oil so that we may be admonished to have works not only cleansed from the leaven of malice and wickedness, but also rich in a love worthy of the divine sight.

Or certainly we offer cakes mixed with oil to the Lord for our consecration when everything we have done grows rich through the inward grace of the Holy Spirit in the devotion of our heart. We offer wafers spread with oil when we show without hesitation, as an example of right living, that what we do outwardly is also spiritual for other people.

Our consecration is completed by these offerings when, through good works and pure thoughts, the Lord grants us the merit of holiness.

When these commands concerning the consecration of Aaron and his sons have been completed, Scripture returns to give instructions concerning the construction of the altar of incense, on which Aaron was to burn incense daily.

## CHAPTER IX. On the altar of incense and its instruments
You shall also make, he says, an altar for burning incense, made of sethim wood, having one cubit in length and another in width—that is, square—and two cubits in height (Exod. 30). If the altar of burnt offering, mentioned above, generally signifies the life of the righteous, who daily make it their practice to crucify their flesh with its vices and desires and to offer it as a living sacrifice to God, what else does this altar made for burning incense signify except the particular life of certain more perfect persons? Nor was it without reason that the flesh of animals was burned on the former and incense was burned on this one: on the former are represented those who do not walk according to the desires of the flesh, but, as though sacrificing these desires to the Lord, dedicate all the senses of their body to his will through the fire of the Holy Spirit; on the latter is represented the type of those who, with greater perfection of mind, after all the enticements of the flesh have been utterly extinguished and put to sleep, offer to the Lord only the vows of their prayers. They possess nothing from the flesh that attacks them, nothing from consciousness of sin by which they may be troubled and afraid; rather, through the outpouring of sweet tears, they desire to come and appear before the face of God.

Therefore this altar is appropriately placed inside, near the veil and the ark, while that altar is placed outside the tabernacle, because those signified by the outer altar shine before all in the sight of holy Church as examples of virtue; those signified by this altar, through the ardor of a higher desire and contemplation of future blessedness, though detained in the body, draw very near. It is also fitting that the outer altar is ordered to be covered with bronze and this one with gold. Bronze is more resonant than other metals and endures for a long time; gold, however, insofar as it is inferior to bronze in sound, surpasses it in brilliance. Thus the bronze altar, on which the flesh was burned and the blood of victims poured out, rightly bears the type of those who, having subdued and, as it were, sacrificed the pleasures of the flesh to God, persevere in completing the way of truth that they once began, and repeatedly proclaim in the sound of preaching that their neighbors too should walk in it.

[Col. 0208D] The golden altar, on the other hand, is suitably assigned to those who are illumined by a greater grace of heavenly brightness but are less able to disclose to others what they taste in secret of inward sweetness. By speaking, they are sufficient to pour forth the gift, but they do not reveal how greatly they themselves are inwardly refreshed by the sweetness hidden in the presence of God.

The altar of incense was appropriately smaller in proportion to the extent to which it surpassed the other in the splendor of its metal, because the holier people are in the Church, the fewer they are. It is fitting that both altars are ordered to be made from the same sethim wood, which we have said resembles white thorn and is imperishable, because there is one firmness of genuine faith; because the hearts of all the elect ought to be fortified and prepared to receive the fire of love and to offer God libations of virtue; and because the Apostle speaks generally to all, the little along with the great, saying: “Let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God” (1 Cor. 7).

Appropriately, the fire was one and the same: it burned victims on this altar and incense on that one, because there is one Spirit who gives life to the minds of all the faithful through the varying grace of his gifts. As for the fact that the altar of incense was square, having one cubit in length and another in width, but two cubits in height: its length refers to the long-suffering of patience, as was said in the exposition of the altar of burnt offering; its width refers to the breadth of love; its height refers to the sublimity of hope, through which, while enduring temporal labors and rejoicing in love, we delight with a sincere mind.

The altar has one cubit both in length and in width when the greatest and most perfect men in the Church bear temporal evils with equanimity, looking toward no other thing than eternal recompense, and by love bestow upon their neighbors whatever good they are able to provide. The altar of incense is rightly ordered to be made square in its length and width, so that it may be shown that the mind of the perfect, with the virtues joined together, is as capable of loving a brother as it is of bearing with him; and as much as it can endure his annoyance through patience, so much can it offer him kindness through the benevolence of its love.

It has two cubits in height because the elect hope to receive a twofold reward in the future life. One is the repose of souls, when they will strip off this corruptible and mortal body and enter the heavenly kingdom; the other is when, having received the same body incorruptible and immortal, they will rejoice more perfectly in the presence of their Creator, when the prophetic promise is fulfilled: “In their land they shall possess double; everlasting joy shall be theirs.”

“From it shall project horns, and you shall cover it with the purest gold, both its grating, its walls, and its horns.” In Scripture horns often signify the prominence of faith and virtues, by which we must blunt and overcome the battles of the ancient enemy that confront us, saying with the Prophet to the Lord: “In you we shall gore our enemies with the horn” (Ps. 43). Immediately afterward he explained which horn he meant, adding: “And in your name we shall despise those who rise up against us.”

Conversely, the battles of vices that strive to overcome us are sometimes signified by the name of horns. The Lord, briefly embracing both meanings through the Prophet, said: “I shall break all the horns of sinners, but the horns of the righteous shall be exalted” (Ps. 74). Hence the law rightly decrees that only horned animals are clean and edible for the people of God. For it is also established that the animals that chew the cud and divide the hoof are horned, so that it may be mystically shown that only those can be incorporated into the spiritual Church of God who are proved invincible in the battles of vices by the strength of faith.

The horns proceed from the altar of incense when the elect do not display their works of virtue superficially before the faces of human beings, but exercise them with a fixed and immovable disposition rooted in the innermost foundation of the mind. The altar is covered with the purest gold when the perfect shine with the true inner light of wisdom; when, in everything they do, the splendor of love, like the glory of their daily way of life, is made manifest beforehand; when they show to all who live with them or hear them that the memory of everlasting brightness is always present to them; and when they make clear that, before all else, they think about and seek the kingdom of God and his righteousness.

It is fitting that both the grating of the altar, its walls, and its horns are ordered to be covered with gold. The grating was inside, in the middle of the altar, prepared to receive the incense; the walls, however, were outside, and the horns appeared outside them, rising higher with a distinctive elevation. The grating is gilded when the grace of Christ shines within our inner person through faith. The walls are gilded when the same grace of the Lord’s love spreads outward through good works. The horns too are gilded when the very confidence of the righteous—the strength by which they have learned either patiently to endure the adversaries of truth or wisely to repel and correct them—flashes with the radiance of inner light in all things.

And because such people can rightly say, “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith. From now on the crown of righteousness is laid up for me” (2 Tim. 4), it is rightly added: “You shall make for it a small golden crown all around.” The small golden crown is made around the altar of incense when the saints await eternal rewards for the good things they remember having done. The crown is made around the altar so that they may be taught that everything they have done is worthy of heavenly recompense.

“You shall make two golden rings beneath the crown, on each side, so that poles may be put into them and the altar may be carried; and you shall make the poles from sethim wood and overlay them with gold.” In these rings by which the altar was carried, the four books of the Gospels may indeed suitably be understood, as was explained above concerning the altar of burnt offering, the ark, and the table. Through faith in and teaching from these books, the saints are carried and, lifted above earthly thoughts, are borne through the wilderness of this life toward the heavenly homeland by daily advances in good works.

But because there it is explicitly commanded that four rings be made—two on one side and two on the other—while here, with the number four left unspoken, two rings are made on each side, the number of the Evangelists is plainly indicated there; here, however, there is also another spiritual mystery, one that especially concerns love of God and neighbor. The altar is surrounded on each side by golden rings because the hearts of the elect are strengthened on both sides by love of God and neighbor. Love is suitably compared to rings because, when prophecy has been abolished, knowledge destroyed, and tongues have ceased, love alone will never cease. There are two rings on each side because the two commandments of love are distinguished by a twofold virtue. The love of God is perfected through sincerity of faith and purity of life.

[Col. 0211A]

You shall place the altar opposite the veil that hangs before the ark of the testimony, before the mercy seat by which the testimony is covered, where I shall speak with you.

The veil that was before the ark, as was explained in its proper place, signified the Lord Savior who hung there; it signifies heaven itself, whose inner sanctuary the Lord entered after conquering death, so that, as the Apostle says, he might now appear before the face of God for us. The altar stands opposite the veil that is hung before the ark when the whole intention of the righteous is directed toward entering the heavenly kingdom. It stands before the mercy seat that covers the ark when a person approaches the vision of his Creator with purity of mind; and although they are enclosed in bodily existence, they nevertheless have their way of life in the heavens.

## CHAPTER X. On burning incense daily upon the altar itself, morning and evening

“And Aaron shall burn upon it fragrant incense in the morning, when he prepares the lamps, and shall burn it when he sets them in place toward evening” (Exod. 30).

It is clear that incense, or thymiama, expresses the power of prayer, as the Psalm says: “Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight” (Ps. 140). In the Apocalypse John saw the saints holding golden bowls full of perfumes (Rev. 5); immediately explaining this, he added that these are the prayers of the saints.

And since Aaron, as was said above, signifies both specifically the high priest himself, namely the Lord Savior, and also the priests of our order, Aaron burns fragrant incense on this altar in the morning when either the Lord himself, having illumined the hearts of the faithful, urges them toward the sweetness of prayer with the new radiance of his grace, or when the participants in his priesthood rouse the faithful by diligent exhortation to seek the face of their Creator.

The priest burns the incense not only in the morning but also in the evening. Incense is burned in the morning so that, at the beginning of every good work that we intend to undertake with God’s inspiration, we may invoke his help to bring it to completion. In the evening, however, it is burned so that, when we have completed a good work begun, we may return vows of thanksgiving to the one from whom we received it, for the things he has granted.

Thus it is rightly said: “And Aaron shall burn upon it fragrant incense in the morning, when he prepares the lamps, and shall burn it when he sets them in place toward evening.” Aaron burns incense upon the altar in the morning when the Lord inflames the hearts of the faithful, in the things they are already able to understand among the mysteries of truth, toward the grace of compunction. He burns it in the evening, when he sets the lamps in place, when, even through those things they are not yet able to grasp—because it is evident that these things are holy and divine—he forms them toward love of heavenly realities, where all secrets are revealed. The incense gives off a sweet fragrance when those who have been suddenly touched by God through compunction find delight in devoting themselves solely to tears and prayers.

It follows appropriately: “He shall burn incense perpetually before the Lord throughout your generations.” For it is necessary that after prayer and weeping the mind not turn aside to idle words or deeds, but preserve, even after prayer has ended, the same strength of devotion that it received in prayer, following the example of Anna, of whom it was said while she prayed: “Her face was no longer changed toward other things.”

“You shall not offer upon it incense of another composition.” In the subsequent part of this book the aromatics from which this incense ought to be composed are named individually: namely, stacte, onycha, galbanum of good fragrance, and the clearest frankincense. All these are understood to pertain to the meaning of eternal things, which are chiefly to be sought from the Lord.

Therefore no incense of another composition is to be offered upon the golden altar except that which the Lord prescribed, because when we pray we ought to seek from the Lord nothing other than what he himself commanded and promised that he would give, and to believe about him nothing other than what he himself taught.

“You shall not offer upon it any victim, nor pour out any libation.” All these things belong to the outer altar, which signifies the life of beginners and of those who are still making progress. The life of the perfect righteous is of such great sublimity that nothing carnal can be found in it which they must slaughter for the Lord.

It is true that wine libations sometimes signify the great power of spiritual grace: that is, either the cup of teaching, or the chalice of suffering, or the fervor of exceptional love, or the reception of the Holy Spirit itself, or something of this kind. But whenever a wine libation is offered together with the flesh of sacrificial victims, it signifies, according to the tropological interpretation, the holiness of those who still possess something among carnal things and desires that opposes purity of spirit and must be burned by the fire of the Holy Spirit on the altar of the heart.

The perfect righteous, however, who can say, “My heart and my flesh have failed; God is the God of my heart, and God is my portion forever” (Ps. 72), as the victims and libations cease—the things belonging to the outer bronze altar—offer inwardly upon the golden altar only the spices of heavenly desire to the Lord. For, having become more secure concerning the remission of sins, they grieve only over the delayed entry into the everlasting kingdom, and every night they water their bed with sweet streams of tears.

Concerning this altar it is suitably added: “And Aaron shall make atonement upon its horns once a year, with the blood of the offering for sin.” Our high priest offered his blood once a year for the sin of the whole world. He did so in that year of which Isaiah says that he came to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord—that is, throughout the whole period in which he graciously joined the Church to himself.

Once also, for each believer, he gave the washing of the sacred font as a mystery of his blood, for loosing the bonds of sins. There is a beautiful correspondence in the figure: once a year the high priest is commanded to make atonement upon the horns of the altar with the blood of the offering, but every day he is commanded to burn fragrant incense upon it. For our Lord and Savior, who renews his faithful daily by kindling in them the grace of inward compunction, redeemed them once for all by the sacrifice of his blood, conquering death.

The faithful themselves, who customarily wash away their daily sins with daily prayers and tears, rejoice that they have been absolved from all sins once for all in the sacrament of his passion. He makes atonement upon the horn of the altar because he not only lived among human beings and prayed for human beings, but even now, seated at the right hand of the Father in heaven, intercedes for us. Dwelling by faith in the hearts of the elect, and stirring them to pray, he is rightly said himself to pray.

“And he shall make atonement upon it throughout your generations. It shall be most holy to the Lord.” Aaron makes atonement upon the altar of incense when, on account of the righteousness of the saints for whom we seek an intercessor and patron, the Lord is made propitious toward us. Thus, when Hezekiah was besieged by enemies and invoked the Lord’s help, he said: “I shall save this city and protect it for my own sake and for the sake of David my servant” (2 Kings 19).

We may also interpret these altars in this way: the bronze altar, on which the flesh was burned and the blood of victims poured out, may signify the whole Church of the present age, in which no one is without sin, even if his life upon earth were only one day. No one is born according to the flesh without the sin of Adam’s transgression, and therefore everyone must be reborn in Christ and purified by the fire of the Spirit.

The golden altar, however, signifies the Lord himself, who in a wondrous and ineffable order took true flesh from Adam in such a way that he was truly free from the sin of Adam’s flesh. For both altars were made from wood of one and the same kind, but both were not covered with gold. On this altar, moreover, nothing carnal was offered; only spices were burned, because the Lord, pouring out prayers or tears, did so not for sins of his own—for he had none—but for our salvation.

Just as the ark placed within the veil signifies the man seated at the right hand of the Lord’s majesty in the heavens, so the altar placed outside the veil but near its entrance can figuratively express the same mediator between God and human beings: living among human beings in human form, yet penetrating the inner regions of heaven by the power of his divinity.

The altar of incense stood in the sanctuary, where the lampstand and table also stood, because the Word became flesh and dwelt among us. The ark stood within the veil because the same Lord Jesus, after his passion and resurrection, was taken up into heaven and sits at the right hand of God.

Aaron makes atonement upon the horns of his altar with the blood that was offered for sin, and he makes atonement upon it when priests, praying for the people of God or for their own ignorance, trust that they are to be helped through his only-begotten Son and saved through the sacrament of his passion. The Apostle urges this when he says: “Through him, therefore, let us continually offer to God a sacrifice of praise, that is, the fruit of lips confessing his name.”

This may suitably be understood of all, including the elect members of the high priest, who pray to the Father in spirit and in truth. For to whom could what is said—“It shall be most holy to the Lord”—belong more fittingly than to this altar? Of him, when he was born into the world, the archangel said to the Virgin Mother: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you” (Luke 1), and so forth.

The construction of the altar of incense has now been described. There remains a description of the bronze basin, in which the priests entering the tabernacle were to wash their hands and feet; but one commandment of the Lord has been passed over, which we too should briefly touch upon and explain according to our ability. It follows:

## CHAPTER XI. On the price commanded by the Lord to be paid for the souls of each member of the numbered people

The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “When you take the census of the children of Israel, each shall give, according to the number, a price for his soul to the Lord, and there shall be no plague among them. Everyone who passes into the census shall give this: half a shekel according to the measure of the sanctuary. A shekel contains twenty obols. Half a shekel shall be offered to the Lord.”

David forgot this command when he numbered the people, and therefore by numbering he brought a plague upon that same people (2 Sam. 24).

In the spiritual sense, the census of the children of Israel signifies the number of all the elect whose names are written in heaven. Each gives a price for his soul to the Lord when he offers him the service of diligent obedience in good works. Otherwise there will be a plague among them when they have been counted. For perpetual punishment awaits those who do not deserve to be joined to the number of the faithful and refuse to offer the Lord the perfect works of faith. It is said of such people: “They shall not give God their reconciliation, nor the price of the redemption of their soul” (Ps. 48).

“For the redemption of a man’s soul is his riches” (Prov. 13), as Solomon says—whether temporal riches, namely when he distributes them and gives them to the poor, “so that his righteousness may remain forever and ever” (Ps. 111); or spiritual riches, that is, the righteousness itself that he has practiced, whether by showing mercy to the poor or by doing other good works.

“Everyone who passes into the census shall give half a shekel,” that is, ten obols. This can be understood most appropriately as observance of the Ten Commandments of the Law. Whoever knows how to understand it correctly recognizes that the whole fullness of faith and works, together with the promise of future recompense, is contained in it.

Indeed, in the first three commandments love of God is comprehended, while in the following seven love of neighbor is comprehended, as the Apostle testifies: “Love is the fullness of the law” (Rom. 13).

Nor should another mystery be passed over, which is contained in the same number ten. The name Jesus begins among the Hebrews with the letter *yod*, and among the Greeks with *iota*; each is the sign of the number ten in its own language. Those offer ten obols as the price of their soul to the Lord who, believing in Jesus Christ, display upon their forehead and in their confession the sign of his name, which begins with the number ten.

Perhaps for the sake of this mystery the Lord testifies in the Gospel that not one *iota* can pass away from the Law, because the power of the Decalogue contained there, and the faith in his name mystically signified there, can never be corrupted by any disturbance caused by unbelievers.

“He who is counted in the census from twenty years old and upward shall give the price.” The number twenty signifies the joining of the two Testaments: the Law, written in five books, and the Gospel, which consists of four. For four times five makes twenty.

A person is therefore counted among the people of God at twenty years of age because only that person is worthy of the company of the elect who, aided by the grace of the Gospel, fulfills according to his measure and capacity the decrees of the Law understood spiritually, and awaits eternal rewards in heaven from the promises of that same grace.

“The rich shall not add to the half shekel, and the poor shall not diminish it.” Whether someone is great in merits and perfect, or still young and advancing in virtue, the same law of the Decalogue—that he love God and neighbor—is imposed upon all.

“You shall receive the money that has been collected from the children of Israel and give it for the use of the tabernacle of the testimony, so that it may be a memorial of them before the Lord and that he may be propitious to their souls.” The money received from the children of Israel is brought as their memorial before the Lord when everything good that we do is preserved in eternal memory with our Creator and Judge, so that he may deign to be propitious toward us on account of the fruits of good works that we have offered him.

The same money is preserved for use when, through the good acts of the righteous, the conduct and deeds of subsequent believers in Christ are strengthened, and the lesser strive to become like those whom they recognize as reigning with the Lord.

It should certainly be noted that the money mentioned is to be given not according to ordinary popular valuation but according to the measure of the sanctuary. The measure of the sanctuary is the disposition of the divine Law, which the Lord commands to be observed in his Church and for whose observance he nevertheless promises eternal rewards in the future.

But if someone strives to serve God according to the pleasure of human will, then, because he has not offered the money of his devotion according to the measure of the sanctuary, he will be struck by the plague of the last judgment, his offering having been rejected and cast aside.

## CHAPTER XII. On making the bronze basin

The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “You shall also make a bronze basin with its base, for washing. You shall place it in the tabernacle of the testimony, between the altar and the tabernacle, and, having poured water into it, Aaron and his sons shall wash their hands and feet in it, whenever they are to enter the tabernacle of the testimony and whenever they approach the altar.”

This basin—or laver, as it is called below—may indeed principally be understood as the water of baptism, by whose washing all who enter the doors of the Church must be cleansed. Yet it was placed between the tabernacle of the testimony and the altar of burnt offering because these same priests were commanded to wash in it twice each day, that is, morning and evening, when they entered to the altar to offer incense to the Lord.

But since the water of baptism permits us to wash only once, this laver more suitably commends to us the offering of compunction and tears, which we always need, but especially when we approach to minister at the heavenly mysteries. The altar of burnt offering, on which the flesh of victims was burned for the Lord, signifies the extinguishing of carnal desires through the fire of the Holy Spirit. The altar of incense signifies the purity of those who, having quieted every enticement of the flesh and ceased the struggle with vices, pour out tears solely in expectation and desire of entering heaven.

The laver is rightly placed after the altar of burnt offering, in which the priests wash before entering the tabernacle to burn incense to the Lord. The condition of tears and compunction is distinguished in two ways. First, it is necessary that anyone converted to the Lord should pray with poured-out tears for forgiveness of the sins he has committed. When, accompanied by worthy fruits of repentance, he has advanced for a long time, it remains for him, now more secure concerning the forgiveness he has received, to desire with longing the time when he may deserve to see the face of his Creator among the most blessed choirs of angels.

Whoever truly acts in this way cannot endure without tears either the length of this life or the delay of the next, saying of the present life: “Woe is me, for my sojourning has been prolonged; I have dwelt with the inhabitants of Kedar” (Ps. 119)—that is, with those who live in the darkness of errors and crimes, which is what the name *Kedar* signifies.

Already sighing for the joys of everlasting light, he finds life exceedingly wearisome, because to the degree that he thirsts for the heavenly homeland, he dreads the company of the wicked among whom he lives as a stranger, saying also of that homeland: “My soul has thirsted for the living God; when shall I come and appear before the face of God?” (Ps. 41).

That he could not bear this thirst without tears is shown by the words that follow: “My tears have been my bread day and night.” It is as though he openly said: The longer I am delayed from seeing the face of the God for whom I ardently thirst, the more sweetly I am refreshed by the bread of tears that I pour out in his memory.

Thus the altar of burnt offering signifies the tears of penitents for the sins they have committed; the altar of incense expresses the weeping of those who rejoice over the good works they have completed with the Lord’s help and desire the rewards that they trust the Lord will grant them. This weeping surpasses the former as gold surpasses bronze, and as the Holy of Holies, where the ark of the Lord was, surpassed the former tabernacle, in which the lampstand and the table of the Lord stood.

The laver was placed beside the altar of burnt offering, in which those entering the altar of incense were to wash, because no one suddenly becomes supreme. As merits advance, each person must first conquer the battles of vices; then, through the compunction of tears, he must humbly ask his Creator to grant him the ability to pour out sweet weeping for entry into the kingdom, when previously he poured out bitter tears through fear of punishments.

What could the base on which the laver was placed more suitably signify than the very desire for the kingdom and heavenly life? For its sake the perfect and supreme men cleanse themselves daily in the fountain of tears and, although they cannot yet possess the joy of inner rest through perfect living, at least taste it by sighing for it.

That this washing, placed between the tabernacle and the altar, signifies the tears of the perfect is testified by the very words that say: “And when water has been poured in, Aaron and his sons shall wash their hands and feet in it.” No one from the people is commanded to wash there; the high priest himself is commanded to do so, together with his sons, namely the priests of a lower rank, because just as the holy life of great men is more perfect, so their compunction is usually more exalted.

We do not say this as though only the ministers of the altar can or ought to possess the power of such compunction, but remembering the blessed Apostle Peter, who, speaking to all the faithful about the cornerstone, which is Christ, says: “You yourselves, as living stones, are being built up as a spiritual house, a holy priesthood, to offer spiritual sacrifices” (1 Pet. 2).

And John says in the Apocalypse: “Blessed and holy is he who has a share in the first resurrection; over these the second death has no power, but they shall be priests of God and of Christ” (Rev. 20).

We admonish all the faithful to be counted under the mystical name of priests, since they are members of Christ, the eternal priest. The blessed Apostle Paul also shows them what victims they ought to offer, saying: “I beseech you, brothers, by the mercy of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God” (Rom. 12).

Therefore Moses placed this laver not only for the ministers of the sacred altar but also for all the perfect, whatever their rank, because the Law of God proclaimed the grace of saving compunction generally to all the faithful.

If we wish to understand the great high priest, the Lord Savior himself, in the person of Aaron, it is clear that he too underwent the washing of this laver before entering to offer upon the altar. Before he burned the incense of his most holy body on the altar of the cross for our salvation, he also shed tears for our sake, as was most famously made known in the raising of Lazarus.

It is rightly added: “So that they may offer incense upon it to the Lord, lest they die” (John 11). Death is to be feared when it concerns the spiritual and eternal soul. If someone chosen for the ministry of the altar neglects to offer God the incense of prayers, death is to be feared. Death is also to be feared if someone presumes to enter the sacred mysteries without the spiritual washing of compunction and to handle the holy things of the Lord with common, unpurified hands.

Let them therefore wash their hands and feet in the water of the bronze laver and then approach the altar. Let them cleanse their actions and conduct with tears, and afterward extend their hands to touch the mysteries of Christ and set the steps of their feet in the courts of the Lord.

I think this command applies equally to those who are to be cleansed through receiving these same sacraments: they should first examine, sift, and purify their actions and thoughts with more careful attention, and then proceed to participate in the sacraments of faith, lest they deserve to hear the Apostle’s words: “Whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself, not discerning the body of the Lord” (1 Cor. 11)—that is, not separating the food of bread and wine from the usefulness of ordinary foods with a cautious and attentive mind.

It should be considered more carefully what is added in conclusion: “It shall be a perpetual ordinance for him and his descendants throughout their generations.” Literally, these observances have ceased; but according to the ancient understanding, they will never cease to be observed spiritually by the saints: “for him and his descendants throughout their generations”—not by being born from the stock of Aaron, but by believing in him whom Aaron believed, together with his grandfather.

## CHAPTER XIII. On preparing the finest ointment for consecrating the tabernacle and its vessels

[Col. 0218B]

The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “Take for yourself the finest spices: five hundred shekels of selected myrrh, half as much—that is, two hundred and fifty shekels—of cinnamon, likewise two hundred and fifty of calamus, and five hundred shekels of cassia, according to the sanctuary’s weight, together with a hin of olive oil. You shall make a holy anointing oil, a compounded ointment made by the work of a perfumer. With it you shall anoint the tabernacle of the testimony, the ark of the testimony, the table and all its vessels, the lampstand and its utensils, the altars of incense and of burnt offering, and all the equipment belonging to their service.

“You shall sanctify all these things, and they shall be most holy; whatever touches them shall be sanctified. You shall anoint Aaron and his sons, and sanctify them so that they may serve me as priests.

“You shall also say to the children of Israel: ‘This shall be my holy anointing oil throughout your generations. No human flesh shall be anointed with it, and you shall not make another according to its composition. It is holy, and it shall be holy to you. Whoever compounds anything like it and gives some of it to a stranger shall be cut off from his people’” (Exod. 30).

Be it observed and noted how he commanded everything to be anointed with the chrism-oil—namely, the tabernacle and the things that were in it—and then said that they would be “holy of holies”: that is, once everything had been anointed, it would be “holy of holies.” What, then, will now distinguish those inner parts that are covered by the veil, and so forth, if everything, once anointed, will be “holy of holies”? This must be investigated more carefully. We nevertheless believe that the following points should be noted, especially when we remember that, just as concerning that altar of sacrifices, which he wished to be called “holy of the holy” after its anointing, it was immediately said, “Everyone who touches it shall be sanctified,” so concerning all the things that were afterward called “holy of holies” because they had been anointed with that oil, the same statement follows: “Everyone who touches them shall be sanctified.”

This can be understood in two ways: either that one is sanctified by touching, or that one is sanctified in order that one may be permitted to touch. Yet it was not permitted for the people to touch the tabernacle when they offered sacrifices, or whatever offerings of theirs were presented to God. For what follows shows that this was not to be said only to the priests, nor only to the Levites, since he says to Moses, “And speak to the children of Israel.” The children of Israel were, of course, the whole people. He commands him to say: “This anointing oil shall be holy for you throughout your generations.
