It shall not be applied to the flesh of a human being, and according to this composition you shall not make another for yourselves in the same way. It is holy, and it shall be your sanctification. Whoever makes one like it, and whoever gives any of it to a foreign nation, shall perish from his people.”

He therefore commands not only the priests but the whole people of Israel not to make such an ointment for human uses. This is what he means by saying, “It shall not be applied to the flesh of a human being.” He thus forbids its being made for similar personal uses, and threatens death if anyone makes a similar preparation—that is, makes an ointment like it for his own use—or gives any of it to a foreign nation. Accordingly, when he says, “It shall be your sanctification,” and commands this to be said to the whole people of Israel, I do not see what else can be understood except that, when they came with their own offerings, they were permitted to touch the tabernacle, and by touching it they were sanctified.

*(From Isidore.)* Because of that oil with which all things were anointed, it was said, “Everyone who touches it shall be sanctified”; yet not in the same manner as the priests, who were also anointed with it in order to exercise the priesthood.

Moreover, the ointment with which the tabernacle is completely anointed is the chrism with which the faithful people are anointed, in whom the divinity dwells as in a tabernacle. This ointment may also be understood as the virtues of the saints, or the fragrance of righteousness spread far and wide, concerning which the Apostle says: “But thanks be to God, who always leads us in triumph in Christ Jesus and manifests through us the fragrance of his righteousness” (1 Cor. 2).

## CHAPTER XIV. On the preparation of incense from the most precious aromatics, and on Bezalel the craftsman

And the Lord said to Moses: “Take for yourself spices: stacte, onycha, sweet-smelling galbanum, and the clearest frankincense. All shall be of equal weight. You shall make incense compounded according to the art of the perfumer, carefully mixed and pure, and most worthy of sanctification. When you have pounded everything into the finest powder, you shall place some of it before the tabernacle of the testimony, in the place where I shall appear to you. The incense shall be most holy for you. You shall not make such a composition for your own uses, because it is holy to the Lord. Whoever makes a similar one in order to enjoy its fragrance shall perish from his peoples” (Exod. 30).

*(From Augustine.)* When he commanded from which spices the incense—that is, the fumigation—was to be made, and said that it was prepared according to the manner of a perfumer, as the work of a perfumer, we must not therefore think that an ointment was to be made, that is, something with which anyone would be anointed. Rather, as has been said, it was incense or fumigation to be placed upon that altar of incense, where it was not permitted to sacrifice and which was inside the Holy of Holies.

*(From Isidore.)* The incense that he compounds from four highly fragrant substances ground to the greatest fineness—namely, stacte, onycha, galbanum, and frankincense—the blessed John shows in the Apocalypse to have been established as a figure of the prayers of the faithful: “And,” he says, “the twenty-four elders fell down before the Lamb, each holding a harp and golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints.”

Although these four fragrances may also seem to signify the form of the four elements by their natures: frankincense, which is translucent, may be compared with air; stacte with water; and galbanum and onycha with earth and fire. Thus, through these, the whole creation—whatever is in heaven, beneath the heavenly assembly, on earth, and in the waters—may be understood as a pleasing incense to God, namely, the prayer of creation’s praise.

We make incense compounded from spices when we emit the fragrance of a multitude of virtues upon the altar of good works. It is made mixed and pure because, to the extent that virtue is joined to virtue, the incense of good works is offered with that much greater sincerity. Hence it is rightly added: “When you have pounded everything into the finest powder, you shall place some of it before the testimony of the tabernacle.”

We grind all the spices into the finest powder when we pound our good deeds in the hidden examination of the heart’s mortar and, if they are truly good, reconsider them minutely. To reduce the spices to powder, therefore, is to wear down the virtues by recollection and to call them back for the subtle scrutiny of hidden examination.

It should also be noted that it is said of this same powder, “You shall place some of it before the testimony of the tabernacle,” because our good deeds truly please the sight of the Judge only when the mind, by more subtle reflection, grinds them down—when what reduces the spices to powder ensures that what is done is not coarse and hard, and that, if the strict hand of reconsideration does not break it into pieces, it does not fail to scatter its fragrance more subtly.

“The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Behold, I have called by name Bezalel, son of Uri, son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah, and I have filled him with the spirit of God, with wisdom, understanding, and knowledge at all times, to devise skillfully whatever can be made from gold, silver, and bronze, from marble and precious stones, and from varieties of wood. Indeed, I have given him Oholiab, son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan, as his companion, and in the heart of every skilled person I have placed wisdom, so that they may make all that I have commanded you,” and so forth (Exod. 31).

What does it mean that, when he commanded Bezalel to be assigned to the works required for making the tabernacle, God said that he had filled him with the divine spirit of wisdom, understanding, and knowledge, so that he might devise and construct every work and practice architecture, and so forth? Are these works, which seem to belong to craftsmanship, also to be attributed to the gift of the Holy Spirit? Or was this said figuratively, so that those things which are signified by these objects might belong to the divine spirit of wisdom, understanding, and knowledge? Nevertheless, even here, although this man is said to have been filled with the divine spirit of wisdom and knowledge, the Holy Spirit is not yet mentioned by that name.

## CHAPTER XV. The commandment concerning the keeping of the Sabbath

The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “Speak to the children of Israel and say to them: See that you keep my Sabbath, because it is a sign between me and you throughout your generations, so that you may know that I am the Lord who sanctifies you. Keep the Sabbath, for it is holy for you. Whoever profanes it shall surely die. Whoever does work on it shall perish from the midst of his people. For six days you shall do work; on the seventh day is the Sabbath, a holy rest for the Lord. Whoever does work on this day shall die. Let the children of Israel keep the Sabbath and celebrate it throughout their generations. It is an everlasting covenant between me and the children of Israel, an enduring sign. For in six days the Lord made heaven and earth, and on the seventh he ceased from all his work” (Exod. 31).

It should be noted that in the Septuagint this passage reads as follows: “An everlasting testament between me and the children of Israel.” What does it mean that, when he commanded the observance of the Sabbath, he said, “It is an everlasting testament between me and the children of Israel”? He did not say “between me and the children of Israel,” but “in me and the children of Israel.” Is this because the Sabbath signifies rest, and we have no rest except in him?

For plainly he calls the whole people “the children of Israel”—that is, the offspring of Abraham, both his Israel according to the flesh and his Israel according to the spirit. For if Israel were to be understood only according to carnal descent, the Apostle would not say, “Behold Israel according to the flesh.” Here he plainly indicates that there is also an Israel according to the spirit, who is a Jew inwardly and possesses circumcision of the heart.

Thus the passage may perhaps be more correctly punctuated: “An everlasting testament in me.” From this there may be another meaning, with “the children of Israel” understood as an everlasting sign—that is, a sign of an eternal reality. In the same way, Christ is the rock because the rock signified Christ.

It should not, therefore, be understood that the everlasting covenant is “in me and the children of Israel,” as though it were in God. Rather, this everlasting covenant is in him, because eternal rest is promised in him; and for the children of Israel there is an everlasting sign, because they received the sign to be observed by which eternal rest is signified: for the true Israelites, that is, the children of promise who will see God face to face as he is.

And when Moses had finished speaking these words, he gave him on Mount Sinai two stone tablets of the testimony, written with the finger of God.

*(From Augustine.)* Although God spoke so many things, nevertheless two stone tablets were given to Moses, which are called the tablets of the testimony. They are a figure of the ark. Clearly, all the other things that God commanded are understood, if they are carefully sought and rightly understood, to depend upon those ten commandments written on the two tablets—just as those same ten commandments, in turn, depend upon the two commandments of love of God and of neighbor, upon which the whole Law and the Prophets depend.

## CHAPTER XVI. On Aaron’s transgression in the fornication of the golden calf

When the people saw that Moses was delayed in coming down from the mountain, they gathered against Aaron and said: “Arise, make gods for us to go before us. For as for this Moses, the man who brought us out of the land of Egypt, we do not know what has happened to him.”

Aaron said to them: “Take the golden earrings from the ears of your wives, your sons, and your daughters, and bring them to me.” The people did what he had commanded and brought the earrings to Aaron. When he had received them, he fashioned them by casting and made from them a molten calf. And they said: “These are your gods, Israel, who brought you out of the land of Egypt.”

When Aaron saw this, he built an altar before it and proclaimed with the voice of a herald: “Tomorrow is a solemnity of the Lord,” and so forth (Exod. 32).

When Aaron commands that the earrings be removed from the ears of the wives and daughters so that he might make gods for them, it may reasonably be understood that he wished to command something difficult, so that in this way he might turn them back from that intention. Yet I thought that the deed itself should be noted as difficult—that the gold should be used to make an idol—because of those who are distressed if they are told that something of this sort was divinely done or commanded to be endured with equanimity for the sake of eternal life.

“The people sat down to eat and drink, and they rose up to play.” Eating and drinking impelled them to play; play dragged them into idolatry. For if the fault of vanity is not carefully restrained, the unwary mind is immediately swallowed up by iniquity, as Solomon bears witness: “Whoever despises small things will gradually fall.” If we neglect to attend to small matters, we are imperceptibly led astray and then boldly commit even greater things.

The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “Go, descend, for your people, whom you brought out of the land of Egypt, have sinned. They have quickly departed from the way that you showed them. They have made for themselves a molten calf, and they have worshiped it and sacrificed victims to it, saying: ‘These are your gods, Israel, who brought you out of the land of Egypt.’”

It can also greatly edify the reader, in accordance with the historical account, if he considers how authority in governing and kindness in providing counsel are mingled in good rulers. Discipline or mercy will be greatly weakened if one is held without the other. Rulers should therefore possess toward their subjects both merciful justice in giving right counsel and a discipline that acts with benevolent severity.

It is a pleasure to contemplate in Moses’ heart mercy joined with severity. Let us see him loving, and acting with pious yet strict severity. Certainly, when the Israelite people had incurred before God an offense almost beyond remedy, so that their ruler heard, “Descend; your people have sinned”—as though the divine voice were saying to him, “Because they have fallen into such a sin, they are no longer mine”—it added: “Now therefore let me alone, so that my anger may burn against them and I may destroy them, and I will make you into a great nation.”

He, once and again opposing himself as a barrier to the assault of the angry God on behalf of the people over whom he ruled, said: “Either forgive them this sin, or, if you will not, blot me out of the book that you have written.” Let us consider with what inward compassion he loved that people for whose life he asked to be blotted out of the book of life.

Yet let us also consider how zeal for righteousness burned against the sins of the same people who bound him by so great a love. Immediately, after obtaining forgiveness by his first petition so that they would not be destroyed, he came to that same people and said: “Let each man put his sword upon his thigh. Go and return from gate to gate through the midst of the camp, and let each man kill his brother, his friend, and his neighbor.” And on that day about twenty-three thousand men fell.

Behold the man who sought the life of all, even at the cost of his own death, yet extinguished the lives of a few by the sword. Within, he burned with the fires of love; outwardly, he was kindled by the zeal of severity. So great was his piety that he did not hesitate to offer himself to death before the Lord on their behalf; so great was his severity that those whom he had feared God would strike, he himself struck with the sword of judgment.

He loved those over whom he ruled so much that he did not spare even himself for them; yet he pursued the guilty whom he loved so severely that, even when the Lord spared them, he cast them down. In both respects he was a strong ambassador, in both respects a remarkable mediator: by prayers he pleaded the people’s cause before the Lord, and by swords he vindicated God’s cause against the people. Within, by supplication, he opposed the divine anger; outwardly, by striking the guilt, he brought it to an end, hastening to aid all through the death made visible in a few.

For this reason almighty God more quickly heard his servant when he acted for the people: he saw that Moses himself would act for God against the people. Thus, in governing the people, Moses mingled both qualities, so that neither discipline would be lacking in mercy nor mercy in discipline.

## CHAPTER XVII. On how Moses softened the Lord’s anger against the people for their idolatry by his prayers, and on his rebuke of Aaron

Again the Lord said to Moses: “I see that this people is stiff-necked. Let me alone, so that my anger may burn against them and I may destroy them, and I will make you into a great nation.”

But Moses prayed to the Lord his God, saying: “Why, Lord, does your anger burn against your people, whom you brought out of the land of Egypt with great strength and a mighty hand? Please do not let the Egyptians say, ‘He brought them out deceitfully, in order to kill them in the mountains and destroy them from the earth,’” and so forth (Exod. 32).

All the saints who oppose the anger of God receive from God himself the power to set themselves against the force of his striking. So to speak, they rise with him against him. The divine power sets them against itself with itself, because while outwardly he allows them to oppose the anger that rages, inwardly the grace of the one who is angry cherishes them and raises up those who serve him inwardly, although outwardly he tolerates them as if they were opponents.

He therefore bears the contradiction of those who pray—a contradiction that he himself inspires—and, as though unwilling, accepts what he commands them to do. For he says to Moses: “Let me alone, so that my anger may burn against them, and I will make you into a great nation.” What does it mean to say to a servant, “Let me alone,” except to offer him the boldness to pray? It is as though he were saying openly: “Consider how much influence you have with me, and understand that you can obtain whatever you ask for the people.”

Yet, although this is so, it moves the reader’s mind less readily when, by the same holy man, the following is said in the account of blessed Job: “No one can resist his anger” (Job 9). It is very astonishing that no one is said to be able to resist the anger of God, when the divine words testify that many have stood against the indignation of heavenly judgment.

Did not Moses resist the anger of God? He stood on behalf of the falling people and restrained the very force of the heavenly blow by offering his own death, saying: “Forgive them this sin; otherwise blot me out of the book that you have written.”

Did not Aaron resist the anger of God when, standing between the living and the dead, he took the censer and tempered the fire of judgment with the smoke of incense?

Did not Phinehas resist the anger of God? He slew those who were indulging in lust with foreigners in the very act of intercourse, offered his zeal to the divine indignation, and appeased the fury with the sword.

Did not David resist the anger of God? He offered himself to the striking angel and, before the appointed time, demanded the grace of appeasement.

Did not Elijah resist the anger of God? After the earth had already remained dry for a long time, he recalled by his word the rains that had been withheld from heaven.

How, then, is it said that no one can resist the divine anger, when examples demonstrate that many have often resisted it?

But if we carefully weigh both the words of blessed Job and the deeds of those men, we recognize both truths: that the anger of God cannot be resisted, and that many have often resisted it. For many saints are shown, as the foregoing order of the narrative teaches, to have resisted the anger of the Lord.

The anger of God cannot be resisted when his indignation, so to speak, moves him from the depths of his being. When it moves him, human opposition cannot restrain it, nor can anyone’s prayer usefully interpose itself, when God has once inwardly determined to be angry.

Thus Moses, who wiped away the guilt of the whole people before the Lord by his prayers and, by offering himself as a barrier, appeased the force of the divine anger, later came to the rock of Horeb and, because he doubted concerning the provision of water, was unable to enter the promised land when the Lord was angry.

For this reason he is repeatedly afflicted when he approaches the matter and is repeatedly troubled as desire stirs him; he who, when the Lord willed it, removed the anger of the planned vengeance from the people, was unable to turn it away from himself. Similarly, because David afterward restrained the angel’s sword by prayer after the people had been struck down, he first fled from his son weeping and wailing barefoot, and he was in no way able to temper God’s anger on his own behalf until he had fully received the punishment for the crime he had committed.

Similarly, although Elijah, as a human being, experienced something small, as it were, of divine judgment—he who had opened the heavens by his word—he was terrified before the anger of a woman, fled through the wilderness, and, weakened on his own account, became fearful, although by intercession he appeased the fury of God on behalf of others.

The anger of God can therefore be resisted when he himself who is angry gives assistance; but it cannot be resisted at all when he stirs himself to vengeance and does not accept the prayer poured out to him.

“The Lord relented from doing the evil that he had said he would do against his people.” According to other copies: “And the Lord was appeased concerning the evil that he had said he would do to his people.” Here “evil” is intended to mean punishment, just as the outcome of those men was considered evil. In this sense it is said that both good and evil come from God—not according to the evil by which wicked people are evil. God is not evil, but he brings evil upon the wicked because it is just.

Moses returned from the mountain, carrying the two tablets of the testimony, written on both sides by the hand of God and made by the work of God. When he drew near the camp, he saw the calf and the dances. He became very angry, threw the tablets from his hand, and broke them at the foot of the mountain.

Moses appears to have been angry when he dashed against the ground and broke the tablets of the testimony written by the finger of God. Yet the repetition of the covenant was represented by a great mystery, because the old covenant was to be abolished and a new one established.

He seized the calf that they had made, burned it, and ground it to powder. He scattered the powder upon the water and gave it to the children of Israel to drink.

But what does this calf, which the children of Israel made in the wilderness, signify? And what does it mean that Moses burned the calf itself in the fire, cut it into pieces, sprinkled it upon the water, and gave the people a drink of it?

If he broke the tablets that he had received, written by the finger of God—that is, by the operation of the Holy Spirit—because he judged those to whom he was to read them unworthy, then, when he wished that the calf made by them should be completely abolished, he burned it, ground it up, scattered it in the water, and submerged it. Why, then, did he also give the people a drink made from it?

Should this deed not stir us to seek and understand its prophetic meaning?

Let attentive minds therefore recognize that the body of the devil is signified in the calf—that is, human beings in all the nations, for the devil is their head, or author, in these sacrileges. It is golden because the rites of idolatry appear to have been established, as it were, by wise men.

The Apostle speaks of them as follows: “Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became futile in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened. Claiming to be wise, they became fools, and exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of an image of corruptible man, and of birds, four-footed animals, and serpents” (Rom. 1).

From this wisdom also comes this golden calf, such as even the leading men of the Egyptians, as though educated men, were accustomed to worship as their creations.

The calf therefore signifies the whole body—that is, the entire fellowship—of the Gentiles devoted to idolatry. The Lord burns this sacrilegious fellowship with the fire of which he says in the Gospel: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth.” And because no one can hide from its heat, when the nations believe in him, the diabolical form in them is dissolved by the fire of his power.

Then the entire body is ground to pieces: that is, separated from the fusion of its evil conspiracy, it is humbled by the word of truth. Once ground up, it is cast into the water, so that the Israelites—that is, preachers of the Gospel—may transfer them from baptism into their own members, that is, into the body of the Lord.

Concerning these Israelites, Peter was told regarding the Gentiles themselves: “Kill and eat” (Acts 10). Why was it not, “Kill and drink”? Thus that calf was absorbed by those whom it had tried to swallow, through the fire of zeal, the edge of the word, and the water of baptism.

And he said to Aaron: “What did this people do to you, that you brought upon them so great a sin?”

He answered him: “Let not my lord be angry. For you know this people, that they are inclined to evil. They said to me, ‘Make gods for us to go before us. For this Moses, the man who brought us out of the land of Egypt, we do not know what has happened to him.’ I said to them, ‘Who among you has gold?’ They took it and gave it to me, and I threw it into the fire, and this calf came out.”

He spoke briefly here, not saying that he himself had fashioned it so that the molten calf might emerge. Or did he lie out of fear, as an excuse, pretending that he had thrown the gold into the fire to be consumed and that, without his doing anything, the form of a calf had emerged?

That he said this with such an intention should not be believed, because Moses could not have been unaware of what was in the man with whom God spoke, and he did not rebuke his brother for lying.

When Moses saw that the people had been stripped—for Aaron had stripped them because of the disgrace of their filth and had placed them naked among their enemies—it should be noted how the whole evil that the people committed is attributed to Aaron, because he had consented to their doing what they had wrongly requested.

It is more properly said that Aaron “stripped” or “dispersed” them because he yielded to them than that they dispersed themselves, since they were the ones who demanded so great an evil.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the vengeance inflicted upon the idolaters; on the Lord’s command that Moses lead the people into the promised land; and on the denial of his own presence during their passage

Standing at the gate of the camp, he said: “If anyone belongs to the Lord, let him join me.” And all the sons of Levi gathered to him. He said to them: “Thus says the Lord God of Israel: Let each man put his sword upon his thigh. Go and return from gate to gate through the midst of the camp, and let each man kill his brother, his friend, and his neighbor.” And the sons of Levi did according to the word of Moses, and so forth.

When Moses says to the Lord, “I beseech you: this people has sinned a great sin, and they have made gods of gold. And now, if you will forgive them their sin, forgive it; but if you will not, blot me out of the book that you have written,” he certainly spoke confidently, so that the reasoning implied by what follows might reach its conclusion: namely, that because God did not blot Moses out of his book, he forgave the people that sin.

Nevertheless, one should consider how great an evil Moses perceived in that sin, since he believed it had to be expiated by such slaughter, although he loved them so greatly that he poured out those words to God on their behalf.

It is rightly asked why, although Aaron is previously said to have stripped or dispersed the people, no vengeance was carried out against him—neither when Moses commanded everyone to be killed who encountered the armed Levites as they went through the camp and returned to the gate, nor when what Scripture says afterward occurred: “And the Lord struck the people because of the making of the calf that Aaron made.” This is especially noteworthy because the matter is emphasized here by repetition.

For it does not say, “The Lord struck the people because of the making of the calf that they made,” but “that Aaron made.” Yet Aaron was not struck.

What of the fact that God’s instructions concerning his priesthood, given before his sin, were fulfilled? He commanded that Aaron and his sons themselves be washed, and thus they were ordained to the priesthood.

He knows, therefore, whom to spare until a change for the better, and whom to spare for a time, although he foreknew that the person would not change for the better; and he knows whom not to spare so that he may be changed for the better, and whom not to spare in such a way that he does not even await his change.

The whole matter returns to what the Apostle exclaims: “How inscrutable are his judgments, and how unsearchable his ways!” (Rom. 11).

We must now investigate what prophetic meaning is contained in the fact that he ordered many of those who had fashioned an idol in his absence to be killed, without any hesitation arising from their relationships. It is easy to understand the killing of those men as signifying the death of such vices as had led them into the same idolatry.

The Apostle commands us to rage against such vices when he says: “Put to death, therefore, your members that are upon the earth” (Col. 3): fornication, uncleanness, lust, evil desire, and greed, which is the service of idols.

“If anyone belongs to the Lord,” he says, “let him come and join me. Let him put his sword upon his thigh. Go and return from gate to gate through the midst of the camp, and let each man kill his brother, his friend, and his neighbor.”

To put the sword upon the thigh is to place zeal for preaching above the pleasures of the flesh. Whoever is eager to speak holy things must necessarily take care to subdue suggestions of the flesh.

To go from gate to gate is to pass by rebuke from vice to vice, through which guilt enters the mind.

To pass through the midst of the camp is to live within the Church with such equality that the person who rebukes the faults of sinners must not deviate in any direction out of partiality.

Hence it is rightly added: “Let each man kill his brother, his friend, and his neighbor.” He kills his brother, neighbor, and friend who, whenever he finds something deserving punishment, does not spare them from the sword of rebuke, even those whom he loves because of kinship.

If, then, the person who is stirred to strike down vices by zeal for divine love is called God’s own, surely the person who refuses, as far as necessary, to rebuke the life of carnal people denies that he belongs to God.

The number of the three thousand who were killed also indicates the threefold form of sins. For every sin is committed either by deed, by word, or by thought.

And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “Go, ascend from this place, you and your people whom you brought out of the land of Egypt, into the land that I swore to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, saying, ‘I will give it to your offspring’” (Exod. 33).

“Go, ascend from here, you and your people whom you brought out.” Otherwise he would have said, “You and my people whom you brought out of the land of Egypt.”

But when they asked for the idol, they spoke in this way: “For this Moses, the man who brought us out of the land of Egypt, we do not know what has happened to him.” By assigning their liberation to a man, they had failed in their understanding. This is now repeated to them when he says, “You and your people whom you brought out of the land of Egypt.” The fault is theirs, not Moses’.

For Moses wanted nothing else than that they should place their hope not in him but in the Lord, and should believe that they had been liberated from that slavery by the Lord’s mercy, giving thanks for it.

Nevertheless, Moses’ merit before the Lord, as that of a most faithful servant, was so great through the Lord’s grace that God said to him, “Let me alone, so that I may be angry with them.” Whether the phrase “Let me alone” is the command of one ordering or the request of one asking, either interpretation appears absurd.

For if God commands, the servant would disobey by refusing; and it would not be fitting for the Lord to request this from a servant as though seeking a favor, especially since he could crush them even against Moses’ will.

The meaning therefore readily apparent is that, by these words, God signified how greatly that man benefited the people in his sight: they were loved by the man whom the Lord loved so greatly. We are thereby admonished that, when our merits weigh against us so that we are not loved by God, we may be raised up before him by the merits of those whom he loves.

For when the Almighty says to a man, “Let me alone, and I will crush them,” what else does he say than, “I would crush them if they were not loved by you”?

Thus “Let me alone” was said as though he were saying: “Do not love them, and I will crush them, because your love for them intervenes with me and prevents me from doing so.”

One ought to obey the Lord when he says, “Do not love them,” if he had said this as a command, rather than as an admonition expressing what held him back from punishing them.

Yet even though Moses interceded, God did not leave the people without the scourge of discipline. In some mysterious way, while Moses himself loved them so greatly, God loved them secretly, terrifying them openly.

The Lord said to Moses: “Go, ascend from here, you and your people whom you brought out of the land of Egypt, into the land that I swore to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, saying, ‘I will give it to your offspring.’”

Immediately, as though he were still speaking to Moses himself by a hidden conversion—which in Greek is called an *apostrophe*—he now speaks to the people themselves, saying:

“I will send my angel before you, and he will drive out the Canaanite, the Amorite, the Hittite, the Perizzite, the Girgashite, the Hivite, and the Jebusite. He will bring you into a land flowing with milk and honey. For I will not go up with you, lest I destroy you on the way, because you are a stiff-necked people.”

Great is the depth and wondrousness of the sacrament here: it is as though an angel could have greater mercy than the Lord, sparing a stiff-necked people.

Yet he also says that, in a certain sense, through his angel—and while absent from them, although he cannot be absent anywhere—he will fulfill what he swore to their fathers. It is as though he were also showing here that he does this because he promised it to those righteous fathers, not because these people were worthy.

What else, then, does this signify, unless perhaps that he is not with those who are stiff-necked because humility and devotion alone make him present as a merciful and saving God?

For God’s being with stiff-necked people means nothing other than his being present in judgment and punishment. When he is not present with the wicked in this way, he spares them by turning away. To this belongs the saying: “Turn your face from my sins” (Ps. 50), because if he does not turn his face away, he overturns them. Just as wax flows before the face of fire, so sinners perish before the face of God.

When the people heard this very grievous message, they mourned, and no one put on his customary adornment.

The people are said to have heard a very grievous message—that is, one most cruel and sorrowful. For what greater benefit can be granted to anyone than to have the grace of God present and to recognize that his Creator is favorable toward him? Or what greater danger is there than to endure the anger of one’s Creator? Whoever is deprived of the grace and presence of his Creator possesses nothing good.

And the Lord said to Moses: “Speak to the children of Israel: You are a stiff-necked people. If I should go up in your midst even once, I would destroy you. Now take off your adornment, and I shall know what to do with you.”

In the Septuagint this is likewise read: “Take off your garments of glory and your adornment, and I shall show what I will do with you.”

Here “to know” must be understood as “to reveal,” just as elsewhere “not to know” means “not to make manifest.” Hence the saying in the Gospel: “Concerning that day and hour no one knows, neither the angels of heaven nor the Son, but the Father alone.”

Moses also took the tabernacle, pitched it outside the camp, far away, and called it the tabernacle of the covenant. Everyone who had any matter to inquire about went out to the tabernacle of the covenant outside the camp. Whenever Moses went out to the tabernacle, the whole people arose, and each person stood at the entrance of his tent. They watched Moses’s back until he entered the tent. When he had entered the tabernacle of the covenant, the pillar of cloud descended and stood at the entrance. He spoke with Moses while everyone saw that the pillar of cloud stood at the entrance of the tabernacle; and they themselves stood and worshiped at the doors of their tents.

The Hebrew people, liberated from Egyptian slavery, stood at the doors of their tents and worshiped when they saw the pillar of cloud while God was speaking. Concerning them it is also said: “Whenever Moses went out to the tabernacle, the whole people arose, and each person stood at the entrance of his tent.” For what does it mean for the people to look upon the pillar of cloud, stand at the doors of their tents, and worship, except that when the human mind glimpses, however obscurely, those higher and heavenly realities, it already strains beyond the barriers of its bodily dwelling through uplifted thought and humbly worships him? Although it cannot see his substance, it nevertheless already marvels at his power through the illumination of the Spirit.

And when Moses enters the tabernacle, the people look upon his back and remain at the entrances of their tents, because whenever a holy preacher speaks lofty things about God, he already enters both tabernacles of the heavenly dwelling. Though the weak cannot fully weigh the power of his preaching, they nevertheless look, as it were, upon his back, because they follow in understanding those latter things that they are able to grasp. Yet even in those smallest matters that they are capable of understanding, they already seem to leave their tents and stand at the entrances, because they strive both to leave the habitations of the flesh and to advance toward the joys of eternal life that they hear proclaimed.

Moses said to the Lord: “You command me to lead this people away, but you do not indicate whom you will send with me, especially since you have said, ‘I know you by name, and you have found favor before me.’” In some copies it is read: “I know you above all others, and you have favor with me,” which is nearly the same. What else does “I know you by name” mean except “I know you above all others,” that is, “I know you specially above all others”? For a person’s particular character is also indicated by his name.

[“Therefore, if I have found favor in your sight, show yourself to me openly, so that I may see you, so that I may continue to find favor before you, and so that I may know that this nation is your people.”]

The Greek has γνωστὸς, *known*. Some Latins translated this as “openly” or “manifestly,” although Scripture did not say φανερῶς, *openly*. It might therefore perhaps more properly be rendered: “If I have found favor in your sight, show yourself to me so that I may see you with understanding.” By these words Moses makes it sufficiently clear that, despite such great intimacy of vision, he did not see God in the manner in which he desired to see him.

All the visions of God that were presented to mortal minds, and through which sound was produced so that mortal hearing might be touched, were displayed in whatever form God wished, so that the divine nature itself would not be perceived by any bodily sense. That nature is wholly invisible everywhere and contained by no place.

And because the whole law depends upon two commandments—love of God and love of neighbor—Moses therefore expressed his desire in both. He expressed love of God when he said: “If I have found favor in your sight, show yourself to me openly, so that I may see you, so that I may continue to find favor in your sight.” He expressed love of neighbor when he said: “And so that I may know that this nation is your people.”

It is asked how God could have said to Moses, “I know you above all others.” Does God know some things more and others less? Or is this according to what is said to certain people in the Gospel: “I do not know you”? This refers to the kind of knowledge by which God is said to know what pleases him and not to know what displeases him—not because he is ignorant of those things, but because he does not approve them. In the same way, an art is rightly said not to know defects when it rejects defects.

God knew Moses above all others because Moses pleased God above all others. It should be noted that Moses himself had earlier said to God, “You told me, ‘I know you above all others,’” and that after Moses himself said this, God is recorded as having said it; previously, however, it is not recorded. We should therefore understand that not everything God said to him was written down. Yet the earlier portions of Scripture must be examined more carefully to determine whether this is truly so.

## CHAPTER XIX  
### On Moses’s desire to contemplate the face of God and on the Lord’s passing before him

The Lord said: “My face will go before you, and I will give you rest.” Moses replied: “If you yourself do not go before us, do not lead us away from this place. For by what means shall I and your people know that we have found favor in your sight, unless you walk with us, so that we may be distinguished from all the peoples who dwell upon the earth?”

The Lord said to Moses: “I will also do this word that you have spoken. For you have found favor before me, and I know you by name.” Moses said: “Show me your glory.” He replied: “I will show you all my goodness, and I will call upon the name of the Lord before you. I will have mercy on whom I wish, and I will be gracious to whomever I please.” Again he said: “You cannot see my face. For no human being shall see me and live.”

And again: “Behold,” he said, “there is a place with me upon the rock. When my glory passes by, I will place you in a cleft of the rock and protect you with my right hand until I pass by. Then I will take away my hand, and you shall see my back; but you cannot see my face” (Exodus 33).

But if it was God with whom Moses spoke face to face, why did he ask to see the one whom he was seeing? This request more clearly establishes that Moses knew that he was to behold, through the radiance of God’s unbounded nature, him whom he had already begun to see through certain images. Thus the heavenly essence might be present to the eyes of his mind, insofar as a created image had been present to him temporally for the vision of eternity.

The fathers of the Old Testament therefore saw the Lord, yet, in John’s words, “no one has ever seen God.” And according to that same saying of the Lord, “No one has seen God and lived.” For those dwelling in this mortal flesh, God could both be seen through certain bounded images and could not be seen through the unbounded light of eternity.

But if, even while still in this corruptible flesh, certain people who were growing in immeasurable virtue could see the eternal glory of God through a certain sharpness of contemplation, this too does not conflict with the meaning of the statement: “No human being shall see me and live.” Whoever has seen Wisdom, which is God, dies completely to this world, so that he may no longer be held by its love.

No one has seen Wisdom while still living according to the flesh, because no one can embrace God and the world at the same time. Whoever has seen God dies by that very act, insofar as he is wholly separated from the loves of this life either in the intention of his heart or in the affection expressed through his deeds. No one, therefore, has seen God and lived. It is as though it were said plainly: No one has ever seen God spiritually while continuing to live carnally in the world.

When Moses had said to the Lord, “Show me your glory,” the Lord replied: “My glory will pass before you, and I will be called by the name of the Lord in your sight; I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will show compassion to whom I show compassion.”

A little earlier he had said: “I myself will go before you,” or, according to another edition, “My face will go before you, and I will give you rest.” How, then, does Moses seem to have understood this as: “I will go before you,” as though the Lord would not be with the people who would be present on the journey? For this reason Moses said: “If you yourself do not come with us, do not lead me away from here,” and so forth.

God did not deny him this, but said: “I will also do this word that you have spoken.” How, then, after Moses had said to him, “Show me your glory,” does he again seem to speak as though he would go ahead and would not be with them: “I will pass before you,” or, “My glory will pass before you”?

This must be understood differently. The one understood to speak and say, “I will pass before you,” is the one of whom the Gospel says: “When the hour had come for Jesus to pass from this world to the Father” (John 13). This passing is also said to be interpreted as the Passover.

This, therefore, is a great prophecy indeed. He himself passes before all the saints from this world to the Father in order to prepare for them the dwellings of the kingdom of heaven, which he will give them in the resurrection of the dead, since he was made the firstborn from the dead, passing before all others.

He strongly commends his grace in the very words: “And I will call upon the name of the Lord in your sight.” This is as though it were in the sight of the people of Israel, whose type Moses represented as he heard these things. In the sight of that nation itself, dispersed throughout the world, the Lord Jesus is called among all the nations.

He said, “I will call,” not “I will be called,” using an active verb in place of a passive one, an unusual form of expression in which a profound meaning is concealed. For perhaps he wished to signify that he himself would bring this about: namely, that by his grace the Lord would be called among all the nations.

When he added, “I will have mercy on whom I have had mercy, and I will show compassion to whom I have shown compassion,” he clearly demonstrated that the calling by which he called us into his kingdom and glory was not on account of our merits but on account of his mercy.

Since he promised that he would bring the nations in by saying, “I will call upon the name of the Lord in your sight,” he emphasized that he would do this mercifully. As the Apostle says: “For I say that Christ became a minister of the circumcision for the sake of the truth of God, to confirm the promises made to the fathers. But the Gentiles are to glorify God for his mercy” (Romans 15).

This, therefore, had been foretold: “I will have mercy on whom I have had mercy, and I will show compassion to whom I have shown compassion.” By these words he prevented human beings from boasting as though of the merits of their own virtues, so that “the one who boasts may boast in the Lord.”

He did not say, “I will have mercy on such and such people,” but “on whom I am merciful,” thereby showing that no one had earned the mercy of so great a holy calling through preceding good works. Indeed, Christ died for the ungodly.

But whether he intended to repeat the same thing when he added, “I will show compassion to whom I have shown compassion,” or whether, as others have translated it, “to whom I am merciful,” I do not know. What was expressed in Greek by two words, ἐλεήσω and οἰκτειρήσω—words that seem to signify one and the same thing—a Latin speaker could not express with different words except by repeating the same mercy in different forms.

If one were to say, “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I have mercy on whom I will have had mercy,” or, “I will have mercy on whom I have had mercy,” it would not seem an entirely suitable expression. Yet the meaning itself is stronger there: God demonstrated the firmness of his mercy by this repetition, just as in “Amen, amen,” or “So be it, so be it,” and as in Pharaoh’s repeated dream and many similar examples.

Alternatively, God may have pronounced in this way that he would show mercy to both peoples, namely the Gentiles and the Hebrews. For the Apostle says: “For just as you once disobeyed God but now have received mercy because of their disobedience, so they too have now disobeyed, so that through the mercy shown to you they too may receive mercy” (Romans 11). God has shut up all in disobedience so that he may have mercy on all.

After this commendation of his mercy, he responds to what had been said to him: “Show me your glory,” or to Moses’s earlier request: “Show yourself to me openly, so that I may see you.”

“You cannot,” he says, “see my face. For no human being shall see my face and live.” He thereby shows that God as he is cannot appear to this life, which is lived through the senses of mortal and corruptible flesh—that is, he cannot appear as he may be seen in the life where, in order to live, one must die to this life.

The Scripture then inserts a transition and says: “And the Lord said.” It continues: “Behold, there is a place with me.” For what place is not with God, who is absent nowhere? Yet by saying, “Behold, there is a place with me,” he signifies the Church, commending it as his temple.

“And you shall stand,” he says, “upon the rock,” because the Lord says: “Upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matthew 16). “As soon as my glory passes by, you shall stand upon the rock.” For after Christ’s passing—that is, after Christ’s passion and resurrection—the faithful people stood upon the rock.

“And I will place you,” he says, “in a cavern of the rock.” He also signifies the firmest protection. Others, however, translated this as “in a watchtower of the rock.” But the Greek has ὀπὴν, which we translate as “a hole” or “cavern.”

“And I will cover you with my hand until I pass by; and I will take away my hand, and then you shall see my back, but my face shall not be seen by you.”

Since he had already said, “You shall stand upon the rock as soon as my glory passes by,” where he is understood to have promised stability upon the rock after his passing, how should we understand his saying: “I will place you in a cavern of the rock and cover you with my hand until I pass by; then I will take away my hand, and you shall see my back”?

It is as though, after Moses had already been established upon the rock, God covered him with his hand and then passed by, although Moses could not be upon the rock except after God’s passing. This must be understood as a recapitulation of an earlier event, a device that Scripture often uses in many places.

Afterward it said what occurred earlier in temporal order. The order is therefore as follows: “I will cover you with my hand until I pass by, and then you shall see my back; for my face shall not be seen by you. You shall stand upon the rock as soon as my glory passes by, and I will place you in a cavern of the rock.”

This took place in those whom Moses’s person then signified, namely the Israelites, who later believed in the Lord Jesus, as the Acts of the Apostles indicate—“as soon as his glory passed by.”

For after he had risen from the dead and ascended into heaven, and the Holy Spirit had been sent from above, while the apostles were speaking in the tongues of all nations, many of those who had crucified Christ were cut to the heart. Had they known him, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory.

“Blindness in part has happened to Israel” (Romans 11), just as it had been said: “I will cover you with my hand until I pass by.” Hence the Psalmist says: “For day and night your hand was heavy upon me” (Psalm 31). He calls it “day” when Christ worked divine miracles, and “night” when he died as a human being and those who had believed during the day stumbled.

This, then, is the meaning: “When I have passed by, then you shall see my back.” When I have passed from this world to the Father, those who are represented by you will believe in me afterward.

Then they were cut to the heart and said: “What shall we do?” (Acts 2). The apostles ordered them to repent and to be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ so that their sins might be forgiven.

The psalm continues after the words, “Day and night your hand was heavy upon me,” namely, “so that I might understand.” For if they had understood, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory.

It continues and joins this to what follows: “I turned in distress while the thorn was being crushed,” that is, “when I was cut to the heart.” Then he added: “I acknowledged my sin, and I did not conceal my iniquity.”

After they saw the enormity of the crime by which they had crucified Christ, those who accepted the counsel to repent and receive forgiveness of sins in baptism said: “I will declare my transgression to the Lord”; and you forgave the wickedness of my heart.

The fact that this was rather a prophecy than something the Lord literally spoke to Moses is sufficiently indicated by what followed. Nothing is subsequently recorded as having visibly happened concerning the rock or its cavern, the covering of his hand, or the vision of his back.

Immediately afterward, with another transition inserted, Scripture adds: “And the Lord said to Moses,” although the Lord himself was certainly speaking the preceding words as well. From that point it continues with what the Lord says next.

## CHAPTER XX  
### On Moses’s obtaining the tablets of the law from God a second time, and on the commandments given to the people

“Cut for yourself two stone tablets like the first ones, and I will write upon them the words that were on the tablets that you broke. Be ready in the morning, so that you may immediately go up Mount Sinai, and stand with me on the summit of the mountain. No one shall go up with you, and no one shall be seen throughout the whole mountain. The sheep and cattle also shall not graze opposite it” (Exodus 34).

The Lord commands Moses to be ready in the morning to go up Mount Sinai immediately, so that he may stand with the Lord on the summit of the mountain. Spiritually, this signifies that those who preside over God’s people should prepare their hearts to receive divine wisdom.

He is therefore ready in the morning to ascend who, after dispelling the darkness of vices and carnal desires, raises his mind to contemplate heavenly things, so that, standing firmly in the Catholic faith, he may become a participant in divine contemplation.

He also forbids the sheep and cattle to graze opposite it, because the simple and those occupied with earthly works are not capable of meditating upon spiritual and divine mysteries.

Moses therefore cut two stone tablets like the former ones. Rising during the night, he went up Mount Sinai as the Lord had commanded him, carrying the tablets with him. When the Lord descended in the cloud, Moses stood with him, invoking the name of the Lord.

What does the Lord’s descending in the cloud mean except that he offers himself for investigation under the veil of mysteries? Hence the Prophet says: “He made darkness his hiding place” (Psalm 17). And in Job: “The cloud is his hiding place” (Job 22).

Thus, according to the Apostle, “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma” (1 Corinthians 13). But then—that is, at the time of the universal judgment—when we have been transferred from death to life and from corruption to incorruption, we shall contemplate the glory of the Lord with unveiled face.

Meanwhile, until the day dawns and the shadows decline, let us, following Moses’s example, remain with him and invoke the name of the Lord. Let us pray more earnestly, so that by his grace and according to the abundance of his mercy he may deign to illuminate us for the things that must be understood and to help us with the things that must be done.

When the Lord had passed before him, he said: “Ruler, Lord God, merciful and gracious, patient and of great compassion, and true, who keep mercy for thousands, who take away iniquity, crimes, and sins, and before whom no one is innocent of himself.”

“No one,” he says, “is innocent of himself before you.” How can anyone be innocent of himself before God, when Scripture says: “There is no one upon earth who does good and does not sin” (2 Chronicles 6)? And elsewhere: “The stars,” he says, “are not pure in his sight, and in his angels he found wickedness” (Job 4).

Therefore each person must necessarily ask to be cleansed by him who alone is without stain, who alone possesses immortality and dwells in inaccessible light. To him the psalm says: “Wash me more thoroughly from my iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin. For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and my mother gave birth to me in sins” (Psalm 50).

And in the Book of Job: “Who can make clean what was conceived from unclean seed? Is it not you alone?” (Job 14).

It continues: “Who repay the iniquity of the fathers upon the children and grandchildren, to the third and fourth generation.”

Although elsewhere the Lord says through the prophet: “The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, nor the father the iniquity of the son; the righteousness of the righteous shall be upon him, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon him,” and so forth (Ezekiel 18), what does it mean that Moses now says to the Lord, “Who repay the iniquity of the fathers upon the children and grandchildren”?

When a different meaning is found in these two statements, the mind of the hearer is instructed to seek carefully the path of distinction.

Original sin is indeed drawn from parents, and unless it is dissolved through the grace of baptism, we also bear the sins of our parents, since we are still, so to speak, one with them. Thus the iniquity of the fathers is repaid in the children when the soul of the offspring is polluted by original sin on account of the parents’ guilt.

Conversely, the iniquity of the parents is not repaid in the children because, when we are freed from original guilt through baptism, we no longer possess the sins of our parents but those that we ourselves commit.

This may also be understood in another way: whoever imitates the iniquity of an evil parent is also bound by guilt arising from that parent; but whoever does not imitate the parent’s iniquity is in no way burdened by that parent’s sin.

Thus it happens that an evil child of an evil father pays not only for the sins he himself has added but also for his father’s sin, because he does not fear to add his own wickedness to the father’s ways—ways by which he knows the Lord was angered.

It is just that those who, under a strict judge, are not afraid to imitate the ways of an evil parent should be compelled in the present life also to pay for the faults of that evil parent.

Hence it is also said there: “The soul of the father is mine, and the soul of the son is mine. The soul that sins shall itself die.” For sometimes, in the flesh, children are killed even because of their father’s sin; but the soul is not held by the guilt of original sin on account of the parents’ wickedness.

For what does it mean that little children are often seized by demons except that the flesh of the child is punished because of the father’s penalty? The wicked father is struck in himself, yet refuses to feel the force of the blow. Often he is struck through his children so that he may burn more fiercely, and the father’s pain is inflicted upon the flesh of his children, so that the wicked mind of the father may be punished through the sufferings of his children.

When not little children but already older children are afflicted because of their parents’ guilt, what else is plainly indicated except that they also suffer the penalties of those whose deeds they followed?

Thus it is rightly said, “To the third and fourth generation.” For the vengeance extends as far as the third and fourth generation because children can see the life of their parents whom they imitate up to that point; the punishment extends to those who have seen that they would follow evil.

Moses quickly bowed forward to the ground and worshiped, saying: “If I have found favor in your sight, Lord, I beg you to walk with us—for the people are stiff-necked—and to take away our iniquities and sins, and to possess us.”

The Lord answered: “I will make a covenant. In the sight of all I will perform signs such as have never been seen upon the earth or among any nations, so that the people in whose midst you are may see the terrible work of the Lord that I am about to do.”

When Moses was praying for the salvation of the people entrusted to him, asking that the Lord grant them his grace and remove their sins and transgressions, why did the Lord answer: “I will make a covenant; in the sight of all I will perform signs such as have never been seen upon the earth,” and so forth?

What are those signs that have never been seen upon the earth? Do those signs perhaps refer to the New Testament—namely, the Lord’s incarnation, passion, and resurrection?

Concerning such signs the prophet Isaiah said to the faithless king who refused to ask for one when commanded by the Lord: “Hear, then, house of David: Is it not enough for you to weary human beings, that you should also weary my God? Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign. Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and you shall call his name Emmanuel. He shall eat butter and honey, so that he may know how to reject evil and choose good” (Isaiah 7).

The covenant was therefore truly made with the people of God when, through Christ’s coming, the Gospel was proclaimed in the world.

“Observe everything that I have commanded you today. I myself will drive out before you the Amorite, the Canaanite, the Hittite, the Perizzite, the Hivite, and the Jebusite.”

What does it mean when Moses is told, “Observe everything that I have commanded you today”? Did he intend to speak about the people, whose teacher he himself was? Yet he himself did not introduce the people into that land where, he says, the testament or covenant was to be established with those who inhabited it.

“Beware lest you ever make an alliance with the inhabitants of that land; let it become a ruin for you. Destroy their altars, break their statues, and cut down their sacred groves. Do not worship a foreign god. The Lord—Jealous is his name—is an emulating God. Do not make a covenant with the people of those regions, lest, when they have prostituted themselves with their gods and worshiped their images, someone invite you to eat of the sacrifices. You shall not take wives for your sons from among their daughters, lest, after they have prostituted themselves, they make your sons prostitute themselves to their gods. You shall not make for yourself molten gods.”

When God was commanding Moses that, once the land had been placed under their control, all idolatry should be overthrown and foreign gods should not be worshiped, he said: “For the Lord God, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God.” That is, the very name by which the Lord God is called is “Jealous,” because God is a jealous God.

He does not do this through the fault of human agitation, but is always and in every way unchangeable and tranquil. Rather, this word indicates that his people will not go unpunished for prostituting themselves with foreign gods.

The word is drawn metaphorically from marital jealousy, which guards a wife’s chastity and benefits us, not God. For who could harm God by this kind of prostitution? It harms the person himself greatly, so that he may perish.

(From Origen.) God forbids this by the most dreadful warning, calling himself jealous. To him the psalm says: “You destroyed everyone who prostitutes himself away from you. But for me, it is good to cling to God” (Psalm 72).

Then Scripture repeats the matters it commended earlier: namely, the three principal festivals, the offering of the firstborn, and the firstfruits of the crops. Since these have already been expounded according to the interpretation of the Fathers, we do not think it necessary to repeat them here.

“Moses was there in the presence of the Lord forty days and forty nights; he neither ate bread nor drank water,” and so forth. He had said the same earlier, when he received the tablets that he broke. Here too he repeats it—not by recapitulating what had happened, but by emphasizing again what had happened.

(From Isidore.) We have already explained what the repetition of the law signifies: the tablets represented the image of the ancient law, which did not cease after a long interval because of the people’s sin. The other tablets, cut again in the likeness of the first, represented the New Testament. They are not broken, to show that the words of the New Testament will endure.

Hence it is fittingly indicated that they were to be read as ten words, so that the figure of the cross might be expressed through the same number. For the form of the cross is contained in the letter X. One straight stroke is drawn from top to bottom, while another, by a different but similar course, is drawn upward across it to form the transverse arms.

Therefore he himself says: “I have not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it” (Matthew 5)—certainly through the passion of the cross, whose image was present in the tablets.

When he says, “He neither ate bread nor drank water,” this is understood to mean that he fasted. Scripture signifies the whole by a part: by the word “bread,” all food, and by the word “water,” all drink.

What does it mean that Moses fasted for forty days? There is a certain figure in the consideration of this number. For Moses, Elijah, and the Lord himself fasted for forty days. We are instructed by the Law and the Prophets, and by the Gospel itself, which has testimony from the Law and the Prophets.

For this reason the Savior shone on the mountain between the two persons, so that we might restrain our appetite from all the enticements of the world as though by a fast of moderation, for as long as the perfection of the Decalogue is proclaimed throughout the four parts of the same world—that is, throughout the whole earth—so that ten multiplied by four may signify the number forty.

“And I wrote on the tablets the ten words of the covenant.” This is said of Moses, that he himself wrote them. A little earlier God had also said to him: “Write these words for yourself.”

When he first received the law, whose tablets he threw down and broke, he is not said to have cut the stone tablets himself. Now, however, it is said: “Cut for yourself two stone tablets,” nor was he then told to write upon them as he is told now, nor is he narrated to have written them himself, as Scripture now says: “He wrote on the tablets the ten words of the covenant.”

At that time, however, it was said: “And he gave Moses, as soon as he had finished speaking with him on Mount Sinai, the two tablets of the testimony, stone tablets written with the finger of God.”

A little later it says: “Moses turned and descended from the mountain, and the two stone tablets were written on both sides; on one side and the other they were written. The tablets were the work of God, and the writing was God’s writing engraved upon the tablets.”

A great question therefore arises: how could those tablets, which Moses was to make with God’s foreknowledge, be called not the work of a human being but the work of God; and not written by a human being but by God’s writing and God’s finger? The later tablets, however, destined to remain for so long and to be kept in God’s tabernacle and temple, were made by a human being at God’s command and written by a human being.

Perhaps God’s grace was signified in the earlier tablets. They were not the work of a human being, because those who turned back in their hearts to Egypt and made an idol had rendered themselves unworthy of grace. They were deprived of that benefit, and for this reason Moses broke the tablets.

The later tablets, however, signified those who boast of their own works. Hence the Apostle says: “Being ignorant of God’s righteousness and seeking to establish their own, they did not submit to God’s righteousness” (Romans 10). Therefore tablets written by human labor were given to signify those who would boast of their own works while the tablets remained with them, rather than of the finger of God—that is, of the Spirit of God.

Certainly, then, the repetition of the law signifies the New Testament, whereas the former tablets signified the Old Testament. The former was broken and abolished, especially since, when the law was given a second time, it was not given with the terror that accompanied the first—with such a great tumult of fires, clouds, and trumpets.

For the people, terrified, said: “Let God not speak to us, lest we die.” This signifies fear in the Old Testament and love in the New.

How, then, is the question resolved: why were the first tablets the work of God, while these are the work of a human being; why were the former written with the finger of God, while these were written by a human being?

Perhaps the Old Testament was signified more especially in the first tablets because God commanded them for himself, but the human being did not make them. For the law was established in the Old Testament to convict transgressors; it entered in so that sin might abound.

It was not fulfilled through fear, since it is fulfilled only through love. Thus it is called the work of God because God established the law. God wrote it, and no human work followed, because the human being did not obey God; rather, the law made him guilty.

In the second tablets, however, the human being made and wrote the tablets with God’s help, because the love of the New Testament fulfills the law. Hence the Lord says: “I have not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it.” The Apostle says: “Love is the fullness of the law,” and “faith working through love” (Romans 13).

Thus what was difficult in the Old Testament became easy for the human being in the New Testament: he possessed faith working through love, and the finger of God—that is, the Spirit of God—wrote it inwardly upon the heart, not outwardly upon stone.

Hence the Apostle says: “Not on tablets of stone but on tablets of fleshy hearts,” because the love of God (Romans 5), by which the commandment is truly fulfilled, “has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.”

This, then, is the first law that was given, where the Old Testament is signified. It is solely the work of God and the writing of God’s finger, of which the Apostle says: “Thus the law is indeed holy, and the commandment holy, righteous, and good.”

The holy and good law is therefore the work of God, in which the human being does nothing because he does not obey; rather, he is weighed down by guilt under a law that threatens and condemns. For he says: “Sin, so that it might appear as sin, worked death in me through what is good.”

But a human being is blessed when this holy, righteous, and good commandment is also his work—but through the grace of God.

## CHAPTER XXI  
### On Moses’s descent from the mountain, on his horned face, which the children of Israel could not see unveiled, and on his explaining the word of the Lord to them; and on the observance of the Sabbath

When Moses descended from Mount Sinai, he held the two tablets of the testimony and did not know that his face had become horned through his association with the word of God.

When Aaron and his sons saw that Moses’s face was horned, they were afraid to approach. They were summoned by him and returned—Aaron as well as the leaders of the assembly. After he had spoken, all the children of Israel also came to him, and he commanded them everything that he had heard from the Lord on Mount Sinai.

When he had finished speaking, he placed a veil over his face. Whenever he entered before the Lord and spoke with him, he removed it until he came out; then he spoke to the children of Israel everything that had been commanded him.

They saw that Moses’s face was horned when he came out, but he covered his face again whenever he spoke to them (Exodus 34).

But when Moses descended again with the tablets, his face appeared glorified, yet it was covered with a veil. This signified that the same law was covered and concealed by a mystical veil, hidden from unbelievers. For the discourse of the law possesses the glory of knowledge, but that glory is secret. It also has the horns of the two Testaments, with which it advances armed against the doctrines of falsehood.

When Moses is read, a veil is placed over their hearts. While unbelievers, through excessive dullness of heart, understand the writings of the Law and the Prophets in a carnal manner, the entire face of Moses is covered for them by a kind of veil, so that they cannot endure the glory of the speaking law. But if they turn to God, the veil will be removed. The letter that kills will die; the Spirit that gives life will be raised up, for the Lord is Spirit, and the law is spiritual. Hence David also prayed in the psalm: “Open my eyes, and I shall contemplate the wonders of your law” (Psalm 118 [119]).

When the whole multitude of the children of Israel had therefore been assembled, he said to them: “These are the things that the Lord commanded to be done” (Exodus 35). “These,” he says, “are the words that the Lord said were to be done,” or, according to another edition, “which the Lord said they were to do.” The wording is ambiguous: is the Lord himself to do these things, or are they to do them? Yet it is certainly clear that they are his, since they are the things that were to be done. Perhaps it is worded in this way so that both senses may be understood, because the Lord acts when he helps those who act, according to the Apostle’s words: “Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling” (Philippians 2). For it is God who works in us both the willing and the working, according to his good pleasure.

“For six days you shall do work; the seventh day shall be holy for you, a sabbath and rest of the Lord.” After Moses descended from the mountain, instructions were given for constructing the works of the tabernacle and the priestly vestment. Before commanding anything concerning their construction, he spoke to the people about observing the sabbath.

Here it is not without reason that a question arises. Since he had received the ten words of the law again on stone tablets—which he himself had hewn and himself had written—why, after descending, did he admonish the people concerning the sabbath alone? If it was unnecessary for the people to hear the ten commandments of the law again, why was it not unnecessary for them to hear again about the sabbath? Why is this also read among those ten commandments? Or is this likewise comparable to the veil with which he covered his face, because the children of Israel could not gaze upon the radiance of his countenance?

Of the ten commandments, this is the only one that he commanded the people in a figurative sense. We have no doubt that the other nine holy commandments are also to be observed in the New Testament. But that one commandment concerning the sabbath was so veiled among the Israelites by the figurative observance of the seventh day, and was commanded as a mystery and represented through a certain sacrament, that it is not observed by us today. Let us consider only what it signified.

In that rest in which people are commanded to cease from servile works, there is the great height of God’s grace. For good works are performed with rest when faith works through love. But fear contains torment; and where there is torment, what rest can there be? Hence “there is no fear in love.” “Love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Romans 5).

Therefore the sabbath is the holy rest of the Lord, that is, a rest to be attributed to God’s grace and not to us as though it came from ourselves. Otherwise our works will be merely human, or sins, or performed with fear rather than with love. And for this reason they are servile and without rest. The fullness of the sabbath, however, will be in eternal rest.

For the “sabbath of sabbaths” mentioned above was not instituted without reason. When God previously spoke of anointing the tabernacle, he said that all those things were sanctified by the same anointing and made “holy of holies.” But he had said that the altar of burnt offering, sanctified by the same anointing, was made “holy of the holy.” This seemed to be the distinction: he called nothing “holy of holies” except what was separated from the holy place by the veil, namely, where the ark of the testimony and the altar of incense were.

Now, however, when he repeated the same matters, he said that the anointed tabernacle and the things within it were sanctified by that anointing and made holy. But concerning the altar of burnt offering, of which he had previously said that it was to be made “holy of the holy,” he now said that by the same anointing it was made “holy of holies.” From this it may be understood that what had been called “holy of the holy” has the same value as what is called “holy of holies.”

Accordingly, all those anointed things—that is, the entire tabernacle and everything that was in it—which he had previously called “holy of holies,” have the same meaning as what he now calls “holy.” Nor does he say that each of them, after this anointing, is merely “holy of the holy,” but also “holy of holies,” as with the altar of burnt offering. Thus, as far as this designation is concerned, there is now no difference between those things that were inside the veil, where the ark of the testimony was, and the other things outside it. The difference is only that the things inside were called “holy of holies” even before the anointing, whereas the others were sanctified by the anointing so that they might receive this name. What these things signified should be examined at leisure.

“Whoever performs work on it shall be put to death. You shall not kindle fire in any of your dwellings on the sabbath day.” He forbids the performance of the necessary works of sinners, and also forbids the kindling of the fire of desire and anger, both in human bodies and in every kind of assembly. Rather, he urges that on the spiritual sabbath one devote oneself to spiritual service and divine contemplation. For just as it is beneficial for all always to burn with the flame of love, so it is harmful for everyone to be unceasingly consumed by the fire of desire.

## CHAPTER XXII  
### Moses, at the Lord’s command, instructs the people to prepare firstfruits and offer them to the Lord with a willing heart for the construction of the tabernacle

And Moses said to the whole assembly of the children of Israel:

“This is the word that the Lord commanded, saying: Set apart among yourselves firstfruits for the Lord. Let everyone who is willing and ready in heart offer them to the Lord: gold, silver, and bronze; violet, purple, scarlet twice-dyed, and fine linen; goats’ hair; rams’ skins dyed red and violet; acacia wood; and oil for preparing the lamps; also spices for making the anointing oil and the most fragrant incense; onyx stones and gems for the adornment of the ephod and the breastpiece” (Exodus 35).

Moses merely made known what works the Lord had commanded to be done: namely, the tabernacle with everything that was in it, and the priestly vestment. He also mentioned certain people to whom he said that the Spirit had been given divinely, so that they could produce these things. Yet many others are understood to have come voluntarily to these works, although they had not been commanded to do so and their names were not mentioned as having been spoken by the Lord to Moses.
