Therefore, those who are mentioned by name were not the only ones to possess this divine gift; perhaps they possessed it especially and more excellently. In all these matters, it is not a mind drawn servilely to its work but one freely and willingly devoted that deserves praise.

“Whoever among you is wise, let him come and do what the Lord has commanded.” We should note that those who are called wise, the makers of the holy works, were also such in character that, when they themselves received everything the people offered, thinking it necessary for completing all those things, they saw that more was being offered than was required and told Moses. He then prohibited the people, through a herald, from offering anything further. They could have offered much more if they wished, but modesty restrained them—or perhaps authority frightened them.

This concerned the tabernacle, its covering, its outer covering, and the rest. The gifts were offered with one purpose, yet they were various: gold, silver, bronze, precious stones, and then fine linen, scarlet, violet, and purple; rams’ skins dyed red and violet; incorruptible wood; goats’ hair for the construction of the tabernacle; and everything necessary for worship and for the holy vestments. Men and women supplied these things together.

“Bracelets, earrings, rings, and armlets. Every golden vessel was set apart as an offering to the Lord. If anyone possessed violet, purple, twice-dyed scarlet, fine linen, or goats’ hair…”

We have already explained more fully above the form of the former tabernacle and of the Church, pursuing it according to the manifold understanding of the Fathers; now, for the sake of remembrance, we repeat the same things briefly.

The faith of the Church is compared with gold; the word of preaching with silver; bronze with patience. The fact that men and women provide what is necessary for the adornment or construction of the tabernacle signifies that within the Church the virtues of the strong, represented by men, and the small works of the weak, represented by women, all find a place and are accepted for the uses of holy edification.

The offering itself is not made under compulsion but voluntarily, because faith is voluntary. The bracelets, which bind the arms, signify the works of leaders who labor vigorously. The earrings signify the obedience of subjects. The rings signify the seal of hidden things: hence teachers conceal certain matters from those who understand less, as though storing them under a seal, lest the mysteries of God be entrusted to the unworthy. Thus the righteous person rejoices and says: “I have hidden your sayings in my heart, that I might not sin against you” (Psalm 118 [119]).

The armlets signify good works and works performed by the right hand. The golden vessel set apart as an offering to the Lord signifies understanding of divinity. This understanding is separated from love of the lower realm to the extent that it is lifted toward the love of those things alone that are eternal.

Violet signifies hope of heavenly things; purple signifies blood and endurance of sufferings, displayed through love of the everlasting kingdom. Twice-dyed scarlet signifies love, which is twice dyed in its perfection, because it is adorned with love of God and of one’s neighbor. Fine linen signifies the spotless incorruption of the flesh and the brilliant whiteness of holiness. Fine linen is white linen. The goats’ hair, from which the roughness of haircloth is woven, signifies the harsh affliction of penitence.

Thus, while some exercise the teaching office through bracelets and rings, others display devout obedience in hearing and upright action through earrings and armlets; some possess a splendid and more subtle understanding of God through the golden vessel; others, through violet, purple, and scarlet, do not cease to hope for, believe in, and love the heavenly things they have heard, even though they do not yet know them through a more refined understanding; some offer the incorruption of the flesh through fine linen; and others, through goats’ hair, harshly lament what they willingly committed.

Behold: from such a great diversity of works one tabernacle is made, just as from different kinds of dust one clod of earth is formed, watered by the infusion of the Holy Spirit.

The incorruptible acacia wood signifies all the saints, incorrupt in mind and body, not perishing with the world but remaining forever eternal. The precious stones signify confessors, apostles, priests, and all the righteous. Blessed Peter the apostle also calls them living stones: “You are to be living stones, built together into the temple of God” (1 Peter 2).

All these things, therefore, are offered for the tabernacle of God, so that no one may despair of salvation. One person offers gold, meaning understanding; another silver, meaning eloquence; another a voice, meaning bronze. Thus many things are made in the tabernacle of God: the table, the lampstand, the altar, the pillars, the bases, the boards, the bowls, the cups, the censers, the basins, the mortars, the snuffers, the pegs, and the tent-curtains. Through these various elements the whole beauty of the tabernacle—that is, of the Church—is distinguished.

For the tabernacle is the Church, in which there is the table, meaning the unity of faith, or certainly the sacred Scripture, by which all the faithful are nourished with spiritual food. The lampstand with its seven lamps is Christ with the seven churches. Its snuffers signify the two Testaments. The pillars are the holy teachers, made firm by the solidity of faith. The bases are the prophets, who bear the structure of the Church upon their foundation.

There are also the boards, namely the apostles, enlarged by the breadth of their preaching. There are the tent-curtains, namely leaders and preachers who labor outwardly against the storms of this world. There are the bowls, meaning the distributions of human beings; and the pegs, namely the rulers and preachers of the Church, from which all kinds of peoples hang as vessels. The cups signify the words or meanings of doctrine.

There are also the censers, namely the virtues of good works or the prayers of the saints, through which an odor of sweetness rises to the Lord. The basins signify the apostles and teachers filled with life-giving waters. There are lilies, meaning the whiteness of virginity; or mortars, meaning endurance of labors and sufferings, through which the members of penitents are put to death.

These forms and administrations of gifts are distributed among the faithful through the Holy Spirit, so that through the individual distributions the perfect tabernacle of Christ may be built, in which God dwells in their midst.

What follows—“The princes offered onyx stones and gems for the ephod and the breastpiece, and spices and oil for preparing the lamps, for making the anointing oil, and for composing the most fragrant incense”—signifies that the apostles and apostolic men, priests and teachers of the faithful, prepare fittingly the beauty of the priestly ministry through wondrous works of virtue, by word and example. Through their zeal and expenditure, the light of knowledge and the example of good works shine in the holy Church: a lucid discourse for instructing hearers, and a good reputation for holy conduct, to commend the grace of holy religion to those who conduct themselves honorably in the house of God, so that their subjects may learn by their example to offer spontaneous vows of heart, mouth, and deed to the Lord.

Hence it follows:

“All the men and women, with devout minds, offered gifts so that the works might be made which the Lord had commanded through Moses. All the children of Israel dedicated voluntary offerings to the Lord.”

They did so certainly not contrary to the Apostle, from sadness or necessity, but with an eager heart and pious devotion, because “God loves a cheerful giver.”

## CHAPTER XXIII  
### Moses, by God’s command, calls Bezalel son of Uri from the tribe of Judah and Oholiab son of Ahisamach to direct the work of the tabernacle

And Moses said to the children of Israel:

“Behold, the Lord has called by name Bezalel son of Uri, son of Hur, from the tribe of Judah. He has filled him with the Spirit of God, with wisdom, understanding, knowledge, and every kind of skill, to devise and make work in gold, silver, and bronze; to carve stones; and to perform carpentry. Whatever can be devised skillfully, he has placed in his heart. Oholiab also, son of Ahisamach, from the tribe of Dan. He has instructed both of them with wisdom so that they may perform the work of the engraver, the embroiderer, the weaver, and the rest” (Exodus 35).

Through these craftsmen of the figurative tabernacle, the spiritual workers of the true tabernacle are represented. Their names also designate their offices. Bezalel is interpreted as “in the shadow of God.” Hur means “fire”; Uri, “my light”; Judah, “confession”; Oholiab, “my father’s protection”; Ahisamach, “strengthening my brother”; and Dan, “judgment” or “judging”—as these names sound in the Latin language.

Therefore the holy teachers who, through their preaching, construct the spiritual building of the house of God may rightly be called the shadow of God, since they trust in divine protection. In their person the Psalmist says: “In the shadow of your wings I shall hope, until iniquity passes away” (Psalm 16 [17]).

They are rightly called fire or light: kindled by spiritual zeal, they offer the light of faith and spiritual knowledge to their hearers and display the standard of catholic confession. Having the protection of God the Father in judgment and justice, they strengthen their brothers through exhortation, so that they may persevere in the catholic faith and in good works.

This too should be considered piously: not only the man who was born from the royal tribe, but also the one who was born from a slave woman, is chosen to direct the work of God. Bezalel came from the tribe of Judah, born from free Leah; Oholiab came from the tribe of Dan, born from Bilhah, Rachel’s slave woman. This spiritually indicates to us that not only the noble but also the lowly, insofar as worldly rank is concerned, are chosen for the governance of the Church. For, according to Peter’s words, God is not a respecter of persons, but in every nation whoever fears God and practices righteousness is acceptable to him.

God does not weigh nobility of flesh but nobility of spirit; and we are distinguished before God from others solely by right faith and good works.

Moreover, in the very election of the craftsmen it may be understood according to the mystery that the Lord wished to have teachers of his Church not only from the Jews but also from the Gentiles. Hence in the Book of Numbers, where the children of Israel camped around the tabernacle, Judah camped in the east and Dan in the north. In the east, therefore, the Lord first established the primitive Church from the Jews. Later, after the calling of the Gentiles—that is, from the pagans, who came to him from the kingdom of the one who is read as having established his throne in the north—he did not wish them to remain without a share in his grace, but decreed that they should receive ecclesiastical dignity and belong to the unity of his body.

## CHAPTER XXIV  
### The erection of the tabernacle and the glory of the Lord appearing over it

In the first month of the second year, on the first day of the month, the tabernacle was set up. Moses erected it, and the rest followed (Exodus 40).

What does it signify that the tabernacle is erected in the first month of the second year, on the first day of the month, except the construction of the Church through the coming of Christ? Understand the first year, therefore, as the entire period of the law before the incarnation of our Savior, so that the second year is understood as beginning with the coming of the Mediator between God and human beings and extending to the consummation of the world.

Thus the tabernacle is erected, as it were, in the first month and on the first day of the month, when at the beginning of grace the entire adornment of the Church is constructed through our Redeemer, and the beauty of the new Jerusalem—the heavenly bride of the King who descended from heaven—is revealed to faithful souls through the thunderous proclamation of the Gospel.

Afterward, that is, at the resurrection of the living and the dead, what is now hidden in an enigma will already be manifested in its visible form. Just as in the first year, when the contributions had been gathered, the prepared material for that structure was reserved for the future work, so the word or work of all the elect who existed from the beginning of the world until the coming of the Lord, suitable for the construction of the holy Church to be built by the Savior himself, is gathered through the writers of the Old Testament. Thus the teachers of the Gospel possess the resources of the ancient law for the testimony of the Gospel and the strengthening of believers’ faith.

It follows:

“After everything had been completed, the cloud covered the tabernacle of the testimony, and the glory of the Lord filled it. Moses could not enter the tent of the covenant, because the cloud covered everything and the majesty of the Lord flashed forth, since the cloud had covered all things. Whenever the cloud left the tabernacle, the children of Israel set out by their companies. If it remained suspended above it, they stayed in the same place. For the cloud of the Lord rested over the tabernacle by day, and fire by night, before the eyes of the people of Israel throughout all their encampments.”

A very remarkable matter must be noted. When the cloud descended and filled the tabernacle—although it is called the glory of the Lord—Moses could not enter the tabernacle, even though, when he first received the law on Mount Sinai, he entered the cloud where God was. Without a doubt, therefore, he represented one person then and another now.

Then he represented those who become leaders and enter into the deepest truth of God; now he represents the Jews, to whom the glory of the Lord that is in the tabernacle—that is, the grace of Christ—is presented as a cloud, because they do not understand it. Therefore they do not enter the tabernacle of the testimony.

We should believe that this happened once, as soon as the tabernacle was established, either for the sake of this interpretation or for some other reason. For the cloud was not always over the tabernacle in such a way that Moses could not enter it. It was not removed except when this sign was given to them that they should separate—that is, move the camp from the place where they were and approach the place to which the cloud led by day and the flame by night. These two likewise remained over the tabernacle after they had set up camp: the cloud by day and the flame by night.

## (Year 834) The Seven Books of Blessed Rabanus Maurus, Abbot of Fulda and Archbishop of Mainz, Containing Expositions on Leviticus

### Prologue to Freculph, Bishop of Lisieux

To the holy and blessed Father, and one greatly venerable among the members of Christ on account of his true piety, Freculph, bishop, Rabanus, a sinner in Christ, sends greetings.

Long ago you commanded me to undertake a difficult work beyond my own strength: to expound for you, in order and according to the spiritual sense, the five books of the Mosaic law, which the Hebrews call the *Torah*. At the beginning of the work I immediately replied that I was amazed that you should choose such a worthless and incapable little man for such a study, especially since I live in remote places and am occupied with many duties, being compelled each day to serve and provide what is necessary for the servants of Christ who live under the Rule of Saint Benedict.

Nor did you accept my excuse that I lacked the leisure either to search out fully the sayings of the Fathers or to undertake the work. I obeyed your command, lest I be accused of disobedience through pride, and I expounded Genesis and Exodus according to the understanding of the Fathers. At last, when I came to Leviticus, I found that it had been expounded sufficiently fully by the venerable Hesychius, priest of Jerusalem. I therefore thought that I should completely abstain from laboring over this book and suggest to you that you satisfy yourself by reading the work of that author.

But your diligence, not content with this answer, commanded me to collect into one work material from the writing of the aforesaid man and also from the writings of other Fathers who had expounded certain passages in the same book, not continuously but individually, so that you might have readily available what each of them had thought concerning it.

I did as you commanded. From the confused order of the sentences, I composed a certain arrangement by alternating and interweaving the opinions of various teachers. If anything in it displeases you, attribute it to yourself, not to me, since you compelled me to do this. In this matter I did not serve anyone’s need, but merely obeyed your will.

Receive the work you requested, and as you read it, turn over in your mind the manifold mysteries of the Book of Leviticus. Its power is so great that blessed Jerome, praising it elsewhere, said that its individual sacrifices—or rather, almost every syllable, and the vestments of Aaron, and the entire Levitical order—inspire heavenly sacraments.

As another teacher says: Just as in the last days the Word of God, clothed in flesh from the Virgin Mary, came forth into this world, and what was seen in him was one thing while what was concealed was another—the appearance of flesh was visible to everyone, but recognition of divinity was given to the few and elect—so also, when the word of God is presented to human beings through the prophets or through the lawgiver, it is not presented without appropriate clothing. For just as there it is covered by flesh, so here it is covered by the veil of the letter: the letter is indeed seen as flesh, while the spiritual meaning hidden within is perceived as divinity.

Let no difficulty of reading deter you. Rather, let the remembrance of divine piety summon you more strongly to study. Through a certain wise man it wished to say: “I love those who love me, and those who watch for me early shall find me” (Proverbs 8). “Come over to me, all who desire me, and be filled with my generations” (Ecclesiasticus 24).

In the Gospel, Truth itself, mercifully inviting our humility to meditate upon its wisdom, says: “Let the one who thirsts come to me and drink, and from his belly shall flow living waters” (John 7). “Come to me, all who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls; for my yoke is easy and my burden is light” (Matthew 11).

May he himself grant that we may feel his piety both in the present and also fully receive it in the future—he who had called us to his grace, Jesus Christ our Lord.

Furthermore, holy brother, I humbly ask your charity to repay me in sacred prayers for the work expended for you, and to persuade all those living with you and using our reading to do the same, so that divine grace may deign to lead me along the way of truth and preserve me in it to the end.

And each day, in praying for me, say this prayer of the Psalmist: “May your good Spirit, O Lord, lead your servant upon the right path; may you make him alive in your righteousness, bring his soul out of tribulation, and in your mercy scatter his enemies; and may you destroy all who afflict his soul, for he is your servant” (Psalm 142).

We desire that you be well and make daily progress in the service of Christ, holy Father. Remember us.

## The Expositions on Leviticus Begin. Book One

### CHAPTER ONE  
#### Concerning the sacrifices of livestock
## (Chapter 1)

Now the Lord called Moses and spoke to him from the Tabernacle of the Testimony, saying: “Speak to the children of Israel and say to them: Anyone among you who offers an offering to the Lord from livestock—that is, from cattle or sheep—shall offer victims.”

*(From Hesychius.)* That God does not delight in those sacrifices which he prescribed for the Jews, Isaiah demonstrates when he says: “Of what use to me is the multitude of your sacrifices?” says the Lord. “[Col. 0248D] I am full; I do not want the burnt offerings of rams, the fat of fattened animals, or the blood of calves, lambs, and goats. When you come to appear before me, who has required these things from your hands?” (Isaiah 1). Thus, in a certain sense, he rejects what he had prescribed concerning sacrifices.

Amos says similar things: “Did you offer me victims and sacrifices in the wilderness for forty years, house of Israel?” (Amos 5). This is not because they had often offered them, but because they displeased him so greatly that he reckoned them as though they had not been offered.

[Col. 0249A] The prophet Jeremiah says the same: “Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel: Add your burnt offerings to your sacrifices and eat meat, because I did not speak to your fathers, nor did I command them on the day when I brought them out of the land of Egypt concerning burnt offerings and sacrifices” (Jeremiah 7).

“But,” you will say, “the very one who denies these things of which we speak commanded them. Why, then, does he deny what he had commanded?” Why? Because those who received the command transgressed the intention of the giver. For since the law was subtle and exceedingly sublime, and since it had been concealed from them beneath the surface of the letter so that, while searching it out, they might learn—after first correcting their own perceptions—the Lord likewise now commanded Moses to portray an image of certain intelligible and rational sacrifices.

Thus, what is called a revocation [Col. 0249B] most clearly intimates a certain dispensation of words or things that look toward higher realities.

But from where does the Lord speak to him? From the Tabernacle of the Testimony, certainly. First, from heaven, because God is affirmed to dwell in heaven. Second, we understand the present Scripture as the Tabernacle of the Testimony, since it was, as it were, a tabernacle, inasmuch as the things being said were images or figures of the mysteries that would follow; for this reason it was called the Tabernacle of the Testimony. The Tabernacle of these words undoubtedly provides them with faith concerning future things.

What does he say, then, and to whom did he give the command? To the children of Israel, certainly. He commanded the one who offered voluntary gifts to offer from cattle or sheep. By either animal or beast of burden he signifies [Col. 0249C] a similar kind of person: one who possesses no sharpness, either toward virtue or toward wickedness, but is drawn along by another. Such are cattle and sheep. For they are exceedingly accustomed to the hand, readily following those who lead them. Therefore these gifts can belong not to everyone but only to the Jews. For them, even if they do not practice some virtue, it is sufficient that they do not act wickedly.

But because we have learned of an intelligible Israel, one that venerates intelligible circumcision, let us apply the sanction of the law spiritually to him, as Paul says: “For he is not a Jew who is one outwardly, nor is circumcision that which is outward in the flesh; but he is a Jew who is one inwardly, and circumcision is of the heart, in the spirit, not in the letter, whose praise is not from human beings but from God” (Romans 2).

“Anyone,” he says, “[Col. 0249D] among you who offers an offering from livestock—that is, from cattle or sheep—shall offer victims. If his offering is a burnt offering, and it is from the herd, he shall offer a male without blemish at the door of the Tabernacle of the Testimony, to make atonement for himself before the Lord,” and so forth.

*(From Origen.)* In this passage, I think that the person whom he called “a human being” and placed first in everything for the offering of a gift to God should be understood as the whole human race. The same person is called a human being because he offers as a burnt offering a calf from the cattle, without blemish.

Now see whether this calf without blemish is not the fattened calf which the father slaughtered for his son who had returned and been restored to him—the son who had perished and squandered all his substance—and for whom he prepared a great banquet and rejoiced, so that the angels in [Col. 0250A] heaven also rejoiced over one sinner doing penance.

Therefore, this human being who had perished and was found again, since he had nothing of his own substance to offer—for he had squandered everything while living extravagantly—found this calf. It had indeed been sent from heaven, but it came from the line of the patriarchs and through the successive generations connected from Abraham. For this reason he did not merely say “a calf” and then stop, so that any commanded calf might be understood, but “a calf from the cattle,” that is, one coming from the generation of the patriarchs. This is the male without blemish.

He is truly male who knows nothing of sin, which belongs to feminine weakness. Therefore only that one is male, only that one without blemish, who committed no sin and in whose mouth no deceit was found.

And he is offered acceptably before the Lord at the door of the Tabernacle.

[Col. 0250B] At the door of the Tabernacle means not inside the door but outside the door. For Jesus was outside the door: he came to his own, and his own did not receive him. He therefore did not enter that tabernacle to which he had come, but was offered as a burnt offering at its door, since he suffered outside the camp. The wicked tenants likewise cast out the son of the householder who came, outside the vineyard, and killed him.

This, then, is what is offered at the door of the Tabernacle, acceptably before the Lord. And what is so acceptable as the sacrifice of Christ, who offered himself to God?

“And then,” he says, “they shall place their hand upon the head of the victim, and shall slaughter the calf before the Lord. The priests, the sons of Aaron, shall offer the blood and pour the blood around the altar, which is at the door of the Tabernacle of the Testimony.”

[Col. 0250C] It may indeed be understood that this was said because Annas and Caiaphas and all the others who, after taking counsel against Jesus, pronounced him guilty of death were sons of Aaron; they poured out his blood around the base of the altar of the Tabernacle of the Testimony. For the blood is poured out there where the altar and its base were, just as the Lord himself said: “It cannot be that a prophet should perish outside Jerusalem” (Luke 13).

Therefore he also placed his hand upon the head of the calf—that is, he placed the sins of the human race upon his own head. For he is the head of the body, his Church.

But perhaps this too does not happen without reason. For after saying above, “He shall bring it to the door of the Tabernacle of the Testimony,” he repeats later and says again, “to the altar which is at the door of the Tabernacle of the Testimony,” as though it would not have been sufficient in the same account to designate the same place once, unless perhaps he wished this to be understood: [Col. 0250D] that the blood of Jesus was poured out not only in Jerusalem, where the altar and its base and the Tabernacle of the Testimony were, but also that the same blood sprinkled the heavenly altar above, where the Church of the firstborn is, as he also says to the apostles: “He has reconciled through the blood of his cross the things that are on earth and the things that are in heaven” (Colossians 1).

If you wish to know that there was a double sacrifice in him, suited to earthly things and adapted to heavenly things, the Apostle, writing to the Hebrews, says: “Through the veil, that is, his flesh.” Again, he interprets the inner veil as heaven, which Jesus penetrated and where he now stands before the face of God [Col. 0251A] for us: “Always living,” he says, “to intercede for them.”

If, then, two veils are understood, through which Jesus entered like a high priest, consequently a double sacrifice must also be understood, by which he saved both earthly and heavenly things.

Finally, the words that follow seem to be more applicable to a heavenly sacrifice than to an earthly one:

“After removing the skin of the victim, they shall cut its limbs into pieces, and shall place fire upon the altar, having first arranged a pile of wood. They shall arrange the limbs that have been cut above it, namely the head and everything attached to the liver, after washing the intestines and feet with water. The priest shall burn them upon the altar as a burnt offering and a sweet fragrance to the Lord.”

[Col. 0251B] It is worthwhile to observe how the flesh of the Word of God, who is here called the calf, is skinned and how it is divided limb by limb.

I think that the priest who removes the hide of the calf offered as a burnt offering—and removes the skin covering its limbs—is the one who withdraws the veil of the letter from the Word of God and exposes its inner members, which are the members of spiritual understanding. He does not place these members, the inner knowledge of the Word, in some lowly place, but sets them in a high and holy place, that is, upon the altar.

He does not disclose the divine mysteries to unworthy people who lead a lowly and earthly life, but to those who are the altar of God, in whom the divine fire always burns and the flesh is always consumed. Upon such people, then, this calf of the burnt offering, divided limb by limb, is placed.

For he divides the calf limb by limb who can explain in order and with appropriate distinctions what it means to have touched the fringe of Christ; what it means to have [Col. 0251C] washed his feet with tears and wiped them with the hairs of one’s head; and how much greater the excellence is of anointing his head with mixed ointment, or of reclining upon his breast.

To explain the reasons for each of these things, and to assign some to beginners, others to those who are already advancing in faith in Christ, and still others to those who are already perfect in knowledge and love of him—this is to divide the calf limb by limb.

The one who knows how to show what the beginnings of the law were, what progress was made in the prophets, what fullness of perfection is found in the Gospels, or who can teach with what milk of the Word the little ones in Christ are to be nourished and with what oil [Col. 0251D] of the Word those who are weak in faith are to be refreshed; the one who also knows what solid and robust food is needed to fatten the athletes of Christ—whoever knows how to divide each of these things according to spiritual reason may be regarded as that priestly teacher who places upon the altar a burnt offering divided limb by limb.

He also adds wood to the altar, so that the fire may be kindled and burn: the one who mingles speech not only about the bodily virtues of Christ but also about his divinity. For his divinity is from above, toward which this fire hastens.

Appropriately, therefore, the heavenly fire seized all these things that were done in the body by the Savior and restored them all to the nature of his divinity. Yet this fire is kindled by the addition of wood. Until the wood, there was Christ’s passion in the flesh; but when he was suspended [Col. 0252A] upon the wood, the dispensation of the flesh was completed.

For, rising from the dead, he ascended into heaven, as the nature of fire shows the direction of his journey. Hence the Apostle said: “Even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him in that way” (2 Corinthians 5).

The burnt offering of his flesh, offered through the wood of the cross, joined earthly things to heavenly things and human things to divine things.

The command also says that the intestines and feet are to be washed with water, proclaiming the sacrament of baptism under the form of a figurative teaching. For he washes the intestines who purifies the conscience; and he washes the feet who receives the completion of the sacrament. He knows that the one who is clean needs only to wash his feet, and that no one can have a share with Jesus unless he has washed his feet (John 13).

[Col. 0252B] But if you wish to incline these matters also toward a moral interpretation, you too have a calf that you ought to offer. Your flesh is a calf, and a very proud one. If you wish to offer it as a gift to the Lord, so that you may keep it chaste and pure, bring it to the door of the Tabernacle—that is, to the place where it can receive the hearing of the divine books.

Let your gift be male; let it know no female, reject desire, flee weakness, and seek nothing dissolute or soft. Also place your hand upon your victim, so that it may be acceptable to the Lord, and slaughter it before the Lord. That is, place upon it the bridle of continence and do not remove from it the hand of discipline, just as the one who said, “I discipline my body and bring it into subjection, lest after preaching to others I myself should be rejected,” placed his hand upon his own flesh.

And slaughter it [Col. 0252C] before the Lord, undoubtedly putting to death your members that are upon the earth.

But let the priests, the sons of Aaron, also offer its blood. The priest in you, and his sons, are the mind that is in you and its faculties, which are rightly called a priest or the sons of a priest. For they alone understand God and are capable of the knowledge of God.

The divine Word therefore wishes you to offer your flesh to God in chastity with rational understanding, according to what the Apostle says: “Your living, holy, and acceptable sacrifice to God, your rational service” (Romans 12).

And this is to offer the blood to the altar through the priest or the sons of the priest: when someone is made chaste both in body and in spirit.

There are others who indeed offer their flesh as a burnt offering, but not through the ministry of the priest. For they do not offer it knowingly [Col. 0252D] or according to the law that is in the priest’s mouth. They are chaste in body, but in soul they are found unchaste.

They are either stained by the desire for human glory, polluted by the greed of avarice, soiled by the misery of envy and jealousy, or tormented by the savagery of raging hatred and anger.

Therefore, whoever is like this, although chaste in body, does not offer his burnt offering through the hands and ministry of the priest. For there is in him no counsel or prudence that performs priestly service before God. He belongs instead to those five foolish virgins who were indeed virgins and preserved bodily chastity, but did not know how to store the oil [Col. 0253A] of charity, peace, and the other virtues in their lamps; and therefore they were shut out from the bridegroom’s chamber (Matthew 25).

For bodily continence alone cannot reach the altar of the Lord if it is abandoned by the other virtues and priestly ministries.

“But if the offering is from livestock, whether a burnt offering from sheep or goats, he shall offer a male a year old and without blemish. He shall slaughter it at the side of the altar that faces north, before the Lord. The sons of Aaron shall pour its blood around the altar. They shall divide its limbs, its head, and everything attached to the liver, and place them upon the wood beneath which the fire is to be set. They shall wash the intestines and feet with water, and the priest shall burn the whole offering upon the altar as a burnt offering and a most fragrant odor to the Lord.”

*(From Hesychius.)* [Col. 0253B] Here he now says the same things that he mentioned above, although with a few alterations. One who carefully investigates the words of the law must understand that Israel was commanded to offer burnt offerings not only from cattle but also from sheep.

Under the name of the ox, the worker of the law is understood—simple and without malice. He is compared to a sheep, as Jeremiah says: “I was like a gentle lamb being led to the slaughter, and I did not know” (Jeremiah 11).

The goat signifies the sinner. Therefore, just as it is permitted to offer not only from sheep but also from goats, and the offering is said to be from livestock, so it is possible for one who is from among sinners to devote himself to simplicity.

The second victim, an offering from sheep, is represented by the lamb—that is, Christ—because of his innocence. This is the lamb brought to sacrifice in Isaiah and shown by [Col. 0253C] John to everyone: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world.”

The lamb is rightly offered in the sacrifice so that the figure of Christ’s innocence and passion might be displayed.

The kid is also rightly offered, because through his death the author of sin, the devil, is recognized as slaughtered; and, having become as a sheep, one may offer his way of life to God as a burnt offering.

That it does not prevent anyone from attaining justification that he was once a sinner, although the Jews did not think so, hear what was said through the prophecy of Ezekiel. After he had inveighed at length against the unrighteous person and said, “He shall surely die; his blood shall be upon him,” he added this:

“But if he begets a son who, seeing all the sins of his father that he commits, does not do likewise; who has not eaten upon the mountains, nor lifted his eyes to the idols [Col. 0253D] of the house of Israel; who has not violated his neighbor’s wife,” and other things of this kind, at the end of which he added: “He shall not die in the iniquity of his father, but shall surely live. And you say, ‘Why has the son not borne the iniquity of his father?’” (Ezekiel 18).

Thus the Jews thought that a son necessarily succeeded to his father’s sin as though by hereditary right.

But why does he command sheep and goats to be killed at the side of the altar facing north before the Lord, when he had not given the same command concerning cattle but had ordained that they be slaughtered before the Lord? The words themselves seem to contain a certain contradiction and distinction, since, although the sacrifice is a burnt offering, each distinction assigns different places.

We must therefore understand that, as far [Col. 0254A] as the surface of the letter is concerned, the legislator indicated the same place in both cases. The altar of the burnt offering, established before the Tabernacle, was at the side of the entrance, so that the entrance would not be blocked for those ministering in the holy places, as the Book of Exodus says concerning the same altar: “He placed the veil at the entrance of the Tabernacle of the Testimony, and set the altar of the burnt offering near the entrance of the Tabernacle of the Testimony.”

Whatever, therefore, was offered for sacrifice stood at the side of the altar, toward the north, and thus the sacrifice was celebrated before the Lord—that is, in the presence of the holy things. For he calls the Holy of Holies the face of the Lord, because the glory of God dwells in them. Hence he did not command the priest to enter them frequently, but only once a year.

The altar of the burnt offering is understood as Christ, in whose remembrance [Col. 0254B] whatever must be offered to God ought to be offered.

The sacrifice of sheep is the simplicity of those who strive. The offering of sheep is not absolute, as is that of cattle, directly before that intelligible altar; rather, it is offered from the side. For the one who fulfills the commandments is directly before it, while the one who abstains from evil is at the side.

Why? Because, just as it is better to enter a royal hall, for example, through the straight entrance, but when this is not easy it is also good to enter through the side entrance, so it is better to offer oneself to God through the perfection of the commandments; nevertheless, it is also good if one offers oneself through abstention from evil. For to offer oneself to God in any way is good.

He necessarily adds that this is to be at the side of the altar toward the north. For this region is almost always clouded. Those who devote themselves entirely to innocence are [Col. 0254C] covered, as it were, by a cloud—that is, by ignorance—and therefore the offering is called a burnt offering even without works of righteousness.

There can be no doubt that the soul is understood by the blood, since the legislator himself says shortly afterward: “You shall not eat blood in any of your dwelling places, because the soul of the flesh is in the blood.”

Therefore we must not spare our soul but give it for Christ.

By the head, the mind is understood. Desire is expressed by the liver; hidden thoughts are signified by the intestines; actions by the feet.

He therefore wishes us to wash our thoughts together with our actions in water, whether the water of baptism or of tears, since in the judgment of the Lord we shall also be held accountable for our thoughts.

But he also commands the divisions, the head, and the liver to be placed upon the wood beneath which the fire is set on the altar, so that we may fit our whole human being to the spiritual Scriptures that have been spoken concerning the intelligible altar of the Lord’s body, [Col. 0254D] living and conducting ourselves according to his imitation:

“And the priest shall burn them upon the altar as a burnt offering and a sweet fragrance to the Lord.”

*(From Hesychius.)* Therefore, when our sacrifice becomes a burnt offering, then a sweet fragrance is found before the Lord. And when we have offered everything upon the intelligible altar, we become imitators of Christ according to our ability, adapting our life or conduct to his imitation. For we have shown above that this is the altar.

“But if the offering of the burnt offering to the Lord is from birds, he shall offer from turtledoves or young [Col. 0255A] pigeons. The priest shall bring it to the altar, and, twisting its head back and cutting it, shall make the blood flow at the place of the wound upon the ledge of the altar. He shall throw its crop and feathers beside the altar, toward the eastern side, in the place where the ashes are customarily poured out. He shall break its wings, but shall not cut it apart or divide it with iron, and shall burn it upon the altar, upon wood beneath which the fire has been placed. It is a burnt offering and an offering of a most fragrant odor to the Lord.”

*(From Hesychius.)* The third sacrifice is said to be the offering of a turtledove. That the turtledove signifies the flesh of Christ is made clear by Solomon, who says: “Your cheeks are beautiful like a turtledove” (Song of Songs 1).

John the Baptist declares that the dove bears the figure of the Holy Spirit when he says: “Upon whomever you see the Spirit descending like a dove, he is the one who baptizes” (John 1).

Thus, through [Col. 0255B] the mystery of the passion, the turtledove and the dove—that is, the flesh of Christ joined to the Spirit—are offered to God as a sacrifice for a sweet fragrance. In this way a human being, that is, Christ Jesus, offers three sacrifices.

Alternatively: The distinction of birds was not included among the foregoing offerings so that it might signify something more perfect and greater, surpassing the capacity of many.

Birds signify people devoted to contemplation, who do not mingle themselves at all with earthly affairs; and if necessity should perhaps demand it, they immediately fly back to higher things, aided by the testimony of the Gospel in which the Lord says: “Consider the birds of heaven, for they neither sow nor reap, and your heavenly Father feeds them” (Matthew 6).

Therefore, if a person devoted to contemplation and perfect in the consideration of higher things—for this is what the preceding [Col. 0255C] matters taught—offers his way of life or conduct as an offering, let him offer his gift from turtledoves or pigeons, that is, in knowledge and spiritual gentleness.

For this knowledge requires that his contemplation of the law not be occupied with vanities. The turtledove, because it possesses knowledge, is shown by Jeremiah, who reproached the people of the Jews through its example: “The turtledove, the swallow, and the stork observed the time of their coming, but my people did not know the judgment of the Lord” (Jeremiah 8).

The dove is clean and simple, and announces the presence of the Holy Spirit. Those who devote themselves to contemplating the Scriptures ought to be like this. Hence Hezekiah says: “I will meditate like a dove.”

One priest shall offer this offering, not many. For the contemplative life does not [Col. 0255D] belong to the multitude: it is for those who offer themselves to God with their whole mind, think of nothing human any longer, continually contemplate heavenly things, and set their minds on the things above, where Christ is, as the Apostle says, seated at the right hand of God (Colossians 3), namely, of the Father. Others offer an offering at the Tabernacle of the Testimony.

This offering, however, is brought to the altar, whose significance you learned in the preceding passages: namely, that it signifies the Lord’s body.

But let us see what is added to these instructions:

“And twisting its head back and cutting it, at the place of the wound”—that is, breaking it away from the skin which lies over the neck, but not separating that skin from the body, so that he would neither tear it apart nor bind it again to the body. This is signified by the place being cut.

For this reason [Col. 0256A] the legislator now commanded not that the bird be killed, but that it be broken or bent *(the reading is uncertain: “cooled” may be intended)*, showing how the true head—that is, the mind—is to be separated gradually and gently from the skin, that is, from the flesh.

For this reason he does not pour out the blood but makes it flow—or, according to the Septuagint, “draws it out” *(the transmitted reading is uncertain)*—so that he may gradually and perfectly despise the contemplation or life of the present age, as one who has offered his whole soul to God.

This is what is signified by the blood being drawn out around the base of the altar, which is Christ. The base of Christ is the Gospel, in which we have learned that we ought especially to despise the present life, as those who offer their whole soul to God.

He commanded the crop and feathers to be thrown away because he wished to purify the bird from both inflation and the investigation [Col. 0256B] of superfluous matters. from both inflation and the investigation of superfluous matters.

Those who possess more abundant knowledge are especially liable to succumb to these passions, as Paul testifies when he says: “Knowledge puffs up.” He therefore does not permit the bird to be puffed up, and for this reason commands the crop to be removed. Nor does he permit us to seek what is greater or higher than we should: “Do not seek what is above you,” he says, “and do not search out what is more sublime than you.”

Therefore he separated the feathers from the victim and commanded them to be thrown away beside the altar, toward the eastern side, in the place where the ashes are customarily poured out.

Toward the east, because the investigation of sublime matters appears to belong there; outside the altar, because it possesses not a necessary but a superfluous and harmful inquiry; and in the place of the ashes, because of the nature of which Abraham says: “I am dust and ashes” (Genesis 18).

Thus, by the place [Col. 0256C] of the ashes, the legislator reproves the aforementioned inflation, as something worthy of ashes. For what is worthy of ashes remains below upon the earth and cannot ascend into heaven.

Then he says: “He shall break its wings, but shall not cut it apart or divide it with iron.” He necessarily commands both wings to be broken, since the one who wishes to become a sacrifice to God must crush and afflict his members.

But he shall not cut it apart or divide it with iron; he shall not make the bird like the ox or the sheep by dividing it into parts. For a person devoted to contemplation and possessing nothing earthly, one who has long since become wholly heavenly, has no body opposed to the soul.

His body, soul, and spirit are kept blameless and whole at the coming of the Lord, as Paul says (1 Thessalonians 5). [Col. 0256D] Therefore a superfluous division of his members is unnecessary.

He is offered whole upon the intelligible altar and upon the wood beneath which the fire is placed. For the sacrifice does not become acceptable in any other way except through meditation upon the spiritual law. Then it is found to be a burnt offering and an offering of a most fragrant odor to the Lord, who always smells our sacrifice and receives the life or conduct of each of us according to the law given by him.

## Chapter 2. Concerning the Offering of Birds

*(Chapter 2.)* “When a soul offers an offering as a sacrifice to the Lord, its offering shall be of fine flour. He shall pour oil over it, place frankincense upon it, and bring it to the priests, the sons of Aaron. [Col. 0257A] One of them shall take a handful of the fine flour and oil, together with all the frankincense, and place the memorial portion upon the altar as a most fragrant odor to the Lord. Whatever remains of the sacrifice shall belong to Aaron and his sons; it is most holy among the offerings of the Lord.”

The fourth sacrifice, in which a soul offers a sacrifice of fine flour, declares the figure of the Catholic Church. It is composed of fitting members, like fine flour gathered from many grains of believers; separated between letter and spirit by the millstone of the Law and the Gospels; united through the water of baptism; anointed with the oil of chrism; solidified by the fire of the Holy Spirit; and made into a sacrifice pleasing to God through humility of spirit.

That he calls the whole human being “a soul” is clear from the statement, “Its offering shall be of fine flour.” For how could the soul by itself [Col. 0257B] bring forward an offering, when it necessarily prays and requires for this purpose the ministry of the body? The passage introduces nothing novel here.

Moses also often calls the whole human being “a soul” elsewhere, as when, enumerating the number of those who went down into Egypt, he says: “All the souls that entered Egypt with Jacob, who came forth from his loins, apart from the wives of his sons, were seventy-two” (Exodus 12).

Luke likewise, when describing Paul’s voyage to Rome, says: “There were in the ship two hundred and seventy-six souls” (Acts 27).

We must consider whether perhaps in this passage he called a gentile a “soul” or “human being.” For above, when speaking of the sacrifices involving blood, he said to the children of Israel: [Col. 0257C] “Speak to the children of Israel: Anyone who offers a victim to the Lord from livestock—that is, from cattle or sheep—shall offer victims” (Leviticus 1).

Here, when prescribing the sacrifice of fine flour, which is without blood, he necessarily does not say, “a human being from among you,” but “when a soul offers an offering,” calling the gentile a soul because previously they were merely natural or soulish people and could not understand the things of the Spirit.

Nevertheless, he is called to the offering, since the just God has mercy on him and saves him through condescension. When he establishes sacrifices for sins, he commands the one who has neither a sheep nor a goat to offer turtledoves or young pigeons; and the one who has not even this, he commands to offer fine flour.

For he is no longer saved by works, since he is poor [Col. 0257D] in virtues, but solely by the knowledge of God.

Although knowledge of God is the beginning of the salvation of the nations, we nevertheless need to pour oil over the fine flour and place frankincense upon it, so that we may mingle God’s grace with almsgiving and prayer.

These things can drive away the sentence—or, according to the uncertain reading, the “knowledge”—of God from heaven. Cornelius is a witness to this. When an angel descended from heaven to him, he said: “Cornelius, your prayers and your almsgiving have ascended before God” (Acts 10).

To understand how prayer is signified by frankincense, investigate and examine its power. Physicians customarily use it against inner ailments and to treat afflictions of the eyes. If someone burns it and receives its smoke, it restrains tears arising in the eyes from weakness.

Prayer accomplishes many things [Col. 0258A] in the same way. It especially heals the passions of the soul; it also cures the wounds of the intelligible eyes, freeing them from ignorance and from the tears that arise from the real sickness—that is, from sin.

After this he commands that a handful of the fine flour be taken. By the handful he signifies faith, and he openly shows that the knowledge or cognition of God acceptable to the Lord is that which faith can grasp.

Just as someone who tries to grasp more than a handful accomplishes nothing—for everything runs through his fingers and falls, and he labors uselessly—so faith is the measure of the knowledge of God.

“For it is necessary to believe,” Paul says, “for the one who approaches God” (Hebrews 11). And, to put it briefly: “Whatever is not from faith is sin,” as the same apostle wrote to the [Col. 0258B] Romans.

Notice also that he commands the fine flour to be taken with oil, openly wishing us to give alms: “Give alms,” the Lord says, “and behold, everything will be clean for you.”

He commands all the frankincense to be taken in the handful. All of it—why? Because we ought always to pray and to give thanks without ceasing, as Paul says.

But who is the one who takes it in the handful? According to the Septuagint, the text does not say, so that it might indicate simply the one who offers. According to the Hebrew truth, however, the priest—that is, one of the sons of Aaron—takes a handful full of fine flour and oil, together with all the frankincense, and places the memorial portion upon the altar as a most fragrant odor to the Lord.

You have learned that this priest is Jesus, through whose ministry we become an offering pleasing to God, and who leads us to the contemplation of God.

*(From Hesychius.)* [Col. 0258C] He himself will offer the memorial of the sacrifice upon the heavenly altar.

The memorial of the knowledge of God is perfect knowledge. We shall always remember it when we become capable of it. It is never destroyed; rather, through its fullness it shows that the knowledge we possess now is only a very small part, not something contrary to it, according to what has been said: “We know in part, and we prophesy in part; but when perfection comes, what is in part will be abolished” (1 Corinthians 13).

How it will be abolished he makes clear by adding: “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face. Now I know in part; then I shall know, even as I am known.”

The legislator rightly called this sacrifice a most fragrant odor to the Lord. For in God, the odor is his knowledge [Col. 0258D] or understanding. And, so that you may not doubt this, Paul, a most truthful witness, also says: “Thanks be to God, who always leads us in triumph in Christ and manifests through us the odor of his knowledge in every place.”

There you have learned, for the present, what the odor of knowledge is. But hear also in what follows concerning the good odor: “We are the good odor of Christ among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing” (2 Corinthians 2).

Then the legislator says: “Whatever remains of the sacrifice shall belong to Aaron and his sons; it is most holy among the offerings of the Lord.”

He speaks of what remains of that perfect knowledge or understanding which is hidden and stored up in the heavens and in Christ: “In him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Colossians 2).

It is most holy among the offerings of the Lord. [Col. 0259A] The knowledge that remains is partial, yet it surpasses all other knowledge and leads to perfection.

It shall belong to Aaron and his sons. Aaron is interpreted as “ark” or “mountainous,” that is, one who understands lofty things concerning God. For the ark, since it contains the law of God and his utterances, is also able to offer the sacrifice mentioned above.

When you offer a sacrifice baked in an oven, namely loaves of fine flour kneaded with oil, and flat cakes, unleavened, spread with oil. (From Hesychius.) By the sacrifice baked in the oven, therefore, he calls the incarnation of Christ to mind. For he was incarnated in order to be sacrificed; and for this reason John the Baptist called him “the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1). Rightly, then, the sacrifice is said in this passage to be baked in an oven, in order to announce his birth, namely in the womb of the God-bearing Virgin [Col. 0259B]: for she is necessarily called an oven. For just as an oven receives loaves and fire from above, so the Mother of God received from above the bread of life—namely, God the Word—in her womb, and also the fire of the presence of the Holy Spirit. “The Holy Spirit,” he says, “will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke 1).

If, then, you offer the offering of the incarnation of the Only-Begotten, which took place in the Virgin’s womb, it is not otherwise acceptable to God unless it is baked from fine flour—that is, unless it proceeds from the knowledge or understanding of God. For from where else have we taken teaching about this matter except from the apostles and the prophets? Take, therefore, the apostles’ words as loaves, and the prophets’ words as flat cakes; for just as loaves are more suitable than flat cakes for nourishment, so the apostles’ words are more suitable than the prophets’ words. [Col. 0259C] Both, however, are unleavened, because they contain no leaven from another doctrine—for example, from secular wisdom, which is what happens among heretics. For when these people attempt to join exterior things to interior things, and to subject and ferment what cannot in any way be fermented, they have fallen away from the unleavened sayings.

But behold: the apostles’ loaves are made with oil, and the prophets’ flat cakes with oil. For both the one and the other have written in harmony that Christ came in compassion for us; but the apostles speak more plainly, since what the prophets narrated as future they already declare to have been fulfilled.

If your offering is from a frying pan, it shall likewise be fine flour kneaded with oil and without leaven; you shall divide it into small pieces and pour oil over it.

By the sacrifice from the frying pan he calls to mind the dispensation of the Only-Begotten’s passion [Col. 0259D], judging the cross to be likened to a frying pan because a frying pan is so strong that, when placed upon the fire, it is itself neither consumed nor subject to any corruption or diminution; yet it quickly renders the foods placed upon it fit for use as soon as they touch the fire—or, if they are harder, after no long interval. So too Christ’s cross was strong enough to subject the whole creation to the one crucified, while it made his flesh—which before the passion was unfit to be eaten (for who could understand eating the flesh of God?)—fit for food after the passion. For if he had not been crucified, we would in no way eat the sacrifice of his body; but now we eat it, receiving food as we commemorate his passion.

[Col. 0260A] The Lord indicated this frying pan through Ezekiel when he said: “And you, take for yourself an iron frying pan, and set it as an iron wall between yourself and the city” (Ezekiel 4). He called it iron on account of the strength mentioned above. “Between yourself and the city,” he says—that is, Jerusalem—because those who most grievously offended him on the Lord’s cross and inflicted sufferings upon him were separated from his knowledge.

The mystery of the sufferings is therefore kneaded with oil, because in his compassion for us he endured death for our sake. That it is also to be without leaven—that is, pure from exterior doctrine—he indicates by saying: “You shall divide it into small pieces,” so that in his passion we may divide the account of what occurred in its several parts: the blows, the blows upon the cheek, the spitting, and the piercing of his side. “And you shall pour oil over it.” But just as he [Col. 0260B], having mercy on us, gave himself over to suffering for our sake, so we too ought to show mercy to our neighbors, taking the Lord’s passion as an example of this compassion.

# Chapter III. On the sacrifice of fine flour with oil and frankincense

(The same passage.) “But if the sacrifice is from a griddle, it shall likewise be fine flour kneaded with oil. You shall offer it to the Lord, handing it over to the priest’s hands; and when he has offered it, he shall take a memorial portion from the sacrifice and burn it upon the altar as a pleasing fragrance to the Lord. Whatever remains shall belong to Aaron and his sons, a most holy thing from the offerings of the Lord.”

He wishes one who is disputing and arguing about the resurrection to discuss similar matters, whose mystery he has not without reason called a griddle. By the griddle [Col. 0260C] he signified death. Just as above we understood the Lord’s cross through the frying pan, so let us understand death—and also burial—through the griddle. The difference between a griddle and a frying pan is wholly unknown to no one: the frying pan is placed upon a fire that is now blazing and kindled, whereas the griddle is placed upon burning coals that were kindled earlier. So too the Lord’s death was not the beginning of some passion, but the underlying reality of the sufferings that had previously been at work in him.

This offering, therefore, is made from fine flour—that is, from the knowledge or understanding of God—which concerns the Lord’s death. For Christ must be called God even in death, and nevertheless the one who died because of mortal flesh must be proclaimed immortal. Yet he will become alive in oil. For one who is discussing the Lord’s death [Col. 0260D] and resurrection must also add to his reasoning the oil of God’s mercy: in compassion for the human race, he both endured death and arranged the resurrection from the dead.

“He shall hand it over into the priest’s hands”—namely, to Christ himself. After he approached the altar that is in heaven—and he approached it in the flesh through the ascension—he is never separated from his divinity. “He shall take a memorial portion from the sacrifice”: the abundance of knowledge or understanding, as we have already taught above. He shall burn it upon the altar, preserving it with himself for the age to come.

“Whatever remains”—that is, as much as he has commanded us to know and investigate—shall belong to Aaron and his sons; that is, he handed it over to those who are able to think and perceive sublime things and things concerning God [Col. 0261A], whom we said above were the sons of Aaron. “A most holy thing from the offerings of the Lord”: in confirming this more strongly, the legislator wrote it thus. All good knowledge is holy, but the most holy is that knowledge of God which is able to discuss him as it ought.

Again, in a moral sense, we offer a calf to God when we overcome the pride of the flesh; a lamb when we correct irrational impulses; a kid when we conquer lust; a dove when we preserve simplicity of mind; and a turtledove when we maintain chastity. For this species of bird is said to preserve a single and chaste union.

We offer fine flour and unleavened loaves when we live this present life without malice and wickedness. For example, one offers fine flour who, whether engaged in agriculture, sailing, or some other activity of ordinary life [Col. 0261B], offers up the conduct of his life, kneaded, however, with oil, since every soul needs the oil of divine mercy, and no one can pass through the present life unless the oil of heavenly compassion is present for him.

It is also necessary to point out that, in accordance with our mortality, the burden of temptations is aptly expressed by the oven; steadfastness of spirit and strength of mind by the frying pan; and manifold opposition by the griddle.

(From Origen.) But perhaps someone among the Church’s hearers says: “Perhaps things were better with the ancients than with us. When sacrifices of various kinds were offered, forgiveness was granted to those who sinned; among us there is only one forgiveness of sins, given at the beginning through the grace of the laver, and afterward no mercy or forgiveness [Col. 0261C] for sin is granted.”

It is fitting that Christian discipline should be strict, for whom Christ died. For them sheep, goats, oxen, and birds were slaughtered, and fine flour was kneaded; for you the Son of God has been slaughtered—and yet you delight in sinning again!

Nevertheless, lest these things raise your spirits toward virtue less than they cast you down into despair, you have heard how many sacrifices for sins there are in the Law; now hear how many remissions of sins there are in the Gospels.

The first is that in which we are baptized for the remission of sins. The second remission is in the passion of the martyrs. The third is given through almsgiving. For the Savior says: “Nevertheless, give what you have, and behold, everything is clean for you” (Luke 11).

The fourth remission of sins comes to us through our forgiving the sins of our brothers. For the Lord and Savior himself says: “If you forgive your brothers [Col. 0261D] their sins from your heart, your Father will also forgive you your sins. But if you do not forgive your brothers from your heart, neither will your Father forgive you” (Matthew 6). And in the prayer he taught us to say: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.”

The fifth remission of sins is when someone turns a sinner back from the error of his way. For the divine Scripture says: “Whoever turns a sinner back from the error of his way saves his soul from death and covers a multitude of sins.”

There is also a sixth remission through an abundance of love, as he himself says: “I say to you, her many sins are forgiven [Col. 0262A], because she loved much” (Luke 7). And the apostle says: “Love covers a multitude of sins” (1 Peter 4).

There is still a seventh remission, though hard and laborious: remission through repentance, when the sinner washes his bed with tears, and his tears become his bread day and night (Psalm 14), while he is not ashamed to disclose his sin to the priest of the Lord and to seek healing, according to the one who says: “I said, I will confess my iniquity against myself, and you forgave the wickedness of my heart” (Psalm 31).

In this is also fulfilled what the apostle James says: “If anyone is sick, let him call the presbyters of the Church, and let them lay hands on him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord; and the prayer of faith will save the sick person, and if he is in sins, they will be forgiven him” (James [Col. 0262B] 5).

You too, then, when you come to the grace of baptism, have offered a calf, because you are baptized into Christ’s death. But when you are led to martyrdom, you have offered a kid, because you have slaughtered the author of sin, the devil.

When you give alms and, with attentive compassion, devote an affection of mercy toward the needy, you have burdened the sacred altar with fattened kids. For if you forgive your brother’s sin from your heart, and, laying aside the swelling of anger, recover within yourself a gentle and simple soul, be confident that you have sacrificed a ram or offered a lamb as a sacrifice.

Moreover, if, instructed by the divine readings, you turn a sinner from his error by meditating like a dove and keeping watch day and night in the law of the Lord, and recall him from the way of wickedness to the simplicity of the dove, and by attaching him [Col. 0262C] to the saints make him imitate the fellowship of the turtledove, you have offered the Lord a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons.

But if love—which is greater than hope and faith—abounds in your heart, so that you love your neighbor not only as yourself but as was shown by the one who said, “Greater love has no one than this: that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John 15), know that you have offered yourself as loaves of fine flour kneaded in the oil of love, without any leaven of malice or wickedness, in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.

But if, in the bitterness of your weeping, you are worn out by mourning, tears, and lamentation; if you have mortified your flesh and made it dry through fasts and great abstinence; and if you have said, “For as in a frying pan my bones have been fried” (Psalm 101), then you have offered a sacrifice of fine flour [Col. 0262D] from the frying pan or from the griddle.

In this way you are found to offer, more truly and perfectly according to the Gospel, the sacrifices that Israel can no longer offer according to the Law.

# Chapter IV. That every offering must be without leaven and with salt

(The same passage.) “Every offering that is offered to the Lord shall be made without leaven, and no leaven or honey shall be burned as a sacrifice to the Lord. You shall offer only their firstfruits and gifts; but they shall not be placed upon the altar as a pleasing fragrance.”

(From Hesychius.) He wishes God’s doctrine to have no communion with exterior knowledge. That he calls leaven an alien doctrine [Col. 0263A], the Lord himself clearly taught when he said to his disciples: “Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees” (Mark 8).

Solomon teaches in Proverbs that honey is to be understood as pagan doctrine, on account of the sweetness of its words and the pleasantness of its speech, saying: “Do not look upon a prostitute, for the lips of a prostitute drip honey, and her throat is smoother than oil; but her end is bitter as wormwood” (Proverbs 5).

What end? When, namely, you have begun to distinguish true wisdom from that which is counterfeit and falsely uses the name. For although he says to the Church in the Song of Songs, “Honey and milk are under your tongue” (Song of Songs 4), he does not contradict the present passage but agrees with it entirely. Nor did he say “on your tongue,” but “under your tongue,” to show that the wisdom of the pagans and the letter of the Jews are subject to the Church’s tongue [Col. 0263B]—that is, to its doctrine.

Therefore he does not wish a complete offering of these things’ doctrine to God. Hence he says: “It shall not be burned as a sacrifice,” which is a whole burnt offering; “you shall offer only their firstfruits.” For he commanded that firstfruits be offered from that wisdom, but not that it be used in full. Thus, when Paul was preaching among the Athenians and said, “As one of your own poets has said, ‘For we are indeed his offspring’” (Acts 17), he found an external saying suitable as an occasion for the knowledge of God. He did not reject it, yet he did not add to it, for he did not multiply further testimonies from that source.

Why? Because, as Paul himself says, “it pleased God through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe,” so that our faith might not rest on human wisdom but on the power of God [Col. 0263C].

For this reason the legislator says: “They shall not be placed upon the altar as a pleasing fragrance.” Although he could have said “they are not placed,” he said “they shall not be placed,” showing that even if we attempt to acquire knowledge of divinity from exterior things, such a sacrifice does not ascend to God’s altar and does not become a pleasing fragrance to the Lord. Rather, such a sacrifice is assigned to inferior things and, since it has its substance from the earth, is brought down to the earth.

“Whatever sacrifice you offer, you shall season with salt. You shall not remove the salt of the covenant of the Lord your God from your sacrifice; in every offering you shall offer salt.”

That he spoke of apostolic wisdom as salt, the Lord plainly showed us when he said to the apostles: “You are the salt of the earth. But if the salt has lost its savor, it will be good for nothing henceforth except to be thrown outside and trampled upon by people [Col. 0263D]” (Matthew 5).

He called apostolic wisdom salt because, just as every food suitable for nourishment is thoroughly seasoned with salt, so every useful word that serves for assistance necessarily has the seasoning of apostolic wisdom. Therefore he commanded that salt not be absent from the sacrifices, but that it be offered in every gift: so that whatever you teach, whatever you correct, and whatever virtue you practice, you may carry out apostolic zeal and imitation, remembering Paul’s saying: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (Philippians 3).

And again: “You are no longer strangers and foreigners, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household, built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the chief [Col. 0264A] cornerstone” (Ephesians 2).

Since, however, he did not simply say “salt,” the legislator indicated that it is intelligible salt: “You shall not remove,” he says, “the salt of the covenant of your God.” If the covenant or testament is rational, then the salt is rational as well. The legislator therefore wishes to forewarn us concerning the salt of the evangelical testament and the apostolic salt.

(From Hesychius.) Likewise, the fact that honey is not offered in God’s sacrifice indicates that nothing pleasurable, nothing sweet in this world, and nothing that lacks some biting element of truth is pleasing to God. Hence the Passover too is eaten with bitter herbs. Conversely, salt is commanded to be mixed into every sacrifice, so that everything we offer for Christ’s honor may always receive the salt of reason and discernment.

That oil was offered in the sacrifice signifies [Col. 0264B] that whatever we expend for the worship of Christ and the devotion of the saints, we should do entirely with cheerfulness: “Nothing,” as the apostle says, “from sadness or necessity, for God loves a cheerful giver” (1 Corinthians 9).

# Chapter V. On the offering of the firstfruits of the crops
## (The Same.)

But if you offer the Lord a gift of the firstfruits of your crops, from ears of grain that are still green, you shall roast them by fire and crush them in the manner of grain, and thus offer your firstfruits to the Lord, pouring oil over them and adding frankincense, because it is an offering of the Lord. From it the priest shall burn, as a memorial portion of the gift, some of the crushed grain and oil, and all the frankincense. *(From Hesiod [sic].)*

He did not command only those who had remained for a long time in the knowledge or understanding of God to offer that knowledge, but also those beginning it, such as Paul. For as soon as he was called, he preached. Therefore, we should understand what is now being said in this way.

The firstfruit offered to God is the person who has newly begun to believe and who previously offered God no fruit of divine knowledge. If, then, we offer him the sacrifice of the word of God, newly beginning his knowledge, and if we offer what is green—as though we were newly learning and newly receiving something—since we are not yet able to expound its mysteries precisely, it is necessary for us to offer it green, roasted, and crushed, rather than as flour or fine flour; or, as the Septuagint says, “fresh, roasted, ripe, and crushed.”

For just as, when we wish to make moist fruits, which cannot yet be ground into flour or fine flour, fit for eating, we crush them by fire and separate their husks while roasting them, so whoever does not yet possess solid knowledge or subtle and exalted theology—for we are not yet capable of discerning it—because we do not possess perfect knowledge of the spiritual Scriptures, needs to roast it in the fire of the Spirit. That is, we need its operation and assistance to be supplied to us, so that from it we may separate the husks of the letter. From this we shall possess an adequate and very swift knowledge of God.

Therefore the intelligible priest receives it. We must, however, pour oil over it and place frankincense upon it, for divine knowledge is brought to perfection in us through almsgiving and prayer. Concerning the priest and the memorial portion placed upon the altar, we have already spoken above, and it is unnecessary to repeat it.

## (Chapter III.)

But if his offering is a sacrifice of peace offerings, and he wishes to offer from cattle, he shall offer an unblemished male or female before the Lord. He shall place his hand upon the head of his victim, which shall be slaughtered at the entrance of the tabernacle, and the sons of Aaron, the priests, shall pour out its blood around the altar. From the sacrifice of the peace offerings they shall offer to the Lord as an offering the fat that covers the inner parts and all the fat that is within; the two kidneys with the fat covering the loins; and the lobe of the liver with the kidneys. They shall burn these upon the altar as a burnt offering, with fire set beneath the wood, as an offering of most pleasing fragrance to the Lord.

*(From Hesychius.)* Since God established different ways of life for human beings through the law, and arranged virtues in the manner of steps [or: ladders], so that one person might be permitted to attain all of them and another only some, yet so that each might be lifted upward from the earth, this too was signified by the difference among the sacrifices.

One person will offer a burnt offering from himself, wishing to offer his entire self to God, just as Paul said: “I have been crucified with Christ” (Gal. II). Another offers a sacrifice of peace or salvation, one who desires salvation but cannot live in an exceedingly exalted manner. For even if someone cannot attain virginity, let him live in a chaste marriage; he receives pardon from the Lord, who said—when he was explaining virginity to the apostles—“Not all can receive this saying.” Yet such a person is necessarily included among those who are saved. The same applies to contempt for possessions, to justice, and to food with thanksgiving: great is the person who can attain great things, and the lesser—though not the least—is the person who can at least attain what is moderate.

Thus, to prove that there are two kinds of conduct leading to the justification of human beings, he established two definitions of voluntary sacrifices. For he says in the Book of Exodus: “You shall make an altar of earth for me, and you shall sacrifice upon it your burnt offerings and your peace offerings, your sheep and your cattle, in every place where my name shall be proclaimed. I will come to you and bless you” (Exod. XX, 25). He first commanded the burnt offering, but then added the peace offering, as belonging to a second rank and degree of virtue.

Therefore, whoever thinks it sufficient merely to be saved will offer from cattle.
