By the bull, as we have said, are meant those engaged in doing the things of the law, whether male or female; nevertheless, let him offer an unblemished gift. Yet, although he commanded that the person offering a burnt offering should not offer a female, he did not in any way exclude the female from this kind of conduct. Rather, he showed that to think perfectly is properly characteristic of men. If a woman possesses this wisdom, she will be called a man, as being courageous, concerning whom Solomon said: “Who will find a strong woman?” (Prov. XXXI). He thereby showed that courage—that is, perfection—is rarely found in women.

The sacrifice of peace offerings, however, belongs to both men and women, for women too must live in a manner suitable to salvation. But why they are commanded to place their hands upon the head of the victim, to slaughter it at the entrance of the tabernacle, and to pour out its blood around the altar, we have sufficiently discussed in the sacrifices of burnt offerings.

What they must offer to God from their own sacrifice if they wish to be saved must now be examined and considered. For from the sacrifice of peace offerings they offer to the Lord the fat that covers the inner parts and all the fat that is within—or, as the Septuagint says, “the fat that covers the belly and all the fat that is in the belly”—signifying the heart by the belly.

In the edition mentioned above, he referred to it twice because, as physicians say, the belly has two functions. Through one part it draws in nourishment; this is what they call the upper belly. Through another it separates excretions; this they call the lower belly. The kidneys are the organs responsible for the vital seeds. They have a connection with the belly and the thighs. For this reason he commands that the first fat, which is above the belly, and the two kidneys, and again the fat that is above them—that is, above the thighs, since these are near the kidneys—be offered, because the kidneys are situated between the thigh and the belly.

He said that pleasure or desire is located in the liver. Hence, according to the Septuagint, the lobe of the liver is also said to be removed with the kidneys, since the liver supplies the kidneys with the force of its activity.

But what does he signify through these things? What does he establish for those who wish to be saved, to whom he has now opened his mouth in parables? He signifies that the victim—that is, the firstfruits and burnt offerings—must be offered to God by those who wish to be saved: intelligible fat, namely desire, which the Greeks call *epithymia* [ἐπιθυμία]. This fat first covers the upper belly, and then the lower, so that we may offer to God both the conception and the fulfillment of desire. For the intention must first be formed and afterward carried out.

The belly of the soul, therefore, is the heart, in which we first propose certain actions and afterward attempt to fulfill them. To form an intention is, in a sense, to desire; but to hasten toward progress may perhaps properly be called a kind of digestion. We must offer to God the desire belonging to both of these—what he called the fat—so that we neither propose nor fulfill anything evil.

He rightly says “the fat that covers the upper belly,” which is the appetite, because the greatest part of desire concerns appetite and intention. To the lower belly he joined the two kidneys. For we have said that the kidneys share a connection with the heart, and therefore David says: “Burn my kidneys and my heart” (Ps. XXV). Hear also the Lord speaking through the prophet Jeremiah: “I am the Lord, searching the heart and testing the kidneys” (Jer. XVII).

Prophecy would never have joined these members together unless they had something entirely in common. Physicians say that the movement of anger lies in the heart, while its memory lies in the kidneys. Therefore David, bearing witness to his innocence, says: “Judge me, O Lord, for I have walked in my innocence” (Ps. XXV); and he asked that his kidneys and heart be burned, since both could bear witness on his behalf.

In these kidneys there is also the source of seed. Hence they are thought to share a connection with the thighs, which themselves provide force for sexual acts. He therefore wishes the desire for marriage also to be offered to God, so that it may produce offspring rather than fornication, and so that marriage and the marriage bed may be honorable and undefiled.

But the irascible element within us must also be offered to God. In this way we shall be able to become angry not for the purpose of committing sin but for destroying sin, and David’s Scripture will be fulfilled in us: “Be angry and do not sin” (Ps. IV). That there is anger pleasing to God, when it serves not to harm but to correct, is clearly demonstrated by what is first written about Moses in Exodus. For it says:

“When he had drawn near to the camp, he saw the calf and the dances; and, becoming exceedingly angry, he threw the tablets from his hand and broke them at the foot of the mountain,” and so forth (Exod. XXXII).

Since desire is thought to reside in the liver, he therefore commanded that its lobe—that is, its summit—be removed with the kidneys and offered upon the altar, so that we might be cleansed from every evil pleasure, knowing that we must offer God the firstfruits of our thoughts, sanctifying both the portion taken from them and the whole mass.

Nevertheless, a person must so order himself that he offers to God every desire, intention, and completion of any action; but he must be cleansed from evil anger and from such pleasure. Therefore he offers the movement of anger and the firstfruits of pleasures, as well as marriage itself, through the lobe of the liver and the kidneys, and he can rightly offer his conduct upon the heavenly altar, upon the burnt offerings and the wood that is upon the fire.

For he lives according to the commands of the Spirit and becomes a sacrifice of most pleasing fragrance to God. God is pleased when he brings forth fruit—not only a hundredfold, but also sixtyfold and thirtyfold.

If his offering is from sheep and is a sacrifice of peace offerings, whether he offers a male or a female, they shall be unblemished. If he offers a lamb before the Lord, he shall place his hand upon the head of his victim, which shall be slaughtered in the vestibule of the tabernacle of testimony. The sons of Aaron shall pour out its blood around the altar, and from the sacrifice of peace offerings they shall offer a sacrifice to the Lord: the fat and the entire tail, together with the kidneys and the fat that covers the belly; all the inner parts and both kidneys, with the fat that is beside the loins; and the lobe of the liver with the kidneys. The priest shall burn these upon the altar as food for the fire and as an offering to the Lord.

If his offering is a goat, and he offers it to the Lord, he shall place his hand upon its head, slaughter it at the entrance of the tabernacle of testimony, and the sons of Aaron shall pour out its blood around the altar. They shall remove from it for food for the Lord’s fire the fat that covers the belly and the fat that covers all the inner parts; the two kidneys with the caul that is above them beside the loins [another reading: “around the inner parts”]; and the fat of the liver with the kidneys. The priest shall burn these upon the altar as food for the fire and as a most pleasing fragrance.

All the fat shall belong to the Lord by perpetual statute throughout your generations and in all your dwellings. You shall eat neither fat nor blood at all.

*(From Hesychius.)* Whom the legislator commanded to offer a bull, whom a sheep, and whom a goat, we explained long ago in the discussion of the burnt offerings. Thus, we showed that the bull signifies the worker of the legal commandments. We said that sheep are the simple, and that goats are also simple, but are people who have been involved in sins and afterward converted.

Yet there he mingled the sacrifice of goats with that of sheep, saying: “If the offering is from the flock, whether from sheep or goats, he shall offer a year-old animal without blemish as a burnt offering.” The Septuagint, however, reads: “If his gift is from sheep, from lambs and kids, he shall offer an unblemished male.”

Since the Old Testament regarded sheep as a kind of category embracing lambs and kids, you will find that not only here but also in Amos goats are called sheep. He says (Chapter VII): “I was not a prophet, nor a son of a prophet, but I was among the people [manuscript: *epolus*], stripping sycamores, and the Lord took me from the flocks of sheep.” Since those who are “among the people” [*epolus*], properly speaking, are called those who feed goats [or: “who pasture goats”], it is clear that he also placed goats among sheep.

Since, therefore, the law calls some of them lambs and others goats, with the lambs signifying those who are simply innocent and have committed no sin, and the goats signifying those who are simple but have sinned and then been converted, their sacrifice was rightly handed down as one and the same in the burnt offerings.

For the person who wishes to think perfectly, even if he was a sinner, must conduct himself, once he has chosen a perfect life, like one who previously did not sin.

In the sacrifice of peace offerings, while he preserved the same requirements in the sacrifice of sheep, goats, and cattle, he preserved one additional requirement in the sheep: he commanded that not only the fat and the caul of the liver—or, according to the Septuagint, the lobe of the liver—but also the kidneys and the tail be offered; or, according to the same Septuagint, the unblemished loin with the kidneys.

Because the simple person omitted many things that he ought to have done, he must offer his virtue to God, so that he may not use his virtue for evil, as the simple person does, but rather for good, and make evident that he has omitted nothing of what he can know and perform.

The simple are rightly made cautious, since through their simplicity they could easily be led according to another’s will, so that they must offer to God not only the kidneys and the fat above them but also the loin located at the kidneys.

As for the phrase added in that same translation, “without blemish,” understand it as “whole.” Explaining this, Symmachus rendered “without blemish” as “whole,” while Aquila rendered it “perfect.” For this reason also he added it with the kidneys, wishing that it be offered whole and perfect in the sense we have explained, so that one part of the simple person might not be offered to God and another to the adversary.

It is enough for such a person to fail to do the things belonging to virtue in order to receive pardon; but when he does evil, he will not have pardon. Therefore the Lord commands the simple to be like doves, because doves possess an excessive kind of simplicity, yet are not entirely free from every kind of wickedness.

The person who offers a sacrifice from cattle, as a worker of the legal commandments, has no need to offer the loin, because he has received this as part of the correction of good actions. But the person who sacrifices from goats, although he belongs to the simple class, is understood to have been converted from among sinners and cannot offer an unblemished loin, for sin once stained it. It is therefore clear that the former, since he had not been in sins, can offer an unblemished loin; but the one who had been in sins will no longer offer the loin in sacrifices, since he is reckoned among the goats, for which the offering of the loin was not established.

This was the reason why, in the sacrifice of peace offerings, he distinguished lambs from goats.

The other requirements are common, and we need not discuss them, since they were sufficiently treated in the offering of cattle.

It is necessary, however, to understand how, where he says, “The priest shall burn these upon the altar as food for the fire and as a most pleasing fragrance,” the Septuagint reads, “The priest shall offer it upon the altar: the entrails, a fragrance of sweetness.” The other interpreters, in the sacrifice of burnt offerings, rendered *entrails* as “burnt offerings,” while others rendered it “offering.” But in this sacrifice of peace offerings one gives “bread,” while others indicate “grain,” clearly showing that although this offering is not one of perfect philosophy—for that is the sacrifice of the burnt offering—it is nevertheless sufficient to nourish a person in matters pertaining to salvation and to give strength to the one who labors.

For the prophet David says that this nourishment provides bread when he says: “Bread strengthens the human heart” (Ps. CIII).

“All the fat shall belong to the Lord by perpetual statute throughout your generations and in all your dwellings, and you shall eat neither fat nor blood at all” (Ps. CIII).

We have said that the fat signifies the desire or longing within us, while the blood represents the soul. Since, therefore, he commanded that the fat be offered forever, it is clear that he wishes our desire or longing to be consecrated to God.

“Forever” means that we must not divide it between God and the world. Therefore he also added, “throughout your generations,” that is, through every age. “Generations” signifies the changes of ages. Jeremiah demonstrates this when he tells the Jewish people in Babylonia to write of seven generations, numbering seventy years.

“In all your dwellings” means in every way of life, whether we pursue a communal life or attain a solitary one. Hence David said: “He makes the like-minded dwell in a house” (Ps. CXII).

He commanded that neither fat nor blood be eaten at all. The prohibition of fat is because he does not wish us to have a desire or longing that is our own—that is, carnal. Therefore James said: “Each person is tempted when he is drawn away and enticed by his own desire” (Jas. I).

The prohibition of blood is so that a person may not rush either toward his own death or toward that of his neighbor. For this belongs to savage beasts. Therefore he said: “You shall not eat any blood.” He commands us not only to spare our neighbors but also ourselves. For he also gave another explicit command to Noah: “You shall not eat flesh with its blood, for I will require the blood of your lives.”

By abstinence from blood he signifies that he wishes human beings to abstain from murder. He did not forbid one to be sacrificed for God or to despise one's life; indeed, he commanded it altogether. Hence he also ordered that the blood be poured around the base of the altar.

## Chapter VI. On sacrifices for the sin of ignorance.

## Chapter IV. Concerning Offerings for the Sin of Ignorance

**(Chapter IV.)** And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “Speak to the children of Israel: When a person sins through ignorance and does something contrary to any of all the commandments of the Lord that he has commanded not to be done, if the priest who has been anointed sins, causing the people to offend, he shall offer to the Lord for his sin an unblemished bull-calf. And he shall bring it to the entrance of the tent of testimony [Col. 0270B] before the Lord, and shall place his hand upon its head, and shall sacrifice it to the Lord. He shall also draw some of the bull-calf’s blood and carry it into the tent of testimony. When he has dipped his finger in the blood, he shall sprinkle some of it seven times before the Lord, toward the veil of the sanctuary. He shall put some of the same blood upon the horns of the altar of the most fragrant incense before the Lord, which is in the tent of testimony. But all the remaining blood he shall pour out at the base of the altar of holocaust at the entrance of the tent. And he shall offer the fat of the bull-calf for the sin, both the fat that covers the entrails and all that is within them, the two kidneys and the fatty covering that is over them beside the loins, and the fat of the liver together with the kidneys, just as it is removed from the bull-calf of the sacrifice of peace offerings. And he shall burn them upon the altar of holocaust.

“But the hide and all the flesh, together with the head, the feet, the entrails, the dung, and the rest of the body, he shall carry outside the camp to a clean place where the ashes are customarily poured out. And he shall burn them upon a pile of wood, which shall be burned in the place where the ashes are poured out.”

The legislator omitted none of the necessary details, indicating the differences among ways of life and showing us, in the offering of sacrifices, the paths by which we ought to conduct ourselves. After this he necessarily explains Christ’s sacrifice, through which the remission and redemption of sins have been granted to us.

First, therefore, understand this above all: he said that sins belong to the soul. For some accuse the body as though it were the cause of sin, but this is not so. If the soul is healthy, the indulgence of the flesh will harm it in no way. When the soul governs it in the proper manner, that indulgence withdraws and ceases. But if you say, “Yet he said that the soul sins unwillingly,” nevertheless it is not compelled by the flesh, but by ignorance of the good, which it suffers through negligence and a change toward worse things, so that it even judges pleasant those things that are harmful.

Observe also how he repeatedly brings the priest into the discussion. He says: “When a person sins concerning any of all the commandments of the Lord that he commanded not to be done, and does something.” Then: “If the priest who has been anointed sins.” Since the anointed priest has sinned, he says that the priest who offers for sins is like the others, because Christ also presented himself to us as like us. Concerning him Paul says: “Therefore he had to be made like his brothers in every respect, so that he might become merciful” (Heb. II). He is the faithful priest in the things that concern God, to reconcile the sins of the people, explaining in Christ a very great part of this law.

But now the matters that follow must also be investigated. Behold, the legislator called the sin of the priest himself the sin of the people, because a negligent visible priest—whether he sins himself or does not punish sinners—incites those who are inexperienced to similar acts. The intelligible priest, however, neither committed sin himself nor neglected us even slightly: together with the natural law, he gave us the written law, and, as Paul says, did not leave himself without testimony.

Nevertheless, since this figure must be fitted to Christ, insofar as possible, so that the color of the image may be brought to completion in every respect, we ought to understand what has been said according to what is worthy of Christ, the intelligible priest. For if someone abuses God’s long-suffering—God who does not wish to destroy the sinner—it seems that God gives him permission to sin. Therefore Isaiah says: “Why have you made us stray, Lord, from your ways? You have hardened our heart so that we would not fear you?” (Isa. LXIII). Habakkuk likewise complains in somewhat similar words: “Why do you look upon those who act unjustly and remain silent, while the impious devours one more righteous than himself, and you make human beings like the fish of the sea, and like a creeping thing that has no ruler?” (Hab. I).

The legislator therefore plainly appears to signify that priest to whom it was said: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek”—the one who was anointed by the Father, to whom David said: “Your throne, O God, is forever and ever; a straight rod is the rod of your kingdom. You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you” (Ps. XLIV).

This priest, therefore, fittingly offered sacrifice for our sins. Concerning him Paul writes to the Hebrews: “So Christ, having been offered once to bear away the sins of many, will appear a second time, apart from sin, to those who await him for salvation” (Heb. IX). Nevertheless, he shall offer himself for his sin. The Seventy add: “because he sinned.” His sin, because he once took it upon himself, is called our sin; hence Paul also said: “We entreat you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God; and he who knew no sin, he made sin for us” (II Cor. V).

He shall offer an unblemished bull-calf to the Lord, that is, to the Father—his own flesh. It is unblemished because he committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth (I Pet. II). He is a bull-calf because on the cross he scattered our intelligible enemies.

But since the Seventy read “a bull-calf from cattle,” we shall understand it as having been said “from cattle” because, according to the flesh, he was from the fathers who had been glorious through the righteousness of the Law.

Where shall he offer the bull-calf—that is, his flesh? “At the entrance of the tent of testimony, before the Lord.” “At the entrance,” so that we may understand Christ’s sacrifice to have been accomplished according to the teachings and traditions of the apostles. For we have already shown that these are the entrances of the tent of testimony, since they provide entry to heaven, which is the tent of testimony; for it is taught and proved that we dwell here in the tent of testimony. Isaiah offers a very clear testimony to this when he says: “He who stretches out the heavens like nothing and spreads them out like a tent for dwelling” (Isa. XL).

“Before the Lord,” because the mystery of the cross was completed while the Father was looking on, to such an extent that the Lord said even to the Father who was looking upon him: “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit” (Luke XXIII).

He commanded him to place his hand upon the head of the bull-calf and slaughter the bull-calf. No one else offered him, nor could anyone sacrifice him unless he himself had handed himself over to suffering. Therefore he not only said: “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again” (John X), but also, in anticipation, sacrificed himself at the supper of the apostles.

Because he carried blood into the tent of testimony, Paul teaches this in the Epistle to the Hebrews: “Christ, being the high priest of the good things to come, entered through the greater and more perfect tent, not made with hands—that is, not of this creation—and not through the blood of bulls and calves, but through his own blood, entering once for all into the holy places and obtaining eternal redemption” (Heb. IX). And again: “For Christ did not enter into holy places made with hands, a representation of the true ones, but into heaven itself, to appear before the face of God on our behalf.”

Let us therefore understand this tent of testimony as heaven, since the prophets testified that God dwells in it: “He who dwells in the heavens will laugh at them” (Ps. II); and, “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven” (John III), as the Only-Begotten himself said concerning himself to human beings.

There he brought in the blood, because, bearing the scars of his sufferings, he rose from the dead. Hence he also offered his body to Thomas to touch, and in this way ascended into heaven.

The following statements prove this: “When he has dipped his finger in the blood, he shall sprinkle some of it seven times before the Lord, toward the veil of the sanctuary.”

He calls the Lord’s flesh by many names, because it also fulfilled many operations. Thus the Lord himself is sometimes called the sacrifice, sometimes the shepherd (Luke XI), and again the vine, the bread of life, and the grain of wheat (John XV, VI, XII), appropriately varying and naming his designations in dispensational language.

Now, therefore, he has called his veil his flesh. We cannot doubt this, since Paul explains the mystery when he says: “Therefore, brothers, since we have confidence to enter the holy places by the blood of Christ, by a new and living way that he opened for us through the veil, that is, through his flesh, and since we have a great priest over the house of God, let us draw near with a true heart in the full assurance of faith” (Heb. X). For this reason it was also called the veil of the sanctuary, since it bore the figure of the flesh of the Holy of Holies.

Since, therefore, the finger of God is said to be his power, he appropriately dips his finger into the blood, so that it may be shown that the sufferings of the Lord’s flesh were accomplished by the power of divinity. For how could such things have happened at that time—the darkening of the sun, earthquakes, the splitting of rocks, and similar events?

Thus, receiving suffering in the power of divinity, he sprinkled his own flesh. He sprinkled it seven times because he did this for the remission of sins and for supplying us with the Holy Spirit; for this number is accustomed to signify both.

That we ought to receive the blood in his passion is proved by Pilate and the crowd of Jews. While he was being handed over to the cross, Pilate himself cried out: “I am innocent of the blood of this righteous man” (Matt. XXVII). But they said: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (ibid.).

Peter also remembers this sprinkling in the Catholic Epistle, calling himself an apostle “according to the foreknowledge of God the Father, in the sanctification of the Spirit, for obedience and sprinkling with the blood of Jesus Christ” (I Pet.).

“And he shall put some of the same blood upon the horns of the altar of the incense most pleasing to the Lord, which is in the tent of testimony.”

This altar signifies the seat of God, that is, the cherubim. What the altar is, Isaiah revealed through his vision of the seraphim. For he says: “And one of the seraphim flew to me, and in his hand was a coal which he had taken with tongs from the altar” (Isa. VI).

The incense, as the Seventy say, consists of “compositions.” He calls the composition of all the virtues an incense, since there is an intelligible incense. Where should the virtues be composed, if not in the seat of God? Even if their manner of life is on earth, they nevertheless descend from heaven. Hence Paul said concerning those who lived in the virtues: “Our way of life is in heaven” (Phil. III).

James says: “But the wisdom from above is first of all pure” (Jas. III), calling wisdom one of the general virtues. After this come fortitude, justice, and charity; and still more, the other virtues are ordered together with these. Since these are four, as I think, they are appropriately called the four horns of the aforementioned altar, because they are the categories of the other virtues.

Isaiah also says: “I will remember the mercies of the Lord, remembering his virtues.” The Lord anoints these with his own blood, granting them greater and more perfect power, so that they may prevail against the forces of their adversaries.

He commanded all the remaining blood of the bull-calf to be poured around the base of the altar of holocaust, which is in the tent of testimony. Let us again understand the altar of holocaust as the body of Christ. For just as he is both priest and sacrifice, so he is also the altar. If one thing is signified under many names, we have said that he must also be understood as the veil; there is nothing in this that can cause difficulty. Since there are many operations in him, there are appropriately many names as well.

Since the intelligible altar is the Lord’s body, blessed Paul also understands this. Listen to him saying: “We have an altar from which those who serve the tent have no authority to eat” (Heb. XIII)—namely, the body of Christ, for it is not lawful for Jews to eat from it.

This altar must necessarily be at the entrance of the tent of testimony, that is, at the entrance of heaven, because through it we have entry into heaven.

But let us now examine the remainder of this sacrifice. Whatever he commanded to be done in the sacrifice of peace offerings, or in the saving sacrifice, he also commanded to be done in this one. He orders the two kidneys to be offered, together with the fatty covering that is over them and the fat of the liver—which the Seventy render “the lobe of the liver.” He orders them to be burned upon the altar of holocaust, dividing the sacrifice into two parts, so that all may be permitted to imitate Christ’s sacrifice: both those whose manner of life is lower—for we have said that the sacrifice of peace offerings is appropriate to them—and those who have a higher understanding, for whom it is sufficient to imitate what follows:

“But the hide and all the flesh, together with the head, the feet, the entrails, the dung, and the rest of the body, he shall carry outside the camp.”

He commanded this so that you would not divide Christ, as some do when they say: “The one who is from Mary suffered, but the one who is from God the Father did not suffer.” For we have one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, who—as Paul said [Ms., “because”]—although he suffered as a human being, nevertheless worked as God in his sufferings (Heb. II).

For all his humanity is called flesh in the Lord, because “the Word became flesh.” Therefore he commanded his flesh to be burned together with the head and the feet—or, according to the other interpreters, “with the head and the extremities,” namely, the feet. Thus, through the words mentioned above, we might understand that the one who suffered for us existed from the beginning and in the last things, concerning whom Paul says: “For in him all things were created, in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or principalities or authorities. All things were created through him and in him. He is before all things, and in him all things hold together. He is also the head of the body, the Church; he is the beginning, the firstborn from the dead, so that he might be first in everything” (Col. I).

Moreover, when he says “with the entrails and the dung,” or, as the Seventy have it, “with the belly and excrement,” he says this so that, because the intelligible belly bears the figure of the mind—as we showed in the sacrifices of the other holocausts—we may by no means fail to understand that the one who suffered for us possessed a mind, which certain heretics deny.

The dung signifies the sins of the human race, which the crucified one took upon himself. These are plausibly called the Lord’s dung: although dung is unclean, it does not pollute the one who carries it. Nor is it part of our nature, although it is within us; so too our sins, which the Lord bore, were alien to him and did not pollute him in any way, for he remained without sin.

Therefore the legislator commands the whole bull-calf—that is, the whole Christ—to be cast outside the camp, in a completely clean place where the ashes are customarily poured out. He plainly strives to signify the place of Christ’s sacrifice, for he suffered outside the camp. Paul testifies to this when he says: “Therefore Jesus also suffered outside the gate in order to sanctify the people” (Heb. XIII).

But what place is clean for ashes? Golgotha, certainly—and so clean that he himself cleansed the whole world. It is rightly called the place of ashes, because the sins of the human race were extinguished in that very place; hence it is called a clean place.

“And they shall burn them upon a pile of wood.”

We have said that the wood in the fire signifies the sacred Scriptures. Whatever took place in the Lord at the time of his passion took place to fulfill what the prophets had said. The Lord makes this clear when he was seized by the Jews, saying: “Have you come out as against a robber, with swords and clubs to capture me? Every day I sat in the temple teaching, and you did not seize me. But this has happened so that the Scriptures of the prophets might be fulfilled” (Luke XXII). And again: “Jesus, seeing that all things had been accomplished, so that the Scripture might be fulfilled, said, ‘I thirst’” (John XIX).

Although the figure of the Lord’s passion appears in each individual detail, nevertheless the legislator seems to portray this mystery more clearly in what follows.

**(Chapter IV.)** “But if the whole congregation of Israel has erred, and through ignorance has done something contrary to the commandment of the Lord, and afterward has understood its sin, it shall offer a bull-calf for the sin. It shall bring it to the entrance of the tent, and the elders of the people shall place their hands upon its head before the Lord. When the bull-calf has been sacrificed in the sight of the Lord, the anointed priest shall carry some of its blood into the tent of testimony. Having dipped his finger in it, he shall sprinkle it seven times toward the veil, and shall put some of the same blood on the horns of the altar [Col. 0275B] that is before the Lord in the tent of testimony. But the remaining blood he shall pour out beside the base of the altar of holocaust, which is at the entrance of the tent of testimony. He shall remove all its fat and burn it upon the altar. He shall do with this bull-calf as he did previously. And when the priest has prayed for them, the Lord will be merciful. But he shall carry the bull-calf itself outside the camp and burn it, as he burned the first bull-calf, because it is for the sin of the multitude.”

The legislator changed nothing in these matters that could be outside the sacrifice already mentioned, which is the sacrifice of the high priest. He commanded the same thing to be offered by the congregation of Israel and by the priest: in both places he mentioned a bull-calf. Similarly, he commands the blood to be brought into the tent of testimony and the bull-calf to be burned outside the camp.

It is shown most plainly in what has been said that the sins of the people and of the priest were the same; for why would the same sacrifice be offered for them if they were not the same?

The alteration made in the sacrifice relates rather to establishing that the sacrifice is one. For in the case of the priest he did not say, “if he has understood his sin.” Nor was the Lord going to be ignorant of the sin for which he became incarnate in order to take it upon himself.

But concerning the congregation—that is, the synagogue or the people—observe what he says: “But if the whole congregation of Israel has erred, and through ignorance has done something contrary to the commandment of the Lord, and afterward has understood its sin.” Thus at the beginning they were ignorant of their sin, but afterward they recognized it. The very words of the Lord show this. He says: “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin; but now they have no excuse for their sin” (John XV), since through his teaching they learned what they had previously not known.

When, therefore, they recognized their sin, they then turned to the sacrifice of the Only-Begotten.

Next, in the priest’s sacrifice, we said that he himself placed his hand upon the head of the bull-calf; here, however, he says that the elders did this. Both things were truly enacted in Christ’s sacrifice: the elders of the people and the scribes, together with Caiaphas the high priest, were intent upon bringing it to completion, and they said: “It is better for you that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation should not perish” (John XVI).

And because it could in no way have been accomplished unless the Lord himself had handed himself over to suffering, he foretold to Peter: “Put your sword into its sheath. Shall I not drink the cup that the Father has given me?” (Matt. XXVI).

For he was hastening to dispense the remission of our sins; this must necessarily be considered in the matters concerning the sacrifice of the synagogue’s bull-calf.

He says: “He shall do with this bull-calf as he did previously. And when the priest has prayed for them, the Lord will be merciful.” For Christ became our propitiation in his blood, as blessed Paul wrote to the Romans. Through him sins were remitted to such an extent that even those who sinned against him might obtain remission. For concerning them he had said: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke XXIII).

But what did the legislator say at the conclusion of the sacrifice? The conclusion of the law itself is sufficient for us to reveal the matters now before us:

“But he shall carry the bull-calf itself outside the camp and burn it, as he burned the first bull-calf, because it is for the sin of the multitude.”

Do you see how he commands nothing to be changed in the second sacrifice except what was done in the first? And why? “Because it is for the sin of the multitude,” he says. Therefore it is clear and indisputable that he understood the sin of the people and of the priest to be the same. For this reason he ordered the same sacrifice in both cases, not even separating them in his wording—something he would not have done unless those things that were then enacted had been figures.

**(The Same.)** “If a prince sins and through ignorance does one of the things prohibited by the law of the Lord, and afterward understands his sin, he shall offer an unblemished male goat as an offering to the Lord, and shall place his hand upon its head [Col. 0276C]. When he has slaughtered it in the place where the holocaust is customarily killed before the Lord, because it is for sin, the priest shall dip his finger in the blood of the sin offering, touch the horns of the altar of holocaust, and pour out the remainder at its base. But he shall burn the fat upon it, as is customarily done with the victims of peace offerings. He shall pray for him and for his sin, and it shall be forgiven him.

“But if a person from the people of the land sins through ignorance, doing any of the things prohibited by the law of the Lord, and commits an offense, and recognizes his sin, he shall offer an unblemished female goat. He shall place his hand upon the head of the sin offering and slaughter it in the place of the holocaust. The priest shall take some of its blood on his finger, touch the horns of the altar, and pour out the remainder at its base. Removing all its fat [Col. 0276D] as the fat is removed from the victims of peace offerings, he shall burn it upon the altar as a sweet fragrance to the Lord. He shall pray for him, and it shall be forgiven him.”

Just as in voluntary sacrifices he established distinctions according to the ways of life and the conditions of those who offer them, so again, in the case of sins, he commands sacrifices corresponding to the sins. Their magnitude is determined not only by the act of sin but also by the person of the sinners.

And rightly so, since the Lord also said to the apostles: “The servant who knew his master’s will and did not prepare himself or act according to his will shall be beaten with many blows; but the one who did not know and did what deserved blows shall be beaten with few” (Luke XII). What did he add? “Everyone to whom much was given, much will be required; and from the one to whom much was entrusted, more will be demanded” (Luke XII).

Understand this one as the person whom the legislator calls the prince. If he sins, he offers a male goat. But if someone from the people—he calls him an ordinary person, or a common person, not one distinguished by lot for the study of the law—sins, he offers a female goat.

For even this person would certainly be called a prince if he were appointed to offer a female goat for a lesser sin, just as the other offers a male goat: this one a female, the other a male.

Just as the offering of the female goat signifies a sacrifice for sin, so the male goat and the female goat, although *hircus* is masculine and *capra* feminine, interpret the power of the sacrifice. The legislator did not attend to this without reason. For “male goat” and “female goat” are rendered by the Seventy in Greek as **χίμαρος** (*chimāros*) and **χίμαιρα** (*chimaira*), which the Latins translated from the same edition as “a male kid from the goats” and “a female kid from the kids.”

Now *chimarrus* and *chimarra* are offspring of goats; *chimerini*, or **χιμέρινοι** (*chimerinoi*), are those born around the time of winter. For goats give birth twice a year: some offspring are born in winter and others in summer.

Since this is how matters stand, he teaches that winter signifies the sorrow of repentance. In sorrow and weeping she gives birth to children here, but nevertheless her children are not approved for the sacrifice.

Hence I think that he commanded penitents to offer kids—that is, **χιμάρους** (*chimārous*)—as wavering persons, so that those who, rising up from their sins amid the changing waves and resisting them, may be saved altogether through mercy. For if they remain in repentance and do not despair, they will be delivered, as though in a storm they were leaving the helm of the soul’s ship. But if they despair, they immediately perish, like certain fearful pilots or sailors.

The Lord also said: “Pray that your flight may not be in winter or on the Sabbath” (Matt. XXIV), calling winter the time of repentance and understanding the Sabbath as the soul’s idleness and cessation from the virtues. The Sabbath was given for rest and freedom from evil deeds, but the Jewish nation used it in the opposite way.

It is grievous to be tempted or to suffer persecution at a time when repentance is necessary, and much more grievous at a time when one is free from all works. Therefore he counted as the final case the person who suffers persecution on the Sabbath, as the greater case.

Since, then, we have learned the power of the male goat, the female goat, and the kid, and the manner of the differences among the sacrifices, let us now see what is done in each of the two sacrifices.

The things they have in common are these: the end of repentance and its general effect is the remission of sins. The legislator plainly states this when he says: “But if a person from the people of the land sins through ignorance, doing any of the things prohibited by the law of the Lord.”

He does not say what particular thing, because whoever transgresses in any one matter sins against the whole law, as blessed James says: “Whoever keeps the whole law but fails in one point has become guilty of all of it” (Jas. II).

When the person who sinned has recognized his sin—for he cannot otherwise repent unless he recognizes his sin—then the prince brings a male goat, or *chimarrus*; but the person from the congregation brings a female goat, or *chimarra*. Both must be unblemished, for repentance must be unblemished.

What is its blemish? Clearly, if the penitent sympathizes with the sin or is a friend of the person for whom he is repenting. He must withdraw from that same sin with a perfect and most earnest resolve.

Then he shall place his hand upon the head of the offering, himself making the sin manifest and offering his confession.

According to the Seventy, he himself does not kill it, but others do. For the assistance of others in prayer is necessary, so that his repentance may be received. Therefore he did not command the priests alone to kill it. He says: “They shall kill it in the place where the holocausts are killed.” He did not add who should kill it. It is permitted in the sacrifice of repentance to make use of the assistance of another.

James testifies to this when he says: “Pray for one another, so that you may be saved” (Jas. V). But let us especially make use of the assistance of the righteous, for he adds: “The continual prayer of the righteous has great power” (ibid.).

Where shall they kill it? According to the Seventy, “in the presence of the Lord.” We must confess sin in the presence of the Lord; therefore David said: “I made my sin known to you, and I did not conceal my iniquities. I said, ‘I will confess my iniquity against myself to the Lord,’ and you forgave the iniquity of my heart” (Ps. XXXI).

For this reason the legislator adds: “The priest shall take and place the blood of the sin offering with his finger upon the horns of the altar of holocaust.” He called it “the blood of the sin offering,” because it is offered for sin.

Christ the priest shall offer its firstfruits upon the horns of the altar of holocaust, namely, through his cross. For if the altar of the Lord’s holocaust is the body of the Lord, then without doubt its horns are the cross, concerning which Habakkuk said: “Horns are in his hands” (Hab. III).

He must offer upon his cross the firstfruits of his blood, which is offered for sin, because the work of the cross and its effect is the perfect remission of our sins.

When he says: “He shall pour the remaining blood at its base,” he assigns all repentance to the preaching of the Gospel, which we have said is the base of the altar. He rightly assigns all repentance to apostolic preaching, because its entire purpose is that every repentant person may be saved by correcting himself. Therefore the Lord also provides its first and authoritative proclamation in the Gospel: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matt. IV).

“He shall remove all the fat as the fat is removed from the victims of peace offerings,” so that all the desire of the penitent may look upward, that is, be directed toward heaven. Only then can the repentance offered be reckoned among the sacrifice of peace offerings.

But to show what the end of these things is, he adds: “The priest shall pray for him, and he shall be forgiven.” We are not capable of forgiving sins for ourselves; Christ, however, accomplishes propitiation for us.

But if he offers a victim from the flock for sin—namely, an unblemished sheep—he shall place his hand upon its head and slaughter it in the place where the victims of holocausts are customarily killed. The priest shall take some of its blood with his finger, touch the horns of the altar of holocaust, and pour out the remainder at its base.

He shall also remove all the fat, as the fat of the ram sacrificed for peace offerings is removed, and burn it upon the altar as incense to the Lord. He shall pray for him and for his sin, and it shall be forgiven him.

Following the same course as before, the legislator has joined the sheep to the offering of the female goat, or *chimarra*, which, as we have said, is offered by those who are from the people and are not occupied in the study of the law. For among the people and the ordinary persons there can also be some simple people for whom the sacrifice of a sheep is appropriate, as has been demonstrated both in the holocausts and in the sacrifices of peace offerings.

The legislator therefore plainly wishes to establish that not only the prince—that is, the person of higher knowledge—nor merely the common person, but also anyone among the common people who is simple, if he should happen to sin, must likewise practice repentance for the redemption of sins. He therefore introduces the sacrifice of a sheep.

He commanded a sheep rather than a ram—that is, a female rather than a male—because he assigned the sacrifice of females to the common people. In this he clearly admonishes those who receive the law: whoever has obtained a position of authority and is superior to others in knowledge must not only display simplicity but must also be prudent, as a serpent, according to the Lord’s saying. But whoever is not such a person—who does not abound in knowledge and therefore remains among the people—even though he is simple, if he happens to sin, will not be forgiven that sin unless he washes it away through the offering of repentance.

Since these matters stand thus, the remaining points do not require further explanation. Since the sacrifice is for sin, he has here ordered both a female goat and a sheep together. Therefore, as we are hastening toward what follows, it is not necessary to linger long over the present passage.

## Chapter VII. Concerning One Who Hears Someone Swearing Falsely

**(Chapter V.)** “If a person sins and hears the utterance of one swearing, and is a witness because he either saw it himself or knows of it, if he does not report it, he shall bear his iniquity.”

**(From St Augustine.)** This seems to say that a person sins when someone swears falsely in his hearing, and he knows that he is swearing falsely yet remains silent. He knows it, however, if he is a witness to the matter about which the oath is sworn—if he either saw it or had knowledge of it; that is, if he came to know it in some manner, either saw it with his own eyes or was informed by the one who swears. For in this way he could be aware of it.

But there is often no small temptation between the fear of this sin and the fear of betraying persons. By warning or forbidding, we may call back from so grave a sin one who is ready to commit perjury. But if he does not listen, and swears falsely before us concerning a matter, whether he should be denounced, should denunciation expose him even to danger of death, is a most difficult question. Yet, since it was not specified to whom this should be reported—whether to the person to whom the oath is sworn, or to a priest, or to someone who not only cannot persecute him by imposing punishment, but can also pray for him—it seems to me that a person frees himself even from the bond of sin if he reports it to persons who can benefit the perjurer more than harm him, either to correct him or to appease God on his behalf, provided that he too employs the remedy of confession.

After mentioning this kind of sin—failing to report another’s perjury—he commanded that no sacrifice be offered for it; but then he added the following.

## Chapter VIII. Concerning a Person Who Touches Something Unclean, or Something Killed by a Beast.

## (SAME PLACE.) The person who touches something unclean—whether an animal killed by a beast, or one that has died of itself, or any other creeping thing—and then forgets his uncleanness is guilty and has committed an offense. And if he touches anything unclean belonging to a human being, according to every impurity by which a person is ordinarily defiled, and afterward, having forgotten it, comes to know of it, he shall be liable for the offense. Here too he did not mention what offering should be made for this kind of sin, but continued and said:

“The person who swears and utters with his lips that he will do either something evil or something good, and confirms the matter with an oath and a verbal declaration, but afterward forgets it and recognizes his offense, shall do penance for his sin and offer a ewe-lamb from the flocks or a she-goat; and the priest shall pray for him and for his sin.”  

### (From Augustine.)

What, then, is the meaning of the fact that he mentioned no sacrifice for someone’s concealed perjury, or for touching a carcass or something unclean, but for that sin in which someone unknowingly swears falsely he said that a ewe-lamb or she-goat should be offered? Or should this sacrifice be understood as applying to all the matters mentioned above? For he wished first to enumerate everything and then to indicate by what sacrifice it could be expiated.

“But if he is unable to offer livestock, let him offer two turtledoves or two young pigeons to the Lord: one for sin and the other as a burnt offering. He shall give them to the priest, who, offering the first as a sin offering, shall bend its head back toward its wings, so that it remains attached to the neck and is not completely severed, and shall sprinkle some of its blood on the wall of the altar. Whatever remains he shall cause to drip at its base, because it is a sin offering; but the other he shall burn as a burnt offering, as is customary. The priest shall pray for him and for his sin, and it shall be forgiven him.

“But if his hand cannot furnish two turtledoves or two young pigeons, he shall offer for his sin a tenth part of an ephah of fine flour. He shall not pour oil upon it, nor place any frankincense on it, because it is a sin offering. He shall hand it to the priest, who, taking a full handful from it, shall burn it on the altar as its memorial portion, praying for and expiating the one who offered it. The remainder he himself shall have as a gift.”

### (From Hesychius.)

Is the legislator repeating the same matter when he had previously said: “But if someone from the people of the land should sin through ignorance, doing any of the things forbidden by the law of the Lord, and should commit an offense”? There he gave a general command concerning every sin and prescribed what should be offered.

For when he said, “But if someone from the people of the land should sin through ignorance, doing any of the things forbidden by the law of the Lord, and should commit an offense,” he showed that Israel was a people possessing understanding: having learned God’s commandments, they ought not to transgress any provision of the law; but, having transgressed, they ought to fulfill what pertains to repentance.

In the present passage, however, when he says, “If a person should sin,” he does not add “from the people of the land.” And he is entirely right, for he is speaking of sins from which, as James says, even those who are from the nations must abstain: things sacrificed to idols, things strangled, blood, and sexual immorality (Acts 15:21). In these matters you will find the following offenses included.

Moreover, in the earlier passage the sin of each individual who transgresses by himself is indicated—what a person has done on his own. Here, however, he points to one who has shared in the sins of others. This is what the touching of an unclean thing, a carcass, or something captured by a beast signifies. He explains openly, not through riddles, what certain people disregard: that when another person leads someone into error, one does not reprove the error but gives consent to it.

Now, therefore, he shows that in this matter too we require an offering, namely the offering that pertains to the absolution of repentance.

“If a person should sin and hear the voice of one who swears, and should be a witness—whether he himself saw it or was aware of it,” that is, if someone sees a theft or fraud committed by another, while the perpetrator gives an oath concerning it, or if in some other way he knows that the person is swearing falsely, but does not expose him, “he shall bear his iniquity.”

And rightly so. For whoever was permitted to rebuke the sin but concealed it has undoubtedly become its accomplice; and whoever has assisted has drawn the sin onto himself.

Nor did he consider only the uncleanness of the aforementioned sin something to be avoided. He also intended to show that if someone touches every unclean thing, or a carcass, or something captured by beasts, these are not bodily but moral acts that render a thing unclean. He did not mean those impurities that the Jewish people imagine.

What those acts are whose fellowship must be avoided as unclean, the Savior taught the apostles when he said:

“Are you also still without understanding? Do you not know that whatever enters the mouth goes into the stomach and is expelled into the sewer? But the things that come out of the mouth proceed from the heart, and these defile a person. For from the heart proceed evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, false testimonies, thefts, blasphemies. These are the things that defile a person” (Matt. 15).

For this reason the legislator understood unclean things—things that pollute those who touch them, that is, those who share in them—as carcasses. A person who has died through sin is like them. Concerning such people the Lord said: “Let the dead bury their own dead.”

A person is “captured by beasts” when, with the devil working within him, he is dragged into some evil action, as Judas was dragged into betraying the Lord. Concerning him the evangelist John says: “After the supper, the devil having put it into the heart of Judas Iscariot, the son of Simon, to betray him” (John 13).

But since in the Septuagint translation he did not say simply “captured by a beast,” but added “unclean”—“one who is captured by a beast”—do you think that someone captured by a beast is not in every way also unclean? We say absolutely not. For not everyone who is captured by a beast is thereby killed by it. Perhaps, after being captured, he may also be freed, as Peter was. He fell into the devil’s snare at the time of his denial, but, repenting, escaped. Thus he says with David: “My soul has been delivered like a sparrow from the snare of the hunters” (Ps. 123).

Such a person, therefore, is not unclean. But certain distinctions are established, according to the Septuagint, among carcasses. Of these, some are said to be livestock, while others are called abominations.

A carcass of livestock is a person who sins through lack of understanding and lives the life of cattle, contrary to the law. Unclean abominations, such as dogs, monkeys, and whatever other animals are like them, are called abominations; these were also worshiped by unbelievers. “Any creeping thing” means whatever drags itself along on its belly.

Through these things he most clearly signifies both idolaters and those living in some other evil way—that is, in deceit, plunder, or other forms of greed. If someone shares by contact in all these things and forgets them—or, as the Septuagint says, if the matter remains hidden from him—then forgetfulness of the soul, darkness of mind, or evil conduct is itself defilement.

By touching such things, therefore, whether by showing indulgence toward those who practice them or by approving such deeds, a person is defiled in every way.

But if he touches anything unclean belonging to a human being, “according to every impurity by which a person is ordinarily defiled, according to all his impurity,” then, by touching whatever makes him unclean, he becomes polluted.

Literally, he speaks of those who suffer an issue of semen, of menstruating women, and of certain others, concerning whom the legislator himself speaks more carefully a little later. We have preserved their explanation there, mentioning here only this: not every human impurity defiles the one who touches it. That is why he said, “according to every impurity by which a person is ordinarily defiled.”

The person who swears and utters with his lips—that is, who openly promises—that he intends either to do something evil or to do something good.

There is sin in these cases when the one who has promised something good lies by failing to do it, or when the one who threatened evil tells the truth. This also happened to Herod, who, because he had sworn to Herodias, beheaded John the Baptist (Matt. 14).

“But afterward, having forgotten it, he recognizes his offense.” When each person perceives and comes to know all these matters that have been mentioned, let him confess the sin he has committed and offer a ewe-lamb from the flocks or a she-goat. For here he is speaking of someone who is from the people, that is, from the common populace, among whom it is possible to find a simple person. He prescribes a ewe-lamb from the flocks as suitable for such a simple person, as we said above.

“And the priest shall pray for him and for his sin.” He uses the customary words, recalling to our memory what he previously commanded to be done in the prayer for sins. Since these matters have already been stated once, we do not need to repeat them.

Let us add only this: if a ruler should commit one of these sins, he is to offer a he-goat from the goats, an offering and repentance appropriate to him. He ought not to have sinned, nor to have shared in the sins of another; for instead of provoking his subjects to virtue, he is found to lead or incite them toward iniquity. For this reason the legislator left the matter unexamined, as though it were something that ought not to occur.

It should also be noted that the legislator sometimes calls “offense” a specific iniquity presumed to be committed against God alone, such as the offense committed against holy things and in an oath. At other times he calls every sin that has come to knowledge an offense. Therefore, whenever knowledge of sin is either placed before or added afterward, he calls it in every respect an offense, to show that every sin, once it is known, is committed against God himself.

For this reason it is called an offense, that is, *πλημμέλεια* (*plēmmeleia*).

The legislator does not use this term frequently without reason. Just as, by indicating different ways of life among human beings at the beginning of the book through burnt offerings and sacrifices of well-being, he did not set them forth without purpose, but wished to open many ways and entrances, so now he has not ordained a single kind but many kinds of offerings for sin, in order to propose more numerous forms of repentance.

For not all people can fulfill every form of repentance, nor is every form of repentance suitable for every sin. When repentance requires sackcloth, fasting, tears, continual prayer, vigils, and similar practices, how, for example, can someone weakened by old age or otherwise infirm in body perform such repentance?

Is such a person, then, rejected from repentance because of infirmity or old age? By no means. He has another way of obtaining the remission of sins. What that way is, the following words show.

“For if he is unable to offer livestock, he shall offer for his sin and for the sin he has committed two turtledoves or two young pigeons to the Lord.”

For this reason it is extremely necessary to remember that we said above that the contemplative life, a life occupied in meditation and pure and simple, is signified by young pigeons and turtledoves.

Therefore, one who cannot remain continually free for affliction and distress, eating his bread with ashes and mingling his drink with weeping (Ps. 101), and practicing other similar forms of repentance—because he is prevented by illness or by some other necessity—can repent in another way. He may offer himself to the contemplation of God and to the examination of his law, consecrating his entire mind to a heavenly way of life and completely restraining himself from earthly matters. Through this he obtains both the remission of his sins and justification.

Thus, of the things offered, one is for sin, that is, for the cleansing of sin; the other is for a burnt offering, as though he were crucifying himself, his conduct or way of life, and is entirely offered in sacrifice to God.

He shall offer these things to the priest, namely to Christ. Both offerings are acceptable only when they are offered according to the Lord’s intention and through him. The one who first offers the sin offering offers it first for this reason: no one can become a burnt offering unless he has first been freed from sin.

But what is the nature of this freedom?

“The priest shall bend its head back toward its wings, so that it remains attached to its neck and is not completely severed.”

By the neck, which the Septuagint translators rendered *spondylus*, the entire body is understood, because the strength, health, and substance of the whole body depend upon the neck.

Since the head is ordinarily understood in divine Scripture as the mind, because the mind holds the chief place in a human being, David therefore says to the Lord: “You have crushed the heads of the dragons upon the waters” (Ps. 73)—that is, the mind is crushed when, with the water of baptism granting remission, the mind of the devil is crushed.

“The priest shall bend its head back toward its wings.” He wants us neither to serve the body nor to sympathize with it, but ourselves to be torn away or turned back, so that the law of sin, which dwells in the members of the body through the habit of sinning, may not contend on equal terms against the law of the mind and lead a person captive, as Paul says (Rom. 7).

But because we ought not to reject the body entirely, nor consider it the devil’s creation, as some suppose, but ought to subject it to the mind, he did not command that the head be separated from the neck. Both belong to one and the same creation.

Let us examine what follows:

“He shall sprinkle some of its blood on the wall of the altar; whatever remains he shall cause to drip at its base, because it is a sin offering.”

The wall of the altar is understood as the body of Christ. Concerning it Christ himself said: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2). Its foundation—or, as the Septuagint translated it, its base—is the Gospel.

Accordingly, in keeping with the meaning of Christ’s sacrifice and evangelical teaching, he commands this sacrifice also to be offered for sins. For this reason he added, “because it is a sin offering.” Nothing can deliver people from sins in the same way as imitation of Christ and obedience to evangelical preaching.

Whoever obeys this “shall burn the other as a burnt offering, as is customary,” that is, in the manner in which a burnt offering ought to be made. The Septuagint expresses this clearly in these words: “He shall make it as it ought to be made.”

For one who rejects father, mother, brothers, and all secular things ought to become a burnt offering, if he wishes his offering to be acceptable and intelligible.

If he does these things—if he is unable to practice repentance through the aforementioned means, namely vigils, sackcloth, and other similar afflictions—then the intelligible priest shall pray for him and for his sin, and it shall be forgiven him.

How greatly to be admired, therefore, is God, the giver of this law. In his clemency he grants pardon to human weakness and finds a way by which the infirm may obtain no lesser benefits.

The matter may be understood differently, according to the moral interpretation, concerning the oath that is uttered and then forgotten, and concerning the offering of a ewe-lamb or she-goat from the flocks, or the offering of turtledoves or pigeons.

### (From Gregory.)

To utter an oath is to bind ourselves by a vow to divine service; and when we promise good works, we pledge ourselves to do what is good. But when we vow abstinence and the mortification of our flesh, we swear that for the present we shall spare ourselves in an evil way.

Yet because no one in this life is so perfect that, however devoted to God, he does not sin amid even his smallest pious vows, he is commanded to offer a ewe-lamb or she-goat for his sin.

What is signified by the ewe-lamb, if not the innocence of the active life? What is signified by the she-goat, which often grazes while hanging upon the highest and most remote cliffs, if not the contemplative life?

Therefore, whoever sees that he is not fulfilling what he has promised and undertaken ought to ascend more earnestly to God’s sacrifice, either in the innocence of good works or in the lofty pasture of contemplation.

The ewe-lamb is rightly commanded to be offered from the flocks, whereas the she-goat is not said to be offered from the flocks, because the active life belongs to many, while the contemplative life belongs to few.

When we do those things that we see many people doing and having done, we give, as it were, a ewe-lamb from the flocks. But when the virtue of the one offering is insufficient for a ewe-lamb or a she-goat, two young pigeons or two turtledoves are added as a remedy of repentance.

We know that young pigeons have the sound of lamentation. What, then, is signified by two young pigeons or two turtledoves, if not the double lamentation of our repentance? When we do not rise to offer good works, we should mourn ourselves in two ways: because we have not done what is right and because we have done what is wrong.

For this reason one turtledove is commanded to be offered for sin and the other as a burnt offering. A burnt offering is called such because it is wholly burned.

We offer one turtledove for sin when we utter a lament over our fault. We make a burnt offering of the other when, because we have neglected good deeds, we set ourselves wholly ablaze and burn with the fire of grief.

It must not be passed over in silence that in this offering of a turtledove or pigeon, which is commanded to be offered for sin, the fact that the head remains attached to the body of the victim after its death allows the person of our Mediator to be understood allegorically.

### (From Gregory.)

The death of our Redeemer availed for the union of his body, that is, the Church, not for its separation. The Mediator of God and human beings—namely, the head of us all and the true sacrifice of purification—by the very means through which he endured death for us, became more truly joined to us.

After the cut, therefore, the head of the turtledove remains attached to its body, because even intervening death does not divide Christ from the Church.

The persecutors therefore accomplished what they had wickedly attempted. They inflicted death in order to sever the devotion of the faithful from him. But from the very point at which the cruelty of unbelievers thought it had extinguished faith, faith grew; and while they thought that by persecuting him they could cut off his miracles, they were compelled, without knowing it, to spread them further.

For who is our head if not the Redeemer of the human race? Of him it is written: “He gave him as head over the whole Church” (Eph. 1), which is his body.

When the Jews persecuted him, they tried to erase his name from the earth. When they saw him crucified and buried, they believed that they had separated him from the love of everyone.

But the head of the turtledove was cut, yet was not severed from its body, because by enduring death for us he joined us more truly to himself in that very death.

### (From Hesychius.)

Since the time for repentance is not always easy—in fact, sometimes it is difficult, namely when we have misused repentance itself and in some way destroyed its power, as happens when someone sins and pretends to repent but returns again to the same conduct—Peter rightly reproved this when he said: “The true proverb has happened to them: The dog has returned to its own vomit, and the washed sow to wallowing in the mud” (2 Pet. 2).

Paul also says: “Let no one be a fornicator or profane person, like Esau, who for one meal sold his birthright. For you know that afterward, when he desired to inherit the blessing, he was rejected; for he found no place for repentance, although he sought it with tears” (Heb. 12).

Since access to repentance is not readily granted to such people, the legislator now gives a sign of it, saying:

“But if he is unable to offer two turtledoves or two young pigeons.”

Whoever cannot offer these cannot possibly offer either a kid or a sheep. Why can he not? The Septuagint says, “He did not find them,” because, having misused the riches of repentance, he did not spend them as he ought.

What, then, shall he do so that despair does not become the cause of his destruction?

“He shall offer for his sin a tenth part of an ephah of fine flour; he shall not pour oil upon it, nor place any frankincense on it, because it is a sin offering.”

This, then, is the form of repentance granted to him. He ought to be anxious and afraid that his repentance may not be accepted, since it has often been insulted and abused. For this reason he does not pour oil over it, as one who doubts whether he is worthy of mercy and compassion. Nor does he place any frankincense upon it, as one who does not know whether the prayer he has so often violated possesses a pleasing fragrance.

Therefore the prophet Joel said to the people of the Jews:

“Return to the Lord your God, for he is gracious and merciful, patient and rich in mercy, and compassionate concerning evil. Who knows whether he will turn and forgive, and leave behind him a blessing, a sacrifice and a drink offering for the Lord our God?” (Joel 2.)

How can there be doubt concerning the merciful, patient, and compassionate God, whether he will turn and relent, and accept sacrifice and a drink offering for sins?

Only because he is speaking to an evil people who love their sins—people who, although they have often repented, have never persevered in pure repentance.

He therefore wishes neither to drive them to despair nor, again, to allow repentant people to presume too much. For this reason he uses doubtful language.

Why should they not readily be given grounds for presumption? Lest presumption make them more negligent in committing other sins, as though their earlier sins had been excused.

The legislator indicates that they are weak and unstable in virtue.

“He shall hand it to the priest.”

The priest is Christ, who is also now understood through the symbolism of the priest. Taking a full handful from it, he shall burn it on the altar as its memorial portion.

The acceptable form of the offering is fine flour, an ephah. The ephah is a measure containing three measures, that is, three *modii*.

Christ, therefore, is the one who offers the sacrifice, and he is himself the sacrifice that is offered. For the ephah, being a measure of three *modii*, clearly indicates the Trinity. It is one measure because the Godhead in it is one, yet it contains three measures, that is, three perfect persons and three subsistences.

Thus it is clear that we do not sin when we call the flesh of the Lord a part of the Trinity, because of its inseparable union with the incarnate Word.

Why is it called a part of the Trinity? Because its glory and power are indivisible, so that Paul says concerning Christ: “In him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily” (Col. 2). John likewise says: “Whoever denies the Son does not have the Father; whoever confesses the Son has the Father also” (1 John 2).

The ephah, therefore, signifies here the incarnate God the Word, since he possesses within himself the fullness of the Trinity.

Its tenth part signifies his flesh. First, this shows the sublimity of his divinity in relation to his humanity; for this reason it is called a part. Second, it signifies that God the Word was incarnate in a complete human being and fulfilled the law.

The tenth signifies both things, because ten is also a perfect number. There are ten commandments of the law. Therefore the law assigned the chief tenth of the tithes to the priest, namely to Christ, since he possesses the first fruits of our lump.

Whoever, therefore, has often violated repentance by repeatedly transgressing, but now wishes to repent again, should do so in hope of Christ. When Peter asked him, “If my brother sins against me, how often shall I forgive him? Up to seven times?” he replied: “I do not say to you up to seven times, but up to seventy times seven.”

This saying gives hope of repentance to those for whom repentance seems impossible.

For this reason he takes a handful from the offering, fills it, makes it a memorial for the one who offered it, and burns it on the altar. In doing so he remembers the word he spoke to the apostles for the salvation of those who came to him: “They shall never perish, and no one shall snatch them from my hand” (John 10).

He saves the person who comes to him for repentance, even if that person has often sinned.

What does he offer by taking a handful for him as a memorial? He offers the word according to which he promised that those who had once come under his hand would not perish.

This memorial he offers upon the altar, his body, which received every sin, even the sin that seemed impossible to save. For this reason he added, “because it is a sin offering,” showing that it belongs to Christ alone to receive the sins of all.

Those who have repeatedly violated repentance by sinning, but at last have repented, possess no hope of repentance because of their repeated violations. Nevertheless, Christ allows even such people to pray—that is, he allows their repentance to be accepted—because of his own word. For he is a merciful and faithful priest before God, who intercedes for the sins of the people.

But let us also learn what the conclusion of this ordinance is. The text continues:

“But the remainder he himself shall have as a gift.”

The Septuagint translated this: “Whatever remains shall belong to the priest, as the sacrifice of fine flour.”

Since we said above that fine flour signifies theology, while this offering pertains not so much to theology as to repentance, the remainder was there assigned to Aaron and his sons. We understand these sons to be those who are able to understand sublime and divine things. They are nourished by the remnants of knowledge, the whole and complete sum of which Christ possesses in the heavens.

It must therefore be considered that this present sacrifice is divided into two parts: into the remission of sins for the repentant person, and into theology for Christ.

For it belongs to God alone to forgive even those sins whose remission seems impossible, because it is written: “What is impossible with human beings is possible with God” (Matt. 19; Luke 18).

Every faithful soul ought to believe that in Christ there is the fullness of knowledge and the power to forgive sins. Therefore every sacrifice ought to be offered to him as to the true priest.

## CHAPTER IX. Concerning the person who, through error, violates the ceremonies of the Lord.

### (CHAP. V.) The Lord spoke to Moses, saying:

“If a person, transgressing through error in matters consecrated to the Lord, should sin, he shall offer for his offense an unblemished ram from the flocks, which can be purchased for two shekels, according to the sanctuary weight. He shall restore what he caused to be lost and add a fifth part to it, giving it to the priest. The priest shall pray for him, offering the ram, and it shall be forgiven him.”

It is good to abstain from every sin, but especially from the sin committed against holy things, because through it God is dishonored.

How serious and how terrible this sin is, the offering that the legislator has set forth here demonstrates. You see that, although he had commanded so many sacrifices to be celebrated, nowhere at the beginning of this book, when the Lord speaks to Moses, does he mention the sacrifice of a ram except in this passage. He wished to show the necessity and usefulness of this sacrifice.

You also see that he did not command a he-goat, she-goat, sheep, or pair of pigeons to be offered, but a ram. From the offering he teaches what sort of sin this is. For the ram is understood as a figure of the Savior.

He not only commanded it to be unblemished, but also specified that it must have a value—or be purchasable—for two shekels, or, according to the Septuagint, for fifty shekels of silver, by the holy shekel.

No one can obtain for himself the sacrifice of the Lord except through the Holy Spirit. For if no one can say, “Lord Jesus Christ,” except in the Holy Spirit (1 Cor. 12), much less can anyone attain his sacrifice without the Spirit’s activity.

Therefore it is not said simply “of fifty shekels.” This number indicates the coming of the Holy Spirit, since he came to the apostles on the day of Pentecost—that is, on the fiftieth day.

The text also says “by the weight of the sanctuary,” or, according to the Septuagint, “by the holy shekel,” so that by adding the word “holy” it might indicate the power and activity of the Holy Spirit.
