Why is the amount specified in shekels? Because a shekel consists of twenty obols, and this number twenty is not subject to sins. Thus those who came out of Egypt when they were twenty years old did not suffer the punishment of the people’s sin. The spiritual person is pure from every sin.

He commanded not only that a ram be offered but also that a fifth part be added. If someone had misused a holy vessel, food, or such anointing oil, the legislator called this a sin committed against holy things.

Such a person shall restore the thing itself and give an additional fifth part—that is, one fifth of its value—to the priest.

This signifies that, since we have five senses, if we have sinned through one sense—for example, if we have employed the eye for adultery at a sacred time and place, or the tongue for slander, the ears for evil speech, the sense of smell for seeking the perfumes of prostitutes, or the hand for profane and unjust touch—we must first abstain entirely from that sin and offer repentance for it through the ram, that is, ask Christ to become our deliverance from the sin committed against him.

Then we must offer the fifth part—that is, the one sense through which the sin was committed—to the priest, namely to Christ, so that we may never again employ any sense for evil action, but consecrate it to God. In this way he will intercede for our sin.

How the ram is offered for sin by the priest is written in another part of the book, where he declared that the sacrifice for sin is equal to the sacrifice made for an offense.

This should now be added: the legislator customarily uses or applies the word “offense” in two ways and calls something an offense. Sometimes he means a sin that has come to knowledge and is no longer unknown as a sin. At other times he means what has been committed against God himself, such as an oath or an offense against holy things.

He calls this an offense for good reason: so that you may recognize that the sin committed knowingly, the sin committed in an oath, and the sin committed against holy things all extend equally against God.

## CHAPTER X. Concerning the offering for one who sins through ignorance or violates the law.

### (SAME PLACE.) If a person should sin through ignorance and do one of the things forbidden by the law of the Lord, and, being liable for the sin, should come to understand his iniquity, he shall offer an unblemished ram from the flocks to the priest, according to the measure and valuation of the sin. The priest shall pray for him concerning what he did unknowingly, and it shall be forgiven him, because he sinned against the Lord through error.

The present passage raises a considerable question worthy of examination. Earlier he commanded that a she-goat or a sheep be offered for sins of this kind. For he said:

“But if someone from the people of the land should sin through ignorance, doing any of the things forbidden by the law of the Lord, and should commit an offense, and should recognize his sin, he shall offer an unblemished she-goat.”

Now, as though he had forgotten what he had commanded, he says:

“If a person should sin through ignorance, and do one of the things forbidden by the law of the Lord, and, being liable for the sin, should understand his iniquity, he shall offer an unblemished ram from the flocks to the priest.”

There appears to be a substantial difference between this sacrifice and the one he prescribed earlier.

Yet he has neither forgotten what came before nor prescribed anything contrary to it. Since we said that the term “person” signifies a gentile, and since such a person might perhaps transgress the commandments of the law through ignorance, the text rightly added, “through ignorance.”

The intelligible ram, namely Christ, rightly wipes away this person’s sin when he is offered in sacrifice for him.

Therefore, if someone is outside the faith of Christ—perhaps a Jew or a pagan—even if he demonstrates repentance for his sins through his conduct and way of life, he will not obtain remission, because he cannot offer the ram, that is, the sacrifice of Christ.

Therefore, wishing in some way to establish a general rule concerning everyone, he did not say, “If a person from the people,” but simply, “If a person should sin,” and should do one of the things forbidden by the law of the Lord.

Accordingly, the statement is rightly understood to concern both the unlearned and the knowledgeable, and every kind of sin.

But since he commands a ram to be offered for an offense, it is perfectly clear that here the legislator uses “offense” to mean an understood sin. Therefore, after saying “through ignorance,” he adds: “and, being liable for the sin, should understand his iniquity.”

Whoever understands the sin has thereby brought it back upon himself and is defiled or burdened by it, until prayer has been made for him through the sacrifice mentioned above.

## CHAPTER XI. Concerning the person who, despising God, denies a deposit or extorts something through false accusation.

## (Chapter 6)

The Lord spoke to Moses, saying:

> [Col. 0290B] The person who sins and, despising God, denies to his neighbor a deposit entrusted to him in confidence, or forcibly extorts something, or brings a false accusation, or finds something that has been lost and, moreover, denies having found it under oath, or commits any other of the several offenses in which human beings commonly sin—when convicted of the offense, he shall restore in full everything he sought to obtain by fraud, and in addition a fifth part to the owner whom he has wronged. For his sin he shall offer an unblemished ram from the flock and give it to the priest according to the valuation and measure of the offense; and the priest shall pray for him before the Lord, and it shall be forgiven him.

You see that, in the same sequence, the Spirit of God hands down both the sin committed against sacred things and that committed through an oath. This is clear from the fact that in both cases he commanded the sacrifice of a ram to be offered. For this is why we said shortly before that a ram was commanded to be offered for every sin: we did so not conjecturing on our own, but following the intention of the lawgiver. But why did he consider the sin committed through an oath and that committed against sacred things together? Because in every respect both pertain to God; and whoever violates an oath harms not only his neighbor but also wrongs God himself, whom he made the mediator.

For it is no small guilt in the sight of God for anyone, against his own conscience, fraudulently to deny to his neighbor a deposit entrusted to him, or forcibly to extort something from him, or to bring a false accusation, or, after finding something his neighbor had lost, to deny it and swear falsely concerning it.

*(From Origen.)* Many people think it is not a sin if they keep something belonging to another that they have found. “God,” he says, “gave it to me; to whom should I return it?” Let them learn, then, that this is like robbery: if someone does not return what he has found, it is a sin.

This is the historical interpretation. But, according to the allegory, a higher meaning must be introduced into this passage. I think that we have received both our soul itself and our body as a deposit from God. And would you like to see another, greater deposit that you have received from God? God entrusted his image and likeness to your very soul.

This deposit, therefore, must be restored to you in its entirety, just as it is evident that you received it. For if you are merciful, as your Father in heaven is merciful (Luke 6), the image of God is in you, and you preserve the deposit intact. If you are perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect, the deposit of God’s image remains in you.

Likewise, all his other qualities—if you are just, holy, pure in heart, and if all that is naturally present in God subsists in you through imitation—the deposit of the divine image is safe with you. But if you act in the opposite way, and instead of merciful you are cruel, instead of devout impious, instead of kind violent, instead of peaceful turbulent, instead of generous a robber, then, having cast away the image of God, you have received the image of the devil within you and denied the good deposit divinely entrusted to you.

Or was this not what the Apostle commanded his chosen disciple Timothy under the mystery, when he said: “O Timothy, guard the good deposit” (1 Timothy 6)?

I add this also: we have received Christ the Lord as a deposit, and we possess the Holy Spirit as a deposit. We must therefore take care that we do not use this holy deposit in an unholy manner. When sins entice us to consent to them, let us not swear that we have not received the deposit; for certainly, if we have this deposit within us, we cannot consent to sins.

But even the rational faculty within me has been entrusted to me, so that I may use it for understanding divine things. Likewise, talent, memory, judgment, reason, and all the movements within me seem to have been entrusted to me by God, so that I may use them in the matters commanded by the divine law. But if a skillful and discerning intellect is turned toward evil arts, and we abuse God’s gifts in matters God does not will, this is to deny the deposit and to turn benefits into treachery.

After this, robbery is discussed. There are evil robbers, and there are good ones. The good are those of whom the Savior says that they seize the kingdom (Matthew 11). But there are also evil robbers, of whom the prophet says: “And the robbery of the poor is in your houses” (Isaiah 3).

The Apostle, however, declares without qualification: “Do not be deceived: neither adulterers, nor the effeminate, nor those who lie with males, nor thieves, nor the rapacious will possess the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians 6).

Yet even in the spiritual understanding there is a culpable kind of seizing, just as those who seize the kingdoms of heaven do so laudably. For example, if a person not yet cleansed of vices and not yet separated from profane and filthy actions should wish secretly to insert himself into the assembly of the saints and hear discourse in which perfect and mystical matters are discussed, such a person has not rightly seized the knowledge of secret and perfect things.

We must remember the Savior’s command, which says: “For no one puts new wine into old wineskins; otherwise the wineskins will burst and the wine will be lost” (Matthew 9). He shows that souls not yet renewed, but remaining in the oldness of malice, should not be entrusted with the secrets of the new mysteries that the world has come to know through Christ.

The lawgiver next adds: “Or if he has harmed his neighbor, or if he has found something lost.” The literal law seems to command that, if someone finds what another has lost and it is sought, he should return it and not swear falsely concerning it. This too is useful instruction for those who hear it.

Likewise, allegorically, we may not inappropriately understand “something lost,” or “a loss,” as it appears in the Septuagint, to mean testimonies that we find wrongly interpreted by heretics. Heretics search the divine Scriptures intensely in order to find a loss from which to construct their error. But if one of them, hearing words being interpreted according to catholic teaching in the Church of God, should come to his senses and understand that what he had found is a loss, he returns what he found—that is, he does not claim another’s error for himself but leaves it with its author.

Let us therefore abstain with all our strength from deceit, since through deceit God, who is truth, is dishonored. Let us also beware of greed, which is signified by money zealously acquired through fraud or seized by force, because Scripture testifies: “Greed is the service of idols” (Galatians 5). “And the desire for possessions is the root of all evils” (1 Timothy 6).

“He shall restore,” he says, “everything he sought to obtain by fraud in full, and in addition a fifth part to the owner whom he has wronged.”

*(From Hesychius.)* Since we say that, in robbery or in a deposit, injustice is done through deceit or perjury both to the person who has suffered the wrong and also against God himself, he rightly commands that a fifth be given to God, toward whom the injury is directed. The fifth, however, is the tongue. We have said that this too is a fifth, although it is one of the five senses.

This, then, is offered to God so that afterward he may not sin, because through the tongue each of the offenses mentioned above is committed. It should be noted, however, that in the Septuagint it is written not that a fifth part but that “fifths” are to be added.

Some explain it in this way: it is not that, for five coins stolen, one coin is added and six coins are returned; rather, whoever stole five coins must return those five and must return another five with one added—that is, eleven.

Let us therefore see, according to the allegory, how these eleven—twice five with one added—are to be returned.

*(From Origen.)* The number five is frequently, indeed almost always, understood as referring to the five senses. We must therefore understand that these five can be restored to the saints in this manner: if we have presumed to misuse them in worldly actions and have devoted their use to things we have done contrary to God, let us make restitution. Let us now devote the five themselves to holy actions and religious services, and add to them another five, which are the senses of the inner person.

Through these, either, having become pure in heart, we see God; or we have ears for hearing what Jesus teaches; or we perceive that fragrance of which the Apostle says, “We are the good fragrance of Christ” (2 Corinthians 5); or we receive that taste of which the prophet says, “Taste and see that the Lord is good” (Psalm 33); or we receive that touch of which John says: “What our eyes have seen and our hands have touched concerning the word of life” (1 John 1).

To all these we add one thing: that we refer them all to the one God.

What should be done concerning the sacrifice of the ram has been explained above.

# Book Two

[Col. 0293]

## Chapter One. On the Law of the Whole Burnt Offering and the Rite of Sacrifices and Libations

*(In the same place.)* The Lord spoke to Moses, saying:

> Command Aaron and his sons: This is the law of the whole burnt offering. It shall be burned on the altar throughout the entire night until morning; the fire shall be kept from the same altar. The priest shall put on a tunic and linen undergarments, and he shall take up the ashes that the consuming fire has burned and place them beside the altar. Then he shall remove his former garments, put on others, carry the ashes outside the camp, and have them consumed to ashes in a very clean place, and so forth.

*(From Hesychius.)* Here the law speaks of the perpetual sacrifice, which it commanded the priests to offer daily in the Book of Exodus. For it says:

> This is what you shall do: on the altar you shall offer two year-old lambs continually each day (Exodus 29).

And shortly afterward:

> As a perpetual offering throughout your generations (ibid.).

It says: “You shall offer one lamb as a whole burnt offering in the morning, and you shall offer another in the evening.”

From this we understand that, among those who belong to the common people, offering a whole burnt offering is left to their will: if they wish, they may offer it. For this reason that sacrifice is called their gift, as a voluntary offering. Perfect wisdom is not demanded of every person; the priest, however, must possess perfect understanding in every respect.

He is commanded to offer the perpetual sacrifice—that is, the continual whole burnt offering—twice a day, morning and evening, so that, beginning with perfect wisdom, he may finish in the same wisdom and shape his whole life toward perfection.

The fire on the altar shall always burn, and the priest shall maintain it. For the person who ought always to kindle the whole burnt offering—that is, the activity of perfect wisdom—must kindle the fire of the Holy Spirit and not allow it to be extinguished. It is extinguished through the negligence of those to whom it has been given. Hence Paul also says: “Do not extinguish the Spirit” (1 Thessalonians 5), as though extinguishing or kindling it lay within our power.

He commanded the fire to be kindled throughout the entire night—not because it was not kindled during the day, for how otherwise would the whole burnt offering be made twice each day? Rather, because the daytime fire was visible, he added the nighttime fire. Since night is the darkness of this life, that is, the ignorance that possesses many—for Paul said of it, “The night has passed, and the day has drawn near” (Romans 13)—he commands us, who have become God’s whole burnt offering, to kindle the fire even at night, so that while others transgress the law and remain earthly, we may be spiritual.

He then added: “The priest shall put on a tunic and linen undergarments.” The priest who offers the whole burnt offering is understood as each person who possesses perfect wisdom, because the priesthood is an example of perfection. Therefore the faithful people are also called “a royal priesthood” (1 Peter 2), since they have received the perfect law of the Gospel.

Whoever wishes to offer a whole burnt offering must put on the tunic, that is, righteousness, and the undergarments, that is, chastity. He wants both the tunic and the undergarments to be made of linen, not wool, because linen clothing is supple and adheres more gently to the body, whereas woolen clothing is rough.

By this he teaches that righteousness and chastity are very pliable and closely joined to the soul. At the same time he teaches that, just as these garments are easy for anyone to possess, so virtues are easy for those who wish to attain them and can quickly be acquired.

He commands the priest, thus clothed, to remove from the altar the ashes of the whole burnt offering that the fire has consumed. What does he teach by this except that, just as the victim is removed—that is, the sacrifice of the completed whole burnt offering—so that another similar offering may again be made, so must we act?

The virtues that we practice with the cooperation of the Spirit we must set aside one by one, so that we may practice others in turn. We must not be content only with what has gone before but must add further virtues, just as a runner, leaving behind the ground already covered, presses on to run the remaining distance, since otherwise he cannot reach the prize.

Therefore, after commanding that the whole burnt offering consumed by fire be removed from the altar, he commanded it to be placed beside the altar. We have said that Christ is the altar of the whole burnt offering.

We therefore remove from him virtues that were long ago completed in practice when we have time to act, lest he fail to credit the earlier virtues to us if, through negligence, we fail to build others upon them. For Christ the just judge preserves for us whatever good we have done, provided that we have not invalidated it through wicked actions.

*(From Origen.)* It should nevertheless be observed that the priest uses one set of garments while engaged in the ministry of sacrifices and another when he goes out to the people.

Paul, the most learned of pontiffs and the most skilled of priests, did this as well. When he was among the assembly of the perfect, as though placed among the Holy of Holies and clothed in a robe and in perfection, he said:

> We speak wisdom among the perfect—not the wisdom of this world, nor of the rulers of this world, who are being destroyed—but we speak God’s wisdom in a mystery, hidden, which none of the rulers of this age has known. For if they had known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory (1 Corinthians 2).

But afterward, as though going out to the people, he changes his robe and puts on another, far inferior to that one. And what does he say?

> I judged that I knew nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified (ibid.).

*(From Hesychius.)* He commands it to be carried outside the camp to a very clean place—that is, to be sent ahead to the future judgment. For the judgment of the future age lies outside the camp of the present age, and it is a clean place, free from every corruption.

But what does he mean by adding: “The fire on the altar shall always burn, and the priest shall maintain it, placing wood on it every morning”?

Just as wood is the fuel of the fire and he commands it to be arranged in the morning, so the testimonies of divine law and meditation on the sacred Scriptures are for us the fuel by which the Spirit is supplied. We have said above that these are the wood.

Therefore we must arrange these things in the morning light—that is, in vigilance and sobriety of soul. For the fire of the Spirit’s supply must suffice for us not only by day but also by night; that is, not only in the time of sobriety but also in the intelligible night of which Paul said:

> Let us not sleep as the others do, who have no hope, but let us watch and be sober. For those who sleep, sleep at night, and those who are drunk, are drunk at night (1 Thessalonians 5).

In this fire we must arrange the intelligible victim and the fat of the peace offerings. “This,” he says, “is the perpetual fire that shall never fail on the altar.” For “God is Spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and in truth” (John 4). Hence the intelligible altar, which is Christ’s body, has an inextinguishable fire supplied by the Spirit.

*(From Gregory.)* Likewise, according to the tropological interpretation: the altar of God is our heart, in which the fire is commanded always to burn, because it is necessary to kindle from it continually the flame of love for the Lord.

Each day the priest must place wood upon it so that it is not extinguished. Every preacher of Christ has become a member of the supreme priest, as the Apostle Peter said to all the faithful: “But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood” (1 Peter 2); and as the Apostle John said: “You have made us a kingdom and priesthood for our God” (Revelation 5).

Therefore, the priest who maintains the fire on the altar must place wood upon it daily. That is, each faithful person, so that the flame of love may not fail within him, must continually gather in his heart both the examples of those who came before and the testimonies of sacred Scripture. For in the exercise of love, supplying either the examples of the Fathers or the Lord’s commands is like providing fuel for the fire.

Because our inner renewal grows old each day through the conduct of this life, this fire must be nourished by adding wood, so that, when our newness is weakened through habitual old age, it may be revived through the testimonies and examples of the Fathers.

And rightly it is commanded that wood be gathered each morning, every day. These things cannot be done until the night of blindness has been extinguished. Or certainly, because morning is the first part of the day, after setting aside thoughts of the present life, every faithful person should first consider how, with whatever strength he possesses, he may inflame the zeal of love that has already nearly failed within him.

For this fire on the altar of the Lord—that is, in our heart—is quickly extinguished unless it is carefully restored by the examples of the Fathers and the Lord’s testimonies.

It is rightly added there: “And, placing the whole burnt offering upon it, he shall burn the fat of the peace offerings.” For whoever kindles this fire of love within himself will certainly place himself as a whole burnt offering upon it, since he burns away every vice that had been living wickedly within him.

When he examines the inner parts of his thoughts and slays his corrupt life with the sword of transformation, he has placed himself upon the altar of his heart and set himself on fire with the flame of love. From this altar the fat of the peace offering gives off fragrance, because the inward richness of the new life, making peace between us and God, produces from us a most pleasing odor.

Because this same love remains unquenchable in the hearts of the elect, it is appropriately added there: “For this is the perpetual fire that shall never fail on the altar.”

This fire will certainly never fail from the altar, because even after this life the ardor of love increases in their minds. For through eternal contemplation it comes about that the more the almighty God is seen, the more he is loved.

*(In the same place.)* This is the law of the sacrifice and of the libations, which the sons of Aaron shall offer before the Lord and before the altar.

The priest shall take a handful of fine flour mixed with oil, and all the frankincense placed upon the fine flour. He shall burn it on the altar as a memorial, a pleasing fragrance to the Lord. Aaron and his sons shall eat the remaining portion of the fine flour without leaven, and they shall eat it in the holy place, in the court of the tabernacle.

It shall not be leavened, because part of it is offered as incense to the Lord. It shall be most holy, like the offering for sin and for an offense. Only males of the lineage of Aaron shall eat it. It is an everlasting statute throughout your generations, from the sacrifices of the Lord. Everyone who touches them shall be sanctified.

> [Col. 0296B] *(From Hesychius.)* The lawgiver appears to be repeating what he explained once before, so that through repeated injunction the readers might recall the command to memory. But, in order to make the reading more necessary through this repetition of the law, he inserts something additional, by which this command might become especially necessary and entirely without excuse.

Just as in the preceding passages he repeated the sacrifices of the whole burnt offerings, mixing in the requirement of their continual observance—as in the statement, “The fire that is on the altar shall always burn and shall never fail”—so now, after bringing the sacrifice of fine flour into the discussion, through which we demonstrated at the beginning of this book that theology is signified, he added that it must be eaten only in a holy place and by males, not everywhere or by everyone.

Observe what he now commands concerning it:

> This is the law of the sacrifice and of the libations, which the sons of Aaron shall offer before the Lord and before the altar.

Those of whom the present discourse speaks—the sons of Aaron, that is, people exalted in wisdom—alone ought to offer it before the Lord, that is, according to God’s will. They must not dispute about divine matters superfluously, but must speak only whatever Christ reveals to us.

Understand “before the altar” in this sense. Since it has been shown that the altar is the humanity of the Only-Begotten, let us establish our theology in those matters that the incarnate Lord handed down to us, so that we may contemplate the Father in him and him in the Father, and know concerning the Holy Spirit that he is also the Spirit of the Son and proceeds from the Father.

> The priest shall take a handful of fine flour mixed with oil, and all the frankincense placed upon the fine flour, and shall burn it on the altar as a memorial, a pleasing fragrance to the Lord.

This is to be done with almsgiving and prayer, for these are signified by the oil and the frankincense, through which theology is necessarily acquired. The assistance of both is necessary, so that those who speak about God may not fall away from the truth; and this is offered as a memorial.

Christ, the intelligible priest, takes the handful, because supreme knowledge remains with him. It is a memorial because it will remain forever in memory. For it is not as our present knowledge is, which is destroyed as progress is made. When the perfect comes, as Paul says, “what is partial will be destroyed” (1 Corinthians 13).

Thus the lawgiver indicates that the highest knowledge and perfect understanding are with Christ.

But pay attention to what he adds:

> Aaron and his sons shall eat the remaining portion of the fine flour.

This means that we should not cease entirely from theology because supreme knowledge is preserved for the future. Rather, the knowledge left and handed down to us by him he commands us to eat and practice.

But we must observe where and how it should be practiced. The text continues:

> Without leaven, and he shall eat it in the place of the sanctuary of the tabernacle.

It is not cooked with leaven—that is, neither according to Jewish teaching nor according to pagan leaven—because he does not want us merely to speak the word, but wants it to be pure from every mixture and without any leaven.

He commanded that it be eaten in the court of the tabernacle of testimony, that is, practiced in the Church. For the tabernacle of testimony is heaven, as Scripture testifies, since God dwells there. The court of the tabernacle of testimony—that is, of heaven—is the Church, not only as the entrance and vestibule of heaven but also as the house of God.

There, therefore, that is, in the Church, one must speak about divinity in every respect and practice theology. For it says in the churches: “Bless the Lord” (Psalm 67).

If someone has a church in his house, Paul says: “Greet Nympha and the church in her house” (Colossians 4). A person has a domestic church when he has sanctified himself for God and ceased from worldly occupations. Such a person may also speak about God and practice theology at home.

These are the people to whom a portion of the sacrifices of the Lord is given—that is, the opportunity to speak about God or to practice theology from the gifts and offerings. Concerning this he added:

> It shall be most holy.

For the saints possess the contemplation of holy things. He added:

> As for the offering for sin and for an offense.

He wished to show that the sacrifice for sin and for an offense is similar. For discourse about God is especially offered for the liberation and cleansing of the soul when the sacrifice of the word of God—that is, theology—is joined with oil and frankincense, namely almsgiving and prayer.

> Only males of the lineage of Aaron shall eat it; it is an everlasting statute throughout your generations, from the sacrifices of the Lord.

It is not therefore for everyone to dispute about God, but only for those who have nothing feminine or weak in their thoughts. He commanded that the everlasting statute be preserved throughout their generations—that is, forever—so that at all times we may be attentive and never presume to dispute about God whenever, through various deviations, we have slipped from the dignity of males into weakness or worldly fantasies.

As for what was finally said concerning the sacrifices—“Everyone who touches them shall be sanctified”—this cannot stand according to the Jewish literal sense. How is everyone who touches the holy sacrifice sanctified if a murderer, a profane person, an adulterer, or an incestuous person touches it? For he excluded no one but said: “Everyone who touches them shall be sanctified.”

A mystical interpretation must therefore be sought. The sacrifice for which all these sacrifices had proceeded as type and figure, the one perfect sacrifice offered, is Christ. If anyone touches the flesh of this sacrifice—that is, if with believing heart he places all his hope of salvation in his passion and resurrection—he is immediately sanctified if he is unclean and healed if he is afflicted with a wound.

*(From Hesychius.)* Every remembrance of God grants sanctification, as Paul testifies when he says:

> Every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving; but it is sanctified through the word of God and prayer (1 Timothy 4).

But when he says that the one who touches is sanctified, he clearly shows that, in disputing about God—that is, in theology—it is sufficient for us even merely to touch him, just as someone who wishes to warm himself touches fire.

For if he thrusts his hand farther into it, he is burned, whereas he could have been warmed. So too whoever presumes to dispute about God more deeply or at a higher level, wishing to say something more glorious, falls into blasphemy because he cannot comprehend the height of divine doctrines.

## Chapter Two. On the Offerings of Aaron and His Sons on the Day of His Anointing
(IBID.) And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “This is the offering of Aaron and his sons, which they are to offer to the Lord on the day of his anointing. They shall offer a tenth of an ephah of fine flour as a perpetual sacrifice: half of it in the morning and half in the evening. It shall be mixed with oil in a pan and fried. The priest who lawfully succeeds his father shall offer it hot, as a most pleasing fragrance to the Lord, and it shall be wholly burned on the altar. For every sacrifice of the priests shall be consumed by fire, and no one shall eat of it.”

Every sacrifice associated with the person of a priest bears the figure of the sacrifice of the Only Begotten, as the present law demonstrates. [Col. 0298C] For it says: “And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: This is the offering of Aaron and his sons, which they are to offer to the Lord on the day of his anointing.” This gift indeed belongs to many priests—for it says “Aaron and his sons”—but it is offered by one anointed priest, because the whole image, firmness, or subsistence of the priesthood is the sacrifice of Christ; for when he alone was offered, the whole was accomplished through him.

And when it says, “On the day of his anointing,” that is, at the time when he was made incarnate—for in the person of the Only Begotten, anointing means incarnation—of this Peter says: “Jesus of Nazareth, how God anointed him with the Holy Spirit and with power” (Luke XXIV). But how and when this took place Gabriel told Mary: “The Holy Spirit,” he said, “will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke I).

What offering, then, did the lawgiver command to be offered after the priest had been anointed, that is, after the incarnation of the Word? “They shall offer a tenth of an ephah of fine flour as a perpetual sacrifice, half of it in the morning and half in the evening, and it shall be mixed with oil in a pan and fried.”

It has already been shown above that the tenth of an ephah of fine flour signifies the humanity of the Only Begotten, just as we rightly said that the ephah, being a measure capable of holding three measures, signifies the Trinity. But if the ephah is the Lord’s flesh, so that the supremacy of his divinity and the inseparability of the Lord’s flesh from it may also be demonstrated, this nevertheless is a perpetual sacrifice, because, as Paul says: “By one offering he has perfected forever those who are sanctified”; hence he is also able to save forever, “approaching God through himself” (Hebrews X).

“Half of it in the morning and half in the evening.” The morning signifies the beginning of the Passion. For from the time when they struck him with blows in the courtyard of Caiaphas and bound him, it continued until evening. Since darkness interrupted it, and since this occurred from the sixth hour until the ninth, the sacrifice is necessarily said to be divided into a morning sacrifice and an evening sacrifice.

“But it shall be mixed with oil in a pan and fried.” The pan should be understood as the Lord’s cross, strong and unharmed by the fire of human sins. It also made the Lord’s flesh, placed upon it, edible for human beings; for unless it had been placed upon the cross, we could in no way have mystically received the body of Christ.

It is mixed with oil because he had compassion on us and, though impassible, endured suffering in the flesh. This whole sacrifice is a most pleasing fragrance to the Lord: for it bestowed salvation upon the human race, and nothing is more pleasing to God, as Creator, than this creaturely nature.

For a fuller explanation that this signifies the sacrifice of the Only Begotten, consider what follows: “The priest who lawfully succeeds his father.” The Septuagint rendered this as follows: “The anointed priest from among his sons shall perform it,” and so forth. That Christ is Jesus, Paul proves by saying: “For us there is one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things” (1 Corinthians VIII).

That Christ is Aaron’s successor, not in his place but on his behalf, with the priesthood transferred to himself, is evident from the fact that, by assuming the priesthood himself, he brought the ministry of that priesthood to an end. The phrase “from among his sons” is also rightly understood of him, since he descended from Jacob’s loins, the line of the Lord’s most blessed mother descending from the same tribe.

We must attend to what follows as the conclusion of this law: “And it shall be wholly burned on the altar. For every sacrifice of the priests shall be consumed by fire, and no one shall eat of it.” What does this affirm, unless it is meant to prevent anyone from saying that the one born of a woman suffered, while the one who descended from heaven did not suffer? “For us there is one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things” (ibid.), whom those who crucified him did not know—of what dignity and power he was. For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory.

Therefore the Passion belongs to the incarnate Word, and it took place in the flesh; for this reason “it shall be wholly burned on the altar.” It belongs to the one who “emptied himself completely, taking the form of a servant, and was found in appearance as a man; he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross” (Philippians II).

The Septuagint said: “It shall be made a complete burnt offering”; Aquila rendered it, “It shall be.” No one, therefore, shall eat of it—that is, it shall not be divided, since it belongs to the teeth to divide and portion out food, which cannot otherwise be chewed. But Christ’s sacrifice has been shown to be indivisible, and therefore it cannot be eaten.

This sacrifice may also be represented under another figure. See whether, as I suspect, this very law promulgated through Moses is the priest’s sacrifice: “Half of it shall be offered in the morning, [Col. 0300A] but the other half in the evening.”

(From Origen.) He commanded this law to be divided into two parts, namely, into letter and spirit. The half that is the letter he commands to be offered in the morning, that is, at the first time of the law, when it brought new light and a new day to those to whom it was then given according to the letter. But he commanded the other half to be offered in the evening. For the Savior’s coming was given to us in the evening, when that half—that is, the meaning or spirit of the law, insofar as the law is spiritual—is offered.

“Mixed with oil, tender.” Oil refers to mercy, which ought to abound in priests; “tender” pertains to subtle and pure understanding. As for the reference to the pan, I think it means that the priest is to be disciplined and, through great continence, dry and parched, with nothing relaxed toward luxury and nothing tending toward lust.

When he called the sacrifice itself one of fragments, as a fragrance of sweetness, I think he intended the fragments of the priests to be understood: when the letter of the law is broken through them, the spiritual food hidden within is brought out, so that the crowds who hear may be refreshed. The Gospels likewise report that the Lord did this: “He blessed the loaves and gave them to the disciples, and the disciples, breaking them, placed them before the crowds; and when all had eaten their fill, he said, twelve baskets of fragments remained” (John VI).

This, then, is the sacrifice made from fragments: when we examine the holy things of the law piece by piece, so that we may receive from them spiritual and pure food. “And this,” he says, “is an eternal law.”

The apostle John says in the Apocalypse that there is an eternal Gospel. Here too we find it written that there is an eternal law. But I would now ask those who wish to follow the law according to the letter: how can the law of this sacrifice be eternal? Once the temple was destroyed, the altar overturned, and all the things called holy profaned, this sacrificial rite could not continue. How, then, will they call eternal what is now known to have ceased and ended long ago?

It remains, therefore, that this law is called eternal according to that aspect by which we say that the law is spiritual and that through it spiritual sacrifices can be offered—sacrifices that can neither ever be broken nor cease. For they do not exist in a place that is overturned or in a time that changes, but in the faith of the believer and in the heart of the one who offers sacrifice.

Indeed, when he says, “No portion shall be taken from the priest’s sacrifice, but it shall be a burnt offering,” it is certain that this refers to the person of our Lord and Savior. His sacrifice is not to be eaten, but shall be a burnt offering.

Here the sacrifice should be understood as the very word and teaching, from which no one eats—that is, no one debates or revises it—but it is a burnt offering: whatever he said, whatever he established, endures through eternal consecration.

No sacrifice is such for almighty God as zeal for souls. Hence the Psalmist says: “The zeal of your house has consumed me” (Psalm LXVIII).

(From Gregory.) How greatly the frying of the heart, which is carried out through spiritual zeal, pleases almighty God is openly shown when the law commands fine flour to be offered as a sacrifice, concerning which it is written: “It is fried in a pan mixed with oil, and the priest who lawfully succeeds his father shall offer it hot as a most pleasing fragrance to the Lord, and it shall be wholly burned on the altar.”

The fine flour is fried in a pan when the pure mind of the righteous is burned through the zeal of holy fervor, and it is commanded to be mixed with oil. Since in Greek *eleos* means “mercy,” oil appropriately signifies mercy, which burns and shines in the sight of almighty God.

Therefore let the mind that is fried in the pan be mixed with oil, because the strictness of holy zeal must burn and shine through the virtue of mercy. For it loves the very one whom it seems to pursue. Hence it is commanded to be offered hot as a most pleasing fragrance to the Lord: if zeal does not possess love, the fine flour offered in the pan has lost its warmth.

It should also be noted who is commanded to offer it: “the priest who lawfully succeeds his father.” That priest lawfully succeeds his father who demonstrates by his conduct that he is a son of almighty God and does not differ from his inner nobility through the ignobility of his deeds.

It is commanded to be wholly burned on the altar, so that it may become a burnt offering. For a burnt offering is called something wholly burned. Hence another translation commands that this same fine flour, which is fried in the pan, be made a burnt offering.

There is this difference between a burnt offering and a sacrifice: every burnt offering is indeed a sacrifice, but not every sacrifice is a burnt offering. Many good deeds are sacrifices, but they are not burnt offerings, because they do not set the whole mind aflame with spiritual love.

Those who perform the things of God in such a way that they do not abandon the things of the world plainly offer a sacrifice and not a burnt offering. But those who abandon everything that belongs to the world and are kindled with the fire of divine love in their whole mind become both a sacrifice and a burnt offering to almighty God.

Thus the fine flour in the pan is the pure mind of the righteous amid the affliction of spiritual zeal, fried through concern for souls, and counted as not only a sacrifice but also a burnt offering to the Lord.

## CHAPTER III. The order in which the sacrifices offered for sin are completed by the priest

(IBID.) The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “Speak to Aaron and his sons: This is the law of the sacrifice for sin. In the place where the burnt offering is offered, the sacrifice for sin shall be slaughtered before the Lord. It is most holy. The priest who offers it shall eat it in a holy place, in the court of the tabernacle. Whatever touches its flesh shall be sanctified. If any of its blood is splashed upon a garment, it shall be washed in a holy place. The earthen vessel in which it was cooked shall be broken. But if it was cooked in a bronze vessel, it shall be scrubbed and washed with water. Every male among the priestly family shall eat of its flesh, because it is most holy.

“But the sacrifice that is slaughtered for sin, whose blood is brought into the tabernacle of testimony for expiation, shall not be eaten in the sanctuary but shall be consumed by fire.”

(From Hesychius.) What is this law? “In the place where the burnt offering is offered, it shall be slaughtered before the Lord; it is most holy.” For this reason these commands are given to Aaron and his sons: to offer a sacrifice for sin—that is, repentance—is the work of those who are exalted and most high, lifted up from the earth, and this is accomplished only by turning away from evil.

Therefore, where burnt offerings are slaughtered, there also the sacrifices for sin are killed, because the one who offers repentance already imitates the one who offered himself wholly to God and in every respect withdrew from the world; hence his offering is also called a burnt offering.

The conduct of both and their offering are before the Lord. It is pleasing to God when it is offered according to his intention; and since it is pleasing to God, it is rightly called most holy. For if the sacrifice of repentance were not the Holy of Holies, he would never have brought the repentant person into the Holy of Holies—the person who had previously been expelled from there through sin.

“The priest who offers it shall eat it.” It says “the one who offers it.” Here this is Christ, who took our sins upon himself and rightly offers our repentance. Learn how he eats it from the place in which he eats it: “In a holy place, in the court of the tabernacle,” or, as the Septuagint rendered it, “in the court of the tabernacle of testimony.”

The court of the tabernacle of testimony is the Church. For it is the court before heaven, the court of the tabernacle of testimony, where Christ works the salvation of the repentant, since his salvation is also called food: “My food,” he says, “is to do the will of my Father” (John IV). His will is that the sinner be converted and saved.

He further says: “Whatever touches its flesh shall be sanctified.” By the flesh of repentance we understand fasting, vigils, sackcloth, prayer with tears, and almsgiving. Repentance consists of these things, and whoever touches them is rightly sanctified.

“If any of its blood is splashed upon a garment, it shall be washed in a holy place.” The blood of repentance is baptism in the proper sense. For just as blood is the life of all flesh, so baptism is the life of repentance [the following transmitted phrase, *domum baptismi*, is corrupt or uncertain]. Anyone who practices repentance but has not received baptism gains nothing from it: repentance is fruitless, dead, and lifeless, because no one lays aside the old person of sin except through the washing of regeneration.

But if you ask, “How, then, do those who were baptized long ago practice repentance?” understand that the power of the preceding baptism is active also in the repentance practiced afterward.

This, then, is the lawgiver’s intention: just as the one who eats the flesh of the aforementioned sacrifice is sanctified, although the offering belongs to another, so it is shown that even one who does not need repentance, if he performs any of these things, is sanctified by practicing repentance.

Similarly, even if someone very young has been baptized—someone who perhaps has not yet sinned—he is cleansed. And what need does he have of cleansing? He needs it because no one is clean from defilement. Even if his life on earth lasts only one day, he nevertheless retains the defilement that he has drawn from Adam through succession and generation.

For this reason, concerning the one sprinkled with the blood of repentance, he did not say that he should be washed as an unclean person. Instead he says: “If any of its blood is splashed upon a garment,” that is, upon the flesh; for the flesh is the garment of the inner person. If it is splashed, it shall be washed there, in a holy place, in the mystical house of the Spirit.

Therefore, if someone has been washed outside, as, for example, in the sprinklings of the pagans, he is not washed, because he has received neither sprinkling nor washing in a holy place.

“The earthen vessel in which it was cooked shall be broken. But if it was cooked in a bronze vessel, it shall be scrubbed and washed with water.”

What an earthen vessel is, and where it lies, Paul shows when he says: “In a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and earthenware; some indeed for honor, others for dishonor.” Those made of earthenware are for dishonor. I understand the great house, since it is the house of God, to be the Church, in which the golden and silver vessels are the righteous, and the earthen vessels are sinners.

Isaiah also spoke of Jerusalem: “Its destruction will come, and it will be crushed as a potter’s vessel is crushed with a mighty crushing, and no fragment of it will be found from which a firebrand might be carried from the burning or a little water drawn from a cistern” (Isaiah III).

Since, then, the vessels in which the flesh of the sacrifice is cooked are in the temple, we have shown from the apostolic words already cited that there are also weak vessels in the temple of God.

Whoever is an earthen vessel in the temple—that is, someone weak and unclean, who has made a habit of sinning, so that he is called a vessel of dishonor as a lover of sins—is broken or crushed by the cooked sacrifice through which the forgiveness of sins is administered. Since he was weak, he received good things wrongly. Seeing sins forgiven, he thinks that it is always permissible to sin; and from the help he receives, another injury and crushing of his weakness arises.

But whoever is strong like bronze and has no rust of sin is not crushed or broken by the cooking of repentance. Rather, he is scrubbed or wiped clean, that is, washed away. And how is he washed away? By being washed with water.

Seeing another person repent, he is moved to contrition and is cleansed, washed with the water of tears.

“Every male among the priestly family shall eat of its flesh, because it is most holy.” Understand the priest who offers the whole sacrifice and eats it to be Christ. He offers our repentance, and he also eats it, because he regards the salvation of sinners as food.

Every male among the priests shall eat the flesh of the sacrifice that pertains to repentance, displaying every kind of strength, to whom it is rightly said: “Act manfully, take courage, and wait for the Lord” (Psalm XXVI).

These things, then, may be understood in this way. But we must consider what conclusion follows: “The sacrifice that is slaughtered for sin, whose blood is brought into the tabernacle of testimony for expiation, shall not be eaten in the sanctuary but shall be consumed by fire.”

And whose blood is brought into the tabernacle of testimony for expiation or supplication? It is the blood of the calf of the congregation, or of the synagogue, and likewise the calf for the sin of the high priest. He stated this fully above.

Since we have shown by many proofs that those sacrifices pertain to Christ, he rightly did not command that they be eaten, but that they be consumed by fire. For it is not through the things by which each person pleads for the remission of sins—through fasting, for example, or vigils, or another similar manner of life—that Christ accomplishes remission. Rather, he accomplishes it through the authority and power of his own divinity.

The sufferings of Christ, through which remission is procured for us, belong not to some mere human being but to God incarnate. Therefore they are not edible by human beings but are consumed by fire, because it belongs to God alone to grant remission to all his creatures; and fire signifies him, for “our God is a consuming fire” (Hebrews XII).

(From Origen.) Some sacrifices belong to God alone, so that no human being participates in them. Some belong to Aaron the priest and his sons; some belong to him, his sons, and his daughters, so that even the priest’s wife may eat of them; some belong to the priests and their sons and daughters, and from some of these the children of Israel may also eat.

In those sacrifices from which the children of Israel may eat, the priests and their sons undoubtedly also participate. Yet it does not follow that, from every sacrifice which a priest may eat, the children of Israel may also eat.

The first sacrifice, therefore, is the burnt offering. For no other sacrifice ought to be named first except the one offered to almighty God. The second sacrifice is the one assigned to the priests for eating. The third is one which even the children of Israel—the very ones who offer it—may touch or eat, though not all the children of Israel, but only those who are clean; for only the clean are commanded to eat from the sacrifices.

But you who are secretly a Jew, do not seek all these sacrifices in visible animals or think that they are to be found in mute beasts that ought to be offered to God. Seek these sacrifices within yourself, and you will find them within your soul.

Understand that within yourself you have herds of oxen, those that are blessed in Abraham. Understand that you also have herds of sheep and herds of goats, in which the patriarchs were blessed and multiplied. Understand that within you there are also the birds of heaven.

Do not be surprised that we say these things are within you. Understand that you are another world in miniature, and that within you there is a sun, a moon, and also stars. For if this were not so, the Lord would never have said to Abraham: “Look toward heaven and see whether you can count the stars; so shall your offspring be” (Genesis XV).

Again, do not be surprised if Abraham is told, “So shall your offspring be, like the stars of heaven”—namely, those who are born from his faith and live rationally, keeping the divine laws and commandments.

Hear something more that the Savior says to his disciples: “You are the light of the world” (Matthew V). Do you doubt that there are within you a sun and a moon, since it is said to you, “You are the light of the world”?

Would you like to hear something still greater about yourself? Perhaps, thinking little and humbly of yourself as though you were worthless, you neglect your life.

This world has its governor; it has one who rules it and dwells in it, almighty God, just as he himself says through the Prophet: “Do I not fill heaven and earth? says the Lord” (Jeremiah XXIII).

Hear, then, what the Lord almighty himself says about you—that is, about human beings: “I will dwell in them and walk among them” (Ezekiel XLIII).

He added something more concerning your person: “I will be their father, and they shall be my sons and daughters, says the Lord.” See how great is the mercy and kindness of God.

And where the burnt offering—that which is offered to God alone—is slaughtered, there the sacrifice for sin is also commanded to be slaughtered, so that the one who has sinned and repents may understand that, having turned to God and slaughtered a sacrifice of a contrite spirit, he stands in the holy place and is joined to the things that belong to God.

The sacrifice for sin is therefore slaughtered where the burnt offering is also slaughtered: “before the Lord,” he says.

Perhaps there is a distinction between offering a sacrifice before the Lord and offering one not before the Lord. Who, then, is the one who offers before the Lord? I think it is the one who has not departed from the presence of the Lord, unlike Cain, who departed from it and became fearful and trembling.

If someone has confidence to stand before the Lord, does not flee from his face, and does not shrink from his gaze because of the consciousness of sin, that person offers sacrifice before God.

This sacrifice offered for sins he calls the Holy of Holies. The discourse wishes to venture something greater, if only your hearing will follow: what is the sacrifice offered for sins and which is the Holy of Holies, except the Only Begotten Son of God, my Lord Jesus Christ?

He alone is the sacrifice for sins, and he is himself the Holy of Holies. But what did he add? “The priest,” he says, “who offers it shall eat it.”

This, then, is the priest who eats and consumes the sins of the people, of whom it is said: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Psalm CIX).

Therefore my Savior and Lord eats the sins of the people. How does he eat the sins of the people? Hear what is written: “Our God is a consuming fire.” What does the fire of God consume? Shall we be so foolish as to think that God’s fire consumes wood, straw, or hay? Rather, God, who is fire, consumes human sins: he destroys them, devours them, and purifies them, according to what he also says elsewhere: “I will purify you with fire completely” (Isaiah I).

This is what it means for the one who offers a sacrifice for sin to eat sin: he took our sins upon himself and, as fire, ate and consumed them in himself.

The law therefore says: “The priest who has offered it shall eat it in a holy place, in the court of the tabernacle of testimony.” It follows that, according to the image of the one who gave the priesthood to the Church, the ministers and priests of the Church should also receive the sins of the people and, imitating their teacher, grant the people remission of sins.

The priests of the Church must therefore be so perfect and so trained in priestly duties that they consume the sins of the people in a holy place, in the courts of the tabernacle of testimony, by not sinning themselves.

What does it mean to eat sin in a holy place? There was a holy place into which Moses had come, as it was said to him: “The place on which you stand is holy ground” (Exodus I).

Likewise, in the Church of God there is a holy place: perfect faith and love from a pure heart and a good conscience (1 Timothy I). Whoever stands in these things in the Church should know that he stands in a holy place.

The priest eats the flesh of the sacrifice in the court of the tabernacle of testimony when he is able to understand what is the meaning and what are the mysteries of the things described concerning the courts of the tabernacle of testimony.

No one approaches these secret and hidden courts; they are open to no one except priests—if indeed they are open, provided that through their knowledge and mystical understanding they can penetrate their secrets.

I know, however, that there are also certain more secret doctrines in the Church, which even priests are not permitted to approach. I mean those places where the ark is kept, where the urn of manna and the tablets of the covenant are found.

Not even the priests themselves are granted access there; entry into this secret is granted only to the high priest, and to him only once a year, after certain prescribed and mystical purifications.

There are also other doctrines of the Church to which even Levites may attain, but they are inferior to those which priests are permitted to approach.

I know also of others to which the children of Israel—that is, the laity—may have access, though not foreigners, unless they have already been enrolled in the Church of the Lord. “An Egyptian shall enter the Church of the Lord in the third generation” (Deuteronomy XXXII).

I believe that the faith of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, in whom everyone who is joined to the Church of God believes, is mystically called the third generation.

Nevertheless, it must be understood that, among the sacrifices that are offered, even though the priests are permitted to eat of them, not everything is granted to them. A portion of them is offered to God and delivered to the altar’s fires, so that we may know that, although we are permitted to grasp and understand some things from the divine Scriptures, there are nevertheless certain things that must be reserved for God.

When they surpass our understanding and their meaning is beyond us, lest we utter them otherwise than the truth requires, it is better to preserve them for the fire. Therefore, here too we have consumed within the tabernacle of the Lord whatever was granted to human beings to eat, insofar as we were able.

But if anything remains—whether it surpasses us in hearing or exceeds us in speaking—let us reserve it for the fire of the altar, as the portion that is commanded to be offered for sin upon the Lord’s altar.

## CHAPTER IV. How the sacrifices for offenses are to be offered

(CAP. VII.) “This also is the law of the sacrifice for an offense: it is most holy. Therefore, where the burnt offering is slaughtered, the victim for the offense shall also be slaughtered, and its blood shall be poured around the altar. From it they shall offer the tail and the fat that covers the vital organs, the two kidneys and the fat that is beside the loins, and the membrane of the liver together with the kidneys; and the priest shall burn them on the altar. It is the Lord’s offering for an offense.

“Every male among the priestly family shall eat this flesh in a holy place, because it is most holy. As the sacrifice for sin is offered, so also for an offense; one law shall apply to both sacrifices. It shall belong to the priest who offers it.”

An offense is sometimes called a recognized sin, but sometimes it means what is committed against God himself, such as what is perpetrated against holy things, as we showed above.

(From Origen.) I nevertheless know also the distinction that seemed correct to some of the wise: an offense occurs when we fail to do what we ought to do, whereas sin occurs when we commit what we ought not to commit. But since we do not always find these terms used with this distinction in the divine Scriptures, we cannot affirm it universally.

(From Hesychius.) Whatever is referred to God has forgiveness with difficulty, so that Eli said to his sons: “If a human being sins against human beings, someone may pray for him; but if he sins against God, who will pray for him?” (1 Samuel II).

Therefore we necessarily said that the ram, bearing the figure of the Lord of whom it was said, “Behold the Lamb of God, behold the one who takes away the sins of the world,” is taken for the sacrifice, since he alone is able to release the sins committed against him.

But it must be asked why every ram is not made a burnt offering, just as the calf was offered for the people and for the priest. For that calf was shown to bear the figure of the sacrifice of the Only Begotten. But in that case, because a general dispensation was made and forgiveness was accomplished for the whole human race, the entire sacrifice of Christ is necessarily offered.

Whatever, therefore, can save people, the lawgiver commanded to be received in Christ’s sacrifice. What are these things? Paul says: “Pursue peace with everyone,” and “holiness, without which no one will see God” (Hebrews XIII). The lawgiver also signified this now through the previously prescribed offering of the inner parts.

For the inner parts are intelligible thoughts; when they have peace, we shall have peace with everyone. By the offering of the kidneys, the lobe, the liver, and the thighs, he signifies the sanctification that has been arranged for our salvation.

(From Gregory.) What is the tail except the end of the body? And he offers well who brings the sacrifice of good works through to the end of his proper action.

Therefore the tail of the sacrifice is commanded to be offered on the altar, so that we may complete every good thing we begin with an enduring conclusion.

(From Hesychius.) Note that whatever he commanded to be done in the sacrifice of peace offerings, he also commanded in this sacrifice. He orders the fat to be offered. For Christ desires to save even the one who has grave sins; and, according to the Septuagint, he offers the loin together with the fat.

For he not only wishes this but is also able to do it. The loin, as a strong member, signifies virtue.

He wishes the two kidneys and the fat that is beside the loins to be cleansed: he especially wishes the inner person of the penitent to be purified. He also wishes the penitent to possess chastity. For this reason he commanded that not only the fat of the kidneys but also that of the loins or thighs be offered, because these are thought to be the organs of intercourse and seed.

Along with these he commanded that the membrane of the liver—or, as the Septuagint says, the small lobe (*pinnula*) of the liver—be removed with the kidneys and offered with the others on the altar as a sacrifice to the Lord.

For he wishes the person who practices repentance not to have his own desire, but to offer it all to God. Since they say that desires or impulses are stirred and nourished in the liver, the first fruits of these are offered through the lobe so that all may be sanctified and corrected.

Having said this, he added: “It is for an offense,” showing that he did not say without reason that this sacrifice differs from the other sacrifices that are for sins, but because it is for an offense—that is, because his sin is directed against God.

“Every male among the priestly family shall eat these fleshly portions in a holy place, because it is most holy. As the sacrifice for sin is offered, so also for an offense; one law shall apply to both sacrifices,” and so forth.

(From Origen.) Accordingly, the sacrifice offered for an offense must be understood in the same way and according to the same tradition as the sacrifice for sin, which we explained above.

Likewise he commands that the fat of the ram around the kidneys and the fat covering the inner parts be placed upon the altar, so that you who hear these things may know that everything within you that is excessively fat and covers your inner parts must be offered to the fire of the altar, so that all your inner parts may be cleansed.

Then you too may say, as David said: “Bless the Lord, O my soul, and all that is within me, bless his holy name” (Psalm CII).

For unless that fatness which covers your inner parts is removed, they cannot receive a subtle and spiritual meaning, nor can they grasp the understanding of wisdom; and therefore they cannot praise the Lord.

But if everything fat is removed from the kidneys and from all the inner organs, then, truly cleansed from every vice of lust, you have slaughtered the sacrifice for an offense and offered a sacrifice to the Lord as a fragrance of sweetness.

“It shall belong,” he says, “to the priest who offers it and has made propitiation for that offense.”

Let the priests of the Lord who preside over the Churches learn that a portion is given to them together with those whose offenses they have made atonement for.

What does it mean to make atonement for an offense? If you take a sinner and, by warning, exhorting, teaching, and instructing him, lead him to repentance; if you correct him from error, reform him from vices, and make him such that, once converted, God becomes favorable toward him, you are said to have made atonement for his offense.

If, then, you are such a priest, and such are your teaching and your speech, a portion is given to you of those whom you have corrected, so that their merit may be your reward and their salvation your glory.

Or does not the Apostle also demonstrate this when he says: “The one who builds upon it will receive a reward” (1 Corinthians III)?

Let the priests of the Lord understand where their portion has been given to them, and let them devote themselves and apply themselves to this. Let them not entangle themselves in empty and superfluous activities, but know that they will have a portion with God in nothing else except what they offer for sins—that is, in turning the sinner away from the path of sin.

The priest who offers the burnt offering shall have its hide; and every grain offering that is baked in an oven, and whatever is prepared on a griddle or in a pan, shall belong to the priest by whom it is offered. Whether it has been mixed with oil or is dry, it shall be divided in equal measure among all the sons of Aaron, each one receiving his share.

We read in the Book of Job that, when the Lord praised Job, Satan replied: “Skin for skin, and all that a man has he will give for his life” (Job 2). [From Hesychius.] Therefore the skin—the surrounding circumstance of riches, as it were, which externally envelops a person—is something that those who wish to become a burnt offering must offer to the intelligible priest. Hence those who believed the apostolic teaching sold their possessions and laid them at the apostles’ feet (Acts 4). Since, therefore, he said, “Skin for skin,” we must necessarily understand the surrounding circumstance of riches, which Job lost, as corresponding to the patience that remained to him. We call patience “skin,” because many useful things arise from it and it provides many benefits to those who acquire it.

That an intelligible burnt offering is being described here is shown by the text itself. For it says: “The priest who offers the victim of the burnt offering”—not of cattle, sheep, or anything similar, but of a human being. Where sacrifices are considered not by those who offer them but by what is offered, mention is necessarily made of animals. Here, however, because he wished to introduce the person of the Lord more openly, he presented a priest offering a human being as a burnt offering. For only Christ will offer our intelligible burnt offerings, and in imitation of him their sacrifices and manner of life are cultivated.

Not only in his teachings, but also in contemplation of him, we possess patience amid sufferings, as Paul says: “Consider him who endured such contradiction from sinners against himself, so that you may not grow weary, fainting in your souls” (Hebrews 12).

After this he said: “Every sacrifice that is baked in an oven, and whatever is prepared on a griddle or in a pan, shall belong to the priest by whom it is offered.” We must remember that we said these sacrifices belong to the theology of the dispensation of the Only-Begotten: that which is from the oven signifies the Virgin’s childbirth; that which is from the pan signifies the passion of the cross; and that which is from the griddle signifies the resurrection from the dead. In each case we have supplied a rationale and added the proofs that were required.

Since these things are close to the theology of the incarnation, they necessarily belong to the priest who offers it—that is, to Christ, who was born, suffered, and rose again. But surely what follows seems new to you: “Whether they are mixed with oil or are dry, they shall be divided in equal measure among all the sons of Aaron, each one receiving his share.” He speaks of the grain offering mixed with oil, which is placed neither in an oven nor in a pan nor on a griddle. We have therefore said that this too is theology, but not concerning the Lord’s incarnation, so that we do not confine all theology to the humanity of the Only-Begotten. We must also discuss the substance of the Father and of the Holy Spirit, and likewise that of the Son, which is from the Father.

For this reason he did not repeat that this sacrifice was to be carried by himself, but assigned it to the sons of Aaron, who advance toward theology through meditation on the Scriptures. He distributed it equally to each, so that they might think alike about God, not differently, but all in agreement. This is clear from the fact that he did not command heretics to partake of such a sacrifice, since they do not think the same things about God, but things very different indeed.

Again he speaks of a grain offering not mixed with oil when a tenth of an ephah, without oil or frankincense, is offered for sin by those who are unable to offer a goat, a sheep, or a pair of turtledoves or pigeons as a sacrifice.

Although this signifies the Savior’s sacrifice, nevertheless, since it is prescribed not for the sake of theology but for the benefit of the one offering it, he also assigned it to the sons of Aaron. (From Origen.)

It is commanded that the offering called salutary be made with oil, as we have already said above; but the offering for sin is not made with oil. For he says: “He shall not put oil upon it, because it is for sin.” Therefore, what is for sin receives neither the oil of gladness nor the frankincense of sweetness. To sinners the Apostle says: “I shall mourn for those who sinned before and did not repent” (2 Corinthians 12). Nor is there any odor of sweetness in it, since it is said in the person of the sinner: “My wounds have become foul and festering” (Psalm 37).

The human heart is therefore an oven. But if vices have kindled that heart, or the devil has inflamed it, it will not cook but burn up. If, however, the one who kindled it is he who said, “I came to cast fire upon the earth,” then the breads of the divine Scriptures and of the words of God that I receive in my heart I do not burn to destruction, but cook for sacrifice.

Perhaps those things are said to be cooked in an oven which are inward and hidden and cannot easily be brought before the common people. There are many such things in the divine Scriptures, as in Ezekiel, when he describes either the cherubim or God and that magnificent vision. If these things are not cooked in an oven, they cannot be eaten as they are, raw. For we must not believe that there is some animal in the form of a lion on which God rides, or another in the form of a calf or an eagle. Such things, and anything similar, must not be brought forth raw; they must be cooked in the oven of the heart.

There are therefore three places in which he says sacrifices must be prepared: in an oven, in a pan, and on a griddle. I think that the oven, according to its form, signifies the deeper and ineffable things in the divine Scriptures; the pan signifies things which, if they are turned over and examined frequently and repeatedly, can be understood and explained; and the griddle signifies things that are plain and visible without any concealment.

We have often said that there is a threefold mode of understanding in the divine Scriptures: historical, moral, and mystical. Accordingly, we have understood that the body, soul, and spirit are present in them, and that the threefold form of this understanding is displayed here by the threefold arrangement of the sacrifices. Elsewhere too we find the same thing, namely, in the passages that speak of sacrifices, where a holy basket of perfection is mentioned, in which three loaves are commanded to be placed.

You see that the forms of all the mysteries correspond to one another. What else should we understand by the basket of perfection, in which three loaves are commanded to be placed, except the divine Scriptures, which set food before their hearers in three ways?

Would you like us to produce examples of a similar mystery from the Gospels? Let us recall the Lord’s words, where he says: “At midnight someone came to his friend, knocked at his door, and said: ‘Friend, lend me three loaves, because a friend of mine has arrived from a journey, and I have nothing to set before him’” (Luke 11). To touch on this briefly: the night is the time of this present life, and the three loaves are one that is cooked in the oven, another in the pan, and a third on the griddle.

After this: “Every sacrifice,” he says, “made with oil or not made with oil shall belong equally to all the sons of Aaron, each one receiving his share”—whether the sacrifice is made with oil or is not made with oil.

## CHAPTER V. Concerning the law of the sacrifice of peace offerings that is offered to the Lord as a thanksgiving

(At the same place.) This is the law of the sacrifice of peace offerings that is offered to the Lord. If the offering is for thanksgiving, they shall offer loaves without leaven, mixed with oil, and unleavened cakes anointed with oil, and fine flour cooked with oil, and cakes mixed with oil. They shall also offer leavened loaves with the sacrifice of thanksgiving, which is sacrificed as a peace offering. From these one shall be offered to the Lord as firstfruits, and it shall belong to the priest who pours out the blood of the sacrifice. Its flesh shall be eaten on the same day, and nothing of it shall remain until morning. (From Origen.)

This sacrifice, which is called salutary, he divides into two parts: one he calls praise, the other a vow. Nevertheless, both sacrifices are called salutary.

(From Hesychius.) You see that the rational and active life is represented by the things he has given us as we pass toward peace or salvation, granting us the power to choose whichever of the two we wish. Since it is a rational sacrifice, it is one of thanksgiving, or, according to the Septuagint, of praise. Hear David, after he rejected the sacrifices that were prescribed according to the Law: “Sacrifice to God a sacrifice of praise, and pay your vows to the Most High.”

(From Origen.) He therefore offered a sacrifice of praise, through whose actions, teaching, word, conduct, and discipline God is praised and blessed. Conversely, there are those of whom it is said: “Through you my name is blasphemed among the nations” (Romans 2).

Hear Paul also, writing to the Hebrews on his own behalf. He says: “Let us therefore continually offer to God a sacrifice of praise, that is, the fruit of lips confessing his name” (Hebrews 13).

How does he command it to be offered? “He shall offer loaves without leaven, mixed with oil, and unleavened cakes anointed with oil, and fine flour cooked with oil, and cakes mixed with oil.” The Septuagint renders it as follows: “And he shall offer fine flour mixed with oil in cakes of unleavened bread, his offerings upon the altar of the salutary praise.”

Understand the loaves without leaven, or unleavened loaves, mixed with oil as the apostolic books; and the cakes anointed with oil as the prophetic books. The former proclaim the mercy of God very abundantly, while the latter, although they too proclaim it abundantly, do not do so to the same extent, since they mingle threats with mercy on account of the disobedience of the Jews. Hence they are said not to be mixed with oil but merely anointed with it.

The cooked fine flour and the cakes mixed with oil—or, as the Septuagint says, “fine flour mixed with oil in cakes of unleavened bread”—we understand as theology joined to almsgiving. Fine flour is so called because of its fineness. Nevertheless, he commanded that the gifts of the sacrifice of peace or salutary offerings be made in unleavened cakes, that is, in the apostolic Scriptures. Above all, the one who desires to be saved must follow apostolic teaching.
