“They shall also offer leavened loaves with the sacrifice of thanksgiving, which is sacrificed as a peace offering. From these one shall be offered as firstfruits to God, and it shall belong to the priest who pours out the blood of the sacrifice.” The Septuagint says: “And he shall offer from all his gifts a praise to God; it shall belong to the priest who pours out the blood of the salutary offering.”

What does this show? That however much a person may act and live, run and attain—or whether he has attained or achieved anything—he cannot obtain or reach salvation without the Lord’s help. Hence Paul also said: “It depends not on human willing or running, but on God who shows mercy” (Romans 9). To the priest who pours out the blood of the salutary offering—that is, to Christ, who ministers and perfects the sacrifice through his own assistance—he commanded that the firstfruits be offered.

Observe also how he concluded the present enactment of the Law: “Its flesh shall be eaten on the same day, and nothing of it shall remain until morning”; or, according to the Septuagint: “The flesh of the sacrifice of salutary praise shall belong to him”—that is, to the one offering it—“and on whatever day he gives it, it shall be eaten; none of it shall be left until morning.”

Here he calls the future age “morning,” since it is wholly light and succeeds the night of the present age. He does not therefore wish any of the flesh of the salutary sacrifice to be left until morning, through which we ought to be saved, knowing that there is no activity remaining in that age.

(From Origen.) We have often said that flesh in the Scriptures indicates solid food and perfect teaching. According to the Scriptures, I know that there is one food of the soul, milk; another food of the soul, vegetables; and another, flesh, just as the Apostle himself says of certain people: “I fed you with milk, not with food, for you were not yet able; indeed, you are not even now able, for you are still carnal” (1 Corinthians 3). Again, elsewhere he says: “One person believes that he may eat everything, while the weak person eats vegetables” (Romans 14). And once more elsewhere: “Solid food belongs to the mature” (Hebrews 5), and so forth.

The flesh of the salutary sacrifice that is offered as praise is therefore commanded to belong to the priest. Of the fine flour offered in three ways, as we said above, only one portion that pleases the priest is assigned to him; the rest belongs to the lay offerer, provided that it is eaten on the same day and that nothing remains of it until morning.

The flesh in which there is solid food and perfect knowledge is assigned to priests, because they ought to be perfect in everything—in teaching, virtues, and conduct. If they do not possess this within themselves, they will not eat of the flesh of the sacrifices. The flesh assigned to the priests from the sacrifices is the word of God that they teach in the Church.

Through these mystical figures they are therefore admonished that, when they begin to bring forth a word before the people, they should not bring forth yesterday’s things, nor speak old things according to the letter, but should always bring forth new things through the grace of God and always discover spiritual things. For if you bring forth today in the Church the things you learned from the Jews yesterday, this is to eat yesterday’s flesh of the sacrifice.

The one portion separated as the principal portion from the three portions prescribed from the fine flour seems to me to designate that part of knowledge about which we spoke above, which signifies perfect and profound teaching.

But perhaps you will ask: since above he entirely excluded leaven from the sacrifices, how does he now command a sacrifice to be placed upon leavened loaves? Consider more carefully: the leavened bread is taken not for the sacrifice but for the service of the sacrifice. Let us therefore see what this means.

In the Gospels the Lord calls the human teaching of the Pharisees, who transmitted human traditions and commandments, “leaven,” when he says to the disciples: “Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees” (Matthew 16; Luke 12).

Human learning is likewise grammar, rhetoric, and even dialectic. Nothing from this learning is to be received for the sacrifice—that is, in the things that ought to be believed about God. But lucid speech, the splendor of eloquence, and the method of argument are fittingly admitted for the service of the word of God.

Or did not the one who said, “Bad company corrupts good morals” (1 Corinthians 15), have the sacrifice of the word of God placed upon this leaven? And likewise the one who said, “Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy gluttons” (Titus 1), and other things similar to these, taken from the leaven of the Greeks?

## CHAPTER VI. On the day when it is permitted to eat from voluntarily offered sacrifices

(At the same place.) If anyone offers a sacrifice by vow or voluntarily, it shall likewise be eaten on the same day. But if anything remains until the next day, it is permitted to eat it; whatever the third day finds, fire shall consume. If anyone eats of the flesh of the peace-offering victim on the third day, the offering shall be invalid and shall not benefit the one who offered it. Rather, whatever soul has defiled itself by such food shall be guilty of transgression.

(From Hesychius.) Every sacrifice of peace or salutary offerings is voluntary. Hence the Lawgiver listed it among the gifts in the earlier part of this book. But although the sacrifice of thanksgiving or praise belongs to the same kind of offering as the one now described, nevertheless, because it is a rational sacrifice, the Law does not add the word “voluntary.” Since we are undoubtedly rational beings, we ought in a certain way to offer to the Creator the principal rational sacrifice that is our due. For this reason the Law is silent about “voluntary” in this case, not excluding it from voluntary offerings.

“Tomorrow” is sometimes understood as the present life and sometimes as the future one. In this passage, however, it refers to the present life, as in what James says in his Epistle: “Come now, you who say, ‘Today or tomorrow we will go into that city, conduct business, and make a profit’” (James 4).

The present age too is called “today,” as David says: “Today, if you hear his voice,” and so forth (Psalm 94).

(From Hesychius.) It is also called “tomorrow,” though not altogether by way of distinction (ἀνὰ διαστολήν) from today, because the intervals of time within the present age are not identical, as Proverbs shows: “Do not say to your friend, ‘Go, and come tomorrow’” (Proverbs 3). For he is not describing the future age, but the time following within the present life. Hence he says: “You do not know what the coming day will bring,” that is, lest you perhaps die on it or be prevented by some other cause.

“Whatever the third day finds, fire shall consume.” By the third day he indicates the future age. In it there is the general resurrection of the dead, which is signified by the resurrection of the Lord occurring on the third day, and this took place in the morning. Hence we said that morning signifies the future age.

Then whatever remains of the sacrifice of peace or salutary offerings will be consumed by fire. Whatever we leave undone that pertains to our salvation is unproductive; what has been wrongly done is also unproductive, and, having become wood, hay, or straw, it will be consumed by this fire, while we shall suffer loss.

But what does he add? “If anyone eats of the flesh of the peace-offering victim on the third day, the offering shall be invalid and shall not benefit the one who offered it. Rather, whatever soul has defiled itself by such food shall be guilty of transgression.”

He did not add these words to the present enactment without reason. Some people, after the end of this life and the resurrection of the dead, have presumed to describe another life like the present one, introducing an age of a thousand years. In it, they say, earthly Jerusalem will be built, its temple and the former Holy of Holies will be restored, and sacrifices will be offered.

Wishing to remove this presumption from our minds, he says: “If anyone eats of the flesh of the peace offerings on the third day”—that is, if anyone proposes in his thought that after the resurrection of the dead he will continue the remnants of this life; if, in a certain manner, he eats by using the foregoing fantasy in his mind as food, hoping that he will eat at a time when eating is impossible, namely, when working is impossible—his offering is not accepted and is not credited to him.

Whoever forms false opinions about the future age harms himself and makes his offering abominable and polluted. Not only this, but he also incurs sin against himself. Hence he says: “Rather, whatever soul has defiled itself by such food shall be guilty of transgression.” He shows that whoever does not form right opinions about Christ’s recompense both lives at a loss of good things and subjects himself to sin.

(From Origen.) Alternatively, in the two days during which it is permitted to eat the flesh of the sacrifice, I think that the two Testaments can be understood. In them it is permitted to seek, examine, and investigate every word that pertains to God—for this is the sacrifice—and to derive from them all knowledge of things.

If anything remains that divine Scripture does not determine, no third Scripture, here called the third day, ought to be accepted as an authority for knowledge. Rather, let us hand over what remains to fire, that is, reserve it for God. For God did not wish us to know everything in the present life, especially since the Apostle also says: “We know in part and we prophesy in part; but when the perfect comes, what is in part will be abolished” (1 Corinthians 13).

This, then, is the fire to which we ought to preserve what remains until the third day. We must not presumptuously claim for ourselves knowledge of everything, lest the same Apostle rightly say to us: “Understanding neither what they say nor about what they make assertions.”

## CHAPTER VII. That no one should touch or eat anything unclean

(At the same place.) Flesh that has touched anything unclean shall not be eaten, but shall be burned with fire. Whoever is clean shall eat it. A polluted soul that eats of the flesh of the peace-offering that was offered to the Lord shall perish from among its people. Whoever touches the uncleanness of a human being or of an animal, or anything whatever that can make one unclean, and eats of such flesh, shall perish from among its people.

(From Origen.) Here the Lawgiver sets forth three causes of uncleanness. The first is that the flesh of the sacrifices must not be touched by any uncleanness. The second is that the one who eats the flesh of the sacrifice must not himself be unclean, with his uncleanness remaining within him. The third is that, even if the flesh is clean and the one who eats it is clean, he must nevertheless not have touched anything unclean, whether from cattle, birds, or anything else that has been declared unclean.

This is the intention of the Law that establishes regulations for the bodily rite of sacrifices. According to the order of our exposition, however, where the holy flesh is understood to be the divine words, the following observance is required.

It often happens that unclean flesh is touched by someone unclean. For example, if someone speaks purely and sincerely about God the Father, his Only-Begotten, and the Holy Spirit, with a fitting understanding of the mystery of deity, and likewise about all rational creatures as made by God for the purpose of apprehending and understanding him, but does not also affirm, in accordance with the mystery, the resurrection of the flesh: his first statement, because he has spoken perfectly and devoutly, is solid food and holy flesh. But when he adds the denial of the resurrection of the flesh—because this is alien to the faith—he has contaminated and polluted the holy flesh by joining it to the preceding perfect and faithful words.

Therefore the Lawgiver commands that such flesh, to which some uncleanness of unbelief has been attached, not be eaten. Hence the Apostle also says: “Let us celebrate the feast, not with the old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” (1 Corinthians 5).

The second kind of uncleanness is that the one who eats the flesh must not himself be unclean, with his uncleanness being within him. This may be understood as follows. Suppose someone has a vigorous nature and a fiery intelligence. He will not immediately be considered suitable for receiving the mysteries of the word of God. It is also required that he first separate himself from profane acts and unclean works, and only then become capable of instruction—provided that he has first become capable of holiness.

The third kind of uncleanness is that in which a clean person touches something unclean and is polluted not so much by his own sin as by another’s contagion. For example, if someone associates in friendship and companionship with an envious, angry, or adulterous person, and does not himself commit his companion’s crimes, but sees him and understands how he hates his brother and is a murderer, or how he plots against another man’s wife and is an adulterer, or how in other matters he is sacrilegious, yet does not withdraw from his companionship after discovering these things: he is the one who touches what is unclean, whether animal, bird, or carcass, and is polluted by another’s uncleanness.

Alternatively: (From Hesychius.) The flesh signifies the virtues of which the salutary sacrifice consists—for example, chastity, almsgiving, and justice. If these touch anything unclean, as when justice and chastity become oriented toward vain glory through pride, or almsgiving arises from injustice, they will be consumed by the fire of the future judgment.

Isaiah demonstrates this when he says: “He who sacrifices an ox is like one who kills a man; he who slaughters a sheep is like one who brains a dog,” and so forth (Isaiah 66).

The proper conclusion of the present commandment is: “Whoever is clean shall eat it; a polluted soul that eats of the flesh of the peace-offering that was offered to the Lord shall perish from among its people.” Here he plainly destroys irony and hypocrisy, for these are the uncleannesses of the soul. Thus the inner person of such a man is called a wolf, when the Lord says: “Beware of those who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravenous wolves” (Matthew 7).

Those who eat of the flesh of the peace or salutary offering that was offered to the Lord—because they perform virtues belonging to God not with virtuous intention but fraudulently—perish from their own people, so that they are no longer called sheep but wolves.

Unclean animals signify those who are occupied with unclean and earthly actions, directing their attention toward the earth like animals. Hence fornicators are also called stallions. “Or anything whatever that can make one unclean”: whoever observes dreams, divinations, and purifications, or keeps particular days and times, and, still more, magicians and sorcerers, is abominable before the Lord.

Anyone who does these things perhaps shares in their evil counsels or actions. Since he has touched a forbidden uncleanness, he cannot eat—or perform—the things that pertain to the salutary or peace offering. For when he attempts to do what pertains to salvation while associating with those who perform evil and what pertains to destruction, he perishes from his people—that is, from those who are being saved.

## CHAPTER VIII. The fat belonging to the Lord’s offering may not be eaten

(At the same place.) The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “Speak to the sons of Israel: You shall not eat the fat of an ox, sheep, or goat. The fat of a carcass and the fat of an animal caught by a wild beast you shall use for various purposes. If anyone eats the fat that ought to be offered as an offering to the Lord, he shall perish from among his people.”

(From Hesychius.) He did not command that the fat of oxen, sheep, or goats be eaten. Although he declared their flesh clean and edible, he forbade the eating of their fat. Nor does he permit us to consume the desire of the one who fulfils the commandment, represented by the ox, of the simple one, represented by the sheep, or of those who repent for sins.

For the goat signifies sacrifices made for sins, since he commanded a she-goat or a he-goat to be sacrificed in such cases. He therefore does not allow us to eat the desire represented by these animals. He commands that it be referred to God and offered to God, so that the desire for each thing that one obtains from those mentioned may not be according to human intention, but may be offered to God alone.

Likewise, the desire of sinners is signified by carcasses and by animals caught by wild beasts. Carcasses signify those who have chosen the death of sin through certain acts of shamelessness and through pride. Paul proves this concerning widows when he says: “She who lives in pleasure is dead while she lives.”

By animals caught by wild beasts are understood those who, neglecting their own vigilance and protection, have been captured and seized by intelligible beasts. To prevent this from happening to us, Peter again says: “Be sober, be watchful; your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour” (1 Peter 5).

He does not permit their fat to be eaten, for it is harmful for us to use their desires. Nor does he command them to be offered to God. “The desire of sinners shall perish.” But what does he command? “You shall use them for various purposes.”

We must therefore transfer that desire to virtue, directing it either toward chastity, almsgiving, justice, or any kind of good action; we must dissolve it and divert it into another form. This is what “You shall use them for various purposes” means, because fat, when it is needed for some useful work, is refined and dissolved.

“If anyone eats the fat that ought to be offered as an offering to the Lord, he shall perish from among his people.” He rightly perishes: namely, the person who compels or otherwise persuades one who has offered himself to God not to direct his desire toward the heavenly gaze, but toward pleasing himself.

“You shall not consume the blood of any animal as food, whether of birds or cattle; every soul that eats blood shall perish from among its people” (Psalm 111). That blood is intended to be understood as the soul has already been sufficiently demonstrated above.

He therefore wants us to attain the virtue of mutual love, and not to eat the blood—that is, not to work toward the death—either of the righteous, whom he signifies here on account of their higher way of life, or of sinners, to whom the designation “cattle” applies because they direct their attention toward lower things.

(From Origen.) It may therefore also be the case here that the command forbidding anyone to eat the fat of what is offered to the Lord means what the Lord says: “Let no one cause one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble” (Matthew 18).

That the blood of no animal is commanded to be eaten may perhaps mean what the Apostle says concerning the Israelites: “You will say, then, ‘Branches were broken off so that I might be grafted in.’ They were broken off because of unbelief; but you stand by faith. Do not be arrogant, but fear” (Romans 11). And again: “Do not boast against the branches”—that is, let no one insult their fall—“lest you too be cut off; and if they do not remain in unbelief, they will be grafted in.”

I think that the blood can appropriately be understood as that people. For they descend not from Abraham’s faith or spirit, but only from his blood.

## CHAPTER IX. The right shoulder and the breast belong to the priest from the peace offerings

(At the same place.) The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “Speak to the sons of Israel: Whoever offers a victim of peace offerings to the Lord shall offer with it the sacrifice—that is, its libations. He shall hold in his hands the fat of the victim and the breast. When he has consecrated both by offering them to the Lord, he shall hand them to the priest, who shall burn the fat upon the altar. The breast shall belong to Aaron and his sons. The right shoulder from the peace offerings shall also belong as firstfruits to the priest who offered the blood and the fat. The one who offers the blood and the fat of the sons of Aaron shall also have the right shoulder as his portion.

“I took the breast of elevation and the shoulder of separation from the sons of Israel, from their peace offerings, and I gave them to Aaron the priest and to his sons as a perpetual ordinance, from all the people of Israel. Whoever offers a victim of peace offerings to the Lord shall offer with it the sacrifice.”

(From Hesychius.) That is, its libations. The Septuagint, however, says: “The one who offers a salutary sacrifice to the Lord shall offer his gift to the Lord from his salutary sacrifice.” The meaning of this interpretation is made entirely clear by what follows: “He shall hold in his hands the fat of the victim.” Or, according to the Septuagint: “His hands shall offer the entrails to the Lord.”

This means that each person must himself perform the things that pertain to peace or salvation, since one cannot be saved through the effort of another, whether friend or relative.

“For as the iniquity of the wicked shall be upon him, so the righteousness of the righteous shall be upon him” (Ezekiel 18).

How ought the sacrifice to be celebrated? “He shall hold in his hands the fat of the victim and the breast.” Or, according to the Septuagint: “He shall offer the fat that is upon the breast and the lobe of the liver, and he shall offer them so that they may be placed before the Lord.”

Here he calls the breast faith and confidence, because these are joined to strength. Strength, in turn, ordinarily designates perfect persons. The breast, signifying faith and confidence, is to be offered to the Lord by the one who desires to be saved, because “without faith it is impossible to please God” (Hebrews 11).

What does he add? “He shall hand it to the priest, who shall burn the fat upon the altar.” Rightly so. For we said that he wants all our desire to become a burnt offering. The breast, however, shall belong to Aaron and his sons; the right shoulder also signifies good actions. Therefore the one who desires to be saved must offer both faith and actions.

But since he assigned the breast to the sons of Aaron, who are exalted in life, and the right shoulder to the priest who bears the image of Christ, the reason is that only the priest can perfect this sacrifice.

The Lawgiver clearly shows that it is ours to believe and to purpose good things—through God’s inspiration—or at least to begin them. But to perfect by works and bring to completion what has been begun belongs to divine grace. Hence Paul says: “It depends not on human willing or running, but on God who shows mercy” (Romans 9).

[Col. 0319A] For it is his alone to direct actions; hence he is also called the arm of God. Isaiah says: “Lord, who has believed our report, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” (Isaiah 53). Since he himself is the true arm, he rightly received our shoulder, or, as the Septuagint says, our arm.

Then, expanding our intention, the legislator added: “He who offers the blood and fat of the sons of Aaron shall have the right shoulder as his portion.” For Christ is the one who offers the intelligible blood of the peace offerings—that is, souls and salutary desires. He is indeed one of the sons of Aaron, not by kinship but by his own dignity: the singular priest and the foremost among human beings. Into his portion passes the right shoulder, or right arm—that is, every good action and the accomplishment of the work. (From Origen.)

No one offers the sacrifice called the sacrifice of salvation to the Lord unless he is sound and conscious of his salvation, giving thanks to the Lord. Therefore no one who is sick in mind and weak in deeds can offer a sacrifice of salvation. Do you wish to see that no sick or weak person can offer that sacrifice? The leper whom the Lord is described as having healed in the Gospel could not offer a victim so long as he was held by the sickness of leprosy. But when he approached Jesus and was cleansed, the Lord then ordered him to offer gifts at the altar: “What Moses commanded,” he says, “as a testimony to them.” Have you seen who ought to offer the salvific victim? Hear now how he ought to offer it: “His hands,” he says, “offer the victim to the Lord.” Does the legislator not cry out clearly [Col. 0319B] that it is not the man who offers the victim, but his hands—that is, his works? For it is the works that commend the victim to God. If your hand is drawn back from giving and extended to receive, your leprosy is still within you, and you cannot offer a salvific victim.

In the place where we read, “His hands shall offer a victim to the Lord,” the Greek has *holokarpōmata*, which means “the whole fruit.” By this he shows that the person who is fruitless cannot offer the whole fruit to the Lord: one who does not bear the fruit of righteousness, the fruit of mercy, or even the fruits of the Spirit, which the Apostle enumerates—love, joy, peace, patience, and unanimity, together with other things like these.

[Col. 0319D] But when he says, “the fats that are upon the breast,” understand your breast to be your heart, from which all evil thoughts must be removed, since they proceed from it, and handed over to the fire of the altar, so that your heart, once made clean, may be able to see God. He also commands the lobe of the liver to be offered. We said earlier that the part of the liver signifies the places of anger or desire. Therefore he offers the lobe of the liver who cuts away from himself every vice of anger and fury.

Thus the fats that are upon the breast are placed upon the altar. But he commands that the breast itself be set apart for Aaron and his sons, and also that the right arm be separated and assigned to them as a gift from the sacrifice of salvation. What, then, is the priest’s breast, and of what kind is it? I think it is one that is full of wisdom, full of every divine understanding—indeed, one that is full of God.

And what is the priest’s arm, which the sons of Israel offer to him for their salvation, by which they are saved? These individual things written in the law are figures of what ought to be done in the Church. Otherwise it would not have been necessary for these things to be read in the Church unless they provided some edification for those who hear them.

If, then, the priest of the Church, through his words and teaching, through great care and the labor of watchfulness, is able to convert a sinner and teach him to follow a better life; if he brings him back to the fear of God, makes him consider the hope to come, causes him to cease from evil deeds, and turns him toward good—if, I say, he has accomplished such a work, it follows that the person saved through his labor should give thanks to God and offer a salvific victim [Col. 0320A] because he has attained salvation.

Nor does it seem to me that what he added—that the breast is called “of presentation” and the arm “of separation” or “removal”—was said without cause. I therefore wish to inquire what must be added to the breast for it to become the breast of presentation. After everything coarse has been removed from your heart, and it has been cleansed of every covering that must be handed over to the fire, it remains that the grace of the Holy Spirit be added to it. Then it will become the breast of presentation.

But how will the arm become the arm of separation or removal? If you know and understand how to distinguish the works of light from the works of darkness, and to separate your actions from darkness so that your works may be in the light, your arm becomes the arm of separation. Or it becomes so when you have separated yourself from every brother who walks disorderly; or certainly, according to the Prophet, when “those who bear the vessels of the Lord” separate themselves and go out from the midst of sinners (Isaiah 52).

## CHAPTER X. On the anointing of Aaron and his sons, and on the ceremonies and garments pertaining to it

(From the same place.) “This is the anointing of Aaron and his sons in the ceremonies of the Lord, on the day when Moses presented them to serve as priests, and what the Lord commanded to be given to them by the sons of Israel as a perpetual religious observance throughout their generations.”

(From Hesychius.) The things that have been said seem in a certain way to concern the anointing of the priests, but the legislator did not intend to discuss this at present. For what connection with the anointing of priests have the sacrifices mentioned above? [Col. 0320D] He intended only either to show the dignity of the things he had spoken of earlier, or to show what advancement they confer upon those who observe them.

For when he says, “This is the anointing of Aaron and his sons in the ceremonies of the Lord,” he referred this back to what precedes—that is, the breast of presentation and the arm of separation. These themselves are the anointing of Aaron and his sons, lest we think that those words were spoken merely about meats, but so that he might teach that those things too are included under the mystery of anointing. Thus you may understand that whoever observes whatever the law said above advances toward the dignity of the priesthood; and by devoting himself to these things, he may be called “a royal priesthood, a holy nation.” Otherwise, he cannot be so called.

For this is the anointing in the ceremonies of the Lord: it is bestowed through the communions that are described in the sacrifices mentioned above. Therefore he added: “On the day when Moses presented them to me, so that they might serve as priests, and what the Lord commanded to be given to them by the sons of Israel.” Thus in these things he gave us anointing, and in these things God called us: “On the day when he presented them.”

When was this? On the day when he anointed them to serve as priests—that is, on the day when he anointed them from among the sons of Israel, through the anointing described here. Those who live or conduct themselves in a more exalted manner are rightly superior to all the people. Hence the legislator very appropriately added: “As a perpetual religious observance throughout your generations,” so that you might know that this religious observance is unshakable before God. No one can excel among the people or among the majority by dignity, wisdom, kinship with the righteous, or anything similar unless he has attained what was commanded above.

Thus someone also becomes a priest according to his kinship with Christ, the true priest, who displayed an undefiled and perfect life. But because he understood the anointing to consist in the things plainly stated above, what follows confirms it: “This is the law of the burnt offering and of the sacrifice for sin and for guilt, and for consecration, and of the victims of the peace offerings, which the Lord established for Moses on Mount Sinai, when he commanded the sons of Israel to offer their offerings to the Lord in the wilderness of Sinai” (from the same place).

You see the different ways of life that unite people to God: either the perfect honor of wisdom, signified by the burnt offering, or the moderate righteousness that is sufficient and capable of accomplishing what pertains to salvation. The law understood these sacrifices of peace offerings—whether they were made through burnt offerings or through an oblation—to be rightly useful, since they bestowed priestly dignity. Therefore, on the day when he commanded Moses on Mount Sinai concerning the law of anointing, he also added the matters concerning sacrifices, briefly enumerating and recalling them all together.

But where did he say that these things were established? “In the wilderness of Sinai.” Sinai is interpreted as “bush” or “temptation.” Temptation resembles a bush, for it is a rough shrub, difficult to grasp by hand. Through it is signified that, just as the crown among those who contend in the contest is attained through sweat and labor, so the crown of a good life is perfected through temptations and tribulations. James sufficiently explained the end of temptations [Col. 0321D] and tribulations for us: “Blessed is the man who endures temptation, for when he has been tested, he will receive the crown of life which God promised to those who love him” (James 1).

(Leviticus 8.) “And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Take Aaron with his sons, their garments and the oil of anointing; a bull for sin, two rams, and a basket with unleavened bread; and gather the whole assembly at the door of the tent of testimony.”

What these things now mentioned signify, the preceding discourse will convey to you: the anointing of Christ is both shared and not shared by those who belong to him. It is shared because they themselves participate in the same anointing; hence we too are called Christians through participation in Christ. It is not shared because God surpasses human beings by an immeasurable sublimity, and by the grace in which we share with him. He is anointed substantially, whereas we are anointed through his operation and grace.

Therefore Aaron’s sons are anointed together with Aaron, but the things performed in their anointing are not such in them as they are in Aaron, as what follows makes clear. But here too we must fix our attention on the fact that we do not accept these things as referring to Christ without reason. Knowing that the legislator is speaking of the mysteries of the Church, he commanded the whole assembly, or synagogue, to be summoned to the door of the tent of testimony—that is, to what the Greeks call the *ekklesiastēs*. This synagogue cannot otherwise share in this law unless it gathers into the Church, in which the truth of these figures [Col. 0322B] is preserved.

“Moses did as the Lord had commanded. When the whole crowd had been gathered before the doors, he said to them: This is the word which the Lord has commanded to be done. Immediately he presented Aaron and his sons; and when he had washed them, he clothed the high priest in a linen undergarment, girding him with a belt, and clothing him in a violet-colored tunic. Above it he placed the ephod, fastening it with a belt and fitting it to the breastpiece, in which were doctrine and truth. He also covered his head with a turban, and upon it, over the forehead, he placed a consecrated golden plate for sanctification, as the Lord had commanded him.”

The things that are mystically done in the Church were commanded by the Spirit of God many generations earlier. Moreover, although above, according to the Septuagint, he had said, “Summon them to the doors of the tent of testimony,” here he says, “He summoned the congregation,” not to the doors but to the door of the tent of testimony. He clearly admonishes our ears that the teachings of the apostles—which the preceding discourse explained to be the doors of the tent of testimony—and the teaching of Christ have been poured into his own tongue, and that they derive from the things by which he himself taught.

“When the whole crowd had been gathered before the doors, he said: This is the word which the Lord commanded to be done.” What word was that? Clearly the one of which David said: “The Lord will give the word to those who proclaim the Gospel with great power” (Psalm 67); and Peter says more plainly: “This is the word which was announced to you” (1 Peter 1).

The present word is evangelical, since the mysteries of the Gospel were announced by him, and in them the grace of baptism is present. But what does it mean that he now explains God to have commanded? “Immediately he presented Aaron and his sons, and when he had washed them”—when the one who is truly the priest, Christ, is offered to the Father. Daniel too remembers his offering when he says: “And behold, one like a son of man came with the clouds of heaven, and he came even to the Ancient of Days. And he was presented before him.”

He is offered for our sake, with us, and on our behalf. Therefore he now says that he was offered with his sons, namely, with those who think exalted thoughts and imitate him as far as is lawful for human beings, such as Paul, who says: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (Philippians 3). But the offering itself is celebrated through baptism; hence he says, “When he had washed them.”

It is certain that Christ was baptized in the Jordan River in order to consecrate the waters of our baptism. These things, then, are common to Aaron and his sons—to Christ and to us. But what follows is not shared with us at all, for it exceeds us and is higher than we are, belonging only to the first and true priest.

“He clothed the high priest in a linen undergarment, girding him with a belt and clothing him in a tunic.” The Septuagint translated this: “He clothed him in a tunic, girded him with a sash, and clothed him in the *hypodytēs*.” Here he plainly follows the incarnation of the Only-Begotten. Because he became incarnate as our whole human being, he is said to have been clothed in a tunic and in the *hypodytēs*. For our condition is twofold: one part of us is from the dust, the other heavenly, yet both are one.

Moses says: “God formed man from the clay of the earth” (Genesis 2). This, therefore, is the earthly part. “And he breathed into his face the breath of life” (same place): this is most clearly the heavenly part.

Christ put on the earthly—that is, the one who is from the earth, the old man—which he also nailed to the cross together with himself. For Paul says: “Our old man was crucified with him, so that the body of sin might be destroyed” (Romans 6). He also put on the heavenly one, which he himself breathed into us. But because he did nothing earthly here, nor anything close to corruption, he is unquestionably called heavenly.

Explaining this, Paul says: “The first man was from the earth, earthly; the second man was from heaven, heavenly” (1 Corinthians 15). This must be understood in two ways. First, our first man—that is, the body—was formed from the earth, and therefore was called earthly; but the soul is from heaven, for it is God’s breathing.

Again, the first man, disobedient Adam, was earthly from the earth because he assigned himself to the works of dust. The second man, the new man, is Christ, who is from heaven—not only because he descended from heaven, but because he preserved the dignity of the heavenly, since he neither did anything earthly nor anything close to corruption.

Therefore here he called the tunic earthly, since the tunic was made of linen, which comes from the earth. Moses says: “And he made for them linen tunics.” But he called the *hypodytēs* heavenly, because *hypodytēs* is a word associated with weight, and it is also violet-colored; this is the color of heaven.

Christ assumed both aspects of our humanity, the visible and the invisible, the earthly and the heavenly—that is, a perfect body and a perfect soul, complete in every respect. For, as creator of both, he saved both.

Notice also this: “And above it he placed the ephod, fastening it with a belt and fitting it to the breastpiece.” The Septuagint, however, gives: “And he placed upon him the *epōmis*, and girded him according to the opening of the *epōmis*, and fastened the shoulder-piece to it.”

Christ’s yoke is gentle—that is, the evangelical life. Since he himself demonstrated it, he rightly carried it upon his shoulders. Concerning it he says: “Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart; for my yoke is easy and my burden is light” (Matthew 11).

But what is the belt with which he girded the tunic and the *hypodytēs*? Learn what the work itself signifies. For, in the construction of the tabernacle, he says: “And you shall make a turban of fine linen and a belt of varied workmanship.” Since the *kydaris* is a head covering, the work of the belt or sash is in a certain way to strengthen and bind the one who is girded.

The legislator intended to show this: Christ, while recapitulating or restoring the whole creation, also strengthens our human substance, whose firstfruits he assumed, in order to administer the mystery of the incarnation. Through it we too have been made strong.

John says what the mode of this dispensation is: “The Word became flesh” (John 1). Therefore Moses says that the *kydaris* and the belt were made of fine linen in varied workmanship. Fine linen, since it comes from the earth, signifies the flesh, which is from our earth. The embroiderer’s work signifies God the Word, who is the craftsman and arranger of the whole creation. He fashioned for himself the flesh taken from us, in a certain way varying within it the mysteries and miracles of creation.

After this he added, according to the Septuagint: “And he placed the breastpiece upon him.” Some manuscripts have, “upon him.” Both expressions, however, refer to the same thing: “Fastening it with a belt, he fitted it to the breastpiece, in which were doctrine and truth.”

The Septuagint gives: “And he placed upon the *logion* the manifestation and the truth.” Elsewhere, when explaining this priestly garment, he called it the rational robe of judgment. According to the rational breastpiece of Christ—that is, according to the teaching and proclamation of future judgment—he is governed.

Thus it has manifestation, that is, disclosure, and with it truth, since he reveals to human beings the previously unknown truth of the mysteries. He commanded that the rational breastpiece be made from four rows—that is, from the four general virtues—and from twelve stones, in a certain way distinct and particular.

What are these? They are the virtues about which Paul wrote: “A bishop must be blameless, as God’s steward” (Titus 1). But how he is to be blameless—that is, clean from accusation and free from every complaint—he shows in what follows: “Not arrogant, not irascible, not addicted to wine, not violent, not greedy for dishonest gain, but hospitable, kind, chaste, just, holy, self-controlled, holding fast to the faithful word that accords with the teaching” (same place).

These things are fitting for everyone to attain, but especially for the priest, since he bears the figure of Christ, who carried the twelve stones mentioned above upon his own breast.

“He also covered his head with a *kydaris*,” or, according to the Septuagint, “He placed a turban upon his head.” But since we know the function of the turban or *kydaris*, and have learned that the Father is the head of Christ, let us hear what follows: “And upon it, over the forehead, he placed a consecrated golden plate for sanctification, as the Lord had commanded him.”

Wishing to lift us upward, the legislator mentioned the turban or *kydaris* as being upon the head, because of the Father. Through the plate and the engraving, or representation, of sanctification, he plainly explained the dignity of the incarnate Word of God, who also became our priest, a dignity which he possesses together with the Father from the beginning. Therefore he places it above the *kydaris* or turban, and opposite the face of the turban [Col. 0325A] or *kydaris*.

He says: “You shall bind it with a violet-colored cord,” or, according to the Septuagint, “You shall place it upon the twisted violet.” By “twisted violet” he understands the humanity of Christ, because it is inseparably joined to divinity.

“And it shall be above the head-covering, projecting over the forehead of the high priest.” Or, according to the Septuagint: “It shall be upon the turban, opposite the face of the turban.” It shall be upon the turban because the Father is in the Son and the Son is in the Father; and it shall be before the face of the turban, because whoever sees the Son is said here to see the Father as well. (From Origen.)

Thus every sanctification is now clearly explained as a mystery of the Only-Begotten.

Alternatively: Let Moses wash you, then—let him wash you himself, and let him himself clothe you. The law, therefore, is what washes you; it cleanses away your filth; if you listen to it, it wipes away the stains of your sins.

This is Moses—that is, the law—which consecrates priests. No one can be a priest whom the law has not appointed priest. If you too have been washed by Moses and have become as clean as the one whom Moses washed, you can reach those garments which Moses brings forth, the robes with which he clothes Aaron his brother and his sons.

But not only garments are needed for priestly insignia; belts are also needed. For he says: “God made tunics of skins and clothed Adam and his wife” (Genesis 3). Those tunics, then, were made from skins taken from animals. It was fitting for the sinner to be clothed in such garments—“in tunics of skin,” which were signs of the mortality he received on account of sin, and of his weakness, which arose from the corruption of the flesh.

But if you have already been washed of these things and purified through the law of God, Moses will clothe you in the garment of incorruption, so that your shame may nowhere appear and so that “this mortal” may be swallowed up by life.

Let us therefore see in what order the high priest is established. “Moses summoned the synagogue,” he says, “and said to them: This is the word which the Lord commanded.” Although the Lord had commanded concerning the establishment of the high priest, and the Lord had chosen him, nevertheless the synagogue is summoned. For the presence of the people is required in the ordination of a priest, so that all may know and be certain that the one who is superior to the whole people, the more learned, the holier, and the more eminent in every virtue, is the one chosen for the priesthood.

He washed him, therefore, and clothed him. In what garment? “In a tunic,” he says, “and he girded him with a sash.” [Col. 0325D] And again: “He clothed him in a full-length tunic,” or, as we read elsewhere, “an inner garment.”

I see the high priest clothed by Moses in two tunics. But what shall we do with the fact that Jesus prohibited his priests—that is, our apostles—from using two tunics? And we had said that Moses and Jesus, that is, the law and the Gospels, agree with one another.

Someone else might perhaps say that Jesus’ command not to have two tunics is not contrary to the law, but more perfect than the law—just as the law forbids murder, whereas Jesus also cuts away anger; and the law forbids adultery, whereas Jesus also cuts away the desire of the heart.

I, however, do not confine the priestly mysteries within the narrow limits of this interpretation. Something more seems to me to be indicated by this form. The high priest whom Moses was then ordaining knew that there was circumcision, and that an uncircumcised high priest could not exist. He therefore had two tunics: one for carnal ministry and another for spiritual understanding.

He knew that spiritual sacrifices ought to be offered to God, yet he also offered carnal sacrifices; for he could not be high priest of those who existed at that time unless he sacrificed victims.

Thus it is appropriately said that that high priest was clothed in two tunics. But the apostles were going to say: “If you are circumcised, Christ will be of no benefit to you” (Galatians 5); and: “Let no one judge you in food or drink, or in respect of a festival, a new moon, or Sabbaths, which are a shadow of things to come” (Colossians 2).

Therefore, since they completely rejected observance of the law according to the letter, so that they might not occupy their disciples with Jewish fables or impose upon them a yoke which neither they nor their fathers had been able to bear, they are rightly forbidden to have two tunics. One is sufficient for them, and that one is the inner garment. They do not want the garment that is outside and appears above—the garment of the law. Jesus permits them to have one garment, and that one the inner garment.

Moses nevertheless places upon the high priest the ephod, which is a kind of ornamental garment formed by wrapping it around the shoulders. The shoulders, however, signify works and labor. He therefore wishes the high priest to be adorned in works as well; knowledge alone is not enough: “He who does and teaches, he shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven.”

“And he girded him,” he says, “according to the workmanship of the ephod.” Already above he had said that he girded him with a sash over the tunic, and now again he is girded according to the workmanship of the ephod. What is this double belt with which he wishes the high priest to be bound on every side?

Let him be bound in word, bound in deed, ready for everything, with nothing slack or disordered. Let him be girded with the virtues of the soul, restrained from bodily vices, fearing no fall of the soul and no fall of the body. Let him always use both belts, so that he may be holy in body and spirit.

“And after these things,” he says, “he placed the *logion* upon him”—that is, the rational breastpiece—and placed upon the rational breastpiece manifestation and truth, and placed the turban upon his head.

But let us see what the *logion*, which is the rational breastpiece, signifies. It is not enough for the high priest to possess wisdom and to know the meaning of everything unless he can also manifest to the people what he knows. Therefore manifestation is placed upon the rational breastpiece, so that he may be able to answer everyone who asks him for an account of faith and truth.

Truth is also placed upon it, so that he may not assert what he has been able to devise by his own ingenuity, but what truth possesses.

But he has not yet finished; another ornament must still be added. He must also receive a crown. Therefore he first receives the *kydaris*, which is either a covering of the head or an ornament, and after this a turban is placed upon it before the face—that is, at the forehead of the high priest—a sanctified golden plate on which the name of God is said to have been engraved.

This ornament of the head, on which the name of God is said to have been placed, is set above all those things with which the lower parts of the body had been adorned. In this he seems to me to indicate that, above everything that can be perceived or understood either concerning the world or concerning the other creatures, the knowledge of God, as the author of all things, is supreme. Since he is the head of all things, this ornament too is placed upon the head above all things. Nothing further is added to the high priest’s head after this.

“He took the oil of anointing with which he anointed the tabernacle and all its furnishings. And when he had sanctified the altar by sprinkling it seven times, he anointed it and all its vessels; he also sanctified the basin and its base with oil.”

(From Hesychius.) It was the Son of God himself who anointed them, and he himself was the one anointed—anointing with the word of his divinity, according to which all things are shared by him with the Father and the Spirit, and from which he is said to be anointed.

For David said that the Father anointed him when he said: “Therefore God, your God, has anointed you” (Psalm 44). Isaiah, however, referred the Son’s anointing to the Spirit, saying: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me” (Isaiah 61).

What the Father and the Spirit do, the Son also does. Therefore, according to his divinity, he is himself the one who anoints himself, and he is himself the one who is anointed according to the human dispensation.

Similarly, he both offers and is offered. Hence Daniel sees him as offered (Daniel 7), but does not see the one who offered him, because he himself was the one offering himself.

Therefore, so that the truth of the figures might be preserved, Moses both anoints and offers, himself also bearing the figure of Christ. Moses therefore sprinkles the altar—namely, the Lord’s body—seven times, because the Lord’s anointing is the whole fullness of the Spirit, who is signified in seven operations, as Isaiah said.

[Col. 0327C] “He also anoints all its vessels”: both the apostles and those who live so similarly to them that they are rightly called the house and vessels of Christ.

“And he poured the oil upon Aaron’s head, anointed him, and consecrated,” or sanctified, “him.” Even if, according to Paul’s word, the head of Christ is understood to be divinity, nevertheless the legislator did not write in this mystery without reason or order that the head of the priest was now anointed. He wished us to understand that, just as the head cannot be separated from the feet, so Christ’s divinity cannot be separated from his humanity after the union.

Whether he is said to be anointed, born, to suffer, to rise, or to be assumed, we must not divide the incarnate Word by saying that the man was anointed but God was not anointed. Rather, he is simultaneously the same God and man.

David also confirms this without any doubt when he says: “Your throne, O God, is forever and ever; the scepter of righteousness is the scepter of your kingdom. You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you” (Psalm 44).

Do you see that the one who was anointed is called God? For it is clear that he claims all things belonging to his flesh for himself, who became incarnate. What was his anointing, unless it was precisely his incarnation?

In this way the head of the intelligible priest was anointed, and he himself was sanctified.

“He also clothed his sons, after they had been presented, in linen tunics, girded them with belts, and placed turbans upon them, as the Lord had commanded.”

Tunics like Aaron’s, belts or sashes like his, and *kydarim* or turbans are placed upon Aaron’s sons. For they put him on, they are bound by him, and they carry him upon their head. Hence Paul says: “Stand, therefore, with your loins girded in truth” (Ephesians 6). Truth is Christ. He also says: “And having put on the breastplate of righteousness”—and this too is Christ, who was made for us by God wisdom and righteousness. Paul also commands us to put on the helmet of salvation, for Christ is salvation.

As Simeon testified: “Now you dismiss your servant, Lord, according to your word, in peace, because my eyes have seen your salvation” (Luke 2). For all who put on Christ put on the Father through him as well.

(From Origen.) Therefore, in the things described by the divine law, each priest ought to look at himself as in a mirror and derive from them the measure of his merit. If he sees himself placed among all the pontifical ornaments explained above; if he is conscious that in knowledge, deeds, or teaching he is such and so great, he should know that he possesses the high priesthood not only in name but also in merit. Otherwise, let him recognize that a lower rank has been assigned to him, even if he has received the name of the first.

We should not pass over something else that an attentive reader may raise, and about which I myself have often been perplexed. In Exodus, where the priestly garments are commanded, I find eight kinds prepared for the high priest. Here, however, only seven are enumerated. I therefore ask what has been omitted.

The eighth kind there is called the *campestre*, or, as we read elsewhere, the linen breeches, about which he is silent here among the other garments. What shall we say? Shall we attribute forgetfulness to the words of the Holy Spirit, so that, after recounting everything else a second time, he overlooked one kind of garment mentioned above? I do not dare to think this of the sacred words.

But let us see whether perhaps, because we said above that this kind of garment seemed to signify judgment concerning chastity—since the thighs appear to be covered, or the loins and lower back restrained—he may perhaps not be saying that these parts were always restrained in those priests who existed then. For at times indulgence is granted concerning the continuation of a lineage and the succession of offspring.

But I would not introduce such an interpretation among the priests of the Church, since I see the matter running according to another sacramental meaning. Priests and teachers in the Church can indeed beget sons, just as the one who said: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Galatians 4).

And again elsewhere he says: “Even if you have countless tutors in Christ, you do not have many fathers; for in Christ Jesus, through the Gospel, I begot you” (1 Corinthians 4).

These teachers of the Church, therefore, in begetting such offspring, sometimes also use restrained breeches and abstain from begetting when they find hearers in whom they know they can bear no fruit.

Finally, it is also reported in the Acts of the Apostles concerning certain people: “We were not able,” he says, “to speak the word of God in Asia” (Acts 16). This means that they had put on breeches and restrained themselves from begetting sons, because their hearers were such that the seed would perish in them and no succession could be obtained.

Thus the priests of the Church, when they see ears incapable of hearing, or when they perceive hearers to be pretenders and hypocrites, should put on the *campestre* and use breeches, so that the seed of the word of God may not perish. For the Lord gives the same command: “Do not give what is holy to dogs, and do not cast your pearls before swine” (Matthew 7), lest they perhaps trample them under their feet and, turning, tear you apart.

(From the same place.) “He also offered a bull for sin. When Aaron and his sons had placed their hands upon its head, he slaughtered it, drew off its blood, and, dipping his finger, touched the horns of the altar around it. After he had purified and sanctified it, he poured the remaining blood at its base. He also burned upon the altar the fat that was over the vital organs, the lobe of the liver, and the two kidneys with their fat; but he burned the bull, with its hide, flesh, and dung, outside the camp, as the Lord had commanded.”

(From Hesychius.) What the force of the sanction mentioned above is, and how each of its parts is to be understood as referring to the sacrifice of the Only-Begotten, the preceding discourse contains. Here we shall say only what differs from that sanction.

There Aaron alone placed his hands upon the bull; here his sons do so as well. He did not preserve this without reason, but also wrote that the anointed placed their hands upon it. For when we too are anointed and offered in baptism, we become companions of the Lord’s passion, whose image baptism bears. Paul’s words teach this as well: “All of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death; therefore we were buried with him through baptism into death.”

The sons of Aaron necessarily place their hands upon the sacrifice, since they share in it.

[Col. 0329C] He also offered a ram as a burnt offering. When Aaron and his sons had laid their hands upon its head, he slaughtered it and poured its blood around the altar. Cutting the ram itself into pieces, he burned its head, limbs, and fat on the fire, after first washing the entrails and feet; and he burned the whole ram upon the altar, since it was a burnt offering of the sweetest fragrance to the Lord, as the Lord had commanded.

*(From the same author.)* For this reason the Law commanded the priest, who in many respects bears the image of the Lord, first to sacrifice a calf for sins and burn it outside the tabernacle: for thus also the Lord’s sacrifice was made for the cleansing of our nature from sins. Now, again, it commanded another sacrifice to be offered to him as a burnt offering, in the form of a ram. For the way of life crucified to and renouncing the world—a burnt offering—has Christ as its first fruits, teacher, and example. Therefore he said, “Whoever does not accept the cross and follow me is not worthy of me” (Matt. X), that is, whoever does not renounce the world as it has been delivered to him by me—for this is what it means to follow him—is not worthy of me.

But for what reason is the burnt offering divided, while its feet and entrails—or, according to the Septuagint, its belly—are washed? The interpretation of the burnt offering given at the beginning of the book has sufficiently explained this. What is changed in the sacrifice must nevertheless be mentioned, because there he said that the parts were made into an offering [*offerings*], thereby signifying that body and soul must be offered. In us these divisions are named because they are opposed to one another, as Paul says; but in Christ there are no divisions. For, taking a human being purified from sin, he became incarnate; he is not divided among the works of the flesh, which the spirit opposes. Therefore the Law made no mention of divisions in that sacrifice.

But by the fact that the priest offers a calf for sin and a ram as a burnt offering, the Law plainly signifies this: since a perfect way of life is recognized through the offering of a burnt offering, a ram must necessarily be offered as the sacrifice. For the ram is accustomed to lead sheep going to pasture and to initiate their departure and entrance from the folds and into the folds. So also Christ is the leader of the perfect way of life: from him it took its beginning, and therefore he commanded the sheep to enter and go out through him.

[Col. 0330B] *(The same author.)* He also offered a second ram at the consecration of the priests, and Aaron and his sons laid their hands upon its head. When Moses had slaughtered it, he took some of its blood and touched the tip of Aaron’s right ear, the thumb of his right hand, and likewise the great toe of his right foot. He also offered Aaron’s sons; and when he had touched the tip of each one’s right ear and the thumbs of his right hand and right foot with the blood of the slaughtered ram, he poured the remainder around the altar. But he separated the fat, the entire tail, all the fat covering the entrails, the lobe of the liver, the two kidneys with their fat, and the right shoulder. Then, taking from the basket of unleavened bread that was before the Lord an unleavened loaf, a cake mixed with oil, [Col. 0330C] and a flat cake, he placed them upon the fat and the right shoulder, and handed everything together to Aaron and his sons. After they had waved these before the Lord, he again took them from their hands and burned them upon the altar of burnt offering, since it was an offering of consecration, a sacrifice of sweet fragrance to the Lord. He also took the breastpiece and lifted it before the Lord; from the ram of consecration he set it apart for himself, as the Lord had commanded him.

*(From the same author.)* This ordinance plainly explains the tradition of the mysteries performed among us and signifies the mystical Passover that Christ ate with his disciples. This is taught by what is commanded to be performed in the several parts of the sacrifice.

Why, however, is the second ram here now called a ram? Because the Lord, having first prefigured the sheep while dining with the apostles, afterward offered his own sacrifice; and, secondly, he himself slaughtered himself as a sheep, as the following words demonstrate:

“And Aaron and his sons laid their hands upon its head. When Moses had slaughtered it,” and so forth.

It was necessary for Aaron and his sons to lay their hands together upon the ram’s head, because Christ celebrated the common supper of the Passover festival with his disciples. But Moses performs this sacrifice because, more than the others, he bears the figure of Christ. At that time above all Christ celebrated his own sacrifice; hence the account begins there. Consider what follows:

“When Moses had slaughtered it, he took some of the blood and touched the tip of Aaron’s right ear, the thumb of his right hand, and likewise the great toe of his right foot. He also offered Aaron’s sons; and when he had touched the tip of each one’s right ear, and the thumbs of the right hand and right foot, with the blood of the slaughtered ram, he poured the remainder around the altar.”

[Col. 0331A] The effect of this sacrifice is shown by the anointing of the ears, hands, and feet. For it is celebrated on account of our obedience, good action, and way of life; therefore our ears too are anointed, so that, lacking Adam’s obedience, we may attain the obedience of the Only-Begotten. After this, the extremities of the hands and feet are anointed, because not only the hands but also the feet signify action. This is proved by what David says: “My foot stood on the straight way” (Ps. XXV); and again: “He set my feet upon a rock” (Ps. XXXIX).

Since we have some good actions and some evil ones, and the left hand bears the figure of evil, the right is rightly anointed. For the things that are anointed are strengthened, while those that are not anointed are destroyed and dispersed. The angel who destroyed Egypt plainly demonstrates this: wherever the anointing of the slaughtered victim was found, he did not strike.

Yet first the priest was anointed with the blood, and afterward his sons according to the Law, because the Lord himself also first received the intelligible blood at the mystical supper, and then gave the cup to the apostles. But observe that here the legislator, after the anointing of Aaron and his sons, added the blood: “He poured the remainder around the altar.” We shall find that Christ did this also. For, drinking himself and giving the apostles to drink, he then poured the intelligible blood upon the altar—namely, his own [Col. 0331C] body.

The body of Christ is the Church and all his people. We find Mark expressly saying: “And taking it, giving thanks, he gave it to them, and they all drank from it. And he said to them, ‘This is my blood of the New Testament, which is poured out for many’” (Mark XIV).

The following corresponds to this: “But he separated the fat and the tail, all the fat covering the entrails, the lobe of the liver, and the two kidneys with their fat, and the right shoulder.” For “tail” the Septuagint gives “loin”; for “entrails,” “stomach”; and for “lobe of the liver,” “liver-lobe.” What these signify in the saving sacrifice, or the sacrifice of peace offerings, has been examined individually. He does not mention them now, in the ram of completion, without reason, but because Christ’s mystical Passover and its reception bring salvation to human beings; and the power of our mystery prepares what follows to build doctrine upon them.

“Taking from the basket of unleavened bread that was before the Lord an unleavened loaf, a cake mixed with oil, and a flat cake.” For “basket of unleavened bread,” the Septuagint gives “basket of completion.” By the “basket of completion” we understand the tongue of the Lord, for he alone introduced a distinctive and perfect teaching. Therefore he said, “I have not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it” (Matt. V), since he himself fulfills what was lacking in the Law.

He fittingly called it a basket because of the interweaving of his sayings, and because he spoke many things in parables, so that the Jews did not understand everything, although it was a dish, just as it was also the table of the whole teaching. Since the mystery was rational, and the things brought into being subsist through reason, he rightly brings forth mystical bread from the basket of completion—that is, from his tongue.

How does he bring it forth? As unleavened bread and a cake mixed with oil—that is, the apostolic teaching together with the Law and the Prophets. For the Law, the prophets, and the apostles make mention of him. The Law says: “This is the bread that the Lord has given you to eat” (Exod. XVI); the prophets say: “Bread shall be given to him, and his waters shall be sure; they shall see the king in his beauty” (Isa. XXXIII). The apostles explain Christ’s mystery more abundantly; hence there is neither a flat cake nor a cake mixed with oil.

[Col. 0332B] The breads are called teachings because they nourish more greatly. Those whom, according to the Septuagint, he called “breads” made with oil, the legislator, in another passage according to the same Septuagint—where he interprets the “cake” in the Feast of Booths as the “basket of completion” received at the priest’s anointing—called a “cake,” signifying by the cake the utterance of the Law.

No one doubts that cakes are inferior to loaves as nourishment. Therefore the sayings of the apostles are placed above the sayings of the prophets and the Law, because they commanded a greater grace, so that Paul said: “God appointed in the Church first apostles, then prophets” (Eph. IV). Then, after the evangelical tradition, they introduce Christ’s mysteries. They introduce them by using testimonies from the Law and the Prophets; for this reason cakes and flat cakes are set beneath and joined to them. But let us consider what he adds to these.

“He placed them upon the fat and the right shoulder, handing everything together to Aaron and his sons.” The Law bears witness that every desire and every good action must be offered to the mystery, if you wish to receive it according to God’s intention and the meaning of the Law. It also says, following the order already mentioned: “Handing everything together to Aaron and his sons.” For Christ first began his mysteries, and then handed them over to us, who through the bath of regeneration have become his sons.

“And they lifted them before the Lord.” The very mystery that he handed over to us he lifted with his flesh into the heavens. By saying, “He lifted them before the Lord,” he explained the manner in which he offered them to those who were to come afterward.

[Col. 0332D] “Again, taking them from their hands, he burned them upon the altar of burnt offering, since it was an offering of consecration, a sacrifice of sweet fragrance to the Lord.” He calls the altar of burnt offering the body of Christ. It is also a sweetest fragrance: for it is plainly said of Christ in the Song of Songs, “Your name is poured-out perfume; therefore the maidens loved you” (Song I).

“Of the sacrifice of the Lord,” that is, of the sacrifice and burnt offering, as the Lord commanded. For he himself commanded: “Whenever you drink this, proclaim the death of the Lord in yourselves” (1 Cor. XI).

“He took also the breastpiece and lifted it before the Lord; from the ram of consecration,” or, according to the Septuagint, “of completion,” “he set it apart for himself, as the Lord had commanded him.” As in the sacrifice of peace offerings, or the saving sacrifice, the breastpiece is offered, so here also the breastpiece of the ram of consecration or completion is set apart for Moses in the intelligible sense—that is, for Christ. For the breastpiece signifies faith and confidence, as we said earlier.

But since the sacrifice belongs to him, must not the faith that is in it also be assigned to him?

“And taking the anointing oil and the blood that was on the altar, he sprinkled it upon Aaron and his garments, and upon his sons and their garments. When he had sanctified them in their vestments…”

That the blood of the Only-Begotten and the anointing of the Spirit are one in operation and power, and that the legislator correctly anointed Aaron with the oil of anointing and the blood of the altar—that is, of the Lord’s body—hear John saying: “There are three that bear witness, and the three are one: the Spirit, the water, and the blood” (1 John V). For they have one effect of sanctification.

The Law rightly distinguished Aaron’s garment from the robes of Aaron’s sons. For although we, who have been adopted by him, possess a garment modeled on the Lord’s, nevertheless we have learned from what precedes how greatly the garment of the high priest differs.

If, then, we have understood that the intelligible Aaron is sanctified by the sprinkling of blood and oil, let us not be surprised at what is said. For Christ himself offered, for our sanctification, the sprinkling of his own blood—that is, his passion for us. Therefore he said that Aaron’s sons and their tunics or robes were sanctified together with Aaron, because whatever takes place in us necessarily leads back to him as the head—indeed, the head of the whole body.

For confirmation of what has been said, let us take the Lord’s words. When he was about to be crucified for us, he spoke the following in the form of a prayer, to instruct the apostles in obedience: “As the Father sent me into the world, so I sent them into the world; and for them I sanctify myself, so that they too may be sanctified in truth.” Thus he plainly called the sacrifice that he offered for us a sanctification, from which sanctification also benefits us.

## CHAPTER XI  
### Concerning Aaron and his sons, that they must not leave the tabernacle before the seventh day of their anointing

*(CHAP. VIII.)* “When he had sanctified them in their vestments, he commanded them, saying: ‘Boil the meat before the entrance of the tabernacle, and eat it there. Eat also the breads of consecration that have been placed in the basket, as the Lord commanded me, saying: Aaron and his sons shall eat them. Whatever remains of the meat and the breads, the fire shall consume. You shall not leave the entrance of the tabernacle for seven days, until the day on which the period of your consecration is completed. For your consecration shall be completed in seven days. As has now been done, so that the rite of the sacrifice might be fulfilled, you shall remain in the tabernacle day and night, observing the Lord’s watches, lest you die. For thus I have been commanded.’ And Aaron and his sons did everything that the Lord had commanded through Moses.”

*(From Augustine.)* What does Moses mean when he says to Aaron and his sons, as they are being sanctified for entering upon the priesthood, “You shall sit at the entrance of the tabernacle of testimony for seven days, day and night, lest you die”? Is it credible that they were commanded to sit in one bodily position in one place for seven days and nights, without moving at all?

Yet neither are we forced to understand this as though something allegorical were signified that did not happen. Rather, we must recognize the scriptural manner of speaking, in which “sitting” means dwelling and remaining. For when it is said of Shimei that he “sat in Jerusalem for three years” (1 Kings II), we must not suppose that he remained seated in a chair throughout that period without rising. Hence places where people dwell are also called “seats,” since the name has acquired the meaning of habitation.

*(From Hesychius.)* The legislator has now provided for and distinguished the principal mysteries. Through what he has contemplated here in figure, he has handed down that these things are to be performed within the Church, and in no way made public to the eyes and ears of the profane, nor made available for profanation by anyone who wishes.

Therefore, since the tabernacle of testimony signifies heaven for God, while the court of this tabernacle signifies the Church, because it has been placed before the entrance to heaven—and since Jerusalem itself bears the image of the heavenly Jerusalem, as we said earlier—he commanded that the flesh of the sacrifice be boiled within it. For he says: “He commanded them, saying: ‘Boil it before the entrance of the tabernacle, and eat it there.’”

How, then, should we not marvel at the wisdom of the Spirit in these things? He left no uncertainty for this kind of understanding, commanding the flesh to be eaten together with the bread, so that we might understand that he was speaking of the mystery that is both bread and flesh, like the body of Christ, the living bread that came down from heaven. This was so that the mystical supper should plainly be celebrated there.

Aaron and his sons rightly eat it. Unless Christ himself comes at the request of the priests, sanctifies the supper, and initiates what is being performed, it cannot in any way become the Lord’s sacrifice.

But he commanded whatever remained of the flesh and bread to be burned in the fire. We now see this also taking place visibly in the Church: whatever happens to remain unconsumed is handed over to the fire—and not merely those portions that have been kept for one day, two days, or many days. For, as is evident, the legislator did not command that; he orders whatever remains to be burned. He did not mention a number of days, so that whatever remains unconsumed for any reason—whether time is responsible or something else—may be subjected to fire and consumption.

Therefore, from what is visibly done, those who attend to it receive the signification of an intelligible reality. When we fail in eating the sacrifice and cannot consume it wholly, perhaps because the mind has grown weary or weakened, we must consider whether what is seen ought to be understood as the Lord’s body—a body upon which not even angels can gaze with their eyes—and whether it must not be left behind. It must also be handed over to the fire of the spirit, so that the spirit may consume what is invisible to us because of our weakness.

[Col. 0335A] How does it consume it? When we consider that what is impossible for us is possible for the power of the Spirit. Hence the legislator seems to argue next. For he says: “You shall not leave the entrance of the tabernacle for seven days.” Why seven? Because the fiftieth day is completed by multiplying the number seven by itself and adding one to it. Hence what follows shows that among Moses’ people it is called the Feast of Weeks.

Luke also delivered things similar to these. He says of the Lord and the disciples: “To whom he also presented himself alive after his passion by many proofs, appearing to them for forty days and speaking of the kingdom of God; and while eating with them, he commanded them not to depart from Jerusalem, but to await the promise of the Father” (Acts I).

Do you see how he was consecrating or perfecting them? He appeared to them, taught them about the kingdom of God, and ate with them. By telling them not to depart from Jerusalem, he did not command them to go forward or leave the door of the tabernacle—that is, he did not permit them to preach until they had received, on the fiftieth day, the promised gift of the Spirit.

When the days were completed, Peter immediately began his preaching, and about three thousand souls were added (Acts II). They too observed this command in every respect, and its meaning is especially fulfilled in what follows: “Observing the Lord’s watches, lest you die; for thus the Lord commanded me. And Aaron and his sons did everything that the Lord spoke through Moses.”

If it is asked why he joins Aaron to his sons, the reason will be found to be wholly necessary and appropriate to the matter under consideration. For they were not to leave the door of the tabernacle of testimony—that is, in the meantime they were not to undertake the evangelical preaching described above.
