Thus Christ appeared with the apostles, and Christ himself did not leave his own door. For he was the one who was to be preached and the one who spoke in the apostles. Therefore Aaron himself was said to be consecrated or perfected together with his sons.

But the legislator did not at all add who it was who consecrated or perfected them. For he says: “For in seven days the consecration is completed,” or, according to the Septuagint, “he completed your hands,” as he also did. It is evident that the one who consecrated or perfected the sons was the same one who was said to be perfected or consecrated in them, as in his own members.

## CHAPTER XII  
### Concerning the completion of the consecration and the sacrifices for himself and the people

*(CHAP. IX.)* “When the eighth day had come, Moses called Aaron and his sons and the elders of Israel. And he said to Aaron: ‘Take a calf for sin and a ram for a burnt offering, both without blemish, and offer them before the Lord. And you shall speak to the children of Israel: “Take a goat for sin, and a calf and a year-old lamb without blemish as a burnt offering, and an ox and a ram as peace offerings. Sacrifice them before the Lord, offering fine flour mixed with oil; for today the Lord will appear to you.”’”

*(From Hesychius.)* He calls the eighth day Pentecost, because Pentecost falls on the day on which the Savior rose, which is believed to be an eighth day because it bears the figure of the first fruits of the future and also of the completion of the present age, which revolves through seven days.

For it was necessary that on the same day on which Christ rose, the Spirit should also come. Therefore he says that Aaron, his sons, and the elders of Israel were called: in a certain manner building the Church through the calling of those who have been named.

For then the Church’s spectacle was first convened, in which the intelligible Aaron—that is, Christ—is believed to be priest. His sons are those whose manner of life is exalted and who are therefore ministers and fellow-workers of the priesthood. The elders of Israel are the order of presbyters. For from these the body of the Church is composed.

Aaron, then, took for himself a calf for sin and a ram for a burnt offering, both without blemish, and offered them before [Col. 0336B] the Lord. For then Christ’s sacrifice began to become known, when the Spirit came and gathered Parthians, Medes, Elamites, and the first fruits of all the nations into the upper room of the apostles (Acts II).

The order of the elders of Israel, which we have said is that of the presbyters, also took these offerings, since it itself bears the lot and figure of teachers and is useful for teaching us and bringing the life of those assembled in the Church to perfection. What were the things it took? A goat for sin, that is, a sacrifice for repentance; and a calf and a year-old lamb, without blemish, as a burnt offering—that is, a perfect and completed life or manner of conduct, signified by victims, namely by burnt offerings; and an ox and a ram as peace offerings.

For the saving or peace offering there is also a moderate manner of life, which nevertheless can save those who offer it, as we said above. He commanded everything to be done before the Lord. Every work of virtue must be performed as though God were watching, and it must not be corrupted or spoiled by our mixing our own will with it.

The sacrifice of fine flour mixed with oil signifies theology together with almsgiving. The sacrifices mentioned above made this known to us when they were carefully examined earlier.

What does he add here? “For today the Lord will appear to you.” This is the conclusion and confirmation, because everything previously mentioned was said concerning Pentecost. For on it the Lord appeared in them—namely, the Spirit of whom Paul said: “The Lord is the Spirit.”

How he appeared in them Luke says: “There appeared to them divided tongues as of fire, and they rested upon each one of them” (Acts II).

They therefore brought everything that Moses had commanded to the entrance of the tabernacle, while the whole multitude stood there. Here he plainly explained the Church: “at the entrance of the tabernacle,” or, according to the Septuagint, “before the tabernacle of testimony,” namely, heaven. For if the Church is the assembly of the firstborn angels who are enrolled in heaven, it is “before the tabernacle of testimony,” that is, before the face of heaven.

Aquila likewise translated it “before the face.” For every contrite soul, every sinner, everyone who needs mercy, and everyone who turns away from error is gathered into this Church. He commanded that not only those from the streets and alleys be called, but also those from the roads and hedges, so that, entering the royal banquet, they might fill it (Matt. XXII).

Moses says: “This is the word that the Lord commanded; do it, and his glory will appear to you.” He plainly shows that the glory of the Lord is the Spirit, as Paul wrote to the Corinthians: “We all, with unveiled face beholding the glory of the Lord, are transformed into the same image, from glory to glory, as by the Lord’s Spirit” (1 Cor. III).

Therefore, so that the glory of the Lord might be seen—that is, so that the coming of the Spirit might be celebrated—he says: “This is the word that the Lord commanded.” It is the mystical word concerning which the Lord had commanded: “Do this in remembrance of me.”

The legislator calls it a “word” according to customary usage, because the administration of this mystery subsists more in a word, especially since the Lord’s word transfers the things that appear into something greater and intelligible.

Thus, when the manna presented the image of the bread of life that came down from heaven, he said: “This is the bread that the Lord has given you to eat; this is the word that the Lord established” (Exod. XVI).

What, then, does the legislator signify through these statements, except that, when they were performing the holy mystery and celebrating the Lord’s supper, the Spirit came? Even if we do not have the matter explained more fully—for divine Scripture omitted much for the sake of brevity—it is permitted to gather it from other passages.

It was the day called the Lord’s Day, on which the apostles absolutely had to perform sacred and mystical acts. We too, following their tradition, set apart the Lord’s Day for divine assemblies.

We also find that Christ was similarly made manifest after his resurrection from the dead through the mystical supper and the breaking of bread. Luke plainly relates this, and the evangelist John also records it.

He said to Aaron: “Approach the altar and sacrifice for your sin; offer the burnt offering and make atonement for yourself and for the people. When you have slaughtered the people’s victim, pray for them, as the Lord commanded.”

Where our translation more plainly has “for yourself and for the people,” the Septuagint gives “for yourself and for your house.” Who the house of the intelligible priest is, learn from Paul. For he says: “But Christ was faithful over his house as a son; and we are his house, if we hold firmly to the end our confidence and the glory of hope” (Heb. III).

Therefore those who have progressed and are more perfect are rightly called his house. He makes supplication for them and for the whole people, since he has become the propitiation for us, and also for himself.

Why for himself, when he does not need propitiation but himself provides propitiation? It is because, taking our sin upon himself, he also makes supplication for himself. This clearly belongs both to the human being and to God: as the human being who receives propitiation, and as God who provides it for himself. For one human being cannot provide propitiation for himself.

*(From Augustine.)* It should certainly be noted that, when sacrifices are offered for the people, the sacrifices commanded to be offered are both a sacrifice for sin and a burnt offering, as well as a saving sacrifice. For the priest, however, there was an offering for sin, a burnt offering, and an offering of completion, but not a saving sacrifice.

The offering of completion was made when the priests were sanctified so that they might exercise the priesthood; Moses offered this for Aaron and his sons. Later, Aaron himself, already sanctified and exercising the priesthood, was commanded to offer for himself a calf for sin and a ram as a burnt offering. He was not commanded to offer an offering of completion for himself, because that offering had then been made so that he might be completed through sanctification and be able to exercise the priesthood that he was already exercising.

Immediately Aaron approached the altar and slaughtered the calf for his own sin. His sons brought him its blood; dipping his finger into it, he touched the horns of the altar and poured the remainder at its base. He burned upon the altar the fat, the kidneys, and the lobe of the liver, which belong to the sin offering, as the Lord had commanded Moses. But he burned its flesh and hide with fire outside the camp.

He slaughtered the victim of the burnt offering also, and his sons brought him its blood, which he poured around the altar. They also presented the victim, cut into pieces, with its head and its individual limbs. He burned all these upon the altar, after first washing the entrails and feet with water (Lev. IX).

*(From Hesychius.)* We have said above why these sacrifices are also performed here. It is therefore unnecessary to speak again, one by one, of the meaning of the things performed in this sacrifice, since we examined them earlier in order and showed without omission what they prefigure.

And since in the Lord’s sacrifice, although it is one, not only is forgiveness of sins granted to us, but also a perfect and completed life in philosophy is produced, it is necessary that it be understood both in the calf sacrificed for sin and in this ram sacrificed as a burnt offering. Hence we see both offered in the person of the priest. Let us now proceed to what follows.

“Offering for the sin of the people, he slaughtered the goat. Having made atonement for the altar, he performed the burnt offering, adding to the sacrifice the offerings of the libation that were to be offered together with it. Burning them upon the altar without the ceremonies of the morning burnt offering, he also slaughtered the ox and the ram as the people’s peace-offering victims. His sons brought him their blood, which he poured around the altar. But the fat of the ox, the ram’s tail, the kidneys with their fat, and the lobe of the liver they placed upon the breasts. When the fat had been burned upon the altar, Aaron separated their breasts and right shoulders, lifting them before the Lord, as Moses had commanded him” (ibid.).

*(From Hesychius.)* What figure the things that have been said bear, and how the goat for sin signifies the sacrifice of repentance, the burnt offerings a crucified manner of life, the fine flour theology, and the saving or peace-offering sacrifice a life capable of saving us, even those who possess only moderate understanding—this has been shown by the preceding examination of the sacrifices before the priest’s anointing. Therefore whoever does not know the explanation of this ordinance should seek it there in detail; he will also learn these things individually.

But we must now add this: the legislator considered that the descent of the Holy Spirit at Pentecost, when the apostles had gathered together and were performing everything according to the law of the Church, was signified by the fact that the priest’s sacrifices were rightly commanded to come first, and afterward those of the people.

For the Church’s teaching must begin with the sacrifice of the Only-Begotten, so that teachers may introduce what the Lord’s passion profited or conferred upon us. Then the word of repentance must follow, which all human beings certainly need. Hence the Lord preaches one teaching—repentance—and the various ways of life, brought to greater perfection, must be added afterward, with theology interwoven among them.

He also adds the things by which, when we correct ourselves or are anointed, we may be saved, even if we do not live in an exalted manner. [Col. 0339B] For the Church must gather people through these things and receive the manifestation of God’s glory.

Without doubt, the Lord’s disciples were occupied especially with these matters during the days of Pentecost. That is why they had then gathered together, as Luke makes clear: “And when the days of Pentecost were fulfilled, they were all together in one accord” (Acts II).

What had they gathered to do except, in every respect, the things that have been described? Even if they were not preaching openly, and for that reason were sitting inside in the upper rooms, not yet spreading the word or speaking publicly—because they had not been commanded to leave the door of the tabernacle of testimony until they should be clothed with the power of the Spirit from on high—it is nevertheless clear that they were performing these things within themselves and did not cease meditating on whatever befits the Church.

For they had Christ himself within them, who is the head of the Church. Hence, after Peter had preached concerning Matthias for the apostleship and had proposed an exposition and testimonies from divine Scripture, they chose him by lot.

Whether preaching means exhorting the people, or interpreting the prophets and joining the clergy, it belonged to the Church’s administration and order. Therefore it is clear that, just as they had gathered in the Church during those days—and the legislator considered that this was signified in every respect—so he consequently added what follows:

“And extending his hand toward the people, he blessed them; and when he had completed the sacrifices for sin, the burnt offerings, and the peace offerings, he descended” (Lev. IX).

(From Augustine.) But where did he do these things except upon the altar—that is, standing at the altar and ministering there? From there, then, he descended, where he had been standing. This testimony seems plainly to assist in resolving the question where we had asked, in Exodus, how one could minister at an altar that was three cubits high. For we were forbidden to understand a stairway there, because God had prohibited it, lest the nakedness of the male organs of the ministering priest be exposed above the altar; and this would certainly happen if a part of the altar were a stairway—that is, if it were constructed as an attached feature. Indeed, he prohibited it precisely where he was speaking of an altar built of masonry. For the altar with its stairway would be one thing, the stairway being part of it, and therefore it was forbidden.

Here, however, where the altar was so high that a priest could not minister properly unless he stood upon something, we must understand that whatever it was which was put in place for the moment of the ministry and then removed was not part of the altar, and therefore did not violate the command prohibiting it from having a stairway. Scripture does not say what this object was, whatever its nature, and for that reason the question arose. But now, when Scripture says that the priest descended after he had performed the sacrifices—that is, after he had placed the victims upon the altar—it clearly shows that he had been standing somewhere from which he could descend; and because he had stood there, he was able to minister at the three-cubit altar.

(From Hesychius.) Observe that he plainly wishes to explain to us the whole figure of the Church. For after saying, “He descended after he had made the offering for sin, the burnt offerings, and the peace offerings,” he shows that he understood the completion of the sacrifices as their exposition, and for that reason said, “he descended”: by the descent signifying the teacher’s seat. From that seat, after the exposition, the priests descend—those to whom Aaron, the intelligible figure, has been entrusted—and through prayer they raise their hands to heaven.

Paul also understood the raising of the hands as prayer. He says: “I desire men to pray in every place, lifting up holy hands” (1 Tim. II). Thus, by stretching out or lifting up his hands, he blessed them, because through the lifting of their hands—that is, through prayer—the priests bless the people.

But from where they bestow the blessing is shown by what follows: “Moses and Aaron entered the tabernacle of the testimony, and afterward came out and blessed the people.” Why, then, do they first enter the tabernacle of the testimony and afterward bestow the blessing, unless so that we may understand that the priests bring forth the blessing from the intelligible tabernacle, namely, from heaven, saying, as Paul also says: “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ” (Eph. I).

The Lord himself also handed this down to us: when blessing the five loaves and again the seven, he looked toward heaven. But why do Moses as well as Aaron bless the synagogue, or the people, unless so that we may learn that priests do not bestow the blessing by their own power, but because they bear the figure of Christ and are able, on account of him who is in them, to provide the fullness of blessing? Hence Moses too, to whom the image of the Lord had been entrusted, is rightly understood as blessing.

The Law also signifies, through the things that have been said, that not only the one who has received the priesthood, but every righteous person who has Christ within himself and bears the figure of his Lord, is capable—through a good manner of life, as Moses was—of bestowing a blessing.

## CHAPTER XIII. The glory of the Lord appears to the multitude, and fire proceeding from the Lord consumes the burnt offering

(The same passage.) “The glory of the Lord appeared to all the multitude, and behold, fire proceeding from the Lord devoured the burnt offering and the fat that was upon the altar.” (From Augustine.) It may be asked whether this happened at the command and will of the Lord, or whether fire came out from the place where the ark of the testimony was. For the Lord is not in one place in such a way that he is not elsewhere. When the crowds saw this, they praised the Lord, falling upon their faces.

(From Hesychius.) Do you suppose that the present words of the Law require any interpretation? For they correspond exactly to what has been written in the apostolic Acts concerning the coming of the Spirit.

“For,” he says, “the glory of the Lord appeared to all the multitude.” How, someone may ask? Certainly in such a form as Ezekiel described when he saw it above the cherubim, or as Micaiah or Isaiah saw it—one of whom saw the seraphim surrounding it, while another saw the heavenly host. But not at all. There was one glory, spiritual and intelligible, which appeared to everyone and everywhere, though, as it was incomprehensible, it presented different visions to those who saw it.

Nevertheless, the present manifestation was similar to that one, because intelligible fire proceeded from the Lord on the day of Pentecost. For this reason he says: “The glory of the Lord appeared, and fire proceeded from the Lord.” Therefore it appeared in the form of fire, just as Luke also explains: “And there came from heaven a sound as of a mighty rushing spirit, and it filled the whole house where they were sitting, and there appeared to them divided tongues as of fire” (Acts II).

The Lawgiver also makes mention of the whole people. Luke explains this in the following manner: “There were dwelling in Jerusalem Jews, devout men from every nation under heaven. And when this sound occurred, the multitude came together and was bewildered.” That it not only came together but was also terrified, he himself demonstrates by saying: “For they were astonished and amazed.” They also fell upon their faces; and if they did not undergo this physically, they nevertheless endured it intelligibly. For they did not understand what had happened.

“Another said to another: ‘These men are full of new wine.’” This was proper to those who were casting the face of their mind prostrate upon the earth. What did the fire that proceeded forth do? It devoured everything that had been placed upon the altar as burnt offerings: the fats from the peace offerings and the offerings for sin that had been laid upon the altar.

The discourse therefore teaches us that it is necessary to place the aforementioned sacrifices and their interpretations upon the intelligible altar of Christ’s body, so that our imitation may hasten toward it; and then they become nourishment for the intelligible fire—that is, for the Spirit—of whom it is said: “The Lord our God is a consuming fire” (Deut. IV). Hence Symmachus now rendered “devour” as “consume.”

## CHAPTER XIV. Concerning Nadab and Abihu, who offered strange fire and were killed by the Lord

(The same passage.) “Nadab and Abihu, the sons of Aaron, took their censers, put fire and incense upon them, and offered before the Lord strange fire, which had not been commanded them.”

(From Augustine.) After the sons of Aaron had died, burned by fire that had gone out from the Lord—for they had dared, after introducing strange fire into their fire pans, to offer incense to the Lord—Moses said: “This is what the Lord said: ‘I shall be sanctified in those who approach me, and I shall be glorified in the presence of all the congregation.’”

He wished those who served in the tabernacle in the priesthood to be understood as approaching the Lord. But was the Lord sanctified in them also by taking vengeance, as happened, so that from this it might be known how little he spares others, if he does not spare them? In this sense it was said: “If the righteous person will scarcely be saved, where will the sinner and the ungodly appear?” (1 Pet. IV).

Or rather, should it be understood according to the statement: “To whom more is given, from him more is required” (Luke XV)? And also: “The servant who did not know the will of his master and did things deserving punishment shall be beaten with few blows; but the servant who knew the will of his master and did things deserving punishment shall be beaten with many blows” (Luke XII).

(From Hesychius.) Here he explained that those who teach what is alien, who blaspheme against the Spirit of God because they interpret otherwise the Scripture inspired by him, concerning which Paul says, “All Scripture is inspired by God and useful” (2 Tim. III), must necessarily be punished by the intelligible fire. The sons of Aaron are said to have the appearance of teachers and to pretend to speak spiritual things; hence their tongues are also called fire.

For we have heard that the Spirit came in the form of fiery tongues. But they place upon the censers—or upon the fires of their tongues—the teachings of the Law and the Prophets, concerning which the Church said to Christ in the Song of Songs: “The fragrance of your ointments is above all spices” (Song IV). Yet they offer strange fire. For they do not interpret according to the intention or power of the Spirit.

From these a fire goes forth from the Lord—not absolutely of the same kind as before. Through the former fire the Lord kindled the sacrifices, and it was called the glory of the Lord. This, however, is a penal fire. The Church possesses both: the former for the illumination of the righteous and the perfection of those who offer, the latter for the punishment of the impious. This fire the priests bring upon those who blaspheme, through the ministry of the Spirit who rests in them, kindling it in them.

For this reason Paul also punishes Hymenaeus and Alexander as teachers of other things. They die before the Lord, who sees them and condemns them in this death, lest by their imitation they give others a cause of death. In this the Lawgiver also expresses great astonishment: those who ought to have enjoyed life—that is, life before the Lord—suffer death because they interpret the divine Scriptures wrongly. They suffer precisely in that from which they ought to have earned a blessing, subjecting themselves instead to a curse.

Observe, however, what he adds: “And Moses said to Aaron: ‘This is what the Lord has spoken: I shall be sanctified in those who approach me, and in the presence of all the people I shall be glorified.’” When Aaron heard this, he was silent—or, as the Septuagint translates it, “Aaron was pierced with grief.”

Where do we find God saying this at all, when he said to Moses: “Go down and testify to the people, lest perhaps they approach God and a multitude of them fall; and let the priests who approach the Lord God be sanctified, lest perhaps the Lord withdraw from them”? Although these words differ from those that have been cited, they nevertheless preserve the same intention without alteration.

For he commanded the people not to approach God and to know—not because he begrudged them the vision, but because he spared those who were imperfect and less capable of such great contemplation. But he commands the priests who approach to be sanctified, so that they may become worthy to see and contemplate God, because no one can seek true knowledge from God without sanctification.

For this reason Paul says: “Pursue peace with everyone, and holiness, without which no one will see God.” By his sight he means his knowledge—that is, his contemplation. Hence, when commanding the priests to be sanctified, see how he threatens in what follows: “Lest perhaps the Lord withdraw from them”—that is, lest that which belongs to God, namely knowledge, flee from them. For the loss of knowledge becomes their destruction.

But now let us take up the words that were spoken through Moses as if from the person of God: “I shall be sanctified in those who approach me.” He calls his sanctification the cleansing of profane or evil persons, which our body possesses. The cleansing of the body is the casting away of filth.

As a good and compassionate God, he works this in those who approach him, according to the abundance of knowledge or according to some divine ministry, so that through them he may inspire fear and be glorified in the presence of the entire people—that is, praised and manifested. For the word “glorification” expresses both things, and David says what praise and manifestation of God arise from this: “For the Lord is righteous; he loved righteousness. His countenance has seen equity” (Ps. X).

Here Aaron was silent—or, according to the Septuagint, “Aaron was pierced with grief.” The Church is meant, since the Church is the intelligible body of Aaron. Hence Christ himself said: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts IX). He also said to his disciples concerning those who receive them: “Whoever receives you receives me.”

Moses called Mishael and Elzaphan, the sons of Uzziel, the uncle of Aaron, and said to them: “Go, take your brothers from before the sanctuary and carry them outside the camp.” They immediately went and carried them away as they lay, dressed in their linen tunics, and cast them outside, as had been commanded.

By those who carried them away, understand those who were lifted up or cast out. Who were the ones who carried them? Mishael and Elzaphan—or Misaddai and Helisaphan. One of these names, Misaddai, is interpreted as “touching God,” while Helisaphan is interpreted as “the watchtower of my God.”

Whoever, then, knows how to touch God and, moreover, to contemplate him—who touches Christ’s flesh and contemplates his divinity through the eyes of the mind, as Thomas touched his flesh with his hand and contemplated his divinity by faith, saying, “My Lord and my God” (John XX)—can remove the fire of alien teaching and cast it out, together with its tunics, from the presence of the saints.

The priests are the persons of the saints. The priests’ tunics are their conduct and life, in which they are clothed in the priestly character. Therefore, when those who have received a share in the priesthood are expelled from the priestly portion, they are driven out not only from the priests but also from the people; hence he added, “outside the tabernacle.”

For the people of the Church are the tabernacle of God. The sons of Aaron’s uncle, or of Aaron’s brother, are reasonably understood to be those who are able to do these things. For if David is the intelligible father of Aaron, and through him the whole body of the prophets is understood, prophecy makes him manifest and, so to speak, gives birth to him for those who are ignorant. But the Gospel is, so to speak, prophecy’s full brother. For everything that happened in the Gospels was foretold by the prophets.

The sons of Aaron’s brother are therefore rightly and most appropriately understood as those who have learned the evangelical manner of life. They are appointed to rebuke and repel those who teach other things, since they possess perfect knowledge. John spoke of this when he said: “Everyone who goes ahead and does not remain in the teaching of Christ does not have God; whoever remains in the teaching has both the Son and the Father. If anyone comes to you and does not bring this teaching, do not receive him into your house, and do not say to him, ‘Greetings’” (2 John V).

It is therefore the proper task of those who have been instructed in evangelical teaching to drive out and cast away from the presence of the saints and the tabernacle those who preach adulterated and alien doctrines.

## CHAPTER XV. Moses forbids Aaron and his sons to uncover their heads and tear their garments on account of the death of those who were killed

(The same passage.) “Moses spoke to Aaron, and to Eleazar and Ithamar, his sons: ‘Do not uncover your heads, and do not tear your garments, lest perhaps you die and indignation arise against the whole assembly. Let your brothers and the whole house of the children of Israel mourn the burning which the Lord has kindled. But you shall not go out from the doors of the tabernacle, lest you perish, for the oil of holy anointing is upon you.’ And they did everything according to the command of Moses.”

(From Augustine.) What does Moses mean when, forbidding Aaron and his remaining sons to mourn the death of those two men, he says: “You shall not uncover the tiara on your head”? Here he clearly shows that the tiaras were coverings for the head, except that mourners did what was contrary to the customary ornament.

Just as, according to our custom, in which the head is usually uncovered, it is covered in mourning, so, because those men adorned themselves with a covering for the head, it had to be uncovered by mourners. He forbids this so that they would not mourn those whose punishment sanctified the Lord—that is, commended reverence for him.

This was not because they were not to be mourned, for he permits others to mourn them, but because those men were not then to mourn, while the days of their sanctification were being observed. The seven days during which he commanded them not to depart from the tabernacle had not yet been completed.

Nevertheless, it might be thought that this was said because they had been sanctified by that oil, so that they should never mourn anyone. For he says: “But your brothers and the whole house of Israel shall mourn the burning with which they were burned by the Lord, and you shall not go out from the door of the tabernacle of the testimony, lest you die; for the oil of anointing, which is from the Lord, is upon you.”

(From Hesychius.) We are not unaware that the tiara signifies the priesthood. Since “the head of every man is Christ God, and the head of Christ is God,” the symbolism of the tiara necessarily signifies, in some manner, both the humanity and the divinity of the Only-Begotten. We demonstrated this earlier also through the composition of the tiara.

He therefore commanded what priests and teachers ought to preserve: that they neither deny nor contradict the divinity or the humanity of Christ, because he is God from God and the Word from the Father. This is what it means not to remove the tiara from the head—not to uncover the intelligible tiara. Nor should they reject or blaspheme the dispensation.

Whoever blasphemes Christ’s dispensation tears the priestly robe, because all human beings who have believed in Christ, and especially priests, are those who have put on Christ: “For all of us who were baptized into Christ have put on Christ” (Gal. III).

When priests do these things, they will neither die nor bring anger upon the congregation. For the vices of those set over others become a stumbling block to their subjects. Much more do the faults of teachers become an occasion of God’s anger for their disciples.

For this reason he wishes the whole house of Israel—that is, the whole Church—to mourn the burning with which they were burned by God, because the loss of one member and any fall whatsoever is damage to the Church, and still more so is the destruction of teachers and priests.

With these matters understood, we must ask how, when by the preceding ordinance he had commanded them to remain in the tabernacle of the testimony for only seven days without going out, after those days had been completed—for these things take place on the eighth day—Moses again commanded them not to go out from the door of the tabernacle.

He is not therefore issuing contradictory commands. Rather, it is clear that here he commanded them to observe another kind of departure from the door of the tabernacle of the testimony, for he added, “lest you die.” He had not written this in the earlier passage. By adding the threat, therefore, he indicated that he had imposed something different.

Because the priests who offered strange fire had perished, he commanded others not to go out through the door of knowledge—that is, through the tradition of Christ—according to what has been said. They were not to transgress the preaching that Christ himself commanded, but to follow the Lord’s command in everything. In this way no one will die.

He gave this command to priests, to whom, as teachers and preachers of the Word, the ministry had been entrusted through the gift of the Spirit. Concerning this the Lawgiver now says: “For the oil of holy anointing is upon you.”

John the Evangelist demonstrates the power of this anointing when he says: “Let the anointing which you received from him remain in you, and you have no need for anyone to teach you; but as his anointing teaches you concerning all things, and is true and is not falsehood” (1 John II).

Moses gave these commands through the Spirit, and the Church keeps them. The Lawgiver therefore appropriately added: “And they did according to the command of Moses.”

## CHAPTER XVI. That Aaron and his sons shall not drink wine when they enter the tabernacle

(The same passage.) “The Lord also said to Aaron: ‘You and your sons shall not drink wine, nor anything that can cause drunkenness, when you enter the tabernacle of the testimony, lest you die. This is a perpetual command throughout your generations, so that you may have knowledge to distinguish between holy and profane, between polluted and clean, and so that you may teach the children of Israel all my ordinances which the Lord spoke to them through Moses.’”

(From Hesychius.) You find this law still being observed in the Churches. For he did not command complete abstinence from wine, but abstinence when we approach the tabernacle of the testimony or ascend to the altar—that is, whenever we undertake any ministry of heavenly teaching.

The altar is a figure of ministry, while the tabernacle of the testimony signifies contact with heavenly realities. Hence Paul also wrote to Timothy: “Use a little wine for the sake of your stomach and your frequent illnesses.” Whoever uses only a little abstains, during the time of ministry—that is, of teaching—from all drunkenness and intoxication.

Likewise, those priests who are devoted to keeping the Law observe this command. For this reason he gives it not only to Aaron but also to his sons, who had attained the higher things.

Paul also wrote something similar to the Ephesians: “Do not become drunk with wine, in which there is debauchery, but be filled with the Spirit” (Eph. V). For drunkenness makes the mind dull and turns its sobriety to the worse, so that what is being done is not understood.

Isaiah testifies to this when he says: “Woe to those who rise early to pursue drunkenness and drink until evening, so that they are inflamed with wine. Lyre and harp, tambourine and flute, and wine are in your banquets, but you do not regard the work of the Lord, nor consider the works of his hands” (Isa. V).

But those who do not see the works of the Lord—how can they distinguish between holy and profane, or between clean and unclean? How can they exhort and enlighten the people from the Scriptures?

Therefore, wishing to show that this command was of a higher order, he says that the Lord himself spoke it. Observe also how he says that the Lord spoke to Moses not “through the tongue” but “through the hand.” Perhaps he wished altogether to display the dignity of the Law: God explained it, Moses wrote it down, and he received it while God commanded what had been ordained.

## CHAPTER XVII. The Lord’s command concerning what Aaron and his sons ought to eat from the sacrifice, and so forth

(The same passage.) “Moses spoke to Aaron and to Eleazar and Ithamar, his remaining sons: ‘Take the sacrifice that remains from the offering of the Lord, and eat it unleavened beside the altar, for it is most holy. You shall eat it in a holy place, because it has been given to you and your sons from the offerings of the Lord, as has been commanded.

“‘You shall also eat the breast that was offered and the shoulder that was set apart in a most clean place, you and your sons and your daughters with you. For they have been allotted to you and your children from the peace offerings of the children of Israel, since the shoulder, the breast, and the fats that are burned upon the altar have been lifted up before the Lord; and they belong to you and your sons as a perpetual ordinance, as the Lord commanded.’”

(From Hesychius.) Since the breast signifies the confidence and faith of those who offer, and the arm signifies the action and correction of the manner of life promised by them, we have sufficiently demonstrated this in the sections where we discussed the sacrifice of the peace offerings, or offerings of salvation, in detail.

But why he assigned these things to Aaron and his sons was explained there by the Lawgiver through their respective distinctions. For when he spoke of the sacrifice that remained from the offering—or from the burnt offerings—of the Lord, he meant what remained of the fine flour. Aquila therefore plainly rendered it: “The gift that remains from the grain.”

This is also explained by what the Lawgiver added: “And eat it unleavened beside the altar.” Everywhere he signifies by this the doctrine of theology, intending the sacrifice of fine flour to be without leaven with regard to external teaching. He likewise shows that theology among us is partial: its fullness is in heaven. Therefore he commanded that what remained—that is, what was left over—should be eaten, to show that the whole exists with him and is preserved.

It must be eaten beside the altar, that is, beside the body of Christ. For all theology is ministered to us from it. But what remained of the fine flour shall belong to Aaron and his sons. The portions from the peace offerings, or offerings of salvation, belong to Aaron and his sons—or, according to the Septuagint, “to his household,” namely, to the whole people.

To study theology does not belong to everyone, but to those who are exalted, who approach the Lord, and who follow Christ. But attaining what pertains to peace or salvation belongs to the entire people.

Meanwhile, when Moses sought the goat that had been offered for sin, he found that it had been burned. He became angry with Eleazar and Ithamar, the remaining sons of Aaron, and said: “Why did you not eat the sin offering in the holy place, since it is most holy and was given to you so that you might bear the iniquity of the multitude and pray for it before the Lord, especially since its blood was not brought inside the sanctuary? You ought to have eaten it in the sanctuary, as was commanded me.”

(From Hesychius.) Since every sin is erased through repentance, and since these men committed the aforementioned sin of another teaching and blasphemy, they were not saved. The Lawgiver explains the cause of the death that came upon them without mercy.

He introduces the goat for sin as an offering of repentance. For, when Moses sought it, he searched carefully, as the Septuagint renders it: “He sought it very diligently.” He became angry with the remaining sons of Aaron because they had not eaten what was for sin in the holy place—that is, because they had not carried out repentance for the sin committed in the Church.

For it was their task to eat what was offered for sin, to pray with the prayer of repentance for the congregation, and to acquire obedience to the command. Why? Because Christ established them in the Churches as his own proper ministers.

But he offered the blood of his own offering, which was offered for our blood, within the sanctuary—that is, in the heavenly dwelling—to the sight of his Father. In the holy place that we call the Church, he commanded this sacrifice to be eaten for the remission and propitiation of sins. Hence Moses said: “As it was commanded me”—that is, “as I commanded and prescribed.” For we have said that Moses also bears the person of Christ.

He investigates without being ignorant. For how could he be ignorant when, in the preceding passage, he added the reason? After saying, “Moses sought the goat for sin with great diligence,” he immediately added: “And it had been burned,” or, “he found it burned.” He showed that, because the sin of another teaching is blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, it had been burned.

For this reason Stephen calls the teachers of the Jews transgressors of the Law and disobedient, stiff-necked and hard-hearted. And when he spoke to those who wrongly interpreted the Law and the Prophets, he said: “You always resist the Holy Spirit” (Acts VI).

Therefore the offering of repentance was necessarily taken away from them by the intelligible fire, namely, the Spirit. For this reason the goat for sin is said to have been burned: although they know that they are sinning willingly, and although they say that they repent, they do not repent purely. Their hearts have been blinded by blasphemy.

For this reason Paul also said: “For if we sin willingly after receiving the knowledge of the truth, there remains no sacrifice for sins” (Heb. X). Just as true repentance can obtain pardon from the most merciful judge, so the simulation of repentance does not appease God but provokes him, because “the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit.”

Concerning this the Apostle mentioned above says: “Do you suppose, O man, that you will escape the judgment of God? Or do you despise the riches of his goodness, patience, and long-suffering, not knowing that God’s kindness leads you to repentance? But according to your hardness and impenitent heart, you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of God’s righteous judgment, who will repay each person according to his works” (Rom. II).

The holy Fathers called this the unforgivable sin and blasphemy against the Holy Spirit: when someone perseveres in errors and crimes until the end of life, and, while he has time, does not wish to turn and implore the mercy of the Lord, despairing more of his own salvation than he trusts in the power of the Redeemer of all. His end will be everlasting destruction.

Aaron answered: “Today the victim for sin was offered as a burnt offering before the Lord. But what you see has happened to me; how could I eat it? Or how could I please the Lord in the ceremonies with a grieving mind?” When Moses heard this, he accepted the explanation.

(From Hesychius.) What period is meant by “today” Paul plainly handed down to us. For after David had said, “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts as in the provocation” (Ps. XCIV), Paul himself interpreted it. He showed that “today” was being used figuratively of the present time, but properly of the time after the Lord’s coming.

See what he added: “Since therefore it remains for some to enter into it, and those to whom it was first announced did not enter because of unbelief, he again establishes a certain day, saying in David, after so long a time, as was said above: ‘Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts.’ For if Jesus had given them rest, he would never afterward speak of another day.”

Thus what has been proclaimed shows that “today” plainly signifies the time after the Savior’s coming, in which the promised rest of the intelligible Sabbath was announced to humanity.

Aaron therefore appears to say this from the person of the Church, since he bears the figure not only of Christ but also of the Church. For because “today” they offered what was for their sin and their burnt offerings—that is, because after the Savior’s coming they were appointed to minister and offer on behalf of repentance—and because they were discovered teaching other things, and such events occurred among them that the Church mourned the death of priests and teachers arising from blasphemy, he could rightly not eat the offering for sin today, nor had repentance obtained prayer, since it was displeasing to the Lord Christ.

Let us therefore examine the passage itself. A goat had been sacrificed for sin and offered as a burnt offering. Moses later sought it, and it had been burned. Moses became angry with Eleazar and Ithamar, the surviving sons of Aaron, saying: “Why did you not eat what was offered for sin in the holy place? Since they are most holy, you ought to have eaten them, so that you might take away the sin of the synagogue, and they ought to be eaten within, as I was commanded.”

When Aaron saw that Moses was angry, he answered him gently: “If today they offered their burnt offerings for their sin before the Lord, and such things have happened to me, shall I eat what they offered today for sin? Will it please the Lord?” Moses heard this, and it pleased him.

Let us consider what these things signify. To commit no sin belongs to God alone; to amend and correct an error, and to repent of sin, belongs to the wise. Yet this is difficult in human life. What is so rare as to find a man who accuses himself and condemns his own deed?

Confession of sin is therefore rare, repentance is rare, and the acknowledgment of the word concerning it is rare among human beings. Nature resists it, and shame resists it. Nature resists because all are under sin, and whoever bears flesh is subject to guilt. Thus the nature of the flesh and the allurements of the world resist it.

Shame also resists innocence and integrity, because each person is ashamed to confess his own fault, thinking more about present things than future ones.

Moses was striving to find a soul free from sin, so that it might lay aside the cast-off garments of error and depart naked of guilt, without any shame concerning itself. But he did not find one, because irrational impulse quickly intervenes, and a certain flame of swift movement feeds upon the soul and burns up its innocence.

Present things outweigh future things; violent things outweigh restrained things; many things outweigh few; pleasant things outweigh serious; soft things outweigh harsh; joyful things outweigh sad; alluring things outweigh severe; and what is premature outruns what is slow.

For iniquity is swift in suggesting opportunities for doing harm: “Their feet are swift to shed blood.” But every virtue is slow and lasting, hesitating before it judges and begins what must be undertaken. Thus the mind that contemplates the good examines its own counsels and first considers what is seemly and honorable.

Iniquity, however, overtakes thought in action. Repentance is therefore sluggish and ashamed, because it is oppressed and held back by shame concerning present things. It attends only to future things, whose hope comes late and whose fruit is slower; therefore the petition itself is slower.

Amid these efforts of hope and virtue, shamelessness runs ahead. By the appearance of present things, repentance is excluded and, as it were, its affection is burned up; it is unwillingly extinguished in this way. The Law seeks it and does not find it.

For it has been scorched by the heat and smoke of iniquity, and a certain indignation of the Law arises. Moses says that repentance ought to have been devoured in the Holy of Holies. He rebukes the priests as though they were too sluggish.

Aaron answered that priestly judgment ought to be prudent, and that the office should not easily be entrusted to an unhealthy conscience, lest the error become worse than the former one. In a foul vessel, oil or wine is easily corrupted and deteriorated.

But how could sin be burned up where there was strange fire, and this before the sight of the Lord, to whom hidden things are known? Can it please the Lord if someone who is still entangled in iniquities and holds injustice enclosed in his heart says that he is repenting?

It is like someone who is sick pretending to be well. He will become more sick, because the pretense of health can do him no good, when it is only shaded by words and supported by no assistance of virtue.

Strange fire, therefore, is lust; strange fire is every burning of unjust desire; strange fire is every ardor of greed. No one is cleansed by this fire; rather, he is burned up.

Where, therefore, this alien fire is present, if someone presents himself before the Lord, heavenly fire consumes him, just as it consumed Abihu and Nadab, together with the things that had been offered upon the sacred altars for sin. Whoever, then, wishes to cleanse his sin should remove alien fire from himself and offer himself only to that fire which consumes guilt, not the human being. What fire this is, hear him say: “For Jesus baptizes in the Holy Spirit and fire” (John I). This is the fire that dried up the flow of blood of the woman who had suffered hemorrhaging for twelve years; this is the fire that removed Zacchaeus’s sin when he said that he would give half of his possessions to the poor and, if he had taken anything from anyone, would repay it fourfold (Luke XIX). This is the fire that wiped away the thief’s guilt. For it is a consuming fire, the one who said to him, “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke XXIII). Thus he healed those in whom he found a simple and pure confession, with nothing malicious and nothing fraudulent.

Finally, Judas could not attain healing when he said, “I have sinned, in betraying righteous blood” (Matthew XXVII), because he was carrying alien fire in his breast, and it inflamed him toward the noose. He was unworthy of healing because he did not groan after turning from his heart’s depths, nor did he earnestly practice repentance. For the Lord Jesus is of such great compassion that he would have granted forgiveness even to him, had he awaited Christ’s mercy.

Priests, therefore, do not remove this guilt, nor the sin of one who presents himself deceitfully and is still intent upon sinning. For they cannot feast upon what is filled inwardly with fraud and the serpent’s scar. The priest’s food is the remission of sins. Hence the High Priest says: “My food is to do the will of my Father who is in heaven.” And what is God’s will except this: “When you have turned and groaned, then you will be saved”? In that deceitful man, therefore, there is no food; indeed, he himself cannot savor the sweetness of feasting, since he has no sincere and pure conscience. The bitterness of fraud covers the sweetness of feasting and does not allow repentance to refresh and nourish the guilty soul.

Therefore such a disposition, such a request, and such repentance are neither useful nor pleasing to priests; and deservedly that goat which was offered as a burnt offering for sin was burned up, because it was not a sincere sacrifice: alien fire was found in its offering. A sacrifice is therefore not pleasing or acceptable to God; it is acceptable only if it has been tested and found rich in sincerity and truth.

# BOOK THREE

[Column 0351]

## CHAPTER ONE. On the animals that ought to be eaten, and on those that are clean or unclean

**(Leviticus XI.)** “The Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying: Say to the children of Israel: These are the animals that you shall eat among all the living creatures of the earth. Whatever among the livestock has a divided hoof and chews the cud, you may eat. But whatever indeed chews the cud and has a hoof but does not divide it, such as the camel and the rest, you shall not eat, and you shall regard it as unclean. The hyrax [*cyrogrillus*], which chews the cud but does not divide the hoof, is unclean. The hare also, for it too chews the cud but does not divide the hoof. And the pig, which, although it divides the hoof, does not chew the cud. You shall not eat their flesh, and you shall not touch their carcasses, because they are unclean for you.”

**(From Hesychius.)** These matters about which the discussion now proceeds, and the divine utterances themselves, appear to contain a very great contradiction. For how, when he said to Noah, “Everything that moves and lives shall be food for you, and just as I gave you green plants, so I have given you everything,” did he now prohibit the eating of some of those things that had previously been permitted? Again, when he made the beasts of the earth according to their kinds, and the livestock and reptiles, it was said: “And God saw that they were good” (Genesis I); and again: “God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good.” Yet nothing that is unclean can be good—especially not very good. Now, however, as though he had forgotten the judgment he had pronounced concerning them, he declared some animals clean and others unclean. Thus some would be good and others not good.

But it is not so. Even if he wished for a little while to chastise the gluttony of the Jews, nevertheless the true consideration of the law is evident, as is the spiritual exposition of the commandments and the kind of intention the legislator has for those who devote themselves to teaching the law. For if “man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” (Matthew IV), then just as bread nourishes the body, so the law of God nourishes the soul, since it is a rational power and substance suited to the rational creature. And just as in the preceding passages, among the things that are sacrificed, he represents those who offer them—signifying the simple person by the sheep, the doer of the commandments by the calf, and the penitent by the kid—so now also he signifies by the animals those who eat them. For he says:

“The Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying: Say to the children of Israel: These are the animals that you shall eat among all the living creatures of the earth.”

The law is common: this commandment applies to everyone, and is the justification of the whole people; for he commanded Moses to speak to the children of Israel, that is, to the entire people. What, then, did he command him to say? “These are the animals that you shall eat among all the living creatures of the earth.” He would certainly not have said “of the earth” unless he intended to distinguish them from the heavenly animals. For Ezekiel (chapter I), describing the cherubim as living creatures, taught that one had the face of a lion, another of a calf, another of an eagle, and another of a human being. Therefore, among the heavenly animals we need no special vigilance or other scrutiny to recognize which are clean: all are alike clean and holy, as is signified by the holy God and those who stand around him.

The animals of the earth, however, are not all clean—not because of their nature, but because of our transgression and because we have corrupted nature through iniquity. How, then, we are to recognize their cleanness or uncleanness must be observed from what follows:

“Whatever has a divided hoof and chews the cud among the livestock, you shall eat.”

The greatest power of animals is thought to reside in their hooves, which also have a kinship with teeth. For it belongs to the hooves to tear apart what is made suitable for eating by the teeth.

**(From Hesychius.)** First, one must know that everything established by God is clean and purified by the very authority of its creation. What, then, is the meaning? In the animals, human dispositions, deeds, and wishes are depicted, and from these human beings themselves become clean or unclean. Thus he says that these are clean:

“Everything,” he says, “that has a divided hoof and chews the cud among the livestock, you shall eat.”

When he said this, he was distinguishing not livestock but human dispositions. In the end, those people are clean who chew the cud, who always carry the divine commandments in their mouths as if they were food. They also divide the hoof, because they believe in the two Testaments—the Law and the Gospels—and establish themselves with a firm step in innocence and righteousness.

The Jews, likewise, chew the words of the Law, but do not divide the hoof. That is, they neither accept the two Testaments nor establish the step of their faith in the Father and the Son; therefore they are considered unclean. Heretics also divide the hoof, believing in the Father and the Son and receiving the two Testaments, but because they do not chew the doctrine of truth in their mouths, they too are nevertheless unclean.

“Whatever,” he says, “chews the cud and has a hoof but does not divide it, such as the camel and the rest, you shall not eat, but shall regard it as unclean.”

The camel is the Jew swollen with pride, such as the scribes and Pharisees, to whom the Lord said: “You strain out a gnat but swallow a camel” (Matthew XXIII). Therefore the scribes and Pharisees eat while chewing the cud, because they glory in meditation upon the letter of the Law, in the observance of the Sabbath, in purification, sacrifices, and other similar matters. But they do not divide the hoof, because they do not distinguish in what they eat the letter from the spirit; therefore their knowledge is unclean.

Such also are those who eat the hare and the hyrax: these too chew the cud, but do not divide the hoof. In the common multitude of the Jews, both are understood, for these animals are said to be weak, as David and Solomon testify concerning the weakness of both animals. Solomon says: “The little hare, an infirm people, has made its dwelling in a rock” (Proverbs XXX). David says: “The rock is a refuge for the hyraxes,” or *chirogrilli* (Psalm CIII). One of them is swift and timid despite its weakness—that is, the hare. The other is indeed weak, but is said to be predatory, beastlike, and deadly—that is, the hyrax. This is found among every common people, but especially among the Jewish people. Of them David said: “Their feet are swift to shed blood” (Psalm XIII).

How timid and weak the children of the Jews are, the divine voice shows when it says: “Woe to timid hearts and slack hands.” But how great was the injustice and ferocity among them, hear Isaiah say: “How has the faithful city, full of judgment, become a prostitute? Justice dwelt in her, but now murderers” (Isaiah I).

After these, he says that the pig is unclean, because it divides the hoof but does not chew the cud. Receive Peter as interpreter and teacher. He called a pig the one who possesses knowledge of divine things but does not use it well, pollutes it by incongruous actions, and gives himself over to an unclean life. He says:

“It would have been better for them not to have known the way of righteousness than, after knowing it, to turn back from the holy commandment handed down to them. What has happened to them accords with the true proverb: ‘The dog has returned to its own vomit,’ and ‘the washed pig to wallowing in the mire’” (2 Peter II).

But when he added to what had been said, “You shall not eat their flesh, nor touch their carcasses, because they are unclean for you,” this means: neither the camel, nor the hare, nor the hyrax, nor the pig, which he judged to be unclean.

For, as we have said, the camel represents the scribes and Pharisees, who through pride are marked by the fault of folly, which is contrary to wisdom; it is characteristic of fools to be proud. The hare, as timid, is contrary to courage; the hyrax, as predatory, is contrary to justice; the pig, as living a sordid and unclean life, is contrary to chastity.

**(From Hesychius.)** Let us not eat the flesh of these, that is, let us not follow the virtue they appear to possess; for they pursue it in hypocrisy and not in truth. Much less should their carcasses be touched, nor should we share in their evil actions. Such men themselves are undoubtedly their carcasses.

“These are the creatures that are produced in the waters and that it is permitted to eat: everything that has fins and scales, whether in the sea or in rivers and ponds, you shall eat. But whatever among the things that move and live in the waters does not have fins and scales shall be abominable and detestable to you. You shall not eat their flesh, and you shall avoid their carcasses. Everything in the waters that does not have fins and scales shall be polluted.”

Since divine Scripture has not openly listed the kinds of fish from which it wishes us to abstain, it is pointless to investigate this at present; nowhere will we find the names of fish in it. In this passage also, therefore, it imitates itself. *(Rabanus.)*

Nevertheless, this should now be noted: just as in the voluntary sacrifices, which the legislator also called gifts, he signified at one time the doers of the Law, at another the simple, and at another the contemplatives through the various forms of offering—and assigned sacrifices of fine flour to those saved from the nations, as to the simple, as he shows by saying, “If a soul offers a gift to the Lord,” without adding, “If a soul from the people of the land,” as he usually does in the descriptions of the other sacrifices—so here also, wishing to show through abstinence from foods what those who meditate upon the Law ought to be, he signified by chewing the cud and dividing the hoof the Jew who ought to fulfill the commandments of the Law, divide the letter from the spirit, and understand the Law spiritually.

By what has now been said, however, he shows that he is speaking about the Gentiles. Hence I think that the fish are mentioned without their names because the Church does not wish the names of her own people to be written upon the earth. Therefore David says of her: “Let these things be written for a future generation” (Psalm CI), namely, for the future in heaven; for there the names of her children are written.

“These are the creatures that are produced in the waters and that it is permitted to eat.”

By these are understood those who have been saved from the Gentiles, since they possess regeneration in the water of baptism. Of them Isaiah also said: “Behold, the nations are like stars of a bucket” (Isaiah XL), or, according to the Septuagint, “like many waters, many nations.”

Therefore what follows also applies to them:

“Everything that has fins and scales, whether in the sea or in rivers and ponds, you shall eat.”

He also commanded those who are from the Gentiles, in other words, concerning their meditation upon the Law. For he wishes them to have fins in their meditation upon the Law and a lofty, heavenly life, but an interpretation of the Law corresponding to this. For this reason he does not wish them to have one fin but fins.

Since ignorance of divine Scripture had possessed the Gentiles—for they had not received the Law or the prophets, nor did they possess any other more refined divine knowledge—he wished them to have scales, which could easily be removed, so that they would not remain afflicted by this persistent and enduring disease. Since scales signify temporary ignorance, from which one can readily be freed, the things written about Paul in the Acts of the Apostles (chapter IX) demonstrate this. When he was persecuting the Church with Jewish zeal and did not know the one whom he was persecuting, he was easily freed from his zeal on account of his ignorance. After he learned whom he was persecuting, when he had been called by Christ and Ananias had evangelized to him, scales fell from his eyes, and immediately he saw. Thus temporary ignorances lay upon him like scales.

Therefore the legislator added with great appropriateness:

“But whatever among the things that move and live in the waters does not have fins or scales shall be abominable and detestable to you.”

For just as certain kinds of fish have a shell in place of skin, whose scale cannot be removed, so are those who neither permit the scales of ignorance to be removed by the word of God nor allow themselves to receive the sword of the Spirit. Even if they are found in the sea of baptism, even if in the rivers of repentance, they are nevertheless abominable in all that moves and lives in the waters. Although they have received life in baptism, they have corrupted their calling and regeneration because they do not have fins and scales—that is, a lofty life and knowledge of divine things, which are heavenly—but retain a blind heart in ignorance. Therefore they are not numbered among those who have scales.

Observe with what subtlety of expression the legislator speaks, signifying through these things the greatest mysteries and wonders. He joined fins to scales. Just as fish that have scales invariably also have fins, so those who possess temporary ignorance, from which they can therefore quickly be freed, are also granted lofty knowledge and a heavenly life.

Therefore, of those who are not such, one ought neither to eat the flesh nor touch the carcasses, nor have any communion with them at all. Paul bears witness to this when he says: “If anyone who is called a brother is a fornicator, or greedy, or serves idols, or is a reviler, or a drunkard, or a robber, with such a person not even to eat” (1 Corinthians V).

An adulterer, a greedy person, a drunkard, or a slanderer does not have fins—that is, he has a sordid and unclean life. But the worshiper of idols is not counted among those who have scales, for he appears to possess a hard, shell-like, and incurable ignorance of divine things. Otherwise, once joined to God, he would never again have served idols.

**(From Gregory.)** Moreover, it should be noted that fish possessing fins and scales are accustomed to leap even above the waters. What, then, are represented by finned fish except elect souls? For they alone pass into the body of the heavenly Church. Now supported by the fins of virtues, they know how to leap through heavenly desire, seeking the contemplation above, although they again slip within themselves because of their mortal flesh.

Therefore they alone pass into the body of the elect as chosen food: while they serve in the depths, they sometimes know how to ascend to higher things through the leaps of the mind, so that they do not always lie hidden in the depths of cares and no breath of supreme love, like free air, touches them. Those who are occupied with temporal matters order external things well when they flee attentively to their inward selves, when they do not love the noise of disturbances outside, but rest within themselves in the bosom of tranquility.

“These are the birds that you shall not eat, and they shall be avoided by you: the eagle, the griffin, and the sea-eagle; the kite and the vulture according to their kinds; and every bird of the raven kind according to its likeness; the ostrich, the owl, the gull, and the hawk according to its kind; the little owl, the cormorant, the ibis, the swan, the pelican, the purple bird, the heron, and the plover according to its kind; also the hoopoe and the bat.”

**(From Hesychius.)** In this matter the legislator did not leave unexamined even the life of those who devote themselves to contemplation. Just as he assigned them a distinct chapter of the Law in the offering of sacrifices, so in the investigation of foods he gave them their own boundaries. Extending and making these boundaries more fearful, he legislates concerning these birds not as he did concerning livestock and fish.

There he said: “These are the animals that you shall eat, among all the living creatures of the earth”; and again: “These are the things produced in the waters that it is permitted to eat.” Here, however, he says: “These are the birds that you shall not eat, and they shall be avoided by you.”

It is truly worthy of abhorrence and must be numbered among what is unlawful and most carefully avoided for anyone devoted to contemplation voluntarily to possess such blemishes as the legislator signifies through the birds he lists. He says: “the eagle, the griffin, the sea-eagle, the kite, and the vulture according to their kind.” By these he signifies those who are rapacious, pursue the food of others wickedly, and delight in unjust profits.

Since some are found in churches among those thought to devote themselves to contemplation who do not devote themselves to it as they ought, but are vainly puffed up, hear Paul say:

“If anyone teaches otherwise and does not assent to the sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ and to the teaching that accords with piety, he is conceited, knowing nothing, but sick with questions and disputes about words, from which arise envy, quarrels, blasphemies, evil suspicions, conflicts among people whose minds are corrupted and who are deprived of the truth, supposing that piety is a means of gain” (1 Timothy VI).

The animals now listed therefore signify those who seek their food through plunder. Some of these attack other birds and are nourished by their hunting; others enter houses and seize whatever they find, not even sparing the food of those who own them. They resemble those who “worm their way into households and capture weak women burdened with sins” (2 Timothy III), whom Paul rebukes.

The vulture delights in quarrels and wars because of the corpses of battles, to such an extent that it even follows an army. Therefore one who devotes himself to contemplation ought not to feed and nourish himself on the misfortunes of others.

The creatures of the raven kind are without affection, as is clear from the fact that when the raven was sent out by Noah, it transgressed from the beginning by flying away. Judas was like it in relation to his teacher and Lord.

The ostrich is indeed a bird, but it cannot fly, and it spends its entire life around the earth. Such are some who serve God but entangle themselves in the business of the world.

The owl—which the Septuagint calls the *glaux*—is said to have sharp sight at night but to enjoy less useful vision when the sun appears. Such are those who glory in contemplation and knowledge of the Law but are unable to receive the light of evangelical conduct.

The gull lives in both elements, water and land: as a bird it flies, and as an aquatic creature it swims. Those who at the same time venerate circumcision and baptism are not improperly compared to it. To them Paul says: “If you are circumcised, Christ will be of no benefit to you” (Galatians V).

The hawk is among the rapacious birds, but it has another characteristic for which it was included by the legislator: it becomes tame and cooperates in acts of rapacity. Those who appear gentle and tranquil in temperament but associate with the powerful, greedy, and rapacious imitate it.

The night-raven is a creature that plunders and works only at night; such are those given over to the works of intelligible night: fornication, impurity, shamelessness, the worship of idols, and similar things (ibid.).

The ibis, the purple bird, the one whom the Septuagint calls the pelican, the swan, the heron, and the plover are said to have long necks and to draw their food from the heights of the earth and the waters. We should imitate these animals and not pluck food from below, but from heavenly things. For the person who devotes himself to contemplation strives toward higher things in his mind and awaits from God not only intelligible food but also sensible food. Hence the Lord says: “Do not be anxious about your soul, what you shall eat, or about your body, what you shall wear. For your heavenly Father knows that you need all these things” (Matthew VI).

The hoopoe is a mournful creature that loves grief. But worldly grief produces death. Therefore the person who loves God ought always to rejoice, pray without ceasing, and give thanks in all things, because joy is the fruit of the Spirit.

Bats fly close to the earth, so that when they walk they use their wings in place of feet. This is unworthy of those who devote themselves to contemplation. For those whose flight is around the earth undoubtedly have their contemplation occupied with earthly things.

Do not, therefore, be unbelieving or doubtful that the legislator also established the animals now listed as figures and representations of those from whom persons devoted to contemplation ought to abstain.

But you will say: How is it that the imitation of these animals, rather than their food, is prohibited? Why did the prophet David compare himself to the pelican and the night-raven, saying, “I have become like a pelican in the wilderness; I have become like a night-raven in a dwelling” (Psalm CI)? And why did Moses represent God himself by the eagle, when he says to Israel, “How I carried you upon eagles’ wings” (Exodus XIX)? The prophets also call Christ a lion, while Peter, conversely, says that the devil is a lion. Yet Christ is not a lion in the same sense in which the devil is called one—far be it from us; far be such impiety. But because the animal is at once royal and also rapacious and savage, possessing a praiseworthy dignity but a blameworthy activity, what it has praiseworthy is understood in the kingdom of Christ, while what is blameworthy in it—rapacity and savageness—is understood in the devil.

When we consider the eagle in the same way, we find this without any doubt. Because of the height of its flight, Moses took it as a figure of God; but because it is rapacious, he said that its food must be avoided.

The prophet David, mourning the human being established in sin, compared him to the night-raven, as one living in the night. By the pelican, as an animal that loves solitude, he represented the person who has perhaps been abandoned by friends or relatives and deprived of the company of others of the same kind.

**(From Augustine.)** But to recapitulate all these matters briefly through the example of the animals: he condemns a shapeless life, twisted by crimes.

**(From Hesychius.)** When he prohibits the pig as food, he certainly condemns a muddy and filthy life that rejoices in the pollution of vices. When he condemns the hare, he condemns men deformed into women. Who, however, would make a weasel into food? Yet he is condemning theft. Who would eat a lizard? Yet he hates the unstable variety of life. Who, finally, could eat a gecko? Thus the Law does not principally prohibit these foods but execrates the stains of minds.

Who eats a hawk, a kite, or an eagle? Yet he hates plunderers who live by violent wickedness. Who eats a vulture? Yet he execrates those who seek booty from another’s death.

Likewise, when he prohibits the raven, he condemns black intentions; when he forbids the sparrow, he reproves intemperance; when he mentions the owl, he hates varieties that flee the light; when he mentions the plover [*casandrium*, or *charandrium*], a kind that loves the court too much, he condemns the intemperance of the tongue; when he prohibits the swan, he marks the pride of a lofty neck; when he mentions the bat, he condemns those who seek the darkness of night, and errors likewise.

“Every creature among the winged animals that walks on four feet shall be abominable to you. But whatever walks on four feet and has longer hind legs with which it leaps upon the earth, you may eat: the locust according to its kind, the *attacus* and the *ophiomachus*, and the grasshopper, each according to its kind.”

Those who profess the contemplative life ought to be pure from every sin and sordid action. Therefore all who resemble winged creatures of the heavenly realm, promising to attain contemplation that leads to heaven, but are compared to creeping things because they feed upon the earth and devote themselves to desires—even though they walk on four feet, that is, even though they pretend to evangelical preaching, which says, “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance” (Matthew IX), and, “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick” (ibid.)—and from whom the thief was saved and the adulteress justified, and those who had been forgiven more were said to love more: nevertheless, because they do not embrace a common life according to truth but abuse the compassion of preaching for their own pleasures, they are unclean and abominable. In such a manner of life and amid such great knowledge, they enter upon a certain shameful and unclean existence.

But those whose hind legs are higher than their feet, so that by means of them they leap from the earth, are consequently placed among the clean. Although they are in the flesh, they do not wage war according to the flesh, but leap away from sordid actions. They mix with worldly people in order to teach and instruct them, so that they sometimes dwell with adulterers and tax collectors, yet do not mingle with their unclean actions. They recoil from them and fly away; while they shun fellowship in their sin, they nevertheless often dwell with sinners so as to free and recall them from the filth of their sins.

Thus the Lord, who “committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (1 Peter II), ate and drank with sinners, justifying them by instruction and teaching and calling them to imitate him, while himself imitating none of their ways and remaining undefiled by them. Therefore the Song of Songs says: “Behold, he comes leaping upon the mountains, bounding over the hills” (Song of Songs II).

We ought, then, to have legs higher than our feet—not like the feet of the Jews, who limp in both their tracks, namely, in the Law and the prophets, but like those of the creatures called cherubim. Of them it is said: “Their legs were straight legs, and their feet were winged” (Ezekiel I).

Let these legs be straight and unwavering in the evangelical feet of which it is said: “Your feet shod in preparation for the gospel of peace” (Ephesians VI). Although such a person walks upon the earth, although he associates with sinners for the sake of a certain dispensation and assistance, fulfilling the apostolic instruction, “If an unbeliever invites you to dinner and you wish to go, eat whatever is set before you, asking no questions for the sake of conscience” (1 Corinthians X), nevertheless he remains winged and clean.
