He knows how to spring and leap away from the earth and not cling to worldly actions.

The legislator appropriately also gave the names of such animals, naming the locust, the grasshopper, the *attacus*, and the *ophiomachus*. What their activity or virtue is, the prophet Nahum sufficiently explains when he says: “The locust spread itself out and flew away; your guards are like locusts of locusts, which settle on the hedges in the day of frost” (Nahum III). Or, according to the Septuagint: “It sprang forth like an *attelaus* mingled with you, like a locust that crosses the wall in the day of frost.”

From this you see that, even if we mingle with sinners, and even if on the day of frost or hoarfrost—that is, of the abundance of sin, for “when sin abounds, the love of many will grow cold”—we should leap over the wall, namely, the thorny accumulation of sins. We should not become like them, but subject them to ourselves so that they may become obedient to instruction; thus we openly save and are saved.

Hence Paul says: “To the Jews I became as a Jew; to those under the Law, as though I were under the Law, although I myself was not under the Law; to those without the Law, as though I were without the Law, although I was not without the law of God but under the law of Christ. I became all things to all people, so that I might win all” (1 Corinthians IX).

Nevertheless, like the locust, we must make an assault and fly away, so that, like the grasshopper or *attacus*—for some say that *attacus* should be understood in this way—we may be able to leap and spring forth. For thus what follows in the same prophet will fittingly apply: “The sun has risen and mounted up, and its place has not been found.” When the sun of righteousness has risen, illuminating hidden things, those who associate with sinners for the comfort of righteousness spring forth and leap away; and their place is no longer recognized as the place whose character they formerly displayed, when in some way they honored those who needed to be saved.

The virtue of the *ophiomachus* is revealed by its name, and it is good to imitate it and oppose the intelligible serpents, remembering that “our struggle is not against flesh and blood but against rulers and authorities, against the cosmic powers of this darkness, against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places” (Ephesians VI). These are the intelligible serpents and poisonous dragons.

“Whatever among the winged animals has only four feet shall be detestable to you; and whoever touches their carcasses shall be polluted and unclean until evening. If it is necessary for someone to carry any of these dead creatures, he shall wash his garments and be unclean until sunset. Every animal that has a hoof but does not divide it and does not chew the cud shall be unclean, and whatever it touches shall be contaminated.”

**(From Hesychius.)** We have shown above that the creeping things among the winged animals that walk on four feet signify those who abuse the evangelical life and pursue a sordid and unclean existence. To divide the hoof, as the Septuagint says here, but not to chew the cud—that is, to meditate upon the Law as one ought and divide the letter from the spirit, but not to practice what is written in it—we have also shown in the preceding passages. Therefore he necessarily commanded us to flee their carcasses, that is, the actions in which they perish through the death of sin, and not to participate in such things in any way or touch them.

Not only are we polluted by touching them, but also by carrying them or receiving anything from them. A person carries sins when he calls evil good, bitter sweet, and darkness light. The prophet Isaiah reproves this, because by doing so he imposes upon himself, in a certain sense, the yoke of what he ought to have forbidden, while exercising another toward iniquity and inviting him to evil (Isaiah V).

No one ought to transfer another person’s sin onto himself. For this reason David also says: “Spare your servant from the sins of others” (Psalm XVIII). If we become participants in the sins of others, we remain unclean until evening—that is, until we practice repentance. David calls this evening: “In the evening weeping will remain, but in the morning there will be joy.” Therefore the legislator also commanded that garments be washed, clearly demonstrating that we are unclean until we wash away our actions with tears.

## CHAPTER TWO. On the uncleanness of an animal’s carcass
(IBID.) “Whatever walks on its hands among all the animals that move on four feet shall be unclean. Whoever touches their carcasses shall be unclean until evening; and whoever carries such carcasses shall wash his garments and shall be unclean until evening, because all these are unclean for you.” ([Col. 0361A] From Hesychius.)

The Law silently passes over no sin. Rather, whatever actions are prohibited through the Gospel Testament, it first concealed under enigmas, so that, learning the harmony of both ordinances, you may confess the God who spoke in them and, fearing him, withdraw from everything they have prohibited.

The one who passes over to evangelical conduct walks on four feet. He “walks on his hands” who pursues it for the sake of gain and shameful profit, quickly laying hands upon it in order to obtain some advantage from it; such a person is rightly counted and compared with the beasts. Whether you call him an adulterer, a covetous man, a murderer, a slanderer, or a blasphemer, he is all of these, since through an unjust laying-on of hands he shares in the sins of them all. Those upon whom he has laid his hands are his carcasses. For in them he suffers the death of sin.

Whoever therefore touches them, and whoever lifts something from them, is rightly polluted. He who touches them—that is, who associates with them—says that they have in no way seized the dignity appropriate to them, although, by peddling it, they were formerly justified in every way through it; yet afterward they remain in their former iniquities. And whoever carries something from them, as one who bears false witness by asserting and calling worthy the person who is unworthy, shall be unclean until evening, which we have explained above as repentance. But when he washes his garments, he shall be cleansed.

“This also shall be reckoned among the polluted things that move upon the earth: the weasel and the mouse, and the crocodile, each according to its kind; the shrew-mouse and the chameleon, and the stellion [Col. 0361C] and the lizard, and the mole. All these are unclean; whoever touches their carcasses shall be unclean until evening.” (From the same author.)

The legislator did not now command these animals to be regarded as unclean by accusing God’s creation. For how would you find them praised elsewhere in divine Scripture? Solomon, indeed, says in Proverbs: “There are four things that are very small upon the earth, and these are wiser than the wise” (Prov. 30). Among them he counted the hare—or, according to the Septuagint, the hedgehog—and the stellion. Of these, the Law above accused one, together with the camel and the hare, as unclean; now it mentions the stellion.

Their nature, therefore, is not unclean, nor is every action associated with them. For how could these things have been praised? Rather, certain actions concerning them are suited to irrational animals [Col. 0361D], actions that require no judgment, that are neither suited to us nor proper to our nature. Consequently, whenever we come into contact with them, they make us unclean.

To crawl upon the earth is not proper to human beings, who have been granted the ability to walk upright and look toward heaven. For to crawl upon the earth is to perform sordid and earthly works, which the legislator signified through the distinction among the animals now enumerated.

The weasel is a deceitful animal, greatly devoted to theft. The mouse, because of its greed for the belly, endures many dangers every day. The crocodile is hard-skinned and malicious, and feeds on mud. The shrew-mouse is an animal contrived—not by nature but by the condition of its life—to provoke ridicule; that is, it is suited to practicing deceit, seizing things, and filling its belly. For this reason it received a composite name from both animals, from which it possesses these vices.

The chameleon pities in an evil manner and, because of its weakness, pretends to be gentle, although it is an untamed animal. The stellion, that is, the *ascalobotis*, is indeed very small or most wretched, yet poisonous. The lizard dwells in tombs. The mole is a blind animal generated from the earth. They say that it is created from earth and rain together, when the earth first receives the rain.

These, then, are unclean among all those that crawl upon the earth—not because other things are not unclean, but because these are especially so, and therefore possess greater pollution, or malice. “Everyone who touches their carcasses shall be unclean until evening.”

The very text therefore aptly proves the legislator’s intention [Col. 0362B]. For if the animals now mentioned were unclean by nature, the person who touched them while they were alive ought also to be unclean. But now only the person who touches their carcasses is unclean.

Their carcasses are the actions mentioned above: deceit, theft, duplicity or irony, occupation with other things, and also haste after earthly matters, by which the eyes of the mind are blinded. Because the soul suffers death in these things, they are rightly called carcasses. Whoever touches them—that is, whoever is polluted in them—is unclean, just as Paul says: “It is good for a man not to touch a woman” (1 Cor. 7). Nothing pollutes a person so much as sin, until evening arrives—the evening of which David said: “In the evening weeping shall remain” (Ps. 29). He is speaking of repentance, the intelligible purification by which we are washed clean.

“And whatever falls upon any of their carcasses shall be polluted, whether a wooden vessel, a garment, a skin, or sackcloth; and whatever object is used for work shall be immersed in water, and they shall be unclean until evening, and afterward they shall be cleansed. But an earthen vessel into which any of these things falls shall be polluted, and therefore it must be broken.” (From the same author.)

Here too the legislator uses an admirable distinction. For sometimes we sin through negligence, and sometimes through the practice and pursuit of evil, as did those of whom Solomon said in Proverbs: “Who has woe? Whose father has woe? Who has anger? Who has strife? Who has wounds without cause? Who has dimness of eyes? Is it not those who pursue wine and devote themselves to drinking cups?” (Prov. 23.) [Col. 0362D]

He placed these among those who touch carcasses: people who, through the negligence of the soul and through stupefaction and the failure of virtues, fall into sin. Thus David rose at midday from his bed, walked on his roof, and saw Uriah’s wife washing herself. Captivated by the woman, who was exceedingly beautiful, he committed both adultery and murder (2 Sam. 11).

The carcasses are said to fall upon such people. For they did not hasten toward sin; rather, they fell into it and, as it were, received upon themselves the sin that fell upon them. But because they accepted it altogether and did not resist, they are rightly unclean.

“Whether a wooden vessel, a garment, a skin, or sackcloth”—that is, whether one has a light and moderate kind of life, such as wooden vessels signify; or something sufficient for covering, as a garment does (or, according to another reading, for covering); or a patient disposition, which the skin signifies; or that which belongs to the suffering, which sackcloth or a sack signifies. In every case, a vessel is something in which the work of virtue can be performed. Thus you understand: “Whatever object is used for work shall be polluted until evening,” that is, until the time of repentance.

It shall be immersed in the water of washing, or in tears, and shall be cleansed.

“But an earthen vessel”—that is, one that is wholly earthly, kneaded from the clay of the age. If a carcass falls into it—that is, if a sin leading to death enters it, penetrates its interior, and gains dominion over it, as David said: “He clothed himself with cursing as with a garment, and it entered like water into his inward parts” (Ps. 108)—then, since he says not only that the curse entered but also that it ruled in the one into whom it entered, the legislator necessarily commanded that vessel to be crushed.

For its uncleanness cannot be cleansed as easily as that of the others. It requires much labor and contrition, and, as it were, the reformation of a mind that has been crushed and humbled, as David says, if it wishes to be cleansed. Hence blessed Paul also so crushed the man who had committed fornication with his father’s wife that he handed him over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that his spirit might be saved through such contrition (1 Cor. 5).

“Every food that you eat, if water is poured upon it, shall be unclean; and every liquid that is drunk from any vessel shall be unclean.” (From the same author.)

We understand food and drink in every vessel to mean good actions. For this reason he says, “the food that you shall eat” and “the liquid that is drunk,” because the food and drink of evil actions are prohibited—that is, participation in them.

If, therefore, in any of the good actions that are found in every vessel—that is, in every person, whether ruler or commoner, wise or ignorant—one of the things called carcasses should fall, that person will necessarily be unclean.

Even if someone did not begin a good action with an evil intention, as those do who feign piety for the sake of business or profit, yet afterward pride, deceit, hypocrisy, or something similar—something said to be a carcass because it introduces a kind of death—should enter into his action, he too will be unclean. For an evil intention entering beneath a good action pollutes it.

Because he added to the law concerning food, “If water is poured upon it,” he shows what the actions are that follow baptism. His statement concerns the faithful and the baptized; he makes no mention of the action of the unbeliever. Blessed Paul proves this when he says: “I wrote to you in the letter not to associate with fornicators—not at all meaning the fornicators of this world, or the covetous, or the rapacious, or those who serve idols; otherwise you would have had to leave this world. But now I wrote to you that if one who is called a brother is a fornicator, or unclean, or covetous, or serves idols, or is a reviler, or a drunkard, or rapacious, with such a person you should not even take food. For what have I to do with judging those who are outside?” (1 Cor. 5.) [Col. 0364A]

He has no concern at all with the conduct or way of life of those who are outside.

## CHAPTER III. Springs and cisterns are clean from carcasses, but earthen vessels are not.

(IBID.) “And whatever falls from such carcasses upon it shall be unclean; whether ovens or cooking-pots, they shall be destroyed, and they shall be unclean. But springs and cisterns and every collection of waters shall be clean. Whoever touches their carcasses shall be polluted.” (From Hesychius.)

If ovens and cooking-pots are contaminated, how much more should collections of water be contaminated, in which it happens that these animals fall and decompose?

But perhaps you ask what the ovens and cooking-pots signify. They signify teachers, in whom the foods of sacred doctrine are cooked, with the fire of spiritual activity placed beneath them.

It is not surprising that ovens and cooking-pots are called so metaphorically, since we know that divine Scripture often uses such names. David called Moab—that is, the nation—a cooking-pot. For he says: “Moab is the pot of my hope” (Ps. 59), because the waters of baptism are heated in them. Ezekiel likewise calls Jerusalem a cooking-pot, but one full of meat—or, according to the Septuagint, of poison—thereby signifying the men who teach wrongly and live wrongly in it.

According to this interpretation, therefore, ovens and cooking-pots in which foods—namely, peoples instructed in doctrine—are cooked can be so called. If a carcass falls into them—that is, if the death-dealing action of one who sins comes upon them—they become unclean and are destroyed, because those who teach others not to steal themselves steal, and those who preach against adultery themselves commit adultery.

The doctrine itself, however, is good and is not unclean. Nor are the divine utterances abominated because some preachers have perhaps become unclean through them. Therefore springs—namely, rich doctrines—and cisterns or pools, signifying tongues that speak ordinary things and possess borrowed doctrine, as well as collections of water, signifying those who gather from every side an abundance of such words, are clean.

The Law rightly added: “Whoever touches their carcasses shall be polluted.” The Septuagint has: “Whoever touches every uncleanness of the soul arising from their carcasses shall be unclean.” They added “of the soul,” lest you suppose that this was said about visible crawling creatures or beasts. For the one who touches the carcasses of such creatures touches uncleanness of the body, not of the soul.

The passage, therefore, is to be understood of teachers who have become unclean through some unclean and evil action. When we attend to their doctrines according to the law of God, we ought in no way to share in their works, handle them, or come into contact with them, remembering the words of the Lord, which he spoke to the people or disciples for confirmation of the present teaching: “The scribes and Pharisees have sat on Moses’ seat. Therefore do and observe everything that they tell you; but do not act according to their works” (Matt. 23).

“If it falls upon seed, it does not pollute it. But if someone pours water upon the seed and afterward it is touched by a carcass, it shall immediately be polluted.” (From the same author.)

The legislator leaves nothing unexamined but discusses everything in what follows, desiring to demonstrate the spiritual perfection of the Law, even though it appeared imperfect to those who looked only at the letter.

Here, therefore, he explains the distinction concerning unbelievers who have not yet been baptized. He calls both groups “seed,” since they have received the proclamation of the kingdom. Concerning them the Lord, presenting the parable of the seed, said: “The good seed are the children of the kingdom” (Matt. 13).

But he called the seed that has not yet been sown “seed for sowing,” as the Septuagint renders it—that is, seed that has not yet been sown but is to be sown. He rightly called those who have not yet been baptized, but are to be baptized, by this name.

If any of the carcasses mentioned above falls upon them, they are said to be clean, because they have not yet received the protection of the mysteries or acquired complete knowledge of God—knowledge that could remove from them the sins that come through negligence. For this reason they are worthy of pardon.

But if water—namely, baptismal water—has been poured upon them, they necessarily become unclean if one of the things called carcasses falls upon them. For participation in so great a gift ought to have made them responsible for guarding themselves. The Spirit of God therefore terrifies those who once received baptism, lest, by sinning through negligence, they become unclean.

“If an animal that you are permitted to eat dies, whoever touches its carcass shall be unclean until evening; and whoever eats any of it and carries it shall wash his garments and shall be unclean until evening.” (From the same author.)

Just as sinners who remain in their sins are abominable, so we must approach the righteous with every diligence, knowing that we are sanctified through them.

But if they have died through the death of a grave sin, we ought not to touch their life or share in their conduct, knowing that whoever touches them shall be unclean until he himself also repents.

Likewise, whoever eats of their carcasses—that is, whoever defends them as an advocate or helper of their sins, and consequently takes their sins upon himself—must wash his garments, namely, his actions, because he too shall be unclean until evening, that is, until he repents.

## CHAPTER IV. Concerning creeping animals.

(IBID.) “Everything that creeps upon the earth shall be an abomination and shall not be taken as food. Whatever walks on its belly among the four-footed creatures and has many feet, or is dragged along the ground, you shall not eat, because it is an abomination. Do not defile your souls, and do not touch any of them, lest you become unclean.” (From Hesychius.)

The legislator has already explained these matters above. He repeats them now in order to move the hearer, through frequent meditation, to keep the Law. For this reason we too must recapitulate them, since he has added something new to the present ordinance, imposing upon them the necessary practice of meditation.

Those that creep upon the earth are those who set their minds on earthly things and feed upon muddy actions. They likewise walk upon the breast or belly, devoting themselves to gluttony.

Those who walk on four feet upon the earth are people who abuse the preaching of the evangelical books—because salvation is preached in them for sinners—for a luxurious life. They do not understand that the preaching summons sinners not to remain sinners but to cease from sins.

To those who walk on four feet he added “and has many feet,” showing that even if they wish to confirm this not only from the evangelical books but also from other Scriptures and from various teachings, as they themselves suppose, they will still be unclean.

In short, “Everything that creeps upon the earth”—that is, everyone who sets his mind on earthly things—we must avoid and flee, knowing that association with them pollutes, and that the person who acts in such a way is likewise unclean, as is the one who joins himself to that action.

“For I am the Lord your God. You shall be holy, because I also am holy. Do not defile your souls with every creeping thing that moves upon the earth. I am the Lord who brought you out of the land of Egypt to be your God. You shall be holy, because I am holy.” (From the same author.)

He altogether forbids us to be companions of those who set their minds on earthly things—whether they are powerful, or pretend to justice or wisdom, or perhaps are clothed with priestly office or some other dignity.

Hence he briefly mentioned all the creeping things that move upon the earth. He did not reject crawling in itself, but crawling upon the earth. To be humbled is indeed good; but to incline toward earthly wisdom is not good, nor is such humility beneficial to souls.

Desiring to free us from it, he says: “I am the Lord your God”—that is, the one whose image you have been made to bear, so that you may set your minds on heavenly things. Hence he says: “Do not defile your souls.”

First, he says this because it has been granted to the soul to be made according to the image of God, and he wants the greatest sanctification to be in it, since it holds authority over every animal.

Next, he shows that the pollution he hates does not concern dead bodies or foods rendered unclean, as some think, but the pollution that comes upon souls through evil actions.

When he says that we must not defile our souls with all the creeping things that move upon the earth, he very appropriately adds: “I am the Lord who brought you out of the land of Egypt to be your God.” Through Egypt he signifies the evils of Egypt and all the works of darkness. For Egypt is interpreted as “darkening.”

If anyone truly wishes to be free from these things and to have as his God the one who truly is God, he must not merely avoid idolatry. If he truly desires to cling to him, then, because he is holy, he must also strive for holiness, without which no one shall see God.

“This is the law concerning animals and birds and every living soul that moves in the water and creeps upon the earth, so that you may know the distinctions between clean and unclean and may know what you ought to eat and what you ought to reject.” (From the same author.)

Foods do not make us clean, nor do they pollute us; rather, we make them so, since we give life to what is eaten. Just as every food is good and nothing is to be rejected when it is received with thanksgiving—for it is sanctified through the word of God and prayer, as Paul says (1 Tim. 4)—so we give life to the things that are eaten, namely, those that nourish the soul, that is, good actions, if we use them well.

But if we use them badly, we do not give them life; we put them to death. For whoever gives alms from iniquity kills the virtue or power of his almsgiving. And those who abstain from foods but slander their brothers with their tongue—of whom David says, “They devour my people as though eating bread” (Ps. 13)—these put their abstinence to death.

## CHAPTER V. How long women remain unclean after childbirth.

(Chapter 12.) “The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to the children of Israel and say to them: If a woman, having received seed, gives birth to a male, she shall be unclean for seven days, according to the days of the separation of her menstruation; and on the eighth day the little child shall be circumcised. She herself shall remain thirty-three days in the blood of her purification. She shall touch nothing holy and shall not enter the sanctuary until the days of her cleansing are completed. But if she gives birth to a female, she shall be unclean for two weeks, according to the rite of menstrual flow, and she shall remain sixty-six days in the blood of her purification.” (From Hesychius.)

In the literal sense, the woman who receives seed is the woman who conceives from the seed of a man. He says that she shall be unclean for seven days. Why is this? Clearly, because the sower is unclean, as the heir of Adam, who became unclean through transgression. Having been mingled with Eve in this condition, he made the whole human race unclean.

This is plainly read in sacred Scripture: after Adam went out from paradise, he knew his wife, and thus the human race began to be propagated. He commanded the woman to be unclean for seven days because Adam, through whose seed she received uncleanness together with the race, also polluted our life.

Alternatively, the number of seven days signifies the period through which the ages revolve. For this reason his rest too is on the seventh day, that is, the intelligible Sabbath is expected.

How did he pollute our life? By bringing a curse upon it and transferring to misery the blessedness that we had received at the beginning. This is clear from what God says to Adam: “Cursed is the earth in your works; it shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you” (Gen. 3).

Therefore the legislator now also says that she shall be unclean according to the days of the separation of menstruation, or, as the Septuagint has it, according to the days of the purification of menstruation.

Other interpreters have expressed the meaning more clearly: Symmachus says, “According to the days of the separation of affliction”; Aquila, “of the separation of misery”; Theodotion, “of the separation of her pain.”

Misery, affliction, and pain began after Adam was separated from paradise and assumed our life, in which we were condemned to eat bread in the sweat of our face.

He added a clearer and indisputable proof of this interpretation when he says: “And on the eighth day the little child shall be circumcised.” Since the eighth day follows the seventh—which is an image of the present life—it bears the figure of the future age, in which we circumcise the flesh of the foreskin by laying aside all the works of the flesh.

Then we shall not only refrain from sinning, but shall neither eat, drink, nor marry. Without doubt, we shall then be, as the Lord says, incorruptible instead of corruptible, like the angels; and in every way we shall be made clean from what was unclean.

Paul says: “It is sown in corruption; it shall rise in incorruption. It is sown an animal body; it shall rise a spiritual body” (1 Cor. 15).

This, therefore, is the reason why he commands the infant to be circumcised on the eighth day. He shows that the uncircumcised shall perish from his people, because before circumcision the flesh is abominable and unclean, for the reasons we stated above. It is cleansed through circumcision, which bears the image of the resurrection of the dead.

But it must be investigated very carefully why, when the Law commands the boy to be circumcised and makes the child himself unclean, it says that the mother is unclean until the day on which the infant is circumcised. For it commanded that he be circumcised on the eighth day, while it says that the mother is unclean for seven days.

Perhaps this is because Eve was deceived on account of disobedience, and through her transgression and disobedience she contracted uncleanness and defilement for us. Therefore the legislator transferred to the woman the greater part of this matter.

It must also be asked why, for this reason, he commanded the woman to remain in the blood of her purification—not in polluted blood, but in clean blood, that is, in the blood of her purification—as is shown in what follows: “She shall touch nothing holy and shall not enter the sanctuary until the days of her purification are completed.”

If, therefore, she remains thirty-three days in clean blood, yet touches nothing holy and does not enter the sanctuary, where shall we find the reason for this except through an examination of the number of days? He prescribed thirty-three days so that, when seven are added, the total may be forty.

(From Augustine.) What does he mean when he says concerning the woman who has given birth that she shall touch nothing holy and shall not enter the sanctuary? What sanctuary is intended, when we read that only priests ordinarily entered the tabernacle, that the second priests entered only as far as the inner veil, and that beyond that veil, where the ark was, only the one high priest entered?

Or could the area before the tabernacle, where the altar of sacrifices stood, also have been called the sanctuary? For even the court itself is often called a holy place, as when it is said: “They shall eat them in the holy place.” Perhaps women used to enter there when they offered their gifts, which were placed upon the altar.

(From Hesychius.) Through this, therefore, the legislator signifies something else. Since the male child is said to be formed over a period of forty days, two things are proved by what has been said [Col. 0369A]: first, that the substance itself of the human race is clean, just as it was created by God.

For everything that God made was very good, and human beings especially so. Therefore he says that the woman remains in clean blood, or in the blood of purification.

But because it was wounded through the succession of transgressing Adam, she necessarily received seed and conceived. She touches nothing holy and does not enter the sanctuary until the days of her purification are completed—that is, until the forty days are completed during which the child is formed.

For the image of God itself is the cleansing of our nature, although that nature has been soiled. We would certainly not have been commanded to enter the sanctuary or touch anything holy unless the image of God, once bestowed upon our race, had granted us access to holy things. For the sake of saving this image, the Lord himself also became incarnate, desiring to save his image.

But in forty days he lifted it to heaven, according to the way in which he grants it to the human being when he forms him in the womb. Then our nature enters the true sanctuary.

These points are clearly proved by the ordinances concerning the female sex. Since females are said to be formed in the womb on the eightieth day, he commanded the same number as the completion of the purification days for women who receive seed. For he says:

“If she gives birth to a female, she shall be unclean for two weeks, according to the rite of menstrual flow.”

Although he ought to have said “fourteen days,” he does not say this, but “two weeks, according to the rite of menstrual flow.” For this reason he directs us to that meaning: namely, that we should understand human life as lasting seven days, while menstrual flow signifies its affliction, pain, and misery.

He said “two weeks,” rightly, because the female sex was punished twofold. For she also bears the curse pronounced against Adam: “In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread”; she also bears the earth producing thorns and thistles; and, having arisen from the earth, she returns to the earth; and she bears a special punishment: “In sorrow you shall bear children, and your turning shall be toward your husband, and he shall rule over you.” Therefore he says, “For two weeks she shall be unclean, according to the manner of menstrual discharge; but for sixty-six days she shall sit in pure blood,” that is, in purification, “touching nothing holy, until the eighty days are completed” [Col. 0369D]. For fourteen added to sixty-six makes eighty, during which the female is formed in the womb.

Thus, without any doubt, the legislator shows that, because our race had been made unclean by the curse, it would in no way enter holy places except through the image of God, which it had once received; and for this reason women who have conceived seed are forbidden the holy things during the days of formation before childbirth. But if you say, “Why, then, are mothers who are pregnant not forbidden the holy things during the days of formation in the womb?” you ask this to no purpose. For it is uncertain to a pregnant woman whether she will bear a male or a female, and how could it have been clear for how many days she ought to be forbidden the holy things? Therefore the reason for which the legislator ordained these matters for them was made clear:

“When the days of her purification have been completed, for a son or for a daughter, she shall bring a yearling lamb for a burnt offering, and a young pigeon or a turtledove for sin, to the door of the tabernacle of testimony; and she shall deliver them to the priest, who shall offer them before the Lord and pray for her, and so she shall be cleansed from the discharge of her blood. This is the law for a woman who has borne a male or a female. But if her hand does not find sufficient means, and she cannot offer a lamb, she shall take two turtledoves or two young pigeons, one for a burnt offering and the other for sin; and the priest shall pray for her, and so she shall be cleansed.”  

(From Hesychius.)

Here the legislator has disclosed his entire intention: it is not natural processes that produce pollution, but sin, of which David said: “For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother gave birth to me” (Psalm 50). He is not accusing his mother of some sin, but calls nature “mother,” signifying that the uncleanness of the sin of Adam and Eve descended upon our whole race. Therefore, when the days of purification have been completed according to the manner stated above, he commands a sacrifice for sin to be offered.

By commanding a yearling lamb to be sacrificed as a burnt offering at that time, he clearly demonstrates and confirms to anyone who considers the matter that the image of God grants perfection to our race. The days indicate formation, while the sacrifice of the burnt offering indicates the perfection of purification.

But here, for the moment, marvel at the legislator’s wisdom. It could happen that those who studied the Law would say: “What need had a woman who had given birth to an infant for this prayer, since she herself had not sinned? For she had conceived not through fornication but from marriage.” Wishing to explain the necessity of this intercession, he added: “And he shall cleanse her from the discharge of her blood,” calling the discharge of blood disobedience, from which its uncleanness and punishment flowed upon the whole human race. Let us therefore also lay it aside, offering for ourselves the sacrifices that have been prescribed: “Two turtledoves or two young pigeons”—meditation upon the Law, contemplation, and knowledge.

It has been shown that the animals mentioned above represent these things. Since neglect of the Law introduced uncleanness among human beings, meditation and knowledge—through which correction plainly comes—can cleanse and free us from the punishment formerly imposed, in Christ Jesus our Lord [Col. 0370D].

Therefore the Lord, remembering our salvation in every respect, was willing not only to become human although he was God, but also, although he was rich, to become poor for our sake, so that by his poverty and humanity alike he might grant us participation in his riches and divinity.

But it is worth pausing briefly to consider why these particular birds were commanded to be offered as the Lord’s sacrifice. For we read that Abraham the patriarch offered them as a burnt offering to the Lord long before the time of the Law; and in many of the ceremonies of the Law, the person who was to be cleansed was commanded to be cleansed through them.

The dove therefore signifies simplicity, and the turtledove chastity. The dove is a lover of simplicity, and the turtledove of chastity, so that if it should happen to lose its mate, it does not concern itself with seeking another [Col. 0371A]. Hence the Lord says in the praises of the Church: “Your cheeks are beautiful like a turtledove’s”; and again: “Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved; behold, you are beautiful; your eyes are like doves” (Song of Songs 1).

The soul that guards itself chaste and free from every plague of impurity has cheeks like a turtledove’s. It has the eyes of doves because, desiring to harm no one, it looks even upon its enemies with simple love.

Both birds mentioned above, because they customarily utter a lament instead of a song, signify the sorrow of the saints in this world. Of this sorrow the Lord is remembered to have said: “Amen, amen, I say to you, you will weep and lament, but the world will rejoice; you will be sorrowful, but your sorrow will be turned into joy” (John 16); and again: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matthew 5).

Rightly, therefore, the turtledove and the dove are offered to the Lord as a sacrifice, because the simple and chaste conduct of the faithful is a pleasing sacrifice of righteousness to him. The one who labors in his groaning, who washes his bed with his tears each night, slaughters a victim altogether most acceptable to God.

Although both birds, because of their customary lamentation, signify the present grief of the saints and their longing for heavenly things, they nevertheless differ in this respect: the turtledove is accustomed to lament in solitude, whereas the dove laments in a flock [Col. 0372A]. The former therefore signifies the private tears of prayer, the latter the public assemblies of the Church.

Jesus the child is rightly circumcised first, and then, after the intervening days, brought to Jerusalem with the sacrifice. For he too, when he had become a young man, first trampled underfoot every corruption of the flesh by dying and rising again; and then, after the intervening days, he ascended to the joys of the heavenly city with that very flesh, now immortal, which he had made a sacrifice to God for our salvation.

Each one of us is first cleansed from all sins by the water of baptism, as by a true circumcision; and then, as the grace of the new light progresses, enters the holy altar to be consecrated through the saving sacrifice of the Lord’s body and blood. The singularly simple and chaste humanity of our Savior, which was offered to the Father for us, may likewise not inappropriately be expressed figuratively through the sacrifice of a dove or a turtledove [Col. 0372B].

At the end of the world, the whole Church will first, in the common resurrection, strip off every earthly stain of mortality and corruption; thereafter, commended to the Lord through the good works of her sacrifices, she will be transferred into the kingdom of the heavenly Jerusalem.

## BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0371]

## CHAPTER ONE

### On the various colors appearing in human flesh and on the plague of leprosy

**(Leviticus 13.)** The Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying:

“If a different color, or a pustule, or something resembling a shining mark appears in the flesh or skin of a man—that is, the plague of leprosy—he shall be brought to Aaron the priest or to one of his sons. When he sees leprosy on the skin and the hairs changed to a white color, and the appearance of the leprosy lower than the skin and the rest of the flesh, it is the plague of leprosy. He shall be separated according to his judgment.

“But if there is a shining whiteness on the skin, and it is not lower than the rest of the flesh, and the hairs retain their former color, the priest shall shut him up for seven days and examine him on the seventh day. If the leprosy has not spread farther and has not passed beyond its former boundaries on the skin, he shall shut him up again for another seven days and examine him on the seventh day. If the leprosy is darker and has not spread on the skin, he shall cleanse him, because it is a scab. The man shall wash his garments, and he shall be clean.

“But if, after he has been examined by the priest and restored to cleanliness, the leprosy again spreads, he shall be brought to him and condemned as unclean.

“If the plague of leprosy is in a man, he shall be brought to the priest, and he shall examine him. When there is a white color on the skin, the appearance of the hairs has changed, and living flesh itself has appeared, it shall be judged to be a very old leprosy, fixed in the skin. The priest shall therefore declare him unclean and shall not shut him up, because it is plainly uncleanness.

“But if the leprosy breaks out and spreads on the skin and covers the entire skin from head to feet, whatever falls under the eyes of the priest, he shall examine him and judge that he is afflicted with the purest leprosy, because it has all turned white; therefore the man shall be clean.

“But whenever living flesh appears in him, then by the priest’s judgment he shall be polluted and counted among the unclean, for living flesh, if it is covered with leprosy, is unclean. But if it again turns white and covers the whole man, the priest shall examine him and decide that he is unclean.”

(From Hesychius.)

The passage partly shows the leprous person to be the Jewish people, as transgressors of the Law in part; therefore the priest drives them out as unclean. But the person leprous over his whole body signifies the Gentile, who transgresses the whole Law; nevertheless the priest judges him clean, since he had not been subject to the yoke of the Law [Col. 0372D].

But, as I think, we must first proceed through the literal exposition. In this way we shall find the spiritual meaning presenting itself spontaneously, since the literal sense, when it fails concerning the causes and cannot extend its meaning to the end, is shown in the present passage to be inadequate.

First, let us attend to who gives the Law and to whom he gives it: “The Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron.” When God speaks, there is a twofold faithful hearing, as the prophet David says: “God spoke once; these two things I heard” (Psalm 61)—namely, the letter and the spirit.

Therefore the spirit, as the higher element, speaks to Moses; the letter, as the subordinate element, speaks to Aaron. Moses was exalted and therefore worthy of the spirit, while Aaron was subordinate and suited to the hearing of the people who needed the letter. God himself said to Moses concerning Aaron: “Learn: he shall speak to the people for you, and he shall be your mouth; but you shall be to him in the things that pertain to God” (Exodus 4).

Thus whatever was higher in the Law was addressed to Moses, for he possessed the things that pertain to God—that is, the things of the spirit. Whatever was subordinate and lower was addressed to Aaron, for he was Moses’ mouth to the people, who received the Law according to the letter. We have promised to expound that letter first.

The appearance of leprosy is either exceedingly or moderately obscure, shaded in a certain manner and hidden for the moment beneath the skin, since the disease has not yet visibly become inflamed; therefore it requires careful deliberation. Another appearance of it is exceedingly clear and entirely evident, so that its recognition is simple and open.

Of these, the first appearance the Septuagint, according to whom nearly this entire passage is expounded literally, rightly called a “scar of signification”—that is, a scar signifying a disease. They divided it into two forms, one highly doubtful and the other less doubtful. One they called *telaugi*, the other *augasma*. The *telaugi* is visible even from a distance; the *augasma*, however, is exceedingly obscure and gives only a slight, doubtful indication of the disease, requiring examination by those nearby, so that those who judge need its brightness, like people who inspect precious stones.

In this case he frequently commands the priest to examine it and not to trust the first appearances that arise or present themselves at the initial inspection [Col. 0373C].

Even if examination shows that the scar has not yet become lower than the skin, and the hair in the place has not been changed by the disease and turned white, nevertheless the person shall be separated for seven days for another examination, and again for another seven days. Perhaps, as the disease becomes inflamed with time, the illness will become more manifest. But if the scar remains obscure and no change occurs in the skin, he calls it a signification, not manifest leprosy.

He did not add what accompanies this signification, preserving it for those who receive the Law according to the spirit and who can reveal and add through contemplative interpretations of the spirit what is less or more deeply hidden. Nevertheless, they have made clear that the signification is not altogether evil.

For how would the priest cleanse him—that is, declare him clean—if he were entirely free and had no need of such a declaration? This is why he called it obscure. Nor, after judgment, would he have counted him among the clean if the signification had arisen from some evil disease.

But if the signification that had appeared on the skin should also become more extensive—if it should spread and advance more broadly on the skin than before, while the hair remained unchanged, for this the passage does not criticize—the priest pollutes him, judging the disease to be leprosy. His recognition of it is doubtful, since the scar is obscure. But if it is white and sends forth hair of the same color as the skin, the priest pollutes him and commands him to be expelled as unclean, even if part of the scar is healthy and contains living flesh [Col. 0374A]—that is, flesh not affected by the disease of leprosy.

Why is this? “Because,” he says, “the leprosy is inveterate.” This is astonishing and introduces into the legal letter either extreme ignorance or, rather, a serious objection. For from what basis should the disease be regarded as curable—from the fact that the body and flesh are alive? Yet there he gives up hope, calls it inveterate leprosy, that is, incurable but lasting, as though the disease were growing old in its place.

Concerning this matter, you will again find what follows still more obscure. He wants the one who is leprous over his whole body, covered by the disease from his feet to his head, to be regarded as clean, the priest making this judgment about him. But if living flesh should ever be seen in him, the priest reverses his judgment and pollutes him. If he turns white again and the whole skin is changed into the condition of leprosy, the priest whose duty it is to judge cleanses him.

Even if these statements are correctly made—and no one says that they are—what defense can we find against this further objection? The leper pays the penalty for a disease that he does not voluntarily choose but unwillingly endures; one who ought to receive mercy from the Law is punished. Though deserving help because of his weakness, he is deprived of it and subjected to guilt. Had he been able to resist, the disease would never have prevailed over him. Nature is blamed for what is attributed to an affliction rather than to his purpose or will. What could he do to avoid falling into this disease?

Someone may say that this disease is the vengeance or punishment of sin, citing first Miriam and then Uzziah. Miriam slandered her brother; Uzziah, although king, presumed to bring incense into the holy places, though this was permitted only to the priests. Therefore, since God did not delay their punishment, they became lepers.

The Law, then, ought to have stated this openly, in order to defend the legislator against those who think that he legislated unjustly concerning lepers. The same objection would also be made concerning those who have injured eyes or ears or other senses, and concerning other sick and paralyzed persons. This is evident from the fact that the disciples, seeing a man blind from birth, asked the Lord about him: “Rabbi, who sinned, this man or his parents, that he should be born blind?” (John 9).

But do not throw Christ’s answer back at me—I know it; rather, I am asking what views many people hold concerning the afflictions that happen to us. The Lord himself, wishing to raise up the paralytic, said: “Your sins are forgiven you” (Matthew 9).

Thus even such persons ought to have been expelled from the tabernacle as hateful to God, and injustice would seem slight if others suffered injustice along with them.

But if you say that sins are punished in every such disease—for he also forbids the man who suffers a discharge of semen from the tabernacle, as well as the woman who suffers a discharge of blood—you speak truly. Yet this is not so much a defense as another accusation against the writer, who condemns the necessities of nature, which he ought either to have defended or not to have unjustly accused the Creator in matters of nature [Col. 0374D].

Therefore we need a contemplative examination of the Law and a useful spiritual interpretation. We must place the eye of the mind before the eye of the flesh, using the former to understand what is decreed and the latter to read.

“The Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying: ‘A man on whose flesh and skin a different color, or a pustule, or something resembling a shining mark has appeared—that is, the plague of leprosy—shall be brought to Aaron the priest or to one of his sons. When he sees leprosy on the skin, the hairs changed to a white color, and the appearance of the leprosy lower on the skin than the rest of the flesh, it is the plague of leprosy, and he shall be separated according to his judgment.’”

(From Hesychius.)

In a simple or general sense, divine Scripture calls “man” the one who preserves the image of God and the dignity of our nature [Col. 0375B]. Therefore hear the wise man saying in Proverbs: “Great is a man, and precious is a merciful man.” But it describes a certain sinful man as a badly formed coin.

By the name “skin,” or “hide,” sometimes each person’s flesh is signified, and sometimes his kinship. Therefore in the Book of Job, in the person of the devil despising what happened to that exceptionally strong man—when, together with his other possessions, he destroyed his sons and daughters, piling the house over them as a tomb—it is said: “Skin for skin, and all that a man has he will give for his life” (Job 2). That is, he lost the skin of his kinship through his children, but it is enough for him that the skin of his flesh remains safe and is not at all corrupted. Therefore he adds: “But stretch out your hand and touch his bone and his flesh, and then you will see whether he will bless you to your face.”

Our edition reads: “A man on whose flesh and skin a different color, or a pustule, or something resembling a shining mark has appeared—that is, the plague of leprosy.” The Septuagint translated it: “If a scar of signification appears on a man’s bodily skin.”

The scar of signification signifies sin, revealing from what appears the hidden and concealed vice of the soul. We understand leprosy as transgression of the Law. For just as a leper, although healthy in every other respect, becomes leprous in one part and gains no benefit from the health of the body that has not become leprous, but is removed from the tabernacle as unclean, so the person who transgresses the commandments of the Law in one part gains no benefit from observing another commandment: “Whoever keeps the whole Law but sins in one point has become guilty of all” (James 2) [Col. 0375D].

He shall be brought to Aaron the priest or to one of his sons. The sons of the priest are his spiritual relations, from whom they receive the dignity of the priesthood. They are those in whom philosophy is perfected and complete, so that they can discern sublime things and judge the hidden movements of the soul.

But how do they judge? They see the leprosy on the skin and whether its hair has been changed to white, and whether the appearance of the leprosy is lower than the skin and the rest of the flesh.

By “hairs” he signifies the thoughts with which the soul is adorned and by which the mind is covered, since it itself produces these thoughts for itself. The head generates hair and is adorned and covered by it; therefore our head-hairs are said to be numbered (Matthew 10)—that is, the thoughts of the mind. The head is so called because it is the ruling part of the soul.

Why are they numbered? Without doubt, he will say that through them the Judge will judge a person: they will either accuse or excuse him, as Paul says, “when our secrets will be judged” (Romans 2).

Therefore we understand why no iron enters the head of a Nazirite, although it may harmlessly be applied to others. For those whose hair is superfluous, cutting it causes no harm and is even beneficial; but for those whose hair is not superfluous, its removal is a loss because it strips away their natural adornment.

So those for whom superfluous thoughts are troublesome are rightly deprived of them by a change of counsels or of passing imaginations, as by a tonsure [Col. 0376B]. But such thoughts are not found in the Nazirite, for he is wholly holy. Therefore iron does not ascend upon his head, since he uses good counsel and possesses necessary thoughts rather than superfluous ones. He does not cut them because he neither considers nor changes to worse things.

If, then, the hair of the person now under discussion is changed to white, turning his thought toward a shameless condition and an open form of sin, and if the appearance of the leprosy is lower than the rest of the flesh and skin—for this is what he examines—and if he sees that extreme weakness has appeared and natural strength has failed, which is what it means for the appearance of the leprosy to be lower than the skin or the rest of the flesh, the priest rightly separates him and judges him unclean, since he is sick through his own purpose and will [Col. 0376C].

But if there is a shining whiteness on the skin, not lower than the rest of the flesh, and the hair retains its former color, the priest shall shut him up for seven days and examine him on the seventh day. If the leprosy has not spread farther and has not passed beyond its former boundaries on the skin, he shall shut him up again for another seven days and examine him on the seventh day. If the leprosy is darker and has not spread on the skin, he shall cleanse him, because it is a scab. He shall wash his garments, and he shall be clean.

But if, after he has been examined by the priest and restored to cleanliness, the leprosy again spreads, he shall be brought to him and condemned as unclean.

(From Hesychius.)

Although it is clear that sin has come under suspicion, nevertheless the mind that has sinned—which is undoubtedly signified by the appearance—has not become lower than the rest of the flesh, according to the tradition of the Septuagint. That is, it has not become weaker than itself or than the condition it has received, nor has it changed its heart through the sin that occurred and become a lover of sins.

This is what is meant by saying that the whiteness is not seen to be lower than the rest of the flesh and that the hairs retain their former color. But, according to the Septuagint, the appearance is darker; and we have said that this signifies the mind. It is still obscure and uncertain because of the single sin committed, yet he does not command that it be removed. Rather, the priest removes the sinner from the tabernacle for seven days and then for the same number again, both for testing and for correction.

After this he restores him to cleanliness if, upon examining it twice, he finds the darker spot neither spreading nor increasing on the skin [Col. 0377A]. For if it had grown, the sin would have increased and passed into the rest of the flesh, and, having spread through the flesh, would have shown that the person who was progressing toward worse things was unclean.

But because it did not grow and remained as it was, the appearance or form remained similarly dark. For what is darker than iniquity? Because of it the eyes grow dim, so that we are not permitted to look clearly either toward God or toward what is expedient.

Or, if you call the darker appearance a doubtful and uncertain suspicion of sin—that is, whether it exists or not—then even this requires a priest, since he knows how to restore the person to cleanliness. He declares it slighter and brief, washing the garments with water—namely, with baptism or repentance.

For the effective water of repentance is a tear. No one errs in calling it a remnant of baptismal grace [Col. 0377B].

Thus, because this is how the matter stands, the Septuagint rendered it “a signification of the disease,” because it disclosed in part what was hidden and did not permit it to remain entirely concealed. It established the priest as having the role of a physician, who ought to apply a remedy—and indeed did apply one.

Since you know that such sin is called a signification, do not conceal the evil from the true priest, even if it is doubtful and hidden from others. Reveal and disclose it. After the priest has separated you for certain days from the holy tabernacle, he will receive you again, provided that you first wash the garment of the flesh in the proper manner, as the legislator says.

But be watchful, and after receiving forgiveness take care not to pollute yourself after having once washed the tunic of the flesh. For if, after this, the signification of the disease should again appear on the skin—or, according to our edition, should increase—and if he should fall back from the better part into sin and be changed, the priest will examine him and, finding him immediately inclined toward worse things, will condemn him as unclean [Col. 0377C].

The Septuagint follows and says that it is leprosy. For plainly the soul of such a person, turning toward profane pleasures, becomes leprous.

Therefore Paul, because the man who committed fornication at Corinth had a manifest disease that was neither hidden nor concealed, removed him from the holy tabernacle and commanded that he be handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh (1 Corinthians 5). But when he examined the disease a second time and saw that it had not increased, and that the sufferer had washed the garment of the flesh through tears of repentance, he ordered him to be received immediately.

Why the priest separates the person taken from the tabernacle for seven days not once but twice is something that diligent students ought to inquire into and understand. The Law commands this to be done twice in order to show that he must be examined not negligently but carefully, and that after a twofold test a strict judgment must be made concerning him.

The sin was evident to the priest, but when he suspected that the mind consented to the disease, he did not yet know this clearly, and therefore necessarily examined him again. For the mind is invisible and difficult to inspect.

For this reason the Lord questions Peter’s mind after his denial not once but a second and a third time, asking what his disposition was (John 21). He did not do so out of ignorance—for Peter himself plainly proves this in his answers, which he directs openly to one who knew and was ignorant of nothing—but because the Lord was searching out the disposition of his mind. He said: “Simon, son of John, do you love me?” He wished to teach us how to search and how to judge, namely, through repeated inquiry [Col. 0378A].

Nor did he establish seven days without reason, but honored as necessary for the present purpose the number that is fitting. For in the seventh day every bond and every obligation under the Law ceased.

The number seven is therefore believed to contain the fullness of the whole present life, which revolves in a cycle of seven days. When this cycle is completed, every sin, every bond of the world, and every servitude rightly cease. For this reason the seventh day is called “rest” in the divine Scriptures.

Thus Paul says concerning Moses: “He has spoken somewhere about the seventh day in this way: ‘And God rested from all his works’; and shortly afterward he adds: ‘Whoever has entered his rest has also rested from his works, just as God did from his own’” (Hebrews 4).

The Ecclesiastes also says: “Give a portion to seven, and indeed also to eight” (Ecclesiastes 11), instructing us to exercise providence concerning the present age and the future.

“If the plague of leprosy is in a man, he shall be brought to the priest, and he shall examine him. When there is a white color on the skin, the appearance of the hairs has changed, and living flesh itself appears, it shall be judged to be a very old leprosy, fixed in the skin. The priest shall therefore declare him unclean and shall not shut him up, because it is plainly uncleanness.”

(From Hesychius.)

The legislator may seem to be adding here once more what he has already explained plainly and sufficiently above, but this is not so. Although the words are similar, the intention is very different. Here he is not speaking simply of some sin, but of an open transgression of the letter of the Law; therefore he called the plague of leprosy the disease itself.

We know that we have called leprosy a transgression of the Law because it causes harm even when it is partial, just as leprosy does, although it affects only a small part of the body.

What Law do they regard as peculiar to the Jews? Not the Law concerning envy, adultery, robbery, greed, or the honoring of parents, for the Gentiles had similar laws. Rather, they regard as peculiar the Law that prescribed sacrifices and purifications: “Do not touch, taste, or handle”; the Law that commanded the flesh to be circumcised. These were its distinctive features, since they were not shared with the Gentiles [Col. 0378D].

If, then, the plague of this leprosy arises in a man, and the priest examines him and perceives a white color on his skin—a manifest transgression, openly expressed in the letter—and if he has acted deliberately and by his own judgment—for this is what is meant by the appearance of the hairs being changed to white, namely, that the mind has plainly turned toward some transgression—then, as we said above, the appearance itself contains living flesh.

This signifies that although he transgresses in one respect, he nevertheless defends the Law in other respects. He would not call it healthy flesh without reason, unless blessed Paul also seemed to have called it this. For he says: “Ordinances of the flesh were imposed until the time of correction” (Hebrews 9).

It shall be judged to be a very old leprosy. For the sin grows old and is not destroyed, because it contains within itself a continual struggle and conflict: in some matters it despises the Law, while in others it defends it.

Therefore the priest pollutes him and does not shut him up—or, as the Septuagint says, separates him—because he is plainly unclean. For how could someone who dishonors the Law be anything other than detestable and unclean, when he confirms through partial observance that the Law is necessary for him?

“But if the leprosy breaks out and spreads on the skin and covers the whole skin from head to feet, whatever falls under the eyes of the priest, he shall examine him and judge that he is afflicted with the purest leprosy, because it has all turned white; therefore the man shall be clean. But when living flesh appears in him, then by the priest’s judgment he shall be polluted and counted among the unclean, for living flesh, if it is covered with leprosy, is unclean. But if it again turns white and covers the whole man, the priest shall examine him and decide that he is unclean.”

(From Hesychius.)

We have learned that leprosy on the skin is a transgression of the letter of the Law. He rightly said “on the skin,” because the transgression of the sabbath, circumcision, or the purifications prescribed by the Law does not inflict injury upon the soul; the letter of the Law restrains the outward person.

If, then, the same leprosy covers the whole skin from head to feet, and whatever falls under the eyes of the priest causes him to declare the person clean, the meaning is this: if someone withdraws entirely from observing the letter of the Law and practices neither circumcision, nor distinctions among foods, nor observance of sabbaths, nor the works of purifications, sacrifices, or any other such matters, but withdraws from all the elements of the Law and, from head to feet—from the first to the last of these commandments—runs toward better and more perfect things, and does this in the sight of the priest, that is, Christ, then Christ, seeing the transgression of imperfect things, receives him.

He will judge him to be afflicted with the purest leprosy, because it has all turned white—that is, toward brightness. He has transferred himself to the conduct of the Gospel, like the people from the Gentiles, to whom it was said: “Let your light shine before men” (Matthew 5), and again: “Let us walk honorably as in the day” (Romans 13). For this reason they are called children of light, not of night or darkness.

“But if living flesh appears in it”—that is, the Jewish commandment, because the words of the Law are considered living not on account of those who receive them but on account of the one who gives them, and even more so on account of those who receive them if they observe them according to the manner in which they were given—it is necessary that the person who neither practices these things nor is polluted by those from which he withdrew be examined in both respects.

Let us therefore present evidence for both points. The legal commandments are called living because they are said to be so. Let us hear Stephen speaking to the Jews about Moses: “This is he who was in the assembly in the wilderness with the angel who spoke to him on Mount Sinai and with our fathers, who received living words to give to us.” There he called the ordinances of the Law “living words.”

What did he add? “Our fathers were unwilling to obey him.” They did obey insofar as the outward appearance of the letter was concerned. But he said that they did not obey the mind and intention of the lawgiver; they obeyed only the letter. Through the multitude of commandments that is regarded as uncleanness according to the Law, the person who is clean is made clean.

So also the people from the Gentiles, through the multitude and perfection of their transgression of the legal letter, are made clean by the Law itself, because they seek not the letter but the spiritual understanding of the commandment [Col. 0380A].

“If flesh and skin in which an ulcer has arisen and been healed, and in the place of the ulcer a scar appears, white or reddish, are found, the man shall be brought to the priest. When he sees that the place of the leprosy is lower than the rest of the flesh and that the hairs have turned white, he shall declare him unclean, for the plague of leprosy has arisen in the ulcer.

“But if the hair retains its former color, the scar is somewhat obscure, and the neighboring flesh is not lower, he shall shut him up for seven days; and if it has spread, he shall adjudge him to have leprosy.”

## CHAPTER TWO

### How the leper is to be shut up for a fixed period so that he may be tested by the priest
(IBID.) But if it remains in its place, it is the scar of an ulcer, and the man will be clean.

(From Hesychius.) Blessed is continual meditation on the Law and continual observance of it, always to have in one’s hands the treasure from which the riches of the knowledge of God proceed. Therefore let us also pursue with all diligence those things that are now hidden in the letter.

An ulcer that has arisen and been healed is sin cured through repentance; for what wounds the soul and fills it with blemishes as sin does? Hence David also said: “My scars have become foul and corrupt because of my foolishness” (Psalm 37). But what, in turn, heals the wound of the soul? It is repentance properly carried out. The place of this wound is the action and intention in connection with which the sin was committed. Thus, in David’s case, the place of the ulcer was bodily desire: because of it he committed both adultery with Bathsheba and the crime of murdering Uriah.

But why, after saying that the ulcer was white, does he nevertheless say that it became white or reddish? He called it white because it arises from a transgression of the legal text, calling the Law “white”; for it had not been warmed by the sun of righteousness and therefore was not red. The red, then, which comes from transgression of the Gospel, is called more evident. Yet both are in Christ, of whom the Church says in the Song of Songs: “My kinsman is white and ruddy” (Song of Songs 5). For the Law is his, and the Gospel is his.

“But what,” you ask, “is the transgression of the Law that pertains to him—namely, to Christ and his mystery?” It is the eating of food sacrificed to idols, of blood, and of what has been strangled. For although these are legal commandments, the apostles nevertheless commanded the Church to observe them, as James shows when he says: “It has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to impose no further burden upon you except these things: to abstain from things sacrificed to idols, and from blood, and from what has been strangled, and from fornication” (Acts 15).

The Gospel command, however, is that which was not according to the Law: “Whoever says to his brother, ‘Fool,’ shall be liable to judgment; and whoever looks upon a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matthew 5).

If, therefore, after the white thing has been healed and the sin cured by repentance, a white or red ulcer appears in the place of the ulcer—that is, in the region of the sin—and some aspect of the aforementioned sin, whether evangelical or legal, is found in the sinner, he necessarily comes before this judgment of the priest. If the priest sees that the place of the leprosy is lower than the rest of the flesh—that is, that the mind has been made lower than itself and the disposition manifestly changed toward wickedness—for this is what is meant by the hairs being turned white—he shall declare him unclean. For he has once become fixed in the condition of sin, and the soul’s evil feeding has settled upon the ulcer. Hence the legislator calls it leprosy, a wound, and a flourishing of the disease.

But if the hair is of its former color and the scar is somewhat dark—that is, the appearance of the penitent—and therefore he commanded him to be shut up for seven days, he wished to set a limit to the suspicion because the man had come under such suspicion. If it has grown and evil boasting has increased, he shall declare it leprosy.

He calls the leprosy of the soul impurity that has grown or flourished, multiplied by later actions. But if it has not multiplied, but has remained in its place—for he is found to have committed no further sin in this matter beyond the one that all knew about, for which he also performed penance—the priest judges him clean. For the scar of a wound shows that he has suffered, not that he is still suffering.

## CHAPTER III. On the plague of leprosy caused by a burn, or on the scar, and so forth

[Column 0381C] (IBID.) “The flesh and skin that fire has burned, and which, after healing, has a white or red scar, the priest shall examine. If it has become white and its place is lower than the surrounding skin, he shall declare him unclean, because the plague of leprosy has arisen in the scar. But if the color of the hairs has not changed, the plague is not lower than the surrounding flesh, and the appearance of the leprosy itself is somewhat dark, he shall shut him up for seven days. On the seventh day he shall examine him. If the leprosy has grown in the skin, he shall declare him unclean. But if the whiteness remains in its place, not sufficiently distinct, it is the plague of a burn; therefore he shall be clean, because it is the scar of a burn.”

(From Hesychius.) Some think that the legislator is speaking here of the same things as before, but that is not so. In one respect he says the same thing, but in another he differs, since he introduces a different disease while nevertheless applying the same judgment concerning the disease.

Above he spoke of an ulcer that occurs, which is produced by an illness of the body and progresses; for Scripture commonly calls such things ulcers. But injuries caused by iron, stones, or some other blow it calls plagues and wounds. Thus, concerning Lazarus, it says that dogs came and licked his ulcers (Luke 16); those wounds were in fact wounds of clean flesh corrupted by hunger and disease. Concerning the man who went down from Jerusalem to Jericho and fell among robbers, it says that they “inflicted wounds on him and departed” (Luke 10). Shortly afterward it prescribes that the Samaritan bind those wounds as injuries. Thus the divine Spirit himself clearly shows through the Scriptures the distinction between an ulcer and a wound or plague.

What, then, is truly the ulcer of our neglected flesh except bodily pleasure, drunkenness, and gluttony? These arise when the body luxuriates and leaps beyond itself. Fire, however, is greater envy—a hidden fire that gradually consumes the one who possesses it. Therefore Isaiah also said: “Jealousy has seized the unlearned people, and now fire consumes the adversaries” (Isaiah 26). He called the jealousy of the ignorant envy. For they are jealous not in order to imitate virtues, but to obstruct them and destroy what is being accomplished.

If, then, a burning caused by envy has befallen someone—that is, a sinner—and he has been healed by repentance, the scar is examined, lest after repentance he fall back into the disease. If the priest finds that it has returned, he shall declare him unclean, rightly judging him impure.

For the earth that often drinks in the rain falling upon it and produces suitable vegetation for those by whom it is cultivated receives a blessing from God; but when it produces thorns and thistles, it is rejected and near to a curse, whose end is burning, as Paul says (Hebrews 6). If, however, envy is not found to have returned to its former wickedness, nor the earlier ulcer to have spread more widely through later activity, the priest judges him clean, since he has once been cleansed through repentance. He also examines the hair to see whether it has changed to white and whether the place is lower than the skin. We have interpreted all these matters fully above; therefore brevity must now be used, so that we may hasten toward what follows.

It continues:

“Whether man or woman has leprosy growing on the head or beard, the priest shall examine him. If the place is lower than the surrounding flesh and the hair is yellow and thinner than usual, he shall declare them unclean, because it is leprosy of the head and beard. But if he sees that the place of the blemish is level with the surrounding flesh and the hair is black, he shall shut them up for seven days. On the seventh day he shall examine them. If the blemish has not grown, the hair is of its own color, and the place of the plague is level with the rest of the flesh, the man shall be shaved, except for the place of the blemish, and shall be shut up for another seven days. If on the seventh day the plague appears to have remained in its place and is not lower than the surrounding flesh, he shall declare him clean. After washing his clothes, he shall be clean” (from Hesychius).

The Law gave this command not concerning just any matters, but concerning necessary ones. It did not pertain only to actions, but also to future divine doctrines. Whenever someone happens to err concerning divinity, he has the blemish of leprosy in his beard and on his head. The priest must examine him. If he sees that the place is lower than the surrounding flesh, and that a more miserable presumption has arisen from blasphemy, how does this happen? It means that the hair is yellow and thinner than usual: even if he has not directed his mind intensely toward blasphemy, he has nevertheless directed it toward it to some small degree. For the hair’s being thin and not flourishing but turning yellow indicates this. The priest shall declare them unclean.

Why? Because it is leprosy of the head and beard—or, as the Septuagint reads, “a wound.” For he has been wounded and struck down by the devil and has reached such impiety.

Since it often happens that someone speaks impiously even against his will, if the priest sees that the place of the blemish is level with the surrounding flesh and the hair is black, so that the wound inflicted upon the soul by demonic activity—that is, the impiety of his doctrines—has not increased, he shall shut them up for seven days. This is not so much for punishment as for strict examination. Time is required in every case, but especially in the case of those whose tongue is occupied with matters concerning the Deity.

Next we must observe how he judges after the period of confinement. The strictness that he preserves against those who act impiously in their doctrines is remarkable. If the blemish—that is, the impiety—has not grown, and the hair is of its own color, meaning that it is not yellow, then, since his thought cannot be known from the denial whether he acted impiously voluntarily or unwillingly, he commands that the man be shaved except for the place of the blemish. He therefore plainly commands that the other hair be shaved and the man disciplined, so that it may perhaps be discovered from him whether he spoke impiously about God through inadvertence, as frequently happens, or maliciously.
