He did not command the old wound to be shaved, because when someone who has sinned once denies the word in which he sinned, it should no longer be judged. For who would judge as guilty of sin the man who denies that he uttered voluntarily what his tongue confessed?

When, judging him in this way, the priest does not find that the blemish has grown and does not see that the impiety has spread in him, then, since the blasphemer has utterly polluted the garment of baptism, he rightly commands him to wash his clothes through repentance, and then he will be clean, because every impiety is cleansed through pure repentance.

Nevertheless, if, after being cleansed in the prescribed manner, he again speaks impiously, the priest does not examine the yellow hair. He does not ask, he says, with what intention he spoke impiously; rather, because he has fallen again into the things for which he repented, he rightly judges him unclean. This is so if the hair is not black—that is, if he does not appear to be mourning his impiety. Mourning belongs not only to one’s outward appearance but also to one’s disposition and thoughts; for it is characteristic of mourners to remain black.

Since the inner person, whom thoughts affect [or, according to the variant, cover: *contegunt*], ought to mourn for sins, he rightly signified his repentance by the black hair. Having spoken sufficiently about the impieties committed against God, whether voluntarily or through ignorance, he now turns his speech to other and milder wounds.

“A man or woman on whose skin whiteness appears: the priest shall examine them. If he detects a somewhat dark whiteness shining in the skin, he shall know that it is not leprosy, but a spot of white color, and the person is clean.”

(From Hesychius.) Since above he had exercised the greatest strictness concerning divine doctrines and their transgressions, now that he has completed his discussion of them, he rightly lays aside the severity of his strictness.

He is speaking both of doctrines according to Jewish Law and of the faults found in them, saying that they are a somewhat dark and shining whiteness. Just as we said that the white scar signifies transgression of the legal text, so let us understand its ignorance as a somewhat dark and shining whiteness.

He does not mean ignorance of everything the Law says, nor of those things that it shares with natural law or with the evangelical commandments. For no one is excused for being ignorant that one must not kill, commit adultery, or steal. Rather, he means ignorance of certain particular and minor commandments—for example, when a menstruating woman must be purified, when an offering must be made for one who has given birth to a male child, and when one has given birth to a female child. For this reason he called it a somewhat dark whiteness, since it possesses the small scars of ignorance concerning particular commandments.

A person of this kind does not need to be cleansed. These commandments were not handed down for the justification of the Jews, but to make their yoke heavier. Therefore God also said through the Prophet: “I gave them statutes that were not good and judgments by which they would not live” (Ezekiel 20).

## CHAPTER IV. On the man whose hair falls from his head

(IBID.) “The man from whose head the hair falls is bald and clean. If the hair falls from his forehead, he is front-bald and clean. But if a white or red color appears on the baldness or front-baldness, and the priest sees it, he shall certainly declare him unclean with the leprosy that has arisen in the baldness.”

We must remember that we have understood the hairs as thoughts.

(From Hesychius.) The hairs were established to adorn and cover the head, just as thoughts adorn and cover the mind. We should not, however, bring disordered thoughts into the discussion, since the disorder of the hair makes the head appear ugly instead of adorned. Moreover, just as some hairs fall while others grow again and never cease growing, so, when the thoughts within us fall away, others grow again.

Here, therefore, he calls a simple person bald—not someone who is entirely foolish or irrational. For who is there who does not have at least a few hairs on his head? He describes the person who, through simplicity, possesses few thoughts, and rightly commands that he be clean. For just as he considers entirely simple the one who is wholly simple, so also he considers clean the one who is simple in part.

He especially means the person whose simplicity is shown in the hair falling from the forehead—that is, becoming sparse—and whom he also calls front-bald. This person is worse than the former. It is better to conceal virtues; if someone reveals their glory, however, the condition is tolerable and near to pardon, and therefore he will be clean.

For divine Scripture says that virtues are revealed openly and before human beings according to their outward appearance, and that through them a person is adorned. Consider Paul’s words: “You look at things according to their outward appearance. If anyone is convinced that he belongs to Christ, let him consider this again within himself: just as he belongs to Christ, so also do we” (2 Corinthians 10).

This applies if no sin is committed through the simplicity of the simple person. But if a white or red blemish appears on his baldness or front-baldness, it is leprosy.

Why? Because no one is so simple that he does not know that he must not put his hand into the fire, throw himself from a precipice, or use a sword against vital parts. If he knows these things, how could he not also know that killing is evil, slander is worst of all, eating food sacrificed to idols is impious, and desiring another man’s wife is wicked?

If, then, the priest finds a man with a white or red blemish on his baldness or front-baldness—that is, in the simplicity that is complete or partial—and finds that he has transgressed the evangelical or legal norm, he shall condemn him or declare him unclean.

Why? Because without doubt leprosy has arisen in the baldness—or, as the Septuagint says, “his blemish is on his head.” That is, he has sinned in serious and necessary matters, in which no sinner deserves pardon. For the natural law, toward which the necessary commandments of the Law tend, and much more the evangelical commandments, are not foreign even to simple souls.

It continues:

“Whoever is marked by leprosy and separated at the priest’s discretion shall have torn garments, his head uncovered, and his mouth covered with a garment. He shall proclaim himself unclean and impure for as long as he is a leper, and he shall dwell alone outside the camp.”

(From Hesychius.) The interpretation of the literal meaning that concerns outward appearance seems altogether ridiculous to many people. For what benefit is there in tearing one’s clothes, having one’s head uncovered, or covering one’s mouth? Nor does the bodily leper who gives off the smell of decay cover his mouth for this reason.

But because the legislator understood the leper to be the person who is unclean through the sins mentioned above, he necessarily commanded that his garments be torn, so that this might reveal that he possesses virtues and powers of the soul that are torn apart—virtues and powers that could have protected him from the heat and cold of sin.

He also commanded that the man have his head uncovered, since he does not possess the helmet of salvation, which Paul commands us to take up among the intelligible weapons (Ephesians 6). Nor did he command that the mouth be covered without reason. Sin is of evil odor and emits every kind of foul breath, but it possesses especially the breath that comes through the tongue. At the same time, the legislator excludes such a person from the dignity of a teacher. For how can one restrain the fall into guilt when one is oneself guilty? How can the thief command others not to steal, or the adulterer command them not to commit adultery?

Hence David also said: “But to the sinner God said: Why do you recount my righteous acts and take up my covenant in your mouth? Yet you hate discipline and cast my words behind you” (Psalm 49).

And indeed he is to remain so always—that is, for the entire time during which he is a leper, for all the days in which the blemish remains in him. What, then, does this signify? Even if he has sinned only once and has not added further sins, he is nevertheless called unclean until he repents, because without repentance the leprosy of sin is never completely cleansed. Therefore the intelligible blemish of leprosy remains in him.

Moreover, the true leper—that is, the sinner—dwells alone and separated, both so that he may be put to shame and so that no one may be harmed by the contagion of his association. Therefore the Lord said to Peter concerning one who had sinned and was refusing to obey the Church, so that he might be converted and corrected: “Let him be to you as a Gentile and a tax collector” (Matthew 18).

“He shall dwell outside the camp.” The commandments of the Law are greatly consonant with the evangelical commandments according to the spirit. Therefore John, separating the intelligible leper from the intelligible tabernacle, writes in the Catholic Epistle: “Whoever comes to you and does not bring this doctrine, do not receive him into your house, and do not say ‘Hail’ to him” (2 John 10).

And so that all these matters may be more easily grasped in memory, I think they should be briefly recapitulated. In certain places, in accordance with what we have found in the sayings of other holy preachers, the wording has been altered while the meaning remains directed throughout toward the same mystery.

Leprosy is false doctrine. Accordingly, lepers may appropriately be understood as heretics, who, lacking the unity of true faith, profess various doctrines of error and mingle falsehoods with truths, just as leprosy disfigures human bodies by varying true and false locations.

We find that the legislator established six kinds of this leprosy in human beings: first, that of the head and beard; second, that of baldness and front-baldness; third, that of flesh and skin; fourth, that of the skin of the body; fifth, that of a white scar with redness and of an ulcer and scar; sixth, that of a burn.

The person who sins against the divinity of the Father, or against the very Head, which is Christ, bears leprosy on his head: “The head of the man is Christ” (1 Corinthians 11). The Jews, Valentinians, Marcionists, Fabians, Manichaeans, Arians, Sabellians, Macedonians, Anthropomorphites, Priscillians, Donatists, Nestorians, Eutychians, and all who hold some perverse opinion concerning the apostles and saints of Christ and falsely claim that they preached some error bear this leprosy on the head.

For just as the beard is an ornament of a man, so the apostles and teachers of Christ are the ornament of Christ’s body.

Those who slander the Church bear leprosy on the body: for example, the Carpocratians, who deny the resurrection of the flesh; the Novatians, who condemn marriage and deny repentance to sinners; the Heraclites, who, among their other errors, do not believe that little children possess the kingdom of heaven; and the Arians,

[Note: This is how it stood in the manuscript; in Isidore’s printed text it is “Eritiani,” but I think “Aeriani” should be read, since this was their heresy.]

who forbid offering sacrifice for the dead.

Those who attempt to persuade people toward carnal or external things bear leprosy in the flesh and skin—for example, the Corinthians, who imagine the future resurrection in bodily pleasure; or the Arians, who say that for those who remain in the faith, sins cannot be counted against them even if they live carnally.

The person who, after the ulcer has been healed, bears leprosy in the scar displays, after acquiring knowledge and receiving God’s healing and the manifestation of the faith he embraced in Christ, some sign of his former error or the unbelief of his old doctrine in that very scar.

The person who bears leprosy in living flesh holds some false opinion concerning the soul, which is the life of the flesh. Such are the Luciferians, who say that the soul is propagated from the substance of the flesh, and the Arabians, who think that the soul dies together with the body.

The Manichaean heretics bear leprosy in the scar of a burn. Through the torment of empty abstinence they burn their bodies and, through unbelief rather than purity, produce leprosy from it.

The Apostle preached against such people: “Some will depart from the faith, giving attention to deceitful spirits and doctrines of demons, speaking lies in hypocrisy and having their conscience seared, forbidding marriage and requiring abstinence from foods that God created to be received” (1 Timothy 4).

He also added the colors of leprosy: pale, red, white, livid, black, and flourishing.

When he speaks of pale leprosy, he signifies a weak and fragile faith of the soul. Having lost the color of sound health, the person languishes through the weakness of error.

When he displays red leprosy, he signifies and brands the mind as stained by the blood of murder.

When he speaks of white leprosy, he means those heretics who call themselves clean, or others who glory in a false merit, such as Pelagius and Novatian.

When he mentions black or livid leprosy, he condemns the marks of envy and rancor.

When he indicates black leprosy, he detests a conscience blackened by the smoke of sacrifices and the pyre of idolatry.

When he says that leprosy is flourishing over the whole body and covering the entire skin from head to foot, he displays the crime of greed. For in the present age it is thought splendid and pleasant to be considered happy in this world and rich in this age. This disease of greed repeatedly stains every class of human beings, as though it were the entire body, through the contagion of this error.

When he speaks of leprosy that has redness mixed with paleness, he signifies the person who, though weak in mind and deceitful, easily erupts into fury and quickly perishes through fickleness of character. Pallor signifies a lying tongue; redness reveals anger.

There is, therefore, a leprosy of sin that is cleansed by sacrificial offerings—that is, by a contrite and humbled heart: “A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit” (Psalm 50).

There is also the leprosy of idolatry, which is washed away by the water of baptism.

There is also the leprosy of heretics, which is held to require seven days of purification outside the camp—that is, it is purified through recognition of the sevenfold Spirit.

There is also a leprosy removed by the priest’s examination through teaching.

But the kind of leprosy that cannot be cleansed at all belongs to those who sin against the Holy Spirit and do not affirm that penitents can obtain forgiveness. Concerning them the Truth says: “Whoever sins against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come.”

When lepers are commanded to leave the camp and sit outside until their leprosy is cleansed, this means that heretics must be expelled from the Church until they are purified from their own error and thus return to the Lord.

Such a person is commanded to sit with torn tunics, his head uncovered, and his mouth covered, awaiting the cleansing of his leprosy: with torn tunics, meaning that all his secrets have been exposed; with his head uncovered, so that his crime may be seen by everyone; with his mouth closed, so that he may no longer teach or speak impiously.

## CHAPTER V. On the leprosy of garments, warp, and woof

[Column 0388A] (IBID.) “A woolen or linen garment that has leprosy in the warp or woof, or a skin or anything made from skin: if it has been infected with a white or red blemish, it shall be reckoned as leprosy and shall be shown to the priest. After examining it, he shall shut it up for seven days. On the seventh day, looking again, if he finds that it has grown, it is persistent leprosy. He shall judge the garment polluted, and everything in which it is found, and therefore it shall be burned in the flames.

“But if he sees that it has not grown, he shall command that the object in which the leprosy is found be washed. He shall shut it up for another seven days. When he sees that its former appearance has not returned, yet that the leprosy has not grown, he shall judge it unclean and burn it in the fire, because the leprosy has penetrated the surface of the garment or the whole of it.

“But if the place of the leprosy is darker after the garment has been washed, he shall tear it away and separate it from the sound material. If it appears again in those places that were previously unblemished, it is a flying and spreading leprosy and must be burned in the fire. If it ceases, he shall wash a second time the parts that are clean, and they will be clean.

“This is the law of the leprosy of woolen and linen garments, of warp and woof, and of every leather object: how they are to be cleansed or declared unclean.”

(From Hesychius.) Some perhaps think the legislator undignified and excessively low-minded because he speaks about the warp and woof, which are commonly called the woven fabric, while leaving aside whatever things might shape the souls of those who hear the Law toward better things.

“What harm,” they ask, “can a stained warp, a leprous woof or woven fabric, or a leather vessel with a blemish do to our life?” Therefore we must not attend only to the letter, but to the fruit of the Spirit, which, just as it is guarded beneath the leaf, is guarded beneath the letter of the legal vine.

Our legislator takes such care for us that he makes us cautious not only about the leprosy that arises from the sins already mentioned, but also about the leprosy that frequently arises even around virtues when someone uses them wrongly.

Some garments, then, belong to the soul, and others to the body. Neither their soiling nor their removal causes grief. For how do matters such as Joseph’s being stripped of his garments by the Egyptians pertain to these things? Or how does John the Baptist’s being clothed in camel’s hair pertain to them? The garments of the soul, however, ought to be clearer.

Solomon said concerning them: “Let your garments always be white” (Ecclesiasticus 9). David also said: “All the glory of the king’s daughter is within, clothed with golden fringes and variegated ornaments” (Psalm 44). He asserts that the soul’s beauty is an inward glory, in golden fringes, which evidently signify virtues.

Some of these garments are woolen and some are linen. Wool is precious, great, and greatly warms the soul; linen is cheap and provides little warmth.

The woolen garment of the soul is virginity; the linen garment is marital chastity. Wool is abstinence from earning or possessing wealth; linen is generosity in distributing acquired possessions. Wool is the philosophy of the desert; linen is propriety or modesty in the city. Wool is striving for the truth even unto death; linen is not speaking falsehood.

Therefore Solomon, symbolically asserting that the Church is clothed in both kinds, said: “She sought wool and flax, and worked with the skill of her hands” (Proverbs 31). Again: “She made for herself a covering; fine linen and purple are her clothing.”

Since the legislator mentions the warp and woof from which garments are woven, let us now explain their subtle meaning. For he desires us to examine not only the virtues, but also that from which they are constituted.

These two things procure true virtue for us: our intention and the divine will or grace. The woof signifies our intention; the warp signifies God’s will. And rightly so. The warp is firmer in a garment, just as God’s will or grace remains unbroken and unchanging within us, supporting the woof of our intention so that the garment of good action may be completed.

By skins—things from which something can be made—he means temptations endured for piety or faith, and tribulations endured for virtue. Why? Because, just as a dead skin can be made into a vessel—perhaps a wineskin, a jar, a bed covering, a tabernacle covering, or something else useful—so tribulations and temptations mortify a person in this world.

They humble him and show him to have been brought very low; yet from them a good and useful vessel is made: endurance and testing, which the Lord invariably crowns.

That skins may appropriately be called tribulations and temptations, hear Job speaking of his tribulations and temptations: “My bone clung to my skin, my flesh having been consumed; and only my lips around my teeth were left. Have pity on me, have pity on me, at least you, my friends, for the hand of the Lord has touched me” (Job 19).

He therefore forbids [pride], whether in perfect virtue—which is a garment—or in virtue that is great or moderate. We said that the difference between woolen and linen garments consists in the appearance of a white or red blemish, or, as the Septuagint reads, a greenish or fiery one.

He calls pride greenish and vainglory fiery. For this was the transgression of the angels, since Christ everywhere commanded that virtues be free from vainglory. He commands us neither to fast nor to show mercy in order to please human beings, and he declares that those who act in this way lose their reward.

For those who wish to be praised by human beings—how can they expect to be praised by the Lord?

Pride is understood as green because it flourishes for a short time, like green vegetation, so that David said: “I saw the ungodly exalted and raised high like the cedars of Lebanon; then I passed by, and behold, he was no more” (Psalm 36). Again, concerning the same people: “They shall fall like grass, and wither quickly like the green plants” (ibid.).

Thus it is plainly proved that he forbids pride or vainglory to cling to virtue.

Nor does he wish the leprosy that has been mentioned to occur in the warp or woof—that is, he does not want us to direct our virtues with pride or vainglory, nor to ask God to grant us such grace. The legislator also does not wish us to endure temptations together with any of these things.

If such a thing should perhaps happen to a person, he wants the priest to examine it. He commands that neither the virtue, nor the intention of virtue, nor endurance in temptation be immediately rejected, but that it be declared unclean and marked by suspicion of pride or vainglory. Nor, again, does he want it regarded as clean; rather, he commands that it be separated for seven days and that the disease be discerned over time.

If it has grown, all the things in which this has occurred are unclean, because the leprosy is persistent. Therefore he commands that it be burned in the flames. This signifies the flame of Gehenna and recalls the future age. For he did not say, “It is burned in the fire,” but, “It will be burned in the fire.”

But if, after the period of confinement, he sees that it has not grown, he shall command that the object in which the leprosy is found be washed. That is, he commanded that it be cleansed through repentance.

Then, after the washing, he again commands it to be shut up for seven days, so that it may be determined whether he finds the blemish of pride or vainglory still remaining. Although it has not grown, it is nevertheless unclean because it has remained unchanged and has not moved toward repentance, and it will be burned in the fire.

For the disease has been strengthened. Therefore the person neither wishes to correct the evil in his virtue nor to direct his attention to it. If the place of the leprosy is darker—that is, if the leprosy is uncertain and doubtful—then, after the garment has been washed through repentance, he commands that the disease be cut away from the garment of virtue and from the other things mentioned above.

How does he cut away pride? By humbling himself exceedingly. Similarly, he must remove vainglory from himself in every way, so that he neither delights nor rejoices in honors, from which the disease of pride is nourished, nor in praises, by which vainglory grows. He must conduct himself in such a way that he does not even fall under suspicion of either one. Then he will be able to be clean.

But if it appears again in those places that were previously stained—that is, in the garment, the woof, the warp, or the skin, meaning in the virtue itself or in the temptations he continues to endure—and if he continues in the same disease for which he was washed or repented, he is judged unclean. The fire of Gehenna receives him, because the leprosy is flying and spreading.

For what was once cleansed of the blemish—that is, after he was once cleansed from suspicion—must be washed again, so that only then may he be called clean.

Thus the legislator most clearly suggests that you should understand this: he wishes a person to repent of the same sin with frequent tears. For frequent remembrance neither allows the wound itself to prevail nor [the source breaks off].

(MAURUS.) Again, in another way: Leprosy in a linen garment can signify loving perversity of conduct in the mind. Hence, under the appearance of justice, some rage against sinners more than they ought, driving them toward despair rather than toward healing, contrary to the Apostle, who says: “Bear one another’s burdens” (Galatians 6). Leprosy in a linen garment signifies those who, out of flattery, do not wish to correct offenders but consent to those who do evil; or, certainly, those who live softly and do not strive to act manfully. Leprosy in the warp can signify the vices of the soul, because just as the warp supports the work of the weaver, so the soul makes the body stand and flourish. [Col. 0391A] Leprosy in the woof, however, consists of sins committed through the body, for the soul subsists in the body as the warp does in the woof. The skin, on the other hand, is external life and the carnal conduct of human beings; hence the Lord is said to have made tunics of skins for Adam and his wife after the sin. Leprosy in the skin is an evil example in the conduct of this life, through which the uneducated are led into error. (From Hesychius.) Since, therefore, the lawgiver also prescribed purifications for stains that arise in virtues, now learn by what means he cleanses the leprous person. For if you consider his intention, you will find that the lawgiver was concerned with that leprosy which is inflicted upon our souls through sins.

## CHAPTER VI. On the offerings to be presented for the cleansing and purification of the leprous person

(CHAPTER 14.) And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: This is the rite of the leprous person when he is to be cleansed: He shall be brought to the priest. The priest, having gone outside the camp and found that the leprosy has been cleansed, shall order the person being purified to offer on his own behalf two living sparrows that may lawfully be eaten, together with cedarwood, scarlet thread, and hyssop. He shall command one of the sparrows to be slaughtered in an earthen vessel over living water. The other sparrow, still alive, together with the cedarwood, scarlet, and hyssop, he shall dip in the blood of the slaughtered sparrow; with it he shall sprinkle the person who is to be cleansed seven times, so that he may rightly be purified, and he shall release the living sparrow, so that it may fly away into the open country.

When the man has washed his clothes, he shall shave all the hair of his body and bathe in water. Then he shall be clean and may enter the camp, but only on the condition that he remain outside his tent for seven days. On the seventh day he shall shave the hair of his head, his beard, his eyebrows, and all the hair of his body; and after washing his clothes and his body again, and so forth.

(From Hesychius.) Since we must not suppose that the lawgiver says anything carelessly, you must note above all that now, when he legislates concerning purifications, he addresses Moses alone, and not Aaron also, as earlier. According to the many modes of interpretation that have been mentioned, Moses especially bears the image of Christ; but the cleansing of common leprosy belongs to Christ alone. For this reason he does not speak of a leprosy of one particular kind, such as that which occurs in a wound, or in a burn, or in some other way; rather, he says: “This is the rite of the leprous person.” [Col. 0391D] By this he wishes to embrace every form of leprosy, because Christ cleansed every kind of sin.

The present subject, therefore, is exceedingly similar to his mystery. We learn this from the fact that the lawgiver commanded the leprous person not to go to the priest, but for the priest to go to him; and he commanded the person who was to be cleansed to be brought in the same way that Christ also came to us, and to those who needed to be cleansed and washed by him. He commanded the priest to go outside the camp to examine the person who was to be cleansed, just as Christ visited us outside the camp through the passion of the cross and through the dispensation then accomplished.

He did not undertake this before he saw that the stain of leprosy had been healed by him—that is, before he saw that we had been freed from error. [Col. 0392A] When not only people from the Jewish multitude believed in him, but also Gentiles came up wishing to see him, and the disciples announced this to him, he said: “The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified” (John 12). When he saw that the human race had been prepared for liberation and salvation through the cross—for he also called this his glory—what did he take up? Two living sparrows that might lawfully be eaten.

Christ possessed these two things, namely divinity and humanity, for Christ’s humanity too is clean and living. It is clean because it had no personal sin; it is living because it was not begotten from a man’s uncleanness, and therefore was not subject to the curse of death.

“He shall take,” he says, “cedarwood,” that is, the cross. Cedar signifies this because cedar is strong among woods. It is also asserted that the ark was made of cedarwood, because Moses mentioned imperishable woods in its construction. He shall also take scarlet, which the Septuagint render as twisted scarlet—that is, the passion. Scarlet is so called because of its dye resembling blood; hence, when he was being led to his passion, the soldiers clothed him in a scarlet cloak. Why did they call it twisted? Because of the union of passibility and impassibility, for in a certain manner passion belonged to him. Hyssop, on account of its good fragrance, is the Spirit cooperating in our purification. Hence David says: “You shall sprinkle me with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed” (Psalm 50).

Concerning the sparrows, which we have said signify Christ, the lawgiver commanded that this one be slaughtered or killed—that is, the one that was passible and could be killed—and that it be killed in an earthen vessel over living waters. For we are an earthen vessel, made from clay; the Only-Begotten, according to the flesh, is killed over living waters, that is, over baptism. His death represents our baptism, as Paul shows when he says: “All of us who were baptized in Christ were baptized into his death” (Romans 6).

In this the living sparrow, the cedarwood, the twisted scarlet, and the hyssop are dipped. All these things are comprehended in the power of baptism, which we have said is a figure and sign of the Lord’s passion. But the living sparrow, which we necessarily understand as the divinity of the Only-Begotten, is dipped both in the blood of the sparrow that was killed and in the water—that is, in the grace of baptism—because we are baptized not into the passion of a human being, but into that of God and man.

After this, the living sparrow is released to fly into the open country. The impassible divinity, therefore, was inseparable from the flesh that suffered. Thus, we are baptized in the blood of the one described as “separable” [reading uncertain], so that the living, impassible one may fly into the open country. It is sent up, so to speak, to the height of contemplation. When our understanding releases it, it is held under this contemplation, detained voluntarily alone, since it cannot be detained by anyone else.

Moreover, the person who has been cleansed washes his clothes—that is, his actions and whatever virtues he may have had—for sin has polluted these also.

He washes through repentance and shaves the hair, that is, he lays aside every thought, because all his thoughts had been unclean. After being washed in the water of repentance or baptism, he is then necessarily cleansed. Although the text earlier called him clean—for it says, “When he appears to have been cleansed, he shall bring two sparrows”—it was speaking of one who was suited for cleansing. For how can someone who is already clean still need to be cleansed?

Then he shall enter the camp, so that he may participate in our assembly, become a companion in intelligible intercourse, and obtain the fruit of that other communion which is held with the faithful. Since sinners who have not yet been cleansed are prohibited from this communion, hear the Apostle saying: “If anyone who is called a brother is an adulterer, or greedy, or a slanderer, or a drunkard, or a robber, with such a one do not even take food” (1 Corinthians 5).

Nevertheless, he remains outside his tent for seven days, still separated from communion with the holy for the sake of more subtle vigilance and gradual advancement toward better things. The tent of each one of us is the attainment of the mysteries: the tent that protects us from frost and heat, the tent in which one dines with God as sons with a father, or as a bride with a bridegroom—or whatever else may be said that more closely expresses the intimacy of kinship.

“On the seventh day you shall shave the hair of your head, your beard, your eyebrows, and all the hair of your body.” Here he commanded that not only the head be shaved, but also the beard, the eyebrows, and, quite simply, every hair on the whole body, including the hair of the hidden parts. He therefore does not wish any old thought to remain in him: [Col. 0393C] not only those thoughts that provide a rational human being with adornment while he debates many matters of various kinds—for these he signifies by the head, on account of its adornment and abundance—but not even those thoughts that make a person contemplative, thinking about lofty and divine matters. This is signified by the eyebrows, which are situated higher up and remain around the organs of the contemplative senses. Nor does he wish to retain those thoughts that contain discernment, rightly signified by the beard, since the beard chiefly distinguishes the male sex from the female.

He gave this command not merely because he wished the man to be without thought, but because he wished him to become wholly new, as though newly born, and to strip off the old man in order to put on the new. For just as new and fresh hair grows for someone who has shaved off the old, so, for one who has shed his former thoughts, new thoughts spring up toward better things.

He is also to wash his clothes again—that is, to make his actions clean—and wash his body again with water. This is a second washing, but for us there is no second baptism: “One Lord, one faith, one baptism” (Ephesians 4). And how is he washed a second time, except plainly through tears? This may be done not once or twice, but a third time and frequently, for David also said: “My tears have been my bread day and night” (Psalm 41).

The text continues:

“He shall take two unblemished male lambs, and one unblemished year-old ewe, and three-tenths of fine flour as a grain offering mixed with oil, and separately one log of oil. When the priest who purifies the man has stationed him, together with all these things, before the Lord at the entrance of the tent of meeting, he shall take one lamb and offer it as a guilt offering, together with the log of oil. After presenting all these things before the Lord, he shall slaughter the lamb where the sin offering and the burnt offering are ordinarily slaughtered, that is, in the holy place. For just as the sin offering belongs to the priest, so also does the guilt offering; it is most holy.

“The priest shall take some of the blood of the guilt offering that was slaughtered and place it on the tip of the right ear of the person being cleansed, and on the thumbs of his right hand and right foot. From the log of oil he shall pour into his own left hand, dip his right finger into it, and sprinkle it seven times before the Lord. What remains of the oil he shall pour from his left hand onto the tip of the right ear of the person being cleansed, and onto the thumbs of his right hand and right foot, and onto the blood that was shed for the guilt offering, and onto his head. He shall pray for him before the Lord, and offer the sin offering. Then he shall slaughter the burnt offering and place it on the altar with its grain offerings, and the man shall be duly cleansed.”

(From Hesychius.) After he commanded that, on the first day on which the priest went outside the camp, a sacrifice be slaughtered for the cleansing of the leprous person, behold, now on the eighth day other sacrifices are again commanded to be made on his behalf. The eighth day has the same force as the first, because the whole present time is divided into weeks, after which comes the eighth day, possessing, as we have said, an equal power with the first—or entirely renewing the first.

This is the day on which the Savior rose, and on which we shall enter the camp. After seven days, the lawgiver commanded the leprous person who had been cleansed to enter the camp on the eighth day. But what sort of camp? Certainly that which the patriarch Jacob saw when, as angels met him, he called the place “the camp of God.” The cleansed leprous person, once justified, comes to this camp at the time of the resurrection, in whose figure the lawgiver received the eighth day, as we have said.

The things commanded to be done on that same eighth day bear the image of the mystery that exists among us. He commanded two unblemished year-old male lambs and one unblemished year-old ewe to be taken. One of the lambs he commanded to be slaughtered as a sin offering, and the other as a burnt offering. All these things bear the figure of the Savior’s sacrifice. He himself was an offering for our sins and transgressions; he himself was the burnt offering.

He commanded a sacrifice to be offered from both kinds in order to show that Christ, slain for us, saved both male and female together. He did not command a year-old animal in both cases without reason, but through this he represented perfection. For year-old animals are perfect in the case of the animals mentioned above, being fit to produce offspring.

But because it is also necessary for the one who is being cleansed to have the faith of the whole Trinity signified in the sacrifice of the Only-Begotten, he commanded three-tenths of fine flour: the Trinity of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, possessing perfection in each person. The number ten is perfect; therefore the Lord also said: “The kingdom of heaven is like a woman who took leaven and hid it in three measures of flour, until the whole was leavened” (Matthew 13).

He commands that these be taken as a grain offering mixed with oil. By the grain offering he means the sacrifice of the Only-Begotten, which is mixed with oil because it was undertaken out of compassion for us. But how do we say that three-tenths of fine flour are offered in him? Either because, although it was through the passion of the Only-Begotten, the mystery accomplished through that sacrifice belonged to the whole Trinity. For baptism is also performed in the name of the Father, of his Only-Begotten Son, and of the Holy Spirit; in baptism we are baptized into Christ’s death, and the whole mystery is sanctified in him.

He also commanded a log of oil to be taken, because each of the things mentioned above is understood and performed through faith. It is rightly called a log, because just as a log is a measure—or, if we use the Septuagint’s term, a cotyle—the same measure admits neither less nor more than its proper amount.

[Note: Col. 0395D. That is: in the printed text it read “the same.”]

[Col. 0395B] The text continues: “For whatever is more is poured out.” It does not admit less because what is diminished can no longer be called a log or a cotyle. So faith too is given according to the measure of our capacity; it neither receives more nor less knowledge than God has distributed to each person. Whatever is less or more tends toward unbelief.

After these things have been received, the cleansed person is brought to the entrance of the tent of meeting—that is, to the entrance of the knowledge of God. The priest takes one lamb and slaughters it as a guilt offering. But if this ordinance concerned bodily suffering, as some think, why would it have been necessary to slaughter a lamb as a sin offering? Since it foreshadows mysteries on account of the weakness of the Jews and hides spiritual understanding within the letter, it also provides certain occasions for contemplation through the letter and through words that signify spiritual understanding.

Thus, when it now commanded one lamb to be slaughtered as a sin offering, it did not say what kind of lamb, because it is undoubtedly the one whom he commanded to be slaughtered for the guilt of the person whose ears were held by leprosy. Why, then, does he do this? Perhaps in order to fortify the hearing and make it cautious, because the person, deceived by the dragon, introduced sin. Through the hand he signifies actions; through the foot he wished to include and anticipate all our movements and ways. Once these have been guarded, through the blood of the intelligible lamb and through faith in him, which has been granted to us through his mercy and compassion, intelligible leprosy can in no way penetrate a person.

Although he also wishes the priest to put the oil of the log, or cotyle, which we have said signifies faith, into his hand, so that the priest’s faith—through which we too are brought forth—may be shown in works. For it does not otherwise manifest its power unless it has been taken up by the hand, that is, confirmed through action and marked by works.

He pours the oil into his left hand and dips his right finger into the oil, as Paul says: “Having conducted ourselves with the weapons of righteousness on the right and on the left, through glory and dishonor, through ill repute and good repute” (2 Corinthians 6), and things similar to these.

Then he sprinkles seven times before the Lord. Such a priest has confidence before God when he is able to cleanse those who are afflicted by necessity and to forgive them their sins. For this reason he sprinkles seven times, because this number has been shown to signify the remission of sins.

But after he has poured the oil onto the tips of the right ears and onto the thumbs of the right hands and feet, as we said above, he pours the remaining oil onto the head of the person called to be cleansed. Through the head he grants sanctification to the whole body, making the cleansed person, through this anointing, the Lord’s anointed.

“Then,” he says, “the sin offering is presented.” He does not say how this is done, for from what has been said concerning guilt offerings, what is done for a sin offering can also be inferred. The two are near and common to one another, since they belong to a common subject.

After this he slaughters the burnt offering and places it on the altar. Thus Christ’s sacrifice first cleanses us from transgressions and sins, and then our own burnt offering is prepared. When, through intelligible purification of the spirit, we have sanctified our whole body and soul and become spiritual, then we are made worthy of ascent to the altar. Then we receive complete cleansing, once we no longer need another.

## CHAPTER VII. What the poor person should offer for his purification

(IBID.) But if he is poor and cannot obtain what has been prescribed, he shall take one lamb as a guilt offering, so that the priest may pray for him, together with one-tenth of fine flour mixed with oil as a grain offering, one log of oil, and two turtledoves or two young pigeons. One of these shall be for a sin offering and the other for a burnt offering.

On the eighth day of his purification he shall offer them to the priest at the entrance of the tent of meeting before the Lord. The priest shall receive the lamb as a guilt offering and the log of oil and shall lift them up together. After slaughtering the lamb, he shall place some of its blood on the tip of the right ear of the person being cleansed, and on the thumbs of his right hand and right foot. He shall put some of the oil into his own left hand, dip the finger of his right hand into it, and sprinkle seven times before the Lord. He shall touch the tip of the right ear of the person being cleansed, and the thumbs of his right hand and right foot, at the place of the blood that was shed for the guilt offering.

The remaining oil in his left hand he shall put on the head of the purified person, to make the Lord gracious toward him. He shall offer one turtledove or young pigeon as a guilt offering, and the other as a burnt offering with its grain offerings. This is the sacrifice of the leprous person who cannot afford everything required for his purification.

(From Hesychius.) The lawgiver uses admirable condescension toward those who receive the law. For behold, he grants indulgence to poverty and commands that moderate sacrifices be offered by the poor, lest they be overwhelmed when greater offerings are required of them than their strength permits.

But since we do not easily find among the poor even any of the things mentioned—for one who has no bread, where will he get a lamb? And one who lacks money, where will he buy a pigeon or a turtledove?—it is clear that the lawgiver intends some contemplation and leads the person who wishes to enter the hidden treasuries of knowledge toward spiritual realities.

Although he could have reduced the number of sacrifices because of the poverty of the one offering them, he omitted to do so. Instead, he requires certain inexpensive things of little value. In this he both excuses poverty and, according to the letter, refuses to deprive the poor person of the profit of sacrifices. But he gives us another understanding: leprosy signifies wickedness, and its cleansing is repentance. Repentance, however, requires works capable of erasing sins through virtues and earnest action.

For this reason John the Baptist said to the Jewish people: “Produce fruit worthy of repentance.” The subtle lawgiver considered those who might not be able to perform everything required by the strict discipline of repentance. Repentance requires earnest prayer, almsgiving, vigils, sackcloth, fasting, and finally even what David says: “My tears have been my bread day and night.” And: “Every night I wash my bed; I water my couch with my tears. I eat ashes like bread and mingle my drink with weeping” (Psalm 6).

There are people who, perhaps because of old age, excessive bodily weakness, or some other necessity, cannot perform all these things, as we have interpreted elsewhere in the present work. He excuses them because they are willing, but their hands do not find the means; they cannot. And because he grants them pardon, he provides them with another path of repentance and requires other kinds of sacrifices.

Above all, he mentions a lamb. For everyone who repents must first turn toward kindness and practice it, since this is easy for anyone who abstains from evil to attain. He commands one-tenth of fine flour mixed with oil—that is, attaining the theology of Christ, who allowed himself to be mingled with our flesh by oil, or mercy.

And he commands one log—or, according to the Septuagint, one cotyle—of oil. We have already shown clearly above that this signifies faith.

But what else did the lawgiver command to be offered with these things? Two turtledoves or two young pigeons. These are easily found by anyone. They signify continual meditation on the law, which is produced not only through reading—for perhaps you might say that even reading is difficult for some—but also through contemplation in the soul and mind. Both of these take the place of sackcloth, fasting, tears, ashes, food, and similar practices.

For if we undertake those practices to humble the flesh and restrain the soul from earthly works, the meditation of the law also accomplishes this, as do continual devotion to these things and the strict contemplation and investigation of divine commandments and benefits. Therefore he necessarily introduced these sacrifices in place of those practices.

David also explains them, saying: “Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly, who has not stood in the way of sinners, and who has not sat in the seat of pestilence” (Psalm 1). This makes clear the sacrifice of the lamb, which is without any wickedness and therefore signifies innocence. “His delight was in the law of the Lord”—that is, in the law of the one who possesses pure knowledge through the contemplation of innocent thoughts.

Paul describes people of this kind as those “who do not have the law, but show the work of the law written in their hearts” (2 Corinthians 3), demonstrating disciplined and chaste thoughts. Such, in a certain sense, is the offering of the turtledove.

“He shall touch,” he says, “the tip of the right ear of the person being cleansed, and the thumbs of his right hand and right foot at the place of the blood that was shed for the guilt offering. The remaining oil in his left hand he shall put on the head of the purified person, to make the Lord gracious toward him,” and so forth.

(From Origen.) Do you see how the ear is purified as the final and highest purification, so that the hearing may remain pure and clean? The right hand is purified so that our works may be clean, with nothing unclean or filthy mixed into them. The feet too must be purified, so that they may be directed only toward good works and no longer fall into the error of youth.

The priest sprinkles seven times before the Lord with oil. After everything has been performed for the purified person, after he has been converted and reconciled to God, and after the sacrifices have been slaughtered, it was appropriate that he should also invoke upon him the sevenfold power of the Holy Spirit, according to the one who had said: “Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and strengthen me with a governing spirit.”

Or again, since the Lord testifies in the Gospel that the hearts of sinners are besieged by seven demons, it is fitting that the priest should sprinkle seven times before the Lord during the purification, so that the expulsion of the seven evil spirits from the purified person’s heart might be declared by the seven shakings of the fingers with the oil.

Thus purification is granted to those who turn away from sin through all the things mentioned above. The gift of the Spirit’s grace is signified by the image of oil, so that the person who turns away from sin may not only attain cleansing but also be filled with the Holy Spirit. Through this he may receive the former robe and the ring, and, fully reconciled to the Father, be restored to the place of the Son.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the leprosy of houses or walls, and a recapitulation concerning every kind of leprosy
(IBID.) And the Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying: “When you enter the land of Canaan, which I shall give you as a possession, if there is a plague of leprosy in a house, the owner of the house shall go and report it to the priest, saying: ‘It seems to me that there is something like a plague of leprosy in my house.’ He shall then order that everything be removed from the house before he enters it and examines whether it is leprous, lest all the things in the house become unclean. Afterward he shall enter to inspect the leprosy of the house. When he sees on its walls what appear to be hollows, disfigured by pallor or redness and lower than the surface, he shall go out through the door of the house and immediately shut it for seven days. On the seventh day he shall return and examine it. If he finds that the leprosy has spread, he shall order that the stones in which the leprosy is found be pulled out and thrown outside the city, in an unclean place; and that the house itself be scraped within, all around, and the dust from the scraping be scattered outside the city in an unclean place; and that other stones be put in place of those removed, and the house be plastered with other mortar. But if, after the stones have been pulled out, the dust removed, and the house plastered with other earth, the priest enters and sees that the leprosy has returned and that the walls are covered with spots, it is a persistent leprosy, and the house is unclean. They shall immediately demolish it, and throw its stones, timbers, and all its dust outside the town, in an unclean place. Whoever enters the house while it is shut up shall be unclean until evening; and whoever sleeps in it or eats anything there shall wash his garments,” and so forth. (From Hesychius.)

“When you enter,” he says, “Moses and Aaron, into the land of the Canaanites.” What land is this? “The land which I shall give you as a possession.” Since seven nations—the Canaanites, Perizzites, Girgashites, Amorites, Jebusites, Hittites, and Arvadites—possessed the land promised to Abraham, these seven bore the image of the seven spirits of iniquity about whom the Lord says in the Gospels: “When the unclean spirit has gone out from a person, it takes with it seven other spirits more wicked than itself, and they enter and dwell there; and the last state of that person is worse than the first” (Matt. XII). These spirits possessed Abraham’s true land, that is, the inheritance of the nations. For it was said to him: “I have made you the father of many nations.”

When Moses and Aaron—that is, the law and the prophets, for they represent them; Aaron, who was called a prophet, was Moses’ mouth, and Moses represented the law—enter among the nations, then through them God expels those spirits that hold tyrannical power over the nations, the intelligible Canaanites mentioned above. He himself grants the nations as a possession to the law and the prophets and to those who proclaim them, for he acquired them by his own blood. He freed us both through the washing of regeneration and through the renewal of the Holy Spirit, which he poured out upon us abundantly, delivering us from those whom we formerly served, so that those who are from the nations might also say Isaiah’s song: “Lord our God, other lords besides you have possessed us; but in you alone we remembered your name” (Isa. XVI).

Whatever belongs to his possession certainly belongs also to his servants and ministers. Therefore, when the prophets and the law have entered into the inheritance of the nations, serving the proclamation of the Gospel, and when the things now spoken concerning the intelligible houses become apparent, the owner of the house shall go and report it to the priest, saying: “It seems to me that there is something like a plague of leprosy in my house.”

What are these household churches? For this reason he says: “The owner of the house shall go.” Let us hear Paul saying: “Greet Prisca and Aquila and the church in their house” (1 Cor. XVI). Therefore, whoever presides over such a household, if he perceives intelligible leprosy—that is, if he detects some meaning of evil and impious doctrine—fearing that what he undertook for righteousness might become judgment against him, should go to a priest who can discern it.

For he is not simply called a priest, as is clear from what Paul wrote again to the Colossians: “Greet Nympha and the church in her house” (Col. IV). Many people, out of zeal and devotion, established churches in their homes and received teachers of divine things and ministers in them, along with those who gathered for their communion and rejoicing.

Therefore, such a person should go to one who bears the image of the true priesthood—men such as Peter, Paul, Timothy, and the others who preserved their teaching and virtues, remaining blameless. For a bishop must be blameless, so that he may judge the sins of others. He shall say: “It seems to me that there is something like a plague of leprosy in the house”—that is, a meaning of impious doctrine has appeared in my household church.

Then the priest shall order everything to be removed from the house, as the Seventy render it; and he shall order the house to be uncovered, and “it shall not flourish throughout the whole house.” That is, he shall order all the people who gathered there to withdraw. They are the roof or structure of the house, as we have often shown. He ordered them to depart, that is, to demonstrate by their conduct that they are strangers to the evil that has appeared in the church and do not share in the punishment to be inflicted upon the impious.

For this reason Moses also, when he was about to lead Dathan and Abiram away for punishment and destruction, ordered the rest of the multitude to withdraw, lest they become participants in the punishment (Num. XVI). This is what is meant by: “Lest everything in the house become unclean.” Then the priest shall enter to inspect the leprosy of the house. “And when he sees on its walls what appear to be hollows disfigured by pallor or redness.” (From Hesychius.)

And so forth. The walls of the house are rightly understood as those who contain it, namely, the orders of those who speak and teach divine things. For the church truly consists of these, and not, as some suppose, of wood and stones. Thus, when Moses was ordered to assemble the church, he summoned not wood and stones and similar things, but the people, the elders, and the Levites. For the same reason James, Cephas, and John were called pillars of the church.

Thus “walls” rightly signify the ministers of sacred things and the teachers, since they themselves support the stability of the church and, in a certain sense, gather the people within themselves. As for the pale, or, as the Seventy have it, greenish, and reddish spot—what it is and of what kind—the interpretation of the preceding ordinance sufficiently demonstrates: it showed that this is empty glory and arrogance. These chiefly characterize the walls of the church, the body of teachers who minister sacred things, when they break out into evil, profane, and impious doctrines.

Therefore, if he sees a wall with hollows or pits—that is, if he perceives that the opinion of the ministers or teachers has become lower, and that it is in some way sinking because of a sin he has detected—he shall go out through the door of the house and immediately shut it for seven days. He imposes a measured rebuke upon the church, which receives the forgiveness of repentance and is absolved; for the number seven signifies the forgiveness of sin.

On the seventh day he shall return and examine it. If he finds that the leprosy has spread, he shall order the stones in which the leprosy is found to be pulled out and thrown outside the city, in an unclean place. This is because he did not find a diffused stain or an overflowing impiety. Thus he forgives those who have sinned, since they are repentant and have sinned from weakness; but dogmas and writings in which intelligible leprosy—the stain of impiety—is found are rightly thrown not merely outside the house but outside the city. They are expelled not only from one particular church but from the universal church.

For the universal church is Jerusalem, the city of the living God, which contains the church of the firstborn enrolled in heaven. Therefore they are thrown into an unclean place, namely, among the assemblies of heretics. This is an unclean place because it receives every dogma of impiety.

And what follows? “The house itself shall be scraped within, all around, and the dust from the scraping shall be scattered outside the city in an unclean place.” Those scrape the house who strive to understand and carefully distinguish the church’s books. They examine all malice diligently, and, sitting in judgment upon teachers through the razor of discernment in corrupt books, they allow no remnants of impiety to remain in the house. Whatever they scrape away they rightly carry to the aforementioned unclean place, as something unclean found among the unclean. “And other stones shall be put in place of those that were removed, and the house shall be plastered with other mortar.”

The stones are to be understood as the dogmas of those who expound the divine law and as writings. When they are sound, the following is appropriately said of them: “Holy stones are rolled upon the earth”; and again: “Whoever builds upon this foundation with gold, silver, precious stones” (1 Cor. II). By “dust,” however, the partial interpretation and teaching is signified, as Moses the lawgiver himself indicates. When he delivered Deuteronomy to the children of Israel, he said to them: “On the day when you cross the Jordan into the land which the Lord your God is giving you, you shall set up great stones and plaster them with dust, and write upon the stones all the words of this law.”

Therefore, when he says that the stones are to be scraped away and other dust brought in, he unquestionably commands that dogmas cleansed from every evil and teaching be brought in to replace those evil ones, and that the church be plastered. For consideration of the law clearly shows this to us.

Did not Paul also, seeing the leprosy of dogmas in the teachers at Antioch, report it to James, as to the great priest (Acts XV)? After the marks of the corrupt teachers’ dogmas had been scraped away, he removed the stones and put in their place the most correct writings of the Jerusalem church, adding their dust—that is, their teaching—and so anointed the church and healed what had occurred.

But if, after the stones have been pulled out, the dust removed, and the house plastered with other earth, the priest enters and sees that the leprosy has returned and that the walls are covered with spots, it is a persistent leprosy, and the house is unclean.

For if, after evil dogmas have been removed and others of sound teaching introduced, the doctrine of impiety is again found sprinkled throughout the house—that is, diffused or overflowing—then the priest recognizes by his own inspection, not merely by hearsay from a distance, that the disease of impiety is persistent and unclean.

The proper judgment concerning such ministers and teachers of the church, in whom impiety has been sprinkled or diffused, is shown by what follows. He says: “They shall immediately demolish it, and throw its stones, timbers, and all its dust outside the town, into an unclean place.”

That is, they must not merely despise the dogmas, but also the persons in whom they are found, those through whose speech the impious church had been constituted; and they must destroy the whole church itself. “I have hated,” he says, “the congregation of the wicked, and I will not sit with the impious” (Ps. XXV), as David said.

Thus it is excluded even from that city established in heaven, namely, the living and true city, and is counted among the unclean heretics.

“Whoever enters this house while it is shut,” that is, while it is subject to punishment or penalty—whoever enters it and in any way shares in its assembly—shall be unclean until he repents. Much more so is the one who sleeps in it. Such a person is not received in any other way unless he washes the intelligible garment with tears.

By “sleeping” in it we understand resting in its words and turning aside to its counsels, not merely visiting them for some customary reason. Likewise, whoever eats in it—that is, presumes to receive its mystical food and partake of the mysteries of the church that the priest destroyed when he found it acting impiously and possessing evil doctrines, the “wood, hay, and stubble”—is unclean.

For this reason he threw out not only its stones, which were not precious, but also its timbers, since they were joined to hay and stubble.

It follows:

“And if the priest enters and sees that the leprosy has not spread through the house after it has been plastered again, he shall purify it, since its health has been restored. For its purification he shall take two sparrows, a piece of cedar wood, scarlet, and hyssop. He shall slaughter one sparrow in an earthen vessel over living water; then he shall take the cedar wood, the hyssop, the scarlet, and the living sparrow, dip everything in the blood of the slaughtered sparrow and in the living water, and sprinkle the house seven times. He shall purify it with the blood of the sparrow, with the living water, with the living sparrow, with the cedar wood, with the hyssop, and with the scarlet. When he has let the sparrow fly freely into the open field, he shall pray for the house, and it shall rightly be cleansed.”

We explained the image represented by these sacrifices, of which the lawgiver speaks, earlier, when he commanded that they be understood also in the case of each leper. This must nevertheless be said here because it plainly appears that the lawgiver is chiefly reproving the iniquity of those who teach in the church, the iniquity that exists in doctrine and is committed against the dispensation of the one who was incarnate for us.

For this reason he commanded that these sacrifices be taken for the cleansing of the house: they represent the mystery of his flesh and passion, which, through the theologies concerning them, can sufficiently heal the tongues of sinners and cleanse all their sins.

It follows:

“This is the whole law concerning leprosy and the plague, leprosy of garments and houses, scars and erupting pustules, a shining spot, and a change of color into various forms, so that it may be known at what time something is clean or unclean.” (From Hesychius.)

“This is the whole law concerning leprosy.” Since he had expounded the ordinance concerning leprosy at greater length, he judged it necessary to repeat its main points. First he presents the genus as a whole, and afterward explains its species individually. When he says, “This is the whole law concerning leprosy,” he presents the genus comprehensively. The species of the genus are the very clear matters he adds afterward, rightly placing the plague first, since this is not an ordinary sin; indeed, we have said that it is the worst of all.

It is the impiety of dogmas that affects certain people among the populace, about whom the lawgiver also says: “A man or woman in whom there is a plague of leprosy.” If he had meant only priests, he would certainly not have mentioned a woman.

After this he placed the leprosy that exists in virtues, for these are the garments of the soul. Then he mentioned what exists among the teachers and priests of the churches. For these have been shown to be the houses and walls of the land of possession. Finally, he makes mention of scars and erupting pustules, describing true leprosy as that which exists in sins, whether doubtful or established.

To all these he added the purpose “so that it may be known at what time something is clean or unclean,” showing that the sinner is unclean when he sins knowingly, whereas when he sins unknowingly he deserves pardon on account of his ignorance. Thus the Lord also said concerning the Jews: “If you were blind, you would have no sin; but now that you say, ‘We see,’ your sin remains” (John IX).

Let us use the eyes of knowledge for the things that are beneficial, so that through them we may avoid sins and seek purity. Let us know the day on which we shall be cleansed, and, knowing it, hasten to meet it. Let us observe the whole law of leprosy, for in this way we shall dwell pure in the Lord’s tabernacles.

# BOOK FIVE

[Col. 0403]

## CHAPTER ONE. Concerning the man who suffers from a discharge of semen, and his cleansing

(LEVIT. XV.) And the Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying: “Speak to the children of Israel, and say to them: A man who suffers from a discharge of semen shall be unclean, and he shall then be judged subject to this condition when at each moment the foul fluid adheres to his flesh and congeals.”

“A man who suffers from a discharge of semen shall be unclean.” The Seventy, however, render it as follows: “For a man, a man to whom it has happened,” and so forth. (From Hesychius.)

Whenever he repeats the person to whom the command is given, he wishes to show the intention of the law and how great the lawgiver’s concern is that none of it should be entirely neglected. Thus he says: “A man, a man from the children of Israel, and from the resident aliens and those joined to them, who offers a burnt offering or a sacrifice and does not bring it to the door of the tabernacle of testimony to offer it to the Lord—that man shall be cut off from his people.” There are other similar passages, concerning the observance of which the lawgiver showed the greatest care.

Here, however, in accordance with the preceding interpretation, he did not say “man, man,” but “for a man, a man,” doubling the person as he did there. Yet he called the recipient of the law “man” because of his strength; by this term divine Scripture customarily signifies one who is more perfect. Solomon demonstrates this when he says: “But who will find a faithful man?” (Prov. XX). Paul likewise says: “Until we all attain to a perfect man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ” (Eph. IV).

(From Gregory.) “A man,” he says, “who suffers from a discharge of semen.” What is speech except semen? When it is emitted in an orderly manner, the mind of the hearer, like a womb that conceives, is made fruitful for the offspring of good works. But if it flows out inopportunely, polluting the one who emits it, it loses the power of generation. In the minds of hearers, the quality of speech heard is the seed of the thought that will follow, because when speech is conceived through the ear, thought is generated in the mind.

For if speech were not seed, it would never have been said of the preacher Paul: “What does this babbler wish to say?” (Acts XVII). Luke also says of him: “He was a leader of speech.” Therefore, semen dedicated to the use of propagation, when it flows improperly, defiles the other members. So too, speech through which knowledge ought to have been born in the minds of hearers, if it proceeds disorderly, stains even what they have understood correctly.

Therefore, whoever suffers from a discharge of semen is declared unclean, because he pollutes himself by excessive talking. If he were to bring forth what he says in an orderly manner, he could produce the offspring of right thought in the hearts of his hearers; but when he flows heedlessly through loquacity, he pours out semen not for the use of generation but for uncleanness.

For this reason Paul, when admonishing his disciple concerning the urgency of preaching, said: “I testify before God and Christ Jesus, who will judge the living and the dead, and by his appearing and his kingdom: proclaim the word; be urgent in season and out of season” (2 Tim. IV). In saying “out of season,” he first added “in season,” because speech destroys itself in the mind of the hearer through its own worthlessness if its untimeliness does not know how to become timely.

When he says, “He shall then be judged subject to this condition when at each moment it adheres to his flesh and the foul fluid congeals,” the discharge of semen—that is, subjection to harmful doctrine—is likewise proved when he devotes himself more frequently to depraved thought and excessive verbal outpouring, seeking temporal glory through arrogance rather than desiring to receive the fruit of an everlasting reward in the heavenly kingdom.

“Every bed on which he sleeps shall be unclean, and everything on which he sits. If any person touches his bed, he shall wash his garments, and, having washed himself with water, he shall be unclean until evening.” (From Hesychius.)

Since there are many kinds of those who teach what is alien to the truth—for some, as Paul said, teach out of envy, others out of rivalry, others through ignorance, others from reckless loquacity, concerning which the Wise Man said, “In much speaking you will not escape sin” (Prov. X), while others turn their teaching into an instrument of certain corrupt desires because they take pleasure in them—the lawgiver rightly indicated some of these in the ordinance concerning leprosy and others in the distinction of foods. Now, through the commandment concerning the man who suffers from a discharge of semen, he has set forth another kind: those who teach other things out of shamelessness and lust.

There are therefore some who shape their doctrinal speech according to their own passions and strive to commend to others what they themselves love. For example, if someone is a lover of adultery, he rejects the commandment concerning chastity; or, if he is a glutton and drunkard, he rejects the law of fasting.

Since such a person is considered a teacher by name but does not teach sound doctrine and instead corrupts the teaching he presents, he cannot beget children for God. Hence he is said to suffer from a discharge of semen.

It is appropriately said: “Every bed on which he sleeps shall be unclean.” The bed of a teacher, since the characteristic of a bed is that its owner rests upon it, signifies in every way the disciple in whom, because of excessive obedience, the teacher himself and his spirit rest. Paul makes this clear in what he wrote to the Corinthians, praising them because they had obediently submitted themselves to Titus: “We rejoiced still more at the joy of Titus, because his spirit was refreshed by all of you” (2 Cor. VII).

Those, therefore, who teach immodest things and oppose the begetting of children, rejecting legitimate marriages in order thereby to introduce fornication, are for this reason also called sufferers from a discharge of semen. They corrupt both the generative seed and the law of marriage. Paul spoke of them as follows: “In later times some will depart from the faith, giving heed to deceitful spirits and doctrines of demons, through the hypocrisy of liars whose consciences are seared, forbidding marriage and abstinence from foods which God created to be received” (1 Tim. IV).

The bed and the vessel, according to the interpretation just given, are those who are so unclean that the lawgiver does not even command their cleansing. For he knows them to be so afflicted by the disease that they are entirely unable to repent. Their doctrine is not infected through ignorance; rather, corrupted and dissolute in their shameless words, they are infected by an evil habit, and for this reason they cling to it so willingly.

“But if anyone touches his bed”—that is, if anyone participates in and receives something from his doctrine, and does not merely sit upon the dogmas of the one who teaches depraved and filthy things, becoming a disciple of his evil words or of his disciples—for these are his vessels and his bed, those who hear him—then that person too is unclean.

Yet he washes his garments through repentance, as we have often said. “And having washed himself with water,” that is, with the water of tears or of baptism, “he shall be unclean until evening,” until he completes the time of repentance. Evening represents this in many passages, and especially because, at the consummation of the ages—that is, at the setting of the present age—Christ preached repentance to us.

It follows:

“Whoever touches his flesh shall wash his garments, and, having washed himself with water, shall be unclean until evening. If such a man casts his saliva upon one who is clean, the latter shall wash his garments, and, having washed himself with water, shall be unclean until evening.” (From Hesychius.)

This means that the one who becomes a participant in the doctrine of a teacher of profane things is to be unclean until he cleanses himself through the repentance commanded by the lawgiver. Or someone may voluntarily become a participant in evil doctrine. This is what is meant by touching the flesh of the man who suffers from a discharge of semen.

Alternatively, the teacher may, through his actions, in a certain way cast himself upon someone and introduce his doctrinal speech. This is what is meant by casting saliva. For this reason Aquila rendered it, “if he spits upon”; Symmachus, “if he spits.”

“The saddle on which he sits shall be unclean until evening.” Just as we said that the bed on which the man who suffers from a discharge of semen rests and the vessel in which he sits signify disciples who cling too closely to him and receive, in a certain sense, his entire doctrine—disciples whose hearts are hard, like earthen, wooden, and stone vessels, which are difficult to change or soften—so here the saddle, or, as the Seventy render it, the saddle of a donkey, signifies a more negligent disciple whose heart is nevertheless more readily disposed to change.

For the lawgiver understood the saddles of the donkey to be soft. Since such a disciple can be shaken loose by good teachers, washed, and reject his evil discipleship—such things are what the Seventy call ἐπισάγματα (*episagmata*), that is, saddlecloths—he too shall be unclean until he turns himself toward repentance.

“And everyone who touches anything that is under him shall be unclean until evening; and whoever carries any of these things shall wash his garments, and, having washed himself with water, shall be unclean until evening.” (From the same source.)

The lawgiver has generally decreed that it is not permissible to touch the fruit of the lips of those who have become subject to teachers of profane things, who have in a certain sense submitted themselves to their words and laid themselves beneath incongruous doctrines. Whoever touches these things, or whoever carries any of them—that is, whoever receives or takes upon himself the sin that has been described—likewise requires repentance according to the foregoing interpretation.

“Everyone whom such a person touches without first washing his hands shall wash his garments and, having washed himself with water, shall be unclean until evening.” (From the same source.)

The lawgiver appropriately used the words just cited, lest we should be driven altogether into despair concerning association with one who teaches evil, but only concerning that association which continues until he turns toward repentance. For this reason they are unclean, whoever is touched by the man who suffers from a discharge of semen, that is, whoever becomes associated with him.

“Without washing his hands with water” means that he has not yet washed his life through repentance. Washing the hands signifies the removal of some dirt and stain. Thus David said: “I will wash my hands among the innocent, and I will go around your altar, O Lord” (Ps. XXV).

“Every earthen vessel that the man who suffers from a discharge of semen touches shall be broken; but every wooden vessel shall be washed with water, and it shall be clean.” (From the same source.)
