In the earlier passages of this law, in which it says that the man who suffers from a discharge of semen touches various people, we say that these are those with whom the teacher of evil has mingled himself and whom he has taken into a certain association with himself. This is plainly what “touching” means.

Hence Paul, warning against improper association with women, said: “It is good for a man not to touch a woman; but because of fornication, let each man have his own wife, and let each woman have her own husband” (1 Cor. VII).

These people have become his vessels. They have received some of his doctrine, even if only a little; for he has not emptied his entire doctrine into them—that is, he has not poured out all his teaching upon them—but he has touched them by handing over a certain part of it.

Thus, since they remain earthen—that is, fragile and earthly—and attend to their own clay and the corruption of clay, they are necessarily shattered, because they are corrupted even by a few words.

But if they are wooden, then, because wooden vessels are stronger than earthen and clay vessels and endure longer, they are cleansed by being washed with water. His doctrine has not settled in them, nor have they received all his evil teaching, as we have said. Therefore they are not so weakened that they cannot be healed through repentance.

The lawgiver’s purpose, then, is to show who should repent and who should not, because salvation is offered to those who repent.

“If the man who suffers from such a condition is healed, he shall count seven days after his cleansing; and, having washed his garments and his whole body in living water, he shall be clean.” (From the same source.)

The cleansing of the man who suffers from a discharge of semen consists in his no longer enduring that corruption of semen. Therefore, if someone who teaches filthy, evil, and profane things ceases to do so, having ceased from such shamelessness, he is rightly called clean.

But because of the filthy words he poured out, he must first count seven days for complete cleansing. This is accomplished through the coming of Christ and the ministry of the Holy Spirit, whose sevenfold gift Isaiah described when he said: “The spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord” (Isa. XI).

All these gifts are needed by those who wish to obtain perfect cleansing from the evil found in speech or in deeds.

They also wash their garments and body with living water. What the garments and body signify has been sufficiently demonstrated above. They wash with living water, namely, that of which Christ said: “Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture has said, rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (John VII). And again: “Whoever drinks from the water that I will give him will become in him a spring of water welling up to eternal life” (John IV).

Therefore the cleansing of one who teaches evil comes through good and legitimate doctrine. For this is the living water, because it grants life to the one who approaches it.

It follows:

“On the eighth day he shall take two turtledoves or two young pigeons and come before the Lord, to the door of the tabernacle of testimony. He shall give them to the priest, who shall offer one for sin and the other as a burnt offering. The priest shall pray for him before the Lord, so that he may be cleansed from his discharge of semen.” (From Hesychius.)

The one who has counted seven days for himself—that is, the works of the Spirit—is commanded on the eighth day, that is, in the grace of Christ, which shone forth or became manifest on the eighth day through the resurrection, to offer a sacrifice.

What sacrifice is this? Two turtledoves or two young pigeons—a sacrifice appropriate for teachers. These animals are birds: the turtledove is, as it were, a contemplative creature, while the dove, because of its frequent reproduction and its simplicity, represents the image of the Holy Spirit.

For a teacher must devote himself to spiritual contemplation. This is why the lawgiver commanded him to take this sacrifice for himself, as priest and teacher. We do not find that this was said in connection with another sacrifice unless it again concerned some priest and teacher.

We showed earlier, in connection with the sacrifices, that bringing the offering to the door of the tabernacle of testimony means bringing it to the teachings of the apostles, and to the veil of the tabernacle of testimony—that is, to Christ’s dwelling and way of life—so that in the future he may perfect his tongue according to the apostolic purpose.

Just as the one who sinned, weakened the priestly status within himself, and rendered it ineffective is commanded to give the offering to a priest and to yield the priestly ministry to another, so the priest who receives the two turtledoves or two young pigeons does the following: he offers one for sin and the other as a burnt offering.

The one sacrifice is beneficial for his cleansing and for the sins he committed by teaching contrary to the law; the other concerns wise conduct in the future, for this is what the burnt offering signifies.

Thus the priest shall pray for him before the Lord, that he may be cleansed from his discharge of semen. No one can otherwise bring about cleansing before the Lord—that is, according to the will and law of God—unless he repents of the things in which he sinned, makes satisfaction through sacrifices of prayer, and afterward lives rightly and gains perfect understanding.

It follows:

A man from whom the semen of intercourse issues shall wash his entire body with water and shall be unclean until evening; he shall wash with water the garment and skin that he has worn, and they shall be unclean until evening. The woman with whom he has intercourse shall wash herself with water and shall be unclean until evening.

*(From Hesychius.)* The Lord himself showed that the human race needs the regeneration of baptism, saying: “Unless someone has been regenerated from water and the Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of heaven” [Col. 0408D] (John 3). The reason for this is that, because defilement has been transmitted into us from Adam through disobedience, David asserted that he was born in iniquities and conceived in sins (Psalm 50), not accusing his mother, but indicating the sin that flows down through the race.

And now the lawgiver commanded the man from whom the semen of intercourse issues—that is, the man who poured out semen for the procreation of children—and also the woman who received it, to wash the body, because she received the semen through which this entire temple of ours, that is, the whole human being, consisting of soul and body, is signified. Since Adam, having become defiled through disobedience, also made his semen defiled, the body too is necessarily unclean, since such semen proceeds from it.

They are said not without reason to be unclean until [Col. 0409A] evening, because Christ, coming at the end of the ages, showed the water by which our race would be cleansed. And that we remained unclean until then is proved by the fact that even those who have not yet sinned—that is, those established in tender age—need the seal of baptism, lest, should death overtake them, they pass away while unclean, carrying within themselves the defilement descended from Adam and therefore unable to enter the kingdom of heaven.

But he commands that the garment and skin which they have when they lie together—namely, that these too are unclean and must be washed—for two reasons. First, he extends and makes clear how greatly the human body was made unclean through a single disobedience, so that even inanimate things are polluted by them. Second, through these things he makes manifest the women who, for the sake of lust, join themselves to men for a certain temporal use, as garments ordinarily serve human beings, and as the abuse of skins is treated—skins that are usually discarded once they have become old. For when friendship grows old, their relationship too is rejected and changed in the manner of garments or skins; indeed, they do not always live with those with whom they fornicate disorderly.

By drawing the Jewish race toward sanctification and chastity—for some of them were excessively devoted to luxury—the lawgiver says these things against those who discharge semen in whatever manner and against those who touch such persons, commanding them to be cleansed, so that, at least under compulsion, they might become chaste and refrain from lustful unions because of the inconvenience of frequent purifications.

For the law has this intention according to the letter in what follows as well, although according to the spirit it signifies something else. I too shall explain this, since I do not pass over the spiritual meaning of the present passage. Just as we understood the man who suffers a flow of semen to be one who corrupts doctrine, so we understand the man from whom the semen of intercourse issues to be one who teaches the doctrine belonging to the Jews. For just as one who emits natural and healthy semen is nevertheless unclean because of Adam’s defilement, so their doctrine, though sound in what concerns the law, is under accusation and blame because it teaches the letter, which brings a curse upon its disciples.

For it is impossible for anyone to be perfectly corrected through that doctrine. Hence it subjects its disciples to the Mosaic curse, and likewise the Jews who are represented by the women who lie with men, since they always cling to and rest beside the teachers of their institutions. It also operates in the same way upon those who are in uncircumcision, whenever they receive the semen of their doctrine; these we say are the garment and the skin, since they receive their teachings temporarily and transitorily, not so that they themselves may produce any legal righteousness. For how could this be possible for those who remain in uncircumcision? Rather, through their words they are understood to become polluted by the curse of the law.

## CHAPTER II  
### Concerning the woman who suffers a flow of blood not at the time of menstruation, and her purification

*(The same passage.)* “When a woman suffers a flow of blood at the return of the month, she shall be separated for seven days [Col. 0410A]. Everyone who touches her shall be unclean until evening; and whatever she sleeps on or sits on during the days of her separation shall be polluted. Whoever touches her bed shall wash his garments, and, after washing himself with water, he shall be unclean until evening. Whoever touches any vessel on which she has sat shall wash his garments, and, after washing himself with water, he shall be unclean until evening.”

*(From Hesychius.)* The lawgiver’s intention is to draw a person away from female lust and, at the same time, to restrain both men and women from intercourse for the sake of shameful union. For what is now being said does not chiefly affirm that this is done for the procreation of children.

He found a way to separate men from entry into women’s company at various times and over many intervals. Since women suffer a flow of blood each month, he commanded that they be unclean for seven days and that even those who touched them by simple contact be unclean until evening. But he says that those who sleep with them are not unclean for one day but for seven days. Thus, under the constraint of many days of continence, both women from men and men from women are necessarily restrained. In this way the literal sense could assist the perceptible Jew and the Israelite according to the flesh.

But the truest assistance is the spiritual consideration enclosed within it. For the flow of blood—which the lawgiver now represented in the figure of a woman, as though feminizing the soul and revealing its lack of the strength of piety—is idolatry: according to the rendering of the Septuagint, its flow is in her body. The shedding of idolatrous blood is the corruption, or destruction, of the human race. For this reason he did not say “from our body”; idolatry was not invented by us, but by demons. It was inflicted upon our race in the body, and corruption was imposed upon human nature.

He also indicates the periods during which idolatry prevailed. Thus Paul said: “Indeed, in the times of ignorance God overlooked, but now he announces that all people everywhere must repent.” The statement “she shall be separated for seven days”—which some rendered “she shall be in her purification,” others “in the separation of her iniquity,” and still others “of her misery”—signifies through the number seven the periods of the Spirit extending to the completion of the ages, at which completion the evangelical proclamation came forth.

During these periods, human beings separated from God through idolatry were necessarily in the separation of iniquity and misery, until we were joined to God through evangelical conduct. This is understood as taking place on the eighth day, because it is in a certain sense the sign, beginning, and pledge of the age to come. For this reason the resurrection of the Savior also took place on the eighth day.

Not only the soul that serves idols, but also the one who touches it—that is, the one who becomes its participant—and still more the one on whose bed it sleeps or on whose seat it sits, as one who becomes a participant in its doctrine and tradition, or the one who has intercourse with it, shall be unclean and shall need purification. Nor is it cleansed in any other way than by being washed with water. What the water is, we have said above.

One must therefore [Col. 0411A] abstain entirely from every evil of idolatry, and not touch either those who serve idols or those whom idolaters use as instruments, beds, or vessels—that is, one must have no communion with them whatsoever.

It follows:

“When a woman suffers a flow of blood for many days, not at the time of menstruation, or when she does not cease to flow after her menstrual blood, for as long as she is subject to this affliction she shall be unclean, as though she were in the time of menstruation. Every bed on which she sleeps and every vessel on which she sits shall be polluted. Whoever touches them shall wash his garments, and, after washing himself with water, shall be unclean until evening.”

*(From Hesychius.)* How much the Spirit of God vindicates the contemplation of the law and the reading of the letter is shown by the things sanctioned in their several parts. Since we said earlier that the man suffering a flow of semen is understood as one who teaches obscene and corrupting things in the law, and that the one from whom the semen of intercourse issues uses Jewish doctrine, those who teach pagan doctrine remained. Behold, he now appropriately adds them as well.

We have said that the flow of blood is the seduction and error of idols, since it belongs to a race of demons that rejoices in blood and commands sacrifices not only of cattle and other irrational animals but also of human beings, so that such rites were celebrated among them in many places. Thus the flow of blood had become so deeply established among them in the mysteries of Dionysus, Diana, and other demons.

Now observe the words used by the lawgiver: “A woman who suffers a flow of blood for many days, not at the time of menstruation.” The Septuagint rendered it thus: “If a woman flows with an issue of blood for many days.” He did not say, “if she sheds blood,” which means serving idols or sacrificing to them, but “if she has flowed with a flow of blood”—that is, if she emits the stain and error of idolatry. Yet she does this not at the time of menstruation, that is, not during the periods in which the service of idols prevailed. That these are the menstrual periods was shown in the words in which we discussed her earlier. Rather, she does it after knowledge has begun and the light of piety has shone forth through evangelical doctrine.

Nevertheless, she flows while unclean and teaches things close to the error of idols, and therefore she is unclean—just as those people of the former times, when the fury of idolatry prevailed, were unclean while teaching whatever belonged to their error. They were then unclean, but they are even more so now, both because their impurity has already been exposed and their error convicted, and because they were unwilling to offer their eyes to the light of true understanding.

We understand the woman who suffers this flow to bear the image of the woman in the Gospels who suffered from a flow of blood (Matthew 9). She spent all her substance, or her life, on physicians—that is, on the philosophers who existed among them—yet she was not healed by them of the disease of her error: “Claiming to be wise, they became fools” (Romans 1).

Although they appeared to be estranged by the worship and frenzy of images, they nevertheless measured the earth, the air, and the heavens, whose origins and boundaries belong to God alone. Thus, touching the fringe of the Lord from behind, she was freed from the flow.

We say that his fringe is his faith. For what reason did Moses command that a fringe be made on garments? Since divinity is to be understood in what is before, we understand humanity in what is behind. We say that the nations, which were situated in the flow of the blood of idols, touched him with this intention.

If we have explained the flow of blood to mean not only those who devote themselves to shedding idolatrous blood but also those who teach matters belonging to pagan doctrine, this is not surprising. For among outsiders it is customary to call abundant eloquence, which pours itself out most freely and readily toward teaching, a “flow” or rhetoric.

It follows:

“If the blood stops and the flow ceases, she shall count seven days for her purification, and on the eighth day she shall offer for herself to the priest two turtledoves or two young pigeons at the door of the tabernacle of testimony. He shall offer one for sin and the other as a burnt offering, and he shall pray for her before the Lord and for the flow of her uncleanness. Therefore you shall teach the children of Israel to beware of uncleanness, so that they do not die in their defilements when they pollute my tabernacle, which is among them.”

*(From Hesychius.)* We have spoken, insofar as necessary, about the virtue of this sacrifice and its character in those who suffer a flow of semen. The law commands similar things there as well. For just as in that passage the lawgiver commanded the man suffering a flow of semen to take turtledoves or pigeons as a sacrifice, because he represented the place and person of the teacher, so now he commands the woman who suffers a flow of blood to do the same; for we said that she represents those who teach matters belonging to the error of idolatry.

Therefore, one who teaches eloquence and participates in eloquence can take for himself the things that contribute to purification. What remains to be interpreted we shall explain in order in what follows.

“You shall teach,” he says, “the children of Israel to beware of uncleanness, so that they do not die in their defilements when they pollute my tabernacle, which is among them.”

*(From Hesychius.)* Although every sin is uncleanness of the soul, idolatry and the things belonging to it are uncleanness above all. The lawgiver wishes the children of Israel to beware of these things and to be fearful in regard to them, so that they do not die the most cruel death of impiety.

For the impious pollute the tabernacle of God, which is in them; and it is the body that is polluted by a flow of blood or semen. But because the wording indicates the impiety that customarily pollutes the whole human being, he therefore says that the children of Israel are to be cautious—or, as the Septuagint has it, fearful—of their uncleanness.

He did not prescribe this concerning lepers or those who had touched corpses, but mentioned the tabernacle of God that is in us. For our whole human being is the tabernacle of God, in which God is believed to dwell: first through the image that he bestowed upon us, and then through the firstfruits that he took from us. “The Word became flesh” (John 1), and through that fortification [or: diminution; *munitionem* [*minutionem*]] he is said also to dwell in the rest of human beings. John proves this by saying: “The Word became flesh, and dwelt among us.”

This is the law concerning the man who suffers a flow of semen, who is polluted by intercourse, concerning the woman who is separated during her menstrual periods, or who continually flows with blood, and concerning the man who sleeps with her.

*(From Hesychius.)* The lawgiver is accustomed to connect these matters with one another, so that for the person who applies himself to the study of the law he may make clear how they ought to be understood and which things are related to which according to the similarity of their meaning.

Since, therefore, it has been established that the man who suffers a flow of semen is the teacher [or: teachers] who corrupt[s] the seed of doctrine and admonishes toward shameful and corrupting things, and that the man from whom the semen of intercourse issues and who becomes polluted is the one who teaches Jewish commandments—in which he himself is polluted by teaching evil things as good and transgressing the intention of the law, while bringing forth what belongs to the letter outside its proper time and, in a certain manner, using the things of the world as the unclean use them—of such people it was said: “To the pure all things are pure, but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is pure; rather, their mind and conscience are defiled” (Titus 1).

Those who suffer a flow of blood during their menstruation have been shown to be those who teach matters tending toward impiety at the time when the human race, held by the error of idols, was in its menstruation—that is, in the separation of wickedness, for it had not been separated from evil.

To show that the law speaks of the same things concerning those who teach depravity, it says nothing according to the letter about a female suffering a flow of semen. Rather, through the woman who suffers a flow of blood it understood the one who pours out the doctrine of idolatry. For this reason it now calls her one who suffers a flow of semen, so that we might learn that the law regards the one who corrupts good doctrine by presenting it shamefully and badly as being like the one who teaches impiety. For the words of both are full of corruption.

## CHAPTER III  
### That Aaron and his sons are not to enter the sanctuary at all times, and what must be offered before entering

*(Chapter 16.)* “The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: after the death of the two sons of Aaron, when they were killed while offering alien fire.”

Behold, now too the Spirit of God makes the law one body and brings together things that cohere with one another.

*(From Hesychius.)* Having earlier made manifest the matters belonging to doctrine that is contrary to the law, and having explained its many and various modes, he now rebukes it by one law, as it were, and sets against it a common commandment, making clear the cause of the disease itself—that is, from where it arises and from where it comes upon them.

You heard when we were investigating the death of the sons of Aaron, those who were consumed by divine fire. When we were then expounding the word of the legal tradition and the history, we said that alien fire meant doctrine alien to God. Therefore those who offered that fire were consumed by divine fire, namely, the fire of the Spirit, because those who teach what is evil [Col. 0414A] and unrighteous openly contradict the divine fire and act against the Spirit.

“And he commanded him, saying: Speak to Aaron your brother, so that he may not enter the sanctuary at all times, which is within the veil before the mercy seat, by which the ark is covered, lest he die, because I shall appear in a cloud above the oracle.”

*(From Hesychius.)* From many things said in the law it can be considered and learned how greatly God shows mercy toward our salvation. Neglecting none of these things, let us direct the eyes of the mind to each one in turn.

The lawgiver rightly displays the greatest diligence, so that teachers may not transgress not only in shameful words, Jewish fables, or some fantasy of idolatry, but also may not fall into impiety under the pretext of theology, as heretics customarily do.

For, investigating the substance of God, they introduce a distinction between the Father and the Son and between the Son and the Holy Spirit. They also seek to investigate other similar matters that exceed our knowledge and are hidden from us, being exceedingly high and of like character, not from divine doctrines but from their own thoughts. In this way they have been cut off from the body of ecclesiastical moderation.

The present words of the law warn us not to suffer this. For it says: “And the Lord said to Moses: Speak to Aaron your brother”—that is, so that priests might command these things to one another, and each of the teachers might impose upon his neighbor the sort of rule that God now commanded Moses to speak to Aaron.

What are these things? “He shall not enter at all times into the sanctuary that is within the veil before the mercy seat by which the ark is covered.” This is a commandment common to all, and here he has set forth a law common to all: first suitable to priests, and then to everyone who wishes to investigate the divine mysteries.

Therefore, according to the Septuagint, he commanded impersonally, saying: “They shall not enter at all times into the inner sanctuary of the veil.” He did not add “all,” clearly wishing to prohibit everyone from this. Because the veil is understood as the body of the Savior, as Paul plainly says: “Having confidence for entering the holy places, which he inaugurated for us as a new and living way through the veil, that is, through his flesh” (Hebrews 10).

He himself is the true and intelligible mercy seat, since he grants us the propitiation of sins. For the same Paul says: “All have sinned and lack the glory of God, being justified freely by his grace, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus, whom God set forth as a propitiation through his blood” (Romans 3).

He plainly forbade teachers, prohibited priests, and restrained all to whom it is lawful to speak about God from investigating God’s substance and examining Christ’s divinity, and from entering into the interior of the intelligible veil. For Christ has flesh as his veil, the covering of his divinity, just as the material veil was the covering of the Holy of Holies.

He called not only the veil but also the ark of the testimony the Lord’s flesh, giving it many names as was necessary, because many operations proceeded from it. Concerning that ark he commands teachers not to enter at all times, so that they may not investigate with excessive curiosity how “the Word became flesh” (John 1), how the one who was in the form of God took the form of a servant, how he “emptied himself” (Philippians 2), and yet remained in heaven.

Faith in these matters brings salvation; inquiry brings danger. Therefore the one who believes this and does not inquire will not die, because, he says, “I shall appear in a cloud above the oracle,” or mercy seat.

Again he calls the Lord’s flesh and the evangelical word a cloud. For he calls the same thing by many names, not through tautology, but by appropriately assigning and distributing names according to the operations of the things signified.

At one time he calls it the veil, signifying that the flesh is the covering of Christ’s divinity. At another time he calls it the ark, that is, the human being whom the Lord himself, explaining this to the Jews, said: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2).

When the Jews, not understanding, said, “This temple was built in forty-six years, and will you raise it up in three days?”, the evangelist explained, saying: “But he was speaking about the temple of his body.”

At another time he calls it a cloud, because a cloud has a body, yet one that is pure and has its substance from the Holy Spirit. For clouds subsist from spirits, that is, from winds. Therefore, showing its subtlety, lightness, and purity, Isaiah said: “Behold, the Lord rides upon a light cloud and will enter Egypt, and the images of Egypt will be shaken” (Isaiah 5).

Similarly, we not incongruously call the evangelical word a cloud, because it is customary for divine Scripture to call the teaching of the Holy Spirit a cloud. Thus, taking away the vineyard of the Jews as fruitless, he said: “I shall command the clouds not to rain rain upon it” (Isaiah 5).

In this cloud God is made known both in the Lord’s flesh and in the evangelical preaching. Therefore, let us who wish to investigate something about God seek nothing beyond this, but only what the evangelical word hands down to us and what we receive from the Lord’s flesh.

It follows:

“He shall offer a calf for sin and a ram as a burnt offering. He shall clothe himself in a linen tunic and cover his nakedness with linen undergarments. He shall gird himself with a linen belt, and place a linen *cidaris* upon his head. For these are holy garments, and he shall put them all on after he has washed himself.”

*(From the same author.)* In an admirable order the lawgiver now makes use of matters that can help and benefit those who read the law and search out the treasure hidden within it.

After saying that it is not permitted to enter the Holy of Holies at every hour—that is, continually or without interruption—lest we presume to approach divine things without fear and circumspection, he did not altogether prohibit deeper investigation. Rather, when and how does he command us to undertake it? When we have perfected or completed ourselves, as he now teaches: Aaron must not enter the holy place unless he has first done these things.

This shows that he commanded not only that one should not enter frequently, but also that one should not enter the higher contemplation of divine things at all without preparation. He called that contemplation the sanctuary, since it concerns God, who is the Holy of Holies and sanctifies the one who uses it well.

The one who is Aaron is the person who possesses an elevated way of life and has advanced so far, ascending toward the sanctification of God, that he can answer, as it were, like the divine ark. For this is what Aaron means.

Upon entering, he shall offer a calf for sin—that is, he enters through the sacrifice of Christ. Since Christ was sacrificed not only for our sins but also grants us perfect life, providing both the remission of sins and perfection in virtues, he seeks and presents the sacrifice of God.

The lawgiver adds: “And a ram as a burnt offering.” But the Septuagint rendered it, “from the calf of cattle,” because Christ according to the flesh came from those oxen who work righteousness—for example, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and David.

For the law knows oxen as those who practice righteousness. Since a ram belongs to the race of sheep but is nevertheless preeminent and the leader of the flock, it rightly signifies Christ, who is from our common mass but is preeminent and surpasses us, and is the leader and king of the human race.

In this one—that is, in Christ—he wishes us to enter the holy places. For Christ and his passion are the beginning of speaking about God. If this had not taken place, and if it had not freed us both from the error of the pagans and from the shadow and darkness of the law, we could not have spoken at all about the divinity of the Father: “No one knows the Father except the Son, and the one to whom the Son wishes to reveal him” (Luke 10).

But whoever is going to speak about God and wishes to contemplate God, insofar as this is possible for human beings, must necessarily arm himself with every virtue.

Observe how he also establishes this. There are four general virtues: justice, chastity, courage, and wisdom.

Therefore, he says, “he shall put on a linen tunic”—that is, justice, concerning which it is written: “Let your priests be clothed with justice” (Psalm 131).

He shall also put on linen undergarments—that is, chastity. He shall wear a belt, for by the belt courage is understood. Thus the Lord says to Job: “Gird your loins like a man” (Job 38).

By the *cidaris*, which is a head covering, wisdom is understood in every respect. For we know that the head contains the organ of wisdom, which is also called the brain, and therefore the head is more honorable than the rest of the body.

He also commanded all these garments to be linen in order to show the ease and rapid acquisition of the virtues, or that they are accessible and pleasing to the one who attains them, like linen garments are to the body.

Although the practice of these virtues is lofty, it can exist on earth. Each of them grows like flax, which has a tall stalk but rises far above the ground and can easily be obtained even by the poor. It is acceptable and pleasing to the one who wears it, as we said above. It cools the one who is hot and warms the one in the cold. This is characteristic of virtue: it cools one in the heat of desires, but in the cold of temptations it warms, raises one to zeal, and does not allow one to feel one’s persecutors.

But so that you do not also lose the central point of salvation, which is baptism, and do not think that virtues without the gift of baptism are sufficient for you, he adds: “For these are holy garments, and he shall put them all on after he has washed himself.”

*(From the same author.)* The whole body is washed through the water of baptism, because it washes and renews our whole human being. Therefore one must first be baptized and be born from water and the Spirit, and then be clothed in the virtues mentioned above and, through them, in Christ.

The entire sequence of the legal words also signifies this. After the lawgiver said that Aaron must not enter the sanctuary at all times unless he had done these things first, he added: “He shall offer a calf for sin, and a ram as a burnt offering; he shall clothe himself in a linen tunic,” and so forth.

He wishes us not only to receive and put on the intelligible ram, Christ, and the true burnt offering, namely perfection in the virtues—for Paul called him the perfect man and the measure of maturity—but therefore also introduced the grace of baptism, since through it above all we are clothed.

When we have attained these things, we shall enter the Holy of Holies, not investigating God’s substance or examining it—for this is forbidden—but applying ourselves with wise doctrines to the matters concerning Christ’s dispensation, his sacrifice for us, and the good things that we enjoy through it. The following words make this especially clear.

“And from the whole assembly of the children of Israel he shall receive two male goats for sin and one ram as a burnt offering. When he has offered the calf and prayed for himself and for his house, and so forth.”

Here the intention of the speaker and of the hearer alike must be great, so that they do not depart from what is right. For the mysteries that the law now expounds are profound, and some stumble over them because they do not know the power of the words. The matters over which they stumble will be explained more carefully below.

But that the things about which the lawgiver has spoken here clearly refer to Christ himself is shown by the forms and effects of the sacrifices, and also by those from whom the sacrifices are received.

He commanded that the sacrifices be received from the synagogue, or from the whole assembly of the children of Israel, because Christ, who was sacrificed for us, was descended from the children of Israel according to the flesh. Thus Paul said: “From them is Christ according to the flesh, who is God blessed forever. Amen” (Romans 9).

Next, he commands some sacrifices to be offered for sins and others as burnt offerings, depicting, as was necessary, the power of Christ’s sacrifice, which is offered for our sins. Hear Paul saying: “Christ, having been offered once to bear the sins of many, will appear a second time, apart from sin, to those who await him” (Hebrews 9).

That the sacrifice of the Only-Begotten was made as a burnt offering—that is, for the perfection and advancement of life and virtues—how can this be doubted when Paul plainly says: “Therefore, brothers, you too have died to the law through the body of Christ, so that you might belong to another, who was raised from the dead, in order that we might bear fruit for God” (Romans 7)?

We showed that the kid, which in Greek is called *chimaros* [*χείμαρος*], is rightly sacrificed by one who practices repentance, since he is situated in storm and turbulence until the sacrifice of his repentance is accepted. But the ram, as one who provides leadership to the flock, is rightly appointed as a burnt offering—that is, it is understood as virtue and perfection of life.

For whose task is it to teach perfection, if not that of those set over others?

With these things established, you say in every respect: If the law commanded goats to be offered for sin, why does it now also command a calf to be offered?

This can be resolved and explained by one short argument: the sacrifice of the Only-Begotten is not of one kind but belongs both to sinners and to the righteous. Therefore the goats are commanded to be offered for a certain class of sinners, so to speak, while the calf is offered for the righteous, because an ox, being an animal made for work, is understood according to the law in the person of the righteous.

Therefore he says of the calf: “He shall pray for himself and for his house,” calling the righteous person the house of God. For God dwells and walks in them; he is their God, and they are his people.

He shall also intercede for him—that is, for the house of his own flesh. For although he committed no sin and no deceit was found in his mouth (1 Peter 2), nevertheless he put on Adam, who needed propitiation because of the curse once imposed upon the human race.

Hear, then, Paul writing such things about Christ to the Hebrews: “He has no need, as the high priests do, to offer sacrifices every day, first for his own sins and then for those of the people; for this he did once for all when he offered himself.”

## CHAPTER IV  
### Concerning the two male goats, one of whom belongs to the lot of God, while the other is sent away as the scapegoat
(IBID.) And when he has offered the bullock and prayed for himself and for his household, he shall make two goats stand before the Lord at the entrance of the tent of testimony, and shall cast lots over the two, one lot for the Lord and the other for the scapegoat. The one upon which the lot for the Lord has fallen he shall offer as a sin-offering; but the one upon which the lot for the scapegoat has fallen he shall set alive before the Lord, to make supplication over it, and shall send it into the wilderness. When these rites have been duly performed, he shall offer the bullock, praying for himself and for his household.

(From Augustine.) Concerning the two goats—one to be sacrificed and the other to be sent into the desert, whom they call *apopompaeus*—there is usually debate. Some understand the one to be sacrificed in a good sense, and the one to be sent away in an evil sense. This interpretation should not, however, be confirmed merely because the man by whose hand the goat is sent into the wilderness is commanded, when he returns, to wash his garments and his body with water and then enter the camp, as though this were also an indication that the goat is to be understood in an evil sense, since the man must be cleansed from its contamination. For he likewise says that the man is to be washed who burns outside the camp the flesh of the other goat, which has been allotted, as well as that of the bullock, since he commands this to be done with both. Their blood is used for sprinkling, and they are offered for sins; therefore the distinction between these two goats must not be treated carelessly in its allegorical significance.

(From Hesychius.) The blind often stumble in the light, and unbelievers are scandalized by the law of God. Peter knew this and said of both the Epistles of Paul, the chosen vessel, and of all divine Scripture: “In them are some things difficult to understand, which the unlearned and unstable distort, as they do the other Scriptures, to their own destruction.” This is also suffered now by those who understand the law of God according to their own will rather than its true intention, and who foolishly suppose that the harmful and pestilential worship of idols is established by the words spoken by the legislator.

For they say: “The law commanded lots to be cast over two goats; one was for the Lord, while the other was commanded to be set apart for sending away. They call the one sent away the devil,” thereby providing an opportunity to worship the Evil One, stopping their ears (*obstrudentes*; Al. *obstruentes*; printed edition *obturantes*) and being so blind in mind. For how could it be reasonable or credible that God Himself should command a sacrifice to be offered to the devil, when through Moses He commanded that a brother, son, daughter, and even an entire city that turns to idols should be destroyed, and cries out: “You shall have no other gods besides me” (Exod. 20)?

If He had accepted the scapegoat as representing some evil person, He would certainly not have cast a lot over it together with the one belonging to God. For in the divine Scriptures you will find no instance of a good person sharing a lot with just any evil person; whenever lots were cast, they were cast among equals, as when the tribes of Israel were divided. Likewise, when it became necessary to choose another for the apostleship in place of Judas, they cast lots over two men equal in virtue and teaching, namely Matthias and Joseph the Just, so that Peter said in his preaching: “You, Lord, who know the hearts of all, show which of these two you have chosen to receive the place of this ministry and apostleship” (Acts 1).

Moreover, before the lot was cast over the two goats, He commanded that they be set before the Lord; and He also commanded that the one upon which the lot for sending away had fallen should be set before the Lord after that lot had fallen upon it and its meaning had become clear, and that prayers should be poured out over it. How, then, is the one who has been set before God and in a certain manner consecrated to Him afterward sent to the devil? Or how can that sacrifice, which is sent to the wicked one, accomplish the propitiation of sins? For if its intention is even to make the righteous sinful, how could it bring propitiation to sinners? And how can that very sinner of whom David says, “Appoint a sinner over him, and let the devil stand at his right hand” (Ps. 108), obtain propitiation for sins? This belongs to God alone, to whom David said: “And be gracious to my sin, for it is abundant” (Ps. 24).

Since these things stand as they do, and this interpretation has everywhere been shown to be incongruous, let us not fail to recognize that the legislator undoubtedly spoke these things chiefly concerning the sacrifice of Christ. Hence, I think that those who envy the glory of the mystery and see its clear testimony in the law wish to sow the tares of a wicked interpretation: for Christ Jesus, who was incarnate for us, was God and man; while preserving the impassible divinity, He offered to suffering only His humanity. The effect of His passion—that is, our propitiation—belonged not merely to the flesh that suffered, but much more to the impassible divinity.

Paul bears witness to this when he says: “Who, being the radiance of his glory and the likeness of his substance, and sustaining all things by the word of his power” (Heb. 1). Showing that all these things are said concerning the divinity of the Only-Begotten, he added: “Having made purification for sins, he sat at the right hand of the Majesty on high,” joining even those things that belonged properly to His flesh to God the Word Himself.

If, then, these things have been suitably said, for this reason two goats are taken and set before the Lord at the entrance of the tent of testimony, so that these things might be performed in them as an image of Christ. For He is the true door that leads to the entrance of the tent of testimony, which is in heaven. Aaron casts a lot over both goats: one, so that by the power and symbolism of the lots we may understand the dispensation to be divided between Christ’s divinity and humanity; yet what belongs to each is divided in such a way that the one suffers while the other strengthens the sufferer, and through the passions working in the humanity both the passions contrary to us are governed and the impassibility of the divinity is revealed.

Then Scripture says that one lot is for the Lord and the other for the scapegoat—no one else but Christ, as we said above: “Aaron shall offer the goat upon which the lot for the Lord has fallen, and shall offer it for sin.” For the intelligible Aaron is the one who presides over our priesthood, of whom Paul says: “As Aaron, so also Christ” (Heb. 5); He did not glorify Himself to become a priest. He will offer His flesh to the Father, and in it He will offer for sin. Of Him Paul wrote to the Hebrews: “After offering one sacrifice for sin, he sits forever at the right hand of God” (Heb. 10).

But the goat upon which the lot of sending away has fallen he shall set alive before the Lord, to make supplication over it. Since we have said that the lot of the scapegoat is figuratively to be referred to Christ’s divinity, he sets this divinity alive, preserving it impassible, so that through it He may make supplication: “No one can forgive sins except God alone” (Luke 5). He sends it into a wilderness, for he calls it deserted by evil, solitary, or inaccessible—a place that intelligible enemies cannot traverse, in which God dwells and appears.

David makes this clear when he says: “O God, my God, to you I keep watch from the dawn. My soul thirsted for you; how manifoldly also my flesh. In a desert, and in an inaccessible and waterless land, so I appeared before you, that I might see your power and your glory.” Therefore the desert and the inaccessible place are holy, the dwelling-place of the Holy of Holies, where the divinity is said to have departed into heaven at the time of the passion—not moving from one place to another, but restraining its own power in relation to the humanity, so as to give room for the passion. In the place worthy of it, namely in the bosom of the Father, it remained where no one approaches except the Son Himself and the Holy Spirit, since He is in the Father and the Holy Spirit, as we have learned from the Gospel writings.

Therefore understand “to depart” as “to be restrained.” For God, who is present everywhere, is said to depart when He restrains His operation. He also bears our iniquities, because it is proper to fire to consume hay, and to divinity to destroy sin. Hence God is called “a consuming fire.”

And Aaron shall offer the bullock as a sin-offering, praying for himself and for his household; he shall sacrifice it, and, taking the censer that he has filled with coals from the altar, and taking in his hand the prepared incense, he shall enter beyond the veil into the holy place, so that, when he has placed the spices upon the fire, their cloud and vapor may cover the oracle that is above the testimony, and he may not die.

(From Hesychius.) The intelligible Aaron therefore sacrifices the bullock, that is, his own flesh. When this victim is understood as a sacrifice for the liberation of the Jewish people, the sacrifice of the bullock is necessarily assumed. For He Himself possessed legal justification to the highest degree, so that He might openly proclaim: “I have not come to abolish the law, but to fulfill it” (Matt. 5). Paul, however, said: “God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law” (Gal. 4). The bullock is suitably understood on account of the yoke of the commandments.

“Praying for himself,” that is, for the humanity. For He bore its figure in Himself; and “for his household,” specifically meaning the people who lived under the law, whom He came to redeem. They were His household because of their knowledge. Therefore Cleopas said: “But we hoped that he was the one who would redeem Israel.”

He shall sacrifice it; for He Himself sacrificed His own flesh. He Himself became the high priest of His sacrifice in Zion, when He gave the cup of the New Testament blood. “And taking the censer that he had filled with coals from the altar”: here he calls the Lord’s tongue the censer, for the Spirit was in it. He therefore takes the censer full of coals, because to His sacrifice He immediately added the teacherly words that were divine and heavenly. Concerning these David said: “Coals were kindled by him” (Ps. 17:9).

John wrote these words at the supper, after Judas had gone out. In them he explains how the Father is in Him, how He Himself, being in the Father, sends the gift of the Spirit, how the Father is the farmer and He the vine, while the apostles are the branches, how the ruler of this world is judged, and other mysteries. These are coals of fire, as it were, warming us toward piety, since they are spiritual in general (John 15).

He also speaks of the altar which, according to the Septuagint, is “before the Lord”; in the opening sections of this book we showed that this is the seat of the cherubim. For the prophet Ezekiel demonstrated that intelligible coals of fire had been placed there. He presents the Lord Himself, clothed in the long robe and girded about the loins, saying: “Enter into the midst of the wheels beneath the cherubim, and fill your hands from the midst of the cherubim” (Ezek. 10).

Since the intelligible altar on which the coals of fire are found must be understood as the seat of the cherubim [Note: [Col. 0421D] “Seat.” In the printed edition there is a punctuation break after “cherubim,” and it continues: “But by two punctuation breaks.”], hear Isaiah saying: “And one of the seraphim came to me, and in his hand was a coal which he had taken with tongs from the altar, and he touched my mouth” (Isa. 6).

What, then, is the altar that is in heaven, if not the seat of the cherubim? For just as the high priest and the king are the same, so he has both a seat and an altar. Signifying this, Paul said to the Hebrews: “For we do not have a high priest who cannot sympathize with our weaknesses, but one who was tested in every respect according to our likeness, without sin. Let us therefore approach with confidence the throne of his glory” (Heb. 4).

He was speaking of this intelligible altar, as the words that follow make clear: “That we may receive mercy and find grace for timely help.” We receive both of these from the altar without any doubt.

But what did the legislator add in what follows? “And taking incense in his hand, he shall enter beyond the veil into the holy place”; or, according to the Septuagint: “And he shall fill his hands with finely compounded incense, and shall offer it within, into the interior of the veil.” This refers to the prayer of which David said: “Let my prayer be directed as incense in your sight.”

When we pray for worldly matters, this prayer is, in a certain sense, coarse and not fine. But when we ask for spiritual things—that is, divine knowledge, the kingdom of heaven, and the remission of sins—it is a certain fine prayer, being spiritual and intelligible, which the intelligible priest offers on our behalf. This is evident from the fact that Christ, when praying for His disciples, requested for them sanctification, unity with Him, freedom in the world, and other such things.

“He shall enter into the holy place,” or, according to the Septuagint, “he shall offer within the interior of the veil,” namely, His flesh. To whom shall He offer it? To the Father, evidently, because these things were brought forth openly before everyone’s eyes, while their inner reality was invisible.

“So that, when he has placed the spices upon the fire, their cloud and vapor may cover the oracle that is above the testimony, and he may not die.” Understand what is said here in two ways. Because Aaron bears the figure of Christ Himself on account of the dignity of the priesthood, he also bears the figure of the body of priests.

Christ places spices upon the fire—that is, prayer upon doctrine—and the vapor of them covers it: this means the power of prayer. The oracle that is above the testimony means His flesh, from which the propitiation of sins was obtained for us, namely, in the saving passion. We showed shortly above that this is the testimony.

“And he shall not die”—that is, with the death of corruption. For His flesh did not see corruption, because it was covered by the vapor of the spices, namely by the power of that prayer with which David says Christ entreated the Father: “For you will not abandon my soul to the underworld, nor will you permit your holy one to see corruption.”

Every priest also, speaking of Christ, places upon the fire the spices of spiritual doctrine—prayer—and the power of prayer covers the oracle that is above the testimony. For it does not permit anyone to inquire into the sufferings of the Lord’s flesh beyond what lies within the power of the one who seeks. “And he shall not die”—that is, he shall not die the death appointed for immoderate investigators who seek things that human beings are not permitted to seek.

He shall also take some of the blood of the bullock and sprinkle it with his finger toward the mercy-seat on the east; or, according to the Septuagint, he shall sprinkle it with his finger upon the mercy-seat on the east. He shall sprinkle before the face of the mercy-seat seven times with his finger.

From these words the sacrifice of the Only-Begotten is clearly shown to be His flesh, while through the power of His divinity and by the Father’s good pleasure it is performed for the remission of our sins and our deliverance, and likewise for the household of the ministry of the Spirit. For the finger signifies the power of divinity. Hence David said: “For I shall see the heavens, the works of your fingers, the moon and the stars which you established” (Ps. 8).

We understand both of these as referring to the power of divinity. The blood of the bullock itself is sprinkled upon the mercy-seat toward the east, for the saving passion was accomplished both for our propitiation and for our illumination. Hence the passion itself is called the mercy-seat, as we have often shown. It is also called “the East.” The prophet Zechariah says of it: “Behold, a man whose name is East, and he shall rise beneath him.” Zechariah, the priest and father of John, likewise says: “In which the East from on high has visited us, to enlighten those who sit in darkness and in the shadow of death” (Luke 1).

He says that it shall also be sprinkled before the mercy-seat, that is, in the presence of the Father, seven times, so that human beings might receive both remission of sins and the gift of the Holy Spirit from the Lord’s blood. The number seven signifies both: there are seven gifts of the Spirit, and the same number also signifies the remission of sins.

For when Peter asked Christ: “If my brother sins against me, how often shall I forgive him, up to seven times?” Christ said: “I do not say seven times, but up to seventy times seven,” multiplying the number seven.

## CHAPTER V. On the Expiation of the Sanctuary through the Blood of the Goat and the Bullock

(IBID.) And when he has slaughtered the goat as a sin-offering for the people, he shall bring its blood within the veil, as he was commanded to do with the blood of the bullock, so that he may sprinkle it opposite the oracle and expiate the sanctuary from the impurities of the children of Israel, from their transgressions, and from all their sins.

(From Hesychius.) Because Christ arose from the Jews according to the flesh, who lived under the yoke of the law, He is rightly called the sacrifice of the bullock. But because, inasmuch as He was incarnate, He was formed from the common mass of humanity, He is again called a goat. For this animal wears a rough garment of hair, and the whole race of living beings is rough, as though filled with sin; nothing is rougher than sin. Therefore, wishing to make this clear, the legislator says: “And when he has slaughtered the goat as a sin-offering for the people.”

Here he understands the entire human race, which once was not a people but is now a people, since Jesus took firstfruits from among us. Thus, to show that Christ is principally from the Jews because of His kinship with Abraham, yet that He bears the firstfruits of our entire nature, which is in sin, and for this reason was also called Adam, the law took both a bullock and a goat as figures of His sacrifice.

Although there is one sacrifice, whether it is called a bullock or a goat, and although the effect is one in both—for the absolution of sins is brought about through it—the things performed with the goat and the bullock are necessarily shared. You see that he also kills the goat before the Lord, namely the Father, and brings its blood into the interior of the veil, that is, to the Father.

“And he shall expiate the sanctuary from the impurities of the children of Israel, from their transgressions, and from all their sins.” He appears to be speaking of the tabernacle, but not of the tabernacle accessible to the senses. For what need would wood have of expiation or propitiation? What need would the skins have, or the other materials from which the Jewish tabernacle perceptible to the senses was constructed? Rather, he means the whole, or the entire human race.

Our mass was holy from the beginning, so that the Spirit of God dwelt in it. This is shown by the fact that God threatened, in anger, to remove it when those who descended from Seth—although they were righteous and were called sons of God—lusted after those who were called daughters of men and became one kind with the wicked and unjust. For He said: “The sons of God, seeing that the daughters of men were beautiful, took wives for themselves from all whom they chose. And the Lord God said: My Spirit shall not remain in human beings forever, because they are flesh” (Gen. 6).

Therefore, if the Spirit of God dwelt in human beings before they all began to follow the passions of the flesh, the mass of humanity was rightly holy. For the Holy of Holies would not have taken firstfruits from it either.

But because it was defiled, He expiated it from the impurities of the children of Israel. According to the interpretation, Jesus was sacrificed as the Israel perceptible to the senses, that is, as a sacrifice, and He offered Himself for the entire human race, for the expiation of the impurities of its natures.

What impurities are these? “From their transgressions,” he says, “and from all their sins.” For the impurity of the soul is not the pollution of a dead body, nor the eating of pork, nor anything else of that kind; it is harming one’s neighbor, sinning against God, or violating the commandments of God.

According to this rite he shall act for the tent of testimony, which is fixed among them in the midst of the portions allotted for their dwelling. No human being shall be in the tent when the high priest enters the sanctuary to pray for himself, for his household, and for the whole assembly of Israel.

(From the same source.) What the law above called “the holy place,” it now calls “the tent of testimony,” which is fixed among them in the midst of the portions allotted for their dwelling. By the same reasoning our mass can be called both holy and the tent of testimony.

If we say that the tent of testimony is heaven, it is rightly called holy: it is our heavenly human being, of whom Paul says: “As we have borne the image of the earthly, let us also bear the image of the heavenly” (1 Cor. 15). Again: “If our earthly house of this habitation is dissolved, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens” (2 Cor. 5).

When Christ enters the holy place—that is, when He became incarnate as the heavenly human being and took firstfruits from us—no one was in the intelligible tent of testimony: neither Gentile, nor circumcised person, nor Levite, nor priest. For “all have turned aside; together they have become useless” (Ps. 52).

At that time no one was following a heavenly way of life, nor did anyone possess a wisdom worthy of the heavenly human being, until He prayed in the holy place of His own flesh through the cross. He then came forth from it under the law of common death, giving up His spirit while leaving His flesh in the tomb; this departure is clearly what is meant.

“No human being,” he says, “shall be in the tent when the high priest enters the sanctuary to pray.” This does not mean that every human being was excluded from the tabernacle during the time of the sacrifice just described. Rather, it signifies that the entire human race at that time had an earthly mind and was in sins, and therefore was rightly not found in the intelligible tent of testimony.

When he has gone out to the altar that is before the Lord, he shall pray for himself, and, taking the blood of the bullock and the goat, he shall pour it over the horns of the altar all around, and shall sprinkle it seven times with his finger. He shall expiate and sanctify it from the impurities of the children of Israel.

(From the same source.) After our going out to the altar that is before the Lord—he is speaking of the altar of incense, which we showed to be the seat of the cherubim—Christ ascended with the flesh, raised our captivity with Him, and together raised us up and made us sit at the right hand in the heavenly places.

He takes the blood and pours it over the horns of the altar that is in heaven all around, sprinkling it seven times with his finger. Through His own passion He expiated and sanctified the horns of the altar that is in heaven—that is, its chief and universal powers: wisdom, strength, justice, and chastity. These horns are rightly the cherubim.

For this heavenly creature bears their figures in the forms it possesses: that of a human being, a lion, a bullock, and an eagle. It bears wisdom in the form of the human being, strength in the form of the lion, justice in the form of the bullock, and chastity in the form of the eagle. We explained these things more fully long ago in our interpretation of the prophet Ezekiel.

“And he shall expiate and sanctify it from the impurities of the children of Israel.” The heavenly things are also expiated by Christ’s sacrifice, so that Paul wished to show the difference between the sacrifices of the law and that of the Only-Begotten when he said: “It is necessary that the copies of the heavenly things should be cleansed by these things, but the heavenly things themselves by better sacrifices.”

Why, then, did the heavenly things need expiation? The legislator shows this by saying: “He shall expiate and sanctify it from the impurities of the children of Israel.” As far as the powers of heaven are concerned, no expiation of any kind was necessary, since they continually live in sanctification. But because the smoke of our sins frequently rises to heaven, concerning which David said: “Smoke rose up in his anger, and fire blazed from his face” (Ps. 17), God said to Jonah: “Arise, go to Nineveh, the great city, and proclaim in it the proclamation that I speak to you, because its wickedness has risen before me” (Jon. 1).

Again, concerning Sodom, He said to Abraham: “I shall go down and see whether they have completed in deed the cry that has come to me, or not” (Gen. 18).

He therefore rightly sanctifies and expiates the heavens from our impurities—or, according to another reading, the heavenly choirs [Al.: “choros”]—so as to remove from them the surrounding abominable odor and the false boast that we have lodged against them. For this reason he does not sprinkle simply once, but seven times, so that you may understand that, through the forgiveness of our sins—which the number seven signifies—the heavenly places are cleansed of the abominable odor and the false boast that we have lodged against them. For this was the cause from which hostility first arose on our part against the things that are in heaven.

It follows: After he has cleansed the sanctuary, the tent, and the altar—or, according to the Septuagint, “and he shall complete his supplication for the holy place, the tent of testimony, and the altar, and shall purify it for the priests.”

(From the same source.) According to their edition, the law rightly made special mention of the priests, so that the figure of the sacrifice of the Only-Begotten might be preserved in every respect. For Christ’s priesthood was received by the company of the apostles, who were also part of the human race for which the Lord offered Himself. Yet He called them, in a certain sense, a special ointment and a distinguished sacrifice, as the Lord demonstrates when He says to the Father: “For them I sanctify myself, so that they too may be sanctified in truth.”

And again He says to them: “No one has greater love than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends. You are my friends if you do what I command you.”

Consider also the order of the legal figure and how it leads to the truth itself. According to the Septuagint he says: “He shall complete his supplication for the holy place, the tent of testimony, and the altar”; that is, he shall bring to an end and complete the supplication made through the cross for the entire human race, and the supplication that was made at the intelligible altar.

After He has been taken up into heaven and has sat at the right hand of the Father, He sends cleansing to His priests through intelligible fire and through the fiery tongues of the Spirit. Therefore He said to them: “But you shall be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now.”

## CHAPTER VI. On the Sending Away of the Goat and the Procession
*(Same passage.)* Then he shall offer the living goat, and, placing both hands upon its head, confess all the iniquities of the children of Israel and all their transgressions and sins; and, having rebuked them upon its head, he shall send it away by the hand of a man prepared for this purpose into the wilderness. And when the goat, bearing all their iniquities, has carried them into a solitary land and has been released in the wilderness, and so forth. *(From Hesychius.)*

[Col. 0426C] We must repeat these things even now for the sake of those who stumble in the light. For it is proved that the things now sanctioned in connection with this living goat are accomplished not for any unrighteous or evil being, but for God himself. First, because the priest places both hands upon the goat’s head. The laying on of hands in a sacrifice signified a blessing, or the remission of sins, or the coming of the Holy Spirit, or intelligible expiation. How, then, could the priest perform upon this goat—concerning which those who belong to that party say that it represents the lot of the enemy and of him who wages war against God—the things just mentioned? Or how could he, in that goat, redeem the iniquities, injustices, and sins of the children of Israel? For the enemy does not allow sins to be confessed; rather, he suggests that we conceal the wounds of the soul, so that we may not find the physician who can apply medicine and provide healing. Therefore, immediately after Nathan rebuked David, he cried out, “I have sinned against the Lord,” and the prophet at once added, “The Lord has taken away your sin; you shall not die” (2 Kings 12). “Nevertheless, because you have caused the enemies of the Lord to blaspheme,” and so forth.

Hence the lawgiver also said that the goat was to be sent into the wilderness by a man prepared for the purpose. By “prepared,” that is, approaching or drawing near, he does not specify the dignity of the person who was to perform this task—whether he was a Levite, a priest, or someone from the people. Thus the goat signifies that Christ is present in all things. For just as, in the first instance, he was sacrificed through the flesh, so now he is called living because of his divinity.

[Col. 0427A] But because he is one, both impassible and passible, the priest necessarily lays his hands also upon the living goat, so that by the laying on of hands it may be shown that the living Word of God—impassible and immortal—assumed flesh for us and accepted the sacrifice. Therefore the priest rightly pronounced upon him the iniquities, injustices, and sins. This is he of whom the prophet Isaiah said: “Lord, who has believed our report, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” (Isa. 53). Calling the Son “the arm of the Lord,” he declares him consubstantial with the Father.

Concerning him he added what follows: “He himself took our infirmities and bore our diseases; he was wounded because of our iniquities, he was crushed because of our transgressions; the discipline of our peace was upon him, and by his bruising we were healed.” Thus he plainly bore upon himself our sins, injustices, and iniquities. Therefore, according to the Septuagint, he says: “He shall place them upon the head of the living goat.” For this is the figure of what Christ also permitted to be placed upon his own head: a crown of thorns, since sins are commonly understood by thorns. For this reason the earth was also commanded to produce thorns for Adam, since he too produced sins through disobedience. Solomon likewise says: “Thorns are born in the hand of the drunkard” (Prov. 26), signifying that his actions are full of sins.

Thus, when you understand the words of the law, you will not be ignorant of its intention and power. You will also find the prepared man by whose hand the living goat is sent into the wilderness. For Christ himself became everything belonging to his sacrifice: priest, sacrifice, knife, and altar. He is also the prepared man, prepared for us for suffering, so that he himself says through Isaiah: “But I did not resist; I did not turn back. I gave my body to those who struck me, and my cheeks to those who plucked them; I did not turn my face away from those who rebuked and spit upon me” (Isa. 50).

[Col. 0427B] To him David also speaks, signifying the mystery of his incarnation, through which he attained our kingship: “The Lord has become king; he has clothed himself with beauty. The Lord has clothed himself with strength and girded himself with power. For he established the world, and it shall not be shaken; your throne is prepared from of old” (Ps. 92).

Christ, therefore, is the intelligible Aaron, even now offering himself through the living goat. He does so through the prepared man, or in the hand of the prepared man—that is, through his own power—for, since he is also the prepared man, he has been manifested as such. And he sends the living goat into the wilderness, or into an impassable and deserted land: his divine nature, immortal and impassible, goes to places inaccessible to us and deserted of all wickedness, in accordance with what John says: “Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he had come forth from God and was going to God.”

[Col. 0427C] “For the priest who has been anointed and whose hands have been consecrated to exercise the priesthood in place of his father shall make expiation”; or, according to the Septuagint: “The priest whom he shall anoint, and whoever shall be completed to consecrate his hands for his father, shall make supplication.” This was said to manifest Christ without any uncertainty. For since Christ had as his fathers, according to the flesh, the chief priests of the Jews—for they too were sons of Abraham, as Christ was—the law showed that, because the Jewish priests could not, as Paul says, “make those who approach perfect” (Heb. 9), since “it was impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins,” Christ himself was rightly anointed for the priesthood and, completing his hands through the cross, makes expiation for us.

Concerning him the law rightly says elsewhere: “The priest whom they shall anoint and complete shall exercise the priesthood with his hands after his father.” First the Father anointed him, as David says: “Therefore God, your God, has anointed you” (Ps. 44). He anointed him when he said: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. 109). Afterwards he was anointed by the human beings who ministered to his passion and sacrifice.

[Col. 0428A] The sacrifice of the cross manifested both our Lamb and Priest and Deliverer. Therefore, for a clearer demonstration and more subtle manifestation of the figure, he says, “Once a year he shall do this”—wishing to show the sacrifice of the Only-Begotten, which was accomplished once for all. Of this it is said: “Christ, having been offered once to bear the sins of many, will appear a second time, apart from sin, to those who await him for salvation” (Heb. 9).

Adamantius, in his homilies on Leviticus, interpreted these two goats differently. He says that the goat sacrificed to the Lord represents those who are saved and belong to the Lord’s lot, like the poor Lazarus who was carried by angels into Abraham’s bosom (Luke 16). But the goat released into the wilderness signifies the reprobate, or the Jewish people, who deserved to be cast away from the sight of the Lord on account of their sins, like the rich man clothed in purple who, after death, was buried in hell.

[Col. 0428B] He understands the prepared man by whom the apompeus (scapegoat) was led into the wilderness to be the Lord Savior or his holy angels, from whom each person receives the fitting recompense for his work.

Hence blessed Ambrose also says in his letter to Simplicianus:

“For just as there are two men in the field, one of whom is taken and the other left behind, so there are two goats: one useful for sacrifice, the other sent into the wilderness. The latter is useful for nothing, neither to be eaten nor to be feasted upon by the sons of the priests. For just as among foods what is good is eaten, while what is useless or bad is thrown away, so we call good works suitable for feasting—works that are fit to be eaten.

“Therefore it will not please the Lord if the priest eats a sacrifice in which there is fraud in the offering and not the sincerity of diligent confession. For this reason this goat must be sent into the wilderness, where our fathers wandered; they wandered there and could not reach the land of resurrection, and the memory of them perished from the earth.

“Finally, there are works suitable for feasting. Hear: ‘The sabbaths of the land shall be food for you.’ For rest in God is suitable for feasting and refreshment; it produces tranquility of spirit. Therefore let us also rest in discourse.”

But since we are setting out the interpretations of different authors, we leave it to the reader’s judgment to decide which should be preferred.

## CHAPTER VII. On sacrifices that may be offered only at the entrance of the tabernacle

(CAP. 17.) And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: [Col. 0429A] Speak to Aaron and his sons and to all the children of Israel, and say to them: This is the word that the Lord has commanded, saying: If any man of the house of Israel kills an ox or a goat within the camp or outside the camp, and does not bring an offering to the Lord at the entrance of the tabernacle, he shall be guilty of blood. He shall be cut off from the midst of his people.

Therefore the children of Israel must bring to the priest their sacrifices that they slaughter in the field, so that they may be sanctified to the Lord before the entrance of the tabernacle of testimony. They shall sacrifice them as peace offerings to the Lord, and the priest shall pour the blood upon the altar of the Lord at the entrance of the tabernacle of testimony, and he shall burn the fat as a pleasing aroma to the Lord. They shall no longer sacrifice their offerings to demons, with whom they have committed fornication. This shall be a perpetual statute for them and for their descendants.

*(From Hesychius.)* [Col. 0429B] This present ordinance shows what he commanded not simply to Moses, but to Aaron and his sons and to all the children of Israel. Yet it plainly makes clear that this commandment of the law does not wish anyone—neither a great person, nor a more perfect one, nor an imperfect one—to be ignorant of what it is useful for them to know: namely, that the law of the letter is temporary, so that, when its time has been completed, we should no longer occupy ourselves fruitlessly and unnecessarily with it.

What, then, is the end of the times? It is the complete destruction of the very place in which he commanded sacrifices to be offered. For he threatened and commanded that anyone who completed God’s sacrifice within the camp or outside it, but outside the tabernacle of testimony, should perish from the people. Thus, when the tabernacle of testimony and the temple—which was made according to its image—have been destroyed, it may be recognized that all the things which the law commanded to be done there have come to an end, and that even those things no longer please God.

For he would not have destroyed the place in which what ought by every means to be performed according to the law was to be carried out. You learn this also from the following: he does not confine righteous actions—namely, not killing, not committing adultery, not stealing, not bearing false witness, honoring father and mother, loving one’s neighbors, making slaves free, fasting frequently, or praying—to a place, because these things are always useful and are shared with evangelical conduct.

[Col. 0429C] But those things which in themselves are superfluous and were established for the sake of some special occasion or purpose he confines to a place, so that they may understand that they are temporary. For everything that serves a place has also been ordained to serve a time.

Sacrifices, therefore, were assigned to a place, as were the cleansing rites for the dead, for those suffering a discharge of seed, for lepers, and for menstruating women, since these too were effected through sacrifices. Likewise the Unleavened Bread, the figurative Passover, the Feast of Tabernacles, Pentecost, the New Moons, and the Sabbaths: sacrifices had to be offered on all these occasions. But because these things contained figures of the mysteries that were to be fulfilled by the Lord, we have sufficiently demonstrated this above.

Therefore whoever now attempts to carry out the figures after the place has been destroyed sheds blood—that is, he pollutes the common way of life and sins in the community. Such people also shed the blood of the one whom they lead into error, since they become the cause of his destruction.

[Col. 0430A] “They shall no longer sacrifice their offerings to demons, with whom they have committed fornication”; or, according to the Septuagint: “They shall no longer sacrifice their sacrifices to vain things.”
