*(From the same author.)* When God had commanded them, “You shall not make for yourself an idol, nor any likeness of the things that are in heaven above, or on the earth below, or in the waters beneath the earth,” they made a molten calf and offered sacrifice to the calf. Because of their greediness of the belly, wishing to consume sacrifices, the law, acting as their pedagogue, commanded them to offer sacrifices to God, so that, occupied with these things, they might abstain from every idolatrous sacrifice. It also sanctioned these practices so that the law, while restraining them from sacrifices to idols, might at the same time teach them the figures of future mysteries.

He rightly called service to idols fornication, teaching us plainly that God betrothed our souls to himself for salvation, and therefore separation from him is called fornication.

[Col. 0430B] Moreover, he frightens those who commit fornication in the flesh and teaches what kind of sin fornication is, so that he called the worship of idols fornication, resorting to demons fornication, and said to them:

“Any man of the children of Israel, or of the foreigners who dwell among you, who offers a burnt offering or a sacrifice and does not bring it to the entrance of the tabernacle of testimony to offer it to the Lord shall be cut off from his people.”

*(From the same author.)* Although the lawgiver seems to say the same things, he nevertheless makes the people, upon whom the law is imposed by him, more cautious. By saying the same thing frequently, he shows that this commandment is necessary and exceedingly useful. Yet he does not repeat it without reason.

Above, he subjected only the one who slaughtered an animal in order to make some sacrifice—not, however, the one who completed every other part of the sacrifice—to punishment. For he says: “Whoever kills an ox or a sheep, whether within the camp or outside the camp, and does not bring an offering to the Lord at the entrance of the tabernacle.” There he is understood to have been forbidden what he attempted. Here, however, the matter is different: whoever offers a burnt offering or a sacrifice and does not bring it to the entrance of the tabernacle of testimony so that it may be offered to the Lord is said to have made a completed or perfect sacrifice, to such an extent that he made it a burnt offering; nevertheless, he is subjected to the same punishment.

For the one who began to undertake this and was forbidden differs in no way from the one who completed it. The punishment of both is also destruction from the people, so that such a person may no longer dwell among the people, glory in circumcision, adorn himself with descent from Abraham, or be called an Israelite, but may be placed among those who possess the foreskin and among foreigners. This is what it means for someone to be destroyed from his people.

[Col. 0430C] Above all, however, this too must be noted: he commanded not only those who are of the children of Israel to observe these things, but also the proselytes, or foreigners who dwell among them—that is, the Gentiles. For these are not joined to them but are among them. We are indeed among them, since we possess their law and prophets and the inheritance promised to them; yet we cleave not to them but to God.

Furthermore, according to the Septuagint, he says “man, man,” although he could simply have said “a man.” He doubles the expression to show that both the one who cleaves to God in circumcision and the one who does so in the foreskin must observe this commandment.

According to the literal sense, the passage says: “Whoever kills an ox, or a sheep, or a goat, whether within the camp or outside the camp, and does not bring an offering to the Lord at the entrance of the tabernacle,” and so forth.

*(From Augustine.)* He is not speaking of animals killed for food or for any other use, but of sacrifices. He prohibited private sacrifices, so that no one might dare in some fashion to be his own priest, but should offer there where sacrifices are offered to God through the priest. Thus they would not sacrifice to empty or vain things either, for he had already warned that this too must be avoided in that practice.

Since sacrifices were not permitted except in the tabernacle, which the temple later succeeded, this explains why Jeroboam, king of Israel, dared to make calves for the people to sacrifice to, so that those who were under his rule would not be compelled by the requirement of this law to leave him and go to Jerusalem to offer their sacrifices in the temple of God. For this act he was condemned by the Lord.

[Col. 0430D] It is reasonably asked, then, how Elijah could lawfully sacrifice outside the temple of God, when he both obtained fire from heaven and defeated the prophets of the demons. This seems to me defensible by no other reasoning than that by which Abraham’s deed is also defended: he wished to sacrifice his son to God because he had been commanded to do so.

When the one who established the law commands something to be done that he prohibited in the law, the command itself is regarded as law, since he is the author of the law. For there could have been no other miracles besides the sacrifice by which the prophets of the groves might be overcome and confuted. But whatever the Spirit of God, who was in Elijah, accomplished in this matter cannot be contrary to the law, because he is the giver of the law.

## CHAPTER VIII. On not eating blood

*(Same passage.)* Any person of the house of Israel, or of the foreigners who dwell among them, who eats blood—I will set my face against that person and cut him off from his people—because the life of the flesh is in the blood, and I have given it to you upon the altar to make expiation through it for your lives; and the blood shall be for the expiation of the soul. Therefore I said to the children of Israel: No person among you shall eat blood, nor any of the foreigners who dwell among you.

*(From Hesychius.)* The Septuagint also says “man, man,” the meaning of which we explained above. Therefore we must observe even the literal sense of this commandment and in no way eat blood. You will find that the apostles also commanded this when a question arising from a dispute over certain Jewish observances was brought before them in the church at Antioch. They settled and determined the question as follows: “It has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to lay upon you no greater burden than these necessary things: that you abstain from things sacrificed to idols, and from blood, and from what has been strangled, and from fornication” (Acts 15).

*(From Augustine.)* There is something vital in blood, because through it especially life is maintained in this flesh, as it is diffused through all the veins throughout the body. He called this the life of the body “the soul”—not the life that departs from the body, but the life that ends in death. In this manner we say that this present life is temporal, not eternal, mortal, not immortal, even though the nature of the soul is immortal. It is this soul that was received by the angels into Abraham’s bosom, and to which it is said, “Today you will be with me in paradise,” and which burned in the torments of hell.

Accordingly, in keeping with this meaning in which even this temporal life is called “soul,” the apostle Paul said: “For I do not hold my soul precious to myself” (Acts 20), wishing to show that he was prepared to die for the Gospel. For according to the meaning in which “soul” denotes that which departs from the body, he was making it all the more precious by acquiring such merit for it.

*(From Hesychius.)* Moreover, let us understand blood properly as homicide, and every bloodshed as every hatred of a brother, because “whoever hates his brother is a murderer,” as John wrote (1 John 3). We therefore call every injustice of deceitful people “blood,” for “the Lord abhors the bloodthirsty and deceitful man” (Ps. 5), as well as anyone who harms the lives of his neighbors through any kind of ambush, so that it may be compared with the shedding of blood in homicide.

[Col. 0432A] Therefore we must abstain from all blood, knowing that God sets his face against the souls that eat such blood—those of whom David said, “They devour my people as though they were eating bread” (Ps. 13). This face is Christ himself, for he is the image of the Father; “whoever has seen the Son has seen the Father.” He is also the judge, and therefore the words “I will cut off” are necessarily used as a threat against those who practice evil. David demonstrates this when he says: “But the face of the Lord is against those who do evil, to destroy their memory from the earth” (Ps. 33).

He destroys this soul that eats blood from his people—that is, from the common race of humanity. But when he says, “The life of every flesh is in its blood, and I have given it to you upon the altar to make expiation through it for your souls,” he signifies the mystical blood of Christ. For his blood shall be for the expiation of the soul. The blood upon the altar for the expiation of our souls, making expiation for the soul, is certainly the blood that the Crucified poured out for us and by which he provided expiation, or propitiation, for the human race, offering the firstfruits.

[Col. 0432B] Therefore he rightly says: “And the blood shall be for the expiation of the soul.” His soul was first formed by him; then, when he became incarnate, he received a soul consubstantial with ours, so that he might pay on our behalf the death that we owed.

Because Christ gave his blood for the expiation of our souls, he teaches us to abstain from every homicide and from every other iniquity that is close to homicide. For this is a common law, extending to everyone:

“Any person of the children of Israel and of the foreigners who dwell among you who catches a wild animal or a bird in hunting or fowling, one that is permitted to be eaten, shall pour out its blood and cover it with earth. For the life of every flesh is in its blood. Therefore I said to the children of Israel: You shall not eat the blood of any flesh, because the life of the flesh is in its blood; whoever eats it shall be cut off. God takes great care that we do not harm one another in any way.”

*(From Hesychius.)* For this reason Jesus commanded that when someone strikes us on the cheek, we should yield and not contend with him in judgment. Likewise, concerning the one who takes away our cloak, he commanded us not even to be provoked by contention into harming our neighbor, but rather to correct the person who acts unjustly against us through our patience.

Nothing constrains our life more than injustice, greed, and mutual oppression. With this in view, the lawgiver did not repeat the command concerning blood without reason.

[Col. 0432C] For some people habitually harm their fellow citizens through frauds, schemes, and various deceits, killing them as though they did not know what was happening. He perceived such plots as well. For observe what he commands: “If he catches in hunting or fowling a wild animal or a bird that is permitted to be eaten, he shall pour out its blood and cover it with earth.”

“Hunting” is often understood in divine Scripture as injustice—especially not every kind of injustice, but injustice directed toward blood and harming, by deceit and fraud, the very life of the person suffering injustice. Hear David say concerning this: “They will hunt the soul of the righteous and condemn innocent blood” (Ps. 93). And again: “Our soul has been rescued like a sparrow from the snare of the hunters” (Ps. 123).

If someone catches game, then—that is, if he sees a sinner who has been exposed to capture through weakness or simplicity—for we say that this is the one who is caught—therefore it says, “a wild animal or a bird that is permitted to be eaten.”

[Col. 0433A] By the wild animal he signifies someone from the common people, yet carnal and devoted to feeding, and without participation in legal disputes. By the bird he signifies one who withdraws himself from earthly matters. Such people are consumed by the violent and greedy in secular lawsuits, by that inappropriate and evil feasting against which Paul warned, saying: “But if you bite and devour one another, take care that you are not consumed by one another” (Gal. 5).

Or perhaps those who were formerly righteous are rightly named among the things permitted to be eaten—that is, among the clean things. Yet if someone sheds the blood of a sinner, as of one lying below and buried in repentance—that is, if he brings out the sin he has committed—he pours out the blood, but he pours it out by approaching prayer and confession, as David says: “I will pour out my prayer before him” (Ps. 141).

Let him cover it with earth. For the earth covers the sins of those who confess, since they remain below and have been put to death through repentance; their cry is prevented from ascending to heaven, as the cry of the Sodomites ascended, for they were unwilling to repent.

[Col. 0433B] With this intention, therefore, the lawgiver added to what has been said: “For the life of every flesh is in its blood.” Then he adds: “Therefore I said to the children of Israel”—that is, I say—“You shall not eat the blood of any flesh, because the life of the flesh is in its blood,” bearing witness that they must abstain from every iniquity.

By this testimony he means that one should not expose the sins of brothers that have been committed unwillingly, but should hand them over to the earth: the blood of the one who has been caught—that is, seen—should be covered by forgiveness and compassion. For the person who defames a neighbor’s sin is rightly considered to eat blood and a soul, since sin is the death of the soul.

## CHAPTER IX. On not eating anything that has died or been seized by a beast

*(Same passage.)* Any person who eats an animal that has died of itself or has been seized by a beast, whether native-born or foreign, shall wash his garments and himself with water and shall be unclean until evening; afterward he shall be clean. But if he does not wash his garments or his body, he shall bear his iniquity.

*(From the same author.)* We said long ago, when the lawgiver was explaining the sacrifices of purification, that the animal that has died of itself signifies a sinner, since he endures the cruel death of sin, while the animal seized by beasts signifies not merely a sinner but a very great sinner, to the extent that evil demons work in him, as was the case with Judas, who, when the devil entered his heart, betrayed Christ.

But there the law speaks of the person who touches an animal that has died or has been seized by beasts—that is, who associates or shares with those previously mentioned. Here, however, it speaks of the person who eats it, that is, who makes the other person’s entire sin his own and fulfills his own evil intention through the evil that the other committed.

Such were Annas and Caiaphas. They did not merely become participants in Judas’s betrayal; they themselves made the purchase and gave him the money for the betrayal. Longing and desiring the Lord’s death, in order to feed and nourish their own intention and satisfy their desire, they prevailed through Judas.

[Col. 0434A] Those who do such things are said to eat animals that have died and those seized by beasts. They must wash their garments and their bodies. The one who washes his garment and body cleanses himself completely—that is, his inner and outer person—for the body is within the garments just as the inner person is within the outer person.

How does he wash himself? Either through baptism or through an abundance of tears that imitate the waters of baptism. But whoever does not do this shall bear his iniquity—that is, the recompense of his injustice. Thus you will find that divine Scripture threatens to restore punishments for sins. Hence Ezekiel represents God as saying: “My eye shall not spare you, nor will I have pity; I will place your ways upon you, and your abominations shall be in your midst.”

## CHAPTER X. On observing the commandments and judgments of the Lord

(CAP. 18.) And the Lord said to Moses: Speak to the children of Israel, and say to them: I am the Lord your God. You shall not act according to the customs of the land of Egypt in which you dwelt, nor shall you act according to the practices of the land of Canaan, into which I am bringing you; you shall not walk in their statutes. You shall carry out my judgments and observe my commandments, and you shall walk in them. I am the Lord your God. Observe my laws and my judgments; the person who does them shall live in them.

*(From Hesychius.)* In commanding the things now mentioned, he says: “I am the Lord your God,” so that, learning that the one who commanded us is Creator and Lord, we may observe with the greatest zeal the things he has commanded. Thus he has explained the intention of the entire ordinance.

What is that intention? That we abstain from every iniquity and practice the things that belong to virtue. By commanding that we do nothing according to the customs of the land of Egypt or according to the practices of the land of Canaan, he commanded us to abstain from every iniquity.

[Col. 0435A] The Septuagint, however, translated “customs” as “pursuits,” because divine Scripture commonly calls wicked inventions and stories “pursuits of evil,” as when Ezekiel, after showing the elders of Israel committing iniquities in the temple, says: “And the Lord said to me: Do you see, son of man?” And again: “When you turn, you will see pursuits greater than these.”

Therefore he commanded us to abstain not only from fornication, greed, and pride, but also from divination, the practices of augury, and magic arts; likewise from magical practices and similar things. Thus Moses said in Deuteronomy:

“When you enter the land that the Lord your God gives you, take care not to wish to imitate the abominations of those nations. Let there not be found among you one who consults an oracle or observes dreams and omens, or a sorcerer, or an enchanter, or one who consults a python, or diviners, or one who seeks the truth from the dead. For everyone who does these things is an abomination to the Lord; and because of these abominations the Lord will destroy them before you.”

[Col. 0435B] We must therefore first abstain from these things. Then he says to us: “You shall carry out my judgments, observe my commandments, and walk in them”—that is, move and conduct yourselves in them, and at no time cease from correcting your conduct according to them.

Then again he adds: “I am the Lord your God. Observe my laws and my judgments; the person who does them shall live in them.”

It is worthy of inquiry and careful consideration why, in one place of the law, he twice says that his judgments are to be carried out and his commandments observed, or why he says twice, “I am the Lord your God.”

There are two Testaments, the Old and the New. Therefore he himself also said through Jeremiah: “I will give you a new covenant, not according to the covenant that I made with your fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt” (Jer. 31).

[Col. 0435C] It is therefore right that he makes mention of judgments and commandments a second time, so that he might also indicate those things that he was later going to sanction. Concerning these he now adds: “The person who does them shall live in them.” For true life is perfected in those who believe in Christ, concerning which the Lord said in the Gospel: “This is the will of my Father, that everyone who sees the Son and believes in him should have eternal life” (John 6).

It is therefore entirely reasonable that he says a second time, “I am the Lord your God,” bearing witness that the same Lord sanctioned both the earlier judgments or commandments and the later ones. The person who does them shall live in them—not in the earlier judgments and commandments.

Observe what he added: “I am the Lord.”

## CHAPTER XI. It is not permitted to approach a near blood-relative in order to uncover that person’s nakedness
(IBID.) No one shall approach any near relation by blood, to uncover his nakedness. I am the Lord. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father or the nakedness of your mother; she is your mother, you shall not uncover her nakedness. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father’s wife, for it is the nakedness of your father. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your sister by father or by mother, whether she was born at home or abroad [Col. 0436A]. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your son’s daughter or your daughter’s daughter, for she is your own flesh. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father’s wife’s daughter, whom she bore to your father; she is your sister, you shall not uncover her nakedness. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father’s sister, for she is your father’s flesh. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your mother’s sister, for she is your mother’s flesh. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your paternal uncle, nor approach his wife, who is related to you by marriage. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your daughter-in-law, for she is your son’s wife; you shall not uncover her shame. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your brother’s wife, for it is your brother’s nakedness. You shall not uncover the nakedness of your wife and her daughter. You shall not take her son’s daughter or her daughter’s daughter in order to uncover her shame, for they are her flesh, and such intercourse is incestuous [Col. 0436B]. You shall not take your wife’s sister in addition to her, nor uncover her nakedness while she is still alive.

(From Augustine.) These matters must be examined more carefully according to the historical sense: “You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father or the nakedness of your mother.” To uncover their nakedness means to lie with one’s mother; for there is the nakedness of father and mother. Later he also prohibits intercourse with the stepmother, when he says: “You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father’s wife, for it is the nakedness of your father.” There he explained how, in the mother of both, there is the nakedness of both father and mother, whereas in the stepmother there is only the nakedness of the father.

“You shall not uncover the nakedness of your sister by your father or by your mother, who was born at home or who was born abroad.” The one born at home is understood to be by the father; the one born abroad is understood to be by the mother, if perhaps her mother had received her from an earlier husband and had brought her with her into the household when she married her father.

Scripture warns a man not to uncover the nakedness of his sister. Here it seems not to have prohibited, but almost to have passed over, intercourse with a sister born of both parents. For it does not say, “You shall not uncover the nakedness of your sister by father and mother,” but “by father or mother.” Yet who does not see that the other case too is most certainly prohibited? If it is not permitted to uncover the nakedness of a sister born of either parent, how much more is it forbidden when she is born of both?

But what does it mean that, after inserting the prohibition of intercourse even with one’s own nieces, whether through a son or through a daughter, he then continues: “You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father’s wife’s daughter”? If he had stopped there, we would understand intercourse with the daughter of the stepmother to have been forbidden—one whom the stepmother had borne from an earlier husband and who was not the sister of the man being prohibited, either by father or by mother. But when he adds, “She is your sister, born of the same father; you shall not uncover her nakedness,” he makes clear that the prohibition concerns a sister born of the father and the stepmother. He had already spoken of her above. Or did he wish to prohibit this again more explicitly because what had been said above was somewhat obscure? Scripture often does this.

“You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father’s brother, nor enter his wife.” He explained what he meant by “the nakedness of your father’s brother,” that is, of your paternal uncle: you shall not uncover it, that is, you shall not enter his wife. In the wife of your paternal uncle he intended the nakedness of the paternal uncle to be understood, just as in the wife of the father the nakedness of the father is understood.

“You shall not uncover the nakedness of your brother’s wife, for it is your brother’s nakedness.” The question is whether this is prohibited while the brother is alive or after his death, and it is no small question. If we say that Scripture is speaking of the wife of a living brother, then this is certainly also included under the general precept by which a man is forbidden to approach another man’s wife. What, then, is the reason that it so carefully distinguishes these persons, whom it calls household relations, from the rest by specific prohibitions? For when it prohibits intercourse with the father’s wife—that is, the stepmother—should this not be understood as referring to the time when the father is alive, and rather to the time after his death? While the father is alive, who does not see that it is all the more forbidden, if the wife of any man at all is forbidden to be defiled by adultery?

It therefore seems to speak of persons who, if they had no husbands, could enter into marriage, unless they were prohibited by law—as is said to have been the custom among the Persians. But again, if we understand the prohibition to concern marrying the wife of a deceased brother, there arises the command that Scripture gives for the raising up of offspring, if he died without children. Accordingly, these prohibitions must be understood in conjunction with that command, so that they do not conflict: namely, that no one may marry the wife of a deceased brother if the deceased left descendants; or perhaps that it is also prohibited to marry a brother’s wife who had separated from her living husband by divorce.

For then, as the Lord says (Mark 10), “Because of the hardness of the Jews Moses permitted the issuing of a bill of divorce.” Through such a dismissal it might be thought that someone could lawfully take his brother’s wife, since adultery would not be feared because she had departed by divorce.

“You shall not uncover the nakedness of a woman and her daughter”—that is, no one should think that he is permitted to marry his wife’s daughter. One may not uncover the nakedness of both the woman and her daughter, that is, have intercourse with both mother and daughter.

“You shall not take her son’s daughter or her daughter’s daughter.” He also prohibited marrying as a wife the wife’s granddaughter, whether through her son or through her daughter.

“Beside her you shall not take her sister in rivalry.” Here he did not prohibit taking a second wife in addition to the first, which was permitted to the ancients because of the abundance of offspring; rather, he did not wish one sister to be taken in addition to another sister. Jacob appears to have done this, either because it had not yet been prohibited by law, or because he had been deceived by the fraud concerning the woman substituted for the other and had come to the one he had agreed to take, whom he later received. Yet it would have been unjust to dismiss the first, lest he make her an adulteress.

But what does he mean by “in rivalry”? Is it placed there so that there may be no rivalry between sisters, something that would not have been objectionable between women who were not sisters? Or rather, is it intended to prevent the act from being done for this reason—that one sister should be taken in addition to another in order to provoke rivalry?

(From Hesychius.) It is worth considering carefully that, when he says, “No one shall approach any near relation by blood, to uncover his nakedness,” he adds, “I am the Lord.” Why was it necessary to add this, when at the beginning of the present enactment he had already said once, “I am the Lord your God”? He plainly shows that the one who enacts these commands is himself the one who has also been joined to us in the flesh and has become a participant in our kinship. Therefore it is unjust for us to dishonor the greatness of his kinship.

Since these things are so, it must be understood that the command is also enacted spiritually. He does not wish us to expose whatever sins have been entrusted to us by relatives or friends, nor to disclose their shameful deeds, lest we suffer what Ham suffered: he saw his father’s nakedness and did not cover it, but, going out, disclosed it to his brothers (Gen. 9).

In the father, mother, sister, and all the other relatives whom he has listed, those to whom Paul refers must be understood along with the bodily relations: “Do not rebuke an older man, but entreat him as a father; younger men as brothers; older women as mothers; younger women as sisters” (1 Tim. 5).

Then, wishing to gather for us a kinship with all who are faithful, with all who share the same faith, he says again: “Though many, we are one body in Christ, and individually members of one another” (Rom. 12). Therefore he called it impious to expose the shame of any of those mentioned above, because the violation of spiritual kinship reaches to God, once we have entered into kinship with him through the bond of the Spirit.

Nevertheless, one who meditates carefully on the words of the law must not pass over this point: according to the Septuagint, the legislator has here set out a number of ten degrees of kinship. The commandments of the whole law are represented by this number, showing that whoever exposes the shame of bodily or spiritual relatives is found to be a transgressor of the whole law.

Why? Because what he does is alien to love, which is the fullness of the law. For what Paul says—“You shall not commit adultery, you shall not kill, you shall not steal, you shall not covet,” and if there is any other commandment—is summed up in this word: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” Love does no harm to a neighbor; therefore love is the fullness of the law (Rom. 13).

The meaning becomes clearer if we examine the wording itself: “No one shall approach any near relation by blood, to uncover his nakedness.” This means that we should not approach relatives under the pretext of knowing the law, and thereby test them, then, after learning their shameful deeds, expose them.

Therefore he very appropriately added, “I am the Lord”—that is, I reveal human sins, but whatever they have confessed and laid open in prayer I cover and scatter, so that not even a trace of them may be found [Col. 0438D].

“You shall not take your wife’s sister in addition to her, nor uncover her nakedness while she is still alive.”

(From Hesychius.) These commands are rightly given, because the Lord God has called us to peace. He wishes us to be at peace with everyone, saying also through Paul: “If possible, so far as it depends on you, live at peace with all people” (Rom. 12). Much more does he wish us to be peaceful with those nearest to us. This peace is overturned if someone joins himself both to a wife and to her sister, so that the sisters live together and rivalry is stirred up between them; from this contention and quarrelling arise.

After this, the law commanded that one should not adopt ecclesiastical observance together with Jewish observance, nor celebrate the Passover—which is in figure—together with what is spiritual; nor, while celebrating the feast of Unleavened Bread, partake of Christ’s supper, which is the true Unleavened Bread; nor preach circumcision and baptism together.

Remember the one who said: “Behold, I, Paul, tell you that if you are circumcised, Christ will be of no benefit to you” (Gal. 5).

But if someone has perhaps followed Jewish observance, let him mortify it by neglecting it—that is, render it ineffective and powerless—and then let him be joined to what belongs to the Church. The Church is indeed its sister, because she has the same law and the same prophets, but she is its rival—not because she herself is jealous, but because the synagogue suffers jealousy on her account. For its riches have passed over to us through her, to such an extent that Paul said to the Galatians, who were from the nations, concerning those who were from the circumcision: “They are zealous for you, but not rightly; they want to exclude you” (Gal. 4).

That it is not the Church that envies the synagogue, but that the synagogue itself is jealous of the Church, is clear from the fact that it is not the second wife who envies the first, but the first who envies the second—just as Leah was jealous of Rachel, evidently because of the desire for the husband that entered between them.

You shall not approach a woman who is suffering her menstrual period, nor uncover her uncleanness.

That is, you shall not approach a menstruating woman; according to the law she was separated because of uncleanness. Since this had already been prohibited sufficiently above, what does it mean that he wished to add it here as well, among the same commandments? Perhaps, because in the earlier passage it was said in such a way that someone might think it was to be understood figuratively, it was also placed here, where matters are prohibited that must unquestionably be observed even in the time of the New Testament, after the removal of the observance of the ancient shadows.

This also seems to have been indicated by the prophet Ezekiel, who, among the sins that are not figurative but plainly iniquities, mentions approaching a menstruating woman, and, among the merits of righteousness, not approaching her. In this matter nature is not condemned; rather, such intercourse is declared harmful to the conception of offspring.

You shall not lie with your neighbor’s wife, nor defile yourself by an emission of seed.

Here again he prohibits adultery committed with another man’s wife, which is also prohibited in the Decalogue. Hence it is apparent that those women whose nakedness he forbids to be uncovered are prohibited even after their husbands’ deaths from being taken as wives.

## CHAPTER XII. He prohibits every form of unnatural uncleanness [Col. 0439D]

(LEVITICUS 18.) You shall not give any of your offspring to be consecrated to the idol Moloch; or, according to the Septuagint, “to be present to the ruler”; and you shall not profane the name of your God. I am the Lord. You shall not lie with a male by a woman’s intercourse, for it is an abomination. You shall not lie with any animal and defile yourself with it; a woman shall not submit herself to an animal or mate with it, for it is a crime.

(From Hesychius.) These interpretations have been suitably joined together in the text. The present intention of the legislator is to restrain the one who receives the law from lusts, impious unions, and fornication, both perceptible and intelligible.

Therefore he commanded him not to unite with a menstruating woman, because of the pollution of unlawful intercourse [Col. 0440A], nor with his neighbor’s wife. Such intercourse is adultery, not marriage. Thus, after saying, “You shall not lie with your neighbor’s wife,” he added, “nor shall you be defiled by an emission of seed,” explaining that this is no longer marriage. For intercourse does not defile the man who unites with his wife, because “marriage is honorable and the bed undefiled” (Heb. 13). But he strives with the greatest zeal to remove us from both perceptible and intelligible fornication. For this reason he added: “You shall not give any of your offspring to serve Moloch,” or, according to the Septuagint, “to the ruler.”

Our translation and the other interpreters indicate which ruler is meant. They consistently rendered Moloch by the expression “to the ruler.” That this was an idol is shown by Stephen in his preaching, and especially by Amos, who prophesied before him. He says: “You carried the tent of your Moloch, and the image of your idols, the star of your god, which you made for yourselves” (Amos 5).

By “offspring” let us understand not only relatives but also all our activity and teaching, so that we do not give our activity to serve idols—for “the root of all evils is covetousness” (1 Tim. 6), which is the service of idols—but teach such things as do not belong to the impiety of idolatrous error.

In this way you will understand that one ought not to approach the menstruating woman in order to uncover her nakedness, so that we do not mingle with the error of the pagans. We have already shown above that the menstruating woman represents this error, when necessity required discussion of menstruating women and women suffering a flow of blood.

Nor should we uncover her uncleanness, so that we do not recount or bring into public view their evil deeds—not as though we were sparing them, but because of those who hear, since such things harm the hearers. Therefore Paul says: “What they do secretly, it is shameful even to mention” (Eph. 5).

But let us avoid the wife of our neighbor, so that we are not defiled by her—namely, the wife of the gentile and idolater, who is called our neighbor both by nature and by kinship. For this reason, when the lawyer asked the Lord, “And who is my neighbor?” (Luke 10), he named as neighbor the man who had gone down from Jerusalem to Jericho and fallen among robbers—that is, demons—and who had been healed neither by the priest nor by the Levite, but by the Samaritan.

You shall not lie with such a woman, so that you may be defiled by such an emission of seed: so that we do not participate excessively in pagan wisdom or devote ourselves so deeply to it that we gather some pollution from it into our doctrine.

Nor should we profane the name of our God. We should understand this generally of everything that has been said. One profanes God’s name not only by the shame of fornication and by engaging in certain idolatrous acts, but also if, from pagan error and from what is called philosophy among them, someone introduces elements into the divine doctrines of the Church. Some who endured this fell into the lot of the heretics and became outsiders to the Church, as polluters of God’s name—that is, dishonoring and in a certain way defiling it.

For it is not right to bring the things of the dead into the realm of life, but Paul’s command, written by the Spirit, must be preserved: “What participation has righteousness with iniquity? Or what fellowship has Christ with Belial?” (2 Cor. 6).

The legislator himself also signifies this in a certain way in the things just mentioned, when he adds, “I am the Lord”—the one whose glory is wholly incommunicable, how much more so to demons, who corrupt souls and the idols belonging to them.

By the very wording he makes the enactment more terrifying. As you see, he placed it in the middle of the matters now under discussion. After the preceding matters that we have just examined, he again declares that a man must not lie with a male by male intercourse, nor lie with an animal. In these two cases he necessarily commands against both, as both are contrary to nature; but he adds that the one is a beast and the other involves a man joining with a man in a shameful intercourse, which must be fled and resisted.

Paul also demonstrated these matters, teaching that punishment, the wrath of God, and destruction overtake those who commit them.

The other interpreters rendered “abomination” as follows: Symmachus, “unspeakable”; Aquila, “defiled”—the latter referring to the act, the former also to the word or account, saying that it is neither bearable nor lawful.

But beyond these meanings let us understand “the male who performs virile acts” as referring to a human being, of whom David said: “Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly” (Ps. 1). And again: “Let your hand be upon the man of your right hand” (Ps. 79).

Such a man must not be made effeminate, nor must the perseverance he possesses in virtue be dissolved. This is appropriately understood by the phrase “to lie with a man by woman’s intercourse.” But just as another person ought not to be made effeminate, so neither should we yield to impious pleasures. These pleasures are rightly called “quadrupeds,” since they are directed toward the earth and lack the actions that befit a man. Quadrupeds look toward the earth and lack the use of hands, whereas hands are understood as instruments of actions worthy of human beings, since it is characteristic of human beings to labor with their hands.

Therefore one ought not to lie with those things by which one is defiled. Whoever remains in pleasures and delights, so that he lies with them, is also said to emit seed, because he is polluted by them, or because he delights in them and, through frequent use, in a certain sense sows them or is sown by them with some seed. This is the seed that the enemy sowed in the world while we were sleeping and negligent, greatly polluting it. Thus such a person ought also to be expelled from the holy tabernacle as a polluter and be excluded from the Lord’s threshing floor, since through evil seed he has become tares.

The law must be observed not only by a man but also necessarily by a woman—namely, the woman whom Solomon praises: “A good woman shall be blessed”; and he praises the fear of God.

## CHAPTER XIII. The people of God shall not follow the contaminations and errors of the nations

(IBID.) Do not defile yourselves by any of these things by which the nations have been defiled, whom I will drive out before your face. For the land has been defiled; I will visit its crimes, so that it may vomit out its inhabitants. Keep my ordinances and judgments.

(From Hesychius.) That defilement in the sins mentioned above is no small matter is demonstrated by the indignation and punishment defined against them. One must not be defiled by any of them. For whoever is defiled by one is defiled by all, because, wishing to show that these matters are connected with one another, the law gathered them all together into one. They are so serious that they destroyed whole nations, defiled the land, caused the defiled land to reject them, and made it vomit out and refuse those who committed such acts in it.

This does not mean that the land could expel or vomit them out, or, as Theodotion renders it, reject them; rather, it means that the land, as though naturally groaning over their transgressions, suffers from those same guilty people, just as Paul says: “The creation itself also groans and labors in childbirth until now” (Rom. 8).

God avenges both its groaning and his own law and creation, since it belongs to him. He shows this by saying, “I will visit its crimes.” The law teaches us these things according to the letter.

Yet the spiritual understanding is joined to this and does not contradict it, if by the nations defiled in all these matters we understand the demons. They are called nations because of their multitude. They are exceedingly wicked and rejoice in every evil, but especially in fornication, impious fornication, and still more in idolatry. In these the body and soul are defiled, and the whole human being, who is also called “land,” is thereby polluted.

But God visits the land—that is, the human race—and its crime. Or, according to the Septuagint, he visits “its injustice upon it,” that is, the injustice committed by it and within it. By it, because sinners are abominable, even if demons draw them toward these things; within it, because the demons, taking occasion from our negligence, inflict insult upon our nature.

It follows:

Nor shall any native or resident alien who dwells among them commit any of these abominations. For the inhabitants of the land who were before you committed all these abominations and defiled it. Take care, therefore, that the land not vomit you out as well, when you commit acts like theirs, just as it vomited out the nation that was before you. Every soul that commits any of these abominations shall perish from among its people.

(From Hesychius.) Both the native inhabitant—that is, one who was brought up by his fathers in the law and taught the Scriptures from childhood—and the proselyte, who has been joined to us, that is, one who has been added to us from outside while we are within, must withdraw from these abominations and in no way commit the acts practiced by those who formerly polluted our land.

Those former inhabitants are older than we are in their creation, because they are invisible creatures. They polluted the human race by suggesting disobedience to Adam and other evils after him, such as lying, murder, and everything similar. Thus the Lord said of the devil: “He was a liar and a murderer from the beginning” (John 8).

They made these suggestions to those whose minds were slippery and inclined toward evil. They could not—or rather, they did not succeed in—making such suggestions to Abel, Seth, Enoch, Noah, or the other righteous. They were mocked by them and withdrew. For the righteous, as the Apostle says, are not ignorant of the enemy’s thoughts: “We are not unaware of his thoughts.”

Knowing them, the righteous guard themselves against them. The intelligible land of ours, visited by God through the coming of the Savior, vomited them out; therefore the intelligible land also rejects and removes them. They are no longer assigned a place among human beings but among demons, and their souls will perish.

This happens in Gehenna, where the place and lot of demons especially are found. Christ makes this clear when he says: “Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25).

Keep my commandments. Do not do what those who were before you did, and do not defile yourselves by them. I am the Lord your God.

(From Hesychius.) Truly, “every word shall stand on the testimony of two or three witnesses.” Wishing to confirm this matter, the legislator now gives the command for the third time: “Keep my commandments; do not do what those who were before you did.” This shows that the commandments belong not to some human being but to God himself [Col. 0443B].

He also showed how they should be kept, not merely in word but in deed, having become incarnate and demonstrating it through his manner of life. We must not do all the things that those who were before us did.

But observe by what words he confirmed the present enactment: “Do not defile yourselves by them, for I am the Lord your God.” He wishes to cleanse us all from defilement because we are surrounded by his image. He necessarily becomes angry when that image is polluted by any of the evil and impious acts that are forbidden, but he is so pleased when it is preserved clean that he even dwells in us.

Paul makes both points clear when he says: “Do you not know that you are God’s temple and that the Spirit of God dwells in you? Whoever destroys God’s temple, God will destroy him. For God’s temple is holy, and you are that temple” (1 Cor. 3).

If, therefore, we preserve completed sanctification, we possess within us the fullness of the Trinity dwelling in us—provided that we are God’s temple, namely, the temple of the Father; and that we are Christ’s body and members, while the Holy Spirit dwells in us, in Christ Jesus our Lord.

# BOOK SIX

[Col. 0443]

## CHAPTER ONE. On guarding the commandments and observing the Sabbath

(LEVITICUS 19.) The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to the whole assembly of the children of Israel, and say to them: You shall be holy, because I, the Lord your God, am holy. Let each one fear his father and his mother. Keep my Sabbaths. I am the Lord your God. Do not turn to idols, nor make cast gods for yourselves. I am the Lord.

(From Hesychius.) He rightly placed sanctification first, because it is the foundation of every virtue. Showing that it must be pursued in every way, the legislator appropriately says: “You shall be holy, because I, the Lord your God, am holy.” That is: if you wish to please God, or wish him to be present with you—or rather, wish to be with him, for God’s presence and union remove from you every ambush and injury—then attain sanctification.

The holy does not permit itself to be joined to the profane. Therefore Paul said: “Do you not know that you are God’s temple and that the Spirit of God dwells in you? Whoever destroys God’s temple, God will destroy him. For God’s temple is holy, and you are that temple” (1 Cor. 3).

Building the commandments upon this foundation, outside which no one can lay another, he says: “Let each one fear his father and his mother.” Through sanctification he commands a pure mind toward the Creator; through honoring father and mother he commands the kindness owed by nature, by which children owe their parents both honor and fear, as the Lord ordained.

Then, wishing to recapitulate the commandments of the law—“You shall not kill, you shall not steal, you shall not commit adultery, you shall not swear falsely, you shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain, you shall not covet your neighbor’s wife”—and to command continence from evil in brief, he reasonably added: “Keep my Sabbaths.” For the true Sabbath is to do no work of corruption.

Moses also commanded that no servile work be done on the Sabbath, plainly instructing the one who wishes to keep the Sabbath according to the law of the Spirit to beware of the works of the flesh, which are fornication, uncleanness, and things similar to these.

Nor should we be ignorant of the reason for the Sabbath, for in this way we shall understand the virtue of the law concerning it. When, therefore, the Lord gave the commandment of the Sabbath, you will find nowhere earlier in divine Scripture the name of Sabbaths, so that it may be clear that the Sabbath commanded abstention from carnal and worldly matters.

Therefore, by prohibiting every work performed for every soul, the law added this and plainly showed that it desires us to abstain from bodily things and to perform those works that contribute to the soul’s help and advancement. The true Sabbath is to do nothing material, nothing that presses a human being down toward the earth and draws him toward carnal corruption.

Along with this, what else does God now command? “Do not turn to idols, nor make cast gods for yourselves. I am the Lord.” Not turning to idols means not accommodating oneself to the things that the law of idols demands in abundance and profusion.

Nor shall you make cast gods for yourselves—not only in the forms of animals, but also in stores of money or masses of gold and silver. Those who make and gather such things make gods of them, and are so placed under their dominion that they fear to touch even the smallest part of them.

But why do we need these things, when we possess, in place of all riches, the one who says: “I am the Lord”—the one who feeds the birds of the air, clothes the lilies of the field, made all things from nothing, nourished what he made, and can again reduce all these things to want?

If you sacrifice a sacrifice of peace offerings to the Lord so that it may be acceptable, you shall eat it on the day on which it is sacrificed and on the following day. Whatever remains on the third day you shall burn with fire. If anyone eats from it after two days, he shall be profane and shall bear his iniquity, because he has polluted what is holy to the Lord; and that soul shall perish from among its people.

(From Hesychius.) Moses, so to speak, commanded all the chapters of the law to the people twice and three times, repeatedly impressing their memory upon his hearers through frequent instruction. He did this especially with the more necessary commandments, as with the present one. He had previously proposed it when giving commands concerning sacrifices, and we discussed it fully in the first book of this exposition of Leviticus. Behold, he has now recapitulated it, so that we too may briefly recapitulate what we said at length then.

By commanding a saving sacrifice to be offered, he rightly signifies the sacrifice in which we perform the works that belong to salvation. For this sacrifice to be acceptable, it must be offered: namely, we must attain by every means the things that are acceptable to God.

Paul spoke of this when, writing to Timothy about how a remote and tranquil life should be pursued in all piety and modesty, he showed: “This is good and acceptable before God our Savior, who desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (1 Tim. 2).

To eat of the sacrifice on the day on which it was offered and on the next day means that in the present life we should perform whatever belongs to salvation. Scripture commonly understands “today” and “tomorrow” as the present age. On this matter let us produce James as a witness, when he writes: “Come now, you who say, Today or tomorrow we shall go into that city,” and so forth (James 4).

The third day, because on it our Lord rose from the dead, bears the figure of the future age and of the resurrection of the dead. In that age it is no longer permitted to work; rather, those who have worked now come there for their recompense.

Whoever therefore lives here as though he were going to perform some of the works of the present life there, and for this reason is said to eat the peace offering—or saving sacrifice—on the third day, undertakes a work prohibited by the legislator. He leaves virtue incomplete, as though he were going to work there. Consequently his sacrifice is not rightly accepted, nor is his life corrected. Rather, one who works such a virtue for himself will bear his iniquity: first, because he works imperfectly; then, because he brings an accusation against the divine law and spreads an impious and alien doctrine.

His soul will perish from his people. He will not be numbered among the people who are saved, because he has left his life incomplete—a life that could have saved him if he had brought it to completion.

## CHAPTER TWO. On care for the poor and resident aliens during harvest and vintage [Col. 0445D]

(IBID.) “When you reap the harvest of your land, you shall not cut it down to the ground over the surface of the land, nor gather the ears that remain; nor shall you collect the clusters and fallen grapes in your vineyard, but you shall leave them to be gleaned by the poor and the resident aliens. I am the Lord your God.” (From Hesychius.)

The lawgiver wishes us to love one another, and desires us to be lovers of the poor and always devoted to almsgiving: at one time giving to those in need, at another not demanding what is owed to us, but even allowing them to gather whatever remnants of all the good things given to us by God they happen to find, and to imitate him who gave—not merely one who is merciful, but one who is “abundant in compassion,” as he is called. Therefore, when reaping or harvesting the grapes, he did not command that the same reaping or vintage be repeated at that time, nor did he ordain that the field be wholly reaped or the vineyard wholly harvested; rather, he commanded that certain remnants from the harvest and vintage be left entirely for the poor and the proselyte, and that thanks be rendered to God, who causes the fruits themselves to grow, through works of thanksgiving.

Mystically, therefore, through what has now been said, the lawgiver commanded the teachers of the Jews not to handle the interpretation of the whole law, but to yield certain portions to the poor and the proselyte—that is, to the teachers of the nations. For these are poor, since they have been commanded to be poor in spirit, and it was said to them: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V). They are proselytes because they now join themselves to the kinship of Abraham and approach God, at least through faith.

Accordingly, what is written—“You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery”—the teachers of the Jews should teach. But whatever requires contemplation and interpretation, such as the matters concerning purifications, sacrifices, and similar things, they should yield to the teachers of the Church. And whatever falls from their harvest—that is, whatever they see passing beyond them, things of which they are ignorant—the Jews cannot gather these clusters for themselves and store them up in their own riches, since they have shown no zeal for their life; they leave them for the poor and the proselyte. For the prophets are with us, as are all the righteous who existed among the Jewish people, to such an extent that their memory is honored by us each year, something that does not happen among them. Thus experience shows the divine utterance to be true.

## CHAPTER III. The commandments are set forth, and just judgment concerning one’s neighbor is required.

(IBID.) “You shall not steal; you shall not lie; no one shall deceive his neighbor; you shall not swear falsely by my name. You shall not profane the name of your God. I am the Lord.” (From Augustine.)

The commandment concerning theft is included in the Decalogue. But when he says, “You shall not lie, and no one shall slander his neighbor,” it is surprising if this is not contained in the commandment stated there: “You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor,” since slander cannot occur without falsehood and is encompassed by the general category of false testimony.

But whether such acts may be admitted in some compensatory circumstance is a major question. The same seems to be true of lying to almost everyone: where no one is harmed, one ought to lie for the sake of someone’s safety. Is this therefore also true of theft? Can theft occur where no one is harmed? Indeed, it can occur even when the person against whom it is committed is being helped—for example, if someone were to steal a sword from a person who wished to kill himself.

As for slander, I do not know whether it can ever be committed for anyone’s benefit, except perhaps when something was done for the sake of a greater joy that they would afterward enjoy—as when Joseph accused his brothers concerning the cup and brought against them the false charge of espionage. Yet if we try to determine these matters by definitions, perhaps theft is not theft unless, when something belonging to another is secretly taken, one’s neighbor is harmed; and slander is not slander unless one’s neighbor is harmed by the imputation of a false crime. But we cannot say that lying exists only when one’s neighbor is harmed. For when someone knowingly says what is false, it is undoubtedly a lie, whether someone is harmed by it or no one is.

Accordingly, the great question concerning lying—whether a lie can sometimes be just—might perhaps be easily resolved if we considered only the commandments and not the examples. For what commandment is more absolute than “You shall not lie”? It is stated in the same way as “You shall not make an idol for yourself,” which can never be just; and as “You shall not commit adultery.” Who could say that adultery might ever be just? Likewise, according to that definition of theft, “You shall not steal” can never permit a just theft. And “You shall not kill”—for when a person is justly killed, the law kills him, not you.

But can it be said in the same way that, when a person lies justly, the law lies? The examples make the question exceedingly difficult. The Egyptian midwives lied, and God rewarded them; Rahab lied on behalf of the spies, and for that reason was delivered. Once the law has said, “You shall not lie,” should we understand that lying is forbidden even in such a circumstance as that in which Rahab is said to have lied? Rather, is it not more credible that the lie was forbidden because it was unjust, and not that it became unjust because it was forbidden?

Perhaps, then, as we said concerning the midwives, what was rewarded in them was not that they lied, but that they rescued the Hebrew infants; and that, because of this mercy, the sin became pardonable, though it should not therefore be thought not to have been a sin. The same should be understood of Rahab: she was rewarded for the deliverance of the spies, so that, because of that deliverance, pardon was granted for the lie. But wherever pardon is granted, it is evident that there is sin.

One must beware, however, lest anyone suppose that the same pardon can be granted for other sins whenever they are committed for the deliverance of human beings. For many intolerable and utterly detestable evils follow from this error.

(From Hesychius.)

The lawgiver shows us the boundaries of good conduct, and at the same time teaches how sins are related to one another. For what we consider small is great, since in lying, so to speak, we are accustomed to sin every day, whether through circumstances or intention, and likewise through violating an oath. These things are so evil that he joined them to theft—and rightly so, because theft is usually accompanied by lying. For this reason the prophet Zechariah showed the sickle that he saw, twenty cubits long and ten cubits wide, sharpened against thieves and perjurers. He says: “It shall enter the house of the thief and of the perjurer” (Zech. III). Lying also cooperates in every sin.

Let us avoid lying, in which some sin under the appearance of truth, slandering their neighbor more in their mind than with their tongue, as did those who said concerning the Lord: “This man said, ‘I can destroy this temple and rebuild it in three days’” (John II). The Lord had indeed said this when the Jews asked him, “What sign do you show us, since you do these things?” He replied to them: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.” But he did not say this with the intention with which those who testified against him repeated it. He was speaking about the temple of his body, whereas they asserted that these words had been spoken about the Jewish temple. Therefore the Spirit called them false witnesses.

For perjury, the Septuagint reads: “You shall not take up my name for an unjust thing.” An oath is unjust not only when it is violated, but also when it is unjustly kept—for example, the oath by which Herod, swearing to the daughter of Herodias, beheaded John the Baptist (Matt. XIV). He ought not to have made such an oath; but once he had sworn, he ought not to have kept it, since God neither wishes such oaths to be initiated nor allows those that have been initiated to reach their fulfillment.

Therefore, after saying, “You shall not take up my name for an unjust thing,” he added, “and you shall not profane the name of the Lord your God.” Jerome’s translation reads: “You shall not profane the name of your God.” How, then, does someone profane it? I mean, by doing evil, because an oath cannot be violated. God desires what is good to such an extent that, even if he has threatened certain people with terrible things and they have repented, he does not delay changing his sentence and retracting his word, in order to show us mercy. For this reason he added, “I am the Lord”—the kind of Lord of whom the prophecy of Jonah speaks, when the Ninevites fasted and prayed and God repented of the evil that he had said he would do to them, and did not do it (Jonah III). The prophets have said many other things of this kind. It follows:

“You shall not slander your neighbor, nor oppress him by force. The workman’s wage shall not remain with you until morning. You shall not curse the deaf, nor place a stumbling block before the blind; but you shall fear your God, because I am the Lord.”

(From Augustine.)

Everything that is forbidden against one’s neighbor should be referred to the one statement: “You shall not harm your neighbor.” For what follows—“You shall not seize”—unless it is understood as meaning that one must not harm by seizing, sometimes it happens that one harms by not seizing. The sword of a madman ought to be taken away, and if someone does not do what is necessary, he may cause greater harm.

(From Hesychius.)

You see how the law gradually cultivates the mind of the one who received it, joining what appear to be small sins to great ones, so that, through fear of the punishment defined for greater sins, we may abstain from lesser ones as well. For just as they are joined in the commandment, so they are joined in the punishment. “Whoever keeps the whole law but fails in one point has become guilty of all of it” (James II).

Nor was it without reason that he joined oppression by force to slander. What difference is there, for one who is deprived of his possessions, whether he is deprived by force, by arms, perhaps by some position of power, by the manipulation of courts, by fraud, or by any other similar means? Likewise, one who has worked all day in order to receive wages by which he and his children, wife, and parents, who are waiting for those wages, are to live—and who does not receive them, but is made to wait—does he not suffer slander and oppression, not only in food but through these things in life itself? For life is sustained by daily food. Thus, even if he receives the wages the next day, because on the day that has passed, during which he endured labor, he remained fasting, he has suffered oppression and been subjected to slander. What constitutes subsistence for others constitutes wages for laborers. Thus the deprivation of these things is rightly called oppression.

The one who curses the deaf also does great harm, as does the one who places a stumbling block before the blind, against which they may strike their feet. The deaf person is harmed when he is cursed, not only because he is slandered, but because he cannot correct or guard against the things for which he is slandered. Nor can the blind person protect himself from the stumbling block placed before him. Both may suffer death from these things: the blind man when he is crushed by the stumbling block; the deaf man through the curse, as though he had slandered a ruler or done something else that would bring danger upon him, while being entirely unable to correct himself.

What appears to be a small matter, and is often committed by many in jest, leads to death. Therefore David very appropriately called blessed the one who did not sit “in the seat of pestilence,” that is, of mockers (Ps. I).

Let us return to the same matters and pursue them further. The law forbade not only financial slander and oppression, but every other kind as well, and especially oppression in spiritual matters: we must not seize another’s glory or draw to ourselves what has been gathered through another’s labor. For this reason Paul said: “Not boasting in another’s sphere about things already prepared” (II Cor. X); and again he says that he was granted the task of evangelizing not where Christ had already been named, lest he build upon another’s foundation (Rom. XV).

The latter statement is an interpretation of the former. He did not wish to preach where another had preached, so as not to seize another’s wages. Concerning these wages the lawgiver says: “The workman’s wage shall not remain with you until morning.” He commands not those who are already preaching, but those who are still learning, not to neglect or leave idle with them the teacher’s word. For the workman of God is the one who preaches his word. His wage is the reward of preaching, as Paul truthfully testifies when he says: “What, then, is my reward? That, when I preach the Gospel, I may offer the Gospel of Christ without charge” (I Cor. IX).

The Septuagint reads: “The wage of your workman shall not sleep with you until morning.” For the Lord shows that those who are negligent are called sleepers, when he commands his disciples: “Watch, because you do not know at what hour your Lord will come”; and when he said that, while people were sleeping—that is, while they were being negligent—the enemy sowed weeds.

“Morning” is the future age, because it follows the night of the present life, and unquenchable light dwells in it. Therefore the word of the teachers ought not to be idle with us throughout all this time, which is followed by the morning of the future age. For in this matter too avarice and injustice are exercised by teachers, who lose the reward owed to them for the progress of their disciples.

By the deaf and the blind, the law indicates those who are held by the disease of disobedience and ignorance, to whom Isaiah said: “Deaf, hear; and blind, look up so that you may see” (Isa. XLII). They are not to be cursed, but admonished, if indeed we wish them to be converted. Therefore Paul commanded the one who teaches to instruct gently those who contradict the teachers of the Church. Nor should we become a stumbling block to them by saying or doing false things. Paul himself prohibited and corrected this when he wrote: “If someone sees one who has knowledge reclining in an idol’s temple, will not his conscience, being weak, be built up to eat things sacrificed to idols?” (I Cor. VIII).

Thus we can be helped by the law both according to the letter and according to the spirit. It follows:

“You shall not do what is unjust, nor judge unjustly; you shall not show partiality to the poor, nor honor the face of the powerful. Judge your neighbor justly. You shall not be a slanderer or a whisperer among your people. You shall not stand against the blood of your neighbor. I am the Lord.”

(From Hesychius.)

The law establishes that not just any justice, but the highest and perfect justice, must be pursued, especially in the present matters. Proceeding in a straight path and order, it first appears to establish the law for the poor, then for the powerful, and afterward for those who possess offices, principalities, and powers, thereby showing that partiality must not be practiced.

Not stealing, slandering, or swearing unjustly may sometimes occur among the rich and powerful; nevertheless, these sins are in a certain sense characteristic of the poor. For through poverty they seem to be compelled to steal, slander, and violate oaths, so that that wise man in Proverbs said: “Give me neither riches nor poverty, lest, being filled, I be enticed to deny, or, compelled by want, steal and swear falsely by the name of my God” (Prov. XXX).

Oppressing by force, depriving people of their wages, and mocking the deaf or the blind—because some of these sins belong to power, while others arise from a kind of extravagant life and pleasures that generate insult—are said to be especially forbidden with regard to the persons of the rich and powerful.

To show partiality in judgment applies to those who preside over magistracies or judicial tribunals. When they judge, they must not show partiality even toward the poor. For no one is more merciful than God, who is called merciful and compassionate above all. Nevertheless, at the time of judgment he does not wish to be called by these names in this respect, but “just,” as David testifies: “God is a just judge, strong and patient” (Ps. VII).

Nor should one show partiality to the powerful in judgment, because no one is more powerful than God, and judgment belongs to him. When we judge, he himself assumes the role of the litigant. Moses is a witness to this when he says in Deuteronomy: “You shall not show partiality in judgment; you shall judge the small and the great alike. You shall not distinguish between persons, because the judgment is God’s” (Deut. I, 16).

Therefore, if you wish to honor the person of the powerful, honor the person of God. You honor it if you place yourself on the side of justice, for there he has a person: “The righteous Lord loved righteousness; his face saw equity” (Ps. X).

For this reason he now also commands that one judge one’s neighbor justly. We must know that by the judgment with which we judge, we shall be judged.

He added: “You shall not be,” he says, “a slanderer or a whisperer among the peoples”; or, as the Septuagint reads, “You shall not walk deceitfully among your people”; “you shall not stand against the blood of your neighbor.”

(From Hesychius.)

He joined deceit to blood, namely, to murder, just as David sings: “The Lord abhors the man of blood and deceit” (Ps. VII); and again: “Men of blood and deceit shall not live out half their days” (Ps. LIV).

Deceit is a hidden sword, a sharpened and concealed blade, so that David again said: “You have practiced deceit like a sharpened razor” (Ps. LI). Let us quickly withdraw from it, fearing it because of its proximity to the sin with which it deserved to be joined. Let us not stand against the blood of our neighbor, but flee every ambush and every association formed for any iniquity. For some people, weak when alone and unable to harm by themselves, habitually mingle with a crowd; and whenever many gather together, it is necessary that a stronger form of wickedness appear. One lends a hand, another a tongue, another gives assent to what is being done, another gives a sign, and thus the madness of wickedness is brought to completion.

It follows:

“You shall not hate your brother in your heart, but openly rebuke him, lest you bear sin because of him. You shall not seek revenge, nor remember the injury done by your fellow citizens. You shall love your friend as yourself. I am the Lord. Keep my laws.”

(From the same author.)

He added, “You shall not hate your brother in your heart,” because we are often compelled to assume, in the case of those who sin, the role of persons who hate them. Therefore Paul commanded the Thessalonians: “If anyone does not obey our word by this letter, take note of him, and do not associate with him, so that he may be ashamed.”

When this is done, it may appear to imply hatred. For whose practice is it, other than that of those who hate and oppose, not to associate with someone? But he did not command this aversion to take place in the heart. He says: “Do not associate with him, so that he may be ashamed and, being put to shame, may be corrected in every way” (II Thess. III). The one who corrected the person with whom he did not associate could not possibly have hated him in his heart. To confirm this he also added: “Do not regard him as an enemy, but correct him as a brother.”

Fulfilling every aspect of justice and establishing the law, in a certain way, for every sphere of life, he adds to the commandments the confirmation that is necessary. If we keep it, no one will be able to harm our riches, and no one will be able to steal our treasure.

This confirmation is: “You shall love your friend”—or, as the Septuagint reads, “your neighbor”—“as yourself.” The whole law is contained in this small commandment, and through this one commandment it is easy for you to keep everything. For Paul says: “Love does no evil to one’s neighbor. Therefore love is the fullness of the law” (I Cor. XIII).

Love also makes our entire life consist in good things. If I love my neighbor as myself, and perhaps I do not have children, riches, beauty, worldly glory, or power, but I see that my neighbor possesses them, I rejoice and am glad as though I myself possessed them. In him, I too possess them.

The same applies to spiritual matters, in which above all we must preserve the love that pertains to our neighbors. We must not envy those who practice righteousness, nor be troubled when others are glorified according to Christ, when they are enriched in the word of teaching, or when they abound in divine gifts. Christ must be imitated, for he loved us to such an extent that he allowed the apostles to perform greater signs than he himself had performed.

Therefore, even now, when he says, “You shall love your friend—or neighbor—as yourself,” he adds: “I am the Lord. Keep my laws.”

Learn how greatly God loved us from his own words. For he says: “No one has greater love than this: that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John XV).

(From Augustine.)

One may ask what it means that, after saying above, “You shall not hate your brother in your heart; rebuke your neighbor directly, and you shall not bear sin because of him,” he then added, “and your hand shall not be avenged.” Does this mean that he is not to be punished? You act with a good intention when you impose discipline for sin upon your neighbor, so that you do not bear his sin by neglecting it. This is the meaning of what he said earlier: “You shall not hate your neighbor in your heart.”

The person being rebuked may think that you hate him, even though this is not in your heart. Or does “your hand shall not be avenged” rather admonish you not to seek vengeance with your hand and not to be carried away by the desire for revenge? For what else is wishing to take revenge than rejoicing or finding consolation in another’s evil?

For this reason it was said: “You shall not be angry with the children of your people.” Anger has rightly been defined as the desire for revenge. Some manuscripts, however, read: “And your hand shall not be avenged,” meaning that, in rebuking, you should not wish to avenge yourself, but rather to benefit the person whom you rebuke.

## CHAPTER IV. That animals of different kinds should not mate, that a field should not be sown with different seed, and so forth.

(IBID.) “You shall not cause your animals to mate with animals of another kind. You shall not sow your field—or, as the Septuagint reads, your vineyard—with different seed. You shall not wear a garment woven from two kinds of material.”

(From Hesychius.)

These things, taken literally, appear in a certain sense ridiculous. Accordingly, we do not find that the prophets and spiritual men observed them in this way, as did the sons of the Jews, who lived weakly and imperfectly, loving milk and unable to receive solid food.

Consider what David said to Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, and Benaiah: “Set my son Solomon upon my mule” (III Kings I). By saying “my” he showed that he himself also rode a mule.

But if the law forbade animals to mate with animals of another kind—that is, a donkey with a horse—and if this was abominable, then surely the things that resulted from such unions, and those born from them, ought also to have been abhorred.

Likewise, if he does not wish a garment to be made from two materials, how does that wise man say concerning the strong woman in Proverbs: “She sought wool and flax and worked with her hands for what was useful” (Prov. XXXI); and again: “Her garments are made of fine linen and purple” (ibid.)?

For the garments are not useful [as printed]. But let us understand him to have called her clothing good, or the garment useful: one garment made of wool and flax, and another made of fine linen and purple.

But Paul clearly writes to the Corinthians what this means: “You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons. You cannot partake of the table of God and the table of demons.” And again: “You who are justified by the law have fallen away from grace.”

The faithful must not be mixed with Jewish seductions or with the error of the nations. Therefore, let us not allow animals—that is, ordinary people—to be joined to animals of another kind; that is, let us not allow them to pursue circumcision and baptism together. Circumcision belongs to another yoke, a heavy and unbearable one. Concerning this Peter said: “Why are you testing God by placing upon the necks of the disciples a yoke that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear?” (Acts XV).
