The baptism of Christ belongs to another yoke, a light one, which Christ placed upon us when he said: “Take my yoke,” and again: “For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.”

Nor should we sow the vineyard or field entrusted to us with varied seed, so that we do not teach the Church things contrary to divine doctrines. Thus the heretics, who think perversely, prepare death for themselves through their impiety: although Christ blessed marriage by his presence and said, “It is not what enters a person that harms him,” they forbid marriage and command abstinence from foods that God created for them (I Tim. IV).

In these matters the Septuagint appropriately adds: “I am the Lord your God,” since he desires us to keep ourselves from all such wickedness. The one who through the Gospel said to those who interpret the law wrongly and according to their own will, “Do not judge according to appearance, but judge a just judgment” (John VII), is the same one.

A person wears the abominable garment woven from two materials who says that he worships Christ while worshiping demons; who claims to be a soldier of the Sun of righteousness while also appeasing the visible sun, which was created for the service of creation, or the other stars, or something of this kind, as the Manichaeans and many other heretics do.

For he does not wish us, although we belong to God, to be mixed with demonic practices, to devote ourselves at once to prayers and incantations, or to wear simultaneously the phylacteries of the Church and of holy men and, conversely, those of wicked sorcerers; nor does he wish us to carry around the things belonging to demons with the Holy Spirit, in whom, Paul says, we have been sealed (Eph. I).

For the Holy Spirit departs, as one who has suffered an insult; the unclean spirit gains possession, and such a person suffers the fate that Saul endured.

## CHAPTER V. What is to be done by one who has slept with a slave woman, and so forth.

(IBID.) “If a man sleeps with a woman in intercourse, and she is a slave who is also of marriageable age but has not been redeemed for a price or granted freedom, both shall be beaten, but they shall not die, because she was not free. For his offense he shall offer to the Lord, at the door of the tabernacle of testimony, a ram. The priest shall pray for him and for his offense before the Lord, and atonement shall be made for him, and the sin shall be forgiven.”

(From Hesychius.)

Through what has now been said, the lawgiver intends to show how great the difference is between freedom and slavery. In the case of a free woman who was betrothed, he asserts that the offense of the man who fornicated with her was adultery, and he decrees that he be subject to the penalty of death.

But in the case of a marriageable slave woman—whom the Septuagint calls “kept for a man,” that is, betrothed—he removes the penalty and commands the one who sinned with her to offer a sacrifice. Through this visible slavery he wishes to indicate an intelligible one.

For he did not command that the offense of fornication be committed with just any slave women, much less with betrothed ones. Rather, by the slave woman betrothed or kept for a man, he means the synagogue of the Jews, which was kept for the law and could not be betrothed to Christ before the letter of the law had died.

Therefore Paul said: “So then, brothers, you also have died to the law through the body of Christ, so that you may belong to another, to him who was raised from the dead” (Rom. VII).

He himself taught that the synagogue of the Jews is a slave woman when he said that Abraham had two sons, one from a slave woman and one from a free woman (Gal. IV). Then, explaining which slave woman he intended, he added: “These things are spoken allegorically. For these are the two covenants: one from Mount Sinai, generating slavery, which is Hagar. For Sinai is a mountain in Arabia, corresponding to the present Jerusalem, which is in slavery” (ibid.).

If someone sleeps with this woman in an act of intercourse—that is, if he becomes a participant in this teaching, to such an extent that he joins and unites himself with it through a life according to the law—for those who are joined to one another in marital fellowship are found, as it were, to be one. We have already shown many times in this book of Leviticus that “seed” must be understood as the word of teaching.

Whoever did these things before she was freed through the coming of Christ was rightly not put to death. For even if he received the law according to the letter and not according to the spirit, as the synagogue of the Jews teaches—and therefore she is rightly called a slave woman, because she was ignorant of the lawgiver’s intention—“the slave,” as Christ says, “does not know the will of his master.” Therefore he was said to sin and needed forgiveness, because he did not strive to follow the Lord’s command according to the Lord’s will.

Nevertheless, because she had not yet been freed, and because the contemplation of the law was therefore hidden, the life according to the letter seemed to have its appointed time. Thus they are not said to be subject to death, and visitation was promised to them.

For what our translation has, “Both shall be beaten,” the Septuagint reads, “There shall be visitation for them, and they shall not die.” “Visitation” means that freedom from slavery to the law was promised to them. It is the custom of divine Scripture to call freedom “visitation.” For we find that God calls liberation from Egyptian slavery visitation, when he said to Moses: “Gather the elders of the children of Israel, and say to them: The Lord God of your fathers has appeared to me, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, saying: ‘I have surely visited you’” (Exod. III).

But because the first Jews needed this salvation and liberation, since they were also deceiving others, forgiveness was granted through sacrifice to the one who slept with her—that is, to the one who mingled with her so as to become a participant in her seed and teaching. But this was through Christ. For, signifying this sacrifice, he commanded a ram to be offered for sin and directed that the priest make supplication through its offering.

Who is this one who first of all made supplication for the world? And who is the ram offered for sin? Why is it led to the sacrifice before the door of the tabernacle of testimony? And what, properly, is to be understood as the sin of the offense?

If, in examining and searching out what was formerly decreed and explained concerning sacrifices, you discover Christ portrayed in them as in an image, you will find that he, sacrificed on the cross, forgave this sin as well as all other sins: the sin committed by the Jewish people and by the one from the nations who was mixed with them and is said to have slept with them—that is, by receiving the law not according to the lawgiver’s intention.

These matters are not inappropriately placed here, but at a highly suitable point, when it was signified that animals should not be joined to animals of another kind: those who have been placed under the yoke of Christ must not take upon themselves the Jewish yoke.

To confirm this, he added what follows, showing that before Christ’s coming, too, whoever from the nations mingled with them needed the sacrifice of the intelligible ram for his propitiation, bringing it to mind and representing the truth to himself through figures.

In this way, by receiving the law spiritually and referring its sacrifices to Christ, he could not only avoid condemnation through the power of the Jewish letter that had come upon him, but also be freed from it and from the death of unbelief.

## CHAPTER VI. Concerning the removal of the foreskins from the trees in the land of Canaan.

(IBID.) “When you enter the land and plant fruit-bearing trees in it, you shall remove their foreskins. The fruit that they produce shall be unclean for you; you shall not eat it. In the fourth year all their fruit shall be sanctified, laudable to the Lord; but in the fifth year you shall eat their fruit, gathering the produce they yield. I am the Lord your God.”

(From Hesychius.)

The lawgiver remains even now with the intention he had earlier, when he sanctioned similar matters in other words, showing that the Jewish people could not bear good fruit before the Lord’s presence.

Why, then, did he say that the fruit of every tree was not edible for three years, nor in any way clean, but that it required purification in the fourth year? And what was this purification? It was neither sprinkling nor sacrifice nor anything of that kind, such as the law elsewhere commanded literally.

Therefore the person who wishes not only to meditate upon the law but also to receive some benefit from it must necessarily turn to the contemplation of the spirit.

God therefore gives the land that it is fitting for him to give: namely, divine Scripture, which bears the fruits of virtues, possesses that life, and is cultivated or worked, as David promises to cultivate and work it. For where can a person please God more than in commandments and good works? He says: “I shall please the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. CXIV). Concerning these things he himself says: “Those who wait for the Lord shall possess the land as an inheritance” (Ps. XXXVI).

For they shall possess the Scripture full of the Spirit of God, together with the good things that come from it. Scripture, as it waits for God, promises the reward of the commandments contained within it.

The sons of the Jews were indeed commanded to enter this land, and they received it first. For they were the first to receive the sacred writings. Therefore they were also commanded to plant the tree that can be eaten—that is, the commandments we have mentioned. Some of them meditated upon them, while others also preached them.

Because meditation on the law and preaching are compared to the planting of trees on account of the progress that comes about gradually, hear David saying: “And he shall meditate on his law day and night, and he shall be like a tree planted beside streams of water” (Ps. I).

Paul wrote concerning the preaching that he preached to the Corinthians: “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth” (I Cor. III).

The commandments, however, were exceedingly good; for this reason the tree is called edible.

But they did not work in the manner they ought, using the law according to the letter. Their fruit, therefore—that is, the practice of the law—was unclean for three years. He calls it “three years” from the time of the law to the time of David, from David to the Babylonian exile, and from the Babylonian exile to the coming of the Lord. Matthew likewise made this division. Since, therefore, in the fourth year he commended all the fruit of the law as holy and praiseworthy to the Lord, yet did not then say to the Jews that it was edible, he clearly demonstrated that the whole fruit of the law belongs to the coming of the Lord. For, according to the sequence of the periods mentioned above, his time may rightly be called the fourth year, holy and praiseworthy to God, because Christ made it fruitful, teaching us likewise that we ought to bear fruit.

It was rightly holy, since it was perfected by the Holy of holies; but it was also praiseworthy. For everything Christ does is of good repute and glorious, so that even ungrateful Jews glorify it. When they saw the paralytic carrying his bed upon his shoulders, they glorified God, who had given such authority to human beings (Matt. IX). Hence the law called this fruit not simply fruit, but fruit praiseworthy to the Lord. It was not yet edible for the people, for they had not yet attained the way of life according to the spirit of Christ; this occurred in the fifth year, that is, in the apostolic generation. From that time the Jewish people themselves—that is, those among them who believed—and all the nations possessed the edible fruit of the law, namely, its practice.

*(From Gregory.)* According to the tropological sense, fruit-bearing trees are works rich in virtues. We therefore remove the foreskins of the trees when, suspicious of the weakness belonging to our beginnings, we do not approve the first stages of our works. We regard the fruits that sprout as unclean and do not adapt them to our consumption, because when the beginnings of a good work are praised, it is fitting that this praise should not nourish the worker’s soul, lest, while the praise received is pleasantly enjoyed, the fruit of the work be eaten prematurely. Whoever receives praise from human lips for a virtue he has begun has, as it were, eaten the fruit of a planted tree before its time.

For this reason Truth says through the Psalmist: “It is vain for you to rise before the light; rise after you have sat down” (Ps. CXXVI). To rise before the light means to rejoice in the night of the present life before the brightness of eternal recompense has appeared. One must therefore sit down first, so that afterward one may rise rightly, because whoever does not now humble himself willingly will by no means be exalted by the glory that follows.

## CHAPTER VII. On Various Ceremonies: Eating, Cutting the Hair, Divination, and So Forth

*(The same passage.)* “You shall not eat with blood. You shall not practice divination, nor observe dreams. You shall not cut your hair in a circle, nor shave your beard. You shall not make cuts in your flesh for the dead, nor make any figures or marks upon yourselves. I am the Lord.”

*(From Hesychius.)* He wishes the faithful person to be pure from every leaven of wickedness. Therefore, at this point, he forbids slavery to the letter of the law and shows Jewish doctrine to be useless. Then he turns his discourse once more to the error of the Gentiles. For not everything now forbidden is practiced, since such practices are not only ridiculous but also harmful to those who engage in them. Ecclesiastes makes this especially clear when he says: “Whoever observes the wind does not sow, and whoever considers the cloud will never reap” (Ecclus. XI).

“Divination,” therefore, refers not only to the call or flight of any bird that either forbids some action or urges one more eagerly to hasten it, but also to the use of signs taken from people who speak, pass by, meet us, or encounter us on a journey, and from similar impediments. It is called divination from birds, but also from the observation of other signs.

 haruspicy, however, consists in watching birds as they pass and, because of them, going out onto a road deserted by human beings, in order to examine what the birds’ flight or calls are like and to learn from them what is going to happen. This is an accusation against God, because it supposes that what God has hidden from the human being—whom he established as ruler over all animals according to his own image—he has entrusted to irrational birds, and that one can learn from them something which cannot be learned even from spiritual men, nor from God, who reveals things to them. Such is the opinion of those deceived by the error mentioned above.

Nor should one cut the hair “in a circle” around the appearance of the head, as Symmachus also rendered it, in the manner practiced by those who cultivate barbarian hairstyles. For this reason the Septuagint called it *sisyn*, perhaps because of the great size of the gathered hair. This ought not to be done; rather, people should be content with their natural adornments and seek nothing else—unless, perhaps, we accuse the Creator of having needed some addition to complete the animal.

Nor should one cultivate curls in honor of demons, making the hair stronger than the rest and dedicating it by a vow. Pagans practice offering the hair of children to demons; hence the lawgiver must be understood to have commanded especially against this. Nor should one shave the beard, or, according to the Septuagint, “corrupt the appearance of the beard.”

Those who mourn over the dead should not make incisions in their bodies, for pagans too are accustomed to this. One ought to grieve over the dead in such a way that neither the face is injured nor the body corrupted. Concerning this Paul says, forbidding us such practices: “I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, so that you may not grieve like the rest who have no hope” (1 Thess. IV).

To do any of the things mentioned above is not to have hope in the resurrection of the dead, because, as though the dead had been corrupted, such people themselves tear apart and corrupt their own bodies. He also forbids the making of marks upon the body, taking care in every respect for its beauty, and not allowing anyone to abuse the flesh through any of these practices, which harm the body itself and make the whole creature repulsive.

The command to “eat upon the mountains,” which the Septuagint placed at the beginning of the present law, is given instead of what our edition has, “You shall not eat with blood.” He prohibited this because of those accustomed to the festivals of idols. Hosea likewise accused the Jewish people, saying: “The spirit of fornication deceived them, and they fornicated against their God; they burned incense upon the mountaintops and sacrificed upon the hills” (Hos. IV).

But let us examine, beyond these matters, what he commands us to avoid according to the spiritual interpretation. We must not eat upon the mountains—that is, we must not feed upon proud thoughts—of which Isaiah says: “Every mountain and hill shall be humbled” (Isa. XL). We must not practice divination or haruspicy, so that, by giving attention to demons, we may not live according to their will. Nor should we hand our heart over to birds, which snatch away from us the seed of piety, as the Lord said in the evangelical parables.

Let us not cut our hair, or, according to the Septuagint, make *sisyn* from the hair of the head. For our hairs are understood as our thoughts; therefore the Lord said: “But even the hairs of your head are all numbered” (Matt. X). All our thoughts are numbered by him, since he is judge and searches the hearts. We must not, therefore, agitate or shake them, nor offer them to the devil, as some do when they offer a lock of their physical hair, as we said above.

Furthermore, as we said, we must not shave the beard, or, according to the Septuagint, corrupt the appearance of the beard, because the beard is a sign of our perfection, while virtues signify our true perfection. It is unfitting to corrupt these by acting falsely, under a deceptive and feigned appearance.

Nor is it good to make incisions upon the soul. There are pleasures in the body that cut into the soul for its harm, wounding and corrupting the body. Let us also understand the marks—that is, the doctrines of evil teaching—in this way: they adhere to and are implanted in the soul through various flatteries, syllogisms, or any other method used by teachers. The law therefore commands us to abstain from these as well, because impressions or insertions, like marks, are difficult to erase once they have been fixed or sunk in.

## CHAPTER VIII. Where He Forbids Prostituting One’s Daughter and Commands That God’s Sanctuary Be Feared

*(The same passage.)* “You shall not prostitute your daughter, lest the land be defiled and filled with guilt.”

*(From Hesychius.)* If fathers, who ought to correct their children, encourage them to fornication by provoking them to it or by living shamefully themselves, so that the children may be enticed to evil through imitation of their parents, the land is filled with guilt—or, according to the Septuagint, with fornication—and advances toward every form of ungodliness, because children have as teachers and guides toward evil those who ought to have been their instructors.

Nor should we prostitute our soul, which is our only-begotten daughter, so that David could say: “Deliver my soul from the lions, my only one from the hand of the dog” (Ps. XXXI, XXXIV), by teaching it to depart from God, lest, when the soul fornicates, the body also fornicate. It is called “land” because it has arisen from the earth and will return to the earth. And it is filled with guilt—or, according to the Septuagint, adultery—because a horse with a drunken rider is driven headlong, and when the soul departs from God, every iniquity rules over the body.

“Keep my Sabbaths, and fear my sanctuary. I am the Lord.”

*(From Hesychius.)* Just as, while there is one particular Sabbath—namely, the seventh day—every other lawful rest is called a Sabbath, so it is when there is a general abstinence from evil. This is what the lawgiver truly seeks as a Sabbath, and through each individual command he orders us to withdraw from evil.

Supporting this, he adds: “Fear my sanctuary,” or, according to the Septuagint, “You shall fear my holy things.” For just as those who approach them in the proper manner are sanctified by them, so those who approach them wickedly, without first cleansing themselves from the filth of malice and then drawing near to what is pure, corrupt or destroy them, like Nadab and Abihu and the sons of Eli. Hence Paul, speaking of those who receive the mysteries without due care, added: “Therefore many among you are weak and sick, and many sleep” (1 Cor. II). For this reason the lawgiver now adds: “I am the Lord,” that is, the holy one who dwells among the holy and necessarily demands vengeance for the holy.

## CHAPTER IX. On Not Following Magicians and Diviners, Nor Resorting to Sorcerers

*(The same passage.)* “You shall not turn to magicians, nor inquire of diviners, lest you be defiled by them.” *(But the Septuagint renders it:)* “You shall not follow ventriloquists, and you shall not join yourselves to sorcerers, lest you be defiled by them. I am the Lord your God.”

*(From Hesychius.)* The investigation of ventriloquists is the greatest form of diabolical error and deception. Thus Paul, when he encountered a girl who had a spirit of Python—even though the demon loudly praised him and Silas, saying, “These men are servants of the Most High God, who proclaim to you the way of truth” (Acts XVI)—nevertheless rebuked the evil spirit and drove it out.

It is also exceedingly wicked to cling to sorcerers, because they pronounce the names of demons that are hostile and destructive to us. Even if, for a short time, they appear to perform something in order to lead people into error—something trivial and insignificant for bodily health, such as inexperienced physicians can also perform—they do not do this as good beings or as those who wish human beings well. Rather, they desire to bring them into slavery and separate them from God.

Nor should we follow ventriloquists—that is, false prophets—who teach and prophesy, in God’s name, things alien to God. They are rightly called ventriloquists, as though they brought forth from the intelligible belly of their heart certain fables, that is, false teachings and prophecies.

It follows:

“Rise before the gray head, honor the person of the old man, and fear the Lord your God. I am the Lord.”

*(From Hesychius.)* It is good, certainly, to honor one who has already reached old age. He undoubtedly possesses something more in the way of experience for prudence. Moreover, the honor we show to those advanced in years will also be deserved by us from those younger than we are; and from this a good order, preserving our life in decency, is established for us.

By the “gray-haired man,” however, he truly understands the old man—that is, the one who has advanced in wisdom—of whom Moses says: “Ask your father, and he will declare it to you; your elders, and they will tell you” (Deut. XXXII). Paul likewise says: “Let the presbyters be considered worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in word and teaching.” It follows:

## CHAPTER X. On Care for Strangers, and on Just Measures, Scales, Rules, and Weights

*(The same passage.)* “If a stranger dwells in your land and stays among you, do not reproach him, but let him be among you as one born among you, and you shall love him as yourselves, for you too were strangers in the land of Egypt. I am the Lord your God.”

*(From Hesychius.)* We said above that the land given to us by God is the cultivation of virtues and his good teaching. If someone approaches this land as a stranger—that is, wishing to turn to our faith and be enrolled as a citizen of that land of which Paul says, “You have approached Mount Zion and the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and the company of many thousands of angels and the church of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven” (Heb. XII)—we must not afflict him; that is, we must not impose a heavier yoke upon him by laying more burdensome commandments upon one newly born and newly believing, lest we sin like the Pharisees and scribes, whom the Lord accused, saying:

“They bind heavy and unbearable burdens and place them upon people’s shoulders, but they themselves do not wish to move them with their finger” (Matt. XXIII).

Therefore, when someone believes in the faith, we must not afflict him by imposing certain legal requirements upon him. Rather, he should be for us like one born among us, who has been nourished in the faith and has grown in piety.

Peter, clearly establishing this, said to those who wished to circumcise believers from the Gentiles: “Why do you test God by placing upon the necks of the disciples a yoke which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear? But we believe that we are saved through the grace of Jesus Christ, just as they are” (Acts XV).

Let us therefore love every stranger—or, as the Septuagint says, proselyte—as ourselves, so that we command them only those things through which we believe that we ourselves, if we practice them, will be saved.

“You shall not act unjustly in judgment, in rule, in weight, or in measure. Your scales shall be just, and your weights equal; your bushel shall be just, and your sextarius equal. I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt. Keep all my commandments and all my judgments, and do them. I am the Lord.”

*(From Hesychius.)* This ordinance is also like the preceding ones, once we have investigated not only the profit of its letter but also its spirit. Earlier he commanded that no injustice be done in judgment. Now he commands that we act unjustly neither in measures, nor in weights, nor in scales, lest we use for injustice the very things that are, as it were, the boundaries of justice.

Measures are given as boundaries of justice to sellers and buyers, and to those conducting any other kind of transaction; likewise weights are given, just as laws are given to judges. Thus, in speaking of not acting unjustly in judgment, not altering scales or weights, and possessing a just sextarius or bushel—that is, every measure of wine or oil—he commands abstention from every injustice practiced against one’s neighbor, both in greater and in lesser matters. For whatever is unjust is everywhere detestable, whereas whatever is just is always pleasing to God.

Moreover, what possession of a field or house is to the rich, a measure of wine or grain, the weight of bread, and other things from which daily life is sustained are to the poor.

Nor should we act unjustly in the judgment of the mind, nor corrupt the measures and scales of the justice naturally implanted in us by judging our own sins one way and those of our neighbor another. For the Lord says: “With the judgment with which you judge, you will be judged, and with the measure with which you measure, it will be measured back to you” (Matt. VII). Explaining how this should be understood, he added: “Why do you see the speck in your brother’s eye, but do not see the beam that is in your own eye?”

Nor should we harm the divine weights, scales, and measures. Rather, let us keep just scales, measures, and weights—that is, the laws of divine Scripture—without imposing our own scale or weight upon them, and without suffering what the Pharisees suffered. Concerning them the Lord said in the Gospels: “Why do you transgress the commandments of God because of your traditions?” (Matt. XV).

To recall that he said these things, the law adds: “I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt. Keep all my commandments and all my judgments, and do them.” It thereby points to the evangelical commandments which the Lord commanded by his authority.

## CHAPTER XI. On Not Sacrificing to the Idol Moloch, Not Clinging to Magicians, and Not Cursing One’s Parents

*(Chapter XX.)* The Lord spoke to Moses, saying:

“Speak to the children of Israel: Any man among the children of Israel or among the strangers who dwell in Israel who gives any of his offspring to the idol Moloch shall be put to death. The people of the land shall stone him, and I will set my face against him and cut him off from the midst of his people, because he has given some of his offspring to Moloch and has defiled my sanctuary and profaned my holy name.

“But if the people of the land, acting carelessly and treating my command as though it were of little importance, let the man who gave some of his offspring to Moloch go and do not wish to kill him, I will set my face against that man and his family, and I will cut him off, together with all who consented with him to fornicate with Moloch, from the midst of his people.”

*(From Hesychius.)* We have often said in the preceding passages why the law sometimes commands the same things two or three times: it does so for the sake of the readers’ memory. Thus, while recapitulating the same commandments, it inserts certain new matters, so that the repetition of the laws may not appear superfluous, and so that, in searching out what is new, we may attend more diligently to what came before.

For this reason, when earlier forbidding certain actions, it left their punishment unmentioned, so that, by asking what that punishment was and of what kind, we might investigate what it later sanctions. In this passage it inserts the punishments that it had previously omitted.

Long ago, therefore, it forbade giving one’s offspring to Moloch, or, according to the Septuagint, “to the ruler.” This was the name of a certain idol or demon. Accordingly, Stephen introduces Amos as saying: “You received the tabernacle of Moloch and the star of your god Remphan, the figures that you made to worship them” (Amos V).

Moloch, or Melchom, as it is also often read, was the idol of the Ammonites. Its name is interpreted as “your king.” “The star of your god Remphan,” that is, “your creations,” you accepted in place of God. It signifies Lucifer, whose worship the nation of the Saracens had embraced in honor of Venus.

Now, therefore, in bearing witness once more against the sinner concerning the same matter, he makes not only the rulers of the people but also the whole synagogue and people judges and avengers. “The people of the land,” he says, “shall stone him.”

Not content with this, he adds: “I will set my face against him, and I will cut him off from the midst of his people,” thereby rousing and provoking everyone against the one who has committed such acts. He also threatens them with terror if they neglect this and do not zealously execute the prescribed punishment upon him with their own hands, since God is so greatly angered that he himself openly pronounces the sentence against him.

Why? Because he gave some of his offspring to Moloch, “to defile my sanctuary and profane my holy name.” Whoever gives a son, relative, disciple, friend, or anyone belonging to his family or teaching to the ruler of this age, who now works in the sons of disobedience, vowing and consecrating him to demons—the one to the sacred rites of demons, the other to a mixture of male and female life—does this.

Both practices were customary among pagans and among those who fell into their error. Concerning them God says through Amos: “Because these were corrupted with fornicators, and they sacrificed with effeminate men.” He defiles God’s holy things. How? Because he defiles his holy name.

He therefore defiles and pollutes God’s name who gives to him one made in God’s image and, through that image, [defiles] the very one who sanctified him and breathed into him the spirit of life from his grace. Such a person is corrupted by an evil spirit opposed to God; he reduces the Lord’s image to the service of demons and allows the royal pearl to be defiled by swine.

The same is true of anyone who offers someone from his family or teaching to avarice, and accustoms to avarice by deeds or words one who is in any way his disciple or relative, making him a devoted slave of demons, consecrated to idols, and a soldier of the evil ruler of this age. “The root of all evils is avarice, which is the service of idols” (1 Tim. VI; Gal. V).

We say the same against those who teach adultery, suggesting wicked actions and persuading others to shame, thereby polluting the holy things of God—that is, the bodies sealed for God, whose flesh is God’s temple and the dwelling place of the Holy Spirit.

For this reason the lawgiver commands that those who teach such evil and abominable things by deeds or words be punished not by one person’s hands but by everyone’s, since they are enemies and adversaries of all and, as was said above, harm everyone’s glory.

“But if the people of the land, acting carelessly and treating my command as though it were of little importance, let the man who gives some of his offspring to Moloch go and do not wish to kill him”—that is, if those who have been nourished in knowledge neglect the one who teaches such things.

For this is the true and upright land, of which David says: “Your good spirit will lead me into an upright land” (Ps. CXLII), because it is especially wicked not to prosecute such a sin but to let it go unpunished.

What is meant by “and against his family”? It means those who strive after similar things, who are his relatives because of the similarity of their actions and teaching. He therefore says: “I will cut him off, together with all who consented with him to fornicate with Moloch, from the midst of his people.”

For it is evil to allow or consent to those outside to fornicate away from God and cling to the intelligible ruler; it is much worse to allow this “from the midst of his people.” This means surrendering the entire flock to wolves and handing all the sheep over to wild beasts.

If we allow enemies to snatch them from the midst of the people, or if we stretch out our hand to the one who is snatching them, we are guilty. Whoever consents and remains silent instead of accusing the person whom it is necessary to rebuke, admonish, or reprove will not escape divine judgment.

God sets his face against him—the face of which David says: “The face of the Lord is against those who do evil, to destroy their memory from the earth” (Ps. XXXIII). This applies not only to those who do such things but also to those who consent to their perpetrators.

It follows:

“The soul that turns to magicians and diviners and fornicates with them, I will set my face against it and destroy it from the midst of its people. Sanctify yourselves and be holy, because I am the Lord your God. Keep my commandments and do them. I am the Lord who sanctifies you.”

It is no ordinary sin to turn to magicians—or, according to the Septuagint, ventriloquists—or to sorcerers, as we have already explained. In either case one departs from God, whether one speaks of physical Python-spirits and sorcerers or of intelligible ones, that is, those who prophesy falsely in the name of God: deceivers and flatterers who, with sorcerous words, corrupt the hearing of many, turning their hearing away from the truth so that they may turn instead to fables and error (2 Tim. IV).

Therefore the judge threatens to set his face against them and destroy them from his people. He adds: “Sanctify yourselves and be holy,” showing that all who have followed them are polluted, abominable, and unclean, since they have consented to abominable words and corrupt doctrines.

He further adds: “Keep my commandments and do them,” thereby showing that they teach transgression of God’s commandments, whether they teach the law or pretend to interpret divine commandments. For this reason he rejects both them and their followers.

He also adds a brief conclusion in these words: “I am the Lord who sanctifies you.” That is: Why do you corrupt yourselves with those who speak things contrary to my law or my teaching? I am the Lord who sanctifies you.

It follows:

“Whoever curses his father or mother shall be put to death. Whoever curses his father or mother, his blood shall be upon him,” or, according to the Septuagint, “he is guilty,” so that this word may be referred to God himself. Isaiah says: “Did not one God make you? Is he not the father of you all?” (Isa. LXIV). And again: “Lord, you are our father; we are clay, and you are our maker, and we are all the work of your hands.”

*(From Hesychius.)* Rightly, therefore, whoever disparages his father, and likewise his mother, is punished with death. He is ungrateful toward nature and blasphemes his benefactors, through whom we receive our existence from God and through whom we were generated as intermediaries. He insults the instruments of the Creator, to say nothing of the labors they endured in our generation.

Because the lawgiver prescribed the greatest punishment against such a person—namely, death—he shows that he has written such a sentence of punishment very rightly and reasonably. He then adds: “Whoever curses his father or mother, his blood shall be upon him,” or, according to the Septuagint, “he is guilty,” mentioning and recapitulating the sin in order to demonstrate the magnitude of the punishment.

If this applies to one who curses physical parents, how much more does it apply to one who blasphemes Christ? Christ regenerated us spiritually. Therefore whoever insults his mystery and the grace of baptism by disobeying the Lord’s voice—“Unless one is regenerated from water and the Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of heaven”—will die a most terrible death, alienated from the kingdom of heaven and suffering the loss of eternal life.

He is guilty for this additional reason: although the Lord preached, and preached nothing harsh or burdensome, nothing requiring time, material, or technical discipline, but only a pure heart and faith, this person willingly turned away from the Lord’s command.

## CHAPTER XII. Adultery and Fornication Are Forbidden, with Punishment Added for Transgressors

*(The same passage.)* “If anyone commits adultery with another man’s wife and commits adultery with the wife of his neighbor, both the adulterer and the adulteress shall be put to death”—that is, both the man who committed adultery and the woman with whom adultery was committed.

*(From Augustine.)* Here he wished to distinguish somewhat between any man and a neighbor, although in many places he uses “neighbor” for every human being. But what kind of expression is this, that after having spoken of a man he repeats the same thing concerning a neighbor, when it follows that one must abstain all the more from a neighbor’s wife if one must abstain from the wife of any man?

If he had first spoken of a neighbor, then, lest anyone think it permissible to commit adultery with the wife of another man, it would have been necessary to add “neighbor” after “any man.” But now, if what is less serious is not permitted, how much less is what is more serious permitted? For if one may not commit adultery with the wife of any man, how much more may one not do so with the wife of a neighbor?

Or perhaps this repetition explains what was said earlier, so that a person may understand how great an evil it is to commit adultery with another man’s wife: if he does this, he commits adultery with the wife of his neighbor.

*(From Hesychius.)* Every human being is the neighbor of every other human being. Therefore, just as physical adultery is evil, so intelligible adultery is worse. The former insults the flesh, the latter the spirit; the former insults a human being, the latter God himself.

Concerning these adulterers Hosea says: “All are adulterers, like an oven heated by the baker” (Hos. VII), accusing intelligible adultery in the heart. This was committed by the whole Jewish people, who corrupted the law and the doctrines of the law.

Whoever therefore commits adultery with the woman of that man concerning whom Paul says, “I betrothed you to one man, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (2 Cor. XI)—that is, whoever commits adultery with the Church, of whom the same apostle says, “Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ loved the Church” (Eph. V)—commits adultery.

He commits adultery by spreading shameful words, teaching not what is proper to her and not what belongs to Christ, as Paul says: “For the sake of shameful gain.”

“Both the adulterer and the adulteress shall be put to death”—that is, the one who sows another’s word over the true word, and the Church that allows such things to be sown within her. Let us understand her as a wife, first of the true husband, namely Christ, and then also of her husband to whom Christ has entrusted the Church, whether priest or teacher.

For all who, out of rivalry with Christ, corrupt the word in hatred of him and thereby suffer shipwreck concerning the faith are adulterers, like Hymenaeus and Alexander, whom Paul handed over to Satan so that they might learn not to blaspheme (1 Tim. I).

Their adultery is reckoned against Christ. But whoever acts in rivalry with human beings who have been appointed to govern churches, doing something of this kind in order to overthrow their teaching, commits the adultery which Paul says Alexander the coppersmith committed.

For he says: “Alexander the coppersmith showed me much harm; the Lord will repay him according to his works. You also avoid him, for he strongly opposed our words” (2 Tim. IV).

Their adultery is reckoned against their neighbor, namely, the priest or overseer, because of rivalry with whom a person advances toward such conduct. This too has death as its punishment. Even if he does not contend specifically against Christ but against a human being, he corrupts Christ’s work and scatters the flock. For this reason, whoever allows himself to be corrupted by him becomes his partner in punishment.

“Whoever sleeps with his stepmother and uncovers his father’s nakedness, both shall be put to death; their blood shall be upon them. If anyone sleeps with his daughter-in-law, both shall be put to death, because they have committed a crime; their blood shall be upon them” (the same passage).

*(From Hesychius.)* The lawgiver spoke of these matters earlier in this book of Leviticus. There, however, he said: “You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father or your mother, nor of your sister, daughter-in-law, or the others in order.” When explaining these passages, we showed that the law commands not only the rejection of shameful and impious intercourse with relatives, but also that we should not reveal what we have learned, nor publicize the sins of our carnal or spiritual relatives.

Here God added, “If he sleeps with,” thereby bringing forward the person who knows that another has committed the same wicked action but nevertheless commits it himself, without being ashamed of sharing in the sin. In this way he becomes an informer, and the lawgiver rightly assigns him the punishment of death.

He appropriately joined the stepmother and the daughter-in-law, because in the first case a son commits an offense against his father, and in the second a father against his son. It is a similar impiety for a son to expose or publicize his father’s sin, or a father his son’s, when they themselves have committed similar offenses.

To such people Paul says: “Therefore you are without excuse, O man, whoever you are who judge; for in judging another you condemn yourself, since you do the same things that you judge” (Rom. II).

“Whoever sleeps with a male as with a female, both have committed an abomination; they shall be put to death; their blood shall be upon them.”

*(From Hesychius.)* Because this sin is an insult to nature, its novelty and its wickedness demonstrate the point. Therefore the law does not decree the penalty of death for it without reason.

We should also reject, even in hearing, such conduct. Let us also beware of the one who is strong in spirit and for that reason is called “male.” In divine Scripture a man is everywhere named as one perfect in virtues. Hence Paul says: “Until we all attain to a perfect man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ” (Eph. IV).

Let us therefore beware of making effeminate by inappropriate words, or dissolving through our actions, the virtue of this soul, lest we ourselves be dissolved together with it. For, as you see, the punishment of both is death.

It follows:

“Whoever takes a woman together with her mother as his wife has committed a crime; he shall be burned alive with them, and such an abomination shall not remain among you.”

*(From Hesychius.)* He has very rightly threatened this offense with such a severe punishment. For when the children born from the mother are considered together with those born from the daughter, and there is one father, it is uncertain whether they ought to be called brothers or maternal uncles. Since they have one father, necessity compels them to be regarded as brothers. But when there are two parents, with one being the mother and the other the daughter, necessity compels those born from the mother to be called maternal uncles of those born from the daughter.

This is carefully observed and guarded according to the letter, so that such incestuous intercourse and confusion of lineage may be avoided.

But since desire is the mother of every sin, we must also understand that this command forbids us to transgress spiritually: whenever sinful desire arises in us, we must resist it to the end and not join an action to it. Whoever joins an action to it is burned in fire—not only the person himself, but also the desire for sin and the action itself.

By what fire? By the fire of which Christ said: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and I desire that it be kindled” (Luke XII), that is, the administration of the Spirit, who will remove sinners from the midst, together with their sins. For Paul says: “If by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the flesh, you will live.”

Whoever lies with an animal or beast shall be put to death; the beast also shall be killed. And the woman who has lain with an animal shall likewise be killed together with it; their blood shall be upon them. The question arises how the beast can be guilty, since it is irrational and in no way capable of the law. Or should we understand this as an instance of the figure of speech called in Greek *metaphor*, by which words are transferred from the animate to the inanimate—as when one says “a wicked wind” or “an angry sea”—and likewise here transferred from the rational to the irrational? For it is to be believed that the beasts were ordered to be killed because, having been polluted by such a crime, they renew the unworthy memory of the deed.

*(From Hesychius.)* The legislator uses exceedingly severe language against the Jewish people, because they were so unjust and devoted to lust that they even strayed toward foreign desires. Therefore, when he mentions intercourse between men or women and quadrupeds, he shows that death is the penalty for such conduct.

But perhaps you will judge this law superfluous for the faithful. “They have no need,” you say, “to be judged by such a statute.” It is not superfluous, however; rather, its spiritual contemplation can greatly benefit us. If we understand quadrupeds as perverse pleasures that look downward toward the earth—for they are devoid of every human activity and are therefore called “quadrupeds,” since quadrupeds do not have hands like human beings, and consequently lack the closest kinship with us—then whoever, man or woman, devotes himself so completely to alien pleasures that he is not merely seized by them through negligence but actually clings closely to them and unites himself with them, maintaining prolonged and enduring intercourse with them, is guilty of death [Col. 0467D].

For this is the end of wicked lusts: when those who practice them are punished, the lusts themselves are rightly said also to die. They do not subsist independently, since sin has no substance in the sinners who commit it; yet when the sinners are destroyed, the sins themselves likewise perish. It follows:

> Whoever takes his sister, the daughter of his father or the daughter of his mother, and sees her nakedness, and she sees her brother’s shame, they have committed a detestable act. They shall be killed in the sight of the people, because they have mutually uncovered their shame, and they shall bear their iniquity.

*(From Augustine.)* What does “he has seen” mean in this passage, except “he has known through intercourse,” just as Scripture says, “He knew his wife,” meaning “he was joined to her”? And what does “they shall receive their sin” mean, when he was speaking about their punishment, except that he wished even the punishment of sin to be called “sin”?

*(From Hesychius.)* Many thought it tolerable to have intercourse with sisters who were daughters of one’s father or daughters of one’s mother, because Abraham also said of Sarah, “She is my sister” (Gen. XII)—a sister on his father’s side and not on his mother’s. Yet the matter is not altogether as the history is commonly understood. For when Moses narrates the sons born to Terah, Abraham’s father, he nowhere mentions Sarah. And if Abraham did marry his sister, was it before he came to know God?

It is therefore wrong to unite oneself to sisters in marriage, and for this reason the law prohibited it. Since these matters stand thus, let us in no way depart from the contemplation already given. “To see” the nakedness of a sister on the father’s or mother’s side—understand that the person who truly sees and takes it is one who not only observes a shameful action committed by a father or mother, that is, an action in which the father or mother transgressed, but also adopts it through a similar and corresponding action. Such a person is detestable: he not only investigates what he ought not to investigate but also builds upon and joins himself to the perversity committed by his parents. This is called his “sister,” as it were the perversity of the perverse.

But why did he expose and disseminate it? The hidden sins of many parents are exposed by their children when the children commit similar acts. Therefore he commanded that such a person be destroyed in the sight of the people—or, according to the Septuagint, “in the sight of the children of his race,” that is, in the sight of those who contemplate and devise similar things. These are rightly called the children of his race. Why, then, “in their sight”? So that, through the punishment of one, the others may learn chastity [Col. 0468C]. When the sinner is killed, the sin also perishes, as we said once before in the preceding discussion. It follows:

> Whoever lies with a woman during her menstrual flow and uncovers her nakedness, and she exposes the source of her blood, both shall be cut off from the midst of their people.

*(From Hesychius.)* The legislator did not command abstention from a menstruating woman without reason. He was urging a person toward the modesty of chastity and wishing him to exercise the care from which sanctification arises, rather than continually mixing with women like pigs and giving himself over to common corruption. He wished him to make use of enforced abstinence as a means to self-control.

But how did he command that they be destroyed from among their people, when earlier he had prescribed purification for the man who slept with a menstruating woman? For he said: “If a man lies with her during the time of her menstrual blood, he shall be unclean for seven days.” Then, after describing the sacrifices of purification, he added: “This is the law for him who suffers a discharge of semen, and for him who is polluted, and for the woman who suffers a discharge of blood during her menstruation; and for the man and woman who suffer a discharge, and for the man who sleeps with a menstruating woman: thus he is to be purified.” He wishes this man, like the others, not to be punished.

Let us therefore contemplate the menstruating woman as the wisdom of the Gentiles: she is far from God, speaking and teaching about the flight of birds, the course of the stars, and the measurements of heaven. It is exceedingly wicked to sleep with her—that is, to take pleasure in her and remain joined to her for a long time—and also to uncover and publicly expose her nakedness [Col. 0468D], by transmitting what is in him [the reading *eletas* is uncertain] and the errors that he has, and by displaying the face of the whole error.

When these things are made public, she also reveals the discharge of her blood—that is, he introduces the things belonging to idolatrous sacrifices. For this reason he did not simply say, “They shall be killed,” but added, “from the midst of their people,” or, according to the Septuagint, “from their race.” For whoever transmits the wisdom of the Gentiles, which transgresses against our Creator, his knowledge, and piety, ought no longer rightly to be called human. By failing to know himself, he has deprived the Creator of the image of God;” therefore he is killed from the midst of the people, or from his race, so that what he possessed may no longer be called wisdom, and so that he may be deprived of the false and fictitious name he bore. Paul bears witness to this when he says: “The wisdom of this world is folly with God” (1 Cor. V).

> You shall not uncover the nakedness of your maternal aunt or your paternal aunt; whoever does this has exposed the shame of his own flesh. Both shall bear their iniquity.

*(From Hesychius.)* The law also forbade intercourse with the sisters of those who begot us, both so that family lines might not be confused and so that we might preserve the fitting reverence owed to our parents, abstaining on their account from their sisters. Understand this similarly in the spiritual sense: not only are the sins of parents to be veiled in silence and handed over to oblivion, but also the sins of those who were joined to them, and who are therefore called their brothers.

Let us be silent about their sins, because when those sins are exposed, even the parents cannot remain hidden. Hence he says, “He has exposed the shame of his own flesh.” But what punishment do those who do this undergo? “Both shall bear their iniquity,” he says. The Septuagint adds, “They shall die without children,” because they do not bear one another’s burdens but expose and disseminate the sins of their relatives, both according to the flesh and according to the spirit. They shall die without virtues. This is the worst sterility, for children do not help us at the time of judgment, whereas virtues do help us, and on account of them we are crowned. It is most wretched for the soul to languish through their sterility. To be adorned with the generation of such children is the condition of blessedness. This is what Isaiah means when he says: “Because of your presence, Lord, we conceived and, as it were, travailed and gave birth; we did not bring forth the spirit of salvation [justice] upon the earth” (Isa. XVI). Understand this, and what follows, in the same way.

[Col. 0469D]

> Whoever lies with the wife of his paternal uncle or maternal uncle and uncovers the shame of his relative, both shall bear their sin; they shall die without children.

According to another edition it is read as follows:

> Whoever sleeps with his female relative shall uncover the shame of his kinship; both shall die without children.

*(From Augustine.)* The question is how far this relationship is to be understood, since it is certainly permissible—and always has been permissible—to take a wife from a more distant degree. It must be understood as referring to those degrees that he prohibited, and the statement must be interpreted according to them: “Whoever sleeps with his female relative.” Here he has left some cases unmentioned but intended them to be understood, such as a sister by both parents and the wife of one’s mother’s brother, that is, one’s maternal uncle. For he first prohibited the wife of one’s paternal uncle, although she is said to be related not by blood but by affinity.

But what does “they shall die without children” mean, since children have been born from such unions in the past and are born even today? Should this be understood as established by God’s law, namely, that whoever is born from such unions is not to be counted as a child and is not to succeed the parents by any legal right?

It follows:

> Whoever takes his brother’s wife commits an unlawful act; he has uncovered his brother’s shame. They shall be without children.

*(From Hesychius.)* The legislator therefore shows that the Creator especially commanded nature to be joined for the sake of children. For it is truly incongruous, and close to the life of animals, to unite oneself with the wives of brothers and relatives—those, namely, who are near to one another.

Elsewhere in the law, in the book of Deuteronomy, he not only commanded this but also compelled it, saying: “When brothers dwell together and one of them dies without children, the wife of the deceased shall not marry another, but his brother shall take her and raise up offspring for his brother,” and similar things. When there was no brother, he commanded that the deceased man’s childless widow be taken by a maternal uncle or by another relative on the father’s side, just as Boaz took Ruth according to the law of kinship.

Thus, for the sake of lust, he forbids intercourse and association with relatives; but when it is necessary again to relieve distress or respond to misfortune, he commands and wishes marriages to be contracted—not in the pollution of corruption, but for the succession of the race. For this reason he also commanded that the man who unites himself in the prohibited manner should die without children. He says: “They shall be without children,” because by misusing the law of procreation they have confused the generation of children.

What, then, does it mean to die without children? This is the principal question to be asked in this law: did he command that the children of those who married the wives of their brothers or uncles be put to death? And how does this agree with the statement, “Parents shall not be put to death for their children, nor children for their parents”? Yet he nowhere commanded that they be killed; he said only that they would die without children, according solely to the edition of the Septuagint interpreters, so that the succession of children would not be reckoned to them, nor would they leave their inheritance to their children.

Symmachus also indicates this by his clearer rendering, as does Theodotion. Instead of “They shall die without children,” both render it, “They shall be without children.” Hence the spiritual interpretation and explanation is similar to those given above.

> Keep my laws and judgments and do them, lest the land into which you are about to enter and in which you are about to dwell vomit you out.

*(From Hesychius.)* It is not enough for us to preserve some portion of the law, or to carry out one command or another for the correction of life. We must keep all the precepts and judgments that the legislator wrote at God’s command. These are the “precepts” he mentions, including those about which he himself, in uncertainty, inquired of God and learned from his judgment, as in the case of the son of an Israelite woman who spoke blasphemy. The laws that were thus issued he calls “judgments.”

By these words he briefly signified the whole law, from which nothing ought to be transgressed, lest the transgressor be expelled, that is, cast out. This is what “remove” means. Symmachus, and likewise Theodotion, rendered it “cast away.” But from where are they to be vomited out? Clearly, from the land into which God promises to bring us. What this land is, learn from what follows.

## CHAPTER XIII  
### On possessing the land and avoiding every impurity in it

*(Ibid.)*

> Do not walk according to the ordinances of the nations that I am about to drive out before you. For they have done all these things, and I have abhorred them. But to you I say: Possess their land, which I shall give you as an inheritance, a land flowing with milk and honey. I am the Lord your God, who separated you from the other peoples.

*(From the same author.)* These words were not spoken only to the Jews, because they believe themselves separated from all nations on account of circumcision and the law of Moses; they were spoken to all who draw near to serve God. For it is above all forbidden to walk according to the ordinances of the Gentiles.

As for the Gentiles—or nations—“whom I am about to drive out before you,” he says, the other translators rendered it, “Whom I drive out from before your face”;” the Septuagint, “From you.” These are the demons whom he drove out from before the faithful. Previously they ruled over them while they persisted in ungodliness: not one ruling over one, but many ruling over one. Mary Magdalene proves this, for from her he cast out seven demons; and the man who was bound with chains says to him, “My name is Legion, because we are many” (Matt. IX).

The things that the law prohibited were therefore committed by those nations, either by the demons themselves acting or by their working in human beings. For this reason God abhorred them and brought us into their inheritance, into a land flowing with milk and honey. He did not say “having” these things, so that you might understand the statement of a sensible earthly land, but “flowing.” What land, then, flows with milk and honey?

He is speaking of the delights of the age to come and of the blessings that God gives us after the resurrection of the dead. He called them “milk and honey” because among the foods we now use nothing is sweeter or more pleasant than these. Moreover, they are food without labor, requiring no work or preparation. In the same way, the blessings of the age to come will be without labor or pain, requiring no effort, preparation, or work [Col. 0471D].

And who gives us these things? The legislator’s following words clearly show: “I am the Lord your God, who separated you from the other peoples.” Christ did this. In the Gospels he distinguishes those who believe in him from all nations, not only intelligible but also visible, saying: “Do not be anxious, saying, ‘What shall we eat?’ or ‘What shall we drink?’ or ‘What shall we wear?’ For all these things the Gentiles seek” (Matt. VI). Thus he clearly wishes us to be separated from the nations by pursuing a higher manner of life.

> Therefore separate the clean animal from the unclean, and the clean bird from the unclean. Do not pollute your souls with animals, birds, or all things that move upon the earth, which I have shown you to be unclean. You shall be holy to me, because I am holy, the Lord, and I have separated you from the other peoples so that you may be mine.

*(From the same author.)* That the law understands animals or beasts as ordinary people, and flying creatures as contemplatives who devote themselves to the heights of knowledge, has been clearly demonstrated by us through scriptural proofs when we discussed the sacrifices and the foods of quadrupeds and birds.

Since, then, every ordinary person is judged by many to be clean because of his simplicity, and likewise those who seem to devote and apply themselves to divine knowledge are also considered clean, although this is not necessarily so, the ordinary person ought to be wise in what is good and, as Paul says, simple in what is evil. Whoever is such is clean; whoever is not such is unclean.

But the person who devotes himself to the contemplation of divine things also needs a clean heart, a clean conscience, and sincere faith. Those who do not possess these things turn to empty talk, understanding neither what they discuss nor what they assert, as it is written to Timothy.

Therefore he necessarily commanded that the clean of both groups be separated from the unclean, so that we may abstain from the latter and unite ourselves to the former. But the legislator also displays great wisdom in the present passage. He distinguishes quadrupeds and birds in one way, but does not make the same distinction among the reptiles of the earth.

Everything that moves upon the earth is unclean: namely, whatever has an earthly mind, whose god is the belly, and which feeds on the poison of pleasures established in the dust. Concerning these things, as you see, he speaks distinctly:

> And all things that move upon the earth, which I have shown you to be unclean.

All who feed upon earthly actions, even if they pretend to wear the appearance of the faithful, are separated as unclean and distinguished among the unclean. He wants us to abstain entirely from their evils. For this reason he added:

> You shall be holy to me, because I am holy, the Lord;

that is, I have become for you a model of conduct. I so rejected earthly things that I did not even have a place to lay my head. I also commanded my disciples: “Do not possess gold, silver, or copper in your belts; no bag for the journey, nor two tunics, nor sandals, nor a staff” (Matt. X).

Thus he earnestly wishes us neither to think nor to act in any way concerning the things that creep upon the earth.

## CHAPTER XIV  
### On diviners and their punishment

*(Ibid.)*

> A man or woman in whom there is a divining or prophetic spirit shall surely be put to death; they shall stone them with stones. Their blood shall be upon them.

*(From the same author.)* To be a diviner or seer—or, according to the Septuagint, an enchanter—is a matter of extreme wickedness. Whoever is such a person is himself corrupted and undoubtedly corrupts others in his own wickedness. Therefore he commanded that such a person be stoned.

We should not engage in anything perceptible, but neither should we devise fables from the heart, like excessive and empty speeches, nor offer certain seductive enchantments through inappropriate discourses of doctrine in order to deceive the ears of ordinary or simple people, desiring by such inquiries to nourish our bellies and satisfy our other pleasures.

Writing to the Romans, Paul, the vessel of election, clearly described intelligible diviners and wicked enchanters:

> We urge you, brothers, to watch those who create dissensions and occasions of stumbling contrary to the teaching that you learned, and to avoid them.

He explained in what follows who these people are:

> For such persons do not serve our Lord Christ, but their own belly, and by smooth speech and blessings they deceive the hearts of the innocent.

## CHAPTER XV  
### How priests ought to conduct themselves in the death of citizens and in taking wives

*(CHAP. XXI.)*

> And the Lord said to Moses: Speak to the priests, the sons of Aaron, and say to them: A priest shall not be defiled by the deaths of his fellow citizens, except only by his blood relatives or close kin—that is, for his father, mother, son, daughter, brother, or virgin sister who is not married to a man. Nor shall he be defiled for a leader of his people.

The Septuagint reads: “He shall not be polluted suddenly among his people, to his defilement.”

*(From Hesychius.)* The literal wording indeed commanded priests to avoid pollution from the dead, but this is not the intention of the law, nor did the legislator set out to speak about this matter. Rather, he understood something greater, something that necessarily had to be said about priests.

For when they neglect the sins of the people, those sins are said to defile them, according to what is written in Hosea: “They shall eat the sins of my people, and they shall lift up their souls to their iniquity” (Hos. IV). Not every sin committed by the people ought to be imputed to them, but the distinction spoken by the prophet Ezekiel must be carefully considered:

> Son of man, I have made you a watchman for the house of Israel. You shall hear a word from my mouth and announce it to them from me. If, when I say to the wicked, “You shall surely die,” you do not announce it to him, and do not speak so that he may turn from his wicked way and live, that wicked person shall die in his iniquity, but I shall require his blood from your hand. But if you announce it to the wicked, and he does not turn from his wickedness and his wicked way, he shall die in his iniquity, but you shall have saved your own soul (Ezek. III).

The present legislator explains this more openly and precisely:

> They shall not defile themselves among the souls of their fellow citizens,

that is, among sinners whose souls are filled with pollution and who in certain ways become the causes of pollution to others, especially to priests and teachers when they neglect them.

Nevertheless, he says, they shall not be defiled by the deaths of their fellow citizens—that is, when they are found not to have omitted anything that would have benefited them, but to have done what was incumbent upon them and proclaimed God’s law, while those who refused to obey brought death upon themselves through disobedience.

Therefore those who preside are not polluted in such cases, but they are polluted by their close and immediate relatives: by their father and mother, sons and daughters, brother and virgin sister who is not married to a man [Col. 0473D].

For a priest ought to exercise care not only over the people, so that they may not sin, but especially over his own household and relatives. Hence Paul says: “Command these things so that they may be blameless. But if anyone does not care for his own, and especially for those of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever” (1 Tim. V). And again: “If anyone does not know how to govern his own household, how will he care for the Church of God?” (1 Tim. III).

In the case of a son, daughter, brother, or virgin sister—namely, when they sin—the priest is necessarily polluted, since he ought daily, indeed every hour, to instruct them in what pertains to salvation and to watch over them so that they do not commit sins deserving death. The same must be understood of mother and father.

The dignity of the priest makes a son a teacher of his priestly father and mother. By specifying a sister who is not married to a man, he shows that if the priest’s relatives separate themselves and, becoming in a certain sense another household, remove themselves from him, he suffers no pollution from their sins. But as long as they remain attached to him, observing the law of proximity and kinship, they rightly become participants in their pollution, since, as cohabitants, they cannot be unaware of their sins; this itself becomes a cause of pollution for them.

Therefore, after saying that they would be defiled by these persons, he subsequently added, according to the Septuagint: “He shall not be polluted suddenly among his people, to his defilement.” What else does this show except that the priest is indeed polluted by a sinful people, but not suddenly?

The sins committed by strangers do not immediately defile the priest. They do so when the sinners persist in their sins and the priests neglect to heal them. He did not add “to his defilement” without reason. By this word he indicates that when a priest is polluted by the sins of the people for the reason stated—namely, because he is negligent and does not do what a priest ought in every way to do—he is found to be profane, that is, stripped of the dignity of the priesthood, one among the many. For those who have not been sanctified are called profane, and rightly so, because they have not done what belongs to a priest. It follows:

*(From the same author.)*

> They shall not shave their heads or their beards, nor make incisions in their flesh.

The law rightly commands priests to restrain even the grief that normally arises from death, since they themselves possess the hope of future life and teach it to the people. Beyond this, it clearly commands them not only to remain watchful and sound-minded in their own sins, but also in the sins of others. Learn how this is to be understood.

The head and beard signify wisdom and our perfection. For this reason Christ is called our head, in whom we ought to possess the highest and most perfect understanding. Paul bears witness to this when he says: “Until we all attain to a perfect man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ” (Eph. IV).

The beard also rightly signifies the perfection of wisdom, because a beard grows on those who have reached youthful maturity and are already capable of understanding what is useful.

Since, then, the Lord—and Paul likewise—calls sinners dead, saying, “When we were dead in our sins, he made us alive together with Christ” (Eph. II), priests above all ought not to shave their head or beard over the dead—that is, over the sinner.

The thoughts that adorn the head like hair, and that likewise adorn our wisdom when they are ordered and sober, ought not to be corrupted by another’s sin. Rather, the priest must preserve them whole, so that he may exhort, entreat, rebuke, and reprimand, according to what Paul wrote to Timothy: “Reprove, rebuke, exhort, with all patience and teaching” (2 Tim. IV).

He added how this is to be done:

> But you, be watchful in all things, endure hardship, do the work of an evangelist (ibid.).

Therefore a priest who does not exhort and rebuke the sinner is not watchful. Whoever is not watchful is rightly said, according to the virtue indicated above, to shave his head and beard.

Nor is it fitting for a priest to make incisions in his flesh over the dead—that is, he must not be scandalized by the sinner, nor be offended when someone sins, nor acquire from this a carnal wisdom that incites him to similar wickedness. For the incision is the wisdom of the flesh, as Paul says of the Jews who live according to the flesh and think earthly thoughts: “Beware of the dogs, beware of the evil workers, beware of the mutilation.”

> They shall be holy to their God, and they shall not profane the name of their God, for they offer the incense of the Lord and the bread of their God; therefore they shall be holy.

How priests profane the name of God was explained by the prophet Malachi:

> You priests who profane my name, and you say, “How have we profaned you?” You offer polluted bread upon my altar (Mal. I).

Adding similar statements, he continued:

> If you offer the blind for sacrifice, is that not evil? And if you offer the lame and the sick, is that not evil? (ibid.)

And again:

> Great is my name among the nations, says the Lord. But you have profaned it by saying, “The table of the Lord is despised” (ibid.).

Thus priests profane the name of God in the sinfulness of their sacrifices. It follows:

> He shall not take a prostitute or a common harlot as wife, nor a woman divorced by her husband, because he is consecrated to his God and offers the bread of presentation. Therefore he shall be holy, because I am holy, the Lord who sanctifies you.

*(From Hesychius.)* If we priests preserve the sanctification given to us by God, then through our sanctification we sanctify him who is holy by nature. He has used this expression only with respect to us, in those conformed to him and sharing in his glory, in whom he wished to be sanctified, speaking figuratively and typically.

Nevertheless, he does not wish those who are sanctified by him to take a prostitute or a common harlot as wife. He is clearly directing his words against the synagogue of the Jews, which is a harlot. Hear the Lord saying through Isaiah:

> How has the faithful city Zion become a harlot, full of judgment? Righteousness dwelt in her, but now murderers do (Isa. I).

And in Hosea:

> I shall remove her fornication from her midst, and her adultery from between her breasts (Hos. II).

David also proclaims her profanation, saying to God:

> You have profaned her holiness on the earth; you have destroyed all her fortifications (Ps. LXXXVIII).

The sanctification of the Jews was undoubtedly their synagogue. In it were the sacrifice and tabernacle, and in it their ordinances were fulfilled. It is she who was rejected by God as by her husband, who had become her husband through election. But when he later found her blameworthy, he rejected her.

Since she was altogether cast out, hear the voice spoken by Hosea:

> Judge your mother, judge her, for she is not my wife, and I am not her husband (Hos. II).

Hear also what the prophet Isaiah transmitted:

> Thus says the Lord: Where is this bill of divorce of your mother, by which I dismissed her? (Isa. L.)

Where there is divorce and dismissal, it is clear that she had been a wife, of whom these things were said.

He does not therefore wish the priest to take her as wife, so that he may not proclaim any of the ordinances belonging to her as lawful, nor use those things that she used according to the letter; that is, those to whom intelligible realities have been entrusted should neither perform sacrifices of irrational animals nor practice sensible purifications.

> If a priest’s daughter is found to have committed fornication and has profaned her father’s name, she shall be burned with fire.

It is serious when the daughter of any man commits fornication, but especially when she is the daughter of a priest, because, as Paul said, “A priest must have his children submissive, with all chastity,” so that what follows may not be said of him: “If anyone does not know how to govern his own household, how will he care for the Church of God?”

For this reason the synagogue of the Jews is found in the prophets to be called not only the wife but also the daughter of God. Yet by corrupting both relationships, she proved unworthy of the gifts and therefore became alienated, so that God said through Isaiah:

> The daughter of Zion shall be left like a shelter in a vineyard, like a hut in a cucumber field, and like a city that is laid waste (Isa. I).

She was herself profaned and adulterated. Concerning her you will find God speaking prophetically through Hosea:

> I shall not have mercy on her children, because they are children of fornication, for their mother has committed fornication (Hos. II).

She was also burned with fire, as is shown by that ancient temple and city, Jerusalem, which still displays the remains of the conflagration. Therefore the spiritual contemplation of the law is true and undeniable. For she was not merely burned; according to the law, she was burned completely [Col. 0476D].

## CHAPTER XVI  
### On the dignity of the high priest, that he may not be polluted, and that he should marry a virgin, etc.

*(Ibid.)*

> The high priest, that is, the greatest priest among his brothers, upon whose head the oil of anointing has been poured, whose hands have been consecrated for the priesthood, and who is clothed in holy garments, shall not uncover his head, tear his garments, or enter at all where any dead person is present. He shall not defile himself even for his father or mother.
