Nor shall he go out from the sanctuary, lest he pollute the sanctuary of the Lord, because the oil of the holy anointing of his God is upon him. I am the Lord.

*(From Augustine.)* He is understood to have prohibited the high priest from doing the things mentioned above in mourning: removing the tiara from his head and tearing his garments. Tearing garments was customary among the ancients in mourning, as is written of Job when he received news that his sons had been crushed in the collapse (Job I).

Uncovering the headgear could be an act of mourning because it is the removal of an ornament.

But what does the Septuagint version mean when it says, “He shall not enter over every dead soul”? It is difficult to understand how it can call a dead body a “dead soul,” although this is a customary expression in Scripture and quite unfamiliar to us.

The soul therefore gives the name of its ruler even to the body deprived of it, because the body will be restored to the soul in the resurrection. In the same way, a building called a church continues to be called a church even when the Church—that is, the human beings—has departed from it.

Yet since the body does not receive the name of the soul in a living human being, it is astonishing that the body should then be called a soul when it has been deprived of the soul.

If we understand “dead soul” as the soul separated from the body, so that the separation itself is called death—that is, so that the soul is dead when separated from the body, not because it has lost its nature—then the expression may be explained. For when we are said to be dead to sin, we are not said to have perished according to nature, but to have ceased to use sin. In this way the soul may be called dead, that is, dead to the body, because it has ceased to use the body while continuing to live in its own nature.

But how can anyone enter over a dead soul, which this priest is forbidden to do, when whoever enters steps over a dead body, not over the soul that has departed from the body?

Or did he call the temporal life “soul,” a life that is indeed dead in the deceased body when that soul departs which cannot die—not because that life itself was the soul, but because it subsisted through the presence of the soul and received its name, just as we distinguished when we were speaking about blood, where it is said: “The soul of every flesh is its blood”? Blood itself is dead in a dead body, but it did not depart when the soul departed.

Therefore Scripture forbade the high priest even to enter over the funeral of his father or mother, a prohibition that it did not impose in the case of others. It follows:

He shall not defile himself for his father or his mother. The order of the words is: “He shall not defile himself for his father, nor for his mother.” And he shall not go out from the holy place, plainly at the time when the funerals of his relatives are being conducted, just as he was forbidden to leave the holy place during the seven days in which he was being consecrated. [Col. 0477D]

But this was not always so. Indeed, if high priests at that time were not forbidden to take wives or beget children, a serious question arises, since the Law declares a man unclean until evening even through marital intercourse, although he has washed his body with water; and the high priest was commanded, because of the continual offering of incense, to enter twice every day beyond the veil, where the altar of incense was. Since it was not lawful for anyone unclean to approach the holy things, how did the high priest fulfill this daily duty if he fathered children?

For if illness had befallen him, who would have acted in his place? If someone asks, it may be answered that, by God’s grace, he did not fall ill. But can the same answer be given concerning the begetting of children? [Col. 0478A] It follows, therefore, either that he was continent, or that the incense was omitted on certain days; or, if it could not be omitted—since it was necessary that it be offered only by the high priest—that he did not become unclean through marital intercourse, because of the excellence of his consecration. Or, if the statement made later concerning all the children of Israel also applies to him—that no one who had contracted any impurity should approach the holy things—we must accept as the explanation that on certain days the incense was not offered.

But since the high priest is forbidden to enter upon the funeral of his father, one may ask how he could already be high priest while his father was still alive, since the Law commands them to succeed their fathers. For this reason it was necessary, before the high priest had been buried, that another priest be appointed immediately, because of the continual incense, which had to be offered daily by the high priest. [Col. 0478B]

Nevertheless, the question concerning the high priest’s illness remains: whether he necessarily had to be ill for some days before dying, unless this too is resolved by saying that high priests usually died suddenly, without a preceding illness, as Scripture testifies concerning Aaron himself.

It should be observed how often God says, “I am the Lord who sanctifies him,” speaking of the priest, although he also said this to Moses: “And you shall sanctify him.” How, then, does Moses sanctify and the Lord sanctify? Moses does not act in place of the Lord. Rather, Moses sanctifies through visible sacraments by his ministry, while the Lord sanctifies through invisible grace by his Spirit, in which lies the whole efficacy even of the visible sacraments; for without this sanctification of invisible grace, the visible sacraments are of no benefit. [Col. 0478C]

It is rightly asked, however, whether this invisible sanctification itself is likewise of no benefit without the visible sacraments by which a person is visibly sanctified. That is certainly absurd. Someone would more tolerably say that this sanctification is not present without those sacraments than that, when it is present, it is of no benefit, since their entire usefulness consists in it. Yet we must also consider how it can rightly be said that this sanctification cannot exist without them. The visible baptism profited Simon Magus nothing, because invisible sanctification was absent from him. But those in whom this invisible sanctification was present and beneficial also received the visible sacraments, being baptized in the same way. [Col. 0478D]

Nor is it shown where Moses, who visibly sanctified the priests, was himself sanctified by those sacrifices or by the oil. But who would dare deny that he was sanctified invisibly, when such great grace excelled in him? The same may be said of John the Baptist. He baptized before he appeared to have been baptized; therefore no one can deny that he was sanctified, although we do not find this accomplished visibly in him before the ministry of baptizing came to him. [Col. 0479A]

The same may be said of the thief to whom the Lord, crucified with him, said: “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23). He was not granted such blessedness without invisible sanctification. It follows, therefore, that invisible sanctification was present and beneficial in some people without the visible sacraments, which have been changed according to the diversity of times, so that at one time they were one kind and now are another. But visible sanctification, which takes place through visible sacraments, can exist without this invisible sanctification, yet cannot be beneficial without it.

Nevertheless, the visible sacrament must not for that reason be despised, for one who despises it can in no way be sanctified invisibly.

This is why Cornelius and those who were with him, although they had already appeared to be sanctified by the invisible infusion of the Holy Spirit, were nevertheless baptized (Acts 10); nor was the visible sanctification considered superfluous, although invisible sanctification had already preceded it. [Col. 0479B]

**(From Hesychius.)** Who is the great priest among his brothers, except certainly the one of whom David said: “Great is the Lord, and great is his power, and of his wisdom there is no number” (Psalm 146)? For who can contemplate his power, count his wisdom, or comprehend it? Since he is God, yet through the dispensation of the deeds and mysteries performed for our sake he also became a priest.

He is therefore rightly called the great priest, since he offered himself for us as a victim and an offering. For this reason he also deigned to call his servants his brothers—that is, the saints, who always do his will. He says: “Whoever does the will of my Father, that one is my brother, sister, and mother” (Matthew 12). [Col. 0479C]

Upon his head the oil of anointing was poured. Concerning this it is said: “Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever; the scepter of uprightness is the scepter of your kingdom. You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Psalm 44). This agrees with the present law, not only because both passages mention anointing, but because, just as David declares him to surpass his companions in that very anointing, so too the legislator calls him greatest among his brothers—that is, superior to them.

What must especially be considered in the present history is that, although according to the Septuagint edition one might expect the text to say, “upon whose head the oil of anointing was poured,” it does not say this, but rather: “the greatest of his brothers, who poured upon his head.” Since it is Christ’s flesh that received the anointing of the divinity communicated to, or united with, him, and since through this flesh we have become his brothers and relatives, it is rightly said: “The high priest, that is, the greatest priest among his brothers, upon whose head the oil of anointing was poured,” so that what must be understood becomes clear: he is the greatest among his brothers, that is, among those of his flesh. [Col. 0479D]

It is this flesh that received the oil of the anointing of this priest. It is also clear that his hands were consecrated—or, according to the Septuagint, perfected—through the fastening of the cross. For then, just as those who are priests according to the Law perfected or consecrated their hands with the blood of a calf and a ram, so he consecrated or perfected his hands with his own blood. Concerning this Paul says: “Although he was a Son, he learned obedience through what he suffered; and, having been perfected, he became the cause of eternal salvation for all who obey him, having been named by God a high priest according to the order of Melchizedek” (Hebrews 5). And again: “For it was fitting that God, for whom and through whom all things exist, in bringing many sons to glory, should perfect the author of their salvation through suffering” (ibid.). [Col. 0480A]

He was also clothed in those garments of which David sang in the Psalms: “The Lord reigns; he is clothed with beauty. The Lord is clothed; he has girded himself with strength” (Psalm 92).

He shall not uncover his head, nor tear his garments. He did not uncover his head because he is not separated from his Father, who is called his head, even while he endured the sufferings of the flesh. Nor does he tear his garments, that is, his flesh. From the time when the Word became flesh, he has been wholly present in his flesh and has never severed himself from it—not from the flesh that was crucified, buried, or subjected to anything else belonging to our nature. [Col. 0480B]

If you wish to hear of his more exalted garments, listen to the prophetic words: “Clothed with light as with a garment; the abyss is as the garment of his covering” (Psalm 103).

**(From Adamantius.)** This is the attire of my great high priest, by which he is judged to be clothed in the profound light of knowledge and wisdom; these are truly holy garments. “He shall not remove,” it says, “the turban from his head.” We have already said that the *cydaris* is a kind of covering placed upon the priest’s head that gives it adornment.

My great high priest, therefore, never lays aside the adornment of his sacred head. But what is the head of Christ? Learn from the Apostle, who says: “The head of Christ is God” (Ephesians 5). [Col. 0480C] Rightly, therefore, does he never lay aside the adornment of his head, which is God, because the Father is always in the Son, just as the Son is always in the Father.

“And he shall not tear his garments.” Truly, he is the one who does not tear his garments, but has always preserved them clean, whole, and chaste.

It follows:

**(The same passage.)** “And he shall not enter at all upon any dead person; nor shall he defile himself for his father or mother.” But the Septuagint says: “He shall not enter upon any dead soul.”

**(From Hesychius.)** But how does the soul die, since it was created immortal? Hear the prophet saying: “The soul that sins, it shall die”—namely, by the death of ungodliness. This is the death of the soul that the nations especially have suffered, since they possessed neither the law of God nor any knowledge of him. [Col. 0480D]

He shall not enter upon a dead soul, or upon any dead person, because although he bore the sins of all, he nevertheless remains undefiled and is not polluted by the sins even of the nations. It is concerning these nations, according to the Septuagint—“every dead soul”—that the statement is made, since ungodliness and idolatry had been poured out against them all.

Nor shall he defile himself for father or mother—that is, for the Jewish people, from whom he is descended according to the flesh, and who are therefore called his father and mother. He shall not go out from the holy place; and although he chose to stoop to sinners, he nevertheless remains holy, rests among the holy, and is surrounded by the saints who are the angels in heaven.

**(From Adamantius.)** Every human being, therefore, is polluted in father and mother; but Jesus alone, my God, entered this generation clean and was not polluted in his mother. He entered an undefiled body, for he was the one who had earlier said through Solomon: “But, being good, I entered an undefiled body” (Wisdom 8). [Col. 0481A]

He was not polluted in his mother, nor in his father either. Joseph contributed nothing to his generation except the mystery and affection; therefore, for his faithful service, Scripture also granted him the title of father. For Mary herself says in the Gospel: “Behold, your father and I have been seeking you sorrowfully” (Luke 2).

This priest alone, therefore, was polluted neither in his father nor in his mother. But let us see whether we can still discover something more sublime and worthy of so great a high priest. God is called the true Father of all; the Apostle calls heavenly Jerusalem the mother. All who sin, therefore, are polluted in the Father, by whom they were created. Whether we have done something ungodly, spoken something ungodly, or thought something against God, when we did not believe God, we were polluted in the Father. Would that this had happened only through unbelief and had ceased once we believed! [Col. 0481B]

Thus we are also polluted in the mother if, while believing God, we harm the Church or defile the freedom of our heavenly mother with an unworthy slavery to sin. But our Lord Jesus Christ alone, who knew no sin, was polluted neither in the Father nor in the mother.

“And he shall not go out from the holy place.” Nor shall he pollute the sanctuary of the Lord, because the oil of the holy anointing of his God is upon him. [Col. 0481C]

**(From Hesychius.)** Therefore, even if you see him associating with tax collectors and prostitutes and saying to sinners, “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance” (Matthew 9), he will nevertheless not be polluted by any of these things, for he does not become a participant in their evil actions.

Thus he does not pollute the sanctuary of God, that is, the Holy Spirit. Concerning him it is said: “Because the oil of the holy anointing of his God is upon him.” He himself also agrees with the words of Isaiah concerning Christ: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me” (Isaiah 60).

Injury to and grieving of the Spirit is the defilement of every sin. Therefore Paul, teaching abstinence from sins, said: “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption” (Ephesians 4). [Col. 0481D]

Thus you understand both the preceding and the following concerning the great priest. For the legislator does not intend him, as the first priest, to be harsh and inaccessible, so that he approaches no dead person; nor does he wish to suggest to us that such great sanctification, with which the high priest is said to be clothed, would be polluted by seeing the dead.

“I am the Lord. He shall take a virgin as wife; he shall not take a widow, a divorced woman, a defiled woman, or a prostitute, but a maiden from his own people, so that he may not mix his offspring with the common people of his nation, because I am the Lord who sanctifies him.”

**(From Hesychius.)** He shows above all that he himself is the legislator and fulfiller of this decree. He necessarily added, “I am God.” What kind of virgin he is speaking of, he teaches in the words that follow: “He shall take a virgin as wife from his own people,” or, according to the Septuagint, “from his own kindred.” It is clear to everyone that, according to the flesh, the kindred of Christ is the whole human race. [Col. 0482A]

From this people he took a virgin wife, namely, the Church of those who believe in him. Concerning her Paul said: “I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ” (2 Corinthians 11).

“He shall not take a widow, a divorced woman, a defiled woman, or a prostitute.” We know that the Synagogue of the Jews is called a widow in the prophets. To it he said: “Cut off your hair and rejoice over your tender children” (Micah 1); “Enlarge your widowhood like an eagle.” Concerning the Jewish people, or Judas the betrayer—for their disgrace is shared—he also says: “Let his children be fatherless, and his wife a widow” (Psalm 108). [Col. 0482B]

We understand the divorced woman and the widow in accordance with what was said shortly before. The Synagogue was divorced from fellowship with God when it fornicated with idols. For this reason he does not permit himself to receive her in marriage, so that you may understand that he forbade the way of life existing in shadows and figures, and does not wish those who expect to cling to him through a good life and faith to share in it in any way.

Therefore, after saying once, “He shall take a virgin maiden from his people,” or “from his kindred,” he was not satisfied, but added that he would not take a widow, prostitute, or divorced woman. According to the Septuagint, “He shall take a virgin from his own kindred,” so that the first statement may be understood of the whole body of the Church, and the second of every individual soul. For just as there is a fellowship of the faithful, so each person’s soul is the bride of God and the Church. [Col. 0482C]

**(From Adamantius.)** If one of us sins, he is rejected, even if he is not rejected by the bishop—whether because this is permitted or because it is sometimes judged expedient for the sake of favor. Nevertheless, he is expelled by the very conscience of his sin, and human favor does not help, since Christ does not receive such a soul, as one rejected, into marriage.

Therefore he will receive neither a widow, as we said above, nor one who has been expelled, nor one who has been polluted. A person is called polluted who, even if he has not completed the sin in deed, is nevertheless polluted by the very fact that he has thought about it, willed it, or desired it, even if he did not commit it. The great high priest does not choose such a person, for he seeks a soul that is very pure, very clean, and sincere, to unite to himself: “Whoever is joined to the Lord is one spirit” (1 Corinthians 6). [Col. 0482D]

This also shows that there are different degrees of sin. Whoever commits a sin leading to death is rejected. Whoever does not sin unto death but commits some lesser offense is polluted. The bride of Christ, however, can be neither rejected nor polluted, but must be a virgin undefiled, incorrupt, and clean.

“He shall not take a prostitute.” What soul is a prostitute? The soul that receives lovers, concerning whom the prophet says: “You have played the prostitute after your lovers.” Who are these lovers who enter the prostituted soul, except hostile powers and demons, who desire its beauty?

For the soul was created beautiful by God, and very lovely. Hear how God himself says: “Let us make the human being according to our image and likeness” (Galatians 1, citation as printed). See what beauty and loveliness the soul possesses: it has the image and likeness of God. [Col. 0483A]

When the hostile powers—that is, the devil and his angels—look upon this beauty, they desire its appearance. Since they cannot become its bridegrooms, they wish to commit fornication with it. If, therefore, you receive the adulterous devil into the chamber of your soul, your soul has prostituted itself with the devil. If you receive his angels, or various spirits that persuade you to sin, your soul has prostituted itself with them.

If a spirit of anger, envy, pride, or impurity enters your soul, and you receive it, consent to what it says in your heart, and take pleasure in what it suggests to you according to its own mind, you have committed fornication with it. [Col. 0483B]

The great priest, therefore, will not take a prostitute and will not defile his seed among his people. What this seed is that he does not wish to be defiled is written in the Gospels: “The one who sows sows the word.” He does not wish the word of God to be defiled by those who sow.

Who are those who sow? Those who proclaim the word of God in the Church. From this seed of the word of God that is sown, Christ is born in the heart of the hearers. The Apostle also says this: “Until Christ is formed in you” (Galatians 4).

The soul, therefore, conceives from this seed of the word, and forms the conceived Word within itself until it gives birth to the spirit of the fear of God. Thus the souls of the saints say through the prophet: “From your fear, O Lord, we conceived in the womb, and were in labor and gave birth; we brought forth the spirit of your salvation upon the earth.” This is the birth of holy souls, this their conception, these the holy marriages that are fitting and suitable for the great high priest. [Col. 0483C]

**(From Hesychius.)** But why does he not wish the woman betrothed to him to share in Jewish conduct? He himself adds: “So that he may not mix the offspring of his kindred with the common people of his nation.” The Septuagint, however, says: “And he shall not profane his seed among his people.”

Therefore the profanation of the faithful consists in their associating with the Jewish manner of life of our priest. These are the seed and people of our priest. For this reason Paul said: “You are severed from Christ, you who are justified in the Law; you have fallen away from grace” (Galatians 5).

To these words he adds: “I am the Lord who sanctifies him.” That is, for this reason he has no need of the figures of the Law, sacrifices, or purifications, because I, the Lord, become sacrifice and purification in place of all these things. And whatever else you may say belongs to that sanctification. [Col. 0483D]

When he mentioned the widow, prostitute, and divorced woman, saying that he would not take them, we say that the legislator also spoke of the gatherings of heretics. They have been widowed from the knowledge of God, and for this reason have been expelled from the fellowship of the godly; they also fornicate through incongruous and impious doctrines.

Therefore he rightly placed the widow first, the divorced woman second, and the prostitute third. The Lord will take none of these into fellowship with himself, so that they may not defile the seed of the faithful, because evil conversations corrupt good morals.

## Chapter 17

A man of the seed of Aaron who has a blemish shall not offer the loaves to God. Also, the priest must beware of the things consecrated by the children of Israel. [Col. 0484A]

**(The same passage.)** And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “Speak to Aaron: Any man of your seed, throughout your families, who has a blemish shall not offer the loaves to his God, nor approach his ministry. If he is blind, or lame, or has a small, large, or crooked nose; if he has a broken foot or hand; if he is hunchbacked, bleary-eyed, has a white spot in his eye, a persistent skin disease, an eruption on his body, or is herniated: no man who has a blemish of the seed of Aaron the priest shall approach to offer sacrifices to the Lord, or the loaves to his God.

“Nevertheless, he may eat the loaves that are offered in the sanctuary, provided only that he does not enter within the veil or approach the altar, because he has a blemish and must not defile my sanctuary. I am the Lord who sanctifies you.” [Col. 0484B]

If we wish to understand this decree literally, how will the legislator’s intention appear just? For bodily blemishes do not happen to people by their own choice. How, then, is it not incongruous to exclude a priest from office for things that do not happen voluntarily?

What if someone, knowing this command of the Law and envying the priest, were to crush one of his limbs—a hand, foot, eye, or something else? Or what if, fighting against foreigners and for the holy things of God, while armed—for Moses commanded in Deuteronomy that priests should preside over wars—he received a wound that caused one of the blemishes listed above? Do you think he would therefore deserve to be removed from the priesthood? [Col. 0484C]

Bodily blemishes are so far from being abominable to God that David says: “The Lord gives sight to the blind” (Psalm 145). He did not choose beauty, a strong body, or a body that appeared well formed. Thus, when Samuel thought that God would be pleased by the appearance of Jesse’s older son, God said to him: “Do not look at his face or at the height of his stature, because I have rejected him” (1 Samuel 16). Yet the one being anointed was a king, not a priest.

Appearance and bodily stature were necessary for a king, but what did God add? “I do not judge according to human appearance. Human beings see what is visible, but God looks at the heart.” He searches the heart to see whether it has a blemish, and he judges those whose mind is without blemish to be chosen. But those who have a blemish in the soul he rejects. [Col. 0484D]

For if lameness of the feet or weak eyes is evil and separates a person from God, why did he permit Isaac and Jacob to grow dim in sight and lose the power of vision? Isaac did not recognize Jacob, who was pretending to be Esau. Concerning Jacob it is said: “The eyes of Israel had grown dim from extreme old age, and he could not see clearly.”

**(From Gregory.)** By bodily blemishes, therefore, he describes defects of the soul. It must be considered very carefully that when an elected bishop undertakes responsibility for the people, he approaches the sick person as a physician. If the passions of his own conduct are still alive in him, with what presumption does he hurry to heal the wounded when he carries the wound on his own face? [Col. 0485A]

The person who is to be drawn in every way toward being an example of life must be one who, dying to all the passions of the flesh, already lives spiritually; who has placed worldly prosperity behind him; who fears no adversity; who desires only inward things; whose purpose is well ordered; whose body neither rebels altogether through weakness nor rebels excessively through contempt; who is not led to desire what belongs to others but gives away what is his own; who is quickly moved to forgive by the compassion of mercy, yet, while forgiving, never bends away from the stronghold of righteousness more than is fitting; who does not perpetrate unlawful acts, but mourns those perpetrated by others as though they were his own; who, moved by affection of heart, sympathizes with another’s weakness; who rejoices in his neighbor’s virtues as in his own progress; who makes himself imitable to others in everything he does, so that inwardly he has nothing, even from his past, for which he must blush; who strives to live in such a way that he can irrigate the parched hearts of his neighbors with the streams of his teaching; and who, through the practice and experience of prayer, has learned that he can obtain from the Lord what he asks. [Col. 0485B]

For this reason bodily defects signify defects of character by a heavenly voice, when the Lord says to Moses:

“Speak to Aaron: Any man of your seed, throughout his families, who has a blemish shall not offer the loaves to his God, nor approach his ministry.” Then he immediately adds: “If he is blind, if he is lame, if he has a small or large or crooked nose; if he has a broken foot or hand; if he is hunchbacked, bleary-eyed, has a white spot in his eye; if he has a persistent skin disease, an eruption on his body, or is swollen.” [Col. 0485C]

The blind person is one who is ignorant of the light of heavenly contemplation. Pressed by the darkness of the present life, he cannot see the light to come because he does not love it, and therefore does not know where to direct the step of his actions. Hence Anna says through the prophet: “He will guard the feet of his saints, and the wicked will be silent in darkness” (1 Samuel 2).

The lame person is one who sees where he ought to go but, because of weakness of mind, cannot perfectly keep to the way of life that he has seen. A habit weakened by decline is not raised to the state of virtue, since the steps of action do not effectively follow the desire with which he leans toward it. Hence Paul says: “Raise up your slackened hands and weakened knees, and make straight paths for your feet, so that what is lame may not go astray, but rather be healed” (Isaiah 55, citation as printed). [Col. 0485D]

The person with a small nose is one who is not capable of maintaining the proper measure of discernment. We distinguish smells and stinks with the nose; therefore discernment is rightly expressed through the nose, since by discernment we choose virtues and reject sins. Hence it is said in praise of the bride: “Your nose is like the tower that is in Lebanon” (Song of Songs 7). For the holy Church sees through discernment what kinds of temptations arise from individual circumstances, and from lofty reflection detects the wars of vices that are to come.

But there are some who, unwilling to regard themselves as dull, often exercise themselves in certain investigations more than necessary and are deceived by excessive subtlety. Hence it is added here: “Or large and crooked in nose.” A large and crooked nose is an immoderate subtlety of discernment, which, when it grows beyond what is proper, itself confounds the uprightness of its action. [Col. 0486A]

The person with a broken foot or hand is one who is altogether unable to proceed along God’s way and remains wholly deprived of good actions, so that he does not merely hold to them lamely despite weakness, but is altogether alienated from them.

The hunchback is one whom the burden of earthly concern presses down, so that he never looks toward heavenly things but attends only to what is trodden underfoot. Even if he sometimes hears something about the good of the heavenly homeland, he cannot raise the face of his heart toward it, weighed down by the mass of perverse habit, because he cannot raise the state of his thoughts; earthly habits of concern keep him bent over.

Concerning people of this kind the Psalmist says: “I have been bent down and humbled exceedingly” (Psalm 118). Truth itself also condemns their fault, saying: “The seed that fell among thorns—these are the ones who hear, but as they go on their way they are choked by the cares, riches, and pleasures of life, and they bear no fruit” (Matthew 13). [Col. 0486B]

The bleary-eyed person is one whose natural intelligence flashes toward knowledge of the truth, but whose carnal works nevertheless obscure it. In bleary eyes the pupils are healthy, but as fluid flows down, the eyelids become diseased and swollen; because they are repeatedly rubbed by the discharge, the sharpness of the pupils is also impaired. [Col. 0486C]

There are some whose understanding is wounded by the activity of carnal life. They could see what is right with subtle intelligence, but through bad practice they grow dim in their actions. The bleary-eyed person, therefore, is one whose nature sharpens his understanding, but whose corrupt way of life confounds it.

To such a person the angel rightly says: “Anoint your eyes with salve, so that you may see” (Revelation 3). We anoint our eyes with salve so that we may see when, in order to recognize the brightness of the true light, we assist the sharpness of our understanding with the medicine of good works.

The person who has a white spot in the eye is one who is prevented from seeing the light of truth because he is blinded by arrogance concerning wisdom or righteousness. The pupil of the eye, being black, sees; when covered by a white spot, it sees nothing. Likewise, when the understanding of human thought recognizes itself as foolish and sinful, it grasps knowledge of inward brightness. [Col. 0486D]

But if it attributes to itself the whiteness of righteousness or wisdom, it excludes itself from the light of heavenly knowledge. It cannot penetrate the brightness of the true light precisely because it exalts itself arrogantly in its own eyes, as it is said of certain people: “Claiming to be wise, they became fools” (Romans 1).

The person who has a persistent skin disease is one over whom the wantonness of the flesh exercises uninterrupted dominion in the mind. In a skin disease, the heat of the inward organs is drawn toward the skin, by which lust is rightly signified. For if temptation of the heart leaps into action, the inward heat bursts outward into the irritation of the skin and now wounds the body externally; while pleasure is not restrained in thought, it also rules in action. [Col. 0487A]

Paul seemed to be treating the itch of the skin when he said: “Let no temptation seize you except what is human” (1 Corinthians 10). It is as though he were saying openly: It is human to endure temptation in the heart, but it is demonic to be overcome by the contest of temptation in action as well.

Whoever is ravaged in mind by greed also has an eruption on his body. If greed is not restrained in small matters, it expands without measure. An eruption occupies the body without pain, and, growing without causing annoyance to the one afflicted, disfigures the beauty of the limbs. [Col. 0487B]

So greed, while it seems to delight the mind it has captured, ulcerates it; while it places before thought whatever is to be acquired, it inflames the mind toward hostility. It causes no pain in the wound because it promises abundance to the heated mind as a result of its fault.

The beauty of the limbs is lost through the eruption because the beauty of other virtues is also distorted by it. It roughens the whole body, as it were, because it undermines the soul through every vice, as Paul attests when he says: “The love of money is the root of all evils” (1 Timothy 6).

The swollen person is one who does not practice disgraceful conduct in action, yet is continually and immoderately burdened by such thoughts in the mind. He is not actually dragged into wicked deeds, but his mind takes pleasure in lust without any obstacle of resistance.

This is the defect of swelling, when the fluid of the inward organs flows into the powers and these swell with the distress of disgrace. The swollen person, therefore, is one who, letting all his thoughts flow toward wantonness, carries the weight of disgrace in his heart. Although he does not perform wicked actions, he is not torn away from them in the contemplation of his mind, nor can he rise openly to the practice of good works, because a shameful weight burdens him in secret. [Col. 0487C]

**(From Hesychius.)** Whoever, therefore, is subjected to any one of these vices is forbidden to offer loaves to the Lord, lest one who is still ravaged by his own sins be unable to cleanse the sins of others. The priest must be without blemish in conduct and mind, just as Moses commanded him to be clean from twelve blemishes; for you will find that twelve are counted according to the Septuagint.

Paul likewise commanded that twelve qualities be preserved in the person who is to receive the priesthood, saying: “A bishop must be blameless, as God’s steward” (1 Timothy 6). And who is blameless except the undefiled?

He then shows in what way one is gathered to be blameless—by being free from what kinds of blemishes or passions—in the following words: “Not arrogant, not irritable, not addicted to wine, not violent, not greedy for dishonorable gain, but hospitable, kind, chaste, just, holy, self-controlled, holding fast to the trustworthy word that accords with the teaching.” [Col. 0487D]

He too wishes the priest to preserve twelve qualities. And why does he impose so many upon him? He said earlier: “A bishop must be blameless, as God’s steward.” Whoever administers the things of God must surpass those over whom he is steward in virtues. For how will he be able to administer or arrange those things for them?

Since the legislator commanded that anyone possessing one of the aforementioned blemishes might eat from the holy things, but might not enter within the veil or approach the altar—that is, the body of Christ—it may perhaps be found that this too is observed in the churches. [Col. 0488A]

For if it is established that a priest once had a blemish of the soul but has ceased from it, he is not forbidden to share in the holy things. But it is not lawful for such a person to minister, or to approach the veil and the altar—that is, the body of the Lord—in order to perform its ministry.

Paul, writing to the Hebrews, taught what this veil and altar are: “We have an altar from which those who serve the tabernacle have no authority to eat,” namely, the body of the Lord. The Jews, because of their unbelief and slavery to the letter, are not permitted to use this.

Learn from the same Apostle that this is called the veil: “Therefore, having confidence for entering the holy places through the veil, that is, his flesh” (Hebrews 10). [Col. 0488B]

Only for this reason does the person who has a blemish of the soul not enter. Why? Because he has a blemish and must not defile my sanctuary. For it is a defilement and an insult to the holy things when such people are offered for ministry—people who offend the faithful and whose blemishes scandalize those who know them.

For this reason Paul also wants a priest to have “a good testimony from those outside” (Colossians 4).

The Law confirmed what has been said when it declared: “I am the Lord who sanctifies you.” I—who? The one who commands and orders: “Be perfect, just as your heavenly Father is perfect.” For whoever has even one of the aforementioned blemishes is not perfect.

[Col. 0488C] Moses therefore spoke to Aaron and to his sons and to all Israel everything that had been commanded him (Chap. XXI). What are these things that he spoke? Namely, those stated above, which God indeed spoke to Moses. Moses, however, delivered them to Aaron, his sons, and the people, as the things now read demonstrate—not without reason does the Law distinguish these matters. Rather, Moses wished to commend and openly demonstrate his dignity: God spoke only a few things to others, but everything to him, because of his righteousness and the image of Christ that he bore. Likewise, he teaches us to attend to whatever those superior to us in rank and perfection may say, knowing that they continually enjoy heavenly activity.

And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: [Col. 0488D] Speak to Aaron and his sons, so that they may beware of the consecrated things of the children of Israel and not profane the name of those sanctified for me, which they themselves offer; I am the Lord. Say to them and to their descendants: Any man of your lineage who approaches the consecrated things that the children of Israel offer to the Lord, while he has some impurity, shall perish before the Lord. I am the Lord (Chap. XXII).

[From Augustine.] Every doubt has been removed: no priest, whether of the highest or of the secondary ranks, ought to have approached the holy things if he had impurity in himself. It followed, therefore, that the priest should practice continence, lest, because of the procreation of children, the continual incense—which only the high priests used to offer twice a day, morning and evening—should not be imposed on certain days; for after marital intercourse he was unclean, even after washing his whole body, until evening, and he was the one by whom it had necessarily to be offered. When he says “which the children of Israel sanctify,” this is to be understood as referring to what they offer to the priests to be offered by them to the Lord. But one should note the kind of sanctification that occurs through the vow and devotion of the one who offers. Yet whether, just as the things offered by human beings are sanctified in this way, human beings themselves are likewise said to sanctify themselves when they vow themselves for some undertaking.

[From Hesychius.] It must be observed in Scripture that the dignity of the priesthood is no ordinary dignity. To him, by lot, it has been granted to be mediator between God and human beings, and through him our race is reconciled to its Creator. In the tongue of priests consists the binding and loosing of our sins. Malachi shows how great the dignity of the priest is and what ought to be expected from him: “For the lips of the priest,” he says, “guard knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Mal. II).

Therefore, in addition to what was previously decreed concerning priests, he also commanded this: “Let them beware of the consecrated things of the children of Israel, and let them not profane the name of those sanctified for me, which they themselves offer.” But if such men, abominably and disorderly, and outside all religious reverence, profane the name of the sanctified things through the people’s offerings and through whatever things are sanctified and offered in any manner—or, according to the Septuagint, “the holy name of God”—then, first, they will cause the one who chose such men to be blasphemed. [Col. 0489C] Then they also compel the people to stumble over holy things and to think that the ministry, righteousness, and judgment of God are superfluous.

How greatly God becomes angry when a priest or his sons—that is, his disciples—sin against holy things is shown by what happened to Eli and his sons. Therefore he added: “I am the Lord.” You shall say to them: “I am the Lord”—that is, the one who becomes angry and exacts vengeance. But what did he say? “You shall say to them and to their descendants: Anyone of your lineage who approaches the consecrated things that the children of Israel offer to the Lord, while he has some impurity, shall perish before the Lord. I am the Lord.”

First, by mentioning the priestly lineage, he clearly signified that he commands not only the priest, but every minister of holy things—even if he has the lowest and most subordinate rank among them—to observe the present decree. In saying “of your lineage,” he showed that this precept must always be observed, by anyone who has the impurity of the soul within himself. For the Septuagint renders it thus: “Let him abstain not only from the ministry and mystical office, but let him neither touch the things that have been offered nor take anything from them.” The clean person must approach clean things. But if someone does not approach in this manner, he shall perish before the Lord; God will always turn away from him, repel him from every participation and communion of the Spirit. This turning away is what is specifically understood here by “perish before the Lord,” as the Septuagint says.

David bears witness, saying: “Do not turn your face away from me, and do not take your Holy Spirit from me” (Ps. L). In these words there is the true destruction, or extermination, of the soul—that is, the destruction of which the Lord said in the Gospels: “Fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna.” Therefore he did not add “I am the Lord” without reason; rather, he showed that the one who says these things is himself the only one who can destroy the soul.

CHAPTER XVIII. A leper or one suffering from a discharge of semen, of the lineage of Aaron, shall not eat of the consecrated things.

(CHAP. XXII.) A man of the seed of Aaron who is a leper or suffers from a discharge of semen shall not eat of the things consecrated to me until he is healed. Whoever touches an unclean thing upon a dead body, or from whom semen goes out as in intercourse, and whoever touches a creeping thing or any unclean thing whose touch is filthy, shall be unclean until evening and shall not eat of the things consecrated; but when he has washed his flesh with water and the sun has set, then, being clean, he shall eat of the consecrated things, because they are his food. They shall not eat an animal that has died of itself or one captured by a beast, and they shall not be defiled by them. I am the Lord.

[From Hesychius.] He does not wish polluted persons to eat holy things until they are cleansed, but neither does he wholly exclude them by abstinence. Therefore he lists here the one who has been polluted by any one of these things as being unclean until evening, saying: “He shall not eat of the things consecrated, but when he has washed his flesh with water and the sun has set.” By evening and the setting of the sun he indicates repentance; by the water with which he washes himself, tears, of which David said: “Every night I wash my bed; I water my couch with my tears” (Ps. VI). He likewise signified evening to us as repentance and the joy arising from it, saying: “At evening weeping shall remain, and at morning joy” (Ps. XXIX).

When, therefore, someone has been cleansed by the tears of repentance, then he shall eat the holy things, because that is his bread, of which the Lord said in the Gospels: “And the bread that I will give is my flesh” (John VI). Now, recalling bread and distinguishing who ought to eat it, he added: “They shall not eat an animal that has died of itself or one captured by a beast, nor shall they be defiled by them; I am the Lord.” Thus, when you hear the words “I am the Lord,” understand that he is saying: “I am the bread that came down from heaven.”

By prohibiting animals that died of themselves and those captured by beasts, he commanded that one must not participate in the Lord’s table and the table of demons. For in these there are truly animals that have died of themselves and animals captured by beasts. What we have frequently said concerning this decree must also be said now, for it benefits the hearers: the legislator does not abominate lepers and those suffering from a discharge of semen in the physical sense. They endure this condition unwillingly and not by choice. Rather, he refers to those who have a leprous soul or suffer a discharge of semen when he says that “a leper and one suffering from a discharge of semen shall not eat until he is healed.” Interpreting how this should be understood, he added: “Whoever touches an unclean thing upon a dead body”—or, according to the Septuagint, “every uncleanness of the soul.”

The uncleanness of the soul is sins, some of which are leprous and some of which suffer a discharge of semen, as we have demonstrated in what was said by us concerning lepers and those suffering from a discharge of semen. And again, when he says: “And from whom semen goes out as in intercourse, and whoever touches a creeping thing and any unclean thing whose touch is filthy,” he makes the meaning of this clear to you. It is especially useful and helpful for understanding this commandment to recognize that he does not wish only priests, but all ministers, to presume to receive holy things without fear. One must contemplate the distinction handed down by the Law, which commands penitents to approach holy things but prohibits them before repentance.

Since you have learned that the priests who are of the seed of Aaron are our priest, Christ, and that Aaron bears his figure, you will understand without any doubt that those who have the adoption of baptism are meant, as well as the seed of his kindred and everything that may rightly be called related to him. Hence they are called an elect race, a royal priesthood, and a holy nation because of their kinship with him.

To them he says what follows: “They shall observe my precepts, so that they may not fall under sin and die in the sanctuary when they have profaned it; I am the Lord who sanctifies them.” Therefore the precepts of the Lord—that is, the Law—require strict observance and untransgressible obedience. Just as they become the cause of sanctification, justification, and salvation for those who fulfill them, so they become the cause of sin and death for those who transgress them. This is true in every law and every commandment, but especially in the reception of holy things. Whoever approaches them in a manner other than is proper takes judgment and death upon himself.

Paul also wrote concerning such people among the Corinthians: “For whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself, not discerning the body of the Lord; therefore many among you are weak and sick, and many sleep” (1 Cor. XI)—that is, they die. In accordance with this saying, therefore, the legislator enacted: “They shall observe my precepts, so that they may not fall under sin and die through them.” And what is the cause that brings death? “When he has profaned it.” For it is an insult to and profanation of the sanctuary for anyone filthy to approach clean things.

“I am the Lord who sanctifies them”—that is, I receive into communion with holy things only sinners who have been cleansed, but I turn away when they remain polluted and unrighteous.

No foreigner shall eat of the consecrated things; a resident of a priest and a hired servant shall not eat them. This commandment is necessary, lest we suppose that the spiritual table is available equally to all the faithful and the impious, or think that, because the mystery of the bread of life is called the Lord’s, even those who are still alienated from the faith ought to receive it.

All who do not accept the law of God and do not become participants in evangelical grace are therefore foreigners. They can understand nothing that is akin or related to God, nor anything related to knowledge of him. Hence they are called foreigners, like those who are led astray by demons and embrace kinship with them. Such people are rightly called alienated both from us and from God. Concerning them David sang: “Rescue me and deliver me from the hand of foreign children” (Ps. CXLIII).

A resident of the priest is one who does not enter his court with pure intent, nor show him the reverence or diligence that is due. Just as a resident acts solely for his own benefit and awaits his departure each day, not caring whether some people plunder or steal the rights of the household, so are those who minister in the divine court for their own advantages—perhaps for glory, monetary gain, or some other such reason—but do not show diligence lest any of them corrupt the order or use the divine courts badly and unjustly.

We say the same concerning hired servants, of whom the Lord says: “The hired servant, who is not the shepherd, whose sheep are not his own, sees the wolf coming, abandons the sheep, and flees; and the wolf seizes the sheep and scatters them. The hired servant flees because he is a hired servant, and he has no concern for the sheep” (John X). He rightly prohibits such people from receiving holy things, for they are not worthy to participate in what they do either negligently or for some advantage.

But the person whom the priest has purchased, and the native-born servant of his household, shall eat of them. Having prohibited foreigners—namely, the impious and unbelieving—from participating in divine things, he shows that if they change from their error and approach Christ, he permits them to receive the holy things. No one is foreign by nature; rather, some have taken alienation from God upon themselves by their will.

Therefore, all those whom the intelligible priest possesses as purchased servants—that is, all whom he purchases through evangelical teaching and grace—for this is the Lord’s acquisition, and true silver is “silver tested by fire, purified from the earth”—he has redeemed, namely those who wish to serve him. No others, as Peter said: “You were bought with a price; do not become slaves of human beings.” His native-born servants, that is, those nourished in his faith and brought up in the intelligible house of Christ, namely the Church, through the faith of their parents, shall eat of his mystical and life-giving breads.

It follows: If the priest’s daughter is married to anyone from the people, she shall not eat of the consecrated things or of the firstfruits. But if she has become a widow or has been divorced without children and returns to her father’s house, she shall be nourished by her father’s food, as she was accustomed when she was a girl. No foreigner has the authority to eat of them.

What our translation has—“If the priest’s daughter is married to anyone from the people, to a foreign man”—teaches us that it is not sufficient for us merely to be nourished in the faith of Christ. We must also remain and grow in it, and we must not unite ourselves to any foreigners—that is, to anything belonging to another doctrine from God, another law, or another way of life. Nor, because we come from faithful fathers, should we presume to partake of holy things unless we ourselves also remain faithful.

Therefore the daughter of the intelligible priest means every soul regenerated by him through baptism. If she is joined to a foreigner—that is, if she acts in ways belonging to foreigners, such as Jews, pagans, or heretics, and embraces their fellowship—she shall not eat of the firstfruits of the consecrated things, that is, of the mystical body.

[Col. 0493A] But if she has become the priest’s daughter through the regeneration mentioned above, has been joined to a foreigner by practicing something heretical, Jewish, or pagan, and then becomes a widow or is divorced—abandoning and, in a manner, burying her error completely, and freeing herself from the unrighteous union—and returns to her paternal house, that is, the Church, and is nourished according to the youth in which she once burned with the sacred doctrines of the faith, becoming young again through the virtues and being called a womanly champion by them, of whom the Spirit of God said to Christ in the Song of Songs, “Your name is oil poured out; therefore the young women loved you” (Song I)—let her eat of her father’s breads, that is, of Christ’s. For if each of us has the Church as mother and Christ as father—

[Col. 0493B] “No foreigner has the authority to eat of them,” that is, one who acts in ways foreign to Christ, his laws, and his glory. For his law is: “You shall not give what is holy to dogs, nor throw your pearls before pigs” (Matt. VII).

It follows:

Whoever eats of the consecrated things through ignorance shall add a fifth part to what he has eaten and shall give it to the priest for the sanctuary; and they shall not profane the consecrated things of the children of Israel that they offer to the Lord, lest they bear the iniquity of their offense when they have eaten the consecrated things. I am the Lord who sanctifies them.

The holy of holies are properly the mysteries of Christ, because they are his body, concerning which Gabriel said to the Virgin: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the holy one who will be born from you shall be called the Son of God” (Luke I). Isaiah also says: “The Lord is holy, and he dwells on high” [Alternative: “His holy name is on high”] (Isa. LVII), namely, in the bosom of the Father. For he prohibited from the sacrifice not only foreigners, residents, and hired servants, but also commanded that no one receive it through ignorance.

He receives it through ignorance who is ignorant of its power and dignity, who does not know that this is truly the body and blood, but receives the mysteries without knowing the power of the mysteries. To him Solomon—or rather, the Spirit who is in him—says: “When you sit to eat with a ruler, carefully attend to what is set before you” (Prov. XXIII).

He himself openly compels and urges the ignorant person to add a fifth part. For this added fifth enables us intellectually to understand divine and mystical things. What this fifth is, the legislator’s own words can teach you. For he says: “He shall add a fifth part to what he has eaten.” And how can anyone add a fifth part of something he has already eaten and consumed? It is not something else or something from elsewhere, but from the very thing itself and together with it; or, as the Septuagint says, he commands that a fifth be added “upon it.”

Therefore, the fifth part added upon it is the word spoken by Christ himself concerning the Lord’s mystery. For he liberates us from ignorance and removes from us the notion that we should regard something carnal or earthly as belonging to the holy things; rather, he decrees that we understand them divinely and spiritually. This is properly called the fifth, because the divine Spirit within us and the word he has delivered bring together the five senses within us.

He does not merely lead our taste toward the mystery, but also our hearing, sight, touch, and smell, so that we suspect nothing in these matters that is of lesser reason or close to a feeble mind, in things that are exceedingly heavenly.

Whoever, therefore, eats the consecrated things through ignorance, being ignorant of their power as we have said, shall add the fifth part of them upon or together with them and shall give it to the priest for the sanctuary. For the sanctification of the mystical sacrifice, and its translation or transformation from sensible things to intelligible things, must be given to the one who is the true priest, namely Christ. That is, the wonder of these things must be attributed and ascribed to him, because through his power and the word spoken by him, they are seen to be consecrated and to exceed the whole sense of the flesh.

Rightly, therefore, he added: “They shall not profane the consecrated things of the children of Israel that they offer to the Lord, lest they bear the iniquity of their offense when they have eaten the consecrated things.” For those who attribute to Christ the sanctification of their ministries, and add to themselves the fifth that has been spoken—namely, his word, which leads our senses toward higher things—do not profane the holy of holies, since they understand what such things ought to mean. Nor do they bring upon themselves the iniquity of an offense by eating the holy of holies. They do not approach as though to ordinary food, but as to something mystical, fearful, and heavenly. Those who approach it rashly are said not merely to sin, but to bear the iniquity of their offense.

An offense is properly called by the legislator a sin committed against God, and we previously demonstrated the matters relating to this in the sacrifices offered for offenses. Hence now, when he had said, “Lest they bear the iniquity of their offense,” he rightly added: “I am the Lord who sanctifies them.” By this he showed that an offense—that is, impiety toward God—is the name given to an unworthy reception of holy things, for it is directed against God who sanctifies.

CHAPTER XIX. The victims offered to the Lord, in order to be acceptable, shall be without blemish.

(IBID.) The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to Aaron and his sons and to all the children [Col. 0494D] of Israel, and say to them: Anyone from the house of Israel or from the resident foreigners who dwell among you who offers his offering, whether in fulfillment of a vow or as a voluntary offering—whatever he offers as a burnt offering to the Lord, to be offered through you—shall be a flawless male from the cattle, the sheep, or the goats. If it has a blemish, you shall not offer it, and it shall not be acceptable. Anyone who offers a sacrifice of peace offerings to the Lord, whether in fulfillment of a vow or as a voluntary offering, shall offer an unblemished animal, whether from the cattle or the sheep, so that it may be acceptable; no blemish shall be in it.

[From Hesychius.] He commands not only that priests be clean from pollution, but also that the offerings presented by the people be clean. Thus you may understand, as one who is faithful to God and has become an offering to him through the intelligible sacrifice of a burnt offering, that your conduct must be clean and undefiled from every pollution. You should strive to be like the priests, because Christ also commanded them to teach all these things to the nations who were learning what the apostles had been commanded to do. For he said: “Go and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe everything that I have commanded you” (Matt. XXVIII).

Whether, therefore, one who has promised a burnt offering to God according to his confession, or according to the whole condition of his life—that is, a perfect life, which is the true burnt offering—his offering must be clean from pollution, for otherwise it will not be accepted. According to the Septuagint, the one who offers by confession is one who, placed in some affliction and pierced by it, promises God a certain way of life by a vow.

According to the edition mentioned above, however, we find “choice” where our version says “voluntary.” The Psalmist sets forth both kinds of offering, whether the one made from necessity or the one made voluntarily, saying: “I will pay my vows to you, which my lips have distinguished, and which my mouth spoke in my affliction.” And again: “Accept the freewill offerings of my mouth, O Lord” (Ps. XCV).

We understand the first of these without any doubt as the vow or confession mentioned above; the choice or voluntary offering is what was said in the second place. Whether, then, the one who offers the burnt offering is a doer of the commandment—for this is the one who offers from the herd—or simple—for this is the one who offers from the sheep—or from the flock—for this is the one who offers from the goats—the offering must be male, that is, it must be presented with a manly, courageous, and steadfast mind and with strong and unwavering faith, so that the one who offers may be like the man whom Solomon said in Proverbs: “It is difficult to find a faithful man” (Prov. XX).

The same applies if someone offers a sacrifice of peace offerings: that is, not the life that is perfect in philosophy, such as the life of renunciation of possessions or virginity, concerning which the Lord said, “Not all accept this word” (Matt. XIX), but the moderate life that procures salvation for us in every way, even if it does not attain what leads to the measure of the prophets and apostles. “For star differs from star in glory,” as Paul said (1 Cor. XV). Even in this case he must offer a male without blemish.

The children of Israel and the resident foreigners—that is, those who have now come to the faith and have been added to us from external error—must likewise observe these things. Once someone has promised God a perfect and complete life, he can no longer claim that he spent a long time in error, because virtue does not require time in order to be learned: as soon as we have desired it, we learn how to practice it.

Nevertheless, if you offer a physical sheep, an ox, a goat, or something of this kind to God—for example, so that firstfruits may be given to priests, or so that the poor may be fed by it, or so that some service may be rendered to the holy, or so that the divine temple may be built, or for any other work that pertains to God himself—then, because it is called a burnt offering, this offering too must be free from pollution.

But what this pollution is, the Law has left unstated, giving us to understand and avoid true pollution. It is offering from robbery, injustice, or any other greed. For such an offering is abominable to God and unacceptable to him.

It follows:

If it is blind, broken, scarred, covered with papules, scabies, or a skin disease, you shall not offer it to the Lord, nor shall you burn any of it upon the altar of the Lord. An ox or sheep whose ear or tail has been cut off may be offered voluntarily, but a vow may not be fulfilled with such an animal. Any animal whose testicles are bruised, shorn, cut, or removed you shall not offer to the Lord, and you shall not do this at all in your land. You shall not offer bread to the Lord your God from the hand of a foreigner, nor anything else they may wish to give, because all such things are corrupt and blemished; you shall not accept them.

[From the same author.] Here the legislator appears to intimate something worthy of much consideration. His subject now is the things offered upon the altar. There are people who are entrusted with the mystical ministry and with holy service. In the preceding decree he commanded that the offering of the people be clean from pollution—a matter that must necessarily be understood in each person’s conduct. Now he enumerates those whom it is not appropriate to offer upon the altar.

First among these he names the blind. How will one who has ignorance of God minister to God? He is neither called to the ministry, knowing its dignity, nor able to explain it to others. Hence he will also be negligent toward them, since he does not know the power of the divine things in which he ministers. Such were certain Jews, concerning whom God said through Isaiah: “Behold, they all lack knowledge; they are all mute dogs, unable to bark” (Isa. LVI).

He placed “broken” or “crushed” second. If someone’s hands or feet—that is, his actions and his paths toward God—are broken or crushed, he too is not worthy to minister at the altar. To him applies what the Psalmist says: “Destruction and misery are in their ways” (Ps. XIII).

Nor is one who has a cut tongue, according to the Septuagint, worthy: that is, someone who has lost the confidence to teach through a filthy life. To him David says: “But to the sinner God said: Why do you recount my righteousness?” (Ps. XLVIII).

One covered with papules or scabies signifies a slanderer, because his disease is most evil and his wound exceedingly harsh. It cannot easily be soothed by any medicine.

One who has a skin disease is a fornicator, for he stains his own body. Therefore Paul said: “The one who commits fornication sins against his own body” (1 Cor. VI).

The legislator’s spirit therefore wishes none of these to be appointed to the ministry of the altar, and for this reason he says: “You shall not offer them to the Lord, nor shall you burn any of them upon the altar of the Lord.” Or, according to the Septuagint: “They shall not offer these to the Lord, and none of them shall be placed upon the altar of the Lord.”

He does not add the sacrifice of peace offerings, as he did above, so that you may understand in every way that he is speaking about those who minister in the mysteries. These too must be a burnt offering, conducting a perfect and complete life.

What did he add to these instructions? [Col. 0497A] “An ox or sheep whose ear or tail has been cut off may be offered voluntarily, but a vow may not be fulfilled with such an animal. Any animal whose testicles are bruised, shorn, cut, or removed you shall not offer to the Lord.”

He employed great precision and a discipline befitting the legislator in making this distinction, and it must also be observed in the matters above. The person with a cut-off ear is one who languishes from the disease of disobedience, delights in slander, takes pleasure in shameful things heard, and rejects good words.

The person with a cut-off tail is one who does not think about the last things, because the tail is the extremity of the body. Those with a cut-off tail are therefore properly those who regard the last things—things that are remote, lowly, and least—as worthless; who store up nothing for themselves in the future ages; who make no provision for the future; who say: “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die” (Isa. XXII).

The person with crushed testicles is one who, as malice gradually grows, crushes the offspring of his virtues and the signs by which a man can be recognized. He is rightly rejected, because in such matters he has harmed himself.

The person with shorn testicles is one who has yielded to temptations and tribulations brought upon him and has lost—or, alternatively, betrayed—the strength of his soul. He must not suffer this, nor yield altogether to the enemy who threatens and afflicts him.

The person with cut-off and removed testicles is one who, through a single wicked and exceedingly impious action—standing like a knife and cutting away, like a savage and plundering hand—has cut himself off and removed himself from union with God, which consists in the virtues. As we have said, he has been deprived of offspring; the following phrase is textually uncertain: “and if anyone has subjected himself to certain [things] of manly understanding.”

One person is gradually crushed, while another suddenly deprives himself of the offspring of the virtues through a single evil action, like Simon, who thought that he could purchase the gift of God with money and consequently became alienated from his lot.

But anyone who has even one of these blemishes just mentioned, or one of those previously enumerated, is not a doer of the commandments. Therefore the calf, as simple, and the sheep are so called; according to the Septuagint, where our translation reads “may be offered voluntarily,” it reads: “You shall slaughter them for yourself,” so that we may not wholly reject them or count them among the enemy, but teach and exhort them: “Will not the one who falls rise again?” (Ps. XL), “or will the one who has turned away not return?” They are said to be slaughtered because they are put to death with respect to sin through admonition, so that they may live for righteousness.

These slaughters are performed for us. We may associate with them, but we must not offer them to God as a vow; that is, we must not appoint them to his mystical ministry.

Therefore, if those who have any of the aforesaid blemishes repent concerning them and are slaughtered through the putting to death of sin, let us indeed receive them and regard them as members of the common body, because Christ came into this world to save sinners (1 Tim. I). But it is not permitted to offer them upon the altar.

Paul, I think, used this distinction when writing to the Corinthians: “I wrote to you in the letter not to associate with fornicators—not, of course, with the fornicators of this world, or the greedy, or the rapacious, or those who serve idols; otherwise you would have had to leave this world. But now I wrote to you not to associate if anyone who is called a brother is a fornicator, or serves idols, or is greedy, or is a slanderer, or is a drunkard, or is rapacious; with such a person do not even eat” (1 Cor. V).

There he calls them brothers who minister at the altar, because this applies especially to those who have received the dignity of teaching and to whom the governance of peoples has been entrusted.

If such people possess any of these traits, their fellowship must be rejected in every way, because those who preside over the people must abound in virtues above the people and must themselves be especially without blemish. For how can they cleanse others from pollution?

Concerning such people the legislator also gave these commands.

“And you shall certainly not do this in your land, nor shall you offer bread to the Lord your God from the hand of a foreigner, nor anything else they may wish to give, because all such things are corrupt and blemished; you shall not accept them.”

Therefore, let us not devote ourselves in our own land to any of these blemishes. Our land is good conduct, which has been commanded through the divine Scriptures and which we have received from God to cultivate.

Nor should we participate when a foreigner—that is, one who has been instructed and brought in from outside—offers such gifts, because there is corruption in them, while we serve the incorruptible God. They have a blemish, whereas we minister in the Church, to which the Bridegroom said: “You are altogether beautiful, my nearest one, and there is no blemish in you” (Song IV). Concerning her Paul said: “That he might present the Church to himself in glory, having no blemish or wrinkle or anything of this kind” (Eph. V). Therefore nothing possessing a blemish is offered by us.

CHAPTER XX. An ox, sheep, and goat shall remain with their mother for seven days after birth; they may be offered on the eighth day, and victims offered in thanksgiving must be eaten on that same day, etc.

[Same place.] And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “When an ox, a sheep, or a goat has been born, it shall remain for seven days at its mother’s breast; but on the eighth day and thereafter it may be offered to the Lord. Whether it is an ox or a sheep, it shall not be slaughtered on the same day as its young.”

Every animal’s mother is, of course, nature; under her every kind of human being, both sinners and righteous, is for seven days, but from the eighth onward no longer. For even if someone is a doer of the commandments—whether simple, sinful, or descended from a sinner—during the seven days, that is, throughout the whole present age, he must endure whatever nature demands, just as Paul dared to say concerning the Savior, showing that, having been made according to our nature in the flesh without sin, he endured everything that belonged to nature. Since the children shared in blood and flesh, he likewise shared in the same things.

But when we have departed from the present life and have been established in the blessed day of the resurrection of the dead, from that time onward, throughout the whole future age, we shall no longer be under the mother who has been mentioned. For we shall no longer be subject to these natural necessities: “On the eighth day it may be offered.”

The Septuagint renders this as follows: “But gifts and sacrifices to the Lord”—that is, those who have prepared their offering perfectly and completely in this life. It must be understood, however, that because our life is changeable and admits many changes and purposes, the offering accepted on the eighth day is made in the future age. Therefore Solomon said: “Before death, praise no one” (Ecclesiasticus 11:28).

Since these things are so, let us again understand the mother as the Church, and the grace that is in her. Concerning her Solomon says in Proverbs: “Hear, my son, the discipline of your father, and do not abandon the law of your mother.” When someone has been begotten through the grace of the Gospel, according to what Paul says—“For in Christ Jesus I begot you through the Gospel” (1 Corinthians 4:15)—he will remain under the intelligible mother, the Church or grace, for seven days, that is, throughout the whole present life, which revolves through seven days, obedient to her laws and ordinances. Thus, on the eighth day, in the time of the resurrection, he will be a gift and sacrifice to the Lord, because the Lord receives such a person not only as a sacrifice of the soul but also as a holy and acceptable sacrifice of the body. [Col. 0499B]

But learn, on account of this and what follows: “Whether it is an ox or a sheep, it shall not be slaughtered on the same day as its young.” Here, through the names themselves, he again indicates something else. Those who celebrate the evangelical Passover, which the Church has handed down to us, ought not to celebrate the legal Passover. The legislator signified this by mentioning the ox and the sheep, since Moses prescribed these for slaughter on the day of Passover, as the book of Deuteronomy can show: “And you shall sacrifice the Passover to the Lord your God, sheep and oxen.”

The young of these animals—whether of this Passover or of the Passover of the Old Testament and of the tradition contained in figures—has a figurative significance of the Lord’s Passover. The former preceded in type; the latter followed in truth. Therefore Christ first celebrated the figurative Passover, but after the supper he handed on the intelligible Passover; and, as time pressed upon him, he changed the hour in place of the day, or rather, even the day itself.

For if the supper of the Jewish Passover feast is celebrated toward evening on the fourteenth day, afterward Christ handed on his own supper. He handed it on, therefore, after the evening of the fourteenth day. But the time after evening is entirely the beginning of another day. This had to occur to make the time clear: when the old came to an end, the new then began.

Or perhaps the old signifies those to whom the law refers, concerning whom Isaiah also said: “A child has been born for us; a son has been given to us” (Isaiah 9:6). These words and what follows were spoken concerning Christ. Thus this young animal—or, according to the Septuagint, “sons”—was not to be slaughtered on the same day on which the calf and the sheep of the Jewish festival were killed. For those who celebrated the Passover on the fourteenth day crucified Jesus on the following day.

The text continues:

“If you sacrifice a sacrifice of thanksgiving to the Lord, so that it may be acceptable, you shall eat it on the same day; nothing shall remain of it until the morning of the following day. I am the Lord. Keep my commandments and perform them. I am the Lord. Do not profane my holy name, so that I may be sanctified in the midst of the children of Israel. I am the Lord, who sanctify you and brought you out of the land of Egypt to be your God. I am the Lord.”

(From Hesychius.) Just as there is no satisfaction if, when the New Testament has begun, someone continues to serve the old and, while the evangelical preaching is advancing, lives according to the letter—for it is an insult to the one who established both if we do not obey him in the times he has distinguished—so there is no excuse for anyone to suppose or even think that, in the future age, any of the things now commanded for us to do will be reserved for action.

“If you sacrifice,” he says, “a sacrifice of thanksgiving to the Lord,” promising him an evangelical way of life. For this is the sacrifice of thanksgiving to the Lord: that a person performs whatever pertains to his praise and glory.
