The Lord demonstrates this to the apostles when he says: “Let your light shine before human beings, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5:16).

It is sacrificed to the Lord so that it may be acceptable. The Septuagint renders this, “You shall sacrifice it as acceptable to you”; that is, let us undertake the aforesaid way of life in a worthy manner, completing it and leaving nothing diminished. Therefore he added: “You shall eat it on the same day; nothing shall remain until the morning of the following day.”

In the time in which this sacrifice has been prescribed, we are permitted to eat it—that is, we must perform and complete it. We must leave nothing of it until the morning, so that we do not preserve for the future age any remainder of our way of life uncorrected, nor anything of our virtues unfinished and unpracticed, when it is no longer permitted to work. “Morning” is rightly spoken, because the present life is night; therefore it is called a mist on account of what is now in it.

“I am the Lord: keep my commandments and perform them. I am the Lord”—who here establishes the law, but there judges; who gave intelligible talents to his servants to work with in the present age, but in the future settles accounts with them and demands the work produced by the talents.

“I am the Lord: do not profane my holy name.” It is a profanation and blasphemy against the Creator if he raises us in the same condition or activity in which we now exist. For what change would there be in this world if we were to remain in the same pains and labors? [Col. 0500D]

“So that I may be sanctified in the midst of the children of Israel.” He did not say, “I am sanctified,” but “so that I may be sanctified,” indicating the future time in which he will be sanctified in the midst of the true children of Israel. The mention of the departure from Egypt was not pointless. It indicates that, just as those who came out of Egypt no longer practiced the things of Egypt, so, when God has led us out of the present life, we will no longer be able to practice the things belonging to it.

For there is an intelligible Egypt, the present world, since “Egypt” is interpreted as “darkening.” The present things are filled with darkness and, as we have said, with mist or gloom, so much so that John said concerning the Lord: “The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it” (John 1:5). Therefore the Lord God leads us out of this intelligible Egypt so that he may be our God—not because he is not so now, but because not everyone confesses him or knows him. Then we shall confess him; then we shall all submit to him; then God will be all in all.

## CHAPTER XXI. Concerning the commandment about observing the festivals and offering sacrifices on them

(CAP. XXIII.) The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “Speak to the children of Israel, and say to them: These are the festivals of the Lord, which you shall call holy. For six days you shall work; the seventh day, because it is the rest of the sabbath, shall be called holy. You shall do no work on it; it is the sabbath of the Lord in all your dwelling places.” [Col. 0501B]

If you attend carefully to these words spoken here by the legislator, you will find that he introduces the intention of the Spirit not only into the contemplation of the law but also into the letter itself. For after saying, “These are the festivals of the Lord, which you shall call holy,”—“These are my festivals”—he immediately added: “For six days you shall work.”

He ought, of course, to have remained silent about this and to have said only what follows: “The seventh day, because it is the rest of the sabbath, shall be called holy.” But by connecting the festivals with the words, “For six days you shall work,” he shows that the first festival, or feast, according to the law, is to work—and to work good things. For this reason he says, “For six days you shall work,” because everything that God established in six days was very good.

The second festival, following these works, is the rest of the seventh day, a feast that no one who has not performed good works worthy of God will be able to celebrate. For it was not without reason that God himself was speaking; God does not speak without reason. First he said, “For six days you shall work,” and afterward, “The seventh day, because it is the rest of the sabbath, shall be called holy.”

This was to show that if someone acts in imitation of God and achieves good things—for this is to work during the six days—then that person rests in the intelligible sabbath. Concerning this Paul said: “Let us fear, therefore, lest, while the promise of entering his rest remains, any of you should appear to have fallen short” (Hebrews 4:1). For whoever has entered his rest has himself also rested from his works, just as God rested from his own.

By adding afterward, with great emphasis, “in all your dwelling places,” he also signified that he was speaking of the future age. The present world is a pilgrimage; the dwelling place is what follows. None of us departs from those mansions or dwelling places that we shall once have received.

The text continues:

“These, therefore, are the holy festivals of the Lord, which you must celebrate at their appointed times. In the first month, on the fourteenth day of the month toward evening, it is the Lord’s Passover; and on the fifteenth day of this month is the solemnity of the Lord’s Unleavened Bread. For seven days you shall eat unleavened bread. The first day shall be most solemn and holy for you. You shall do no servile work on it, but you shall offer a sacrifice by fire to the Lord for seven days. The seventh day shall be most solemn and holier, and no servile work shall be done on it.” [Col. 0502A]

Now, if it is permitted, let us ask the Jews why he did not command a festival on the fourteenth day, on which the figurative Passover was celebrated, but merely made mention of it. Instead, he determined that a festival should be held on the first day of Unleavened Bread, which followed it. It is clear from this that the one who receives the law desires to know the difference between figure and truth, and that, although it is right to know the figures because they lead to the truth, it is worthy to celebrate the festival when the truth contained in the figures has arrived.

He makes mention of the fourteenth because it contained the figure. But he commanded that the festival be celebrated on the fifteenth because on that day the true Passover is present, concerning which Paul said: “Christ our Passover has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5:7).

Let us now examine the actual words: “These are the holy festivals of the Lord, which you must celebrate at their appointed times.” Why did he not say “festivals for the Lord,” but “festivals of the Lord”? Or perhaps the law is thereby bearing witness to the hearer that it did not command these festivals, of which it is speaking, to be celebrated for God in some ordinary sense, but because they are his own.

For just as the festivals of an emperor are those on which he has raised victories and trophies against his enemies, saved nations, and acquired cities, so these are the festivals of Christ, on which he saved our race, conquered our captivity, and established for himself an inheritance from the nations—a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for his possession (1 Peter 2:9).

By saying “at their appointed times,” he did not speak in this way concerning their festivals. He shows that these festivals belong not to those who serve the figure but to the faithful who receive the festival. One of them is the feast of which he says: “In the first month, on the fourteenth day of the month toward evening, it is the Lord’s Passover.”

We rightly call the first month the time of the Lord’s Passion, in which these words spoken by God to Moses especially find their fulfillment: “This month shall be for you the beginning of months; it shall be the first among the months of the year” (Exodus 12:2).

For it is the beginning and entrance of the new life and of the way of life now begun by us. John taught that it should be called an evening time, at which the Lord came. For he said: “Little children, it is the last hour” (1 John 2:18).

The Lord’s Passover occurred toward evening. He who suffered did not immediately bring the time to an end, but left the remnants of the last and evening hour, in which the preaching ought to run its course and the saving word penetrate the whole earth.

But toward evening, or in the middle of the evening, Christ also celebrated his own Passover beforehand, anticipating it. On the day of the figurative Passover festival, which was the fourteenth, after the supper he handed over to the disciples the supersensible true Passover belonging to its mystery. Therefore it was already night when Judas, receiving the bread from that supper, went out to betray the Lord.

On the following day, which was the fifteenth, he fulfilled the Passover of the cross. Therefore the legislator commanded that this festival be celebrated on the fifteenth day of the month, and proclaimed that celebration to be the solemnity of the Lord’s Unleavened Bread.

For if we wish to celebrate his Passover properly and truly, we must be unleavened, free from every evil, and especially from Jewish error and antiquity. Therefore, after Paul said, “Christ our Passover has been sacrificed,” he added: “Let us therefore keep the feast, not with the old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” (1 Corinthians 5:7–8).

We must be free from the leaven of the world’s evil not for a limited time but throughout our whole life. Therefore he says: “For seven days you shall eat unleavened bread,” prescribing through the number seven that this apply to our whole life.

“The first day shall be most solemn and holy for you. You shall do no servile work on it.” The Spirit indicates what kind of work is entirely servile when the Lord says: “Amen, amen, I say to you, everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin” (John 8:34). If we celebrate the true Passover, let us flee the service of sin, because Christ, who suffered for us, freed us from sin and from its servitude.

This does not mean that he commanded no servile work to be done on the first day but, for that reason, commanded servile works to be done on the other days. See what he added: “But you shall offer a sacrifice by fire to the Lord,” or, according to the Septuagint: “You shall offer burnt offerings to the Lord for seven days. The seventh day shall be more solemn and holier, and no servile work shall be done on it.”

By commanding burnt offerings to be offered for seven days, therefore, he also commanded abstention from every servile work during them. For how could someone offer a burnt offering to God while being worthy of the devil or performing servile works?

Then he named not only the first day but also the seventh, so that through the first and the seventh he might encompass the whole human life: the former has the beginning, while the latter has the end, in which everything is included.

The text continues:

“And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to the children of Israel, and say to them: When you have entered the land that I will give you, and have reaped the grain of your land, you shall bring to the priest a sheaf of the firstfruits of your harvest. He shall lift up the sheaf before the Lord, so that it may be acceptable for you; on the day after the sabbath he shall consecrate it. On the same day on which the sheaf is consecrated, an unblemished male lamb one year old shall be slaughtered as a burnt offering to the Lord.

“Libations shall be offered with it: two-tenths of fine flour mixed with oil, as incense to the Lord, a most pleasing aroma; and a wine offering, a fourth part of a hin. You shall not eat bread, roasted grain, or parched grain from the harvest until the day on which you offer it to your God. This shall be an everlasting ordinance throughout your generations and in all your dwelling places.

“You shall count, therefore, beginning with the day after the sabbath on which you offered the sheaf of the firstfruits: seven full weeks, until the day after the completion of the seventh week—that is, fifty days. Then you shall offer a new sacrifice to the Lord from all your dwelling places: two loaves as firstfruits, from two-tenths of fine flour fermented, which you shall bake as firstfruits for the Lord. With the loaves you shall offer seven unblemished male lambs one year old, one bull from the herd, and two rams. They shall be a burnt offering with their libations, a most pleasing aroma to the Lord.

“You shall also make a male goat for sin, and two male lambs one year old as sacrifices of peace offerings. When the priest has lifted them up with the loaves of the firstfruits before the Lord, they shall become his use. You shall call this day most solemn and most holy. You shall do no servile work on it. It shall be an everlasting ordinance in all your dwelling places and throughout your generations.”

Some Jews are found to celebrate the feast of Pentecost by counting from the first day of Unleavened Bread, rather than from the day on which the sheaf of the firstfruits is offered—that is, from the following day, the second day—and they proclaim that Pentecost should be celebrated on that basis.

Therefore, reproaching them because they did not fulfill the law even according to the letter, the Lord said: “And none of you fulfills the law” (John 7:19). But the Church does fulfill it, as is now shown:

“The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to the children of Israel, and say to them: When you have entered the land, and so forth.”

We have frequently taught that the land given by God signifies evangelical teaching and conduct. It is called land because of the fruits of virtue that arise from it, and it was given by God himself. He did not employ a mediator for it but proclaimed it by his own mouth.

When, therefore, they entered it and reaped its grain—those who received the saving word—for they are also the reapers of the intelligible harvest, to whom the Lord said: “The harvest is indeed abundant, but the workers are few. Therefore ask the Lord of the harvest to send workers into his harvest” (Luke 10:2). To them he also entrusted the mystery of the word, for the harvest was then so ripe that the Lord said: “Lift up your eyes and see the regions, for they are already white for harvesting” (John 4:35).

The intelligible priest, Christ, offered his own body as the sheaf of the firstfruits. For the head, or sum, of the harvest—namely, of the word and of the divine preaching—was the resurrection of the dead. Therefore, as the true sheaf and true firstfruits of our intelligible harvest, Christ the priest raised his own body from the dead. Concerning this Paul said: “But now Christ has risen from the dead, the firstfruits of those who sleep” (1 Corinthians 15:20).

But when did this happen? “On the day after the first,” the priest shall offer it. What we have said above shows that the first day was the day of the Lord’s Passion, on which the Lord, not without reason, administered his sacrifice.

Since this first day was called the first day of Unleavened Bread and the first day of the Passover festival, while the following day of the Passion was the resurrection, the legislator first shows the priest offering the sheaf of the firstfruits, and afterward says: “And on the same day on which the sheaf is consecrated, an unblemished male lamb one year old shall be slaughtered as a burnt offering to the Lord.”

He wishes us, on the day when we celebrate the Lord’s resurrection and the intelligible offering of the sheaf, not to forget the Lord’s sacrifice, from which the offering of the sheaf comes. Instead, we are to slaughter the unblemished male lamb one year old as a burnt offering to the Lord, mystically slaughtering and offering the intelligible Lamb of the Lord in his handing-over.

He also made remembrance of the one who slaughtered him as a sacrifice. For otherwise, but through his mediation and power, the things accomplished in that sacrifice would not be transferred from the sensible to the intelligible. And that this is the sacrifice is shown by the words: “Two-tenths of fine flour mixed with oil.”

We must contemplate perfect humanity and perfect divinity, that is, their coming together as one, in the oil—that is, through the compassion that he has toward us. In this way the sacrifice is found to be a sweet aroma to the Lord, when we understand from it what things are worthy.

The following words show in whom and through whom the sacrifice is performed and how the offering of the intelligible Lamb is celebrated. God does not receive a sacrifice from us in blood or through irrational animals, as what follows demonstrates. He says: “And a wine offering, a fourth part of a hin, bread, roasted grain, and parched grain.”

Perhaps it was uncertain from whom the mystery of the sacrifice that is through Christ was celebrated, the sacrifice of which we spoke above. Behold the offering of the intelligible Melchizedek, which is completed in bread and wine. In it, a fourth part of a hin is offered in the wine offering, so that through the fourth part the evangelical tradition contained in four books might be signified, while through the libation the word of the Lord is signified, when he says: “This is my blood, which will be poured out for you” (Mark 14:24; Matthew 26:28; 1 Corinthians 11:25).

The legislator appeared to signify the mystery of Christ without diminution. Therefore he also added: “You shall not eat roasted grain or parched grain from the harvest until the day on which you offer it to your God. This shall be an everlasting ordinance throughout your generations and in all your dwelling places.”

The offering of the present gifts, which we have shown to be the mystery of the Only-Begotten, reconciled us to God and provided us with food of the new roasted grain and parched grain.

While saying these things and describing the manner of the resurrection in the way required, the legislator joins his discourse to the Pentecost that we celebrate:

“You shall count, therefore, beginning with the day after the sabbath on which you offered the sheaf of the firstfruits: seven full weeks, until the day after the completion of the seventh week—that is, fifty days. Then you shall offer a new sacrifice to the Lord.”

It has been sufficiently shown above that the Jewish people observe neither the time nor the number of this Pentecost. We, however, observe it both contemplatively and according to the letter.

For the legislator, wishing to demonstrate his intention more clearly, commanded that fifty days be counted from the day after the sabbath on which the sheaf was offered, plainly intending the Lord’s day to be understood. For this is the day after the sabbath. On it the resurrection took place, and seven weeks are counted until the day after the completion of the week.

Again, on the Lord’s day we celebrate the feast of Pentecost, on which we received the advent of the Holy Spirit. It was not without reason that we observe the arrival after seven weeks, but so that we might understand that God commanded those who desire to receive him to do nothing old, nothing worldly, and nothing close to ancient corruption.

At that time he also commanded a new sacrifice to be offered to the Lord. For when the Spirit came, he renewed our whole life, confirming the tradition of Christ and establishing the way of life that he perfected in them. He says: “He will take from what is mine and declare it to you” (John 16:14).

Therefore he did not come on another day of the week, but on the day on which the resurrection took place and the intelligible sheaf was offered. This also proves that the new way of life, which renewed us by freeing us from the corruption of antiquity, was corrected through Christ’s resurrection and the advent of the Holy Spirit.

The offering itself makes clear the kind of sacrifice he commanded:

“Then you shall offer a new sacrifice to the Lord from all your dwelling places: two loaves as firstfruits, from two-tenths of fermented fine flour, which you shall bake as firstfruits for the Lord. With the loaves you shall offer seven unblemished male lambs one year old, one bull from the herd, and two rams.”

By calling it a new sacrifice, he excluded the sacrifices of the law as old and introduced evangelical sacrifices in their place.

Then, by adding “from your dwelling places,” he signified the Church and adapted the things mentioned to be offered to her. For he did not say “from all dwelling places,” but “from all your dwelling places,” plainly indicating a particular dwelling place, concerning which David says: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house” (Psalm 83:5); and again: “One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I will seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life” (Psalm 26:4).

The two loaves of the firstfruits signify the law and the Gospel, for they are loaves containing food for faithful souls. [Col. 0506C]

They are also firstfruits—or, according to the Septuagint, “set apart”—because, although they are preeminent in every kind of wisdom, they are separate and set apart from the wisdom that is external.

They are made from two-tenths of fermented fine flour, from the teaching that hands on perfect divinity and perfect humanity. They cannot be baked in any other way except through such teaching, and they are firstfruits for the Lord.

For the Lord was first to perfect the law and the Gospel, and afterward to teach: “You have heard that it was said to the ancients, ‘You shall not kill’; but I say to you, everyone who is angry with his brother without cause shall be liable to judgment” (Matthew 5:21–22). Here he joined the law to the Gospel; therefore they are called his firstfruits.

Luke also confirms this and shows us the true firstfruits when he writes: “I made my first account, O Theophilus, concerning all the things that Jesus began to do and teach” (Acts 1:1).

He commanded seven unblemished male lambs one year old to be offered with them, signifying the gifts that are of the Spirit, concerning which Solomon said in Proverbs: “Wisdom built herself a house; she erected seven pillars” (Proverbs 9:1).

Isaiah presented the matter more clearly: “And the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him” (Isaiah 11:2). He did not leave unsaid what the gifts were or what their number was, but added: “The Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety; and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isaiah 11:2–3).

He calls these gifts lambs to show that the Holy Spirit is one with Christ. Concerning him it was said: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sin of the world” (John 1:29). Therefore no one can say, “Jesus is Lord,” except in the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 12:3).

Thus it is not without reason that the present offering contains, together with the seven lambs, one bull from the herd. It clearly signifies him who was made from the herd of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and David according to the flesh.

He joined to this two unblemished rams, signifying the excellent commandments and virtues that we must follow as though they were sheep. In these we possess protection and security, since they drive away the intelligible enemy as with a fan.

What are these commandments? “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have and give to the poor, and come, follow me” (Matthew 19:21).

The greatest commandment is to sell what one has and give to the poor; it is also the greatest thing to follow Christ, so that, despising the possession of anything, we may strive to do everything according to the Lord’s will. For this is what it means to follow him.

These commandments, therefore, established for an unblemished and perfect life, are called rams because rams are superior to the whole flock.

Their sacrifices and libation—namely, knowledge and correction—are a sweet aroma to that Lord concerning whom Paul said: “Thanks be to God, who always leads us in triumph in Christ Jesus and manifests through us the aroma of his knowledge, because we are the good aroma of Christ” (2 Corinthians 2:14–15).

Nevertheless, he did not bring the offering of Pentecost to an end with these things. He also speaks of what remains, because perfection especially belongs to the Spirit whose festival has been described.

What does he say? “You shall also make a male goat for sin,” introducing the subject of repentance. “And two male lambs one year old as sacrifices of peace offerings,” signifying those commandments of Paul: “Pursue peace with everyone and holiness, without which no one shall see God” (Hebrews 12:14).

Because these were expressed through the apostolic tongue, he commanded them to be offered with the loaves of the firstfruits, which we have said signify the teaching of Christ.

In what follows he again adds: “When the priest has lifted them up with the loaves of the firstfruits before the Lord.” According to the Septuagint, the text reads: “And the priest shall separate them with a separation, with the loaves of the firstfruits before the Lord, with the two lambs,” signifying for which Lord they are offered. “And they shall become his use,” that is, the use of the priest who offers them, namely Christ.

For he is our priest, and he is also our Lord. His are both the loaves of the firstfruits and the lambs of the commandments mentioned above. For he was the one speaking in Paul; he offered everything that has been said. The peace concerning which Paul commands was first announced by the Lord to his disciples, and he preserved holiness above all as the Holy One of holies.

For he was the one concerning whom Gabriel said to the Virgin: “Therefore also the holy one who will be born from you shall be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35).

Nevertheless, if you wish to grasp the excellence of the day under discussion, consider the confirmation of what has been said about it:

“You shall call this day most solemn and most holy. You shall do no servile work on it. It shall be an everlasting ordinance in all your dwelling places and throughout your generations.” [Col. 0508A]

What, then, does it possess that makes it excel among these days? Behold, he also calls other days holy, but of this day he first says, “You shall call this day most solemn,” and afterward, “and most holy,” so that you may recognize both what it has in common with the others and what is proper to it.

On this day the calling of the nations not only began to be proclaimed but also began to be accomplished, when Parthians, Medes, and Elamites, and those who inhabit Mesopotamia, Judea, and Pamphylia—all the remaining nations whom Luke enumerated—began to hear the apostles speaking in their own languages of the mighty works of God and preaching.

Let us therefore do no servile work on that day—that is, nothing belonging to slavery—but let us keep the everlasting ordinance in all our dwelling places and throughout our generations, doing nothing servile in the time when the Spirit came to us, because, as Paul writes, “Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (2 Corinthians 3:17).

The text continues:

“After you have reaped the grain of your land, you shall not cut it down to the ground, nor shall you gather the ears that remain; you shall leave them for the poor and for the strangers. I am the Lord your God.”

Since the things now commanded by the law are full of piety, it is clear that they ought to be observed according to the letter as well. But contemplation possesses their greater profit.

Note this about them: although he had commanded similar things above, he did not establish the same things here. The change in the wording itself demonstrates this. There he said: “You shall not complete your harvest.” Here, however: “You shall not cut it down to the ground.” We are therefore to understand the difference through the alteration of the words.

We have frequently shown that the land mentioned by the law signifies the way of life of those who believe in God. Its harvest flourished after the Savior’s resurrection from the dead and the coming of the Holy Spirit.

The word of preaching does not impart all the knowledge that we shall possess when we come to God himself. There are things it leaves behind, things that cannot now be lifted up for us. Therefore he inserted this law among the festivals mentioned above and said: “After you have reaped the grain of your land, you shall not cut it down to the ground.”

By saying, “You shall not cut it down to the ground,” he signified the things lacking for us in full and perfect knowledge. Therefore he added: “Nor shall you gather the ears that remain,” so that we may not contend or strive vainly after things that elude our knowledge.

For this reason we can neither gather what is said to fall from the harvest, but must leave it to Christ. Signifying him, the legislator added: “You shall leave them for the poor and for the strangers.” According to the Septuagint: “You shall leave them for the poor and the proselyte.”

And who is this? Hear what follows: “I am the Lord your God.”

He is also called poor because, although he was rich, he became poor for our sake, so that by his poverty we might become rich. He is also called a stranger, because although he came among his own, his own did not receive him (John 1:11).

You shall therefore leave these things for him. He alone knows what remains for us. Therefore we cannot gather the things that have been set apart for him to gather, as Paul bears witness when he says: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and unfathomable his ways!” (Romans 11:33).

The text continues:

The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “Speak to the children of Israel: On the first day of the seventh month you shall have a sabbath of memorial, with the sounding of trumpets, and it shall be called holy. You shall do no laborious work on it, and you shall offer a burnt offering to the Lord.”

Many things demonstrate that the number seven bears an evident and unmistakable figure of completion, whether of each one of us or universally; but this demonstrates it most of all: [Col. 0509B] that God ceased from His works on the seventh day, thereby giving us also an indication of our own rest, concerning which Paul says: “For whoever has entered into that rest has himself also rested from all his works, just as God did from His own.” But the beginning of the completion of the ages is the Lord’s advent; therefore the Evangelist John called it “the last hour,” for he says: “Little children, it is the last hour.” James likewise says: “Behold, the judge stands before the door.” The law rightly called this time—the first day of the seventh month—the beginning of completion.

It is rest for us because He has made us free from evil works and liberated us from a heavy yoke. “Come,” He says, “all who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. XI). And again: “Learn from me, [Col. 0509C] because I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls.”

This is also a memorial of trumpets: for it proclaims the Savior’s resurrection, which is a memorial of the common resurrection of the dead. That resurrection will take place at the sound of great and terrible trumpets, at the Lord’s command, at the voice of the archangel and the trumpet of God, as Paul taught. This time shall be called holy to the Lord, because it possesses the calling that is in sanctification, through which adoption belonging to Him is brought about for those who are called.

“You shall do no laborious work on it, and you shall offer a burnt offering to the Lord.”

For it is no longer the time to perform servile works, since the past time is sufficient for the will of the nations, in which servile works were done. Just as we [Col. 0509D] presented our members as weapons of unrighteousness for iniquity, so we must present our members as weapons of righteousness for sanctification: for this is the true burnt offering. It continues:

The Lord also spoke to Moses, saying: “On the tenth day of this seventh month there shall be a most solemn day of expiation, and it shall be called holy; you shall afflict your souls on it, and you shall offer a burnt offering to the Lord. You shall do no work during this day, because it is a day of propitiation, so that the Lord your God may be propitiated for you. Every soul that is not afflicted on this day shall perish from its people; and whoever does any work, I shall destroy that person from among his people. Therefore you shall do no work on it. It shall be an everlasting ordinance [Col. 0510A] for you throughout all your generations and dwellings. It is a sabbath of rest, and you shall afflict your souls. From the ninth day of the month, from evening until evening, you shall celebrate your sabbaths.”

The legislator wishes to show us that propitiation—that is, liberation from sins—is acquired through humility and the affliction of the soul. We must undertake this beginning in the evening, that is, beginning with repentance itself, because Christ also made repentance the beginning of His preaching. But we must build a good and perfect life upon repentance, bringing it to completion through virtues; therefore he added: “And you shall offer a burnt offering to the Lord.” “You shall do no work during this day.” By the burnt offering he indicates a life brought to completion and perfectly attached to God; by [Col. 0510B] doing no work he indicates abstinence from every earthly activity.

Therefore he added with great appropriateness: “Because it is a day of propitiation, so that the Lord your God may be propitiated for you,” showing both things: that this is the time granted to us by God for propitiation, in which the Lord, coming among us, washes away our sins, and that, while we await these things, we must undertake nothing earthly.

Then, extending the law and providing an advocacy for Christ, who said, “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matt. XI), he says: “Every soul that is not afflicted on this day shall perish from its people.” For the person who does not follow Christ, who established these things and humbled Himself so greatly that Paul said of [Col. 0510C] Him, “He humbled Himself, becoming obedient unto death—even death on a cross” (Phil. II), will perish. “And whoever does any work, I shall destroy him from among his people.”

You shall do no work, therefore, on it. It shall be an everlasting ordinance for you throughout all your generations and dwellings.

He spoke in this way as though the command had been given to the Jewish people; yet this is not so, for the law is common to all. The Lord also said to everyone: “Work not for the food that perishes,” wishing us to undertake nothing earthly.

Therefore, wishing to lead the guardianship of the calling toward greater contemplation, he added well and wisely: “It is a sabbath of rest,” or, according to the Septuagint, “It shall be a Sabbath of Sabbaths for you,” so that through this spiritual meaning we may understand a sabbath [Col. 0510D] that surpassed the weakness of the Jews, just as the Holy of Holies did. For this reason they did not even possess sabbaths, nor “Song of Songs”: they do not understand the power of the things written there. Whatever receives interpretation according to the anagogical sense of the law, we should understand as exceeding the measures of the Jews.

Now observe the expressions he used: “You shall afflict your souls; from the evening of the ninth day of the month until evening you shall celebrate your sabbaths.”

He repeats the word of humility, because Christ frequently taught it and established it for the apostles as a crown, foundation, virtue, and subsistence. When asked who was greatest in the kingdom of heaven, He answered, “Whoever humbles [Col. 0511A] himself,” and so forth.

When he said, “From evening until evening,” he plainly wished us always to strive for freedom from superfluous and vain things. Hence the Lord does not even permit us to plead our cause: He commanded that we should not dispute over a tunic or garment, nor consider what we should eat, drink, or wear. Rather, teaching us and announcing the sabbath of sabbaths—in which every work ceases and only the things of God are displayed, while only those things that are useful and beneficial to the soul are corrected—He continues:

The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “Speak to the children of Israel: From the fifteenth day of this seventh month there shall be the feast of tabernacles for the Lord, for seven days. The first day shall be called most solemn and most holy. You shall do no laborious work, and [Col. 0511B] for seven days you shall offer burnt offerings to the Lord. The eighth day shall also be most solemn and most holy, and you shall offer a burnt offering to the Lord. For it is an assembly and a gathering; you shall do no laborious work on it.”

By this, he says, the legislator signifies not only that we must surpass the wisdom of the world and recognize its transience and temporality, but also that we ought to keep our eye upon the age to come.

You will find this represented without any doubt both through the number and through the tabernacles. He commanded the feast to begin on the fifteenth day. This number is composed of seven and eight, one of which represents the present age and the other the future. Therefore, while commanding the feast to be completed in seven days, he again mentioned other most solemn and most holy days; he did not count [Col. 0511C] the eighth day together with the seven, but placed it afterward and separate from the others, just as the future age follows the present age, yet is something other than it.

He called it the feast of tabernacles for seven days. Whoever uses the present world as a tabernacle can have a feast in it and rejoice because of his expectation of the future. So too can whoever knows that, if the earthly house of this dwelling is dissolved, a building not made with hands will receive him in the heavens.

He called the first of the seven days most solemn and most holy. Whoever knows how to use present things as a tabernacle begins the first day—that is, the beginning and origin—with the sanctification of his calling. Therefore he says with great appropriateness: [Col. 0511D] “You shall do no laborious work,” because those who regard the world and the things in it as a tabernacle and as transitory serve no one in this age.

He also commanded burnt offerings to be offered for seven days, showing that a perfect manner of life must be followed throughout the whole period. When, therefore, we pass through the present life in this way, then we possess the most solemn and most holy eighth day—namely, the future age—when the one who called us in this manner of life calls us to the good things prepared for the saints.

For the Septuagint rendered it as follows: “The eighth day shall be a day of convocation; it shall be holy.” Then we offer to the Lord the burnt offering that we have prepared here. “For it is an assembly and a gathering,” or, according to the Septuagint, “an exodus,” because here there is departure, while there [Col. 0512A] is dwelling there, as Paul says: “I desire to depart and to be with Christ” (Phil. I).

We shall do no laborious work, because at that time we shall be like the angels of God. Observe also how he says the same things about the first and the eighth day, because in a certain way the virtues of both are one: for the day of resurrection, which is the substance of the future age, is its beginning and foundation.

The first day is the beginning in Christ of our manner of life and the beginning of future things; the eighth day is the one that succeeds the present age, which the number seven is said to represent.

These are the feasts of the Lord, which you shall call most solemn and most holy, and in which you shall offer offerings to the Lord—burnt offerings and libations according to the rite of each day—apart from the sabbaths of the Lord, your gifts, [Col. 0512B] those that you offer by vow, and those that you give freely to the Lord.

Observe those apostolic words: “Rejoice always, pray without ceasing, give thanks in all things.” These words appear to correspond with the present terms of the Mosaic ordinance. For when the legislator set forth certain principal feasts, which he also called most solemn and holy, he mingled daily libations and sacrifices with them: “These,” he says, “are the feasts of the Lord, which you shall call most solemn and most holy.” And when he ought to have spoken of this feast or that one, he did not speak in that way, but added: “You shall offer in them offerings to the Lord, burnt offerings and libations according to the rite of each day.”

He also wishes us to rejoice, to keep a feast, and to pray without ceasing. For this is the daily libation and sacrifice, or burnt offering, which we can offer when [Col. 0512C] we present our bodies to God as a living sacrifice and put to death our members that are upon the earth, ready to go to God and saying with Paul: “For I am already being poured out, and the time of my departure is at hand.”

For this reason he added: “Apart from the sabbaths of the Lord, your gifts, and those that you offer by vow, or those that you give freely to the Lord,” clearly handing down this teaching: that, beyond the turning away from evils—for this is the sabbath—and beyond the other acts of righteousness that we promise to God according to the time, we sometimes promise Him a fast, sometimes an offering of possessions, whether in dangers that come upon us or voluntarily.

From the fifteenth day of the seventh month, therefore, when you have gathered [Col. 0512D] all the produce of your land, you shall celebrate the feast of the Lord for seven days. On the first day and on the eighth day there shall be a sabbath, that is, rest. You shall take for yourselves on the first day the fruit of a beautiful tree, branches of palms, branches of a tree with dense foliage, and willows from the torrent; and you shall rejoice before the Lord your God. You shall celebrate His solemnity for seven days each year. It shall be an everlasting ordinance throughout your generations. In the seventh month you shall celebrate the feast, and you shall dwell in shelters for seven days. Everyone who is of the race of Israel shall remain in tabernacles, so that your descendants may learn that I made the children of Israel dwell in tabernacles when I brought them out of the land of Egypt. I am the Lord your God.”

And Moses spoke concerning the solemnities of the Lord to the children of Israel.

[Col. 0513A] From the fifteenth day of the seventh month, therefore: we have said that the seventh month signifies the completion or fullness of the times. The fifteenth, being composed of seven and eight, signifies the evangelical preaching, which consists of the present life and the future one, joining the former and preparing the latter.

When we have gathered all the produce of the land—that is, when we have ceased from earthly works—let us celebrate a feast for seven days, meaning that we should devote our entire life to celebrating the divine feast. On the first day there is rest, and on the eighth day there is rest.

Once he had proposed that the feast be celebrated during seven days, he no longer included the seventh day with that number, but appointed the eighth. First, because those who hold the law according to the letter are not permitted to celebrate the feast: a new people has been separated from them, one that knows [Col. 0513B] how to receive the law according to the spirit and to honor the eighth day, which we have said signifies the resurrection of the dead.

Second, because the first and the eighth possess one virtue. The eighth is itself also the first, because it is the beginning of the future age. Furthermore, the first day, which is the beginning of the preaching established at the end of the ages, contains rest: it makes us rest when it liberates us from the labors of sins through the gift of baptism.

Here, when the legislator had proclaimed a feast lasting seven days, he called its first day rest. He is silent concerning the succeeding days, thereby indicating that we ought to devote ourselves to virtues. Then he transfers rest to the eighth day, showing that the true rest of the believer and of the person who serves the law of God is the future age.

What, then, must we work at throughout our entire life, [Col. 0513C] and from where must we begin our work?

“You shall take for yourselves on the first day the fruit of a beautiful tree, branches of palms, branches of a tree with dense foliage, and willows from the torrent, and you shall rejoice before the Lord your God; and you shall celebrate His solemnity for seven days.”

That we ought to devote ourselves to virtues throughout our entire life is confirmed beyond any doubt by the number seven itself, which he signified through the fruits and branches of the trees mentioned above.

Since we must begin from the calling itself, from which the spiritual rest of Christ previously mentioned derives—and this is the first day of the feast—it is clear that the day which above he called a day of rest is now the day on which he commands us to take the fruit of a beautiful tree. These are the fruits that David sang of in the first [Col. 0513D] psalm: “And he shall be like a tree planted beside streams of water, which shall give its fruit in its season” (Ps. I).

He also commands us to take branches of palms—that is, the young shoots of righteousness: “The righteous shall flourish like a palm,” as David said (Ps. XCI). But since there is nothing on the palm, just as there is nothing among those who live righteously, that can be rejected, take also branches of a tree with dense foliage.

These signify all the fruits of the virtues, but especially mercy. For mercy ought to be continuous and enduring, as Ecclesiastes commends it: “Let oil not fail from your head” (Eccles. IX). And in Proverbs: “Do not say to your friend, ‘Go and return, and tomorrow I will give to you,’ when you are able to give immediately.” [Col. 0514A]

Take also willows; and, according to the Septuagint, the chaste-tree (ἄγνου), but not its branches, signifying continence and chaste marriage. The willow signifies continence because it bears no fruit, just as the continent, who are true eunuchs and have castrated themselves for the sake of the rest of heaven, produce no sensory fruit. To them God says through the prophet Isaiah: “Let not the eunuch say, ‘I am a dry tree,’ for I will give them in my house and within my walls a place and a name better than sons and daughters; I will give them an everlasting name” (Isa. LVI).

We also say that the willow bears the figure of prayer and likewise of repentance. Thus we should understand what was said by David: “By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept when we remembered [Col. 0514B] you, Zion. On the willows in its midst we hung our instruments” (Ps. CXXXVI). These are the tears of prayer and repentance, concerning which Isaiah says: “Like willows beside flowing waters” (Isa. XLIV).

But these are to be taken from the torrent—that is, from the present life. The torrent is rightly so called because of its passing or flowing onward, and also because of the winter it contains, namely, the various temptations and tribulations. Thus David spoke of Christ, who Himself tasted the world and its tribulations, having become like us: “He shall drink from the torrent on the way; therefore He shall lift up His head” (Ps. CIX). For He lifted it up while hanging on the cross; He was crucified because He once chose to drink from our torrent.

Whoever does these things for seven days—that is, throughout the whole [Col. 0514C] period—can rejoice. But he must rejoice before the Lord, not with the joy of the impious and sinners. “There is no joy [or, according to the transmitted text, ‘peace’] for the impious,” says the Lord (Isa. XLVIII), since they celebrate in pleasures and corruptions. Rather, he must rejoice in the Lord.

What does it mean to rejoice before the Lord? It means to believe in Him and to suffer for Him.

“You shall celebrate His feast for seven days each year. It shall be an everlasting ordinance throughout your generations. In the seventh month you shall celebrate the feast, and you shall dwell in shelters for seven days,” so that throughout the whole present age we may use it as a tabernacle.

Thus Hezekiah called it when he said: “My generation has departed; it has been taken away and rolled up from me like a shepherd’s tent.” For we do not ignore its passing or flowing onward while gathering riches or building [Col. 0514D] large houses. Rather, as Paul says, let us direct our attention to this: “The time is short, so that those who buy should be as though they did not buy, those who possess as though they did not possess, and those who use this world as though they did not use it; for the form of this world is passing away.”

“Everyone who is of the race of Israel shall remain in tabernacles, so that your descendants may learn that I made the children of Israel dwell in tabernacles when I brought them out of the land of Egypt. I am the Lord your God.”

Do you see that these figures and images of greater mysteries were given to the Jewish people? For this reason they were commanded to dwell in tabernacles and to celebrate the feast of tabernacles, so that they would not forget the Egyptian liberation—but this was according to the letter.

Spiritually, [Col. 0515A] however, it was so that we might remember that we have been liberated from the spiritual Egypt, that is, from the slavery of the spiritual Pharaoh, which is slavery according to the corruption of the bricks of the present age. Whoever wishes to be completely free from this must dwell in tabernacles, imitating his God, who says: “Foxes have dens, and the birds of heaven have nests; but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay His head” (Matt. VIII; Luke IX).

Everyone who is of the race of Israel shall remain there—or, according to the Septuagint, “the native-born,” that is, the truly noble person, the true Israelite, heir of Abraham, who left his country, his lineage, and his ancestral homes, and dwells in tabernacles with Isaac and Jacob, fellow heirs of the promise.

[Col. 0516A] Since the legislator wishes the true Israelite to dwell in tabernacles not merely for seven days, but signifies the whole of life through this number, the sons of Jonadab, the sons of Rechab, and what is written about them in the prophecy of Jeremiah teach us this. For it says:

“We obeyed the voice of Jonadab son of Rechab, our father, in everything that he commanded us, so that throughout all our days we did not drink wine—we, our wives, our sons, and our daughters—and we did not build houses in which to dwell. We had neither vineyard nor field nor seed, but we dwelt in tabernacles and obeyed, doing according to everything that Jonadab our father commanded us” (Jer. XXXV).

## BOOK SEVEN

[Col. 0515]

### CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0515B]

#### On the oil to be offered for preparing the lamps in the tabernacle of the Lord

**(CHAP. XXIV.)** The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “Command the children of Israel to bring you pure, clear oil of olives for preparing the lamps continually outside the veil of testimony in the tabernacle of the covenant. Aaron shall set them from evening until morning before the Lord, with perpetual observance and rite, throughout your generations. They shall always be placed upon the most pure lampstand in the presence of the Lord.”

We say that the lampstand is the evangelical manner of life, in which Christ caused virtues to shine like a lamp. For He says: “No one lights a lamp and places it under a bushel, but upon a lampstand, so that it may shine for all who are in the [Col. 0515C] house” (Matt. V).

Almsgiving is added as oil to these lamps, because fasting, virginity, prayer, righteousness, and every good action are watered and preserved unquenchable through the mercy of love for the poor. This is shown by the five lamps of the foolish virgins, who, because they possessed too little oil of love for the poor, were excluded by the bridegroom (Matt. XXV).

The oil must be of the purest olives, so that we may serve love for the poor neither from injustice nor from rapacity, nor for the sake of display. It is “of olives” when it is produced from good labors and from the resources or possessions of righteousness; these olives are rightly called shady and fruitful. It must be “clear” so that we do not give alms for human glory.

Therefore this lamp must always be lit outside the veil—namely, the body of Christ; that this is the intelligible veil [Col. 0515D] has been demonstrated through many preceding passages. It is in the tabernacle of the covenant—or, according to the Septuagint, “of the testimony”—that is, in heaven, where it is clear that God dwells.

The legislator has therefore said both things. For if He who became poor for our sake counts whatever we do for the poor as having been done for Himself, the lamps of almsgiving are rightly lit before the Lord’s body. Yet they are also lit in heaven, for there the merciful send their treasures ahead.

For this reason Aaron shall kindle it—or, according to the Septuagint, “Aaron and his sons shall kindle them.” Christ, who is the true priest, embraced compassion for the poor; and all who wish to gain adoption through Him imitate Him.

“Aaron shall set them,” or, as the [Col. 0516B] Septuagint has, “Aaron and his sons shall kindle them,” from evening until morning—that is, without ceasing. Solomon also said: “Let oil not fail from your head” (Eccles. IX), thereby showing that the lamp of almsgiving ought to be kindled continually.

And this is to be done “before the Lord,” as the Lord Himself said: “When you give alms, let your left hand not know what your right hand is doing, so that your almsgiving may be in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you” (Matt. VI).

Let us keep this law with perpetual observance and rite [Col. 0516C] throughout our generations, upon the purest lampstand—that is, the evangelical manner of life, as we have already said. For this manner of life is free from all irony and hypocrisy, since it kindles the lamps of almsgiving before the Lord and not before human beings.

Let us kindle them until morning—that is, during the present age. For when the morning of the future age has dawned, there will no longer be time for prayer and almsgiving. Solomon plainly signifies this when he says: “Do not say to your friend, ‘Go and return, and tomorrow I will give to you,’ when you can give immediately; for you do not know what the coming day may bring forth” (Prov. XXVII). That is: hasten and do not delay, lest you be led to places where you have no time to work, but must there render an account of what you have done here.

Moreover, [Col. 0516D] it is time for us to unfold the legislator’s meaning: the pure lampstand is so called because He had no sin, nor was deceit found in His mouth; it is a lampstand because He is the true light that enlightens every person coming into this world (John I).

Upon this lampstand the lamp of the Holy Spirit is kindled. For He is fiery in substance and operation; therefore He descended upon the disciples in the form of fiery tongues.

We ought to offer Him the purest oil—that is, a pure life—knowing that it is not given to everyone to kindle Him, but only to the spiritual Aaron and his sons. Christ Himself was full of the Spirit, saying: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon [Col. 0517A] me; therefore He has anointed me” (Isa. LX). The Spirit descended upon Him from heaven in the form of a dove; and He also said: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and I desire that it be kindled” (Luke XII).

By this He signified the fire of this lamp. For He Himself also handed it on to His sons when, breathing upon the apostles, He said: “Receive the Holy Spirit,” and the rest (John XX).

But this lamp is not kindled in any other way except through a pure life and a most clear, or radiant, manner of life. Whoever is not such will have the Spirit extinguished in him. For Paul did not testify without cause: “Do not extinguish the Spirit” (1 Thess. V), clearly showing that it lies with us either to kindle His operation and to extinguish it, by striving after the things through which it is kindled or by neglecting them.

### CHAPTER TWO

[Col. 0517B]

#### On providing fine flour for making the bread of the Presence
**(The same passage.)** “You shall also take fine flour and bake twelve loaves from it. Each loaf shall contain two tenths; you shall place them in two rows of six on the purest table before the Lord, and you shall put upon them the clearest frankincense, so that it may be for the bread as a memorial offering to the Lord. On every Sabbath they shall be changed before the Lord, having been received from the children of Israel as an everlasting covenant. They shall belong to Aaron and his sons, so that they may eat them in a holy place, because it is most holy, from the sacrifice of the Lord, by perpetual right.”

Remember the mystical table from which no one is commanded to take anything except the intelligible Aaron, that is, Christ. For he himself first consecrated it, and also his sons, who through him were made christs and clothed with him; yet they were commanded to eat it in a holy place. It is also the Holy of Holies, so that they may possess a special and inviolable sanctification.

Those loaves are made from two tenths, for they belong equally to God and to man, each being perfect in both. Six are placed on each side. The mystical table is placed here, and it will also be placed in the age to come. Six loaves form one arrangement, because six is a perfect number, just as the mystery itself is perfect and makes perfect those who partake of it. This visible creation was made in six days, and on the sixth day the human being was produced, for whose sake Christ prepared the mystical table.

Nevertheless, taken together, they are rightly twelve loaves, because the apostles, who were twelve in number, first ate the Lord’s supper.

**(From Adamantius.)** We may also speak in another way. Every word of God is bread, but there is a difference among breads. There is one kind of word that can be delivered to the common hearing and can teach the people about works of mercy and every form of benevolence; this is the bread that appears common. There is another kind that contains hidden things and discusses the faith of God or the knowledge of realities. This bread is pure and made from fine flour. It must always be placed in the presence of the Lord and set forth upon a clean table. It is set apart for the priests alone and granted to the sons of Aaron as an eternal gift.

But lest you think that we are recounting these things as inventions of our own understanding, rather than observing them in the divine books, I shall bring forth for you from the Scriptures how, among various men, the difference of bread was maintained according to the merit of each.

It is reported in Genesis (chapters XVIII and XIX) that the patriarch Abraham received angels as guests, and likewise Lot. But Abraham, who excelled in merit, is described as having set before them loaves made from fine flour, which he also called *eucrifias* [Greek: εὐκρυφὰς], that is, things secretly and sacredly seasoned. Lot, however, because he did not have fine flour, set before his guests loaves made from ordinary flour—not because he was so poor that he lacked fine flour, since he is described as being no less wealthy than his uncle, but because the difference between their merits is indicated by these signs.

The one to whom mysteries were to be revealed by the Lord, to whom it was said, “Shall I hide from my child Abraham what I am about to do?”—the one who was to be instructed and taught concerning the hidden and secret things of God—is described as having loaves made from fine flour. But the one to whom no sacramental mystery was entrusted, but only the account of present salvation and life, is described as having loaves made from ordinary flour alone.

You also, therefore, if you possess knowledge of secret things, if you can speak with knowledge and prudence about the faith of God, the mystery of Christ, and the unity of the Holy Spirit, will offer loaves made from fine flour to the Lord. But if you use ordinary exhortations addressed to the people, and know only how to treat the moral sense that belongs to everyone, know that you have offered common bread.

Let us now see how these loaves of the Presence, which are always commanded to be placed before the Lord, are made. “Let one loaf be made from two tenths,” he says. He mentions two tenths, but does not explain of what measure these tenths are. Yet surely, if he wished the quantity of the fine flour to be understood, it would have followed that he should name the measure of which he commanded two tenths to be taken.

What, then, is this thing whose measure and extent could neither be comprehended nor named? The number ten is found to be perfect everywhere, for the reckoning and origin of the whole number arise from it. Appropriately, therefore, God, the author and origin of all things, appears to be indicated under this number.

Now, if in the Church I speak only about the Father and proclaim the praises of the Father alone, I have made the bread of one tenth. Or if I speak only about Christ, enumerate his passion, and proclaim his resurrection, I have offered the bread of one tenth.

But if I say that the Father is always with his Son and that he himself performs his works; or if I say that the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father, that whoever sees the Son also sees the Father, and that the Father and the Son are one, then from two tenths of pure fine flour I have offered one loaf—the true bread that gives life to this world (John VI).

Heretics do not make one loaf from two tenths. For they deny that the Creator God is the Father of Christ, nor do they make the Old and New Testament one loaf and confess one Father in both instruments. We, however, say that one and the same Holy Spirit is present in the Law and in the Gospels, and in this way also we offer one loaf of the Presence from two tenths.

Those, therefore, who separate Christ from God the Father, his Creator—the heretics—and the Jews, who receive the Father alone but do not receive his Word and Wisdom, Christ, do not make one loaf from two tenths.

We, however, cannot comprehend or discover the name or account of the measure itself, that is, of the substance. Yet while confessing the Father and the Son, we make one loaf from two tenths—not so that one loaf should be made from one tenth and another from the other, with the two tenths remaining separate, but so that these two tenths may be one mass and one loaf.

How do two tenths become one mass? Because I do not separate the Son from the Father, nor the Father from the Son: “Whoever sees me,” he says, “sees also the Father” (John XIV). Thus each loaf is made from two tenths, and they are presented in two arrangements, that is, in two rows.

For if there were one arrangement, the word concerning the Father and the Son would be confused and mingled. But now there is one loaf—for there is one will and one substance—yet there are two arrangements, that is, two distinct properties of persons. We say that the Father is the one who is not the Son, and that the Son is the one who is not the Father. In this way we preserve two tenths in one loaf and confess two arrangements before the Lord.

But truly, to preserve these measures carefully and to balance the discourse concerning the Father and the Son—joining them where it is fitting and separating them again where appropriate, so that neither do the two measures ever disappear nor does the one loaf ever cease to appear—is, so to speak, the work of a great and highly skilled painter.

Twelve loaves, therefore, are commanded to be made from this fine flour, according to the number of the tribes that at that time constituted carnal Israel. In this I believe the form of the whole rational nature to be contained. For there are thought to be twelve general orders of rational creation, whose figure was represented in those twelve tribes.

One order was royal, called Judah. Another was sacerdotal, called Levi. There was also another order neighboring Judah, called Benjamin; in this order the temple of God and the altar were placed. There was another order of Issachar and Zebulun and Ephraim, and others whom divine Scripture designates by name. It is not appropriate to explain their meaning at the present time.

There is a loaf before the Lord for each tribe or order. Although there may be a tribe descended from Israel not from a free woman but from a concubine, and therefore partly free and partly servile, nevertheless a loaf made from two tenths is presented before the Lord on behalf of all, and throughout the whole arrangement the two tenths of fine flour remain.

They are commanded to be presented before the Lord on a clean table. Who among us possesses such a clean table that loaves may be offered upon it to the Lord? In this person’s heart, in this person’s mind, loaves are offered to the Lord.

If you sit down to eat intelligibly at the table of this powerful person, understand what is set before you (Proverbs XXIII)—that is, attend spiritually to what is spoken by him, so that you too may be able to do what is added. For he says: “Knowing that you must prepare such things.”

Upon these loaves the clearest frankincense is placed—or, according to the Septuagint, also salt, but frankincense first. Frankincense signifies thanksgiving, that is, the offering that holds the chief place in the Lord’s supper—not only because it is sacrificed to God, but also because, as physicians say, it heals many disorders of the eyes.

Salt signifies the teaching of the apostles, to whom it is said: “You are the salt of the earth” (Matthew V). In many places the apostles themselves and their teaching are rightly placed upon the mystical table, because just as the Lord handed on to them the communion of the divine supper, so they handed it on to us.

The twelve loaves on the table of the tabernacle are therefore the twelve apostles, together with all their followers in the Church. Since they do not cease to nourish the people of God with the food of the word until the consummation of the age, the twelve loaves of the Presence never depart from the table of the Lord.

And rightly these same loaves are commanded to be made not from ordinary flour but from fine flour, because whoever ministers the word of life to others must first devote himself to the fruits of virtue, so that what he urges by preaching he may also commend by doing.

It is also fitting that these loaves are commanded to be placed six on each side of the table, on account of the harmony of charity and fellowship. For the Lord is also said to have sent his disciples to preach two by two, figuratively indicating that holy teachers never differ from one another either in their assertion of truth or in the affection of love.

The clearest frankincense is also placed upon the loaves as a memorial of the Lord’s offering, when prayer is purely added to the devout action and teaching of the saints. By these two things being rightly joined, the memory of the sacred offering may always appear in the presence of the supreme Judge.

The loaves are rightly commanded to be changed before the Lord every Sabbath. The loaves had been placed upon the Lord’s table while work was being done for six days; on the Sabbath they are changed for new ones, when each teacher of the holy Church, having completed the period of his holy labor, is rewarded with eternal rest in heaven and leaves others after him to labor at the same work of preaching the word, under the same hope of reward.

According to Josephus, the loaves were baked before the Sabbath, two and two separately, and on the morning of the Sabbath they were offered and placed upon the sacred table, six on each side and turned toward one another. Two golden dishes filled with frankincense were placed above them; these remained until the next Sabbath, when other loaves were brought in their place. The former loaves were given to the priests, and after the frankincense had been burned in the sacred fire in which all the burnt offerings were made, additional frankincense was placed upon the other loaves.

The loaves were therefore placed on the Lord’s table on the Sabbath with this intention: that, once the Sabbath had passed, they should remain there through seven days of labor, and, when these too had passed and another Sabbath arrived, they should be consumed as nourishment by the high priest and his sons. For at the beginning of our life devoted to God, rest and eternal life are promised to us, but on this condition: that we must reach them through the labors and works of a good temporal life.

**(From Hesychius.)** He commanded that Aaron and his sons alone should partake of this food, and that they should eat it not everywhere but in a holy place. Let the holy place for us be, first, the court of God, and then our bodies, when they are clean from pollutions, so that these words of Paul may also apply to us: “The temple of God is holy, which you are.”

Moreover, raising its glory and exalting the dignity of the mystery, he added: “It is most holy, from the sacrifice of the Lord, by perpetual right.” Therefore prayer is holy, the reading of divine Scripture is holy, and the hearing of its interpretation is holy. In short, everything that is said and done in the Churches of God according to his law is holy.

But the Holy of Holies from the sacrifice of the Lord—that is, from everything offered and done for his glory—is the table that Christ sets forth from his own sacrifice.

## CHAPTER III. On the blasphemer, and how he was condemned to death by the Lord’s command

**(The same passage.)** “Then the son of an Israelite woman went out. She had borne him to an Egyptian man, and he quarreled in the camp with an Israelite man. When he had blasphemed the name of the Lord and cursed him, he was brought to Moses. His mother was called Salamith, daughter of Dabri, of the tribe of Dan. They put him in custody until they might know what the Lord would command. Then he spoke to Moses, saying: ‘Bring the blasphemer outside the camp, and let all who heard him place their hands upon his head; then let the whole assembly stone him.’”

**(From Adamantius.)** Scripture has set before us two men who were quarreling: one entirely an Israelite, who did indeed quarrel but did not sin; the other, whose sin it identifies, it indicates to be largely of Egyptian descent, against whom the Israelite is quarreling—and perhaps he is quarreling appropriately and reasonably.

For in Exodus also the Israelite prevails and the Egyptian falls. Therefore, if today I defend the truth and struggle on behalf of the ecclesiastical faith against one who partly believes in Christ and receives the Scriptures but does not receive their meaning wholly or faithfully, I am quarreling against the same kind of person: one who is Israelite by his mother but Egyptian by his father.

If someone is Christian and Catholic both in the faith he believes and in his profession of the name, he is an Israelite on both sides. But whoever is Christian in profession and heretical and perverse in his understanding of the faith has an Israelite mother but an Egyptian father.

How does this happen? When someone reads the Scriptures, follows the letter but rejects the spiritual understanding, he has an Israelite mother—that is, the letter—but because he does not follow the spiritual sense and instead follows the carnal sense, that Egyptian is his father. Therefore he quarrels against the Catholic, who is an Israelite on both sides: an Israelite according to the letter, but not an Israelite according to the spirit. Thus according to the letter he is an Israelite, but according to the spirit he is an Egyptian.

What, then, is necessary for the two who are quarreling? The one who follows the carnal sense, as though deriving his ancestry from Egypt, names and curses the Name. For he names the name of God while cursing it: he denies that God is the Creator and denies that he is the Father of Christ.

We, however, who are Israelites from both lines, defend both the letter and the spirit in the holy Scriptures, and quarrel against those who appear to be Israelites only in part. We say that one must neither curse according to the letter nor blaspheme according to the spiritual understanding. For by the judgment of the apostle Paul, the one who curses is excluded from the kingdom of God—not only one who curses God but also one who curses his neighbor.

See how the Apostle says: “Do not be deceived: neither fornicators, nor adulterers, nor the effeminate, nor those who lie with males, nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor the cursing will possess the kingdom of God” (1 Corinthians VI).

Observe among what crimes—among adulterers, those who lie with males, and the greedy, whom he elsewhere says serve idols—he also placed those who curse, and excluded them equally with the others from the kingdom of God.

Let those therefore consider who almost by daily habit accustom their mouths to this vice what danger threatens them. Thinking that this is a light and easy sin, they do not easily guard against it. But let them consider the Apostle, how he excludes the one who curses from the kingdom of God, and how God through Moses commands the one who curses to be punished.

I have therefore been greatly astonished that in this passage of Scripture which we have before us it did not expressly identify the one of Egyptian descent as having cursed God, but merely said that, while naming him, he cursed, leaving it uncertain whether he cursed God or a human being.

It seems to me that for this reason it did not wish to state expressly that he cursed God: lest it appear to have granted license to curse human beings as well. Thus it remained silent about whether the curse was directed against God or man, so that both might be avoided.

But since we have brought forward the Apostle’s sentence that those who curse are to be excluded from the kingdom of God, this passage demands some word of consolation, lest we seem altogether to impose despair upon those who are carried away by an almost daily habit of cursing and neglect to place a guard or door upon their mouths.

The form of the future promise is not one and the same, nor is its appearance simple. The Lord himself taught this in the Gospel when he calls the poor in spirit blessed and affirms that the kingdom of heaven belongs to them; then he calls the meek blessed, yet promises them not the kingdom of heaven but the inheritance of the earth. He calls the peacemakers blessed, but he does not grant them the kingdom of heaven either; nevertheless he declares that they are sons of God.

Although he promises different things to different people, he calls all blessed who attain the promises; yet he has not granted the kingdom of heaven to all.

It can therefore happen that someone is corrected and perfected in other works and actions, yet is overtaken by a fault of the mouth and a lapse in speech. Even if, according to the Apostle’s sentence, the kingdom of heaven is denied to such a person, he is not thereby cut off from a place among the other blessed. Nevertheless, the more perfect someone is in other matters, the more he must also labor in this matter, lest the creeping fault of an evil habit deprive him of the kingdom of heaven, which is the summit of all blessedness—although the Lord said: “In my Father’s house are many dwelling places” (John XIV).

We may also add that the nature of sin resembles material consumed by fire. The apostle Paul says that sinners build wood, hay, and straw upon Christ’s foundation (1 Corinthians III).

In this he clearly shows that some sins are so light that they may be compared with straw, upon which fire cannot long remain. Others resemble hay, which fire also consumes without difficulty, though it remains there somewhat longer than upon straw. Others are compared with wood, in which, according to the quality of the crimes, the fire finds abundant and prolonged fuel.

Thus each sin pays a just penalty according to its quality or magnitude.

Yet what need is there for the faithful and for those who have known God to think about the different qualities of punishments? Why should we place wood, hay, or even straw upon Christ’s foundation? Why do we not instead place gold, silver, and precious stones upon the precious foundation, so that when fire comes it may find nothing to consume?

For if it comes upon straw, it will make ashes and cinders from the straw; but if it comes upon gold, it will make the gold purer.

Let these words be understood as spoken for those who neglect to cut away the habit of cursing with their mouths. Even if they do not curse from the heart, even if they do not utter curses with deliberate intention or an evil purpose, they nevertheless incur uncleanness of lips and pollution of the mouth, according to the word of Isaiah (Isaiah VI).

This man, however, although he had an Israelite mother, was nevertheless born from an Egyptian father. He went out and, naming the Name, cursed. I think that if he had not gone out, he would not have quarreled against the true Israelite or, while naming the Name, cursed.

For he went out from the truth, from the fear of God, from faith, and from charity, as we said above.

If someone goes out from these things and thus goes out from the camp of the Church, even if he is not expelled by the voice of a bishop—as, conversely, it sometimes happens that someone is driven out and sent outside through the mistaken judgment of those who govern the Church—yet if he himself did not go out beforehand, that is, if he did not act in such a way as to deserve to go out, he suffers no harm from appearing to have been expelled by human beings through an unjust judgment.

Thus it sometimes happens that the one who is sent outside is inside, while the one who appears to be retained within is outside.

**(From Hesychius.)** It is therefore not right for the Israelite woman—that is, the wisdom of spiritual Scripture—to unite with external wisdom, so that she becomes subject to it and the one born from them, namely the one taught by both, becomes not only the son of an Israelite woman but also the son of Egypt, since he understands Egyptian things, joins himself to external wisdom, and wishes to maintain the doctrines that come from there.
