If this should ever happen, and someone of this kind should be found among the sons of intelligible, faithful Israel in the camp—which is the Church, as Jacob, seeing it figuratively in a dream, said, “These are the camps of God” (Genesis XXXII)—and if one who is of the Israelite woman and an Israelite should quarrel, then the one who is great and pure, who has given himself wholly to the wisdom of God and says, as Paul says, “We speak wisdom among the mature, but not the wisdom of this world or of the rulers of this age, who are being destroyed” (1 Corinthians II), may quarrel with him over words or doctrines.

If the son of the Israelite woman blasphemes the Name—for this happens when one who has been harmed by external wisdom makes mention of Christ—observe how the lawgiver, following an exceedingly subtle distinction, says, “When he had blasphemed the Name.” He does not say what name it was, because at the time when this was enacted it was not yet known: the one who was incarnate from the Virgin and the Holy Spirit had not yet been born. Of him Gabriel said, “You shall call his name Jesus, for he himself will save his people from their sins” (Luke I).

But Paul, showing how great this Name is, said: “God gave him the name above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Philippians II).

When, therefore, the one who trusts in and attends to external wisdom—which calls the small great and the greatest, and seeks degrees where this is impossible—blasphemes the Name of Christ, he is blaspheming the Son by saying that he is lesser than the Father. He must necessarily be expelled outside the camp and led out from the Church.

Those who heard him shall place their hands upon his head, indicating through the head that Christ is the head of man and God is the head of Christ, because whoever blasphemes the Son blasphemes the Father in him.

The entire people stoned him—that is, they killed and destroyed the one who had blasphemed. But it is also worth noting the words of this enactment: how they brought him to Moses.

Moses does not act on his own authority or pronounce a sentence against him. Rather, he placed him in custody so that he might judge the matter by the command of the Lord. What command? The command of those who say: “Whoever does not believe in the Son has already been judged” (John III); and again: “If you do not believe that I am he, you will die in your sins” (John VIII), along with many other such statements made in the evangelical commandments.

The text continues:

“You shall speak to the children of Israel: Whoever curses his God shall bear his sin; and whoever blasphemes the name of the Lord shall surely be put to death. The whole assembly shall stone him to death, whether he is a citizen or a resident alien. Whoever blasphemes the name of the Lord shall surely be put to death.”

Here there is something new that troubles the ears of many. According to the edition of the Septuagint, he commanded as follows: “Any man, any one who curses God shall receive sin; but whoever names the name of the Lord shall surely be put to death.”

To name the name of the Lord while blaspheming God is the more serious offense. The former merely receives sin, but the latter also suffers the punishment of death.

What difference is there between the Lord and God? Is he not the very one who said: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one Lord”; and again: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart”? How, then, does the one who curses God receive sin, while the one who names the name of the Lord die?

Or for what reason is the one who names the name of the Lord subjected to punishment at all? For you will find Isaiah rejoicing in this and saying: “Lord, apart from you we know no other; we name your name.”

What, then, is the name of the Lord which, when someone names it, causes him to fall under a curse and the punishment of death? If the lawgiver is now speaking of some hidden name unknown to us, a name not revealed in sacred Scripture, how could anyone name what he has not learned and cannot bring forth publicly?

But observe what God made known to us through Moses. When the Lord descended in a cloud, he stood with Moses, who invoked the name of the Lord. As he passed before him, he said: “Lord, Lord God, ruler, merciful and gracious” (Exodus XXXIV).

He would not have revealed this to us if he had wished us not to name it.

But through the present passage the lawgiver demonstrates something else. He means that the blasphemy which someone commits knowingly is subject to the greatest punishment and is not pardonable. He says openly what the Lord says in the Gospels: “Every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven to human beings, but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come” (Matthew XII).

He calls the blasphemy of the Spirit that which is committed with knowledge of God, since knowledge is especially the gift of the Spirit, so that Paul said: “To one is given through the Spirit a word of wisdom, and to another a word of knowledge” (1 Corinthians XII).

Accordingly, you now understand that the one who blasphemes God without knowledge curses him. For this reason Symmachus did not write “blaspheme,” as in the case of the son of the Israelite woman, but “revile.” He says: “A man who reviles his God.”

This especially demonstrates that through excessive ignorance he speaks about God those things that he knows concerning a human being, things in which reviling has a place. Nevertheless, even so he receives sin, because when he ought to possess knowledge, he does not possess it.

But by “naming the name of the Lord” he means the one who blasphemes knowingly. Those who have sought his knowledge through the Spirit properly name the Lord. For no one can say, “Lord Jesus,” as Paul says, except in the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians XII).

Since they blaspheme knowingly, they are rightly without pardon, whether they received knowledge from their fathers and are therefore called citizens, or whether they have learned it recently and are therefore resident aliens.

When they name the name of the Lord, they will rightly die—that is, when they both name and blaspheme. For you see that the son of the Israelite woman, because he named the Name and blasphemed, brought punishment upon himself.

In this enactment also, what appears doubtful is made clearer by Aquila. He says: “When a man blasphemes his God, he shall incur iniquity; and he who explicitly names the name of the Lord shall surely die.”

He did not say “naming,” but “denominating,” so as to show that the man about whom the present passage speaks both blasphemes and names the Name.

Therefore the lawgiver commanded that the one who blasphemes and names the name of the Lord—that is, the Spirit, for Paul says, “The Lord is the Spirit” (2 Corinthians III)—should die and be killed. This is the one who blasphemes knowingly, as we have said once already.

## CHAPTER IV. On the law of retaliation for striking or killing one’s neighbor

**(The same passage.)** “Whoever strikes and kills a human being shall surely be put to death. Whoever strikes an animal shall make restitution, life for life. Whoever inflicts a blemish upon any of his fellow citizens, as he has done, so shall it be done to him: fracture for fracture, eye for eye, tooth for tooth. Whatever blemish he inflicted, he shall be compelled to suffer the same. Whoever strikes an animal shall repay another. Whoever strikes a human being shall be punished. Let there be equal judgment among you, whether resident alien or citizen has sinned, because I am the Lord your God.”

“Whoever strikes and kills a human being”—or, according to the Septuagint, “Whoever strikes the soul of a human being shall surely be put to death.”

Who strikes the soul of a human being except the one who entices him to impiety, who draws him into blasphemous words, in which he earns the worst death of sin, which is the true death of the soul? For this reason he commanded that the one who is such should die the death.

Yet by saying “the soul of a human being,” he especially means an animal-like human being, that is, one who cannot understand the things of the Spirit. Paul says of him: “The natural person does not receive the things of the Spirit” (1 Corinthians II). For folly is involved for him, and he cannot understand that he is being spiritually deprived of life. Whoever strikes such a person shall surely be put to death.

But if he strikes an animal—that is, one who lives like cattle, of whom David says, “A human being, when he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared with senseless beasts and became like them” (Psalm XLVIII)—he shall make restitution, life for life.

For merely because he caused a sinner or an ordinary person, lacking subtle discernment concerning God, to go astray, he is not entirely deserving of pardon. But if he did not strike him in such a way as to lead him completely into impiety and make him entirely go astray from God, yet said or did certain things to him and inflicted upon him a blemish of sin, he will likewise suffer punishment according to this.

He says: “Whoever inflicts a blemish upon any of his fellow citizens, as he has done, so shall it be done to him: fracture for fracture,” or, according to the Septuagint, “crushing for crushing”; “eye for eye, tooth for tooth.”

Whether he crushed the virtue possessed by a fellow citizen or neighbor by teaching evil, persuading, causing scandal, reviling, or slandering; whether by any of these actions he blinded his eye—that is, his knowledge—or knocked out his tooth, that is, the power of his words—for Scripture customarily understands teeth as words, as David shows when he says, “The teeth of human beings are weapons and arrows, and their tongue is a sharp sword” (Psalm LVI); and the patriarch Jacob said of Christ in his blessings, “His eyes are more beautiful than wine, and his teeth whiter than milk” (Genesis XLIX), for Christ’s clear and manifest evangelical words are superior to legal milk—then, necessarily, whoever harms another in any of the things mentioned will himself suffer a similar blemish in the future judgment.

If he harmed or crushed another’s virtue, his own will be crushed. If he obscured another’s knowledge, his own knowledge will be counted as nothing. If he harmed another’s teaching, the Judge will render his own words fruitless and useless.

For this reason Paul also said: “The one who troubles you will bear the judgment, whoever he may be” (Galatians V)—whether small or great, whether possessing much knowledge or little, whether he has learned it recently or long ago, whether he is a citizen by faith or a resident alien.

Since these things are so, the sanction of the letter was necessary for the Jews, because they were unable to hear: “If anyone strikes you on your right cheek, turn to him the other also” (Matthew V).

But since they were malicious, each person would demand this from his neighbor and would not do it himself. Therefore they were rightly told to give eye for eye and tooth for tooth, so that fear of reciprocal punishment might restrain them from violence and homicide.

The text continues:

“Moses spoke to the children of Israel, and they brought the one who had blasphemed outside the camp. They stoned him, and the children of Israel did as the Lord had commanded Moses.”

We have now heard how he brought the one who had blasphemed outside the camp and commanded that he be crushed with stones. Therefore he added deed to indignation and showed you the law confirmed by the experience itself, so that you too might fear to blaspheme God and flee that sin, recognizing its magnitude, since he commands not only the leaders but the whole assembly to avenge it.

The struggle against blasphemers ought to be shared by all, because they attempt to revile our common benefactor and the source of our common life, from whom we all have both existence and well-being. They do no harm to his glory, but they wish to separate us from him and drive us away.

## CHAPTER V. On the rest of the seventh year after entering the holy land
## Chapter XXV

And the Lord spoke to Moses on Mount Sinai, saying: Speak to the children of Israel, and say to them: When you enter the land that I shall give you, let the land keep a sabbath to the Lord. For six years you shall sow your field, and for six years you shall prune your vineyard and gather its fruits; but in the seventh year there shall be a sabbath of rest for the land, a sabbath of the Lord. You shall not sow your field, nor prune your vineyard. You shall not harvest what the ground produces of itself, nor gather the grapes of your firstfruits as a vintage; for it is a year of rest for the land. But these things shall be food for you: for you, your male and female servants, your hired worker, and the sojourner who dwells with you. For your cattle and livestock, everything that grows shall provide food. [Col. 0527D]

The land which it has pleased God to give us, and which it is advantageous for us to receive, is the land from which we can seek true life—that is, a good way of life according to his law and the commandments he has given us. Of this David says: “Teach me to do your will, for you are my God; your holy Spirit will lead me in a straight land” (Psalm 142).

If we enter this land, we can sow our field for six years, prune the vineyard, and gather the fruits that grow in it—that is, so long as we are in this life and in this visible creation, which the number six rightly signifies, because all visible things were established in six days. [Col. 0528A]

But in the seventh year there shall be a sabbath and rest for the land. When our intelligible sabbath arrives—that is, the rest of the present age, of which Paul says, “Therefore a sabbath-rest remains for the people of God” (Hebrews 4)—the seventh day signifies it, because on the seventh day God rested from all his works, namely, the visible works. Therefore it is not then the time for activity. Consequently, at that time we can neither sow the field of the Law nor prune the evangelical vineyard. [Col. 0528B]

The field is rightly understood by us as the Law, since the elder son, who is jealous of the younger people and bears the image of the Jewish people, is said to return from the field—that is, from the practice of the Law. The vineyard, without any doubt, is preaching the Gospel, for Christ gave it its occasion and substance when he said: “I am the vine, and you are the branches, and my Father is the cultivator” (John 15).

Therefore, after our departure from this life, or our passage beyond it, we shall not be able to cultivate either the legal or the evangelical commandments. Nor shall we harvest what grows of itself—that is, anything that the natural law suggests for human action. This is what grows spontaneously, because apart from the study of books and every form of instruction, it suggests and urges what is useful and supplies us with thoughts that assist the soul.

Nor shall we then need to harvest the grapes of the firstfruits, or, according to the Septuagint, the grape of sanctification. Those who have been initiated into the mysteries of Christ know what the grape of sanctification is.

“But these things shall be food for you: for you, your male servant, your female servant, your hired worker, and the sojourner who dwells with you, your cattle and your livestock.” [Col. 0528C] Whatever we accomplish now, we shall receive the fruit of it there. The saying of the Psalm will apply to us: “Blessed are all who fear the Lord: you shall eat the labors of your hands; blessed are you, and it shall be well with you” (Psalm 127).

For he describes the blessedness of the coming age, in which it is blessed to find food: “Blessed,” he says, “is the one who will eat bread in the kingdom of heaven” (Luke 14).

It is much more blessed, however, to have male and female servants, hired workers, and sojourners, cattle and livestock—or, according to the Septuagint, beasts. These are various classes of those who provide discipleship for us in the holy way of life before God.

The male and female servants are all who have submitted themselves to us for discipleship, or who have been bought by us from an external servitude. Our hired workers are those whom we have invited, but who are not so subject that they are called male and female servants. The sojourners—or, according to the Septuagint, resident aliens—are those who dwell alongside us. The text does not say “the resident aliens,” but “the resident alien who dwells alongside you.” These are all who, in this life, are like resident aliens through philosophy; yet they do not dwell alongside external things but alongside us, who have entered the good land, possess it, and possess what belongs to it. [Col. 0528D]

If we help some ordinary or common person, these are the cattle. Moreover, if we cause some unbeliever or ungodly person—properly called livestock, or, according to the Septuagint, tame beasts—to leave the forests and come into our land, these too are included.

According to the edition of the Septuagint, where it reads, “When you enter the land that I shall give you, and the land that I shall give you keeps sabbaths to the Lord: for six years you shall sow your field, and for six years you shall prune your vineyard and gather its fruit. But in the seventh year there shall be a sabbath, a rest for the land, a sabbath to the Lord”:

### From Augustine

It is asked how we should understand the passage: “When you enter the land that I shall give you, and the land rests, for six years you shall sow your field,” and so forth—as though the command were to be carried out when the land had already rested, whereas the land rests precisely because this command is carried out.

He clearly wishes the land’s rest to be understood as occurring in the seventh year, in which he commanded that no one work it through agriculture. But a very long hyperbaton creates obscurity in this meaning. The order of the words therefore seems to be:

“When you enter the land that I shall give you, and the land that I shall give you keeps sabbaths to the Lord, you shall not harvest what grows of itself in your field, nor gather the grape of your sanctification; it shall be a year for the land to rest. And the sabbaths of the land shall be food for you, your male servant, your female servant, your hired worker, and the resident alien who dwells alongside you, and for your livestock and the beasts that are in your land: everything that grows from it shall be food.” [Col. 0529A]

He then inserted an explanation of how the land rests, saying: “For six years you shall sow your field, and for six years you shall prune your vine and gather its fruit. But in the seventh year there shall be sabbaths, a rest for the land, sabbaths to the Lord. You shall not sow your field, and you shall not prune your vine.”

By saying “you shall not prune,” we must understand that every kind of cultivation is prohibited in that year. For if it is not to be pruned, neither is it to be plowed, supported with props, or subjected to anything else belonging to its cultivation. But just as a part is often used to signify the whole, so all cultivation is signified by pruning. And by “field” and “vineyard,” since he prohibits sowing the one and pruning the other, every kind of field must be understood. For nothing is to be done in an olive grove or in a field of any other kind, although these were not mentioned. [Col. 0529B]

When he says, “And the sabbaths of the land shall be food for you, your male servant, your female servant,” and so forth, he makes the matter sufficiently clear. He does not prohibit the owner of the field from eating what grows spontaneously that year without cultivation; rather, he prohibits him from gathering the fruit for storage.

Thus he is permitted to take something from it as food, as one does while passing through: he may take only what he immediately consumes by eating, not what he stores for later use. [Col. 0529C] [Col. 0529D]

## Chapter VI. On the observance of the Jubilee and its laws

### The same context

You shall count seven weeks of years for yourself—that is, seven times seven—which together make forty-nine years. And you shall sound the trumpet in the seventh month, on the tenth day of the month, at the time of atonement, throughout all your land. You shall sanctify the fiftieth year and proclaim release to all the inhabitants of your land; for it is the Jubilee. Each person shall return to his property, and each shall return to his former family, because it is the Jubilee, the fiftieth year.

You shall not sow, nor harvest what grows spontaneously in the field, nor gather the firstfruits of the vintage, because of the sanctification of the Jubilee; rather, you shall eat it as soon as it is brought forth. In the year of the Jubilee everyone shall return to his property.

Here the Jews should be questioned: If the legislator, as they themselves say, honored the seventh day and commanded that it be kept free from agricultural and similar works, why did he also command that work cease in the fiftieth year? If the weeks of weeks are counted as forty-nine years, it was not necessary for the fiftieth to be kept free—unless perhaps it signified something and the Law was expounding mysteries that it was not yet time to disclose openly because of the weakness of its hearers. [Col. 0530A]

Now hear what these mysteries are. God introduces a twofold consummation of all visible things: one belonging to each of us individually, and another common to the human race and to those things themselves that constitute the present way of life.

God also indicates when each of these will occur, and he does so very knowingly in these and the preceding words. In the preceding passage he suggests the end of each individual; in this passage he signifies the consummation of the entire human race and of the visible world. [Col. 0530B]

“You shall count seven weeks of years for yourself,” or, according to the Septuagint, “You shall count seven sabbaths of years for yourself.” The other interpreters rendered *sabbata* as “rests.” What does this mean?

He says seven weeks of years, seven times, and these are seven weeks of years—forty-nine years. Since the entire human age is divided into a week of days, when this same age has been multiplied within itself and the whole cycle of the age has been completed—the period whose duration the Creator determined—it reaches its end after turning through its full course. [Col. 0530C]

Therefore that end of the time of the weeks is rightly called the forty-ninth year. But the following fiftieth year must also succeed it, as the legislator says here, and in it the resurrection of the dead takes place.

After the end comes the resurrection. Paul says how and in what manner it will occur, and the legislator likewise adds the same teaching in the words before us. He says: “And you shall sound the trumpet in the seventh month throughout all your land,” signifying the trumpet of which Paul writes to the Thessalonians: “For the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the trumpet of God; and the dead who are in Christ will rise incorruptible” (1 Thessalonians 4). The trumpet that raises the dead must precede the resurrection. [Col. 0530D]

Therefore, in the forty-ninth year—the year in which, as we have said, the common consummation takes place—he commands that the trumpet be sounded. “In the seventh month, on the tenth day of the month, at the time of atonement, you shall sound the trumpet throughout all your land.” He rightly gives this command, making the matter clear through the atonement: because of God’s goodness toward us and his mercy toward the whole human race, he administers the mystery of the common resurrection, showing mercy to Adam, who was commanded to return to the earth because of his disobedience.

If God had not had mercy and been reconciled, he would not have freed Adam from earthly corruption. He says “throughout all the land” because the resurrection will belong to the whole human race.

By the seventh month and the tenth day, he understands the one who accomplished these things, namely Christ. For he came in the seventh month of the age of the world. We call the first month the period that was in paradise; the second, the period up to the Flood; the third, up to Abraham; the fourth, up to the time when the descent into Egypt occurred; the fifth, up to the captivity in Babylon; the sixth, up to the advent of Christ; and the seventh, the advent of the Lord himself. [Col. 0531A]

Even if these ages do not all have an exact distinction from one another, they nevertheless have signs of the times, like months. He adds the tenth day because of imperfection, for ten is the perfect number. Christ accomplished our atonement through the cross and his Passion. Therefore the sheep that Moses commanded to be sacrificed was also commanded to be perfect and to be set apart on the tenth day, bearing the image of the one about whom we are now speaking. [Col. 0531B]

What else did he add?

“You shall sanctify the fiftieth year and proclaim release to all the inhabitants of your land.” The Septuagint adds: “This year of release shall be a sign for you, and it shall be sanctified.” That is, await it in holiness and think holy thoughts about it. Correct your sanctity within it, remembering the one who said: “Pursue peace with all people, and holiness, without which no one will see God.”

Let us also proclaim release to all who are on the earth from the sentence pronounced against us on account of Adam. This is what the passage signifies. The resurrection of the dead is a sign of Christ’s victory, through which he conquered the enemy, subjected all things to himself, and destroyed death, as Paul says: “For he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet. The last enemy to be destroyed is death” (1 Corinthians 15). [Col. 0531C]

This signification is brought about through evangelical preaching. When Christ came, he signified and proclaimed it. Then each person will return to his property, and everyone will return to his former family—or, according to the Septuagint, to his former homeland.

Our property is the acquisition [source: *indemptio*; corrected reading: *adeptio*] and possession of the coming age, because we shall possess it not temporarily but forever. It is not sometimes this possession and sometimes that one; it is always the same firm possession, one that cannot be taken away. Of it the Lord said: “Store up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust corrupts, and where thieves do not break in and steal” (Matthew 6). [Col. 0531D]

But we return to our former family—or, according to the Septuagint, we shall go to our homeland. There is a clear homeland, or family, of those who love hospitality, over which Abraham presides; a clear homeland of the chaste, whose leader is Joseph; and a clear homeland of the zealous, in which Elijah holds primacy.

We receive the inheritance of these when the release from the things of this life and the signification of victory over death have been accomplished—in the fiftieth year, which follows the week of weeks, that is, after the common end, as has already been shown.

Then no one can sow or harvest what grows spontaneously in the field, nor gather the firstfruits of the vintage. For it is not then the time for us to acquire any holiness through activity—holiness which we did not acquire in this life—but to enjoy what we accomplished here.

It follows:

When you sell anything to your fellow citizen or buy it from him, do not oppress your brother. Buy from him according to the number of years of the Jubilee, and let him sell to you according to the reckoning of the crops. The more years remain after the Jubilee, the greater the price shall be; and the fewer years you count, the lower the purchase price shall be, for he is selling you the time of the crops. Do not afflict your fellow countrymen, but let each person fear his God, for I am the Lord your God.

That there is a kind of sale whose transaction takes place without silver, Isaiah clearly taught us when he said: “All you who thirst, come to the waters; and you who have no silver, hasten, buy, and eat” (Isaiah 55). [Col. 0532A]

For this reason Peter spoke as follows when condemning Simon: “May your silver perish with you, because you thought that the gift of God could be possessed with money.” What is good and truly blessed is spiritual; yet its possession is not something that may rightly be acquired with money.

The Law now proposes such a spiritual sale and possession. For it says: “When you sell anything to your fellow citizen or buy it from him”—that is, some teaching—or “when you give or receive,” that is, when you teach or are taught. This is the good possession that leads onward to possession of the coming age.

He appropriately joined the two phrases: “When you sell anything to your fellow citizen or buy it from him.” For wealth is reciprocal, and possession is reciprocal, between disciples and teachers. Paul demonstrates this when he writes to the Corinthians: “You are our glory, just as we are yours, on the day of our Lord Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 1). [Col. 0532B]

Therefore, a person must not oppress his brother—that is, we must not impose upon disciples what exceeds their strength, but only what is possible for them: virginity for one to whom virginity is possible, namely the person of whom Paul says: “He who has stood firm in his heart, not being under compulsion, but having authority over his own will, and has determined in his heart to keep his virgin unmarried” (1 Corinthians 7). [Col. 0532C]

Marriage should be given to one who cannot contain the word of virginity. For Paul also says: “He who gives his virgin in marriage does well, and he who does not give her in marriage will do better.” And again: “But if anyone thinks that he is behaving improperly toward his virgin because she is past the bloom of youth, and it ought to be so, let him do what he wishes; he does not sin—let her marry.” And again: “It is better to marry than to burn.”

The same applies to every virtue: God himself requires from each person what is according to that person’s ability, and he wishes us to serve one another in these matters. Thus he reproved the Pharisees for imposing burdensome commands on others, saying: “They bind heavy and unbearable burdens and lay them on people’s shoulders” (Matthew 23). [Col. 0532D]

The legislator therefore very appropriately adds: “But according to the number of years of the Jubilee you shall buy from him,” or, according to the Septuagint, “According to the number of years after the signification you shall possess from your neighbor.” By “signification” he understands, as has already been said, the advent of the Lord and the evangelical preaching concerning him, which signifies to us the future victory over death and the rest of the coming age.

From the time this signification occurs, no one bears a harsh yoke or carries a heavy burden. Rather, he acts according to the number of years—that is, according to his own virtue—for years reveal a person’s age, from which it becomes evident what he can do according to the body. [Col. 0533A]

Explaining this further, he adds: “According to the reckoning of the crops he shall sell to you.” In proportion to the ability he has to work and bear fruit, the disciple should return fruit to the teacher.

“The more years remain after the Jubilee, the greater the price shall be. And the fewer years you count, the lower the purchase price shall be. For he is selling you the time of the crops.”

If a person can accomplish much, you will demand much fruit from him; if little, a small amount. One person is required to bear thirtyfold fruit, another sixtyfold, and another a hundredfold.

The legislator does not treat this carelessly but attends to it on the basis of actual work. For he again says: [Col. 0533B] “Do not afflict your fellow countrymen, but let each person fear his God, for I am the Lord your God.”

A person must not afflict his fellow countryman—that is, he must not impose a heavy burden upon him or one exceeding his strength. Rather, let each person fear his God, who says: “Take my yoke upon you, for it is gentle, and my burden is light” (Matthew 11).

“I am the Lord your God”—that is, the one who commanded the apostles concerning virginity and said: “Not everyone can receive this word, but whoever can receive it, let him receive it” (Matthew 19). Thus he requires from each person what accords with that person’s ability. [Col. 0533C]

This is the profit of the spiritual interpretation. The literal sense also contains no small instruction: one should show compassion toward one’s neighbor even in material contracts, and should in no way be harsh or burdensome toward anyone. One should not trade upon the necessities of the poor, nor strive or hasten to acquire their possessions for oneself, joining house to house and adding field to field. Rather, one should give to those in need and gradually receive back what they have given from the produce gathered from the fields. To give the debt itself away, and not even to reclaim what was lent, belongs to the perfect life—a life that not everyone can receive, but those who can receive it are blessed.

It follows:

Do my commandments, observe my judgments, and fulfill them, so that you may dwell in the land without fear. Then the earth will give you its fruits, and you shall eat them to satisfaction, fearing no attack.

We are not permitted to remain idle, for we are weak in the practice of the Law. Yet God unquestionably wishes each person to work according to his ability. Our conscience bears witness to our ability, as Paul says: “Their thoughts alternately accusing or defending them” (Romans 2). [Col. 0533D]

Therefore let us first observe all the righteousness of God and all his judgments, and afterward perform them. Let us observe them without corrupting their intention, but guarding them strictly and immutably.

For example, if someone wishes to practice almsgiving, he must do so without harming his neighbor. Nor should a poor person himself rob the money of the rich in order to give it to the poor. God wishes almsgiving to be offered with righteousness.

We say the same concerning every commandment: first let us preserve its intention and purpose, and then let us advance to its practice. Then we shall dwell confidently in the intelligible land—namely, in the divine Law of spiritual Scripture and in the good way of life—which God commands us to possess and cultivate, when we have not transgressed its intention. [Col. 0534A]

Then it will produce its fruits for us to eat to satisfaction, and we shall fear no attack. Whoever guards the intention of the Law and puts it into practice will gather its fruits and eat them to satisfaction, and will dwell in it without fear, because he does not transgress the legislator’s intention and is not conscious of living contrary to the Law within God’s Law.

It follows:

But if you say, “What shall we eat in the seventh year, if we do not sow or gather our crops?” I shall give you my blessing in the sixth year, and it shall produce the crops of three years. You shall sow in the eighth year, and you shall eat the old crops until the ninth year; until the new crops grow, you shall eat the old.

It is very appropriate that we should first be helped—that is, that we should first seek to understand the usefulness of the literal sense and pursue this kind of profit. When he commands the land to rest for two years, he does not wish those who receive the Law to lack food or be troubled about what or from where they will eat. Rather, he says: “I shall give you my blessing.” [Col. 0534B]

What blessing is this? “Human beings do not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” (Matthew 4).

How, then, do some accuse Christ’s command as impossible and burdensome when he said: “Do not worry about tomorrow”? See, the Law also gives a similar command, ordering those who attend to the legislator’s virtue not to worry about three complete years.

Moreover, through the three years we necessarily understand the consummation of each one of us and the common recompense that follows the resurrection. In each of these we shall eat whatever we have accomplished here. [Col. 0534C]

Therefore he says: “But if you say, ‘What shall we eat in the seventh year?’”—that is, at the consummation of each one of us. For it is clear that in the common consummation, in which the resurrection occurs, we shall likewise have the same food as our recompense.

Hear the answer that God gives you concerning these matters through the Law: “I shall give you my blessing in the sixth year, and it shall produce the crops of three years.”

The Son is the blessing of the Father. He destroyed the curse imposed upon Adam. Therefore the psalmist and prophet David taught us that we must be blessed in him: “The blessing of the Lord is upon you; we bless you in the name of the Lord” (Psalm 28). [Col. 0534D]

He plainly calls the Son the name of the Lord, because just as a name reveals each person, even one who is not seen, so Christ, appearing, caused the Father—although invisible—to be known in himself.

He came in the sixth year, as in the time of perfection, for the number six signifies this, so that restoration might again occur at the end of time. Humanity was formed during the number of these days. Therefore, just as the sixth day is called the day of formation, so the sixth year is rightly called the year of restoration.

The sixth day is mentioned there, but the sixth year here, because many intervals of time passed between our formation and our restoration.

The legislator therefore did not mention the sixth year without reason: [Col. 0535A] Christ came in that year and enabled us to acquire fruits by which we can be nourished at the individual consummation of each of us and at the common resurrection and recompense. He granted the human race the power to produce virtues abundantly—so abundantly that those who were hired to work at the eleventh hour received the denarius of wages along with those who had been hired in the morning.

It follows:

The land also shall not be sold permanently, because it is mine, and you are sojourners and settlers with me. Therefore all the region of your possession shall be sold under a right of redemption.

### From Augustine

“And the land shall not be sold for profanation.” Other manuscripts read, “for confirmation.” I think this textual corruption occurred earlier in the Greek in one or the other reading because of the similarity of the words’ sound: *bebēlōsis* (βεβήλωσις) means “profanation,” whereas *bebaiōsis* (βεβαίωσις) means “confirmation.” [Col. 0535B]

The first sense is clear: “The land shall not be sold for profanation,” that is, no one should dare sell the land he received from God to profane persons who would use it for impiety and the worship of foreign and false gods.

The other reading, “The land shall not be sold for confirmation,” is somewhat obscure. I think it should be understood to mean that the sale must not be confirmed in such a way that the seller does not receive the land back at the time of release, as has been commanded.

What follows can agree with either interpretation, whether one reads “The land shall not be sold for profanation” or “for confirmation.” For he immediately adds: “The land is mine.” Therefore proselytes and resident aliens you are before me. “Throughout the land of your possession you shall give payment for the land.” Other manuscripts read, “You shall give redemption for the land.” [Col. 0535C]

The meaning is therefore this: The land shall not be sold for profanation—that is, to those who would use it to insult the Creator—or for confirmation, that is, so that the buyer would possess it forever and would not, at the appointed interval of years, restore it to the seller according to God’s command.

“For the land is mine,” he says; therefore you must use it according to my command.

And to show that the land belonged to him and not to them, he appropriately adds what they themselves were in it: “Therefore you are proselytes and resident aliens before me.”

That is, although the proselytes among you are foreigners—people joined to your nation from other peoples—and resident aliens, dwelling not in their own land, [Col. 0535D] nevertheless all of you are also resident aliens and sojourners before me.

God says this either to the Israelites, because he gave them the land of other nations whom he expelled, or to every human being, because before God, who always remains and, as it is written, fills heaven and earth with his presence, every person is a sojourner by being born and a resident alien by living, since death compels him to migrate.

If your brother becomes impoverished and sells a small part of his property, and if his near relative wishes to redeem what he sold, he may redeem it. But if he has no near relative, and he himself is able to find the price of redemption, he shall calculate the fruits from the time when he sold it and return whatever remains to the appointed time; thus he shall recover his property. [Col. 0536A]

But if his hand does not find enough to repay the price, the buyer shall possess what he bought until the year of the Jubilee. In the Jubilee, however, every sale returns to the Lord and to the former owner.

### The same context

### From Hesychius

The possession of every person is therefore the good way of life that we have received by lot from God. Paul spoke of this when he said: “Let each person remain, brothers, in the calling in which he was called” (1 Corinthians 7).

Before God, one person possesses virginity, another a chaste marriage, another a life of righteousness, another silence and withdrawal from disputes, one the priesthood, another the protection of the poor, and another something else. Each possesses his own portion according to his particular ability.

But when our thoughts have been weakened through indolence, then we fall in part from our own possession. [Col. 0536B]

“If your brother becomes impoverished”—or, according to the Septuagint, “If your brother who is with you comes into poverty”—he understands our brother who is with us as a fellow believer. When sin enters his thought, he falls into poverty and is truly poor, having lost spiritual riches.

He becomes like the one of whom David spoke when he described a person established in sinful thoughts: “I am needy and in labors from my youth; though exalted, I have been humbled and brought to shame” (Psalm 87).

When someone of this kind sells part of his own good possession, which had fallen to him by lot, by accepting a sinful thought, he sells his mind to the adversary. As God said to the Jews: “Behold, you have been sold because of your sins” (Isaiah 30). [Col. 0536C]

Then his kinsman and near relative comes—his spiritual kinsman and fellow believer—demonstrating the law of kinship through his deeds, and he frees the sale of his brother, fulfilling what Paul wrote: “Brothers, if a person is caught in any transgression, you who are spiritual should restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness, taking care that you yourself are not tempted. Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Galatians 6).

If we bear one another’s burdens through exhortations, admonitions, and timely counsel, we can free and redeem our brother from the poverty into which he fell through negligence, having sold his possession when he ought not to have done so. In this way the possession becomes common.

But if he has no near relative or kinsman—perhaps because he failed to show compassion toward another at the appropriate time—he must save himself, redeem his own substance, and therefore the text says: [Col. 0536D]

“But if he has no near relative, and he himself is able to find the price of redemption, he shall calculate the fruits from the time when he sold it and return to the buyer whatever remains; thus he shall recover his possession.”

Who among us is capable of freeing a mind sold through negligence or perversity, so that it may not perish completely through alienation, unless by a good life and action that repels whatever sins we are found to be committing in the mind?

Therefore we must consider for how long we have sold our minds to the one who habitually purchases them through evil thoughts and reduces them to slavery. [Col. 0537A]

If, for example, a thought of avarice has invaded our desire, let us recover our mind by despising even money and possessions acquired justly. If the suggestion of captivity to gluttony has invaded us, let us recover our resolve through strict fasting and abstinence from all foods. In this way we can recover our possession from the stronger enemy whom we have defeated.

But if this does not happen, learn what follows: “If his hand does not find enough to repay the price.” For, as we have said, when no spiritual kinsman has previously stirred us, and when we repel evil thoughts without harm, thought and action must follow, by which we may be freed from whatever we have been found wrongly to have alienated. [Col. 0537B]

“The buyer shall possess what he bought until the year of the Jubilee; for in that year every sale returns to the lord and to the former owner.”

If, therefore, we have corrected our thoughts neither through fraternal instruction nor through some virtue, and have not recovered what was alienated from our possession, the one who acquired it through our negligence will rule it. The sin is carried through to its completion, and we do not otherwise recover our intelligible possession except at the time of the Jubilee—or, according to the Septuagint, of release.

This is the perfect year, which contains within itself all hours and the cycle of every kind of time. When sin has been completed and has remained for a long period, it cannot otherwise be corrected, nor can the mind over which the one who wrongly acquired our possessions has ruled be freed, except through perfect repentance, in which fasting, prayer, sackcloth, almsgiving, and tears are practiced.

Through these things full release is acquired for us. [Col. 0537C]

Whoever sells a house within the city walls shall have the right to redeem it until one full year has passed. If he does not redeem it, and the year has run its course, the purchaser shall possess it, and his descendants after him, forever; and it shall not be redeemable even in the jubilee. But if the house is in an unwalled village, it shall be sold according to the law governing fields; if it has not been redeemed beforehand, it shall return to its owner in the jubilee. The houses of the Levites that are in the cities may always be redeemed; if they have not been redeemed, they shall return to their owners in the jubilee, because the houses of the Levitical cities are their possessions among the children of Israel. Their outlying lands, however, are not to be sold, because they are an everlasting possession.

If the legislator had intended only this—that possessions should not pass from some people to others—this would indeed have been useful, since, as we have said, the law takes care concerning sufficiency. Why, then, do you suppose that, when they have not been redeemed within a year, as he says, they are ordered to become the property of the purchasers—not simply so, but while preserving a certain subtle distinction? Whatever houses are within the walls of fortified cities may be redeemed only within a year; whatever are in unwalled places, he allowed them always to have the right of liberation; but the houses of the Levites, whether they are in walled or unwalled places, he ordered always to be redeemable, while he prohibited the sale of all fields.

This distinction is as unfruitful on the face of the letter as it appears, because the law did indeed at times derive benefit from the letter, but not always, nor in every matter. For this reason spiritual contemplation is necessary to it; and a perpetual usefulness, concerning every commandment of the law, comes from directing one’s attention to this.

Let us now examine the force of the present enactment. In the preceding passage, when he proposed the possession of an individual, he said: “If your brother becomes poor and sells his little possession.” Without doubt he was explaining the particular conduct of each person. Here, however, he is no longer speaking about a particular conduct, but about the whole Synagogue or the Church. In these terms, the Synagogue of the Jews remains, even to the present, in servitude to the enemy and adversary who has acquired it, whereas the Church of the Gentiles in some manner receives liberty. He also explains, in a manner befitting God, how certain Jewish communities are saved through certain intelligible Levites—that is, through the apostles—when he says:

“Whoever sells a house within the city walls shall have the right to redeem it until one full year has passed.”

Let us understand this as referring to the Synagogue of the Jews. It was indeed inhabited; for this reason God established it through Moses, so that it might be inhabited, although it itself did not preserve those by whom it was meant to be inhabited. Therefore the Lord also said to the Jews: “My house shall be called a house of prayer, but you have made it a den of thieves” (Matthew 21).

It was in a walled city, in Jerusalem; for it had the wall of the law. Someone sold it—but he does not identify the seller as “a brother,” “a kinsman,” or “a neighbor,” as he did above. For there was not one person who sold it, but the entire Jewish people, living wickedly, who deserved to be called neither brother nor kinsman. For this reason God also called that people the people of Sodom and Gomorrah through the prophet Isaiah: “Hear the word of the Lord, rulers of Sodom; give ear to the law of our God, people of Gomorrah” (Isaiah 1).

Elsewhere the prophet again said to them: “To which creditor did I sell you? Behold, you have been sold because of your iniquities” (Isaiah 50).

They were nevertheless permitted to redeem this sale within the year in which Christ proclaimed the redemption of sins to the whole human race, and especially to the Jewish people. The legislator now alludes to that year; Isaiah openly displayed it:

“The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because the Lord has anointed me. He has sent me to announce good news to the meek, to heal the brokenhearted, to proclaim release to captives and opening to those who are imprisoned, to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord and the day of vengeance of our God.”

But if it has not been redeemed until the year is completed, “the house that is in the walled city shall be confirmed as the property of the purchaser and his descendants forever, and it shall not be redeemable even in the jubilee” (Isaiah 61).

The enemy who purchased the Jewish Synagogue has exercised dominion over it and over its descendants forever—that is, throughout the whole present age. This is what is meant by “its descendants” or “generations,” as the Septuagint renders it, because he has power throughout the present age against those who join themselves to him. And it shall not be redeemable even in the jubilee, or, according to the Septuagint, “in the remission.”

What remission could this be except that which the crucified Lord pronounced for them: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing”? But after the remission had been granted, they renewed their sin by becoming malicious. Their former sin was not enough for them; they added worse things, which they perpetrated around the tomb, after the resurrection, and after the ascension into heaven, against Christ himself and against the company of the apostles.

But if the house is in an unwalled village, it shall be sold according to the law governing fields; if it has not been redeemed beforehand, it shall return to its owner in the jubilee.

The prophet Isaiah demonstrates to us that the houses in the village are to be understood as the Church of the Gentiles, saying: “Praise, barren woman who do not bear; sing praise and neigh, you who did not bear, because the children of the deserted woman are more numerous than those of her who has a husband, says the Lord” (Isaiah 54).

Thus the houses in the village—or, according to the Septuagint, “in the courts”—are understood as the Church of the Gentiles. This is shown even more clearly later in the same prophecy: “Fix firmly; do not spare; stretch out your ropes and strengthen your pegs. Extend farther to the right and to the left; your offspring shall inherit the nations, and they shall inhabit deserted cities.”

Behold, he called the deserted cities—cities without walls—those of the Gentiles. For they did not have the wall of the law, and they were deserted through the error of idolatry. Their houses, therefore, in the villages—which the Septuagint called “courts,” and which we have said are the Churches—shall be sold according to the law governing fields; or, according to the Septuagint, “shall be assessed according to the field of the land.”

Whose field is this? Certainly the one of which the Lord says: “The kingdom of heaven is like a treasure hidden in a field. When a man finds it, he hides it, and for joy over it goes and sells everything he has and buys that field” (Matthew 13).

He calls the field the Gospel, in which the mystery is Christ, the treasure. According to the law of this field, then, they shall be sold, or they shall be assessed in relation to this field, because they are near to it and not to the law. Therefore they can always be redeemed; or, according to the Septuagint, they shall be completely liberated.

From the time the Lord came until his second coming, the Gentiles are redeemed by parts and escape through the remission that he procured for the whole human race through the cross. For the cross is the true remission.

The houses of the Levites that are in the cities may always be redeemed; if they have not been redeemed, they shall return to their owners in the jubilee, because the houses of the Levitical cities are their possessions among the children of Israel.

Let no one say that the Levites are called the apostles without reason. For it was said concerning the Levites: “You shall possess nothing in their land, nor shall you have a portion among them; I am your portion and your inheritance in the midst of the children of Israel.” This was fulfilled particularly in the apostles, who confidently said to the Lord: “Behold, we have left everything and followed you; what, then, shall be ours?” (Matthew 9).

Their houses, therefore, which are in the cities—or, according to the Septuagint, “the houses of their cities”—all the possessions that followed them in faith and conduct are rightly understood as the Jewish communities. For Christ first commanded them, on their account, to go to “the sheep that had been lost, the house of Israel.” Those people therefore belonged to their lot and possession, and they could always be redeemed. The history of the Acts of the Apostles also demonstrates this, for it says that many Jewish communities were liberated from error through the apostles.

It was not only the apostles who were permitted to carry out this redemption, but also their disciples. Nevertheless, it had to be accomplished according to their teaching, so that it might be credited to those who had provided the beginning of the work and established its doctrines.

“If they have not been redeemed, they shall return to their owners in the jubilee.”

Why this was said follows: “Because the houses of the Levitical cities are their possessions among the children of Israel”—that is, because of their relationship with the apostles. For the possession of the intelligible Levites, the apostles, was in the midst of the children of Israel, as we have learned, since Peter and John received the apostolic lot in preaching to those who were of the circumcision.

But in another way also, possession among the children of Israel belonged to the apostles. They themselves had circumcision, and they had always lived according to the law. Therefore those city houses were theirs, since they had been liberated by them; and whoever was saved was saved through them.

Although they were unworthy because of the blasphemy they had committed against the cross, and which they had again dared to commit after the resurrection, they were nevertheless received into the faith on account of the honor due to the apostles, who had believed before the cross, on the cross, and even after the cross.

Since this is true, learn it from Isaiah, who says: “Unless the Lord of hosts had left us offspring, we would have become like Sodom, and we would have been made like Gomorrah” (Isaiah 1). For if the apostles’ offspring had not been left, nothing would have prevented the entire Jewish people from perishing in the manner of Gomorrah and Sodom. But because of the apostles, not all perished.

What their virtues and possessions were like, consider in these few words: “Their outlying lands, however, are not sold, because they are an everlasting possession.”

Whose? The apostles’, plainly. For these were called Levites. Their outlying lands, or fields, are not sold—that is, their conduct, virtues, and teachings. They cultivated these in place of fields, so that Paul could say of them: “Who plants a vineyard and does not eat of its fruit?” (1 Corinthians 9). And again: “The laborer is worthy of his wages” (1 Timothy 5). And again: “Does God care about oxen? Or does he certainly say this for our sake? For the one who plows ought to plow in hope, and the one who sows in hope ought to receive a share of the harvest” (1 Corinthians 9). And again: “If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it a great thing if we reap your material things?” (ibid.).

These teachings, therefore, were distinct from their cities. The cities existed through them and were saved through them, while the teachings could not be sold, because it was said to them: “You received without payment; give without payment.”

For this reason he deprived Simon, who wished to purchase the gift of the Spirit, of its share or lot.

*(From Adamantius.)*

According to the tropological sense, let us apply these things to ourselves. If we follow the law of Christ, it does not permit us to possess either estates on earth or houses in cities—and what do I mean by houses? It does not even permit us to possess several tunics or a great amount of money. For it says: “Having food and clothing, with these we shall be content” (1 Timothy 6).

How, then, shall we observe the laws given concerning houses, whether they are placed within a walled city or in villages without walls? We find in other passages of Scripture that the divine word gives “house” a greater sacramental meaning, as when it speaks of Jacob and presents this almost as his praise: “Jacob was a simple man, dwelling in a house” (Genesis 25).

Again, I find it written concerning the Hebrew midwives: “Because they feared God, the midwives made houses for themselves” (Exodus 1). We see, then, that fear of God was the reason the midwives made houses, while Jacob’s simplicity and innocence gave him the reason to dwell in a house.

Finally, because Esau was evil, it is not written of him that he dwelt in a house. Nor is it written of anyone else that he built a house for himself if he did not have the fear of God.

What, then, is this house, and what kind of building is it? The apostle Paul explains more clearly when he says: “We have a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens” (2 Corinthians 5).

This, then, is the house that no one can build unless he fears God. This is the house that no one can construct or inhabit except in simplicity of mind and purity of heart.

But how does it happen that even someone who has built well, and has constructed a heavenly house by acting well, living well, and believing rightly, nevertheless incurs the debt of some sin and is compelled to sell this house to a cruel moneylender and transfer his labors to another? Here the piety and mercy of the legislator come to his aid, so that the house may be redeemed within a fixed period: “If your hand finds the price that you can restore,” he says.

What price is this? Without doubt, one gathered through the tears of repentance and found by the hands—that is, through the labor—of good works.

This year can be understood as the year that the Lord came to call the acceptable year, in which he releases the brokenhearted into remission and grants salvation to those who confess their sins (Isaiah 61).

When he speaks of a house in a walled city, he rightly says, as I think, that the house in heaven is understood as being in a walled city. The wall of such houses is the firmament of heaven itself. But only a few can possess such a house—perhaps those who, while walking upon the earth, have their conduct in heaven, and of whom the Apostle says: “You are God’s building” (1 Corinthians 3).

The others have houses in villages without walls. Nevertheless, they have beside them a fertile field—perhaps those who prepare a dwelling for themselves in the land of the living, in that land which the Lord promises to the meek, saying: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth as an inheritance” (Matthew 5).

If someone happens to fall into these houses, therefore, as we explained above, there is always the possibility of recovering them. To give an example: if some moral fault overtakes us—not a mortal crime, not blasphemy against the faith, which is enclosed by the wall of ecclesiastical and apostolic doctrine, but a fault consisting either in speech or in conduct—this is to have sold the house that is in the field or in the village without a wall.

Such a sale, and such a fault, can always be repaired; it is never forbidden to you to do penance for offenses of this kind.

But concerning graver crimes—that is, persisting in unbelief, continuing in iniquity with an unrepentant heart until the end of life, and despairing of the mercy of almighty God, which is blasphemy against the Holy Spirit—the judgment of truth itself makes clear to us in the Gospel what must be thought.

These ordinary faults, however, into which we frequently fall, always admit repentance and are continually redeemed.

“But if it is a priestly house,” he says, “or a Levitical one, wherever it may be, whether in a city or in a field, it always has a redeemer.”

Here I seek the priestly meaning and the Levitical understanding. If it is possible, the hearer of these things ought not to be inferior to the one who wrote and established them.

What, then, does it mean that the priest and the Levite always have redemption for their house, and that wherever it may be, it has redemption, in the spiritual understanding?

A priest is said to be a mind consecrated to God; and a Levite is one who continually stands before God and ministers to his will. Therefore perfection in understanding and in work, in faith and in deeds, is to be understood as the priest and Levite.

If, then, it should at some time happen to this perfect mind that it sells the house it possesses—not made with hands, eternal in the heavens—and hands it over to another, as happened at one time to the great patriarch David when, from his roof, he looked upon the wife of Uriah the Hittite, it immediately redeems it and immediately restores it, for he immediately says: “I have sinned.”

Indeed, we must look still more deeply into this meaning. How are the houses of priests and Levites—that is, of perfect minds—always redeemed from sins and continually cleansed? Whenever we read the divine Scriptures and recount in them certain sins of the holy Fathers, if we say according to the judgment of the apostle Paul, “All these things happened to them in figure, and they were written for our instruction” (1 Corinthians 10), then their house is always redeemed in this way.

For purification and satisfaction are continually supplied for their faults by teachers who show from the divine Scriptures that these events were forms and images of future things—not forms by which the sins of the saints were condemned, but by which it was shown that sinful and impious people could be brought into the portion and fellowship of the saints.

Therefore a priestly possession is never separated from the priest, even if it is taken away for a time, even if it is sold. It is always redeemed and always restored. It is as though he were saying: “Love, which is perfect, bears all things, hopes all things, endures all things; love never fails” (1 Corinthians 13).

So also the possession and house of all such people never falls, is never taken away, and is never separated from their right.

For how can the house that has been built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, in which Jesus Christ himself is the cornerstone, be separated from the priests? (Ephesians 2.)

But that this house can at some time be sold—that is, that such a building can fall into sin—hear the apostle Paul, who says elsewhere: “As a wise master builder I laid the foundation, and another builds upon it. But let each one take care how he builds upon it. For no one can lay another foundation besides the one that has been laid, which is Jesus Christ. Now if anyone builds upon this foundation gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, or straw…” (1 Corinthians 3).

You see, then, that wood, hay, and straw can be built upon the foundation of Christ—that is, works of sin. Whoever builds such things has undoubtedly sold his house to the worst purchaser, the devil, from whom each sinner receives the price of sin, the satisfaction of his desire.

If anyone should incur this—may it be far from us—let him redeem it quickly and restore it quickly, while there is time for restoration and while there is opportunity for repentance. Let us pray together that we may not be deprived of dwelling in the eternal house, but may be deemed worthy to be received into the eternal tabernacles.

## CHAPTER VII. On Not Taking Interest

*(The same passage.)* “If your brother becomes poor and weak in hand, and you receive him as a newcomer and resident alien, and he lives with you, do not take interest from him, nor more than you gave. Fear your God, so that your brother may live with you. You shall not give him your money at interest, nor shall you demand an excess of produce from him. I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, to give you the land of Canaan and to be your God.”

*(From Hesychius.)*

In the present law there are two things that one must admire in the legislator: wisdom and piety. Wisdom, because he explains lofty matters through things that appear humble; and piety, which is found both in the preservation of the letter and in spiritual contemplation.

The letter demands assistance for the poor. It does not permit us to close our compassion toward one who asks for a loan, nor to conduct business upon his poverty by demanding an excess, receiving interest, and seeking profit from an act of piety.

The Spirit, through the anagogical sense, demonstrates how we ought to treat those who have been made poor by that poverty concerning which David cried: “Let your mercy quickly come to meet us, because we have become exceedingly poor” (Psalm 78).

Let us therefore attend in order to the things that have been said: “If your brother becomes poor and weak in hand, and you receive him as a newcomer and resident alien, and he lives with you.”

Here he calls each person’s equal in dignity and conduct “brother.” If this brother has become weak in the practice of the virtues—for this is what “weak in hand” means—therefore Aquila says, “If your brother goes beyond measure and his hands fail with you,” assist him.

According to the sense of the Septuagint translators, he wants us to receive him as a proselyte and resident alien. Our proselyte, or newcomer, is one who now comes to the faith; our resident alien is one who does not yet have a house of his own but needs our admonition and careful instruction in order to be protected, rather than wandering here and there without a home.

Thus we assist the weak brother so that he may live with us and in no way die by becoming alienated from the conduct required by God—living with us, that is, through us and through our teaching, as one strengthened by certain good foods.

We ought to accommodate ourselves to him as to a sick person and heal what is appropriate to his virtue. For this reason he adds: “Do not take interest from him, nor more than you gave.” Let us not, because he has become weak and diminished from his former rule, demand from him a more abundant practice of virtue. Instead, let us encourage him and sustain his hand as one who is weak, demanding from him only the head of the law and of the divine commandments—that is, that he not sin.

Therefore he added most appropriately: “Fear your God,” and, “I am the Lord your God.” His yoke is easy. He requires a human being in every way not to sin, but he requires virtues according to ability.

For this reason, when establishing the rule concerning virginity, he says: “Not everyone can receive this.” And when teaching about renunciation of possessions: “If you wish to be perfect” (Matthew 19).

In the commandment he said beforehand: “If, then, your brother lives with you, you shall not give your money at interest, nor shall you demand an excess of produce.” But imitate Paul, who says: “I became weak to the weak” (1 Corinthians 9). Do not demand more from them for the account of virtue than they possessed before.

But if you perhaps say that they are able, while pretending to be weak, this is no longer your concern, but belongs to the one who knows what we are truly able to do. He said to the one who hid the talent: “You ought to have given my money to the money-changers, and when I came I would certainly have demanded it with interest” (Luke 19).

He was not condemned because he did not receive interest, but because he did not give the money. The master of the household reserved the demand for interest for himself.

See, then, what conclusion he added to the commandment: “I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, to give you the land of Canaan, to be your God.”

Why did the legislator need to mention this in the present passage? He wished in every way to demonstrate that, just as he brought the people out of the land of Egypt and out of a sinful people, and introduced them again into the land of Canaan, another sinful people, so he brought them out of there in order that, if they still inhabited the land of the Egyptians, they would not remain under Egyptian domination. He introduced them into the land of the Canaanites because, after the nations had been expelled, they were no longer to be reduced to their service, and because the cleansed land was free of evil inhabitants.

So God does not permit us to be brought under the domination of sinners, nor to embrace their fellowship while they remain sinners. But when their land has been cleansed, he commands us to be with them, to dwell together with them, and to give them our money.

## CHAPTER VIII. How the One Who Serves Another from among the Children of Israel Must Be Treated

*(The same passage.)* “If your brother, compelled by poverty, sells himself to you, you shall not oppress him with the service of slaves, but he shall be like a hired laborer and a tenant. He shall work for you until the year of the jubilee; afterward he shall go out with his children, return to his kindred, and return to the possession of his fathers. For they are my servants, and I brought them out of the land of Egypt. They shall not be sold as slaves. Do not oppress him by force, but fear your God.”

The letter itself is full of piety, but the spiritual understanding is much more so. For just as the freedom of the soul is better than the freedom of the body, so spiritual contemplation grants to those who can enjoy its fruit things more glorious than the letter.

The letter does not at all wish us to abuse what happens to our brothers—that is, to our fellow believers. Even if one of them has been sold to us because of some necessity of humiliation, it absolutely does not permit us to demand slave service from him.

Once we have received someone as a brother through the adoption of Christ, how can we thereafter treat him as our slave? Therefore Paul, writing about Onesimus to Philemon, said: “For this reason he was separated from you for a time, so that you might receive him forever, no longer as a slave, but in place of a slave, as a most beloved brother—especially to me, but how much more to you, both in the flesh and in the Lord.”

And again: “Those who have believing masters must not despise them because they are brothers” (1 Timothy 6).

Moreover, the Spirit also commands something else. When we discover that one of our brothers—our equal in calling and conduct—has been sold, yet humbled in virtues, that is, weakened, and when we turn him back through corrections and exhortations, we must not abuse him in any way. Rather, we must approach him modestly and humbly.

For this reason, attend to the very words: “If your brother, compelled by poverty, sells himself to you, you shall not oppress him with the service of slaves, but he shall be like a hired laborer and a tenant.”

For poverty is the weakness of the soul in attaining the virtues.

If, then, a humbled brother has been sold to you, a faithful person who worships God, and if, while receiving the ransom and price of his soul—that is, your teaching and exhortation—and considering you as his master, he should serve you, let him not serve you with the service of a slave. Let him indeed submit, but with that freedom of which Paul says: “With the freedom with which Christ freed us” (Galatians 5).

Elsewhere you will find him writing again: “You were bought with a price; do not become slaves of human beings” (1 Corinthians 9).

For this reason the legislator says: “He shall be like a hired laborer and a tenant,” or, as the Septuagint has it, “a resident alien.” Each of these is indeed subject to the one whose house he inhabits and in whose field he works, since poverty has deprived him of both a house and a field of his own. Yet the dignity of freedom is not taken away on that account.

So also, when someone has been converted from sin through us, if before his sin he was our brother according to the equality of grace and the honor of his conduct, we ought to treat him accordingly. Even if he now has neither his own house of righteousness nor his own field of virtue, though he once possessed them, the legislator does not say: “He shall be a hired laborer, a tenant, or a resident alien,” but: “He shall be like a hired laborer, a tenant, or a resident alien to you.”

He needs to dwell in our house and work in our field—that is, according to the exhortations, rules of life, and examples that he receives from us. Nevertheless, there is hope that he will return to his own dignity when he has completed a full and perfect repentance.

The legislator made this clear when he added: “He shall work for you until the year of the jubilee.”

After perfect repentance, having been completely cleansed and therefore made perfect, he can work both for himself and in his own place. “Afterward he shall go out,” as the Septuagint says, “in remission,” with his children.

For he himself is not the only one who is made free; the virtues born from him before he was reduced under the sale of sin are also liberated.

Therefore he shall return to his kindred and to the possession of his fathers, receiving the lot of his conduct and the share of grace that he had received by lot from the beginning, from God, who is properly our Father. Concerning him Paul says: “Because you are sons, God sent the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, ‘Abba, Father’” (Galatians 4).

Why does God use such great piety when establishing these things? The law itself demonstrates this in its words: “For they are my servants, and I brought them out of the land of Egypt.”

Those who once became his servants, and through him were freed from the intelligible slavery of Egypt, he does not wish to see lose this dignity. Nor, because someone has fallen for a short time, does he desire to destroy his former dignity forever. Therefore he says: “They shall not be sold as slaves.”

He says something similar through Paul: “You were bought with a price; do not become slaves of human beings” (1 Corinthians 9).

He also adds: “Do not oppress him by force, but fear your God.”

We must moderate the yoke of those who are being converted and fear our God, who said: “With the judgment with which you judge, you will be judged, and with the measure with which you measure, it will be measured back to you” (Mark 4).

## CHAPTER IX. Let Male and Female Slaves Be from Other Nations, Not from the Children of Israel

*(The same passage.)* “Let a male slave and a female slave be yours from the nations that are around you, and from the resident aliens who dwell among you, or from those who are born from them in your land. You shall have them as servants, and you shall transmit them by hereditary right to your descendants and possess them forever. But you shall not oppress your brothers, the children of Israel, by force.”

The nations around us, which have not yet believed but nevertheless possess the hope of faith and salvation, are those to whom the Gospel has been sent. Thus Paul said to the Jews in Antioch: “Behold, we turn to the Gentiles, for thus the Lord has commanded us” (Acts 13).

From these, then, let male and female servants be acquired—that is, those who are taught through the word. For this reason they call those who taught them “masters,” as is demonstrated by the prison guard at Philippi, who said to Paul and Silas: “Masters, what must I do to be saved?” (Acts 16).

Let us also acquire servants from the resident aliens—or, according to the Septuagint, “from the children of the resident aliens”—who dwell among us.

Here he calls Jews resident aliens: they dwell in our light, but are unwilling to turn toward it the eyes of their minds, hiding its lamp under a bushel.

For this reason the Septuagint did not simply render the word “resident aliens,” but “the children of the resident aliens who are among you.” The same thing is expressed more clearly by Theodotion and Symmachus: “From the children of the resident aliens who dwell among you.”

David spoke of them: “They shall dwell and hide” (Psalm 55). For there are among us people who possess the law itself and the prophets, which we also possess, yet they dwell among us without holding the same understanding of the law and the prophets as we do.

They seek to establish their own righteousness and are not subject to the righteousness of God. Yet they hide this, and rightly dwell among us, like those who exclude themselves from free and confident habitation.

Therefore the Lord, implying that they dwell among us because of their unbelief, said: “A slave does not remain in the house forever” (John 8)—which is characteristic of those who dwell in it.
