But the legislator says, according to the Septuagint: “And from the kindred of these, whoever they may be in your land, they shall be your possession.”

The kindred of the Jews are heretics because of their unbelief. They do not think fully as the Jews do, and although they proclaim the same mysteries to us, they do not hold the same correct, perfect, and complete doctrines concerning God.

Thus they are indeed in our land, but they are resident aliens.

“You shall have these,” he says, “as servants, and you shall transmit them by hereditary right to your descendants and possess them forever.”

Whoever from the Gentiles and unbelievers, or from the Jews or heretics, we have won and offered to God, acquiring them as male and female servants while spending the money of our teaching on them, these are in our perpetual possession. We may also divide them among our children—that is, among our disciples—and hand over their discipleship to them.

Paul makes this clear. His children were his disciples Titus and Timothy. He wrote to Timothy, his beloved son in the faith, and to Titus, his beloved son according to the common faith. Then he assigned the Ephesians to one and the Cretans to the other.

To Timothy he wrote: “As I urged you when I was going to Macedonia, remain in Ephesus, so that you may instruct certain people not to teach differently” (1 Timothy 1).

To Titus: “For this reason I left you in Crete, so that you might set right what remains and appoint presbyters in each city, as I directed you” (Titus 1).

Now, wishing to teach us what distinction remains between those whom we have won from outside and our equal brothers who perhaps have been humbled and are being corrected, the legislator wrote the following concerning the common instruction of the matters already mentioned:

“But you shall not oppress your brothers, the children of Israel, by force.”

He did not command us to reduce to external slavery or wear down with labor the others whom we have won. Nowhere does he appear to have said this in the present enactment. Rather, he teaches that we cannot exercise equal authority over the former and the latter.

For one thing is an unbeliever brought to faith; another is a believer who has fallen and has been admonished by us.

## CHAPTER X. Concerning the Redemption of the One Who Has Sold Himself to a Newcomer or Resident Alien
**(IBID.)** If the hand of an immigrant or resident alien prevails among you, and your brother, reduced to poverty, sells himself to him [Col. 0548A] or to anyone of his lineage, he may be redeemed after his sale by any of his brothers who wishes: his uncle, his paternal cousin, his kinsman, or his relative by marriage may purchase him. Since the law shows that, according to the literal sense, it concerns the freedom of native Israelites, it therefore does not permit one of them who, because of poverty or some other necessity, has fallen into a worse condition to serve proselytes or resident aliens—those born outside Israel but attached to them. Rather, it commands that he be redeemed by one of his relatives.

See how this ought also to be observed according to the spiritual allegory. For it says: “If the hand of an immigrant or resident alien prevails among you”—or, according to the Septuagint, “of a resident”—“and your brother, reduced to poverty, sells himself to him or to anyone of his lineage.” That is: if someone newly joined to our faith from the Gentiles, or from the Jews, [Col. 0548B] or even from the heretics, is distinguished by virtues, so that he is powerful in reproving and exhorting sinners—for his hand particularly “prevails,” or, as the Septuagint has it, “he finds,” since through his conduct he can find a way to influence the conduct and exhortation of others—and then your brother, who was formerly instructed in the word and who is also your equal in the condition of his way of life—for this is the “brother reduced to poverty,” that is, one who does not find someone to exhort and advise him—sells himself to an immigrant, resident alien, or resident, that is, to one who has newly come to believe from the Gentiles, the Jews, or, as we said, the heretics, and sells himself to him by offering the teacher’s word on account of his manner of life: since it is unfitting for one who was formerly renowned for his knowledge and conduct [Col. 0548C] to live under one who has only recently come to the faith, he is rightly redeemed. For discipleship is no small matter, but requires a considerable passage of time in a life directed toward perfection.

“Any of his brothers who wishes may purchase him”: that is, someone of equal honor, equal knowledge, and equal conduct may redeem him through his teaching, and make him no longer need correction from those whom he himself ought to have corrected, since he has advanced in knowledge beyond those who have only recently been born.

“His uncle, therefore, and his paternal cousin, his kinsman, and his relative by marriage shall redeem him.” Our fathers according to the spirit are those who begot us through the teaching of Christ. Hence Paul also wrote to the Corinthians: “For although you have countless pedagogues in Christ, you do not have many fathers; for in Christ Jesus I begot you through the Gospel” (I Cor. IV). Therefore, as many of their brothers—that is, priests, as they themselves are, and teachers—or sons of their brothers, or disciples of those brothers who have advanced into the same knowledge and teaching as the man in question—for they are called the father’s brothers—may rightly redeem him. Those who are his kinsmen and relatives by marriage, that is, those who have shared his dignity and manner of life, redeem him once again when he needs advice and exhortation, mindful of Paul’s words: “But if anyone does not care for his own, and especially for those of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever” (I Tim. V). And again: “Let us do good to all, but especially to those who are of the household of faith” (Gal. VI). For these are our kinsmen according to the flesh of Christ [Col. 0549A], because we are of his flesh and of his bones.

The text continues:

“But if he himself is able, he shall redeem himself, calculating only the years from the time of his sale until the jubilee year, and calculating the money for which he was sold according to the number of years and the rate of a hired laborer. If the years remaining until the jubilee are many, he shall pay the price according to them; if they are few, he shall reckon with him according to the number of years and shall repay the buyer what remains for the years during which he served, reckoning them as wages. He shall not oppress him violently in your sight. But if he cannot be redeemed by these means, he shall go out in the jubilee year with his children; for the sons of Israel are my servants, whom I brought out of the land of Egypt: I am the Lord your God.”

The law speaks so much about our freedom, dignity, glory in good things, and confidence in the Holy Spirit that it commands each one of us who has been placed under the bondage of sin to be redeemed through virtues and corrections—if, for example, we wish to obtain sackcloth and ashes, tears, and the confession contained in these things. All the practices that together constitute the year of jubilee, or remission, are set forth as a test of this kind.

“But if he himself is able to redeem himself, calculating only the years from the time of his sale until the jubilee year.” If someone who was formerly rich in virtues and corrections has been made poor through sin, he rightly frees himself, provided that he is sufficient for his own exhortation. Yet even he must not place complete confidence in himself: having once become weak and needing exhortation and counsel [Col. 0549C], he calculates within himself—that is, he deliberates and argues with himself. He calculates from the year in which he sold himself to that person until the jubilee year, or year of remission: from the time when, as a sinner, he needed counsel and teaching until he completes a full and complete repentance, in which he receives remission and becomes equal to one who has not sinned at all.

What will he consider? By what virtues and corrections he may attain and surpass the remission that comes through earnest repentance. Just as the man who repays money to his redeemer did not need to wait for the year of remission—for it was the fiftieth year and was called the jubilee—so the man who seeks equal or corresponding virtues to erase his sin anticipates repentance through good works, redeeming himself. Zacchaeus demonstrates this: although he had taken away very much from many people, he did not need sackcloth, ashes, tears, and prayer. For this is for us the year of remission, thus possessing everything that produces remission for us. For his sins were financial; he himself promised to restore fourfold what he had taken and to distribute half of his possessions to the poor. Therefore Christ said to him: “Today salvation has come to this house” (Luke XIX), receiving the money of his redemption.

“If the years remaining until the jubilee are many, he shall pay the price according to them; if they are few, he shall reckon with him according to the number of years and shall repay the buyer what remains for the years during which he served, reckoning them as wages” [Col. 0550A]. First, therefore, according to these provisions he pays the price—that is, according to the sins committed by the man who wishes to redeem himself. If, for instance, he sinned through gluttony, let him correct it through fasting; if through excessive talk, let him cultivate silence; if, through carelessness of the eyes, he fell into desire for a woman, let him practice not looking at women and not meeting them at all.

Then, if he wishes to prepare a swift redemption for himself, let him devote himself to the money of his acquisition—that is, to the word and teaching that caused him to understand his own sin and submit to the one who admonishes him. And if he sees that much is still lacking before the year of remission, that is, before the correction imposed by a defined penance, let him work more earnestly at virtues and gain a laborious repentance [Col. 0550B]. If he has done too little of this, then, if not through virtues, he must necessarily obtain the remedy for his sin through tears, sighs, and similar means.

“And you shall not oppress him through labor in your sight.” What does this mean? Do not impose upon one who has rejected sin through virtue the burden of a severe penance; he has already redeemed himself through good works. Therefore the text very appropriately adds what follows:

“But if he cannot be redeemed by these means, he shall go out in the jubilee year with his children.” The one who has not redeemed himself through virtues equal to his sin is nevertheless commanded to be redeemed in the year of jubilee, or remission—that is, in perfect and severe repentance, as we have frequently said. The good works that each of us performed before sinning are also his children [Col. 0550C].

If you wish to know what perfect repentance is, consider the Ninevites. They proclaimed a fast, clothed themselves in sackcloth from the greatest to the least, cried earnestly and wholeheartedly to God, and each turned away from his evil way and from the injustice that was in his hands (Jonah III). God accepted their repentance, so that the prophet added: “God had compassion concerning the evil which he had said he would do to them, and he did not do it.”

What is the cause that makes repentance erase sins and brings about a pure redemption for the penitent, so that he no longer needs someone else to admonish him or has to live under another’s teaching? “For the sons of Israel are my servants, whom I brought out of the land of Egypt.” How did he bring them out? Sighing, as the book of Exodus demonstrates for us. In the same way, even now he frees each person who sighs in repentance and redeems him from the intelligible Egypt.

## CHAPTER XI. Where God forbids the making of idols and the erecting of monuments.

**(CHAP. XXVI.)** “I am the Lord your God, who did those things and commanded these things. You shall not make for yourselves an idol or a carved image; you shall not erect monuments, nor set up a conspicuous stone in your land, in order to adore it. For I am the Lord your God. Keep my sabbaths and fear my sanctuary: I am the Lord.”

The law commands not only that we should know how to possess freedom when we sin, but also that we should not need another’s teaching or exhortation, so that the prophetic word might be fulfilled in us: “And they shall no longer teach each one his neighbor and each one his brother, saying, ‘Know the Lord,’ because all shall know me, from the least to the greatest of them; for I shall be merciful toward their iniquities, and I shall remember their sins no more” (Jerem. XXXI).

How will this happen? It will happen if we abstain not only from the overt worship of idols, which the literal wording of the law forbids, but also from hidden idolatry. Paul said of this: “The root of all evils is avarice, which is the service of idols” (Ephes. V). Thus the spirit of the law also now commands us to abstain.

“And we shall not make for ourselves an idol or a carved image”—or, according to the Septuagint, “fashioned houses,” building houses and possessing certain fields, but not making carved images in them, thereby in some way wearing down our mind through love of them [Col. 0551B]. Nor shall we erect for ourselves monuments, or statues, in these things, wishing through them to extend our memory into future generations. Nor shall we erect a conspicuous stone: a heap of gold or silver, for example, or stones that seem precious. For these stones too are of the earth and are equal to other stones; and thus the sight of the greedy is deceived by them just as the sight of pagans is deceived by idols. Hence it is called a “conspicuous stone.”

Let us suffer none of this. Let riches not become conspicuous stones for us, so that we live according to their purpose, according to the understanding of the Septuagint interpreters. Let us not do whatever they command, serve their desires, adore and worship them, and preserve them.

Let us also keep the sabbaths from every other evil, devoting ourselves to abstinence and vocation, and acting so that we may be free from the works of the present world and rest from them. For this is the intelligible and true sabbath, which belongs not to an ungrateful people but to God himself, as he said through Isaiah: “Blessed is the man who does this, and the son of man who holds fast to it, keeping the sabbath so as not to profane it” (Isa. LVI). If he did not intend to distinguish it from those sabbaths of which he said at the beginning of the prophecy: “I will not endure your new moons and sabbath and great festivals” (Isa. I).

What God’s sabbath is, and how one can avoid profaning it, he adds immediately: “Cease to act perversely,” and so forth. Therefore abstaining from evils is the fulfillment of the sabbath.

There is also a sanctuary: let us fear it, devoting ourselves to holiness, that is, to chastity and purity. For this is the principal or culmination of a perfect and completed life. Hence he placed this last. Then God says to us: “I am the Lord your God, who am holy and also rest among the holy, destroying and scattering all who pollute my tabernacle and violate my temple with the pollutions of pleasures.”

## CHAPTER XII. The good things promised to those who keep the Lord’s commandments, and the evils promised to those who violate them.

**(IBID.)** “If you walk in my commandments, keep my precepts, and do them, I will give you rain in its season, and the earth shall produce its fruit, and the trees shall be filled with fruit. The threshing of the harvest shall overtake the vintage, and the vintage shall overtake the sowing; you shall eat your bread to satiety, and dwell in your land without fear. I will give peace within your borders; you shall sleep, and there shall be no one to terrify you. I will remove the evil beasts, and the sword shall not pass through your borders. You shall pursue your enemies, and they shall fall before you; five of you shall pursue a hundred strangers, and a hundred of you shall pursue ten thousand. Your enemies shall fall before you by the sword. I will look favorably upon you and make you increase; you shall multiply, and I will establish my covenant with you. You shall eat the oldest of the old, and you shall cast out the old when the new arrives. I will set my tabernacle in your midst, and my soul shall not reject you. I will walk among you and be your God, and you shall be my people. I am the Lord your God [Col. 0552B], who brought you out of the land of Egypt so that you would not serve them, and who broke the chains of your necks so that you might walk upright.”

Since we find that all these things were fulfilled literally among the Jews, this requires attention. Many of God’s prophets, keeping his commandments and walking in his precepts, were placed in great affliction and ate their bread not in satiety but in want, as Ezekiel did, to whom this was commanded by God himself. Paul also, explaining those who were justified in the law and the prophets, said: “They wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins, humbled and afflicted, of whom the world was not worthy” (Hebr. XI).

We should attend more closely to what has been said, because the law has placed thirty blessings in the present life for those who keep God’s commandments. You will find them by numbering each blessing as distinguished from the next by a conjunction in the Septuagint edition. For the Lord, of whom Paul says, “until we all attain to a perfect man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ” (Ephes. IV), came to baptism when he had reached the age at which he was baptized, in order to announce and demonstrate the perfection of the gift. Thus, having been made perfect according to the appointed time, he began to preach the Gospel, in which there is the fullness of all life, gift, conduct, and recompense—things signified here.

For he says: “I will give you rain in its season.” The Word of God, descending from heaven as grace, speaks of this, as Moses said: “Give ear, O heaven, and I will speak; and let the earth hear the words from my mouth. Let my speech be expected like rain” (Deut. XXXII). To receive this good at its proper time is no ordinary matter, but a clear manifestation of God’s goodness. Just as failing to receive it is a sign of rejection, so God, angered with the Jewish people, threatened through the prophet Isaiah, saying: “I will abandon my vineyard, and it shall not be pruned or dug; thorns shall rise up in it as in an untilled field, and I will command the clouds not to rain rain upon it” (Isa. V).

What benefit does it bring us to receive rain in its season and for the earth to produce its fruit—that is, for our body to produce its fruit? The fruits of this good are chastity, sobriety, and abstinence. “And the trees shall be filled with fruit”; or, according to the Septuagint, “the trees of the field shall give their fruit.” The trees of the field are the movements of the soul, since they are higher than the movements of our intelligible earth, namely, the flesh. Their fruits are truth, justice, gentleness, compassion, and similar qualities.

**(From Origen.)** We have within ourselves trees of the field that produce their fruit. What are these trees of the field, someone in the audience may ask? What does this word-spinner say again? Why does he gather words from everywhere in order to escape through an explanation of the reading? How will he teach that trees and wood exist within us? If you do not rashly slander me, you will hear now: “A good tree cannot produce evil fruit, nor can an evil tree produce good fruit” (Matt. VII). We therefore have trees within us, whether good or evil; those that are good cannot bear evil fruit, just as those that are evil cannot bear good fruit.

Do you want me to explain to you the names and designations of the very trees that are within us? There is no fig tree, apple tree, or vine, but one tree is called justice, another prudence, another fortitude, and another temperance. And if you want a still greater multitude of trees, learn what kinds might rightly be considered to have been planted in God’s paradise. One tree, therefore, is piety; another is wisdom; another is discipline; another is the knowledge of good and evil. Above all there is also the tree of life. Let me call the wisest Solomon as witness, when he says of wisdom: “She is a tree of life to all who embrace her” (Prov. III).

If wisdom is the tree of life, then undoubtedly there is also another tree of prudence and another of justice. For it would not logically be said that, among all the virtues, wisdom alone deserved to be called the tree of life, while the other virtues by no means received names of the same kind.

“The trees of the field shall give their fruit. The threshing of the harvest shall overtake the vintage, and the vintage shall overtake the sowing.”

**(From Hesychius.)** Since the threshing of the earth gathers fruits, the vintage rightly comprehends or overtakes the fruits of the body—or the fruits of the soul—because this is especially a blessing: to possess at one and the same time a stable and fruitful body and soul in virtues.

“The vintage shall comprehend or overtake the sowing.” For the soul, gathering its virtues, immediately desires others until it reaches those riches toward which Paul hastened. Therefore he said: “Brothers, I do not consider that I have apprehended it; but forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead, I pursue according to my purpose toward the prize of the heavenly calling of Christ” (Phil. III).

Therefore good seed follows, full of salutary actions, so that what follows may fit well: “And you shall eat your bread to satiety.” If our bread is virtue, concerning which the Lord said, “Work not for food that perishes, but for food that endures to eternal life” (John VI), then the one who continually desires it eats this bread to satiety—that is, he practices it continually.

“And you shall dwell in your land without fear; I will give peace within your borders”; or, according to the Septuagint, “war shall not pass through your land.” Our translation says shortly afterward: “The sword shall not pass through your borders, and I will give peace in your land.” If the body is stable and the soul bears fruit, we shall dwell securely in our land, because “the flesh does not desire against the spirit” (Gal. V). Hence war will not pass through the land, for it will have no opportunity in the resurrection of the desires of which James says: “From where are wars and quarrels among you? Is it not from your desires, which wage war in your members?” Once these have been destroyed, peace in our land, restrained by the law of God, is brought about.

“And you shall sleep,” he says. Scripture has also placed this among the forms of recompense. Sleep, as rest, is called the death of the saints; but it is not so for the wicked. Ecclesiastes bears witness to this: “The abundance of the rich does not allow him to sleep” (Eccl. V).

Therefore he appropriately adds: “And there shall be no one to terrify you.” Whoever has lived in the manner described above will have no one to terrify him at the time of death, which is sleep for us because of the hope of the resurrection of the dead. He will have no one to terrify him, since he is conscious of nothing for which he should be afraid.

“I will remove the evil beasts,” namely, demons. They are beasts because of their similar wickedness: first because they lie in wait, and then because they possess an unbearable and deadly poison. “You shall pursue your enemies.” They cannot stand before those who live according to the law. “And they shall fall before you.” By what death? Certainly by fasting and prayer. In this way our intelligible enemies, the demons, are slain, so that they can never again rise against us.

Hence, when the apostles asked the Lord why they had been unable to cast out the mute and deaf demon, he answered: “This kind is not cast out except by fasting and prayer.”

“Five of you shall pursue a hundred strangers” (Matt. XVII); or, according to the Septuagint, “fifty shall drive out.” We call the spiritual man “one hundred and fifty,” because on the day of Pentecost the Spirit descended from heaven. Therefore that spiritual man of whom Paul said, “the spiritual person judges all things, but is himself judged by no one” (I Cor. II)—that is, the person who possesses perfect knowledge for the subtle discernment of what ought to be done—can overcome and conquer even a powerful demon, for example one of those above a hundred, called Legion because of the multitude of evil spirits obeying and cooperating with it.

“And a hundred of you shall pursue ten thousand.” Whoever possesses not only subtle knowledge but also a perfect and completed life is, in a certain sense, doubly spiritual. Therefore he is honored by the number one hundred, as bearing a double fruit in the spirit and as perfect. Concerning such a person Christ says that there is no greater measure, when he frequently described the good soil as bearing “thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and a hundredfold” (Matt. XIII). He can therefore subdue thousands of enemies, namely all opposing powers, since he possesses the perfection of virtues.

How does he subdue them? Certainly through the word of God. For he says: “And your enemies shall fall before you by the sword” [Col. 0555A]—the sword which Paul explained when, after first mentioning the thousands of enemies, saying, “we do not wrestle against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places,” he adds: “Therefore take the armor of God,” and, counting its pieces one by one, says: “And the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God.”

“I will look favorably upon you.” What is better than to be regarded favorably by God, whose regard is salvation? Rejection is death.

“And I will make you increase, and you shall multiply.” He increases us when he makes the small good things we do appear great; he multiplies us when he causes a few things to grow into many. Did he not, increasing and magnifying our virtues, say: “As long as you did it to one of the least of these, you did it to me” (Matt. XXV)? And again, multiplying, he caused Paul to write: “You shall not kill, you shall not commit adultery, you shall not covet, and if there is any other commandment, it is summed up in this word: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself’” (Rom. XIII), making many commandments into this one commandment, so that by attaining it we may become rich.

The following words are therefore especially appropriate: “I will establish my covenant with you.” The things mentioned above are his covenant; through recompense he confirms it. The following words make this clear:

“You shall eat the oldest of the old”—or, according to the Septuagint, “the things promised to you through the law and the prophets, and the ancient things of the ancients, which he promised through the patriarchs in their blessings.” “And you shall cast out the old when the new arrives.” What are the new things? The Gospel, certainly. For although the things promised through the patriarchs, the law, and the prophets are very great, greater things have been promised through the Gospel. Therefore, in comparison with these, those earlier things are judged by us to be superfluous.

For behold, he adds a statement that confirms the whole blessing, namely the grace accomplished and fulfilled through the Gospel: “I will set my tabernacle in your midst”; or, as the Septuagint has it, “I will establish my covenant with you.” This is the covenant in which he promised new things, of which the prophet Jeremiah recalls: “I will establish for you a new covenant, not according to the covenant which I made with your fathers” (Jerem. XXXI).

To these words the following are especially joined: “And my soul shall not abhor you.”

**(From Augustine.)** God calls his will his soul. He is not an animal possessing a body and a soul; nor is his substance of the kind that his creature is, which is called a soul and which he himself made, as he himself testifies elsewhere, saying: “I made every breath”—and the context shows that he is speaking of the human soul.

Therefore, when he speaks of his eyes, lips, and the other names of bodily members, we do not understand him to be defined by bodily form. Rather, by all those names of members we understand only the effects of operations and powers. Thus, when he says, “my soul,” we ought to understand his will. That perfectly simple nature called God does not consist of body and spirit, nor is it changeable even in spirit as the soul is. God is spirit, and he always remains the same; with him there is no change (James I).

From this the Apollinarists took an opportunity to argue that the mediator of God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, did not possess a soul, but consisted only of Word and flesh, since he said: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death.” Yet from his very action, which is made known to us through the Gospel narrative, the functions of a human soul are so clearly apparent that it would be madness to doubt them.

“I will walk among you and be your God, and you shall be my people.”

**(From Hesychius.)** These words too were plainly foretold by the prophet, as the Septuagint edition contains them: “This is our God; no other shall be reckoned beside him. After this he appeared on earth and lived among human beings” (Baruch III). He would not have done this if he had rejected us. He did not therefore abhor us, but wished to walk among us in the flesh and become our God, although he had been our God previously but was unknown because we were joined to error. From the time when he purchased us with his own blood, he became our God and made us, who were not his people, his people.

And who is the one who did these things? “I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt so that you would not serve them.”

If you wish to understand these words, examine in order both the words of Exodus and those of the Gospel. The Lord said to Moses: “I have seen the affliction of my people in Egypt, and I have heard their cry because of the harshness of those who preside over their labors. Knowing their suffering, I have come down to free them from the hands of the Egyptians and to bring them out of that land into a good and spacious land flowing with milk [Col. 0556C] and honey” (Exod. III).

And who is the one who brings them into the promised land? The same God who said these things to Moses shows this when he says: “Behold, I send my angel before you, to go ahead of you, guard you on the way, and bring you into the place that I have prepared.” He calls the angel “son,” because he announced the Father’s will to us. Isaiah says of him: “A child is born to us, a son is given to us, whose rule is upon his shoulders; and he shall be called the angel of great counsel, Wonderful, Counselor, Mighty God,” and so forth (Isa. IX).

## CHAPTER XIII. The many punishments of those who transgress God’s commandments are foretold.

**(IBID.)** “But if you do not listen to me and do not perform my commandments; if you reject my laws and despise my judgments [Col. 0556D], so that you do not do what I have established and bring my covenant to nothing, I too will do these things to you. I will swiftly visit you with poverty and an inflammation that will consume your eyes and waste away your souls. You shall sow seed in vain, and your enemies shall devour it. I will set my face against you, and you shall fall before your enemies; you shall be subjected to those who hate you, and you shall flee when no one pursues you.”

The law sufficiently stated above what good things await those who obey God’s commandments. The things now decreed show what it threatens will happen to transgressors. When we examine each of them literally, we find that the Jewish people suffered some of them according to the letter, but all of them according to the spirit.

“But if you do not listen to me and do not perform my commandments; if you reject my laws and despise my judgments, so that you do not do what I have established and bring my covenant to nothing.” Who are those who do not listen to God’s commandments and despise his judgments? Surely those who, attending to the tradition of the elders and transgressing the legislator’s intention, explained the law according to what seemed right to them. They said, as the Lord reports: “Whoever says to father or mother, ‘Whatever gift from me might benefit you,’ and does not honor his father and mother” (Matt. XV)—that is, whoever says to his parents, “The things I possess are vows to God; I have offered them as a gift and offering,” is not compelled to honor those who gave him birth.

Who are those who do not perform all his commandments? Surely those who tithe dill, cumin, and mint, but leave aside judgment, mercy, and faith (Matt. XXIII), although God says to them through the prophet: “I will show you, O human being, what the Lord requires of you: to do judgment, to love mercy, and to walk carefully with your God” (Mic. VI). Therefore the Lord said to them, since they did not fulfill all the precepts of the law, but abandoned what was weightier and practiced what was lesser: “These you ought to have done, without neglecting the others.”

Those who preserve the outward appearance of God’s commandments but not his intention also properly transgress his commandments and are especially disobedient to them.

Aquila, Theodotion, and Symmachus are therefore found to have rendered the passage more clearly. Aquila says: “If you reject my ordinances”; Theodotion and Symmachus say: “If you refuse my subtleties” [Col. 0557C]. They transgress God’s doctrines and the subtlety that lies in the spiritual understanding of the commandments, wishing by this means to weaken the grace of the Gospel, which agrees with the New Testament. Rebuking them, he says: “And you bring my covenant to nothing.”

What does he threaten through this? The punishment is very similar to their transgression: “I too will do these things to you.” How? “I will swiftly visit you with poverty.” For the Lord made them exceedingly laborious through his word, to such an extent that they said to one another: “This is a hard saying; who can hear it?” (John VI). Just as they deliberately transgressed the meaning of the law in order to nullify the Gospel covenant, whose origin lay there, so he also spoke obscure words to them and made the understanding of his doctrines difficult [Col. 0557D].

But now recognize what follows: “An inflammation that will consume your eyes”; or, according to the Septuagint, “Scab and a fever burning your eyes, while your soul wastes away.” Scab is a disease of the body, but it is visible on the surface and runs over the skin. The fever, that is, hecteria, arises from inflammation; it too is visible on the surface of the flesh and runs over the skin, especially attacking the eyes. Neither of these diseases can remain hidden.

Such were the manifest and evil diseases of the Jewish souls, no longer hidden. For, jealous of the Lord’s words and miracles, they could no longer conceal their illnesses, but cried out and proclaimed openly: “What are we to do? This man is performing many signs. If we let him go on like this, the Romans will come and take away both our place and our nation” (John XI).

They did not therefore refuse to obey his words because he taught things contrary to the law or the prophets—for he taught things exceedingly consonant with them—but because of their love of themselves and their own interests. Struck by this disease, they consumed their eyes and wasted away their souls, not only burning with fury and corrupted by envy, but also, once their minds had become diseased and their thoughts were no longer sufficiently sound for discerning deeds or words, consuming their inner eyes and wasting away their soul in the Lord’s words and miracles. Thus they cried out to him: “How long will you take away our soul? If you are the Christ, tell us openly” (John X). This was because their souls were subject to the wasting away of unbelief.

But John also says this about them: “For this reason they could not believe,” because Isaiah again said: “Blind the heart of this people, and make their ears heavy, lest they should ever see with their eyes, hear with their ears, and understand with their heart” (Isa. VI). You see that, just as they acted, so Christ also acted toward them: because they sought to annul his covenant or testament, he rightly blinded their eyes and heart, and gave them the burning fever—or hectic fever—that consumed their eyes and souls.

But what did he add to these words? “You will sow your seed in vain; it will be devoured by enemies.” For the seeds of the prophets and the Law are brought forth for them in vain [Col. 0558C], and teachers sow discourses among them without finding fertile soil for the fruit of intelligible doctrines. Hence they do not enjoy their nourishment, but their adversaries devour it—the adversaries who believe in Christ, whom they themselves made their opponents through unbelief and envy.

“And I will set my face against you,” according to that prophetic utterance: “But the face of the Lord is against those who do evil, to destroy their memory from the earth, and you will fall before your enemies” (Ps. XXXIII). The Gentiles, whom they judge to be their enemies, fall before them, stumbling at their salvation. Hence Symmachus, instead of “you will fall,” says “you will stumble before your enemies.”

What else did he add? “Those who hate you will pursue you, and you will flee when no one is pursuing you.” Here what is said seems in a certain way contradictory [Col. 0558D]. If they suffer persecution from enemies, how do they flee when no one is pursuing them? But the legislator did not understand “they will pursue you” as meaning that they would pursue them in order to drive them away; rather, they would press upon them as they ran, hastening toward their salvation. Hence, instead of “they will pursue you,” Symmachus says, “they will reduce you to servitude”; Theodotion rendered it, “They will discipline you.”

Paul likewise shows us such a persecution: “I pursue, if indeed I may apprehend that for which I was also apprehended” (Phil. III). Thus the Gentiles, even if, together with David, they say concerning the Jews, “Do I not hate those who hate you, O God?” (Ps. CXXXVIII), nevertheless press on toward their salvation, hasten toward it, and pray. For he knows that “their acceptance,” as Paul says, “is life from the dead,” and that “their fullness is the salvation of the world” (Rom. XI).

But these flee when no one is pursuing them. For just as they envy our salvation, we do not envy theirs; therefore we neither pursue them nor, when they turn away from us, turn away from them. Rather, we fulfill what the prophet Isaiah said: “Say to those who hate you: ‘You are our brothers’; and to those who abhor you: ‘May the name of the Lord be glorified, and may he be seen in their rejoicing, while they themselves are put to shame’” (Isa. LXVI).

It follows:

**(Same passage.)** “But if you will not obey me even after this, I will add sevenfold chastisements for your sins, and I will break the stubbornness of your pride. I will make your heaven above like iron and your earth like bronze. Your labor will be consumed in vain; the earth will not produce its growth, and the trees will not yield their fruit. If you walk contrary to me and refuse to hear me, I will add your plagues sevenfold for your sins. I will send against you the wild beasts of the field, which will consume both you and your cattle and reduce everything to a small number, and your roads will become deserted. But if even then you will not accept discipline, and you walk contrary to me, I too will advance against you in opposition and strike you seven times for your sins. I will bring upon you the sword that avenges my covenant. When you take refuge in your cities, I will send pestilence among you, and you will be delivered into the hands of your enemies. After I have broken the staff of your bread, so that ten women will bake your bread in one oven and return it by weight, you will eat and not be satisfied.”

The legislator did not employ such divisions without reason. For now he says, “But if you will not obey me even after this”; then, after enumerating certain chastisements, he adds, “If you walk contrary to me”; and again, setting forth other plagues, he adds, “But if even then you will not accept discipline, and you walk contrary to me.” He used these distinctions, as we have said, because Christ frequently wished to receive the Jewish people, but they did not obey him, so that he cried out to them: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those who are sent to you, how often I wanted to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were unwilling.”

Let us especially attend to this point in what has been said. Although he threatened seven chastisements, he introduced them as follows: he threatened to break the stubbornness of their pride, to give them an iron heaven and a bronze earth, to consume their labor in vain, and to prevent the earth from producing its growth or the trees from yielding their fruit. These are six, not seven. You will find the same thing as you review the remaining chastisements. It is therefore evident that the number seven is a figure and sign of the whole present life, which revolves according to the number seven.

Because he threatened to inflict seven chastisements, acts of vengeance, or plagues upon them—that is, complete punishment and entire vengeance, as upon those whose sins were neither pardonable nor worthy of repentance—thereby the prophetic utterance would receive its fulfillment in them: “What are you plotting against the Lord? He himself will bring about complete destruction. Affliction will not rise a second time, for just as thorns embrace one another, so their banquet companions, drinking together, will be consumed. Like straw filled with dryness, one has gone forth from you, plotting evil against the Lord and devising transgression in his mind” (Nahum I).

From whom did an evil thought against the Lord go forth—one devising evil and opposing his commandments—if not from the Jewish people? Isaiah spoke of them: “Woe to them, because they devise an evil plan against themselves, saying: ‘Let us surround the righteous, because he is useless to us’; therefore they will eat the fruit of their deeds” (Isa. III). [Another reading: “Woe to their soul, for evil has been repaid to them. Say to the righteous that it is well with them, for they will eat the fruit of their inventions.”]

Observe the order that the legislator uses in threatening them: “But if you will not obey me even after this, I will add your chastisements sevenfold for your sins” [Col. 0560B]. The Septuagint, however, rendered it: “If you will not hear me even after these things,” meaning, “up to that point which the preceding words indicated,” where he spoke of poverty and burning fever. We have explained above how these things should be understood.

If, therefore, they remain disobedient up to the point that they are not corrected even by the things that have been said, he says that they will be chastised seven times—that is, that perfect chastisement will come upon their sins. What he does not say explicitly is that we should understand their sins to be precisely this: that they were not corrected by the preceding punishments.

When he adds, “And I will break the stubbornness of your pride,” he refers to the fact that they refused to accept Christ’s freedom, saying: “We are Abraham’s seed, and we have never been enslaved to anyone” (John VIII). He broke the stubbornness of their pride by making them serve the Gentiles.

“I will make your heaven above like iron.” For they received no visitation from it at all. “And your earth like bronze.” The earth of divine Scripture, which they possess, is unfruitful for them because they do not understand it in the manner they ought; therefore it is bronze. To demonstrate this he added: “Your labor will be consumed in vain.” The labor that they display in the divine Scriptures, devoting themselves to the tradition of the letter, is consumed in vain, since they cannot fully use the Law according to the letter, with the place removed in which the letter confined the whole worship of God prescribed by the Law.

What follows therefore agrees very closely: “The earth will not produce its growth, and the trees will not yield their fruit.” Their outward man, which is called “earth,” does not bear fruit, for they live in gluttony, and it was said of them: “Their god is their belly, and their glory is in their shame” (Phil. III). Nor do their minds, which are the trees of the fields, bear fruit—although they are implanted in the body, they are nevertheless higher than it and ought to offer fruit to God, who wishes us to germinate in piety.

“If you walk contrary to me.” They do not walk toward God with an upright heart. They turn his way aside, overthrowing the meaning of the Law and the prophets in order thereby to cultivate their own disobedience and transgression. Therefore he adds: “And you refuse to hear me, I will add your plagues sevenfold for your sins.” These are no longer chastisements but plagues; he now sets forth a stronger punishment, corresponding to their iniquities:

“I will send against you the wild beasts of the field, which will consume you and your cattle and reduce everything to a small number, and your roads will become deserted.” Because they drove themselves away from the way of God, the wild beasts of the field—demons—are rightly sent upon them and permitted to rule over them; they consume them.

For whatever acts of righteousness they appear to perform, God does not credit to them, as Paul demonstrates: “Seeking to establish their own righteousness, they have not submitted to the righteousness of God” (Rom. X). And again: “Israel, pursuing the law of righteousness, did not attain the law of righteousness” (Rom. IX).

It is therefore necessary that demons consume the people whose cattle—that is, people resembling cattle, namely, the perverse and ignorant people—they consume, since there is no understanding in them. They are not accustomed to think of anything worthy of God’s service, but, like beasts, they are led as though by a bridle by the foolish traditions of their rulers. For this reason they become food for demons and are reduced to a small number, both in quantity and in dignity. Their roads become deserted, since they possess neither the water of life nor intelligible reception or hospitality, nor anything that brings them forth, leads them by the hand, or guards them.

“But if even then you will not accept discipline, and you walk contrary to me, I too will advance against you in opposition.” I will use an adverse punishment, just as their transgression is opposed to the Law. Although they appear to meditate upon it, they do not preserve its intention. Thus I too will bring upon them an adverse punishment, no longer chastising them with those things with which I scourged them earlier, when I brought upon them deadly serpents, fire, chasms in the earth, and similar things, but with other punishments. What these are, we shall learn as we read what follows.

“And I will strike you seven times for your sins.” First he chastises, then he strikes; as the punishment proceeds, it becomes stronger, since it is directed against the disobedient.

“And I will bring upon you the sword that avenges my covenant.” We have often said that the sword of the Spirit is the word of God. This word, spoken through the tongues of the teachers of the Church, avenges the judgment of the covenant or testament of the Gospel. For it convicts those who transgress the New Testament and are unable to keep even the Old. The Gospel is vindicated when the enemies of the Law are exposed, because they transgress the grace of the Gospel.

But marvel also at the legislator’s wisdom, how appropriately he adds: “When you flee to your cities, I will send pestilence among you.” The intelligible cities are the prophets; this is clear. God said to Jeremiah: “Behold, I have made you today a fortified city” (Jerem. I).

Therefore, just as one who flees to walled cities is saved if he is a friend, but if he is an enemy is more easily destroyed when enclosed within them, so those who flee to the prophetic books and to their testimonies as friends of the faith find fortification and salvation; but enemies and unbelievers are quickly captured and perish. Hence, when the Jews take refuge in the prophets, avoiding the spiritual sword that is present among learned men, he says that he will send pestilence among them. There they die even though no one accuses them, since they are unable openly to resist all the prophecies concerning Christ.

“And you will be delivered into the hands of your enemies”—that is, intelligible enemies.

“After I have broken the staff of your bread.” For the bread of teaching, especially the bread that brings salvation, has become scarce among them. How so? Hear what follows:

“So that ten women will bake bread in one oven and return it by weight, and you will eat and not be satisfied.” The Jews have nothing that gives their doctrine the power to nourish, except the Ten Commandments, because they flee the true interpretation of the prophets as agreeing with the dispensation of our Savior. They do not wish to understand the rest of the Law intelligibly or to receive it spiritually, but only according to the letter—a position that cannot stand.

First, the place in which sacrifices, purifications, offerings, and the other matters belonging to service according to the letter were performed has been destroyed. Furthermore, many things contained in the Law were more worthy of ridicule than of serious observance and practice. The commandment concerning the Sabbath is not a contradiction, for although it is included among the Ten Commandments, it is not one of them. If, therefore, we regard as a separate commandment the words, “I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, from the house of slavery,” we shall find the complete number of ten commandments.

Furthermore, it clearly signifies intelligible rest, in which we are permitted to perform no work of this kind. These commandments alone produce bread for the Jewish people in one oven—namely, the legal oven—and return the aforementioned bread by weight, that is, according to sensible strictness. They neither expand the teaching as the Gospel does, nor teach the doctrine of adultery in such a way as to guard against even looking at a woman; nor do they teach against murder, or even against anger. Hence those who are nourished by them are not satisfied with the bread of the Jews, receiving a narrow doctrine that possesses no abundance or spiritual generosity.

**(Same passage.)** “But if you will not hear me even after these things, but walk contrary to me, I too will advance against you in my contrary anger, and I will chastise you with seven plagues for your sins, so that you will eat the flesh of your sons and daughters. I will destroy your high places and break your images. You will fall among the ruins of your idols, and my soul will abhor you to such an extent that I will reduce your cities to solitude and make your sanctuaries desolate. I will no longer receive the most fragrant odor, and I will destroy your land. Your enemies will be astonished at it when they become its inhabitants. I will scatter you among the nations, and I will unsheathe the sword after you; your land will be desolate and your cities destroyed.

“Then the land will enjoy its Sabbaths throughout all the days of its desolation, when you are in the land of your enemies. The land will keep Sabbath and rest during its Sabbaths of desolation, because it did not rest during your Sabbaths when you dwelt in it. Those of you who remain, I will place fear in their hearts in the regions of their enemies. The sound of a flying leaf will terrify them, and they will flee as though from a sword. They will fall with no one pursuing them, and each will collapse upon his brother as those fleeing from war. None of you will dare resist your enemies. You will perish among the nations, and the hostile land will consume you.

“But if some of you should remain even after these things, they will waste away in their iniquities in the land of their enemies, and because of the sins of their fathers and their own sins they will be afflicted, until they confess their iniquities and those of their ancestors, by which they transgressed against me and walked contrary to me. I too will walk against them and bring them into the land of their enemies, until their uncircumcised mind is ashamed. Then they will pray concerning their ungodliness, and I will remember my covenant, which I established with Jacob, Isaac, and Abraham. I will also remember the land, which, when it has been abandoned by them, will enjoy its Sabbaths, enduring desolation on their account.

“They themselves will pray concerning their sins, because they rejected my judgments and despised my laws. Nevertheless, while they are in the land of their enemies, I will not utterly reject them, nor will I despise them so as to destroy them completely and annul my covenant with them. For I am the Lord their God, and I will remember my first covenant, when I brought them out of the land of Egypt in the sight of the nations, so that I might be their God; I am the Lord God.”

Because not only was Moses the legislator, but he was also a prophet, he himself demonstrated this concerning Christ, prophesying specifically in these words: “The Lord will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers, like me” (Deut. XVIII).

He carefully preserved the likeness of Christ, for, apart from the other respects in which he bore Christ’s likeness, just as the Lord spoke concerning the end of the world, so Moses here wrote in the present Law what would happen to the Jewish people. They experienced many captivities and endured many scourges, but the things he now describes in parts refer to that captivity which came upon them because of the iniquity committed against Christ, when the Romans ravaged them.

You can learn what happened to them, if you wish to know it more precisely, from Josephus’s *History*, in which he described how they ate their children and endured the other events contained in these threats. Many of these things still lie before our eyes to behold: their land is deserted, their cities plundered, their province devastated by enemies, and they themselves live as exiles among their Gentile enemies in continual fear.

Nevertheless, they suffered these things not only according to the letter but also in their spiritual meaning. For because they sinned doubly, transgressing the Law and blaspheming the legislator, they rightly endure a double punishment. Learn this in the following way.

They walked contrary to Christ, overturning his miracles and disparaging his teaching. When, through envy, they plotted against him, they deceitfully alleged that the teacher of divine love was acting against God. Yet he himself, having become their adversary in anger, acted toward them in this way. Since judgment was being carried out, and the captivity they endured was the punishment for the iniquity committed against him, he nevertheless did not cause the Romans to inflict it on that account.

For the Romans were not yet vindicating his glory. But because they resisted Roman rule, though they had formerly been subject to it and obedient to Roman tributes, laws, and magistrates, God, exercising anger against them in opposition, brought wrath upon them through the Roman power, so that he might be vindicated through the Roman empire, as though they had been his preachers.

“And he chastised them with seven plagues,” according to their sins, multiplying their punishment. He did not avenge himself upon them in only one way, because they too did not sin in only one way. They eat the flesh of their sons and daughters—that is, they consume their disciples, whom they adopt as sons, as it were, for the same doctrine, through crafty words that corrupt the soul.

He also brought their high places to desolation and broke their images. Their high places are their rulers and teachers, whom they ought to have looked upon as established on high—or, according to the Septuagint, their statues—as models by which they should order their lives. But because they possessed nothing sound or strong, but everything consisted of weak and corruptible patterns of virtue and imitation that decay and rot with time, the Septuagint therefore called them “wooden works made by hand.” He laid them waste, exposing their empty hypocrisy.

Together with them he also destroyed the common people who looked to them. He placed their corpses among the ruins of their idols—that is, he heaped the members and actions of the people upon the actions of their Pharisaic and scribal idols, whom they used as idols, abandoning God and attending to their seductions.

Therefore he says: “My soul will abhor you.” What soul? The soul that he gave for us, in order to redeem us from the slavery of sins and death. This soul will therefore abhor the Jews and turn away from them forever, because, so far as they were concerned, they brought his work to nothing by rejecting the gift granted through it.

Therefore he reduced their cities to solitude and made their sanctuaries desolate. They find no fruit in the prophetic books, nor are they able to devote themselves to any holiness. He does not receive their most fragrant odor, for he does not accept their prayer. He destroyed their land—that is, the whole Old Testament—not because he made it entirely desolate in itself, but because he made it desolate and inaccessible to them, while he caused the nations to dwell in it.

Therefore he says: “Your enemies will be astonished at it when they become its inhabitants.” The nations are the enemies of the Jews because the Jews chose to be enemies of God and of those whom Paul calls “enemies of the cross of Christ” (Phil. III). The nations dwell in the land of the Jews, in the Old Testament, and as they dwell there they marvel at him who spoke such things in the Law and the prophets, and who founded there the beginnings of life.

He further says: “I will scatter you among the nations,” not only in a visible dispersion but also in an intelligible one. Learn what this is: “I will unsheathe the sword after you, and your land will be desolate and your cities destroyed.” The word of God, which is the sword of the Spirit, runs everywhere among the nations and surrounds the whole earth; it consumes the children of the Jews and expels them from the saints of God, showing that they have no communion with them. Thus the land and cities are found deserted after they have been expelled from their habitation.

[Col. 0565A] “Then the land will enjoy its Sabbaths throughout all the days of its desolation, when you are in the land of your enemies. It will keep Sabbath and rest during its Sabbaths of desolation, because it did not rest during your Sabbaths when you dwelt in it.”

We have often shown that the land is the intelligible Scripture of God and the way of life contained in it: the Old Testament belongs to the Jews, while the New belongs to the nations that are hostile to the Jews.

Since the Sabbath signifies cessation, the legislator now especially intimates this to the Jews: they find nothing now in the Law and the prophets that they themselves wish to practice, while nearly the entire surface of the letter has been destroyed. For this reason they have come to be in the land of their enemies—that is, in the evangelical Testament. They came to be there, even if not willingly, nevertheless by necessity. For the Gospel caused sacrifices, purifications, the Feast of Unleavened Bread, the festivals of Tabernacles, and the other rites to cease, even against their will. Enduring difficulty, they withdraw into the study of it; sacred Scripture accepts this cessation from them in place of the Sabbath, and will rejoice even more than it did in the former Sabbaths, because it has become desolate to them.

But why? “Praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner” (Ecclus. XV).

He says: “Those of you who remain, I will place fear in their hearts in the regions of their enemies; the sound of a flying leaf will terrify them.” For all those who remain among them and still devote themselves to sacred Scripture are afraid in the land of their enemies, in the New Testament, as we have said. Through folly and a blinded heart they fear association with it, and this saying is fulfilled: “There they trembled with fear where there was no fear” (Ps. XIII).

Therefore the legislator, expressing his wonder, says: “The sound of a flying leaf will terrify them,” calling the letter of the Law a leaf. Its sound pursues them and makes them fear us. For example, they hear that the Sabbath must be kept, but they see that we understand nothing contemptible or earthly in the same commandment, nor anything concerning the cultivation of the earth; rather, we understand cessation from evil action. They stumble at this in us and avoid mingling with us.

The leaf is rightly understood as the letter of the Law, because just as the fruit of trees is covered by leaves, so the Spirit is hidden beneath the letter of the Law. Therefore we, of whom it was said, “If grape-gatherers had entered upon you, they would at least have left you a gleaning” (Obad. III), strip away the leaf of the letter in order to find the fruit of the Spirit. Those who do not know this regard us as enemies and flee from us as one flees from a sword.

“And they will fall when no one is pursuing them.” We do not pursue them; rather, they suffer persecution because of the hardness of their own hearts. Consider what he adds: “They will collapse, each upon his brother, like those fleeing from war.” When we speak with them and bring against them the testimonies of the Law and the prophets concerning Christ and the mysteries of the Gospel, some, constrained by one point, say one thing, while others say another, and each falls upon his brother. For all of them speak weakly and therefore cannot stand firm in their arguments against one another; they are disturbed like those fleeing from war, with no one pursuing them. We do not pursue them to harm them, but to help them and win them over; this is why we argue with them.

What, then, do they suffer from this? “None of you will dare resist your enemies. You will perish among the nations, and the hostile land will consume you.” The evangelical Testament consumes them, crushing the substance of all their error. Therefore they cannot resist their enemies, who wish to save them through faith. They also perish among the nations, stumbling over the cornerstone, and they do not even wish to look upon the letter of the Law, since they have no confidence in it.

“But if some of them should remain, they will waste away in their iniquities in the land of their enemies.” Whoever among them has been converted yet remains devoted to the study of the Law will also perish because of his sins in the land of his enemies—that is, in the evangelical Testament, as we have said—because of his transgression of it. These are the sins that are committed there in every way: “Because of their own sins and because of the sins of their fathers, because they transgressed and despised me.”

They attribute the things that have now happened to them to the sins of their fathers; therefore they waste away in those sins, confessing on their behalf that they transgressed against God in earlier times—not with a good but with an evil intention, in order to soften the punishment that has come upon them because of the iniquity they committed against Christ. For he adds: “And they walked contrary to me; I too will walk against them and bring them into the land of their enemies.”

Just as they think that they can deceive God by walking contrary to him and offering interpretations of the Law and the prophets in place of one another—interpretations that confirm the mystery of Christ, which is characteristic of those who oppose him—so he too will walk against them and bring them into the land of their enemies, that is, into the Gospel that he gave to the nations. From this they perish in two ways: first, because it destroys Jewish righteousness; and second, because it is among the nations, toward whom they are envious, and, in a contentious spirit against them, they are unwilling to be saved. Thus God said through Moses: “I will provoke you to jealousy by a non-nation” (Deut. XXXI). Paul says: “According to the Gospel, they are enemies for your sake” (Rom. X); and again: “For just as you, when you were enemies, were reconciled to God” (Rom. XI; V), “so these too have now disbelieved because of your mercy.”

“Then their uncircumcised mind will be ashamed, and then they will pray concerning their iniquities”—or, according to the Septuagint, “they will regard their sins as acceptable,” that is, the punishments they suffer because of their sins. Thus we understand what is said in Hosea: “They will eat the sins of my people” (Hos. IV).

What this means he made clear in what follows: “They will lift up their souls for their iniquity.” Therefore, to eat the sins of the people means to endure punishments on their behalf. They will say that they are suffering punishments worthy of their sins. Even if they confess some of their sins, they conceal others—the sins they committed against Christ.

“And I will remember the covenant that I established with Jacob, Isaac, and Abraham.” Why did he not begin with Abraham, according to the order of time and descent, but with Jacob? Or, as the Septuagint has it, they do not say “the testament of Jacob, and Isaac, and Abraham,” but “the testament of Jacob, the testament of Isaac, and the testament of Abraham.” You will find, in a certain sense, three testaments, so that they might commend the Law, the prophets, and the Gospel.

Because the Law is the oldest, the prophets are second, and the Gospel is last, they wished to display this order. Although the Gospel is last in time, it is preferred by grace and by God; therefore he mentions it first in his intention. He first mentioned Jacob, who is last in time and order, and then joined together those who are related to one another. In those passages where he mentions the Law and the prophets, he says that he is also mentioning the Gospel.

What follows confirms this especially: “I will also remember the land, which, when it has been abandoned by them”—or, according to the Septuagint, “which is abandoned by them.” Since it is the greatest blessing for the land to be remembered by God, God, who lovingly remembers the intelligible land—that is, his Scriptures—has ensured that their memory and the Scriptures themselves are not abandoned in oblivion by the Jews. For by interpreting them maliciously, they did not meditate upon them properly; they dishonored them, first by saying and not doing, and then by interpreting them contemptuously and concealing the excellent spiritual understanding contained in them.

Therefore he adds next: “It will enjoy its Sabbaths,” that is, while it remains desolate from them. The Law of God rejoices in the desolation that the Jews themselves brought upon it. Therefore he said that it would endure that solitude on their account.

“They themselves will pray concerning their sins, because they rejected my judgments and despised my laws.” He says that, after the Jewish populace has been expelled, double blessings have come forth from the sacred Scriptures. For the Scriptures themselves have not been dishonored; therefore they rejoice that the Jews no longer read them. They do not read them as before, since they have been scattered and deprived of every presumption; they themselves have also become conscious of their sins and of their transgression of the divine Law.

It is also remarkable that, as the conclusion and culmination of the entire enactment, he added this—and we must understand that the one who spoke openly in Moses also spoke in Paul and in all the apostles.

“Nevertheless, while they are in the land of their enemies, I will not utterly reject them, nor will I despise them so as to destroy them completely and annul my covenant with them. For I am the Lord their God, and I will remember my first covenant, when I brought them out of the land of Egypt in the sight of the nations, so that I might be their God; I am the Lord.”

If you wish to know these matters individually, read Paul and see how God did not despise them in the land of their enemies—that is, in the evangelical Testament—nor destroy them so as to annul his first covenant. He did not abolish it completely; rather, he left a hope of salvation, though not for all, but for a remnant, as Paul says, bringing forward the testimony of the prophet Isaiah: “Though the number of the sons of Israel be as the sand of the sea, a remnant will be saved” (Rom. IX).

He says: “Has God rejected his people? Certainly not.” He will also remember his first covenant, when he brought the sons of Israel out of the land of Egypt. And in what way will he remember it? So that he might be their God in the sight of the nations.

For a clear demonstration of this, let these words of apostolic wisdom suffice: “For I do not want you to be ignorant of this mystery, brothers, lest you be wise in your own estimation: a hardening has come upon Israel in part, until the fullness of the Gentiles enters, and thus all Israel will be saved” (Rom. XI).

Therefore, in bringing the entire discourse to a conclusion, the Lord rightly said: “I am the Lord God,” who desires the salvation of all human beings and who, for this reason, will save a remnant of the Jews despite so many iniquities.

It follows:

“These are the commandments, judgments, and laws that the Lord gave between himself and the sons of Israel on Mount Sinai through the hand of Moses.”

Do not attend carelessly to what has been said. The legislator added a conclusion in his own words, by which he clearly showed that he wished the letter of the Law to remain firm until a certain time, without any doubt.

He therefore specifically called “judgments” those matters that were spoken when God judged certain cases about which ignorant people had asked questions. He called “commandments” those matters that the legislator himself enacted, not in response to questions, but on his own authority.

Then, wishing briefly to complete the dispensation of the entire enactment, he added: “And laws, which the Lord gave between himself and between the sons of Israel.” For this reason the other translators, except the Septuagint, rendered the word as “laws,” wishing by this expression to indicate the distinction within the Law.

But what does “between” mean, unless undoubtedly it indicates the time until he himself comes, concerning whom Isaiah says: “He himself will come and save us. Then the eyes of the blind will be opened, and the ears of the deaf will hear” (Isa. XXXV), together with all that is contained in that prophecy?

Then the Law must no longer be kept according to the surface of the letter, but as he himself will have expounded it: transferred to evangelical grace and to a more perfect way of life.

**CHAPTER XIV. How a man or woman ought to observe a vow that he or she has made.**
## Chapter XXVII

And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “Speak to the children of Israel, and say to them: A person who makes a vow and promises God his own life shall give a price according to the valuation. If he is male, from twenty years up to sixty years he shall give fifty shekels of silver, according to the sanctuary measure; if female, thirty. From the fifth year up to the twentieth, a male shall give twenty shekels, a female ten. From one month up to the fifth year, five shekels shall be given for a male, three for a female. From sixty years onward, a male shall give fifteen shekels, a female ten. If he is poor and cannot pay the valuation, he shall stand before the priest, and he shall give whatever the priest has assessed and judged him able to pay.”

These words of the legislator are also full of prudent foresight and most aptly adapted to circumstances. Having prescribed above what ought and ought not to be done, he now explains through these words the dignity of those who perform these things, whether wholly or in part. He has set forth the different ages, explaining what the perfect life is, what is still in progress, what possesses the beginning of knowledge of God, what proceeds through conspicuous and perfected works of virtue, and also what has become weak but has not withdrawn from it.

He says as follows: “A person who makes a vow and promises God his own life”—that is, whoever promises his life to God and wishes to offer his entire life to him—“the valuation of the male shall be from twenty years up to sixty years, fifty shekels of silver according to the sanctuary measure.”

If, then, someone is twenty years old—that is, mature, strong, vigorous, and capable of practicing every virtue and subjecting the intelligible enemies through all his actions and works—consider what the Law says concerning this age: “Every male from twenty years old and upward.” It has given testimony in the words mentioned above concerning all who walk in their own strength, for that period is especially one of strength for those who undertake such things, so that at that age a person can run, carry weapons, and possess great ardor and warmth for action. The valuation of such a person—that is, his manner of life, his life itself, and the recompense that he offers and promises to God for himself—is fifty shekels, or drachmas.

The number fifty signifies the spiritual life, because on the fiftieth day the coming of the Holy Spirit took place; and in the fiftieth year liberation from every debt and the restoration of the land occur, along with many other good things arranged for the Jews through the Law.

“From twenty years up to sixty years.” Within these periods a person possesses mature understanding, strength, and the begetting of children, so that from sensible things we may contemplate intelligible realities. Therefore, whoever possesses mature and perfect understanding, together with the strength to perform what he has understood, can acquire other children for God by devoting himself to a virtuous life or to teaching.

The valuation of such a soul, fifty didrachmas, is the perfect fruit and crown of perfection. It includes martyrdom, contempt for worldly things, and all that perfection which the Lord said: “You shall be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect” (Matthew 5).

This applies when he is male—that is, when he is always strong; for here he calls the steadfast person “male.” The valuation of a female shall be thirty shekels, or didrachmas, making sixty drachmas: namely, the sixtyfold fruit, itself great, but less than the hundredfold. For this reason he introduces the figure of a female, which is inferior to the male.

Thus women too, when they have reached the highest measure and advanced toward perfection, can be called strong, since they have transcended their weakness and taken up again the purpose of strength. Therefore the Spirit of God also says in Proverbs: “Who will find a strong woman?” (Proverbs 31)—one who lacks contempt for worldly things.

She performs another work perfectly: the Law commands her who lives according to it to practice continence with respect to all things. Her valuation is thirty shekels, or didrachmas—that is, the sixtyfold fruit. Paul also represented this when he said: “Let a widow be enrolled if she is not less than sixty years old” (1 Timothy 5). Through the age and number of years he wished to manifest what virtues and actions the widow chosen by God must display, the widow who is recorded in the divine books and who can dwell within the number of the heavenly Jerusalem.

Therefore he added, indicating that his concern was not so much with her age or years as with the virtues signified through them: “The wife of one man, if she has brought up children, if she has shown hospitality, if she has washed the feet of the saints, if she has assisted those suffering tribulation, if she has followed every good work.”

These things concern the person who is perfect and complete in every respect. But observe also the one who lacks this, yet desires to advance toward it:

“From the fifth year up to the twentieth, a male shall give twenty shekels,” or, according to the Septuagint, didrachmas.

Here he speaks of one who is not yet perfect, but is a sensible person who has begun to make progress. Understanding is indicated by the number five, because there are five senses; progress toward youth and perfection extends from five years up to twenty years. The Law numbered those twenty years and older among the strong and able to fight, as the Book of Numbers shows.

The valuation of such a person will be twenty didrachmas—that is, forty drachmas and four hundred obols. The number forty signifies progress in fasting and prayer, because we learn that Moses, Elijah, and the Lord himself fasted for that many days when he was tempted by the devil.

What the number four hundred signifies, and what manner of life it indicates, is shown by what is said in the Book of Kings, when it recounts the return of the ship sent by Solomon to Sophira. According to the Septuagint it says: “And he came to Sophira.” *Sophir* is interpreted as “good.” “And from there he received four hundred and twenty talents of gold and brought them to King Solomon” (3 Kings 9).

What, then, is this? The good is such: through fasting and prayer to exercise oneself and advance toward that life toward which Moses and Elijah, building upon fasting and prayer, also advanced through other virtues. The Lord likewise, when he began to make himself known to the human race through preaching and signs, made fasting and prayer the beginning of his manner of life.

Whoever, then, is sensible and begins to make progress, but not excessively—only moderately—so that he cannot be adorned by the presumption of a life of fasting, has a valuation of ten didrachmas, that is, twenty drachmas and two hundred obols.

His manner of life consists in keeping the ten commandments, which are doubled according to letter and spirit. Fasting is not among these commandments; the manner of life belonging to it is more exalted, and it befits the legislators, prophets, and all who have made progress. His manner of life does not yet possess perfection. He needs gentleness and perfect charity, which is found in zeal for Christ; nevertheless, it leads him toward perfection.

“From one month up to the fifth year, five shekels shall be given for a male, and three for a female.” By “one month” understand the person who has now been born in faith.
