Peter said to him: “As newborn infants, desire the rational milk without deceit, so that you may grow unto salvation, if indeed you have tasted that the Lord is sweet” (1 Peter 2).

His valuation up to the age of five years—that is, his manner of life and conduct—is five didrachmas of silver, namely ten drachmas and one hundred obols. The manner of life of one newly born is five didrachmas, so that through the ministries he may possess the twofold sense: that is, so that what he hears sensibly he may receive intelligibly. The same applies when he sees, tastes, smells, and touches; for this leads him toward perfection. Therefore his valuation is one hundred obols. The number, as has been said, is perfect.

Without doubt, therefore, this signifies the person who has now become a participant in the mysteries but has not yet advanced to action and is meanwhile being tested in faith, like an infant who does not yet have the time needed to display virtues.

But if such a person is even less advanced, so that the figure of the female applies to him—less advanced because he is simpler and not especially discerning—his valuation is three didrachmas. These signify faith in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, so that he does not go beyond it, but believes in his heart, as Paul says, and confesses with his mouth.

Thus, for one who confesses these three not only with his tongue but also believes them in faith, the three become two drachmas; and such faith brings him to moderate perfection. For three didrachmas are six drachmas, and six drachmas are sixty obols. Such a number bears moderate perfection. For this reason the people of Israel also numbered six hundred thousand—sixty myriads.

Visible Israel possessed people who were moderately perfect and who, established within the Law, practiced the evangelical manner of life to some extent. There were also those whose concern was only moderately devoted to the Law and the Prophets; therefore their number was likewise represented by myriads. Yet perfection was not always found among them in a thousand thousands or in myriads of myriads; for that belongs to the angels and to those who live according to the Gospel. Angels themselves also become such when they make progress.

“From sixty years onward, a male shall give fifteen shekels, or didrachmas; but a female ten.”

Who is this person who has undertaken the highest manner of life—for example, through virginity or through the virtue of possessing nothing that he promises to others—and afterward has become weak? You know that the legislator placed the one from twenty years up to sixty years above all the others.

Then, after all the others, he mentions the one who is sixty years old and above. By saying “above,” he plainly signifies the old age and weakness of the soul of the person who had undertaken the highest manner of life.

Accordingly, one who promises and undertakes a manner of life through virginity or contempt for possessions, and afterward becomes weak and fails to fulfill his purpose, hears Paul say: “But if anyone thinks that he is behaving dishonorably toward his virgin, because she is past marriageable age” (1 Corinthians 7). He shows a purpose that has become weak and been brought into old age; and thus, he says, what the person wishes should be done: “Let him do what he wishes; he does not sin if she marries.”

And again: “If you marry, you have not sinned; and if the virgin marries, she has not sinned. Nevertheless, such persons will have tribulation in the flesh. But I am sparing you. This, however, I say, brothers: the time is short. From now on, let those who have wives live as though they had none; and those who mourn as though they did not mourn; and those who rejoice as though they did not rejoice; and those who buy as though they did not possess; and those who use this world as though they did not use it. For the form of this world is passing away. But I want you to be without anxiety” (ibid.).

Therefore his valuation will be fifteen didrachmas, which are thirty drachmas. He set forth three fruitfulnesses of life from the good soil of Christ: through the hundredfold, he signified virginity and the renunciation of possessions; through the sixtyfold, continence; and through the thirtyfold, the life of chaste marriage.

But if such a person is weaker—for perhaps one of this kind has fallen into fornication—he is therefore called “female,” yet he is not to be rejected even so. He has a valuation of ten didrachmas. For he offers to God the keeping of the commandments, which we have shown to be twenty drachmas and two hundred obols, and in this he has his manner of life: justified through keeping the commandments.

But if you ask how the Lord was thirty years old, although he alone was truly perfect, when we say that perfection is represented by the number one hundred, followed by sixty, and then by thirty, learn that he alone was truly perfect. Nevertheless, as teacher of all and firstfruits of the entire mass of humanity, he became and set forth a manner of life composed from all these forms.

If you wish virginity, he was himself a virgin born of a virgin, and he taught virginity. If you wish marriage, he commanded marriage and blessed those who marry. If you wish abstinence, he also taught this. The same applies to the course of faith, whether it belongs to the perfect or to the simple.

Since, then, he indicates distinctions in the present passage and in a certain way differentiates human life, saying that the valuation of one is fifty didrachmas, of another thirty, of another twenty, of another ten, of another five, of another three, of another fifteen, and of another ten, these numbers together amount to somewhat less than one hundred fifty. What, then, is represented by what falls short of one hundred fifty?

When divided into five, these numbers come close to thirty. Observe how neither the legislator overlooked the proportion that Christ established in our life and conduct, nor did the Evangelist overlook a number possessing proportion. Therefore he says that Christ came to baptism when he was not yet fully thirty years old: “And Jesus himself was beginning to be about thirty years old” (Luke 3).

Why is this? Because neither the person who pursues a very perfect life, nor the one who pursues a moderately perfect life, nor the one who pursues an inferior life reaches the measure perfectly. Each has something excessive, since perfection belongs to God alone; but each also falls short only to the extent that pardon is granted for what is lacking. Hence one hundred fifty is short by seven; for the number mentioned above adds up to one hundred forty-three, and through the number seven pardon is clearly signified.

“But if he is poor and cannot pay the valuation, he shall stand before the priest, and he shall give whatever the priest has assessed and judged him able to pay.”

Now he speaks of one who has sinned greatly. For this reason Aquila rendered “if he has exceeded” for “poor.”

If such a person wishes to be offered to God, he shall stand before the priest, so that the priest may assess him according to what he sees him able to do, imposing upon him a rule of life according to virtue and the measure of philosophical discipline, prescribing what he has judged him capable of bearing.

For example, if he is wealthy, he is commanded to distribute his money; if he is healthy, to devote himself to fasting, prayers, and other good works; if he is both wealthy and healthy, he is commanded to do whatever his wealth and health suggest. If he possesses neither, he is to weep in prayer. In short, he is to perform whatever the priest sees him capable of accomplishing through his body, his resources, his health, or his other abilities.

“An animal that may be sacrificed to the Lord, if anyone vows it, shall be holy, and it may not be exchanged”—that is, neither may a worse thing be given for a better, nor a better for a worse. “But if he exchanges it, both the exchanged animal itself and the one for which it was exchanged shall be consecrated to the Lord.”

The legislator has explained that the offerings presented from ourselves possess certain degrees and distinctions. For even among those who in some manner become like us—so that they are also called our animals, either because they are exceedingly subject to us or because we do not use them for our service as we use animals—he explains through these words when the offering is holy.

He commands that we should not repent of what we offer to God. If, then, we offer animals of the kind customarily offered to God—and it is customary for immaculate and clean animals to be offered—our gift is immediately sanctified, and it is no longer lawful for us to repent of it.

Similarly, if we offer to God a son, a disciple, a servant, or another person under our authority, we must not exchange a bad one for a better or a good one for a bad one. Here he calls “bad” whatever is not wicked in every respect but is clean; if it is unclean, it is not among those things customarily offered to God.

The legislator has said that this offering must be among those animals that may be sacrificed to the Lord, but here he calls “bad” what is inferior. Symmachus likewise clearly transmitted the passage in this sense: “He shall not give a better thing for an inferior, or an inferior thing for a better.”

Thus, when we offer a son or servant to the service and ministry of the Lord, we may not wish to take him back for our own service and advantage, promising perhaps to offer a better or a worse one. For this is not permitted. Therefore Hannah also said concerning Samuel: “If you will indeed look upon the humiliation of your maidservant and remember me, and give your maidservant a male child, I will give him as a gift before you until the day of his death” (1 Samuel 1).

“But if he exchanges it, both the exchanged animal itself and the one for which it was exchanged shall be consecrated to the Lord.”

Thus we sanctify to God both the one whom we offered previously and the one whom afterward we offered in exchange with the first offering, and we grant both to God. For this does not permit us to repent concerning what we offer; rather, it strikes the enemy who suggested repentance to us, when he sees our offering doubled—the offering that he wished to intercept through our repentance.

## Chapter XV

### Concerning one who vows an unclean animal, his house, or his field, and what must be done

**The same passage.** “An unclean animal that cannot be sacrificed to the Lord, if anyone vows it, shall be brought before the priest. The priest, judging whether it is good or bad, shall establish its price. But if the one who offers it wishes to give it, he shall add a fifth part to the valuation.”

A Jew must be asked how this command can stand according to the letter. If it is not lawful for the animal to be offered and the gift will not be acceptable, how did the legislator write both statements as though they opposed and contradicted one another?

But in every respect he indicates something close to evangelical generosity and to the condescension known by grace. Let us therefore understand the words in this way.

It was not permitted that animals be offered to God unless they both divided the hoof and chewed the cud. The Law called animals lacking these qualities unclean.

What was signified enigmatically by not dividing the hoof? It signified the person who does not distinguish the letter of the Law from its spirit. What was signified by not chewing the cud? It signified the person who does not continually meditate on the Law and who recalls it for meditation with the tongue alone, not also with the heart.

If, then, someone offers to God such a son, servant, or disciple—one who, with respect to meditation on the sacred Scriptures or the division of contemplation, is inferior not through wickedness but through weakness—he is not yet truly a gift to God. The legislator does not mention him as though he had forgotten him; rather, he brings him before the priest.

The priest establishes his valuation, judging whether he is good or bad. In condescension toward the imperfect, he imposes upon him a moderate yoke: that is, a manner of life midway between good and evil, or a turning away from evil and progress toward better things.

Perhaps we may properly understand this as the distinction between inferior and better. For instead of the words “whether it is good or bad,” Symmachus rendered: “The priest shall establish its price, seeing whether, by making progress, it can become a gift among those things offered to God.”

“But if the one who offers it wishes to give it, he shall add a fifth part to the valuation.”

What does this mean? There are five senses; the fifth part of these is the mind. For the senses are governed by it, whether or not we make much use of them.

The five virgins who were not received into the marriage feast represent these five senses. They lacked wisdom, and therefore were simply called foolish (Matthew 25).

If, then, someone wishes to redeem the person who, for the reasons mentioned above, is compared with unclean animals, he must sharpen his understanding and make him intelligent. In this way he will be able to govern himself and will no longer need another pedagogue.

The text continues:

“If a person vows his house and sanctifies it to the Lord, the priest shall examine it to determine whether it is good or bad, and it shall be sold according to the price established by him. But if the one who made the vow wishes to redeem it, he shall give a fifth part above the valuation, and he shall possess the house.

“But if he vows and consecrates to the Lord a field belonging to his possession, its price shall be assessed according to the measure of seed. If the land is sown with thirty *modii* of barley, it shall be sold for fifty shekels of silver. If he vows the field immediately from the year when the jubilee begins, it shall be valued at whatever it can be worth. But if he vows it after some time has passed, the priest shall calculate the money according to the number of years remaining until the jubilee, and the amount shall be deducted from the price. But if the one who made the vow wishes to redeem the field, he shall add a fifth part of the assessed money and possess it.”

This is no ordinary question. A little later, at the end of the legislation, the legislator says: “Everything that is consecrated to the Lord, whether it is a person, an animal, or a field, shall not be sold or redeemed.” How, then, does he prohibit the redemption of things offered there, while here he commands that a house and field be redeemed after they have been sanctified?

Or perhaps here he recognizes one intention and there another on the part of the person offering. There, the person is not to deal further with what he has offered, but is to consecrate it wholly to God. Therefore he does not say, as here, “If he consecrates his house or the field belonging to his possession,” but “Everything that is consecrated to the Lord.” For nothing that was offered to God was thereafter permitted to return to human use. Not even the priest could use it.

The history of the Amalekites demonstrates this. Saul was commanded that all the spoils of Amalek should be under the ban. Because he permitted the people to take some of the flocks and herds, he endured a great curse and anger. This did not suffice to excuse him when Samuel was angry and asked: “What is this sound of the flocks in my ears, and the sound of the cattle that I hear?” (1 Samuel 15).

Saul answered the prophet in these words: “From Amalek I brought what the people acquired, the best of the sheep and cattle, to sacrifice to the Lord your God; we destroyed the rest.”

Thus it is one thing to sanctify something to God—something that the legislator now shows us is permitted to the person who sanctified it—and another thing to place something under the ban. The use of the latter is forbidden.

A similar meaning must be adopted for contemplation. We shall speak of the ban when we reach that section of the legislation. For now, let us explain what it means to sanctify a house and what it means to sanctify a field, with the Spirit suggesting the matter to us.

First, we say that it is one thing to sanctify something to God and another for it to be holy; one thing to offer something to him and another for it not to need an offering, but simply to belong to God and not require the offerer.

What is sanctified and offered begins to be sanctified through the offering by which it is offered. Previously, therefore, it was not holy. What begins to be sanctified needs progress and increase by stages.

But what has long been holy and has long belonged to God lacks nothing; it is perfect and needs no addition. Therefore it is good to use the teachings of others for sanctification, but it is better to progress so far that one can bring both oneself and those who belong to oneself to sanctification. This does not belong to every person, but only to the sensible one.

These are the things the legislator intends to signify in this passage.

A person sanctifies a house to God when he wishes his family, his relations, and his intelligible household to live in holiness, so that it may be and be called a church. Thus many of the faithful made their houses churches for the sake of sanctification, as we hear from Paul’s writing to the Romans: “Greet Prisca and Aquila, my fellow workers in Christ Jesus, who risked their own necks for my life. Not I alone give thanks to them, but also all the churches of the Gentiles, and the church in their house” (Romans 16).

Whoever therefore has this intention but is not himself capable of bringing what he intends to completion, the priest shall examine his house to determine whether it is good or bad, and it shall be as he assesses it.

Why does he say “whether it is good or bad”? Because a house consists of many different persons, among whom many need condescension and are unable to do or understand what is perfect. The priest should impose nothing burdensome upon them, but weigh each person’s virtue and command them to turn away from evil and advance toward virtue.

“But if the one who made the vow wishes to redeem it, he shall give a fifth part above the valuation, and he shall possess the house.”

That is, if the master of the house, who wishes to sanctify it although it was not previously holy and could not yet be called a church—for if it were sanctified it would indeed be a church, but it is not yet so and is only beginning its sanctification—wishes to redeem his house, cleansing it completely from whatever made it need sanctification and the necessary exhortation of the priest, what will he do?

He shall give—or, according to the Septuagint, add—a fifth part above the valuation. To the priest’s teaching, to which he initially offered his house so that the priest might assess it—that is, impose the rule according to which it ought to stand and live—he himself will add understanding. This is the fifth part: that he receive what is said and build upon the priest’s words. For frequent repetition makes people sensible and intelligent.

In this way he will possess the house. He does not lose its being sanctified to God, nor does it become a loss to him; rather, he will possess it because the sanctification of his own house is ascribed to him, not merely as its offerer but also as its teacher. Thus, when he presides well over his own house and recovers it for himself, he is found in a certain sense to be a priest.

Paul raised to the election and dignity of the episcopate the person who knows how to preside over his own house (1 Timothy 3).

Therefore, for the words “the one who sanctified it shall redeem it,” Aquila rendered: “If the sanctifier brings it to completion.”

What do we learn from this? If the one who sanctified a house claims authority and governance over it and wishes to acquire it himself, then “to bring it to completion according to the Law” means to be placed over others as their kinsman and to perform what the legislator has now commanded.

Since these things are so, that silver properly signifies the exhortation of the teacher of the divine utterances, hear David saying: “The words of the Lord are pure words, silver tested by fire, proven, purified sevenfold” (Psalm 11). And Jeremiah says: “The refiner has refined in vain; his dross has not been consumed” (Jeremiah 6).

He is speaking about the Jews, because the words of those who exhorted them profited them nothing. But hear Paul also saying: “If anyone builds upon this foundation gold, silver, precious stones” (1 Corinthians 3).

“But if he vows and consecrates to the Lord a field belonging to his possession, its price shall be assessed according to the measure of seed.”

No one doubts that the field signifies the divine Scripture. Christ is properly its vine, and the Father is its farmer. In it lies the hidden treasure, namely the saving proclamation; whoever finds it, the worker of the field, will sell everything he has, as the Lord says in the Gospels (Matthew 13), in order to buy that field.

Within this field each person’s possession is different—that is, the measure of what he is able to acquire from it for understanding.

If a person consecrates this field to the Lord, although it was not previously holy but now begins to be consecrated, he should choose a priest as the governor of his conduct, since he is not capable of governing himself.

The legislator has called the things assigned to the priest “consecrated.” “Its price shall be assessed according to the measure of seed,” that is, according to how much has been sown in him, or taught to him. Divine Scripture commonly receives the word of teaching as seed.

The priest indicates as much to him as he has been instructed in good, lawful, and spiritual teaching—not in what deceitful people, pagans, Jews, or heretics teach.

Therefore, after saying “according to the measure of seed,” he adds: “If the land is sown with thirty *modii* of barley, it shall be sold for fifty shekels of silver,” or, according to the Septuagint, “fifty didrachmas of silver.”

Understand in these figures the Old and New Testaments. Through the *modius*, or measure, or heap of barley, he indicates the Old Testament, because its seed is a richer food. Through the fifty didrachmas he indicates together what is spiritual and what is perfect; for perfect teaching is also spiritual.

When this rule or definition must be imposed upon him in its entirety, and when it should be reduced through condescension, learn from what follows:

“If he vows the field immediately from the year when the jubilee begins, it shall be valued at whatever it can be worth. But if he vows it after some time has passed, the priest shall calculate the money according to the number of years remaining until the jubilee, and the amount shall be deducted from the price.”

Here he recalls two years of remission, or jubilee, plainly indicating baptism and repentance. Each is a year of remission: one possesses perfect remission through the gift of grace, while the other belongs to those who devote themselves to prayer, fasting, and other works that complete repentance.

If someone wishes to be governed by the priest and brought forward on the path of grace that he has chosen, the priest should require of him what he commanded when he was being taught through perfect and spiritual doctrine, showing him no condescension. For he has no need of it, since he has been renewed through the gift; the priest makes him remain fully in the teaching he received.

But if he lacks something of the gift he received and has fallen away from it in his conduct—this is what it means to consecrate the field after some time has passed in the jubilee or remission—the priest will rightly calculate the silver for him according to the remaining years up to the year of remission or jubilee, thereby assigning him the time that remains for repentance.

“And the amount shall be deducted from the price.” For what he did less well, the loss he suffered, and the inferior manner of life he adopted diminish the gift; he has become weaker and therefore more rejected, and he is no longer what he was when he received the gift.

Nevertheless, he too can, if he wishes, redeem his field: that is, he can govern and teach himself, adding a fifth part of the silver to its price. He adds his own understanding to the priest’s teaching, so that by understanding and being instructed he may become the governor and teacher of himself.

Thus the intelligible field that the offerer consecrated to the priest will be possessed by him, and not by another: the conduct and virtue that he strives to attain, whether wholly or in part, will be reckoned to the one who practices it.

Pay attention to the legislator’s division: he wishes the person who intends to sanctify or consecrate a house or field first to make the consecration, and then he commands him to redeem what has been sanctified. “And then,” he says, “he shall possess it.”

Without doubt he commands this because we ought to govern our conduct through the teaching, rule, and laws of the priests when we first sanctify it; but we ought also to make progress and add our own understanding to their teaching.

Therefore Paul wrote to Timothy: “Understand what I say, for the Lord will give you understanding in all things” (2 Timothy 2).

Then we shall properly possess the things we have done, which are close to sanctification. But if we fail to observe this division, see what we shall suffer. The text continues:

“But if he does not wish to redeem it, and it is sold to someone else, the one who made the vow shall no longer be able to redeem it. For when the day of the jubilee comes, it shall be sanctified to the Lord, and the consecrated possession shall belong by right to the priests.”

Here the legislator plainly reveals the loss of the person who always needs to be governed by another, makes no progress, and receives no benefit from the teaching of others, but is always his own guide in doing what is useful.

The person who consecrated the field and afterward redeemed it is the one who permitted another to govern his conduct, and who afterward received help and acquired understanding, so that he became, as the prophet says, teachable by God and able to determine within himself what would be expedient in the future. By recovering his field for himself, he acquired it.

But the person who makes no progress under another’s governance and acquires no understanding, who always needs to be taught by another and remains like certain Jews to whom God, reproaching them through the prophetic voice, said: “They were chosen from the womb, taught from infancy to old age” (Hosea 11); and again: “Ephraim is like a senseless dove without a heart” (ibid.)—if he encounters wicked teachers, he does evil in every respect, since he lacks the discernment by which he might seek the reward of the virtue he has practiced.

Therefore he is said not to redeem his own field. When the jubilee comes—that is, when the time of remission has passed, during which remission has its place, namely, the present life—observe what and how great is what he will suffer:

“The possession shall be sanctified to the Lord.” For the conduct that he once acquired, even if another was governing it, shall be holy to the Lord.

But how is “the consecrated possession” said to belong “by right to the priests”? His possession and profit will be reckoned to the one who continually governed him.

If a field has been bought and has not been sanctified to the Lord from the possession of evil men, the priest shall calculate its price according to the number of years remaining until the jubilee, [Col. 0579B] and the one who made the vow to the Lord shall pay it. But at the jubilee it shall return to the former owner who sold it and had received it as part of his inherited possession. Every valuation shall be weighed according to the sanctuary shekel. The shekel contains twenty obols.

The firstborn that belong to God no one may sanctify or vow: whether it is an ox or a sheep, they are the Lord’s.

The letter and the spirit of the law display the greatest justice. The letter did not forbid the possessor of a field belonging to another to sanctify it to God and offer it to the priests, so that the field would be regarded as theirs, because he did not offer what was specifically his own. For just as it was then purchased by him, so what had belonged to the seller’s possession is rightly regarded as another’s. Therefore the priest is commanded to calculate the field’s price up to the jubilee, and to pay that price for it; but at the jubilee [Col. 0579C] it is to return and be restored to its former owner—that is, to the one who, because of poverty, sold his property and alienated it for a fixed period.

From this he passes to the spiritual understanding:

“If a field has been bought, and has not been sanctified to the Lord from the possession of ancestors, the priest shall calculate according to the number of years remaining until the jubilee.”

The one who possesses a field that he has bought, and that is not from his ancestral possession, is able to exhort the one suffering spiritual poverty, rebuke him, and move him to repentance. For he possesses the intelligible land of which David sang: “Your good Spirit will lead me into a level land” (Psal. XIV). He possesses it by not allowing it to be wholly corrupted, but gaining the virtue or life of the brother from which that brother fell through negligence. [Col. 0579D]

If, then, he sanctifies it to the Lord—that is, offers it to the priest—for you have heard that in the present passage he calls those things sanctified to God which have fallen by lot to the priests—how is it to be offered? It means that the one who has been at fault must be corrected and his manner of life made holy.

“The priest shall calculate its price according to the number of years remaining until the jubilee, and the one who made the vow to the Lord shall pay it.”

It is rightly the priest, together with the one who moved the brother to repentance, because the former, as one who corrected him, strictly examined his conduct and manner of life, while the latter, as a priest, recognized and calculated the true and complete redemption—that is, determined what sort of repentance ought to be imposed upon him. [Col. 0580A]

They calculate up to the price of the jubilee—that is, from those things concerning repentance which have been declared in the divine Scriptures. That valuation itself is the year of jubilee, or remission.

“And the one who made the vow to the Lord shall pay it”—or, according to the Septuagint, “and he shall repay the price on that day as holy to the Lord.” For at the time when, according to this rule, the matters concerning repentance are defined or imposed upon him, the definition itself is found to be holy to the Lord, when it is necessary.

He said well, “he shall pay,” or, as the Septuagint has it, “he shall repay,” not “they shall pay.” For although the definition of the repentance to be imposed is established by the common counsel of the priest and the one who moved the sinner to repentance, nevertheless it is the latter who offers him—the one who caused the offending brother to be pierced with remorse. The offender will obey him. But he himself also becomes bound in the correction of the one who is doing penance, since he was the one who once initiated his correction. [Col. 0580B]

The one who is not immediately cleansed completely when the penance is defined, but only when he has performed it perfectly, is the reason for the statement:

“But at the jubilee he shall return to the former owner who sold him.”

Thus the definition of the penance will indeed be made at once on that holy day, when, through divine Scripture, the priest and the exhortation of the one who is to undertake penance assess how he ought to perform it.

The penitent will receive his possession, field, and manner of life when he reaches the year of jubilee, or remission.

“Every valuation shall be weighed according to the sanctuary shekel.” The shekel, or didrachma, contains twenty obols, so that every valuation or definition may be made according to holy weights—that is, according to those things derived from sacred Scripture. External weights, such as those of the philosophers, with which they too weigh lives and manners of life, are not holy, because they possess imperfect knowledge. Nor are the weights of heretics holy: their conscience has been branded. But those measures are holy which are found in the divine Scripture, in which there are twenty obols.

The shekel, or didrachma—that is, the ten commandments—must be understood according to both the letter and the spirit, as the evangelical grace teaches, and as the one who says in the Gospel indicates: “Do not think that I have come to abolish the law or the prophets; I have not come to abolish but to fulfill” (Matth. V).

Therefore whoever either nullifies the law or holds to the Gospel does not possess the didrachma, nor do we receive his teaching as sanctifying. We reject heretics and Jews alike, since some deny grace and others deny the law.

“The firstborn that belong to God no one may sanctify or vow, whether it is an ox or a sheep: they are the Lord’s.”

In the preceding passages we said that cattle signify those who obey us—sons, servants, and disciples. Their firstborn means the one who is so obedient and submissive to us that he also provides other people with leadership in obedience and submission. [Col. 0580D]

For this reason he is called “firstborn” here; elsewhere the legislator says of him: “Everything male that opens the womb shall be called holy to the Lord” (Exod. XXXIV). For he opens the womb for the begetting of sons when he begins to obey according to God and with devout submission.

For example, Timothy was such a one to Paul. Therefore Paul wrote to the Corinthians about him: “He is my beloved son in the Lord; he will remind you of my ways which are in Christ Jesus.”

Let no one sanctify one who is such—not because he is unworthy of sanctification, but because he does not need to be sanctified: he has long been holy. You have learned how we said above that it is one thing for something to be holy to God, and another to begin to be sanctified. The former is better and higher, since it has long been perfected and requires no improvement.

Therefore the son who honors his father and mother so greatly that he becomes an example of such honor to others—honoring them out of piety, that is, out of obedience to the law, and knowing that he offers this honor to God, who commanded that a father be honored—has fulfilled the first of these commandments, the one that includes a promise, and also the second, of which Paul spoke.

Servants who submit themselves purely to the Lord because of the commandment—those of whom Scripture says, “Servants, obey your earthly masters with fear and trembling, in the simplicity of your heart, as you would Christ; not serving merely for appearance, as people-pleasers, but as servants of Christ” (Ephesians 6)—demonstrate obedience to God.

The disciple will do the same, thus obeying [his] teacher for the honor of God, who established through Paul: “Obey your leaders and submit to them, for they keep watch over your souls”; and again, “Obey and be subject” (Hebrews 13).

Each of these is clearly said to refer what belongs to this obedience and submission to God. Whether one pleases God through good simplicity, or through diligent performance of the commandments, anyone who for this reason ought to be called an ox or a sheep belongs to the Lord.

“But if the animal is unclean, the one who offers it shall redeem it according to its valuation and shall add a fifth part of its price; and if he does not wish to redeem it, it shall be sold to another.”

That every sinner is unclean is clear: “Every wicked person,” Solomon says, “is unclean before the presence of the Lord.” He is wicked because the legislator commanded that one both meditate upon and discern the law, as an animal ruminates and divides the hoof. Whoever lacks one of these qualities—that is, whoever is obedient and very submissive to a father, master, or teacher, but does not know how to meditate upon or distinguish the law as he ought—is indeed a firstborn among the cattle, as a leader in obedience, but is unclean because he does not possess what the legislator commanded the clean animal to possess. [Col. 0581D]

If, then, the father, master, or teacher wishes to redeem him, he shall be redeemed according to his valuation, and a fifth part of the price shall be added. He shall add a fifth by offering him instruction together with understanding, guiding him into wisdom, and not ruling him foolishly. For it belongs to an unintelligent father, master, or teacher to teach the obedience that pertains to himself to a son, disciple, or servant, but not to order his life so that he acts according to knowledge of the law, allowing him to remain ignorant and inexperienced in the law.

Let him therefore add understanding to submission [Col. 0582A] and instruction. For at present he alone is lacking in this respect, which is why it says, “He shall add a fifth part of the price,” since obedience has a price. Hence it does not say, “The priest valued him,” as it said above, but, as before, speaks of one having a price.

But if someone does not redeem the son, servant, or disciple whom he possesses—for it belongs to him to redeem him and to make him intelligent through prudent admonition, according to the manner that has been described—he is alienated from this possession.

## CHAPTER XVI  
### What is consecrated to the Lord cannot be redeemed but must remain in his possession

(IBID.) “Everything that is consecrated to the Lord, whether it is a human being, an animal, or a field, shall not be sold and cannot be redeemed. Whatever has once been consecrated shall be most holy to God. Every consecration offered by a human being shall not be redeemed, but shall surely die.”

We have shown, through the matters discussed above, what difference there is between anathematizing and sanctifying according to the letter. We said that what has been anathematized may in no way return to human use, not even to that of a priest, according to the history of the Amalekites.

But this is not all. Whatever spoils were taken by right of war from enemies with whom it was not proper to join friendship, after victory and plunder, they made anathema—not on their own initiative, but at God’s command. For whatever the prophets command are clearly God’s commandments. Therefore we too, when fighting against intelligible enemies—that is, demons—with whom we may not form friendships and against whom we have an unchanging enmity—ought to consecrate to God whatever, whether human being, animal, or field, we have acquired as spoil from the war against them and as victory; but we must consecrate it so as to retain in it nothing of our own will. [Col. 0582D]

For this reason the Lord said: “I have not come to bring peace upon the earth, but a sword,” and therefore “he will divide a man against his father and a daughter against her mother” (Matth. X). He severs the compassion of kinship, so that, leaving below the compassion of the flesh, we may more easily destroy our bodiless enemies.

Whether, on conquering intelligible enemies, we have acquired one who is his own master—for this is truly a human being, by which we mean one who is not at all subject to us but is our equal in manner of life—or one who is subject to us and is therefore called an animal; or whether, from the field of our possession—that is, that which we received by lot—we have taken a manner of life among the spoils and trophies while fighting intelligible enemies: we can neither sell these things nor need to redeem them, because everything consecrated is most holy to the Lord.

But hear how this is to be understood: no one can strip an enemy before he has completely subdued him, just as the Lord said to the Jews: “How can anyone enter the house of the strong man and plunder his goods, unless he first binds the strong man, and then plunders his house?” (Luc. XI). [Col. 0583A]

We fully subdue the intelligible enemy—that is, the devil—and can bind him, plunder him, and consecrate his spoils to God when we have overcome all his schemes, crushed his entire head, avoided every form of sin, and conquered all the desires of the world. Then we have him bound, and we may proclaim him.

By plundering him in this way and defeating him through the victory just described, whatever we plunder we rightly offer to God. We possess the most holy thing as something perfect and complete, needing neither our exhortation nor that of others, requiring neither addition nor further advancement. For how could it be otherwise? It has escaped every sin, performed every virtue, been alienated from the world, and been crucified to the world.

He therefore added very appropriately: “Every consecration offered by a human being shall not be redeemed, but shall surely die.”

By what death? By the death of which Paul said: “I live, yet it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” And again: “So you also must consider yourselves dead to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus.”

Such a person, advancing to the summit of virtue and reaching its full measure, possesses perfection. He is dead to the age, alienated from present things, and has long departed from the wisdom of the world. He is rightly most holy to the Lord, having imitated, according to his ability, what is most holy.

## CHAPTER XVII  
### Concerning the tithes of the land from crops and fruits, and how they may be redeemed

(IBID.) “All the tithes of the land, whether from crops or from the fruits of trees, belong to the Lord and are sanctified to him. If anyone wishes to redeem his tithes, he shall add a fifth part of them. Every tithe of ox, sheep, and goat that passes under the shepherd’s staff—whatever comes as the tenth—shall be sanctified to the Lord. It shall not be selected, whether good or bad, nor shall it be exchanged for another. If anyone exchanges it, both what was exchanged and that for which it was exchanged shall be sanctified to the Lord and shall not be redeemed.”

Perhaps you ask why the law commands that the tithe of the fruit of the land may be redeemed, but does not command this concerning oxen and sheep. A Jew cannot explain this, because he serves the letter alone. In that letter the legislator inserts many matters that admit of questioning, so that those who are constricted may run to the spirit and understand that the letter is good when they use it as an instrument and servant of the spirit.

Here, then, he sets forth the distinction among the disciples of the law. Just as, among the clean and unclean firstborn, some have acquired both obedience and good meditation upon and knowledge of the law, while others possess obedience alone, so here some who perform the commandments possess earthly wisdom and therefore necessarily need redemption; others neither need to be redeemed nor ought to be exchanged, as those who are always perfect and complete.

Thus by “crops” the present law means the harvest that comes from seed; likewise, by “fruits of trees,” it means the fruit according to its season.

According to the law, a tenth part of these is owed to God. Both of these must be understood as referring to the fruitfulness of the law. The Lord, explaining in the parable of the Gospel seeds those who receive the word and do it, spoke of the good land that bears fruit thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and a hundredfold.

David now cries out: “The righteous shall flourish like the palm tree” (Psal. XCI); and again: “But I am like a fruitful olive tree in the house of God” (Psal. LI). Now, briefly describing the righteous, he says: “He shall be like a tree planted beside streams of water, which shall yield its fruit in its season” (Psal. I). [Col. 0584B]

The tithe of such a person is holy. Their action and labor are holy, because the one who performs the commandments of the law while placing his hope in present rewards has an earthly mind, like certain Jews to whom the Lord spoke as people clinging to the earth: “You are from below; I am from above.”

Paul also said of them: “Those who are earthly-minded,” whereas “our citizenship is in heaven” (Philip. III).

This is what the present passage now suggests. For it does not simply say, “All the tithes of the land,” but first says “all the tithes of the land,” and then adds, “whether from crops,” openly proclaiming that the person who performs the commandments of the law with his intention fixed upon earthly goods, even if his tithe—that is, his performance of the commandment—is holy, nevertheless receives no great benefit from such performance with respect to the reward. Such a reward should not be expected from God by those who yearn for earthly things.

Therefore, if anyone wishes to acquire this tithe for himself, let him add a fifth—that is, understanding—so that he may set his mind on things above and seek the things above (Coloss. III), as Paul wrote. For the one who performs the commandments of the law in this way does not lose their profit, because his tithe becomes his own.

Thus the tithe of the one who is earthly-minded is indeed holy, but it is not holy to him, because he does not perform the commandment intelligibly, nor does he know what profit to expect from it or what reward to hope for.

But “the ox, the sheep, and whatever passes under the number and under the staff”—for he speaks of those who are numbered under the staff of the cross, to whom the faith and friendship of God grant that they be numbered. Whoever is faithful to God is found to be his friend.

Abraham demonstrates this, for it is said of him: “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness,” and he was called “the friend of God” (Rom. IV).

Those who are deemed worthy of being counted among the friends of God, even if they are an immeasurable multitude, and even if they exceed not merely a number but also a measure, should hear David saying: “Your friends, O God, have been greatly honored by me; their dominion has been greatly strengthened. I shall count them, and they shall be multiplied beyond the sand” (Psal. CXXXVIII).

These people do not possess earthly wisdom, nor do they seek a corruptible reward in what they do. Therefore no particular one of their works, but whatever they do, is a commandment holy to God.

Nor shall one be selected between good and bad—that is, between what is worse and what is better. Their distinction is not easy. Even if they surpass one another, like star differing from star in glory, all are nevertheless in heaven. As genuine followers of heavenly things, they are recognized only by the one who is able to discern the holy.

According to this understanding one must interpret the words: “It shall not be selected, whether good or bad, nor shall it be exchanged for another.”

Since none of them can be rejected, whom will you exchange for another, or what will you choose as better? It does not belong to our virtue to judge this.

Building upon these things, he added what follows:

“If anyone exchanges it, both what was exchanged and that for which it was exchanged shall be sanctified to the Lord and shall not be redeemed.”

Since the course of all of them is divine and lofty, close to heavenly conduct, you try in vain to reject one. It is not yours to introduce another in his place and consecrate him to God as though he were better. It is not yours to make such distinctions, nor to call one of the saints worse than another. Learn this also from the event recorded in history.

Paul and Barnabas once contended with each other. Barnabas said that Mark ought to be taken along; Paul, however, said that the one who had once withdrawn from Pamphylia and had not joined them in the work should not be taken along. A disagreement arose between them, so that they separated from one another. Barnabas took Mark and sailed to Cyprus, while Paul chose Silas and was commended to the grace of God (Act. XV).

You see how he exchanged the one whom he judged better for the one he judged worse. [Col. 0585C] Yet both the one who was exchanged and the one in whose place he was exchanged became holy. Paul chose Silas as more suitable than Mark for the ministry of preaching, but Mark was not expelled. Barnabas took him and went to Cyprus, and preached with him. He was so great that he also became one of the four evangelists.

Therefore Paul, reconsidering the matter and recognizing that none of the saints should be rejected, and that no one among those who have made perfect progress can call one worse or another better, again took Mark with him and wrote to Timothy: “Take Mark and bring him with you, for he is useful to me in the ministry” (II Tim. IV).

Do not therefore consider which among these is good or bad, nor exchange one for another; and he shall not be redeemed. For one who lacks nothing, what need is there of redemption?

In addition to the matters stated in the present passage, the legislator wishes to show that those who are taught by us, when they become perfect, no longer need our instruction. Therefore he says that the firstborn of the unclean are to be redeemed, but not those of the clean; nor are those things that have been consecrated to God to be redeemed; nor are the things now under discussion. For they have been shown to be perfect, since they carry a divine and heavenly intention.

Observe in what follows what end the spirit intended for this book.

“These are the commandments that the Lord gave to Moses for the children of Israel on Mount Sinai.” [Col. 0586B]

Why does it say not that the commandments were given to the children of Israel themselves, but that they were given to Moses for the children of Israel? Because the people were weaker and unable to grasp so great a sanction of the law, in which God displayed, as in mirrors, the clear forms of its mysteries.

You, therefore, if you do not wish to belong to the common multitude but to be like Moses, present yourself obedient, with all the senses of your soul purified, and say to God: “Open my eyes, and I shall contemplate the wonders of your law” (Psal. CXVIII).

Leave behind the material things of the flesh and follow the riches of the spirit. Say with David: “How sweet are your words to my throat, O Lord, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth” (ibid.), so that he may command his wisdom to you and entrust it to you, just as he did to Moses.

“For her commerce is better than silver and gold of the first quality; her fruits are more precious than all riches, and all that is desired cannot be compared with her. Length of days is in her right hand; in her left are riches and glory. Her ways are beautiful ways, and all her paths are peaceful” (Prov. III).

“She is a tree of life to those who grasp her, and blessed is the one who holds her. My son, hear the instruction of your father”—that is, of God—“and do not forsake the law of your mother”—that is, of wisdom—“for she will give a crown of graces to your head”—that is, Christ—“and a golden necklace around your neck” (Prov. I)—that is, the Holy Spirit—“to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.”

[Col. 0587]

## (YEAR 834) THE FOUR BOOKS OF RHABANUS MAURUS, ABBOT OF FULDA AND ARCHBISHOP OF MAINZ, CONTAINING EXPOSITIONS OF THE BOOK OF NUMBERS

### PREFACE TO FRECULPHUS, BISHOP OF LEXOVIUM

[Col. 0587]

[Col. 0587A] The judgments of the holy Fathers reveal the Book of Numbers as wrapped in manifold obscurities of mysteries. In it the number of the children of Israel is mystically recorded, and the encampment of each tribe around the tabernacle of testimony is referred to the form of the holy Church. There the distribution of the Levites in the service of God, and the offering of the princes, are prefigured according to the correspondence of the divine sacraments.

Finally, after the explicit mysteries of many different things and effects, a catalogue is given of all the stopping-places from Egypt to the promised land at which the Israelites encamped as they traveled. This demonstrates to us how, having gone forth from spiritual Egypt, we ought to hasten through the Red Sea and the vast wilderness of the present age toward our promised homeland in heaven. [Col. 0587B]

But because, holy brother Freculphus, you asked that these matters be explained to you through our labor by a spiritual interpretation, after my initial excuse—by which I wished to release myself from so great a burden in your sight, lest I perhaps be branded with the charge of disobedience—I applied myself to obeying your commands and to gathering from every side the judgments of the holy Fathers for this work.

Where I found something less clearly explained by their judgments, I did not omit it because of their ignorance, but perhaps because of some other occupation. Trusting in heavenly grace, which opens the mouths of the mute and makes the tongues of infants eloquent, I attempted to insert many things in accordance with the traces of their understanding. I did not do so secretly, however, lest I be accused of the fraud of theft. [Col. 0587C] Instead, I marked them openly with the prefatory designation of my name, [Col. 0588A] as I remember having done already in certain other little works of ours, so that the reader might know with what confidence he could read the sayings of the Fathers and with what caution he ought to examine our own.

If any of the things I have set down offend the reader as improperly expressed, let him attribute this more to my weakness and inexperience than to presumption or malice. Let him examine it carefully, and if he sees that it agrees with sound faith, let him not rashly condemn it because of the poverty of its expression.

But if in any place he discovers that I have erred in meaning, let him, prompted by charity, hasten to obtain pardon for me from the most merciful Judge, from whom nothing of human weakness is hidden. He also deigned to take our weaknesses upon himself, bear our illnesses, and pour out his most precious blood for the redemption [Col. 0588B] of our sins, so that although we could not be saved by our own merits, we might be saved through his grace.

As for you, venerable Father, I wish to have you as a corrector in necessary matters and as a defender against superfluous criticism. I therefore beg you to assist my frailty with your prayers before the Most High, so that in this present life he may cause me, strengthened by the shield of his faith, always to perform some part of his service, and, after my soul’s departure from the body, command me to receive eternal life in his presence.

May almighty God, author and restorer of our salvation, preserve you unharmed for a long time for the advancement of many, and, at the end, having joined you to the assembly of the saints, make you a participant in eternal glory.

## THE EXPOSITIONS ON NUMBERS BEGIN. BOOK ONE

[Col. 0587]

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0587C] The Lord’s speech to Moses concerning the numbering of the twelve tribes and the princes of the individual tribes, and what they signify spiritually.

## Chapter I

[Source cols. 0588C–0599B]

The Lord spoke to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai, in the tabernacle of the covenant of the Lord, on the first day of the second month, in the second year after their departure from Egypt, saying.

Near the end of Exodus, where the erection of the tabernacle is described, it is written: “Thus, in the first month of the second year, on the first day of the month, the tabernacle was assembled; and Moses erected it,” and so forth. Now, at the beginning of Numbers, it is stated: “The Lord spoke to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai, in the tabernacle of the covenant, on the first day of the second month, in the second year after their departure from Egypt.”

Here we should note that, at the twelfth encampment—that is, in the wilderness of Sinai, where Moses ascended to the Lord and the Lord descended upon Mount Sinai, giving his law to his people—the tabernacle was constructed. There the variety of sacrifices, the diversity of vessels, the vestments of the high priest, and the rites of the priests and Levites were prescribed. There also were written the enumeration of the people and of the Levites, the distribution of the people among the individual tribes, the offerings of the leaders, and the remaining sacred ordinances belonging to this encampment.

Yet, although it was the same year, it was not the same month in which the tabernacle had been erected when the number of the children of Israel was recorded. What, then, does the second year, or the second month of the second year, signify, except the time of the New Testament, which, after Christ’s coming, passion, and resurrection, will extend to the end of the world?

After the baptism bestowed through Christ’s grace—the baptism in which we came forth from the spiritual Egypt, once Pharaoh had been submerged—it is necessary for us to walk in newness of life for the remaining time, journeying through the wilderness of Sinai toward the promised land. Sinai is interpreted as “bush,” by which the Church is signified. In it the apostles preach to us, and in it we must wage spiritual battle against spiritual wickedness.

There the Lord speaks to Moses, who established the law for the instruction of believers, that is, of spiritual Israelites:

“Take the sum of the whole congregation of the children of Israel, according to their clans and their households, and the names of each individual, every male, from twenty years old and upward, all the men of Israel who are fit for war. You and Aaron shall number them according to their companies; and the leaders of the tribes and of the households in their clans shall be with you.”

Not everyone is worthy to be included among the divine numbers; rather, those who are to be counted within God’s number are marked out by certain privileges. This book, which is entitled Numbers, contains clear evidence of this matter. It relates that, by the Lord’s command, women are not brought into the census, plainly because of the impediment of feminine weakness; nor is any slave counted, as being degenerate in life and conduct. Nor is any Egyptian counted among those who had joined themselves to the people, plainly because they were foreigners and barbarians. Only Israelites are counted.

And not all of these, but only those from twenty years old and upward. Nor is age alone observed: it is also asked whether a person displays strength suitable for war. For the word of God prescribes that everyone who advances in strength is to be counted. Thus, Israel requires not age alone but strength.

Childhood is not counted, nor is it considered suitable for the divine reckoning, unless the children are firstborn or descend from a priestly or Levitical line. These alone among children are brought into the number. No woman whatsoever is brought into it.

But what are we to think? Can these things be empty of mysteries? The Holy Spirit, who dictated that they be written, is believed to have attended to this alone: that we might know who were then counted among that people and who remained outside the number.

And what benefit will this provide for those who eagerly desire instruction from the sacred books? What advantage is there in learning this, or what does it contribute to the soul’s salvation, if one knows that one part of the people was counted in the wilderness while another part was left unnumbered?

But if, following Paul’s judgment that the law is spiritual (Rom. 7), we believe that the things it contains are to be heard spiritually, an immense benefit for the soul will appear in what has been written.

The present reading teaches that, if I pass beyond the ignorance of childhood; if I cease to be a child in understanding and, having become a man, put away the things of childhood; if, I say, I become a young man—and a young man of such a kind that I overcome the evil one—I shall appear suitable for those of whom it is written: “All who advance in the strength of Israel.” I shall be counted worthy to be included among the divine numbers.

But as long as any of you possess either a childish and unstable understanding, or feminine and enervated sluggishness, or exhibit Egyptian and barbarian ways, we do not deserve to be held by God within the holy and consecrated number.

Solomon says that those who perish are without number, but that all who are saved are numbered. Do you wish me to show you that the number of the saints is kept by God? Hear how David speaks of the heavenly stars: “He counts the multitude of the stars and calls them all by their names” (Ps. 146).

The Savior not only placed his chosen disciples under a number; he also said that the hairs of their heads were numbered. For he says: “But the hairs of your head are numbered” (Matt. 10).

By this he was certainly not speaking of those hairs that are accustomed to be cut off with iron and cast away, or to fall out and perish with the passing of time. Rather, the hairs of the head that are numbered before God are those that existed among the Nazirite men, in whom there was the power of the Holy Spirit to cast down foreigners.

Thus he called the powers of the soul and the multitude of perceptions that proceeded from the ruling mind, as from the head of the apostles, “the hairs of the head.” But we have reached this point by a kind of digression; let us now return to our subject.

“And the Lord spoke,” he says, “to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai.” He means all those matters that we summarized above, where it is commanded that everyone from twenty years old and upward who advances in the strength of Israel be counted.

Therefore, if someone advances in strength, that person is counted—not in just any strength, that is, not in the strength of the Egyptians, nor in that of the Assyrians, nor in that of the Greeks, but in the strength of Israel. Such a person is counted before God.

There is a strength of soul that the philosophers of the Greeks teach. But this does not belong to the number of God. It is exercised not for God but for human glory.

There is also the strength of the Assyrians, or of the Chaldeans, which is praised in the study of astrology. But this is not Israelite strength and therefore does not belong to God.

There is also the strength of the Egyptians, in what they call secret wisdom. But this too is not added to the Lord’s reckoning.

Only Israelite strength is counted before God—that is, the strength taught by God, learned through the divine Scriptures, and handed down through evangelical and apostolic faith. Therefore he says that only those are to be counted who advance in the strength of Israel.

But let us consider why the people are not counted immediately upon leaving Egypt. Pharaoh was still pursuing them. Nor are they said to have been counted when, after crossing the sea, they came into the wilderness. They had not yet been tested, nor had they yet been attacked by the enemy.

They fight against Amalek and conquer, but even then they are not counted, for one victory is not sufficient for someone striving toward perfection.

They receive manna as food and draw water to drink from the following rock, but even then they are not counted, for they had not yet matured in those things said to be suitable for the reckoning.

The tabernacle of testimony is built, but even there the time for numbering the people has not arrived.

The law is given through Moses; the practice of sacrifices is handed down; the rites of purification are taught; the laws and sacred ordinances of sanctification are established.

Set these things down, hearer, in your heart twice and three times. See how much you must pass through, how much you must endure, through how many journeys, how many temptations, and how many battles you must fight and win, so that you may belong to the divine number; so that you may be reckoned in some account before God; so that you may be deemed worthy to be numbered among the holy tribes; so that you may be visited and entered by God’s priests, Aaron and Moses, in the registers of the census.

You must first receive the law of God and the law of the Holy Spirit; sacrifices must be offered; purifications must be completed; everything taught by the law of the Spirit must be carried out, so that at last you may belong to the Israelite number.

Therefore I still perceive something further in the mystery of this book of Numbers. The arrangement of the tribes, the distinction of ranks, the association of families, and the ordering of all the camps disclose to me signs of immense sacred mysteries, while the apostle Paul scatters among us the seeds of spiritual understanding.

Come, then, let us see what this entire reckoning of numbers and what the diversity of ranks contain in the way of mystical understanding.

We have a certain expectation of the resurrection of the dead: when those who are living and remain will not precede, at Christ’s coming, those who have fallen asleep, but, joined together with them, will be caught up in the clouds to meet Christ in the air (1 Thess. 4). That is, they will leave the corruption of this place and the dwellings of death, or perhaps some will be transferred to paradise, or to any of the many dwelling places that are with the Father (John 14).

The diversity of the transfer and of the glory will unquestionably be granted according to each person’s merits and deeds. Each will occupy the rank to which the achievements of his merits have brought him, just as Paul himself declares concerning those who rise: “Each in his own order” (1 Cor. 15).

Then, in the resurrection, each person will come to be assigned through spiritual indications to the tribe of Reuben, plainly because in conduct, deeds, or life he possessed something similar and akin to Reuben.

Another will belong to the tribe of Simeon, perhaps because of obedience. Another to the tribe of Levi, I think because he governed the priesthood well, or because, ministering well, he acquired for himself a good rank.

Another will belong to the tribe of Judah, without doubt the one who possessed religious spirits and well governed the people within him, namely, the mind and the thoughts of the heart.

Each person will likewise be associated with the individual tribes according to whatever he possessed in deeds or conduct that was related to each one of them.

Such, then, will be the ranks in the resurrection of the dead, as the Apostle indicates. The type and figure of these ranks seem to me to have been prefigured in this book.

We have given these matters a general indication, wishing briefly to comprehend the mystical content of this entire sacred volume. Thus, having received from these things an opportunity for spiritual understanding, each person may pursue a similar investigation in the remaining passages—or, if God reveals more to anyone, a higher and more exalted one.

But lest we seem to pass over the very meanings of the tribes and the names of their leaders untouched—for no small measure of understanding lies hidden in them, and the same matters are repeated in many places in this book—we have taken care, after interpreting their names and what they signify mystically, to note them briefly in a separate exposition.

Of the tribe of Reuben, it says, there was Elisur, son of Sedeur.

Behold how the law and the priesthood, by a spiritual reckoning, count among the chief offices of the Church and the ministries of individuals. For, according to what is contained in the law of the Lord, the entire ecclesiastical order ought to be arranged through the ministry of true priests.

Reuben, who is Israel’s firstborn and is interpreted as “seeing sons” or “seeing in the midst,” can bear the type of the primitive Church that was in Jerusalem. The Savior himself founded it first, during the time of his incarnation, in his apostles.

Elisur can signify this same thing, since his name means “my father is strong.” For the one whom the Prophet calls “the King of glory, the Lord strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle” (Ps. 23) is rightly called strong.

Thus this Reuben, established under such a leader, “sees sons” when he sees a great number of believers flocking to him. Hence, in Acts of the Apostles (chap. 2), it is recorded that, when Peter preached, about three thousand were baptized in a single day.

A little later in the same book it is written: “The multitude of those who believed were of one heart and one soul” (Acts 4). Again: “The multitude of men and women who believed in the Lord increased still more” (Acts 5).

More generally, the leader of the tribe of Reuben can signify those who, living among their brothers, care for those subject to them. Proceeding well in both speech and example, they desire to have many imitators whom they may send into the service of God in the place of sons.

Thus, in this tribe—that is, in spiritual Reuben—Elisur, who, as we have said, is interpreted as “my father is strong,” or, uncertainly, “my father is constricted,” holds the leadership. He is the son of Sedeur, which is interpreted as “hidden.”

For the person who uses the authority of teaching well, rightly presides over his subjects with paternal discipline, and does everything inwardly—not to seek human praise outwardly, but for the glory of God in the hidden place of the heart—is rightly described as leader of the tribes and households according to their clans.

He knows how to maintain the proper order of governance according to God’s will, caring for both married and celibate persons, for men and women alike, in both sexes and at every age.

In the tribe of Simeon, the leader was Gamaliel, son of Surisaddai.

What is expressed in Simeon, whose name is interpreted as “hearing” or “being heard,” except the devotion of the Church from the nations? Concerning it the Lord said through the Prophet: “A people whom I did not know served me; at the hearing of the ear it obeyed me” (Ps. 17).

Gamaliel—that is, “God is my peace”—rules in this tribe when our Redeemer, who according to the Apostle is our peace and “has made both one” (Eph. 2), and whose rule, according to Isaiah’s prophecy, will be multiplied and whose peace will have no end (Isa. 9), daily displays the signs of his power in the voices and works of the faithful.

More generally, Simeon signifies the entire order of those who obey.

Their leader, then, is Gamaliel, whose name in Latin means “God repays me,” or, as we stated above, “God is my peace.” He is the son of Surisaddai, that is, “one who restrains from evil.”

When a person considers God’s just retribution toward everyone and, living a peaceful life in a tranquil heart generated by true humility and the fear of God, appears worthy of all reverence in the assembly of the faithful, he is such a person. For, according to the word of Truth: “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 14).

Such people turn all their intention toward pleasing God, and confidently promise to obey his teaching according to what is contained in the sacred Scriptures. They say with the Prophet:

“To you I lift up my eyes, you who are enthroned in the heavens. Behold, as the eyes of servants look to the hands of their masters, and as the eyes of a maidservant to the hands of her mistress, so our eyes look to the Lord our God, until he has mercy upon us” (Ps. 122).

In the tribe of Judah, the leader was Naasson, son of Aminadab.

Judah, from whom kings arose, is interpreted as “confession” or “praise” and signifies the ecclesiastical people. The head of this people is the Lion from the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, namely, the Lord Christ.

And rightly is that people called “confession” or “praise,” because true confession of the sacred faith was praise—that is, right preaching—is found only in the Catholic Church.

Naasson, whose name is interpreted as “serpentine” or “omen,” is the son of Aminadab, that is, “spontaneous people.” He is rightly understood as the Savior himself, descended from the patriarchs, the servants devoted to God. Through death he destroyed the one who holds the power of death, namely, the devil.

For in the serpent, through which the first cause of death—that is, sin—entered our first parents, death itself was prefigured. Accordingly, the death of Christ and the mystery of the holy cross were prepared for the salvation of believers.

Hence the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life” (John 3).

All who rightly invoke the name of the Lord and do not dissent in word from the rule of the Catholic faith can also be reckoned under the name of Judah.

Naasson is rightly their leader: that is, the one who not only provides instruction to others by preaching, but also strives to kill within himself the poisonous darts of vices by disciplining his body, according to the apostolic saying: “I chastise my body and bring it into subjection, lest perhaps, after preaching to others, I myself should be found disqualified” (1 Cor. 9).

In the tribe of Issachar, Nathanael, son of Suar, was leader.

Issachar is interpreted as “reward”; Nathanael as “my God,” or “house of God”; and Suar as “little.”

Those who remember that they were redeemed by the price of Christ’s blood and devote themselves piously to good works in order to receive a reward in heaven have as their leader Nathanael, son of Suar.

For the Lord Christ, who appeared small among human beings through the dispensation of his incarnation, is shown to be the leader of all the elect, since he is the guide of his own on the way, and, when they arrive, their blessed life and most joyful reward.

Issachar can also appropriately represent the person of monks. Having entirely rejected all the business of the world, and with God’s gift guiding them—that is, under the protection of the Holy Spirit—they seek the heavenly reward through a strict life and the restriction of pleasures.

By despising the pomp of the world, they choose what is humble and despised before human beings, and desire to please God inwardly.

In the tribe of Zebulun, the leader was Eliab, son of Helon.

Zebulun, which is interpreted as “dwelling of strength,” has as its leader Eliab, interpreted as “my God is father.” He is the son of Helon, that is, “oak.”

The holy Church, which can rightly be called a dwelling of strength—that is, one that endures unconquered—powerfully defends and protects her children against heretics and schismatics. She has over her as leader God, who is the Father of the faithful and, with eternal power, disposes, orders, and governs all things.

Alternatively, Zebulun can represent those who endure. Surrounded by the protection of the virtues against every adversity inflicted upon them, they persevere unconquered.

Their leader is God alone, because without his gift they can do nothing; rather, through his grace they hope to overcome everything. They say with the Apostle:

“Who will separate us from the love of God? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword?” (Rom. 8).

And again: “I am sure that neither death nor life, nor angels nor rulers, nor things present nor things to come, nor powers, nor height nor depth, nor any other creature will be able to separate us from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus” (ibid.).

Among the sons of Joseph, from Ephraim, the leader was Elisama, son of Ammiud.

Joseph is interpreted as “increase”; Ephraim as “fruitful” or “increasing”; Elisama as “my God hears”; and Ammiud as “my illustrious people.”

What does Joseph signify, from whom two tribes arose, except our Redeemer, who is the father of two peoples? He became the cornerstone and joined together in himself two walls coming from different directions.

There Ephraim, younger in age than the firstborn Manasseh, is preferred by the judgment of his father, because the Gentile people, who flocked to the faith after Christ’s resurrection and ascension into heaven, multiplied through the abundance of faith and are preferred to the Jewish people.

Hence the Lord, praising the centurion’s faith, says in the Gospel: “Amen, I say to you, I have not found such faith in Israel” (Matt. 8). And again: “Many will come from east and west and recline with Abraham and Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven. But the children of the kingdom will be cast into the outer darkness; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (ibid.).

The tribe of Ephraim also has Elisama as its leader. Whom can we better understand as Elisama than our Savior, concerning whom the Apostle says: “He became obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross” (Phil. 2)?

The Lord himself says of himself in the Gospel: “He who sent me is true, and what I have heard from him I speak in the world” (John 8).

He is the son of Ammiud, that is, of “the illustrious people,” because, descending from the line of patriarchs, prophets, and kings, he came into the world to redeem the human race.

Again, in the leader of the line of Ephraim we can understand those who listen attentively to and meditate upon the word of God. They strive to do this not fruitlessly but productively, so that, according to James, they may be “doers of the word, and not hearers only” (James 1).

For, as Truth testifies, those who hear the word with a good and excellent heart and retain it bear fruit with patience: one a hundredfold, another sixtyfold, and another thirtyfold (Matt. 3).

Moreover, Gamaliel, son of Phadassur—that is, “of strong redemption”—rules in the tribe of Manasseh, whose name is interpreted as “forgotten” or “forgetful.”

Our Redeemer, whom the Father sent into the world to summon the Jewish people, found in his kingdom a forgetful nation. Hence the Lord himself says through the prophet Hosea:

“My people is silent, because it has no knowledge. Because you have rejected knowledge, I will reject you from serving as my priest; and because you have forgotten the law of your God, I too will forget your children” (Hos. 4).

And again: “Israel has forgotten his Maker and has built sanctuaries” (Hos. 8). “And Judah has built fortified cities.”

Yet not all of them perished, for God did not reject his people whom he foreknew (Rom. 11), but a remnant was saved according to the election of grace.

And when, according to the Apostle, the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel will be saved.

In another way, we may understand Manasseh together with the leader of his lot as those who, laboring because of their desire for eternal life and sweating in good works, do not value highly whatever works of virtue they have accomplished, but desire still greater works. In accordance with the Apostle, they forget what lies behind and stretch forward to what lies ahead, striving somehow to reach the prize of the heavenly calling (Phil. 3), so that they may receive the crown of life which God, the righteous judge, will bestow upon all who love him in truth.

From the tribe of Benjamin, Abidan, son of Gideon, was leader in the tribe itself.

Benjamin means “son of the right hand”; Abidan, “my father is judge”; and Gideon is interpreted as “temptation of iniquity” or “temptation of my humility.”
