Thus, in the name of Benjamin, earthly Jerusalem is represented, since it belonged to the tribe of Benjamin. Its people, according to the prophecy, were Rachel’s *Benoni*, that is, “son of sorrow,” because they afflicted their mother with great sorrow by shedding the blood of the prophets. Moreover, by conspiring in Christ’s death, they impiously cried out and invoked the curse: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27).

But just as he was a son of sorrow for unbelievers, so among believers, according to the prophecy of the father, he is rightly called “son of the right hand.”

Nor does anything prevent us from understanding in the figure of Benjamin the Gentile people, who were first “sons of sorrow” in persecuting Christians, but afterward, by believing in Christ, became “sons of the right hand.”

The apostle and preacher of this people was Paul, whom the holy teachers often place in the signification of Benjamin.

This people can therefore be called “son of the right hand” either because, at the final judgment, it will stand among the elect on the right hand of the judge, or because it strives to perform works of the right hand—that is, blessed works.

Abidan, son of Gideon, is the leader of this people, because our Savior—the one whom Jewish unbelief despised when he came to it in humility, and whom the ancient enemy presumptuously attempted to test unjustly—is the head of believers and will come at the end as judge of the living and the dead, to render to each according to his works: rewards to the righteous and the punishment owed to sinners.

Again, by Benjamin, “son of the right hand,” we can understand those who, through zeal for virtue, fight bravely against their enemies and press down the goads of temptation manfully. They do not permit anything feminine, soft, or pleasure-loving to rule within them. Armed with zeal for God, they are always prepared to fight against spiritual wickedness and the allurements of the world.

In the tribe of Dan, Ahiezer, son of Ammishaddai, held the leadership.

Dan is interpreted as “judgment” or “judging.” Ahiezer means “my brother is helper,” and Ammishaddai means “my people is sufficient.”

What prevents us from understanding the Gentiles in this person, those who, withdrawing from the coldness of unbelief, fled to Christ’s grace? Hence Dan is later described as having first encamped on the northern side beside the tabernacle.

Ahiezer is therefore the leader of the tribe of Dan, and he is the son of Ammishaddai when the apostles of Christ among the Gentile churches—like brothers of the nations, since they were generated from the earlier people—are established as teachers sufficient in word and good works. Instructing them with brotherly love, they strive to summon them to fellowship in spiritual grace.

Alternatively, in Dan we may understand those who do everything according to just judgment and strive to preserve discernment in all matters. They lead a sufficient people because they live discreetly.

They also establish “my brother is helper” as their leader, because they intend to do everything according to the teaching of the holy preachers and the authority of canonical instruction. Whatever good they do, they attribute not to themselves but to God, saying with the Prophet:

“Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory, because of your mercy and your truth” (Ps. 113).

And with the Apostle: “We are not sufficient of ourselves to think anything as from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God, who also made us competent ministers of a new covenant, not of the letter but of the Spirit” (1 Cor. 13).

Over the tribe of Asher presided the leader Phegiel, son of Ochran.

Asher, which in Latin is called “blessed” or “having riches,” signifies the number of the elect, rich in virtues.

Among these Phegiel holds the leadership—that is, “the Lord’s encounter”—the son of Ochran, which is interpreted as “he troubled them.”

This is because the mediator of God and human beings, who mercifully comes to the aid of the human race when it is in danger and collapsing under the burden of sins, troubled the enemies who harmed them—that is, by driving away the evil spirits.

Hence in the Gospel the Samaritan is described as coming to the aid of the man who fell among robbers. He approached him, bound his wounds, pouring in oil and wine; then he placed him on his own animal, brought him to an inn, and cared for him (Luke 10).

Again, in Asher we may understand those who do everything with counsel and desire to be rich not in perishable things but in virtues. They consider the wealth of this world of little value; indeed, they distribute all their possessions to the poor, so that they may store up treasures in heaven, where neither rust nor moth destroys, and where thieves do not break in and steal (Matt. 6).

They diligently consider the Lord’s saying in the Gospel: “When you give a banquet or a dinner, do not invite your brothers, or your friends, or your rich neighbors; instead invite the poor, the weak, the blind, and the lame. And you will be blessed, because they cannot repay you; for you will be repaid in the resurrection of the righteous” (Luke 14).

In the tribe of Gad, the leader was Eliasaph, son of Duel.

Gad is interpreted as “girded”; Eliasaph as “the protection of my God” or “ascent”; and Duel as “knowing God.”

Whom could Gad more fittingly represent than the people of the faithful? They always gird the loins of the mind with righteousness and, equipped with the shield of faith and spiritual weapons for battle, are always ready to fight against spiritual wickedness.

Christ our Savior, sprung from the line of the holy Fathers who truly knew God and obeyed his commandments, watches over this army. He directs his soldiers into battle and mercifully protects them by the power of his strength, so that they do not fall before the enemy.

We may also understand the holy teachers under the name of Gad. They stand prepared for battle and are always ready to resist their enemies.

They rightly excel among those designated by the name Eliasaph, that is, “ascent,” because when they lift their hearts to God and seek help from him, they cannot be overwhelmed by enemies below.

Concerning such people Solomon says: “A rooster girded about the loins, and a ram—there is no king who can resist him” (Prov. 30).

By the rooster he means the holy preachers who proclaim the true morning amid the darkness of this night. They are girded at the loins because they restrain the flowing excesses of lust from their members.

The ram in this passage likewise signifies these same men: that is, the first order within the Church, the order of priests, concerning whom it is written: “Bring to the Lord the sons of rams” (Ps. 20). Through their examples they draw along the people who walk behind them, as a flock of sheep following.

No king can wholly resist those who live spiritually and rightly. For even if some persecutor confronts them, he cannot hinder their purpose.

In the tribe of Naphtali, Ahiram, son of Enan, held the leadership of his lot.

Naphtali is also interpreted as “turned” or “enlarged,” and it signifies the people of the Church. Turned away from error, this people has been enlarged through the abundance of faith throughout the three regions of the world.

Isaiah says to it: “Enlarge the place of your tent, and lengthen your cords,” and so forth (Isa. 54).

Ahiram, that is, “the friend of my brother,” the son of Enan, meaning “fountain of sorrow,” was set over this people.

Christ, the Son of God, was a friend to his brotherly people—that is, the Jewish people—when he gave them the law and granted them knowledge of himself. Now, caring for the Gentile people through the sorrow of true repentance, he turns them to his faith, so that, counted among his army, they might enjoy his leadership and governance in battle.

Again, in Naphtali we can understand all holy men who, enlarged by brotherly love, extend the power of their affection not only to friends but also to enemies.

Their leader is Ahiram—that is, the Lord himself. He governs and protects through the leadership of his love those whom he has deigned to enroll not among servants but among friends, saying to them with the apostles:

“I no longer call you servants, but friends, because everything that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John 15).

These were the most noble leaders of the multitude, according to their tribes and clans, and the heads of the army of Israel. They are also the leaders of the multitude of the faithful, distinguished in virtue and outstanding in doctrine, and therefore rightly shown to be eminent and placed in authority within the Church.

Moses and Aaron took these men, together with the entire multitude of the people, and assembled them on the first day of the second month. They reviewed them according to their clans, households, families, heads, and individual names, from twenty years old and upward, just as the Lord had commanded Moses. And they were counted in the wilderness of Sinai.

### From Augustine

It is rightly asked what is meant by the fact that, throughout all the tribes, whenever the children of Israel are counted at military age, they are said to have been reviewed according to their clans, households, families, heads, and individual names—as though “according to clans” meant one thing, “according to households” another, “according to families” another, “according to heads” another, and “according to the names of individuals” yet another—when these seem rather to signify the same names in different words.

The repetition draws attention to itself, because the same things are described so carefully throughout all the tribes that anyone can see that this was not done without reason, even if he does not understand it.

Without doubt, therefore, the number itself conveys some sacred meaning, so that the same thing is repeated in five different ways. For this number, just as in the five books of Moses themselves—that is, the number five—is especially prominent in the Old Testament.

The four items connected afterward—“male,” “from twenty years old and upward,” “everyone who advances in strength,” and “their review,” as it appears in the Septuagint interpreters—have a necessary distinction.

When the number of the entire multitude belonging to one tribe was being given, sex had to be distinguished; hence the words “all male” were inserted.

And lest children also be counted, “from twenty years old and upward” was added.

Again, lest the age of feeble old age be included in the number, “everyone who advances in strength” was added.

Everything is concluded by the word designating the work by which this was done: “their review.” A review was carried out when these thousands of men were counted.

Thus the five items—clans, households and families, heads, and individual names—and then the four items—sex, age, strength, and review—perhaps signify something through their very numbers.

For if one of these two numbers, the number five and the number four, is multiplied by the other—if four is taken five times, or five four times—the result is twenty.

That number also signifies the age of young men. It is mentioned when they enter the promised land and that age of twenty years is described as not having turned aside to the right or to the left.

Here I think the holy faithful who hold the true faith from both Testaments are signified. For the Old Testament is especially distinguished by the five books of Moses, and the New by the four Gospels.

## Chapter II

On the Levites not being numbered with the children of Israel, but being appointed over the tabernacle of testimony.

(Same place.) And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “Do not number the tribe of Levi, nor include their total among the children of Israel; but appoint them over the tabernacle of the testimony, over all its vessels, and over everything pertaining to the ceremonies. They shall carry the tabernacle and all its equipment; they shall minister to it, and encamp around the tabernacle. When it is time to set out, the Levites shall dismantle the tabernacle; when it is time to encamp, they shall erect it.”

What is expressed by the tribe of Levi if not the priestly order, which was appointed over the tabernacle of the testimony so that it might exercise proper care over the holy Church, in which the divine covenants have been duly deposited? Thus all its vessels—that is, all the faithful and holy men who are vessels chosen for God, suitable for spiritual ministry and remaining unharmed by error and the stains of vice—may be preserved intact.

This order must attend to everything pertaining to the ceremonies of God’s law, because it has been entrusted with teaching the people of God how, walking according to God’s law, they ought to conduct themselves honorably and orderly in the Church of God. They shall carry the tabernacle and all its equipment, because, by bearing with the conduct of the weak through compassion and assisting them with timely consolations, they carry the holy Church, as it were, upon the shoulders of labor and patience.

They shall also encamp around the tabernacle, because, lest any part be left open to attacking enemies, they provide pastoral care on every side. They dismantle the tabernacle when it is time to set out, and erect it when it is time to encamp, when by word and example they arrange both how each person, prostrate in humility, should advance in the progress of the virtues, and how, raised up by hope, he should stand firmly in the state of right faith and steadfastness in good works.

And rightly the Levites are not permitted to be numbered with the other tribes, because the teaching and conduct of priests ought to be distinctive and not mixed with the common multitude. Hence Paul also commanded that a bishop be blameless and that deacons have no accusation against them (1 Tim. III). He likewise writes to Timothy that he should be an example to the faithful in word, in conduct, in love, in faith, and in chastity (1 Tim. IV). For it is not fitting that one who is superior to others in rank should be inferior in the practice of good works.

(From Augustine.) Concerning what he says about dismantling the tabernacle [Note: [Col. 0599D] In Saint Augustine, *distenaendo*.], carrying it, and erecting it: “Whoever of the outsiders approaches shall be put to death”; or, as it is found in the Septuagint, “and the foreigner who approaches shall die.” Here “foreigner” must also be understood to include those among the children of Israel who were not of the tribe that had been commanded to serve the tabernacle—that is, anyone who was not of the tribe of Levi.

It is strange that this person is improperly called a “foreigner,” a term that more properly signifies a person of another race, that is, ἀλλογενής, rather than ἀλλόφυλος, which signifies a person of another tribe. Scripture more commonly uses the latter term for people of other nations, calling them *allophyli*, as though they were people of other tribes.

Mystically, however, whoever unworthily approaches the sacred ministry is bound by the guilt of presumption, and will not escape the punishment of pride if he does not take care to recognize his proper measure. No one should usurp an illicit honor or seek, through arrogance, a higher rank; rather, let him be one who has been called by the Lord, like Aaron (Heb. V), and whom divine election has foreknown and predestined.

Thus King Uzziah, who unlawfully sought the dignity of the priesthood, was struck with leprosy on his forehead (2 Chron. XXVI) and withdrew in disgrace.

## CHAPTER III. What the camps of the children of Israel around the tabernacle of the covenant signify spiritually in the Church

[Col. 0600C] (CHAP. II.) And the Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying: “The children of Israel shall encamp, each by his companies, standards, banners, and ancestral houses, around the tabernacle of the covenant.” Or, according to another edition: “Let each man, according to his order and his standards, according to the houses of his families, place the camps of the children of Israel opposite and around the tabernacle of the testimony.”

Moses says: “Let each man proceed in the camp according to his order, his standards, and the houses of his family”; and Paul says: “Let all things be done honorably and according to order” (1 Cor. XIV). Does it not seem to you that there is one Spirit of God who speaks both in Moses and in Paul? Moses commands that the camps proceed according to order; Paul commands that all things in the Church be done according to order.

Moses, who ministered to the law, commands that order be maintained in the camps; but Paul, as a minister of the Gospel, wishes the Christian to be orderly not only in his actions but also in his very appearance. Therefore he says: “Women likewise, in orderly attire” (Tit. II).

I therefore think that they intend order to be observed not only in duties and appearance, but also indicate that there is an order in the soul, concerning which it is said that each person must proceed according to his own order. This order is chiefly revealed by the fruits of one’s works, but also by the grandeur of one’s understanding.

For it often happens that someone who possesses a lowly and degraded understanding, and whose thoughts are earthly, occupies a lofty priestly rank or the teacher’s chair; while someone who is spiritual, and so free from earthly conduct that he can examine all things and himself be judged by no one, either holds an inferior ministry or is even left among the common multitude. But this is to disregard both the ordinances of the law and of the Gospel, and to do nothing according to order.

If one of us is concerned with food and drink, devotes all his care to worldly matters, and assigns only one or two hours from the entire day to God—even if he comes to church for prayer or hears the word of God in passing—he does not fulfill God’s command that a person proceed according to his own order, or that all things be done according to order.

For the order established by Christ is to seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness (Matt. VI), believing that these other things will be added to us by God afterward. Let each person therefore recognize his own order and understand what is worthy of the order he has received. Let him regulate his actions, his speech, his manner of walking, and even his appearance so that they agree with his profession of that order, lest he hear God say to him: “Because of you my name is blasphemed among the nations” (Isa. LII).

But what does he mean by “according to their standards”? Let us see. I think that standards are those features by which each person’s individual character is marked. For example, all human beings are alike, but each person has a distinctive characteristic, whether in the face, stature, posture, or appearance, by which, for example, Paul is identified as Paul and Peter as Peter, and Peter is not Paul.

Sometimes, even to those who do not see, the difference of each person’s sign is conveyed, so that from his voice and speech one recognizes who is speaking. According to the sign of his distinctive character, each person can be known even without bodily sight.

I think that there are likewise different signs in souls. The movement of one soul is envy; another is mild, peaceful, tranquil, and even-tempered; another is turbulent, boastful, harsh, excitable, and insolent; one is circumspect, cautious, prudent, attentive, and energetic; another is lazy, negligent, and careless. And among these, one possesses more and another less.

I venture to declare that perhaps as great as the diversity of human faces is, so great also is the difference found among souls. I remember that the most wise Solomon says somewhere: “As faces differ from faces, so also the hearts of human beings differ” (Prov. VII).

But let each person, as Moses says, proceed according to his own standards—that is, let one whose standards are lowly and despised not walk more proudly and loftily than the standards of his soul demand.

It is possible, however, that through zeal for good works we may rise from inferior standards to better and more magnificent ones. For if we have rightly understood that all the things written in the law are forms of the good things to come, and of that age which we hope will arise through the resurrection, then it is certainly true that, if in the present life we devote ourselves to better things and, according to the Apostle’s teaching, forget what lies behind and stretch forward to what lies ahead (Phil. III), then in the resurrection of the dead, where star differs from star in glory, each person’s merits will likewise shine. We shall be able to be transferred from inferior standards to better and brighter ones and be made equal to more radiant stars.

Indeed, human nature can advance so far in this life that in the resurrection of the dead it may be made equal not only to the glory of the stars but even to the splendor of the sun, according to what is written: “The righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of God” (Matt. XIII).

This, then, is why it is said of the lesser ones: “According to their standards, by the houses of their families.” In the phrase “by the houses of their families,” the Greek has the same expression that the Apostle uses where he says: “For this reason I bend my knees before the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, from whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named” (Eph. III).

Thus the fatherhoods that Paul names here are rendered “families” by the Latin translator there. The same expression is found in the Greek. These, therefore, are the fatherhoods or families that Paul has already shown to exist in heaven, while Moses describes them still under the legal figures on earth. He urges us to proceed according to them, so that we may be joined to the heavenly fatherhoods.

As Paul declared above, these should be called either families or fatherhoods in heaven. Among them, perhaps, is also that which the same Paul names elsewhere: “the church of the firstborn enrolled in heaven” (Heb. XII). We shall be granted fellowship with it if we proceed according to order and do everything according to order; if nothing disorderly, nothing restless, and nothing dishonorable is found in us. Then we shall shine like the firmament and gleam like stars and the sun in the kingdom of God through Christ.

To the east, Judah shall pitch its tents by the companies of its army, and its leader shall be Nahshon son of Amminadab. The total of those in his army shall be seventy-four thousand six hundred. Around the tabernacle all the children of Israel shall encamp, three tribes on each side, so that none of them may be left over or missing.

Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun therefore pitched their tents to the east; Reuben, Simeon, and Gad to the south; Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasseh to the west; Dan, Asher, and Naphtali to the north.

What does the tabernacle signify in this passage if not the Church of both the Old and the New Testament? The twelve leaders who encamp around the tabernacle signify the patriarchs or apostles, by whose prayers and teaching the Church is defended.

But the fact that the position and arrangement of the camps are described through a certain association of tribes and connection of encampments undoubtedly pertains to some condition in the resurrection of the dead. Three tribes are said to have been placed to the east, three to the west, three toward the sea, and the final three to the north, which is called the harsh wind.

Nor do I think it insignificant that the tribe of Judah, which is royal, is placed in the east, from which our Lord arose. Nor is it without meaning that Issachar and Zebulun are joined to it, or that this group of three is arranged in the four regions.

Although these groups have different qualities in their arrangements, all are nevertheless contained within the number three. And because throughout all four regions this same trinity is gathered into one number, this undoubtedly signifies that, under the one name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, all those who come from the four regions of the world and invoke the name of the Lord are counted together, reclining with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of God (Matt. VIII).

Let us say something further that may assist the reader, so that from these brief observations he may infer greater things.

The four regions of the world, in whose designation the encampment of the children of Israel around the tabernacle is described, signify, according to the mystery, the calling and arrangement of the holy Church.

The east, where the entrance into the tabernacle was open, signifies the beginning of conversion, the confession of the Catholic faith, and the initial reception of baptism, as well as the primitive Church founded in Jerusalem by the apostles after the Lord’s coming.

And rightly the tribe of Judah is assigned to this region, together with the tribes of Issachar and Zebulun, because the confessors of Christ have access through that entrance to the dwelling of strength where they will labor for an eternal reward. He said: “I am the door; if anyone enters through me, he will be saved” (John X). And again: “I am the light of the world; whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life” (John VIII). Concerning him Zechariah also says: “The dawn from on high has visited us, to illuminate those who sit in darkness and the shadow of death” (Luke II).

The southern region, alongside which the southern side of the tabernacle was extended, designates that ancient people of God who, having long ago received the light of legal knowledge, used to burn with love for their Creator. Reuben, Simeon, and Gad encamped there.

And rightly so, because the holy fathers, who sharpened the gaze of their minds in order to see the will of God, duly devoted themselves to obedience, girding themselves with the armor of righteousness, so that they might always be armed to resist the wicked enemy who, according to Peter’s word, “prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour” (1 Pet. V), as well as the noonday demon.

The northern region, along which the other side of the tabernacle was situated, represents the multitude of the nations. It had not ceased to languish in the darkness and cold of unbelief until the time of the Lord’s incarnation. Dan, Asher, and Naphtali were not improperly commanded to encamp there, because, when the Jews rejected the word of the Lord, the people of the Church, enlarged by the multitude of the faithful from the nations according to God’s just judgment, does not cease to hope for and seek eternal blessedness.

The western region, receiving both walls of the tabernacle and bringing them together in its union, signifies the completion of the whole holy universal Church, which is perfected at the end of the world. Then the elect, as they increase in good works, are tested by the persecution of the Antichrist; and that hour approaches when the wicked have been handed over to the oblivion of eternal death, and the righteous will be placed at God’s right hand to reign eternally with the Lord.

Therefore, rightly, by this region Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasseh were commanded by God to pitch their camps.

The Levites were also close to the tabernacle for this reason: the other tribes stood around them on every side in the four regions, so that those whose duty it was to care for the tabernacle might devote themselves without fear to the divine service, while they were protected externally by their brothers against the assault of enemies.

So also in the present time it is right that the common order should provide for the ecclesiastical order in matters external, so that the ministers of God may devote themselves without hindrance to the word and the divine service.

Ascend now, therefore, O listener, if you can, and lift the gaze of your mind and the sight of your heart above earthly perceptions. Forget earthly things for a little while; walk with the step of your mind above the clouds and beyond heaven itself. There seek the tabernacle of God. There Jesus, the forerunner, has entered for us, and now stands before the face of God, interceding for us.

There, I say, seek those four orders and stations of the camps. There behold the Israelite armies and the watches of the saints; there examine the mysteries of the firstborn that we are now seeking.

But I do not dare to ascend there alone. I do not dare to plunge into these so-secret retreats of the mysteries without the authority of some great teacher. I cannot ascend there unless Paul goes before me and shows me the way of this new and difficult journey.

That greatest of the apostles, who knew that there are many Churches not only on earth but also in heaven, among which John names certain seven (Rev. III), nevertheless, wishing to show that there is also another Church of the firstborn, writes to the Hebrews: “You have not approached a blazing and tangible fire; rather, you have approached Mount Zion and the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and the multitude of angels praising together, and the Church of the firstborn enrolled in heaven” (Heb. XIX).

Moses, then, divided the people of God on earth into four camps, while the Apostle describes four orders of the saints in heaven, and says that each one of us approaches one of them.

For not everyone approaches all of them. Some approach Mount Zion. Those who are somewhat better approach the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem. Those who are more eminent among these approach the multitude of angels praising together. Those who are above all these saints approach the Church of the firstborn enrolled in heaven.

Since you have understood from these things what the order of the firstborn is and what the mystery of this name signifies, prepare yourself and strive with all your strength. Perhaps through your actions, life, conduct, faith, and disciplines you may advance, so that you can approach the Church of the firstborn enrolled in heaven.

If you are not yet able to reach that height but are somewhat lower, approach the multitude of angels praising together. If you cannot approach that, hasten and strive toward the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem. If you are not fit even for this, strive only toward Mount Zion, so that you may be saved on the mountain.

Only do not remain on earth or stay in the valleys; do not persist in low and sunken places (Gen. XIX).

The tabernacle of the testimony shall be lifted by the services and companies of the Levites. As it is erected, so also it shall be dismantled. The erection and dismantling of the tabernacle signify the condition of the Church, which is raised up daily in believers and dismantled in those who deny. In the elect it is exalted through the services of the priests and the sacred orders; in sinners it is likewise humbled by the judgment of the priests through excommunication.

## CHAPTER IV. The sons of Aaron and their ministry; likewise, the Levites and their service

(CHAP. III.) These are the generations of Aaron and Moses on the day when the Lord spoke to Moses on Mount Sinai, and these are the names of Aaron’s sons: Nadab the firstborn, then Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar.

These are the names of the sons of Aaron, the priests who were anointed and whose hands were filled and consecrated so that they might perform the priesthood. Nadab and Abihu died when they offered unauthorized fire before the Lord in the desert of Sinai, without children. Eleazar and Ithamar performed the priesthood before Aaron their father.

The four sons of Aaron were chosen together with their father for the priesthood; but while two remained in their position, the others were consumed by divine fire because they placed unauthorized fire upon God’s altar.

By this event, if I am not mistaken, it is indicated that, although many gathered from the four regions of the world and exalted in divine ministry may appear to hold preeminence in the Church, only those properly persist in their ministry who, after sound doctrine has been tested by the fire of the two Testaments and the Holy Spirit, carry out their preaching. Kindled by zeal for God through love of God and neighbor, they strive to accomplish whatever they can for the salvation of their neighbors.

But those who introduce foreign doctrines fashioned by human teaching, and who, inflamed by worldly desire, unworthily perform what is divine, are justly consumed by the fire of vengeance directed against them by the Lord.

## CHAPTER V. How the Lord took the Levites for the ministry of his tabernacle in place of the firstborn of the children of Israel

(CHAP. III.) And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “Bring forward the tribe of Levi and make them stand before Aaron the priest, so that they may minister to him, keep watch, and observe everything pertaining to the worship of the congregation before the tabernacle of the testimony; and let them guard the vessels of the tabernacle while serving in its ministry.

“You shall give the Levites as a gift to Aaron and his sons; they have been given to them by the children of Israel. You shall appoint Aaron and his sons over the priestly worship.”

The Septuagint: “And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: ‘Take the tribe of Levi and set them before Aaron the priest, and they shall minister to him; and they shall guard the guards of the children of Israel before the tabernacle of the testimony.’”

(From Augustine.) The things that the Greek calls φυλακαί, some of our translators have rendered “guards,” others “watches.” But surely “watches” is the better term, since watches customarily consist of periods of three hours. Hence it is written: “In the fourth watch of the night he came to them, walking on the sea” (Matt. XIV)—that is, after the ninth hour of the night, after three watches.

In many places in Scripture our translators have rendered φυλακαί, which the Greeks use, as “watches.” There is no doubt that these signify periods of the night. I think that this meaning should also be understood here.

How are the Levites commanded to observe the watches of Aaron and the watches of the children of Israel—that is, the φυλακαί—unless perhaps this was said lest they should think that, because of the honor in which they served the tabernacle, they ought to be exempt from observing the watches that are customarily maintained in camps? They too had to take their turn, on account of the work of the tabernacle, in observing the watches that were maintained in the other camps of the children of Israel all around.

But the outsider who approaches to minister shall die.

One must ask how Leviticus says, “Whoever touches the tabernacle shall be sanctified,” whereas here it says, “The foreigner who touches it shall die,” intending to refer to those who were not of the tribe of Levi. Or did he perhaps use “touches” here in the sense of approaching for the service of ministry, which he commanded to be performed at the tabernacle only by the Levites? For this was the subject under discussion.

(Same place.) And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “I have taken the Levites from among the children of Israel in place of every firstborn who opens the womb among the children of Israel, and the Levites shall be mine. For every firstborn is mine. From the day when I struck down the firstborn in the land of Egypt, I sanctified to myself everything that is firstborn in Israel, from man to beast. They are mine; I am the Lord.”

(From Augustine.) Why does God assign the Levites to himself in place of the firstborn of the children of Israel, so that, when the firstborn of the people were counted, those found more numerous than the Levites were redeemed with silver, as Scripture testifies later in this book—five shekels being given for each one—whereas this was not done for the animals, even though God wished the animals of the Levites to belong to him in place of the firstborn of Israel’s animals?

How, thereafter, did their firstborn, or the firstborn of their animals, belong to God, when he commanded the human firstborn to be exchanged for sheep? How would the sons of the Levites thereafter not be counted in place of those firstborn? The same tribe remained in their descendants, and could have been counted in place of later firstborn—unless the point is that it was just that those born from those who already belonged to the Lord as his portion, having been given in place of the firstborn who came out of Egypt, should already be God’s own, as his from his own, and could not rightly be counted in place of those firstborn who thereafter were owed to God.

For from the whole people and all the people’s animals, a portion was given to God in place of the firstborn; and this portion consisted of the Levites and their animals. Now, if anything was born from those belonging to God, it belonged to God and could not be given as though it came from the people, since it was not the people’s property.

Therefore, thereafter the firstborn owed to God had to be rendered to him, and the descendants of the Levites or of their animals could not be counted in their place.

“And the Levites shall be mine,” he says, “for every firstborn is mine. From the day when I struck down every firstborn in the land of Egypt, I sanctified to myself everything firstborn.”

It is known from the historical account how the firstborn of the Egyptians were struck down when the people of Israel were led out of Egypt. This, then, is what is indicated here: the firstborn of Israel were not sanctified until the firstborn of the Egyptians had been struck down. He presents the hour of their destruction and death as the cause of their sanctification.

Hence it must also be understood here that there are certain firstborn among the Egyptians—that is, among the opposing powers—chosen, as it were, in wickedness and first among the demons. Unless these are struck down and destroyed, the firstborn of Israel cannot receive sanctification at all.

Who, then, struck down the firstborn of the Egyptians, that is, the principalities and powers of the demons? Was it not my Lord Jesus Christ, who is the firstborn of all creation, who led the opposing principalities and powers in triumph, triumphing over them on the cross?

If he had not struck them down, the sanctification of the firstborn could in no way have come to us. But in order to give us the blessings of the firstborn, he first became the firstborn from the dead, so that he himself might hold first place among human beings (Col. I). He then took us who believe in his resurrection as firstborn and placed us in the order of the firstborn, provided that we retain the grace of the blessings firm to the end, aided by the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ.

But when he says “in place of the firstborn who opens the womb,” anyone who is firstborn ought immediately to be regarded as worthy of sanctification. For we also read in the Psalms: “Sinners have been estranged from the womb; they have gone astray from the belly; they have spoken falsehood” (Ps. LVII).

This cannot possibly be understood according to the literal sense. For when could anyone have gone astray from the way of God immediately upon leaving his mother’s womb? Or how could one who had just been born, still an infant, have spoken falsehood or uttered any kind of speech?

Since it is impossible for anyone either to go astray from the womb or to speak falsehood from the belly, it will be necessary to seek a womb and belly to which the statement can apply: “Sinners have been estranged from the womb; they have gone astray from the womb; they have spoken falsehood.” It is also necessary to consider the womb that every firstborn who is sanctified opens.

At one time God opened Leah’s womb, which had been closed, and she bore the patriarchs. Likewise, he opened Rachel’s womb so that she too might give birth, she whose sight was keen and whose appearance was beautiful.

But in many other passages of Scripture you will find wombs being opened. If you consider each of them in its proper place, you will discover both how sinners go astray from the womb and how others, by opening the womb, are sanctified into the order.

The Lord spoke to Moses in the desert of Sinai, saying: “Count the sons of Levi who are firstborn, according to their ancestral households and families, every male from one year old and upward.” Moses counted them as the Lord had commanded, and the sons of Levi were found according to their names: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari. The sons of Gershon were Libni and Shimei. The sons of Kohath were Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel. The sons of Merari were Mahli and Mushi, and so forth.

Behold: when Moses, by God’s command, counted the tribe of Levi from one month old and upward, the order of enumeration was distributed among the individual families of the sons of Levi; and it was arranged how they should be suitably assigned to the service of the tabernacle, to carrying its burdens, and to pitching their camps around the tabernacle. Nor should we believe that this, too, occurred without a great mystery. But, touching briefly on a few matters among many, in keeping with the smallness of our understanding, we shall leave the greater matters to be explained by those who are more perfect.

We have therefore said that the Levites signify the ecclesiastical order; the meaning of the name itself makes this clear. For Levi is interpreted as “added” or “taken up.” The order of teachers may rightly be called “taken up” or “added,” because, raised from the world by heavenly grace to fulfill divine service, it has been added and united to the assembly of the holy angels. Hence the Savior says to the apostles in the Gospel: “I chose you from the world, so that you may go and bear fruit, and that your fruit may remain” (John 15). Elsewhere, when discussing the true resurrection and the glory of the saints, he answered the Jews who were testing him: “For in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are like the angels of God in heaven.”

The three sons of Levi therefore designate those same holy preachers, distinguished by their confession of the Holy Trinity and greatly admirable in faith, hope, and love. Nor does the interpretation of their names in any way contradict this exposition; rather, it agrees with it very closely. Gershon is interpreted as “stranger”; Kohath as “patience” or “molars”; Merari as “bitter” or “bitterness.” Whoever is rightly devoted to divine service acknowledges that he is a stranger and pilgrim in this world. Applying himself to patience, he does not shrink from grinding and breaking up the divine word with the teeth of discernment according to the capacity of his hearers. Moreover, by showing that the world has become bitter to him, he does not cease to turn others away from, and call them back from, the pleasures of the world.

These men are counted from one month of age, because it is most fitting that the beginning of the conduct of holy teachers should be dedicated to God, lest, after becoming blameworthy through many crimes, they give others an occasion to blaspheme the name of God if they are chosen, unworthy, for this sacred work. Hence Paul also commanded that a bishop should be blameless, the husband of one wife, chaste, sober, prudent, modest, well ordered, hospitable, a teacher, not addicted to wine, not violent but gentle, not quarrelsome, not greedy, presiding over his own household and having children submissive with all chastity (1 Timothy 3).

Furthermore, in what has been related about the encampment of the sons of Levi, a most fitting order is shown in this place: those who were first in rank were to guard the eastern region, namely Moses and Aaron with their sons, having charge of the sanctuary in the midst of the sons of Israel. Next, the Kohathites, from whom Moses and Aaron had sprung, occupied the southern region under the care of Eleazar the priest, who was the senior among Aaron’s sons. After these, the Gershonites pitched their camp on the western side, likewise placed under the care of Eleazar the priest. Finally, the Merarites encamped on the northern side, under the custody and direction of Ithamar, the younger son of Aaron.

This, of course, while preserving the allegory, indicates according to mortal life that the ministers of the Church should honorably maintain the ranks in which they have been placed and should not seek greater things than their position requires.

Mystically, the eastern region signifies the beginning of faith. There Moses—whose name is interpreted as “drawn from water”—and Aaron, that is, “mountain of strength,” are commanded to encamp with their sons. For those who rightly hold episcopal authority in the Church, and to whom the keys of the heavenly kingdom have been entrusted, ought to know the entrance and the order themselves and continually preach them to others. Each person must enter in the light of faith through the gate of catholic confession and the water of baptism, so that, being “drawn from water,” he may become a son of adoption; and, begetting sons of good works through the strength of steadfastness, he must guard the entrance of faith by which he entered the Church, lest, having become idle and useless, he be cast out from it.

The southern region, beside which the Kohathites encamp under Eleazar the priest, signifies that, after receiving the light of knowledge, each person must discreetly bestow upon his neighbors the word and consolation of patience, and must do so under Eleazar, that is, under the help of God. For, according to the Psalmist’s saying: “Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain. Unless the Lord guards the city, those who guard it labor in vain” (Psalm 126).

The Gershonites, who are likewise placed under Eleazar’s care, pitched their camp in the western region, where the sun usually closes the day and all the stars seem to die. By this figure they express that the ministers and guardians of the true tabernacle must flee the desire of the world and, with God’s help, mortify carnal desires within themselves. Thus they should await the final day and the end of their present labor. Though dead to the world and alive to God, they can say with the apostle Paul: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Galatians 6).

The Merarites, last of all, under Ithamar the son of Aaron—whose name is interpreted as “where it is bitter” or “where there is a palm”—received the northern region, where winter endures in icy cold. This type admonishes all, especially the bishops and ministers of the Church, not to grow sluggish through harmful security. Although they have already entered the Church through the gate of faith, have already received the light of knowledge, and have crucified the desires of the flesh within themselves, they have not yet attained perfect sweetness, that is, eternal blessedness. Something bitter still remains. They must contend with him who raises his throne toward the north; it is not easy—indeed, it is impossible—to soften his hardness. Hence the Lord speaks to Job under the figure of Leviathan: “His heart will be hardened like a stone, and will be compressed like a blacksmith’s anvil” (Job 41). When this enemy has been overcome and perfectly vanquished, then there will be exultation, then joy, then blessed life, when no danger of life remains.

All the Levites whom Moses and Aaron counted, according to the Lord’s command, by their families, male by male, from one month old and upward, numbered twenty-two thousand.

And the Lord said to Moses: “Count the firstborn males among the sons of Israel, from one month old and upward, and you shall have their total. You shall take the Levites for me in place of every firstborn among the sons of Israel—I am the Lord—and their animals in place of all the firstborn animals of the sons of Israel.”

Moses counted the firstborn of the sons of Israel as the Lord had commanded, and the males, according to their names, from one month old and upward, numbered twenty-two thousand two hundred and seventy-three.

The Levites were counted separately; they had not been counted with the sons of Israel. Their number is recorded as set apart and distinguished from the others: all together they were found to number twenty-two thousand, so that neither more nor fewer than this number were found.

After this the Lord commanded that the firstborn of the sons of Israel also be counted in the same order in which the Levites had been counted, that is, from one month old and upward. The firstborn of the sons of Israel were found to number twenty-two thousand two hundred and seventy-three.

Do you suppose that by these things Moses wished to teach us only history, and that he enclosed no mystery, as was his customary manner, in these differences of numbers? Does it seem that there is no reason why the firstborn of the sons of Israel are said to exceed the number by only two hundred and seventy-three, while the Levites are recorded as neither exceeding nor falling short of twenty-two thousand?

If anyone observes the number twenty-two in the divine Scriptures, he will frequently find that it has been assigned to certain principal matters. For, first, the Hebrews are traditionally said to have twenty-two letters of the alphabet. Again, from the first-created Adam up to Jacob, from whose seed the twelve tribes take their beginning, twenty-two fathers are counted. If anyone examines many other passages of Scripture more carefully, he will find that numerous things have been consecrated under this number.

For this reason the Levites—that is, those who serve God—and the firstborn of the sons of Israel are both associated with this admirable and sacred number. But the two hundred and seventy-three by which the sons of Israel exceed it does not seem to me to be without purpose; nor do I see an easy way of explaining it, unless the Lord should deign to open for us and remove the veil placed over these letters in Moses.

The generation of the human race in the flesh, as those skilled in such matters assert, remains in the womb for nine months. Yet it is said not to begin moving toward birth until three days of the tenth month have also passed. Thus it is found that this number—two hundred and seventy-three—indicates the days gathered from nine months and three days of the tenth month. Together these make two hundred and seventy-three days, during which the human race is granted entry into this world.

Thus, in the number twenty-two, the sum of the mystical principles of all creatures is brought together. But in the excess found among the firstborn of Israel, the mystery of human generation is also set forth.

Since the Levites signify the ecclesiastical order, which serves in holy things and meditates upon and teaches the law of the Lord, they are appropriately associated with the number twenty-two, because, as stated above, the number of the Hebrew letters is contained in twenty-two elements. The sequence of the Old Testament also, according to some, is enclosed in the same number of books. This is so that the ministers of the Lord, moved by this enumeration, may live, work, and teach according to what is contained in the law of the Lord, and may in no way presume to go beyond it and transgress it; rather, everything should be done under its instruction.

But the fact that the total of the firstborn among the sons of Israel exceeds this number by two hundred and seventy-three, and that each of these is commanded to be redeemed for five shekels, teaches, if I am not mistaken, figuratively that whoever wishes to consecrate the beginning of his conduct, will, or work to God should carefully guard the five senses of the body, lest through wantonness he slip into error or worldly desires. Rather, according to the sanctuary shekel, which is measured at twenty obols—that is, according to the teaching of the Ten Commandments, which consists in the two commandments of love—he should labor to bring all his works into the house of the high priest and his sons.

## CHAPTER VI. Concerning the service of the sons of Kohath in the ministry of the Lord

**(CHAPTER IV.)** The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “Take the census of the sons of Kohath from among the Levites, according to their ancestral households and families, from thirty years old and upward to fifty years old, all who enter to stand and minister in the tabernacle of the covenant. This is the service of the sons of Kohath: Aaron and his sons shall enter the tabernacle of the covenant and the Holy of Holies when the camp is to be moved. They shall take down the veil that hangs before the entrance, wrap the ark of the testimony in it, and cover it again with a covering of violet-colored skins. They shall spread over it a wholly violet cloth, insert its poles, and so forth.”

**(From Isidore.)** The sons of Levi have already been counted from one month old and upward. Now the sons of Levi are counted from thirty years old—or, according to the Septuagint, from twenty-five years old—not as in the other census, but up to fifty years old; and this is a particularly distinguished and select number.

For it is said of them: “Everyone who comes forward to minister in the works of the tabernacle of the testimony.” These are those who are counted by a better and more distinguished number. Just as it was said concerning the sons of Israel, “Everyone who comes forward for battle among the sons of Israel,” so here it is said, “Everyone who comes forward for the ministry, to perform the works in the tabernacle of the testimony.”

After this the works of the sons of Kohath are described, among the tribes of the sons of Levi, in the tabernacle of the testimony. “Aaron and his sons,” it says, “shall enter when the camp has been raised, and they shall take down the veil with which the holy things are covered, and with that veil they shall cover the ark of the covenant.”

After this, seven kinds of objects are enumerated that are commanded to be covered. First, the ark of the covenant itself, more precious than all the rest, is to be covered with the veil with which it had previously been veiled; it is also to be covered above with violet-colored skin, and another violet covering is added over it. Second, the table is covered; third, the lampstand; fourth, the golden altar; fifth, the vessels of the ministry; sixth, the covering of the altar is put in place with certain coverings; seventh, the basin is covered. Nothing of all these is left bare or uncovered.

Finally, a command of this sort is added: “Do not destroy the tribe of the clans of Kohath.” They would know themselves to be liable to destruction if they were sent to put their hands to these things before each one had first been covered by the priests.

Let us now return to this tabernacle of the Church of the living God and see how each of these things ought to be observed in the Church of God by the priests of Christ. If there is a priest to whom the sacred vessels—that is, the secrets of the mysteries of wisdom—have been entrusted, let him learn from these things and observe how they ought to be guarded within the veil of conscience and not readily brought forth into public view. Or, if circumstances require him to bring them forth and hand them on to those beneath him, that is, to the inexperienced, let him not bring them forth naked, display them openly, or leave them wholly exposed; otherwise he commits murder and destroys the people.

Everyone who touches secret and ineffable mysteries before being transferred, by merit and knowledge, into the order and rank of the priesthood is destroyed. For only the sons of Aaron—the priests—were permitted to see the ark of the covenant, the table, the lampstand, and whatever else we have listed above, bare and uncovered. Others are to see these things covered; indeed, they should carry them veiled upon their shoulders. The sons of Kohath, although they themselves are not priests, are nevertheless close to the priests, and therefore can carry these things upon their shoulders. Others place their burdens and their ministries not upon their shoulders but on carts.

The Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying: “Do not destroy the people of Kohath from among the Levites, but do this for them, so that they may live and not die when they touch the Holy of Holies. Aaron and his sons shall enter, and they shall arrange the work of each one and divide what each person ought to carry. Let no others, out of curiosity, look at what is in the sanctuary before it has been wrapped; otherwise they will die.”

First, let us understand the things that are related according to the letter; then, with the Lord’s help, let us rise from the understanding of the letter to the understanding of the spirit.

Understand, then, first the arrangement of the tabernacle of the testimony itself. Understand also the Holy of Holies, which is separated from the holy place by an intervening veil and which no human being may look upon except the priests alone. Then understand how, when the time comes for the sons of Israel to move their camp, the tabernacle is dismantled, and Aaron and his priestly sons, within the Holy of Holies, cover each object with its coverings and veils. Leaving them covered, they bring in the sons of Kohath, who have been assigned to this service, and make them lift upon their shoulders all that the priestly hands had covered.

For this reason the Lord says: “Do not destroy the people of Kohath from their tribe,” as though they would be destroyed if they touched the Holy of Holies bare and open [the printed reading *patientia* appears to be an OCR corruption of *patentia*]. They were not only forbidden to touch these things, but were not even permitted to look upon them unless they were veiled.

If you have understood what the order of the history contains, now ascend to the splendor of the mystery and contemplate the light of the spiritual law, if the eye of your mind is pure.

If someone among those who minister to God is worthy to receive and see divine mysteries, which others are less capable of contemplating, he should be understood as an Aaron or a son of Aaron, who may enter into things that it is not lawful for others to approach.

If someone is such a person, the ark of the covenant lies open to him alone, revealed. He sees the jar containing manna; he considers and understands the mercy seat; he beholds both cherubim, the holy table, the lampstand of light, and the altar of incense. He considers these things and understands them spiritually—that is, he devotes himself to the word of God and the mysteries of wisdom, and is free for God alone in holy things.

Let the person to whom these things are revealed and entrusted for spiritual contemplation know that it is not for him alone to open and disclose them to those to whom they may not be disclosed. Rather, he must cover each thing and hand the covered objects over to those less capable, to be carried and placed upon their shoulders and necks.

When the learned and perfected teachers, instructed by mystical words, assign works to the people, and the people carry out and fulfill what is commanded, yet do not understand the meaning of what they are doing, what else is happening except that the works and the veiled Holy of Holies are being carried upon their shoulders?

To make what I am saying clearer, we shall instruct you with examples drawn from the divine books. Moses undoubtedly understood what true circumcision was; he understood what the true Passover was; he knew what the true new moons and true Sabbaths were. Yet, although he understood all these things in the spirit, he veiled them in words and through the forms and shadows of bodily things.

Although he knew that Christ was the true Passover to be sacrificed, he commanded the bodily celebration of the Passover. Although he knew that the festival ought to be celebrated in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth, he nevertheless gave instructions concerning unleavened loaves made from flour.

These and similar things were therefore the Holy of Holies. When Moses handed them over to others to be carried—that is, to be fulfilled in things and works—he nevertheless handed them over covered and veiled, in the common language of words. We have often shown in many passages of Scripture that shoulders signify works.

In ecclesiastical observances, moreover, there are certain things of this kind that everyone must indeed do, though their meaning is not clear to everyone. For example, I do not think it is readily understood by everyone why we bend our knees when we pray, or why, from all the regions of heaven, we turn toward the eastern region alone and pour out our prayer.

Likewise, who can easily explain the meaning of the Eucharist—whether of receiving it or of explaining the rite by which it is celebrated—or of the words, actions, arrangements, and questions performed in baptism?

Yet we carry all these works, veiled though they are, upon our shoulders when we fulfill and perform them in the manner in which we have received them as handed down and commended by the great high priest and his sons.

Whenever we perform all these and similar things without attaining their meaning, we lift them upon our shoulders and carry veiled and covered divine mysteries. Unless someone among us is an Aaron or a son of Aaron, to whom it is granted to see these things bare and revealed, such a person must know that he is to veil and cover them when reason requires them to be given to others and put into practice.

After this it is said concerning the Levites that all who enter upon the ministry of the tabernacle of the covenant are taken from thirty years old and upward to fifty years old; or, according to the Septuagint edition, the Levites are taken from twenty-five years old and upward to fifty years old, all who proceed to the work of works and to the works carried by the tabernacle of the testimony.

Observe the distinction in the language of divine Scripture. When it speaks of the works of the sons of Israel, it does not say “works of works,” but simply “works.” But when it speaks of the duties of the Levites, it says not merely “works,” but “works of works.”

Just as there are certain holy things, while there are other things that are holy of holies, so there are certain works and other works of works. It therefore seems to me that when Moses perceived certain works that were visible but contained within themselves another, interior, mystical and hidden understanding, he called them not merely works but “works of works.” But those works that he understood to be common and belonging only to the present time he called simply “works.”

There are therefore certain works of works, which I think include all those matters that are commanded under hidden mysteries either in the present reading, in Exodus, or in other passages—some to be fulfilled in the present and others in the future. Nevertheless, as we have said, these works of works are commanded to be entrusted not to everyone but to the Levites alone. Even among the Levites themselves, no one is called to these works before he reaches the age of twenty-five, and this continues until the age of fifty.

Nor are the numbers twenty-five and fifty years without sacramental significance. In the number twenty-five the perfection of the five senses is indicated, since it is five times five. This shows that the person called to perform the works of works in the ministry is one who, with his senses multiplied and purified in every respect, is found to be perfect.

If, however, we wish to read the number thirty, so that the Levites enter upon the ministry of the tabernacle under that number, we should know that this too is not without sacred mystery. For the number thirty, in which the number ten is multiplied three times, signifies the integrity of faith together with the perfection of good works, without which no one is fit for divine ministry.

The number thirty is also found in countless places in Holy Scripture to be adapted to the mysteries of Christ and the Church. Joseph, who—prefiguring the resurrection and the New Testament—protected the Egyptians from famine for eighty years, assumed the government of the kingdom at the age of thirty, after washing away the filth of the prison. David began at the same age the reign that the number seventy, that is, perpetual rest, would complete. Ezekiel, at thirty years of age, when the heavens were opened to him, obtained the gifts of prophecy.

Because through faith one must endure adversity with patience and hope for rewards on high, the height of the ark and of the temple, as well as the length of the tabernacle, is measured at thirty cubits.

We have often and abundantly shown in many passages of Scripture that the number fifty contains the mystery of the promise of pardon. For the fiftieth year is the year in which remission is made of possessions, slavery, and debt; and the fiftieth day after Passover is handed down in the law as a feast (Leviticus 25).

In the Gospel, when the Lord was teaching the parable of promise and pardon, he says that the debtors he introduces were liable, one for fifty denarii and another for five hundred. Fifty and five hundred are related numbers: ten times fifty makes five hundred.

The number is also sacred in another respect. Seven weeks, when the perfection of the number one is added, make fifty days. Likewise, seventy weeks, when the completion of one decade is added, make five hundred.

If anyone wishes to gather still more of the mysteries of the numbers fifty and five hundred, we have in this very book of Numbers, which is in our hands, the passage where, from the spoils of the enemy, some offer in the house of God a fiftieth portion, namely those who did not go out to war, while others offer a five-hundredth portion. Certainly, the number fifty is not found here without purpose.

Likewise, in Genesis, when the Lord was discussing the pardon of the Sodomites and whether they might perhaps be worthy of forgiveness, the patriarch Abraham, aware of such mysteries, begins his supplication to the Lord for the pardon of Sodom from the number fifty and says: “If fifty are found in the city, will you not spare the city for the sake of the fifty?” (Genesis 19).

But let us return to our subject. The Levites must therefore work in the holy things until the age of fifty: those of lesser rank in works, those of greater rank in works of works. The latter are to serve in spiritual duties, enter the Holy of Holies, cover there what must be covered, and hand it over to the sons of Kohath to be carried upon their shoulders and conveyed by their hands, and likewise to the others, each according to what we have often explained above.

But lest such excessive caution concerning coverings and veils produce a certain despair and sorrow in our hearers, we shall attempt to disclose a few matters that it is safe for us to reveal and lawful for you to contemplate. For, as we said earlier, we have been called “a royal race and priesthood, a holy nation, a people for possession,” and therefore we shall try to open these things.

Let us understand, then, that the tabernacle of the testimony consists of all the saints who are reckoned under God’s covenant. In this tabernacle there are some who are loftier in merits and superior in grace. Of these, some are called the lampstand—perhaps the apostles themselves, who illuminate those who approach God. If there are others who, in this tabernacle of God, display the light of knowledge and teaching to all who enter, let all such be called the mystical lampstand.

Others are the sacred table: possessing the bread of God, they refresh and feed souls that hunger for righteousness.

Others are the altar of incense: all who devote themselves day and night to prayers and fasts, praying in the temple of God not only for themselves but also for the whole people.

Those to whom God has entrusted secret mysteries and committed the hidden secrets of his providential judgments may be called the ark of the covenant of God.

Those who, with complete confidence, reconcile God and human beings through sacrifices of prayers and supplications, and intercede for the sins of the people, may be called the mercy seat.

Those who have earned an abundance of knowledge and overflowing riches in the knowledge of God may be understood as cherubim. In our language, cherubim is interpreted as “multitude of knowledge.”

All those designated by each of the things enumerated above must be carried, and carried upon shoulders. Hence, perhaps, as I think, the angels who have been appointed for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation are themselves the ones who carry each of those whom we have mentioned.

When this tabernacle has been dismantled, and we begin to enter those holy places and proceed to the place of promise, those who are truly holy and are counted among the Holy of Holies advance, undoubtedly carried by angels. They are transported upon shoulders and lifted in hands until the tabernacle comes to rest.

The prophet foresaw this in the spirit when he said: “For he has commanded his angels concerning you, that they may lift you up in their hands, lest you strike your foot against a stone” (Psalm 90).

The devil thought that this saying was to be understood of the Savior; but, blinded by wickedness, he did not understand the mystical words. Our Savior did not need angels so that he would not strike his foot against a stone. The devil slanders divine Scripture when he presents these words as spoken of the Savior. They are spoken not of him but of all the saints: “God has commanded his angels concerning his people, so that they may not strike their foot against a stone.”

Everything written in this psalm also applies more to the righteous than to the Savior. God delivers from ruin, and from the demon of noonday, not the Savior—far be it from us to understand it in that way—but every righteous person. It is the righteous who need the help of God’s angels, so that they may not be overthrown by demons and so that their hearts may not be darkened by the arrow that flies in darkness.

Under the same mystery, Paul confirms through the angels that some are to be carried in the clouds when he says: “But we who are alive, who remain, shall be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet Christ in the air” (1 Thessalonians 4).

Those who have been thoroughly cleansed and made light by freedom from sins are therefore caught up by angels. Those who are still weighed down by certain remnants of sin are carried.

The pillars of the tabernacle, the courts, and the other things related by Scripture are also carried—not by the Israelites but by the Levites—according to this interpretation, which we seem briefly to have touched upon in passing, leaving it to the understanding of our hearers.

If anyone burns with a greater desire for these matters, let him kindle for himself the light of knowledge and contemplate greater things with a more discerning eye.

## CHAPTER VII. Concerning the expulsion of the leper from the camp

**(CHAPTER V.)** The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “Command the sons of Israel to expel from the camp every leper, everyone who suffers from a discharge, and anyone who has been defiled by a dead person; expel both male and female, lest they defile the camp in which they dwell with you.” And the sons of Israel did so: they expelled them outside the camp, as the Lord had spoken to Moses.

The lepers who are commanded to be expelled from the camp are heretics, who are polluted by various stains of doctrine and do not wish to have a uniform color of teaching or faith. Lacking knowledge of the true faith, they profess various doctrines of error. They do not even conceal their ignorance; instead, they bring it into the light as though it were the highest expertise and display the boastfulness of their speech.

No false doctrine exists that does not mix in some truth. Truth mixed disorderly with falsehood, appearing in a person’s single argument or account like a bodily color, signifies leprosy—like the colors that vary and stain a human body with patches of true and false.

The person who suffers from a discharge should be understood as one who is foul with lustful thoughts and burns with the luxury of carnal desires.

The person defiled by a dead body is one who follows the examples of those who are dead in sins and ungodliness and is polluted by the filth of vices.

All these, therefore—unfruitful in thought, unclean in speech, and diseased through contact—must be separated from the camp of the Church, lest through the contagion of their conduct they pollute the life of the innocent, until they themselves wash away their crimes.

## CHAPTER VIII. Concerning the expiation of the priests’ sins of negligence
(IBID.) And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “[Col. 0617C] Speak to the children of Israel: When a man or woman commits any of the sins that people ordinarily commit, and through negligence transgresses the Lord’s command and incurs guilt, they shall confess their sin and restore the principal itself, adding a fifth to it, to the person against whom they sinned. But if there is no one to receive it, they shall give it to the Lord, and it shall belong to the priest—apart from the ram that is offered for expiation, so that it may be an acceptable sacrifice.”

The Septuagint reads: “A man or woman, whoever commits any of the human sins, and, treating the matter with utter contempt, incurs guilt, that person shall declare the sin that he has committed, restore the offense, and add a fifth of it to the amount, and repay it to the one against whom he sinned. But if the person has no near relative, so that he may repay the offense to him, the offense that he repays to the Lord shall belong to the priest, [Col. 0617D] apart from the ram of expiation, by which he has made atonement for him in that matter.”

Here we must understand those sins whose commission concerns matters that can be repaid with money. For otherwise Scripture would not explain how they are to be restored, unless they involved financial loss. They are commanded to restore the principal and a fifth—that is, the entire amount, whatever it may be, together with a fifth of it—apart from the ram that was to be offered as a sacrifice to expiate the offense. He commands that what is restored shall belong to the priest—that is, the principal and the fifth—if the person against whom the offense was committed has no near relative. Everywhere, then, it is to be understood that what belongs to the priest is to be returned to the Lord if the person who suffered the loss is no longer alive, nor is there a relative of his whom, I think, Scripture intended to be understood as his heir; yet Scripture says nothing about the man himself. Nevertheless, when it says, “if he has no near relative,” it briefly indicates that his relative is to be sought if he himself is absent; but if he has no relative either, the amount shall be restored to the Lord, so that what was lost may not remain unpunished. Yet it is not to become part of the sacrifice, but shall belong to the priest. Thus the words of Scripture should be punctuated: “But if the man has no near relative, so that he may repay the offense to him”—for “to him” is an addition required by the construction. Or perhaps “to him” means “that which belongs to him,” that is, which he himself possesses. Then follows: “The offense that is restored to the Lord shall belong to the priest.” He calls it an “offense” when the thing that was taken through the offense is restored.

One may ask how Exodus says: “If anyone steals a calf or a sheep, he must restore five calves or four sheep if he has killed or sold it; but if what he took is found alive in his possession, he shall restore double,” whereas here he commands the restoration of the principal and a fifth—which is far from double, and even more so from fourfold or fivefold restitution. Perhaps the reason is that here he says, “A man or woman, whoever commits any of the human sins,” and thereby intends human sins committed in ignorance. It can happen that, through insufficient attention, a person negligently transfers another’s property into his own. This is a sin because it would not have been committed had he paid careful attention. Such a person he intended to restore the principal and the fifth, not to undergo the penalty prescribed for theft.

But if here we understand thefts and frauds—not committed through ignorant negligence, but with the intention of stealing and defrauding, and therefore called “human” because they are committed against human beings—then, if I am not mistaken, the solution to this question will be that the offender is to restore only double because he is neither apprehended nor convicted; rather, when no one knows who committed the offense or even whether it was committed, he himself declares his guilt. For after Scripture had said, “A man or woman, whoever commits any of the human sins, and, treating the matter with utter contempt, incurs guilt”—that is, commits these things contemptuously—it added: “That person shall declare the sin that he has committed, and restore the offense, the principal and its fifth.” Perhaps, then, this is the sole reason: that he himself declared it, and therefore was not to be punished with the penalty appropriate to a thief who had been apprehended or convicted.

[Col. 0618D] Mystically, however, this chapter admonishes us that if we have carelessly committed something through negligence, we should strive to correct it through confession and repentance. And if the person against whom we sinned by inflicting some injury is still alive, we should perhaps do penance before him and restore the loss. But if the person whom we injured is no longer alive, we should take care to make satisfaction to the Lord for this through confession, worthy fruits of repentance, and works of almsgiving. By the fifth part that he commands to be added to the sum, he teaches us that through the bodily faculty by which we sinned, inflicting some evil, we should likewise strive to do some good. The offering of the ram signifies Christ’s Passion, in which we must place our greatest confidence, because our effort accomplishes nothing unless his grace assists us. He is also the priest who reconciles us to the Father through the offering of his flesh. Therefore every gift of our devotion must be offered to him, so that through his mercy we may deserve to obtain complete forgiveness.

“All the firstfruits that the children of Israel offer shall belong to the priest, and whatever is offered by individuals and delivered into the hands of the priest shall be his.”

“All the firstfruits,” he says, “that the children of Israel offer”—that is, the firstfruits of good will in words and deeds that the children of the Church, who are the true Israelites because they diligently gaze upon God with the eyes of the mind, bring forward—belong to the priest, namely, the priest who offered himself to the Father for us.
