And whatever [Col. 0619B] is offered by individuals in the sanctuary and delivered into the hands of the priest shall belong to that priest, namely, our Lord Jesus Christ, because whatever is offered to the Lord by individuals in the sanctuary of the Lord—that is, in the holy Church—or whatever is offered collectively by all, belongs to his grace.

## CHAPTER IX. On the law of jealousy.

(IBID.) And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “Speak to the children of Israel and say to them: If a man’s wife goes astray, despises her husband, and sleeps with another man, but her husband cannot discover it, the adultery remains hidden and cannot be proved by witnesses because she was not found in the act, if a spirit of jealousy stirs the husband against his wife, whether she is polluted or is being accused on the basis of a false suspicion, he shall bring her to the priest and offer on her behalf a tenth part of a satum (a dry measure) of barley flour. He shall not pour oil over it or place frankincense upon it, because it is a sacrifice of jealousy and an offering that investigates adultery. The priest shall offer it and set her before the Lord. He shall take holy water in an earthen vessel and put into it a little dust from the floor of the tabernacle. When the woman stands in the presence of the Lord, he shall uncover her head and place in her hands the sacrifice of remembrance, the offering of jealousy. He himself shall hold the water of extreme bitterness, into which he has put the accursed curse, and he shall adjure her and say: ‘If no other man has slept with you, and if you have not been polluted by leaving your husband’s bed, these waters of extreme bitterness into which I have put the curse will not harm you. But if you have turned away from your husband, have been polluted, and have slept with another, you shall be subject to these two curses: May the Lord make you a curse and an example to all his people. May he cause your thigh to waste away and your swollen womb to burst. May these accursed waters enter your belly, and, as your womb swells, may your thigh waste away.’ And the woman shall answer: ‘Amen, amen.’

“The priest shall write these curses in a book and wash them away with the waters of extreme bitterness into which he has put the curse, and he shall give them to her to drink. When she has drained them, the priest shall take the sacrifice of jealousy from her hand and lift it before the Lord. He shall place it upon the altar, but only after first taking a handful from what is offered and burning it upon [Col. 0620A] the altar; then he shall give the woman the waters of extreme bitterness to drink. When she has drunk them, if she is polluted and, having despised her husband, is guilty of adultery, the waters of the curse shall pass into her, her belly shall swell and her thigh waste away; and the woman shall become a curse and an example to all the people. But if she has not been polluted, she shall be innocent and shall bear children. This is the law of jealousy.

“If a woman has turned away from her husband and has been polluted, and her husband, stirred by a spirit of jealousy, brings her before the Lord, and the priest does to her according to all that is written, the husband shall be without guilt, and she shall bear her iniquity.”

The written words are what the priest is to say to the woman when her husband brings her forward on suspicion of adultery: “May the Lord make her a curse and an object of execration.” The Greek has *enorkion* (ἐνόρκιον), a word that seems to signify an oath expressed through execration—as when someone says, “May such-and-such not happen to me”; or, alternatively, swears in this way: “May such-and-such happen to me if I have done, or have not done, this.” Thus it is said here: “May the Lord make you a curse and an object of execration,” as though it meant that people should swear by you with oaths of execration: “May this not happen to them,” or “May this happen to them,” unless they have done that thing.

This man whose wife went astray while despising her husband signifies the shepherd and teacher of the Church. His wife, likewise, is each subordinate who ought to obey the word of the teacher in everything, just as a good wife obeys her lawful husband. But if, through contempt, this wife goes astray and departs from such a husband and seeks an adulterous union—that is, becomes involved in heretical teaching—and although this crime does not appear openly nevertheless falls under suspicion, the teacher, inflamed with zeal for justice, shall bring her to the priest, namely, to the priest of whom it is said through the Prophet: “You are a priest forever, according to the order of Melchizedek” (Psalm 109). He leaves everything to that priest’s judgment, lest, contrary to the Apostle’s command, he judge an uncertain matter before the proper time—the Apostle who said: “Do not judge before the time, until the Lord comes, who will illuminate the hidden things of darkness and reveal the counsels of hearts” (1 Corinthians 4).

“And he shall offer on her behalf a tenth part of a satum (a dry measure) of barley flour.” Barley flour, therefore, signifies knowledge of the Old Law. It is rightly compared with barley, because just as barley, after great labor, is cleansed of its husks and reduced to flour, so the letter of the Law, crushed in the mill of discernment, produces the flour of spiritual meaning. And rightly is a tenth part of an ephah commanded to be offered: for the Law itself consists of ten commandments, and its tenth part is any one commandment, against which the perverse wife is found to have acted. Thus the woman is offered by her husband to the priest with an offering of a tenth part, when she is reserved for condemnation or acquittal according to the judgment of Christ and the divinely given Law.

“He shall not pour oil over this offering or place frankincense upon it, because it is a sacrifice of jealousy.” Therefore it is not fitting that a sinful person be soothed with the oil of flattery or the frankincense of excessive praise, nor that an impenitent heart be smeared with the oil of indiscriminate mercy or the frankincense of disordered prayer. Rather, in zeal for justice and according to the Lord’s commands, the vice must be pursued persistently and in an orderly manner.

“He shall offer her,” he says, “and the priest shall set her before the Lord; he shall take holy water in an earthen vessel and put into it a little dust from the floor of the tabernacle,” and so forth. The priest sets the woman whom he is offering before the Lord because the sinful soul is adjudged by divine judgment. The holy water in an earthen vessel is divine wisdom contained in the lowly letter of the Law. The priest mixes with it a little dust from the floor of the tabernacle when, by Christ’s decree, a remembrance of the patriarchs, prophets, and apostles is found introduced into it.

Scripture therefore calls this water extremely bitter because of the punishment for sin that is manifested in it, mixed in this way and attested by divine action. The woman drinks it so that her contempt may be revealed—whether for her own correction or for the correction of others, or in the future for her condemnation—for, according to the word of Truth: “Nothing is hidden that will not be known” (Matthew 10). And again: “The word that I have spoken to you will judge you on the last day” (John 12).

The priest then takes a handful of the sacrifice and burns it upon the altar, when the confession of the Holy Trinity is found in the sacrifice of the Law and is worthily offered to God upon the altar of faith. The fact that the priest writes in a book the curses he has pronounced against the sinner and washes them away with the waters of extreme bitterness into which he has put the curse signifies that the punishment destined for sinners is found explained in Holy Scripture.

Then whoever drinks in Holy Scripture with a devout and believing heart, fears the punishments of sinners narrated in it, and strives to guard himself from sins, finds the water life-giving. But whoever, despising God’s threats, hears the Holy Scriptures without benefit, will have his thigh waste away as his belly swells, and will become a curse and an example to all the people. For when the contemptuous soul is punished by God’s just judgment, all its deeds and desires will come upon it as a reproach.

## CHAPTER X. On the rite of the Nazirite and his offering.

(CHAPTER VI.) The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “Speak to the children of Israel and say to them: When a man or woman makes a vow to consecrate themselves and wishes to dedicate themselves to the Lord, they shall abstain from wine and everything that can cause intoxication. They shall not drink vinegar made from wine or from any other drink, nor anything pressed from grapes. They shall not eat fresh or dried grapes throughout all the days during which they are consecrated to the Lord by their vow. They shall eat nothing that comes from the vine, from the raisin even to the grape seed. Throughout the entire period of their separation, no razor shall pass over their head until the day is complete on which they are consecrated to the Lord; they shall be holy, allowing the hair of their head to grow.”

What, then, is signified by the name “Nazirites” except the life of those who abstain and practice continence? In their case, luxury is prohibited in wine, and every earthly pleasure in strong drink. For strong drink is made from various ingredients; so pleasure arises from the varied passion of vices. Those drink wine and strong drink who, in order to deceive people, pretend to possess certain shadows and images of virtues. They eat a single raisin who, for the sake of human eyes, stain themselves with the pallor of abstinence in order to obtain glory from people.

Those drink vinegar who, after a holy way of life, fall back into the former state of their vices and take pleasure in the corruption of their old wickedness. God therefore commanded that those who display the title of holiness should be free from all these vices and seek no disturbance of this kind.

In what he adds—“No razor shall pass over his head until the day is complete on which he is consecrated to the Lord”—he admonishes those who practice continence not to harbor deceit or malice in their minds, lest the hair of their head—that is, all the thoughts of their minds—be polluted. Rather, they should preserve innocence until the end, namely, until the end of the present life. For otherwise they will not have made their vow of holiness acceptable to God unless they have carefully guarded their minds and striven to persevere in this until the end, according to the judgment of Truth: “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew 12).

“Throughout the entire period of his consecration he shall not approach a dead person, nor shall he be defiled by the funeral of his father, mother, brother, or sister, because the consecration of his God is upon his head. Throughout all the days of his separation he shall be holy to the Lord.”

Why, then, does he forbid the Nazirite to approach a dead person, unless it is because he does not want one who has vowed his continence to God to imitate the examples of those who are dead in sins or to enter the path of their iniquity? Otherwise he might lose his labor, and all his deeds might be rejected—those in which he trusted that he had previously done something acceptable to the Lord—because it is not the one who began a good work, but the one who perseveres in goodness, who will be crowned.

For this reason he is also kept away from the funeral of his father, mother, brother, or sister, because every carnal attachment must be cut away when one strives to please God alone. No relationship with those close to us that draws us into sin is permitted to remain associated with us. Rather, in accordance with the Gospel: “If your right hand or foot causes you to stumble, cut it off and throw it away from you. It is better for you that one of your members perish than that your whole body go into Gehenna” (Matthew 5).

Every person, every dignity, and every blood relationship must be placed after the love of Christ; nothing should be joined to us that prevents us from being united with Christ. For “the consecration of his God,” he says, “is upon his head”—that is, the grace of the Holy Spirit has been poured into his heart. Hence Paul also says: “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption” (Ephesians 4).

“Throughout all the days of his separation he shall be holy to the Lord.” It is therefore entirely necessary that this be the object of his vow, his aspiration, and his labor: that throughout all the time in which he wishes to be consecrated to the Lord through continence or abstinence, he strive to persevere without contamination by sin or transgression until the end. The text continues:

“But if someone should suddenly die in his presence, the head of his consecration shall be polluted. He shall shave it immediately, and on the same day of his purification, and again on the seventh day he shall shave it. On the eighth day he shall offer two turtledoves or two young pigeons to the priest at the entrance of the tent of testimony. The priest shall make one for sin and the other as a burnt offering, and shall intercede for him because he sinned by being present over the dead. He shall sanctify his head on that day and consecrate to the Lord the days of his separation, offering a year-old lamb for sin; nevertheless, the earlier days shall be nullified, because his consecration has been polluted.”

What does the legislator’s concern that someone’s sudden death might occur before the Nazirite and thereby contaminate the Nazirite’s consecration signify, except the commission of the death of sin? If, upon observing this, one who practices continence sees himself fall into the delight of sin or consent to it, he must know that his conscience has been polluted. Therefore he must understand that his head must immediately be shaved—that is, his mind must be cleansed of evil thoughts and harmful delight—on that very day of his purification and again on the seventh day.

At the very time of his compunction, when he recognizes that he has sinned, he must hasten to cleanse himself from guilt and fear that a similar fall may occur throughout the rest of his life. “On the eighth day he shall offer two turtledoves or two young pigeons to the priest at the entrance of the tent of testimony.” The eighth day signifies the time of the resurrection; the two turtledoves signify chastity, and the young pigeons simplicity.

Whoever therefore wishes to belong to the resurrection of the blessed and attain the future immortality of the saints should offer to our priest, who offered himself for us, chastity both of body and of heart, and simplicity of soul in the Catholic faith. Through him he remembers that he enters the Church, so that through the help of so great a high priest he may be cleansed from the contagion of sin.

“The priest shall make one for sin and the other as a burnt offering,” when he causes the man to groan over his sins through fear of Gehenna and also to sigh more earnestly through desire for eternal life. Our priest is said to intercede for us either because, in his humanity, he is our advocate with the Father, or because through the Spirit of his grace he makes us pray for ourselves in a saving manner. Hence Paul also says: “The Spirit himself pleads for us with inexpressible groanings” (Romans 8). This does not mean that the Spirit himself groans, since by nature he is incapable of suffering, but that through his inspiration he makes us groan over our sins.

“This priest shall sanctify the Nazirite’s head on that day and consecrate his days of separation to the Lord,” when he grants a mind rescued from carnal desire to display spiritual continence irreproachably. He offers a year-old lamb for sin—that is, an innocent life in place of a criminal one, Christian simplicity in place of diabolical cunning—yet in such a way that the man presumes nothing for himself from his former way of life or takes pride in past acts of righteousness. Rather, he must rely solely upon the grace of the heavenly Author, by whose gift he should receive forgiveness of his sins and attain eternal grace.

Hence it is written here: “The earlier days shall be nullified, because his consecration has been polluted.” For, as it is said through the Prophet: “On whatever day the righteous person turns away from his righteousness and commits iniquity, all his righteousnesses shall be consigned to oblivion” (Ezekiel 3).

“This is the law of consecration: When the days that he had determined by his vow have been completed, he shall bring him to the door of the tent of testimony and offer his offering to the Lord.”

After instructing the Nazirite how he should cleanse himself if his consecration had been polluted by a dead person, the legislator also added an account of how, after completing his vow, he should present himself to the Lord with an offering of thanksgiving. Mystically, he indicates that a life of continence, together with an offering of good works and purity of heart, will be pleasing to the Lord at a good end.

“He shall offer an unblemished year-old lamb as a burnt offering, an unblemished year-old ewe for sin, and an unblemished ram as a sacrifice of peace.”

He offers an unblemished year-old lamb to the Lord as a burnt offering who places all his hope in the spotless Lamb, whom John pointed out with his finger and said: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1). He offers him as a burnt offering when, for his love, he mortifies the desires of the flesh and consecrates his whole life to the Lord, consumed by the spiritual fire of true charity.

He offers the unblemished ewe for sin when he faithfully believes in Christ’s innocent death, accomplished for the absolution of sins and the redemption of the human race. He brings the unblemished ram as a sacrifice of peace when he trusts that Christ is the one who, through the dispensation of his incarnation, reconciled heavenly and earthly things, abolishing every principality and power. God the Father exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of the Lord Jesus every knee should bow—in heaven, on earth, and under the earth—and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father (Philippians 1).

Tropologically, he offers an unblemished lamb as a burnt offering when he presents to God simplicity of heart together with the devotion of charity. He offers the ewe when he provides innocence in action as an example to others. He also offers the ram as a sacrifice of peace when he strives to govern himself well and lead himself along the path of God’s commandments, subjecting rebellious flesh to the rule of the spirit and laboring to unite them. Then the text adds:

“He shall also offer a basket of unleavened loaves mixed with oil, and unleavened wafers anointed with oil, together with their libations; and the priest shall offer them before the Lord, both for sin and as a burnt offering.”

The basket in which the loaves are placed and offered signifies Holy Scripture, in which there is spiritual nourishment: the teaching of the Gospel mixed and joined with the oil of gladness, namely, the grace of the Holy Spirit. There are also wafers anointed with oil, signifying the Old Law, consecrated by the same Spirit, smoothed and tempered for the benefit of those who hear it. These are without the leaven of malice and wickedness, together with the libations of each person, because spiritual grace is rightly evident both in the Law and in the Gospel to all who understand them.

The priest offers these before the Lord when the Redeemer of the human race presents before the divine presence, in rewarding them, each person’s merit, the labor he has undertaken in God’s service, and his meditation upon and observance of the divine Law. He brings the person, enriched with spiritual gifts through the entrance into life and the covenantal struggle of good works, to the contemplation of God the Father.

“He shall sacrifice the ram as a sacrifice of peace to the Lord, offering with it the basket of unleavened bread and the libations that are prescribed according to custom.”

This occurs when he shows the person worthy of the reward of perpetual rest, on account of the leadership and governance by which he has been accustomed to govern himself well and lead himself along the straight path of God’s commandments, ordering his life according to the teaching of the Holy Scriptures and the grace of spiritual gifts.

[Col. 0625B] “Then the Nazirite shall shave the hair of his consecration before the door of the tent of testimony. He shall take the hair of his head and place it upon the fire that is laid upon the sacrifice of peace offerings.”

What is meant by the Nazirite’s allowing his hair to grow, except that through a life of great continence thoughts of presumption increase? But what is meant by the command that, when his devotion is complete, the Nazirite should shave his head and place his hair in the fire of the sacrifice, except that we reach the summit of perfection when we overcome our outward life in such a way that we also cut away superfluous thoughts from the mind? To burn these in the fire of the sacrifice is to kindle them with the flame of divine love, so that the whole heart burns with love of God, and perfection of devotion consumes the superfluous thoughts like the Nazirite’s hair.

[Col. 0625C] “He shall give into the hands of the Nazirite, after his head has been shaved, the cooked shoulder of the ram, one unleavened cake from the basket, and one unleavened wafer. Then he shall receive them back from him and lift them before the Lord; and, once sanctified, they shall belong to the priest, like the breast that was commanded to be set apart and the thigh,” and so forth.

The priest gives the cooked shoulder of the ram into the Nazirite’s hand when the Savior of the world grants him to offer acceptably to God the strength of good works, cooked and tested by the fire of tribulation. He also gives him the unleavened wafer when he grants him to bring the knowledge of the Law to completion through the gift of the Holy Spirit.

“For after his head has been shaved,” he says, “he shall receive it back from him and lift it before the Lord.” Once the Nazirite’s head has been shaved, he receives the offering and lifts it before the Lord because, when he has stripped him of the corruption of the flesh and freed him from the burden of worldly cares, our Redeemer will deem it worthy to present before the divine presence the offerings of the virtues that the continent man himself has practiced, and by his own gift will cause him to be rewarded with an everlasting recompense in the heavenly kingdom.

Hence it is also added: “And, once sanctified, they shall belong to the priest, like the breast that was commanded to be set apart and the thigh.” For whatever his fellow servants either understood, rightly desired, or brought to completion in a good work will pertain to Christ’s glory, as Paul testifies when he says: “For God is the one who works in us both to will and to accomplish according to his good pleasure” (Philippians 2). Hence James also says: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no change or shadow caused by turning” (James 1).

Let us therefore see what Scripture says about the Nazirite after the perfect offering. “After this,” it says, “the Nazirite may drink wine.” After this, then—that is, after right intention, after a reasonable promise, after the perfection of good works, after the completion of all labor, and after the repayment of a just reward—the Nazirite may drink wine, that is, fully imbibe the spiritual gift. For the more freely he receives it, the happier he is; and the greater his capacity, the more abundantly he receives the gift of heavenly grace, according to the Apostle: “Now we see through a mirror, in a riddle; but then face to face. Now I know in part; then I shall know fully, just as I have been fully known” (1 Corinthians 13).

## CHAPTER XI. Where the Lord commands how the children of Israel are to be blessed.

(IBID.) And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “Speak to Aaron and his sons: Thus you shall bless the children of Israel, and say to them: May the Lord bless you and keep you. May the Lord show his face to you and have mercy on you; may the Lord turn his face toward you and give you peace.”

What, then, is expressed in Moses except the Law, and what in Aaron and his sons except the ecclesiastical priesthood? The Lord therefore instructs through the Law and teaches through the order of priestly teachers, whose duty is to build up God’s people by the word of preaching and strengthen them through constant prayer and blessing. He teaches them how to bless the ecclesiastical assembly and establish a form of prayer over it.

“Thus you shall bless,” he says, “the children of Israel, and say to them: May the Lord bless you and keep you.” In the words “May the Lord bless you,” he wishes the gifts of spiritual graces to be poured out upon them from heaven. In what follows—“and keep you”—he teaches that we must altogether ask him to preserve within us by his grace what we receive through his blessings, because Truth himself says: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15). Concerning this the Psalmist also says: “Unless the Lord keeps the city, those who keep watch over it labor in vain” (Psalm 126). And again: “The Lord keeps all who love him, but he will destroy all sinners” (Psalm 144).

Another form of blessing follows: “May the Lord show his face to you and have mercy on you.” The showing of God’s face signifies his favor and the granting of true salvation. Hence the Prophet prays to the Lord, saying: “Show us your face, and we shall be saved” (Psalm 79). And again: “Show us, Lord, your mercy, and grant us your salvation” (Psalm 84).

Then he set forth a third form of blessing in this way: “May the Lord turn his face toward you and give you peace.” The turning of God’s face expresses the coming of his mercy, just as the turning away of his face expresses his indignation. Hence the Prophet says to the Lord: “Look upon me and have mercy on me” (Psalm 85). And again: “Why,” he says, “do you turn your face away, forgetting our poverty and our affliction?” (Psalm 43).

“May the Lord turn his face toward you” is an entreaty, because the sins we have committed rightly compelled him to turn his help away from us. We must therefore ask his clemency again to deign, through his boundless mercy, to turn his face toward us anew, so that, rescuing us from all enemies, he may grant us perpetual peace.

Note that in this blessing, formed in three parts, the Lord’s name is invoked three times, so that you may understand that the Holy Trinity is equal, through whom and in whom all honorable, good, and salutary things are to be desired, sought, and enjoyed, because “from him and through him and in him are all things; to him be glory forever and ever.”

As for what follows—“They shall invoke my name over the children of Israel, and I will bless them”—it belongs to the same meaning, because it is the priests’ office to invoke the Lord’s name, while it is the Lord’s office to accomplish the very thing for which he is invoked. Therefore human presumption must not arrogate to itself through proud display what belongs solely to the Holy Trinity, who bestows it by his grace upon whom he wills.

## CHAPTER XII. On the offering of the princes of Israel: namely, six covered wagons with twelve oxen for the service of the tabernacle.

(CHAPTER VII.) It happened on the day when Moses completed the tabernacle and erected it, and sanctified and anointed it with all its vessels, and likewise the altar and its vessels.

Moses has different and not always the same significance in various passages of Holy Scripture. At times he bears the type of the Jewish people, as in the passage in Exodus where he was commanded to hold the serpent’s tail; for this signifies that the Jews will come to the faith of Christ near the end of the world.

At times he figuratively represents Christ, as in the passage where he led the people out of Egypt through the Red Sea, signifying that Christ leads his chosen ones out of spiritual Egypt through the water of baptism and delivers them from the most savage enemies. The same is true of the passage mentioned here, where Moses completed, erected, and anointed the tabernacle with all its vessels, and likewise the altar and its vessels.

The tabernacle of the Lord, therefore, is the present Church, which Christ completed and erected when, redeeming it by his blood, he made it perfect in devotion and raised it in faith and hope toward the glory to be sought in the future. He also anointed and sanctified it with the oil of gladness, the grace of the Holy Spirit, together with all its vessels—that is, the elect who have been appointed within the Church for various ministries.

The altar likewise signifies either the Church in general, or all the perfect, in whom the fragrance of virtues and holy prayers is perceived; or, most especially, it signifies Christ’s humanity, in which he presented to God the Father the acceptable gifts of our redemption, because he is both priest and victim. The fact that he offered himself to the Father for us also makes him the altar, because, holding death in his own power, he accepted it by his own will and brought the sacrament of his Passion to completion.

Hence he himself says: “No one takes my life from me, but I lay it down, and I take it up again.” And to Pilate: “You would have no power over me unless it had been given to you from above” (John 19).

And the princes of Israel and the heads of the families, who were the leaders of each tribe and had been counted, offered gifts before the Lord. The princes of Israel and the heads of the families are therefore the patriarchs, prophets, and apostles, who gave acceptable gifts to God—some through teachings, some through exhortations, and some through good examples and works of virtue—and, for the instruction of the holy Church, contributed whatever they could with joyful hearts. Or, according to the tropological sense, “princes” may be understood as those who, instructed in apostolic teaching, know how to rule and govern properly both the senses of the body [Col. 0628B] and the affections of the soul. Their virtues are believed to be most pleasing to God, because they are shown to spring from the root of unity and concord, as Truth herself bears witness, saying: “For if two of you should agree on earth about anything whatsoever that they ask, it will be done for them by my Father, who is in heaven” (Matt. 18).

Six covered wagons with twelve oxen. Two leaders offered one wagon, and each one ox; and they offered them in the presence of the tabernacle. “Six,” he says, “covered wagons with twelve oxen.” Historically, by covered wagons he means either wagons covered with planks, so that they could contain loads inside, or even wagons spread with certain cloths, so that they might receive the equipment of the tabernacle with greater dignity. Mystically, however, the wagons that the children of Israel offered to the Levites for transporting the tabernacle signify the supports of temporal life that devoted disciples of the truth contribute to the Levites—that is, to the holy preachers—in return for the word, so that, having received bodily sustenance from them, they may more easily and without the hindrance of earthly affairs devote themselves to winning souls and to divine service. Hence the Lord also ordained that those who proclaim the Gospel should live from the Gospel. And Paul, writing to the Corinthians, says: “If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it a great matter if we reap your material things?” (1 Cor. 9). And to the Galatians: “Let the one who is instructed in the word share all good things with the one who instructs him” (Gal. 6).

These wagons are suitably comprehended by the number six, so that the perfect devotion of the faithful who serve Christ’s preachers from their own resources may be signified. They are also rightly read as being sound and complete, as though fully adorned, and most splendid in the affection of mercy; for this reason they are shown to be acceptable to God. The twelve oxen, moreover, are appropriately assigned to the wagons, to demonstrate that those who piously labor in the service of the saints, established under the yoke of apostolic teaching, ought to do everything honorably and according to order. Or we may understand the oxen as the teachers themselves, who work worthily in God’s field; concerning them Scripture commands: “You shall not muzzle the ox when it is treading out the grain” (Deut. 25). The Apostle interprets this statement of the Law as referring to the teachers of the Church, saying: “Is God concerned about oxen? Or does he say this entirely for our sake? Indeed, it was written for our sake, because the one who plows ought to plow in hope, and the one who threshes ought to do so in hope of receiving the fruit” (1 Cor. 9). Those, therefore, who preserve the apostolic rule in preaching and conduct are rightly nourished by the benefits of their subjects.

That two leaders offered one wagon, and each one an ox, shows that the office of charity is acceptable when it is displayed both from the heart and through the body, because, as the Apostle testifies, “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Cor. 9). The oxen were offered individually by individual leaders in order to show that unity of faith and simplicity of good intention, together with pious labor, are especially pleasing to the Lord in teachers.

There are nevertheless some among teachers who do not require bodily support from their hearers but, laboring with their own hands, prepare food for themselves, so that they may receive from God the proper reward of their labor. Hence Paul says to the Corinthians: “For if I preach the Gospel, it is no glory to me; necessity is laid upon me. Woe to me if I do not preach the Gospel! For if I do this willingly, I have a reward; but if unwillingly, I have been entrusted with a stewardship. What, then, is my reward? That, in preaching the Gospel, I may offer the Gospel without cost, so as not to misuse my authority in the Gospel” (1 Cor. 9).

Nor, I think, should it be left unsaid that the number twelve seems to embrace each human being and the fullness of time and the arrangement of the world. For a human being consists of seven parts: three qualities in the soul and four in the body. Whether one takes the four parts, or multiplies the three by four, it is clear that the number twelve encompasses the whole human being. The world, too, is bounded by twelve winds. The years likewise revolve through twelve months, just as the days revolve through hours. From all this we gather that every human being, in every place and time, ought to hasten toward God’s tabernacle with worthy virtue.

And so, when Moses had received the wagons and oxen, he handed them over to the Levites. He gave two wagons and four oxen to the sons of Gershon, according to what they needed; and he gave four other wagons and eight oxen to the sons of Merari, according to their duties and service, under the direction of Ithamar, son of Aaron the priest. But to the sons of Kohath he gave neither wagons nor oxen, because they serve in the sanctuary and carry the burdens on their own shoulders.

It was written above that the sons of Kohath were to carry on their own shoulders the tabernacle of the covenant, the Holy of Holies, the ark, the altar, the table, and the lampstand, together with all their vessels wrapped in coverings. The duties of the Gershonites, however, were to carry the curtains of the tabernacle and the covering of the covenant, another covering, and above all the violet veil, as well as the tent hanging at the entrance of the tabernacle of the covenant, the curtains of the court, and the veil at the entrance before the tabernacle; everything pertaining to the bronze altar, the cords, and the vessels of the ministry. The Merarites were to carry the boards of the tabernacle and its bars, its pillars and their vessels, as well as the pillars of the court all around, with their bases, pegs, and cords. [Col. 0630A]

Consider now how such a division is made among the duties of divine service, and how those things that are holy are not assigned to dumb animals to carry, but must be borne by rational human beings, who carry on their shoulders the vessels with which service is performed within the Holy of Holies. Those things, however, that are heavier and more burdensome are assigned to be carried not so much by rational beings as by dumb animals. Yet even among these there is a distinction. For those who undertake the harder and heavier services have more animals. Four wagons, indeed, are given to the sons of Merari; but only two wagons suffice for the sons of Gershon, who were near the sons of Kohath. From this it is shown that for harder and, so to speak, more material works, there are more who serve in an animal-like manner; whereas few who appear less instructed or educated approach the matters that are administered by rational beings. But no merely animal person approaches those things that are mystical, hidden in secret, and open only to priests; indeed, not even those who seem to possess some practice and learning, but who have not yet ascended in mind and life to priestly grace.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the offering of the leaders of the Israelite people and the dedication of the Lord’s altar

(IBID.) Therefore the leaders offered their offering for the dedication of the altar on the day when it was anointed, before the altar. The dedication of the altar is the consecration of the Church. The day on which the altar was anointed is the time of the Lord’s incarnation, when, after the Lord’s resurrection and ascension, the entire assembly of believers gathered in the upper room of Zion was sanctified through the outpouring of the Holy Spirit. It is therefore rightly said that the leaders offered their offering for the dedication of the altar, because each of the faithful ought to offer, as divine mercy grants him the ability, an offering of right faith, holy teaching, and good works for the advancement and honor of the holy Church. The text continues:

The Lord said to Moses: Each leader shall offer gifts on separate days for the dedication of the altar. Why, then, did he command the individual leaders to offer gifts on separate days, unless he spiritually intimates to us that our leaders—that is, our holy preachers [Col. 0630D] and guides along the right path—although they bring the same kinds of spiritual gifts, whether through instruction in the Catholic faith or through examples of good works, nevertheless distribute them according to the suitability of place or time and do not present them all at once, as the one who has ordained what is useful and beneficial determines, in whose hand all places, times, matters, and effects subsist? Let us now see what gifts those leaders offered according to the command of the lawgiver.

On the first day Naasson, son of Amminadab, of the tribe of Judah, offered his offering. It contained a silver bowl weighing one hundred and thirty shekels, and a silver basin weighing seventy shekels according to the sanctuary weight; both were full of fine flour mixed with oil for a sacrifice; a small golden mortar of ten shekels, full of incense; a bull, a ram, and a yearling lamb for a burnt offering, and a goat for sin; and, for a sacrifice of peace offerings, two bulls, five rams, five goats, and five yearling lambs. This was the offering of Naasson, son of Amminadab.

These various vessels, made for presenting libations, [text corrupt; apparently: “signify divine [things] variously according to the differing capacity of the hearers”]. For the same teaching cannot suit everyone alike; the wise must be taught in one way, the foolish in another; the rich in one way, the poor in another; the healthy in one way, the sick in another. The Jewish people, then still unformed and remaining under the shadow of the Law, had to be instructed in one way; but the Christian people now, seeing the mysteries of the Law explained in the truth of the Gospel, must be nourished in another way until they reach maturity.

In the end, the bowls, which have a narrow opening above, express mystically the narrowness of the letter of the Law and the obscurity of prophetic speech. The basins, however, which are made originally from glass—for the Greeks call glass ὕαλος, and they are wider at the upper opening—signify the brightness and clarity of the Gospel meaning, in which all the mysteries of the Law and the prophets have been explained, and the plain expression of apostolic teaching, in which those things that had previously lain hidden in a riddle have been brought into the light and expounded.

The bowls are rightly described as one hundred and thirty shekels of silver, because of the Decalogue of the Law and the age of the lawgiver, which was one hundred and twenty years. The basins, too, are described as seventy shekels, where the number ten, multiplied seven times, shows that the fulfillment of the commandments can be accomplished only through the grace of the Holy Spirit, who was given more manifestly in the New Testament. These vessels are appropriately commanded to be made full of fine flour mixed with oil for a sacrifice, because it is evident to all who rightly believe and properly understand that spiritual knowledge is present in the Law and in the Gospel; through the dispensation of the grace of the Holy Spirit, it was written and proclaimed for the salvation of human beings. Thus the sacrifice is rightly made, because nothing is so acceptable to God as meditation on the divine Law together with the performance of good works.

A golden mortar, weighing ten shekels and full of incense, is likewise commanded to be offered. And what is signified by a golden mortar except the heart of the elect, full of divine wisdom and containing within itself the spices of virtues? [Col. 0631D] Nor do I think it incongruous to speak of the heart of the elect in the singular, since it is written in the Acts of the Apostles concerning the unity of the saints: “The multitude of believers had one heart and one soul” (Acts 4). It is rightly described as full of incense to the weight of ten shekels, because, through the fulfillment of the Ten Commandments, it knows how to produce the sweet fragrance of doctrine and sacred prayer, so that at the end we may deserve to receive the tenfold measure of eternal blessedness.

After these vessels mentioned above, he commands various animals to be offered: a bull from the herd, a ram, and a yearling lamb for a burnt offering, and a goat for sin. This variety signifies the persons of the fathers who preceded us and were given to us as examples: some performed the office of teacher; some were appointed to leadership and the governance of their subjects and were rationally set over them; some were most pleasing through the simplicity and gentleness of a modest way of life; and some were especially acceptable through the repentance that they undertook vigorously and worthily for their sins. Divine Providence has placed many examples of all these in the holy Scriptures for our instruction, so that we might consider their teaching in their sayings and their examples in their actions, which they nobly displayed while living among their own people for imitation, and strive always to reform our lives for the better.

Thus, according to the laws of tropology, he offers a bull, representing one who contributes usefulness in the Church of God for the salvation of his neighbors. He offers a ram, representing one who hastens not only to govern his own life properly but also to direct others onto the way of righteousness. He offers a yearling lamb when he displays holy simplicity and true innocence. All these are for a burnt offering, because he strives to do everything for the love of God alone and from desire for eternal life. Yet amid these he does not forget to offer a goat for sin, because he does not cease to repent of past sins and to pray for the offenses of human life.

Furthermore, as commanded above, he offers two bulls as a sacrifice of peace offerings: the person who fulfills the two commandments of charity through good works—showing love for God by keeping his commandments, and love for his neighbor by attending to his needs—for on these two commandments the whole Law and the prophets depend. He offers five rams, five goats, and five yearling lambs when he vigorously leads his five bodily senses along the way of truth, restrains them from sins, and displays in them the signs of good simplicity.

Every Catholic teacher, every ecclesiastical master, and every Christian person must undoubtedly present these gifts to his Creator, because no one is so devoid of divine gifts that he owes nothing to the divine glory; by God’s gift he has the very fact that he is, and whatever good there is in him. For, according to Paul’s statement, “In him we live and move and are,” since “from him and through him and in him are all things” (Acts 17).

Nor is it without a mystery that, after listing the leaders with their offerings, which they offered to God on separate days according to the order assigned to them, he finally counts together how many vessels of each kind there were and what the total weight of all of them was—that is, the silver vessels separately—and how many animals there were of each kind, which were commanded to be offered both as burnt offerings and as peace offerings. For it is written:

These were offered at the dedication of the altar by the princes of Israel on the day when it was consecrated: twelve silver bowls, twelve silver basins, and twelve golden mortars, so that one bowl contained one hundred and thirty silver shekels, and one basin seventy shekels—that is, the total weight of all the silver vessels was two thousand four hundred shekels according to the sanctuary weight. [Col. 0633A]

Twelve golden mortars full of incense, each weighing ten shekels according to the sanctuary weight—that is, one hundred and twenty golden shekels in all. Twelve bulls from the herd for burnt offerings, twelve rams, twelve yearling lambs, and twelve goats for sin offerings, together with their libations. For peace offerings: twenty-four bulls, sixty rams, sixty goats, and sixty yearling lambs.

What, then, should we understand by the silver vessels, which together amounted to two thousand four hundred shekels according to the sanctuary weight, except the perfect teaching of the utterances of God, which consists in the two Testaments? If we obey it properly, the chariot of virtues—that is, prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance—leads us to eternal blessedness; these numbers truly indicate this to us. For the doubled number one thousand shows that the twofold Testaments reveal to us the way by which we are to come to eternal blessedness. The number four hundred signifies that we must arrive there with the perfection of good works, in the chariot of the virtues, because unless one runs by means of good works, one arrives there not at all.

The twelve golden mortars, each weighing ten shekels, and together described as one hundred and twenty shekels of gold—what do they signify except the hearts of the elect observing the knowledge of the Law in all things as apostolic teaching instructs it to be observed? Twelve times ten makes one hundred and twenty. By this number the primitive Church in Jerusalem also received the Paraclete Spirit on the day of Pentecost. Hence it is rightly added that the shekel must be according to the sanctuary weight. [Col. 0633C]

The sanctuary of the Lord is the Catholic Church. If we follow its rule of faith and understanding, we must believe that everything written in the Law and the prophets is salutary for us. Whatever, on the other hand, is thought, understood, or observed outside the unity of the Church will most certainly produce not the salvation of the soul but condemnation.

The bulls, rams, and yearling lambs offered as burnt offerings are included in the number twelve. I believe this signifies that whether someone performs the office of teacher in the Church, holds the honor of some authority, or chooses a simple life, he ought to do everything according to apostolic and prophetic teaching. Likewise, the twelve goats offered for sin figuratively instruct those who repent to strive to complete their repentance according to the rule of faith.

Moreover, the twenty-four bulls, sixty rams, sixty goats, and sixty yearling lambs offered as peace offerings seem to signify nothing other than spiritual knowledge in the perfection of good works. The number twenty-four, because the course of the day is completed in that many hours, signifies that the light of knowledge and right faith is necessary for every Christian. The number sixty, because it contains ten multiplied six times, demonstrates the perfection of the commandments. It is therefore necessary that superiors and subjects alike, the righteous and the penitent, do everything according to ecclesiastical teaching, so that their offering may preserve before the Lord the rite and order of peace offerings and may merit God’s grace rather than his displeasure. [Col. 0634A]

And when Moses entered the tabernacle of the covenant to consult the oracle, he heard a voice speaking to him from the mercy seat that was above the ark of the testimony, between the two cherubim; from there he spoke to him. Moses’ entering the tabernacle of the covenant to consult the oracle of the Lord mystically instructs the preachers and teachers of God’s people how they should care for the spiritual word: namely, that they should enter the tabernacle of the covenant—that is, diligently meditate on sacred Scripture—and from there hear what the Lord God speaks to them.

From the mercy seat—or, as it is read in Exodus, above the mercy seat—the Lord speaks to Moses all that through him the Lord commands the children of Israel, because [Col. 0634B] through the grace of divine propitiation it came about that, after the guilt of transgression, God deigned to appear to human beings and to show them the way of truth after their error. He speaks from between the cherubim because God appeared through an angelic vision, and not in his own substance. He spoke to Moses, as the Apostle bears witness: “The Law was given because of transgressions, until the offspring should come to whom the promise had been made, ordained through angels by the hand of a mediator” (Gal. 3).

Again, the Lord speaks from between the two cherubim because, through the words of both Testaments, he teaches us the faith of truth with harmonious voice. Or certainly he speaks from the midst of the cherubim because, through his Only-Begotten Son, who appeared in the flesh between the two Testaments, God the Father deigned to reveal his will to the human race.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the lampstand and its lamps

(CAP. 8.) And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Speak to Aaron and say to him: When they have set up the seven lamps, let the lampstand be erected on the southern side. Therefore give this command: the lamps are to face northward, opposite one another, and they shall shine toward the table of the bread of the Presence, toward the side opposite the side that the lampstand faces.

The table and the lampstand of the tabernacle signify the temporal benefits of God, by which we are refreshed and enlightened in the present, so that, strengthened and assisted by them for a time, as the grace of our merits increases, we may be able to enter heaven to eat the bread of angels and to behold the true light of the world. Both are outside the veil, because only in this life do we need either the holy Scriptures and teachers or the other mysteries of our redemption. In the age to come, the Lord will announce the Father to us openly—that is, he will openly show the Father to us.

We said elsewhere that the southern side of the tabernacle signified the ancient people of God, who first received the fervor of divine reading; whereas the northern side of the same tabernacle indicated the Church gathered from the Gentiles, which had remained longer in darkness and the shadow of death. Hence, by a proper distinction, the lampstand, which is placed on the southern side, can also signify the grace given to the earlier people. The table, however, which stood on the northern side, signifies the benefits of God that have been granted to us. [Col. 0635A]

The lampstand is rightly said to have been placed opposite the table, because the Scripture of the Law and the prophets looks in every respect toward the grace of the Gospel, bearing witness to it and signifying that through it Scripture is to be revealed in its spiritual meaning.

And Aaron did so and placed the lamps on the lampstand, as the Lord had commanded Moses. The seven lamps are the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, which always remained in the Lord our Redeemer and were distributed among his members—that is, among all the elect—according to his will. The seven lamps are therefore placed upon the lampstand because upon our Redeemer, the firstborn from the root of Jesse, rested the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and fortitude, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord filled him (Isa. 11).

And, again, he himself speaks through the same prophet: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because the Lord has anointed me” (Isa. 61). What is said about their shining opposite one another is what the prophet subsequently added: “He has sent me to announce good news to the meek, to heal the brokenhearted, to proclaim release to the captives and opening to those who are imprisoned, to proclaim an acceptable year of the Lord and the day of vengeance of our God” (ibid.).

This was the construction of the lampstand. From beaten gold he made both the central shaft and all that arose from either side of the branches, according to the model that the Lord had shown Moses; thus he made the lampstand. We have said that the lampstand itself—that is, the central shaft of the lampstand from which the branches proceeded—designates the Lord the Savior, from whose grace the righteous have received whatever good they possess. Hence, when he had said to his disciples in the Gospel, “I am the vine; you are the branches,” he immediately added: “As a branch cannot bear fruit by itself unless it remains in the vine, so neither can you unless you remain in me” (John 15).

The entire work of the lampstand—that is, both the central shaft and the branches proceeding from it, with all their adornment—is made from gold, because the Lord himself appeared in the world uniquely free from sin and altogether distinguished by works of righteousness, while his members, insofar as they are able in this present life, imitate that same innocence and righteousness; in the future, by truly adhering to him, they will bring them to perfection.

Appropriately, this same gold was beaten into shape. Beaten gold is produced by striking, because our Redeemer, who from conception and birth existed as perfect God and man, endured the pains of sufferings and thus reached the glory of the resurrection. And all who wish to live piously in him suffer persecution (1 Tim. 3). They too, like metal expanded by hammering, advance through the insults of suffering toward the grace of immortality.

## CHAPTER XV. On the purification of the Levites

(IBID.) The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Take the Levites from among the children of Israel and purify them according to this rite. Let them be sprinkled with the water of purification, and let them shave all the hair of their bodies.

Thus, when the Lord gives the Levites this command through Moses, he instructs the ecclesiastical order concerning how one may properly approach the priestly order. He shows how they must be purified before approaching divine service. First he commands them to be sprinkled with the water of purification, which we may understand either as the sacrament of baptism or as the shedding of tears, through which the stains of sins are rightly washed away.

Next he commands them to shave all the hair of their bodies. The hair of the body represents every superfluity of human corruption. The hair of the body represents the thoughts of the former life, which we cut away from the mind in such a way that we are troubled by their loss with no pain. A Levite is so called because he has been taken up. Therefore all Levites ought to shave the hair of their bodies, because the one who is taken up into divine service must appear pure before God’s eyes from every thought of the flesh. [Col. 0636B]

Let the mind not produce illicit thoughts and, like fruitful hairs, render the beautiful appearance of the soul deformed. But however far, as we have said, the virtue of holy conduct may have elevated someone, something from his old condition still grows within him and must be endured. Hence the Levites were commanded to have their hair shaved, not plucked out. When the hair is shaved, its roots remain in the flesh, and it grows again so that it may be cut off again. Thus superfluous thoughts must indeed be cut away with great diligence, but they can never be cut out completely. For the flesh always generates something superfluous, which the spirit must always cut away with the sword of vigilance. We perceive these things more subtly, however, when we penetrate the heights of contemplation.

And when they have washed their garments and been cleansed, let them take a bull from the herd and its libation, fine flour mixed with oil. To wash the garments is to cleanse one’s works and to keep one’s entire conduct pure in the sight of the Divinity, as well as to present oneself blameless before human eyes.

He also commands the purified to offer a bull from the herd and its libation, fine flour mixed with oil. What should we understand in this bull except the Lord’s body, descended from the herd of patriarchs and prophets? Its libations—that is, the mysteries of its passion—when treated and understood through spiritual knowledge by the faithful, are to be believed most salutary and most pleasing to God. This is so, however, only if the Levite, who is certainly the Lord’s spiritual minister, presents himself inwardly and outwardly clean and worthy to receive such mysteries.

The text continues: But you shall take the other bull from the herd as a sin offering. The other bull, which was offered for sins, is the same mediator between God and human beings, through whose sacrifice our sins have been wiped away. No one should find it incongruous that we have said that the Lord’s incarnation is signified by both bulls. Although Christ’s passion is one and the same, it nevertheless carried out a twofold operation in us, because it cleansed us from sins and granted us sanctification.

Hence Peter also says in his Epistle: “Christ died once for our sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, that he might bring us to God—put to death in the flesh but made alive in the spirit. Therefore, girding the loins of your mind, being sober, hope perfectly in the grace that is offered to you, at the revelation of Jesus Christ, as obedient children; do not be conformed to the former desires of your ignorance, but according to the one who called you, the Holy One, be holy yourselves in all your conduct” (1 Pet. 1).

For this reason the Apostle Paul also, writing to the Corinthians, after listing the principal crimes by which human life is polluted, added: “And such were some of you. But you were washed; you were sanctified in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God” (1 Cor. 6).

These two bulls—one of which was to be offered for sin and the other as a burnt offering, as will be demonstrated below—can indeed express two kinds of action. By one we strive to wash away, through the lament of repentance, the things we have done wrongly; by the other we strive, through the fruits of good works and the pursuit of virtues, to merit the grace of the Creator and the blessedness of the heavenly reward.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the Levites being received in place of the firstborn of the children of Israel for the service of the Lord

(IBID.) And he shall bring the Levites before the tabernacle of the covenant, after gathering the entire assembly of the children of Israel. The Levites are brought before the tabernacle of the covenant when the ministers of the Lord, chosen for service at the altar, are led into the apostolic teaching through which one enters the true tabernacle of the Lord. They are rightly brought before the tabernacle of the covenant if, according to the words and examples of the holy Fathers, they begin the course of their conduct and strive to persevere in it to the end. This must also be done with the testimony of many. Therefore he added, “after gathering the entire assembly of the children of Israel,” because the election of God’s ministers ought to be known to many, and a worthy examination and testing ought to be carried out concerning them, so that no one may be able justly to criticize their life. Hence Paul commands that they have a good reputation among outsiders, so that they may not fall into reproach and the devil’s snare.

And when the Levites are before the Lord, the children of Israel shall place their hands upon them, and Aaron shall offer the gift before the Lord on behalf of the children of Israel, so that they may serve in his ministry. The children of Israel are commanded to place their hands upon the Levites and thus offer them as a gift before the Lord through Aaron, because the consent of good subjects ought, through the affection of true charity, to accompany the teachers they choose with suitable assistance. They place their hands upon them when they grant their devoted assent to their election and strive to persevere in good works at their command, so that the Lord’s ministry may be worthily fulfilled through those who have been offered for service.

The Levites also shall place their hands upon the heads of the bulls, one of which you shall make a sin offering and the other a burnt offering to the Lord, to make atonement for them. The Levites place their hands upon the heads of the bulls when ministers hasten, through their own labors, to consecrate the beginnings of their works to the Lord, so that whether repentance for the offenses of human life is required or works are to be devoted to the pursuit of virtues, they may strive to complete them not feebly but effectively.

You shall also set the Levites before Aaron and his sons, and consecrate those offered to the Lord, and separate them from among the children of Israel, so that they may be mine; and afterward they shall enter the tabernacle of the covenant to serve me. Observe that the Levites are commanded to be separated from among the children of Israel so that they may belong to the Lord, and afterward to enter the tabernacle of the covenant to serve God. A minister of the Lord ought not to be content with the discipline of the common people; rather, whether in conduct or in teaching, he must become set apart and distinguished, and thus devote himself to the Lord’s service.

Thus you shall purify and consecrate them as an offering to the Lord, since they have been given to me as a gift by the children of Israel. In place of every firstborn in Israel who opens the womb, I have taken them. For every firstborn of the children of Israel is mine, both human and animal. From the day on which I struck down every firstborn in the land of Egypt, I consecrated them to myself.

It is not unknown that the firstborn of the Egyptians signify the beginnings of the vices by which human life is corrupted. For every soul, when it reaches maturity and a certain natural law within it begins, as it were, to defend its rights, undoubtedly produces its first impulses according to the desire of the flesh—impulses stirred by the inciting force of the tinder of lust or anger. Hence, as something exceptional and not shared with other human beings, the prophet says of Christ alone: “He shall eat butter and honey” (Isaiah 7); “before he does or utters evil, he will choose the good. For before the child knows good or evil, he will resist wickedness, so that he may choose what is good.”

Elsewhere the Prophet speaks as though of himself, saying: “Remember not the sins of my youth and my ignorances” (Psalm 24). Since, therefore, these first impulses of the soul, brought forth according to the flesh, rush into sin, these first beginnings are rightly assigned to the Egyptians’ *immortali* place [the reading is materially uncertain], and they are extinguished insofar as the conduct of the rest of life directs its course toward improvement.

When the vices that are the devil’s firstborn, or the harmful works of the flesh by which nature is defiled, have been extinguished, good morals must be maintained, so that a worshiper of God, not a servant of demons, may truly appear through a spiritual way of life. But whoever still wishes to be a minister of the Lord must be clothed with more perfect conduct than the multitude of the people can possess. Therefore, in place of the firstborn of the Egyptians, the firstborn of the Israelites are commanded to be offered to the Lord.

Likewise, in place of the firstborn of the children of Israel, the Levites are commanded to be taken into divine service, so that through a spiritual exchange a righteous life may be offered in place of a sinful life, and a holy and perfect life in place of a righteous one. Thus the true Levite may be worthily fitted in the Lord’s sanctuary for the altars of Christ and the divine mysteries.

“And I took the Levites in place of all the firstborn of the children of Israel, that they may serve me in place of the children of Israel in the tabernacle of the covenant and pray for them, lest there be a plague among the people if they should dare to approach the sanctuary,” and so forth.

Let bishops, priests, ministers of the Lord, and the entire clergy observe how necessary it is for them carefully to guard the rights of their office, lest they surrender themselves, together with the unlearned multitude, to earthly profits and worldly pleasures. For it is proper to their order and office that they serve in the tabernacle of the Lord’s covenant and pray for the peoples, lest there be among them a plague that destroys.

Otherwise, if they themselves lead their lives negligently and serve the profits and desires of the world instead of the service of God, they will cast themselves into perdition and will not save the people. Of them it will be said in the prophetic word: “I have no pleasure in you, says the Lord of hosts, and I will not accept an offering from your hand” (Malachi 1). And elsewhere: “Their clergy will not profit them.”

## CHAPTER XVII. On the order of the Levites: when they are ministers and when they become guardians of the vessels

### (ibid.)

The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “This is the law of the Levites. From twenty-five years of age and upward they shall enter to minister in the tabernacle of the covenant. When they have completed their fiftieth year, they shall cease to serve; they shall be ministers of their brothers in the tabernacle of the covenant, to guard what has been entrusted to them, but they shall not perform the actual work.”

Or, according to the Septuagint:

“From the twenty-fifth year and upward they shall enter to minister in the ministry, in the works, in the tabernacle of testimony; and from the fiftieth year they shall withdraw from the administration and shall work no longer. Their brothers shall minister in the tabernacle of testimony, to guard the guards; but they shall not perform the work.”

The meaning is obscured by the *hyperbaton* (ὑπέρβατον), which has been so confused that the phrase “to guard the guards” seems to have been spoken of the brother himself, whereas it is spoken of the one who withdraws from the work and remains in the tabernacle of testimony “to guard the guards”; “but he shall not perform the work.” His brother shall perform it—that is, the one who has not yet reached the age of fifty, beginning to work from the age of twenty-five.

The passage should therefore be punctuated as follows: “From the fiftieth year he shall withdraw from the administration and shall work no longer; and his brother shall minister.” Then it returns to the man of fifty about whom it was speaking and explains the remainder, saying: “In the tabernacle of testimony, to guard the guards; but he shall not perform the work.”

For when it says “to guard the guards,” it is customary even in Latin expressions for an infinitive verb to be used in place of a finite one.

In the mystical sense, what is signified by the twenty-fifth year, in which the flower of youth springs forth, except the wars waged against each of the vices? And what is signified by the fiftieth year, in which the rest of the Jubilee is contained, except the inward rest expressed after the battle of the mind has been subdued? What else are the vessels of the tabernacle than the souls of the faithful?

The Levites therefore serve the tabernacle from their twenty-fifth year, and from their fiftieth year become guardians of the vessels, so that those who still endure the struggles of contending vices may not presume to take charge of others. For the elect, while they are still in temptation, must be subject and serve, so that they may be wearied by obedience and labor. But when they have conquered the battles of temptations and are already secure within themselves through inward tranquility, they are entrusted with the guardianship of souls.

When the age of the mind is tranquil and the heat of temptation has withdrawn, they are guardians of the vessels, because they become teachers of souls.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0639]

## CHAPTER I. On the time of Passover

### (Chapter 9)

The Lord spoke to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai, in the second year after they had gone out from the land of Egypt, in the first month, saying: “Let the children of Israel celebrate the Passover at its appointed time, on the fourteenth day of this month at evening, according to all its ceremonies and ordinances.” And Moses commanded the children of Israel to celebrate the Passover. They celebrated it at its appointed time, on the fourteenth day of the month at evening, at Mount Sinai; according to everything that the Lord had commanded Moses, the children of Israel acted.

Although in the Old Testament the time of Passover is commanded to be observed by three indications of its proper reckoning—namely, after the equinox, in the first month, and in the third week of that month, that is, from the evening of the fourteenth day of the moon, which is the beginning of the fifteenth, until the evening that marks the end of the twenty-first—the rule imposed upon us from the time of the Lord’s resurrection is that, when the equinox has passed and we see the fourteenth day of the first month’s moon rising in the evening, we should not immediately rush to celebrate Passover.

Rather, we should await the Lord’s day on which he himself, by rising again, graciously accomplished Passover—that is, the passage from death to life, from corruption to incorruption, and from punishment to glory—and finally celebrate the appropriate solemn rites of Passover on that day.

If anyone objects that the Lawgiver did not establish the memory of the equinox but only the first month and its third week, let him know that, even though the equinox is not expressly named, nevertheless, by commanding that Passover be celebrated from the full moon of the first month, he fully indicates the passage of the equinox. For it is indisputably established that, when the moon has encountered its full orb at the first passage of the equinox, it belongs to the first month.

Whenever, therefore, we have the Lord’s day immediately approaching the fifteenth day of the moon, our paschal time does not differ at all from the legal one, although we celebrate the solemnities of that same Passover through other kinds of mysteries. But whenever that Lord’s day occurs two, three, four, five, six, or seven days later, even then we do not abolish the Law or the Prophets. For just as the whole observance of the paschal ceremonies is full of sacred mysteries, so too is the entire period during which it was commanded to be performed.

First, in celebrating the Lord’s Passover we take care, according to the decrees of the Law, to pass beyond the equinox, so that the solemnity in which the Mediator of God and human beings, having destroyed the power of darkness, opened for the world a path of light may also reveal outwardly, through the order of time, what it contains inwardly. And the solemnity that promises us the light of eternal blessedness is celebrated especially at the time when the light of the sun, increasing annually, first gains victory over the shadow of night.

Next, we observe the first month of the year, which is also called the month of new things, in which we celebrate Passover. It is the month in which this world was formed and the human being was first placed in the seat of paradise, because through the mysteries of this solemnity we hope to recover our first garment and to find again the first kingdom of heavenly blessedness from which we departed into a distant land.

Concerning the glory of that kingdom, the blessed apostle Peter says: “We await new heavens and a new earth according to his promise, in which righteousness dwells” (2 Peter 3). John likewise says in his Apocalypse: “And he who sat upon the throne said, ‘Behold, I make all things new’” (Revelation 12).

We also observe in Passover the third week of that month, because it most aptly corresponds to the joys of the Lord’s resurrection: his own most holy resurrection took place on the third day, and in the third age of the world—that is, with the coming of heavenly grace—his entire dispensation in the flesh, which was consummated in the glory of the resurrection, appeared to the world.

He graciously chose to illuminate the first periods of the world in stages through the natural law, the middle periods through the natural law and the prophets, and the final periods through the spiritual anointing, coming himself.

The moon’s own change at that time also provides us with a most beautiful spectacle of heavenly mystery. As we said above, the moon, made in the form of a sphere, receives light from the sun. It is therefore always bright on the half of its orb that faces the sun, while the other half is always dark. From the first day up to the fifteenth, it has an increase of light toward the earth but a decrease toward the heavens; from the fifteenth onward, until the final increase of that same light, it turns away from earthly things and gradually returns toward heavenly things.

This change of the moon rightly signifies the mysteries of paschal joy, by which we are taught to turn all the glory of our mind away from lowly pleasures and passing favors and to direct it solely toward the light of heavenly grace through contemplation.

Or, if one prefers to interpret both of its changes positively, we may understand the moon’s increasing light toward human eyes to signify the grace of the virtues through which the Lord, appearing in the flesh, illumined the world. Of these it is said: “And Jesus advanced in wisdom and age and grace with God and human beings” (Luke 2).

Its increasing return toward the heavens, however, may signify the glory of his resurrection and ascension. That glory immediately came to perfection in him, but in the minds of the faithful, through certain advances of its light, it does not cease to increase until the end of the world.

For after rising from the dead, the Lord appeared first to individuals and pairs, and then to larger numbers—at one time to seven, at another to eleven, at another to twelve, and at another to more than five hundred brothers at once—and finally to all the disciples. In their sight, as he was about to ascend into heaven, he commanded them to be witnesses of his dispensation in Jerusalem, throughout all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth (1 Corinthians 15).

And fittingly, when the moon grows before our eyes, it gradually moves away from the sun; but when it returns toward the heavens, it comes back with equal * intervals [the printed text is uncertain]. This is what he himself said: “I came forth from the Father and came into the world; again I leave the world and go to the Father” (John 10). And the Psalm says of him: “His going forth is from the end of heaven, and his circuit reaches to its end” (Psalm 18).

Since, therefore, the moon’s increase of light as it leaves the sun and unfolds before our eyes signifies the teaching and virtues of the Lord and Savior in the flesh up to the time of his Passion, while its return toward the sun and gradual withdrawal toward the heavenly face invisible to us demonstrates the miracles of his resurrection and subsequent glory, it is rightly proclaimed suitable for the joys of the paschal vow from the fifteenth day onward.

In addition to these indications of the paschal season taken from the observance of the Law, we, the heirs of the New Testament, also join to them the Lord’s day, which Scripture calls the one or first day of the week (Matthew 28), and not without reason. It excels through the condition of the first light, is distinguished by the triumph of the Lord’s resurrection, and remains always desirable to us because of our own resurrection.

The seven days of the moon—from the fifteenth through the twenty-first—during which the Lord’s day proceeds according to the natural order, plainly proclaim the universality of the Church, which throughout the world has been redeemed through the paschal mysteries. Scripture often uses the number seven to signify universality.

Thus, when the Prophet says, “Seven times a day I have praised you” (Psalm 118), nothing better is understood than what he says elsewhere: “His praise shall always be in my mouth” (Psalm 33). John also testifies that the entire progress of the catholic Church is specially represented by this number when, writing to the seven churches of Asia, he disclosed the mysteries of the universal Church throughout the world (Revelation 1).

Therefore, in all the exhortations that he writes to the seven churches individually, he took care to weave in this verse: “Let anyone who has ears to hear listen to what the Spirit says to the churches” (Revelation 2). What he had said to each one, he thereby showed that he had said to all the churches.

The paschal seasons also commend to us a moral meaning. In the very name “Passover” we are taught to make a spiritual passage daily from vices to virtues.
