In the month of new things, when mature fruits announce by their arrival the cessation of old things, we are taught: “Putting off the old man with his deeds, let us renew the spirit of our mind and put on the new man, who has been created according to God in righteousness and the holiness of truth” (Colossians 3).

Thus, strengthened by the truth of various virtues and covered, as it were, by their leaves like the shade of a pleasant tree, let us sprout like joyful and fruitful crops at the full moon, bearing the perfect brightness of the assent of faith and being separated from the darkness of sin.

When the same lunar light turns back toward the heavens, beginning at the fifteenth moon, we are taught to humble ourselves in all things the more we become great, saying individually with the Apostle: “By the grace of God I am what I am.”

Since this grace, the gift from above, was poured out more manifestly in the third age of the world, a most beautiful sequence of figures is displayed: the light of the moon’s week, which had until then increased toward the earth, now begins to increase toward heavenly things.

We are beautifully commanded to observe this in Passover, so that, never forgetting the grace we have received, we may remember, by obeying its giver through each stage of our spiritual passage, to consider the return we owe.

Or certainly, in the moon’s increase toward human beings, the type of the active life is shown to us; in its return toward the heavens, the type of the contemplative life. Or in this change the love of neighbor is signified, and in that one the love of our victorious Lord.

Its movement toward us, with the progress of its light, admonishes us to perform good works outwardly; its movement away from us, toward that place, admonishes us to perform those same good works solely with a view to the heavenly reward. Here we are taught, “Let your light shine before human beings, so that they may see your good works”; there, “so that they may glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5).

On the one day of the week, whose solemnity belongs properly to the New Testament, we are instructed that, in hope of our future resurrection in Christ, we must patiently endure in the present every adversity for Christ’s sake, even the injury of death, hearing the Apostle say: “If the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Christ Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit dwelling in you” (Romans 8).

That Spirit, which possesses a sevenfold grace, may appropriately be understood as indicated by the same number of seven lunar days through which the aforementioned one day of the week—that is, the Lord’s day—is carried.

But if anyone wishes to know more fully about the mystery of the time of Passover, let him read the letter of the blessed Aurelius Augustine to Januarius concerning the reckoning of Passover.

## CHAPTER II. On those who could not celebrate Passover at the time appointed for them

[Col. 0643D]

### (ibid.)

“Behold, certain persons who were unclean because of a human soul and could not celebrate the Passover came to Moses and Aaron on that day and said to them: ‘We are unclean because of a human soul. Why are we defrauded, so that we cannot offer an offering to the Lord at its appointed time among the children of Israel?’ Moses replied to them: ‘Stand here, that I may consult what the Lord commands concerning you.’

“The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: ‘Speak to the children of Israel: If anyone is unclean because of a human soul, or is on a distant journey among your people, let him celebrate the Passover for the Lord in the second month, on the fourteenth day of the month at evening. They shall eat it with unleavened bread and wild lettuce. They shall leave none of it until morning, and they shall not break any of its bones. They shall observe every rite of the Passover,’” and so forth.

At the time of Passover, certain people who had become unclean because of a human soul—that is, because of a dead person—asked how they should celebrate Passover, since according to the Law they had to be purified from uncleanness for seven days. Moses consulted the Lord and received the answer that anyone to whom such a thing had happened, or who was situated on such a distant journey that he could not arrive, should celebrate Passover in another month, on the fourteenth day of the month, when the reckoning of the moon was observed.

But if it is asked what they should do if such uncleanness should also occur in the second month, I think that what was said concerning the second month should be retained as a rule, so that they would observe it in the third month; or certainly that, because of such necessity, their failure to celebrate Passover would not be counted as guilt.

But what does the second mystery signify—that those who live farther away, or who were unclean in soul, were commanded to celebrate Passover in the second month? It is surely understood as a type of the people of the nations, who, having fornicated with all the demons, appeared unclean in soul but, cleansed by a saving confession, are commanded to pass over into a second birth, as it were in the second month.

Two circumstances were set forth because of which no one could celebrate the first Passover: if he were unclean because of a human soul, or if he were on a distant journey.

A person is unclean in soul when he is polluted by diabolical deception through the worship of idols and the enormity of sins. He is on a distant journey when, hearing the word of salvation, he chooses to abandon idols and receive faith in God, but has not yet reached the sacrament of baptism, through which one enters the Church—namely, Jerusalem, the city of peace, where the temple of God and the Holy of Holies are.

They are commanded to eat the flesh of the lamb in one house, because outside the holy Church it is not permitted to eat the flesh of the true Lamb, that is, the Lord’s body.

Therefore, since the gentile people could not celebrate the first Passover according to the Law, in the second month—that is, in the time of grace—now cleansed from all the uncleanness of sins and restored to the household where it is permitted to celebrate Passover properly, they shall eat the lamb toward evening, with unleavened bread and wild lettuce. They are commanded to leave none of it until morning and not to break any of its bones, but carefully to observe every rite of the Passover.

The person who eats unleavened bread is one who practices what is right without the corruption of empty glory and who performs the commandments of mercy without any mixture of sin, lest he become perversely foolish.

Wild lettuce, however, is extremely bitter. The flesh of the lamb must be eaten with wild lettuce so that, when we receive the body of the Redeemer, we may afflict ourselves with tears for our sins, so that the very bitterness of repentance may wipe from the stomach of the mind the perverse love of life.

None of it shall remain until morning, because his words must be examined with the greatest diligence, so that before the day of resurrection appears, all his commandments may be penetrated through understanding and practice during the calling of the present life.

But because it is exceedingly difficult for the whole utterance of the Lamb to be understood, or for all his mystery to be penetrated, the text rightly adds: “But if anything remains, you shall burn it with fire.”

We burn with fire what remains of the lamb when we humbly entrust to the power of the Holy Spirit what we cannot understand concerning the mystery of his incarnation. No one should arrogantly dare either to despise or to denounce what he does not understand; rather, he should hand it over to the fire by reserving it for the Holy Spirit.

Those who celebrate Passover are forbidden to break the bones. The Lord’s bones were not broken on the cross, as the Evangelist testifies when he says: “You shall not break any of his bones” (John 19).

Christians shall observe every rite of the Passover, because whatever was commanded historically in the Law to be done in the celebration of Passover is observed spiritually in its entirety in the Church of Christ.

“But if anyone is clean, has not been on a journey, and nevertheless does not celebrate the Passover, that soul shall be exterminated from its peoples, because it did not offer the sacrifice to the Lord at its appointed time; it shall bear its sin itself.”

Here he instructed those who were under the old Law by threatening them, so that they would not neglect to observe the lawful time of Passover and thereby incur the destruction of life if they failed to take care to observe the Lord’s command. Indeed, he also admonishes those who have been placed under the grace of Christ not to neglect to celebrate the spiritual Passover at its appointed time.

Concerning this time, the Apostle Paul says: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Corinthians 6). Whoever does not take care to celebrate in worthy faith the redemption of the human race, accomplished through the sacrifice of the true Lamb, and does not strive to turn his life toward better things during this mortal existence, nor hasten to pass from vices to virtues, will certainly have no share in the glory of the resurrection that will be granted at the end to the true worshipers of Christ.

Rather, that soul will be exterminated from the fellowship of all the saints, and it will not be permitted to have any communion with them in the most joyful assembly of the saints.

What follows—“If a sojourner and a resident alien is among you, let him celebrate the Passover for the Lord according to its ceremonies and ordinances. There shall be one ordinance among you for both the resident alien and the native”—shows that with the Lord there is no distinction of persons.

Whoever, whether Jew or gentile, male or female, slave or free, has been converted to the catholic faith, washed in Christ’s baptism, and received the unity of the Church may rightly share in the mysteries of Christ’s resurrection.

## CHAPTER III. How the children of Israel should set out

### (ibid.)

“On the day, therefore, when the tabernacle was erected, the cloud covered it. From evening onward there was something like the appearance of fire over the tent until morning; so it happened continually. By day the cloud covered it, and by night there was something like the appearance of fire.

“When the cloud that protected the tabernacle was taken away, then the children of Israel set out; and in the place where the cloud had stood, there they pitched camp. At the command of the Lord they set out, and at his command they pitched their tents.

“All the days that the cloud remained over the tabernacle, they stayed in the same place. If it happened that it remained over it for a long time, the children of Israel kept watch at the Lord’s watch and did not set out for as many days as the cloud was over the tabernacle.

“At the command of the Lord they erected their tents, and at his command they took them down. If the cloud was from evening until morning and then left the tabernacle at dawn, they set out. If it withdrew after a day and a night, they dismantled their tents.

“But if it was over the tabernacle for two months, or one month, or a longer period, the children of Israel remained in the same place and did not set out. As soon as it withdrew, they broke camp.

“By the word of the Lord they pitched their tents, and by his word they set out. They kept the Lord’s watch according to his command through the hand of Moses.”

In the Septuagint translators the chapter is also contained as follows:

“On the day when the tabernacle was established, the cloud covered the tabernacle, the house of testimony, and in the evening there was over the tabernacle something like the appearance of fire at night. When the cloud went up from the tabernacle, afterward the children of Israel moved forward. Wherever the cloud had stood, there the children of Israel placed their camp.

“By the command of the Lord the children of Israel placed their camp, and by the command of the Lord they moved forward. All the days during which the cloud overshadowed the tabernacle, the children of Israel were in camp. When the cloud remained over the tabernacle for many days, the children of Israel would keep the Lord’s watches and would not move forward.

“When the cloud covered the tabernacle for a number of days, by the voice of the Lord they would remain in camp, and by the command of the Lord they would move forward. When the cloud was from evening until morning, and the cloud went up in the morning, they would move forward by day or by night.

“If the cloud went up, they would move forward. Or if the cloud remained over it for a day, a month, or as many days as the cloud overshadowed it, the children of Israel would remain in camp and would not move forward, because they would move forward by the command of the Lord. They kept the Lord’s watch by the command of the Lord through the hand of Moses.”

This entire passage must be explained carefully, because it has been obscured by unusual forms of expression.

“And on the day,” it says, “when the tabernacle was established, the cloud covered the tabernacle, the house of testimony.” It called the same tabernacle the house of testimony. “And in the evening it was over the tabernacle like the appearance of fire until morning”: this happened continually.

It then carefully explains what happened continually: “The cloud covered it by day, and the appearance of fire by night.”

“And when the cloud had gone up from the tabernacle, afterward the children of Israel shall move forward.” This sentence is not obscure except because of the addition of the conjunction “and.” The order of the words remains complete even if the conjunction itself is absent, so that it reads: “And when the cloud had gone up from the tabernacle, afterward the children of Israel shall move forward.” Indeed, even if “afterward” were absent, the sentence could still be complete.

Then it continues: “And in the place where the cloud had stood, there the children of Israel would place their camp.” Referring all that they did to the command of the Lord, it summarizes it as follows: “By the command of the Lord the children of Israel shall place their camp, and by the command of the Lord they shall move forward.”

He calls the command of the Lord the sign itself that appeared in the cloud, whether when it stood, overshadowing the tabernacle so that they might remain in camp, or when it rose and moved farther on, so that they might follow it after breaking camp.

In this sentence the narrator has indeed changed his manner of speaking and, as though predicting and announcing beforehand, has begun to use verbs in the future tense. For he does not say, “By the command of the Lord the children of Israel placed their camp,” but “shall place.” Nor does he say, “By the command of the Lord they moved forward,” but “shall move forward.”

He preserves this manner in what follows as well—a manner exceedingly unusual in Scripture. We know that future events are often predicted through verbs in the past tense, as in: “They pierced my hands and my feet” (Psalm 21); “He was led like a sheep to the slaughter” (Isaiah 53); and countless similar passages. But for a narrator of completed events to use verbs in the future tense, as in this passage, can scarcely be found in Scripture.

After saying, therefore, that the people would move forward or remain according to the sign, day and night, lest anyone think that they traveled by night but were accustomed to remain in camp by day—and that they did this on all days—he confidently adds:

“All the days during which the cloud overshadows the tabernacle, the children of Israel shall be in camp. And when the cloud remains over the tabernacle for many days,” he then warns that this does not happen from their own necessity but from the will of God: “the children of Israel shall keep the watch that God commanded, and they shall not move forward.”

And as though someone were to ask, “When then shall they move forward?” he says: “It shall happen when the cloud covers the tabernacle for a certain number of days”—that is, for a definite number, which number is pleasing to God—“by the voice of the Lord they shall be in camp, and by the command of the Lord they shall move forward.”

He seems to call the voice of the Lord the sign that he gives concerning the cloud’s standing and movement, because the voice of one who speaks is unquestionably a sign of his will. What he says, therefore, “by the command of the Lord,” should, I think, be understood as referring to this same sign, although “the voice and command of the Lord” could also be understood as the word that he spoke, as he commonly did to Moses, commanding this to be done.

For they would not know that they were to move forward when the cloud moved forward and stand when the cloud stood unless this had first been commanded to them.

In the statements already given it has not yet appeared whether they traveled only by day or also by night, according to the sign given by the cloud through its movement. For although they remained in camp for many days while the cloud did not move forward, it could nevertheless have been supposed that the cloud did not usually rise from the camp or give the sign for departure except by day.

Therefore the text continues and says: “It shall happen when the cloud is from evening until morning, and the cloud rises in the morning, that they shall move forward by day.”

Here the conjunction “and” has been placed according to the custom of Scripture. If it is removed, the sense is complete in this form: “It shall happen when the cloud is from evening until morning, and when the cloud rises in the morning, they shall move forward by day.”

Then, because they also moved forward at night if the cloud rose and undertook a night journey when they received that sign, he adds: “Or by night, and if the cloud rises, they shall move forward.”

But the expression is more unusual. The word *et* (“and”) has not merely been placed there; it has been placed in a manner in which it is not ordinarily used. It therefore seems to me that the order of the words has been reversed, as often happens even in Latin expressions—a figure called *antistrophe*.

Accordingly, if it is read, “or also by night, if the cloud rises, they shall move forward,” or, “if the cloud also rises by night, they shall move forward,” the sense is perfectly clear.

As he continued thinking, another question arose: whether, just as it had become known that they were accustomed to travel by day and night at the sign of the cloud, or to remain in camp by day and night, so they were also accustomed to remain for entire days, even on nights during which they traveled.

I think Scripture indicates this in what follows when it says: “By day, or by a month of days, while the cloud overshadows it, the children of Israel shall be in camp and shall not move forward.”

Since he had said, “Or by night, if the cloud rises, they shall move forward,” it remained, as it were, for him to say: “But by day, if it does not rise, they shall not move forward,” even when they seemed as though they ought to move forward.

But because this could also happen for many days—that they would travel by night when the cloud moved forward, while by day, when it remained, they would not travel—he therefore said, “by day, or by a month of days.”

He did not say simply “by a month,” lest the nights of that same month also be understood; rather, he said “by a month of days,” that is, a month insofar as it was composed of those days, not insofar as it was composed of nights.

“By day, or by a month of days, when the cloud abounded, overshadowing”—that is, when it abounded in overshadowing, or overshadowed more abundantly—“over it,” namely, over the tabernacle, “the children of Israel shall be in camp and shall not move forward.”

Finally, he repeats that this occurred by divine authority, which certainly ought not to be resisted, adding: “because by the command of the Lord they shall move forward.”

“They kept the Lord’s watch by the command of the Lord through the hand of Moses.” He returned to the verb in the past tense, saying “they kept.” What he placed at the end, “through the hand of Moses,” is a very common expression in Scripture, because God gave these commands through Moses.

According to the allegorical interpretation, the cloud that covered the tabernacle and led the people through the wilderness, giving by its position a sign of when the children of Israel were to travel and when they were to pitch camp, signifies the incarnation of Christ. Through his mercy he protected the tabernacle of the Church; through his goodness he orders its condition; and through his wisdom he directs its passage along the way of the present age.

The same is also the pillar, because he is upright and firm, supporting our weakness, and shining by night but not shining by day, so that those who do not see may see and those who see may become blind (John 9).

It may also appropriately be understood in this way: the mystery of Christ was manifested as in daytime, in the flesh as though in a cloud; but at the judgment it will be as though in nighttime error [*errore nocturno*], because then there will be great tribulation in the world like fire. It will shine for the righteous and burn the unrighteous.

According to the tropological interpretation, terrors are shown in the fire, while in the cloud is shown the gentle consolation of vision. Day signifies the life of the righteous, and night the life of the sinner. Hence Paul says to those who have been converted from sin: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Ephesians 5).

Therefore, by day the column was shown by means of a cloud, and by night by means of fire, because almighty God will appear gentle to the righteous and terrible to the unrighteous. When he comes in judgment, he soothes the righteous through the gentleness of his mildness; but he terrifies the unrighteous through the justice of his severity. Again, when this column of fire and cloud is examined through subtle investigation, it can also be understood in another way. What, then, does it mean that the column of cloud, which went before the people in the wilderness with the brightness of fire, shone not by day but by night, except that our Redeemer, offering himself as guide to those who follow him through the example of his conduct, showed no light to those who were confident in their own righteousness, but kindled the fire of his love in those who recognized the darkness of their sins? [Col. 0649B]

## CHAPTER IV. On the manner of the trumpets

**(CHAP. X.)** And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “Make for yourself two silver trumpets, beaten out, with which you may summon the multitude when the camps are to be moved. When you sound the trumpets, the whole assembly shall gather to you at the entrance of the tabernacle of the covenant. If you sound only once, all the princes and leaders of the multitude of Israel shall come to you. But if a longer and broken blast is sounded, those who are encamped on the eastern side shall move their camps first.”

For the army is led by means of two trumpets, because through the two Testaments—or through the two commandments of charity—the people are summoned to the battle array of faith. They are commanded to be made of silver so that the words of preachers may shine with brilliance and not confuse the minds of their hearers through any obscurity of their own. They are made beaten out because it is necessary that those who preach the life to come should grow through the blows of present tribulations.

As for what follows—“If you sound only once, the princes and leaders of the multitude of Israel shall come to you”—to sound the trumpets once means to bring forth the force of the word of teaching according to the unity of faith and the harmony of Catholic understanding. The princes and leaders of the multitude ought to gather at this sound, because it is entirely fitting that those who preside over others, united in one faith and one love, should discuss peacefully their own salvation and that of those subject to them, and offer others an example of peace and concord. Otherwise, if they should sound differently, the apostolic authority would rightly rebuke them. Writing to the Corinthians, it says: “Since there is jealousy and contention among you, are you not carnal and walking according to human standards?” (1 Cor. I.) And again: “When you come together in the church, I hear that there are divisions among you, and in part I believe it” (1 Cor. XI).

Rather, they should follow what the same Apostle says to those same Corinthians: “I beseech you, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you all say the same thing and that there be no divisions among you. Be perfected in the same understanding and in the same knowledge” (1 Cor. I).

It is rightly said, “When a broken blast is sounded, the camps shall move,” because when the word of preaching is treated more subtly and in finer detail, the minds of the hearers are stirred more ardently to the struggles against temptations. “The camps shall move first,” he says, “which are on the eastern side.” Who are those who move camp toward the eastern side, except those upon whom the light of faith first shone?

Therefore, after the preachers of the Gospel had been arranged in order, the Savior first commanded: “Do not go on the road of the Gentiles, and do not enter the cities of the Samaritans, but go rather to the sheep that have perished from the house of Israel” (Matt. X). To them the Truth himself, dwelling bodily among them, preached the Gospel. But after the passion and resurrection of our Redeemer had been accomplished, the same Redeemer appeared to the disciples and said: “All power has been given to me in heaven and on earth. Go, therefore, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. XXVIII).

Thus the tribe of Judah, together with the others who dwelt with it toward the east, moved camp first; afterward the remaining tribes moved according to their order. For it was necessary that the primitive Church first be established in Judea, and afterward that the Gentiles from all the nations throughout the world be summoned to faith.

When the people are to be gathered, they shall sound with a simple blast of the trumpets and not with a broken one. At the summoning of the people, the blast of the trumpets is commanded to be simple and not broken, because whoever preaches the word of faith to a multitude ought to use simple and open speech, so that many may understand what is said and many may be edified by it. Otherwise, if the teacher devotes himself to obscure speech and inserts unfamiliar words, the hearer may depart empty, without the fruit of edification.

For this reason the teacher of the Gentiles says to certain people who were boasting about the diversity of languages: “Brothers, if I come to you speaking in languages, what good shall I do you unless I speak to you either in revelation, or in knowledge, or in prophecy, or in teaching? Yet things without a soul that give sound, whether flute or harp, if they do not produce a distinction of sound, how will what is played on the flute or harp be known? Indeed, if the trumpet gives an uncertain sound, who will prepare himself for battle? So also you, unless you give a clear word through the tongue, how will what is said be known?” And again: “What is it, then, brothers? When you come together, each of you has a psalm, has a teaching, has an apocalypse, has a language, has an interpretation: let everything be done for edification” (1 Cor. XIV).

Although good teachers have, or ought to have, such great care in teaching that, if a word is excessively obscure or ambiguous, it cannot properly be Latin, nevertheless it should be expressed according to the usage of ordinary people, so that ambiguity and obscurity may be avoided. It should not be spoken as educated people customarily speak, but rather as the uneducated are accustomed to speak.

For what benefit is there in correctness of expression when the hearer’s understanding does not follow it, since there is no reason for speaking at all if those for whose understanding we speak do not understand what is said? Therefore, whoever teaches will avoid all words that do not teach. And if instead of these he can use some correct words that are understood, he will choose those all the more readily. But if he cannot—either because such words do not exist or because they do not occur to him at the moment—he will also use less correct words, provided that the matter itself is taught and learned correctly. [Col. 0651A]

This principle must be observed not only in conversations, whether they take place with one person or with several, but much more among the people when a discourse is delivered so that it may be understood. The best manner of speaking is that by which the hearer hears the truth and understands what he hears; and the mark of excellent minds is to love the truth in words, not the words themselves.

For what good is a golden key if it cannot open what we wish? Or what harm is there in a wooden one if it can do so, when we seek nothing except that what is closed may be opened? The text continues:

“And the sons of Aaron the priest shall sound the trumpets, and this shall be a perpetual ordinance throughout your generations.”

The sons of Aaron will sound the trumpets when holy teachers preach the word of God and demonstrate to their hearers the way of righteousness, or the practices by which they may walk with the steps of good works in the path of God’s commandments and persist in avoiding the way of the ungodly. Notice that not just any others, but the sons of Aaron, are commanded to sound the trumpets, because it is properly the duty of priests to preach the Gospel of Christ to the peoples. Through the prophet they are told: “Cry out, do not cease; raise your voice like a trumpet” (Isa. LVIII). And again: “Raise your voice with strength,” he says, “you who proclaim good news to Zion; raise it, do not fear,” and so forth (Isa. XL). [Col. 0651B]

“If you go out to war from your land against the enemies who fight against you, you shall sound the trumpets with a wailing blast, and you shall be remembered before the Lord your God. And you shall be delivered from the hands of your enemies.”

The trumpets are sounded with a wailing blast when, before the assembled peoples, speech is turned toward awakening repentance and the compunction of tears, and the hearts of the hearers are urged to implore the Lord’s mercy. “That you may be delivered,” he says, “from the hands of your enemies.” For it is necessary to seek help against every hostile power and against spiritual wickedness, so that by his grace he may protect those who have confidence in nothing except his compassion.

“And whenever you have a feast, festival days, and new moons, you shall sound the trumpets over your burnt offerings and peace offerings, so that they may be for you a remembrance of your God. I am the Lord your God.”

We must consider that the lawgiver commands the trumpets to be sounded in adversity and prosperity, because scarcely any time exists that is not suitable and opportune for proclaiming the divine word. At one time there is an occasion for using readings, at another for devoting oneself to divine song, at another for praying, at another for teaching, at another for exhorting, and at another for rebuking, because the speech of teachers must always be adapted to the character of their hearers.

Hence the Psalmist also says: “It is good to confess to the Lord and to sing praise to your name, O Most High, to proclaim your mercy in the morning and your truth during the night.” And again he says: “I will bless the Lord at all times; his praise will always be in my mouth” (Ps. XXXII). Hence Paul too, writing to his disciple, says: “Preach the word; be urgent in season and out of season; reprove, entreat, rebuke, with all patience and teaching” (2 Tim. IV). And elsewhere he says: “Pray without ceasing; give thanks in all things. For this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for all of you.” [Col. 0652A]

“In the second year, in the second month, on the twentieth day of the month, the cloud was lifted from the tabernacle of the covenant; and the children of Israel set out by their companies from the wilderness of Sinai, and the cloud came to rest in the wilderness of Paran,” and so forth (1 Thess. V).

At the twelfth encampment the children of Israel came into the wilderness of Sinai, on the forty-seventh day after they had departed from Egypt. Scripture bears witness to this in Exodus, saying: “In the third month after the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt, on this day they entered the wilderness of Sinai. Having set out together from Rephidim, they came into the wilderness of Sinai and encamped in the wilderness. Israel settled there opposite the mountain, and Moses went up to the Lord. And the Lord called him from the mountain, saying,” and so forth (Exod. XIX).

And again: “Go,” the Lord said, “to the people and sanctify them today and tomorrow. Let them wash their garments and be ready for the third day, because on the third day the Lord will descend upon Mount Sinai in the sight of all the people” (ibid.). This was done. They washed their garments and abstained from intercourse with their wives, and on the third day the Lord descended upon the mountain. As it smoked, and flashes of lightning, thunder, darkness, and the sound of a trumpet terrified the hearts of mortals, Moses spoke and the Lord answered him.

Let us calculate the number, and we shall find that on the fiftieth day after Israel’s departure from Egypt, the law was given at the summit of Mount Sinai. Hence the solemnity of Pentecost is celebrated, and afterward the mystery of the Gospel is completed through the descent of the Holy Spirit.

It would be lengthy to recount what was commanded in the law, how the tabernacle was constructed, what varieties of sacrifices there were, what diversity of vessels, what garments of the high priest, what rites of the priests and Levites, what they did, and how the people were numbered. I shall say only this: half of Exodus, the entire book of Leviticus, a considerable portion of the commandments of Numbers, the distribution of the people among the individual tribes, and the offering of the princes are described in this encampment. The discussion of many volumes could scarcely suffice for this passage. [Col. 0652C]

Sinai is interpreted as “of the bushes”—not one bush, as above in the wilderness of Sin, but many—so that there it is the beginning, whereas here it is perfection; there, a solitary number, here, a multiple one. For it is one thing to possess one grace, and another to possess all graces.

Thus Israel, after familiar conversation with God, after remaining beside Mount Sinai for one year and four days, departed through a marvelous arrangement of the camps into the wilderness of Paran, which is interpreted as “wild ass” or “wildness.” There it succumbed to the evil beast, scorning the heavenly bread and desiring the flesh of the Egyptians. At that time a sudden fire devoured many, and, when Moses interceded, the voracious flame consumed one. Then they received quail and devoured them to the point of nausea and vomiting.

Seventy elders are chosen. They go to the entrance of the tabernacle. Two remain behind, Eldad and Medad—not through contempt for authority, but in submissive humility, since they considered themselves unworthy of the honor. Hence they prophesy while absent. When the people had been filled, while food was still in their mouths, the wrath of God rose against them and killed their fat ones, and struck down the chosen men of Israel, lest they run swiftly toward evil (Ps. LXXVII). Hence the place was called “Graves of Lust,” or, as we read in the Septuagint, “the memorial of desire.” [Col. 0653A]

From all this we are taught that, having abandoned secular wisdom and despised the Egyptian pots, we must not murmur against the heavenly bread of the Scriptures, nor seek the pungent fare of Egypt, consisting of abundant flesh, but must seek the simple food of manna. Otherwise, if we should once again desire those things, we shall devour them to the point of nausea and immediately be tormented by the Lord’s fire; and our desire will be turned into burial mounds, so that we become whitewashed tombs, which appear outwardly beautiful to people but inwardly are full of the bones of the dead and every impurity (Matt. [Col. 0653B] XXIII).

## CHAPTER V. On Hobab, son of Raguel the Midianite and kinsman of Moses, and on the departure of the children of Israel from Mount Sinai

**(IBID.)** And Moses said to Hobab, son of Raguel the Midianite, his kinsman: “We are setting out for the place that the Lord will give us. Come with us, so that we may do good to you, because the Lord has promised good things to Israel.”

He answered him: “I will not go with you, but I shall return to my land, in which I was born.”

And he said: “Do not leave us, for you know in which places we ought to camp in the wilderness, and you will be our guide. When you come with us, whatever is best among the possessions that the Lord will hand over to us, we shall give you.”

We can often persuade the proud of what is useful more effectively if we say that their advancement will benefit us rather than them, and if we ask that their improvement be bestowed more upon us than upon themselves. Pride is easily bent toward what is good if it is believed that its bending will benefit others as well.

Thus Moses, who under God’s direction was proceeding through the wilderness with the aerial column as his guide, wished to lead his kinsman Hobab away from pagan association and subject him to the dominion of almighty God. He said: “We are setting out for the place that the Lord will give us. Come with us, so that we may do good to you, because the Lord has promised good things to Israel.”

When Hobab answered him, “I will not go with you, but I shall return to my land, in which I was born,” Moses immediately added: “Do not leave us, for you know in which places we ought to camp in the wilderness, and you will be our guide.”

Moses was not constrained by ignorance of the route—a knowledge which his acquaintance with divinity had expanded for the purposes of prophecy, which the column led outwardly before him, and which the diligent and familiar speech of God supplied inwardly through their communion. Rather, the prudent man, speaking to a proud hearer, asked him to provide assistance on the journey, so that he himself might become Hobab’s guide to life.

He therefore acted so that the proud hearer would become all the more devoted to the voice urging him toward better things when he acknowledged that he was necessary; and from the very point at which he believed himself to precede his exhorter, he would be brought low beneath the words of the exhorter.

So they set out from the mountain of the Lord for a three days’ journey, and the ark of the covenant of the Lord went before them for three days, seeking out a place for the camps. [Col. 0654A] The cloud of the Lord was also over them by day as they proceeded.

What does it mean that the ark of the covenant of the Lord went before the children of Israel for three days, seeking out a place for the camps, except that the incarnation of the Lord directs the journey of the present life for the elect from the beginning of the world and truly provides them with guidance to the holy land? Formerly it led the fathers of the Old Testament under a figure; now in truth it shows us the way of righteousness.

The three-day journey is therefore the faith of the Holy Trinity, faithfully showing the path of truth and righteousness to those who follow it through three periods: before the law, under the law, and under grace.

When it says that the cloud was over them by day as they proceeded, it signifies that, through the grace of the Holy Spirit, divine protection has defended the elect from the beginning and preserved them for future rest. [Col. 0654B]

Whenever the ark of God was lifted up, Moses said: “Arise, Lord; let your enemies be scattered, and let those who hate you flee from your presence.” But when it was set down, he said: “Return, Lord, to the multitude of the army of Israel.”

Thus, according to the tropological sense, the lawgiver instructs by his example the leaders and rulers of God’s people not to become sluggish or negligent in pastoral care and in the task entrusted to them. Rather, following the pattern of his action, at the beginning and completion of every undertaking they should faithfully commend the flock entrusted to them to the chief Shepherd, so that, protecting his own sheep through his aid, he may put enemies to flight, drive away hostile forces, and, dwelling among his people, graciously preserve them forever.

## CHAPTER VI. Where the people murmur and are consumed when struck by fire; and concerning the eating of flesh, about which the mixed multitude murmured together with the children of Israel

**(CHAP. XI.)** Meanwhile, a murmur arose among the people, as from those suffering because of their labor, against the Lord. When the Lord heard it, he was angry. The Lord’s fire was kindled against them and devoured the farthest part of the camp. When the people cried out to Moses, Moses prayed to the Lord, and the fire was extinguished. He called the name of that place “Burning,” because the Lord’s fire had been kindled against them.

What does it mean that the fire kindled by the Lord devours the murmuring people, except that the fire of just vengeance in the future torments those who, with a tongue inflamed by Gehenna, readily rush into murmuring and slander? Hence Wisdom says: “The whisperer and the double-tongued person are accursed” (Ecclus. XXVIII). And again: “Blessed is the one who is protected from an evil tongue. Its death is an evil death, and hell is more useful than it. Those who forsake God will fall into it; it will burn within them and will not be extinguished” (ibid.).

It is rightly added that this same fire devours the farthest part of the camp. The farthest part of the camp is the end of present actions, where the Lord judges what the end of each person has been. Hence it is written: “The Lord will judge the ends of the earth.” Whoever persists in the evil he has conceived without correction until death will be burned by perpetual punishment, both in soul and also in body. Nothing will remain unexamined, when everything that he has done through an evil work or even word, once conceived in thought, is punished in the prison of hell.

Hence in the Gospel the Truth himself says to the obstinate person: “Be reconciled with your adversary, lest perhaps your adversary hand you over to the judge, and the judge hand you over to the officer, and you be thrown into prison. Amen, I say to you, you will not come out from there until you have paid the last penny” (Matt. V).

The mixed multitude that had gone up with them burned with a desire for flesh. Sitting and weeping, joined together with the children of Israel, they said: “Who will give us meat to eat? We remember the fish that we ate freely in Egypt. The cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions, and garlic come to mind. Our soul is dry; our eyes see nothing except manna,” and so forth.

The hard minds of carnal people are prepared to endure what is harsh through love of the world, like certain soft and pleasurable things, while they strive to seize the heights of worldly affairs in this life. The Lord commands cessation from the labors of the world and persuades them to the sweetness of holy rest; yet the insane mind of the wicked rejoices more in pursuing harsh things carnally than in possessing gentle things spiritually. It feeds more on the bitterness of toil than on the sweetness of rest.

The Israelite people openly demonstrated this in themselves. Although they had received the refreshment of manna from above, they desired from Egypt the pots of flesh, melons, leeks, and onions.

For what is signified by manna except the food of grace, sweet to the taste and given from above for the refreshment of the inner life of those who devote themselves rightly? And what is signified by the pots of flesh except carnal works, which must be cooked with difficulty through the labors of tribulations, as though through fires? What is signified by melons except earthly pleasures? What is expressed by leeks and onions—which often cause those who eat them to shed tears—except the difficulty of the present life, which is endured by those who love it not without struggle and yet is loved with tears?

Therefore, abandoning manna, they sought leeks and onions together with melons and flesh, because perverse minds despise the sweet gifts of rest through grace and desire, in place of carnal pleasures, the laborious paths of this life, full even of tears. They disdain having a place where they may rejoice spiritually and, desiring it, seek a place where they may groan carnally.

And the Lord said to Moses: “Gather for me seventy men from the elders of Israel, whom you know to be elders and teachers of the people of Israel, and bring them to the entrance of the tabernacle of the covenant, and make them stand there with you. I shall descend and speak with you, and I shall take from your spirit and give it to them, so that they may bear the burden of the people with you and you may not bear it alone,” and so forth.

Just as young men are often called those who are not weighed down by the gravity of counsel, so sacred Scripture is not accustomed to call people elders merely because of the length of their years, but because they are mature through the greatness of their character. Hence a certain wise man says: “Honorable old age is not of long duration, nor measured by the number of years. The gray hairs of a person are understanding, and the age of old age is an undefiled life” (Wis. IV).

This is why he says to Moses: “Gather for me seventy men from the elders of Israel, whom you know to be elders of the people.” What else is sought in them than old age of heart, since those who are elders are commanded to be chosen? If bodily old age were being sought in them, they could be known by as many people as could see them. But when it is said, “whom you know to be elders of the people,” it is plainly indicated that old age of mind, not of body, is to be chosen.

In the mystical sense, when Christ descended in the cloud of flesh, the grace of the Holy Spirit was spread throughout the world over the peoples chosen from the seventy languages of the nations [or: through faith]. And that gift of heavenly power which had once been in Moses and the prophets came upon them all.

And Moses said: “There are six hundred thousand foot soldiers of this people, and you say, ‘I shall give them meat to eat for a whole month.’ Will flocks of sheep and herds of cattle be slaughtered so that it may suffice for food? Or will all the fish of the sea be gathered together so that they may be satisfied?”

He answered him: “Is the hand of the Lord powerless? Now you shall see whether my word will be fulfilled in deed.”

**Septuagint:** “And Moses said: ‘There are six hundred thousand foot soldiers, among whom I am included, and you have said, “I shall give them meat, and they shall eat for a month of days.” Shall sheep and cattle be slaughtered for them, and will it suffice for them? Or shall every fish be gathered together for them, and will it suffice for them?’”

It is customary to ask whether Moses said this out of distrust. If so, the question arises why the Lord did not reproach him for it, as he reproached him when, at the rock from which water flowed, he appears to have doubted the Lord’s power.

But if we say that he said this while asking how it would happen, the Lord’s response—when he said to him, “Will the Lord’s hand not be sufficient?”—seems to rebuke him, as though he had not believed these things. Yet I think it better to understand that the Lord answered in such a way that he did not wish to tell Moses the manner in which the future event would occur, which Moses was asking about, but rather to demonstrate his power through the deed itself.

For likewise, when Mary said, “How will this happen, since I do not know a man?” (Luke II), detractors could have objected that she had believed too little; yet she had asked about the manner and had not doubted the Lord’s power. To her answer was given: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you” (ibid.). He could have answered in the same way as here: “Is anything impossible for the Holy Spirit, who will come upon you?”—as though the same meaning were preserved.

Zacharias, however, when saying something of this kind, is accused of unbelief and punished by the suppression of his voice. Why, except because the Lord judges not words but hearts?

Otherwise, the words of Moses at that rock from which water flowed could also have been excused, unless the divine judgment had made clear that he had said such things out of distrust. For his words are as follows: “Hear me, you unbelievers: shall we bring water for you from this rock?” (Exod. XVII.) Then it follows: “And Moses lifted up his hand and struck the rock twice with his staff, and abundant water came out, and the congregation and their livestock drank” (ibid.).

Certainly, he gathered the people for this purpose, took the staff with which he had performed so many miracles, struck the rock with it, and obtained from it the customary result of divine power. The words in which he said, “Shall we bring water for you from this rock?” could therefore be understood as if he had said: “Indeed, according to your unbelief, water cannot be brought from this rock”—so that, by striking it, it might be shown that what they did not believe because of their unbelief could in fact be accomplished by divine power, especially since he had not said, “Hear me, you unbelievers.”

These words could indeed be understood in this way, unless God, who examines the heart, indicated with what intention they had been spoken. Scripture continues and says: “And the Lord said to Moses and Aaron: ‘Because you did not believe me, to sanctify me in the sight of the children of Israel, for this reason you shall not bring this assembly into the land that I have given them.’”

Thus it is understood that Moses spoke those words as though he had struck the rock uncertainly, so that, if the result had not followed, he would have been thought to have foretold this when he said: “Shall we bring water for you from this rock?” What lay hidden in his mind would have remained entirely unknown unless God’s judgment had revealed it.

By contrast, in this passage we ought to understand Moses’ words concerning the promised flesh as those of one asking how it would happen rather than of one distrusting, since the Lord’s judgment did not follow to punish him, but rather to instruct him.

## CHAPTER VII. On the seventy elders chosen to teach the people

**(IBID.)** Moses therefore came and recounted the words of the Lord to the people, gathering seventy men from the elders of Israel and making them stand around the tabernacle. The Lord descended in the cloud and spoke with him, taking from the Spirit that was in Moses and giving it to the seventy men. When the Spirit had rested upon them, they prophesied and did not cease thereafter.

“And Moses went out,” he says, “to the people and spoke the words of the Lord.”

As long as Moses hears the words of God and is taught by him, he is within, remains in the interior, and is held in secret places. But when he speaks to the crowds and ministers to the people, to the one who cannot remain within he is said to go out.

What, then, does this form and such speech contain except that every doctor and teacher of the Church, when he raises something from the deeper mysteries, when he brings forth among the perfect some hidden secret from the wisdom of God, is said to be within and to remain in the interior as long as he is moving through profound understandings?

But when he speaks to the crowds and brings forth what is sufficient for those who are outside, and what the common people can hear, he is said to go out and speak the words of the Lord to the people.

I see Paul doing this as well. He was certainly within when he said: “We speak wisdom among the perfect—not the wisdom of this world, which is being destroyed, but we speak God’s wisdom in a mystery, hidden, which none of the rulers of this world has known” (1 Cor. II).

Do you see how Paul is within and penetrates the inward and hidden things of divine wisdom when he says these things? But when he comes out to the people, hear what he says: “Let no evil word proceed from your mouth. Whoever was stealing, let him steal no longer” (Eph. IV). And: “Let each man have his own wife, and let each woman have her own husband” (1 Cor. VII).

Paul speaks these and similar things to the people, going out according to the pattern of Moses. [Col. 0658A]

But let us examine another passage, in which it is reported that Moses chose seventy men from the elders of Israel and had them with him before the tabernacle of testimony, and that God took from Moses’ Spirit and gave it to the seventy elders. “And when the Spirit had rested upon them,” he says, “they all prophesied.”

When it says that God took from Moses’ Spirit and gave it to the seventy elders, do not understand the spirit as though God removed some material and bodily substance from Moses, divided it into seventy portions, and thus gave a small piece to each of the elders. It is impious to understand the nature of the Holy Spirit in this way.

Rather, consider the figure of this mystical expression in the following manner: Moses and the Spirit that was in Moses were like a lamp of exceedingly bright light, from which God lit seventy other lamps. The splendor of that original light came to them in such a way that the source of the light itself suffered no loss through the process of transmission.

In this way it is piously understood that it is written that the Lord took from Moses’ Spirit and gave it to the seventy elders.

But let us see what follows: “And the Spirit rested upon them, and they all prophesied.”

We do not read that the Spirit rests in just any people, but in the blessed and holy. The Spirit of God rests in those who are pure in heart and in those who put their souls to death with respect to sin.

Conversely, concerning one who dwells in a body subject to sins—even if he dwells in it at some time—the text adds that the Holy Spirit cannot have fellowship with sin or partnership with an evil spirit. For it is certain that, at the time of sin, an evil spirit is present in the heart of every person and performs its own role.

When room is given to it and it is received by us through evil thoughts and wicked desires, the Holy Spirit, being grieved and, so to speak, constricted, is driven away from us. Hence the Apostle, knowing that these things occur in this way, warned us, saying: “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption” (Eph. IV).

Therefore, when we sin, we grieve the Holy Spirit; but when we act justly and holily, we prepare a place of rest for him within us. Hence, when he now says of the seventy elders that the Spirit rested in them, he has set forth the praise of their life and their virtues.

[Col. 0658D] Finally, because the Holy Spirit rested on account of the purity of their hearts, the sincerity of their minds, and the capacity of their understanding, he immediately also works in them; nor does he tolerate idleness where worthy material for working is supplied. For Scripture says: “And the Spirit rested upon them, and they prophesied.” Therefore, the Holy Spirit rested in all who prophesied; yet he did not rest in any of them as he rested in the Savior. Hence it is also written about him: “A shoot went forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower rose from his root, and the Spirit of God rested upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and piety; and the spirit of the fear of the Lord filled him” (Isa. XI).

But perhaps someone will say: “You have shown nothing more written about Christ than about other human beings. For just as it is written of the others that the Spirit rested upon them, so it is said of the Savior, ‘The Spirit of the Lord rested upon him.’” But observe that nowhere else is the Spirit of God described as resting with sevenfold power. Through this, without doubt, that very substance of the divine Spirit—which could not be expressed under one name and is therefore explained by various terms—is prophetically said to rest upon the shoot that would proceed from the stock of Jesse.

I have another testimony by which I can show that in the Lord and Savior the Holy Spirit rested in a remarkable way, and far differently from the manner in which he is said to rest in others. John the Baptist says of him: “He who sent me to baptize in water said to me: ‘Upon whomever you see the Spirit of God descending and remaining upon him, he is the one’” (John I). If he had said only “descending,” and had not added “and remaining upon him,” Christ would appear to possess nothing exceptional in comparison with the others. But he added “and remaining upon him,” so that this might be the sign distinguishing the Savior, something that could be shown in no one else. For it is again written that the Holy Spirit remained upon him.

And lest anyone think that in this I am disparaging the prophets, they themselves know that I do not disparage them by preferring my Lord Jesus Christ to them. For each of them recalls his own words and finds that it was said of no one else: “He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth” (Isa. LIII). Since he alone committed no sin, therefore the Holy Spirit remained and continued in him alone.

For if he is the one of whom something singular and exceptional is said—namely, what we mentioned above, that he committed no sin—it is clear that all the rest were under sin. If all, then necessarily the prophets also. And how can it be fitting for us to say that the Holy Spirit remained in them during the time of sin? Or, if it seems incredible to you that the prophets could have sinned after receiving the Holy Spirit, let us return once more to Moses himself, whom we have before us, who is certainly the greatest and most eminent of the prophets. He himself records and testifies about himself that he sinned in what he said: “Hear me, you unbelievers: shall we bring water for you from this rock?” (Exod. XVII).

In these words he did not sanctify the Lord at the water of contradiction—that is, he did not trust in God’s power and say, “God is able to bring water for you from this rock, or from this one”; rather, as though answering out of a certain weakness of distrust, he said: “Can we bring water for you from this rock?” Since, therefore, the Lord counts this as sin in his words, it is certain that when he spoke them he was not speaking from the Holy Spirit but from the spirit of sin.

If the testimony of Scripture shows that so great a prophet, Moses, at one time possessed the Spirit of God and at another time did not possess him—namely, during the time of sin—it is certain that the same pattern must be maintained concerning the other prophets. What, moreover, shall I say about David, who prays as though the Holy Spirit could be taken away, asking that he not be taken away, and says: “Do not cast me away from your presence, and do not take your Spirit from me” (Ps. L)? [Col. 0660A] In what follows, as though reclaiming the gift taken from him because of his guilt, he says: “Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and strengthen me with your governing spirit” (ibid.).

What, too, should I recall about Solomon? No one, surely, will say that he either judged judgments without the Holy Spirit, or built a temple for the Lord, or again, in the Holy Spirit, built temples for demons, or turned his sides toward impious women. Even that prophet who, in the Third Book of Kingdoms, was sent by the Lord to Bethel spoke his words in the Spirit of God; nevertheless, we must not suppose that he transgressed in the Spirit of God the Lord’s command by which he had been ordered not to eat bread at Bethel; for this reason he was killed by a lion (III Kings XIII).

But it would be lengthy to go through them one by one. Although I do not venture to pronounce universally, I nevertheless think that there are certain ordinary actions of human beings which, although they are not free from sin, do not seem worthy of our saying that the Holy Spirit is present in them. For example, lawful marriages are indeed free from sin; nevertheless, at the time when conjugal acts are performed, the presence of the Holy Spirit is not granted, even if the one fulfilling the duty of generation should appear to be a prophet.

But there are many other matters in which human power alone suffices, and in which neither does the matter require, nor is it fitting, that the presence of the Holy Spirit be present. But we have entered upon these matters by a kind of digression while wishing to show that the Spirit of God remained upon the Lord and Savior Jesus alone, whereas in all the other saints—as also in the seventy elders, from whom the present discussion began—the Spirit of God merely rested and was understood to have worked what was expedient for those through whom he worked and useful for those to whom they ministered.

Two men, however, had remained in the camp, one named Eldad and the other Medad, and the Spirit rested upon them. For they too had been enrolled, but they had not gone out to the tabernacle. They remained in the camp not out of contempt for the Lord’s command, but rather out of humble devotion, judging themselves unworthy to receive so great a gift. Therefore the examiner of hearts judged them worthy of the grace of his Spirit, for their whole intention had been adorned with the virtue of humility.

While they were prophesying in the camp, a boy ran and reported to Moses, saying: “Eldad and Medad are prophesying in the camp.” Immediately Joshua son of Nun, Moses’ assistant, chosen from among many, said: “My lord Moses, forbid them.” But he replied: “Are you jealous on my behalf? Would that all the people might prophesy, and that the Lord might give them his Spirit!”

The mind of a pious shepherd seeks not his own glory but that of the author, and wishes what he does to be assisted by all. A faithful preacher desires, if it could be so, that the truth—which he is not sufficient to proclaim alone—might sound from the mouths of everyone. Therefore, when Joshua wished to oppose the two men who had remained in the camp and were prophesying, Moses said to him: “Are you jealous on my behalf? Would that all the people might prophesy, and that the Lord might give them his Spirit?” [Col. 0661A] All wish to prophesy who do not begrudge others the good they themselves possess.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the eating of quail meat

(IBID.) “Moses and the elders of Israel returned to the camp. Then a wind going forth from the Lord, seizing quail from across the sea, brought them and cast them down in the camp, as far as a day’s journey can be made, all around the camp; and they flew in the air two cubits above the ground. So the people rose and gathered quail throughout that entire day and night and the following day. He who gathered least gathered ten homers. And they dried them all around the camp. The meat was still between their teeth, nor had such food failed them, when behold, the fury of the Lord was aroused against the people, and he struck the people with a very great plague. That place was called ‘Graves of Desire,’ because there they buried the people who had desired meat.”

Thus the carnal people of the Jews, scorning heavenly food, desired the pleasure of carnal things. But divine providence so tempered its judgment that it punished the desire of those who sought pleasure while not denying the frail their appropriate nourishment. Indeed, in the very granting of their request it indicated something spiritually. For when they asked that meat be supplied to them, he did not give them the flesh of wild beasts, quadrupeds, or terrestrial animals to eat, but of birds, so that from the very reception of their food they might learn to desire heavenly things more than earthly things, spiritual things rather than bodily things.

The nature of birds first proceeded from the waters, but acquires its dwelling in the air. Therefore those who partake of the flesh of birds are admonished to lift their hearts from the depths to heavenly things, so that although they dwell in earthly bodies, they may nevertheless always aspire in mind to celestial things, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying: “Although we walk in the flesh, we do not wage war according to the flesh. Our commonwealth is in heaven” (II Cor. XII).

After leaving the Graves of Desire, they came to Hazeroth and remained there. This is the fourteenth encampment in the wilderness of Paran, which is translated “court.” In this place Aaron and Miriam murmured against Moses on account of the Ethiopian woman. And, prudent reader, observe this: after virtue had been completed in the number twelve, Israel became proud and desired Egyptian meats in the Graves of Desire; then he lays another foundation and courts—that is, he enters the vestibules of virtue—showing us that those who stand can fall and those who have fallen can rise again. For Jesus has been appointed “for the falling and rising of many” (Luke II). And he himself speaks through the Prophet: “Will not one who falls rise again?”

## CHAPTER IX. On Aaron’s and Miriam’s murmuring against Moses on account of his Ethiopian wife

(CHAP. XII.) “Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses on account of his Ethiopian wife, and they said: ‘Has the Lord spoken through Moses alone? Has he not also spoken through us?’ When the Lord heard this, he became angry. For Moses was a very meek man, more than all the men who dwelt upon the earth,” etc.

(From Augustine.) It is usually asked whether she was Jethro’s daughter, or whether he took another wife [Al.: “took an additional wife”]. But it is credible that she was the same woman. For she was from the Midianites, who are found to be called Ethiopians in Chronicles, when Jehoshaphat fought against them. In these regions, moreover, Scripture says that the people of Israel pursued them, where the Midianites dwell, who are now called Saracens. But scarcely anyone now calls them Ethiopians, just as the names of places and peoples are often changed by the passage of time.

Allegorically, however, we say that Miriam represented the earlier people, while Moses—that is, the law of the Lord—passed over to marriage with this Ethiopian woman, who had been gathered from the nations. Moses, therefore—that is, the spiritual law—took her as his wife. For this act Miriam, who is the Synagogue, becomes indignant and slanders him together with Aaron, that is, together with the priests and Pharisees.

To this day that people disparages Moses, who has been placed with us, and regards him as disgraceful because he does not teach among us the circumcision of the flesh, nor the observance of the Sabbath, nor new moons, nor sacrifices of blood; rather, he urges circumcision of the heart, leisure for prayer, feast days in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth, and sacrifices of praise—not the slaughter of animals now, but of vices.

God therefore judges these matters and confirms the marriage with the Ethiopian woman. He willingly allows Moses to live and rest with her, but expels Miriam outside the camp and makes her remain far from the tabernacle of testimony, while Aaron is not expelled as well; moreover, Miriam is afflicted with leprosy.

Now look upon that people and see how great is the leprosy of sin among them, how great the darkness of understanding, how great the foulness of observance, and how great the deformity of their appearance. Nevertheless, this leprosy does not remain forever. When the week begins to be completed, she will be recalled to the camp. For at the end of the world, when the fullness of the nations has entered, then all Israel will be saved (Rom. XII); and this will be when the leprosy has ceased from Miriam’s face. She will receive the beauty of faith and the splendor of the knowledge of Christ, and her face will be restored when the two become one flock and one shepherd. Then it will truly be said: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God” (Gal. III), because he has shut up all under sin so that he might have mercy on all, in Christ Jesus our Lord, as the Apostle says: “All these things happened to them as a figure, but they were written for our admonition” (I Cor. X).

I ask what admonition we should receive from what has been read to us: Aaron and Miriam slandered Moses, and for this they were reproved; Miriam, moreover, became leprous. So great was the seriousness of this correction that, while Miriam completed the period of a week in leprosy, the people of God did not journey toward the promised land, nor was the tabernacle of testimony moved.

First, I am warned—and rightly and necessarily warned—by this event not to slander my brother, not to speak evil of my neighbor, and not to open my mouth to disparage not only the saints but any of my neighbors, seeing how great was God’s anger on account of this, and how great a vengeance proceeded from it.

Finally, we see that the Lord is moved with a similar indignation against this sin even in the Psalms, where he says: “When you sat and spoke against your brother, and placed a stumbling block against your mother’s son” (Ps. XLIX). Likewise, in another psalm, from the person of the righteous, you will know how greatly this displeases God, where it is said: “The one who secretly slandered his neighbor, I pursued” (Ps. CX).

From all these words of divine Scripture, therefore, as from certain double-edged swords, let us cut away the vice of slandering our brothers and disparaging the saints. For leprosy follows those who disparage and the *aecologi* (ἀεικολόγους?; perhaps “habitual evil-speakers,” though the reading is uncertain)—[Col. 0663B] and afterward let us pass from moral instruction to mystical understanding. Although a few things have already been said above, we shall add what seems to have been lacking.

Let us therefore see who it is that disparages Moses and who speaks evil of him. It is not only the Jew, but also the heretics who do not receive the law and the prophets; they themselves slander Moses. Indeed, they commonly bring even a charge against him, saying that Moses was a murderer: for he killed an Egyptian, and with blasphemous mouth they compose many other accusations either against him or against the prophets.

Those, then, who disparage Moses have leprosy in their soul and are leprous in the inner person; therefore they are held outside the camp of the Church of God. Whether they are heretics who disparage Moses, or members of the Church who slander their brothers and speak evil of them, there is no doubt that all who are driven by this vice are leprous in their soul.

Miriam, indeed, through the intervention of Aaron the high priest, is healed on the seventh day. But if we fall into leprosy of the soul through the vice of slander, we shall remain leprous and unclean in soul until the end of the world’s week—that is, until the time of the resurrection—unless, while the time for repentance remains, we correct ourselves and, turning to the Lord Jesus and entreating him, are cleansed through repentance from the uncleanness of our leprosy.

I think, however, that it is not only that earlier people, nor only the heretics whom we mentioned above, who disparage Moses. Anyone who misunderstands his writings and receives the spiritual law in a carnal manner disparages Moses, because he teaches people carnally from holy words.

You have heard what judgment and what condemnation slanderers and evil-speakers acquire. Now hear also how much benefit they bring to those whom they slander. You will never find God speaking such great praises of Moses his servant as those we now see spoken when men have disparaged him.

Hear, then, in what follows what he says, and with what praises the Holy Spirit extols Moses:

“And the Lord descended in a pillar of cloud and stood at the entrance of the tabernacle of testimony. And Aaron and Miriam were called, and both stood there. And he said to them: ‘Hear my words. If there should be a prophet of the Lord among you, I will make myself known to him in visions, and I will speak to him in dreams—not so with my servant Moses, who is faithful in all my house. Mouth to mouth I shall speak with him, in appearance and not in riddles, and he sees the glory of God. Why, then, were you not afraid to disparage my servant Moses?’ And the anger of the Lord’s fury rose against them, and they departed; and the cloud withdrew from the tabernacle. And behold, Miriam became leprous, like snow.”

You see what punishment the slanderers brought upon themselves, and what praise they sought for the one whom they had slandered. For themselves they sought disgrace, but for him splendor; for themselves leprosy, but for him glory; for themselves reproach, but for him magnificence.

Nevertheless, before Moses had taken the Ethiopian woman, it is not written that God spoke with him “in appearance and not in riddles.” But after he took the Ethiopian woman, God says of him: “Mouth to mouth I shall speak with him, in appearance and not in riddles.”

For now, when Moses has come to us and has been joined to this Ethiopian woman of ours, the law of God is recognized no longer in figures and images as before, but in the very appearance of truth. What was formerly represented in riddles is now fulfilled in appearance and truth.

Therefore the one who explained the appearances of figures and riddles says: “We know that all our fathers were under the cloud, and all were baptized into Moses, in the cloud and in the sea; and all ate the same spiritual food and drank the same spiritual drink. For they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them; and the rock was Christ” (I Cor. X).

Do you see how Paul unfolds the riddles of the law and teaches the appearance of those riddles? He says that the rock was an enigma with Moses before Moses was joined to this Ethiopian woman of ours; but now, in appearance, the rock is Christ.

Now God speaks mouth to mouth through the law. Formerly, baptism was in a riddle, in the cloud and in the sea; but now, in appearance, regeneration is in water and the Holy Spirit. Then manna was food in a riddle; but now, in appearance, the flesh of the Word of God is true food, as he himself says: “For my flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink” (John IX).

Thus now Moses, placed among us and joined to this Ethiopian woman, does not speak to us—or the Lord to him—in a riddle, but in appearance.

Here it is also added: “And he saw the glory of the Lord.” When did Moses see the glory of the Lord? I say that he saw it when the Lord was transfigured on the mountain, and Moses was there with Elijah, and they were speaking with him. Therefore he rightly adds in what follows: “Why were you not afraid to disparage my servant Moses?”

This is evidently directed at those who appear to receive the Gospels but disparage Moses. And rightly are they reproved, because although they learn through the Gospel that Moses, together with Elijah, saw the glory of the Lord, they have dared to disparage the law and the prophets. Therefore let us not slander Moses, nor disparage the law, but let us be not only hearers of the law but doers, so that we may deserve to be glorified together with Moses.

I think, however, that those also provide material for disparaging Moses who, for example, when the Book of Leviticus or a reading from Numbers is being read, do not show how the things written in riddles are to be understood in their visible meaning—that is, those who do not expound spiritually the things read in the law.

Those who hear the rite of sacrifices, or Sabbaths, or similar matters read in the Church will necessarily take offense and say: “Why is it necessary to read such things in the Church? What benefit do Jewish commandments and the observances of the rejected people bring us? These things belong to the Jews; let the Jews take care of them.”

Therefore, so that such stumbling blocks may not come to the hearers, care must be devoted to knowledge of the law. In accordance with the fact that the law is spiritual, the things that are read must be understood and explained, lest because of the teachers—or rather, because of their laziness and negligence—the unskilled and uninstructed disparage Moses.

But let us also turn to the Lord, so that he may remove from us the veil of the letter, and so that Moses’ face may appear to us not deformed but glorious and beautiful. Then we shall not merely refrain from slandering him, but, because of the greatness of our understanding, shall confer praise and glory upon him.

“And the anger of the Lord’s fury rose against them, and they departed; and the cloud withdrew from the tabernacle. And behold, Miriam became leprous, like snow.”

The anger of the Lord’s fury comes upon those who speak evil and slander. Nevertheless, when it says that the cloud withdrew from the tabernacle and that Miriam became leprous like snow, this must be considered carefully: the cloud withdraws first, and then she is filled with leprosy. This shows that even if the grace of the Holy Spirit is in someone and he slanders and disparages, it withdraws from him after the slander, and then his soul is filled with leprosy.

That earlier people also possessed the grace of God within them. But after they extended their blasphemous tongues against the true Moses, our Lord Jesus Christ, the cloud departed from them [Col. 0665C] and passed over to us on the high mountain, when our Savior was transfigured and a shining cloud overshadowed his disciples; and a voice came from the cloud saying: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. XVII).

After this, therefore, Miriam became leprous like snow. As long as the cloud was present, Miriam was not leprous; but when it departed, she became so. For as long as God’s visitation was among that people, it was not leprous. But when he departed, the disgrace of its face covered it.

Let us fear, therefore, lest we perhaps drive this cloud away from ourselves by speaking evil, acting badly, and thinking badly; then the leprosy of sin will appear in us.

Aaron looked upon Miriam, and behold, she was leprous. And Aaron said to Moses: “I beg you, lord, do not lay this sin upon us, for we did not know that we had sinned. Let her not become like death and like a miscarriage expelled from its mother’s womb, which consumes half her flesh.”
