By this he wishes to show that that people was indeed formed in the womb of its mother, the synagogue, but could not attain a complete and fully developed birth. For just as a miscarriage is an imperfect and malformed birth, so that people remained for a certain time within the womb of its mother—that is, within the institution of the synagogue—but, because sins intervened, could not be fully formed and brought to life.

Therefore they were cast out like an imperfect and premature miscarriage, with sin consuming half, as he says, of its flesh. Yet sometimes a miscarriage is also called good. A miscarriage is called good when it is compared with something else, as Ecclesiastes says: “And I said: A miscarriage is better than he.” Which “he”? “He who proceeds in vanity and walks in darkness” (Eccles. VI).

He does not, therefore, call a miscarriage absolutely good, but better than a life spent in vanities and in the darkness of ignorance.

And Moses cried out to the Lord, saying: “God, I beg you, heal her.” And whom was it fitting to pray for the healing of that people except Moses? Moses prays for them, and perhaps he prays for this when he was speaking with the Lord Jesus Christ, when he was transfigured on the mountain, asking him that, when the fullness of the nations had entered, all Israel might be saved (Rom. XI).

And the Lord said to Moses: “If her father had spit in her face, would she not be ashamed for seven days? Let her be separated outside the camp for seven days, and afterward she shall enter.”

What does it mean: “If her father had spit in her face, would she not be ashamed for seven days”? We have placed Miriam in the position of the synagogue. Her father spat in her face. Spitting in the face is a sign of repudiation. In the law, finally, it is written that when a man refuses to marry his deceased kinsman’s wife, she is to approach him and remove his sandal; then she spits in his face (Deut. XXV). This too was given as a sign of repudiation.

Thus Miriam—that is, that people—is said to be spat upon in the face when it is repudiated by God. We also have an indication of the meaning of spittle in another passage, when Isaiah says: “All the nations are as a drop from a bucket, and are counted as spittle” (Isa. XL). This passage shows that that people too, like the other nations that are counted as spittle, was cast away.

And indeed, if you consider its former honor, when the priestly order flourished among them, with the insignia of the priests, the Levitical ministries, the majesty of the temple, the prophetic splendor, and their heavenly fellowship upon earth—what honor was that, what glory? And if again you look at them now, at how greatly they shudder at their loss of beauty—without a temple, without an altar, without sacrifice, without prophecy, without priesthood, and without any heavenly visitation, scattered throughout the whole earth and living as fugitives—who would not clearly recognize how “her father spat in her face” and covered their faces with disgrace?

For seven days, therefore, she is separated outside the camp. We have already said above that these seven days signify the week of this world. In the week of days, the substances of the entire visible creation appear to have been produced. Then what did not exist came into being. In the week of the whole world, however, what was then produced is unfolded according to a hidden dispensation known to God.

Meanwhile, during this week in which Miriam has been secluded, the camp of the children of Israel is not moved; they remain enclosed in one place, and there is absolutely no progress for them until Miriam is cleansed from her leprosy.

## CHAPTER X. On the twelve spies sent by Moses into the land of Canaan and on what happened there

(CHAP. XIII.) “The people departed from Hazeroth and pitched their tents in the wilderness of Paran. There the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: ‘Send men to inspect the land of Canaan, which I am going to give to the children of Israel, one from each tribe, from among its leaders.’”

Hazeroth is interpreted as “a perfect house.” Thus the people set out, after Miriam had been cleansed, from perfect houses and came to Paran, which is interpreted as “a visible mouth.” It can be understood that the Word became flesh and that the invisible became visible; and this is signified after the end and completion of all that had to be done concerning that people had come. Then he passes over and comes to the one whom, before the Word became flesh, he had not believed.

It should be noted, however, that Paran is not the proper name of a single encampment, but of a wilderness that contained several encampments within it, as is demonstrated in what follows in this book, where the complete catalogue of the encampments is given. For there it is related that, after departing from Hazeroth, the children of Israel camped at Rithmah; then at Rimmon-perez; then at Libnah; and so in order all the way to Ezion-geber. That is, up to the thirty-second encampment, the encampments are included under the name of the wilderness of Paran.

From this encampment, therefore—that is, Rithmah, which was fifteenth in order—up to the thirty-second, the following events are contained: twelve spies are sent to the holy land; a cluster of grapes is brought back on wood, and the passion of Christ is briefly indicated; the Jewish people murmur, fearing the attack of giants; they fight against Amalek and the Canaanite contrary to God’s will, and are defeated; they learn what sacrifices they must perform in the holy land; Dathan and Abiram and the sons of Korah rise up against Moses and Aaron and are swallowed by the opening of the earth; the high priest, armed with a censer, enters between the dead and the living, and the advancing wrath of God is stopped by the priest’s voice; Aaron’s staff produces both flower and leaves, and its greenness, despite its dryness, is consecrated as an eternal memorial.

Nor have even the temple attendants, nor yet the priests and Levites, offered sacrifices; and the mystical discourse describes their respective portions. A red heifer is burned as a whole burnt offering, and its ashes are a purification sprinkled upon others. All these figures demand their proper explanations, which will be given in their appropriate places.

[Col. 0667D] Moses therefore sent them to inspect the land of Canaan and said to them: “Go up through the southern region. When you have come to the mountains, inspect the land, what it is like, and the people who inhabit it, whether they are strong or weak, few in number or many; whether the land itself is good or bad; what the cities are like, whether fortified or without walls; whether the soil is fertile or barren; wooded or without trees. Take courage and bring us some of the fruits of the land.”

(From Augustine.) He is understood to have explained in what sense he said: “Whether they are strong or weak”—that is, whether they are few or many. For it is asked how, looking out from the mountain, they could perceive the strength of human forces.

Another interpretation may be much more consistent with the truth. When he says, “Go up into the mountain,” he refers to the land itself which they wished to inspect. For the spies could not easily be understood to have been investigating everything as though they were travelers. If we suppose that they viewed and inspected the land from the summit of the mountain, how could they have investigated everything that Moses commanded them to investigate? How could they have entered the cities, which Scripture says they entered? How could they have taken a cluster of grapes from another valley, on account of which the place itself was named and called the Valley of the Cluster?

The land was inspected on the mountain because the mountain itself was the land that was being inspected; and there was indeed a lower place there, a valley from which the cluster was taken.

When they had gone up, they explored the land from the wilderness of Zin as far as Rehob, at the entrance to Hamath. They went up toward the south and came to Hebron, where Ahiman, Sheshai, and Talmai, the sons of Anak, were. Hebron had been founded seven years before Tanis, a city of Egypt. Proceeding as far as the Valley of Eshcol, they cut off a branch with its cluster of grapes, which two men carried on a pole. They also took some of the pomegranates and figs [the text reads *deficis*, evidently for *ficis*, “figs”] of that place, which was called Nahal Eshcol, that is, “Valley of the Cluster,” because the sons of Israel had carried a cluster from there. [Col. 0668B]

The sending of twelve spies to explore the fertile land, who terrified the people so that they would not believe that they could receive from the Lord the promised land, prefigured the testimony of the scribes and Pharisees. For just as those men were sent through Moses to examine only the fertility of the land with careful observation, so these men were commanded through the Law and the Prophets to watch for the Lord’s coming by investigating the Scriptures. In him there was the land—that is, the holy land—in which they could attain the kingdom of God, the abundance of spiritual fruits, and eternal life. [Col. 0668C]

But just as those men terrified the people by despair, so that they would not trust in God’s promise, so these scribes and Pharisees persuaded the Jewish people not to believe in Christ. They desired to return to the Egypt of this age, rejecting the manna of faith, seeking the black pots of sins, the foul onions of blasphemies, and the melons withered by the corruption of vices and lusts.

That cluster of grapes which two bearers brought from the land of promise on a piece of wood—the cluster hanging from the wood—was certainly Christ, promised to the nations from the wood of the cross, from the land of his mother Mary, poured forth according to the flesh from the inward parts of an earthly lineage. [Col. 0668D]

The two bearers who walked beneath the burden of that cluster are the two peoples. The first of them is the Jewish people, blind, hostile, and ignorant of the grace that was hanging there, weighed down by the burden of the one suspended, to whom it is subjected as judge. Of them it is said: “Let their eyes be darkened, so that they may not see, and bend their backs continually” (Psalm 68).

The people who came afterward represented the nations. Believing and having Christ before their eyes, they see him while continually carrying him; and, like a servant following his lord and a disciple following his teacher, they follow him, just as the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him take up his cross and follow me” (Matthew 16).

This is the cluster which the pomegranate accompanied, followed by innumerable seeds: namely, our mother, the Church, containing within herself, in the number of the seeds, a multitude of peoples, flashing with the red sign of Christ’s blood. [Col. 0669A] It also contains distinct seeds within, as the Apostle says: “The charisms and gifts are divided and distributed by the grace of the Holy Spirit” (1 Corinthians 12).

The unbelievers, judging themselves unworthy of all these things, did not merit to receive the land of Christ’s flesh, flowing with milk and honey; his servants, that is, the Christian people, have attained it through faith. Concerning its teaching the Church says daily: “How sweet are your words to my throat, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth” (Psalm 118).

We are taught by the examples of the Gospel that the fig which they brought from the land of promise together with the cluster represented the Law. The cluster, likewise, is clearly shown to represent the Savior, as the Church says of Christ in the Song of Songs: “My brother is like a cluster of henna” (Song of Songs 1). For neither can Christ exist without the Law, nor the Law without Christ. [Col. 0669B]

The spies returned from exploring the land after forty days and came to Moses and Aaron and to the whole assembly of the sons of Israel in the wilderness of Paran, which is Kadesh. The wilderness of Paran contains eighteen encampments. At the last of these the spies returned to Moses and reported what they had seen in the land of promise, bringing back a cluster on a pole together with the pomegranates and figs of that place.

Hence, and in what follows, it is written: “Setting out from Ezion-geber, they camped in the wilderness of Zin, that is, Kadesh.” Kadesh, however, does not mean “holy,” as many think, but “changed” or “transferred.” At this encampment Miriam dies and is buried; and because of the waters of contradiction Moses and Aaron offend the Lord and are forbidden to cross the Jordan. [Col. 0669C]

## CHAPTER XI. On the Murmuring of the People and the Vengeance Inflicted upon Them for It

**(There.)** When they had spoken to them and to the whole multitude, they displayed the fruits of the land and reported, saying: “We came into the land to which you sent us. It truly flows with milk and honey, as can be recognized from these fruits. But its inhabitants are exceedingly strong, and its cities are very large and fortified. We saw the race of Anak there,” and so forth. [Col. 0669D]

The account concerns the spies of the land, who were sent to report that the land was indeed good and wonderful, but that the sons of giants lived in it. Jesus, however, does not despair; rather, together with Caleb, who was from the tribe of Judah, he confirms the faith of the people, and they say: “If the Lord loves us, he will bring us into this land.”

What, then, is this land according to the spiritual understanding—a land that is holy and good, yet has an impious inhabitant? Who are these enemies who dwell in the land of the saints, and how are they to be driven out, so that once they have been expelled, the saints may take their place?

Let us return to the Gospels; let us return to the Apostle. The Gospels promise the kingdoms of heaven to the saints. The Apostle says: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3). In heaven, therefore, is the place of the inheritance promised to the saints. Do we suppose that in these places promised to you there is no inhabitant whom you must drive out from there by fighting?

How, then, does the Lord say: “From the days of John the Baptist until now, the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and those who use force seize it” (Matthew 12)? Unless there were those against whom violence was to be used, unless there were those who ought to be driven out and excluded from it, it would never be said that the kingdom of heaven must be seized by force. [Col. 0670A]

And unless there were those with whom we had a struggle and a battle, the Apostle would never say: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this age, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places.” Of these also that word of God through the prophet seems to be understood, where he says: “My sword is drunk in heaven” (Isaiah 34).

It is necessary that the spiritual wickednesses said to be in the heavenly places, who are the true Canaanites, be conquered by you and expelled from the heavenly places, so that you may dwell there in their place.

I know, nevertheless, that they are giants. Everyone who resists God is called a giant. Whoever, therefore, opposes God and is contrary to the truth—what those beings principally do—is rightly called a giant. To you, therefore, it is granted that you may drive out the giants and enter their kingdom. [Col. 0670B]

Is it not written of one of them: “Who will take spoil from the giant?” Of him the Lord also says in the Gospel: “No one can enter a strong man’s house and plunder his goods unless he first binds the strong man” (Mark 3).

For now, insofar as we are compared with human and demonic nature, we are locusts and they are giants—especially if our faith is uncertain and unbelief frightens us. In that case they will truly be giants, and we will be locusts. But if we follow Jesus, believe his words, and are filled with his faith, they will be as nothing in comparison with us. [Col. 0670C]

Hear how he exhorts us and says: “If the Lord loves us, God will bring us into this land, which is good and whose fruit is wonderful.” The type and figure that came before in the fathers is fulfilled in us. They expelled the nations and received their inheritance; they received all the land of Judea and Jerusalem, the city and Mount Zion. These things were fulfilled in them.

But what is said to you? “You have not approached,” he says, “things that are visible, but invisible things. For you have approached the mountain of the living God, the city Jerusalem, and a multitude of angels” (Hebrews 12). [Col. 0670D]

In another place the same Apostle says: “But the Jerusalem above is free, and she is the mother of us all” (Galatians 4).

If anyone does not grant faith to the Apostle’s words that Jerusalem is heavenly, he can also reject these words of ours. But if faith is to be given to Paul’s words, and we believe that Jerusalem is heavenly, then we shall refer what is written about this earthly Jerusalem to that heavenly one as its type. [Col. 0671A]

Therefore, as Paul says, we have approached the heavenly Jerusalem, and without doubt the heavenly Judea. Just as they expelled the Canaanites, Hivites, and the other nations from earthly Judea, so we who have approached the mountain of God and the heavenly kingdoms must expel from them the opposing powers and the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places.

Just as they expelled the Jebusite from Jerusalem—and what had previously been called Jebus was afterward called Jerusalem—so we too must expel the Jebusite from Jerusalem and thus receive his inheritance.

They did these things with visible weapons; we do them with invisible ones. They conquered through bodily battles; we hope to conquer through spiritual struggle.

If you wish to hear how Paul fought this battle—Paul, who is not only the teacher of the nations but also the teacher of this warfare—listen to what he himself describes, as we mentioned above: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of this world’s darkness, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 6). [Col. 0671B]

Therefore, for those who are going to wage this spiritual and invisible battle, he prepares spiritual weapons and invisible arms, saying: “Put on the breastplate of love and the helmet of salvation, taking up the shield of faith, with which you will be able to extinguish all the flaming darts of the evil one. And take up,” he says, “the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (ibid.).

When you have armed yourself with such weapons, following Jesus as your leader, do not fear those giants. You will see how Jesus will subject them to you. And just as the fathers trampled the necks of the nations, so you too will trample upon the necks of human beings.

For he himself says to those who faithfully follow him: “Behold, I have given you authority to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy” (Luke 10).

Jesus always wishes to perform wonderful things. He wishes to conquer giants through locusts and to overcome the heavenly wickednesses through those who are on earth.

Perhaps this was what he said in the Gospels: “Whoever believes in him will not only do the things that I do, but,” he says, “will do greater things than these” (John 14). [Col. 0671C]

Indeed, it seems greater to me if a human being, placed in the flesh—fragile and subject to decay—armed only with the faith of Christ and his word, conquers the giants of demons than if he does what Christ himself does. Although it is Christ who conquers in us, he nevertheless says that what he conquers through us is greater than what he conquers through himself.

The essential point is that we should always be armed with these weapons and that our citizenship should always be in heaven; indeed, that all our movement, every action, every thought, and every word should be heavenly. For the more ardently we ascend there, the more precipitately they will descend from it. And the more we increase, the lower they become.

**(Chapter 14.)** When the whole multitude cried out and wished to crush them with stones, the glory of the Lord appeared over the roof of the covenant tent, before all Israel. And the Lord said to Moses: “How long will this people insult me? How long will they refuse to believe me, despite all the signs that I have performed before them? Therefore I will strike them with pestilence and consume them; but I will make you the leader of a great nation, stronger than this one,” and so forth. [Col. 0671D]

Twelve men were sent from among the sons of Israel to examine the land that had been promised to them. After forty days they returned and reported different things. Some of them drove the people into despair, so that they wished, after rejecting Moses, to choose another leader and return to Egypt. Two others, however, reported good things and urged the people to remain in faith, saying: “If the Lord loves us, he will bring us into this land.”

But the people, driven headlong by the despair of unbelief, rushed to stone those who brought good news. The majesty of the Lord protected them in the cloud, and the Lord said to Moses: “I will strike them with death and destroy them, and I will make you and your father’s house into a nation, much greater than this one.” [Col. 0672A]

This great threat is made by the Lord not to show that the divine nature is subject to suffering and the fault of anger, but so that through these words both Moses’ love for the people and God’s goodness, which surpasses every mind, might become known.

For it is written that God grows angry and threatens the people with destruction in order to teach that a human being holds such a place and such confidence before God that, even if there is some indignation in God, it may be softened by human supplications; and that a human being may obtain so much from him that he even changes his own decrees. [Col. 0672B]

The goodness that follows the anger both shows Moses’ confidence before God and teaches that the divine nature is free from the fault of anger. At the same time, the passage contains a mystery to be fulfilled in the future ages: God promises that, after rejecting this people, he will raise up another.

He says: “I will strike them with death and destroy them, and I will make you and your father’s house into a great nation, much greater than this one.”

This threat is not anger but prophecy. Another nation was to be taken up—that is, this people from the nations—but not through Moses. Moses excused himself, for he knew that the great nation that was promised was not to be called through Moses, but through Jesus Christ, and that the people were to be called not Mosaic but Christian.

Therefore Moses pleads at greater length for that people. The Lord, meanwhile, dispenses the measure of correction with balanced moderation and says: [Col. 0672C]

“For the men who came out of Egypt, who tested me and remained unbelieving, will fall in this wilderness. And they will not see,” he says, “the land that I swore to their fathers; but their children, who are with me here, all who do not know good or evil.”

Perhaps there is also some hidden mystery in the Lord’s words: “Their children, who are with me here.” Where are they “with me here”? Or how are they with him? “Let the one who has ears hear.”

For the present we say that our fathers were that earlier people; but we, their children, have risen and been established in their place, we who did not know good or evil. For we are from the nations, because we knew neither the good things that come from God nor the evil things generated from sin. [Col. 0672D]

If, however, we who succeed those who were rejected fear the example of so great a fall, let us hear Paul’s warning: “Consider, therefore, the severity and goodness of God: severity toward those who fell, but goodness toward you, if you continue in goodness. Otherwise you too will be cut off, and they, if they do not continue in unbelief, will be grafted in” (Romans 11).

After this the Lord adds and says: “Your children will dwell in the wilderness for forty years.” And he explains what mystery this number contains, saying: “According to the number of the days during which you examined the land—forty days—you shall bear your sins for forty years, one year for each day.” [Col. 0673A]

I fear examining the secrets of this mystery. For I see that in it an accounting both of sins and of punishments is contained. If one year of punishment is assigned to each person’s sins for the sin of a single day, and if, according to the number of days in which one sins, an equal number of years must be spent in punishment, I fear that perhaps the ages of ages themselves may not suffice for us, who sin daily and perhaps have passed no day of our lives without sin, to pay the penalty.

In the fact that the people are tormented in the wilderness for forty years because of the sin of forty days and are not permitted to enter the Holy Land, a certain likeness of the future judgment seems to be shown, where an accounting of sins must be examined—unless perhaps there is also some compensation through good works, or through the things that each person receives as evil in this life, as Abraham taught concerning Lazarus (Luke 16). [Col. 0673B]

But no one can know these things fully except the one to whom the Father has entrusted all judgment.

That a day of sin is reckoned as a year of punishment is shown not only in this book, in which there is nothing at all that can be doubted, but similar things are also indicated in the little book of the Shepherd—if, indeed, anyone considers that writing acceptable.

Perhaps someone may deny that it accords with God’s goodness to repay a single day of sin with a year of punishments. But perhaps someone will also say: If he repays day for day, although that may be just, it does not nevertheless appear merciful or kind.

Hear, then, whether we can perhaps explain the difficulty of the matter through clearer examples.

If a wound is inflicted on the body, or the connection of the nerves is severed, the wounds of this world can occur to bodies within the space of a single hour, but afterward, once torments and pains have been endured, they are scarcely healed over a much longer period. How many fears arise at the site, how many torments are generated! [Col. 0673C]

But if it happens that in the same wound or the same fracture someone is wounded again and again, and is broken more frequently, with what punishments can this be treated, with what torments can it be healed, and over what period of time—if indeed it can be restored to health?

Even then it will scarcely be healed in such a way that the person escapes either bodily weakness or the disfigurement of a scar.

Now pass from the example of the body to the wounds of the soul. Whenever the soul sins, it is wounded. And so that you may not doubt that it is wounded by sins as by arrows and swords, hear the Apostle’s admonition: “Take up the shield of faith, with which you can extinguish all the flaming darts of the evil one” (Ephesians 6). [Col. 0673D]

You see, therefore, that the sins of the evil one are darts directed against the soul. But the soul suffers not only the wounds of darts; it also suffers fractures of the feet, when snares are laid for its feet and its steps are tripped.

How long, then, do you think these and similar wounds can take to heal?

If only we could see, with respect to each sin, how our inward person is wounded, how an evil word inflicts a wound. “Have you not read,” they say, “that swords have wounded, but not as the tongue has wounded?”

The soul is therefore wounded through the tongue; it is wounded through thoughts and evil desires; it is broken and crushed through the works of sin. [Col. 0674A]

If we could see all these things and feel the scars of the wounded soul, it is certain that we would resist sin unto death.

But just as those who are filled with a demon or deprived of their minds do not feel when they are wounded because they lack their natural senses, so we too, made foolish by the desires of the world or intoxicated by them, cannot feel how many wounds and how many crushings of the soul we acquire by sinning.

Therefore it is entirely reasonable that the period of punishment—that is, of healing and treatment—should be extended, and that for each wound the time of healing should be prolonged according to the severity of the injury. [Col. 0674B]

Thus God’s justice and goodness are made evident even in the punishments of the soul, so that the one who has sinned, hearing these things, may repent and sin no more.

Conversion and fruitful repentance carried out in the present life will provide swift medicine for such wounds, because repentance not only heals a past wound but also prevents the soul from being wounded by sin thereafter.

Indeed, I shall add this by way of example: If I am a sinner, will the punishment be the same for me if I have sinned once, as it will be if I sin a second and third time, or if I sin more frequently? It will not be so. The amount of punishment must also be measured according to the manner, number, and measure of the sin.

For God will give us the bread of tears and give us to drink tears—but in measure. That measure will be what each person has acquired for himself in this life by sinning more greatly or more extensively.

It is also said that the cup in the Lord’s hand is full of pure wine mixed [with something]. It is therefore undoubtedly mixed for each person, and his judgment will be made not only from the evils he has done but also from the good things. Yet, when both are mixed together, its dregs—which I think means the portion of evils—will not be completely emptied. But these matters, as we have said, are in God’s hand. [Col. 0674C]

Our task is to hasten more quickly toward correction, to turn without dissimulation to repentance, to mourn past sins, to beware of future ones, and to invoke God’s help.

For as soon as you turn and groan, you will be saved. You will find an advocate who intercedes for you with the Father: the Lord Jesus, far greater than Moses, who nevertheless prayed for that people and was heard.

Perhaps for this reason Moses is written to have intervened for the sins of the earlier people and obtained pardon, so that we might have much greater confidence that our advocate Jesus will secure for us an unquestionable pardon from the Father, provided that we turn to him and our heart does not turn back, as John says in his Epistle: “I write these things to you, little children, so that you may not sin” (John 2). “But if anyone among you does sin, we have an advocate with the Father, the righteous one, who intercedes for our sins.” [Col. 0674D]

Moses spoke all these words to all the sons of Israel, and the people mourned greatly. And behold, rising early in the morning, they went up to the summit of the mountain and said: “We are ready to go up to the place of which the Lord spoke, because we have sinned.”

Moses said to them: “Why are you transgressing the word of the Lord? It will not succeed for you. Do not go up. For the Lord is not with you, lest you fall before your enemies. The Amalekites and the Canaanites are before you; you will fall by their sword, because you were unwilling to obey the Lord.”

But they, blinded, went up to the summit of the mountain. The ark of the Lord’s covenant and Moses, however, did not leave the camp.

Then the Amalekites and the Canaanites who dwelt in the mountain came down, struck them down, cut them to pieces, and pursued them as far as Hormah. [Col. 0675A]

O marvelous obstinacy of the human mind, and dreadful foolishness produced by the blindness of an evil heart! God commands them to believe his promises and trust in his patience, and thus to enter into possession of the land. Human foolishness refuses to believe this and scorns to obey salutary commands.

Conversely, God announces to them, because of their sins and faithlessness, that they will not possess the land previously promised to them, and he denies them his help. But they, blinded, wish to invade it against God’s will. [Col. 0675B]

Would that we did not have imitators of them in our own times! For, alas, there are not a few today who, although they condemn the ancients for their obstinacy and criticize their unbelief, nevertheless themselves remain their followers in conduct. They neither strive to attain the good things promised through the divine Law nor cease involving themselves in the forbidden evils of sinning.

But just as it did not prosper for those people, so this obstinacy will not prosper for these either. For the spiritual Amalekites and Canaanites who dwell on the mountains of pride will strike them down and cut them to pieces, pursuing them as far as Hormah.

The Amalekites are interpreted as “the people licking blood,” and the Canaanites as “traders” or “movements.” Hormah is interpreted as “anathema.” [Col. 0675C]

Therefore the heavenly forces of wickedness, which desire our destruction and wish to entangle us in earthly desires, will cut us down with flaming darts and lead us to perpetual anathema if we persevere in sins and do not cease ascending the mountains of pride.

Thus, not following Pelagianism, we must not presume upon our own strength without God’s grace. Rather, humbly considering our weakness, let us humbly believe that what is decreed by the Lord’s mouth must be obeyed and followed in all things. In this way all our enemies will be made subject to us, and by the Lord’s mercy we shall prevail in reaching the joys of our heavenly homeland, which have been promised to us.

## CHAPTER XII. On the Rite of Sacrifices According to Their Several Kinds

**(Chapter 15.)** The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “Speak to the sons of Israel and say to them: When you have entered the land of your dwelling, which I will give you, and you make an offering to the Lord as a burnt offering or a sacrifice of peace offerings, fulfilling vows or making freewill offerings, or when at your festivals you burn offerings as a pleasing aroma to the Lord, from cattle or sheep, whoever offers a victim shall offer as a sacrifice a tenth part of an ephah of fine flour mixed with oil. It contains a quarter of a hin as its measure; and he shall give wine of the same measure for drink offerings, as a burnt offering or as a victim.

“For each lamb and ram there shall be a sacrifice of two-tenths of fine flour, mixed with oil amounting to a third of a hin; and he shall offer wine for a libation, a third of the same measure, as a pleasing aroma to the Lord.

“When you make a burnt offering from cattle or a sacrifice to fulfill a vow, or peace offerings, you shall give for each bull three-tenths of fine flour mixed with oil, which shall amount to half a hin; and for libations you shall offer wine of the same measure, as an offering of the sweetest aroma to the Lord.

“You shall do this for each bull, ram, lamb, and kid,” and so forth. [Col. 0675D]

Josephus, recalling this passage in the third book of his *Antiquities*, reports:

“The Law also commanded that in private and public sacrifices the purest flour should be added: for a lamb, one measure; for a ram, two; and for a bull, three. They sanctify this upon the altar, mixed with oil. For oil is also offered by those who sacrifice: for a bull, half a hin; for a ram, a third of this measure; and a quarter for a lamb.

“The hin, an ancient Hebrew measure, contains two Attic *choes*, according to which measure they offered oil. The ephah, as is read in the book of Ruth, is a measure of three *modii*. The hin, according to those who have written about weights and measures, holds the measure of a sextarius. It was so named because it is the sixth part of a *congius*.” [Col. 0676A]

What, then, does this command mean—that those entering the land of promise should add a sacrifice for each kind of animal that could be offered—except that it teaches us spiritually that we who, through the Lord’s grace, have entered the land of the Church should apply spiritual knowledge in meditation upon the divine Law through each kind of good work? [Col. 0676B]

The measure of the ephah, which contains three other measures, signifies faith in the Holy Trinity. Its tenth part is commanded to be offered—that is, belief in the incarnation of Christ, which is commended to us most fully in the Law, or observance of the Decalogue itself.

We are likewise commanded to offer oil, that is, love and mercy. We are also commanded to offer wine as a libation, that is, spiritual grace or participation in Christ’s passion. These offerings are made according to the proportion of the hin, that is, according to the distribution of perfect devotion.

The number six, being a perfect number, signifies the perfection of each thing.

What else, then, does it mean to offer at the sacrifice of a lamb a tenth part of an ephah of fine flour mixed with oil according to a quarter of a hin, and wine of the same measure for libations, except to present simplicity of conduct together with knowledge of the divine Law and evangelical prudence? [Col. 0676C]

For it is not fitting for anyone who desires to make his offering acceptable to God to have simplicity without prudence, or prudence without simplicity. Hence the Savior commanded his disciples in the Gospel, saying: “Be prudent as serpents and simple as doves.”

For every kind of foolishness, as well as every kind of cunning, is hateful to God; therefore it must be driven out by every means from the Catholic soul, in which Christian simplicity alone must always flourish. [Col. 0676D]

Likewise, in the offering of a ram he commands two-tenths of fine flour to be offered, together with a third part of a hin of oil and wine. Because the ram signifies the order of rulers, it is fittingly offered with two-tenths, when a person who holds the Decalogue of the Law both in understanding and in practice is appointed to the office of ruler. [Col. 0677A]

In this offering, oil and wine amounting together to a third part of a hin are presented when love, mercy, and the grace of spiritual teaching are diligently expended by the ruler in caring for those subject to him.

Likewise, in the offering of a bull, three-tenths of fine flour are commanded to be offered, together with half a measure of a hin of oil or wine. What else is signified under the name of the bull than the order of the holy preachers, who cultivate the Lord’s field and, uprooting the thorns of vices with the evangelical plow, multiply the harvest of virtues?

They are offered with three-tenths of fine flour because, rightly holding the Decalogue of the Law in knowledge, practice, and teaching, they are proved to be true defenders of faith in the Holy Trinity.

Therefore they ought to have especially great love and, by showing mercy in attending to the needs of their neighbor, to provide others with a good example. [Col. 0677B] They must also strive to advance in divine grace as far as is possible for mortals and to reach the perfection and holiness of life, in accordance with the Lord’s command: “Be holy, because I, the Lord your God, am holy” (Leviticus 19).

Yet what is lacking to them in this life they ought to hope will be brought to perfection in themselves, by the Lord’s grace, in heavenly blessedness.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the Firstfruits to Be Given to the Lord

**(There.)** The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “Speak to the sons of Israel and say to them: When you have entered the land that I will give you and have eaten the bread of that region, you shall set apart firstfruits for the Lord from your food. Just as you shall set apart firstfruits from the threshing floors, so also you shall give the first portion of your cooked food to the Lord.” [Col. 0677C]

What does it mean that the Israelites are commanded to offer the firstfruits of their food to the Lord—that is, that just as they shall set apart firstfruits from the threshing floors, so also they shall give the first portion of their cooked food to the Lord?

We said above that the land which they enter and in which they are to offer oblations or firstfruits to the Lord signifies the present Church. Therefore whoever enters the Church through faith and baptism must diligently exercise the land of his flesh—that is, his bodily life—in the fear of God, so that he may cause the fruit of virtues to grow in it, from which eternal nourishment may be prepared for him.

We are commanded, therefore, to consecrate firstfruits to the Lord not only from the threshing floors but also from cooked food.

What does it mean to set apart firstfruits from the threshing floor except to consecrate to the Lord the beginnings of labor in the ministry of preaching? [Col. 0677D]

And what does it mean to offer the first portion from cooked food except to dedicate to the Lord the beginning of good will in the domestic disciplines that each person ought diligently to practice in himself?

Whether someone devotes himself to the practice of virtues within himself, or expends pious labor for the salvation of others by teaching, exhorting, and urging them through good examples, it is necessary that he attribute this not to himself but to divine grace, so that the beginning of every good thing may be consecrated to him from whom it is right to hope for the completion of all perfection.

## CHAPTER XIV. On Sins of Ignorance

**(There.)** “But if through ignorance you have overlooked any of these things that the Lord spoke to Moses and commanded through him to you, from the day on which he began to give the command and thereafter, and if the multitude has forgotten to do them, it shall offer a bull from the herd as a burnt offering, as a most pleasing aroma to him, together with the libations required by the rites, and a goat for sin. The priest shall intercede for the whole multitude of the sons of Israel, and it shall be forgiven them, because they sinned unintentionally,” and so forth. [Col. 0678A]

**(From Augustine.)** It is rightly asked what these sins of the unwilling are—whether they are committed by those who do not know, or whether something that a person is compelled to do can properly be called the sin of one who is unwilling. For it is also customary to say that someone does this against his will.

Yet in any case he wills the reason for which he does it. If someone threatens another with death unless he does something, he wishes to live. He therefore wishes to do the act because he wishes to live. He does not desire by himself to swear falsely, but he wishes to live by swearing falsely.

If this is so, can such acts be called the sins of the unwilling, such as those said here to require expiation? For if the matter is carefully considered, perhaps no one wishes to sin itself, but the sinner does what he wishes for the sake of something else.

All people who knowingly do what is not permitted would wish it to be permitted. To such an extent does no one desire sin for its own sake, but rather for the sake of what follows from it.

If this is so, they are not the sins of the unwilling except in the sense that they are the sins of the ignorant, and these are distinguished from the sins of those who act willingly. [Col. 0678B]

Mystically, the children of Israel offer a bull from the herd as a burnt offering when believing peoples, with complete faith, believe and confess that the Lord’s body, sacrificed on the altar of the cross for the salvation of the human race, is a pleasing fragrance to the Lord [Col. 0678C]. They offer his sacrifice and libations as the rites require when, in the sacrament, they bring bread and wine upon the altar in remembrance of his passion and, partaking of them, confidently believe that they have truly received his body and blood. They offer a goat for sin when we believe that he assumed his very humanity not as sinful, but in the likeness of sinful flesh—that is, sharing our mortality—and offered it for the dissolution of our sins. The priest himself, who is our advocate with the Father, intercedes for the sins of his people, and pardon will be granted him, because, in Paul’s words, “in the days of his flesh, offering prayers and supplications to him who was able to save him from death, with a loud cry and tears, he was heard because of his reverence” (Hebr. V). Moreover, they are commanded to offer incense for themselves and for their sin and error. Thus those offer incense for their sins who offer prayer to God together with fasting and almsgiving; through these, God is appeased and grants pardon to those who rightly ask for forgiveness of their error.

The text continues:

> “But if a person sins unknowingly, he shall offer a year-old she-goat for his sin, and the priest shall intercede for him, because he sinned unwittingly before the Lord; and he shall obtain pardon for him, and it shall be forgiven him,” etc.

Thus he offers a year-old she-goat who performs penance for his sin not lukewarmly but fervently, and withdraws from that same sin with a completely earnest and zealous resolve, taking care thereafter to avoid it and daily asking forgiveness for his offenses. Groaning, he says with the Prophet: “Do not remember the sins of my youth and my ignorances, O Lord; according to your great mercy, remember me, O Lord.” The intercession of the supreme High Priest will also help him obtain pardon: he entered once for all into the holy places, not by the blood of goats and calves but by his own blood, having obtained eternal redemption.

## CHAPTER XV. On sins committed through pride

(IBID.) “But the person who commits anything through pride, whether he is a citizen or a sojourner, because he has rebelled against the Lord, shall be cut off from his people,” and so forth.

(From Augustine.) What sins are committed “with a high hand”—that is, committed through pride—the Scripture itself sufficiently explains in what follows, where it says: “Because he has despised the word.” To despise the commandments is one thing; to value them highly but act against them either through ignorance or when overcome or unwilling is another. These two forms perhaps belong to the sins committed by the unwilling, concerning which he instructed us above how they are to be expiated when God has been appeased. He then added the sins of pride, when someone acts wrongly through pride—that is, by despising the commandment. He did not say that this kind of sin ought to be cleansed by any sort of sacrifice, judging it incurable by that particular remedy which was carried out through sacrifices, such as this Scripture commands to be performed. If these are considered merely in themselves, they can heal no sin; but if the realities whose sacraments they are are investigated, purification from sins can be found in them.

Thus, when it is written, “When the sinner has come into the depths of evils, he despises” (Prov. XVIII), the one whom Scripture here says sins “with a high hand” is signified. This, therefore, cannot be abolished without punishment for the one who commits it, and for that reason it cannot go unpunished. When it is healed through repentance, the very affliction of the penitent is the punishment of sin, although it is medicinal and salutary. Sin is rightly judged great when pride despises the commandment. Yet, so that it may be healed, God does not despise a contrite and humbled heart.

Nevertheless, because it does not occur without punishment, the following statements are made here: “This person,” it says, “provokes God,” because “God resists the proud.” “That person shall be exterminated from his people,” because such a person is in no way numbered among those who belong to God. “Because he has despised the word of the Lord and scattered his commandments, that person shall be crushed by contrition.” Why he shall be crushed by contrition, the text adds in what follows, saying: “His sin is in him.” Therefore, if through repentance he himself applies to himself the contrition due for such a sin, God does not despise the contrite heart, as has been said.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the man gathering wood on the Sabbath, and on making fringes at the corners of garments with violet cords

(IBID.) It happened that, when the children of Israel were in the wilderness, they found a man gathering wood on the Sabbath [Col. 0680A]. They brought him to Moses and Aaron and to the whole congregation. They shut him in prison, not knowing what they ought to do with him. Then the Lord said to Moses: “Let this man be put to death; let the whole congregation stone him outside the camp.” When they had led him out, they stoned him, and he died, as the Lord had commanded.

What does it signify that, by God’s command, he was slaughtered so atrociously by the whole people—a punishment readily promised by unbelievers? Let them understand, then, that all these things happened to them as types, for they were written for our correction. That former carnal man, who dared to violate the Sabbath while gathering wood, and was therefore punished, signified the one who today, having been marked with Christ, is found to perform a carnal work—that is, to gather wood, hay, and straw suitable for the food of eternal fire [Col. 0680B]. When he gathers these things to his own destruction, if he is discovered, he is driven away by all and immediately put to death while he is judged by spiritual persons. Thus everything that happened to those Jews through the law is to be understood figuratively.

The Lord also said to Moses: “Speak to the children of Israel and tell them to make fringes for themselves at the corners of their garments, placing violet cords in them. When they see them, they will remember all the commandments of the Lord, so that they do not follow their own thoughts and eyes, committing fornication through various things; but, rather, remembering the Lord’s commandments, they shall observe them and be holy to the Lord their God. I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt so that I might be your God.”

According to the historical sense, therefore, the Lord commanded through Moses that the children of Israel make violet fringes at the four corners of their garments, so that the Israelite people might be distinguished. Just as circumcision on their bodies gave the Jewish nation its sign, so their clothing was to possess a distinctive feature. They were also to be reminded that, since by God’s command they differed from the other nations in their dress, they should likewise differ from them in religion: they were to worship the one God, rejecting all the idols of the nations, and strive with the greatest devotion to preserve his commandments.

Allegorically, however, this instructs us to understand that the commandments which appear to be the least important in the habit of the law, if they are observed for the sake of the heavenly life—which the violet cord signifies, expressing the color of the air—are of great benefit. For whoever despises the smallest matters gradually falls away. Therefore it is necessary, according to the Apostle’s teaching, that whether we eat or drink or do anything else, we do everything for the glory of God.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the revolt of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram against Moses, and their punishment

(CAP. XVI.) Behold, Korah son of Izhar, son of Kohath, son of Levi, and Dathan and Abiram, sons of Eliab, and On son of Peleth, of the sons of Reuben, rose up against Moses; and with them two hundred and fifty men of the children of Israel, leaders of the congregation, men who were summoned by name at the time of the assembly. When they stood against Moses and Aaron, they said: “Let it be enough for you, since the whole multitude is holy and the Lord is among them. Why do you exalt yourselves above the people of the Lord?” When Moses heard this, he fell prostrate on his face. He spoke to Korah and to the whole congregation: “In the morning the Lord will make known who belong to him; he will draw the holy ones to himself; and those whom he chooses will approach him,” and so forth.

(From Isidore.) Through the destruction of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram, who claimed for themselves against Moses and Aaron the priest the license to offer sacrifice and paid the penalty for their attempts, those are signified who endeavor to create heresies and schisms and deceive many by drawing them along with themselves. They despise the priests of Christ, separate themselves from his clergy and from the fellowship of his people, and dare to establish churches, another altar, and another prayer; by unlawful utterances, they profane the reality of the Lord’s sacrifice through false sacrifices. Those who strive against God’s order, because of the audacity of their presumption, will be swallowed up in the prepared vengeance of eternal judgment when the joints of the earth are broken and the deep chasm opens—not only those who are their leaders, but also those who, by consenting, have become participants with them.

The Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying: “Separate yourselves from the midst of this congregation, so that I may suddenly destroy them,” and so forth.

(From Augustine.) It should be noted that the Lord then commands physical separation to take place when vengeance already threatens the wicked. Thus Noah and his household are separated from the others who are destined to perish in the Flood; thus Lot and his household are separated from Sodom, which was to be consumed by heavenly fire; thus that very people is separated from the Egyptians, who were to be overwhelmed by the waves of the sea; thus these men are now separated from the congregation of Korah, Abiram, and Dathan, who wished through sedition to tear themselves away from the first fruits.

Yet the holy people had previously lived and associated with them, and although God reproves the others in the words with which he rebukes them, they could not be contaminated by them. Nor were they commanded to separate themselves when the Lord was either postponing vengeance or employing a form of vengeance through which the innocent could not be endangered or harmed: for example, through the bites of serpents or through a slaughter by which God struck whomever he wished, as he wished, while leaving another untouched. This was not like the water of the Flood, the rain of fire, the water of the sea, or the opening of the earth, which would carry away the mixed multitude together—not because God could not preserve his own even there, but because what need was there for a miraculous test where separation could take place, so that the water, fire, or chasm of the earth might carry away those whom it found?

So also at the end the wheat will be separated from the weeds, and while the flames burn the wicked, the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father.

As soon as he finished speaking, the earth beneath their feet was split open. It opened its mouth and swallowed them, together with their tents and all their possessions. They descended alive into the underworld, covered by the earth, and perished from the midst of the congregation.

It should be noted that “the underworld” is here used in an earthly sense, that is, of the lower parts of the earth. In Scripture the name “underworld” is used in various ways and with multiple meanings, according to the sense demanded by the matters under discussion; it is especially accustomed to refer to the dead. But since these people are said to have descended alive into the underworld, and the narrative itself makes clear what happened, it is evident—as I have said—that the lower parts of the earth are called the underworld in comparison with this upper earth, upon whose surface people live.

Likewise, in comparison with the higher heaven, where the dwelling of the holy angels is, Scripture says that the sinful angels, cast down into the darkness of this air, are being kept in reserve for punishment as though in the prisons of the underworld. For, it says, “If God did not spare the angels when they sinned, but thrust them into the prisons of the darkness of the underworld and handed them over to be kept for punishment at the judgment” (I Pet. III), while the Apostle Paul calls the devil “the ruler of the power of the air,” who works in the sons of disobedience.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the censers of the rebels, removed from the fire by Eleazar the priest

(IBID.) The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “Command Eleazar, son of Aaron the priest, to remove the censers that lie in the fire and scatter the fire here and there, because they have been sanctified through the deaths of sinners. Let him make them into beaten plates and fasten them to the altar, because incense was offered in them before the Lord; and they have been sanctified, so that they may be a sign and memorial for the children of Israel.”

Here it is asked why the Lord did not speak to Moses and Aaron, as in the preceding passages, but to Moses and Eleazar, Aaron’s son. For the moment, this reason occurs to me: the question concerned the priestly lineage, that is, from what family priests ought to come. Since men of another family had dared to usurp the priesthood and had perished through such a terrible and miraculous punishment, God wished to speak not to Aaron, who was already the high priest, but to Eleazar, who was to succeed him and was already serving in the second priesthood, so that in this way he might commend the allotment of the lineage that was to exist in the succession of priests.

But it should be noted that, in a new manner, their punishment is called sanctified—the punishment of those by whom this sin had been committed—because through them an example was given to the others of how they should be afraid. As to why he wished a covering for the altar to be made from them, he added: “Because they were offered before God and were sanctified; they have been made a sign for the children of Israel.” He did not therefore wish it to be rejected that they had been offered by such men. Rather, he wished people to consider and attend to before whom they had been offered: namely, before the Lord, so that the name of the Lord, before whom they had been offered, might have greater force in them than the extremely bad merit of those by whom they had been offered.

Scripture had already mentioned this in Exodus, when it says that the altar was constructed. From this it is understood that accounts of events have been distributed among the books, rather than being arranged in a continuous chronological order.

Mystically, however, Korah represents those who rise up against ecclesiastical faith and the teaching of truth. It is written concerning Korah and his company that they offered incense with alien fire in bronze censers. God commands that the alien fire be scattered and poured out.

But concerning the censers he says: “Because they have been sanctified, make them into beaten plates and surround the altar with them, because they were offered before the Lord and have been sanctified.”

By this figure, it seems to me, the following is shown: the censers that Scripture calls bronze represent divine Scripture. Heretics place alien fire upon this Scripture—that is, they introduce a sense and understanding alien to the Lord and contrary to the truth—and thus offer to the Lord not a pleasing but an accursed incense. Therefore an example is given to the priests of the churches: if something of this kind should arise, whatever is alien to the truth must indeed be completely removed from the Church of God; but if, even in the words of heretics, certain meanings drawn from divine Scripture are found inserted, they must not be rejected together with those things that are contrary to truth and faith. For the things brought forth from divine Scripture and offered to the Lord have been sanctified.

This may also be understood in another way, namely, that the censers of the sinners are commanded to be joined and attached to the altar. First, the fact that they are called bronze will not appear meaningless. Where there is true faith and an unimpaired preaching of the word, things are called either silver or gold: gold, to indicate the purity of faith like a flash of lightning; silver, tested by fire, to signify tested utterances.

But those things called bronze consist only in the sound of the voice, not in the power of the Spirit, and are, as the Apostle says, “sounding brass or a clanging cymbal” (I Cor. XIII). If, therefore, we bring these bronze censers—that is, the voices of heretics—to the altar of God, where the divine fire is and where the true preaching of the faith is found, the truth itself will shine more brightly through comparison with falsehood.

For example, if the sayings of Marcion, Basilides, or any other heretic are brought forth and I refute them through the words of truth and the testimonies of the divine Scriptures, as though with the fire of the divine altar, will not their impiety become more evident by comparison? For if ecclesiastical doctrine were simple, with no external opposition from the assertions of heretical teachings, our faith could not appear so clear and so thoroughly tested. But for this reason the teaching of the Catholics is besieged by the opposition of those who contradict it: so that our faith may not grow sluggish through idleness but may be polished through exercise.

For this reason the Apostle also said: “There must also be heresies, so that those who are approved may become manifest among you” (I Cor. XI). This means: the altar must be surrounded by the censers of heretics, so that the difference between the faithful and the unfaithful may become certain and manifest to all. When ecclesiastical faith begins to shine like gold and its preaching gleams to those who look upon it like silver tested by fire, then, by the greater contrast of ugliness and beauty, the voices of heretics will be sullied by the cheapness of dark bronze.

## CHAPTER XIX. On the murmuring of the people against Moses and Aaron, and the fire sent among them for this reason

(IBID.) While the Lord was speaking to Moses, the whole congregation of the children of Israel murmured against Moses and Aaron on the following day, saying: “You have killed the people of the Lord.” When sedition arose and the tumult increased, Moses and Aaron fled to the tabernacle of the covenant. After they had entered it, the cloud covered the tabernacle, and the glory of the Lord appeared, and so forth.

We do not previously read that the cloud covered the tabernacle of the testimony, that the majesty of the Lord appeared, and that he received Moses and Aaron within the cloud, except here, when the people rose up against them and wished to stone them. Let us learn from this how great is the benefit of persecutions for Christians, how much grace is bestowed, how God becomes their defender, and how abundantly the Holy Spirit is poured out. For the Lord’s grace is especially present when human savagery is stirred up. We have peace with God when we suffer wars from human beings on account of righteousness.

“For where sin abounded, grace abounded still more.” The cloud therefore covered the tabernacle, the synagogue rushed upon Moses and Aaron, and the glory of the Lord appeared. Although Moses and Aaron were great in the merit of their lives and powerful in the virtues of their souls, the glory of God could not have appeared to them unless they had been placed amid persecutions, tribulations, dangers, and even death itself.

Therefore do not think that the glory of the Lord can appear to you while you sleep and remain idle. Did not the Apostle Paul deserve to obtain the Lord’s grace in these circumstances? Does he not enumerate above all others that he was in tribulations, necessities, prisons, shipwrecks, dangers of the sea, dangers of rivers, dangers from robbers, and dangers from false brothers (II Cor. XI)? The more these things abound, the more they confer the glory of God upon those who endure them patiently.

The Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron, saying: “Withdraw from the midst of this congregation, and I will destroy them at once.” And they fell upon their faces.

In Sodom, when at least ten were sought, through whom—if perhaps they could be found—the inhabitants of the five cities of the Sodomites might barely be saved, now even two are considered sufficient, if only such men as Moses and Aaron are found, for the whole Israelite nation to be saved. What, then, shall we say is present in these two? What virtue or merit is so great that six hundred thousand and more may be delivered from the destruction of the destroyer?

I believe that Moses signifies the law, which teaches human beings the knowledge and love of God, while Aaron represents the pattern of praying to God and entreating him. If, then, it should ever happen that God is angry with us, or with the whole people of the Lord, so that a sentence of vengeance proceeds from him, let the law of God return to our heart, reminding us and teaching us to turn to repentance, make satisfaction for our offenses, and plead for our faults. Immediately his anger will cease and his indignation will be calmed. The Lord will be appeased, as though Moses and Aaron were interceding for us and pleading for the whole people.

But if God’s indignation should ever arise and a fierce correction come because of sins, while our hearts become hardened and we do not turn to the Lord or humble ourselves in his presence so as to mitigate his movement and anger through the confession of those who plead; if instead we say, “God does not care about the life of mortals; these matters do not concern God. He abandoned us long ago, and such things do not come to his knowledge”—if we think such things in our hearts and they proceed from our mouths, it is certain that Moses and Aaron are not in us: neither knowledge of the law nor the fruits of repentance, through which we might escape the destruction of the impending ruin.

I think that this also happened to that people who lived before us, when all turned aside, together became useless, and there was no one who did good—not even one. For if there had been one, the Lord would certainly never have abandoned them. But let us also fear lest something similar be found in us. I fear that sentence in which our Lord and Savior, who knows all things beforehand, speaks doubtfully: “Do you think that when the Son of Man comes, he will find faith upon the earth?” (Luke XVIII).

While they were lying upon the ground, the Lord said to Moses and Aaron: “Take the censer, draw fire from the altar, place incense upon it, and go quickly to the people to pray for them. For wrath has already gone out from the Lord, and the plague is raging.” When Aaron had done this and had run to the people and to the middle of the congregation, which the fire was ravaging, he offered incense (thymiama). Standing between the dead and the living, he pleaded for the people, and the plague ceased.

Those who were struck numbered fourteen thousand seven hundred, apart from those who had perished in the rebellion of Korah. Moses and Aaron are therefore commanded to leave the midst of the congregation so that the congregation may be destroyed at once. But let us see what these men do. They are holy and perfect; they are even more disciples of the Gospel than of the law. Therefore they also love their enemies and pray for their persecutors. When those who had come to kill them appeared, they fell upon their faces on the ground.

Moses said to Aaron: “Take the censer, place fire from the altar upon it, and put incense upon it; carry it quickly into the camp and plead for them. For wrath has gone forth from the presence of the Lord, and it has already begun to destroy the people.”

Since we have reached this passage, I wish to remind the disciples of Christ of the goodness of God, so that none of you may be disturbed by heretics if a dispute should arise, when they say that the God of the law is not good but just, and that the law of Moses contains not goodness but justice.

Let those who accuse both God and the law observe how Moses and Aaron themselves acted first in the way that the Gospel later taught. Behold, Moses loves his enemies and prays for his persecutors—something that Christ certainly teaches should be done in the Gospels. Hear how, falling upon their faces on the ground, they pray for those who had risen up to kill them.

Thus the power of the Gospel is also found in the law, and the Gospels are understood to rest upon the foundation of the law. I do not call the law the Old Testament if I understand it spiritually. The law becomes an Old Testament only for those who wish to understand it carnally. For them it has necessarily become old and has grown aged, because it cannot retain its strength.

But for us, who understand and expound it spiritually and in an evangelical sense, it is always new; and for us both Testaments are new—not by the passage of time, but by the newness of understanding. Does not the Apostle John also express the same thought in his Epistle when he says: “Little children, I give you a new commandment, that you love one another” (I John II)? He certainly knew that the commandment of love had long ago been given in the law. But because love never fails, and the commandment of love never grows old, he declares that what never grows old is always new.

For those who constantly observe and keep it, the commandment of love continually makes them new in spirit. But for the sinner who does not keep the bonds of love, even the Gospels grow old. The New Testament cannot be new to one who does not put off the old man and put on the new, created according to God, so as to offer incense in the camp and plead for the people.

“For,” he says, “the people has already begun to be destroyed.” In the spirit Moses saw what was happening. He saw the power go forth into the camp and ravage and kill sinners. For this reason he urged the high priest to take the censer, place fire from the altar upon it, and, after putting incense upon it, go out and stand between the dead and the living, so that the destruction might proceed no farther—or, more accurately, as the wording of Scripture has it, so that the breach might cease.

But first, if it seems good, let us describe the image of the historical event itself. When the appearance of what happened has been made clear, then we may investigate whatever mystical meaning is present in the passage.

Understand, then, that the people of Israel were arranged in the camp according to the order of their tribes and families. Consider a certain power sent by God, not spreading randomly, but beginning from some first part and ravaging the people with death, advancing in order and producing a slaughter of the dead.

After this, understand that the high priest, clothed in the priestly vestments, advanced carrying the censer and the fire, bearing incense, and went toward the place to which death, brought by the destroying angel, had reached. He stood in the place where death had ended its work among the first and was near the last.

Look upon the high priest standing there and, by a kind of opposition through his presence, dividing the living from the dead. Consider the power of his propitiation and the mystery of the incense, by which the destroying angel was checked. In this way death was brought to an end and life restored.

If you have understood the order of the historical account and, so to speak, been able to see with your eyes the high priest standing between the living and the dead, now ascend to the higher heights of this word. See how the true High Priest, Jesus Christ, took up the censer of human flesh, placed upon it the fire of the altar—that magnificent soul, without doubt, with which he was born in the flesh—and added incense, which is the spotless spirit. He stood in the midst between the living and the dead and did not allow death to advance farther. Rather, as the Apostle says, “He destroyed him who held the power of death, that is, the devil, so that whoever believes in him might no longer die but live forever” (Hebr. II).

This, then, was the mystery that the one who was later to ravage the people already feared at that time. He recognized the figure of the censer, the fire, and the incense, and foresaw what kind of offering was to be presented to God by the one who stood in the midst of the dead and the living. At that time the prefigured image saved them; for us, the reality of salvation itself has arrived.

For that destroying angel would not have been put to shame by the high priest’s garments woven of purple, wool, and fine linen. Rather, he understood the garments that were to belong to the great High Priest and yielded to those before whom the whole creation was inferior.

I think, moreover, that this form was fulfilled not only at the first coming of our Lord and Savior but perhaps will also be preserved at the second. “The Son of Man will come,” and when he comes again, he will certainly find some dead and others living. We may understand this in one way: some will still be found in the condition of life in which we now exist, while many will already have gone before us in death.

It may also be understood in another way, so that we take the dead to mean bodies and the living to mean souls. I remember that some who interpreted this passage before us said that the dead are those understood to be dead in their sins through the enormity of their crimes, while the living are those who have persevered in works of life.

However it is understood, this great High Priest and our Savior will also stand in the future in the midst of the living. But perhaps he will then be said to stand in the midst of the living and the dead when he places the sheep at his right hand and the goats at his left and says to those on his right: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom of the world,” and so forth (Matt. XXV).

But to those on his left he will say: “Go into eternal fire, workers of iniquity, which my Father prepared for the devil and his angels, because I do not know you.” Those who are sent into eternal fire are indeed dead, while those who are sent into the kingdom are living.

## CHAPTER XX. On the twelve rods of the tribes, brought to the tabernacle at the Lord’s command, among which only Aaron’s rod had put forth leaves
(CAP. XVII.) The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “Speak to the children of Israel and take from them one staff for each of their ancestral houses, one staff from all the leaders of the tribes, and write each man’s name upon his staff. Aaron’s name, however, shall be in the tribe of Levi, and one staff shall contain all their families. You shall place them in the tabernacle of the covenant before the testimony [Col. 0687D], where I shall speak with you. The one whom I choose, his staff shall sprout; and I shall restrain from myself the complaints of the children of Israel, with which they murmur against you,” and so forth.

Twelve staffs, corresponding to the twelve tribes, were commanded to be placed in the tabernacle, and behold, the staff of Levi blossomed. It showed what power—or rather, what distinction in number—Aaron possessed. What, plainly, is suggested by this sign except that all of us who lie in death until the end of the world remain, like the other staffs, in dryness? Yet while all the staffs remained dry, the staff of Levi returned to flower, because the body of the Lord, truly our priest, placed in the dryness of death, burst forth into the flower of resurrection.

By this flower Aaron is rightly recognized as a priest, because through this glory of resurrection our Redeemer, who arose from the tribe of Judah and Levi, is shown to be our intercessor. Behold, then: Aaron’s staff flowers after its dryness, but the staffs of the twelve tribes remain dry, because the Lord’s body now lives after death, while our bodies are still deferred from the glory of resurrection until the end of the world.

Therefore, as we have said, Aaron’s staff, which flowered after being dried, signifies the flesh of Christ. After it had been cut from the root of Jesse, it came back to life, having been put to death in a manner all the more truly alive. Thus the staff that became green after its dryness is Christ rising after death. We understand the staff and the flower to be the same thing, so that in the staff his reigning power, and in the flower his beauty, may be displayed. Hence the same one says in the Song of Songs: “I am the flower of the field and the lily of the valleys” (Song II).

Others think that this staff, which produced a flower without moisture, signifies the virgin Mary, who without intercourse gave birth to the Word of God. Of her it is written: “A staff shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise from his root” (Isa. XI), namely Christ, who, bearing beforehand the type of the future Passion, was purple with the bright light of faith and the blood of the Passion: the flower of virgins, the crown of martyrs, and the grace of the continent.

Tropologically, all the leaders of the tribes and all peoples likewise have a staff. No one can govern a people unless he has a staff. Hence the apostle Paul, because he was a leader of the people, said: “What do you want? Shall I come to you with a staff, or with love and a spirit of gentleness?” (I Cor. XI).

Therefore all the leaders of the tribes necessarily have their staffs, but there is one alone, as Scripture reports: the high priest Aaron, whose staff sprouted. But since, as we have often seen, Christ is the true high priest, he alone is the one whose staff not only sprouted but also flowered and brought forth the fruit of all the faith of believing peoples.

What, then, is this fruit that it brought forth? “A nut,” he says. This fruit is bitter in its first covering; in the next it is fortified and enclosed; in the third it nourishes and feeds the one who takes it. Such, then, is the doctrine of the Law and the Prophets in Christ’s school.

At first, the surface of the letter is quite bitter: it commands circumcision of the flesh, gives prescriptions concerning sacrifices, and contains the other matters represented by “the letter that kills.” Cast all these aside like the bitter shell of a nut. In the second place you will reach the protection of the hard shell, in which either moral teaching or the discipline of self-restraint is signified. These are necessary for guarding what is kept within, although they must eventually be broken and certainly dissolved.

For example, abstinence from food and the chastisement of the body are undoubtedly necessary so long as we are in this corruptible and suffering body. But when it has been broken and dissolved, and at the time of resurrection has been restored incorruptible from corruptibility, and spiritual from animal, then no corruption will any longer dominate the body—not through the labor of affliction or the discipline of abstinence, but by its own condition. Thus the discipline of abstinence now appears necessary, but afterward it is not to be sought.
