In the third place you will come to what is stored within these things, the hidden and secret meaning of the mysteries of the wisdom and knowledge of God, by which the souls of the saints are nourished and fed, not only in the present life but also in the future. This is the priestly fruit, concerning which it is promised to those who hunger and thirst for righteousness that they shall be satisfied.

In this way, throughout all the Scriptures, the pattern of this threefold sacrament runs its course. Thus Wisdom also admonishes us to describe these things for ourselves three times in our heart, “in order,” it says, “to answer with a word of truth those who propose questions to us.” Thus the patriarch Isaac dug three wells (Gen. XXVI), and only the third did he call Rehoboth, that is, “width” or “breadth.”

Because of this priestly sacrament and the staff of the nut, I think that Jeremiah also, who was one of the priests of Anathoth (Jer. I), saw a staff of almond wood and prophesied about it those things that are written—whether concerning the almond staff or concerning the burning cauldron or pot—as though he were showing through these things that life is in the almond staff and death in the burning cauldron. For life and death are placed before our face.

Christ is life in the sacrament of the nut, while the devil is death in the figure of the burning cauldron. If, therefore, you sin, you will place your portion with the burning cauldron. But if you act justly, your portion is made to be with the almond staff, together with the great high priest.

In the Song of Songs, moreover, the bride is said to descend into the garden of nuts, where she is also described as having found, together with the nuts, in a certain manner, a great abundance of fruits belonging to the priesthood.

There were twelve staffs, apart from Aaron’s staff. [Col. 0689C] When Moses had placed them before the Lord in the tabernacle of the testimony, he returned the following day and found that Aaron’s staff, in the house of Levi, had sprouted, and that flowers had burst forth from its swelling buds. When its leaves had spread wide, they were transformed into almonds.

Behold, Aaron’s staff sprouted in the house of Levi. This is undoubtedly the one thing that had been promised. But other things are added and said: “It produced leaves, brought forth flowers, and sprouted nuts.” Since only a sprout had been promised, see how much God bestows: it produced not merely a sprout but also leaves; not merely leaves but also flowers; and not merely flowers but also fruit.

What, then, should we gather and contemplate from these things? First of all, the sacrament of resurrection from the dead. A dry staff sprouts when an extinguished body begins to live again. What are the four things that will be granted to the body when it rises? That what was sown in corruption may rise in incorruption; what was sown in weakness may rise in power; what was sown in dishonor may rise in glory; and that the animal body that was sown may rise as a spiritual body. These are the four things that the dry staff of our body will sprout at the resurrection.

In the second place we say this also: just as in these matters God gave his promise fourfold and bestowed much more and more precious things than he promised, so much more, in all the passages of Scripture where some promise of God is contained, if one is nevertheless found worthy to attain it, will he be prepared for many things in the future. Thus that saying of the Apostle will truly be fulfilled: “Eye has not seen, nor ear heard, what God has prepared for those who love him.”

We may still understand the differences among the things that had sprouted on the staff in this way. Everyone who believes in Christ first dies, and afterward is born again; and this too is represented by the fact that the dry staff later sprouts.

The first sprout, therefore, is a person’s first confession in Christ. Secondly, it puts forth leaves, when the one who has been reborn receives the gift of the grace of Christ through the sanctification of God. From there he brings forth flowers, when he begins to make progress, to be adorned with the sweetness of good works, and to pour forth the ardor of mercy and kindness. Finally, he bestows life.

When he has reached perfection and brings forth from himself a word of faith and a word of the knowledge of God, and wins others, this is to have brought forth fruit by which others may be nourished. Thus each individual believer sprouts from Aaron’s staff, which is Christ. These four distinctions are designated in other passages of Scripture as four stages, which the apostle John embraces in his epistle with a mystical distinction. For he says: “I have written to you, little children; I have written to you, adolescents; I have written to you, young men; and I have written to you, fathers” (I John II).

In these words he establishes not distinctions of bodily age but distinctions in the soul’s progress, so that in this also we may observe the sprouts of the priestly staff being signified.

All these things, then, are found not so much in Aaron’s staff as in that staff which came forth from the root of Jesse, and the flower rose from its root, upon which the Spirit of the Lord rests. In this it does not appear meaningless that the staff is said to come forth and the flower to rise.

Although Christ is one in substance, he nevertheless becomes different for individuals according to the understanding of the one in whom he works. For the person who is slower and more negligent with respect to discipline, Christ becomes a staff; and in the staff he is said not to rise but to come forth. One who is inert and sluggish must come forth from the state in which he does not stand rightly and pass into another state, as though driven by a staff—that is, admonished by the more rigid truth of doctrine.

But the one who is righteous, because “the righteous shall flourish like the palm,” is said to have Christ rise within him. Thus the one who needs blows has the staff come forth for him, while the one who advances toward righteousness has the flower rise within him. It rises until he brings forth the fruits of the Spirit, which are love, joy, peace, wisdom, and the remaining virtues.

Now Scripture has recounted in this book how the matter concerning Aaron’s staff came about, so that, sprouting flowers, it might divinely indicate his election to the priesthood. Yet concerning that same staff it is said in Exodus that it was to be placed in the holy of holies together with the manna in the ark, when the command was given concerning the construction of the tabernacle—or at any rate, the command had been given long before the tabernacle itself was built and completed.

The tabernacle stood in the first month of the second year after they had gone out from Egypt, while this book begins in the second month of that same second year, on the first day of the month. Hence it is clear, if we consider the order of the books, that these things are recalled by recapitulation—that is, by remembering earlier events—which those who attend less carefully suppose to have happened in the same order in which they are narrated.

## CHAPTER XXI. On Aaron’s priesthood and the ministry of the Levites

(CAP. XVIII.) “And the Lord said to Aaron: You and your sons and your father’s house with you shall bear the iniquity of the sanctuary; and you and your sons together shall bear the sins of your priesthood,” and so forth.

These are the sins that are called sacrifices for sins. Accordingly, they are called “the sins of the holy things,” not because holy people commit them, but because the expression “of the holy things” derives from the fact that they are holy things offered in the holy places. They are called “sins” because they are sacrifices for sins. For this reason they are called “the sins of the holy things” and “the sins of your priesthood,” that is, the very sacrifices that are offered for sins. Leviticus likewise makes this clear and says that they belong to the priest.

Alternatively: Those who are better always take upon themselves the faults and sins of their inferiors. Thus the Apostle also says: “You who are stronger must bear the weaknesses of the weak” (Rom. XV).

If an Israelite sins—that is, a layman—he cannot remove his own sin, but seeks a Levite and needs a priest; indeed, he seeks something even more eminent than these: he needs a high priest in order to receive remission of sins. But if a priest or high priest sins, he can cleanse his own sin, provided that he does not sin against God.

We must inquire how some people are called holy while their sins are written about. For some think that as soon as someone begins to be holy, he can no longer sin and must immediately be regarded as without sin. If a holy person did not sin, it would certainly not have been written: “You shall take the sins of the holy things.” If a holy person were without sin, the Lord would not have said through the prophet Ezekiel to the angels whom he sent to punish sinners: “Begin with my holy ones” (Ezek. VIII).

Writing to the Corinthians, the Apostle says: “Paul, called an apostle of Jesus Christ.” And shortly afterward: “To the church of God that is at Corinth, sanctified in Christ Jesus, called holy” (I Cor. I). Listen, then, to how many sins he rebukes in those whom he calls sanctified and holy. For he says later: “Since there are jealousy and strife among you, are you not carnal and walking according to human ways?” (I Cor. III). Again: “As though I were not coming to you, some have become puffed up” (I Cor. IV). A little later: “Fornication is actually heard of among you, such as does not occur even among the Gentiles” (I Cor. V). In what follows he says: “And you have become puffed up, and have not rather mourned” (ibid.).

In this he left no one exempt, assigning to some the charge of fornication and to others the charge of puffed-up pride. It would be lengthy and unsuitable to the present occasion to produce many testimonies proving that those who are called holy are not thereby immediately understood to be without sin. But we shall say as much as the present passage requires.

Those who have devoted themselves to God and separated their life from the society of the crowd in order to serve the Lord are called holy, and also sinners. According to the fact that such a person has devoted himself to the Lord after cutting himself off from other activities, he is called holy. Yet it can happen that even in the very service by which he serves the Lord he does not conduct everything as it ought to be conducted, but falls short in some matters and sins.

For just as someone who separates and withdraws from all other activities in order to attain, for example, the discipline of medicine or philosophy is not immediately so perfect, as soon as he has handed himself over to such disciplines, that he cannot be found to sin in anything—in fact, by committing many faults he may scarcely reach perfection at some point—yet as soon as he has given himself to such schools, it is certain that he is counted either among physicians or among philosophers; so it must be understood concerning the holy that as soon as someone devotes himself to the pursuits of holiness, he is called holy according to what he has undertaken. But according to the fact that he must fall short in many things until, through practice, discipline, and diligence, the habit of sinning is cut away from him, he will also be called a sinner, as we said above.

I add something further: unless someone has a holy purpose and pursues holiness, when he sins he does not know how to repent of sin or seek a remedy for wrongdoing. Those who are not holy die in their sins. Those who are holy repent of their sins, feel their wounds, recognize their falls, seek a priest, ask for healing, and seek purification through the high priest.

Therefore the language of the Law carefully and significantly indicates that high priests and priests take upon themselves the sins not of just anyone, but only of the holy. For the holy person is the one who cures his sin through the high priest.

But let us return to our high priest, the great high priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus our Lord, and let us see how he himself, together with his sons—that is, the apostles and martyrs—takes upon himself the sins of the holy.

Everyone who believes in Christ knows that our Lord Jesus Christ came to take away the sin of the world and that by his death he erased sins. But how his sons also take away the sins of the holy—that is, the apostles and martyrs—we shall attempt, if we can, to prove from the divine Scriptures.

First hear Paul saying: “I will gladly spend myself and be spent for your souls.” And in another place he says: “I am no longer being sacrificed, and the time of my departure or release is at hand.” For those to whom he was writing, the Apostle says that he spent himself and was being sacrificed. A victim is sacrificed so that the sins of those for whom it is slaughtered may be cleansed.

Concerning the martyrs, John writes in the Apocalypse: “The souls of those who were slaughtered for the name of the Lord Jesus stand beside the altar” (Rev. VI). Whoever stands beside the altar is shown to perform the office of a priest. The duty of a priest is to intercede for the sins of the people.

Therefore I fear that, since martyrs are no longer being made and the sacrifices of the holy are no longer offered for our sins, remission of our sins may not be taking place. I fear, consequently, that while our sins remain in us, what the Jews say about themselves may happen to us: because they have no altar, temple, or priesthood, and therefore offer no sacrifices, they say that their sins remain in them, and for that reason no pardon follows.

Yet the Lord knows those who are his, and among those in whom no hope is placed he has his own treasures. For God does not see as a human being sees. I do not doubt that in this gathering also there are some known only to him who are already martyrs before him, prepared by the testimony of their conscience, if anyone should demand it, to pour out their blood for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. I do not doubt that there are some who have taken up their cross and follow him.

Although these things seem to have been said in a kind of excess, they nevertheless appear necessary, so that we might understand how, through the high priest and the sons of the high priest, remission of sins takes place among the holy.

The Lord continues speaking to Aaron, saying: “You and your sons shall minister in the tabernacle of the testimony. The Levites shall keep watch according to your commands and over all the work of the tabernacle, but only so that they do not touch the vessels of the sanctuary or approach the altar, lest they die and you perish with them. Let them be with you and keep watch in the guardianship of the tabernacle and in all its ceremonies; no outsider shall join himself to you. Keep watch over the guardianship of the sanctuary and in the ministry of the altar, lest indignation arise against the children of Israel,” and so forth.

Behold, the Lord commands Aaron the priest and his sons to minister in the tabernacle of the testimony, to oversee the sacred vessels, and to care for everything pertaining to the service of the altar and everything that is within the veil. The other Levites, however, are to keep watch at the commands of Aaron and his sons, in the guardianship of the tabernacle and in all its ceremonies; nevertheless, they are not to approach the altar or touch the sacred vessels.

What else should we understand by Aaron and his sons except the more perfect members of the Church and the holy teachers or overseers of the churches of God? Their duty is to handle the divine mysteries with their hands, to examine and sift the sacred vessels—that is, the mystical words of Holy Scripture—through investigation, and to hasten to bring them to understanding; and whatever things are difficult in practice, they must strive to complete by their own works.

The rest of the company of the faithful, however, needs to meditate with a vigilant mind on the easier things that they themselves can grasp in understanding, and to guard them diligently—those things that they are commanded by their teachers to preserve. For the capacity of the understanding of those already perfect in knowledge is not the same as that of beginners still in the faith, nor is the energy of the talented equal to that of the dull.

Hence Paul says to some who were less capable of his teaching: “I gave you milk to drink, not solid food; for you were not yet able to receive it. Indeed, even now you are not able” (I Cor. III). Elsewhere, speaking of certain more perfect people, he says: “We speak wisdom among the perfect, which none of the rulers of this age has known” (I Cor. II).

This is what occurred in the Gospel when the apostles gathered up the fragments left over by the crowd fed by the Lord and filled twelve baskets. Hence Truth itself, discussing the higher virtues, says: “Let the one who can receive it receive it.” And to the lawyer he says: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me” (Matt. XIX).

Therefore it is especially fitting for those who glory in the priestly order to observe more diligently and attend to the things that are written, so that they may know that what the divine Law has commanded them must be observed.

“You and your sons,” he says, “with me in the presence of the tabernacle of the testimony, keep watch over your duties, those of the altar, and those of the tabernacle.” The commands are certain and clear: we must keep watch over the tabernacle and the priesthood.

But who observes and does what has been commanded to priests, and who makes use of the rank and honor of the priesthood but does not observe the commands established for priests, only the one who searches hearts and minds can know.

The priests are commanded to guard not only the things that are outside, but also, he says, to care especially for the things that are within the veil—as though he were saying: Let it be the priests’ concern to fulfill the evident and manifest commands of the divine Law and to contemplate with complete discernment its hidden and veiled ministries.

If you wish to apply the tabernacle of the testimony to the human being, since Paul calls the human body a tabernacle, saying: “For we who are in this tabernacle groan, being burdened, although we do not wish to be unclothed but to be clothed upon” (II Cor. V), then, if we refer the tabernacle to the human being, we call the inner regions behind the veil, where inaccessible things are concealed, the ruling faculty of the heart, which alone can receive the mysteries of truth and be capable of the secrets of God.

As for the two altars, the inner and the outer, since an altar is an indication of prayer, I think they signify what the Apostle says: “I will pray with the spirit; I will pray also with the mind” (I Cor. XIV).

When I pray in my heart, I enter the inner altar. I think this is also what the Lord says in the Gospels: “But when you pray, enter your room, shut your door, and pray to your Father in secret” (Matt. VI). Whoever prays in the manner I have described enters the altar of incense, which is within.

But when someone pours out prayer to God in a loud voice and with words spoken aloud, as though building up those who hear him, he prays in the Holy Spirit and appears to offer a sacrifice on the altar outside, which was established for the burnt offerings of the people.

Therefore priests ought especially to care for and guard the things that are concealed within the inner veil, so that nothing polluted and nothing unclean may be found there. That is, they must care for the inner person and the secrets of the heart, so that the cherubim and the mercy seat may remain undefiled there.

“Cherubim” is to be understood as knowledge of the truth. The interpretation of “cherubim” indicates a multitude—that is, the perfection—of knowledge. And what other knowledge is perfect except to have recognized the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit?

These, then, must be cared for by priests, so that they may be preserved undefiled and unharmed. The jar containing the heavenly food of manna, moreover, clearly signifies the treasury of the divine word; and the golden ark in which are the tablets of the covenant, I think, signifies nothing other than our mind, in which we ought to have the Law of God written.

This golden table must be pure and precious, so that we may always have the Law of God written upon it, as the apostle Paul says: “Written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of fleshly hearts” (II Cor. III). This is what is said concerning certain people who show that the work of the Law is written in their hearts.

But who wrote it in their hearts except God with his finger? It is the natural law, certainly, which God wrote for the human race and in the minds of all.

“If an outsider,” he says, “approaches, he shall be put to death.” According to the historical sense, he calls outsiders—or, as he said above, foreigners—those who are not from the tribe of Levi and to whom the service of performing God’s ministry in the tabernacle was not entrusted. For it was not permitted for just anyone from another tribe to be present at the altar or to serve there.

Hence King Uzziah, who was from the tribe of Judah, as is read in the Book of Chronicles, when he attempted to burn incense on the altar of incense in the manner of priests, namely the sons of Aaron, was struck by the Lord with leprosy on his forehead. He was disgracefully expelled from the temple by the priests and lived in a separate house until the day of his death (II Chron. XVI).

## CHAPTER XXII. Where he grants all the offerings of the children of Israel and the firstfruits to the priests and Levites
(SAME PLACE.) The Lord spoke to Aaron, saying: “Behold, I have given you charge of my firstfruits. Everything that is sanctified by the children of Israel I have given to you and to your sons, for the priestly office, as a perpetual ordinance, etc.”

The law commands that the firstfruits of all crops and of all livestock be offered to the priests, so that everyone who possesses a field, vineyard, olive grove, or even a garden, [Col. 0695C] and whatever else is cultivated on the land, as well as anyone who raises livestock of any kind, should offer to God from these whatever is first—that is, should bring it to the priests. For it says that what is given to the priests is offered to God.

This is also what we learn from the law: no one may lawfully or legitimately make use either of the fruits produced by the earth or of the animals brought forth by livestock, unless from each and every kind firstfruits—that is, offerings to the priests—are presented to God. I therefore think that this law must also be observed according to the letter, as must several others. For there are certain commandments of the law that even the disciples of the New Testament preserve with necessary observance.

And if it seems appropriate, let us first discuss those very matters that, although written in the law, are to be observed as though they were in the Gospels. When these have become clear, [Col. 0695D] we shall then inquire what ought also to be understood spiritually in them. There are some who say that, if anything at all is to be observed according to the letter, everything must nevertheless be discerned spiritually. We, however, moderating the presumption of both assertions, shall attempt to set forth from the authority of the divine Scriptures what rule ought to be observed in discussions of this kind concerning the law.

For it is written in the eighteenth Psalm: “The law of the Lord is blameless, converting souls; the testimony of the Lord is faithful, giving wisdom to the young. The commandment of the Lord is bright, enlightening the eyes. The fear of the Lord is holy, enduring forever and ever; the justifications of the Lord are right, gladdening hearts; the judgments are true, justified in themselves; more desirable than gold and a precious stone exceedingly, and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb” (Psalm 118). [Col. 0696A]

Now, if these several things were not each distinct from the others, divine Scripture would certainly never have assigned to each its own particular distinctions, so as to say one thing about the law of the Lord, another about the commandment, another about justifications, and another about judgments. Thus, as we have shown in these matters, the law is one thing, the commandment another, the testimony another, justification another, and judgment another.

The law itself also indicates a clearer distinction among these when it says: “This is the law, and the commandments, and the justifications, and the precepts, and the testimonies, and the judgments that the Lord commanded Moses.” Since, then, the testimonies of the law itself establish that these things are so and differ from one another by these distinctions, we must attend more carefully to what is recited from [Col. 0696B] the law. For whenever, for example, it is written that something is a commandment, it should not immediately be understood as the law. Likewise, wherever it is written, “These are the justifications,” they should not be taken as the law or as a commandment. Similarly, wherever testimonies or judgments are written, each should be understood as distinct from the others, not confused into one with the rest.

If, then, we read that “the law has a shadow of future good things” (Hebrews 10), should we immediately believe that the commandment, or the justifications, or the riches, concerning which this has not been written, are also shadows of future good things? To give one example among many, it is not written, “This is the commandment of the Passover,” but, “This is the law of the Passover” (Exodus 12). And because the law is a shadow of future good things, there is no doubt that the law of the Passover is a shadow of future good things. [Col. 0696C]

When, therefore, I come to that passage written about the Passover, in that carnal sheep I must understand a shadow of the future good and perceive that “Christ our Passover has been sacrificed.” In the same way, you will find that the unleavened bread and the observances of the other feast days are also written about in this manner. Since all these things are written in the law under the title of “law,” and since the law signifies future good things through a present shadow, I must ask what the unleavened bread of future good things is. I find the Apostle saying to me that we should keep the feast “not with the old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” (1 Corinthians 5).

Circumcision, too, is written of as follows: “This is the law of circumcision” (Genesis 17). Since circumcision is therefore reckoned under the title of law, while the law is a shadow, I ask what the shadow of circumcision contains of future good things, lest Paul say to me, while I am placed within the shadow of circumcision: “If you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing.” For “that circumcision which is outward in the flesh is not circumcision”; nor is the one who is outwardly a Jew in the flesh a Jew, “but he who is a Jew inwardly,” and “circumcision is of the heart, in the spirit and not in the letter, whose praise is not from human beings but from God” (Galatians 5). [Col. 0696D]

You will therefore find that nearly all these individual things, which he says are by no means to be observed entirely according to the letter, are designated by Moses under the title of law.

But where he says, “You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal,” and so forth (Exodus 20), we do not find that he prefaced these with the title of “law”; rather, they appear to be commandments. Therefore, among the disciples in the Gospel, this Scripture is not abolished but fulfilled, because, as I have said, it is not the commandment but the law that is said to have the shadow of future good things. Consequently, these commandments must be kept by us according to the letter. [Col. 0697A]

Likewise, elsewhere: “Justly pursue what is just” (Deuteronomy 16). Why should we seek an allegory in these matters, when the letter itself also builds up? We have therefore shown that there are certain things that absolutely are not to be observed according to the letter of the law, and also certain things that must not be altered at all through allegory, but must be observed in every respect as the Scriptures contain them.

Now I ask whether there are any things that can indeed stand according to the letter, but in which an allegory must nevertheless necessarily be sought. And see whether we can support this with apostolic and evangelical authority. [Col. 0697B]

For it is written in the law: “For this reason a man shall leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh” (Genesis 2). That these words contain allegorical mysteries, Paul declares when, having used this very example in his Epistle, he says: “This mystery is great, but I speak with reference to Christ and the Church” (Ephesians 5).

That this must also be observed according to the letter, the Lord and Savior himself teaches when he says: “It is written: For this reason a man shall leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh. What God has joined, let no human being separate” (Matthew 19). By saying, “What God has joined, let no human being separate,” he plainly declares that these things must also be observed according to the letter. [Col. 0697C]

In another Epistle, when he says that Abraham had two sons, one by a slave woman and one by a free woman (Galatians 4), who can doubt that these things must stand according to the letter? For it is certain that Isaac, from Sarah, and Ishmael, from Hagar, were Abraham’s sons. Yet the Apostle adds to this and says: “These things are allegorical,” and he turns them toward the two covenants. He calls the offspring of Sarah, as of one who gives birth in freedom, the children of the New Testament; but the offspring of Hagar, as of one who gives birth in slavery, he calls the children of the earthly Jerusalem.

We have shown, I think, from the authority of divine Scripture, that among the things written in the law some must be wholly rejected and avoided, lest they be observed according to the letter by the disciples of the Gospel; while others must be retained in every respect as they are written. Still others possess a truth according to the letter itself, yet usefully receive, as necessary, an allegorical meaning as well. [Col. 0697D]

Thus it will be the task of a wise and learned scribe, instructed concerning the kingdom of God, who knows how to bring forth new and old things from his treasures, to know how, in each passage of Scripture, either to reject entirely the letter that kills and seek the spirit that gives life, or to confirm it in every respect and prove the teaching of the letter useful or necessary, or, while the history remains, to introduce the mystical meaning appropriately and fittingly. I think this is also suitable in the discussion we now have in hand.

For it is fitting and useful that firstfruits also be offered to the priests of the Gospel. Thus the Lord ordained that those who proclaim the Gospel should live from the Gospel, and that those who serve at the altar should share in the altar. [Col. 0698A]

And just as this is fitting and worthy, so, conversely, it is unfitting and unworthy—indeed impious—that someone who worships God and enters the Church of God, who knows that priests and teachers stand at God’s altar and serve either the word of God or the Church, should not offer firstfruits to the priests from the fruits of the earth that God has given by bringing forth his sun and providing his rains.

Such a soul does not seem to me to have remembrance of God, nor to think or believe that God gave the fruits it has gathered, since it stores them away as though they were alien to God. For if it believed that they had been given to it by God, it would certainly know, by counting the priests, to honor God with his gifts and offerings.

And, so that the very words of the Lord may teach us more fully that these things must also be observed according to the letter, we shall add the following. The Lord says in the Gospels: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who tithe”—that is, who give tithes of mint, dill, and cinnamon—“and neglect the weightier matters of the law. Hypocrites, these things ought to have been done, and those not omitted” (Matthew 23). [Col. 0698B]

Consider, therefore, more carefully how the Lord’s discourse wants the weightier matters of the law to be done in every respect, yet does not want those things that are designated according to the letter to be omitted.

But the firstfruits that the children of Israel vowed and offered, he gave to you and to your sons and daughters as a perpetual right. Everyone who is clean in your household shall eat them. All the best of the oil, wine, and grain, whatever firstfruits they offer to the Lord, I have given to you. All the firstfruits of the produce that the soil brings forth and that are brought to the Lord [Col. 0698C] shall pass into your uses, and so forth.

This, however, must necessarily be pointed out: the word “law” is used in two ways. In general, all these things—that is, commandments, justifications, precepts, testimonies, and judgments—are called “law.” In a special sense, however, some particular part of what is written in the law is called “law,” as are the matters about which we discussed above.

The general law is signified, for example, when it is said of the Savior that he did not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it (Matthew 5). Likewise, elsewhere: “The fullness of the law is love” (Romans 13). In this statement he plainly called everything written in the law, taken together, “the law.”

We have said this while asserting that the commandment concerning the firstfruits of crops or livestock must also stand according to the letter. Now let us see how it also receives an allegorical—that is, spiritual—understanding. [Col. 0698D]

Let us ask whether, apart from the matters mentioned above, we find the firstfruits named anywhere in the Scriptures. For he did not say: “All the firstfruits of oil, wine, and grain—the firstfruits of all these things that are offered to God—you shall dedicate to me.” I therefore now ask where firstfruits are named apart from these.

If all firstfruits belong to the high priest, then we must necessarily also seek the high priest to whom those firstfruits ought to belong that we find mentioned in other passages of Scripture. First of all, we read that the Lord Christ himself is “the firstfruits of the dead” (1 Corinthians 15). He too, then, is firstfruits in some respect.

Again, we find the Apostle saying of certain people that they are the firstfruits of Asia, and of others that they are the firstfruits of Achaia (1 Corinthians 16). It follows, therefore, that in the several churches certain believers whom the apostolic spirit has approved are called firstfruits. [Col. 0699A]

Among these, I think, is that Cornelius who, together with those of the Caesarean church with whom he was worthy to receive the Holy Spirit, may rightly be called firstfruits (Acts 10). Indeed, Cornelius may perhaps be called not only the firstfruits of that church but also of all the nations. For he was the first among the Gentiles to believe and the first to be filled with the Holy Spirit; therefore he will rightly be called the firstfruits of the nations.

But perhaps you will ask who offers these firstfruits to God, or who the high priest is to whom they belong by right. I think that, according to the Lord’s word, the field is called “this world.” The field of the earth, however, should be understood not only as the soil but also as human hearts, which the angels of God have undertaken to cultivate (Matthew 13). [Col. 0699B]

They themselves therefore possess and hold the fruits of their cultivation—namely, those who labor under stewards and managers and have not yet reached the summit of perfection. But if some people’s hearts have been carefully cultivated and brought to perfection, they offer these, as chosen and distinguished from the rest, as firstfruits to the great high priest.

We may therefore say that perhaps in the future, when all the fruits are gathered into the threshing floor, some will be the portion of Christ the high priest, and others will be the portion of the Levites, as we said above, or will be set apart for angels or heavenly powers. I think, however, that some will be the portion of human beings—namely, those who in this life were prudent and faithful stewards of the word of God. [Col. 0699C]

For I think this is signified by the Lord in the Gospels when he says to the one to whom he had entrusted five minas and who had made ten from them: “Have authority over ten cities” (Luke 19). To the one to whom he had entrusted one and who had made five from it, he says: “Have authority over five cities.” For what authority over cities is to be understood here except the governance of souls?

“All the firstfruits of the sanctuary that the children of Israel offer to the Lord, I have given to you and to your sons and daughters as a perpetual right.” [Col. 0699D]

Therefore, from all sanctified fruits, holy firstfruits must be offered to the spiritual high priest. Concerning the spiritual firstfruits that we offer, hear what fruits the Apostle enumerates: “The fruit of the Spirit,” he says, “is love, joy, peace, patience,” and so forth (Galatians 5).

What firstfruits, then, shall I offer to the true high priest from the fruit of love, which is the first fruit of the Spirit? I think they are these firstfruits of love: that I should love the Lord my God with all my heart, with all my soul, and with all my mind. These are the firstfruits.

What, then, is the second thing that we ought to have from this fruit of love? That I should love my neighbor as myself. Those firstfruits of love are offered to God through the high priest; these, which come second, are left for my own uses.

I think there is still something from this fruit that should be held in third place: that I should also love my enemies. In the same way, one can find similar firstfruits among the other fruits of the Spirit.

Joy is described as the second fruit of the Spirit. [Col. 0700A] If, then, I rejoice in the Lord, rejoice in hope, and, having suffered injury, rejoice for the name of the Lord—in all these things and others like them I have offered to God, through the true high priest, the firstfruits of joy.

If I bear with joy the seizure of my possessions, and if I endure with joy tribulations, poverty, or any kind of insult, this too is for me a fruit of joy, in second place among the fruits of the Spirit.

But if I rejoice over worldly matters, honors, or riches, these are false joys arising from vanities of vanities. If, however, I rejoice in evils and exult in the downfall of others, these are not merely empty but diabolical joys; indeed, they should not be called joys at all. “There is no rejoicing for the wicked,” says the Lord (Isaiah 57). What follows.

[Col. 0700B] “It is an everlasting covenant of salt before the Lord, for you and for your sons.”

He calls the totality of the offerings that belonged to the ministry or the right of the priests “the covenant of salt.” Hence what is written in Leviticus: “Whatever sacrifice you offer, you shall season with salt; and you shall not remove the salt of the covenant of your God from your sacrifice. In every offering you shall offer salt” (Leviticus 2).

Figuratively, however, this shows that wisdom properly belongs to priests and to preachers of the divine law. God does not want us to use merely external wisdom, but apostolic wisdom, concerning which Paul says: “We speak wisdom among the mature”—not the wisdom of this world, nor of the rulers of this world, who are being destroyed, but “we speak God’s wisdom in a mystery, hidden, which God predestined before the ages for our glory” [Col. 0700C] (1 Corinthians 2).

And from where is it certain that he used salt for apostolic knowledge? The Lord clearly shows this to us when he says to the apostles: “You are the salt of the earth. But if the salt has lost its savor, it is good for nothing from then on, except to be thrown outside and trampled by people” (Matthew 5).

He therefore called salt apostolic wisdom because, just as every food suitable for nourishment is seasoned in every respect with salt, so every useful discourse for seeing necessarily possesses, in every respect, the seasoning of apostolic wisdom.

Thus, for Aaron and his sons, the covenant of salt is everlasting, because wisdom is necessary not only for the first rank of the Church, held by bishops, but also for the other lower ranks—namely, priests, deacons, and the entire ecclesiastical order.

And this is “before the Lord,” because heavenly wisdom must be loved, learned, and taught pure and without any admixture of cunning or malice. For the wisdom of this age is hostile to God; it always loves boastfulness and empty disputes. [Col. 0700D]

Therefore the Apostle James, in his Epistle written to the dispersed, forbidding quarrels and disputes, says: “If you have bitter jealousy and disputes in your hearts, do not boast and be liars against the truth. This is not the wisdom descending from above, from the Father of lights, but earthly, natural, demonic. For where jealousy and dispute are, there are instability and every evil work. But the wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, compliant, agreeing with what is good, full of mercy and good fruits, judging without hypocrisy. The fruit of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace” (James 3). [Col. 0701A]

## CHAPTER XXIII. On tithes being given for the use of the Levites.

(SAME PLACE.) And the Lord said to Aaron: “You shall possess nothing in their land, nor shall you have a share among them. I am your share and inheritance in the midst of the children of Israel. To the children of Levi I have given all the tithes of Israel as a possession, for the ministry by which they served me in the tent of the covenant, so that the children of Israel may no longer approach the tabernacle, nor incur a deadly sin, while only the children of Levi serve in the tabernacle and bear the sins of the people. It shall be a perpetual ordinance throughout your generations.

“They shall possess nothing else, content with the offering of tithes, which I have set apart for their use and necessities.” [Col. 0701B]

In both the Old and the New Testament, the ministers of the altar and the servants of the temple of the Lord are commanded to receive sustenance from the generosity of offerings and the giving of tithes; nor are they permitted in any way to aspire to acquire earthly possessions.

Therefore, in the Gospel, the Lord commanded the apostles and preachers of the Gospel, saying: “Go and preach, saying, ‘The kingdom of heaven is near.’ Heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse lepers, cast out demons. You have received freely; give freely. Do not possess gold, nor silver, nor money in your belts; no bag for the road, nor two tunics, nor sandals, nor a staff. For the laborer is worthy of his food” (Matthew 10).

Hence also Paul, speaking to the Corinthians, says: “Do you not know that those who work in the sanctuary eat the things that are of the sanctuary? Those who serve at the altar share with the altar” (1 Corinthians 9). Thus the Lord also ordained that those who proclaim the Gospel should live from the Gospel. [Col. 0701C]

Hence also, writing to Timothy, he says: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in worldly business, so that he may please the one to whom he has proved himself. And he who competes in the contest is not crowned unless he has competed lawfully. The farmer who labors must first partake of the fruits of the earth” (2 Timothy 2).

For it is not fitting that the one who ought always to stand at the divine service should be occupied in acquiring earthly profit.

If anyone asks what the tithes signify mystically, let him know that in them one may understand either observance of the law, or the integrity of the Catholic faith, or the perfection of good works. This especially befits those who ought to offer special service to God according to the election by which they were chosen for divine ministry. [Col. 0701D]

For in the number ten, knowledge of creation and of the Creator is comprehended, because the number seven refers to eternal nature, while the three signify the power of the soul. Hence it is also written in Deuteronomy: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your strength” (Deuteronomy 6). The body, however, consists of the four most familiar elements. Therefore, if you add to the number seven the number three, which expresses faith in and confession of the holy Trinity, you will properly complete the number ten.

[Col. 0702A] The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “Command the Levites and announce to them: When you receive from the children of Israel the tithes that I have given you, offer their firstfruits to the Lord—that is, a tenth part of the tithe—so that it may be reckoned to you as an offering of firstfruits. From the threshing floors as well as from the winepresses, and from everything whose firstfruits you receive, offer to the Lord and give them to Aaron the priest,” and so forth.

In allegorical exposition, I think this can be understood as follows: if someone distributes to the needy or performs some good work, he has offered a gift to God in obedience to the commandment. But he offers the firstfruits of this gift if he not only gives food, for example, or money, but also has an attitude of mercy and compassion.

For this is what God requires from a human being: that the mind itself be filled and formed with pious and merciful affections, and that firstfruits be offered from all their sacrifices. Spiritual sacrifice is the one of which we read: “Offer to God a sacrifice of praise, and pay your vows to the Most High” (Psalm 49). To praise God and offer vows of prayer is to sacrifice to God.

But the firstfruits of such a sacrifice will be offered through the high priest if we pray not only with words and voice but also with the mind and heart. As Paul also admonishes: “I will pray with the spirit; I will pray also with the mind” (1 Corinthians 14). “I will sing a psalm with the spirit; I will sing a psalm also with the mind.”

For even now the angels of God, the cultivators and farmers of our heart, stand by and inquire whether in any one of us there is a mind so attentive that it has received the word of God as a divine seed with complete eagerness; whether, as soon as we rise for prayer, it has displayed fruit—that is, whether, having gathered and collected its senses within itself, it prays to God, or whether it wanders in mind and flies away in its thoughts, so that while the body is bent in prayer, the senses run in different directions. [Col. 0702B]

If anyone, I say, understands himself to be present in such earnest and directed supplication, and to stand in the very sight and presence of that ineffable light, and there pours out his prayers, supplications, petitions, and thanksgivings, undistracted by any external image of fantasy, let him know that through the angel who stands at the altar he has offered the firstfruits of his sacrifice to the great and true high priest, Christ Jesus our Lord. [Col. 0702C]

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the red heifer and its ceremonies, and on the purifications made from its ashes.

[Col. 0702D] **(CHAP. XIX.)** And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying:

“This is the rite of the sacrifice which the Lord has appointed. Command the children of Israel to bring you a red heifer, sound and without blemish, which has never borne a yoke. You shall hand it over to Eleazar the priest, who, after it has been led outside the camp, shall slaughter it in the sight of all. Dipping his finger in its blood, he shall sprinkle it seven times toward the entrance of the tabernacle, and he shall burn it while all look on. Its flesh, hide, blood, and dung having been committed to the flames, the priest shall also cast cedar wood, hyssop, and scarlet twice-dyed into the fire that consumes the heifer. Then, after washing his garments and his body, he shall enter the camp; but he shall be unclean until evening. The man who has burned it shall also wash his garments and his body, and he shall be unclean until evening. A clean man shall gather the ashes of the heifer and pour them outside the camp in a very clean place, so that they may be kept for the congregation of the children of Israel, for the water of sprinkling, because the heifer was burned for sin.”

Strength is usually signified by the masculine gender, weakness by the feminine. What, then, is represented by the heifer except the weakness of the Lord’s assumed incarnation, taken for sacrifice? Of this it is written: “Though he was crucified in weakness, yet he lives by the power of God” (II Cor. XIII).

This heifer is rightly also called red, since his humanity was reddened by the blood of his passion. Hence in the Song of Songs the bride describes him, saying: “My beloved is white and ruddy” [Col. 0703B] (Cant. V): white, clearly, through his divinity; ruddy through his blood; white through the justice of his life; ruddy through the blood of his passion.

“Sound in age, in which there is no blemish.” The age of God’s humanity is sound, and all his work is perfect. In that humanity there was no blemish, for it is truly written of him: “He committed no sin, neither was deceit found in his mouth” (Isa. XXXV).

It is rightly added: “Nor has it borne a yoke.” For it is written: “Everyone who sins is the slave of sin” (John VIII). Since, therefore, the Lord submitted to no sin, he bore no yoke.

It follows: “You shall hand it over to Eleazar the priest, who, after it has been led outside the camp, shall slaughter it in the sight of the Lord.” Why is this heifer handed over to the priest for slaughter except because the incarnate Lord, [Col. 0703C] who made himself a sacrifice for our redemption, is delivered into the hands of the people in the judgment, and was also slaughtered outside the camp in the sight of the Lord, since he suffered outside the gate? Hence the apostle Paul says: “Jesus, in order to sanctify the people through his own blood, suffered outside the gate” (Hebr. XIII). Let us therefore go out to him outside the camp, bearing his reproach. For we have no abiding city here, but we seek the one that is to come.

He suffered outside the gate in order to lead us out from the manner of life of the present age, as from a city, and to persuade us to tear our hearts away from earthly dwelling.

It is rightly said that “he shall slaughter it in the sight of the Lord.” Our Redeemer was, as it were, extinguished in the sight of human beings, [Col. 0703D] but is sacrificed in the sight of the Father, because what was punishment before the eyes of human beings was sacrifice before the eyes of the Father.

“And he shall dip his finger in the blood.” What is signified by the finger except the discernment of our activity? To dip one’s finger in the heifer’s blood, therefore, is to consecrate our works in the passion of the Lord’s incarnation, so that we may imitate the passion which we acknowledge, as it is written: “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you should follow in his footsteps.”

Thus Eleazar the priest both slaughters and dips his finger in the blood, because the Jewish people, on the side of the reprobate, persecuted the Lord’s humility even to his passion, while, on the side of the elect, it imitated the activity of his humility.

“And he shall sprinkle toward the entrance of the tabernacle.” What, then, is meant here by the tabernacle except the whole synagogue together? Whoever has dipped his finger in his blood should sprinkle that same blood toward the entrance of the tabernacle—that is, whoever imitates the ways of his passion should offer to the unbelieving and contradicting synagogue, through good examples and upright preaching, a sign of right living.

To sprinkle the heifer’s blood toward the entrance of the tabernacle is to display, through upright preaching and holy works, the examples of his passion to the resisting Jewish people.

It is rightly said that the finger is to be dipped and the blood sprinkled seven times. In the number seven perfection is understood. Hence the whole of time is completed in seven days, and the Holy Spirit is called sevenfold [Col. 0704B]. To dip the finger in his blood seven times, therefore, is to imitate the mystery of his passion through perfect action. To sprinkle seven times against the synagogue is to proclaim, through perfect preaching, the sacraments of his incarnation and passion to unbelievers.

“And he shall burn it outside the camp while all look on, its hide and flesh, its blood and dung having been committed to the flames.” What are signified by the flesh and hide, by the blood and dung of the heifer, except the carnal sacrifices contained in the Old Testament, which proclaimed the Lord’s weakness? Once these had later been understood spiritually by the Fathers, they were called dung in respect of the outward ministry. Hence Paul, speaking of carnal sacrifices, says: “Because of these things I suffered the loss of them all, and count them as dung” (Phil. III).

They are committed to the flames because, although they were first offered in a carnal manner, they were afterward consumed by the fire of understanding through the Holy Spirit.

Nevertheless, in the same heifer—that is, in the very weakness of the Lord’s incarnation—we can understand the flesh, hide, blood, and dung as representing individual works. What is signified by the flesh and hide except his external works? What by the blood except the subtlety and inward power that gives life to his external deeds? What by the dung except weariness, thirst, hunger, fear of death, and everything else which he chose to endure from the human condition? Whatever he possessed as a result of the defect of our mortality had, as it were, to be cast away as dung.

Yet all these things which he assumed from weakness, because he offered them for our redemption, are to be consumed by fire—that is, understood according to the power of the Holy Spirit—so that whatever he did bodily may be recognized as ordered through the incorporeal Spirit of his divinity.

Hence it is fittingly added: “The priest shall also cast cedar wood, hyssop, and scarlet twice-dyed into the fire that consumes the heifer.”

Cedar is both a lofty and incorruptible wood. Hyssop, however, is a very humble herb which nevertheless removes the inflation of the lungs. What is signified by the cedar except lofty and persevering contemplation? What by the hyssop except the humility of a gentle heart? Whoever is already lifted toward heavenly things through lofty contemplation must necessarily descend through the compassion of humility to those below, and must not exalt himself because of what he possesses, but freely impart by preaching whatever he has even to those who do not possess it.

What, then, is expressed by the scarlet twice-dyed except the virtue of charity? It is called twice-dyed scarlet because charity, kindled by the flame of holy love, is commanded to be displayed in two precepts: love of God and love of neighbor. Twice-dyed scarlet, therefore, is charity formed by the double commandment: God must be loved in such a way that one does not abandon one’s neighbor, and one’s neighbor must be loved in such a way that one does not despise God.

Into this flame that consumes the heifer the priest casts cedar, hyssop, and twice-dyed scarlet. For all who believe in Christ are priests. Hence it is written: “You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood” (I Pet. II).

Whatever we understand through lofty contemplation, whatever we display through the gentleness of humility, whatever we offer through the fire of charity, we must immerse in the spirit of the Lord’s passion, so that everything within us may imitate him from whom it comes. For if we do anything apart from imitation of his passion, we perform not so much a virtue as a vice.

Let the cedar, therefore, be cast into the flame that consumes the heifer—that is, let the perseverance and loftiness of our contemplation be burned by the fire of the Lord’s passion. Let the hyssop be cast into that flame—that is, let the truth of the humility of our hearts derive gentleness from participation in the Lord’s passion. Let the twice-dyed scarlet be cast into that flame—that is, let charity, which arouses us to love God and neighbor, compel us continually to contemplate the Lord’s passion, so that in it we may learn the right works we ought to perform.

This may also be understood in another way: by the cedar is signified hope, which seeks what is high; by the hyssop—which by its heat also cleanses the stomach of uncleanness—is signified faith, which patiently endures adversity in lowly circumstances, so that it may cleanse what had been contracted from former sins. By the scarlet, as has been said, charity is expressed.

Let each one of us, therefore, cast cedar, hyssop, and twice-dyed scarlet into the flame that consumes the heifer—that is, let us offer hope, faith, and charity in the sacrifice of the Lord’s passion—lest we hear of the passion of our Redeemer to no purpose unless we also necessarily add these works to it.

Of these three the apostle Paul says: “But now faith, hope, and charity remain; but the greatest of these is charity” (I Cor. XIII). Hence the scarlet is placed last, because when faith and hope have been completed and we come to our eternal homeland, only charity will finally be increased in us.

This priest, or the man who burns the heifer’s flesh, hide, blood, and dung, may signify the order of the Jewish priesthood together with the people who joined in the Lord’s death. Hence what follows is also fittingly added:

“And then, after washing his garments and his body, he shall return to the camp, but he shall be unclean until evening.”

What do we understand by evening except the end of the world? This priest, or the one who commits the heifer to the fire—that is, the Jewish people—is unclean until evening, because it remains unbelieving until the end of the world.

But after washing his garments and body, he enters the camp at evening, because when the end of the world comes, after the works of its unbelief have been cleansed, the Jewish people also returns to the knowledge of its Creator, as it is written: “Though the number of the children of Israel be as the sand of the sea, a remnant shall be saved” (Rom. IX). And again it is written: “Until the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, and so all Israel shall be saved” (Rom. XI).

At evening, therefore, after washing his garments, the priest returns within the camp; he who was unclean before evening does so because the unbelieving Jewish people remains until the end of the world outside the commandments of life, as though outside the camp, defiled by evil works.

But when it is washed with the water of baptism and repentance, then at evening—that is, at the end of the world—it returns to the knowledge of faith, as though into the camp.

It may also be understood that this priest is said to have washed his garments and yet to be unclean until evening because the same Jewish people, on the side of those who have believed, has already washed its garments, but on the side of those who have not yet believed it remains unclean until evening.

He washes his garments and body who, by believing, cleanses both his external works and his inward mind from evil actions. He then fully returns to the camp when he is perfectly recalled to the faith.

But because, while Judaea persists in unbelief and in the portion of the reprobate, the Gentile enters into faith and understands the mysteries of the divine incarnation, it is rightly added there:

“A clean man shall gather the ashes of the heifer”—that is, the Gentile people, already cleansed by faith. Hence it is written: “Cleansing their hearts by faith” [Col. 0706C] (Acts XV).

He gathers the ashes of the heifer who recognizes the subtle mysteries of the divine incarnation. The clean man gathers the ashes of the heifer which the priest burned because the Gentile people understands the most subtle mysteries of the Lord’s weakness, which the Jewish people slaughtered in his death.

It is rightly continued: “And he shall pour them in a very clean place outside the camp,” because the same Gentile people, which recognizes the hidden things and mysteries of the divine incarnation, does not cease to preach the good things it has received, so that what it has itself learned may become known even to others who do not know it.

But because the hidden things and mysteries of the Lord’s incarnation are not to be entrusted to wicked and polluted hands, it is rightly said: “He shall pour them in a very clean place outside the camp.”

All the Gentiles had been outside the camp, because they were outside the law, outside the sacrifice, and outside the synagogue. Yet, when it came to faith, it cleansed its heart, and the ashes of the heifer are poured into it, because the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation is entrusted to the clean heart of the Gentiles.

Many converts from the Gentiles became preachers and handed over the mysteries to the same Gentiles who were coming to faith in the Redeemer.

Thus the clean man pours the ashes of the heifer in a very clean place when any teacher taken from the Gentiles seeks hearts of the Gentiles cleansed through humility and does not cease to hand over to them the mysteries of our Redeemer.

When this is done, the faith of the Gentiles increases, divine power is acknowledged, and the discipline of the commandments is maintained. Hence it is rightly added:

“So that they may be kept for the congregation of the children of Israel.” [Col. 0707A]

Israel is interpreted as “seeing God.” The converted Gentiles are not inappropriately called Israel, since they now contemplate God through faith.

These ashes, therefore, become a safeguard for the congregation of the children of Israel, because the subtle sacraments entrusted to the clean hearts of the Gentiles are transformed into a fortification of the mind.

It is rightly added: “And for the water of sprinkling.” Because of action, the ashes are kept for our protection; because of baptism, we use the ashes in the water of sprinkling, so that, while we consider his works and bring our own deeds under discipline, we may preserve the ashes of the heifer as our safeguard. By attending through imitation to the hidden and subtle operation of the Lord, we provide ourselves through it with both purity and perseverance.

It is fittingly added: “Because the heifer was burned for sin.” We then carefully guard our protection when we attentively consider that our Redeemer suffered for our sins. We weigh what he repays to the good, since he chose to die for the wicked. We weigh what grace we owe, having been brought to the justice of faith, since even while placed in sins we received the intercession of his death.

The ashes become a safeguard because the heifer was burned for sin: as we attentively contemplate the mysteries of his passion, we learn what works we ought to perform, since we know that our Redeemer died even for us, the unrighteous.

In a moral sense, we slaughter the heifer when we extinguish the flesh's wantonness of pleasure. We offer it with hyssop, cedar wood, and scarlet when, together with the mortification of the flesh, we burn the sacrifice of faith, hope, and charity.

Whoever has offered himself as a sacrifice to God, if he desires perfection, must take care to extend himself not only to the breadth of action but also to the heights of contemplation.

Meanwhile, it must be known above all that the temperaments of souls are greatly different from one another. Some people are so sluggish in mind that if the burden of occupation overtakes them, they collapse amid the very work itself. Others are so restless that if they are given relief from labor, they suffer more grievously, because they endure the tumult of the heart more intensely the more freely they are idle in thought.

Therefore a tranquil mind must not stretch itself toward an immoderate exercise of work, nor must a restless mind constrict itself toward the pursuit of contemplation. Often those who could contemplate God in quiet have fallen under the pressure of occupations; and often those who would have lived well while occupied in human affairs have been destroyed by the sword of their own leisure.

For this reason some restless spirits, while seeking through contemplation more than they can contain, break out into perverse doctrines. And while they neglect humbly to be disciples of the truth, they become teachers of errors.

“They shall have this, both the children of Israel and the resident aliens who dwell among them, as a sacred right forever.” And he says: “It shall be an everlasting ordinance for the children of Israel and for the proselytes who are joined to them.”

What else does this show except the baptism of Christ, which the water of sprinkling signified and which was destined to benefit both Jews and Gentiles—that is, the children of Israel as natural branches, and the proselyte grafted into the richness of the root as a wild olive?

Who would not be made attentive by the fact that after the washing of each person it is said: “And he shall be unclean until evening”? This is not said only here but in all such purifications.

Here I do not know whether anything else can be understood except that every human being, after the fullest remission of sins, contracts something by remaining in this life through which he is unclean until the end of that same life, when this day is, in a certain sense, closed—something signified by evening.

Then Scripture begins to explain how people who have become unclean are purified by that water of sprinkling.

“Whoever touches the corpse of a human being and is unclean for this reason for seven days shall be sprinkled with this water on the third and seventh days, and so he shall be cleansed. If he is not sprinkled on the third day, he cannot be cleansed on the seventh. Everyone who touches the corpse of a human soul and is not sprinkled with this mixture defiles the tabernacle of the Lord and shall perish from Israel, because he has not been sprinkled with the water of purification. He shall be unclean, and his uncleanness shall remain upon him,” and so forth.

“Whoever touches,” he says, “the dead, every human soul shall be unclean for seven days. He shall be purified on the third day and on the seventh, and he shall be unclean.”

Here I see nothing else to understand except that contact with a dead person signifies human iniquity. I think the uncleanness of seven days is spoken of on account of soul and body: the soul in the number three, the body in the number four. In accordance with this, I think the prophet said: “For three transgressions and for four I will not revoke it.”

He adds and says: “But if he is not purified on the third day and on the seventh, he shall not be clean. Whoever touches any dead human soul and is not purified on the fourth day and on the seventh”—that is, if he dies before he has been purified after touching the dead—“defiles the tabernacle of the Lord; that soul shall be cut off from Israel.”

It should be noted that in these books it is very difficult to find anything more explicit written about the life of the soul after death.

“He shall be purified on the seventh day, and he shall wash his garments and bathe in water, and he shall be unclean until evening.”

The water of sprinkling is one kind of water, and the water with which he washes his garments is evidently another. “And he shall bathe in water,” which I think is to be understood spiritually by signification, not according to its literal nature.

For without doubt it was visible, like all those shadows of things to come. Accordingly, whoever is rightly washed by the sacrament of baptism—which that water of sprinkling prefigured—is cleansed spiritually, that is, invisibly, in flesh and soul, so that he may be clean both in body and in spirit.

“A vessel that has no covering or binding over it shall be unclean.” The covering of the lid or the binding signifies the restraint of discipline, because whoever is not held in check is rejected as an unclean and polluted vessel.

Just as a vessel without a covering or binding becomes polluted, so the person who lies open through pursuits of self-display is polluted when he is covered by no veil of silence.

“If anyone in the field touches the corpse of a slain man or of one who died naturally, or a human bone or a tomb, he shall be unclean for seven days.”

According to another edition it is read as follows: “Everyone who touches on the surface of the field one wounded or dead, or a human bone or a monument.”

It may be asked why it says “wounded or dead.” If it wished to understand “wounded” or “dead” as two different things, care must be taken lest it be thought that even someone who touches a wounded living person is unclean, which is certainly absurd.

But since the dead can also be wounded, it is understood to have decreed that we should understand “wounded dead”: that is, one killed by a wound, or one dead without a wound.

“They shall take some of the ashes of the burning of the sin offering and pour living water over them in a vessel. A clean man shall dip hyssop in it and sprinkle it over the tent, all its furnishings, and the people polluted by such contamination. In this way the clean man shall purify the unclean on the third and seventh days. After he has been purified on the seventh day, he shall wash himself and his garments, and he shall be unclean until evening,” and so forth.

Since he says that the water of sprinkling is to be sprinkled with hyssop—and we have said above that this herb signifies faith—what else comes to mind except what is written: “Cleansing their hearts by faith”? Baptism is of no benefit if faith is absent (Acts XV).

He said that this was to be done by a clean man, signifying ministers who bear the person of their Lord, who is truly a clean man. Of these ministers he says in what follows: “And the one who sprinkles the water of sprinkling shall wash his garments,” that is, he shall attend also to his body; “and whoever touches the water of sprinkling shall be unclean until evening. Everything that the unclean man touches shall be unclean, and the soul that touches him shall be unclean until evening.”

**CHAPTER XXV. On the Israelites’ rebellion at the water of contradiction.**

**(CHAP. XX.)** The children of Israel and the whole congregation came into the desert of Zin in the first month, and the people remained at Kadesh. Miriam died there and was buried in the same place.

When the people lacked water, they gathered against Moses and Aaron and turned to rebellion, saying: “Would that we had perished among our brothers before the Lord! Why have you brought the assembly of the Lord into this wilderness, so that both we and our cattle may die? Why have you made us come up from Egypt and brought us to this most wretched place, where nothing can be sown, which produces neither figs, vines, nor pomegranates? Moreover, it has no water to drink.” [Col. 0709D]

Moses and Aaron entered the tabernacle of the covenant, leaving the congregation, and fell prostrate on the ground. The glory of the Lord appeared over them, and so forth.

The thirty-third encampment is in the desert of Zin; this is Kadesh. *Sin* is interpreted as “holy,” by the figure of antiphrasis, as with *lucus* (“grove”), when it does not shine at all, and *bellum* (“war”), although it is dreadful.

At this encampment Miriam dies and is buried. In Miriam we may see prophecy having died; in Moses and Aaron, that an end was imposed upon the law and the Jewish priesthood: neither could they themselves cross over into the promised land, nor could they lead the believing people out of the wilderness of this age, except Jesus alone—that is, the Savior, the true Son of God.

At this encampment also Moses offended the Lord because of the water of contradiction and was forbidden to cross the Jordan. Disturbed by the murmuring of the people, he struck the rock uncertainly with the rod, as though God could not cause water to flow from the rock, although he had already done so.

What, then, does Moses’ faith suggest here, since he faltered about bringing water forth from the rock? We rightly understand this to have been a prophecy concerning Christ.

Although Moses assumes one person or another in the holy Scriptures to signify different things, at this point he represented the Jewish people placed under the law and temporarily prefigured it through prophetic utterance.

For just as Moses, striking the rock with the rod, doubted the power of God, so the people held under the law given through Moses, fastening Christ to the wood of the cross, did not believe that he was the power of God.

But just as the struck rock poured out water for the thirsty, so the wound of the Lord’s passion became life for believers. We have a most distinguished apostolic testimony concerning this, when he says: “The rock was Christ” (I Cor. X).

God therefore commands this carnal despair concerning Christ’s divinity to die upon Christ’s own height, when he commands Moses’ bodily death to take place on a mountain.

For just as Christ is the rock, so Christ is also the mountain. The rock is humble strength; the mountain is exalted greatness. For just as the Apostle says, “The rock was Christ,” so the Lord himself says: “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden,” asserting that he himself is the mountain and that his faithful, founded in the glory of his name, are the city.

The wisdom of the flesh lives when Christ’s humility is despised on the cross, as though the rock had been struck. “Christ crucified is a stumbling block to the Jews and foolishness to the Gentiles”; but the wisdom of the flesh dies when Christ is recognized as exalted, like the height of a mountain.

To those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God.

When Moses raised his hand and struck the rock twice with the rod, very abundant waters came forth, so that the people and the cattle could drink. *(From Augustine.)*

The spiritual grace flowing from Christ was therefore signified, by which the inner thirst was refreshed. But the striking of the rock with the rod signifies the cross of Christ. When wood approached the rock, grace flowed forth. And because the rock is struck here, it signifies the cross more clearly. For the cross consists of two pieces of wood. [Col. 0710D]

The Lord said to Moses and Aaron: “Because you did not believe me, so as to sanctify me before the children of Israel, you shall not bring this people into the land which I have given them.”

“This is the water of contradiction, where the children of Israel quarreled against the Lord, and he was sanctified among them.”

What is said of that water which flowed from the rock is this: “This is the water of contradiction, where the children of Israel quarreled against the Lord”; or, according to what is found in other copies, “the children of Israel cursed before the Lord, and he was sanctified among them.”

They first cursed when they spoke against the Lord’s benefaction by which they had been brought out of Egypt; afterward he was sanctified among them when his holiness was declared through the miracle of the flowing water.

Or perhaps he indicated two kinds of people: those who contradict the grace of God and those who receive the grace of Christ. For the former it is the water of contradiction; for the latter, the water of sanctification.

Of the Lord himself, too, it is read in the Gospel: “And for a sign that shall be contradicted” (Luke II).

**BOOK THREE**

[Col. 0711]

**CHAPTER ONE. On the Israelites’ journey from Kadesh to Mount Hor, and their battle and victory over the Canaanites.**

**(CHAP. XX.)** Meanwhile Moses sent messengers from Kadesh to the king of Edom, saying:

“This is what your brother Israel commands. You know all the hardship that has overtaken us: how our fathers went down into Egypt, how we lived there for a long time, how the Egyptians afflicted us and our fathers, and how we cried to the Lord and he heard us and sent an angel who brought us out of Egypt.

“Behold, we are stationed in the city of Kadesh, which is at the extremity of your borders. We beg you to allow us to pass through your land. We will not go through fields or vineyards; we will not drink water from your wells. We will travel by the public road until we have crossed your borders,” and so forth.

Among the commands Moses gave to the king of Edom, he says, among other things, “Nor will we drink water from the reservoir.” This is to be understood freely—that is, “we will not drink your water without payment.” He makes this clear later, saying: “But if I and my cattle drink your water, I will pay you for it.”

“We will not turn aside to the right or to the left.” It is expressed in the plural with respect to the things that are on the right or the things that are on the left.

When they had moved their camp from Kadesh, they came to Mount Hor, which is at the borders of the land of Edom. There the Lord spoke to Moses:

“Let Aaron go to his people. He shall not enter the land which I have given to the children of Israel, because he was unbelieving toward my word concerning the water of contradiction,” and so forth.

The thirty-fourth encampment is at Mount Hor, at the farthest borders of Edom. There Aaron ascended according to the Lord’s command and died in the fortieth year after the exodus from Egypt—that is, in the year in which the new people was about to enter the promised land.

Although on the mountain he left the priesthood to his son Eleazar, and although the law leads those who fulfill it to the summit, nevertheless that very height does not extend beyond the waters of the Jordan, but remains at the outer limits of earthly works.

The people mourned him for thirty days. Aaron is mourned; Jesus is not mourned. In the law there is descent to the underworld; in the Gospel there is migration to paradise.

**(CHAP. XXI.)** When the Canaanite king of Arad, who lived in the south, heard that Israel had come by the route of the explorers, he fought against them, prevailed, and took captives from them.

Israel then bound itself to the Lord by a vow and said: “If you deliver this people into my hand, I will destroy its cities.” The Lord heard Israel’s prayers and delivered the Canaanite into its hands. Israel killed him after overthrowing his cities and called the name of that place *Horma*, that is, “anathema.”
