*(From Augustine.)* Or, as it is read in other copies: “Israel vowed a vow to the Lord and said: If you deliver this people subject to me”—that is, “if you subject him so that he may be delivered to me”—“I will anathematize him and his cities.”

Here we must consider how what is vowed is called *anathema* and yet is used for a curse, as is also said concerning this people: “If anyone preaches to you a gospel contrary to what you received, let him be anathema” (Galat. III).

From this it has entered common usage that one is said to “devote” someone. For scarcely anyone says that he “devotes” another except when cursing him.

“And he anathematized him and his cities, and the name of that place was called anathema.” Hence there are two senses of *anathema*, so that something may appear detestable and abominable.

Since the victor was to carry nothing away from it for his own use, but was to vow the whole of it to punishment, this was to anathematize it, as it is commonly called, to devote it.

The origin of this word is in the Greek language, from things that had been vowed and discharged—that is, promised and given back—and were placed above in temples: **ἀπὸ τοῦ ἀναθέσθαι**, that is, “to place above,” either by fastening or by hanging.

The Canaanite also heard that Israel had come to the place of the explorers. There, where they knew that the people had once offended, they entered battle and took Israel captive.

Again battle is waged in the same place: the victor is defeated, and the defeated prevail. By this we understand that when enemies invade us after we have been deprived of God’s help and have led us captive, we should not despair of salvation but arm ourselves again for battle.

It can happen that we conquer where we were defeated and triumph in the very place in which we were captives.

**CHAPTER TWO. On their departure from Mount Hor, their weariness of the journey, and the people’s murmuring; why they were punished with fiery serpents and healed by the raising of a bronze serpent as a sign.**

**(IBID.)** The children of Israel set out from Mount Hor by the road leading to the Red Sea, in order to go around the land of Edom. The people began to grow weary of the journey and the hardship.

They spoke against God and Moses, saying: “Why have you brought us up from Egypt, so that we might die in the wilderness? There is no bread, there is no water, and our soul is already nauseated by this worthless food.”

Therefore the Lord sent fiery serpents among the people. When many had been wounded and had died from their bites, they came to Moses and said: “We have sinned, because we spoke against the Lord and against you. Pray that he may take the serpents away from us.”

Moses prayed for the people, and the Lord said to him: “Make a bronze serpent and set it up as a sign. Whoever has been bitten and looks upon it shall live.”

Moses therefore made a bronze serpent and set it up as a sign. When those who had been bitten looked upon it, they were healed.

The thirty-fifth encampment is at Zalmonah. The thirty-sixth encampment is at Punon. These two encampments are not found in the sequence of the historical narrative.

At them Aaron having died, the Israelite people murmurs against the Lord and Moses, grows weary of the manna, and is wounded by serpents.

But what does it signify that the deadly bites of the serpents were healed when the bronze serpent was lifted up and looked upon, except that now, in a type of the Savior who triumphed over the ancient and savage serpent on the gallows, the poisons of the devil are overcome, so that whoever has truly and clearly looked upon the image of the Son of God and his passion may be preserved?

This is also signified by the words of the Lord himself: “As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, that everyone who believes in him should not perish but have eternal life” (John III).

What, then, is the bronze serpent? The one who was himself suspended on the wood. Bronze is usually more durable than other metals. Fittingly, therefore, the bronze serpent was suspended on wood, so that the Lord might be signified as dead in the serpent and eternal in the bronze: dead, namely, through humility, yet like bronze, eternal through divinity.

Beautifully, too, the first encampment, Zalmonah, is interpreted as “low bonds,” because there the image of the Savior was expressed through the bronze serpent that hung upon the wood.

Likewise, the second, Punon, is beautifully interpreted as “mouth,” because after we recognize the passion of the Son of God, we proclaim with the mouth what we believe in the heart, reading the words of the apostle Paul: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. X).

Having set out, the sons of Israel encamped at Oboth. [Col. 0713C] The thirty-seventh station is at Oboth, which is rendered “magicians” or “Python-spirits.” From this it is shown that, after the image of God—which is manifested in the reasoning of the heart—and the confession of faith, which is uttered by the mouth, serpents arise, and magical arts provoke us to battle. But we, surrounding our heart with a guard, harden our ears lest we hear the voices of enchanters, and disregard the songs of the Sirens.

From there they departed and pitched their tents at Jeabarim, in the wilderness that faces Moab, opposite the eastern region. The thirty-eighth station is at Jeabarim, on the borders of Moab; it signifies “heaps of stones of those who are passing through,” that is, the saints who hasten through this age toward other stations. There are holy stones that roll over the earth—light, polished, and by their roundness resembling the courses of wheels. There are also others whom he commands to be removed from the road, lest the feet of those walking stumble over them. Who are these walkers? Certainly travelers and passers-by, who hasten through this age toward other stations.

But the statement that they were on the borders of Moab, and the earlier statement that they were in the wilderness facing Moab toward the sunrise, shows according to the literal sense that until this point they had been within the boundaries of the land of the Edomites, and now were coming to the borders of Moab, passing from one province to another. For one must not always devote oneself to a single virtue; rather, as it is written, “They will go from strength to strength” (Ps. LXXXIII), one must pass from one to another, because they cling to one another and are so interwoven that whoever lacks one lacks them all. Yet to pass from one to another belongs properly to those who contemplate the rising of the Sun of righteousness.

And from there they moved the camp and came to the torrent of Zared, and so forth. The thirty-ninth station was at Dibongad, as will be made clear in what follows, where the sequence of the stations is described. For Dibongad is interpreted as “a temptation understood with fortitude.” But in this place, in the order of the narrative, something else is found written. After they had encamped at Jeabarim, on the borders of Moab, opposite the sunrise, we read: “From there they departed and turned toward the torrent of Zared.” Departing from this place, they encamped beyond Arnon, which is in the wilderness of the borders of the Amorites, since Arnon lies [Col. 0714B] on the borders of the Moabites and the Amorites.

After this they came to the well, where Israel sang this song: “Rise up, well, which the princes dug, and which the leaders of the peoples opened, with the lawgiver and with his staff.” From the wilderness they went to Mattanah; from Mattanah to the torrent of God; from the torrents to the high places; from the high places to the valley that is in the region of Moab, at the summit of Phasga, which looks toward the wilderness.

Some interpreters, considering these places to be within the borders of the Amorites, think that they are not stations but passages, and that they ought not to prejudice the catalogue of stations by introducing them into the ordinary exposition. Others, comparing spiritual things with spiritual, do not want regions to be signified, but rather, through the names of the places, progress in the virtues: that after the magicians and the assembly of stones we frequently come to the torrent of Zared, which means “a descent into what is alien”; and, having been placed in that descent, we pass to Arnon, which conveys the sense of “curse.” It is situated on the borders of the Amorites, who are either bitter enemies or, swollen with pride, speak many words.

But if we cross the borders of Moab—who was begotten through incest and departed from his true father—a well immediately meets us. No common person dug it, no man of low status, but princes and leaders who give laws to the peoples. Singing a song over the water of the well and rejoicing in the gifts of God, they prophesy where they will pass and at what places they will arrive: namely, that from the wilderness they come to Mattanah, which is interpreted as “gift”; from Mattanah to Nahaliel, which is called “the torrents of God”; and from Nahaliel—which is interpreted as “the high places” [Col. 0714D] or “the coming of death”—when we are conformed to the death of Christ.

From Bamoth a valley of humility meets us. Yet it is situated at the summit of Mount Phasga, which is interpreted as “hewn,” since it has nothing shapeless or rough about it but is polished by the craftsman’s hand. This mountain looks toward the wilderness, which in Hebrew is called Jeshimon. For when we have been established at the summit of the virtues, then we look upon the ruins of the whole world and the desolation of all sins.

As our discourse hastens onward, we have almost forgotten to explain why Dibongad is interpreted as “a temptation understood with fortitude.” After Dibongad, war is waged against Sihon king of the Amorites and Og king of Bashan. We say that when we have reached the summit, and have drunk from the spring of princes and kings, ascending Mount Phasga, we must not be lifted up into pride; rather, we must recognize the anxiety set before us in opposition to this. For “before destruction a man’s heart is exalted, and before glory it is humbled.”

As for what is inserted into the narrative—“Therefore it is said in the Book of the Wars of the Lord: As he did in the Red Sea, so may he do in the torrents of Arnon. The cliffs of the torrents were bent down, so that they might rest in Arnon and recline on the borders of the Moabites”—the author did not mention in what book this was written. Nor is there any book among those whom we call canonical Divine Scripture in which this is found written. Such passages provide opportunities for those who try to insert apocryphal books into the ears of the unwary and the curious, in order to persuade them of fabulous impieties.

But here it says that it was written “in a book”; it does not say that it was in the book of some prophet or holy patriarch. Nor should we deny that books already existed—whether of the Chaldeans, from whom Abraham came; or of the Egyptians, where Moses had learned all their wisdom; or of any other nation—in one of which this might have been written. Yet such a book should not for that reason be admitted among those Scriptures by which divine authority is commended, just as neither should the Cretan prophet whom the Apostle Paul mentions, nor Greek writers, philosophers, or poets. The same apostle, speaking before the Athenians of something truly great and truthfully expressed, confirms that they said: “In him we live and move and are” (Acts XVII).

Although he may have wished to take from them, because he found it true, a testimony in support of divine authority, he does not thereby affirm that everything written there is to be accepted. Why this has been mentioned at this point is not evident, unless perhaps the matter was conducted as a war in order to establish boundaries between the two peoples there; and the people of that region, because of the war’s greatness, called it “the War of the Lord,” so that it might be written in some book of theirs as “the War of the Lord.”

## CHAPTER III

Where the Lord gave water from the well to the sons of Israel, and concerning the song spoken over it.

**(CHAP. XXI.)** From that place the well appeared, concerning which the Lord spoke to Moses: “Gather the people, and I will give them water.” This, he says, is the well of which the Lord said to Moses: “Gather the people, and I will give them water to drink.” It is recalled as though somewhere earlier the Lord were read to have said this to Moses. But since it is found nowhere, we must understand that here the people who had complained of the lack of water also drank there.

For what is the meaning of God’s commanding Moses with such emphasis to gather the people, so that he might give them water to drink from the well? It is as though the people would not also come of their own accord to the well for the sake of drinking. Why, then, is so great a matter commanded through the mouth of the prophet—that by his own effort and labor he should gather the people to draw water from the well? Hence the poverty of the literal sense sends us back to the richness of spiritual understanding.

Therefore I think it appropriate to gather the mysteries of wells from other passages of Scripture as well, so that, by comparison with many passages, whatever obscurity the present discourse contains may be brought to light. Thus the Spirit of God says through Solomon in Proverbs: “Drink water from your vessels and from the spring of your wells; and let not waters be poured out for you beyond your spring” (Prov. V), although in other copies we have read, “and let waters be poured out for you beyond your spring.” “Let your waters be for you alone, and let no stranger share in them.”

Thus, as these words signify, each of us has a well within himself. Indeed, we say something more: each of us has within himself not one well but many wells, and not one vessel but many vessels. For he did not say, “Drink waters from your vessel,” but “from your vessels”; and he did not say, “from the spring of your well,” but “from the spring of your wells.”

We read that the patriarchs also had wells. Abraham had them, Isaac had them, and Jacob also had them. Beginning from these wells, run through all Scripture, seeking wells, and come as far as the Gospel. There you will find the well beside which the Savior was sitting and resting after the labor of his journey. Then, when the Samaritan woman came and wished to draw water from the well, the power of the well—or of the wells—according to Scripture is explained, and a comparison of waters is made, where the mysteries of the divine teaching are also revealed (John IV).

For it is said: “If anyone drinks from these waters, which that earthly well contained, he will thirst again. But whoever drinks from those waters which Jesus gives will become in him a spring of water welling up into eternal life.” Accordingly, on the basis of what we set forth as written in Proverbs, where wells are named together with a spring, the word of God must be understood. A well is so called if it conceals something profound within its mysteries; a spring, if it flows out abundantly to the peoples.

But it is not without purpose that we must ask how we can explain a plural number of wells and a singular number of a spring, since Wisdom says in Proverbs: “Drink waters from the spring of your wells” (Prov. V). Let us therefore consider whose wells have one spring.

I think that the knowledge of the unbegotten Father may be understood as one well; but the recognition of his only-begotten Son ought to be understood as another well. For the Son is other than the Father, and the Son is not the same as the Father, as he himself also says in the Gospel. He is indeed other, and the Father bears witness to this. Again, I think that a third well may be seen as the knowledge of the Holy Spirit. For he too is other than the Father and the Son, as it is likewise said of him in the Gospels: “The Father will send you another Paraclete, the Spirit of truth” (John XIV).

Thus there is a distinction of three persons—in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—which corresponds to the plural number of wells. Yet these wells have one spring, one substance, and one nature: the Trinity. In this way the distinction made by Holy Scripture when it speaks of “the spring of the wells” is found not to be idle.

Then Israel sang this song: “Let the well rise up.” They sang together: “The well which the princes dug and which the leaders of the multitude prepared, with the lawgiver and with his staffs.”

There are therefore many wells, which, as we have said, are within the soul. There are also very many others that are understood in the individual words and meanings of the Scriptures. Yet this well is more eminent and outstanding than the others, of which Scripture also says in the present passage that it was dug not by just any ordinary people, but by princes, and by those still higher than these, whom it called kings.

For this reason it is also sung to God beside this same well. It does not seem to have been said without purpose that Moses—that is, the law—should gather us to this well. Someone may appear to come to this well, but unless he is gathered there through Moses, he is not acceptable to God.

Marcion seemed to himself to have come to this well, and Basilides and Valentinus likewise. But because they did not come through Moses, and did not receive the law and the prophets, they cannot praise the Lord God from the springs of Israel. Therefore such people do not come to the well that the princes dug and the kings excavated.

But do you wish me to show you from the Scriptures to which wells these people come? There is a certain false valley, and in that valley are wells of bitumen. Every heresy and every sin is in a valley, and in a false valley. For sin and iniquity do not rise upward but always descend toward the lowest places and the underworld.

Thus every heretical opinion and every act of sin is situated in the valley, salty and bitter. For what sweetness or pleasantness can sin possess? But it has something more. If you come to a heretical doctrine, if you come to the bitterness of sin, you have come to wells of bitumen. Bitumen is fuel and nourishment for fire.

Therefore, if you also taste water from these wells—if you take in a heretical opinion, if you begin to drink the bitterness of sin—it will prepare within you fuel for fire and the flames of Gehenna. For this reason it is said to those who do not wish to drink water from that well which the princes dig and the kings excavate, but instead drink from those that are in the valley of sin and feed the materials of fire: “Walk in the light of your fire and in the flame which you have kindled for yourselves” (Isa. L).

What, then, is sung beside this well? “Sing to the well,” he says. “The princes dug it; the kings excavated it.”

The princes and kings may indeed be understood as the same people. But if a distinction must be made, let us understand the prophets as the princes. They placed the meaning and prophecy concerning Christ, dug out and submerged, in the depth of the letter.

The kings, then, who are able to search out such profound and hidden things of the well, we shall rightly call the apostles, one of whom said: “But God has revealed them to us through the Spirit. For the Spirit searches everything, even the depths of God” (1 Cor. II).

Since through the Spirit they can search out even the depths of God and penetrate the mysteries of the well, both high and deep, they are therefore called kings. They excavated this well even in rock and penetrated the hard and difficult secrets of knowledge.

That the apostles can also be called kings may, I think, easily be proved from the statement made concerning all believers: “But you are a royal race, a great priesthood, a holy nation” (1 Pet. II). If those who believed through their word are called kings, how much more must those themselves be regarded as kings who make others kings?

For the apostles are especially the kings of the nations: they gathered the nations into obedience to the faith and made the knowledge of Christ available to all, in whom are hidden the treasures of wisdom and knowledge.

The whole Scripture of the law and the prophets, together with the evangelical and apostolic writings—all of it together—is one well. No one can dig or excavate it unless kings and princes are found there. Truly they must be regarded as kings and princes who can remove the earth from this well, clear away what lies upon the surface of the letter, and bring forth from the inner rock, where Christ is, spiritual meanings like living water. This is fitting for those alone who are either kings or princes.

They are kings also for this reason: they have driven the reign of sin out of their bodies and established the reign of righteousness in their members.

[Col. 0718B] “From the wilderness to Mattanah; from Mattanah to Nahaliel; from Nahaliel to Bamoth, which is a valley in the region of Moab, at the summit of Phasga, which looks toward the wilderness.” After this, he says, “they departed from the well to Mattanah; from Mattanah to Nahaliel; from Nahaliel to Bamoth; and from Bamoth, which is in the plain of Moab, to the grove at the summit of the hewn mountain, which looks toward the face of the wilderness.”

These names, which appear to be names of places and to express their meanings in their own language, seem to indicate more the sequence of mystical realities than the designation of places. For he says that, departing from the well, they come to Mattanah. Mattanah is interpreted as “their gifts.”

You see, then, that if someone drinks from this well which the kings and princes dug, he immediately advances [Col. 0718C] to the point of possessing gifts to offer to God. But what can a human being offer to God? The very thing that is written in the law: “My gifts, my offerings.” Thus, with what God has given, human beings nevertheless offer gifts to God.

What did God give to humanity? Knowledge of himself. What does a human being offer to God? His faith and his deed—what God seeks from a human being.

From Mattanah we come to Nahaliel, which is interpreted as “from God.” What does “from God” mean? After we have offered ourselves and what comes from us, we come to the point of attaining what comes from God. For when we have offered him our faith and our devotion, then he also bestows on us the various gifts of the Holy Spirit, concerning which the Apostle says: “But all things are from God” (1 Cor. III).

From Nahaliel we come to Bamoth, which is interpreted as “the coming of death.” Whose death should we understand as coming here except the death of the one who dies with Christ so that we may also live with him, by whom we must put to death our members that are upon the earth? And again: “For we were buried with him through baptism into death” (Col. II).

Therefore, if anyone follows the order of this saving life, he ought to act in accordance with what we have mentioned and, after many stages, come to this place which we have said signifies the coming of death.

“And from Bamoth,” he says, “to the grove, which is in the plain of Moab, from the summit of the hewn mountain which looks toward the wilderness.” If we travel by this route—whose explanation has asserted that its order consists not so much in the names of places as in the progress of the soul—after all these things we come to the grove, or, as it is found in other copies, to Janam, which is interpreted as “ascent,” or “the summit of the mountain.”

Through these things we come either to that most famous grove of the divine paradise, to the pleasant delights of the dwelling of the ancients, or certainly to the summit of perfection and the height of blessedness, so that you too may say: “He raised us up with him and made us sit in the heavenly places in Christ.”

You see how far one reaches from the well. You see by what stations—or rather, by what advances—the journey of the soul is prepared for heaven. If you examine these carefully, investigating your daily progress within yourself and considering in what places you are and how near you are to the kingdom of heaven, you will perceive it, like the one of whom the Lord said: “You are not far from the kingdom of God” (Matt. XII).

## CHAPTER IV

Concerning the fact that the people of Israel fought against Sihon, king of the Amorites, and, after defeating him, possessed his land.

**(IBID.)** Israel sent messengers to Sihon king of the Amorites, saying: “I ask that you allow me to pass through your land. We will not turn aside into fields or vineyards; we will not drink water from your wells. We will walk along the royal road until we have passed through your borders.”

But he was unwilling to allow Israel to pass through his territory. Instead, after gathering an army, he came out to meet them in the wilderness, came to Jahaz, and fought against him; and he was struck by the edge of the sword.

The historical account is clear, but let us beseech the Lord that we may be able to perceive something worthy in the inward meanings. Sihon has a twofold interpretation: either “a fruitless tree” or “exalted.”

Israel therefore sends envoys to Sihon: he sends them to a fruitless tree; he sends them to the exalted and proud one. This Sihon is king of the Amorites, who themselves are interpreted as “those who bring into bitterness” or “those who speak.”

Moses therefore sends to Sihon king of the Amorites, the king who provokes to bitterness, with peaceful words, saying: “We will pass through your land.” If, according to spiritual understanding, we say that Sihon the king represents the devil, because he is exalted and fruitless, I think you should not be surprised that I have called him a king, since you hear our Lord and Savior himself saying of him in the Gospel: “Now the ruler of this world is coming, and he finds nothing in me” (John XIV). And again: “Now the ruler of this world will be cast out” (Ps. LXXI).

If, then, he is called in the Gospels the ruler of the whole world, it ought not to seem absurd if Sihon, king of the Amorites, or even any other kings of the nations, is compared with him. He is called the ruler of the world not because he created the world, but because there are many sinners in this world. Since he is the ruler of sin, he is therefore also called the ruler of the world—in those, that is, who have not yet abandoned the world and turned to the Father.

For this reason it is also said: “Every human being is placed in evil.” What benefit is there in our saying that Christ is our ruler if our deeds and actions prove that the devil holds rule within us? Is it not evident under what ruler the immoral and unjust person acts? Can such a person say, “I do these things while placed under Christ,” even if he appears to be counted under Christ’s name? Where Christ exercises rule, no impurity and no iniquity is admitted. Unjust desire cannot have any place there.

Accordingly, in this sense Christ is rightly called the ruler of the virtues, and the devil the ruler of wickedness and of every iniquity.

Israel therefore sends envoys to the king of the Amorites—the king who provokes to bitterness, the fruitless king, the proud king. How will the devil be shown to be proud and exalted? He is the one who said: “By my strength I will act, and by the wisdom of my understanding I will remove the boundaries of the nations, and I will plunder their strength. I will shake the inhabited cities, and I will seize the whole earth in my hand like a nest” (Isa. X).

And again this exalted and proud one says: “I will ascend into heaven; above the stars of heaven I will set my throne. I will sit on the high mountain, above the lofty mountains that are toward the north. I will ascend above the clouds; I will be like the Most High” (Isa. XIV).

Do you still ask whether he is exalted and proud? Rather, both he himself is proud and exalted, and so is the one who is, as it were, his only-begotten son, of whom it is written: “He will be exalted above everything that is called God or worshiped” (1 Thess. II), so that he sits in the temple of God, displaying himself as though he were God.

Everyone, therefore, who is exalted and proud is either the son of this exalted one, or his disciple and imitator. For this reason the Apostle says of someone: “Lest, being puffed up, he fall into the judgment of the devil” (1 Tim. III), showing by this that everyone who is exalted will be condemned by a judgment like the devil’s.

We are therefore the ones who wish to pass through this world so that we may reach the holy land promised to the saints. We send peaceful words to Sihon, promising that we will not dwell in his land or remain with him, but will merely pass through and travel along the royal road, turning aside nowhere—not into a field or into a vineyard—and promising that we will not drink water from his cistern.

Let us see, then, when we made these promises and when we announced these words to the devil. Let each of the faithful recall when he first came to the waters of baptism, when he first received the seals of faith and approached the fountain of salvation, what words he used there at that time: that he renounced the devil and would not use his spectacles, his works, or obey any of his services and desires.

This is what is prefigured in these words of the law: Israel shall not turn aside into his field or into his vineyard, nor promise to drink water from his cistern. He will no longer drink from the discipline of the devil, astrology, magic, or any teaching whatsoever that teaches something contrary to the worship of God.

The faithful person has his own springs and drinks from springs of salvation. He will not drink water from the cistern of Sihon. He will not abandon the fountain of living water and dig for himself cracked cisterns. Rather, he professes that he will walk along the royal road.

What is the royal road? Without doubt, the one that says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV). And rightly is it royal. For he is the one of whom the Prophet says: “O God, give your judgment to the king” (Ps. VII).

We must therefore walk along the royal road and turn aside nowhere—not into his field or into his vineyard. That is, the minds of the faithful must no longer turn aside either to the devil’s works or to his thoughts.

How, then, do we wish to pass peacefully through the borders of the Amorites? The Amorites may be understood as a portion of the unbelievers who are in this world. But, as we said above, they are interpreted as “speakers” or “those who bring bitterness.” How unbelievers and the faithless bring God into bitterness requires no explanation.

The word “speakers,” however, can be applied to that aspect because the unbelievers who act under the devil as ruler know only how to speak, and they speak empty things. For example, their poets, astrologers, and even some philosophers speak empty and vain things.

But the kingdom of the faithful, which is from God, does not consist in speech but in power.

We therefore wish to pass peacefully through the world. Yet this very thing provokes the ruler of the world all the more: that we say we do not wish to remain with him, linger with him, or touch anything belonging to him. Because of this he is more greatly embittered, exalted, and angered; he stirs up persecutions against us, raises dangers, and threatens torments.

Therefore it says: “The wicked Sihon gathered his people and went out to fight against Israel.” Who is this whole people of Sihon whom he stirs up against Israel?

But what does Israel do? “He came,” it says, “to Jahaz,” which is interpreted as “the fulfillment of the commandment.” If we too come to this place—that is, to the fulfillment of the commandments—even if this exalted Sihon, the proud devil, comes against us with his entire army and fights against us, even if he rouses all his demons against us, we overcome him if we fulfill God’s commandments.

For to fulfill the commandments is to overcome the devil and his entire army. Then the Apostle’s prayer will be fulfilled in us: “The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet” (Rom. XVI). And also what the Lord says: “Behold, I give you authority to tread on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy, and nothing will harm you” (Luke X).

None of all these things will be able to harm us if we come to Jahaz—that is, if we keep the commandments and precepts of our Lord Jesus Christ.

And Israel possessed his land from Arnon as far as the Jabbok and the sons of Ammon, because the borders of the Ammonites were held by a strong fortress. Israel therefore took all his cities and dwelt in the cities of the Amorite, namely in Heshbon and its villages, and so forth.

Israel struck him with the sword and ruled over his land from Arnon as far as the Jabbok, as far as the sons of Ammon, because Jazer is the boundary of the sons of Ammon. All Israel took these cities, and Israel dwelt in all the cities of the Amorites, in Heshbon.

Here Israel certainly possessed the cities of the Amorites whom he had overcome in war, because he did not devote them to destruction. For if he had devoted them to destruction, he would not have been permitted to possess them or to take any spoil from them for his own use.

It should rightly be noted how just wars were conducted. Innocent passage was denied, although by the law of human fellowship it ought most justly to have been permitted. But now, so that God might fulfill his promises, he helped the Israelites, to whom the land of the Amorites was to be given.

When Edom likewise denied them passage, the Israelites did not fight against that people—that is, the sons of Jacob did not fight against the sons of Esau, the two brothers, the two twins—because God had not promised that land to the Israelites. Instead, they turned away from them.

“And the sons of Israel ruled,” he says, “over all his land.” This entire earthly region is indeed the land of Sihon; but Christ rules in his Church over the whole land of Sihon.

“And they ruled from Arnon as far as the Jabbok.” Arnon and Jabbok were cities of the region of Sihon. Arnon was the beginning of his kingdom, and Jabbok its end. Therefore it is said that they ruled from Arnon as far as the Jabbok.

Arnon is interpreted as “their curses.” The beginning, then, of the kingdom of Sihon, the exalted and fruitless one, consists of curses; its boundary is Jabbok, which is interpreted as “struggle.”

For everyone who wishes to leave the kingdom of the devil and escape his borders must encounter struggle, and combats must be stirred up against him by the devil’s ministers and attendants. But if he struggles and conquers, Jabbok will no longer be a city of Sihon; it will be a city of Israel (Gen. XXIII).

This is precisely what we also read concerning the patriarch Jacob. When he came to a certain place, a struggle was prepared for him. Having wrestled there all night, and having prevailed and grown strong with God, his name was called Israel.

“And Israel took,” he says, “all these cities, and Israel dwelt in all the cities of the Amorites.” [Col. 0722C] This Israel, who is Israel in Christ, who is not Israel according to the flesh and is not a Jew outwardly, dwells in all the cities of the Amorites, as the churches of Christ are spread throughout the whole world.

But each of us was previously a city of the region of Sihon, the exalted king. Folly, pride, impiety, and everything belonging to the devil’s side ruled in us. But when the strong one is defeated and overcome, and his vessels are plundered, we become cities of Israel and the inheritance of the saints—provided that the power which formerly ruled in us has been completely cut down, the fruitless tree has been cut down, and the exalted king has been cast down, and we are under the rule of the king who says: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble in heart” (Matt. XI).

After this he enumerates individually the cities of the proud and fruitless king and says: “In Heshbon and in all its neighboring places.” Why did he name Heshbon as the principal city of the kingdom of Sihon? Heshbon is interpreted as “thoughts.”

Rightly, therefore, the greatest portion of the devil’s kingdom and the greatest part of his power rule in thoughts. For the Lord also said: “For from the heart proceed evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, thefts, false testimonies, blasphemies; these are the things that defile a person” (Matt. V).

Therefore this city is necessarily set on fire and burned with fire. With what fire? Certainly with the fire of which the Savior says: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and how I wish that it were already kindled” (Luke XII).

A little later, however, the account speaks of the city.

For this reason it is said in the proverb: “Come to Hesebon, so that [Col. 0723A] the city of Sihon may be built and reconstructed. Fire has gone forth from Hesebon, a flame from the town of Sihon, and it has devoured Ar of the Moabites and the inhabitants of the heights of Arnon.” Therefore, he says, the enigma-speakers will say: “Come to Hesebon, so that the city of Sihon may be built and reconstructed, because fire has proceeded from Hesebon and a flame from the city of Sihon, and it has devoured Ar of the Moabites.” Sihon, as we have said, was a king whose city was Hesebon.

The order of the words is therefore to be understood as follows: these enigma-speakers say, “Come, so that Hesebon, which was the city of Sihon, may be built and reconstructed.” But let us now inquire who these enigma-speakers are. An “enigma” is figurative speech. Enigma-speakers, then, are those who speak figuratively. And who else has spoken in figures except the Law and the Prophets? For hear how David says: “I will open my mouth in a parable; I will speak riddles from the beginning” (Ps. XLVIII). Isaiah likewise explains in this way that what he wrote consists of enigmas. “The words of the book,” he says, “will be like the words of a sealed book. When they give it to a man who does not know letters and say to him, ‘Read this,’ he will say, ‘I do not know letters.’ But when they give it to one who knows letters, he will say, ‘I cannot read, for it is sealed’” (Isa. XXIX). A book is called “sealed” because it is entangled in figures and wrapped in enigmas.

These enigma-speakers therefore say: “Come to Hesebon, so that it may be built.” That first Hesebon has fallen—or rather, it has been overthrown and burned; another must be rebuilt. But to show how this happens, let us take an example.

Consider a Gentile placed in a shameful way of life and in the error of religion. You should have no hesitation in saying of him that he is this city of Hesebon in the kingdom of King Sihon. For an unfruitful and arrogant king reigns in his thoughts. If an Israelite approaches him—that is, a son of the Church—and applies the darts of God’s word, draws against him the sword of the Spirit, destroys within him all the fortifications of Gentile doctrines and the arrogance of his arguments, and burns them with the fire of truth, say of him that the city of Hesebon, the city of Sihon, has been overthrown.

Yet the person in whom the Gentile doctrines have been overthrown is not immediately abandoned and left desolate. For it is not the discipline of the children of Israel to leave destroyed the cities that they have destroyed. Rather, when they have demolished and overturned evil thoughts and impious perceptions in a person, they rebuild in his heart the good [Col. 0723D] thoughts that they had destroyed and implant pious perceptions; they hand on the teaching of truth, transmit the practice of religion, teach the order of life, and immediately display moral integrity and observance. Then these enigma-speakers truly say to one another: “Come, let us build Hesebon, which was the city of Sihon.”

For they themselves—that is, the sons of the Church—are also called enigma-speakers, because they understand spiritually the figures and enigmas of the Law. This is likewise what Jeremiah designates in figurative speech when the Lord says to him: “Behold, I have put my words in your mouth; behold, today I have appointed you over nations and kingdoms, to uproot and overthrow, to rebuild and to replant” (Jer. I). What does he uproot and overthrow? The city of Hesebon, which belonged to King Sihon. What does he uproot in it? Impious and impure thoughts. What does he rebuild and replant in it? Pious and chaste thoughts. Thus Hesebon becomes the city of Sihon—not of the Amorites, but of the children of Israel.

Moab, which is interpreted as “from the father” or “paternal water,” conceived through incest and drunkenness, and in a certain sense appearing to have been begotten while the father was absent—or rather, unaware—signifies secular wisdom, which has the mind as its author. And because it is generated from God’s creation, it appears to be born from a father, which is what Moab signifies. But because it is adulterous and an adversary of the people of God, it is generated from incest, a cave, and night. Hence, according to Isaiah’s prophecy, it perished in the night—that is, in everlasting error.

The city of the Moabites, moreover, which is interpreted as “antidicus,” that is, “adversary,” shows that this wisdom, which is hostile to God, is consumed by the fire of truth when ecclesiastical speech contends against it. By that fire the inhabitants of the heights of Arnon are also devoured. For Arnon, as was said above, is interpreted as “their curse” or “their illumination,” because all who trust in the pride of eloquence and human wisdom—which appears luminous to the children of darkness—fall, are hurled down, and are consumed.

“Woe to you, Moab; you have perished, people of Chemosh. He has given his sons to flight and his daughters into captivity to Sihon, king of the Amorites. Their yoke has perished from Hesebon to Dibon. The weary have reached Nofe as far as Medaba.”

Chemosh is interpreted as “gathering” or “as it were, a touching.” Dibon signifies “understanding abundantly,” or “their temptation” or “their flowing.” Nofe means “blowing” or “breathing,” and Medaba means “from the leap.”

There is indeed woe for those who trust in the spiritual Moab, who gather for themselves treasures of wisdom that is hostile to God, and who raise themselves through pride against God’s power. Yet their audacity will not prevail; rather, it will be turned into a figure and delivered into captivity to the king of the spiritual Amorites. For their yoke will perish from Hesebon to Dibon—that is, their knowledge will flow away from the root of thought to the depth of understanding.

Then, weary and blowing forth the vanity of words, breathing out the foul odor of a rotten understanding, they will reach an infertile forest, where there are no fruitful trees but where wild beasts dwell. Against these the Prophet entreats the Lord, saying: “Do not hand over, O Lord, the souls of those who confess you to the beasts” (Ps. LXXIII).

Israel lived in the land of the Amorite. Moses sent men to explore Jazer, whose villages they captured and whose inhabitants they possessed. “Moses sent messengers,” he says, “to explore Jazer, whose villages they captured and whose inhabitants they possessed.”

Who are those messengers whom Moses—that is, the Law—sent, except the holy preachers? They were sent to explore Jazer, which is interpreted as “their strength”: that is, the strongest doctrines of the heretics, constructed by dialectical art, in which the world seems to have the strength of its error. When the holy preachers investigated these things and perceived that they were empty and fragile, they captured the villages—that is, the gatherings of peoples—and possessed their inhabitants, when they converted to the catholic faith those whom they had freed from error. By sound teaching and good examples they directed them onto the way of truth, so that, through their correction and progress, they might obtain a dwelling in the heavenly homeland.

## CHAPTER V. The battle of the Israelites against Og, king of Bashan

**(IBID.)** They turned and went up by the road to Bashan. Og, king of Bashan, came out against them with all his people to fight at Edrei. The Lord said to Moses: “Do not fear him, for I have delivered him into your hand, together with all his people and his land. You shall do to him as you did to Sihon, king of the Amorites, who lived at Hesebon.” They struck him, therefore, together with his sons and all his people, until they had utterly destroyed them, and they possessed his land.

After the children of Israel had taken possession of the cities of the Amorites, they also went up by the road leading to Bashan, where Og, king of Bashan, was. But they do not even deem it worth sending ambassadors to him or asking permission to pass through his land; instead, they immediately engage him in battle and defeat both him and his people.

Let us therefore see what Bashan is. Bashan is interpreted as “shamefulness.” It is therefore fitting that no ambassadors are sent to this people and that no passage through its land is requested. There ought to be no passage for us, no approach, to shamefulness; rather, it must be attacked from the outset and avoided in every way.

Og, who is said to be king of Bashan, is interpreted as “confinement.” He may represent all carnal and material things, by whose love and desire the soul is held fast, shut out, and separated from God. Against these, therefore, war must be waged in such a way that no living thing from them is left. Nothing living ought to be left by the children of Israel in the kingdom of shame and disgrace. Rather, Israelite virtue should cut away and excise whatever is shameful, rebuild whatever is pious in the mind, and plant whatever is honorable and religious.

Nothing of this sort is written concerning the kingdom of Sihon: “Let no living thing be left,” nor concerning the kingdom of Moab. Perhaps some use could be made of those things, and we need some of them for the struggles and exercises of this life. Otherwise, we ought to have departed from this world. But from Bashan—that is, from shamefulness—we have absolutely no need. Let us leave nothing of it behind. All the works of shamefulness must be cut away; all must be overturned. For nothing that is shameful can in any respect be honorable.

## CHAPTER VI. Balac, king of the Moabites, Balaam the diviner, and his she-ass

**(CHAP. XXII.)** They set out and pitched their camp in the plains of Moab, where Jericho is situated beyond the Jordan. Balac, son of Sephor, saw all that Israel had done to the Amorite, and that the Moabites had been terrified of him and could not withstand his attack. He said to the elders of Moab: “Now this people will devour all those who dwell within our borders, just as an ox is accustomed to crop the grass down to its roots.” He himself was king in Moab at that time.

He therefore sent messengers to Balaam, son of Beor, a diviner who lived by the river of the land of the children of Ammon, to summon him and say: “Behold, a people has come out of Egypt and covered the surface of the earth, sitting opposite me. Come, therefore, and curse this people, which is stronger than I. Perhaps I may somehow be able to strike it and drive it from my land,” and so forth.

First of all, then, we must acknowledge that in certain circumstances words can have greater power than bodies. For what an army of many nations cannot accomplish, and what cannot be obtained with shield and weapons, may be achieved by words. I do not mean holy words or the words of God, but certain words that are current among human beings.

For example, there were enchanters and magicians in Egypt. What human strength of body can transform a staff into a serpent, as is reported to have been done by them? Or who by bodily strength can turn water into blood? Yet the Egyptian enchanters and magicians did these things. Moses had done them first. But because the king of Egypt knew that such things could be accomplished by a certain verbal art current among human beings, he supposed that Moses had done them not by God’s power but by magical art, and that he was pretending that what he had done by human art had been accomplished by God’s power.

He immediately summoned the Egyptian enchanters and magicians and set a contest between Moses, who was acting by God’s power, and those who invoked demons. Our God causes suffering and then restores; the opposing power, however, can inflict harm, but cannot restore completely. We have prefaced all this so that we may understand Balaam’s works and words.

There are also various kinds of magicians. Some have greater power, others less. This Balaam was very famous in the magical art and exceedingly powerful in harmful incantations. For he did not possess the power to bless. Demons are summoned for cursing, not for blessing.

It is therefore written: “Moab said to the elders of Midian: Now this assembly will lick up all who are around us, as a calf licks up the grass of the field.” This is plainly because a calf tears the grass from the field with its mouth, cutting whatever it finds with its tongue like a sickle. Thus this people, like a calf, fights with its mouth and lips and has weapons in its words and prayers.

Knowing this, he sends to Balaam so that Balaam too may bring opposing words and prayers against prayers. Do not be surprised that such a thing exists in magical art. Scripture itself indicates that this art exists, although it forbids its use. Scripture also indicates the existence of demons, but forbids their worship and invocation.

It rightly forbids the use of magic, since the ministers of magicians are rebellious angels, evil spirits, and unclean demons. No holy spirit obeys a magician. A magician could not invoke Michael; he could not invoke Raphael or Gabriel. Still less can a magician invoke almighty God, or his Son, Jesus Christ our Lord, or his Holy Spirit. We alone receive the power to invoke God the Father; we alone have the power to invoke his only-begotten Son, Jesus Christ.

Therefore, through a certain art and arrangement of words, demons had entered, so to speak, into friendship with Balaam. Relying on their friendship, he appeared great in the eyes of human beings. For this reason the king sent to him and said: “Come now and curse this people for me, because it is stronger than we are. Perhaps we may be able to strike some of them and drive them from the land.”

It seems to me that this king did not place complete confidence in Balaam the diviner. I believe that he had been terrified by hearsay of the powers that had been manifested among the people of God, and therefore said “perhaps”: perhaps Balaam’s curses might prevail to such an extent that he could strike some of them, while frightening and driving the rest away from their land.

He added: “For I know that those whom you curse are cursed, and those whom you bless are blessed.” I do not believe that the king knew that whoever Balaam blessed would truly be blessed. Rather, it seems to me that he said this to flatter him, so that by praising and exalting his art he might make him more ready to undertake the crime. Magical art does not know how to bless, because demons do not know how to do good. Isaac and Jacob know how to bless, as do all the saints; no impious person knows how to bless.

At last the ambassadors came to Balaam.

“For the elders of Moab and the elders of Midian came,” he says, “holding the price of divination in their hands,” or, according to another edition, “their instruments of divination in their hands.” In those arts of divination that human curiosity has devised, there are certain objects that Scripture indeed calls “instruments of divination.” Gentile custom calls them tripods, curtains, or other names of this kind. As though consecrated for this very purpose, they are accustomed to be moved and handled by the diviners.

Divine Scripture also uses the vernacular term *ephod* for a certain object among the prophets, which they say is the garment of those who prophesy.

When Balaam had received the instruments of divination, and the demons were accustomed to come to him, he saw that the demons had been driven away but that God was present. Therefore he says that he is consulting God, because he nowhere sees the demons accustomed to obey him. God came to Balaam—not because Balaam was worthy of God’s coming to him, but so that those who were accustomed to attend him for cursing and doing harm might be driven away. For God was already making provision for his people.

God therefore came and said to him: “Why have these men come to you?” Balaam said to God: “Balac, son of Sephor, king of Moab, sent them to me, saying: ‘Behold, a people has come out of Egypt and covered the face of the earth, and it has settled beside me. Come now and curse it, if perhaps we may be able to strike it and drive it away.’”

The Lord said to Balaam: “Do not go with them, nor curse the people, for it is blessed.”

Here a profounder question arises. I do not know whether it is appropriate to uncover and disclose a matter of such deep mystery to the crowds—and to such crowds as come to hear the word of God for only a few days, then depart immediately and do not remain longer in meditation on the word. Nevertheless, for those who are eager and thirst to hear, and who are able to grasp a spiritual meaning, we shall say a few things from among many.

Someone might object as follows: Let Balaam invoke demons and curse the people; let the demons do whatever they are able to do when invoked. Surely God can defend the people from demons and destroy their power to do harm? Why, then, was it necessary for God himself to come to Balaam and prevent the demons accustomed to him from approaching, lest they even attempt or endeavor to harm God’s people?

To this we reply, although not everything that may arise can be stated here, that God does not wish to condemn the race of demons before the appointed time. For the demons themselves know that their present time includes this age. Accordingly, they asked the Lord not to torment them before the time or send them into the abyss.

For this reason he did not remove the devil from his authority over this age either, because his work is still necessary for the contests and victories of the blessed. If freedom of choice were taken away from demons, no one would thereafter assault the athletes of Christ. But if no one assaults them, there will be no contest; and when the contest is removed, there will be no prize and no victory.

God therefore follows this course: the still inexperienced people, who had only recently begun to be withdrawn from the worship of demons, would not be handed over to demons; answers would be given to the magician who invoked them; and the race of demons would not be stripped of the power of choice.

Thus God anticipated Balaam and forbade him to approach and invoke demons for the purpose of cursing—if only he had ceased from his greed. But because he persisted in his desire for money, God once more permitted him to go, in accordance with the freedom of his choice. He nevertheless placed his word in Balaam’s mouth, preventing a curse from being uttered through the demons, so as to make room for blessings and cause Balaam to proclaim blessings and prophecies instead of curses—prophecies capable of building up not only Israel but also the other nations.

For if his prophecies were inserted by Moses into the sacred books, how much more were they recorded by those who at that time inhabited Mesopotamia, among whom Balaam was held in high esteem and who are known to have been his students? From this source, indeed, the race and institution of the magicians is said to have flourished in the regions of the East. They possessed written records of everything that Balaam had prophesied, including this statement: “A star shall arise from Jacob, and a man shall rise up from Israel” (Num. XXIV).

The magi had these things written among themselves. Therefore, when Jesus was born, they recognized the star and understood the fulfillment of the prophecy—more readily than the people of Israel, who had refused to listen to the words of the holy prophets.

The princes returned and said to Balac: “Balaam was unwilling to come with us.” Again he sent men more numerous and more distinguished than those he had sent before. When they came to Balaam, they said: “Thus says Balac, son of Sephor: Do not hesitate to come to me. I am ready to honor you and to give you whatever you wish. Come and curse this people.”

Balaam replied: “Even if Balac were to give me his house full of silver and gold, I could not alter the word of the Lord my God, so as to speak either more or less,” and so forth.

As we said above, Balaam was a diviner, serving demons through magical art and sometimes foreknowing future events. King Balac summoned him to curse the people of Israel. The ambassadors came; the nations stood in astonishment, anxiously awaiting what Balaam would answer, since they were convinced that he was worthy of divine utterances.

See how the wisdom of God now makes this vessel prepared for dishonor serve the benefit not merely of one nation but of almost the whole world. To this man, to whom demons had been accustomed to appear, God appears, forbidding the path of an evil deed. Balaam is astonished and marvels at the authority of the one who forbids him. He had not been accustomed to displease the demons, but meanwhile he sends the ambassadors back, saying that he could do nothing except speak the word that God would give him.

The ambassadors return; he asks again, troubles God again, and again desires to hear. For one who is greedy is not easily deprived of his greed, nor does he easily lack rewards.

What, then, does he hear from God a second time? “If these men have come to call you, rise and go with them.” In this God yields to the will of his greed, so that what is written may be fulfilled: “I gave them over to the desires of their heart; they shall go in their own pleasures” (Ps. LXXX). Yet the purpose of the divine dispensation is also fulfilled. For God says to him: “The word that I give you, you shall speak.”

If Balaam had been worthy, God would have placed his word not in his mouth but in his heart. But because the desire for reward and the greed for money were in his heart, the word of God is placed not in his heart but in his mouth.

A marvelous and great dispensation was taking place. Since the word of the prophets who were confined within the Israelite court could not reach the nations, the mysteries concerning Christ were to be made known to the nations through Balaam, whose authority was trusted by all the peoples. Thus he would bring forth to the nations a great treasure, carried not so much in his heart and understanding as in his mouth and speech.

But so that we do not linger over every detail—for it is not now the time to unfold everything—Balaam mounted his she-ass and went along the road. An angel met him. The angel who unquestionably attended the children of Israel opened the mouth of the she-ass, so that Balaam might be reproved through her and that the one who appeared to be a diviner and wise might be refuted by the voice of a dumb animal.

After this, however, it seems appropriate to touch upon something of the allegory. Balaam, whose name is interpreted as “vain people,” seems to me to represent the scribes and Pharisees of the Jewish people. Balac, whose name is interpreted as “exclusion” or “devouring,” should likewise be understood as representing one of the spiritual powers opposed within this world, which desires to exclude and devour Israel—not Israel according to the flesh, but Israel according to the spirit.

That opposing power, wishing to destroy and utterly extinguish spiritual Israel, uses no other ministers than the chief priests, scribes, and Pharisees. It invites them and promises them rewards and prizes. But they, as Balaam did, pretend to refer everything to God and to act out of zeal for God.

They say: “Search the Scriptures and see that no prophet arises from Galilee” (John V). Again they say: “We have a law, and according to the law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God” (John XIX). In each of these statements the scribes and Pharisees appear to possess zeal for God, but it is feigned.

The she-ass on which Balaam sat may be understood as the portion of believers, in accordance with Scripture: “You will save humans and beasts, O Lord” (Ps. XXXV). It is compared with animals either because of its foolishness or because of its innocence. Thus the Apostle also says: “Consider your calling, brothers: not many of you were wise according to the flesh, not many powerful, not many noble. But God chose what is foolish in the world to confound the wise” (1 Cor. I).

Such people, therefore, as the Gospel events enacted in parables signify, were in a certain way subjected to and bound by those wicked masters, the scribes and Pharisees, but they are released by the Lord—not by the Lord himself, but by his disciples. For he says to the disciples: “Go into the village opposite you, and you will find a she-ass tied up, and her colt with her. Untie them and bring them” (Matt. XXII).

Thus, just as in the Gospel the Lord himself does not untie the she-ass but the disciples do, so here the mouth of the she-ass is opened not by God himself but by the angel. And just as in the Gospels those who do not see rebuke those who do see, so here those who were mute rebuke those who speak.

This is what the Lord was saying: “Father, I give you thanks because you have hidden these things from the wise and revealed them to infants” (Matt. X). The scribes and Pharisees, therefore, were those who sat upon this she-ass and kept her bound. The angel is consequently angry with them also; and were it not for a certain foreknowledge of future things, he would have destroyed them while preserving the she-ass, which saw and revered him who came to the vineyard and stood among the vines.

Nevertheless, she pressed the feet of the one sitting upon her against the wall, and therefore her former rider could neither proceed nor come to him who says: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened,” and so forth (Matt. XI).

The she-ass, however, comes when brought by the disciples; and the one on whom the money-loving Balaam once sat is now ridden by God. Do not be surprised if you see the one whom we have said represents the scribes and teachers of the people prophesying about Christ. We read that Caiaphas did the same when he said: “It is expedient for you that one man should die for the whole people” (John XI). The Evangelist adds: “Since he was high priest that year, he prophesied.”

Balaam, therefore, also prophesied about Christ. For this reason let no one exalt himself even if he prophesies or is deemed worthy of foreknowledge. Let him return to the Apostle’s saying, by which, looking toward these matters, he declares: “Whether prophecies will be abolished, or tongues will cease, or knowledge will be destroyed.” What, then, remains? “Faith,” he says, “hope, and love. But the greatest of these is love.” And love alone, he says, is what never falls away. Therefore love must be held and cultivated above prophecy, above knowledge, above faith itself, and even above martyrdom, as Paul teaches. And because “God is love” (1 Cor. XIII), and Christ is the Son of Love, may he grant us the perfection of love.

Nor do I think this should be left unsaid: this she-ass of the diviner Balaam represents the type of the Gentiles. Once Balaam himself—that is, the seducer into idolatry—had subjected the Gentiles like a brute animal, incapable of retaining any reason, to whatever error he wished.

But this Gentile people both saw and reverenced the angel of God whom the man could not see, and it spoke. Thus we may recognize that, later, at the coming of the great angel of God, that mute Gentile people, hardened by stupidity, would speak with its natural tongue loosed by God, so that the people formerly subjected to unbelief would burst forth into the voice of faith and confession.

It is also possible to understand our flesh as an animal. For often, when the flesh is touched by affliction, it reveals God to the mind through its own scourging—God whom the mind itself, presiding over the flesh, did not see. Thus, through the anxiety of the spirit that longs to advance in this world, as though journeying along a road, the flesh impedes it until the invisible one who opposes it becomes known.

Hence Peter rightly says: “The beast of burden, mute, speaking with a human voice, restrained the prophet’s madness” (2 Pet. II). A madman is reproved by a mute beast of burden when the afflicted flesh reminds the exalted mind of the good of humility, which it ought to possess. Balaam, however, did not obtain the gift of this reproof because, as he proceeded to curse, he changed his voice but not his mind.

## CHAPTER VII. Balaam’s arrival at Balac and his prophecy

**(CHAP. XXIII.)** Balaam therefore said to Balac: “Stand beside your burnt offering until I go, in case the Lord may meet me; and whatever he commands, I shall tell you.”

When he had gone away swiftly, God met him, and Balaam spoke to him: “I have erected seven altars,” he said, “and placed a calf and a ram upon them.” The Lord then put a word in his mouth and said: “Return to Balac, and speak these things.”

When he returned, he found Balac standing beside his burnt offering, together with all the princes of the Moabites. Taking up his parable, he said: “Balac, king of the Moabites, brought me from Aram, from the mountains of the East.”

“From Aram,” or, as another edition has it, “from Mesopotamia,” he says, “Balac, king of Moab, summoned me—from the mountains of the East.”

By Mesopotamia he means the land lying between the rivers of Babylon, concerning which it is written: “By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept when we remembered you, Zion” (Ps. CXXXVI).

If someone is among these rivers of Babylon, if someone is washed by the streams of lust and surrounded by the heat of luxury, he is not said to stand but to sit. Therefore those who were captured there said: “By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat when we remembered you, Zion.” But they cannot even weep beforehand unless they have remembered Zion. For remembrance of good things makes the causes of evil lamentable. Unless someone remembers Zion, unless he looks upon the Law and the mountains of Scripture, he does not begin to weep for his evils.

From these rivers, therefore, Balaam is summoned, and from these mountains of the East he is invited. These mountains are not holy mountains; they are not the mountains of which it is written: “Its foundations are in the holy mountains” (Ps. LXXXVI). Again: “Jerusalem, which is built as a city whose participation is in unity. The mountains surround it, and the Lord surrounds his people” (Ps. CXXI).

The mountains of Mesopotamia are not such mountains, but those of which it is said: “Dark mountains.” Again, they are the mountains of which it is said: “Behold, I am against you, corrupt mountain.” These are the mountains in which there is every height exalting itself against the knowledge of God.

From these mountains, therefore, this Balaam too is summoned. And just as these mountains are, so is their East. For the one who transforms himself into an angel of light also possesses the rising of his own light. He possesses that light of which it is written: “The light of the impious will be extinguished.” Just as this is the light of the impious, and as the light that transforms itself into an angel of light is opposed to the light that said, “I am the light of the world” (John VIII), so this East is opposed to that East of which it is written in Jeremiah: “Behold, a man; East is his name.”

From the borders of that East, therefore—not this one—Balaam came, unquestionably illuminated by that Lucifer of whom it is said: “How Lucifer fell from heaven, who rose in the morning” (Isa. XIX). But let us see what Balac, that king of Moab who summoned him from the midst of the rivers and from the mountains of the East, says.

“Come,” he says, “and curse Jacob; hasten and denounce Israel. How shall I curse one whom God has not cursed? How shall I denounce one whom the Lord does not denounce? From the highest rocks I shall see him, and from the hills I shall consider him. The people has dwelt alone and shall not be reckoned among the nations. Who can count the dust of Jacob or know the number of the offspring of Israel?”

Balaam seems to set forth a curse against Israel with greater force and stronger intensity than against Jacob. For as long as someone is merely Jacob—that is, occupied only with lower actions and works—he is attacked by curses. But when he has made progress and has begun to sharpen and arouse the inner person to see God, with the eye of the mind uncovered, then he will be attacked by the enemy not only with curses but with denunciations added to curses—that is, with more violent darts of cursing.

At that time, however, Balaam’s mouth was full of cursing and bitterness, and under his tongue were labor and pain, and he sat in ambush with the rich (Ps. IX). For he was expecting rewards from the wealthy king and was secretly seeking to kill the innocent.

But God, who alone always works wonders, brings salvation out of enemies. He placed a word in Balaam’s mouth, although his heart could not yet receive the word of God. For there was still in his heart the desire for payment, because even after the word of the Lord had been placed in his mouth, he said to Balac: “Come, and I will give you counsel.” He taught him how to set a stumbling-block before the children of Israel, so that they would eat food sacrificed to idols and commit fornication. Because of this the people fell, and a great plague broke out among them, until Phinehas, after killing the Israelite who was fornicating with the Midianite woman, appeased the Lord’s fury.

And after this, he says, Phinehas led an army against the Midianites, and they slew twelve thousand men—and Balaam son of Beor by the sword. But we have introduced these matters here prematurely, by a certain digression, in order to show that Balaam had the word of God not in his heart, but only in his mouth. Meanwhile, what he utters and says, he says from the word of God, and therefore what he says is the word of God. He says, then: “How shall I curse one whom the Lord has not cursed?” And so forth.

What, then, shall we say? The Lord does not curse Jacob, nor Israel—but perhaps you think that he curses someone else. We read that the Lord says to the serpent: “Cursed are you among all the beasts of the earth” (Gen. III). And again to Adam: “Cursed is the earth in your works” (ibid.). Also to Cain: “And now you are cursed by the earth, which has opened its mouth to receive your brother’s blood from your hands” (Gen. IX). And: “Cursed is everyone who makes a carved or cast image” (Deut. XXVII).

But lest you think that such things are contained only in the ancient writings, you will also find similar statements written in the Gospels. For it is written that the Lord will say to those who are on his left: “Depart from me, you accursed, into eternal fire” (Matt. XXV). Likewise when he says: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites” (Matt. XXIII); and: “Woe to you who are rich” (Luke VI); and each of the statements of this kind. What else does he seem to be doing than pressing them with curses?

But what are we to make of the fact that a command is given through the Apostle, who says: “Bless, and do not curse”? Does he himself, then, do what he commands human beings to do, he who sets before everyone an example of life? It is not so. When God curses certain people, he designates the merit of the one who is cursed and pronounces a sentence, since neither the character of the sin nor the consequence of the sinner escapes him.

But a human being, because he can neither endure nor perform such things—for no one can see another’s purpose and mind, or grant pardon—therefore, even if he utters a curse with the intention of judging or pronouncing a sentence, it cannot be a just reason for cursing when the outcome of the sinner’s conduct is unknown. This is especially so because human weakness knows how to utter curses when it has perhaps been provoked by insults or injuries.

Wishing to cut away this fault, so that we do not answer curses with curses and insults with insults, the Apostle establishes the necessary command that we should bless and not curse (Rom. XII). His purpose is to cut away the vice of reviling, not to abolish the truth of judgment—which is hidden from human beings—or the authority to pronounce sentence. Nevertheless, let us more carefully hear from Balaam himself—in fact, from the word that God placed in his mouth—what the reason is that the Lord does not curse Jacob or Israel.

## “From the summits of the rocks I shall see him, and from the hills I shall observe him”

Or, according to another edition: “Because from the peaks of the mountains,” he says, “I shall behold him, and from the hills I shall understand him.”

“Because,” he says, “Israel has been placed upon lofty mountains and high hills”—that is, in an elevated and arduous life, which no one can easily contemplate or understand unless he ascends to eminent and lofty knowledge—“therefore,” he says, “God does not curse him.” His life is high and exalted, not lowly and cast down.

Yet this does not seem to me to have been said about that Israel who is Israel according to the flesh, but about the one whose conduct, while he walks upon the earth, is in heaven. Or, if these words must also be referred to that people, he speaks with a distinction—“that I may behold and understand”—so that he may indicate a future time, namely, without doubt, the time when all Israel will come to faith in Christ and be saved: by those, certainly, who, rising with Christ, have practiced an exalted and heavenly life upon the earth.

The statement, moreover, “I shall see Jacob, but I shall understand Israel,” must also be received as a most appropriate distinction: one part refers to visible actions, the other to invisible faith and intelligible knowledge. Or, if we turn it toward the future age—that is, toward the time of the resurrection—“I shall see Jacob” may be understood as referring to bodies, while “I shall understand Israel” signifies the spirits and souls of those who rise.

## “Behold,” he says, “the people shall dwell alone, and shall not be reckoned among the nations”

This can also stand according to the literal sense. The people of Jacob was not mixed with other human beings, nor was it counted among the other nations. It possessed particular privileges in its observances and ordinances, by which it was kept separate from the other nations. Thus, too, the tribe of Levi was not mixed among the other tribes, nor was it numbered with them.

These things existed in that people as a pattern of future blessings. But the true Jacob and spiritual Israel truly dwelt alone among the nations. For if we have approached Mount Zion and the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and have come to the spiritual Judea, which is God’s portion, and, though placed on earth, have our conduct there, then truly we are not reckoned among the other nations, nor are the boundaries of the remaining nations mingled with our boundaries.

Even if Sodom should be restored to its former condition and Egypt return to its own state—and if anything of this sort has been written in the prophets—nevertheless, once those Jacobites and spiritual Israelites have ascended to the Church of the firstborn, no one among them will be made equal to them or mixed with them, even if those nations should be restored according to the prophetic statements.

For unless the branch of the wild olive has been grafted in and made a companion of the richness of the olive root, how can it be associated and joined to Jacob or Israel? Without that root, no one can be called Jacob, nor Israel. Therefore, if anyone from Jacob or Israel sins, he cannot be called Jacob or Israel; nor, if someone from the nations enters the Church of the Lord, will he henceforth be reckoned among the nations.

## “Who can investigate the seed of Jacob, and who can number the peoples of Israel?”

This resembles what is written concerning Abraham: God led him outside and said to him, “Look toward heaven, and count the stars, if you are able to count them.” And he said: “So shall your seed be.” And Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness (Gen. XIII).

But Abraham—and any other human being, or even angels, and perhaps also the higher powers—could not count the stars, nor Abraham’s seed, concerning which it is written: “So shall your seed be.” God, however, of whom it is written, “He numbers the multitude of the stars and calls them all by their names” (Ps. CXLVI), and who said, “I have given command to all the stars,” can investigate the seed of Jacob and number the peoples of Israel. For he alone knows who is truly Jacob and who is truly Israel.

He does not look to the one who is a Jew outwardly, nor to circumcision that is outward in the flesh; rather, he sees the one who is a Jew inwardly, and the one who is circumcised in heart, not in flesh.

He alone, therefore, is able to number and investigate. According to his ineffable and incomprehensible wisdom, and with reference to that heavenly pattern which he alone can know, he also established these Numbers that we have in our hands. In them he commanded that, according to their clans and according to the houses of their families, every male should be numbered by name, head by head, from twenty years of age and above—everyone who goes forth in the strength of Israel.

A certain sacred number is gathered, about which we have already spoken above, insofar as the Lord granted us to do so. But this number is sacred and pleasing to God only when it is counted at his command. If, however, someone wishes to number contrary to the Lord’s command—even if he belongs to God, even if he is a great prophet—he acts against the law, is reproved through the prophet, and suffers what we read written in the Second Book of Kings.

Therefore, he alone who numbers the multitude of the stars, and who has brought forth all things in measure, number, and weight (Wis. II), investigates the seed of Jacob and numbers the peoples of Israel.

After this, he seems to prophesy certain things about himself when he says: “May my soul die the death of the righteous, and may my end be like theirs.” But, insofar as this concerns the person of Balaam, and of that Jacob and that Israel, it neither did happen nor could happen. For he did not die among them, but because of them.

Rather, as we have said, these words will suit the person of those who, although in the present place or age they were regarded as a vain people, nevertheless, at the end of the age, when the fullness of the nations has entered and all this prophecy spoken about Israel has been fulfilled in spiritual Israel, will have their soul die together with the souls of the righteous.
