For they will receive the faith of Christ within themselves, so that they may say: “We who have been baptized into Christ Jesus have been buried with him through baptism into death” (Rom. VI). And again: “As we suffer death with him, so shall we also reign with him” (2 Tim. II). Thus Balaam will be fulfilled in an intelligible sense, so that his soul may die among the souls of the righteous.

As for what he says, “And may my end be like theirs,” or, as another edition has it, “May my seed be like the seed of the righteous,” this could indeed be understood of that Balaam. The magi who came from the East and were the first to worship Jesus may appear to have been from his seed, either through succession of lineage or through the transmission of teaching.

It is clearly established that they recognized the star which Balaam had foretold would arise in Israel, and that they came and worshiped the king who had been born in Israel.

Nevertheless, this will also suit the person of the people, according to what we have said: it is not so much they themselves as their seed that will become like the seed of the righteous—namely, like those who, believing from among the nations, have been justified in Christ.

Hence it is clear that, as the Apostle says: “Neither circumcision is anything, nor uncircumcision, but faith working through love” (Gal. VI). Therefore, let no one boast in the antiquity of circumcision, nor glory in the novelty of uncircumcision. Rather, as the Apostle says: “Let each one test his own work, and then he will have glory in himself” (ibid.).

Thus, too, the Prophet says: “Behold the human being and his work.” And a reward is said to be before the Lord, so that he may repay each person according to his works.

This sentence can also usefully be understood according to the laws of allegorical interpretation. For there are some within the holy Church who offer prolonged prayers to the Lord but do not possess the life of those who pray. The heavenly promises follow their petitions, but their works flee from them.

Sometimes they experience tears in prayer; but when, after the time of prayer, pride assails their mind, they immediately swell with the arrogance of self-exaltation. When avarice incites them, they at once boil with the fires of greedy thought. When lust has tempted them, they immediately pant after illicit desires. When anger advises them, the flame of madness quickly burns up the gentleness of their mind.

Thus, as we have said, they experience weeping in prayer, yet, once their prayers are completed and they are assailed by the suggestion of vices, they do not remember that they wept from a desire for the eternal kingdom.

Balaam clearly revealed this about himself. Seeing the tents of the righteous, he said: “May my soul die the death of the righteous, and may my end be like theirs.” But when the time of compunction had passed, he offered counsel against the life of those whom he had asked to resemble even in death. When he found an opportunity through avarice, he immediately forgot what he had desired for himself concerning innocence.

Therefore, it must be carefully considered that the wicked are often moved uselessly to compunction for righteousness, just as the good are often harmlessly tempted toward guilt.

A wonderful measure of the inner disposition occurs, according to the demands of their merits: while the wicked do something good, which nevertheless they do not complete, they grow proud amid the very evils that they fully perpetrate; while the good are tempted by an evil to which they do not consent, through humility they all the more truly fix the steps of their heart in righteousness insofar as they had wavered through weakness.

Balaam, looking upon the tents of the righteous, said: “May my soul die the death of the righteous.” But Paul said: “I see another law in my members, fighting against the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin, which is in my members” (Rom. VII). He is tempted for this very reason: so that, from the awareness of his weakness itself, he may be made more firmly established in the good.

What, then, is the reason that the one is moved to compunction and yet does not draw near to righteousness, while the other is tempted and yet is not stained by guilt? It is this, which is plainly demonstrated: imperfect good deeds do not help the wicked, nor do incomplete evils condemn the good.

Prayer has no weight of virtue when it is not held together by the perseverance of continuous love. In contrast, it is rightly said of Hannah, who was weeping: “Her face was no longer changed in different directions” (1 Sam. I). For her mind did not afterward lose through wanton, foolish joy what it had sought with groaning and firmness during the time of her prayer.

Balac said to Balaam: “What are you doing? I called you to curse my enemies, and instead you are blessing them.” He answered him: “Can I say anything other than what the Lord commands?”

Balac said: “Come with me to another place, from which you may see part of Israel but may not see all of it; from there curse him.” And when he had led him to a lofty place upon the summit of Mount Phasga, Balaam built seven altars. After calves and rams had been placed upon them, he said to Balac: “Stand here beside your burnt offering,” and so forth.

Thus King Balac, as though stunned and struck by what he saw being said contrary to his expectation—for he was hearing blessings instead of curses—could bear Balaam’s words no longer. He interrupted him and said: “What have you done to me? I called you to curse my enemies, and behold, you have blessed them with a blessing.”

The bitter king could not tolerate the blessing of sweetness; he sought curses and demanded curses. For he was acting from the thought of the one to whom the Lord said: “Cursed are you among all the beasts of the earth” (Gen. III).

But the one into whose mouth God had placed his word answered him: “Shall I not observe speaking whatever God puts into my mouth?”

At this Balac, thinking that Balaam had been frightened by the multitude of the Israelite people and therefore had not dared to utter curses, believed that a change of place would benefit him. He said to him: “Come with me once more to a high place, from which you will not see him in his entirety, but will see some part of him without seeing them all; and curse him for me from there.”

He was mad to believe that the grace of Israel could be concealed by the obstruction of a place, and he did not know that a city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden (Matt. V).

“And he took him,” he says, “to the lookout of the field, upon the summit of a cut mountain; and he built seven altars there, and placed a calf and a ram upon each altar. Balaam said to Balac: ‘Stand beside the sacrifice; I shall go on to inquire of God.’”

God came to meet Balaam, placed a word in his mouth, and said—and certainly it was God who said it: “Return to Balac, and speak these words.”

But he—that is, Balac—was standing beside his burnt offerings, with all the princes of Moab with him. Balac said to him: “What did the Lord say?”

The matter concerned a profane sacrifice, and divination was being sought through magical art. Yet God, wishing to make grace abound where sin had abounded, deigned to be present and did not shrink from matters that were being conducted according to the error of the nations.

He was present not at the sacrifices, but to meet the one who came to him; and there he gave his word. There he foretold mysteries of the future—precisely where the faith and wonder of the nations most depended—so that those who do not wish to believe our prophets might believe their own diviners and seers.

But he took up his parable and said:

“Stand, Balak, and listen; hear, son of Sephor. God is not like man, that he should lie, nor like a son of man, that he should change. Has he said, and will he not do it? Has he spoken, and will he not fulfill it? I have been brought for blessing; I cannot prevent the blessing. There is no idol in Jacob, nor is an image seen in Israel. The Lord their God is with them, and the victorious shout of the king is among them. God brought him out of Egypt; his strength is like that of a rhinoceros. There is no augury in Jacob, nor divination in Israel. In their times it shall be said to Jacob and Israel what God has done. Behold, the people will rise like a lioness, and like a lion it will rise up. It will not lie down until it has devoured its prey and drunk the blood of the slain.”

Another edition reads as follows:

“And taking up his parable,” he says, “he spoke: ‘Rise, Balak, and hear; attend with your ears, son of the witness, Sephor. God is not frustrated like a man, nor is he terrified like a son of man. When he has spoken, will he not act? Will he speak and not stand by it? Behold, I have been taken up for blessing; I shall bless and shall not turn him away. There will be no toil in Jacob, nor will pain be seen in Israel. The Lord their God is with him; the splendor of princes is with him. God, who brought him out of Egypt, is to him like the glory of a unicorn. For there will be no augury in Jacob, nor divination in Israel. In due time it shall be said to Jacob and Israel what God will accomplish. Behold, the people will rise like a lion’s cub, and like a lion it will exult. It will not sleep until it has eaten its prey and drunk the blood of the wounded.’”

This is the substance of Balaam’s second prophecy. Let us first examine what he says: “Rise, Balak, and hear.” If the preceding passage had not said that he was standing beside his burnt offering, there would be no particular reason to ask why he said, “Rise, Balak.” But since he now urges him to rise whom he had just said was standing, the prophetic statement must not be passed over casually.

What, then, the earlier passage indicates by saying that he was standing beside his burnt offering is that he was not standing rightly. He was standing in idolatry, and he was standing as an enemy of God; and that is more truly not standing but falling. Thus, as one who had taught him to fall from that position—or rather, as one who had caused him to fall—he now commands him, in prophetic understanding, to rise, since by appearing to stand in idolatry he had fallen.

Let such a person rise: let him rise in spirit, let him rise in faith, and let him become a witness to faith. But if he remains unbelieving, let him be a witness to his own condemnation.

But let us hear what he announces to him:

“God,” he says, “is not frustrated like a man, nor is he himself terrified like a son of man.”

“Do not hold this opinion about God,” he says, “so as to think that he is like a man who can be frustrated in what he says.” Human beings are hindered by many circumstances and faults from making what they say true. They may speak in anger, and when the anger has passed, they have spoken in vain; or they may speak from fear, desire, boastfulness, or from other similar motives. Whatever they have said while dominated by such a fault will certainly be futile and empty.

But God, in whom there is no passion and no frailty, says everything he says according to the merits of the circumstances. Therefore he can never be frustrated, because whatever is brought forth by reason cannot be deprived of reason. God, then, is not like a man who speaks in vain, nor is he like a son of man who is terrified—or, as we still read in other copies, “nor does he terrify like a son of man” [Col. 0739A].

Among human beings, someone sometimes changes his decision and issues threats. But God, who is above all things—by whom could he be terrified, so that he would change his decision?

If, however, we understand the reading found in the other copies, namely, “nor does a son of man terrify,” this seems to mean that human beings sometimes make threats and issue menaces out of boastfulness, even against those whom they may sometimes be unable to harm. God, however, does not terrify human beings in this way, as though he were unable to punish them. If he terrifies, he terrifies rationally. He terrifies in order to correct a person through the experience of tribulation, so that the one who does evil, terrified by the word of warning, may reform and the punishment of his deeds may not overtake him.

God, therefore, does not terrify in the manner of a human being. A human being, as we have said, terrifies out of boastfulness; God terrifies for the sake of correction.

After this he says:

“When he has spoken, will he not act? Will he speak and not stand by it?”

The passage should be read as though he were speaking with the feeling of one asking a question:

“He”—that is, God—“when he speaks, will he not also act? And what he has spoken, will he not stand by?”

Human beings, through the fault of human frailty, do not do what they say and do not stand by what they speak. A human being is changeable, but God is unchangeable.

Someone may object and say: How, then, did God not stand by what he said concerning Nineveh, that after three days it would be overthrown (Jonah III), nor by what he said concerning David, when three days of death had been foretold to lay waste the people, yet within a single day it ceased by the hour of the meal?

It may perhaps appear that these statements, expressed as questions, should not be taken as absolute, but that this is a certain figure of speech which seems to indicate something intermediate, without declaring the outcome of a sentence as entirely definite and irrevocable. Thus the statement, “When he has spoken, will he not act?” may be understood more moderately, as though it had been written: “When he has spoken, he will certainly act.”

Yet even in the prophetic words themselves, we should understand not so much the words of God as those of the prophets, who uttered them in accordance with the merits of each person; but through God’s mercy the things threatened were suspended, so that they would not come upon them.

Likewise, through Jeremiah the Lord says:

“At the end I will speak”—that is, “I will speak with a definitive judgment”—“against a nation and against a kingdom, to uproot and destroy them. And if that nation turns from its evils, repenting of all the evils that I had thought to do to them, I will repent. And at the end I will speak against a nation and a kingdom, to rebuild and replant them; and if it does evil in my sight, so that it does not hear my voice, I will repent of all the good that I had spoken of doing to them” (Jeremiah XVIII).

How, then, can we place before these words, spoken absolutely through Jeremiah, those spoken conditionally through Balaam, unless it is because the former are to be confirmed for the negligent and contemptuous, while the latter are to be perceived more secretly by the more perfect?

After this Balaam says:

“Behold, I have been taken up for blessing; I shall bless and shall not turn him away.”

Balaam was engaged by Balak for blessing, but by God, who placed in his mouth the word by which he was to bless the people. Balaam did not turn this blessing away; nor could he, even if he wished, alter the word of God with a human tongue.

After this he says:

“There is no idol in Jacob, nor is an image seen in Israel.”

How can this be understood historically, when the carnal Israelites themselves, the descendants of the patriarch Jacob, are repeatedly accused by the prophets of the idolatry they practiced?

It is better understood of the future people—that is, of the true and spiritual Israelites—in whom there is no worship of idols, but the service, religion, and perpetual worship of the one almighty God, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

But as the other edition reads, “There will be no toil in Jacob, nor will pain be seen in Israel,” these words plainly announce the condition of the future life. Who, after all, passes through this present life without toil and pain? Even if someone were Peter, or if he were Paul, how could he be without toil and pain, when he is beaten with rods, stoned once, suffers shipwreck three times, and spends a day and night in the depths of the sea (1 Corinthians XII), besides enduring countless other hardships that he writes about in connection with his labors and sufferings?

But this will be fulfilled there where it is said: “Pain, sorrow, and groaning shall flee away.” This, however, is not referred to everyone, but only to those who have the merits of Jacob and Israel. Such was Lazarus, who passed his present life in toil and pain.

There, however, it is said to the rich man:

“Remember, son, that you received good things in your life, and Lazarus likewise evil things. But now he is comforted here, while you are tormented” (Luke XVI).

He, then, is Israel and Jacob, upon whom toil and pain do not come.

That rich man was indeed rich, and he too was an Israelite according to the flesh. For it is said to him: “Your brothers have the law; let them hear them” (ibid.). But because he was not Israel according to the spirit, toil and pain came upon him.

Next follows:

“The Lord their God is with him, and the victorious shout of the king is among them.”

He says this about the preaching of the Gospel among the Christian people, where it is proclaimed openly how Christ the King triumphed over the devil through the trophy of the cross and acquired an everlasting kingdom for himself.

Therefore, after he had risen from the dead, he appeared to his disciples and said: “All authority has been given to me in heaven and on earth,” and so forth (Matthew, last chapter).

Paul also says:

“Christ became obedient for us to the Father unto death, even death on a cross. Therefore God exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth, and every tongue should confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (Philippians II).

But according to the other edition, the reading is:

“The Lord God is with him; the splendor of princes is with him.”

God never abandons his Israel. Let us see, then, whose splendor of princes is with this Israel.

“The splendor of princes” means the power, authority, and kingdom of rulers. But since there are also certain rulers who are either to be expelled from their authority or perhaps have already been expelled, and since those who are truly Israelites are to be introduced into their place and authority, this Israel and Jacob, who wrestled and prevailed, will receive all those splendid things that the princes who did not preserve their authority but abandoned their eternal dwelling places possessed in heaven. Thus the splendor of princes will be with him [Col. 0741A].

“God brought him out of Egypt; his strength is like that of a rhinoceros.”

Or, according to the other edition:

“His glory is like the glory of a unicorn.”

That Israel was indeed brought out of the earthly Egypt; but this spiritual Israel has been brought out of the Egypt of the age and from the power of darkness, and his strength or glory is like that of a unicorn.

The unicorn is said to be an animal formed in the shape indicated by its name. We frequently read of this animal in the divine Scriptures, but especially in Job its power and strength are explained through God’s words; and in these passages Christ is understood to be signified, as in very many others.

In the divine Scriptures we often find the horn used for a kingdom, as the prophet also says: “The four horns are four kingdoms” (Daniel VII).

Under the name “unicorn,” this seems to be shown in Christ: everything that is one belongs to his horn—that is, his kingdom is one. For the Father has subjected all things beneath his feet, until the last enemy, death, is destroyed; and, like a unicorn, Christ holds the one kingdom of all things, because, as it is written, “there will be no end of his kingdom” (Isaiah IX).

“Therefore,” he says, “there will be glory for him”—that is, for that spiritual Israel—“like the glory of a unicorn.”

For the Lord himself says in the Gospel:

“Father, grant them that just as you and I are one, so they too may be one in us” (John XVIII).

Therefore glory like the glory of a unicorn will also be given to Israel, especially when he transforms the body of our humiliation, making it conform to the body of his glory.

“There will be no augury in Jacob, nor divination in Israel. In due time it shall be said to Jacob and Israel what God will accomplish.”

Since it has seemed worthwhile to examine each point more carefully, it is not unreasonable also to investigate what augury and divination are—things that Scripture has chosen to mention—so that no one may perhaps fall into them through ignorance.

It seems to me that foreknowledge of future events, considered in itself, is something intermediate: that is, neither properly good nor properly evil. For foreknowledge of future things can sometimes come to human beings even from the devil.

Without doubt, when the time and the occasion require it, and when God wills, foreknowledge is also given to human beings by God in the form of prophecy. Therefore we have said that what sometimes comes from evil cannot properly be called good, nor can what sometimes descends from God properly be called evil.

For in the Book of Kings, the priests and diviners of the Philistines gave counsel by divination concerning the return of the ark of God, because of the plague that had come upon them on account of it. They advised that it should be sent toward the land of Judah on a new cart drawn by cows.

Thus there is a certain operation of demons in this sort of foreknowledge. Those who have enslaved themselves to demons gather it by various arts: sometimes through what they call lots, sometimes through what they call auguries, sometimes through the observation of the entrails (*fibrarum*, “fibres/entrails”), which they call extispicy, and through other similar deceptions. This appears to be the operation of this kind of foreknowledge [Col. 0742A].

These arts advanced so far in deceiving the human race that even Manasseh, the son of the exceedingly righteous Hezekiah, was deceived by this error and, as Scripture says, built an altar to the whole army of heaven in both houses of the Lord (2 Kings XXI).

I think that this army of heaven is the one of which Paul writes: “the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Ephesians VI).

Unless there had been great deception and error in these arts, I do not think that the son of so great a man, brought up in the law of the Lord, could have fallen into those impieties that are reported about him in the Fourth Book of Kings.

Our divine and heavenly religion rejects all these practices. In Leviticus it expressly states:

“You shall not practice divination or augury.”

And shortly afterward:

“Do not follow ventriloquists, nor associate with enchanters, lest you be defiled by them. I am the Lord your God” (Leviticus XIX).

God does not want us to become hearers and disciples of demons. Nor does he want us, if we wish to learn something, to learn it from demons. It is better to be ignorant than to learn from demons. It is also better to learn from prophets than to inquire of diviners.

Some people think that divination is given divinely, but in my view it received its name rather through antiphrasis—that is, from its opposite—as though it were something practiced by human beings filled with a demon.

The ritual of the Gentiles, however, considers everything divine that is spoken through any kind of spirit. But God commands us to learn nothing from such sources, lest we become their companions and fall into what Isaiah says:

“Your words shall be brought low to the earth, and your speech shall sink beneath the earth; your voice shall be like one speaking from the earth, and your voice shall become weak in the dust” (Isaiah XXIX).

For this reason our God Jesus does not deign to accept testimony from demons, but says:

“Be silent and come out of him” (Luke IV).

His apostle Paul imitates him. Being distressed, he turned and said to the spirit of the python:

“I command you in the name of Jesus Christ, come out of her” (Acts X).

Therefore, he says, “there will be no augury in Jacob, nor divination in Israel.”

But what is added to this?

“In due time,” he says, “it shall be said to Jacob and Israel what God will accomplish.”

What does “in due time” mean? It means: when it is necessary and beneficial—in due time.

If, then, it is beneficial for us to know the future beforehand, it will be declared by God through God’s prophets and through the Holy Spirit. But if it is not declared or announced, know that it is not beneficial for us to know what is to come.

If, because it is not beneficial for us to know these things, we nonetheless desire through various arts and invocations of demons to know the future, we are doing nothing other than desiring to learn what it is not beneficial for us to know.

Jacob is to be understood here as everyone who wrestles against principalities and powers and against the rulers of this world. Israel is to be understood as everyone who sees God through purity of faith and cleanness of mind.

Someone may say: If we must learn about the future from God alone, and must accept neither a diviner, nor an augur, nor anything else of this kind, then surely Balaam himself is not to be accepted by us either. For he is one of those whom the divine judgment forbids us to admit.

But consider the matter more carefully, and remember what we read above, where it is said that “the Lord placed his word in his mouth.” We are not now speaking these things from Balaam, but from the word of God that had been placed in his mouth.

For if these were not the words of the Lord, he would certainly not have revealed them to his servant Moses. Moses was far away, yet when they were spoken to Balak the king, it is certain that Moses could not have known them unless they had been revealed to him by God.

After this he says:

“Behold, the people will rise like a lioness or a lion’s cub, and like a lion it will exult.”

In these words it seems to me that he describes the confidence of the people who believe in Christ, the freedom they possess in faith, and the exultation they display in hope.

It is compared to a lion’s cub while it is advancing joyfully and swiftly toward perfection. It is compared to a lion when it already possesses what belongs to maturity.

For just as a lion, a lioness, or a lion’s cub fears no animal or beast, but all things are subject to them, so all things are subject to and trampled beneath the feet of the perfect Christian who takes up his cross and follows Christ. He can say:

“The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Galatians VI).

He despises and rejects everything that is in this world, and imitates him who is called the Lion from the tribe of Judah and the Lion’s Cub.

For just as he himself is the light of the world and gave his disciples also to be the light of the world, so, although he himself is the lion and the lion’s cub, he also assigns the name of lion and lion’s cub to those who believe in him [Col. 0743C].

Observe that these words are clearly spoken not of the people who were then in authority, but of the people who were to come.

He says:

“Behold, the people will rise like a lion’s cub, and like a lion it will exult.”

He says that the people will rise—certainly, the people who were to come. For if he were speaking of the people whom he saw, he would undoubtedly have said: “Behold, the people have risen like a lion’s cub.”

But it is certain that he is speaking of that people of whom it is also written:

“The heavens will proclaim his righteousness to a people that will be born, whom the Lord has made” (Psalm XXI).

This people, then, is a lion’s cub while they still desire, like newly born infants, rational and pure milk. But it is an exultant lion when, having become mature, it has put away the things that belonged to childhood.

“It will not sleep until it has eaten its prey and drunk the blood of the wounded.”

In these words, what defender of the historical interpretation will be so contentious—or rather, who will be so brutish—as not to recoil at the sound of the literal wording and, compelled by the very necessity of the case, flee to the sweetness of allegory?

How could this people, so praiseworthy and so glorious, of whom the discourse enumerates such great praises, come to the point of drinking the blood of the wounded, when blood as food is prohibited by such forceful commands? We too, although called from the Gentiles, necessarily seem to abstain from blood just as we abstain from things sacrificed to idols.

Let them therefore learn from us who this people is that makes a practice of drinking blood.

These were the things that those who followed the Lord from among the Jews heard in the Gospel, and they were scandalized and said:

“Who can eat flesh and drink blood?” (John VI).

But the Christian people, the faithful people, hear these words, embrace them, and follow the one who says:

“Unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood, you will not have life in yourselves. For my flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink” (ibid.).

And certainly the one who said these things was wounded for human beings. For “he was wounded for our sins,” as Isaiah says (Isaiah LIII).

We are said to drink the blood of Christ not only through the rite of the sacraments, but also when we receive his words, in which life consists, as he himself says:

“The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life” (John VI).

He himself, then, is the wounded one whose blood we drink—that is, whose words of teaching we receive.

But those who preached his word to us were also wounded. When we read the words of his apostles and obtain life from them, we likewise drink the blood of the wounded.

Therefore, he says:

“It will not sleep until it has eaten its prey.”

This people, which is compared with a lion’s cub or a lion, will not rest or sleep until it seizes its prey—that is, until it plunders the kingdom of heaven. For “from the days of John the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and those who use force seize it” (Matthew XI).

But so that you may recognize more clearly that these words are written about our people, which has been joined in covenant with the sacraments of Christ, hear how Moses also proclaims similar things elsewhere:

“Butter of cattle and milk of sheep, with the fat of lambs and rams, of the offspring of bulls and goats, with the fat of the kidneys of wheat; and they shall drink wine, the blood of the grape” (Deuteronomy XXXII).

This blood that is called the blood of the grape is also the blood of the grapevine that comes from the vine of which the Savior says:

“I am the true vine, and the disciples are the branches; the Father is the cultivator” (John XV).

He purifies them so that they may bear abundant fruit.

You, then, are the true people of Israel, who know how to drink blood and know how to eat the flesh of the Word of God and drink the blood of the Word; and who draw the blood of that grape which comes from the true vine and from those branches that the Father purifies.

The fruit of those branches may rightly be called the blood of the wounded, which we drink from their words and teaching—provided that we are like lion’s cubs rising up.

Balak therefore said to Balaam:

“Do not curse.”

And he replied:

“Did I not tell you that whatever God commanded me, I would do?”

Balak said to him:

“Come, and I will take you to another place, in case it should please God that you curse them from there.”

When he had brought him up to the summit of Mount Phogor, which overlooks the wilderness, Balaam said to him:

“Build me seven altars and prepare seven calves and an equal number of rams.”

Balak did as Balaam had said, and placed a calf and a ram upon each altar.

This unfortunate Balak thought that Balaam was a diviner and that the opportunity of the place, rather than the will, had been lacking for cursing. He therefore judged that it would be more effective to change the location.

“Come,” he says, “and I will take you to another place, if it pleases God, so that you may curse him from there.”

Balak took Balaam to the summit of Mount Phogor, which extends toward the desert.

Those whom God calls he sets upon the summit of Mount Sinai. But this Balak, who is opposed to God, sets Balaam upon the summit of Mount Phogor.

Phogor is interpreted as “pleasure.” This Balak places people upon the summit of pleasure and lust. He is therefore a lover of pleasure more than of God. For this reason he places them upon the height and summit of pleasure, so that God may exclude them.

For Balak is interpreted as “excluding” and “devouring.” Thus Phogor ultimately extends toward the wilderness—that is, toward matters that are wild and desolate with respect to God.

Balaam said to Balak:

“Build me seven altars, and make me seven calves and seven rams.”

Balak did as Balaam had said. He offered a calf and a ram upon the altar.

The Apostle’s statement is clear:

“What the Gentiles sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons and not to God” (1 Corinthians X).

The prophet likewise says:

“They sacrificed to demons and not to God.”

Nevertheless, since the law of God also gives commands concerning sacrifices and transmits the rite of sacrificing to the children of Israel, perhaps it should be asked why these sacrifices, although they appear to have been dedicated to demons, are also commanded to be offered to God.

There is a simple and immediate answer: just as we have shown elsewhere that the granting of a bill of divorce was not God’s will—for he did not wish to separate what he had joined—but that Moses wrote this specifically because of the hardness of the Jews’ hearts (Deuteronomy XXIV), so it may also be understood here that God, as he says through another prophet, does not eat the flesh of bulls or drink the blood of goats (Psalm XLIX).

Likewise, as it is written elsewhere:

“I did not command you concerning sacrifices and victims on the day when I brought you out of the land of Egypt.”

But Moses gave them these commands because of the hardness of their hearts and the evil custom with which they had been imbued in Egypt, so that those who could not abstain from sacrificing might at least sacrifice to God and not to demons.

Nevertheless, we must consider whether there may be some more hidden and secret reason for sacrificing to God. Perhaps, I say, the sacrifices offered to God were made as a distinction from those sacrifices that were offered to demons, so that, since souls are wounded by the former, they might be healed by the latter, just as those skilled in medicine affirm.

They say that the poisons of snakes are likewise driven out by substances cut from snakes. In the same way, then, the poison of demonic sacrifices is driven out by sacrifices offered to God, just as the death of Jesus does not allow the death of sin to rule over believers [Col. 0745D].

For as long as the time permitted, sacrifices were set against sacrifices. But when the perfect offering and the spotless Lamb came, who was to take away the sin of the whole world, those sacrifices that had been offered individually to God appeared superfluous, since one offering had driven away the entire worship of demons.

But this Balaam—whether according to the interpretation by which we said that he represents the teachers and Pharisees of the unbelieving people—still renews sacrifices and orders offerings to be prepared.

In these things place their hope those whose heart does not reject faith in Christ.

But what follows?

## Chapter XXIV

When Balaam saw that it pleased the Lord that he should bless Israel, he did not go away as he had gone before to seek an augury. Instead, turning his face toward the wilderness and lifting up his eyes, he saw Israel dwelling in tents according to its tribes. And when the Spirit of God rushed upon him, he took up his parable and said:

It may perhaps be asked how Balaam saw that it was good in the sight of the Lord to bless Israel. It may be thought that he understood this from the sacrifices he had offered. When he saw that no demon was present, that no opposing power dared to stand beside his victims, and that all the ministers of wickedness whom he used for cursing had been excluded, he could have understood from these things that it was good in the sight of God to bless Israel.

I, however, understand it rather in this way: that the people who was born, and those teachers who, not believing in Christ, hold the people in vanity, will at some time see—that is, in the last days, when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered and all Israel begins to come to faith in Christ. Those who now have eyes but do not see will then see.

They will lift up their eyes through a higher and spiritual understanding, and they will see and understand that it is good in the sight of the Lord to bless spiritual Israel.

For he will see him arranged according to tribes, houses, and families, and each person attaining the glory of the resurrection in his own order.

And, taking up his parable, he will understand the things written in parables, which now, because of the veil placed over their hearts, they neither see nor understand.

Finally, he says:

“He did not go away, as was his custom, to meet the omens.”

For he will not be carried away according to his customary manner by foolish and empty perceptions, considering God in dumb animals and beasts, as do those who gather omens from such things. Rather, he himself will recognize that God is concerned neither with bulls, nor with sheep, nor with birds, nor with other animals, but that these things were written for the sake of human beings, and he will understand what has been written.

If anyone is troubled by the fact that, according to the edition of the Seventy translators, the text reads, “The Spirit of God came upon him”—that is, upon Balaam—he should know that this must not be understood as though the Spirit of God were a created thing when it says, “the Spirit of God came to be.” Rather, “it came upon him” means that it came to be upon him; that is, it happened that it was upon him.

In the same way:

“He who comes after me has come before me” (John I)

means that it happened that he was before me, that he was placed before me, because, he says, he existed before me.

Likewise:

“The Lord became my helper” (Psalm CXVII).

The Lord did not become a created thing; rather, it happened that he helped me.

And:

“The Lord became a refuge for the poor” (Psalm IX)

means that it happened that the poor fled to him.

And:

“The hand of the Lord came upon me” (Ezekiel III)

means that it happened that it was upon me.

Many similar expressions are found in the Scriptures.

But let us now see what Balaam speaks in his third prophecy.

Having taken up his parable, he said:

“Balaam son of Beor said: The man whose eye is closed said; the hearer of the words of God said; he who beheld the vision of the Almighty, who falls, and thus his eyes are opened.”

What does it mean that it is written of Balaam that he was “the man whose eye was closed,” and that he “spoke as the hearer of the words of God, beholding the vision of the Almighty”? How did he see the vision with his eye closed? Historically, this does not mean that, in a dream, when his bodily eyes had already been shut, he learned through a vision—communicated by angelic agency—the things that were to be said. Allegorically, however, it is shown that the eyes of the mind may be open in one respect and closed in another. They were open for recognizing future mysteries, but closed for correcting his error. He had the revealed perception of his heart for discerning the sacrament of prophecy, but he did not have it for worshiping and venerating the author of the prophecy himself.

“All those,” he says, “bear his type who do one thing in knowledge and another in conduct; who show one thing with their mouth and another by their deeds.” Concerning such people the Apostle says: “Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks; but they became futile in their reasoning, and while claiming to be wise, they became fools,” and so forth (Rom. I). Elsewhere it is written: “They profess to know God, but by their deeds they deny him” (Tit. I).

Hence Balaam is interpreted as “a vain people,” or “one who makes them rush headlong,” and Beor as “one who impels.” Since all who act contrary to the true religion—in which the one God is truthfully worshiped and honored through faith working by righteousness—are rightly called “a vain people,” they are also called sons of Beor, that is, sons of the devil who impels them: for he continually drives and provokes them to sin.

It follows: “He who falls, and thus his eyes are opened.” Often some people admire the eternal judgments, love the proclamation of the heavenly homeland when they hear it, and are astonished at the wondrous works of the inward ordering of things; yet, although they love and behold these things, they neglect to rise toward those same works. Thus, while lying prostrate, they contemplate God’s miracles: they weigh his power by knowing it, but do not love it by living accordingly. Through contemplation they stretch out the eyes of their understanding toward it, yet by the direction of their will they do not raise themselves from the earth.

This statement may also be understood tropologically in another way. “The man whose eye is closed,” he says, “spoke; the hearer of the words of God spoke, who beheld the vision of the Almighty, who falls, and thus his eyes are opened.” The wicked person does not know the evils he commits until he has begun to be punished for those very evils. Balaam gave counsel against the Israelites; afterward, in his punishment, he saw what he had previously committed through guilt. The elect, however, because they take care not to sin, have their eyes open before the fall. The unrighteous person opens his eyes after the fall, because after his guilt, in his punishment, he sees that he ought to have avoided the evil he committed.

It should be noted, however, that this passage is read differently according to the Septuagint: “Balaam son of Beor blessed. The truly seeing man said; the one hearing the words of the Mighty One said, who saw God’s vision in a dream, his eyes having been revealed.”

It is certainly astonishing how Balaam should receive such a lofty description, when, having taken up his parable, he pronounces these things about himself. For it is extremely surprising that Balaam should be called “a truly seeing man,” since he practiced divination and augury, and even devoted himself to magic, as we showed above—unless perhaps these great praises are thought to have been written about him because it was previously said that the spirit of God had come upon him and that the word of God had been placed in his mouth.

Neither Moses nor any other prophet is easily found to have been exalted with such praises. Therefore it seems to me more likely that this should apply to that people at the time when, having already turned to the Lord, it laid aside the veil that was over its heart. “The Lord is the Spirit.” Hence, finally, he says, “his eyes having been revealed,” as though they had previously been closed and were now uncovered through the Spirit of God that had come upon him.

It is therefore now that he truly sees and truly hears the words of the Mighty One, and sees God’s vision in a dream—that is, he will see fulfilled the things whose times were symbolically indicated in dreams to the prophet Daniel, and he sees those visions that were conveyed to him in dreams; that is, he understands and recognizes them. With revealed eyes he becomes like those of whom it is said: “We all, with unveiled face, behold the glory of the Lord, being transformed into the same image, from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord” (II Cor. V).

But if someone wishes to accept these words also according to the historical sense, then, because Balaam saw that it was good in the sight of the Lord to bless Israel, his eyes are shown to have been revealed and he is shown to have become a truly seeing man. For he truly saw what was to come concerning Israel or Jacob. He may also be said to have heard the words of the Mighty One when God came to him and spoke to him in a dream: “The word that I shall put in your mouth—observe this, that you may speak it.” This was the vision of God that he saw in a dream. By these words he asserts that Balaam’s eyes were revealed, because he was able to see what he saw.

This, then, is what may be said concerning the things that Balaam appears to have prophesied about himself in his preface. Let us now see what he says in what follows.

## “How beautiful are your tabernacles, Jacob, and your tents, Israel! Like wooded valleys, like gardens beside irrigated streams; like tabernacles that the Lord has planted, like cedars beside the waters.”

I do not think that this refers to earthly dwellings enclosing them. For no such thing is recorded as having existed among them, especially in comparison with the other nations. But let us see whether, perhaps because the people was divided into tribes, each tribe into peoples, the peoples again into kindreds, and the kindreds into family households, while they were counted according to the number of names and heads—that is, every male who was twenty years old or more and able to go forth to war—Balaam, beholding these tabernacles in the spirit, magnifies and extols them.

Yet the meaning should not be considered solely in terms of the letter, since Balaam speaks what he says after taking up his parable. Therefore let us also hear in parables what is said. If you consider those divisions and ranks of the peoples that will exist in the resurrection among the people of the true Israel, when each person will rise in his own order, then, if you can, behold those tribes, peoples, and kindreds, in which kinship consists not so much in flesh and blood as in mind and spirit. Then you will understand how beautiful are the tabernacles of Jacob and the tents of Israel.

If you wish to read the passage according to another edition, it runs as follows: “How good are your houses, Jacob, and your tabernacles, Israel; like shady groves, like paradises beside rivers.” If you ask about the difference between his houses and tabernacles, and likewise about the distinction between Jacob and Israel, the following differentiation should be made.

A house is something founded and stable, enclosed within definite boundaries. Tabernacles, however, are dwellings belonging to those who are always on the road and always journeying, without ever finding the end of their route. Accordingly, Jacob should be understood as representing those who are perfect in deeds and works, while Israel should be understood as representing those who devote themselves to the pursuit of wisdom.

Since completed works are enclosed within a definite end—for the perfection of works is not without limit—when someone has fulfilled everything he ought to do and has reached the completion of his works, that perfection of works is called his good house. But those who love to devote themselves to wisdom and knowledge have no end. For what limit will there be to the wisdom of God? The more someone approaches it, the deeper he will find it; and the more someone searches it out, the more ineffable and incomprehensible he will discover it to be. For the wisdom of God is incomprehensible and immeasurable.

Therefore, for those who walk the path of wisdom, he does not praise houses. They have not yet arrived at the goal; rather, he marvels at their tabernacles, in which they are always walking and always advancing. The more they advance, the more their path of advancement increases and extends into immensity. Thus, beholding their progress through the Spirit, he calls them the tabernacles of Israel.

Indeed, if someone has made some progress in knowledge and acquired some experience in such matters, he knows perfectly well that when the soul has arrived at some theoretical understanding and recognition of spiritual mysteries, it dwells, as it were, in a certain tabernacle. But when, from what it has found, it again searches out other things and advances to other understandings, it moves onward from there toward higher things, as though its tabernacle had been lifted up. There it establishes itself, fixing its seat in the depths through the stability of its perceptions. From there it again discovers other spiritual meanings arising from those very meanings which, without doubt, the sequence of its earlier perceptions has disclosed.

Thus, always extending itself toward what lies ahead, it appears to journey through a kind of tabernacle. There is never a time when the soul, kindled by the spark of knowledge, can be idle and at rest; rather, it is always summoned from good things to better, and again from better things to higher ones. Balaam has therefore described this journey of God’s wisdom with sufficient grace and great beauty, saying:

“Like shady groves, like paradises beside rivers, and like tabernacles that the Lord has planted; like cedars beside the waters.”

Those who walk this way walk through shady groves. The groves are shady for them, and the paradises are the whole assembly of the righteous and the chorus of the holy and the prophets. Under the shadow of the meanings that they find written among them, their souls are refreshed; and in their teachings they delight, as though walking through the shaded spaces of groves. They are like paradises beside rivers, resembling and belonging to that paradise in which the tree of life is found.

By “rivers” we may understand either the evangelical and apostolic Scriptures, or also the assistance given by angels and heavenly powers to souls of this kind. For by these they are watered and cleansed, and nourished toward every kind of knowledge and recognition of heavenly realities. Our Savior, too, is a river that makes glad the city of God; and the Holy Spirit is not only himself a river, but also causes rivers to flow from the belly of those to whom he has been given. God the Father says: “They have forsaken me, the fountain of living water”—from which fountain, of course, these rivers flow.

Thus, when the tabernacles of Israel have been cleansed by these rivers, they are like those that the Lord has planted.

Perhaps, however, the hearer may be troubled by the fact that the present passage mentions two kinds of tabernacles. For it says: “How good are your houses, Jacob; your tabernacles, Israel; like shady groves and like paradises beside rivers.” Then again it compares tabernacles with tabernacles and says: “And like the tabernacles that the Lord has planted.”

Another exposition may therefore be received in addition to those proposed above: we may say that the houses of Jacob are the Law, and the tabernacles of Israel are the prophets. For he does not praise Jacob himself, but his houses; nor Israel himself, but his tabernacles. And he praises them when his eyes have been revealed. As long as the veil remains over the reading of the Law and the prophets, neither the good tabernacles nor the praiseworthy house can be seen. But when the veil has been removed, and it begins to be understood that the Law is spiritual, and likewise the prophecy, then the houses of Jacob are good and wonderful. The tabernacles of Jacob, too, become worthy of admiration when, after the removal of the letter that kills, you begin to receive from them the Spirit that gives life.

It may still be understood in another way: the bodies and souls of the believing people—and indeed of this people gathered from the nations by Christ—may together appear to be praised. Jacob may be called the house in reference to the bodies, just as it is also written in a certain little book that Jacob is the house of Israel: that is, Jacob is called its body, and Israel its soul.

Likewise, the bodies of all the perfected may be called praiseworthy houses of Jacob. A body is praiseworthy when marked by self-restraint and chastity, and sometimes when it is adorned by martyrdom. The tabernacles, however, may be referred to perfected souls, to whom the name “Israel”—those who see God—is also appropriate.

“These tabernacles,” he says, “are like shady groves, like paradises beside rivers, and like tabernacles that the Lord has planted.” He thus shows that there are other tabernacles that the Lord has planted, and that the tabernacles of Israel resemble them.

I should proceed beyond this point and see what the tabernacles are that the Lord has planted. They are surely those that he showed to Moses when he was constructing the tabernacle in the wilderness, saying to him: “See that you make everything according to the pattern that was shown to you on the mountain” (Exod. XXV).

Israel, therefore, ought to make tabernacles in imitation of those tabernacles that the Lord planted, and each one of us ought to prepare and construct his own tabernacle.

For this reason it does not seem accidental that Peter and Andrew and the sons of Zebedee were first found to be fishermen, while Paul had previously been a maker of tabernacles. Since those who were called from the craft of catching fish are thought to have become fishers of human beings, when the Lord said, “Come after me, and I will make you fishers of human beings” (Matt. IV), there is no doubt that Paul also, because he too was called by the Lord Jesus Christ to be an apostle, was transformed through a similar craft and calling. Just as they became fishers of human beings from being fishers of fish, so he was transferred from making earthly tabernacles to constructing heavenly tabernacles.

Paul constructs heavenly tabernacles by teaching each person the way of salvation and showing the path to blessed dwellings in heaven. Paul makes tabernacles when, by establishing churches, he fills the regions around Jerusalem as far as Illyricum with the Gospel of God. In this way he also makes tabernacles in the likeness of the heavenly tabernacles that God showed to Moses on the mountain.

But each one of us—provided that he has come out of Egypt and dwells in the wilderness—ought to live in a tabernacle and celebrate the feast in tabernacles. For just as departure from Egypt is commemorated through Passover and Unleavened Bread, so remembrance of the wilderness is commemorated through tabernacles. Our fathers lived in tabernacles in the wilderness.

From what else should these tabernacles be made, if not from the words of the Law and the prophets, from the sayings of the Psalms, and from everything contained in the Law? For when the soul advances through what has been written, continually forgetting what lies behind and stretching itself toward what lies ahead, proceeding from a lower place, growing and advancing toward higher things through an increase of virtues and the very transformation involved in its progress, it is rightly said to dwell in tabernacles.

See whether those tabernacles that the Lord has planted are not also the ones that the Savior mentions in the Gospel when he says: “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of unrighteousness, so that when it fails, they may receive you into eternal tabernacles” (Luke XVI). They are called planted by God because they are not carried about by every wind of doctrine.

These tabernacles are also “like cedars beside the waters.” Here he does not mean other cedars, in which culpable arrogance is indicated, but the cedars of God that look up toward the shoots of that vine transplanted from Egypt, and in which rests the fruit whose shade covered the mountains.

If you have understood how much rest, grace, and sweetness the path of wisdom possesses, do not dissemble and do not neglect it. Undertake it, and do not shrink from the solitude of the wilderness. For when you dwell in such tabernacles, heavenly manna will meet you, and you will eat the bread of angels. Only begin, and do not let the solitude of the desert pass you by. Soon the angels too will come into your company, because, as the grace of your merits increases, you ascend to eat the bread of angels and to behold the God of gods. I think that they are indicated under the figure of cedars.

## “Water will flow from his bucket, and his seed will be in many waters.”

According to the historical sense, he shows that a great multitude of peoples will grow abundantly from the nation of Israel. For, he says, water is a multitude of people.

Allegorically, however, it signifies the abundant grace of evangelical teaching, which from the primitive Church in Jerusalem, through the ministry of the apostles, was poured generously throughout the whole world. The apostles themselves arose from the stock of Abraham and, filled with the blessing of Christ, who is the true seed of Abraham, filled the whole world with their preaching.

Hence it is written: “Their sound has gone out through all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. XVIII). For this reason Isaiah also says: “All who see them will recognize them, because they are the seed that the Lord has blessed.”

## “His king will be taken away because of Agag, and his kingdom will be removed.”

This statement shows that the first king of the Jews, Saul, lost his kingdom because of Agag, king of the Amalekites, because he spared him contrary to the Lord’s command.

Another edition, however, has this passage very differently. It contains a prophecy concerning Christ and his kingdom. Let us see how it is written:

“A man will come forth from his seed, and he will rule many nations. Gog will be exalted, and his kingdom will increase, and his kingdom will grow.”

Christ, therefore, is the one who came forth from the seed of Israel according to the flesh. How he rules the nations requires no explanation, especially for one who reads what the Father said to him: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession to the ends of the earth” (Ps. II).

But what does he mean by saying, “Gog will be exalted, and his kingdom will increase”? Gog is interpreted as “above the roofs.” In this passage it is not used as the name of some nation, as is commonly thought; rather, as in several other places, the Hebrew word itself has been left untranslated, and for this reason it appears to refer to some nation.

The sequence of the passage is therefore as follows: “His kingdom will be exalted above the roofs, and his kingdom will increase.” To be exalted above the roofs refers to the perfection of believers; to increase refers to the multitudes.

Thus the kingdom of Christ is exalted above the roofs in those who are perfect—that is, even above those who are in the heights and dwell in higher places. For perhaps there are also beings in heaven from whom those who are in the kingdom of Christ may advance further and be exalted higher. For this reason, I believe, the Savior himself said: “Let the one who is on the roof not come down to take anything from his house” (Matt. XXIV), warning those who have attained lofty perfection not to descend again to the low and base things of this present world, which is now called a house.

The other saying, “What you have heard, preach upon the roofs” (Matt. I), likewise refers to this. Thus his kingdom will be exalted above Gog, and his kingdom will increase. It increases as the churches multiply and the number of the faithful grows, and the kingdom of Christ increases until the Father places his enemies beneath his feet. After this, he will also destroy the last enemy, death.

The passage continues with another statement concerning Christ:

“God brought him out of Egypt; his strength is like that of a rhinoceros.”

This appears to have been fulfilled when, after Herod’s death, he was recalled from Egypt, as the Gospel indicates when it says: “Out of Egypt I called my son” (Matt. II; Hos. XI). Some think that this saying was taken from this passage and inserted into the Gospels; others think that it is itself a prophecy.

It may nevertheless also be understood allegorically: after he came into the Egypt of this world, the Father led him out and took him to himself, so that he might prepare a way for those who were to ascend from the Egypt of this world to God.

“And the glory of his unicorn.”

For Christ, overthrowing all the kingdoms of the demons, established his one kingdom in glory, like the kingdom of the true unicorn. We have often shown that a horn signifies a kingdom.

“They will devour the nations, his enemies; they will crush their bones and pierce them with arrows.”

By the enemies of the Lord Christ he means the ungodly Jews. Concerning them the Truth himself, in the Gospel parable about a nobleman who went away to a distant country to receive a kingdom for himself and return, says: “But his citizens hated him, and they sent an embassy after him, saying, ‘We do not want this man to reign over us’” (Luke XIX).

Against these nations they gathered with the Roman emperors Vespasian and Titus, in order to destroy them. They broke and crushed the strength of their empire, and with military weapons they utterly overthrew Jerusalem, their capital, and destroyed the nation, in vengeance for the innocent blood of the Lord that had been poured out.

Mystically, however, the nations will devour those same enemies when holy preachers chosen from the nations convert many of them to the Catholic faith by their preaching and transfer them through baptism and saving confession into the body of Christ. They crush their bones when they soften their stubbornness and pride through godly admonitions. They pierce them with arrows when, through the testimonies of divine Law, they penetrate their hearts and provoke them to compunction and repentance for their sins.

Hence, according to another edition, this passage is read as follows: “He will eat the nations of his enemies and drain their fat to the marrow.”

He will indeed eat those nations that his enemies possessed, destroying the enemy’s power; and he will drain their fat to the marrow when he makes all their coarse and carnal understanding thin and turns it toward spiritual understanding.

That fatness is censured in Scripture is shown by the passage: “The heart of this people has grown fat” (Isa. VI). Elsewhere: “He grew fat and thick and became rebellious, the beloved one” (Deut. XXXII).

He will therefore eat the nations, and he has as his food those who believe in him, just as he says in the Gospel: “My food is to do the will of my Father who sent me” (John IV). His will, of course, was that the nations should be converted to the faith.

If, as we taught above, fatness is considered blameworthy, then, conversely, subtlety should be considered praiseworthy. For the Spirit of wisdom, who is said to be intelligible, holy, only-begotten, and manifold, is likewise declared to be subtle.

“And with his arrows he will shoot the enemy.”

As we said above, his arrows are his words, by which he conquered the devil and all his enemies, and even now overcomes and pierces those who oppose him. Everyone who sins is his enemy while he is sinning. But if he hears the words of God, recognizes his sins, is pierced and moved to compunction by them, and turns to repentance, then, pierced by the word of truth, he too is said to have been struck by his arrows.

## “Lying down, he sleeps like a lion, and like a lioness, whom no one will dare to rouse.”

Or, as another edition has it: “Reclining, he rested like a lion and like a lion’s cub; who awakened him?”

He rested like a lion when, placed upon the cross, he stripped the principalities and powers and triumphed over them on the wood of the cross. He was like a lion’s cub when he rose from the sleep of death.

The fact that he is compared at once to a lion, a lioness, and a lion’s cub may also be understood as follows: the lion represents those who are perfect; the lioness—that is, the lesser sex—represents those who are weaker in understanding; and the lion’s cub represents those who are foolish and inexperienced.

When it says, “whom no one will dare to rouse,” it signifies that no one—neither angel nor human being—could raise Christ’s flesh from the dead. Only divine majesty recalled it from the dead. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “No one takes my life from me, but I lay it down of my own accord, and I take it up again” (John X).

But if we read according to another edition, “Who awakened him?”, then, because he is now said to have been raised by the Father, and because he himself also says that he will raise the temple of his body after three days, the wording rightly conveys the attitude of one asking a question.

## “Whoever blesses you shall himself be blessed, and whoever curses you shall be counted accursed.”

It is certain that those who bless Christ are blessed and are admitted to share in the Father’s blessing. Those who curse him, however, are accursed. For if you look at that people which curses Christ, it is found, even in a lamentable way, to be accursed. What else could happen to those who curse wisdom, who curse truth, who curse life, except that they should be cast out and lie as exiles, deprived of all these good things? For Christ is all these things. Whoever curses Christ, as though cursing all these things, is condemned to perpetual condemnation or curse.

I nevertheless think that it is not only the person who utters a curse against Christ who curses him. The one who acts badly and behaves shamefully under the Christian name also curses him, whether by disgraceful words or by dishonorable actions, because he causes his name to be blasphemed among the nations.

Conversely, the one who blesses the Lord with words alone should not be thought to be the only person who blesses him. Rather, the one who causes the Lord’s name to be blessed by all through his deeds, life, and conduct is the true blesser.

In such people what Balaam’s third prophecy indicates will be fulfilled: those who bless Christ will be blessed, and those who curse him will be accursed. Therefore let us take every possible care that the name of Christ not be blasphemed through our works and actions. Rather, let us act so that we may deserve to share in his blessings.

## “Balaam became angry with Balak, and clapping his hands, he said: ‘I called you to curse my enemies, but instead you have blessed them three times. Return to your place. I had decided to honor you magnificently, but the Lord has deprived you of the honor I had arranged.’”

These words show that Balak too understood that Balaam was no longer being deceived through the agency of demons, but was being transferred by the power of God to better things. Hence he says, “The Lord has deprived you of your honor.”

But let us pass over what is clear and come to what follows.

Balaam answered Balak: “I said to your messengers whom you sent to me: ‘If Balak were to give me his house full of silver and gold, I could not transgress the word of my God, to utter from my heart either good or evil; but whatever the Lord says, that I shall speak.’”

Knowing that answers were not being delivered to him through his customary ministers, but by the one who possesses power over all, Balaam rightly appears to have declared that he could not transgress the word of the Lord or make it, whether small or great, subject to his own judgment.

For he was not speaking to one who could be changed by sacrifices and gifts, but to one with whom there is no change and no shadow of alteration. A priest therefore cannot be changed by payment where God is not moved by gifts.

As Balaam is about to depart, he begins to prophesy again and says: “Nevertheless, as I go to my people, I will give counsel concerning what your people shall do to this people at the end of time.”

According to another edition, it is read as follows: “Come, I will give you counsel concerning what this people shall do to your people in the last days.”

Having taken up his parable, he says again:

But before we come to the explanation of the prophet’s words, I would like to ask what meaning or order of words is intended by the statement, “Come, and I will give you counsel.” He does not appear to give any counsel, but says: “What this people will do to your people in the last days.” The natural sequence would indeed seem to be that Balaam was prophesying about what the people of Israel would do to the people of Balak or to the other nations—what it would accomplish by its power, so that none of the cities of Moab would be left with anyone surviving.

The prophecy concerning Christ that he joins to this in what follows also appears to be appropriately placed if the text had read: “Come, and I will prophesy to you.” For it says: “A star shall arise from Jacob, and a man shall rise from Israel, and he shall destroy all the princes of Moab.”

But what shall we say about the fact that the text reads: “Come, I will give you counsel concerning what this people shall do to your people”? Let us therefore inquire how the statement “I give you counsel” should be understood.

After frequently considering this question within myself, I do not think I can find any way out of the difficulty. Let us suppose that the words “I give you counsel” are spoken in the ordinary and familiar sense. Yet I find the following interpretation more suitable: “I give you counsel” should be understood to mean, “I disclose and reveal to you the divine counsel that is to be fulfilled in the last days, now revealed to me, so that you may know what this people will do to your people.”

In this way, it seems to me, the statement “I give you counsel concerning what this people will do to your people” can stand: that is, “I announce and make known to you the counsel of God.”

As I was asking myself whether something similar might occur anywhere in the divine Scriptures under this expression, it seemed that the Apostle’s statement should also be understood in the same way: “For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor?” (Rom. II).

Here, “who” does not mean “no one,” but “who among the few or the exceptional?” For how did his only-begotten Son know the mind of the Lord, when he says: “No one knows the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him” (Luke X)? What else is it to know the Father than to know his counsel and mind?

The Holy Spirit too, who searches even the depths of God—what else does he know than his mind? The Son and the Holy Spirit therefore know the mind of the Lord, as do those to whom the Son chooses to reveal it.

If the Son knows the mind of God, then he is also his counselor. This should not be understood as though the Son and the Holy Spirit give counsel to one who is ignorant of what he is doing. In the same way, Balaam, because he was making Balak a participant in and knower of the counsel that God had revealed to him, says: “Come, I give you counsel.”

Balaam son of Beor said:

“The man whose eye has been closed said; the hearer of the words of God said—he who knows the knowledge of the Most High and sees the vision of the Almighty, who, falling, has his eyes open. I shall see him, but not now; I shall behold him, but not near.”

How can this be understood as worthy of Balaam, that he should know the knowledge of the Most High, when he even taught Balak the king how to place a stumbling-block before the children of Israel, so that they might eat what had been sacrificed and commit fornication? [Col. 0756C] One will scarcely find it said even of the holy prophets or apostles that they know the knowledge of the Most High. Although Paul said that he had heard “unspeakable words, which it is not lawful for a human being to utter” (II Cor. XII), he nevertheless did not claim to possess the knowledge of the Most High. Therefore let us attend more carefully, in case God may deem it worthy to reveal something to us concerning this expression.

In the book which among us is usually counted among Solomon’s writings and is called Ecclesiasticus, but which among the Greeks is called *The Wisdom of Jesus Son of Sirach*, it is written: “All wisdom is from the Lord” (Eccles. I). Perhaps we can understand this as meaning that even the wisdom of this world, which is said to be destroyed, and the wisdom of the rulers of this world, and whatever else there is by which false knowledge is commended, comes from God—unless the same little book went on to say: “For the discipline of wickedness is not wisdom.” By this it plainly teaches that every discipline which asserts something false—even if it appears forceful, plausible, and difficult to overthrow—must nevertheless in no way be assigned the title of wisdom.

What, then, does he mean when he says, “All wisdom is from the Lord”? (Eccles. I.) It seems to me that he meant that every skill, whether it is considered necessary for human use in some art or is knowledge of any kind of thing, is called wisdom given by the Lord. Thus it is written in Job: “Who gave women the knowledge of weaving and the varieties of crafts?” But also in Exodus: “The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Behold, I have called by name Bezalel, son of Uri, son of Hur, from the tribe of Judah, and I have filled him with the divine Spirit, with wisdom, understanding, and skill, so that he may understand in every work and be an architect, to work in silver, gold, and bronze, and stones for setting, and every work of craftsmanship, and in wood, so as to work according to all the works for which I have appointed him. And Eliab, son of Ahisamach, from the tribe of Dan. And I have given understanding in the heart of every wise person, so that they may make everything that I have commanded you” (Exod. XXXI).

Let us reread what is written in Daniel concerning Daniel himself and his three companions, whom King Nebuchadnezzar entrusted for three years to be educated, wishing them to become highly learned in his own—namely, the native Babylonian—wisdom. There it is written: “God gave them understanding and prudence in every grammatical art”; and, “Daniel understood every vision and dreams” [Col. 0757B] (Dan. I). And shortly afterward: “They stood in the presence of the king, and in every matter of wisdom and knowledge about which the king questioned them, he found them ten times superior to all the enchanters and magicians who were in his whole kingdom.”

From all this, then, it can be understood how Balaam also said of himself, “He who knows the knowledge of the Most High”—namely, so that it may be understood that the origin of all knowledge received its beginning from him. Through the fault of human wickedness, however, and because demons also aspire to and steal these things, what was granted for usefulness has been turned toward destruction.

We have examined, as far as our ability allowed, what he said: “Knowing the knowledge of the Most High.” Let us therefore see what he means when he says in what follows: “I shall see him, but not now; I shall behold him, but not near.” This is believed to refer to the coming of the Savior, namely the Lord Christ, concerning whom he also says in what follows: “A star shall arise from Jacob, and a man shall rise from Israel.”

He says that he is to be seen, but not now—that is, not at the time when he was speaking these things. “For in the last days, when the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son.” But if we wish to read it according to other copies in this manner: “I shall show him, and not now; I shall bless him, and he does not approach,” the words will refer not to this Balaam, through whom these things are spoken, but to those whose person we have said is represented here.

For those teachers of the law and scribes show Christ, prophesied in the law and the prophets, but not now—that is, not at the time when he came. Rather, when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered and all Israel begins to be saved, then they will show him, and then they will bless the one whom they now blaspheme. But the time when these things will occur is not near; it is far off and must be awaited at the very end of the age. Therefore he says, “I shall show him, but not now”—to that people, namely, which will then be saved.

After this he says:

“A star shall arise from Jacob, and a scepter shall rise from Israel; he shall strike the rulers of Moab and lay waste all the children of Seth; and Edom shall be his possession. The inheritance of Seir shall pass to his enemies.”

We have spoken of these things above, because he clearly proclaims the star that appeared to the Magi in the East. Guided by it, they came to Judea seeking the one who had been born King of Israel; when they had found him, they worshiped him after offering gifts.

But I am troubled by the fact that, after the Gospel says that the star went before the Magi as far as Bethlehem and, when it came, stood above the place where the child was (Matt. II), it is not subsequently said whether it departed from there, vanished, was taken up, or whether the Gospel narrative indicated anything else about it. It says only that it came and stood above the place where the child was.

Perhaps, therefore, just as at the time of Jesus’ baptism, when Jesus had been baptized and came up from the Jordan, the heavens were opened to him, and John saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove and remaining upon him, and heard a voice from heaven saying, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. III), so also this star, which came above the place where the child was and stood there, likewise remained in Christ. Just as the Holy Spirit is said to have come in the form of a dove and remained in him, and just as we understand that the Spirit of God came upon him and remained in him to mean that the Spirit of God never departed from him, so I think we should understand the star that came and stood above him as having stood above him in such a way that it was never moved from there. For this reason, I believe that star to have been an indication of his divinity.

Accordingly, the order of the prophecy also subsequently shows the same thing, when it says of his divinity, “A star shall arise from Jacob,” but of his human nature, “A man shall rise from Israel.” Thus Christ is clearly shown as prophesied in both respects, according to his divinity and according to his humanity.

“And he shall lay waste the rulers of Moab.” We understand Moab to be a nation whose rulers can be no others than the spiritual wickednesses and those principalities against whom our struggle is waged. This man from Israel will lay them waste when he strips away principalities and authorities and fastens them to his cross. For he could not save the Moabites and bring them to the knowledge of God unless he had first devastated those rulers who had held them under the domination of impiety.

“And he shall plunder all the children of Seth.” Seth was the son of Adam, concerning whom Eve said when he was born: “For God has raised up another seed for me in place of Abel, whom Cain killed” (Gen. V). This, then, is Seth, from whom the whole human race in this world is descended. For those who had been born from Cain perished in the flood.

Therefore all human beings who are in this world are sons of Seth.
