When it is said, “He shall plunder all the children of Seth,” understand the plunder in the way we interpreted it above: having defeated the opposing demons, Christ receives all the children of Seth, those who had been held under their domination, as the spoils of victory; he leads them as his booty and carries away the spoils of salvation. Thus it is also written elsewhere concerning him: “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive” (Ps. LXVII). He led captive, namely, that captivity of the human race which the devil had taken for destruction; he took it captive again and recalled it from death to life.

Would that Jesus always hold me captive to himself, lead me as his spoil, and keep me bound in his chains, so that I too might deserve to be called “a prisoner of Christ Jesus,” as Paul boasts concerning himself:

“And Edom shall be his inheritance, and the inheritance of Esau shall belong to his enemies” (Eph. III).

Edom is the same as Esau. Historically, he is indeed an enemy of Israel; but at the coming of Christ, he says, even he will be Christ’s inheritance [Col. 0759A]—that is, he will be received into the faith and will not be excluded from Christ’s inheritance.

If, however, we attend to the matter spiritually, Edom is understood as the flesh, which opposes the spirit and is its enemy. At the coming of Christ, therefore, when the flesh has been subjected to the spirit through the hope of the resurrection, even the flesh itself will come into the inheritance. For it is not the soul alone, but also the flesh—which had once been hostile—that will, through the obedience of the spirit, become a partner in the future inheritance.

“Israel, however, shall act valiantly.” This means that Edom or Esau—that is, the nature of the flesh—will then be called into fellowship in the inheritance when Israel, namely the soul, has been made strong in virtue and has been fittingly filled with virtues. For if the soul does not attain virtue but persists in indolence, the flesh too will not come into the inheritance, but into the judgment of him who can destroy soul and body in Gehenna (Matt. V).

“From Jacob there shall arise one who rules, and he shall destroy the remaining cities.”

This is plainly the Lord Christ, who was born according to the flesh from the seed of Jacob and came into the world. According to the testimony of the holy Gospel, all authority in heaven and on earth was given to him (Matt. ult.), so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth—and every tongue should confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father (Phil. II).

He himself, together with the city of God joined to him, namely the Catholic Church, will destroy the remaining cities: unquestionably, the assemblies of heretics and the defenses of philosophical doctrines that think and act contrary to the Catholic faith.

Nor do I think we should be silent about the fact that in certain copies this passage reads as follows: “Jacob shall rise,” he says, “and shall destroy the one delivered from the city.” Not only in this passage, but in almost the whole prophetic style, the things that are said are expressed in a sufficiently veiled and obscure manner. He did not despise the holy men who wished these things to be written, so that they might be placed openly—as one might say—under the feet of the unlearned to be trampled. Rather, he arranged matters so that, although they appear to be publicly available, they would nevertheless be preserved in mystery, concealed in the obscurity of their words and covered in secret places.

Here, therefore, when he says, “He shall destroy the one delivered from the city,” the meaning will appear very difficult unless you attend to the prophetic convention concerning which it is said: “No prophecy can be established by its own interpretation” (II Pet. I). Let us nevertheless see whether it can perhaps be explained in this way.

Let us understand the city as this world, just as the Gospels also say concerning the prodigal son who squandered his father’s substance: “He went,” it says, “to a certain prominent man of that city in that region, and, having been received by him, was sent into his field to feed swine” (Luke XV). That city, then, of which the prominent man was ruler, is understood as this world.

Accordingly, he will destroy the one delivered from this city—that is, the one whom Christ delivers from this world. For he says to him: “He who loses his soul for my sake will save it” (Matt. XVI). Jesus will destroy him with a saving destruction when he has delivered him from the city of this world.

We too, then, who wish to come to salvation and be delivered from this world, must lose our souls through a useful and necessary destruction. He loses his soul according to Christ who restrains its desires, cuts away its cravings, chastises its luxury and dissipation, and does not at all do its will, but the will of God. Through these things the soul is said to perish. For its former life perishes, and it begins to lead the new life that is in Christ.

A similar saying is also this: “If we die together with him, we shall also live together with him” (II Tim. II). And this: “If you have died to the elements of the world, why, as though living in the world, do you make judgments?” (Col. II.) These things therefore make the necessity clear: the one who dies with Christ loses his soul in this world; and the one who has thus lost it will find it, undoubtedly where the Apostle says: “Your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Col. III).

When he saw Amalek, he took up his parable and said: “Amalek is the beginning of the nations; his end shall perish.” [Col. 0760B]

At the outset, I think it necessary to investigate in the divine Scriptures the places and times in which the name Amalek is written, and from what lineage this nation descended. What is sought is recognized more easily if passages written concerning the same matter are brought forward from several places.

Accordingly, in the reading from Genesis, where five kings gathered to attack the four kings who were reigning in Sodom, the account shortly afterward says: “They came to the spring of Masphat, which is Kadesh; and they struck the whole region of the Amalekites and the Amorites who dwelt in Asasonthamar” (Gen. XIV). I remember that Amalek is first mentioned in this passage.

But perhaps it should be asked whether there were two nations of the same name, since Amalek is also mentioned in the catalogue of the sons of Esau and of the chiefs who descended from his lineage. For it is written:

“These are the generations of Esau, the father of Edom, on Mount Seir. These are the names of his sons: Eliphaz, son of Adah, the wife of Esau; and Raguel, son of Basemath, his wife. The sons of Eliphaz were Theman, Omar, Zepho, Gathan, and Genez. Thamna was the concubine of Eliphaz, son of Esau, and she bore him Amalek.”

And shortly afterward:

“These are the chiefs of the sons of Esau, the sons of Eliphaz, Esau’s firstborn: chief Theman, chief Omar, chief Sephu, chief Cenez, chief Chore, chief Gathan, chief Amalek” (Gen. XXXVI).

This Amalek, then, was the son of Eliphaz, the firstborn son of Esau, born from a concubine named Thamna.

But let us return to the first mention of Amalek, [Col. 0760D] where those who had turned back and came to the spring of judgment, which is called Kadesh, were to kill all the rulers of Amalek. Kadesh is interpreted as “licking up the people.” Therefore those who turn back to the holy place and turn themselves toward sanctification kill and destroy Amalek—namely, the one who washes away the people or turns the people aside.

Who else is there who turns the people away from God except the opposing power and the spiritual wickednesses? Who, then, are their rulers? Without doubt, those principalities against whom the saints have their struggle. Their contests are against principalities and authorities and the rulers of this world; yet they will not be able to overcome them unless they turn themselves toward holiness.

That holiness itself, however, which is Kadesh, is the spring of judgment. For everyone who turns himself toward holiness always has the spring of judgment before his eyes. He looks toward the day of judgment, and with a purified heart he contemplates both the punishments of the wicked and the blessedness of the godly. By doing this, he casts down and overthrows all the rulers of the Amalekites.

But if some do not turn themselves toward Kadesh—that is, toward holiness and the spring of judgment—and do not consider the future day of judgment, they are subject to the rulers of Amalek.

Now let us consider this Amalek also, the son of Eliphaz, Esau’s firstborn, whom his concubine Thamnas bore to him. His father is Eliphaz, whose name is interpreted, “God has scattered me.” His mother is Thamnas, whose name is first [uncertain reading: *deneger*], and then is interpreted as “agitated falling-away.” Necessarily, then, one who is begotten by such parents is an enemy of Israel, or one who turns the people aside.

He was the first to attack the Hebrews, who had come out of Egypt, in battle at Raphidim, at the time when Moses said to Jesus: “Choose men for yourself, go out, and engage Amalek in battle tomorrow. Behold, I shall stand on the top of the hill, and the rod of God shall be in my hand.” And Jesus did as Moses told him, and engaged Amalek in battle. Moses, Aaron, and Hur climbed to the top of the hill. And it happened that whenever Moses raised his hands, Israel prevailed; but whenever he lowered his hands, Amalek prevailed (Exod. XVII).

Shortly afterward it is written again that Jesus put Amalek to flight and struck down his people with the sword, at the time when the Lord said to Moses: “Write this for a memorial in the book, and give it into the ears of Jesus: I shall utterly blot out the memory of Amalek from under heaven.” And Moses built an altar and called its name, “The Lord is my refuge,” and said: “Because with a hidden hand—that is, an invisible one—the Lord was warring against Amalek from generation to generation.”

But in Deuteronomy it is written as follows: “Remember what Amalek did to you there on the way, and how he cut off your rear, all those who were laboring behind you. You were hungry and weary, and he did not fear God” (Deut. XXV).

Observe here also how Amalek opposed Israel on the way. Yet he could not cut off its head, but only its tail; that is, he was able to prevail against those who were positioned behind, who followed last and did not forget the things that were behind, stretching themselves toward the things that lay ahead.

For this reason, I think that the Lord commanded in the Gospels: “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke IX). And rightly so. For if someone looks backward, Amalek will cut him off at the tail.

As for the statement, “Amalek is the beginning of the nations,” it is certain that it cannot in any way refer to that Amalek who then existed in the flesh. For he was not first in the origin of antiquity. Rather, it is better referred to the invisible Amalek, who, by turning peoples away from God and making them Gentiles, is named Amalek among those who had been worshipers of God.

Therefore he is rightly called “the beginning of the nations,” as though he were a certain opposing power that first gave occasion for human beings to become Gentiles, changing “the glory of the incorruptible God into the likeness of the image of corruptible human beings and birds and four-footed animals and serpents,” serving the creature rather than the Creator.

Just as Christ is written to be the beginning in the people of God, so, conversely, in the people who turn away from God and become Gentile, Amalek is the beginning. “His end shall perish”—that is, his end will be death, not this bodily death, but the spiritual death that is everlasting.

Or, as another edition has it, “Their seed shall perish.” Their seed is the persuasion and teaching by which they taught human beings to turn away from God. Therefore this evil seed and most wicked teaching will perish, not the people in whom it has been sown. For when those people have turned back and groaned, they will be saved.

And see whether this interpretation does not also suitably answer those who accuse the God of the law of harshness and cruelty. The prophecy declares that not only the nation of Amalek but also its seed will perish, when the nation is understood as referring to the spiritual wickednesses, while its seed is explained as the doctrine of Gentile superstitions, the worship of idols, and every sect that persuades the people to turn away from God.

After Amalek, the prophecy mentions the Kenite, saying:

“He also saw the Kenite and took up his parable and said: Your dwelling is indeed strong; but if you place your nest in the rock and are chosen from the stock of the Kenite, how long will you be able to remain?”

Kenite is interpreted as “possessor.” Who are those who possess the things of the present except those who are skilled through the ingenuity of secular wisdom? They truly build a strong dwelling for themselves in this world if, through humility, they have become little in their own eyes and are nourished in the sublimity of Christ; if they recognize themselves to be weak and, known by lofty humility, place in the Redeemer the trust that must be cherished in the mind. Let them not seek what is exalted, but transcend everything that passes away on the wings of the heart.

Let us see how the holy man places his nest in the rock. For he says: “Our citizenship is in heaven.” And again: “When he raised us up and made us sit in the heavenly places,” he places his nest in the rock, because he fixes his purpose in the realms above (Phil. III). He does not wish to cast his mind down into fleeting things; he does not wish to dwell in the lowest places through the degradation of human conduct.

Perhaps Paul was being held in prison when he testified that he was sitting with Christ in the heavenly places. But he was there where he had already fixed his ardent mind, not where the still sluggish flesh necessarily held him.

“And if you are chosen,” he says, “from the stock of the Kenite, how long will you be able to remain?” Kenite is interpreted as “my nest,” or “possession.” Those who are chosen from the stock of the Kenite—that is, from the number of the wise—and are found to be true investigators of the truth can remain for a long time, because they will live an enduring life forever.

Hence it is said through the prophet: “Seek the Lord, and your soul shall live” (Ps. LXVIII). And elsewhere, through Wisdom itself, it is said: “Those who elucidate me will possess eternal life” (Eccles. XXIV).

Another edition, however, has the passage as follows: “If you place your nest in the rock, and Beor becomes for you a nest of cunning, the Assyrians will lead you captive.”

It seems to me that he does not name the Kenite in a particularly blameworthy way. He is the one to whom Saul said earlier: “Depart from the midst of Amalek, and I will not strike you, because you showed mercy to Israel when it came up from Egypt.”

Concerning him, therefore, it is now also said that his dwelling is strong if he places his nest in the rock. The rock is Christ. If he places his nest in the rock, his dwelling is strong—provided that Beor does not become for him a nest of cunning.

Beor is the father of Balaam, and he can be understood in the person of heretics. The meaning may therefore be that the Kenite can be saved if he places his nest in the rock—that is, if he places his hope in Christ—and is not surrounded and ensnared by the cunning of heretics. For if this happens, it will profit him nothing that he appears to be placed in the rock, which is Christ.

He will be led captive by the Assyrians—namely, by the malignant powers that lead into captivity and take into their power those whom heretical error has entangled. [Col. 0763B]

Certainly, according to the interpretation we have given of the Kenite, the conjunction also seems to disturb the sense. But we should know that this is characteristic of the Hebrew language: it frequently uses conjunctions, so that sometimes one appears superfluous even in necessary expressions, as though it had been inserted into our language. This should be accepted with indulgence. Every language has some peculiarity which may appear faulty in another language.

Here, therefore, the conjunction should also be regarded as apparently abundant and superfluous.

Let the Kenite beware, then—the one whose name is interpreted as “possessing.” Let him beware, I say, even if he possesses and merits this grace, that he is in the Church of Christ, lest perhaps the cunning of Beor circumvent him, and he turn toward corrupt and perverse doctrines and be handed over by this means to the Assyrians.

For those who blaspheme while placed in the Church are handed over to Satan, as were Phigelus and Hermogenes, concerning whom Paul says: “I handed them over,” he says, “to Satan, so that they may learn not to blaspheme” (I Tim. II).

Therefore he is handed over to the Assyrians because he has turned toward heretical blasphemy, since Assyrians are interpreted as “those who direct.” For this reason they are handed over to them—not so that they may perish or be utterly destroyed, but so that they may be directed and corrected, and, as Paul himself says, so that they may learn not to blaspheme.

After this Balaam concludes the speech of his prophecy with the following words:

“And he took up his parable again and spoke: Alas! Who shall live when God does these things? They shall come in ships from Italy; they shall overcome the Assyrians, they shall lay waste the Hebrews, but finally they themselves shall perish.” [Col. 0763D]

The fact that Balaam is said to speak in a parable at each point instills shame in the reader, lest he think that anything stated here was spoken not as a parable but according to the literal sense.

He therefore says: “Who will live when God has done these things?” Here he names not this ordinary life, but the life that is second. His meaning is that, while all these things are happening—when the star has arisen from Jacob, the man has risen from Israel, Amalek has been destroyed, and his seed has perished—that is, when Christ has come, destroyed the worship of idols, and subjected the power of all demons—who will be so blessed and fortunate as to see these things, that is, to perceive, understand, and believe that God has done them in this way?

“They shall come in ships from Italy; they shall overcome the Assyrians, they shall lay waste the Hebrews, but finally they themselves shall perish.”

Insofar as the literal sense is concerned, this seems to foretell in prophetic fashion that, around the time of the Lord’s incarnation, the Roman leaders, advancing from Italy with an army, would overcome the kingdom of the Assyrians, the Hebrews, and all the eastern peoples, and turn them into their own dominion. They themselves would later lose that very kingdom according to Daniel’s prophecy, because, according to the vision of the statue, one part of the feet was iron, while another part was clay.

According to the allegorical sense, however, it signifies the Lord’s coming at the end of time. The western part of the city represents the fact that all the kingdoms of the world will be subdued by the sword of the Spirit—that is, by the word of the Gospel—and, by being turned away from carnal understanding, converted to spiritual insight.

Another edition gives the passage as follows: “They shall come out of the hands of the Citians and afflict the Assyrians.”

Citians are interpreted as “the wound of the end.” Those, therefore, who turn to the Lord and are instructed by Christ, escaping the wound that will come upon the impious at the end of the age, will themselves afflict the Assyrians. That is, those who are engaged in the contest of godliness and crush Satan beneath their feet will themselves afflict the Assyrians, the nation of demons.

For they will tread upon serpents and scorpions and upon every power of the enemy. “And they shall afflict the Hebrews, and they themselves shall likewise perish.”

Hebrews are interpreted as “those who pass over.” This same people is therefore called Hebrew because it passes from Egypt to the promised land, from darkness to light, and from death to life.

But since, as we have said, it cannot obtain these things without struggle and without great conflict, it is now, as it were, engaged in combat: at one moment it afflicts, at another it is afflicted; at one moment it strikes its adversary, at another it is itself struck by its adversary.

The Assyrians, therefore, will also afflict the Hebrews—that is, the people of God—in the same way as they are afflicted by them. But they themselves—that is, the Assyrians—when they have done these things and have poured out all their strength in afflicting the Hebrews, will immediately perish themselves.

When he says, “They shall afflict the Hebrews, and they themselves shall likewise perish,” this should not be understood as though the Assyrians would perish together with the Hebrews. Rather, “likewise” means “immediately”: as soon as they have done these things, as soon as they have afflicted the Hebrews, they themselves too will perish. For the Greek expression uses the word “likewise” in the sense of “immediately.”

This, then, will be the end of all things: that even Assur, to whom those who were sinning from among the people of God were believed to have been handed over—either so that the flesh might be destroyed and the spirit saved, or so that they might learn not to blaspheme—will perish.

For he will perish at the hands of the one who has authority to destroy in Gehenna. For it is said to them by the just Judge: “Go into the eternal fire which God prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. XXV).

There, then, Assur will perish.

And indeed, just as sometimes even one sheep out of a hundred sheep is sought and found by the good shepherd, who leaves the ninety-nine sheep in the mountains, descends into the valley—this valley of our tears—and searches for it, places it upon his shoulders, carries it back, and adds it to the number that had remained safe above, so I do not know whether this Assur, who is said to perish at the end of all things, can at some time be sought or found.

He perishes, therefore, not through error but through judgment; not stirred by a fall, but enduring in perseverance.

Balaam rose and returned to his place. And Balak returned by the way he had come. After Balaam had finished his prophecy, he is said to have returned to his place, and Balak to have gone back by the way he had come. Nor does he relate anything here about the counsel Balaam gave for deceiving Israel; he merely says that Israel settled at Shittim, and that the people were defiled by fornication with the daughters of Moab, who invited them to the sacrifices of their idols. The people ate of their sacrifices, and worshiped their idols. And Israel was initiated into the worship of Baal-peor, and the Lord was angered with Israel in great fury.

In this is demonstrated what we have often mentioned: that after Balaam, constrained by God’s power, was not permitted to curse Israel, yet wishing to please King Balak, said to him, as it is written, “Come, I will give you counsel”; but there he did not disclose what counsel he had given. In the later parts of this book of Numbers the matter is reported in writing, but more fully in the Revelation of John: “You have there,” he says, “those who hold the teaching of Balaam, who taught Balak to place a stumbling block before the children of Israel, so that they might eat food sacrificed to idols and commit fornication” (Rev. II).

From this it is therefore evident that Balaam employed wickedness and gave the king counsel of this sort, saying to him: “This people conquers not by its own strength but by worshiping God, and preserves its chastity. If you wish to conquer it, first destroy its chastity, and they will be defeated of their own accord. But against these people one must fight not by the valor of soldiers but by the beauty of women; not by the hardness of weapons but by the softness of females. Away with the hands of armed men, therefore—remove them far away—and gather a chosen company of beautiful girls. Let them play with their feet and clap their hands. Beauty conquers the armed; loveliness captures iron. Those who cannot be conquered in battle will be conquered by appearance.

“But when the Moabite or Midianite women perceive that the men have given themselves over to lust and bowed their necks to sin, let them not offer themselves to those who desire them until the men have consented to taste the sacrifices of the idols, so that, compelled by lust, they may obey the women’s counsels and first be initiated into Baal-peor, which is an idol of obscenity.”

These were Balaam’s counsels. Having received them, King Balak immediately prepared an army composed not of weapons or strength but of feminine splendor; inflamed not with the fury of war but with the flame of lust.

These, then, are the matters taught us by the historical text. But since John, in his Revelation, brings forward what is written in the Law according to its history and teaches that certain divine mysteries and sacraments are contained in it, it also seems necessary for us, in accordance with his understanding, to follow the rule of interpretation he has given. First, then, let us recall what he says in writing concerning the glory of a certain church: “You have there some who hold the teaching of Balaam, who taught Balak to place a stumbling block before the children of Israel, so that they might eat food sacrificed to idols and commit fornication” (Rev. II).

Thus, in the time of the apostle John, there were some in that church to which he was writing who taught the teaching of Balaam. Should we understand this to mean that in those days there were people who said that they taught what Balaam had taught, and who professed to be teachers of his doctrines and traditions? Or should we rather observe that anyone who does the work Balaam did appears to teach the teaching of Balaam?

In the same Revelation the teaching of Jezebel is likewise mentioned—not because someone teaches from Jezebel’s disciplines what she handed down, but because if someone, for example, persecutes God’s prophets as she did, or deceives people through idols, or destroys the innocent by false contrivances, that person is said to hold the teaching of Jezebel.

So also, if someone generates scandals among God’s people by evil counsels and provokes divine offense and heavenly wrath against the people, whether by sharing in sacrifices to idols or by serving fornication and lust, that person must be said to hold the teaching of Balaam.

Bodily fornication, then, is also accursed. For what is so accursed as to violate the temple of God, to take away the members of Christ, and to make them members of a prostitute? Yet far more accursed is that general fornication in which every kind of sin is contained alike.

General fornication is said to occur when the soul, which has been admitted into fellowship with the Word of God and in a certain way joined to his marriage, is corrupted and violated in faith by some other alien power—namely, by the adversary of that husband who betrothed it to himself.

The bridegroom and husband of the pure and chaste soul is therefore the Word of God, who is Christ the Lord. As the Apostle says or writes: “I wish to present you all as a pure virgin to one husband, Christ. But I am afraid that, just as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, so your minds may be corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ Jesus” (II Cor. XI).

Therefore, so long as the soul clings to its bridegroom, listens to his word, and embraces him, it undoubtedly receives from him the seed, the Word of God. And as he said: “Because of your fear, O Lord, we conceived in the womb and gave birth, and by the spirit of your salvation we brought forth upon the earth.” If the soul has thus conceived Christ, it bears children concerning whom it may be said of her that she will be saved through the bearing of children, if she remains in faith and love with sobriety.

From this a noble offspring will be born; from this chastity will arise; from this, justice; from this, gentleness and love; and a venerable progeny of all the virtues will follow.

But if the unhappy soul abandons the holy marriage of the divine Word and, deceived by the allurements of the devil and other demons, gives itself over to adulterous embraces, it will undoubtedly bear children from that union as well—children of whom it is written: “The children of adulterers will be imperfect, and the offspring of an unlawful union will be destroyed” (Wis. III).

All sins, therefore, are children of adultery and children of fornication. Hence it is shown that in each thing we do our soul gives birth and generates children—namely, the thoughts and deeds it produces. If what you do is according to the Law and, according to the Word of God, produces a spirit of salvation, then you will be saved through the bearing of children.

Nevertheless, Israel settled at Shittim, as Scripture relates.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the People’s Fornication with the Daughters of the Moabites

**(CHAP. XXV.)** “At that time,” he says, “Israel was dwelling at Shittim, and the people committed fornication with the daughters of Moab, who invited them to their sacrifices. They ate and worshiped their gods. And Israel was initiated into the worship of Baal-peor.”

In the interpretation of Hebrew names, we find that *Shittim* is said in our language to mean “answer” or “refutation.” Israel therefore settled at an answer or refutation. It did not settle well. Consider, finally, what befell it. While it was staying in this place, it fornicated with the women of the Midianites and was rejected by God, because it not only fornicated but was also consecrated to the idols of the nations and ate from what had been sacrificed to idols—things that are surely accursed before God. For what agreement is there between the temple of God and idols?

It is therefore right also to be astonished at what the apostle Paul writes to the Corinthians: “If someone sees you, who possess knowledge, reclining at table in an idol’s temple, will not his conscience, being weak, be built up to eat what has been sacrificed?” (I Cor. VIII). He seems to pronounce not so much the act itself to be grievous as the offense of the person who sees it and is provoked by a similar example, though he is not fortified by similar knowledge. Thus he shows that the person who possesses knowledge and reclines in an idol’s temple becomes guilty not so much of his own harm as of another’s.

But see whether perhaps the Corinthians did not merely recline in an idol’s temple and eat what had been sacrificed to idols. Perhaps, since they were devoted to Greek literature and lovers of philosophy, they were still held by a longing for their former studies and ate the doctrines of philosophers as though they had been sacrificed to idols.

Such things might perhaps not destroy those who had received complete knowledge of the truth. But those who possessed less instruction in Christ could be wounded and entangled in the various errors of differing doctrines if, seeing such persons read such works and still pursue those studies, they imitated them.

If this was what happened—so that one person was destroyed—how could the one who possessed complete knowledge of the truth not also be harmed? But since love does not seek what is useful to itself but what is useful to many, care must be taken to take in such food of the Word as not only builds us up and delights us but also does not offend those who see it.

There is therefore not only food sacrificed to idols but also words. And I think that just as every word that teaches piety, justice, and truth is consecrated to God and sacrificed to God, so every word that looks toward immodesty, injustice, or impiety is sacrificed to idols; and whoever attends to it eats as though it were food sacrificed to idols.

“The people ate of their sacrifices, and they worshiped their idols.” They not only ate but also worshiped. Observe the sequence of evil. First desire deceives the servants of the Lord; then come the belly and gluttony; finally impiety takes them captive. And the payment made to impiety is fornication.

“They worshiped their idols, and they were consecrated to Baal-peor.” Baal-peor is the name of an idol worshiped especially by the women among the Midianites. In the mysteries of this idol Israel was therefore consecrated.

When we investigated the interpretation of the name more carefully, among the Hebrew names we found only this written: that Baal-peor is a form of obscenity. The interpreter did not wish to explain what kind or what sort of form it was, or whose obscenity it represented—he was, I believe, consulting decency, so that the hearing of his listeners might not be polluted.

Since there are many forms of obscenity, one among the many forms of obscenity is called Baal-peor. Hence it must be understood that everyone who commits something shameful and turns toward some form of obscenity is consecrated to Baal-peor, the demon of the Midianites.

Moreover, through each sin we commit—especially if we sin not through some sudden seizure but deliberately and with intention—we undoubtedly consecrate ourselves to that lord whose concern it is to make the sin we have committed effective in us.

“And the Lord was angry with Israel and said to Moses: Take all the leaders of the people and hang them before the sun on gallows, so that my fury may be turned away from Israel.”

The Lord, angered by Israel’s fornications, both carnal and spiritual—for they had shamefully mingled with the daughters of Moab and had been consecrated to idols—said this to Moses, commanding him to display the leaders of the people before the Lord and before the sun.

In this word it is understood that he commanded them to be crucified, so that the meaning is: “Display them before the Lord against the sun,” that is, publicly, in the sight of this light. For the Greek text says *paradeigmátison* (παραδειγμάτισον), which may be rendered “make them examples,” since *paradigma* means “example.” Apart from the translators of the Septuagint, Aquila is said to have rendered it “fix them,” or rather “fix them up,” which is *anápēxon* (ἀνάπηξον). Symmachus, however, uses the more explicit word “hang.”

And Moses said to the judges of Israel: “Let each one kill his fellow tribesmen who have been initiated into Baal-peor.”

It is truly remarkable that Scripture has ceased to relate whether this command was carried out according to the Lord’s order—which I cannot see how anyone could have dared to disregard—or whether, if it was disregarded, it could have been disregarded with impunity.

But if the matter was also merely left unmentioned, why does Scripture testify that when Phinehas, the son of Eleazar, pierced the adulterers, the Lord was appeased and the plague ceased? It would seem that, although the leaders had been crucified as the Lord had commanded and the indignation still continued, it had to be appeased in another way. Yet surely what the Lord had declared and promised could not be false when he said: “Take the leaders of the people and display them before the Lord against the sun, and the anger of the Lord’s indignation will be turned away from Israel.”

If this had been done, who would doubt that the Lord’s anger had been turned away from Israel? Why, then, was it still necessary for Phinehas to take vengeance in this way on the adulterers in order to appease God, and why does Scripture bear witness that he appeased the Lord in this manner?

Unless perhaps we understand it as follows: when Moses was preparing to fulfill what had been commanded concerning the leaders of the people, he wished also to punish such crimes and sacrilegious audacity according to the Law. He therefore ordered each person to kill his fellow tribesman who had been wickedly consecrated to foreign gods. Meanwhile Phinehas also carried out his act, and thus, once the Lord’s anger had been appeased, it was no longer necessary for the leaders of the people to be crucified.

This severity, appropriate to that time, shows with sufficient clarity to the understanding of the faithful how great an evil fornication and idolatry are.

You see what is required of the leaders of the people. They are accused not only on account of their own offenses but are compelled to give an account for the people’s sins, lest it be their fault that the people sinned—lest perhaps they failed to teach them or were not diligent in reproving those who first began the wrongdoing, so that the contagion would not spread to many.

For all these duties fall upon leaders and teachers. If, because they did not perform them and did not show concern for the people, the people sins, they themselves are displayed and brought to judgment. Moses—that is, the Law of God—accuses them as negligent and idle, and God’s anger turns against them and ceases from the people.

If people considered these things, they would never desire or strive for leadership over the people. It is enough for me if I am accused for my own offenses. It is enough for me to give an account for my sins on my own behalf. Why must I also be displayed before the sun on account of the people’s sins—before that sun before which nothing can be hidden or obscured?

## CHAPTER IX. On the Vengeance Carried Out by Phinehas, Son of Eleazar, Son of Aaron the Priest, against the Israelite Fornicator and the Midianite Woman

**(IBID.)** “Behold, one of the children of Israel entered before his fellow tribesmen to the Midianite prostitute, while Moses and the whole assembly of the children of Israel saw it; they were weeping before the doors of the tabernacle. When Phinehas, son of Eleazar, son of Aaron the priest, saw this, he rose from the midst of the assembly, seized a dagger, went after the Israelite man into the brothel, and pierced them both at once—the man and the woman in their genital parts. And the plague ceased from the children of Israel.”

These actions built up the former people. But you, who have been redeemed by Christ, from whose hands the bodily sword has been taken and to whom the sword of the Spirit has been given, seize this sword.

If you see an Israelite understanding fornicating with Midianites and prostitutes—that is, wallowing with demonic thoughts—I do not want you to spare it; I do not want you to conceal the matter. Strike immediately; kill immediately. Examine and penetrate the very womb—that is, the hidden places of nature—and cut away the very tinder of sin, so that it may no longer conceive or give birth, and so that the accursed offspring of sins may not defile the Israelite camp.

If you do this, you will immediately calm the Lord’s anger. You anticipate the day of judgment, which is foretold as a day of wrath; and once the tinder of sin—the thing now called the womb of the Midianite woman—has been destroyed in you, you will come safely to the day of judgment.

It follows: “And twenty-four thousand men were killed.”

The slain are appropriately numbered by the twenty-four thousand, because those who abandon the light of truth and justice and plunge themselves into the blindness of idolatry and fornication, deprived of the light of the eternal sun, experience the darkness of perpetual death.

For twenty-four hours the worldly sun illumines the whole earth on every side and drives away the darkness of night by its circuit. Whoever illumines the eyes of the mind with the light of faith preached through the apostles and prophets strives to avoid the darkness of sins.

But, on the contrary, whoever does not take care to possess the light of right faith and refuses to walk along the path of justice, when the righteous enjoy eternal light, will be punished with sinners and the devil by the torments of hell.

And the Lord said to Moses: “Phinehas, son of Eleazar, son of Aaron the priest, has turned away my anger from the children of Israel, because he was moved by my zeal against them, so that I did not destroy the children of Israel in my zeal. Therefore say to him: Behold, I give him the covenant of my covenant, and it shall be for him and for his offspring the covenant of an everlasting priesthood, because he was zealous for his God and made expiation for the crime of the children of Israel.”

It is rightly promised to Phinehas, son of Eleazar the priest, a covenant of everlasting priesthood because of the zeal he exercised in the matter of fornications. Whoever, pierced by zeal for God, strives to restrain the impulses of his flesh, or who rightly rebukes and restrains those subject to him so that through wantonness and lust they do not turn aside from the path of truth, will worthily possess the dignity of an everlasting priesthood in the Church of God.

This dignity properly belongs to that priest of whom it is written: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. CXIX), and with him he will possess an everlasting kingdom perpetually in the heavenly light.

Phinehas is interpreted as “sparing with the mouth,” or “he rested with the mouth,” or “the omen of the mouth.” Eleazar means “my God is helper,” or “the help of God.” Aaron means “mountain of strength,” or “strong mountain.”

These names appropriately express the same meaning we have proposed. For whoever refrains from speaking what is wicked with his mouth and rightly expounds the heavenly mysteries to his hearers in words, completing his devout labor through the help of God, will ascend by good works and happily reach the mountain of strength, concerning which it is written through the prophet: “The mountain of the house of the Lord shall be established on the top of the mountains, and it shall be exalted above the hills” (Isa. II).

The name of the Israelite man who was killed with the Midianite woman was Zambri, son of Saul, a leader from the family and tribe of Simeon. The Midianite woman who was killed with him was called Cozbi, daughter of Zur, a most noble prince of the Midianites.

This Israelite fornicator, who fornicated with the Midianite woman, represents those who separate themselves from fellowship with the Church either through error or through evil deeds, and who by their wickedness provoke blasphemy among unbelievers more than they encourage them by good works to glorify God.

To such people the Apostle said: “Through you the name of God is blasphemed among the nations” (Rom. II).

Their names also sufficiently reveal this. Zambri is interpreted as “psalm” or “song.” Saul means “regarding temptation.” Simeon means “he has heard sorrow,” or “the name of the tabernacle.” Cozbi means “boundless cup,” or “sacrifice to me.” Zur means “wall” or “distress,” and Midian means “contradiction” or “answer.”

Whom, then, does this Zambri better represent than a bodily or spiritual libertine and fornicator who arouses among the enemies of Christ not a song of praise but a psalm of reproach or mockery? Concerning such people the prophet said: “All day long I am their psalm” (Lam. III). And elsewhere: “They sang against me, those who drank wine” (Ps. LXVIII).

This man, therefore, regarding temptation—that is, consenting to temptation—under the name of a dwelling place, that is, under the name of one who is ecclesiastical, brings sorrow through his fall upon all the faithful dwelling with him. Filled with love for the boundless cup—that is, serving the allurements of gluttony—he has sacrificed himself to the devil by handing his members over to lust.

By his evil work causing a response of contradiction from the adversaries of God, he will plunge himself into the walls of the eternal prison and into the distress of perpetual condemnation, where he will be tormented day and night. Nor will he depart from there until he has paid the last penny (Matt. V).

## CHAPTER X. On the Second Census of the Israelites, Conducted by Moses and Eleazar, Son of Aaron the Priest

**[Col. 0771B] (CHAP. XXVI.)** After the blood of the guilty had been shed, the Lord said to Moses and Eleazar, son of Aaron the priest: “Count the entire number of the children of Israel, from twenty years old and above, according to their houses and clans—all who are able to go forth to war.”

At the Lord’s command the people were therefore first counted. But because those who had initially been enrolled fell on account of their persistence in sins, the second people, which by a renewed generation succeeded to the place of those who had fallen, is now called to the census. What had not been said concerning the former people is said concerning these.

For after the number had been collected by tribes, peoples, houses, and families, the Lord says to Moses: “To these the land shall be distributed by lot, and you shall give a small inheritance to the small.”

If it had been said concerning the former people that “to these the land shall be distributed by lot,” it would certainly have been false, because they fell in the wilderness on account of their sins. What was not said to the first people is therefore said to the last, for whom everything that was promised has also been fulfilled.

But do not think that these matters are confined to the text of history alone. They are mysteries written through the image of the Law. The former people, who are in circumcision, is rejected, and a second people, gathered from the nations, is introduced; it is this people that receives the paternal inheritance.

And from whom does it receive it? Not from Moses but from Jesus. For even if Moses gives some people an inheritance, he does not give it within the Jordan but outside the Jordan. He gives land that does not flow with milk and honey but is suitable for livestock. Dumb animals and irrational beasts will be nourished better there than rational human beings.

But my Jesus gives the second people a land flowing with milk and honey—a honeycomb, indeed, and the fullness of honey, but surpassing every land.

Moses does not give an inheritance among the clergy, nor distribute it by lot, nor can he weigh the merits of individuals by divine lot through peoples, houses, families, and names. Jesus alone does this, for the Father has handed all judgment over to him.

He knows how to distribute his people not only by tribes, families, and houses but also by names, assigning each one a worthy and appropriate dwelling.

There are nevertheless some among these who rise above the condition of the lot and are not brought to the lot at all. All the Levites—that is, those who remain attentively and continually in the ministry of God and keep watchful guard in his service—do not receive a lot among the others.

Nor is their lot in the land at all. Rather, the Lord himself is said to be their lot and inheritance.

By these, it seems to me, are signified those who, dulled by no bodily obstacles of nature but having surpassed the glory of all visible things, devote the use and practice of their life solely to the wisdom of God and his Word, seeking nothing bodily and nothing foreign to reason.

They desired wisdom; they desired knowledge of God’s secrets. “For where their heart is, there also is their treasure” (Matt. VI).

These therefore do not have an inheritance on earth, but rise beyond the highest summits of heaven and there continually delight in the Lord, continually in his Word, continually in his wisdom and in the will of his knowledge. This will be their food; this their drink; these their riches; this their sign.

Such, then, will be those among whom the Lord himself will be the inheritance. Those who are lower and have not reached this summit of progress will receive an inheritance of earth, though they may be more exalted and powerful in some respect.

The land of the living is promised to them—a land called the land of the living because it does not know death.

These too are great and blessed; but more blessed are those who will see God face to face, no longer through a mirror and in an enigma, nor in bodily substances, but face to face, illumined by the radiance of wisdom and made capable of the marvelous divinity through purity of heart. Their portion is not in a creature but in the Creator, who is God over all, blessed forever.

The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “To these the land shall be divided according to the number of their names, as their possession. To the larger group you shall give a larger portion, and to the smaller group a smaller one. To each, as they have now been counted, possession shall be given, provided only that the lot divides the land among the tribes and families. Whatever falls by lot, whether to the larger or the smaller group, they shall receive.”

This teaches that if a tribe is found to be larger in population, it should receive larger stretches of land by lot. But if one is reckoned smaller in number, it should be content with a shorter possession.

Since we say that this division and earthly inheritance hold the form and image of future goods and display the shape of that heavenly inheritance which is accomplished among the faithful and saints, I ask who are the many and who are the few in the inheritance that is to be hoped for. I find that the blessed are fewer than the many.

For those who travel by the broad and spacious way that leads to destruction are called many; but those who proceed by the narrow and constricted way that leads to life are called few.

And again it is said elsewhere: “How few there are who are saved!” (Matt. XIX). And elsewhere: “When iniquity abounds, the love of many grows cold” (Matt. XXIV)—not of the few.

But in the ark constructed by Noah, whose dimensions are given from heaven, the length in the lower part is three hundred cubits and the breadth fifty cubits. When its structure rises toward the higher levels, it is narrowed and gathered into a confined space of a few cubits, so that its summit is completed within the space of a single cubit.

This is because in the lower parts, where there were broad and spacious areas, beasts and cattle were placed; in the higher parts, birds; but in the highest places, which were narrower and more confined, the rational human being was placed.

The summit itself is gathered into one cubit. For everything is reduced to unity. Nevertheless, this number of three hundred cubits signifies the mystery of the Trinity. And man is placed close to this mystery, as a rational being capable of God.

From this let us also gather indications of the difference between the few and the many. Take the whole number of the human race and choose the faithful from all the nations. Without doubt they are fewer than the whole.

Then from the number of the faithful choose the better ones. It is certain that a much smaller number will remain. Again, from those whom you have chosen, choose the more perfect. You will surely find that the further you proceed in choosing, the more scant and very few they become, until at last you come to one who confidently says: “I labored more than all of them” (I Cor. XV).

Those who are many in this world will therefore receive more earth and more bodily inheritance. But the few will obtain only a little of the earth, because they have more in the Lord.

Others will receive no earth at all, if they are found worthy to be priests and ministers of God. For the Lord himself will be the entire inheritance of these.

And who is so blessed as to receive a little earth among the few, or, among the chosen priests and ministers, to deserve to receive God alone as an inheritance by lot?

Although they receive some land on account of their livestock, it is land adjoining cities and attached to towns.

This saying, which declares that the inheritance is to be increased for the larger number, can still be understood in another way. One righteous person, insofar as he is accepted by God, is counted as many.

Thus it is written: “Through one wise man a city shall be inhabited, but the tribes of the wicked shall be laid waste.” One righteous person is reckoned for the whole world, whereas the wicked, even if they are many, are considered few and worthless before the Lord.

There is therefore also a praiseworthy multitude, as we saw when the Lord brought Abraham outside and said to him: “Look up at the heavens; if you can count the stars, so shall your offspring be.”

Observe also in this passage how the righteous person is inward and always remains in the interior, because inwardly, in secret, he prays to the Father; and “all the glory of the king’s daughter,” that is, of the royal soul, is within.

Yet God brings him outside when circumstances require it and when the order of visible things demands it again.

In this way also the inheritance can be multiplied for those many who are like the stars of heaven, while a small inheritance can be assigned to those who are few—namely, those who, even if numerous in number, are considered few because of the unworthiness and baseness of their life.

“By lot,” he says, “the inheritance shall be distributed.” This is indeed commanded. But when I come to the Scriptures, I see that Moses himself, although commanded to do so, does not use the lot in the division of the inheritance of Reuben, Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh.

Joshua son of Nun also gives an inheritance outside the lot to the tribe of Judah, and gives Caleb one outside the lot in the tribe of Ephraim and to the half-tribe of Manasseh. In the remaining cases the lot is cast. The first lot comes forth for Benjamin, and thereafter for the remaining tribes.

Hence I think that in that blessed inheritance of the kingdom of heaven there will also be some who do not come to the lot and are not numbered with the others, although they are holy. Their inheritance will be distinguished and exceptional, as was that of Caleb, the tribe of Judah, and Joshua son of Nun.

For just as, when after a battle provinces and spoils are divided among the victors, the distinguished and outstanding warriors are not brought to the lot with the other soldiers in the division of the spoils, but the best things and the special rewards are assigned to them in accordance with their merit in virtue, while the others use the lot by the ordinary right of victory, so, it seems to me, my Lord Jesus Christ will act.

For to some whom he knows to have labored more abundantly than the others, and whose magnificent deeds and sublime virtues he himself recognizes, he assigns the foremost and most distinguished honors and glories—if I may dare to say so, honors like his own.

Does he not seem to confer something resembling his blessedness upon his dearest disciples when he says: “Father, I desire that where I am, they also may be with me” (John XVII)? And again: “You also will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. XIX). And again: “As you, Father, are in me and I am in you, so may they also be one in us” (John I).

All these things are not determined by lot but bestowed by the prerogative of election by him alone who sees the hearts and minds of human beings.

May he also deign to bring us, even if not among the distinguished and chosen, and those who are above the lot, into the lot of the saints.

## CHAPTER XI.

## (Chapter XXVII)

Then the daughters of Zelophehad approached—he was the son of Hepher, the son of Gilead, the son of Machir, the son of Manasseh, [Col. 0774D] who was the son of Joseph. Their names were Maacah, Noah, Eglah, Milcah, and Tirzah. They stood before Moses and Eleazar the priest, and before all the leaders of the people, at the entrance of the tabernacle, and said:

“Our father died in the wilderness. He was not among the rebellion that was stirred up against the Lord under Korah; he died because of his own sin. He had no male children. Why should his name be removed from his family because he had no son? Give us a possession among the kinsmen of our father.”

Moses brought their case before the judgment of the Lord. The Lord said to him: “The daughters of Zelophehad have made a just request. Give them a possession among the kinsmen of their father, and let their father’s inheritance pass to them.”

Everyone who knows that these laws are observed not only among the children of Israel but among all people who live under laws can plainly see what force these matters have according to the historical sense. It is therefore evident that the liberty granted to the daughters of Zelophehad not only bestowed an inheritance upon them but also gave them perpetual rights of life. You see how great, even in the historical sense, is the usefulness of the law of God. Who could ever abolish these laws, which the whole world employs?

Nevertheless, let us inquire how we too may be spiritually edified. It may happen that I have neither daughters according to the flesh nor any piece of land whose inheritance can be received. What then? Will this law accomplish nothing in one who is such, and will what was sanctioned by the divine voice be useless for anyone? Let us therefore inquire, even according to the spiritual law, who these five daughters are, who, even if their father has died [Col. 0775B] because of some sin, may themselves receive an inheritance from the word of God.

Earlier, when we were discussing spiritual sons, we taught that the virtues of the soul and the perceptions of the mind were sons. It therefore seems undoubtedly appropriate and fitting that daughters should receive the works accomplished through the service of the body. For this reason, finally, the number five is assigned to them: there are five bodily senses, through which every work is accomplished in the body.

These five daughters, therefore—that is, the perfection of works—even if they are deprived of their father and remain orphans, are nevertheless not rejected from the inheritance or excluded from the kingdom. Rather, in the midst of the people of God they receive a share of the inheritance.

But let us see who their father is, of whom it is said that he died. “Zelophehad,” it says. Zelophehad, however, is interpreted as “shadow in his mouth.” The father of works is understanding. It often happens, therefore, that there are not a few among our brothers in whom there is no higher or deeper understanding, but in whom the faculty of perception is dead. Yet if such a man begets daughters—that is, works of service, works of obedience, works of God’s commandments—he receives an inheritance in the land together with the people of God.

He will not, indeed, be numbered among those whose portion is the Lord and whose inheritance is God. He cannot be admitted into the number of ministers and priests; nevertheless, in the order of the common people he will receive the inheritance of the land of promise. For “many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. XX).

The reason is also shown by the interpretation of the name itself: this Zelophehad could not beget sons, but daughters. For, as we said, it is interpreted as “shadow in his mouth.” You see that if someone has the shadow of the law in his mouth, and not the reality of the things themselves, then, because he is unable to perceive anything spiritual or profound in understanding, but has only the shadow of the law in his mouth, he cannot beget living and spiritual perceptions. He can nevertheless beget works and actions that belong to a simpler way of life and service.

In this, therefore, the mercy of God is revealed: even those who are more innocent, though deficient in understanding, nevertheless possess good works and are not excluded from the inheritance of the saints.

“When a man dies without a son, his inheritance shall pass to his daughter. If he has no daughter, you shall give his inheritance to his brothers. If he has no brothers, you shall give his inheritance to his father’s brothers. But if he has no paternal uncles, you shall give his inheritance to the one who is nearest to him among his family.” [Col. 0776A] “This shall be a sacred ordinance for the children of Israel, by a perpetual law, as the Lord commanded Moses.”

A law concerning succession is established: first the son succeeds; the daughter succeeds second; the brother third; the father’s brother fourth. The fifth degree does not designate any particular person, but whoever is nearest to him from the whole family is to succeed him.

In these matters the historical sense is so complete and perfect that it seems to require nothing from outside. Yet if someone is well instructed in spiritual laws and illumined by the fuller light of knowledge, he can understand these various degrees of succession.

The first, then, is the order of heavenly inheritance: the degree of teaching and knowledge, represented by the male child. The second is the prerogative of works, represented by the daughter. The third is that of compassion and imitation, for which reason the person is called a brother.

There are some who do nothing of their own accord or through their own understanding. Yet, placed among brothers, they seem, by imitating the others, to do what those also do who are moved by their own understanding. An inheritance is therefore given even to these, under the title of brother.

The fourth degree, which names the father’s brother, can perhaps be understood as that class of people who, having heard what was handed down by their fathers and received the narratives of the ancients, strive to fulfill them. They do good not so much because they are moved by their own perceptions or stirred by the teaching of the present, but because they have been formed by the tradition or mere custom of the ancients.

The final degree is written concerning the person who, by whatever means, is nearest to these, as though it said: Whether through opportunity or through the truth of teaching someone has done something good, the reward of the good work will not perish. Rather, through the generosity of the Lord, he will receive a place in the inheritance.

These interpretations may perhaps seem boldly presumed and brought forward by us. Nevertheless, it will not be absurd if, setting spiritual things before spiritual things, we make them eager to pursue and desire a more secret understanding.

## Chapter XII

### Moses Is Commanded to Ascend the Mountain, and It Is Foretold to Him That He Will Not Enter the Land of Promise; Jesus Is Appointed Leader of the People in His Place

**(There.)** The Lord also said to Moses: “Ascend this mountain of Abarim, and from there behold the land [Col. 0776D] that I will give to the children of Israel. When you have seen it, you too shall go to your people, as your brother Aaron went, because you offended me in the wilderness of Zin, in the contradiction of the multitude, and you were unwilling to sanctify me before them over the waters. These are the waters of contradiction at Kadesh in the wilderness of Zin.”

Consider first of all how the perfect man, who is also blessed, does not complete his course in a valley, on some level stretch of land, or on some hill, but on a mountain—that is, in a lofty and difficult place. The completion and perfection of his life is found on high.

He is commanded to look upon the whole land of promise with his eyes and to examine everything carefully from an elevated perspective. For one who was about to attain the highest perfection, it was necessary that nothing remain unknown to him, but that he possess knowledge of all things that are seen and heard. I believe that this was so that he might swiftly grasp the reasons and causes of all things: while still placed in the flesh, he had begun with bodily sight, but, having become spiritual and hastening with every faculty of his mind toward the things heard and toward discipleship in wisdom, he would attain their meaning.

For what benefit would there be in showing a man who was about to depart from the world and immediately reach the end of this life places whose labor he would not endure and whose grace he would not receive?

The following statement truly frightens me and makes me hesitant and trembling to speak: concerning that great Moses, servant and friend of God, to whom God spoke face to face, and through whom wondrous signs and virtues were accomplished, such grave and perilous things are reported. What does God say to him?

“You also shall be gathered to your people,” he says, [Col. 0777B] “as your brother Aaron was gathered on Mount Hor.” And, explaining the cause of his death, he says: “Because you transgressed my word in the wilderness of Zin, when the assembly resisted, so that I might not be sanctified. You did not sanctify me in the water before them.”

Therefore Moses too is at fault; he too incurs the charge of transgression; he too has come under sin. For this reason, I believe, the Apostle confidently said: “Death reigned from Adam to Moses.” It reached even to Moses and did not spare him (Rom. V). And so, I think, he said that “sin entered this world, and through sin, death,” in which all sinned (Rom. VII). And again: “God has enclosed all under sin, so that he may have mercy on all.”

But thanks be to our God through Jesus Christ, who delivered us from this body of death, so that where sin abounded, grace might abound still more (Rom. II). For how could Moses have freed anyone from sins when it is said even to him: “You transgressed my word in the wilderness of Zin, and you did not sanctify me in the water before the children of Israel”?

Thus it is made clear to everyone that the one who alone did not commit sin, and in whose mouth no deceit was found, is the one who alone ought to be sought.

Nevertheless, this mystery must be considered: neither the priesthood that was instituted, represented by Aaron, nor the law, represented by Moses, brings the people of God into the land of the inheritance that is eternal. Rather, Jesus does so, in whom there was a type of the Lord Jesus Christ—that is, grace through faith.

Aaron died before Israel entered any part of the land of promise. While Moses was still alive, the land of the Amorites was captured and possessed; but he was not permitted to cross the Jordan with them. In some respect, therefore, the law is observed in the Christian faith, for there are commandments in it that Christians are still commanded to observe today. But that priesthood and those sacrifices have no place in the Christian faith, except insofar as they were performed and completed as shadows of things to come.

When it is said to both brothers, Aaron and Moses, that they are to be gathered to their people, it is clear that God’s anger was not directed against them in a way that separated them from the peace of the holy and eternal fellowship. It is therefore shown that not only their offices but also their deaths were signs of things to come, not punishments inflicted in God’s anger.

But for the moment let us consider Moses’ greatness. As he is about to depart from the world, he prays that God will provide a judge for the people, saying:

“Let the God of the spirits of all flesh provide a man who shall be over this multitude and be able to go out and come in among them, to lead them out and bring them in, so that the people of the Lord may not be like sheep without a shepherd.”

What are you doing, Moses? Are Gershom and Eleazar not your sons? Or, if you have some doubt concerning them, are they not the sons of your great and distinguished brother? Why do you not pray to God for them, asking him to appoint them as leaders of the people?

Let the leaders of the churches learn from this not to designate as their successors those who are joined to them by blood relationship, nor those connected with them by kinship of the flesh; let them not hand down leadership as an inheritance, but refer the matter to the judgment of God. Let them not choose the person commended by human affection, but leave the whole matter of choosing a successor to the judgment of God.

Could Moses not have chosen a leader for the people—and chosen one with true judgment and a correct and just decision? God had said to him: “Choose elders for the people, whom you yourself know to be elders” (Num. II). And he chose such men, of whom it is immediately said that the Spirit rested upon them and that they all prophesied.

Who, then, could have chosen a leader of the people as Moses could? Yet he does not do so. He does not choose one. He does not dare. Why does he not dare? So that he might not leave posterity an example of presumption.

But listen to what he says: “Let the Lord,” he says, “provide a man over this assembly, who shall go out before them and come in before them, who shall lead them out and bring them in.”

If that great and extraordinary Moses does not presume to rely on his own judgment in choosing a leader of the people and appointing a successor, who would dare to do so? Who, whether from the common people—who are often accustomed to be stirred by cries raised either for favor or perhaps for battle—or even from the priests themselves, would judge himself suitable for this, unless the Lord should reveal it to someone who prays and asks him?

As the Lord also says to Moses: “Take Joshua the son of Nun, a man in whom is the Spirit of God, and lay your hand upon him. He shall stand before Eleazar the priest and all the congregation. You shall give him commandments in the sight of all, and you shall give him a share of your glory, so that the whole congregation of the children of Israel may hear him. Whenever anything must be done, Eleazar the priest shall consult the Lord for him. At his word he shall go out, and all the children of Israel with him, and the whole congregation.”

You hear the appointment of the leader of the people described so clearly that it scarcely requires interpretation. There is no acclamation of the people, no consideration of blood relationship, no regard for kinship. Let inheritance of fields and estates be left to relatives. Let governance of the people be entrusted to the one whom God has chosen—namely, a man who, as you have heard written, has the Spirit of God within himself, before whom the commandments of God stand, and who is very well known and familiar to Moses: a man in whom there are the glory of God and knowledge, so that the children of Israel may hear him.

When he says, “You shall give him a share of your glory,” this should not be understood as though he were saying, “Make him a partner in your glory.” Things of this kind are not diminished by being divided into portions; rather, they are wholly possessed by all and wholly possessed by each person who shares in them.

“Whenever anything must be done,” he says, “Eleazar the priest shall consult the Lord for him. At his word he shall go out and come in,” and so forth.

This statement instructs us morally: whoever receives authority over the people of God must do and arrange everything according to the teaching of the divine law, which is especially entrusted to us in the office of the priest. He must order and govern his entire life, and the lives of those committed to him, according to that teaching.

For this reason it is also said through the prophet Malachi: “The lips of the priest guard knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord of hosts” (Mal. II).

But since everything is filled with mysteries, we cannot omit the more precious matters, even if what is commanded according to the literal sense seems necessary and useful. Let us therefore consider what Moses’ death means.

It is undoubtedly the end of the law—but of the law understood according to the letter. What is its end? The interruption of sacrifices, certainly, and of the other observances that are commanded in the law in the same manner.

When these things therefore reach their end, Jesus assumes the leadership. “For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes.” And just as it was said concerning those earlier matters, that “all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea” (1 Cor. X), so let it also be said concerning Jesus that all were baptized into Jesus in the Holy Spirit and water.

For Jesus is the one who crosses the waters of the Jordan, and in them he already then baptizes the people, in a certain sense. He is also the one who distributes the land of the inheritance, the holy land, to all—not to the first people, but to the second.

The first people fell in the wilderness because of their transgression. Concerning the time of Jesus it is said that “the land rested from wars.” This could not be said of the time of Moses, but it is said of Jesus my Lord, not of that Joshua son of Nun.

Would that my land too might cease from wars—and might be able to cease! If, therefore, I faithfully served under Jesus my prince, and if I also obeyed my Lord Jesus, my flesh would never rise up against my spirit, nor would my land be attacked by hostile nations—that is, by the various desires that incite it.

Let us all pray that Jesus may reign over us, and that our land may cease from wars and from the attacks of carnal desires. When these have ceased, then each person will rest beneath his own vine, beneath his own fig tree, and beneath his own olive tree. Under the shelter of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit the soul that has recovered peace between flesh and spirit will rest. Amen.

# Book Four

[Col. 0779]

## Chapter I

[Col. 0779B] [Col. 0779C]

### Concerning the Individual Kinds of Sacrifices Offered to the Lord at Various Festivals—that Is, on the Sabbath, at the New Moon, in the First Month, in the Month of Firstfruits, and in the Seventh Month

**(Chapter XXVIII.)** The Lord also said to Moses: “Command the children of Israel, and say to them: You shall present my offering, my bread, and the incense of a most pleasing fragrance at their appointed times. These are the sacrifices that you must offer: two unblemished yearling lambs each day as a perpetual burnt offering. You shall offer one in the morning and the other in the evening. You shall also offer a tenth of an ephah of fine flour mixed with the purest oil, together with a quarter of a hin. This is the continual burnt offering that you offered on Mount Sinai, as a most pleasing fragrance, an offering made by fire to the Lord. [Col. 0779D] Offer one lamb in the sanctuary to the Lord, and offer the other lamb in the evening in the same manner, according to the whole rite of the morning sacrifice and its libations, an offering of most pleasing fragrance to the Lord.”

Since, then, we have the laws of the festivals in our hands, and our discourse now concerns them, let us inquire more carefully what the order of the festivals is, so that from their order and the rite of the sacrifices we may gather how each person can prepare a festival for God through his own holy actions and manner of life.

The first festival of God is therefore the one called “unceasing.” For it concerns the sacrifices that are offered unceasingly and without any interruption at all, in the morning and in the evening.

In commanding the festival, therefore, the law does not immediately come first to the festival of Passover, nor to Unleavened Bread, nor to the Feast of Booths, nor to the others concerning which commandments are given. Rather, it placed first this festival, in which an unceasing sacrifice is commanded to be offered, so that whoever wishes to be perfect and holy may recognize that a festival is not something to be practiced for God at one time and not at another, but that the righteous person ought always and unceasingly to keep a feast.

The sacrifice that is commanded to be offered unceasingly, both in the morning and in the evening, indicates that one should persist with unceasing devotion in the law and the prophets, which point to the morning, and in the evangelical teaching, which points to the evening—that is, to the coming of the Savior at the evening of the world.

The Lord therefore says concerning such festivals: “You shall observe my feast days.” The Lord’s feast day exists if we offer him an unceasing sacrifice, if we pray without interruption, so that our prayer may rise before him like the morning sacrifice, and the lifting up of our hands may become for him an evening sacrifice.

The first solemnity, then, is that of the continuous and unceasing sacrifice. Those who cultivate the Gospel must fulfill it in the manner explained above.

But since, as the prophetic word has taught, the feast days of sinners are turned into mourning and their songs into lamentation, it is certain that the one who sins and observes the days of sin cannot keep a feast day. Therefore, on the days when he sins, he cannot offer God an unceasing sacrifice. Only the one who unceasingly guards righteousness and preserves himself from sin can offer it.

On whatever day he interrupts this and sins, it is certain that on that day he does not offer an unceasing sacrifice to God.

The command to offer two unblemished lambs each day as a burnt offering, one in the morning and the other in the evening, signifies that we must present to God not only innocence of action but also purity of heart, both at the beginning of our way of life and at its end, through the fire of love and the fervor of the Holy Spirit. For “the one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. XXIV).

At the same time, a tenth of an ephah of fine flour mixed with the purest oil is commanded to be offered with the lamb, and a quarter of a hin of wine as a libation. This means that innocence will then be pleasing and acceptable to God if, according to the knowledge of the divine law and evangelical teaching, it is applied honorably and tempered by grace. Scripture shows this when it says: “The one who is innocent in his hands and pure in heart, who has not received his soul in vain and has not sworn deceitfully to his neighbor” (Ps. XXIII). The measure of an ephah or a hin has already been explained above.

On the Sabbath day you shall offer two unblemished yearling lambs, and two-tenths of fine flour mixed with oil as a sacrifice, together with the libations that are properly poured on each Sabbath as a perpetual burnt offering.

What is the festival of the Sabbath except that of which the Apostle says: “A sabbath observance remains” (Heb. IV)—that is, the observance of the Sabbath for the people of God?

Leaving behind the Jewish observances of the Sabbath, let us see what the observance of the Sabbath ought to be for a Christian. On the Sabbath day one ought to perform none of the works of the world. If, therefore, you cease from all secular works and do nothing worldly, but devote yourself to spiritual works; if you come to church, lend your ear to the divine readings and teachings, think about heavenly things, concern yourself with the hope of the future, keep the coming judgment before your eyes, and do not look toward present and visible things but toward invisible and future things—this is the observance of the Sabbath for a Christian.

But the Jews too ought to observe these things. Indeed, even among them, if a smith, a builder, or any other such artisan should arise on the Sabbath day, the reader and teacher of the divine law does not cease from his work, and yet he does not profane the Sabbath.
