For he says to them: “Have you not read that the priests in the temple violate the Sabbath and are without guilt?” (Matt. XII).

The one who ceases from the works of the world and devotes himself to spiritual actions is the one who offers the Sabbath sacrifice and keeps the feast of Sabbaths; he does not carry burdens on the way. Every sin is a burden, as the Prophet also says: “Like a heavy burden, they are too heavy for me” (Ps. XXXI).

He does not kindle a fire either—the fire of which it is said: “Go in the light of your fire and in the flame that you have kindled.”

“On the Sabbath, let each person sit in his own place and not go out from it.” What, then, is the place of the spiritual soul? Righteousness is its place; truth, wisdom, sanctification, and everything that Christ is are the soul’s place. It ought not to leave that place if it is to keep the true Sabbaths and celebrate the feast day with the sacrifices of Sabbaths.

Thus the Lord also said: “The one who remains in me, and I in him” (John VI).

When we speak of true Sabbaths, if we inquire more deeply into what the true Sabbaths are, the true observance of the Sabbath lies beyond this world. For what is written in Genesis—that God rested on the Sabbath day from his works (Gen. II)—we do not see to have happened then on the seventh day, nor do we see it happening now.

For we always see God at work. There is no Sabbath on which God does not work, on which he does not make his sun rise over the good and the evil and send rain upon the just and the unjust; no Sabbath on which he does not bring forth grass on the mountains and plants for human use; on which he does not strike and heal, bring down to the underworld and bring back; on which he does not kill and make alive.

Therefore, when the Jews challenged him concerning work and healing on the Sabbath, the Lord also answered them in the Gospels: “My Father is working until now, and I am working” (John V).

By this he shows that on no Sabbath of this age does God rest from the administration of the world and from his providence for the human race. For he made the creatures in the beginning and brought forth as many substances as he knew, as the creator of all things, would be sufficient for the perfection of the world. Yet until the consummation of the age he does not cease to provide for and govern them.

There will therefore be a true Sabbath on which God will rest from all his works: the age to come, when pain, sadness, and groaning will flee, and God will be all in all.

On that Sabbath may God grant us also to celebrate a feast with him, to keep festivals with the holy angels, offering a sacrifice of praise and fulfilling our vows to the Most High. Then perhaps our unceasing sacrifice, which we explained above, will be offered more perfectly. For then God will be better able to be present unceasingly, and the sacrifice of praise will be offered through the great High Priest, who is a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek (Ps. CIX).

The Sabbath offering consists of two unblemished yearling lambs, two-tenths of fine flour mixed with oil as a sacrifice, and the libations that are properly poured on each Sabbath. These signify nothing other than that we should live soberly, righteously, and piously in this present age, awaiting the blessed hope and the coming of the glory of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ.

Whatever we are able to do by divine grace, let us earnestly strive to accomplish it in order to attain the Father’s rest.

The one who offers two yearling lambs to the Lord presents before the divine presence simplicity of mind and innocence of action. The one who gives two-tenths of fine flour mixed with oil as a sacrifice, together with the libations, is filled with spiritual grace and, while the Holy Spirit teaches him, commends to his hearers the knowledge of the two Testaments through both words and examples.

All this, as we have said, they strive to expend not for the gain of temporal profit but for the attainment of eternal life.

The third festival is the day of the new moon, on which an offering is made, as it is written:

“On the Kalends—that is, at the beginnings of the months—you shall offer a burnt offering to the Lord: two bulls from the herd, one ram, seven unblemished yearling lambs, three-tenths of fine flour mixed with oil for each ram, and a tenth of a tenth of fine flour mixed with oil as a sacrifice for each lamb, a burnt offering of most pleasing fragrance and incense to the Lord,” and so forth.

“New moon” (*neomenia*) means the new moon. This festival therefore occurs when the moon is renewed. It is called new when it has come close to the sun and has become very closely joined to it, so that it lies hidden beneath its radiance.

But it may perhaps seem remarkable, indeed superfluous, for divine law to command this. What religious benefit is there in observing a festival for the new moon—that is, when it is joined to and adheres to the sun? If these things are considered according to the letter, they will seem not so much religious as superstitious.

But the Apostle Paul knew that the law was not speaking about these things, and that the Holy Spirit did not command the rite that appears to be observed by the Jews. Therefore, to those who had received faith in God he said: “Let no one judge you concerning food or drink, or in respect of a festival, or a new moon, or a Sabbath: [Col. 0783B] these are a shadow of things to come” (Col. II).

If the Sabbath is a shadow of things to come, concerning which we have explained as much as we could above, and if the new moon too is a shadow of things to come, it is certain that the other festivals are likewise shadows of things to come.

But now let us consider the new moon. We have said that the festival of the new moon is observed when the moon begins to be renewed, becomes close to the sun, and is completely joined to it.

Christ is the Sun of righteousness. If the moon—that is, his Church, which is filled with his light—is joined to him and adheres to him completely, so that, according to the Apostle’s word, “the one who is joined to God becomes one spirit with him,” then she celebrates the festival of the new moon.

For she becomes new when she has put off the old person and put on the new person, who was created according to God. Thus, by the merit of her renewal, she rightly celebrates the solemnity that is the festival of the new moon.

This occurs, finally, when she can neither be seen nor grasped by human eyes. For when the soul has joined itself entirely to the Lord and has wholly entered into the splendor of his light; when it thinks of nothing earthly, seeks nothing worldly, and strives not to please human beings, but has wholly devoted itself to the light of wisdom and wholly surrendered itself to the warmth of the Holy Spirit; when it has become subtle and spiritual—how can it be seen by human beings or grasped by human eyes?

The merely natural person cannot understand or discern the spiritual person. Therefore, the soul most worthily keeps the feast and sacrifices the new-moon offering to the Lord, having been renewed by him.

If, according to the rule of allegorical interpretation, someone wishes to know what these offerings that are offered to the Lord as a burnt offering signify—namely, two bulls, one ram, seven yearling lambs, and the other kinds that were commanded to be offered together—he can understand, according to the understanding of the orthodox, in the two bulls the delight of good work, through soul or body, and the teaching of the two Testaments fittingly offered to God in the two commandments of love.

In the one ram, he may understand the governance of discipline according to the unity of faith, presented not weakly but courageously and nobly.

In the seven unblemished yearling lambs, he may understand simplicity and gentleness of character, rightly displayed by the faithful, through the grace of the sevenfold Spirit, for future rest in heaven, both for their own salvation and as an example to others.

The faithful person therefore offers God three-tenths of fine flour mixed with oil as a sacrifice for each bull when, illuminated by the oil of gladness, he presents spiritual knowledge in faith in the holy Trinity together with good works.

He offers two-tenths of fine flour mixed with oil for each ram when he strives to apply the Decalogue of the law, with sober understanding, to the two commandments of love for his own benefit and that of his neighbors, and through it to dedicate his entire life to the Lord as a sweet fragrance.

He also offers a tenth of a tenth of fine flour mixed with oil as a sacrifice for each lamb when he strives to establish and adorn the simplicity of his conduct according to the rule of the Holy Scriptures, with the grace of the Holy Spirit working within him.

All these things are rightly commanded to be offered to the Lord as a burnt offering, because we ought to do everything with this sole intention: not to seek human praise or present recompense, but to please God, the giver of all good things, in everything, and to deserve to receive eternal life from him, the most just rewarder, in the future.

In the first month, on the fourteenth day of the month, there will be the Lord’s Passover, and on the fifteenth day a solemn festival; for seven days they shall eat unleavened bread, of which the first day shall be venerable and holy. You shall do no servile work on it; and you shall offer as a burnt offering to the Lord, for a pleasing fragrance, two young bulls from the herd, one ram, and seven unblemished yearling lambs, together with the offerings for each animal, made of fine flour mixed with oil: three-tenths for each bull, two-tenths for the ram, and one-tenth of a tenth for each lamb—that is, for seven lambs—and one male goat as a sin offering, to make atonement for you, in addition to the morning burnt offering, which you shall always offer.

Thus you shall do on each of the seven days, as fuel for the fire and as a most pleasing fragrance to the Lord, which shall rise from the burnt offering and the sacrifices of each animal. The seventh day also shall be most solemn and holy for you. You shall do no servile work on it.

Fourth among the festivals of God in this passage is the solemnity of Passover, at which the lamb is slaughtered. If you understand it rightly, it is the true Lamb, the Lamb of God, the Lamb who takes away the sins of the world; and say that “our Passover has been sacrificed, Christ.” Let the Jews eat the flesh of the lamb in a carnal sense; but let us eat the flesh of the Word of God. For he himself said: “Unless you eat the flesh of me, you will not have life in yourselves” (John 6). What we are now discussing is the flesh of the Word of God, provided that we do not offer it as though to the weak vegetables, or as though to children nourishment of milk. If we speak of perfect things, of robust and strong things, then we set before ourselves the flesh of the Word of God to eat.

For wherever mystical discourse is proclaimed, wherever a doctrinal teaching filled with faith in the Trinity is set forth in solid form, wherever the sacraments of the spiritual law are disclosed after the veil of the letter concerning the future age has been removed, wherever the soul’s hope, torn away from earthly things, is cast into the heavens and placed among those things “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart” (1 Corinthians 2)—all these are the flesh, the words of God. Whoever is able to eat this with a perfect understanding and a purified heart offers the sacrifice of the true festival of Passover, [Col. 0785A] and keeps a feast with God and with his angels.

After this—or rather, as a continuation of it—comes the festival of unleavened bread. You will celebrate it rightly if you drive out from your soul all leaven of malice and wickedness and preserve the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth. For one must not suppose that almighty God wrote laws for human beings concerning leaven, and for that reason commanded a soul to be exterminated from the people if it happened that a little of this leaven, mixed into flour, were found in its house; nor that this concern over such leaven mattered so greatly to the divine majesty that he would say he was offended by it to such an extent that he commanded the soul which he himself made in his image and likeness to be exterminated and destroyed on this account. This does not seem to me to be the divine understanding of the divine laws, [Col. 0785B] but rather that greater matter which God dreads—and rightly dreads—if the soul is weakened by the spirit of malice, anger, or wickedness and swells toward sinful deeds.

God does not want the soul to be this; and if we cast such leaven out of the house of our soul, we shall rightly be exterminated. But do not disregard it even if you see only a small amount of malice fermenting within you, because “a little leaven corrupts the whole lump” (1 Corinthians 5). Therefore do not neglect even a small sin, since one sin gives rise to another. For just as justice gives birth to justice, and chastity to chastity, so if someone first begins to be chaste in a modest way, apart from the leaven of chastity he becomes daily more chaste. Likewise, whoever once stores within himself, even in a small amount, the leaven of malice becomes daily more wicked and worse than himself. Therefore, if you wish to celebrate the festival of unleavened bread with God, do not permit even a little leaven of malice to remain within you.

The Day of Firstfruits also, when you offer new produce to the Lord after the weeks have been completed, shall be venerable and holy. You shall do no servile work on it, and you shall offer a burnt offering as a most pleasing fragrance to the Lord: two young bulls from the herd, one ram, and seven unblemished lambs, together with their sacrifices—three-tenths of fine flour mixed with oil for each bull, two-tenths for the ram, and one-tenth of a tenth for the lambs, which together are seven lambs. You shall also offer the male goat slaughtered for expiation, in addition to the perpetual burnt offering and its libations. You shall offer everything unblemished, together with its libations.

After this comes the sixth festival, which is called that of the New Things, that is, the firstfruits are offered from the new produce. When a field has been carefully sown and cultivated, and the crop has reached maturity, then the festival of the Lord is celebrated in the perfection of its fruits. Therefore, if you too wish to celebrate with God the festival of the New Things, see how and where you sow, so that you may reap such fruits as will make God rejoice and enable you to keep the festival.

You will not be able to fulfill this in any other way than by hearing the Apostle say: “Whoever sows in the spirit will reap eternal life from the spirit” (2 Corinthians 9). If you sow and reap in this way, then you truly celebrate the festival of the New Things. Therefore the prophet also admonishes, saying: “Renew your new-ploughed fields, and do not sow upon thorns” (Jeremiah 4). Whoever renews his heart and his inner person from day to day renews his new-ploughed fields for himself and does not sow upon thorns, but upon good soil, which will return to him fruit thirtyfold, or sixtyfold, or a hundredfold.

This, then, is the person who sows in the spirit and gathers the fruits of the spirit. The first fruit of the spirit is joy. And rightly does the person who reaps joy celebrate the festival of new fruits. Above all, let him reap peace, patience, and goodness together with it, and gather gentleness and other fruits like these, celebrating most worthily the festival of new fruits for the Lord.

## (CHAP. XXIX.)

The first day of the seventh month shall also be venerable and holy for you. You shall do no servile work on it, because it is the day of the sounding and of the trumpets. You shall offer a burnt offering as a most pleasing fragrance to the Lord: one young bull from the herd, one ram, and seven unblemished yearling lambs. With their sacrifices, you shall offer three-tenths of fine flour mixed with oil for each bull, two-tenths for the ram, and one-tenth for each lamb; together there are seven lambs.

You shall also offer a male goat as a sin offering for the expiation of the people, in addition to the burnt offering of the Kalends with its sacrifices, and the perpetual burnt offering with its customary libations. You shall offer these according to the same rites as a most pleasing fragrance, an offering to the Lord.

Next comes the festival of the Seventh Things. For just as among seven days every seventh day is observed as a sabbath and is a festival, so among the months every seventh month is the sabbath of the months. A festival is therefore celebrated in it which is called the Sabbath of Sabbaths; and on the first day of the month there is a memorial of trumpets—unless someone is able to commit to memory and store in the treasure-house of his heart the prophetic, evangelical, and apostolic Scriptures, which resound like a kind of heavenly trumpet.

Whoever does this and meditates on the law of the Lord day and night keeps a festival of memory. But if someone is able to earn those gifts of the Holy Spirit by which the prophets were inspired, and, singing psalms, to say, “Blow the trumpet at the beginning of the month, on the notable day of its solemnity” (Psalm 80), and if he knows how to rejoice in him with psalms, he worthily celebrates the solemnity of the Trumpets for God.

The tenth day of this seventh month shall also be holy and venerable for you, and you shall afflict your souls. You shall do no servile work on it, and you shall offer a burnt offering to the Lord as a most pleasing fragrance: one young bull from the herd, one ram, and seven yearling lambs. With their sacrifices you shall offer three-tenths of fine flour mixed with oil for each bull, two-tenths for the ram, and one-tenth of a tenth for each lamb; together there are seven lambs. You shall also offer a male goat as a sin offering, in addition to those offerings customarily made for guilt, as an expiation and a perpetual burnt offering, with their sacrifices and libations.

There is yet another festival, when people afflict their souls and humble themselves before God while celebrating the festival. O marvelous festival! The festival day is called the affliction of the soul. “This day,” he says, “is the day of propitiation, the tenth day of the seventh month.” You see, then, that if you wish to celebrate a festival, if you wish God to rejoice over you, afflict your soul and humble it. Do not permit it to fulfill its desires, nor allow it to wander into wanton pleasures; but, insofar as this can be done, afflict and humble it.

Finally, the festival of Passover and of Unleavened Bread is also said to have the bread of affliction. No one can celebrate a festival unless he has eaten the bread of affliction and eaten Passover with bitterness. “You shall eat unleavened bread,” he says, “with bitterness.” You see, then, what the festivals of God are like. They do not admit bodily sweetness; they desire nothing relaxed, pleasurable, or luxurious, but demand affliction of soul, bitterness, and humility. For “whoever humbles himself will be exalted before God” (Luke 14).

This, then, is what the day of propitiation also demands. For when the soul has been afflicted and humbled in the presence of the Lord, then God is propitiated toward it; and then there comes to it the one whom God “put forward as a propitiation through faith in his blood”: Jesus Christ, its Lord and Redeemer.

But on the fifteenth day of the seventh month, which shall be holy and venerable for you, you shall do no servile work on it. Rather, you shall celebrate a solemn festival to the Lord for seven days, and you shall offer as a most pleasing fragrance to the Lord thirteen young bulls from the herd, two rams, and fourteen unblemished yearling lambs. With their libations you shall offer three-tenths of fine flour mixed with oil for each bull—together there are thirteen bulls—and two-tenths for one ram, that is, for the two rams together, and one-tenth of a tenth for each lamb—together there are fourteen lambs—and a male goat as a sin offering, in addition to the perpetual burnt offering, its sacrifice and libation, and so forth.

Now let us see what the final festival of God is, the festival in which God rejoices in the human being: “the Feast of Tabernacles,” he says. He rejoices over you when he sees you dwelling in tabernacles in this world; when he sees that you do not have your mind and purpose fixed and founded upon earthly things, nor desire what is earthly, nor regard the shadow of this life as your own perpetual possession, but consider yourself to be passing through and hastening toward that true homeland, the paradise from which you came, saying: “I am a sojourner and a pilgrim, as all my fathers were” (Psalm 118).

For the fathers also dwelt in tabernacles, and Abraham lived in huts—that is, in tabernacles—with Isaac and Jacob, co-heirs of the same promise. Therefore, when you are a sojourner and a pilgrim on earth, and your mind is not fixed and rooted in earthly desires, but you are ready to pass quickly into the land flowing with milk and honey and to receive the inheritance of future things—if, I say, God sees you placed in this condition, he rejoices in you and keeps a festival over you.

These things concern the present. But if you wish to consider how the festivals will be celebrated in the future, raise your thoughts a little from the earth, if you can, and for a while forget what is visible. Picture for yourself how heaven and earth will pass away, and what the whole inhabited world is like here; then imagine a new heaven and a new earth established. Remove also from your sight the light of this sun, and give that coming world sevenfold the light of this sun—or rather, according to the authority of Scripture, give it the Lord himself as its light.

Place before yourself the attending angels of glory; place the powers, thrones, dominions, and every glorious name among the heavenly powers—not only those named in the present age, but also those that will be named in the future. Consider all these things together, and imagine how the festivals of the Lord can be celebrated there: what festivals, what joys, what greatness of gladness there will be.

For regarding the spiritual festivals we mentioned above, although they are great and true, especially when they are celebrated spiritually in the soul, they are nevertheless partial, not complete. For just as the Apostle said, “We know in part, and we prophesy in part” (1 Corinthians 13), so it follows that we celebrate a festival in part. To understand that this is so, let us return to Paul’s own discourse, in which he spoke about festivals and new moons. See how he described the person who observes them: “Therefore let no one judge you in food or drink or in a part of a festival day.” In this world we celebrate the festival in part, not completely.

Even if we do not wish it, we are interrupted by the burden of the flesh; we are assaulted by its desires and pierced by cares and anxieties. “The corruptible body,” as the wisest writer says, “weighs down the soul and presses down the mind occupied with many thoughts” (Wisdom 9). In this world the saints celebrate a festival in part, because they know in part and prophesy in part. But when what is perfect has come, these partial things will be destroyed. For just as partial knowledge yields to perfect knowledge, so this partial festival yields to the perfect festival.

This world cannot contain what is perfect, since, as we have said, the necessity of the body supplies at one time food, at another drink, at another sleep, and at yet another raises whatever concern for the necessities of the present life may be required. All these things undoubtedly interrupt the continuity of God’s festival.

But when what has been said concerning those who will be restored among the holy has come—if we are worthy to be among those who are to be restored—then they will neither hunger nor thirst nor sleep nor labor, but will remain ever wakeful, like the life of the angels. They will be called ever wakeful when they are deemed worthy to be restored to that order. Then there will be a true and incorruptible festival, whose prince, bridegroom, and lord will be Jesus Christ, our Savior.

The Apostle Paul, knowing that there are certain first beginnings for instruction and that afterward, in due course, one also comes to perfection, wrote to some people: “For although by this time you ought to be teachers, you again need someone to teach you the elements of the beginning of the words of God; and you have become those who need milk, not solid food. For everyone who is nourished by milk is inexperienced in the word of righteousness, for he is a child. But solid food belongs to the mature, who, according to their capacity for receiving it, have faculties trained through practice for distinguishing good and evil” (Hebrews 5).

And again, in another letter, he declares that the letter of the law and every such Scripture are the elements of the world. Even now, therefore, those things which pertain to people being instructed in the first elements seem modest to us at first hearing. For anyone among the hearers who wishes to learn the things pertaining to salvation will indicate, insofar as mere hearing is concerned, that the letters concerning sacrifices of rams, goats, and bulls contribute nothing useful to him.

But if someone is found who can remove the veil placed over the reading of the Old Testament and inquire within it what the true sacrifices are that purify the people on the festival days, then he will see how wondrous and magnificent are the things indicated through these sacrifices—things that the ignorant call superfluous and superstitious.

These matters Paul, and those like him, may have understood more fully from wisdom itself and from the Word of God. We, however, insofar as we can gather from their writings—in which they have given us, as it were, through a shadow and image, certain indications for our common edification—will attempt to examine briefly some matters concerning the rite of sacrifices.

At the festival of Passover, a lamb is written of as the one who purifies the people; in other passages, a bull, a male goat or ram, or a she-goat or heifer, as you have learned from the passages that were read. One of these animals, therefore, which are taken for the purification of the people, is the lamb. That lamb is said to be our Lord and Savior. For John, who is greater than all the prophets, understood it in this way and pointed to him, saying: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sin of the world” (John 1).

If the lamb given for the purification of the people refers to the person of our Lord and Savior, it seems to follow that the other animals also contribute something to the human race through these same acts of purification. Consider, then, whether perhaps, just as our Lord and Savior, led as a lamb to slaughter and offered as a sacrifice on the altar, granted forgiveness of sins to the whole world, so perhaps also the blood of the other saints and righteous people, shed from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of the prophet Zechariah, who was killed between the temple and the altar (Matthew 23), was poured out as the blood of one person like a heifer, and of another like a male goat, she-goat, or some other such animal, in order to make expiation for the people in some measure.

Whether these things should be referred to the persons of the righteous and prophets who were slaughtered in this world, or to those who say, “For your sake we are put to death all day long; we are regarded as sheep for slaughter” (Psalm 43), or even to the higher powers to whom the administration of the human race has been entrusted—who would readily dare to affirm this? For these animals must not be thought to refer to this or that person according to their outward form, but figuratively.

Our Lord Jesus Christ is not called a lamb because he was changed and transformed into the form of a lamb. He is called a lamb because his will and goodness, by which he reconciled God to human beings and granted forgiveness of sins, were such for the human race as the sacrifice of an unblemished and innocent lamb, by which God is believed to be reconciled to human beings.

So perhaps, if any of the heavenly angels and powers, or any righteous human beings, has been offered as a sacrifice for divine reconciliation, like a ram, bull, or male goat, in order to obtain purification for the people, this may be understood. Or does it not seem that Paul offered himself as a burnt offering for the people like a ram or male goat when he said: “For I myself could wish to be accursed from Christ for the sake of my brothers, my kinsmen according to the flesh” (Romans 9)?

Do you wish to know that Paul also offers himself as a victim to be slaughtered? Hear him saying elsewhere: “For I am already being offered, and the time of my departure—or, as we read in the Greek books, of my return—is at hand” (2 Timothy 4).

If it can therefore be understood figuratively that one person is offered for the festival of the New Things, another for the festival of the Sabbath, and another for the festival of Tabernacles, as a male goat, bull, or ram, to reconcile God to human beings, then, as long as there are sins, it is necessary that sacrifices for sins also be sought.

Suppose, for example, that there had been no sin. If there had been no sin, it would not have been necessary for the Son of God to become a lamb, nor would it have been necessary for him, having taken flesh, to be slaughtered; rather, he would have remained what he was in the beginning: God the Word.

But since sin entered this world, and the necessity of sin requires propitiation, and propitiation does not take place except through a sacrifice, it was necessary that sacrifices for sin be provided. And since sin itself had diverse and varied qualities, sacrifices of different animals were commanded, unquestionably corresponding to the varieties of sins.

Thus one of the saints and angels, or, as we have said, of human beings, becomes a bull who intervenes at a particular festival for the offenses of the people; another becomes a ram at another festival, through whose intercession purification from sins takes place. If human beings can be purified from sins and become purer, the sacrifices also decrease. For if sacrifices are offered for sins, and they are multiplied according to the multitude of sins, then without doubt they also decrease according to their smallness.

We have indications of this in the present passages of Scripture, namely, in the final festival of the Feast of Tabernacles, when sacrifices are commanded to be offered for eight days. On the first day, as though sins were still abundant, fourteen bulls are commanded to be offered. On the second day, when the sins have been diminished, the sacrifices are also diminished: fourteen bulls are offered; on the third day, twelve; and after this, eleven. Thus, as the multitude of sins gradually diminishes through the purifications over the days, the successive numbers of sacrifices also decrease.

Understand, then, the principle of purification also with regard to the dispensation of the whole world. For purification is needed not only by the things that are on earth, but also by those that are in heaven. Destruction also threatens the heavens. Thus the prophet says: “The heavens will perish, and all of them will grow old like a garment; and as a cloak you will wrap them up, and they will be changed” (Psalm 101).

Consider, therefore, the purification of the world—that is, of heavenly, earthly, and underworld things. See how many sacrifices all these things require; how many bulls, how many rams, how many male goats they require. But among all these there is one lamb who was able to take away the sin of the whole world. Therefore the other sacrifices have ceased, because this sacrifice was such that one alone was sufficient for the salvation of the whole world.

The others forgave sins through prayers; he alone forgave them by his authority. For he said: “Son, your sins are forgiven you” (Matthew 9). Thus the world is first instructed to seek remission of sins through various sacrifices, until it comes to the perfect sacrifice, the complete sacrifice: the yearling lamb, perfect, who takes away the sin of the whole world. Through him it celebrates spiritual festivals, not for the satisfaction of the flesh, but for the advancement of the spirit, offering spiritual sacrifices through the purification of the mind.

For it is fitting that the sacrifice of the heart and the offering of a contrite spirit be sacrificed to God, rather than flesh and blood being slaughtered. For even if we have known Christ according to the flesh at one time, now we no longer know him in that way. Therefore let us celebrate the festival in the spirit, and slaughter spiritual festivals.

Let these matters concerning the diversity of sacrifices be considered by us according to our abilities. He to whom all things are naked and revealed knows their complete understanding; no creature is invisible in his sight.

## CHAPTER II. On Fulfilling a Man’s Vow

Moses recounted to the children of Israel everything that the Lord had commanded him, and he spoke to the leaders of the tribes of the children of Israel: “This is the word that the Lord has commanded. If any man makes a vow to the Lord or binds himself by an oath, he shall not invalidate the word of God, but shall fulfill everything that he has promised.”

If a woman makes any vow and binds herself by an oath while she is in her father’s house and still of maidenly age, and if her father learns of the vow that she has promised and of the oath by which she has bound her soul and remains silent, she shall be liable for the vow. Whatever she has promised and sworn, she shall also fulfill in action.

But if her father contradicts her immediately upon hearing it, both her vows and her oaths are invalid, and she shall not be held liable for the pledge, and so forth.

The law did not wish a woman under her father before marriage, or under her husband after marriage, to make a vow against her soul to God—that is, to abstain from certain things that are lawful and permitted—in such a way that the authority in those vows belonged to the woman rather than to the man. Thus, if her father had permitted her, while still unmarried, to fulfill her vows, but she married before fulfilling them and her husband, having learned of them, did not approve, she shall not fulfill them and shall be entirely without sin, because the Lord has cleansed her—that is, has judged her clean.

This must not be thought to be done against God, since God himself commanded and willed it. But a widow or a divorced woman shall fulfill whatever vows they make. The passage then continues concerning widows or women rejected by their husbands—that is, women not placed under the authority of a husband or father—and says in this way that their vows are free to be fulfilled: “The vow,” he says, “of a widow and of one who has been expelled, whatever she has vowed against her soul, shall remain binding upon her.”

## CHAPTER III. On a Woman’s Vow

(SAME PASSAGE.) If a wife in her husband’s house binds herself by a vow and an oath, and her husband hears it and remains silent, not contradicting the pledge, she shall fulfill whatever she promised. But if he immediately contradicts it, she shall not be held liable for the promise, because her husband contradicted it, and the Lord will be merciful to her.

If she makes a vow and binds herself by an oath to afflict her soul through fasting or abstinence from other things, it shall be in her husband’s discretion whether she does it or not. But if her husband hears and remains silent, postponing his decision until the next day, she shall fulfill whatever she vowed and promised, because as soon as he heard it, he remained silent.

But if he contradicts her after learning of it, he himself shall bear her iniquity. It is clear that the law wished a woman to be under her husband in such a way that she should fulfill none of the vows she made for the sake of abstinence unless her husband authorized it by permitting her. For when it wished the matter to pertain to the husband’s sin—if he had first permitted her and afterward prohibited her—it nevertheless did not say that the woman should do what she had vowed because her husband had previously permitted it. It said that the sin belonged to the husband, because he rejected what he had previously allowed; yet even on this account it did not grant the woman permission to be condemned when her husband had first permitted her and afterward prohibited her.

Whether this also applies to a vow of continence and abstinence from intercourse is rightly questioned, lest perhaps only those things which concern food and drink should be understood as vows made against the soul. This seems also to be signified by what the Lord says: “Is not the soul more than food?” (Matthew 6). And when fasting is commanded, it is commanded in this way: “You shall afflict your souls” (Leviticus 16).

I do not know whether anywhere one can read that a vow concerning abstinence from intercourse is called a vow made against the soul, especially since here the law grants authority to the husband and not to the woman who is subject to her husband: the woman’s vows are to be fulfilled if the husband approves, but if he refuses, they are not owed.

Yet when the Apostle spoke about intercourse between married people, he did not give greater authority to the husband than to the wife: “Let the husband,” he says, “render the due to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband. The wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband; likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife” (1 Corinthians 7).

Therefore, when he wished the authority in this matter to be equal for both, I think he suggests that we should understand this rule concerning intercourse or abstinence from intercourse not to apply to those vows in which husband and wife do not have equal authority, but in which the husband is greater and the authority belongs almost solely to him. For the law does not say that a husband need not fulfill his vows if his wife prohibits him, but that a wife need not fulfill hers if her husband prohibits her.

Therefore, it does not seem to me that, among such vows, decisions, and obligations made against the soul, those agreements which husband and wife have made with one another concerning intercourse or abstinence from intercourse should also be included.

These are the laws that the Lord established through Moses between husband and wife, and between a father and a daughter who is still of maidenly age or who remains in her parent’s house. For these laws are also called “ordinances,” or “justifications,” as certain copies have it; and we remember that other ordinances are mentioned under this name in Exodus, such as the piercing of a slave’s ear and anything similar.

It is not unreasonable to understand something figuratively here as well: just as many abstinences imposed by ceremonies are irrational and sometimes even hostile to the truth, perhaps this is what is intended here—that they are valid when they are rational; that is, when reason approves them. Reason ought to rule every animal impulse, not only in desiring but also in abstaining.

Thus, if the mind and reason determine that something should be done, let it be done; but if the counsel of reason disapproves it, let it not be done. If, however, reason afterward disapproves what it previously decided should rightly be done, let the sin be attributed to the counsel, but in such a way that the impulse consents only to reason.

According to the mystical sense, no one can offer vows except one who has something within himself and in his substance to offer to God. It is not enough for the outward person to receive the law of God or to offer vows alone. For he cannot possess anything worthy of God. Rather, it is the inner person who has more within himself to offer to God.

For in the inner person is the dwelling-place of the virtues; in him is all understanding of knowledge; in him is the renewal of the image. When he has recovered his form, which was made by God in the beginning, and rediscovered the beauty of the virtues of his former shape, then he can offer vows to God; and then he is called not merely “a human being,” but truly “a human being.”

For whoever does not cultivate the inner person, who does not care for him, who does not instruct him in the virtues, adorn him with good conduct, exercise him in divine teachings, seek the wisdom of God, or devote himself to knowledge of the Scriptures, cannot be called a human being in the full sense, but remains a human being nevertheless—a carnal human being.

I know that various vows are recorded in the Scriptures. Hannah vowed to God the fruit of her womb and consecrated Samuel in the temple (1 Samuel 1). Another person vowed to God whatever should meet him upon his return after victory; when his daughter met him, he fulfilled the vow with tears (Judges 11). Others offer to God bulls, rams, houses, or other such things lacking reason.

But the one who is called a Nazirite devoted himself to God (Numbers 6). This is the vow of the Nazirite, which is above every vow. For if someone offers a son or daughter, livestock, or an estate, all this lies outside us. But to offer oneself to God, and to please him not through another’s labor but through one’s own, is more perfect and excellent than all vows.

Whoever does this is an imitator of Christ. He gave the human being the earth, the sea, and everything in them for service; he also gave heaven, and granted the sun, moon, and stars for human use; he bestowed rains, winds, and everything in the world upon human beings. But after all these things, he gave himself.

“For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son for the life of the world” (John 3). What great thing, then, does a human being do by offering himself to God, when God himself first offered himself?

Therefore, if you take up your cross and follow Christ (Matthew 16); if you say, “I live, yet it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2); if our soul desires and thirsts to return and be with Christ, as the Apostle also said; if it does not delight in the allurements of the present age; and if it fulfills spiritually the whole law that was given to Nazirites, then it has offered itself—that is, its soul—to God.

But we must pray to God to grant understanding, if it is worthy, so that we may be able to perceive and understand these things from the words of God as we ought.

All of us who live under the law of God and belong to his Church are governed, some under fathers and some under husbands. If the soul is still small and at the beginning of divine instruction, it should be understood as acting under a father. But if it has grown more mature, so that, like a man, it is capable of conceiving the seed of the Word of God and receiving the secrets of spiritual teaching, it is said to be placed under a husband.

Thus Paul also said concerning the Corinthians: “I wish to present you as a chaste virgin to one husband, Christ” (1 Corinthians 11). But of those who are more perfect and eminent, it is not said that they are under a husband. Rather, hear how Paul pronounces concerning himself and those like him: “Until we all come,” he says, “to a perfect man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ” (Ephesians 4).

Therefore, no one rules over the vows of the soul that has come to a perfect man; it possesses authority and freedom over its own vows. But if the soul is still of the feminine gender, so that either a husband or a father rules over its vows, the fault is not always in the soul itself; sometimes it returns to husbands or to parents.

## CHAPTER IV. On Vengeance against the Midianites and Balaam the Diviner
### Chapter XXXI.

The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “First avenge the children of Israel upon the Midianites, and afterward you shall be gathered to your people.” Since the scandals that had befallen the Israelites had occurred through the treachery of the Midianites—for they had procured women who deceived them into sinning before the Lord—they indeed endured vengeance for their sin, yet more moderately and sparingly; but those who had caused them to sin are subjected to a much more severe punishment. From this we are taught that it is far more serious to provide the occasion for sin than for each person to sin himself.

Thus also the Lord indicates this when he says that it would have been better for a man not to be born, or for a millstone to be fastened around his neck and for him to be thrown into the depths of the sea, than for him to scandalize one of these little ones (Matt. XVIII). We must also observe that some people improperly assume the name “scandal.” By scandal I mean that in which, along the straight path of walking, some deception is contrived toward sin and an occasion for sinning is supplied—as the Midianites, while the Israelites were walking in the law of the Lord and observing chastity, procured women who would deceive them into sinning.

To provide an occasion for sin, therefore, is to scandalize. Nevertheless, vengeance is exacted, but it is much more severe against those who scandalized and supplied the occasion for sin than against those who sinned. Observe also what he added: “And finally, you too shall be gathered to your people.” Whenever we are speaking with the Samaritans, since they deny the resurrection of the dead and do not accept faith in the future age, let us refute them by these words in which the Lord says to Moses that he is to be gathered to his people. For no one is gathered to those who do not exist. Hence it is clear that there is a people to whom Moses is said to be joined after the end of this life.

Since the Samaritans do not believe the prophets, from whom the faith in the resurrection of the dead is more broadly established, they must at least be convicted and corrected from those books of Moses that they accept and whose authority they confess—if, indeed, Babylon ought also to be corrected. This passage, then, clearly demonstrates the resurrection of the dead. For it indicates both that there is a people to whom Moses is to be joined after his death and that he is to be transferred to them according to his merits.

Immediately Moses said: “Arm from among yourselves men for battle who can exact the Lord’s vengeance from the Midianites. Let a thousand men from each tribe be chosen from Israel and sent to war.” And they gave a thousand from every tribe, that is, twelve thousand equipped for battle. Moses sent them with Phinehas, son of Eleazar the priest. He also entrusted to him the holy vessels and the trumpets for sounding.

When they had fought against the Midianites and conquered them, they killed all the males, as well as their kings, Evin, Raon, Sur, Ur, and Rebe, five princes of the nation. Earlier the children of Israel had numbered six hundred thousand armed men who advanced against Midian, and all were defeated because sin was among them. Now, therefore, the victorious Midianites, who had put six hundred thousand to flight, are themselves defeated by twelve thousand, so that you may know that Israel conquers neither by the multitude nor by the number of its soldiers, but by the justice and piety that are in it.

For this reason it is said finally in their blessings that, if Israel keeps the law of the Lord, one will pursue a thousand and two will put ten thousand to flight. You see, therefore, that one holy person is far more powerful in prayer than countless sinners in battle. The prayer of a holy person penetrates heaven; how then could it not also conquer an enemy on earth? Therefore, one must strive in every way first to seek and preserve the justice of God. If you offer and observe it, it will itself subject all your enemies to you.

If, as the Apostle says, you are clothed with the breastplate of justice and girded with truth; if you have received the helmet of salvation, the sword of the Spirit, and above all the shield of faith, with which you can extinguish all the flaming arrows of the evil one (Eph. VI), then equipped with such weapons you will put to flight the entire camp of the devil and all his army. With confidence you will sing: “Though an army encamp against me, my heart will not fear; though battle rise against me, in this I will hope” (Ps. XXVI).

They also killed Balaam son of Beor with the sword. A question may arise concerning how, when the Israelites defeated the Midianites, Scripture says that Balaam was killed, since he had been hired to curse the people of Israel, although earlier, when he was compelled to bless them, Scripture concluded the account of that compulsion by saying: “And Balaam arose and went to his place. Balak went to himself.”

If Balaam had therefore returned to his place, how was he killed, since he had come from such a distant region, namely Mesopotamia? Nevertheless, it may also be understood that he returned to “his place” in the sense that he went back from the place where he had been offering sacrifices to the place from which he had come out—that is, where he had lodging as a stranger. For Scripture did not say “to his house” or “to his homeland,” but “to his place.” Every stranger, moreover, has a place where he dwells for a time.

Of Balak himself, who had hired him, Scripture does not say that he went “to his place,” but “to himself,” that is, to the place where he lived as a ruler. Thus one could say “to his place” of either a ruler or a stranger; but “to himself”—I do not see how this could be said of a stranger, since he had come to his lodging.

They captured their women and little ones, all their livestock and all their possessions, and plundered everything they had been able to possess. Both the cities and the villages and fortified settlements were consumed by fire, and so forth.

Thus twelve thousand advanced against the Midianites and killed, as Scripture says, all their males, their kings, and Balaam son of Beor with the sword, together with the rest of their wounded. What we were seeking earlier—how it could be proved from Scripture that, on Balaam’s advice, Midianite women had been procured to deceive the children of Israel into fornication—the present passage of Scripture clearly demonstrates. It says that he was killed with the sword as the author of the scandal that had been brought upon the children of Israel.

The following passage speaks of him even more explicitly: “And Moses said to them: Why have you spared every female? For these are the very ones who, according to Balaam’s word, caused the children of Israel to apostatize.” The kings of the Midianites were also killed. Those who had earlier been defeated by the women now, after expiation had been made and repentance had been performed, even conquer kings.

From this let us understand how powerful conversion to God is and how beneficial correction from sins can be. All the males and all the kings of the Midianites are conquered and killed by those who have been corrected and amended through returning to the Lord and repenting of their deeds.

Five kings of the Midianites are reported to have been overcome by the Israelites. Scripture also took care to record their names: “Evim, Raon, Sur, Ur, and Roboc.” These are the kings who reign among the Midianites, whom everyone who serves God must overcome and utterly destroy.

Evim is interpreted as “bestial” or “feral.” How will you be able to please the one who has tested you if you do not cut away from yourself and utterly destroy bestial and feral conduct? How will you reach the blessedness of the meek unless you first kill Evim and consign the ferocity of all anger to death?

I think that divine Scripture did not recount these names merely for the sake of history, but adapted them to the causes and realities they signify. For do you suppose that anyone was so foolish as to give his son the name “bestial”? Rather, I believe that the divine word provided for the instruction of souls, wishing to show us that we must wage war against such vices and drive them from the dwelling places of our flesh, putting these kings to flight from the kingdom of the body. “Therefore let not sin reign in your mortal body.”

Do you wish to see how names are adapted to realities not only among holy people but also among gentiles and barbarians? Among the holy this is well known: Abram was called Abraham, Sarai Sara, and Jacob Israel. Let us show, however, that this custom also exists among barbarians.

Was not one of the children of Israel given the name Joseph by his parents? When he went down into Egypt and stood before Pharaoh, Pharaoh changed his name and called him ψομθομφανήχ—“Psomthomphanech”—a name that Pharaoh formed in his own language to signify the revelation of secrets or dreams. Joseph was not the only one whose name was adapted by Pharaoh to the reality; Daniel in Babylonia was also called Belteshazzar, and Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael were called Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego.

You see, therefore, that the names of Israelites and of barbarians alike are assigned in the law not by chance but according to realities and causes.

Accordingly, Moses called the king of the Midianites what he judged him worthy to be called: “Bestial ferocity,” he says, “is what reigns among the Midianites.” But not only this; another king among them was named Raon, which in our language means “emptiness.” Emptiness, therefore, reigns among the nation of the Midianites.

There is indeed much emptiness and vanity in this world—rather, “vanity of vanities, and all is vanity” (Eccl. I)—which the soldier of God must overcome sincerely. He conquers emptiness who does nothing vainly, nothing superfluously, and nothing irrelevant; he who remembers that command of the Lord in which he says that people will give an account even for every idle word on the day of judgment (Matt. XII).

In this life almost everything that people say and do is idle and empty. Every action and every word in which there is no outward purpose for God or for God’s command is called empty.

There is another king of Midian, Ur, and this name is interpreted as “irritation.” You see what sort of kings reign among the Midianites. All of them must be opposed; indeed, they ought to be killed and destroyed by those who follow God.

For it is not so much the names of kings as the names of the vices that reign in human beings that are recorded in the law. Nor are the wars of nations described so much as the wars of carnal desires that wage war against the soul.

Finally, those who reign in vices are said to be five kings, so that we may be taught most clearly that every vice that reigns in the body depends upon the five senses. These five senses, therefore, must be killed and removed from the kingdom of the Midianites, so that vices may no longer reign through them, but justice may reign instead; and so that what they see may not serve as an occasion for scandal, but for edification.

### Chapter 5. Where Moses is angry on account of the Midianites

**(Ibid.)** Moses, Eleazar the priest, and all the leaders of the assembly went out to meet them outside the camp. Moses became angry with the leaders of the army, the tribunes, and the centurions who had come from the battle, and said: “Why have you spared the women? Are these not the ones who deceived the children of Israel at Balaam’s suggestion and caused you to transgress against the Lord in the matter of the sin of Peor, for which the people was also struck down? Therefore kill every male, including the little ones, and slaughter every woman who has known a man in intercourse. But preserve for yourselves the young girls and all the women who are virgins, and remain outside the camp for seven days.”

When Balaam gave this evil counsel—that women should be presented to them as enticements through whom they would commit fornication not only bodily but also spiritually by worshiping an idol—Scripture did not say; nevertheless, it appears that it happened, since it is mentioned here. Thus Balaam himself, who had already gone to his place, could also have returned, if we understand “his place” as the place of his sojourn, although Scripture has kept this silent.

In the mystical sense, the person who returns from battle and preserves a woman as booty is one who restrains outward evil actions and destroys them through good zeal, yet still hides carnal delight within the secrecy of his heart. But he is rightly rebuked by Moses—that is, by the law—because whoever wickedly entertains carnal delight in the secret place of his mind will readily fall openly into the guilt of an evil action.

Thus every male, including the little ones, and every woman who has known a man in intercourse, is commanded to be slaughtered, because we are commanded utterly to kill and completely extinguish within ourselves the disgraceful desire and the delight of the flesh that conceives iniquity and gives birth to sin.

But the young girls and virgin women—that is, that part of delight which is not inclined toward sin but rather burns more ardently to seek what is good—we ought to preserve, so that we may always desire those things that we know our Creator has commanded us through the sacred Scriptures.

### Chapter 6. Concerning the division of the booty of the Midianites

**(Ibid.)** Eleazar the priest also spoke as follows to the men of the army who had fought: “This is the ordinance of the law that the Lord commanded Moses. Gold, silver, bronze, iron, tin, lead, and everything that can pass through fire shall be purified by fire; but whatever cannot endure fire shall be sanctified by the water of purification. You shall wash your garments on the seventh day, and after you have been purified you shall enter the camp.”

Thus, in accordance with the Lord’s commands, the wars against the Midianites were completed by the children of Israel. Abundant spoils were brought back from them—gold and silver, an immense quantity of the other movable goods, and a very large number of captured animals and prisoners.

But because all these things are called unclean among the Israelites, an appropriate purification is applied to each. Things made of metals are purified by fire; things that are more fragile and cannot endure fire are commanded to be purified by water.

Let two equal portions therefore be made from all the spoils: one for those who went out to war [and one for those] who remained in the camps. They are also commanded to offer gifts to God from these: those who went out to war, one head from every five hundred; those who remained in the camps, one from every fifty. The total number of all these is then reported together.

This is the historical account. But let us see what spiritual meaning it indicates among the people of God. There are some, as the Apostle says, who serve as soldiers for God—those, undoubtedly, who do not entangle themselves in worldly affairs (II Tim. II). These are the ones who go out to war and fight against hostile nations and against spiritual wickedness on behalf of the rest of the people and of those who are weaker, whether because of age, sex, or purpose.

They fight with prayers and fasts, justice and piety, gentleness and chastity, and all the virtues of self-control, equipped with them as with weapons of war. When they return victorious to the camps, even the unarmed and those who are not called or are unable to go out to battle share in the fruits of their labors.

It must nevertheless be understood that everything taken from these nations is unclean, and perhaps everything whatever that is taken from this world or seized in battle is unclean and requires purification. Some of these things must pass through fire; for others purification by water will suffice.

People and animals are also taken from the battle, when every intellect is taken captive for obedience to Christ. Unless we fight with the word of God, we cannot take captive the intellects of those who think differently from Christ and lead them into obedience to Christ.

Few are able to fight and complete these battles. Of more than six hundred thousand armed men who appear to serve God, only twelve thousand are chosen; the rest remain in the camps. Consider now the people of God who are in the Church: how many among them are able to resist those who contradict and who know how to conduct the wars of the word.

Blessed are those who can fight on behalf of the whole people, defend God’s people, and bring back abundant spoils from the enemy. Nevertheless, even the remaining part of the people, which appears weak, may remain quietly in the camps, provided that it lives in silence and does not depart from Moses but remains in the law of God; it too will receive a share of the spoils.

For the portion will be equal—not according to number, but in this way: whatever is given to the whole remainder of the people is also given to the twelve thousand by whose victory the spoils were captured. Who, hearing this, would not be invited to God’s service? Who would not be encouraged to fight for the Church and resist the enemies of truth—those who either teach people to attack the doctrines of the Church or to devote themselves to pleasure and luxury?

Whoever overcomes these enemies and destroys vices either in himself or in those near him will receive many spoils, multiplied fiftyfold in comparison with the others. The quantity appears to increase to such a number when the twelve thousand are compared with the six hundred thousand.

Nevertheless, both portions are commanded to offer something to God: those who conquered, one out of five hundred; those who remained at home, one out of fifty. Hence the text continues:

“And the Lord said to Moses: Take the sum of what has been captured, from human being to livestock, you and Eleazar the priest and the leaders of the people. You shall divide the booty equally between those who fought and went out to war and all the remaining multitude. You shall separate for the Lord a portion from those who fought and were in the battle: one person out of every five hundred, both from the human beings and from the cattle, donkeys, and sheep, and you shall give it to Eleazar the priest, because they are the first fruits of the Lord. From the half belonging to the children of Israel you shall take one out of every fifty human beings, cattle, donkeys, sheep, and every living creature, and you shall give it to the Levites who keep watch over the duties of the tabernacle of the Lord.” Moses and Eleazar did as God had commanded, and so forth.

Scripture testifies that the number fifty and the number five hundred are holy. Hence the Savior said in the Gospels: “A certain moneylender had two debtors. One of them owed five hundred denarii, the other fifty. Since they had nothing with which to repay, he forgave both” (Luke VII).

Seven weeks, moreover, with one unit—that is, one—added, make the fiftieth day, which is called the feast of Pentecost. Similarly, seventy weeks, with the perfection of one decade added, produce the number five hundred. But just as seventy weeks are more than seven, so the number five hundred is more excellent and perfect than fifty.

For this reason, in the Gospel parable that we explained above, our Savior declares that the one to whom five hundred denarii were forgiven loves more than the one to whom fifty were forgiven.

In the present reading, finally, Eleazar the priest is not said to have spoken to the whole people, but only to those who returned from battle. For he says: “And Eleazar the priest spoke to the men of valor who were returning from battle.” You see, therefore, how the word of the Lord speaks to men of valor: men of valor are those who go out to war.

But if someone does not wish to fight or serve as a soldier, if he does not wish to undertake the contest of spiritual disciplines and self-control, he does not wish to fulfill what the Apostle said: “Everyone who competes in the contest exercises self-control in all things” (I Cor. IX). Whoever does not compete in the contest is not self-controlled in all things; nor does he wish to train himself in the word of God and meditate on the law of the Lord day and night. Even if he is called a man, he cannot be called a man of valor.

The time of war is therefore ours in this world. Fight against the Midianites—whether against the vices of our flesh or against hostile powers. The choir of angels watches us, and the pious expectation of the heavenly powers hangs over us, awaiting when and how we shall return from this battle, and what booty each of us will bring back.

They look on with great care and examine anxiously to see which of us will carry more gold from here, which will bring there the weight of silver, and which will carry precious stones. They also inquire whether anyone will bring bronze, iron, or lead; whether someone perhaps brings a wooden or earthen vessel, or something else of this kind that is necessary for the uses of a great house.

For in a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also wooden and earthen vessels. Thus, when we have gone there, what each of us brings will be carefully examined; and according to what he has brought, according to how his labor is shown by the contemplation of his spoils, the merit of his dwelling will also be assigned to him.

Then all these things will be tested: what is to be tested by fire, by fire; what is to be tested by water, by water. For the fire will test what sort of work each person’s work is.

Therefore it says: “This is the ordinance of the law that the Lord established for Moses: Gold, silver, bronze, iron, lead, and tin—every object that passes through fire, pass it through fire, and it shall be purified. But everything shall be purified in the water of purification. Whatever does not pass through fire shall pass through water. You shall wash your garments on the seventh day, and you shall be clean; after this you shall enter the camp.”

You see how everyone who has gone out from the battle of this life requires purification. If I may dare to say something according to the authority of Scripture, no one who departs from this life can be clean.

Consider carefully what the historical text indicates. These men went out to fight on behalf of the children of Israel and killed the Midianites. Insofar as the order of the history and the letter of the law are concerned, by killing them they pleased God, for they fulfilled God’s will. Yet by the very fact that they killed their adversaries, they are said to have become unclean. Therefore it is said to them: “You shall wash your garments on the seventh day, and you shall be clean; after this you shall enter the camp.”

Those who fight are therefore defiled by the very fact that they came into contact with unclean enemies, attacked them, and engaged them in battle.

I too, then, will strive either to repel the unclean and evil thoughts that are now suggested to my heart as they come, or, if they have entered, to kill them within myself so that they do not reach fulfillment. Yet even if I am able to trample upon the head of the dragon, I must nevertheless be defiled and polluted by the very fact that I have striven to trample one who is polluted and unclean.

I shall indeed be blessed because I was able to trample him; yet I am unclean and polluted because I touched one who was polluted, and for this reason I require purification.

Therefore Scripture says, and rightly so, that no one is clean from defilement. We all require purification—indeed, purifications. For many and various purifications await us.

But these things are mystical and ineffable. Who could explain to us what purifications are prepared for Paul or Peter, or for others like them, who fought so greatly, destroyed so many nations, won such great spoils, cast down so many enemies, seized so many triumphs, and returned from the slaughter of their enemies with bloodstained hands? Their feet were dipped in blood, and they washed their hands in the blood of sinners.

For they killed all the sinners of the earth in the morning and exterminated their image from the city of the Lord. They conquered and destroyed various nations of demons. If they had not conquered them, they could not have taken from them as captives all this multitude of believers, led them into obedience to Christ, subjected them to his gentle yoke, and laid upon them his light burden.

Who, then, is so blessed as to succeed them in these battles, kill all the Midianites, and be justified by their blood? The one who rescues those over whom demons rule is said to shed the demons’ blood.

He will be washed from this blood and purified in the kingdom of God, so that, purified and made clean, he may enter the holy city of God, when Jesus Christ our Lord opens the door for him—indeed, he who is himself also the door of that city of God.

The text continues:

“When the leaders of the army, the tribunes, and the centurions approached Moses, they said: ‘We, your servants, have counted the number of the warriors whom we had under our command, and not one of them is missing. For this reason we offer as gifts to the Lord, each of us, whatever gold we were able to find among the spoils: anklets, bracelets, rings, armlets, and necklaces, so that you may entreat the Lord for us.’ Moses and Eleazar the priest received all the gold in its various forms, weighing sixteen thousand seven hundred and fifty shekels, from the tribunes and centurions. For each man’s share of what he had taken in the spoils belonged to him. And they took it and brought it into the tent of testimony, and so forth.”

Another edition reads as follows:

“All those who had been appointed leaders of the tribes in the army, tribunes and centurions, approached Moses and said to him: ‘We, your servants, have collected the total number of our warriors, and not one of us has dissented. We have offered a gift to the Lord, each man whatever he found: a golden vessel, a necklace or golden bowl, a ring, an armlet, or a chain, to make atonement for us before the Lord.’”

There is therefore much diversity in the order of those who are called warriors. There is also some difference among the noncombatants themselves. For not all of them are called noncombatants equally or in the same way.

Some are so incapable of battle that they can never become warriors: old age, the entire female sex, and the condition of slavery. Childhood, however, is incapable of battle in such a way that it retains the hope of becoming a warrior at some time.

When it reaches mature manhood, the measure of age, children hope not only to become warriors but also to join the ranks of the warriors, be chosen, and be counted among the twelve thousand—or even to be preferred to them and become leaders of the chosen.

Consider now the condition of the present age. See how everything is filled with wars and how the whole of human life is pressed by invisible battles and attacks of demons. Yet among the people of God there are some so strong, armed with faith and virtues, that they wage daily battles against such enemies.

Always standing ready for battle, they protect not only themselves but also the others who, because of sex, age, or the condition of slavery, cannot fight, guarding them against the enemy’s snares and strengthening them by the word of instruction, by the example of their life, and by constant exhortation—provided, however, that faith is not lacking in them.

For whether they are warriors or noncombatants, it is impossible to be saved without faith. Yet among the warriors themselves there are those who truly serve as soldiers for God.

Consider others who are so unencumbered that they do not entangle themselves at all in worldly affairs, so that they may please the one who has tested them, but meditate on the law of God day and night. These are called the total number of the warriors.

They are the ones who have captured the greatest amount of gold by fighting, and who offer to God all the gold and every ornament—whether of the head, the arms, or the fingers—that is, whatever understanding and whatever works they possess.

For they know that these things have been given by God’s gift, and therefore not one among them is divided. They could not offer gifts to God while living in dissension.

I think that these are, according to the Gospel, the people who carefully observe that command which the Lord and Savior gives: “If you are offering your gift at the altar and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go first to be reconciled to your brother; then come and offer your gift” (Matt. V).

Thus they raise their hands to God without anger or dissension: every golden vessel, golden necklace, ring, armlet, or chain.

A necklace signifies the ornament of wisdom. For in Proverbs it is said of wisdom that whoever acquires it should place a golden necklace around his neck (Prov. I). A bowl and a ring are ornaments of the hands, in which the signs of works are marked. The same is true of the armlet. Chains indicate the connections of word and teaching.

“To make atonement,” he says, “for us before God.” If we were to say that God becomes favorable to human beings because of gold, consider how absurd—or rather, how impious—that would be judged. Even in a good man it is considered shameful if he is pleased by receiving gold from inferiors; how much less is it appropriate to think this of God?

Therefore I believe that the ecclesiastical interpretation of this passage is more sound: the forms of gold indicate the virtues of the soul and the deeds of good works, which alone it is worthy for human beings to offer to God, and on account of which alone it is fitting for God to become favorable to human beings.

“And Moses and Eleazar the priest received,” it says, “the gold from all the tribunes and centurions, and brought it into the tent of testimony as a memorial for the children of Israel before the Lord.”

You see that what is spoken of is referred not to visible sight but to the memory of the mind. Blessed is the one who remembers having performed some good work before the Lord and having offered gifts pleasing to the Lord—the virtues of the soul and the ornaments of piety.

After this follows the history concerning the inheritance of Reuben, Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh. We intend to discuss certain matters concerning it and to raise the minds of our hearers toward contemplation of its spiritual meaning.

Everything that is said must be weighed not only from the speech itself that is spoken, but also, and very carefully, from the person who speaks [the text reads “said” (*dicenda*), corrected to “weighed” (*pensanda*)]. The text continues:

### Chapter 7. Where part of the people—that is, the tribe of Reuben, the tribe of Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh—requested that the Lord’s inheritance be given to them beyond the Jordan
(CAP. XXXII.) The sons of Reuben and Gad possessed many herds, and they had an immeasurable wealth of livestock. When they saw that Jazer and Gilead were lands suitable for raising animals, they came to Moses, Eleazar the priest, and the leaders of the assembly, and said:

“‘Ataroth, Didon, Jazer, Nimrah, Heshbon, Elealeh, Sebam, Nebo, and Beon—the land that God struck down before the sons of Israel—are regions [Col. 0804A] exceedingly rich for feeding animals. And we, your servants, have very many livestock. We ask that, if we have found favor in your sight, you grant this land to us, your servants, as a possession, and do not make us cross the Jordan.’”

Moses answered them: “Will your brothers go to war while you sit here? Why do you turn aside the minds of the sons of Israel, so that they do not dare to cross into the land that the Lord is going to give them? Did not your fathers act in the same way when I sent them from Kadesh-barnea to explore the land?” And so forth.

As the tradition of our ancestors maintains, the Holy Spirit narrates these things. For how could Moses have narrated either the events that took place at the origin of the world or those that were to occur at its end, except through the inspiration of the Spirit of God? How could he have prophesied about Christ except through the Holy Spirit [Col. 0804B] speaking in him? For Christ himself both bears witness to this and says: “If you believed Moses, you would certainly believe me also; for he spoke of me. But if you do not believe his writings, how will you believe my words?” (John 5).

It is therefore clear that these things were spoken through the Holy Spirit, and for that reason it seems appropriate to understand them in keeping with the dignity of the speaker. I also consider it most fitting to recall here that when Abraham heard the rich man, who had been placed in torment, ask that he be sent and, on coming, warn his brothers to live piously lest they descend into that place of torment, he answered him: “They have Moses and the prophets; let them listen to them” (Luke 15). He certainly did not mean human beings physically present when he spoke of Moses and the prophets; rather, he called “Moses” the things that had been written through Moses at the dictation of the Spirit of God. [Col. 0804C]

Someone may say: Since these things have been written in this way, if Abraham sends me to what Moses said, so that by reading it I may escape that place of torment, how will it help me to flee Gehenna if I read how the sons of Reuben, the sons of Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh receive an inheritance from Moses beyond the Jordan, because they had more livestock than the other tribes? And how will it help me that Moses says to them: “See that you do not provoke God, as did those ten who were sent with Jesus and Caleb to explore the land and said that the land was such and such, and that we could not take possession of it”? And how will it help me that the sons of Reuben and the others with them replied to this: “Give us this land and its inheritance, and we will no longer seek an inherited land beyond the Jordan with our brothers; [Col. 0804D] but here we will leave our livestock, our baggage, our wives, and our children, while our men will go together and cross the Jordan”? And how will it help me that afterward Moses commends them to Jesus son of Nave and to Eleazar the priest, son of Aaron, on the condition, nevertheless, that they cross with the sons of Israel and fight alongside them against the enemies who were beyond the Jordan until the land was freed from them? Then they were to receive the land they had requested—the land of King Sihon and King Og—and to them alone Moses gave an inheritance beyond the Jordan, while all the others received theirs within the Jordan.

Someone therefore says: What benefit do these things have for what Abraham says—“They have Moses and the prophets; let them listen to them”—so that by reading these things they may not come into that place of torment? [Col. 0805A]
