We have said these things, then, to rouse the minds of our hearers, so that they may attend more watchfully to what is read or spoken and, removing the veil of the letter from the writings of Moses, understand what has been written in such a way that they may find themselves in each of those to whom these things are spoken. If these things are understood and observed, the hearers may be prevented from being led to that place of torment to which the rich man who had despised hearing these things, written in secret, was taken away; rather, may they enter the bosom of Abraham, where Lazarus rests.

Let us pray from the heart to the Word of God, his only-begotten Son, who reveals the Father to whom he wishes, that he may deem us also worthy to have these things revealed to us. For within them are the mysteries of the promises that he promised to those who love him.

It has often been said, both by our predecessors and by us, that the figure of departing from Egypt is understood in two ways. [Col. 0805B] When someone is led from the darkness of error to the light of knowledge and is converted from an earthly way of life to spiritual practices, he appears to have gone out from Egypt and come into the wilderness—that is, into that condition of life in which, through silence and repose, he is trained in the divine laws and instructed in heavenly utterances. Once he has been formed and guided by these, when he has crossed the Jordan, he hastens all the way to the promised land; that is, through the grace of baptism, he reaches the practices of the Gospel.

We have also said that there is another figure of departing from Egypt: when the soul leaves behind the darkness of this world and the blindness of bodily nature and is transferred to another age. This is indicated either by Abraham’s bosom, as in the case of Lazarus, or by paradise, as in the case of the thief who believed from the cross; [Col. 0805C] or, if God knows there are other places and other dwellings, by these also, as the soul passes through them while believing in God and reaches that river which makes the city of God glad, and within it receives a portion of the inheritance promised to the fathers.

Since, then, as we have said, departure from Egypt is designated in two ways, and one passes into the wilderness and from there goes on to the inheritance of the holy land, let us now see what is signified by the inheritance of Reuben and Gad and half the tribe of Manasseh, which is transmitted through Moses and assigned beyond the Jordan.

In the twelve tribes of the sons of Israel, through certain hidden and mystical meanings, the figure of the entire human race is contained—or at least of all human beings who have come to the knowledge of God. Some of them obtain an inheritance beyond the Jordan [Col. 0805D] through Moses; others cross the Jordan and receive their inheritance in the promised land through Jesus.

Those to whom an inheritance is assigned beyond the Jordan are the firstborn. Although they are less noble, although they are not without blame, they are nevertheless the firstborn. Reuben is Jacob’s firstborn; although he defiled his father’s bed, he is nevertheless the firstborn. Manasseh also, whose half-tribe receives an inheritance beyond the Jordan, although he was born of an Egyptian woman, is nevertheless the firstborn.

All these, then, are firstborn, and therefore they signify the earlier people, who receive the portion of their inheritance beyond the Jordan not through Jesus Christ our Lord but through Moses. Consider more carefully, however, the reason [Col. 0806A] why those who are earlier, who are beyond the Jordan, and who are separated from the others, obtain an inheritance.

“We also have many livestock and herds.” This, then, is the reason why the earlier people could not reach the inheritance of that land which flows with milk, abounds in honey, and is a honeycomb above every land; nor could they recognize the Word as flesh, because they had many livestock and many herds. The animal person could not perceive the things of the Spirit of God, nor judge them spiritually, because “a human being, when he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared with senseless animals and became like them” (Psalm 48). For this reason they received their inheritance beyond the Jordan’s waters and made themselves strangers to the holy land.

That people therefore received an inheritance through Moses; they received only the land of two kings. [Col. 0806B] For Moses could kill no more than two kings whose land he could distribute to peoples who possessed many animals and many herds.

For those who cross the Jordan, Jesus divides the land. Although they too have animals and herds, they do not have so many that these prevent them from crossing the Jordan. Together with their wives and children, they strive to cross the Jordan and reach the promises made to the fathers.

But those others, because of their herds, livestock, wives, and children, could not cross the Jordan or enter into the faith of Christ, which is the promised land. Moses nevertheless rebukes them and says to the sons of Reuben and the sons of Gad: “Will your brothers go on to battle while you sit here? And why do you turn aside the hearts of the sons of Israel, so that they do not cross into the land that the Lord is giving them?”

When he had rebuked them with these words, “the sons of Reuben and the sons of Gad approached him,” it says, “and said: ‘We are building here sheepfolds for sheep and cattle, and cities for our livestock [and stalls for the livestock, and cities for our little ones]; but we ourselves, armed and in the first rank, will march before the sons of Israel until we bring them to their place.’” [Col. 0806C]

By making these promises, they appeased Moses, so that he himself commended them to Jesus and Eleazar. For it is written:

“Moses brought them before Eleazar the priest, and Jesus son of Nave, and the leaders of the families of the tribes, and Moses said to them: ‘If the sons of Reuben and the sons of Gad cross the Jordan with you, all armed for battle before the Lord, and you take possession of the land before you, you shall give them the land of Gilead as a possession.’” [Col. 0806D]

We find the name “land” placed in the divine Scriptures with various meanings. In the first place, the land on which we live was not called “land” from the beginning, but “dry ground.” Later, what had previously been called dry ground received the name “land.” Likewise, this visible heaven was not called “heaven” at the beginning, but first “firmament,” and afterward it was designated by the name “heaven.”

Nevertheless, at the beginning of creation God is said to have made heaven and earth, and afterward the dry ground, and afterward the firmament. For as long as we are unfruitful and produce no fruit of chastity, no fruit of justice, and no fruit of piety, we are dry ground. But if we begin to cultivate ourselves and rouse our sluggish minds toward the fruit of virtue, we become earth out of dry ground, [Col. 0807A] multiplying the seeds of the word of God that have been received in us with joyful fruit.

There is therefore a certain land in the kingdom of God that is promised to the meek, and a land called the land of the living, and a land placed on high, concerning which the Prophet says to the righteous: “I exalted you so that you might inherit the land.”

The soul that believes in God will obtain the inheritance of this land after it has gone out from the Egypt of this world. Some who lived under the Law receive their inheritance in one place; others, who have been governed through the faith and grace of Jesus Christ, receive theirs elsewhere.

Nevertheless, those who appear to be first and who have been ordered through Moses do not receive the inheritance assigned to them until they themselves cross over with those whom Jesus orders, fight with them against their enemies, and establish them in their dwellings. Thus they too obtain the inheritance [Col. 0807B] that they earned under the leadership of Moses.

But unless these things are proved from the divine Scriptures, they will seem like fables. Let Paul therefore be produced as a reliable witness to them. In his Epistle to the Hebrews, where he describes all those fathers, patriarchs, and prophets who pleased God through faith, after listing them all he says in his final conclusion concerning them:

“And all these, although they had received approval through faith, did not obtain the promises, since God had provided something better for us, so that they might not be made perfect without us.”

It is as though he were saying: For this reason these nine and a half tribes did not receive the promise of that land which had been assigned to them beyond the Jordan through Moses, because God had provided something better for us, so that they might not be made perfect without us.

Therefore let them cross over with us, armed for battle, and help us in warfare to overthrow our enemies. But those cross over [Col. 0807C] who are armed, who are strong and powerful men; all the others, with feeble and unmilitant hands, remain beyond the Jordan.

If there are strong men among them, let them abandon their animals, their herds, and every impediment, and fight against the enemy together with us until our enemies are conquered, until we take possession of the good land, the land of milk and honey.

For who doubts that all the holy fathers both help us with their prayers and strengthen and encourage us by the examples of their deeds? They also fight for us through the books they left written for us as reminders, teaching and instructing us how to wage war against hostile powers and how to endure the contests of our struggles. [Col. 0807D]

They fight on our behalf, and they themselves march armed in the first rank before us. Having them as our example and seeing through the Spirit their mighty deeds, we arm ourselves for spiritual battle and fight against spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places.

Thus, in the end, those who serve under Jesus son of Nave kill more than thirty kings and receive their lands as an inheritance by lot. For when spiritual wickedness has been driven from the heavenly places, they receive the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom, as Jesus our Lord distributes it.

A third mode of interpretation may also be understood: among the sons of Israel—that is, among the people of the Church—some may be understood to be spiritual and to receive an inheritance within the Jordan, taking in the sweetness of wisdom and knowledge from the land flowing with milk and honey. The city of God is surrounded and watered by their river, which is filled with the waters of divine understanding. [Col. 0808A]

Others, however, are carnal, abounding in animals and cattle—that is, in gross and solid perceptions—as were those of whom the Apostle said: “Are you so foolish? Having begun with the Spirit, are you now being perfected in the flesh?” And: “O Galatians, who has bewitched you not to obey the truth?” (Galatians 3).

Unless each one of us arms himself and, casting aside brutal and bestial perceptions, hastens toward spiritual understanding, he will remain outside the Jordan and will not be able to proceed along the river of wisdom that makes the city of God glad—that is, the soul capable of receiving God. He will not attain the inner meanings of the Lord’s utterances, which are sweeter than honey and the honeycomb; [Col. 0808B] instead, he will obtain only that land in which two kings were killed, where it is said to him: “I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (1 Corinthians 2).

But whoever is able to cross the Jordan and penetrate to the interior, following Jesus Christ our Lord, will kill more than thirty kings—perhaps those of whom it is said: “The kings of the earth stood forth, and the rulers gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ” (Psalm 2).

After these kings have been driven out and cast down, he will recognize the more secret mysteries, until he comes even to that place where the throne of God is, the Jerusalem that is the city of the living God—not this Jerusalem, which is in bondage with her children on earth, but the Jerusalem that is free and is the mother of us all.

## CHAPTER VIII. [Col. 0808C] On the forty-two encampments of the sons of Israel
(CAP. XXXIII.) These are the encampments of the children of Israel, who went out from Egypt in their companies, under the leadership of Moses and Aaron. Moses recorded them according to the locations of the camps, which were changed at the Lord’s command.

We read that the Apostle Paul, after recalling the ancient history contained in the books of the Law and the Prophets, said: “Now all these things happened to them as a figure; for they were written for our instruction, upon whom the ends of the ages have come. I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, that all our fathers were under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea; and all ate the same spiritual food, [Col. 0808D] and all drank the same spiritual drink. For they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them; and the rock was Christ” (I Cor. X).

If, then, a portion of the history of the journey from Egypt is understood spiritually, the other matters also—those which the Apostle omitted because of the constraint of time—will be shown to belong to the same interpretation. And in the Psalm: “Open my eyes, and I shall contemplate the wonders of your law” (Ps. CXVIII). Paul too says: “The law is spiritual.” And the Lord himself says: “If you believed Moses, you would also believe me; for he wrote about me” (John V). And the Gospel according to Luke says: “Beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things that had been spoken about him” (Luke, last chapter).

Let the Jews, therefore—little children who cannot swallow solid food but are still nourished with the milk of infancy—read of a material Pharaoh and a Red Sea across which one sails to India, and manna resembling coriander, and hear bodily of everything that has been written: the leprosy of houses, the leprosy of skin and of warp, the ox guilty of homicide, the beast accused of adultery, and the Hebrew who wished to serve because of his wife and children, with his ear pierced by an awl.

But we, leaving Capernaum, once a most beautiful field, and going out with Jesus into the desert, are fed with his breads: if we are foolish and like beasts, with barley loaves; if we are rational animals, with wheat loaves made from ground grain—the grain which, falling into the earth and dying, produced abundant fruit.

Egypt was struck by nine plagues. Pharaoh was broken so that he might release God’s people; finally, he lost his firstborn, so that the firstborn of Israel might be consecrated to the Lord. Those who had previously wished to hold them back now drive them out urgently. The Destroyer passed through, but did not dare touch the pastoral land of Goshen, watered by rains. Their doorposts had been marked with the blood of lambs, and by their deed they proclaimed: “The light of your countenance has been marked upon us, O Lord” (Ps. IV).

Hence the solemnity itself is called Passover (*Phase*), which we may call “passing over,” because, proceeding from the flocks toward better things, we leave behind dark Egypt. “These,” he says, “are the encampments of the children of Israel, who went out from the land of Egypt in their companies, under the leadership of Moses and Aaron.”

The Greeks call these places διαμοναί (*diamonai*), “sojourns” or “abodes”; we, because of the character of our language, translate them more meaningfully as “encampments” (*mansiones*), or, when the word concerns an army, as “camps.” A catalogue of the encampments is made from the first to the last, and together they number forty-two. Matthew speaks of these: “From Abraham to David, fourteen generations” (Matt. I)—that is, forty-two generations altogether.

Through these the true Hebrew travels, hastening to pass from earth to heaven; leaving behind the Egypt of this age, he enters the promised land. Nor is it surprising that, through that sacred symbolism of the number, we arrive at the kingdoms of heaven, under which the Lord and Savior proceeded from the first patriarch to the Virgin, as if to the Jordan, which, flowing in a full torrent, overflowed with the graces of the Holy Spirit.

When Scripture says that they went out “under the leadership of Moses and Aaron,” understand the Law and the priesthood: works and the worship of God, one of which requires the other. For it is of no benefit to practice virtues unless you know the Creator; nor does reverence for God advance salvation unless you fulfill the commandments of the founder.

By these two encampments, as by two seraphim, we break forth into confession of the Holy Trinity, saying: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts.”

Moses is said to have written these encampments according to the locations of the camps, which were changed at the Lord’s command. You have heard what Moses wrote through the word of the Lord. And why did the Lord wish these things to be written? Surely so that this writing of the encampments made by the children of Israel might benefit us in some way.

Finally, according to the spiritual interpretation, we are commanded to go out from Egypt in two ways: either when, abandoning a pagan life, we approach the knowledge of the divine Law, or when the soul departs from the dwelling of this body. These encampments, then, which Moses now records through the word of the Lord, refer to both.

Concerning those encampments, indeed, in which the soul, stripped of the body—or rather, clothed again in its own body—is to drink, the Lord declared in the Gospel, saying: “There are many dwelling places with my Father; otherwise I would have told you: I am going to prepare a dwelling place for you” (John XIV). There are, therefore, many dwelling places which lead to the Father. What is the reason for each one, what benefit the soul receives from its sojourn, and what instruction or illumination it receives, is known only to the Father of the age to come, who says of himself: “I am the door” (John X). “No one comes to the Father except through me” (John XIV).

Perhaps he will become a door for each soul in each of these dwelling places, so that through him it may enter, and through him go out, and find pasture. Then it will enter another, and from there another, until it reaches the Father himself.

But if we return to the second interpretation mentioned above, and understand these as the soul’s advances while it is placed in this life—when, converted from a pagan life, it follows not so much Moses as the Law of God, and not Aaron so much as the priest who remains forever—then, before it reaches perfection, it dwells in the desert. There it is trained in the Lord’s commandments, and there its faith is tested through temptations.

When it has conquered one temptation, and its faith has been proved in it, it proceeds from there to another, and passes, as it were, from one encampment to another. When there it has obtained whatever things befall it and has borne them faithfully, it proceeds to another. Thus, through each trial, the advances of life and faith are said to provide encampments, in which increases of virtue are sought one by one, and in them what is written is fulfilled: “They will go from strength to strength” (Ps. LXXXIII), until one reaches the final—or rather, the highest—degree of virtue, crosses the river of God, and receives the promised inheritance.

Setting out, therefore, from Rameses in the first month, on the fifteenth day of the first month, on the day after Passover, the children of Israel went out with a high hand, in the sight of all the Egyptians, while they were burying their firstborn whom the Lord had struck down (for he had also carried out vengeance upon their gods), and they encamped at Succoth.

Some interpret Rameses as “turbulent commotion,” or “the bitterness and commotion of the moth.” We, however, think that it more truly expresses “the thunder of joy.” To this city, which lay at the farthest borders of Egypt, the people who wished to go into the desert gathered, because, abandoning the tumult of the world, they were moved away from their former vices and from the moth of sins that had previously consumed them, so that, turning all bitterness into sweetness, they might hear the voice of God thundering from above on Mount Sinai.

That divine words and the utterances of the Scriptures are called thunder in the wheel of this age and world, the Psalmist declares, saying: “The voice of your thunder is in the wheel” (Ps. LXXVI). When they heard the voice of God the Father at the baptism, they thought it was thunder.

And when we have been moved by the evangelical trumpet and roused by the joy of thunder, we go out in the first month, when winter passes away and departs, when spring begins, when the earth gives birth, and when all things are renewed. We go out on the fifteenth day of the first month, on the day after Passover, in the full light of the month, after eating the spotless lamb, with our feet shod according to the Apostle and our loins girded with chastity (Eph. VI), with staffs prepared in our hands.

Although in Egypt we ate the lamb on the fourteenth day of the month, celebrating Passover, the full light is completed for us when, with a high hand, we leave Rameses behind. It is called “high,” either because it struck Egypt or because it protected Israel in the sight of the Egyptians. They marvel that we go out from the world and are tortured by envy; afterward, wishing to hold us back, they are suffocated in persecutions, when the Egyptians also bury their firstborn, and dead fathers, overwhelmed by earthly works, bury their dead sons.

It seems to me that the firstborn of the Egyptians are the doctrines of the philosophers, by which they held deceived and entangled human beings. When living Israel has escaped them, they surround their dead, lest they imitate the example of those who are departing.

Moreover, concerning what follows—“In their gods he carried out judgments,” or, as the Septuagint translated it, “vengeances”—the Hebrews maintain that on the night when the people went out, all the temples in Egypt were destroyed, either by an earthquake or by the touch of lightning. Spiritually, however, we say that when we go out from Egypt, the idols of error collapse and the whole worship of perverse doctrines is shaken.

Others think one should ask how God carries out vengeance upon demons, since the day of vengeance and judgment has not yet come. But I think that vengeance is carried out upon demons when one who had been deceived by them into worshiping idols is converted through the word of the Lord and worships God; through the very work of conversion, vengeance is inflicted upon the one who had deceived him.

Likewise, if one who had been deceived by demons into fornication is converted to chastity, loves purity, and laments that he had gone astray, the demon is burned and consumed by the tears of his repentance, and thus vengeance is inflicted upon the author of the deception. Likewise also, if someone returns from pride to humility or from luxury to moderation, through each of these acts he scourges and torments the demons who had deceived him into such things.

How great do you suppose their torments are when they see someone, according to the word of the Lord, sell all that he possesses, give it to the poor, take up his cross, and follow Christ? (Luke XVIII.) But beyond all kinds of torment and above every punishment, it is for them the greatest torment if they see someone devote himself to the word of God, seeking with attentive study knowledge of the divine Law and the mysteries of the Scriptures. In this [uncertain text] lies all their flame; in this they are consumed by a complete conflagration, because they had darkened human minds with the shadows of ignorance and had thereby secured that God would be unknown, while the devotion of divine worship was transferred to them.

What vengeance, do you think, is inflicted upon them; what flame of punishment is brought upon them when they see these things opened by the light of truth and the clouds of their fraud stripped away through knowledge of the divine Law? They possess all who live in ignorance—not only those who are still in ignorance, but they often thrust themselves even upon those who have come to know God and again attempt to work the deeds of ignorance in them.

For no sin is completed without them. When someone commits adultery, it is certainly not without a demon. Or when [uncertain text] is carried away, or when he seizes another’s property, and when one who sits slanders his neighbor and places a stumbling-block against the son of his mother, it is not without a demon.

Therefore we must act lest, if we give them room to work in us the things God hates, we perhaps raise up in ourselves the firstborn of the Egyptians—or their gods—which the Lord struck and destroyed. But if we restrain ourselves from all these things in the manner described above, the Lord will carry out vengeance upon all the gods of the Egyptians, and they will suffer punishment on account of our amendment and conversion.

“Setting out,” he says, “from Rameses, the children of Israel encamped at Succoth.”

The second encampment. In this place they bake unleavened bread and first pitch their tents; hence the place received its name. For Succoth is interpreted in our language as “tabernacles” or “tents.” And from this, on the fifteenth day of the seventh month, is the solemnity of Tabernacles.

When, therefore, we have gone out from Egypt, we first pitch a tabernacle, and we must know that we are to proceed farther. For then we do not eat of the leaven of Egypt, the leaven of malice and wickedness, but we eat the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth (I Cor. V), completing the Lord’s commandments in practice: “Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees” (Luke XII).

In this encampment we are commanded always to remember our departure from Egypt, to celebrate the passing over—that is, the Lord’s Passover—and to consecrate the firstborn of our womb and of all our virtues in place of Egypt’s firstborn, who were struck down by the Lord.

And setting out from Succoth, they encamped at Etham, which is at the edge of the wilderness. The third encampment follows the tabernacles. In it the Lord is first seen at night in a pillar of cloud, so that he may go before the people and be the guide of their journey.

Etham corresponds for us to “strength” or “perfection,” of which David also sings: “You broke the streams of Etham” (Ps. LXXIII), that is, “of the strong.” Great is the strength required to leave Egypt and dwell at the farthest edge of the wilderness. From this we understand that Succoth was still near the regions of Egypt.

For in the statement that it is “at the farthest borders of the wilderness,” it is shown to lie between the boundaries of the desert and Egypt. It should also be noted that another edition has Buthan in place of Etham. Buthan, therefore, is called a valley.

We have said that there is an advance in virtues in these places. Virtue, however, is acquired only through struggle and labor. It is tested not so much in prosperity as in adversity. One therefore comes to the valley. In valleys and lower places the contest is waged against the devil and the opposing powers. In the valleys, therefore, the contest must be conducted, and in the valleys one must fight.

Finally, Abraham also fought barbarian kings in the Valley of Salt, and there he obtained victory. Our traveler descends to those who are in the depths and lowest places, not to remain there, but to gain victory there.

Let us prepare strength for ourselves; let us assume perfect vigor, so that amid the darkness of errors and the confusion of night the light of the knowledge of Christ may appear. Let our day also have a protective cloud, so that under these guides we may be able to reach the holy land.

Setting out from Etham, they came opposite Pi-hahiroth, which faces Baal-zephon, and encamped opposite Migdol.

The fourth encampment is Pi-hahiroth, which is interpreted as “the mouth of nobles.” It is written with the letter *beth*, ב. Some incorrectly think that *hiroth* means villages; and the error is obvious, because in place of the aforesaid element they read the letter ν.

Baal-zephon is translated into our language as “Lord of the north,” or “the lookout of ascent,” or “the one possessing secrets.” Migdol, moreover, means “greatness” or “tower.”

Having therefore assumed strength, we are ennobled in the Lord, while we despise the secrets of Baal-zephon, the idol, and avoid its magnificence and tower-like pride. For he is not from the south, from which the Lord comes, nor from the region of the south where the bridegroom reclines among flowers; rather, he is the possessor of the north, the coldest wind, from which evils blaze forth upon the earth. Although he is extremely cold, he is called “right” by name, falsely assuming the title of virtue and the right hand, when he is wholly on the left.

And setting out from Pi-hahiroth, they passed through the midst of the sea into the wilderness. They traveled for three days through the wilderness of Etham and encamped at Marah.

The fifth encampment is Marah, which is interpreted as “bitterness.” They could not have reached the waters of the Red Sea and seen Pharaoh perish with his army unless they had first had nobility in their mouth and virtues in confession of the Lord. After the preaching of the Gospel, after the tabernacles of those who are migrating, after strength has been assumed, and after the nobility of confession, dangers again arise.

From this we learn always to beware of snares and to invoke the mercy of God, so that we may escape the pursuing Pharaoh and have him drowned for us in spiritual baptism.

After they had gone out from the Red Sea, the wilderness of Shur, which is also called the wilderness of Etham, met them. Entering it for three days, they had no water; and they came to Marah, which received its name from bitterness. The spring had water, but it had no sweetness. The people murmur when they see the water and cannot endure drinking it.

Understand Marah as the waters of the letter that kills. If the confession of the cross is cast into them, and the mysteries of the Lord’s passion are joined to them, everything that seemed undrinkable, sad, and harsh will be turned into sweetness.

Hence it is also written: “God established for the people a statute and judgments, and he tested them.” For where there is a greatness of grace, there is also a greatness of testing. Do not be terrified if, after victory, you come to bitterness, because those who truly celebrate Passover eat unleavened bread with bitter things; temptation produces testing, testing produces hope, and hope brings forth salvation.

Among physicians also, a certain antidote that tempers harmful humors is named from bitterness; it proves sweet by restoring health. So, conversely, pleasure and luxury must be tempered by bitterness, as Scripture says: “What makes your throat fat for a time, at the end you will find more bitter than gall.”

Setting out from Marah, they came to Elim, where there were twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees, and there they encamped.

Do you see what pleasant places receive you after bitterness and after the harshness of temptations? You would not have come to the palms unless you had endured the bitterness of temptations; nor would you have come to the sweetness of the springs unless you had overcome what was sad and harsh.

This does not mean that there is already an end and the perfection of all things in these earthly places. Rather, God, the steward of souls, inserts into the journey itself certain refreshments amid its labors, by which the restored soul may return more eagerly to the remaining labors.

Elim, however, is interpreted as “rams.” Rams are leaders of flocks. Who are the leaders of Christ’s flock except the Apostles, who are also the twelve springs? But because our Lord and Savior chose not only twelve but also another seventy, therefore not only twelve springs but also seventy palm trees are recorded. They too are called apostles.

Thus Paul himself says, when explaining the Savior’s resurrection: “He appeared to them,” he says, “the eleven; then he appeared also to all the apostles” (I Cor. XV). In this he shows that there were other apostles besides the twelve.

This pleasantness after bitterness, this rest after labor, this grace after temptation, will receive you. But from there also they departed and pitched their tents beside the Red Sea: “Setting out from Elim, they encamped at the Red Sea.”

The Red Sea, which in Hebrew is called *yam suph*, is the seventh encampment. It is asked how, after crossing the Red Sea and reaching the spring of Marah and Elim, they came again to the Red Sea—unless perhaps, as they continued on their journey, a certain inlet of the sea appeared, beside which they encamped. For it is one thing to cross the sea and another to pitch tents nearby.

From this we are warned that even after evangelical discipline and the sweetest foods of triumphs, a sea may sometimes appear to us, and past dangers may be placed before our eyes. Yet there is a great difference between crossing the sea and seeing the sea from a distance.

The Hebrew expression *yam suph* is composed of the words for “sea” and “red.” *Suph*, however, is called both “red” and “reed.” Hence we may conjecture that they came to some marsh or lake full of reeds and rushes.

There can be no doubt that Holy Scripture calls every gathering of waters “the sea.” This encampment is not found in Exodus; instead, it is written there that they came from the Red Sea to the wilderness of Sin, which lies between Elim and Sinai, on the fifteenth day of the second month after their departure from Egypt—that is, the thirty-first day after they went out from Rameses.

“And setting out from the Red Sea, they encamped in the wilderness of Sin.”

This is the eighth encampment, although according to the order in Exodus it is the seventh. It should be understood that the whole wilderness up to Mount Sinai is called Sin, and that, from the name of the entire province, one place also received the name of an encampment. Thus Moab is likewise the name both of a city and of a province.

There are five encampments in this wilderness: Yam Suph, of which we spoke above; the wilderness of Sin; Dophkah; Alush; and Rephidim, concerning which we shall speak in what follows.

Sin, however, is interpreted as “bush” or “hatred.” Both meanings contribute to the mystical interpretations. When we have come to the place from which the Lord is to speak to us, may we deserve the great hatred of the enemy. Then we shall see the bush burning without being consumed; the Church inflamed by persecutions, yet not perishing because the Lord speaks within it.

Notice also that in the eighth encampment, in which our winepresses are found—and hence the eighth Psalm is prefaced by this title—we take the wilderness of the bush, because “the children of the desolate woman are more numerous than those of her who has a husband.”

And setting out from the wilderness of Sin, they encamped at Dophkah.

The ninth encampment. Among the Hebrews this name is called κροῦμα (*krouma*), that is, “a knocking,” in accordance with the Lord’s saying: “Knock, and it will be opened to you.” In the book of Hebrew Names, however, we translated it as “adhesion” or “remission.” This should not trouble the reader, nor should he think that we are writing contradictory things.

There we published according to the common reading, if the middle word is written with the letter *beth*. Here, however, in the Hebrew volume I found it written with *pe*, a letter that signifies “knocking” more than “gluing.” The meaning is clear. After the Lord’s answers, after the number eight, we begin to knock at the mysteries of Christ’s resurrection.

And setting out from Dophkah, they encamped at Alush.

The tenth encampment is not found in Exodus. It is believed to be contained within the wilderness of Sin, as the same book relates: “The whole multitude of the children of Israel set out from the wilderness of Sin by their encampments, according to the word of the Lord, and they came to Rephidim” (Exod. XIII). From this it is evident that several encampments are designated by the name of one region.

Alush is interpreted as “leaven,” which the woman took and mixed into three measures of flour until the whole was leavened (Matt. XIII). In this wilderness the people murmur because of hunger, and, turning, they look toward the cloud at a distance, the glory of God. In the evening they receive quail, and in the morning of the next day, manna.

Notice that in the tenth encampment leaven is placed, and that after the eating of meat manna is supplied, fulfilling the Scripture: “He gave them the bread of angels to eat.” The people set out from Alush and encamped at Rephidim, and there was no water for the people.

This is the eleventh encampment. In the book of Hebrew Names I found it interpreted rather forcefully as “a sufficient mouth saw them,” or, alternatively, “the defect of the mouth of the strong.” It is better translated as “the dissolution of the strong,” or “the health of the strong,” or, according to the character of the Syriac language, “the loosening of hands.”

This place is also read about in Exodus after the departure from the wilderness of Sin. The people complain there because of the burning thirst; a spring bursts forth and flows from the rock of Horeb; and it receives the name of temptation, that is, Massah.

Moses ascends the mountain, while Jesus wages war against Amalek. Through the sign of the cross the enemy is overcome; when the hands of the one praying are lowered, the enemy pursues victoriously. Moses sits upon the stone mentioned by Zechariah, which had seven eyes, and in the book of Samuel is called Abenhaazer—that is, “the stone of help.” Aaron and Hur—that is, “mountainous” and “luminous”—support both his hands.

After the adversary has been defeated, Jethro arrives. He brings Zipporah and both sons; he gives the counsel of the seventy elders; and, as a type of the Church gathered from the Gentiles, the diminution of the Law is completed with the Gospel supplying what was lacking.

It is fitting that Rephidim is called “the dissolution” or “health of the strong,” either because Amalek was dispersed or because Israel was healed. If Rephidim is called “the loosening of hands” according to the Syrians, we shall say that the name was given because of the offense of the people, since they murmured against the Lord.

We touch upon these matters rather than explain them, content to indicate briefly that after the leaven of Alush and the Massah of the Church, manifold temptations of demons ordinarily rise up against us.

And setting out from Rephidim, they pitched their camps in the wilderness of Sinai.

This is the twelfth. Let the number of the apostles immediately come to mind. It is one among many, but greater than all; it is not separated in order, but excels in merit.

They reach this place on the forty-seventh day, as Scripture says: “In the third month after the children of Israel had gone out from Egypt, on this day they entered the wilderness of Sinai,” and so forth. This has been explained more fully above, in the second book.

And setting out from the wilderness of Sinai, they encamped at the Graves of Lust.

This is the thirteenth encampment. Its name, together with its interpretation, is published among the Hebrews as *Kibroth-hattaavah*. Its meaning is that passage from the Gospel in which Jesus, after being baptized, was immediately led by the Spirit into the desert and tempted by the devil (Matt. IV).

Thus Israel too, after familiar conversation with the Lord, after dwelling beside Mount Sinai for one year and four days, departed through a marvelous arrangement of the camps into the wilderness of Paran, which is interpreted as “wild ass” or “wildness.” There it succumbed to the evil beast, disdaining the heavenly bread and desiring the meat of the Egyptians, when a sudden fire devoured many and, at Moses’ intercession, the earth-consuming flame consumed them.

And setting out from the Graves of Lust, they encamped at Hazeroth.

This is the fourteenth encampment in the wilderness of Paran, which is interpreted as “courts.” In it Aaron and Miriam murmur against Moses because of the Ethiopian woman; and, as a type of zeal against the Church gathered from the Gentiles, the Jewish people are covered with the filth of leprosy and do not return to the tabernacle to recover their former health until the appointed time of the fullness of the Gentiles has been fulfilled.

And setting out from Hazeroth, they encamped at Rithmah. In place of this, above in the same book, we read: “After the people had departed from Hazeroth, they encamped in the wilderness of Paran.”

This is the fifteenth encampment. It should be noted that the remaining nineteen encampments, whose catalogue is now briefly described, from Rithmah to Ezion-geber—that is, to the thirty-second encampment—are included under the name of the wilderness of Paran.

In them we understand all the things that are written to have occurred at different times: the sending of the twelve spies to the holy land and the report of the cluster of grapes carried from it on a pole; the murmuring of the Jewish people, who feared the attack of the giants; their battle against Amalek, by whom they were defeated; Dathan and Abiram and the sons of Korah, together with the vengeance inflicted upon them; Aaron’s rod that blossomed; and the red heifer burned as a whole offering, with its ashes used for sprinkling. All these matters have been explained above in the book.

Rithmah is translated as “sound” or “juniper,” although many among the Greeks maintain that ἄρκευθος (*arkeuthos*) signifies another kind of tree. “Juniper” is also expressed by the first of the Gradual Psalms according to the Hebrew truth, where it is written: “What shall be given to you, or what shall be added to you, against a deceitful tongue?” (Ps. CXIX). And the Prophet answers: “The sharp arrows of the mighty, with coals of juniper” (ibid.). In our version, this is rendered “desolating.”

It is said that this wood preserves fire for a very long time, so that if a coal is covered with its ashes, it may last until the following year. From this we learn that, after the Graves of Lust, we must pass through vestibules to the wood that retains heat for a long time, so that we may be fervent in spirit and proclaim the Gospel with a clear sound, raising the Lord’s voice on high.

And setting out from Rithmah, they encamped at Rimmon-perez.

This is the sixteenth encampment. In Greek it is interpreted as ῥοιᾶς ἀποκοπή (*rhoias apokopē*), in Latin, “the cutting of a pomegranate,” which others call “a pomegranate fruit.” The fruit of this tree is understood in Scripture in two ways: either as the Church, which covers the whole multitude of believers with its rind, or as the diversity and harmony of virtues, according to what is written: “The multitude of believers was of one heart and one soul” (Acts IV).

Thus the individual ranks are diverse, yet all are held together by the same structure.

From there they departed and came to Libnah.

The seventeenth encampment, which we may translate as “bricks.” Some, translating Libnah, have incorrectly interpreted it as “whiteness.” We read in Exodus of the Egyptians’ bricks, which the people made with groaning. We read in Malachi of the bricks which Edom, after its destruction, attempts to replace with polished stones; and in Ezekiel of the brick on which the image of besieged Jerusalem is depicted.

From these things we learn that on the journey of this life, as we pass from one thing to another, we sometimes grow and sometimes decline, and that after the ecclesiastical order we often pass over to works of bricks.

And from Libnah they encamped at Rissah.

The eighteenth encampment is translated as “bridles.” For if, after advancing, we descend again to works of clay, we must be bridled; and once more, as wanderers and headlong travelers, we must be directed by the restraints of the Scriptures.

As far as my memory recalls, I do not know of having found this word anywhere in the Holy Scriptures among the Hebrews, except in the apocryphal book which the Greeks call Μικρογένεσις (*Mikrogenesis*). There it is placed in the construction of a tower as a racecourse, in which boxers and athletes train and the speed of runners is tested.

The Psalmist also says: “Constrain their jaws with a bridle, who do not draw near to you” (Ps. XXXI). And the Apostle: “Do you not know that those who run in the stadium all run, but one receives the prize? So run that you may obtain it” (I Cor. IX).

And setting out from Rissah, they encamped at Kehelathah.

The nineteenth encampment is interpreted as “Church.” The steps of wandering runners are drawn back by bridles to the Church, and they hasten to enter again through the doors they had previously left.

From there they departed and encamped at Mount Shepher.

The twentieth encampment is interpreted as “beauty,” and it is established on the mountain of beauty. From this the beginning of the fourteenth Psalm also sounds: “Lord, who will dwell in your tabernacle, or who will rest upon your holy mountain?” (Ps. XIV).

See what the bridles accomplish: they draw us back from vices, introduce us to the choirs of virtues, and make us dwell in Christ, the most beautiful mountain.

According to Daniel, this is the stone cut from the mountain without hands, which grew into a great mountain and filled the whole earth (Dan. II). According to Ezekiel, it wounded the prince of Tyre. To this mountain, in Isaiah and Micah, the peoples flock, saying: “Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord and to the house of the God of Jacob; and he will announce his ways to us, and we will walk in his paths” (Isa. II).

And setting out from Mount Shepher, they came to Haradah.

The twenty-first encampment is translated as “miracle.” What a beautiful order of advances, what an excellent texture of believers! After the work of bricks we are bridled; after the bridles we are introduced into the Church; after dwelling in the Church we ascend to Christ on the mountain.

Placed upon it, we are astonished and marvel, so that our speech in his praises is surpassed, discovering in him things that “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have entered into the heart of man” (I Cor. II).

From there they departed and encamped at Makheloth.

The twenty-second encampment is interpreted as “assemblies.” In it the multitude of believers, the Church of the firstborn, and the harmony of all virtues are found. Then we can truly say: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is when brothers dwell together in unity” (Ps. CXXXII). And the Lord makes those of one mind dwell in a house.

And setting out from Makheloth, they encamped at Tahath.

The twenty-third encampment may also be understood as “beneath.” But it is better interpreted as “fear.” You have come to the Church; you have ascended the most beautiful mountain; through awe and wonder you confess the greatness of Christ. You see there many companions in virtue. Do not be high-minded, but fear.

For “the Lord resists the proud but gives grace to the humble.” And whoever exalts himself should beware lest he fall. “The mighty will suffer mighty torments.” Fear is the guardian of virtues, while security readily leads to a fall.

Hence, in a certain Psalm, after the Prophet had said: “The Lord governs me, and I shall lack nothing; he has placed me in a place of pasture,” he joins the fear that guards blessedness and adds: “Your rod and your staff, they themselves have comforted me.” The meaning is: “While I feared punishments, I preserved the grace I had received.”

From Tahath they encamped at Terah.

The twenty-fourth encampment is translated by some as “malice” or “pasture.” They would not be mistaken if it were written with the letter *ayin*. But now, since there is a double aspiration in the final syllable, the cause of the error is obvious.

I find the patriarch Abraham written with this same word and the same letters in the aforementioned apocryphal volume of Genesis. After driving away the ravens that were ravaging human grain, he received the name “driver away” or “repeller.”

Let us therefore imitate Terah and more diligently prevent the birds of heaven which hasten to devour the wheat sown beside the road. For the patriarch Abraham also, as a type of Israel, divided the limbs of the sacrificial victims and did not allow them to be devoured by birds. And ravens pluck out the contemptuous eye from the valleys.

The true Moses leads the Ethiopian woman, and Elijah is fed by ravens. If you have fear, you will be watchful; if you are watchful, the lion will not be able to enter the folds of your sheep. This may refer either to the overseers of the churches, or to…

It refers to the guardianship of your soul, into which the devil tries to enter through the various openings of vices. Hence they departed and pitched their tents at Methea.

The twenty-fifth station is translated as “sweetness.” You have ascended on high, marveled at the choirs of virtues, feared a fall, and driven away the ambushers [Col. 0819B]; immediately the sweet fruit of your labor follows you. In accordance with the nature of letters, the sweetness of the fruit will compensate for the bitterness of its roots, and you will say: “How sweet are your utterances to my palate, sweeter than honey to my mouth.” You will also hear your Bridegroom singing to you: “Honey drips from your lips, my sister, my bride.” For what is sweeter than discipline, what better than instruction, what sweeter than the Lord? “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet.”

Thus Samson, who had driven the birds away from his fruits, had tied up the foxes that destroy the vineyards, and had killed the roaring lion, found a honeycomb in the mouth of the dead. From Methea they set out and encamped at Hesmona.

The twenty-sixth station, in our language, signifies “haste.” In accordance with what is written in the Psalm: “Envoys will come from Egypt” [Col. 0819C] (Psalm 67 [68]). In Hebrew, instead of “envoys,” we read “those who hasten,” so that, after we have harvested the sweet fruits of our labor, we may not be content with rest and leisure; and, hastening again toward what lies farther ahead, may forget what is past and stretch ourselves toward the future.

They departed from Hesmona and came to Moseroth.

The twenty-seventh station signifies “bonds” or “disciplines,” so that we may proceed with rapid step to our teachers, tread their thresholds, and regard the precepts of virtue and the mysteries of Scripture as eternal bonds. In accordance with what is said in Isaiah: “And the lofty men of Saba will pass over to you and will be yours. After this they will walk, bound with manacles.” And Paul was “a prisoner of Jesus Christ.”

There are two kinds of bonds in the Scriptures, which Samson broke, and he overcame his enemies. And we read concerning the prostitute: “A bond is in her hands” [Col. 0819D]. And in the person of the Lord, who says: “Let us break their bonds and cast their yoke from us” (Psalm 2). And elsewhere: “The snare has been broken, and we have been freed” (Psalm 128 [129]). But the bonds of Christ are voluntary, and they are transformed into embraces. Whoever has been bound will say: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand will embrace me” (Song 2).

From Moseroth they set out and encamped at Benejaacan.

The twenty-eighth station is Benejaacan, which by interpretation is rendered “sons of necessity” or “sons of gnashing.” If you begin with the number one and gradually add until you reach seven, the number twenty-eight is produced. Who these sons of necessity are, the Psalm itself teaches us: “Bring to the Lord, sons [Col. 0820A] of God; bring to the Lord the sons of rams.”

What is this great necessity that is imposed upon the unwilling? When you have been instructed in the divine Scriptures and know their laws and testimonies of truth, contending with adversaries, you will bind them and lead them captive; and from those who were once enemies and captives you will make free children of God, so that suddenly you may say with Zion: “I was barren and did not give birth; I was exiled and captive—and who raised these? I was abandoned and alone—and where were these?”

Moreover, what we have translated as “sons of gnashing” should be referred to this meaning: out of fear of punishment and of that place where there is “weeping and gnashing of teeth,” the crowds of believers submit their necks to Christ the Lord, abandoning the devil’s bonds.

They departed from Benejaacan and came to Mount Gadgad.

The twenty-ninth station is interpreted as “messenger,” or “expedition” and “girding” [Col. 0820B]; or rather, as we more correctly judge, κατακοπή (*katakopē*), that is, “cutting down.”

We, as teachers of disciples and believers, cannot otherwise make them sons of necessity unless we slay their instructors and are cruel in killing them. Let not our hand spare the shoulder or the tip of the ear when drawing them from the lions’ mouths. “Cursed is the one who performs God’s work negligently and withholds his sword from blood.” Hence David also says: “In the morning I was killing all the sinners of the land” (Psalm 118 [119]).

Concerning the “messenger” and the “girding,” we can briefly say that we should offer the sons of necessity great incentives to virtue when we announce to them the rewards of the future and teach those who are girded to enter into battle. Whatever the teacher does in these three respects, [Col. 0820C] he stands upon the mountain.

They departed from Mount Gadgad and encamped at Jetebatha.

The thirtieth station is interpreted as “goodness,” so that, when we have reached the perfect man, the priestly rank, and the fullness of Christ’s age—in which Ezekiel also was beside the river Chobar—we may sing with David in the thirtieth Psalm: “Lord, in you I have hoped; I shall not be put to shame forever.” For “the good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep.”

They departed from Jotbatha and encamped at Ebrona.

The thirtieth station is interpreted as “passage” or “crossing over.” To this place comes the true Hebrew and passer-over, who can say: “As I pass by, I will see this great vision.” Of him the Psalmist also says: “And those who were passing by did not say, ‘The blessing of the Lord be upon you’” (Psalm 128 [129]). [Col. 0820D] “For the form of this world is passing away.” Therefore the saints desire to pass over to better things; they are not content with their present condition but groan daily: “These things I remembered, and I poured out my soul within me; for I shall pass into the place of the wondrous tabernacle, even to the house of God” (Psalm 41 [42]).

They departed from Ebrona and encamped at Asiongaber.

The thirty-second station is Asiongaber, which is rendered “the wood of a man.” These “woods of a man”—the forests and all kinds of trees—may signify the multitude of nations.

Up to this point, the wilderness of Paran contains eighteen stations, which, although listed in the catalogue, are not placed on the preceding route.

From there they set out and came to the wilderness of Sin, which is Kadesh.

It is asked [Col. 0821A] why the eighth station is now said to be the thirty-third. But it should be understood that the earlier one is written with the letter *samekh* and is interpreted as “bush” or “hatred.” This one, however, is written with *sade* and is rendered “commandment.” The word joined to it, Kadesh, does not mean “holy,” as most suppose, but “walled” or “transferred.”

We read in Genesis (chapter 38), according to the Hebrew truth, where Judah, thinking Tamar to be a prostitute, sends gifts, and the bearer of the gifts asks: “Where is the *kadesha*?”—that is, the prostitute, whose dress has been altered from that of other women. We find the same thing in many passages.

But if it is interpreted as “holy,” it must be understood *κατ’ ἀντίφρασιν* (*kat’ antíphrasin*), that is, by antiphrasis—just as the Parcae are named from *parcere* (“to spare”), although they spare no one; and *bellum* (“war”), although it is not at all *bellum* (“beautiful”); and *lucus* (“grove”), although it does not shine at all.

In this station also [Col. 0821B] Miriam dies and is buried; and because of the waters of contradiction, Moses and Aaron offend God and are forbidden to cross the Jordan. Messengers are sent to Edom, and passage is requested but not obtained.

Who would have feared, after so many advances, the murmuring of the people, the offense of the teachers, and the denial of a route across? Note also that, after the death of the prophetess and the waters of contradiction, they cannot cross the fleshly and earthly Edomite; although they seek a road with many prayers and great effort, they do not obtain it. Instead, Edom comes out against them with a great multitude and a strong hand.

The interpretation of the name also agrees with death, offense, and the denial of passage. For where there is a commandment, there is sin; where there is sin, there is offense; where there is offense, there is death.

This is the station of which the Psalmist sings: [Col. 0821C] “The Lord will shake the wilderness of Kadesh.”

Having set out from Kadesh, they encamped at Mount Hor, on the farthest borders of the land of Edom. Aaron the priest ascended Mount Hor at the Lord’s command, and there he died in the fortieth year after the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt, in the fifth month, on the first day of the month, when he was one hundred twenty-three years old. The king of Arad, a Canaanite who lived in the south, heard that the children of Israel had come into the land of Canaan. The thirty-fourth station is one which most interpret as “light”; nor would they be wrong if it were written with the letter aleph. Others interpret it as “skin,” and they too would be right if an ayin had been used. Some interpret it as “hole,” which could be accepted if its element were beth. But when it is read with he, “mountain” is more clearly understood, and it can be read as follows: [Col. 0821D] “Aaron the priest ascended into the mountain of the mountain,” that is, to the summit of the mountain. From this we also understand that the pontiff died not simply on a mountain, but on the mountain of the mountain, so that a place worthy of his merits might be indicated.

He dies in the year when the new people were about to enter the land of promise, at the farthest borders of the land of the Idumeans; and the people mourn him for thirty days. Aaron is mourned; Jesus is not mourned. In the Law there is a descent to the underworld; in the Gospel, a migration to paradise. The Canaanite also hears that Israel has arrived and, at the place of the spies where he had once known that the people had offended, brings on a battle and takes Israel captive; then he fights again at the same place in fulfillment of a vow. The victor is conquered; the conquered prevail. The place is named [Col. 0822A] Hormah, that is, “anathema.”

It is not burdensome for me to say the same things again, though it is necessary for readers: the human condition always fluctuates on the road of this age, and one person dies in a valley, another in a plain, another on a mountain—not simply on a mountain, but on the mountain of the mountain, that is, on its lofty summit. And when the enemy attacks us, deprived of God’s help, and leads us away captive, we must not despair of salvation but arm ourselves again for battle. It may happen that we conquer where we were conquered, and triumph at the very place where we had previously been captives.

Having departed from Mount Hor, they encamped at Zalmonah. From there they set out and came to Punon. These two stations, the thirty-fifth and thirty-sixth, are not found in the order of the narrative; instead, it is written [Col. 0822B] in their place: “They set out from Mount Hor by the way of the Red Sea and went around the land of Edom.” This shows that they were situated on the borders and in the circuit of the land of Edom. Nor is it read according to the usual form, “Having departed from Mount Hor, they encamped at Zalmonah or at Punon,” but after going around the land of the Idumeans the account reaches its conclusion and says: “The children of Israel set out and encamped at Oboth.” It did not say that they set out from one place and came to the next, because it had passed over the two stations in silence. What it had omitted in its reckoning, it restores in the summary.

The first station, Zalmonah, is interpreted as “a little image.” The second, Punon, understand as a diminutive of *os*, “mouth,” not of *os*, “bone.” At these places, after Aaron’s death, they murmur against the Lord and Moses; they grow tired of the manna; they are wounded by serpents; and, as a type of the Savior, who triumphed on the cross over the true and ancient serpent, the poisons of the devil are overcome. Hence the “little image,” the true and exact image of God the Son, is preserved as it gazes upon his Passion; and what it believes in its heart it proclaims with its mouth, reading the Apostle’s words: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Romans 10).

Having departed from Punon, they encamped at Oboth. The thirty-seventh station is at Oboth, which is interpreted as “magicians” or “python-spirits,” signifying spiritual serpents and magical arts that provoke us to battle. These we must overcome through divine protection, keeping watch over the heart. From Oboth they came to Iye-abarim, which is on the borders of the Moabites.

The thirty-eighth station signifies “heaps of stones of those who cross.” There are holy stones that roll over the earth—light, polished, and, by their roundness, resembling the course of wheels. There are also others that the prophet removes from the road, lest the feet of those walking stumble over them. Who are these walkers? Surely travelers and passers-by who hasten through this age toward other stations. The statement that they were on the borders of Moab, toward the rising of the sun, shows according to the literal sense that up to this point they had been on the borders of the land of the Idumeans; now they come to the boundaries of Moab, passing from one province to another, as has already been said above.

For one must not always devote one’s labor to a single virtue; rather, as it is written, “They shall go from strength to strength” (Psalm 83), and one must pass from one virtue to another, because they adhere to one another and are so closely joined that whoever lacks one lacks them all. Yet passing from one to another properly belongs to those who contemplate the rising of the sun of righteousness.

Having departed from Iye-abarim, they pitched their tents at Dibon-gad. The thirty-ninth station is interpreted as “a temptation firmly understood.” In its place I find something else written in the order of the narrative. For after they had encamped at Iye-abarim, on the borders of Moab toward the rising of the sun, we read: “From there they set out and turned aside toward the torrent Zered. And departing from that place, they encamped beyond the Arnon, which is in the wilderness of the borders of the Amorites,” and so forth.

After Dibon-gad, war is waged against Sihon king of the Amorites and Og king of Bashan. We learn that when we have reached the summit and drunk from the spring of princes and kings, ascending Mount Pisgah, we must not be lifted up in pride; instead, we must recognize the wilderness set before us. “Before destruction the heart of a man is exalted, and before glory it is humbled.”

From there they departed and encamped at Almon-diblathaim. The fortieth station is interpreted as “contempt of wounds,” or “of reproaches.” Through this we learn that all the sweetness and allurements of pleasures in this age are to be despised, and that we must not become drunk with the wine of the world, in which there is wantonness. Honey is not offered in God’s sacrifices, and the other sweet things do not shine in the tabernacle; rather, there is the purest oil, which is produced from the bitterness of the olive. For honey drips from the lips of the adulterous woman.

I think that Jonathan tasted of this according to the mystical meanings, and, when discovered by lot, was scarcely delivered through the prayers of the people. But that reproaches are to be despised, and that even when falsely inflicted they produce blessedness, the Savior teaches most fully.

Having departed from Almon-diblathaim, they came to the mountains of Abarim, opposite Nebo. The forty-first station is interpreted as “the mountains of those who cross,” and it is opposite the face of Mount Nebo, where Moses dies and is buried, having previously seen the land of promise. Nebo is interpreted as “conclusion,” in which the Law ends and no memory of it is found. But the grace of the Gospel extends without limit. “Its sound has gone out into all the earth, and its words to the ends of the world” (Psalm 8).

At the same time, consider that the dwelling-place of those who cross is situated in the mountains and still requires progress. For after many mountains we descend to the plains of Moab and the streams of the Jordan [Col. 0823D], which is interpreted as “descent.” Nothing, as we have often said, is more dangerous than the desire for glory and vainglory, and a mind swollen with consciousness of its virtues.

Having departed from the mountains of Abarim, they crossed over to the plains of Moab, above the Jordan opposite Jericho. There they encamped from Beth-jeshimoth as far as Beth-shittim, in the flatter regions of the Moabites.

In the forty-second station, which is the final one, let us briefly recount what took place. While the people remained there, they were blessed, at God’s command, by Balaam the diviner, whom Balak son of Zippor had hired, and the curse was changed into praise. He hears the Lord’s words and makes them resound through his profane mouth:

“A star shall rise from Jacob, and a man shall arise from Israel; he shall strike the princes of Moab, lay waste the sons of Seth, and Edom shall be his inheritance.”

They fornicate with the daughters of Midian, and Phinehas son of Eleazar, zealous with the zeal of the Lord, pierces Zimri and the Midianite woman with a dagger. For this he received as a reward, for eternal remembrance, the shoulder of the sacrificial victim.

The people are counted again, and the Levites are also counted, so that after the wicked have been killed the new people of God may be enrolled. Five daughters of Zelophehad intervene, and by the Lord’s judgment receive an inheritance among their brothers; the female sex is not excluded from God’s possession.

Jesus succeeds Moses on the mountain and learns from the Law what he must offer spiritually in the Church: first, what is to be offered each day; then what is to be offered on the Sabbath, what on the Kalends, what at Passover, what at Pentecost, what at the New Moon [Col. 0824B] of the seventh month, what at the fast on the tenth day of that month, and what at the Feast of Booths, when the tabernacles are set up, on the fifteenth day of the aforementioned month.

The vows of wives and daughters are recorded, when made without the authority of fathers and husbands; the war against the Midianites, the death of the divine Balaam, the division of the booty, and the offering from it in the tabernacle of God are also recorded.

First Reuben and Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh, receive possession opposite the Jordan in the wilderness. For they had very many animals and had not yet come to the point where they could dwell with the temple. The people are instructed to destroy the idols in the holy land and to preserve nothing from their former habitation. The province once desired is described, and the inheritance of the two-and-a-half tribes is separated. The leaders of the tribes who are to enter the holy land are counted.

The Levites receive forty-two cities with their suburbs, extending one thousand paces around them—equal in number to the stations. Six other cities of refuge are added, three on this side of the Jordan and three beyond the Jordan, making forty-eight altogether. It is explained who among those seeking refuge should be received, who should be killed, and who should be kept until the death of the high priest.

Deuteronomy, the second law and the mediator of the Gospel, follows. There we briefly learn what Moses said to the people between Paran, Tophel, Laban, Hazeroth, and the gold-bearing places, after abandoning the most wretched Judas; namely, during an eleven-day journey from Horeb by the way of Mount Seir as far as Kadesh-barnea. He sings his final song, in which the Synagogue is most openly cast off and the Church joined to the Lord:

“He grew fat, grew thick, and became swollen, and the beloved kicked; and he forgot God his Savior” (Deuteronomy 32).

And again:

“They are a wicked generation, uneducated children. They provoked me to jealousy with that which was not God; they angered me with their carved images. And I will make them jealous through a people; against a foolish nation I will anger them.”

The children of Israel are blessed, and again the pitiable Judas is excluded among Simeon. Moses ascends Mount Nebo to the summit of Pisgah, which is opposite Jericho, and the Lord shows him all the land of Gilead as far as Dan and Naphtali, and Ephraim and Manasseh, and the whole land of Judah as far as the Great Sea toward the south; and the plain of Jericho, the whole city of palms, as far as Zoar [Col. 0825A].

Who can know such great mysteries? Who, standing at the borders of the Law and of this life, understands that he must always fight, and that complete victory is granted only if he has been in the plains? If, in Abel-shittim, which is interpreted as “the mourning of thorns,” he mourns ancient sins and the thorns that choked the seed of God’s word, of which the Prophet says: “I have been afflicted while a thorn is fixed in me” (Psalm 31).

Nor, I think, should we pass over the fact that some consider it necessary to inquire to which years the forty-two stations of the children of Israel in the wilderness, which are reckoned here in the final part of the Book of Numbers, should be assigned—whether to the years of that very long journey by which that people was led from Egypt to the land of promise.

But I think sufficient answer has been given in the letter of the presbyter Bede, which he wrote to Acca the bishop on this matter. We have judged that most of it should indeed be inserted in this work of ours in order to resolve this question. The camps or stations are properly assigned to only three years: the first, the second, and the fortieth after the departure from Egypt.

The first year contains twelve stations, distinguished in a definite order. The first, Rameses, was entered on the fifteenth day of the first month; the last, the wilderness of Sinai, was added on the first day of the third month and was not left for eleven continuous months, while the tabernacle was being built and the Law taught. Of these twelve stations, the Book of Exodus names only nine explicitly; the remaining three it passes over indiscriminately under the name of the wilderness of Sin, which is said to lie between Elim and Sinai.

The second year contains twenty-one stations. In the order of the narrative all of these are indiscriminately included under the name of the wilderness of Paran; only the first, second, and last—that is, the Graves of Lust, Hazeroth, and Kadesh—are distinguished by name. But in the catalogue of the stations, all are carefully shown, both in number and in name.

The first of these stations, namely, the Graves of Lust, was entered in the second month of that second year, on the twenty-second day of the month. For in the second year, as Scripture says, on the twentieth day of the second month, they moved their camp from the wilderness of Sinai; and, it says, the cloud rested in the wilderness of Paran. They set out from the mountain of the Lord for a journey of three days, until they came to the place of the station which, appropriately, received the name Graves of Lust because of the people’s desire for Egyptian meat.

But it is not stated on what day or in what month of that same year the last of these stations, Kadesh, was entered. Nevertheless, because it too was situated in the wilderness of Paran, and because it was added in that same year, this is not left unmentioned. For it is written:

“The people did not move from that place until Miriam was recalled; then they set out from Hazeroth and pitched their tents in the wilderness of Paran, where the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Send men to inspect the land of Canaan” (Numbers 12).

To prevent this from being thought to have been commanded and carried out at the station immediately after Hazeroth, and to make it understood instead as having been fulfilled at the last of those included under the name of the wilderness of Paran, let us see what is written below.

When the spies returned from the land after forty days, having traversed the whole region, they came to Moses and Aaron and the entire assembly of the children of Israel in the wilderness of Paran, which is at Kadesh. But in Deuteronomy, Moses himself speaks to the people in the first chapter:

“When you had come to Kadesh-barnea, I said to you: You have come to the mountain of the Amorites, which the Lord our God is about to give us. See the land which the Lord your God will give you; go up and possess it. And you all approached me and said: Send men to inspect the land, and so forth.”

That they approached this same station in the second year after departing from Egypt, although because of the sin of murmuring they deserved to turn back from it, wander in the wilderness for a long time afterward, and fall here and there, Moses testifies in what follows, saying:

“You remained at Kadesh-barnea for a long time. Then, setting out from there, we came into the wilderness that leads to the Red Sea, as the Lord had said to me, and we went around Mount Seir for a long time” (Deuteronomy 1).

And below:

“The time during which we journeyed from Kadesh-barnea until we crossed the torrent Zered was thirty-eight years, until the entire generation of fighting men from the camp was consumed, as the Lord had sworn” (Deuteronomy 2).

Zered is the name of a station—I mean one of those forty-two—but it is also the name of the torrent to which, as we read in the Book of Numbers, they came after crossing the twenty-eighth station, named Iye-abarim. “Leaving it,” he says, “they encamped at the Arnon, which is in the wilderness and projects into the borders of the Amorites.”

That this took place in the fortieth year is clear. This fortieth year, which is also the final one, contains ten stations along the very long road through the wilderness. The first is Kadesh of the wilderness of Sin, reached again after great labor: thirty-eight years earlier, as has been said, they had turned back from it and left it behind because their transgression demanded it.

Of it, it is written:

“The children of Israel and the whole multitude came into the wilderness of Sin in the first month, and the people remained at Kadesh. Miriam died there and was buried in the same place. When the people lacked water, they gathered together against Moses and Aaron,” and so forth, up to what is written: “This is the water of contradiction, where the children of Israel quarreled against the Lord, and he was sanctified among them” (Numbers 20).

It should be noted that Scripture reports this same Kadesh as being both in the wilderness of Paran and in the wilderness of Sin. From this it may be inferred that, according to the customary manner of naming places, the wilderness of Paran, where Kadesh is located, was also specifically called Sin.

But this Sin is not the same Kadesh which they crossed immediately after passing through the Red Sea, between Elim and Sinai; rather, it is entirely different and is written with different letters among the Hebrews.

The second station of that same fortieth year is Mount Hor, where Aaron died on the first day of the fifth month. The final station is the plain of Moab above the Jordan opposite Jericho, where they remained meditating on Deuteronomy until, after Moses’ death, they crossed the depths of the Jordan’s riverbed on dry ground under the leadership of Joshua, on the first day of the tenth month.

Thus the stations of the first year number twelve; those of the second, twenty-one; and in the final year the twenty-first station likewise is Kadesh, followed by nine others—forty-two altogether.

Here one must look more carefully at why the legislator, having written out the catalogue of three years with such diligence, preferred to pass over the remaining years in silence, so that the stations of so long a period, distinguished by no specific span of time, are connected in the continuous text of the narrative as though succeeding one another immediately.

“Having departed from Ebronah, they encamped at Ezion-geber. From there they set out and came into the wilderness of Sin, that is, Kadesh. Having departed from Kadesh, they encamped at Mount Hor” (Numbers 33).

Since the preceding passages, examined more carefully, show that in the second year of their journey they came from Ezion-geber to Kadesh, and that after the long winding course of thirty-eight years they came from that same Kadesh, reached again, to Mount Hor, understand that this was not written and arranged without purpose, but for the sake of a great mystery.

Without entering into a more subtle treatment, I think it should be understood morally that the sequence of these stations leads those liberated from Egyptian slavery to the land of promise, as blessed Jerome explains more fully in his book written on them. It is the high-reaching ascent of spiritual virtues, by which the Churches of Christ and every faithful soul, taken up in hope of freedom, hasten and strive to ascend from the valley of tears to the place appointed for them—that is, to see the God of gods in Zion—until, while progressing in the sound movement of our good works, we go “from strength to strength,” conducting through the wilderness of the world, under God’s leadership, camps and stations that are perfectly ordered and most worthy of God’s sight, while we thirst for him.

But whenever we are overcome by any plunderers and stray after taking a winding road, we cannot immediately ascend to the higher degrees of virtue. In the meantime, through repentance, we must gradually return upward from the lowest failures of our wretched mind, until, having performed worthy fruits of repentance, we come back to the very condition and summit of spiritual grace from which we had fallen.
