Thus we may begin again the interrupted journey of the virtues, having stripped off the old person with his deeds and put on the new, who was created according to God in righteousness, holiness, and truth.

The death and burial of sinful fathers in the wilderness, and the vigor of youth born and matured there, signify this: a youth worthy to enter the kingdom of the heavenly promise after conquering the river of death. Thus it comes about that, with the youth of our good conduct renewed like that of the eagle, we are able, when confronting such great and powerful evil spirits, to establish camps of heavenly progress—camps that are pleasing not only to the divine gaze but also most worthy of the writings and praise of spiritual fathers.

## CHAPTER IX. The Lord’s command to Moses concerning the destruction of idols

**(The same passage.)** The Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Command the children of Israel and say to them: When you have crossed the Jordan and entered the land of Canaan, destroy all the inhabitants of that region. Crush their calves and statues, and lay waste their high places, cleansing the land and dwelling in it; for I have given it to you as a possession, which you shall divide among yourselves by lot. To the greater number you shall give a wider portion, and to the fewer a narrower one. Each person shall receive an inheritance according to the lot that falls to him. The possession shall be divided among tribes and families.

What is meant by the Lord’s command that, when the Israelites have crossed the Jordan and entered the land of Canaan, they should destroy all the inhabitants of that region, crush the calves, and lay waste all the high places, cleansing the land of their habitation, except that after receiving baptism we should strive to uproot from our flesh every army of vices, cleansing the land of our heart so that, enriched by the gift of virtues, we may live in it healthfully?

He, therefore, has crossed the Jordan who washes away the crimes of his sins in the water of baptism. He enters the land of Canaan, that is, the land of promise, who acquires for himself the possession of virtues, so that, having put off the old person with his deeds, who is corrupted according to the desires of error, he may put on the new, who is renewed in the knowledge of God according to the image of the one who created him.

This person destroys all the inhabitants of that region when, pierced by fear of Christ, he strives to crush from his mind the evil spirits with their suggestions and the phantasms of vices. Of him the Psalmist says: “Blessed is he who shall seize and dash his little ones against the rock” (Psalm 136).

He lays waste the high places when he hastens to tame the pride of his flesh. Thus he possesses the clean land of his habitation by hereditary right when he keeps his flesh cleansed from the filth of sins and at rest from the battles of vices.

But the command that a wider possession be given to the greater number and a narrower one to the fewer, each according to the lot that falls to him, signifies that those who possess an abundance of virtues should hope for a breadth of rewards. Those, however, who are content with a small number of virtues should also be content with rewards corresponding to their merit.

Thus Paul, urging the Corinthians to generosity in almsgiving, says: “He who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and he who sows in blessing will reap from blessing eternal life” (2 Corinthians 9).

It follows:

**(The same passage.)** But if you are unwilling to kill the inhabitants of the land who remain, they will be like nails in your eyes and spears in your sides; they will oppose you in the land of your habitation, and whatever I had intended to do to them, I will do to you.

It is as though he were saying: Whoever does not take care to drive the spiritual enemies from his heart and does not strive to keep them from the boundaries of his actions and thoughts will be pierced by the nails of his self-restraint and will in no way be able to have rest in his conduct. Rather, from the just retributor he will deserve to experience not the comfort of friends but the destruction wrought by enemies.

## CHAPTER X. On the distribution of the land of promise to Israel by lot
### Chapter XXXIV

And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: “Command the children of Israel, and say to them: When you have entered the land of Canaan, and it has fallen to you as a possession by lot, it shall be bounded by these limits.”

For it is written in the Book of Numbers, in which the whole Promised Land is divided in brief words according to its four regions. The southern portion shall begin from the wilderness of Sin, which is beside Edom, and its boundary on the east shall be the Salt Sea. They shall go around the southern region by the ascent of Scorpion, so that they pass into Senna and reach the south as far as Cadesbarne. From there the boundaries shall go out to a settlement called Adar and extend as far as Asemona. The boundary shall run in a circuit from Asemona to the Brook of Egypt, and shall end at the shore of the Great Sea.

For this reason, in the final vision of Ezekiel it is said: “The southern region, that is, the south, from Thamar as far as the waters of [Col. 0829B] Masibor” (Ezek. ult.), that is, of contradiction. Cades also, and the brook as far as the Great Sea—which signifies the very broad extent of Sin, which is beside Edom—and to circle the boundary at the Red Sea, to pass by the ascent of Scorpion and through Senna and Cadesbarne, and through the court or settlement of Addar and Asemona, reaching as far as the Brook of Egypt, which flows into the sea beside the city of Rhinocorura.

This boundary of the southern region begins at Thamar, a city in the wilderness, which Solomon also built with marvelous works and which today is called Palmyra. In Hebrew the name is Thamar, which in our language means “palm,” and it extends as far as the waters of contradiction, Cades, which is undoubtedly in the wilderness; then the brook enters the Great Sea, the sea that stretches along the shores of Egypt and Palestine. [Col. 0829C]

The Book of Numbers continues: “The western region shall begin from the Great Sea, and shall be closed by the same boundary,” that is, from sea to sea. Namely, from the brook of Rhinocorura, which flows into the sea, as far as the place where Emath, a city of Syria, is situated. Ezekiel gives both the name and the region in this quarter, saying: “The region of the sea, the Great Sea, from the boundary in a straight line until you come to Emath,” which is now called Epiphania, its name having been changed by Antiochus, the most savage of tyrants. For his surname was Epiphanes.

“Then,” he says, “the boundaries of the northern region shall begin from the Great Sea, reaching as far as the highest mountain; from there you shall come to Emath, as far as the borders of Sedada. The boundaries shall go on as far as Zephrona and the settlement of Enan. These shall be the boundaries on the northern side.” [Col. 0829D]

The Hebrews say that the northern region begins from the Great Sea, which extends along the coasts of Palestine, Phoenicia, Syria, which is called κοίλη [“hollow,” i.e. Coele], and Cilicia, and stretches through Egypt toward Libya. As for the words “reaching as far as the highest mountain,” the Hebrews maintain that this signifies either Mount Anianus or Mount Taurus, the latter seeming more likely to us.

“The boundaries shall go on,” he says, “as far as Zephrona”; for this reason they today call a town of Cilicia Zipheum. What follows, “and the settlement of Enan,” for which Aserenan is written in Hebrew, meaning “court of the spring,” refers to the boundary of Damascus.

And from north to north is the northern region. “From there,” he says, “they shall mark out the boundaries toward the eastern region, from the settlement of Enan as far as Sephama. From Sephama the boundaries descend to Rebla, opposite the spring of Daphnim. From there they shall reach eastward to the Sea of Cenereth, and shall extend as far as the Jordan; finally they shall be closed by the most saline sea.” [Col. 0830A]

Thus, from the end of the northern region—that is, from the court of Enan—the boundaries extend as far as Sephama, which the Hebrews call Apamia. From Sephama the boundaries descend to Rebla, which is now called Antioch of Syria. And so that you may know that this Rebla signifies the city that is now most famous in Coele-Syria, the text continues: “opposite the spring,” which clearly signifies Daphnim; from this spring the aforementioned city receives a very abundant supply of water.

“From there,” he says, “the boundaries reach eastward to the Sea of Cenereth,” that is, to the Lake of Tiberias. It is called a sea, although its waters are fresh, according to the idiom of the Scriptures, which call collections of waters “seas.” “And they shall extend,” he says, “as far as the Jordan, and finally they shall be closed by the Dead Sea”; or, as others think, by the tongue of the Red Sea, on whose shore Achila is situated. [Col. 0830B]

And Moses commanded the children of Israel, saying: “This shall be the land that you shall possess by lot, and which the Lord commanded to be given to the nine tribes and a half-tribe.”

For the tribe of the children of Reuben, according to their families, and the tribe of the children of Gad, according to the number of their clans, and half the tribe of Manasseh—that is, two and a half tribes—received their portion beyond the Jordan, opposite Jericho, on the western side. In the earlier division of the lands beyond the Jordan, the land was divided by Moses among the two tribes, Reuben and Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh; within the Jordan, however, it was divided between Joshua son of Nun and Eleazar son of Aaron.

Judah possessed the southern region, and Ephraim and half the tribe of Manasseh the northern region. Later, when explorers had been sent from Shiloh through each tribe and a description of the land had been brought to Joshua and Eleazar, Benjamin received its possession beside Judah in the south and beside Ephraim and half the tribe of Manasseh. [Col. 0830C]

Second, the tribe of Simeon received its inheritance within the tribe of Judah, so that what was written concerning Levi and Simeon might be fulfilled: “I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel” (Gen. XLIX).

Third, Zebulun received Galilee, in which Mount Tabor is situated.

Fourth, Issachar received the region where Jezreel is, as far as the Jordan.

Fifth, Asher received the land as far as Mount Carmel, which overlooks the Great Sea, and Tyre and Sidon.

Sixth, Naphtali received the region in Galilee as far as the Jordan, where Tiberias is situated, formerly called Cenereth.

Seventh, Dan received the land as far as Joppa, where the towers of Achiloan are, and Emmaus, and Selebi, which is now called Nicopolis—although afterward we read that they took for themselves, after crossing through the territories of the other tribes, the city of Leshem in the tribe of Dan, which today is called Paneas.

This passage that we have before us contains a shadow of future good things. It follows, and is necessary, that everything which is described in the Law as though it concerned earthly matters should be understood as a shadow of heavenly good things; and that the entire inheritance of that land, which in Judea is called the holy land and the good land, should be an image of heavenly good things, of which, as we have said, the things called good on earth preserve the shadow and image. [Col. 0830D]

No one doubts that in the land of Judea every place, every mountain, every city, and every village is designated by particular names; nor is there any place at all without a name, but each thing is marked by its own proper designation—for example, the places in which the Canaanites were named, the Perizzites likewise in their places, and the Amorites or Hivites, or even the Hebrews.

Thus, according to the judgment of Paul, who says that earthly things are a shadow and likeness of heavenly things, perhaps in the heavenly regions there will likewise be distinctions among places according to their names. The word of God therefore describes in the divine Law the land of Judea, and these things must be referred to the image of heavenly realities.

The Apostle clearly declares that Jerusalem is in heaven, as is Mount Zion. It follows, therefore, that just as other cities, villages, and various regions are situated around earthly Jerusalem, so also that heavenly Jerusalem, according to the image of earthly things, has around it other cities and villages and different regions. In these the people of God and the true Israel are to be placed by Jesus the true one, whose image that Jesus son of Nave bore, when he is also to receive his inheritance through the distribution of lots—that is, through consideration of merits. [Col. 0831B]

If, then, the Lord now says in the distribution of the land, for example, that the boundaries of one tribe are these and those of another are different, this may be because the merits of those who obtain the inheritance of the kingdom of heaven are different. For this reason, in these tribes the distinction of boundaries is commanded to be observed, so that we may know that such differences of merit are to be discerned in each individual.

For example, someone may have lived so negligently that, on account of his faith, he deserves to be counted among the children of Israel, but because of the negligence of his conduct and the slothfulness of his deeds he must be reckoned among the tribe of Reuben or Gad, or half the tribe of Manasseh, and receive the lot of his inheritance not within the Jordan but beyond it.

Another person, however, may have rendered himself through amendment of life and conversion of purpose such that, according to reasons known only to God, he must be reckoned either in the tribe of Judah or in the tribe of Benjamin, in which Jerusalem itself and the temple and altar of God are situated; another in one tribe, and another in another.

In this way the things now written in the Book of Numbers may be a kind of shadowing of the future lot in heaven, at least for those who, through Jesus our Lord and Savior, are to receive, as we have said, the inheritance of the kingdom of heaven. [Col. 0831D]

There, I believe, even those privileges of the priests that are shadowed here will be carefully observed—those privileges by which the places near the cities and joined to the very walls are commanded to be set apart from the children of Israel.

Some think that the position of each star, and the assembly of stars, may be called or regarded as a city in heaven. I do not dare to determine this. For I see that every creature, although subjected in hope because of the one who subjected it, is waiting, and yet undoubtedly works toward freedom, the redemption of the children of Israel, and something more excellent and sublime.

If, therefore, as we have said, the Law contains a shadow of future good things, and those who serve in the Law serve the copy and shadow of heavenly things, then those who shall be worthy will dwell in heaven—now through a mirror and in an enigma, but then face to face.

If, therefore, by the logic of events and by the covenant of the promises, we must be transferred from earth to heaven, I think that in those heavenly places our Jesus the Lord, not without regard to merits, will establish each person in one or another part and dwelling-place of heaven.

For just as there is much difference on earth—for example, between living in fertile, productive places abounding in every good thing, where a temperate climate, human education, and liberal institutions are also present, and living in barren places, desolate through lack of resources, or scorched by heat, or numbed by cold and frost, or certainly in places where there are no laws but only savage and monstrous barbarism, where there is always war and never rest—so there will be something of this kind in those places also. Nothing that is a shadow of heavenly things will be altogether without meaning on earth. [Col. 0832B]

There will therefore, as we have said, be some city of refuge there also, and another in the wilderness, like Bosor in the inheritance of Reuben. Reuben is said to be a city in the wilderness. But another city must likewise be attained or received.

For if, when God was scattering the children of Adam, he established the boundaries of the nations “according to the number of the angels of God,” or, as we read in other copies, “according to the number of the children of Israel at the beginning of the world,” and if the children of that Adam were scattered according to what either their merits or the consideration of Adam himself required, what shall we say will happen when the last Adam, who was made not into a living soul but into a life-giving spirit, begins to scatter his children—not at the beginning but at the end of the world? And not as those who all died in Adam, but as those who are all made alive in Christ?

There will undoubtedly be a division and distribution of this kind, to be weighed not only according to the merits that are apportioned, but also according to the consideration of the last Adam, in whom all are said to be made alive.

But who among us is such that he may deserve to come from such a distribution to that lot of heavenly inheritance? Who will be so blessed that his lot will be Jerusalem’s, so that he may be where the temple of God is—or rather, so that he himself may be the temple of God?

Who is so blessed that he may celebrate the feast days there where the divine altar is kindled with perpetual fires? Who is so blessed that he may place his sacrifice and incense of sweetness upon that fire of which the Savior said, “I have come to cast fire” (Luke X)?

Who is so blessed that he may always celebrate Passover there, in the place that his Lord has chosen; that he may keep the day of Pentecost there, and the festival of propitiation, and the solemnity of Tabernacles—not now through the shadow, but in the very form and truth of the realities?

Who among us will be judged worthy of the choice of the blessed lot, when God begins to distribute the children of the last Adam—not one to whom he says, “You shall have authority over five cities” (Luke XIX), nor one to whom he says, “You shall have authority over ten cities” (Luke XIX), nor one to whom he says, “Enter into the joy of your lord” (ibid.), but one to whom he says, “You also, sit with me upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Luke XXII), and of whom he says, “Father, I will that where I am, these also may be with me” (John XVII)?

And that these also may be kings: where I am King of kings, I wish these also to have dominion, just as I am Lord of lords.

Blessed are those who shall attain this supreme blessedness. Blessed are those who shall climb to these heights of merit. And blessed is our God, who has promised these things to those who love him. These are truly numbered by those sacred numbers before God; indeed, they are those whose very hairs of the head have been numbered through Jesus Christ our Lord.

## Chapter XI. On the Cities of Refuge [Col. 0833B]

### Chapter XXXV

The Lord said to Moses: “Speak to the children of Israel, and say to them: When you have crossed the Jordan into the land of Canaan, determine which cities are to be places of protection for fugitives who have shed blood unwillingly. When a fugitive has fled into one of them, the kinsman of the slain person shall not be able to kill him until he has stood before the assembly and his case has been judged.

“Of those cities that are set apart as refuges for fugitives, three shall be beyond the Jordan and three in the land of Canaan, both for the children of Israel and for resident aliens and sojourners, so that anyone who has shed blood unwillingly may flee to them.”

How this was done is made clear by the book called Joshua son of Nave (chap. XX), when it records that Joshua, at the Lord’s command, appointed six cities of refuge for those who had committed homicide without intending it. These were: Cades in Galilee, in the hill-country of Naphtali; Sichem in the hill-country of Ephraim; and Cariath-arba, which is Hebron, in the hill-country of Judah. Beyond the Jordan, opposite the western region of Jericho, was the city of Bosor, situated in the plain wilderness, from the tribe of Reuben; Ramoth in Gilead, from the tribe of Gad; and Gaulon in Bashan, from the tribe of Manasseh. [Col. 0833C]

These cities were established for all the children of Israel and for the resident aliens who lived among them, so that anyone who had unknowingly struck and killed a person might flee to them and not die at the hand of the one who wished to avenge the shed blood, until he had stood before the people and presented his case.

Behold, you have the six cities of refuge. Enter them, if you please. And if perhaps, because of the awareness of your sins, you do not dare to enter those that are in the Promised Land—that is, in the Church—there is Bosor beside the Jordan in the wilderness, which is interpreted as “narrowness,” that is, a small or modest monastic cell. It will suit you very well that it belongs to the lot of Reuben, who himself unlawfully defiled his father’s bed.

There is also Ramoth from the lot of Gad, which is interpreted as “exalted death” or “vision of death.” Truly, penance ought to be called an exalted death, since through the mortification of the members a person is led to the heights of heaven, from which he had previously fallen. Or, in comparison with that humble death which generally threatens all flesh, it is reasonably called exalted, because it is far nobler to die through penance [Col. 0834A] than to be dissolved by this common death.

If we wish to understand it as the vision of death, it can be explained in this way: when we are established in penance and place before our eyes the torments of hell, we see the very form of death from which we are freed through the benefit of penance.

You must remember that you are doing penance in the city of the son of the slave-woman, because everyone who sins is a slave of sin; and, taking the form of a servant, you must humble yourself even unto death.

There is Gaulon within the borders of Manasseh, which is interpreted as “rolling about,” so that you may remember that you must roll about in sackcloth and ashes. And this is within the borders of Manasseh, which is interpreted as “forgetfulness,” so that you may forget the things you formerly did and stretch forward to what lies ahead.

Dwell here, therefore, so that through the narrowness of death and rolling about you may escape the wrath of the persecutor and find hope of salvation. [Col. 0834B]

Then, after you have done something beneficial in these places, you will also be able to reach Cades in the Promised Land, which is in Galilee and is interpreted as “holy.” When, in tribulation, you have cast off corruptions, access to the holy Church may also be granted to you, so that in the lot of Naphtali—whose name is said to mean “a vine let loose”—you may deserve to participate in the mystery of the Lord’s blood.

Nor is Hebron’s entrance closed to you. Hebron is interpreted as “union” or “marriage.” For your soul will return to its husband, that is, to the Spirit of God, from whom it had been widowed for a time because of its sins.

Thus one who has also attained the sixth city, Sichem, which our Joseph received as an inheritance because he was buried there, will be able to enter it. Sichem is interpreted as “shoulder” or “labor,” so that you may show that through the labor of penance you have been carried back from your error upon Christ’s shoulders, joined to the ninety-nine sheep and made the hundredth, because Sichem is said to have been purchased from foreigners for one hundred lambs.

## Chapter XII. On the Judgment of Homicides

### The Same Context

“If anyone through hatred has pushed a man, or thrown something at him by ambush; or, being his enemy, has struck him with his hand, and he has died, the striker shall be guilty of homicide. As soon as the kinsman of the slain person finds him, he shall kill him.

“But if he has done any of these things by accident, without hatred or hostility, and this has been established with the people hearing it, and the case has been examined between the striker and the blood-relative, the innocent man shall be freed from the hand of the avenger and restored by judgment to the city to which he had fled. He shall remain there until the great priest who has been anointed with holy oil dies.”

According to the historical sense, the meaning is clear: it condemns malice and makes provision for carelessness, since it is one thing to kill someone through wicked deliberation and calculated action, and another to bring danger upon one’s neighbor through accidental circumstance.

Allegorically, however, it indicates that if anyone through envy or hatred strikes another with the sword of malice and reduces him to the death of the soul, he himself will be liable to eternal death. Hence Truth itself says: “Whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it would be better for him that a millstone be hung around his neck and that he be sunk into the depth” (Matt. XVIII).

And John says: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer. And you know that every murderer does not have eternal life abiding in him” (1 John III).

According to the text of Exodus, such a person is commanded to be torn away from the Lord’s altar, because, being unworthy of the Lord’s mysteries, he is rightly removed from participation in the sacred altar and in no way deserves to be recalled to forgiveness through worthy penance.

But whoever has injured someone not through a desire for malice but through carelessness or ignorance has cities of refuge—namely, the Catholic Church—where, constraining himself through the narrowness of penance, he should remain throughout the whole time of the present life, devoting himself to good works. And if he places his hope in the death of the supreme priest, namely his Redeemer, he will undoubtedly be saved forever.

If the homicide is found outside the boundaries of the cities assigned to exiles, and is struck by the one who is the avenger of blood, the person who kills him shall be without guilt. For the fugitive ought to have remained in the city until the death of the priest. But after the priest has died, the homicide shall return to his own land. [Col. 0835B]

Thus the homicide who is found outside the boundaries of the cities assigned to exiles is killed without guilt, since the unrepentant sinner, and for that reason withdrawn from the fellowship of the saints and from the unity of the Church, is punished deservedly for his perversity.

The avenger of blood who kills him is innocent, because the sentence of the heavenly Judge—for through the assumption of flesh he is our neighbor—will be irreproachable when he strikes the one who neglected to be concerned for his own salvation.

The fugitive ought to have remained in the city until the death of the priest—that is, the penitent, remaining in the Catholic faith, ought to have hoped for forgiveness of his crime only through the death of the Mediator between God and humanity.

But after the priest has died, the homicide shall return to his own land: when the sinner, after penance has been worthily completed, deserves to receive the homeland of paradise.

For what does it mean that the homicide returns to absolution after the death of the supreme priest, except that the human race, which by sinning inflicted death upon itself, received absolution from guilt after the death of the true priest, namely Christ our Redeemer?

“Do not pollute the land of your dwelling, which is stained by the blood of the innocent. Nor can it be cleansed in any other way except by the blood of the one who shed another’s blood; and so your possession shall be cleansed, while I dwell among you.”

For he pollutes the land of his dwelling who performs bloody and wicked deeds, through which he does not fear to scandalize and spiritually kill his neighbors. But unless the blood of the one who shed another’s blood is poured out, the land of the possession will remain polluted, because unless the desires of the flesh are slain through confession of sins and worthy penance, the land of his body will in no way be cleansed. Nor will the Creator of all be able to dwell in his soul when he sees the squalor of a filthy way of life ruling there. [Col. 0835D]

The text continues: “For I am the Lord who dwell among the children of Israel.”

That is, among faithful men who behold God with their hearts, and among saints who obey his commands in all things. Concerning this it is written: “For God says, ‘I will dwell in them and walk among them; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people.’ Therefore, ‘Come out from their midst and be separate,’ says the Lord, ‘and do not touch what is unclean; and I will receive you. And I will be a father to you, and you shall be sons and daughters to me,’ says the Lord Almighty” (Isa. LII).

## Chapter XIII. On the Daughters of Zelophehad, That They Should Marry Their Near Relatives

### Chapter XXXVI

The heads of the families of Gilead, the sons of Machir, the son of Manasseh, from the clans of the sons of Joseph, also approached and spoke before the leaders of Israel. They said:

“The Lord commanded you, our lord, to divide the land by lot among the children of Israel, and to give to the daughters of Zelophehad our brother the possession due to their father. If they marry men from another tribe, their possession will follow them; and, transferred to another tribe, it will be diminished from our inheritance.

“Thus it will happen that when the jubilee arrives—that is, the fiftieth year of remission—the distribution by lots will be confused, and the possession of some will pass to others.”

What is meant by the fact that the heads of the families of Gilead, the sons of Machir, the son of Manasseh, the son of Joseph, spoke to Moses on behalf of the daughters of Zelophehad, asking him to take care that the lot of their possession not be transferred to another tribe if they married men of another tribe, except that devout thoughts ought to take forethought lest the possession of good merits pass into the dominion of strangers, but remain perpetually with its rightful heir?

For this reason they think that Moses—that is, the Law—must be consulted, so that from it they may learn how to become perpetual possessors of what belongs to them. Their names express this through their interpretation.

Gilead is interpreted as “heap of testimony”; Machir, “selling”; Manasseh, “forgetting”; Joseph, “increasing”; and Zelophehad, “shadow of fear.”

Thus the heads of the families of Gilead, the sons of Machir, the son of Manasseh, from the clan of the daughters of Joseph, speak on behalf of the daughters of Zelophehad when the thoughts and counsels of a devout mind, ordered according to the testimonies of the sacred Scriptures, contend for the faithful soul, which sells the labor of the present life for a future reward; and, forgetting the things that are behind, stretches forward to what lies ahead, so that through the increase of good works it may obtain eternal rewards.

It was said above that the five daughters of Zelophehad—that is, “the shadow of fear”—signified outward works, which are properly carried out through the five senses. [Col. 0836D]

It is necessary, therefore, that those who now labor in good works under the shadow of the present life should strive through the fear of God to preserve them, lest they lose the labor they have expended.

The heads of Gilead therefore fear that their possession may be transferred to another tribe. So it is necessary for every faithful person carefully to foresee how the works he performs may be preserved for his salvation, lest perhaps, if they are undertaken with a perverse intention, they be seized by alien possessors—that is, by evil spirits.

The worker’s intention is perverse when he spends uselessly, out of desire for earthly things, the works that he ought to have performed with a view to eternal recompense. It is necessary that what has been taken away from him be held by an alien possessor, when an evil spirit hastens to draw such things to its own side because of the negligent worker.

Hence Truth itself says to his disciples in the Gospel: “Take heed that you do not perform your righteousness before men, in order to be seen by them” (Matt. VI). “Otherwise you will have no reward with your Father who is in heaven.”

Moses answered the children of Israel and, at the Lord’s command, said: “The tribe of the children of Joseph has spoken rightly. And this is the law that the Lord has proclaimed concerning the daughters of Zelophehad: Let them marry whom they wish, provided that they marry men of their own tribe, so that the possession of the children of Israel may not pass from tribe to tribe.

“For all the men shall take wives from their own tribe and clan, and all the women shall take husbands from the same tribe, so that the inheritance may remain within the families and the tribes may not be mixed with one another, but remain as they were separated by the Lord.”

Paul the Apostle wrote similar things to the Corinthians when he discussed marriage: “A woman is bound by the law as long as her husband lives. But when her husband has died, she is freed from the law of her husband. Let her marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord” (1 Cor. VII).

Moses therefore commanded that the daughters of Zelophehad marry whom they wished, provided that they married men of their own tribe, so that the possession of the children of Israel might not pass from tribe to tribe.

So also the Apostle commands that a woman marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord—that is, a Catholic man—lest she lose the possession of good works and a righteous life if she joins herself to a pagan or a heretic.

According to the allegorical sense, a woman—that is, a pure intention—may through good action join herself to whatever labor she wishes, provided that she preserves Christian piety and religion in all things, lest she suffer loss of the work for which she ought to have hoped to possess an eternal inheritance if she joins herself to something alien—that is, to error.

And the daughters of Zelophehad did as they had been commanded. Maalah, Tirzah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Noah married the sons of their paternal uncle, from the family of Manasseh, who was the son of Joseph. And the possession that had been allotted to them remained in the tribe and family of their father. [Col. 0838A]

The names of these women—that is, the daughters of Zelophehad—may not inappropriately be transferred to the sense stated above. For Maalah is interpreted as “weakness”; Tirzah, “pleasing”; Hoglah, “this solemnity” or “calf”; Milcah, “its king”; and Noah, “movement.”

Whoever strives above all to possess within himself the virtue of humility, and, in his weaknesses, is pleased in accordance with the Apostle’s teaching, celebrates a solemnity and offers acceptable gifts to God; and, being cautious, as king and ruler of his own way of life, is moved forward by the progress of the virtues.

According to the Psalmist: “They shall go from strength to strength; the God of gods shall be seen in Zion” (Ps. LXXXIII).

The daughters of Zelophehad therefore married the sons of their paternal uncle from the family of Manasseh, who was the son of Joseph, when any one of the number of those who believed from among the Jews joins himself to a teacher who believes from among the Gentiles, so that, joined to his instruction, he may be able to beget children—that is, to display works of piety.

For teachers chosen from among the Gentiles may in a certain sense be designated by the name “paternal uncle,” because they are brothers of the holy preachers who were established in Judea.

There must be no schism in spiritual kinship, where there is one faith in the profession of belief. The Savior says to his disciples in Matthew XXIII: “Do not call anyone your father on earth. For one is your Father, who is in heaven. But you are all brothers.”

And elsewhere he says: “I have other sheep that are not of this fold. I must bring them also, and they will hear my voice; and there will be one flock and one shepherd” (John X).

Thus the possession is lawfully preserved in the same tribe, when every devout action is energetically offered in the Catholic Church for the love of Christ and in the service of God. The end of this labor is an everlasting reward, which may the almighty Father deign to grant to his faithful through our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.

[Col. 0837C]

### (Year 834.) Four Books of the Exposition on Deuteronomy by Blessed Rabanus Maurus, Abbot of Fulda and Archbishop of Mainz

## Preface to Freculph, Bishop of Lisieux

[Col. 0837]

To the devout father Freculph, Rabanus, the least of the servants of the Lord, sends greetings.

Having completed, in obedience to your commands, the earlier books of the Law, I finally came to consider the Deuteronomy of Moses, so that, agreeing in some measure with your holy will, I might search out its spiritual mysteries and gather the sayings of the Fathers into a single volume.

But since I did not find a proper exposition of this book by anyone, I had to draw upon the completed expositions of the preceding books in order to unravel the questions of this one. These things, however, which I found newly inserted by the Lawgiver, I have taken care to explain, with the generosity of divine grace, according to the modest capacity of my little intellect, however small that may be.

Deuteronomy also, as blessed Jerome says in one of his letters to a friend, is the second law and a foreshadowing of the evangelical law. Thus it contains the earlier things in such a way that everything is nevertheless new.

For this reason the matter requires laborious resolution: namely, that the old things should be arranged historically in such a way that all things may be shown spiritually to be new, and that the letter of the Law may disclose through figures the mysteries that the sacred text of the Gospel contains within itself.

Therefore, holy brother, we especially need your assistance in this matter, so that through constant prayers you may obtain from the almighty Father that what you command us, sluggish as we are, to do for your benefit and that of your people may be granted to us through his help—the one who gives generously to all and does not reproach anyone, and who promised his faithful ones in the Gospel, saying:

“Ask, and it shall be given to you; seek, and you shall find; knock, and it shall be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives, and whoever seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it shall be opened.”

I therefore implore your petitions because I believe that, through your holy merits, they are most acceptable to God.

For our part, in this very matter, though our prayers are not worthy, we nevertheless persist in them with the greatest humility, asking that the heavenly Judge who dwells on high and regards the humble in heaven and on earth, who raises the needy from the dust and lifts the poor from the dung heap, may deign, through the generosity of his gift, to grant us some small portion of his gifts, so that we may be able to fulfill his service in his holy Church, to his praise and for our salvation.

Behold, as you requested, you have the Pentateuch of Moses, explained to some extent with its mysteries by a spiritual pen—the same five words by which the Apostle boasts that he speaks in the church (1 Cor. XIV).

Be a devout investigator of the Law and a faithful executor of the commands of the Most High, so that, just as you are a sharer in their order, you may also be a fellow worker with the holy apostles.

Remember the teacher of the Gentiles and the exhortation with which, instructing his disciple, he says:

“Command and teach these things. Let no one despise your youth, but be an example to the faithful in word, in conduct, in charity, in faith, in chastity. Until I come, attend to reading, exhortation, and doctrine. Do not neglect the grace that is in you, which was given to you through prophecy with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery. Meditate on these things; be occupied with them, so that your progress may be evident to all. Pay attention to yourself and to doctrine; persist in them. For by doing this you will save both yourself and those who hear you.”

May the Most High grant that you do and fulfill these things for your salvation and that of many. Farewell, holy Father, and always remember your Maurus in your sacred prayers.

## The Exposition on Deuteronomy Begins. Book One

[Col. 0839]

### Chapter One [Col. 0839C]

The words of Moses which he spoke to Israel beyond the Jordan, in the plain wilderness, after the killing of Sihon and Og, kings of the Amorites.

## (Chapter I)

“These are the words that Moses spoke to all Israel beyond the Jordan, in the Arabah, opposite the Red Sea, between Paran and Tophel, Laban and Hazeroth, where there is an abundance of gold, eleven days from Horeb by the way of Mount Seir, as far as Kadesh-barnea, in the fortieth year, in the eleventh month, on the first day of the month.”

The beginning of this book thus appears, in a certain sense, to be both the title and the index of the entire work, because it identifies the person who performed the work and the work that was performed, and at the same time includes the place and time at which it occurred. Hence, by grace, it demonstrates not only the very name of the book but also the beginning of the New Testament. For Deuteronomy, which in Latin is interpreted as “the second law,” signifies the Gospel, which, after the establishment of the Old Testament, mystically expounds and explains all the same sacraments according to their spiritual meaning.

The Book of Deuteronomy is therefore a repetition of the preceding four books of the Law. For while those books contain their own proper subjects, this one nevertheless repeats everything. It too possesses innumerable sacraments of its own, some of which, insofar as divine grace grants us the ability according to the sayings of the Fathers who came before us, we have decided to explain for the exercise of the reader.

“These are the words,” he says, “that Moses spoke to all Israel.” Here some think that a question must be raised: since Moses is recognized as the author of this book, how does he speak of himself as though of another? For he says that Moses himself spoke these words. But it must be understood that it is customary for the writers of sacred history to speak of themselves as though of another person. Thus, in the Book of Numbers, the same Moses wrote: “Now Moses was a man exceedingly meek, above all the men who dwelt upon the earth” [Num. 12:3]. So too, in the Book of Job, Job himself says at the beginning of his work: “There was a man in the land of Uz whose name was Job. And that man was simple and upright, fearing God and departing from evil” [Job 1:1]. John likewise says of himself in his Gospel: “This is the disciple who bears witness concerning these things and wrote them, and we know that his testimony is true” [John 21:24].

But since these things are so, let us see what Moses signifies, who spoke to all Israel beyond the Jordan, in the Arabah, opposite the Red Sea, in the places that are subsequently mentioned. It is evident to all that Moses bears the type of the old Law, since he taught the people beyond the Jordan, in the Arabah. The Jordan, because the Savior was baptized in it, bears the type of baptism. Moses taught Israel beyond the Jordan because, before the institution of baptism and the grace of the New Testament, the Law instructed the earlier people concerning the commandments of God. And it did so in the Arabah—that is, in the barrenness of the carnal people, who did not know how to produce the spiritual fruit of virtues.

It was opposite the Red Sea because the hard heart of the reprobate in no way believed that the washing away of sins took place in the blood of Christ.

“Between Paran and Tophel and Laban and Hazeroth.” These four places signify divine mysteries through the interpretation of their names. Paran is interpreted as “increased”; Tophel as “insipidity”; Laban as “whitening”; and Hazeroth as “courts.”

The people to whom the divine Law was expounded were indeed increased, both in the multitude of human beings and also in the gift of the Law and the prophets, which divine mercy bestowed upon them. But they were insipid, because they did not love the salt of spiritual wisdom. They were also whitened by the ceremonies of the Law and by empty purifications, which they believed they possessed by the Law’s command. They may rightly also be called “courts,” that is, a people, because through the divine Scriptures they were prepared for entry into faith.

Therefore many of them, taught by the Law and instructed by the utterances of the prophets at the coming of our Savior, were able to arrive more easily at belief in that same mediator between God and human beings, because they had recognized him beforehand in the sacred writings. Hence Philip says to Nathanael in the Gospel: “We have found him of whom Moses in the Law and the prophets wrote: Jesus, the son of Joseph, from Nazareth.” And Nathanael said to him: “Can anything good come from Nazareth?” Philip said to him: “Come and see” [John 1:45–46].

The statement that there is a great abundance of gold in the place where the repetition of the Law took place signifies that the books of the Law and the prophets contain manifold mysteries and the spiritual treasury of divine wisdom. This is plainly evident to those who seek devoutly and understand rightly.

But what does it signify that the Law itself was expounded through Moses over eleven days, except the fall of the Jewish people through their transgression of the commandments of the Decalogue—from Mount Horeb, by way of Mount Seir, as far as Kadesh-barnea? For the Law began at Horeb, that is, at the mountain of God. Passing through Seir—that is, through the hairy and filthy people of the Jews, covered with every vice—it reached Kadesh-barnea.

Kadesh-barnea is interpreted as “changed,” “chosen,” or “notable,” signifying that through the Gospel the carnal practice of the old Law has been nobly changed into spiritual observance.

“For all these things,” as the Apostle says, “happened to them in figure. And they were written for our correction, upon whom the ends of the ages have come” [1 Cor. 10:11]. And the Savior says in the Gospel: “I have not come to abolish the Law, but to fulfill it. For not one iota or one stroke will pass from the Law until all things have taken place” [Matt. 5:17–18].

What, then, do the forty years signify figuratively, after which the sons of Israel, having completed their arduous journey, crossed into the land of promise? Through these forty years, surely, the entire period of the world is signified, during which the Church lives amid labors and perilous temptations, hoping for what it does not see through patience, until it reaches the promised homeland of eternal blessedness.

For this reason also the Lord fasted for forty days and was tempted for forty nights in the wilderness. Since his body is the Church, it must suffer temptations and labors in this world until the time arrives when, after temptations, it receives consolations.

“In the eleventh month,” he says, “on the first day of the month, Moses spoke to the children of Israel everything that the Lord had commanded him to say to them.” What the number eleven signifies has already been stated above. But we must consider what is mystically indicated by the statement that Moses spoke to Israel on the first day of that same month.

Just as the transgression of the Law was expressed in the eleventh month, so on the first day of the month the lawgiver’s watchful intention to teach is shown. For once the disobedient people no longer feared to transgress by receiving the commandments, he immediately endeavored, through the light of preaching and correction, to make the Lord’s will known to them, and never ceased to correct them and summon them to better things by words and examples.

“After he struck down Sihon, king of the Amorites, who dwelt in Heshbon, and Og, king of Bashan, who remained in Ashtaroth and in Edrei, beyond the Jordan in the land of Moab.”

It should also be noted that, after the two Amorite kings had been killed—namely, Sihon, the king who dwelt in Heshbon, and Og, the king of Bashan—the Law is recapitulated and the people instructed. Once all stumbling blocks have been removed and the throngs of vices overcome, instruction is appropriately pursued and the light of faith worthily opened to those who desire it.

Although the historical event is recognized in these kings, a spiritual meaning is nevertheless supplied through the qualities and interpretations of their names. Sihon is interpreted as “useless sprout” or “temptation of the eyes.” Through him the devil is represented, for he transforms himself into an angel of light and, through heresy or schism, falsely presents himself as truth in order to deceive the unwary.

The Amorites—that is, “those who make bitter”—have him as their king. For unless some imitation of truth comes first, there are no “bitter ones,” no schisms of those who embitter the Church. This king is killed in each person when that person condemns imitation and loves the truth.

Og, however, the king, is interpreted as “closure,” while Bashan means “confusion.” The devil always strives to close the way to the Lord by setting up his idols, so that people will not believe in Christ. Closure therefore comes first as king, and confusion follows as the people. For those whom he has now closed off from believing in Christ will all be confounded when Christ appears.

Sihon is said to have dwelt in Heshbon because the devil, the root of all vices, mingles with human thoughts and encircles the mind with useless anxieties, lest it utter words of truth and perform works of piety. Heshbon is interpreted as “thought” or “a girdle of sorrow.”

Scripture likewise records that Og, king of Bashan, remained in Hazeroth and in Edrei. What does Hazeroth mean except “vestibules”? Or what do Achia and Edrai signify—namely, “the cleansing of evils”—except unbelief together with wicked works?

For the devil strives to ensure that all whose king he is never enter through the door of faith, but remain outside in unbelief and persist always in wicked works.

“Moses began to explain the Law and said:”

## Chapter II. Remembrance of the words of God, by which he commands Israel to go into the land of Canaan, and concerning the appointment of the seventy elders among the people

“Then the Lord our God spoke to us in Horeb, saying: ‘You have stayed long enough on this mountain. Turn and come to the mountain of the Amorites and to all the neighboring places, the Arabah, the mountains and the lower regions opposite the south, and the seacoast, the land of the Canaanites and Lebanon, as far as the great river Euphrates,’ and so forth.”

In the Book of Numbers he narrates the departure of the children of Israel from the wilderness of Sinai, but he relates the Lord’s command to Moses concerning that same journey. Rather, he tells of the cloud that covered the tabernacle and, whenever it was time to depart, withdrew from the tabernacle. Going before them until they came to the place of the encampment where the tabernacles were to be set up, it then stood above that place.

For thus it is written: “In the second year, in the second month, on the twentieth day of the month, the cloud was lifted from the tabernacle of the covenant. And the children of Israel set out according to their companies from the wilderness of Sinai, and the cloud rested in the wilderness of Paran” [Num. 10:11–12].

It is clear, however, that the whole journey was arranged by divine command, even though this is not mentioned where the same journey is narrated. The present book, with Moses as narrator, makes clear that everything happened in this way. The Book of Numbers also demonstrates the same thing elsewhere, where it says: “At the command of the Lord they pitched their tents, and at his command they took them down” [Num. 9:18].

“And I said to you at that time: ‘I cannot bear you alone, because the Lord your God has multiplied you, and today you are as numerous as the stars of heaven. May the Lord, the God of your fathers, add many thousands to this number and bless you as he has spoken. I cannot alone bear your affairs, your burden, and your quarrels. Choose from among yourselves wise and experienced men whose conduct is approved in your tribes, so that I may set them as your leaders,’” and so forth.

The division of authority is discussed in Exodus before the Israelites reached Mount Sinai, and it is related that Jethro, the priest of Midian and Moses’ kinsman, gave Moses this advice. Hence it may be asked how the two accounts agree, both in their circumstances and in their timing.

I think the matter can be resolved in this way: what is written here as having been said by Moses to the people at that time—“I cannot bear you alone”—does not refer specifically to the time when they were departing from Horeb, but to the entire period during which, after departing from Egypt, they were dwelling in the wilderness. Moses persuaded the people to do what he here says he persuaded them to do, not from his own invention, but after accepting the counsel of his kinsman.

Here we must consider how carefully the statement in Scripture is to be observed: “My son, do not let your activities be many; even here there is enough” [Eccli. XI]. We must then consider the words of Jethro when he gave Moses his advice. He says: “Now therefore listen to me, and I will give you counsel, and God will be with you” [Exod. 18:19].

Here it seems to me to be signified that a mind excessively absorbed in human affairs is, in a certain way, emptied of God. This happens all the more fully as the mind extends itself more freely toward heavenly and eternal things.

## Chapter III. Concerning the twelve scouts sent into the land of Canaan, and concerning the Lord’s indignation against Israel

“And you all approached me and said: ‘Let us send men to inspect the land and report by which road we ought to go up and toward which cities we should proceed.’ And when the proposal had pleased me, I sent twelve men from among you, one from each tribe.”

It is also written in the Book of Numbers that the Lord said to Moses that men should be sent to inspect the land of Canaan. Although what is written here in Deuteronomy and what is read in the Book of Numbers concerning this matter may appear different, the meaning is easy to understand: the people first spoke to Moses about sending scouts, and Moses, referring the matter to the Lord’s counsel, then received from him the command to send men who would explore the land of Canaan.

“When they had gone and ascended into the mountains, they came as far as the Valley of the Cluster. After inspecting the land, they took some of its fruits to display its fertility, brought them to us, and said: ‘The land that the Lord our God is going to give us is good.’ But you were unwilling to go up. Disbelieving the word of the Lord our God, you murmured in your tents and said: ‘The Lord hates us. That is why he brought us out of the land of Egypt: to deliver us into the hands of the Amorites, to destroy us,’” and so forth.

Twelve scouts were sent from the children of Israel to inspect the land that had been promised to them. After forty days they returned and gave differing reports. Ten of them drove the people to despair, so that they wished to reject Moses, choose another leader, and return to Egypt. The other two brought a good report and urged the people to remain in faith, saying: “If God loves us, he will bring us into this land” [Deut. XVIII].

But the people, driven headlong by the despair of unbelief, rushed to stone those who brought the good report. The majesty of the Lord protected them in the cloud, and the Lord said to Moses: “I will strike them with death and destroy them, but I will make you and your father’s house into a great and numerous nation, greater than this one” [Num. 14:12].

The Lord made this great threat not to show that the divine nature was subject to suffering or the defect of anger, but so that through it both Moses’ love for the people and God’s goodness, which surpasses every mind, might become known.

Mystically, however, the twelve scouts sent to explore the fertile land, who terrified the people so that they would not believe that they could receive the promised land from the Lord, represented the judgment of the scribes and Pharisees. For just as those men were sent through Moses to investigate the fertility of the land carefully, so these others were sent through the Law and the prophets to observe the Lord’s coming through the investigation of the Scriptures.

In that land there was the earth—that is, the holy flesh—in which they could attain the kingdom of God, the abundance of spiritual fruits, and eternal life. But just as those scouts terrified the people through despair, so these scribes and Pharisees persuaded the Jewish people not to believe in Christ. They desired to return to the Egypt of this world, rejecting the manna of faith and seeking the black pots of sins, the rotten onions of blasphemies, and the melons withered by the corruption of vices and lusts.

The cluster of grapes that the two bearers brought from the land of promise on a piece of wood was a cluster hanging from wood. It clearly signified Christ, promised to the nations through the wood of the cross, brought forth from the land of Mary his mother, from an earthly stock according to the flesh.

The two bearers who walked beneath the burden of that cluster represent the two peoples. The first, the Jewish people, was blind and turned away, ignorant of the grace hanging before it and weighed down by the burden of the one suspended upon the wood. To this people the judgment is applied: “Let their eyes be darkened, so that they may not see, and bend their backs continually” [Ps. 68:24].

The second, who came behind, represented the people of the nations. Because it believes and has Christ before its eyes, it sees him while always bearing him. Like a servant following his lord and a disciple following his teacher, it follows him, as the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him take up his cross and follow me” [Matt. XVIII].

This is the cluster that poured out, for our salvation, the wine of his blood through the crushing of the cross, and offered the cup of his passion to the Church. This is the cluster that the accompanying pomegranate-grace followed upon the shoulders.

The Church, as a mother, contains within herself a multitude of peoples represented by the number of the seeds. She bears the redness of Christ’s blood as a seal, with the seeds distinguished even within it, and, as the Apostle says, diverse charismata and gifts of the Spirit distributed by grace.

Because the unbelievers judged themselves unworthy of all these things, they did not deserve to receive the land of Christ’s flesh, flowing with milk and honey. The servants of Christ—that is, the Christian people—have obtained it through faith. Concerning its teaching the Church says every day: “How sweet are your words to my palate, sweeter than honey to my mouth!” [Ps. 119:103].

The fig that they brought from the land of promise along with the cluster represented the Law, as we are taught by examples from the Gospel. The cluster likewise plainly shows the figure of the Savior, just as the Church says concerning Christ in the Song of Songs: “My brother is like a cluster of henna” [Song 1:14]. For neither can Christ exist without the Law, nor the Law without Christ.

“Nor is the Lord’s indignation against the people surprising, since he was also angry with me because of you and said: ‘You too shall not enter there, but Joshua son of Nun, your minister, shall enter in your place. Encourage him and strengthen him, and he shall divide the land by lot among Israel,’” and so forth.

It may be asked how Moses says that the Lord, because of them, told him: “You too shall not enter there”—that is, into the land of promise—when the Book of Numbers reads as follows: “And the Lord said to Moses and Aaron: ‘Because you did not believe in me, so as to sanctify me before the children of Israel, you shall not bring these people into the land that I will give them’” [Num. XXVII].

The following statement seems in some way to resolve the question: “This is the water of contradiction, where the children of Israel quarrelled against the Lord, and he was sanctified among them.” The quarrel and rebellion of the people were the cause of the Lord’s anger and of the punishment inflicted both upon the people and upon Moses and Aaron.

It seems to me that in Miriam the prophecy died; in Moses and Aaron an end was imposed upon the Law and the Jewish priesthood. For neither did they themselves wish to ascend into the land of promise nor lead the believing people out of the wilderness of this world—unless it were by Jesus alone, that is, by our Savior, the Son of God.

At the thirty-third encampment, because of the water of contradiction, Moses offended the Lord and was forbidden to cross the Jordan. Disturbed by the murmuring of the people, he struck the rock with his staff in doubt, as though God could not bring water forth from the rock, although he had already done so.

What, then, does the faith of Moses suggest here, since it had wavered over the bringing forth of water from the rock, except that we should rightly understand this too as a prophecy concerning Christ? For although Moses bears one person or another in the sacred Scriptures according to what is being signified, at this point he bore the person of the Jewish people placed under the Law and represented it prophetically.

Just as Moses, striking the rock with his staff, doubted God’s power, so that people, held under the Law given through Moses, did not believe Christ to be the power of God when they fastened him to the wood of the cross. But just as water flowed from the struck rock for those who were thirsty, so the wound of the Lord’s passion became life for believers.

We have concerning this matter a most excellent and faithful apostolic utterance, spoken when the Apostle said: “The rock was Christ” [1 Cor. 10:4].

God therefore commands that this flesh, which despaired concerning Christ’s birth, die upon the height of Christ himself, when he commands Moses’ death to take place on the mountain. For just as Christ is the rock, so Christ is also the mountain. The rock is humble strength; the mountain is lofty greatness. For just as the Apostle says, “The rock was Christ,” so the Lord himself says: “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden” [Matt. 5:14], calling himself the mountain and asserting that his faithful, founded upon the glory of his name, are the city.

The wisdom of the flesh lives when, like a rock that has been struck, Christ’s humility is despised upon the cross. “Christ crucified is a stumbling block to the Jews and folly to the nations” [1 Cor. 1:23]. But the wisdom of the flesh dies when, like the height of a mountain, Christ is recognized as exalted. For to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God [1 Cor. 1:24].

## Chapter IV. Concerning the prohibition against the Israelites’ fighting the Moabites and Edomites

“When you had armed yourselves and were going toward the mountain, the Lord said to me: ‘Say to them: Do not go up, and do not fight. For I am not with you, lest you fall before your enemies.’ I spoke, and you listened; but you opposed the Lord’s command and, swollen with pride, went up toward the mountain. Then the Amorite who dwelt in the mountains came out and, meeting you, pursued you as bees are accustomed to pursue. And you fell from Seir as far as Hormah,” and so forth.

This statement strikes at human pride, which presumes upon its own strength and does not trust in God’s power. The Amorites, then, who, as we said above, are interpreted as “those who make bitter,” are spiritual enemies who dwell in the mountains of pride and kill those who presume upon themselves.

From Seir as far as Hormah—that is, because one does not fear being stained by the squalor and filth of vices, one must be handed over to the fires of Gehenna according to one’s former merits. For the heavenly powers of wickedness, which desire our destruction and wish to entangle us in earthly desires, if we persist in sins and do not cease ascending the mountains of pride, will cut us down with fiery arrows and lead us to perpetual anathema.

Therefore, contrary to the Pelagians, we must not presume upon our own power without the grace of God. Rather, considering our weakness, we should humbly believe that what is decreed by the Lord’s mouth must be obeyed and followed in all things. In this way all our enemies become subject to us, and by the Lord’s mercy we shall prevail in reaching the joys of the heavenly homeland promised to us.

### (Chapter II)

“Then the Lord said to me: ‘Do not fight against the Moabites, and do not engage them in battle, for I will give you nothing of their land, because I have given Ar to the sons of Lot as a possession. The Emim were its first inhabitants, a great and powerful people, so tall that they were thought to be giants, like the descendants of Anak. The Moabites call them Emim.’”

Ar is the metropolis of the Moabites, situated on the bank of the Arnon. It was once possessed by the ancient Emim and later retained by the sons of Lot, that is, by the Moabites, after they had overthrown its inhabitants. It is still shown today on the summit of that mountain. A torrent also descends through steep ravines and flows into the Dead Sea.

Ar is interpreted as “he has raised up,” and Emim as “terrible ones.” They signify spiritual enemies who continually stir up quarrels and contentions and prepare weapons of wickedness against God’s servants.

The Enakim too, who were descended from the stock of Anak and equaled giants in stature, similarly signify spiritual wickedness, as their name testifies. For Enak is interpreted as “a necklace upon a lofty neck.” Spiritual enemies, raised up by the arrogance of pride, attribute all the preparations of their wickedness to their own power.

They are therefore easily overcome by those who trust not in their own strength but in God’s power. Such people can say with the Psalmist: “The Lord is my strength and my praise, and he has become my salvation” [Ps. 118:14].

The Horites formerly dwelt in Seir. After they had been expelled and destroyed, the sons of Esau dwelt there, just as Israel did in the land of its possession, which God gave it.

Seir is a mountain in the land of Edom, where Esau lived in the region of Gebal. Because Esau was hairy and shaggy, the region received the name Seir, that is, “hairy ones.” The Horite lived in these places before him; Chedorlaomer killed him. Isaiah also mentions Mount Seir in his vision concerning Edom.

These Horites and the other nations whom those descended from the seed of the patriarchs overcame mystically signify evil spirits or various vices. Those can rightly overcome them who follow the footsteps, teachings, and examples of the holy Fathers and genuinely wage spiritual warfare under Christ the King.

Concerning such enemies the Apostle says: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” [Eph. 6:12].

## Chapter V. Remembrance of the journey from Kadesh-barnea to the crossing of the Zered, namely, thirty-eight years

“Therefore we arose to cross the torrent of Zered, and we came to it. The time during which we travelled from Kadesh-barnea to the crossing of the torrent of Zered was thirty-eight years, until the entire generation of men of war was consumed from the camp, as the Lord had sworn. His hand was against them, so that they perished from the midst of the camp.”

Kadesh-barnea is a place in the wilderness adjoining the city of Petra in Arabia. Miriam and Moses died there; there, after the rock was struck, water was given to the thirsty people. Even to the present day Miriam’s tomb is shown there. The leaders of Amalek were also killed there by Chedorlaomer.

That the same people came in the second year after their departure from Egypt into the wilderness of Paran, which is Kadesh, where, after the scouts returned and reported what they had seen while bringing back the fruits of the land of Canaan, they murmured against Moses and Aaron, and because of this died, exhausted by the weariness of the long journey and struck by mortality—this passage of Scripture will make clear.

Here it should be noted that the forty-two camps or encampments through which the children of Israel migrated from Egypt as far as the Jordan seem to correspond to only three periods of years: the first, second, and fortieth years after their departure from Egypt.

The first year contains twelve encampments in a definite sequence. They entered the first, Rameses, on the fifteenth day of the first month; the last, the wilderness of Sinai, was entered on the first day of the third month. It was not abandoned for eleven continuous months, because of the construction of the tabernacle and the teaching of the Law. Of these twelve encampments, the Book of Exodus names only nine explicitly; it passes over the remaining three without distinction under the name of the wilderness of Sin, which is said to lie between Elim and Sinai.

The second year comprises twenty-one encampments. In the historical sequence all of them are indiscriminately included under the name of the wilderness of Paran. Only the first, second, and last—namely, the Graves of Lust, Hazeroth, and Kadesh—are distinguished by their names. But in the catalogue of the encampments, all are carefully displayed, both in number and in name.

The first of them, the Graves of Lust, was entered in the second month of that second year, on the twenty-second day of the month. “In the second year,” Scripture says, “in the second month, on the twentieth day of the month, they moved their camps from the wilderness of Sinai. And the cloud,” it says, “rested in the wilderness of Paran. They set out from the mountain of the Lord on a journey of three days, until they came to the place of the encampment, which received the name Graves of Lust because of the people’s desire for Egyptian meat” [Num. 10:11–12, 33; 11:34].

It is not stated on what day or in what month of that same year the last of these encampments, Kadesh, was entered. Nevertheless, it is not concealed that it too was situated in the wilderness of Paran and was added in that same year.

For it is written: “The people did not set out from that place until Miriam was called back. And they departed from Hazeroth and pitched their tents in the wilderness of Paran, where the Lord spoke, saying: ‘Send men to inspect the land of Canaan’” [Num. 12:15–13:2].

To prevent us from thinking that this command was given and carried out at the encampment immediately following Hazeroth, and so that we may instead understand it to have been fulfilled at the last encampment included under the name of the wilderness of Paran, let us consider what is written below:

“The scouts returned after forty days, having traversed the whole region, and came to Moses and Aaron and to the entire assembly of the children of Israel in the wilderness of Paran, which is Kadesh.”

But in Deuteronomy Moses himself speaks to the people: “When you came to Kadesh-barnea, I said to you: ‘You have come to the mountain of the Amorite, which the Lord your God is going to give you. See the land that the Lord your God will give you; go up and possess it.’ And you all approached me and said: ‘Send men to inspect the land,’” and so forth.

That they visited this same encampment in the second year after their departure from Egypt is testified by Moses in what follows, although because of the sin of their murmuring they deserved to turn back from it, wander through the wilderness for a long time, and fall everywhere. He says [ibid.]: “You remained at Kadesh-barnea for a long time. Then we departed from there and came into the wilderness that leads to the Red Sea, as the Lord had said to me. And we went around Mount Seir for a long time.”

And below: “The time during which we travelled from Kadesh-barnea to the torrent of Zered was thirty-eight years, until the entire generation of men of war was consumed from the camp, as the Lord had sworn.”

Zered is not the name of an encampment—I mean one of those forty-two—but the name of a torrent. According to the Book of Numbers, they came to it after passing through the twenty-eighth encampment, named Iye-abarim. “Leaving it,” he says, “they camped opposite Arnon, which is in the wilderness and extends along the borders of the Amorites.” It is clear that this took place in the fortieth year.

The Book of Numbers indicates what the fortieth and final year contained: the encampments of a very long journey through the wilderness. The first encampment of that year had to be recovered with great labor: it was Kadesh itself, in the wilderness of Sin, which, as has been said, they had left behind thirty-eight years earlier because of their transgression.

Concerning it, this is written: “The children of Israel and the whole assembly came into the wilderness of Sin in the first month. The people stayed at Kadesh, and Miriam died there and was buried there. And when the people lacked water, they gathered together against Moses and Aaron,” and so forth, up to what is written: “This is the water of contradiction, where the children of Israel quarrelled against the Lord, and he was sanctified among them” [Num. 20:1–13].

It should be noted that Scripture reports the same Kadesh as being both in the wilderness of Paran and in the wilderness of Sin. Hence one may conjecture that, according to the customary usage of place-names, part of the wilderness of Paran, where Kadesh is located, was specifically called Sin.

This Sin, however, is not the same Kadesh that they crossed shortly after crossing the Red Sea, between Elim and Sinai, but an entirely different place, written among the Hebrews with different letters.

The second encampment of that same fortieth year was at Mount Hor, where Aaron died on the first day of the fifth month. Beyond the Arabah of Moab, beside the Jordan opposite Jericho, they remained there meditating upon Deuteronomy until, after Moses’ death, under Joshua’s leadership, they crossed the depths of the Jordan River on dry ground on the first day of the tenth month.

Thus there were twelve encampments in the first year; twenty-one in the second; and, in the final year, Kadesh itself, which was the twenty-first, together with nine others—forty-two altogether.

## Chapter VI. Recapitulation: how Moses sent messengers to Sihon, king of Heshbon, and Og, king of Bashan
(IBID.) “So I sent messengers from the wilderness of Kedemoth [Col. 0850D] to Sihon king of Heshbon, speaking peaceful words: ‘We will pass through your land; we will travel along the public road. We will not turn aside either to the right or to the left. Sell us food for money, so that we may eat. Give us water for money, and so we shall drink. Only grant us passage, as the sons of Esau who dwell in Seir and the Moabites who dwell in Ar did, and so forth.’”

We said above that Sihon signifies the devil, who is a useless shoot, or a fruitless tree, or else one who is exalted. Israel, therefore, who wished to pass through his land, signifies the Christian people, who wish to pass along the road of the world. We wish to pass through this world so that we may reach the holy land, [Col. 0849A] entered on the fifteenth day of the first month; the final wilderness, Sinai, having been added on the first day of the third month and not left during the continuous eleven months devoted to constructing the tabernacle and teaching the Law. Of these twelve encampments, the book of Exodus expressly names only nine; it passes over the other three indiscriminately under the name of the wilderness of Sin, said to lie between Elim and Sinai.

The second year comprises twenty-one encampments. Although, in the order of the history, all of them are indiscriminately included under the name of the wilderness of Paran, only the first, second, and last—that is, the Graves of Craving, Hazeroth, and Kadesh—are distinguished by their own names. But in the catalogue of encampments, all alike are carefully shown, both how many there were and what they were called. [Col. 0849B] The first of these encampments, namely the Graves of Craving, was entered on the twenty-second day of the second month of that same second year. “For in the second year,” as Scripture says, “in the second month, on the twentieth day of the month, they moved camp from the wilderness of Sinai; and the cloud,” it says, “settled in the wilderness of Paran. And they set out from the mountain of the Lord for a journey of three days, until they came to the place of encampment which received the name Graves of Craving because the people desired the meats of Egypt” (Num. X).

But on what day or in what month of that year they entered the last of these encampments, Kadesh, is not stated. Yet it is not left unsaid that it too was situated in the wilderness of Paran and was added in the same year. For it is written: “And the people did not move from [Col. 0849C] that place until Miriam was recalled. And they set out from Hazeroth and pitched their tents in the wilderness of Paran, where the Lord spoke, saying: ‘Send men to survey the land of Canaan’” (Num. XII). Lest this command and its execution be thought to have occurred at the encampment immediately after Hazeroth, but rather be understood to have been fulfilled at the last one included under the name of the wilderness of Paran, let us see what is written below. When the scouts returned after forty days, having traversed the whole region, they came to Moses and Aaron and to the whole assembly of the children of Israel in the wilderness of Paran, which is at Kadesh. But in Deuteronomy Moses himself says to the people: “When you came to Kadesh-barnea, I said to you: ‘You have come to the mountain of the Amorite, which the Lord your God is going to give you. See [Col. 0849D] the land that the Lord your God will give you; go up and possess it.’ And all of you came near to me and said: ‘Send men to survey the land,’ etc.”

That they reached this same encampment in the second year after their departure from Egypt—and that, because of the sin of murmuring, they deserved to turn back from it, wander long through the wilderness, and fall here and there—Moses testifies in what follows, saying (IBID.): “You remained at Kadesh-barnea a long time. Setting out from there, we came into the wilderness that leads to the Red Sea, as the Lord had told me.
