And we went around Mount Seir for a long time.” And below: “The time during which we travelled from Kadesh-barnea to the brook Zered [Col. 0850A] was thirty-eight years, until the whole generation of fighting men had perished from the camp, as the Lord had sworn.” Zered, however, is not the name of one of the forty-two encampments, but the name of a brook, to which, as is read in the book of Numbers, they came after passing the twenty-eighth encampment, called Iye-abarim. Leaving it, it says, they encamped opposite Arnon, which is in the wilderness and projects into the borders of the Amorite; and it is well known that this occurred in the fortieth year.

That fortieth, that is, final year of the very long journey through the wilderness contains the encampments recorded in Numbers. The first of these was revisited with great difficulty: the very same Kadesh in the wilderness of Sin, which, as stated, they had left behind thirty-eight years earlier when the guilt of transgression compelled them to turn back. Of it it is written: “The children of Israel and the whole multitude came into the wilderness of Sin in the first month; and the people remained at Kadesh, and Miriam died there and was buried in the same place. When the people lacked water, they assembled against Moses and Aaron,” etc., up to what is written: “This is the water of contradiction, where the children of Israel contended against the Lord, and he was sanctified in them” (Num. XX).

It should be noted that Scripture reports the same Kadesh as situated both in the wilderness of Paran and in the wilderness of Sin. Hence arises the conjecture that, according to the customary usage of place-names, the part of Paran where Kadesh lies was specially called Sin. But this Sin is not the same as the Sin through which they passed immediately after crossing the Red Sea, between Elim and Sinai; it is entirely another, written with different letters among the Hebrews. [Col. 0850C] The second encampment of that same fortieth year was moved to Mount Hor, where Aaron died on the first day of the fifth month. Beyond the plains of Moab, above the Jordan opposite Jericho, they remained while studying Deuteronomy, until, after Moses’ death, under Joshua’s leadership, they crossed the dry depths of the River Jordan on the first day of the tenth month. Thus the encampments of the first year number twelve; those of the second, twenty-one; and those of the final year, the twenty-first itself, which is Kadesh, together with the other nine: forty-two in all.

## CHAPTER VI. Recapitulation: how Moses sent messengers to Sihon king of Heshbon and Og king of Bashan

(IBID.) “So I sent messengers from the wilderness of Kedemoth, [Col. 0850D] to Sihon king of Heshbon, speaking peaceful words: ‘We will pass through your land; we will travel along the public road. We will not turn aside either to the right or to the left. Sell us food for money, so that we may eat. Give us water for money, and so we shall drink. Only grant us passage, as the sons of Esau who dwell in Seir and the Moabites who dwell in Ar did, and so forth.’”

We said above that Sihon signifies the devil, who is a useless shoot, or a fruitless tree, or else one who is exalted. Israel, therefore, who wished to pass through his land, signifies the Christian people, who wish to pass along the road of the world. We wish to pass through this world so that we may reach the holy land [Col. 0849A] that was promised to the saints; and we send peaceful words to Sihon, promising that we will neither go into his land nor remain with him, but will merely pass through and proceed along the royal road. We will not turn aside anywhere, either into his field or into his vineyard, but will drink water from the well.

Let us see, then, when we made these promises and when we announced these words to the devil. Let each believer recall when he first came to the waters of baptism, when he first received the seals of faith and approached the saving font, what words he then used there and what he announced to the devil: that he would not use his pomp or his works, nor serve him in any way, nor obey his desires.

This is what is portrayed in these words of the Law: Israel is not to turn aside either into his field or into his vineyard; nor does it promise that it will drink water from his well. The people will no longer take instruction from the devil’s discipline, astrology, magic, or any teaching whatsoever that teaches anything contrary to the devotion owed to God. The believer has his own springs and drinks from the springs of Israel; he drinks from the springs of salvation. He does not drink water from Sihon’s well, nor does he abandon the spring of living water to dig for himself broken cisterns.

He also declares that he will proceed along the royal road. What is the royal road? Surely that which says, “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV). And rightly is it called royal; for he is the one of whom the Prophet says, “O God, give your judgment to the king” (Psalm LXXI). We must therefore proceed along the royal road and turn aside nowhere, neither into his field nor into his vineyard—that is, the mind of the faithful must no longer turn aside either to his works or to his devilish thoughts.

How, then, do we wish to pass peacefully through the territory of the Amorites? The Amorites may be understood as a portion of the unbelievers who are in this world. But they are interpreted, as we said above, as “speaking” or “adding to bitterness.” How unbelievers and the faithless bring God to bitterness requires no explanation. But the interpretation “speaking” can be applied in this way: all unbelievers and those who act under the devil as their prince know only how to speak, but they speak empty things. For example, their poets, their astrologers, and also some of their philosophers speak empty and vain things. But the kingdom of the faithful, which is from God, is not in speech but in power.

We therefore wish to pass peacefully through the world. But the very thing we say—that we do not wish to remain with the prince of this world, linger with him, or have anything to do with what belongs to him—provokes him all the more. For this reason he is embittered, for this reason he is lifted up and grows angry, and he stirs up persecutions against us, raises dangers, and threatens torments.

Therefore Scripture says: “The wicked Sihon gathered his people and went out to fight against Israel.” Who is all the people of Sihon whom he rouses against Israel? The rulers and judges of the world, and all the ministers of wickedness, who are always attacking and persecuting the people of God.

But what does Israel do? “It came,” he says, “to Jahaz,” which is interpreted as “fulfillment of the command.” If, then, we too come to this place—that is, to the fulfillment of the commandments—and if this exalted Sihon, this proud devil, comes against us with his entire army and fights against us; if he rouses all his demons against us, we overcome him if we fulfill the commandments of God. For to fulfill the commandments is to overcome the devil and all his armies. Then the Apostle’s prayer will be fulfilled in us: “But God will crush Satan under your feet speedily” (Romans XVI).

And likewise the Lord says: “Behold, I give you authority to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy, and nothing shall harm you” (Luke X). None of all these things will be able to harm us if we come to Jahaz—that is, if we keep the commandments and precepts of the Lord our God Jesus Christ.

“But Sihon king of Heshbon would not grant us passage, because the Lord your God had hardened his spirit and made his heart obstinate, so that he might be delivered into your hands, as you now see, and so forth.” In saying this while addressing the people, Moses recalls something like what was said in Exodus: “I hardened Pharaoh’s heart.” And what is read in the Psalms: “He turned their heart so that they hated his people.”

The reason for this hardening is not passed over here, since it says, “so that he might be delivered into your hands,” as on this day—that is, so that he might be defeated by you. But this would not have happened unless he had resisted; and he would not have resisted unless his heart had been hardened. If we seek the justice of this matter, God’s judgments are inscrutable. Yet there is no iniquity in him. It should indeed be noted that a heart can be said to have been strengthened even for evil.

“We struck him and his sons and all his people, and at that time we captured all his cities, killing their inhabitants, men, women, and children. We left nothing in them except the livestock, which became the portion of the plunderers, and the spoils of the cities that we captured. From Aroer, which is on the bank of the torrent Arnon, the town situated in the valley, as far as Gilead, there was no village or city that escaped our hands, and so forth.”

This is the Israel who is Israel in Christ, who is not Israel according to the flesh and is not a Jew outwardly. He dwells in all the cities of the Amorites, while the churches of Christ are spread throughout the whole world. But each one of us was previously a city of King Sihon, the exalted king. Folly, pride, impiety, and everything belonging to the devil reigned in us. But when the strong man has been assaulted and overcome and his goods have been plundered, we become cities of Israel and the inheritance of the saints—provided that the power which formerly ruled us has been utterly cut down in us, the fruitless tree has been felled, the exalted king has been cast down, and we are under the rule of the king who says, “Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matthew XI).

The names of the places themselves, with their interpretations, also support this meaning. Aroer, therefore, is interpreted as “one who raises up”; Arnon as “heap of righteousness”; and Gilead as “heap of testimony.” From Aroer, which is on the bank of the torrent Arnon—the town situated in the valley—as far as Gilead, no village or city escaped the hands of the Israelites. For every person, whatever his rank, who relies on the arrogance of pride or on worldly display, together with the persecutors of Christians who afflict them with various tribulations, even to the assemblies of heretics who, by corrupting the testimonies of the holy Scriptures according to their own sense, wage war against the Church, is utterly unable to resist the Catholic truth through the agency of the holy teachers. Instead, falling into the hands of the victors, together with all his habitations and fortifications, he is reduced to the dominion of spiritual Israel.

## CHAPTER VII. That no city or town in the kingdom of Og escaped without being destroyed, and that their land was given to Reuben, Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh

[Col. 0853B] (CHAPTER III.) “Then we turned and went up by the road to Bashan. Og king of Bashan came out to meet us, with all his people, to fight at Edrei. The Lord said to me: ‘Do not fear him, for he has been delivered into your hand, together with all his people and his land. You shall do to him as you did to Sihon king of the Amorites, who dwelt in Heshbon.’ So the Lord our God delivered Og king of Bashan also into our hands, together with all his people. We struck them down to destruction, destroying all his cities at one time.”

After the sons of Israel had taken possession of the cities of the Amorites, they also went up by the road that leads to Bashan, where Og king of Bashan was. But they did not deem it necessary to send messengers to him or to ask him for permission to pass through his land. They immediately fought with him and defeated both him and his people.

Let us see, then, what Bashan is. Bashan is interpreted as “shamefulness.” It is therefore rightly the case that no messengers are sent to this nation, and that passage through its land is not requested. We ought to have no passage, no access, to shamefulness; rather, it must be attacked immediately from the beginning and avoided in every way.

Og, who is called the king of Bashan, is interpreted as “confinement.” He can represent all carnal and material things, by whose love and desire the soul is held captive, shut out from God, and separated from him. Against these, therefore, war must be waged in such a way that none of them is left alive. Nothing living ought to be left by the children of Israel in the kingdom of shamefulness for service to God. Rather, Israelite virtue ought to cut out and excise all that is shameful, rebuild whatever is godly in the soul, and plant whatever is honorable and religious.

It is not written concerning the kingdom of Sihon that no living thing should be left, nor concerning the kingdom of Moab. Perhaps we need something from those things, and need some of them for the struggles and exercises of this life. Otherwise we ought to have departed from this world. But from Bashan—that is, from shamefulness—we have absolutely no need. Let us leave nothing of it behind; everything must be cut out and overturned. The works of strength must be subverted, for nothing that is shameful can be honorable in any respect.

What follows also confirms this interpretation: “There was no town that escaped us, when we destroyed sixty cities, the whole region of Argob, the kingdom of Og in Bashan, and so forth.” The number sixty, like the number six, signifies the perfection of any kingdom. It is therefore fitting that sixty cities are said to have been destroyed in the kingdom of Og, king of Bashan—that is, of the devil, who loves shamefulness—because this signifies that the whole pleasure of vices must be perfectly destroyed. Argob is likewise interpreted as “cursed height,” by which earthly pride, which rules among the sons of wrath, is expressed.

After all the cities have been destroyed, he describes the men, women, and children alike as having been killed. But the livestock and the spoils of the cities, taken away as plunder, indicate to us that, once the devil’s fortress has been overcome, whatever rebellious and wanton thing we perceive in our flesh, together with childish thoughts, must be crushed by zeal for God. Whatever virtues we are able to find for the service of God in a simple and pure mind, or in unadorned speech, must be preserved for him.

“And at that time we took possession of the land from Aroer, which is on the bank of the torrent Arnon, as far as the middle of Mount Gilead. I gave its cities to Reuben and Gad. The remaining part of Gilead, and all Bashan, the kingdom of Og, I gave to half the tribe of Manasseh,” and so forth.

All these matters are explained more fully in the book of Numbers. But since they have been recapitulated here, that is, in Deuteronomy, we shall show what they signify mystically.

There are many in the Church who despise being little ones and do not cease to consider themselves exempt from humility. You will often see such people raised to honors, enjoying pleasures, and expanding through an abundance of possessions. They frequently desire nothing so much as to rule over others; they rejoice to be feared by many; they neglect to live rightly but desire to possess a reputation for right living. They seek flattery and swell with favor; and because they are ready for the things presently available to them, they do not seek the joys that are to come.

When manifold activity occupies them, it also shows them to be alienated from themselves. Yet if some temptation against the faith arises, because they at least maintain the appearance of faith, they defend it with words and shouting. They claim the heavenly homeland, but do not love it.

These people are well represented by Reuben and Gad and half the tribe of Manasseh, who possessed many flocks and herds. Because they desired the plains they had seen beyond the Jordan, they did not wish to have an inheritance in the land of promise, saying: “The land that the Lord struck down before the children of Israel is an exceedingly fertile region for feeding animals. And we, your servants, have very many livestock. We ask that, if we have found favor in your sight, you give it to your servants as a possession and do not make us cross the Jordan.”

Those, therefore, who possess very many livestock refuse to cross the Jordan, because those occupied by many entanglements of the world do not seek a dwelling in the homeland of the heart. Yet the faith that they hold, at least outwardly, reproaches them so that they do not grow sluggish through the delight of idleness and, by their example, break the endurance in labor and the pursuit of perseverance in others: “Will your brothers go to war while you sit here? Why do you turn away the minds of the children of Israel?”

But because they are ashamed not to defend what they confess, they hasten to battle for the very faith they have professed, and they claim it not for themselves but for their neighbors. “Therefore they say to Moses: We have built sheepfolds and stalls for the livestock, and fortified cities for our little ones. But we ourselves, armed and girded, shall proceed to battle before the children of Israel.”

They immediately come forth as strong men for the sake of others, free the land of promise from its enemies, and leave it; then they go beyond the Jordan to feed their herds, because against the faith of baptism they serve with their whole mind and every desire the things that are destined to perish. Yet, as we said, when a temptation against the faith arises, they gird themselves with the weapons of defense, defeat the enemies of faith by slaughtering them, and do not love the inheritance of the land of promise—that is, the fruit of faith. Thus they fight for it while nevertheless placing their own pledges outside it. Because they have little ones outside, they do not possess the effect of dwelling in it.

Therefore they return to the plains, because they slip down from the lofty peaks of the mountains, as from hope in heavenly things, and beyond the land of promise they nourish brute animals. For they labor to feed the irrational movements of their souls with empty desires; they do not know how great is the splendor of eternal light; they are blinded by occupations that pass away; and while they grow proud in earthly things, they close off for themselves access to the heavenly light.

This may also be understood in another way. Reuben is Jacob’s firstborn. Although he defiled his father’s bed, he is nevertheless the firstborn. Manasseh also, half of whose tribe received its inheritance beyond the Jordan, although he was born of an Egyptian woman, is nevertheless a firstborn.

All these, therefore, are firstborn, and for this reason they signify the earlier people, who receive the lot of their inheritance beyond the Jordan not through our Lord Jesus Christ but through Moses. Consider more carefully, however, the reason why this people is first and receives its inheritance beyond the Jordan, separately from the others. “We have many livestock and sheep,” it says. This, then, is the reason why the earlier people could not reach the inheritance of that land which flows with milk, abounds in honey, and is a honeycomb above every land; nor could they recognize the Word made flesh, because they had many livestock and many sheep.

The animal person could not perceive the things of the Spirit of God, nor judge spiritually. For when a human being was in honor, he did not understand; he was compared with senseless beasts and made like them. Because of these things he received his inheritance beyond the waters of the Jordan and made himself alien to the holy land.

That people therefore received its inheritance through Moses; it received the land of only two kings. For Moses could not kill more than two kings whose land he might divide among people possessing many animals and many sheep. But for those who cross the Jordan, Jesus divides the land. They too may have animals and sheep, but not so many as to exclude them from crossing the Jordan. With their wives and children they strive to cross the Jordan and reach the promises made to the fathers.

## CHAPTER VIII. Moses’ exhortation to Israel to keep the Lord’s commandments and judgments

(CHAPTER IV.) “And now, Israel, hear the commandments and judgments that I teach you, so that by doing them you may live and, entering, possess the land that the Lord, the God of your fathers, is going to give you. You shall not add to the word that I speak to you, nor shall you take anything away from it. Keep the commandments of the Lord your God that I command you, and so forth.”

He teaches the rule of equity and strikes every heresy with this sentence, because he forbids adding anything from elsewhere to sound doctrine by means of corrupt inventions, and prohibits taking anything away from what has been proclaimed according to the truth of the right faith.

We must proceed along the royal road. No one may turn aside either to the right or to the left, because the Lord will not hold innocent the person who abandons the straight road and turns into crooked paths. For the ways of the Lord are straight, and the righteous walk in them.

We read something similar in the Apocalypse of John: “Blessed,” he says, “is the one who keeps the words of the prophecy of this book” (Revelation I). And shortly afterward: “I testify,” he says, “to everyone who hears the words of the prophecy of this book: If anyone adds to these things, God will add to him the plagues written in this book. And if anyone takes away from the words of the prophecy of this book, God will take away his portion from the book of life, from the holy city, and from the things written in this book.”

This is true wisdom and understanding before the peoples: that, when they hear all these commandments, they say, “Behold, a wise and understanding people, a great nation; for there is no other nation so great that has gods so near to it as the Lord our God is near to us in all our prayers,” and so forth.

He calls it a great nation on account of the dignity of its gifts, not on account of the number of its people. The Jewish nation did not surpass other nations in number or excel them in power. Rather, the divine favor shown to the fathers raised it up, as Moses himself testifies later, saying: “It was not because you surpassed all the nations in number that the Lord joined himself to you and chose you, since you are fewer than all peoples; but because the Lord loved you and kept the oath that he had sworn to your fathers.”

## CHAPTER IX. Concerning the prohibition against making images of all living creatures and livestock that are upon the earth

[Col. 0856D] (IBID.) “Therefore guard your souls carefully. Have you ever seen any likeness on the day when the Lord spoke to you at Horeb from the midst of the fire? Lest, perhaps, being deceived, you make for yourselves a carved likeness, or the image of a male or female.”

(From Augustine.) It is customary to ask what difference there is between likeness and image. Here, however, I do not see what difference he intended, unless he signified one thing by these two terms, or called it a likeness if, for example, a statue or image was made that had a human form, but did not reproduce the features of any particular human being, as painters or sculptors do when they look upon those whom they paint or model.

No one would doubt that this is called an image, according to the distinction by which every image is also a likeness, but not every likeness is also an image. Thus, if two twins resemble one another, the resemblance of one to the other may be called a likeness, but not an image. If a son resembles his father, however, he is rightly called an image as well, since the father is the source of the whole from which that image appears to have been expressed. Some images are of the same substance, as the Son is; others are not of the same substance, as a painting is not.

Therefore, when it is written in Genesis, “God made the human being in his own image” (Genesis I), it is clear that this was said in such a way that the image that was made is not of the same substance. For if it were of the same substance, it would be said to have been begotten, not made.

But because he did not add “and likeness,” although it had previously been said, “Let us make the human being in our image and likeness,” some have thought that likeness is something greater than image, reserved for the later restoration of the human being through the grace of Christ.

I wonder, however, whether he did not mention the image alone afterward for this reason: wherever there is an image, there is also a likeness. Moses therefore forbids a likeness and an image to be made here, according to the form—or perhaps the reasoning—that we have described.

In the Decalogue, however, it is said generally that no likeness is to be made, and image is not mentioned. For when no likeness is made, plainly no image is made either, since if there is an image, there is certainly also a likeness. But if a likeness is made, an image does not immediately follow. Nevertheless, if there is no likeness, it follows that there is no image.

Finally, where he prohibited likeness and image, he intended the human being to be understood: in the case of a likeness, any human being, not this or that particular person; and in the case of an image, this person or that person specifically. But when he was speaking of livestock and irrational animals, he mentioned likeness alone. Who can be found who would make a dog, or something similar, for himself, so that, looking at its image, he might paint or model it? This is customary in the case of human beings.

“A likeness of all the livestock that are upon the earth, or of the birds that fly beneath the sky, and of the reptiles that move upon the earth, or of the fish that dwell beneath the earth in the waters.”

But what does he mean when he says, “the likeness of every fish that is in the waters beneath the earth”? Did he perhaps also wish water to be understood as earth because of its tangible corporeality? And, in accordance with what is written there, “God made heaven and earth,” should we understand the waters in this way? Scripture frequently wishes the whole world to be understood by mentioning these two parts, according to the saying, “My help is from the Lord, who made heaven and earth” (Psalm CXX), and countless similar passages.

Or was “beneath the earth” said because, unless the earth were above the waters, it could not be inhabited by human beings or bear earthly animals?

“Lest, lifting your eyes to heaven, you see the sun and the moon and all the stars of heaven and, deceived by error, worship and serve them, which the Lord your God created for the service of all the nations that are beneath heaven, because the Lord your God distributed them among all the nations that are beneath heaven.”

This is not said as though God commanded them to be worshiped by the nations but forbade them to be worshiped by his own people. Rather, it was said either because he foresaw that the nations would offer worship to these heavenly bodies and nevertheless created them, while he foresaw that his own people would not worship them; or “distributed” was said so that their use might be understood—the use commended in Genesis, “that they may be for signs and for seasons and for days and years.”

The people of God shares this use of them with all nations, but not the worship that other nations offer them.

“Take care lest you ever forget the covenant of the Lord our God that he made with you, and make for yourself a carved likeness of those things that the Lord prohibited from being made; for the Lord your God is a consuming fire, a jealous God, and so forth.”

Here, certainly, speaking generally, he used “likeness” and remained silent about “image,” since if there is no likeness, plainly there is no image: wherever there is an image, there is immediately a likeness, although wherever there is a likeness, there is not immediately an image.

“But in the latter days you will return to the Lord your God and hear his voice, because God is merciful, and the Lord your God, and so forth.”

Here he foretells the conversion of the Israelite nation to the faith of Christ, when, according to the Apostle Paul’s statement, “after the fullness of the Gentiles has come in, then all Israel will be saved” (Romans XI).

[Col. 0858C] “Inquire about the former days, which were before you, from the day when God created man upon the earth, from one end of heaven to the other, whether such a thing has ever happened or whether it has ever been known that a people heard the voice of the Lord speaking from the midst of the fire, as you heard and saw, and so forth.” One must ask how it is said, “Inquire about the former days, which were before you, from the day when God created man upon the earth, from one end of heaven to the other”—with “inquire” understood. For it seems to signify the whole inhabited world. But why he says “from one end of heaven to the other,” rather than “from one end of earth to the other,” is not easy to discern. There is a somewhat similar expression in the Gospel, when the Lord says that his elect will be gathered [Col. 0858D] “from the ends of the heavens to their boundaries.” Unless perhaps here he wishes it to be understood that it had never been heard, either among human beings or among angels, that which he commends as having uniquely occurred among this people. For what follows is: “Has anything been done according to this great word, or has anything like it been heard? Has a nation heard the voice of the living Lord speaking from the midst of the fire, as you heard and saw?” But if this means that such a thing had never been heard either among human beings or among angels, what then is that saying in the Gospel, “from the ends of the heavens to their boundaries,” when unquestionably the Lord said this while speaking of the final gathering of his elect?

**CHAPTER V**

“Moses summoned all Israel and said to them: Hear, Israel, the ceremonies and judgments that I speak in your ears today. Learn them and put them into practice. The Lord our God made a covenant with us at Horeb. He did not make this covenant with our fathers, but with us, who are here today and alive. The Lord spoke with us face to face from the mountain, in the midst of the fire.”

What does he mean by saying, “The Lord our God established a covenant with us at Horeb”? The Lord did not establish this covenant with our fathers, but with you—namely, with all of you who are alive today. The Lord spoke with you face to face on the mountain, from the midst of the fire. Or is it because those who did not enter the promised land—for they all died—do not belong to this covenant, since the census of them was made when those aged twenty years and older, up to fifty years, were counted as fit for war? How, then, did the Lord speak to those who are alive today? Perhaps because many who were then under twenty years of age could have remembered these things well, being exempt from the punishment that God imposed upon those who were then counted: that they should not enter the promised land. He calls these people “you,” even though they were not yet twenty years old or older when God spoke on the mountain and therefore could not have been included in that census. They could nevertheless have been nineteen, or younger—even of an age still called childhood—that was capable of seeing and hearing what had happened and retaining it in memory.

But what does he mean by saying, “The Lord spoke with you face to face,” when shortly before he took great care to remind them that they had seen no likeness [Col. 0859C], but had heard only a voice from the midst of the fire? Did he use these words on account of the evident reality and, so to speak, the manifest presence of the divinity, about which no one could doubt? If so, what prevents us from understanding the same thing of Moses himself, when it is said that the Lord spoke with him face to face, so that he too saw nothing with his eyes except the fire? Or is he understood to have seen something more because it is written that he entered into the cloud or mist where God was? But even if he saw something more than they did, it cannot be understood from those words of his that he saw the substance of God with mortal eyes. For he said to God: “If I have found favor before you, show yourself to me, so that I may see you.”

Nor should we suppose that this people to whom Moses was speaking [Col. 0859D] saw God face to face at that time, when he was speaking on the mountain from the midst of the fire, in the manner in which the Apostle says that we shall see him at the end, where he says: “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face.” What this means, and how great it is, he subsequently made clear by saying: “Now I know in part, but then I shall know even as I am known” (1 Cor. 13). This statement itself must also be received cautiously, lest one suppose that human beings will possess as much knowledge of God as God now possesses of human beings. Rather, they will know him according to their own measure, perfectly, so that nothing further will be expected to be added to their knowledge: just as God now knows the human being perfectly, but as God knows a human being, so then the human being will know God perfectly, but as a human being knows God. For although it is said, “Be perfect, as your heavenly Father is perfect,” we ought not therefore to hope for the equality with the Father that the only-begotten Word possesses, although there have been some who have thought that even this will come to pass—unless perhaps we understand their meaning poorly.

**CHAPTER X. On Moses’ saying that he was mediator and judge between the Lord and Israel on Mount Sinai**

“I was mediator and stood between the Lord and you at that time, to announce his words to you. For you feared the fire and did not go up the mountain.”

What does he mean by saying, “I was mediator and stood between you and the Lord,” or, as another edition has it, “I stood between the Lord and between you at that time, announcing the words of the Lord to you”? It is as though the Lord were in a place—namely, on the mountain, from which they heard his voice. This must be understood in such a way that we do not infer from it that the substance of God exists in any bodily place. He is wholly everywhere and neither draws near nor withdraws through intervals of space. Rather, his manifestations are presented to human senses in the creature that is not what he himself is.

Therefore, wishing to remove from our minds this sort of suspicion, by which God is thought to be contained in some place, the Lord says: “The hour is coming when you will worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem. You worship what you do not know; we worship what we know, because salvation is from the Jews. But the hour is coming, and now is, when true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth. For the Father also seeks such people to worship him. God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth” (John 4:21–24).

Moses called himself “mediator,” not because there was some spatial interval between the substance of God and the people, but because it pleased God that through him the people should hear the remaining words of God, after they had been greatly terrified on hearing the voice of God, speaking the Decalogue from the midst of the fire.

It is rightly asked, however, how these words of Deuteronomy are to be understood, when Moses says: “And I stood between the Lord and you at that time, to announce the words of the Lord, because you feared the face of the fire of the Lord and did not go up the mountain, saying: I am the Lord your God,” and so forth. These too are the words of God that the Decalogue contains. What, then, does he intend by adding “saying”? For if we suppose that there is a hyperbaton, so that the order of the words is: “And I stood between the Lord and you at that time, to announce to you the words of the Lord, saying: I am the Lord your God,” it will not be true. The people did not hear these words through Moses, but from the midst of the fire. When they could not endure hearing the Decalogue, they asked to hear the remaining words through Moses.

It remains, therefore, to understand the word “saying” as standing for “so that he might say,” so that the sense is this: “And I stood between the Lord and you at that time, to announce to you the words of the Lord, saying: Because you feared the face of the fire and did not go up the mountain, when he said, ‘I am the Lord your God’”—with “when he said” understood to mean, of course, when the Lord said it. For when the Lord spoke these words, and all the words that he subsequently recalls from the Decalogue, then the people feared the face of the fire, did not go up the mountain, and asked that they might hear the words of the Lord through Moses instead.

These are the words that Moses recalls in Deuteronomy as having been spoken to him by the people, when they no longer wished to hear the voice of God but asked that, through him, what God was saying should be told to them: namely, “Behold, the Lord our God has shown us his glory, and we have heard his voice from the midst of the fire,” and so forth.

The words are not exactly the same in Exodus, where the events now repeated were first narrated. We should understand—as I have already mentioned several times—that it should not be counted as falsehood when the same meaning is expressed in different words. This is also evident in the words of the Evangelists, which are criticized by the ignorant and contentious as though they contradicted one another. It would not have been difficult for Moses to attend to what he had written in Exodus and repeat it in precisely the same words, unless it belonged to the purpose of our holy teachers to suggest this very lesson to those learning: that in the words of speakers they should seek nothing other than the intention for which the words were instituted.

And he says: (same passage) “I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, from the house of slavery. You shall have no other gods before me. You shall not make for yourself a carved image, nor any likeness of all that is in heaven above, or on earth below, or in the waters beneath the earth. You shall not worship foreign gods. For I am the Lord your God, a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children to the third and fourth generation of those who hate me, and showing mercy to many thousands of those who love me and keep my commandments.”

There are some who explain what is written in the Law—“visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children to the third and fourth generation”—by applying the statement to the human soul. They say that the father is the slight movement of the senses within us and the incitements to vice; the son, when thought has conceived sin; the grandson, when one has carried out in deed what one has thought and conceived; and the great-grandson, the fourth generation, when one has not only done what is evil and wicked but has also gloried inwardly in one’s crimes, according to what is written: “When the ungodly comes into the depth of evils, he despises” (Prov. 18).

He significantly added, “of those who hate me”—that is, punishment for sin will be reserved for those who hate God through inherited evil and impiety. For it is otherwise unjust and perverse to charge the sins of fathers to children and grandchildren who have not sinned, especially since the Lord says through Ezekiel: “The soul that sins shall die. The father shall not bear the iniquity of the son. The righteousness of the righteous shall be upon him, and the impiety of the impious shall be upon him” (Ezek. 18).

This statement can also be understood in another way, where it says, “visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children to the third and fourth generation,” so that it is not a sign of harshness but of mercy: namely, the postponement of punishment. For when it is written, “The Lord God is compassionate and merciful, patient and of great mercy,” and it is added, “visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the sons and daughters,” this indicates that he is so merciful that he does not punish immediately but delays the sentence of punishment.

But if the vengeance for sinners is delayed until the third and fourth generation, what happens in the case of righteous and holy men? It is precisely what follows: “He preserves righteousness and mercy for many thousands, for those who love him and keep his commandments.”

**CHAPTER XI. On the ten commandments of the Law given on Mount Sinai and written on two tablets**

(Same passage) “You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain, because the one who takes his name over a vain matter will not go unpunished. Observe the sabbath day, to sanctify it, as the Lord your God commanded you. Six days you shall labor and do all your work; the seventh day is the sabbath, that is, the rest of the Lord your God. You shall do no work on it—you, your son, your daughter, your male servant, your female servant, your ox, your donkey, and every animal of yours, and the foreigner who is within your gates—so that your male servant and your female servant may rest as you do. Remember that you too were a servant in Egypt, and that the Lord your God brought you out from there with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm. Therefore he commanded you to observe the sabbath day. Honor your father and your mother, as the Lord your God commanded you, so that you may live long and it may be well with you in the land that the Lord your God will give you. You shall not kill. You shall not commit adultery. You shall not steal. You shall not speak false testimony against your neighbor. You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife, nor his house, nor his field, nor his male servant, nor his female servant, nor his ox, nor his donkey, nor anything that belongs to him.”

The first commandment of the Decalogue concerns God the Father, when it says later: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one Lord.” The point is that, on hearing this, you should worship one God the Father and not pour out your fornication upon many fabricated gods.

The second commandment concerns the Son, when it says: “You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain.” That is: do not think that the Son of God is a creature, since every creature is subject to vanity, but believe that he is equal to the Father: God of gods, the Word with God, through whom all things were made.

The third commandment, concerning the sabbath, pertains to the Holy Spirit, by whose gift eternal rest is promised to us. Because the Holy Spirit is so called, God also sanctified the seventh day. For on the other days of creation no sanctification is mentioned, except on the sabbath, where it says, “God rested.” Therefore this commandment pertains to the Holy Spirit, both because of the name of sanctification and because of the eternal rest belonging to the dwelling of the Holy Spirit.

For it says there: “Remember to sanctify the sabbath day. Six days you shall labor and do your works; but the seventh day is the sabbath of the Lord your God; you shall do no work.” The work of the six days contains the work of six thousand years. In the seventh day, the time of that blessed kingdom’s rest is revealed—a rest that Jews sin by celebrating in a carnal manner.

And so that we do not adapt this to faith as a deceiving falsehood, the Lord cries out through the prophet: “My soul has hated your new moons and sabbaths.” How, then, can those sabbaths that God hated be sanctified? That sabbath has been sanctified in which, after the good works of this life, eternal rest is promised to us. Therefore, whatever we do, if we do it for the sake of the rest of the age to come, we truly observe the sabbath.

After these come three commandments. The number seven precedes the commandments pertaining to love of neighbor, and it begins with honoring parents, although this is fourth in the order: “Honor your father and your mother.” A person first opens his eyes through his parents, and this life takes its beginning from their love. Thus this commandment is first among the seven, just as the Lord also says in the Gospel: “Honor your father and your mother,” which is “the first commandment” (Matt. 15).

But how is it first, since it is fourth? It is first in the number seven, which pertains to love of neighbor, and therefore it is first on the other tablet. For this is why two tablets of the Law were given.

In this commandment, therefore, children are ordered to honor their parents, not to be insulting toward them, but to offer them the reverence due through the duty of filial devotion. For one who does not know how to honor his parents—whom can he spare, if he hates his own?

Fifth: “You shall not commit adultery,” that is, no one should mingle with women other than his wife, outside the bonds of marriage, to fulfill lust. A man commits adultery in the proper sense when, in addition to his own wife, he approaches another.

Sixth: “You shall not kill.” For it is not only the person who commits murder by an act who becomes a murderer. The person who encounters someone hungry and naked, who might die unless he is helped by being given clothing and food, will likewise be held a murderer.

Seventh: “You shall not steal,” which concerns rapacity.

Eighth: “You shall not give false testimony,” which concerns the crime of lying and falsehood.

Ninth: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife.” In this commandment he forbids the intention of adulterous thought. For one thing is to do something of this kind with a woman other than one’s wife; another is to desire another man’s wife. That is why there are two commandments: “You shall not commit adultery”; “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife.”

Tenth: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s property.” In this commandment he condemns worldly ambition and restrains the coveting of possessions.

Thus the first of these forbids theft, the second error, the third destroys love of the world, the fourth impiety, the fifth crushes fornication, the sixth cruelty, the seventh rapacity, the eighth destroys falsehood, the ninth adulterous thought, and the tenth desire for the world.

It should be noted that, just as the Egyptians were struck by ten plagues, so the tablets were inscribed with ten commandments, by which the peoples of God are governed and the demons are slain.

“These words the Lord spoke to all your assembly on the mountain from the midst of the fire, the cloud, and the darkness, with a loud voice, adding nothing further; and he wrote them on two stone tablets, which God gave to me, and so forth” [Col. 0864A].

Why was the Law written on two tablets, unless either to signify the two Testaments or because of those two commandments of love of God and neighbor, “on which the whole Law and the Prophets depend”? These commandments are explained on the individual tablets. On one tablet are three commandments belonging to love of God; on the other are seven belonging to fellowship with one’s neighbor.

But why were those same tablets made of stone, unless to signify the stony heart of the Jews? Through the insensibility of stone, he signifies the hard solidity of their mind, concerning which the prophet says: “I will take away from you the heart of stone, and I will give you a heart of flesh” (Ezek. 11). Hence the Apostle also says: “Not on stone tablets but on tablets of fleshly hearts” (2 Cor. 3).

He does not mean by “fleshly tablets” that we should think carnally. Rather, because flesh has sensation in comparison with stone, which is without sensation, the hardness of stone signifies a heart that does not understand, and the sensitivity of flesh signifies an understanding heart.

“What is all flesh, that it should hear the voice of the living God speaking from the midst of the fire, as we have heard, and yet live? You draw near instead, and hear everything that the Lord our God says to you; then you shall speak to us, and we will hear and do it.”

When the Lord heard this, he said to me: “I have heard the voice of the words of this people, which they have spoken to you. They have spoken everything well. Who will grant them such a mind that they may fear me and keep all my commandments at all times, so that it may be well with them and with their children forever?”—and so forth.

What does Moses mean by saying that the Lord told him concerning the Hebrew people: “Who will grant that their heart may be such that they fear me and keep my commandments”? Is he secretly indicating here that, by his grace, this gift is granted, so that the righteousness of God exists in human beings through faith, rather than as something proper to them, as though it came from the Law?

He signifies this through the prophet, saying: “I will take away from them the heart of stone, and I will give them a heart of flesh” (Ezek. 11)—a statement made because of the sensation that flesh possesses and stone does not, using a transferred expression.

He says the same thing elsewhere: “Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will complete a new covenant over the house of Israel and over the house of Judah—not according to the covenant that I established with their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt—for this is the covenant that I will establish with them after those days: placing my laws in their heart, and I will write them upon their mind; and I will no longer remember their iniquities and their sins” (Jer. 31).

This is what distinguished the New Testament from the Old: in the Old, the Law was given on stone tablets; in the New, it is given in hearts, which takes place through grace. Hence the Apostle also says: “Not on stone tablets but on tablets of fleshly hearts.” And elsewhere: “He made us,” he says, “competent ministers of the New Testament, not of the letter but of the spirit” (2 Cor. 3).

“Hear, Israel: the Lord our God is one Lord. You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your strength.”

The faith of the Holy Trinity is commended to the rational soul, which consists of memory, understanding, and love, in the statement: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your strength.” But this perfection of love belongs to the vision of the beauty of God, when we shall see our Creator as he is.

For now, let us strive toward it by the rightness and perfection of our course: by chastising our body and subjecting it to service; by giving alms; by gladly and wholeheartedly forgiving the sins committed against us; by persevering without ceasing in prayer; and by doing these things in sound doctrine, through which right faith, firm hope, and pure love are built up.

This is the condition of hope for the present. For the reality itself—what is believed and hoped for, rather than what is seen and possessed—will follow. But love, which is greater than these three, will not be taken away; rather, it will increase and be fulfilled, contemplating what it believed and attaining what it hoped for. In that fullness of love the commandment will be fulfilled: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind.”

For while there remains any carnal desire that must be restrained by self-control, God is not loved with the whole soul. The flesh does not desire apart from the soul, although the flesh is said to desire because the soul desires carnally.

Then the righteous person will be entirely without sin, because no law in his members will oppose the law of his mind. Rather, with his whole heart, whole soul, and whole mind he will love God, which is the first and greatest commandment.

Why, then, should this perfection not be commanded to human beings, even though they do not possess it in this life? One does not run correctly if one does not know where one ought to run. And how would one know, if it were not shown through commandments? Let us run, therefore, so that we may attain.

All who run correctly will attain—not as in a theatrical race, where all run but one receives the palm. Let us run by chastising the body; by gladly and wholeheartedly giving good things as alms and forgiving evils; and by praying so that the strength of those who run may be helped. Let us thus hear the commandments of perfection, so that we may not neglect to run toward the fullness of love.

**CHAPTER XII [Col. 0865D]. On loving God with the whole soul and with the whole strength, and on binding God’s commandments in human hearts and proclaiming them to one’s descendants throughout all generations**

(CHAPTER VI.) “You shall love,” he says, “the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind; and you shall love your neighbor as yourself.” On these two commandments the whole Law and the Prophets depend. The end, therefore, of the commandment is love. It is twofold: love of God and love of neighbor. You fulfill it if you understand yourself as a whole—that is, soul and body—and your neighbor as a whole—that is, soul and body; for a human being consists of soul and body.

No category of things that ought to be loved has been omitted from these two commandments. Since the love of God comes first and its measure is prescribed, everything else is seen to flow into it. Nothing seems to have been said about love of oneself; but when it is said, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself,” love of oneself by oneself is not omitted.

The person who lives justly and piously is the one who is an undistorted evaluator of things. Such a person orders love properly, so as not to love what should not be loved, fail to love what should be loved, love more what should be loved less, or love equally what should be loved either less or more.

No sinner, insofar as he is a sinner, is to be loved. Every human being, insofar as he is human, is to be loved for God’s sake; God, however, is to be loved for his own sake. And if God is to be loved more than every human being, each person ought to love him more than himself.

Likewise, another human being is to be loved more than our own body, because all these things are to be loved for God’s sake. A human being can enjoy God together with us, which the body cannot do, because the body lives through the soul, by which we enjoy God.

All people, however, are to be loved equally. But since you cannot benefit everyone, you should especially care for those who, through the circumstances of place, time, or any other conditions, are more closely joined to you, as though by a kind of lot.

“And these words that I command you today shall be in your heart, and you shall recount them to your children, and you shall meditate upon them while sitting in your house, while walking on the road, while sleeping and rising. You shall bind them as a sign upon your hand; they shall be and shall move before your eyes; and you shall write them on the threshold and doors of your house,” and so forth.

The sense of this passage, then, is as follows: Let my commandments be in your hand so that they may be fulfilled in action; let them be before your eyes so that you may meditate upon them day and night.

The Pharisees, interpreting this badly—as the Gospel bears witness—used to write the Decalogue of Moses, that is, the ten words of the Law, on little strips of parchment. They folded them, bound them to their foreheads, and made something like a crown for their heads, so that the words might always move before their eyes. The Babylonians do this even today, and whoever possesses such an object is judged religious among the people.

Because the Lord, disputing against the Pharisees, had said to his disciples, “They do all their works so that they may be seen by human beings,”—a charge he had made in general—he now divides it into particulars. These learned men called such things “phylacteries,” as though anyone who possessed them had them for his own protection and nourishment, while the Pharisees did not understand that these things should be carried in the heart, not on the body. Otherwise, cupboards and chests also contain books, yet do not possess knowledge of God.

“You shall fear the Lord your God, and you shall serve him, and you shall swear by his name,” and so forth.

What he says concerning the Lord—“And you shall swear by his name”—must not be understood as though he commanded us to swear. Rather, he prohibited swearing by the name of any other god. It is better, however, if, in accordance with the Gospel, you do not swear.

This is not because a true oath is evil, but lest the ease of swearing lead to perjury. For one who swears can swear not only what is true but also what is false. The person who does not swear at all, however, remains far from perjury.

**CHAPTER XIII. On expelling the seven nations of the Canaanites from the promised land and gradually destroying them**

(CHAPTER VII.) “When the Lord your God has brought you into the land that you are entering to possess, and has destroyed before you many nations—the Hittite, the Girgashite, the Amorite, the Canaanite, the Perizzite, the Hivite, and the Jebusite—seven nations much more numerous than you and stronger than you—and when the Lord your God has handed them over to you, you shall strike them down to complete destruction. You shall make no covenant with them, nor shall you show them mercy.”

These seven nations are the seven principal vices, which every spiritual soldier is admonished to overcome and utterly exterminate through the grace of God.

The reason they are said to be more numerous is that there are more vices than virtues. Thus seven nations are enumerated in the catalogue, but in the account of their conquest they are mentioned without a number: “And he will destroy many nations before you.” The people of carnal passions, which proceeds from this sevenfold source and root of vices, is more numerous than Israel.

From gluttony arise feasting and drunkenness. From fornication arise obscene speech, buffoonery, frivolity, and foolish talk. From avarice arise lies, fraud, deeds, perjury, the desire for shameful gain, false testimony, violence, brutality, and rapacity. From anger arise murders, shouting, and indignation. From sadness arise resentment, faintheartedness, bitterness, and despair. From acedia arise idleness, drowsiness, untimeliness, restlessness, transgression, instability of mind and body, talkativeness, and curiosity. From vainglory arise quarrels, heresies, boastfulness, and presumptuous novelty. From pride arise contempt, envy, disobedience, blasphemy, murmuring, slander, and many other similar things.

Although these are far more numerous than the virtues, once those seven principal vices from whose nature these others proceed have been defeated, all the rest immediately subside and are likewise destroyed through continual attention directed against them.

That these destructive nations are also stronger, we clearly perceive from the very struggle against our nature. The pleasure of carnal passions fights more powerfully in our members than the pursuit of virtues; and the virtues are not acquired without the greatest contrition of heart and body.

The command that we should beneficially possess the territories of these destructive nations is understood as follows. Every vice has its own station in our heart. But if, together with the people of Israel—that is, with the virtues fighting against them—the vices have been overcome, the place in our heart that the spirit of lust or fornication had held will thereafter be occupied by chastity. The place that anger had seized will be reclaimed by patience. The place that sadness producing death had occupied will be possessed by saving joy in its fullness. The place that acedia had devastated will begin to be cultivated by courage. The place that pride had devastated will begin to be cultivated by humility.

And so, once each vice has been expelled, their places—that is, the soul—see God.

When Abraham spoke of those who would see God, Scripture does not record him as enumerating seven nations, but ten, whose land was promised to be given to his offspring. That number is most clearly completed by adding the idolatry of the nations, the blasphemy of the Jews, and the error of heretics.

Before the knowledge of God and the grace of baptism, the multitude of the impious Gentiles and the blasphemous Jews is subject to these powers, until the intellectual Egypt is mentioned. But if someone renounces these things, departs from them, and reaches the spiritual desert through the grace of God, then, freed from the struggle against three nations, he will undertake battle only against the seven enumerated through Moses.

[Col. 0868B] “Do not be afraid, but remember what the Lord your God did to Pharaoh and to all the Egyptians: the great plagues that your eyes saw, and the signs and wonders, and the mighty hand and outstretched arm by which the Lord your God brought you out. So will he do to all the peoples whom you fear. Moreover, the Lord your God will send hornets against them until he destroys and scatters them all.”

Nowhere in the history of the Old Testament is it recorded that the Lord sent hornets or wasps before the children of Israel against their enemies. Through these animals, however, which fight with stings, he signifies the stings of fear among their enemies, by which they were terrified and put to flight.

“‘The great and terrible God himself will consume these nations before you, little by little and in stages [Col. 0868C]. You will not be able to destroy them all at once, lest perhaps the beasts of the earth multiply against you. And the Lord your God will deliver them before you, and he will kill them until they are utterly destroyed.’ He says: ‘The great and terrible God.’ He calls God great and terrible. He is great because he is almighty in delivering his own, and terrible in justly judging his adversaries. ‘He himself will consume these nations,’ because Scripture truly ascribes the victory to him alone when all the enemies are overcome.

“But when he says that the nations are not to be destroyed all at once, lest the beasts multiply against them, he shows us that we must beware lest, after sins have been driven from our flesh, spiritual beasts suddenly arise and attack us—that is, boasting, or pride, or certainly vainglory—which may creep in and will be uprooted with greater labor than carnal vices [Col. 0868D]. For Lot, placed on the mountain, was polluted by an illicit intercourse, although while dwelling in Sodom he had restrained himself from sinning. Therefore, whatever vice we expel, a virtue must immediately be planted in its place, lest the expelled spirit return and find our house empty.

“Yet we should know that, often by the dispensation of almighty God, it happens that to those to whom he grants greater gifts he does not grant certain lesser ones, so that their mind may always have something for which to reproach itself. Thus, while they desire to be perfect and cannot be, and labor over what they have not received without nevertheless prevailing through their labor, they do not exalt themselves over what they do possess. Rather, they say [Col. 0869A] that they do not have greater goods from themselves, since they cannot overcome within themselves even their small and lesser vices.

“For this reason, when the Lord had led Israel into the promised land, destroying all its strong and foremost adversaries, he preserved the Philistines and Canaanites for a longer time, so that, as it is written, Israel might be tested by them. For sometimes, as has been said, he leaves certain small reprehensible things even in those to whom he grants great things, so that they may always have enemies against whom to wage war and may not lift up their minds after conquering great foes, when lesser adversaries still weary them.

“What, then, is this but that one and the same mind should, in a wondrous manner, possess strength through virtue and grow weary through weakness? Thus, partly built up and partly seeing itself not yet built up, it may preserve humbly what it has through the good it seeks but cannot possess [Col. 0869B]. But what wonder is it that we say this of a human being, when that heavenly region itself suffered losses in part among its citizens and yet in part stands firm, so that the elect angelic spirits, seeing others fall through pride, might stand all the more strongly because they stood more humbly? That region therefore profited even through its loss, being more solidly built for the state of eternity by its partial destruction. Thus, in every soul, something is done for the preservation of humility: sometimes the greatest gains are secured through the smallest loss.”

## Chapter VIII

“‘Every commandment that I command you today, take care diligently to do, so that you may live and multiply, and entering, possess [Col. 0869C] the land for which the Lord swore to your fathers; and you shall remember the whole journey by which the Lord your God led you for forty years through the wilderness, in order to afflict and test you, and to make known what was in your mind, whether you would keep his commandments or not.’”

Here it is stated more openly what is expressed elsewhere in a form of speech that is obscure, where we read: “‘The Lord your God is testing you, to know whether you love him.’” This is understood to mean that “to know” has been used in the sense of “to make known,” just as it is clearly said here: “to test you and make known what is in your heart.” For he does not say, “and that he might know.” Had he said that, it would have to be understood as “that he might make known.”

## Chapter XIV [Col. 0869D]  
### Concerning the manna given to the Israelites and their guidance in the wilderness

“‘He afflicted you with want and gave you manna for food, which neither you nor your fathers knew, to show you that man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of the Lord. Your garment, with which you were covered, did not wear out through age, and your foot was not worn down, and so forth.’”

Here spiritual food is commended to us, by which souls destined to live forever are nourished. For the manna given from heaven signifies the flesh of Christ. “‘I am,’ he says, ‘the bread of life that came down from heaven’ (John 6). ‘And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us’ (John 1). ‘Whoever eats,’ says Truth itself, ‘my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life’ (John 6).”

Therefore the one who does not eat this bread or drink this blood does not possess that life. Human beings who are not in his body by faith can nevertheless have temporal life in this world; but they can never have eternal life, which is promised to the saints.

Alternatively: What he says—“Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” (Matthew 4)—signifies the twofold substance of our nature. Man consists of body and soul. Therefore that which is from the earth is nourished by earthly food, while the soul lives only by the word of God. The Spirit of God, who dwells within him, gives life to the human spirit—provided that the person himself is in the body of Christ and lives by faith in the Son of God [Col. 0870A].

That is why he says [Col. 0870B] that the garment does not wear out with age: the conduct of the new human being ought to issue forth in newness of life. His foot will not be worn down when the steps of good works are preserved unharmed, because, as Scripture testifies: “The Lord knows the way of the righteous, but the way of the ungodly will perish” (Psalm 1).

“‘Observe and beware lest you ever forget the Lord your God, and neglect his commandments, judgments, and ordinances that I command you today, and so forth.’”

Some have wished to establish [Col. 0870C] the following distinction among commandments, judgments, and ordinances: commandments are the ten words of the law written on the two stone tablets; judgments are those regulations that the Lord, through Moses, established for the Jewish people at various times by speaking and commanding them after the law had been given, and which are called “justifications” in the Book of Exodus; ordinances are circumcision, the various festivals of the law, and the divine rites of sacrifices.

Thus blessed Father Ambrose, in his exposition of the Apostle Paul’s Letter to the Romans, says:

“Indeed, the law is threefold: the first part concerns the mystery of God’s divinity; the second accords with the natural law, which forbids sin; the third concerns the works of the law—that is, Sabbaths, new moons, and so forth.”

“‘He who brought you out of the land of Egypt, from the house of slavery, and was your guide in the great and terrible wilderness, in which there was a serpent burning with its breath, a scorpion, and a dipsas, and no water at all, and so forth.’”

A dipsas is a kind of asp, called in Latin situla, because whoever is bitten by it dies of thirst. This serpent is said to be so tiny that, when it is stepped on, it cannot be seen; its venom kills before it is felt, so that death overtakes its victim more quickly than grief can arise in the dying person [Col. 0870D]. These various serpents signify the diverse heresies of schismatics. They are indeed different from one another, but all are deadly; whoever they attack, they destroy.

## Chapter IX

“‘Know therefore that the Lord your God has not given you this excellent land to possess because of your righteousness, since you are a stiff-necked people. Remember, and do not forget, how you provoked the Lord your God to anger in the wilderness. From the day you came out of Egypt until this place, you have always contended against the Lord,’ and so forth.”

Certainly [Col. 0871A] these are the people who, for that reason, did not deserve to perish in the wilderness, because they did not know right hand or left. Behold, they are now called stiff-necked. Therefore we must see that this was spoken mystically, and that their merits are not being commended. For lest anyone suppose that these people had suddenly become blameworthy although previously they had deserved praise, it is said shortly afterward:

“‘Remember, and do not forget, that you provoked the Lord your God in the wilderness. From the day you came out of the land of Egypt until you came to this place, you remained unbelieving in matters concerning the Lord.’”

If some of them were such, while others were faithful and good, then the promised land is nevertheless not given to those who do not know right hand or left, if we understand this as referring to the times when they offended the Lord. Their fathers, who died and were not permitted to enter that same land, are likewise found to have been such that some of them were even good. Therefore the Apostle says that not all of them, but certain ones, offended, and recalls their sins: “You are like your fathers.” Thus he teaches more clearly that this passage of Deuteronomy adds what follows: “And at Horeb you provoked the Lord.” Certainly those provoked him who, because of their evil merit, were not brought into the promised land [Col. 0871B].

## Chapter XV  
### The account of how Moses, fasting for forty days on Mount Sinai, obtained the tablets of the law

[Col. 0871D]

“‘And the Lord gave me two stone tablets written with the finger of God, containing all the words that he spoke to you on the mountain from the midst of the fire, when the assembly of the people had gathered. When forty days and an equal number of nights had passed, the Lord gave me two tablets of the covenant of the law and said to me: Rise and go down quickly from here, because the people whom you brought out of Egypt have quickly abandoned the way that you showed them; they have made themselves a molten calf,’ and so forth.”

Moses therefore recalls here how he received from the Lord the tablets of the law written with the ten commandments. He then relates how, because of the people’s sin, he shattered them, and how, fasting and praying again, he obtained other tablets on which the commandments had been written.

But here a question of no small importance arises. For it is written as follows:

## Chapter X

“‘At that time the Lord said to me: Hew out for yourself two stone tablets like the former ones, and come up to me on the mountain; and make a wooden ark. I will write on the tablets the words that were on those that you broke before, and you shall place them in the ark. So I made an ark of acacia wood. When I had hewn two stone tablets like the former ones, I went up the mountain with them in my hands, and he wrote on the tablets, according to the former writing, the ten words that the Lord spoke to you on the mountain from the midst of the fire, when the people had gathered; and he gave them to me,’ and so forth.”

And rightly [Col. 0872A] the question is asked how Deuteronomy can say this while Moses recalls and repeats what happened, when Exodus, where these things are first narrated, says:

“‘And the Lord said to Moses: Write these words for yourself. For in these words I have made a covenant with you and Israel. And Moses was there in the presence of the Lord for forty days and forty nights. He neither ate bread nor drank water, and he wrote on the tablets the ten words of the covenant’ (Exodus 34).”

Since Exodus recalls that Moses himself wrote the ten words of the law on the tablets—the same words—it follows that, when we were treating the matter briefly in Exodus and committed to writing what seemed to us concerning this difference, we explained why the first tablets, which were shattered, are said to have been written by the finger of God [Col. 0872B], while Moses himself is said to have written the second tablets, which were to remain in the ark and the tabernacle.

Thus, as we have said, the two Testaments are signified by this difference: in the Old Testament the law is commended as the work of God, in which human beings have done nothing, because the law could not be fulfilled through fear. For when the work of the law is truly done, it is done through the love of righteousness, not through fear; and this love is the grace of the New Testament. Therefore in the second tablets a human being is read to have written the words of God, because a human being can perform the work of the law through the love of righteousness, though he cannot do so through fear of punishment.

Now, when Deuteronomy speaks of the second tablets, it says:

“‘And I hewed two stone tablets like the former ones, and went up the mountain, and the two tablets were in my hands; and he wrote on the tablets [Col. 0872C], according to the former writing, the ten words.’”

For it does not say, “and I wrote,” but “he wrote”—that is, God—just as he had said shortly before, when reporting the words of God spoken to him: “Hew out for yourself two tablets as the former ones, and come up to me on the mountain, and make yourself a wooden ark, and I will write on the tablets the words that were on the former tablets.”

A question therefore arises for examination: here God is read to have written both sets of tablets, the first and the second, not a human being. But even if the words of God are read in Exodus, where he commands Moses to hew out these second tablets, nothing else is found except that God himself promised that he would write them. For Exodus 34 says:

“‘And the Lord said to Moses: Hew out two tablets for yourself like the former ones, and come up to the mountain; and I will write on the tablets the words that were on the former tablets that you broke.’”

Apart from the Book of Deuteronomy [Col. 0872D], then, Exodus alone contains this question, since the Lord said, “I will write on the tablets the words that were on the former tablets,” while shortly afterward we read:

“‘Write these words for yourself. For in these words I have made a covenant with you and Israel. And Moses was there in the presence of the Lord for forty days and forty nights. He neither ate bread nor drank water. And he wrote on the tablets the ten words of the covenant.’”

If the earlier statement [Col. 0873A]—“Write these words for yourself. For in these words I have made a covenant with you and Israel”—belongs to what precedes, then the Lord was commanding that these words not be written on two stone tablets but in that book of the law in which many things were recorded. Certainly what follows—“And Moses was there in the presence of the Lord for forty days and forty nights. He neither ate bread nor drank water. And he wrote on the tablets the ten words of the covenant”—quite plainly says that Moses himself wrote these ten words on the tablets, not God.

Unless, perhaps, we are compelled—indeed by force, but by a certain necessity—to understand that where it says, “And he wrote on the tablets the ten words of the covenant,” the implied subject is not Moses but God. For it was stated above: “And Moses was there in the presence of the Lord,” so that the ten words may be understood to have been written on the tablets by the Lord, in whose presence Moses was, during the forty days and forty nights when he ate no bread and drank no water, just as he had promised earlier.

If this is so [Col. 0873B], then the distinction between the two Testaments that seemed to us to be commended by these words can still be maintained, even when God, not a human being, wrote both the first and the second tablets.

Nevertheless, this difference certainly admits no doubt: the Lord both made and wrote the first tablets. For at that time Moses was not told, “Hew out two tablets for yourself,” but rather it is said:

“‘And Moses turned and went down from the mountain, and the two tablets of the testimony were in his hands.’”

The tablets were the work of God, and the writing on the tablets was the work of God. For he had already said above that those same tablets were written with the finger of God, speaking as follows:

“‘And he gave Moses, as soon as he had finished speaking with him on Mount Sinai, two stone tablets of the testimony, written with the finger of God.’”

Thus [Col. 0873C] the tablets were the work of God, and their writing was made by the finger of God. Moses himself was commanded to hew out the second tablets, so that they would certainly be understood to have been hewn through human work, although God himself wrote on them, as he had promised when he commanded them to be hewn.

Moreover, if we attend more carefully, both statements are made concerning the second tablets because God, through his grace, performs the work of the law in a human being, while a human being, receiving God’s grace through faith and belonging to the New Testament, becomes a fellow worker with the God who assists him.

In the first tablets, however, only the work of God is mentioned because unbelievers do not cooperate with the assistance of grace. Ignorant of God’s righteousness and wishing to establish their own, they are not subject to God’s righteousness. Thus the law serves for their condemnation, which is signified by the breaking of the tablets [Col. 0873D].

Certainly we are not compelled to supply by a forced interpretation the idea that God wrote where Scripture says:
