“‘And Moses was there in the presence of the Lord for forty days and forty nights. He neither ate bread nor drank water. And he wrote on the tablets the words of the covenant.’”

Here the wording strongly indicates that Moses wrote. But God earlier promised that he would write, and in Deuteronomy he is narrated not only to have promised this but also to have written himself, so that what the Apostle says may be signified: “For it is God who works in us both to will and to work according to his good pleasure” (Philippians 2). This is in those who receive grace through faith and do not wish to construct their own righteousness, but to be subject to the righteousness of God, so that they themselves may be the righteousness of God in Christ [Col. 0874A].

For there too the Apostle speaks of both: God working and themselves working. For if they themselves were not working, how could he say to them: “Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling”? He works, therefore, and we cooperate. He does not confer it, but assists the free choice of a good will.

## Chapter XVI  
### The journey of the children of Israel from Beroth to Musra, where Aaron died and was buried

“‘The children of Israel moved their camp from Beroth of the children of Jaakan to Musra, where Aaron died and was buried. His son Eleazar served in the priesthood in his place. From there they came to Gadgad. Departing from that place, they encamped at Jotbathah [Col. 0874B], a land of waters and streams,’ and so forth.”

It may be asked how Deuteronomy says that Aaron died and was buried at Musra, when the Book of Numbers describes him as having died on Mount Hor (Numbers 33). Perhaps, however, the same place had two names. Beroth of the children of Jaakan is a place in the wilderness, as is Musra, where Aaron died. As we read in books of places, it is still situated at the summit of a mountain, at the tenth milestone from the city of Petra [Col. 0874C].

Josephus holds a similar view. In the fourth book of the Antiquities, he writes as follows (chapter 3):

“Moses,” he says, “led the people through the wilderness and through Arabia, and came to a place that the Arabs consider their metropolis, first called Archim, but now known as Petra. Since this was a high mountain, Aaron climbed it. Moses had declared that he was about to die, and the entire army watched—for the place where the people were stationed was opposite. Aaron removed his high-priestly robe and handed it to his son Eleazar, who, because of his age, succeeded to the high priesthood. Then he died in the sight of the people, in that very year in which his sister was also said to have died, having lived one hundred and twenty-three years,” and so forth.

“He died on the second day of the month, at its beginning. Among the Athenians this month was called Hecatombaeon (Ἑκατομβαίων), among the Macedonians Loos, among the Hebrews Shebat, and among the Romans August. When the people’s mourning for him had lasted thirty days, it then ceased.

“Moses then took the army from there and came to the river Arnon, which descends from the mountains of Arabia, flows through the entire wilderness, and empties into the Asphaltite Lake, dividing Moabitis from Ammonitis. This land is fertile and rich enough to sustain the multitude of people born there.”

[Col. 0874D]

“‘For this reason Levi had no portion or inheritance with his brothers, because the Lord himself is his inheritance, as the Lord your God promised,’ and so forth.”

Unless the entire royal priesthood belonging to the New Testament is represented by this tribe, a man who was not from that tribe could in no way have seemed to say, “The Lord is my portion.” And in another Psalm: “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance” (Psalm 15).

# Book Two

[Col. 0875]

## Chapter I  
### The command to circumcise the foreskin of the heart, and the commendation of orphans, widows, and foreigners

[Col. 0875A]

“‘Circumcise, therefore, the foreskin of your heart, and do not harden your neck any longer, because the Lord your God is himself Lord of lords and Lord of rulers.’”

Here, through the lawgiver, both spiritual circumcision and the truth of the Gospel are commended and expressed to us: namely, vigilance of mind and abstinence from unlawful things. What, then, is signified by the foreskin in this circumcision, except an explicit command: “After you extinguish lust from the flesh, also cut away superfluous thoughts”?

Certainly, when someone hears circumcision preached [Col. 0875B], no one should understand it as commanding continence of only one member—as though it were sufficient merely to be safe from fornication, to use lawful marriage temperately, or to glory in virginity—without the cultivation of the other virtues. Rather, the command concerns the chastening of all the senses that we bear in heart or body.

Moses, who received the purest words of God, complained that he was uncircumcised in lips. And Stephen said to the unbelieving Jews: “Uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit” (Acts 7).

He, therefore, has been cleansed by true circumcision who stops his ears so as not to hear bloodshed and closes his eyes so as not to see evil; who guards his ways so as not to sin with his tongue and takes care lest his heart be weighed down by overeating and drunkenness. So long as breath remains in him and the Spirit of God is in his nostrils, he does not speak wickedness with his lips; he washes his hands among the innocent and keeps his feet from every evil way; above all, he chastens his body and subjects it to slavery, and guards his heart with complete vigilance, because from it life proceeds [Col. 0875C].

Even a good deed itself, when performed in secret, needs circumcision no less: when I fast, pray, or give alms, I must seek glory inwardly. For if I stand at the street corners, disfigure my face, and sound a trumpet before me so that I may be seen and praised by human beings, I appear circumcised outwardly; but, remaining unclean in heart, I incur punishment for a righteousness that I have feigned.

The Shechemites [Col. 0875D] provide an example. Although they seemed to imitate the circumcision of the patriarchs, they did not do it for the covenant of the Lord but for the sake of lust. They not only failed to gain any reward, but on the third day, when the pain of the wounds is severe, they perished amid the ruins of their city.

Such people, having forgotten the prophetic admonition, “Circumcise yourselves to the Lord and remove the foreskins of your hearts,” will, when the time of resurrection comes, find emptied those virtues in which they trusted, and they will be sent into eternal death. Therefore the Apostle diligently commends circumcision hidden in the heart, whose praise is not from human beings but from God [Col. 0876A].

“‘A great and powerful God, terrible, who does not accept persons or gifts. He executes judgment for the orphan and the widow, loves the foreigner, and gives him food and clothing. You too, therefore, love foreigners, because you yourselves were foreigners in the land of Egypt,’ and so forth.”

There are two commandments of charity: love of God and love of neighbor. Through love of neighbor, love of God is generated; and through love of God, love of neighbor is generated. For whoever neglects love of God certainly neglects love of neighbor. We make fuller progress in love of God when, within the embrace of that same love, we are first nourished by love of neighbor.

Because love of God generates love of neighbor, when the Lord was about to say through the law, “You shall love [Col. 0876B] your neighbor,” he first said, “You shall love the Lord your God.” Thus he first planted the root of his love in the soil of our breast, so that brotherly love might afterward spring forth through its branches.

Again, because love of God grows warm through love of neighbor, John testifies when he rebukes us, saying: “Whoever does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see?” (1 John 3).

This divine love, however, is born through fear, but as it grows in affection it is transformed. Often almighty God, so that it may become known how far someone is from his love and the love of his neighbor, or how far that person has progressed in it, orders all things in a wondrous manner: he humbles some through scourges and supports others through success. And when he temporarily abandons certain people, he reveals what evil lies hidden in the hearts of others [Col. 0876C].

For often those who persecute you in your misery are the very people who, without comparison, honored you in your prosperity. When someone is loved while placed in prosperity, it is highly uncertain whether the prosperity or the person is being loved. The loss of happiness tests the power of love.

Thus a certain wise man rightly said: “A friend is not recognized in good fortune, nor an enemy in misfortune.” Prosperity does not reveal a friend, nor does adversity conceal an enemy. For the former is often hidden by reverence for our prosperity, while the latter is revealed by the confidence of affection.

## Chapter II  
### That the promised land is not like the land of Egypt, flat and irrigated, but mountainous and rugged, awaiting rain from heaven

[Col. 0876D]

“‘The land that you are entering to possess is not like the land of Egypt, from which you came, where, after sowing seed, they lead in irrigation water as in gardens; but it is mountainous and level country, awaiting rain from heaven, which the Lord your God always visits, and his eyes are upon it from the beginning of the year to its end.’”

What, then, does the land of Egypt signify except the prosperity of the present life, which lies below and has no desire at all for what is above? There, therefore, water is led in as in gardens, because all carnal people who desire above all to possess present happiness labor at this: with great exertion they strive and apply themselves to possess an abundance of worldly goods together with pleasures [Col. 0877A].

But the spiritual Israelite, who has departed from Egypt under the guidance of Moses—that is, through the instruction of the law—has learned to abandon the desire for earthly pleasures. Through the dispensation of Jesus Christ, he believes that he will possess the promised land, namely, the blessedness of eternal life. He enters a mountainous and level region, namely, the holy Church, where there is both the height of virtues and the purity of good works.

That land always awaits rain from heaven because it desires to have divine grace from above. The Lord God always visits it [Col. 0877B] because he fills it with a heavenly gift. His eyes are upon it from the beginning of the year to its end because his mercy directs the course of life continually, from the beginning of good will to the perfection of good work.

Hence the Psalmist says: “The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are toward their prayers” (Psalm 33). The same prophet asks with great desire to receive such a gift, saying: “His mercy will go before me” (Psalm 58). And again: “His mercy,” he says, “will follow me all the days of my life, and I shall dwell in the house of the Lord for length of days” (Psalm 22). And again: “One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I shall seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord for length of days” (Psalm 26).

Hence the Apostle also says: “For it is God who works in us both to will and to perfect according to his good pleasure” (Philippians 2) [Col. 0877C].

“‘If, therefore, you obey my commandments, which I command you today, so that you love the Lord your God and serve him with all your heart and with all your soul, he will give rain to your land, early rain and late rain, so that you may gather your grain, wine, and oil.’”

What do we understand by rain in this passage except the words of sacred preaching? Thus, concerning the holy teachers whose preaching was withheld from offending Judea, it is written: “I will command the clouds not to rain rain upon it.” We are watered by the drink of sacred preaching when, with true humility, we acknowledge the dryness of our heart [Col. 0877D].

Hence the Psalmist rightly says to God: “My soul is as land without water, for you” (Isaiah 55). The Prophet urges us to be drenched by these streams of teaching, saying: “You who thirst, come to the waters.”

When, at the end of the world, we receive the words of sacred preaching, we are watered, as it were, by the late rain. This late preaching has come to us from the sacrifice of the one who says through the Psalmist: “Let the lifting up of my hands be an evening sacrifice.” Because our Redeemer endured the power of his persecutors near the end of the world, he offered himself as a sacrifice for us.

Therefore, for the people about to enter the promised land, early and late rain is promised—and we already see this fulfilled spiritually. He gave early rain because in the earlier age he granted his chosen ones the understanding of the law. He also gave late rain because he causes the mystery of his incarnation to be preached in the final days.

[Col. 0878A]

“‘When you sit in your house, walk on the road, lie down, and rise, you shall write them on the doorposts and gates of your house, so that your days and the days of your sons may be multiplied in the land that the Lord swore to your fathers to give them,’ and so forth.”

What does Moses mean when, commending the words of the Lord, he commands, “You shall write them on the thresholds of your houses,” when no Israelite is remembered or read to have done this according to the literal sense? For no one could do so unless perhaps he divided them into many parts throughout his house. Or is this a hyperbolical exhortation, like many other statements?

## Chapter III  
### Concerning the prohibition against offering burnt offerings to the Lord in every place, and against eating firstfruits and tithes except in the place chosen by the Lord

[Col. 0878B]

### CHAPTER XII

“Take care not to offer burnt offerings in every place that you see, but only in the place that the Lord will choose. In one of your tribes you shall offer sacrifices, and you shall do whatever I command you, and so forth.”

What does it mean that the law forbids the Israelites to offer burnt offerings in every place, but only in the place that the Lord will choose, except that by this it cuts off the opportunity to sacrifice to idols? For this reason he commanded them to offer sacrifices in the temple and on the altar of the Lord: so that where true religion existed, there also the appropriate worship might be presented.

Mystically, however, he indicates to us that no sacrifice and no gift is acceptable to God outside the Catholic Church, because it is itself the place that the Lord chose, in order to place his name there and dwell in it.

Hence it follows:

“You may not eat in your towns the tithe of your grain, wine, and oil, the firstborn of your herds and flocks, or any of your vows, or the firstfruits of your hands. Rather, before the Lord your God you shall eat them, in the place that the Lord your God will choose—you and your son and your daughter, your male servant and your female servant, and the Levite who dwells within your towns—and you shall rejoice and be refreshed before the Lord your God in all that you undertake.”

According to the tropological sense, sacred Scripture contradicts us, lest we eat in our towns the tithe of our grain, wine, and oil. For it is very disgraceful that we should ascribe to our own strength or goodwill the gifts that we have received from the divine generosity and offer to the Lord God of all.

Therefore, whoever attributes the tithe of grain, wine, or oil in his towns either to his own good will, to spiritual grace, or to the assistance of the virtues gained by his own merits or assigned to his own power, offers it in his towns; and he gravely offends God by seeking his own praise rather than God’s.

He therefore duly and properly fulfills his vows in the place chosen by God who attributes to divine mercy, and not to his own strength, whatever good he recognizes in himself. For the disposition of true humility and innocence is unquestionably the place that the Lord has chosen. Whoever diligently practices good works in that place undoubtedly offers God an acceptable gift.

For this reason the law commands son and daughter, male servant and female servant, and Levite to rejoice and be refreshed before the Lord, because this commandment was established generally for all: that they preserve before God—that is, in sincerity and purity of mind and without pretense—the virtue of humility and gentleness, and that they do there whatever good they are able to do.

“For man sees what is before his eyes, but God looks upon the heart.”

He truly rejoices who is refreshed by spiritual and heavenly joy. Hence the teacher of the nations also exhorts us, saying:

“Rejoice in the Lord always; again I say, rejoice. Let your moderation be known to all people” (Philippians IV).

And again:

“Whoever boasts,” he says, “let him boast in the Lord” (1 Corinthians I).

Scripture demonstrates how necessary humility is for us, saying:

“The greater you are, humble yourself in all things” (Ecclesiasticus III).

And the Apostle says:

“By the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace toward me has not been empty, but his grace always remains in me” (1 Corinthians I).

Hence Peter says:

“Be humbled under the powerful hand of God, so that he may exalt you at the time of visitation, casting all your anxiety upon him, because he cares for you.”

The Truth himself also admonishes the disciples, saying:

“Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matthew XI).

And again:

“Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted. Take care not to abandon the Levite throughout all the time that you dwell in the land, and so forth” (Luke XIV).

By this statement the law of the Lord commends to us the ministers of the word, so that we may provide them with their due support. For just as the Levites in the Old Testament were suitably nourished by the tithes, firstfruits, and gifts that the people offered to the Lord, so in the New Testament it is fitting that good subjects should serve those who preside over them in the Lord with complete devotion.

Thus the Apostle writes to the Thessalonians:

“We ask you, brothers, to recognize those who labor among you and preside over you in the Lord and admonish you, and to esteem them very highly in love because of their work. Be at peace with them” (1 Thessalonians V).

And elsewhere:

“Let the one who is instructed in the word share all good things with the one who instructs him” (Galatians VI).

Hence the Lord also ordained that those who proclaim the Gospel should live by the word and by the Gospel.

### CHAPTER IV  
### The commendation of the Levites and the prohibition against eating blood

(IBID.) “And if you desire to eat meat, which your soul desires, you shall kill from the herds and flocks that you possess, as he commanded you; and you shall eat in your towns as you please. Just as the gazelle and the deer are eaten, so you shall eat them. The clean and the unclean alike shall eat together. Take care only not to eat blood.”

I ought also to observe the literal force of this commandment and in no way eat blood. You will find that the Apostles also commanded this when, after a dispute concerning certain Jewish observances had arisen in the Church at Antioch, the question was referred to those who established the law, resolving and defining the matter as follows:

“It has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us to impose no further burden upon you than these necessary things: that you abstain from things sacrificed to idols, from blood, from what has been strangled, and from fornication” (Acts XV).

Moreover, by blood let us understand, properly, homicide; and by all blood, every hatred of a brother. For whoever hates his brother is a murderer, as John wrote.

We therefore understand all blood as the injustice of deceitful people:

“The man of blood and deceit the Lord will abhor.”

And we should understand as blood whatever harms the life of our neighbors through any kind of treachery, so that it may be compared with homicide. For this reason we must abstain from all blood, knowing that God—namely Christ—sets his face against the souls that eat such blood, of whom David said:

“Who devour my people like a morsel of bread” (Psalm XIII).

“For he is the image of God the Father,” because whoever has seen the Son has seen the Father. He is also the judge.

“For the blood is for the life; and therefore you must not eat the life with the flesh, but you shall pour it out upon the earth like water, so that it may go well with you and with your children after you, when you do what is pleasing in the sight of the Lord.”

Therefore blood is said to be the life of the flesh because something vital exists in the blood: through it, above all, life is maintained in this flesh, since it is diffused throughout the body into all the veins. He called the life of the body “soul”—not the life that departs from the body, but the life that ends in death.

Since, then, the Lord’s command makes clear that the flesh of irrational animals has been granted to human beings for food, while the eating of blood has been forbidden, the truth of the historical sense being preserved, we are given this mystical indication: when carnal people, dead to their former way of life, join with us in the unity of faith and good works, we must in no way convert the errors of their former life to our own use. Rather, we must pour them out upon the earth—that is, having brought them forth through confession, we must assign them to earthly weakness and cast them away as unworthy of spiritual men.

Hence the Apostle writes to the Ephesians:

“This, therefore, I say and testify in the Lord: you must no longer walk as the Gentiles walk in the vanity of their mind, having their understanding darkened, alienated from the life of God because of the ignorance that is in them, on account of the blindness of their heart. They, having become despairing, have given themselves over to immorality, for the practice of every impurity and greed. But you did not learn Christ in this way, if indeed you heard him and were taught in him, as the truth is in Jesus: that you should put off, according to your former manner of life, the old man, who is corrupted according to the desires of error. Be renewed, however, in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man, who has been created according to God in righteousness and the holiness of truth.”

### CHAPTER V  
### The testing of prophets: that those who prophesy vain things or dream falsehoods should not readily be believed; and concerning the prohibition against cutting the flesh or making baldness over the dead

### (CHAPTER XIII)

“If a prophet should arise in your midst, or someone who says that he has seen a dream, and he foretells a sign or portent, and what he has spoken comes to pass, and he says to you, ‘Let us go and follow other gods whom you do not know, and let us serve them,’ you shall not listen to the words of that prophet or dreamer. For the Lord your God is testing you, to make known whether you love him or not with all your heart and with all your soul. You shall follow the Lord your God and fear him; you shall keep his commandments and listen to his voice. You shall serve him and cling to him, and so forth.”

In the edition of the Seventy it is written as follows:

“But if a prophet or a dreamer of dreams should arise among you and give you a sign or wonder, and what he has spoken comes to pass, saying, ‘Let us go and serve other gods whom you do not know,’ you shall not listen to the words of that prophet or of the dreamer of that dream, because the Lord your God is testing you, to know whether you love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul.”

The Latin interpreters did not render this in the same way—“to know whether you love”—although the meaning appears to be the same. In truth, the word “to know” more readily refers to them, so that we should understand it in this way: “He tests you in order to know,” as if it were said, “By testing you, he makes you know.” Here he also intended that, if the things spoken by diviners not according to God should come to pass, what they command and what they worship should not therefore be accepted as true. Nor does God show himself to be without power because these events occur in this way. Rather, as though someone were asking why he allowed them to happen, he explained that the purpose was to test and discover their love—whether they possess it toward their God—not for him to discover it, since he knows all things before they happen.

Throughout this entire chapter the legislator acts against idolaters, and especially against heretics, commanding every believer to beware of the deceptions of the pagans, to guard against the seductions of heretics, and to separate himself from such people, remembering the Lord’s command:

“If your eye causes you to stumble, tear it out and throw it away from you. And if your hand or your foot causes you to stumble, cut it off and throw it away from you. For it is better for you that one of your members should perish than that your whole body should go into Gehenna” (Matthew V).

Hence he foretells the punishment that will come upon those who remain uncorrected and impenitent: how the sword of ultimate vengeance will kill them and everlasting fire will consume all their possessions—that is, their pursuits and works.

For that city, which is described as rebellious through error and turned away from the Lord, is the city of the devil: namely, great Babylon, with which the kings of the earth committed fornication and from whose fornication all the nations drank; in it is the dwelling place of demons and the prison of every unclean spirit and the prison of every unclean and hateful bird.

All the reprobate belong to this city. Its overthrow is written by John in the Apocalypse as follows:

“Woe, woe, that great city Babylon, that strong city! For in one hour your judgment has come. And the merchants of the earth will weep and mourn over her, because no one will buy their merchandise any longer: merchandise of gold and silver, precious stone and pearl, fine linen and purple, silk and scarlet, every kind of citrus wood, every vessel of ivory, every vessel of precious stone, bronze, iron, and marble, cinnamon and spice, perfume, ointment and frankincense, wine and oil, fine flour and wheat, cattle and sheep, horses and chariots, slaves, human beings, and souls. And the fruits desired by your soul have departed from you; and all fat and splendid things have perished from you” (Revelation XVIII).

They mourn the failure of all the world’s pomp and of those things that are either pleasing to the bodily senses or useful for external purposes. The forms of metals belong to sight; perfumes to smell; ointments to touch; wine, wheat, and oil to taste.

By the terms “cattle” and “slaves,” the remaining aids of human society are understood to perish in two ways, as I have said: either because these things fail as the world dies, or because the wretched survivors lament the destruction of those who, by death, have abandoned the joys of the world, as though they were mourning the ruins of their own city.

“Be sons of the Lord your God. You shall not cut yourselves or make baldness over the dead, because you are a holy people to the Lord your God.”

Cutting the flesh and making baldness over the dead were signs of mourning. Certain nations have the custom, in such mourning, of cutting their own bodies. God forbade those whom he counted as sons to do this. One ought to grieve over the dead in such a way that one neither wounds one’s face nor corrupts one’s body.

Paul forbids us to do these things, saying:

“I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, so that you may not grieve like the others who have no hope” (1 Thessalonians IV).

For to do any of the things mentioned above is not to possess hope in the resurrection of the dead. Such people, as though the dead were already corrupted, scatter and corrupt themselves.

Spiritually, all the hairs of the head have been numbered. They are, as is evident to the judge who searches hearts, a figure of all our thoughts. No one, therefore, ought to stir or shake them, nor should anyone offer them to the devil, as some do when they offer a lock from their bodily senses—that is, from their hair—as we said above.

### CHAPTER VI  
### Clean and unclean animals, and what it is permitted or forbidden to eat

### (CHAPTER XIV)

“You shall not eat what is unclean. These are the animals that you may eat: the ox, the sheep, the goat, the deer, the gazelle, the buffalo, the tragelaphus, the pygarg, the oryx, and the giraffe. Every animal that divides the hoof into two parts and chews the cud you may eat, and so forth.”

First, it must be understood that everything established by God is clean and has been purified by the authority of its very creation.

What, then, is the meaning? In animals, human character, actions, and desires are depicted, through which people themselves become clean or unclean.

He therefore declares these animals to be clean:

“Everything,” he says, “that has a divided hoof and chews the cud among the livestock you may eat.”

When he said this, he was distinguishing not livestock but human conduct. In the end, those people are clean who chew the cud, who continually carry the divine commandments in their mouths as though they were food.

They also divide the hoof, because they believe the two Testaments—the Law and the Gospels—and establish themselves with a firm step in a state of innocence and righteousness.

The Jews likewise chew the cud, but they do not divide the hoof. That is, they neither receive the two Testaments of the Law nor establish the step of their faith in the Father and the Son; for this reason they are considered unclean.

Heretics, too, although they divide the hoof by believing in the Father and the Son and accepting the two Testaments, are nevertheless unclean, because they do not chew the doctrine of truth in their mouths.

“Of those, however, that chew the cud but do not divide the hoof, you shall not eat the following: the camel, the hare, and the rock badger. Because they chew the cud but do not divide the hoof, they shall be unclean for you. The pig also, because it divides the hoof but does not chew the cud, shall be unclean. You shall not eat their flesh, and you shall not touch their carcasses.”

(From Hesychius.)

The camel is the Jew swollen with pride, such as the scribes and Pharisees were, to whom the Lord said:

“Straining out a gnat and swallowing a camel” (Matthew XXIII).

Therefore the scribes and Pharisees eat what chews the cud, because they glory in meditation upon the letter of the Law, in the observance of the Sabbath and of purification, and in sacrifices and other similar practices. But they do not divide the hoof among the things they eat, nor do they distinguish the letter from the spirit; for this reason their knowledge is unclean.

The same applies to those who eat the hare and those who eat the rock badger. These animals also chew the cud, but they do not divide the hoof.

Among the common multitude of the Jews, both meanings are found. These animals are said to be weak, as David and Solomon testify concerning the weakness of both animals. Solomon says:

“The little hare, a weak people, has made its dwelling in the rock” (Proverbs XXX).

David says:

“The rock is a refuge for the hedgehogs or rock badgers.”

One of them is swift and timid together with weakness—that is, the hare. The other, they say, is weak but rapacious, savage, and deadly—that is, the rock badger. This is characteristic of the entire common people, but especially of the Jewish people. David said of them:

“Their feet are swift to shed blood” (Psalm XIII).

The divine voice shows how timid and weak the sons of the Jews are when it says:

“Woe to their fearful hearts and weakened hands.”

Hear Isaiah on the injustice and savagery that existed among them:

“How has the faithful city, full of judgment, become a prostitute? Righteousness dwelt in her, but now there are murderers” (Isaiah I).

After these, he says that the pig is unclean, because it divides the hoof but does not chew the cud. Receive Peter as interpreter and teacher: he called a person a pig who possesses knowledge of divine things but does not use it well, pollutes it by incongruous actions, and gives himself over to an unclean life.

He said:

“It would have been better for them not to have known the way of righteousness than, after knowing it, to turn back from the holy commandment delivered to them” (2 Peter II).

The true proverb has happened to them:

“The dog has returned to its own vomit, and the washed sow to wallowing in the mud.”

But here he added what has been said: “You shall not eat their flesh, nor touch their carcasses, because they are unclean for you.” Thus he did not count the camel, the hare, the rock badger, or the pig among the clean animals.

The camel, as we have said, represents the scribes and Pharisees, who are marked by the vice of foolishness through their pride; foolishness is contrary to wisdom. For it is characteristic of fools to be proud.

The hare, as timid, is opposed to courage. The rock badger, as rapacious, is opposed to justice. The pig, living a filthy and unclean life, is opposed to chastity.

We must not eat the flesh of these animals—that is, we must not follow the virtue that they appear to possess. For they pursue it in hypocrisy and not in truth. Still more, we must not touch their carcasses, nor share in their evil actions. Such things are unquestionably true carcasses.

“These you may eat among all that move in the waters: whatever has fins and scales you may eat. Whatever does not have fins and scales you shall not eat, because they are unclean.”

By these are understood those among the nations who have been saved, possessing regeneration in the water of baptism. Isaiah also says of them:

“Behold, the nations are like a drop from a bucket” (Isaiah XL);

or, according to the Seventy:

“Like many waters, many nations.”

Accordingly, what follows also applies to them:

“Whatever has fins or scales, whether in the sea, rivers, or ponds, you may eat.”

He also commanded that the same things should be preached to those who are from the nations concerning meditation upon the Law, though in other words. For he wants them to possess fins in their meditation upon the Law and to have a lofty and heavenly life, together with an interpretation of the Law like this.

For this reason he does not want them to have merely one fin but fins. Since ignorance of divine Scripture had taken possession of the nations—they had not received the Law or the prophets, nor any other more refined divine knowledge—he did not want them to remain permanently and continually afflicted by this disease. He therefore wants them to have scales, which are easily removed.

Because scales signify temporal ignorance, and ignorance that can easily be removed, he demonstrates this from what is written about Paul in the Acts of the Apostles. When he was persecuting the Church out of Jewish zeal, he easily lost that zeal because of his ignorance after he learned whom he was persecuting, having been called by Christ, and after Ananias had evangelized to him:

“For scales fell from his eyes, and immediately he saw.”

Thus temporal ignorances lay upon him like scales. Hence the legislator appropriately adds:

“Whatever among the things that move and live in the waters does not have fins or scales shall be abominable and detestable to you.”

There are certain kinds of fish that have a shell instead of skin and whose scales cannot be removed. Such are those who neither permit the scales of ignorance to be removed by the word of God nor allow the summit of the spirit to be received.

Even if they are found in the sea of baptism, and even if they are in the rivers of repentance, they are abominable in all that moves and lives in the waters. Although they have received life in baptism, they have nevertheless corrupted their calling and their regeneration, since they do not have fins or scales—that is, a lofty life and knowledge of divine things, which is heavenly—but retain a blind heart in ignorance. For this reason they are not counted among those that have scales.

Consider with what sublimity of language the legislator speaks, signifying through these things the greatest and most wondrous mysteries. He joined fins and scales because, just as fish that have scales also invariably have fins, so those who have temporal scales may quickly be rid of them. To these are added lofty knowledge and a heavenly life.

Those who are not such must neither eat their flesh nor touch their carcasses, nor have any association with them at all. Paul attests to this, saying:

“If anyone who is called a brother is a fornicator, or greedy, or an idolater, or a reviler, or a drunkard, or a rapacious person, with such a one do not even take food” (1 Corinthians V).

An adulterer, a greedy person, a drunkard, or a slanderer does not have fins—that is, he has a filthy and unclean life. The worshiper of idols, who does not have scales, is not counted among them. He appears to possess a hard ignorance of divine things, like shell, and one that cannot be healed. Otherwise, after he had been joined to God, he would never again serve idols.

Furthermore, it should be noted that fish possessing fins and scales are accustomed to leap even above the waters. What, then, are winged fish meant to signify except chosen souls, which alone pass into the body of the heavenly Church? Supported now by the fins of the virtues, they know how to leap through heavenly desire, seeking contemplation of what is above, although they may again fall back into themselves from mortal flesh.

Therefore only those pass into the body of the elect as chosen food who, while serving in the depths, know at times how to ascend to what is above by leaps of the mind, lest they always lie hidden in the depths of cares, and lest any breath of the highest love, like the air of freedom, touch them.

Those who are occupied with temporal affairs arrange external matters well when they diligently retreat to lower things, when they by no means love the noise of disturbances outside, and when they rest within themselves in the embrace of tranquility.

[Column 0885D] “Eat all the clean birds; you shall not eat the unclean. Namely, the eagle, the griffin, the sea eagle, the ixion, the vulture, and the kite according to its kind, and every bird of the raven kind; the ostrich, the owl, the gull, and the hawk according to its kind; the heron, the swan, the ibis, the diver, the purple waterhen, the night raven, the pelican, and the plover, each according to its kind. The hoopoe also and the bat, and everything that creeps and has fins, shall be unclean and shall not be eaten.”

The legislator did not leave unexamined even those who devote themselves to the contemplative life. Just as he assigns them a distinct chapter of the Law in the offering of sacrifices, so in the investigation of foods he gives them their own boundaries.

He makes them more fearful and more awe-inspiring by teaching that they should know these things as well, not only what concerns cattle and fish. There he says:

“These are the animals that you may eat from all the living creatures of the earth.”

And again:

“These are the things that are born in the waters, and which it is permitted to eat.”

But concerning the birds he says:

“These are the birds that you shall not eat, and they must be avoided by you.”

It is truly worthy of abhorrence, and should be counted among the unlawful and most carefully avoided things, for someone devoted to contemplation willingly to possess such stains as the legislator signifies through the birds he enumerates.

He says: “The eagle, the griffin, the sea eagle, and the kite according to its kind.” Through these he signifies rapacious people who pursue what belongs to others wickedly and rejoice in unjust profits.

Since some are found in the Church among those thought to devote themselves to contemplation who do not devote themselves to it as they ought, but are vainly puffed up, hear Paul saying:

“If anyone teaches otherwise and does not assent to the sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ and to the doctrine that is according to godliness, he is puffed up, knowing nothing, but languishing over questions and disputes about words, from which arise envy, strife, blasphemies, evil suspicions, conflicts among people corrupted in mind and deprived of the truth, who think that godliness is a means of gain” (1 Timothy VI).

The animals now enumerated signify such people, who obtain their livelihood through rapine. Some of these birds attack other birds and are nourished by their prey. Others, entering houses, seize what they find and spare not even the provisions of those who possess them. Such are like certain people who enter houses and take captive little women burdened with sins; Paul rebukes them.

The vulture rejoices in quarrels and wars because of the corpses of battle, to such an extent that it even follows an army. Therefore a person devoted to contemplation must not feed and nourish himself on the misfortunes of others.

Animals of the raven kind are without affection. This is evident from the fact that, when sent out by Noah, the raven flew away from him at the first opportunity. Judas was like it in relation to his teacher and Lord.

The ostrich is a bird, but it cannot fly and spends its whole life occupied around the earth. Such are those who serve God but entangle themselves in the affairs of the world.

The Seventy called the owl “glaukos.” They assert that it has keen sight at night but, when the sun appears, derives less benefit from its eyes. Such are those who boast of contemplation and knowledge of the Law but are unable to receive the light of evangelical conduct.

The gull is an animal that lives in both elements, water and land. It flies like a bird, but swims like an aquatic creature. Those who venerate circumcision and baptism simultaneously may appropriately be compared with it.

To them Paul says:

“If you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing” (Galatians V).

The hawk is among the rapacious birds, but it has another characteristic for which the legislator included it. It becomes tame and assists in rapine. Those who imitate it appear to be gentle and tranquil in disposition, but they associate with the powerful, the greedy, and the rapacious.

The night raven is an animal that creeps and works only at night. Such are the nations, who belong intellectually to the works of darkness: fornication, impurity, filth, the worship of idols, and similar things.

The ibis and the purple waterhen—which the Seventy call the pelican—the swan, and the plover are said to have long necks and to draw their food from the heights of the earth and the waters. We must not imitate these animals or pull food from what is below, but from heavenly things.

A person devotes himself to contemplation when he strives toward what is above in his mind and expects not merely intelligible food from the Lord. Hence the Lord says:

“Do not be anxious for your soul, what you shall eat, or for your body, what you shall wear. For your heavenly Father knows that you need all these things” (Matthew VI).

The hoopoe is a mournful animal that loves what is sorrowful. But worldly sorrow produces death. Therefore the person who loves the Lord ought always to rejoice, pray without ceasing, and give thanks in all things, because joy is the fruit of the Spirit.

Bats fly close to the earth, so that when they walk they use their wings instead of feet. This is nevertheless unworthy of those who devote themselves to contemplation. Those whose flight is around the earth undoubtedly also have minds occupied with earthly things.

Do not therefore be incredulous or doubt that the legislator also set down these animals now enumerated to display figuratively those things from which people devoted to contemplation ought to abstain.

But you will say: How is it that the food of these animals, rather than their imitation, is forbidden, when it is written:

“I have become like a pelican in solitude; I have become like a night raven in a dwelling” (Psalm CI)?

By the eagle Moses himself signifies the Lord, who says to Israel:

“How I carried you upon the wings of eagles.”

The prophets also call Christ a lion. Yet the Apostle Peter says that the devil is a lion. Nevertheless, according to this, Christ is not a lion in the same sense in which the devil is called one. Far be such impiety from us.

Rather, because the lion is at once royal, rapacious, and savage, and because it possesses an honorable dignity but exercises a blameworthy activity, what it has honorable is understood in Christ, while what it has blameworthy—rapacity and savagery—is understood in the devil. Considering the same thing in the eagle, we find it without any doubt.

Because of the height of its flight, Moses applied it to the Lord. The prophet David, however, mourning a person established in sin, compared him to the night raven, as one living in darkness.

Through the pelican, as an animal that loves solitude, he represented someone who has perhaps been deserted by friends and deprived of the company of relatives and others like them.

“And everything that creeps and has fins shall be unclean and shall not be eaten.”

He commanded that those who profess the contemplative life should be clean from every sin and filthy action. Therefore whoever resembles flying creatures—that is, professes to attain the contemplation of heavenly things that leads to the heavens—but is compared to reptiles of the earth and devotes himself to desires, is unclean and abominable, even if he walks on four feet.

That is, even if he imitates the Gospel, which says:

“I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance,”

and:

“Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick” (Luke V);

even though the thief was saved and the adulteress justified, and those who had been forgiven more were said to love the innocent one more—nevertheless, because they do not embrace a communal life according to the truth but abuse the compassion of preaching for their own pleasures, they are unclean and abominable. They enter upon a shameful and unclean life in such a way of living and with such great knowledge.

“Eat everything that is clean; you shall not eat anything that has died of itself. Give it to the sojourner who is within your gates, so that he may eat it, or sell it, because you are a holy people of the Lord your God.”

He commanded that everything clean be eaten because he permits the use of good actions and honorable conduct. He prohibits eating what has died because he commands us to abstain from the works of the dead.

Rather, he permits it to be given to the sojourner, because he casts it away as unclean and belonging to a pagan or heretic, who is alien and exiled from the Christian religion, when he sees that such a person is unwilling to abstain from the filth of sins.

Hence the Apostle says:

“To the clean all things are clean; but to the defiled and unbelieving nothing is clean” (Titus I).

For this reason the Savior in the Gospel permitted the demons expelled from human beings to go into pigs. And to the disciple who asked leave to bury his father he replied:

“Let the dead bury their own dead; but you go and proclaim the kingdom of God” (Matthew VIII).

### CHAPTER VII  
### On not boiling a kid in its mother’s milk; on giving tithes; and on the prohibition against shearing the firstborn of sheep

(IBID.) “You shall not boil a kid in its mother’s milk.”

Here the kid is introduced under the figure of the sinner. Therefore the sinner must not be boiled in his mother’s milk—that is, he must not be cleansed by the ordinary and tender disciplines of the Church. Rather, the sins of one whose crimes are great must be boiled away through more severe commandments, so that the person who has destroyed himself through the allurements of lust may redeem himself through stricter discipline.

“From all the produce of your crops, which are harvested year by year, you shall set apart a tenth in the presence of the Lord your God, in the place which he will choose so that his name may be invoked there: a tenth of grain, wine, and oil; and the firstborn of your herds and flocks, so that you may learn to fear the Lord your God at all times. But when the journey is longer and the place which the Lord your God will choose is far away, and he has blessed you so that you cannot carry all these things to him, you shall sell everything, convert it into money, carry the money in your hand, and set out for the place which the Lord your God will choose. With that same money you shall buy whatever pleases you, etc.”

What does it mean that he commands those who lived farther away from the place where God’s tabernacle or temple had been established to sell a tenth of their grain, wine, and oil, as well as the firstborn of their cattle and sheep, except that he is instructing those who live as settlers in this world and are far from the perfection of the saints, who cannot ascend to the practice of the virtues or devote themselves to divine contemplation, to carry out devoutly and humbly whatever good they are able to accomplish by divine grace? Thus, from earthly and transitory things, they may purchase for themselves eternal rewards and heavenly treasures.

Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Store up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither rust nor moth destroys, and where thieves do not break in or steal” (Matt. VI). And elsewhere he says: “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of unrighteousness, so that when it fails, they may receive you into the eternal dwellings” (Luke XVI). There one must feast; there one must rejoice with friends—that is, with the saints, the elect, and the angels—where the joys once begun will not cease but will endure in perpetual blessedness.

“In the third year you shall set apart another tenth of everything that is produced for you at that time, and you shall store it within your gates. Then the Levite, who has no other portion or inheritance with you, and the foreigner, the orphan, and the widow who are within your gates shall come, eat, and be satisfied, so that the Lord your God may bless you in all the works of your hands that you do.”

In the Septuagint edition it reads as follows:

“After three years you shall bring forth the whole tenth of your fruits. In that year you shall place it in your cities. And the Levite shall come, because he has no portion or lot with you, and the orphan and the widow who are in your cities shall come; and they shall eat and be satisfied, so that the Lord your God may bless you in all your works, whatever you do.”

Regarding this tenth, he did not say that the person himself should eat it with his household. Rather, through the Levites, orphans, foreigners, and widows, he commanded that it be expended. But the wording is obscure, because this tenth is not distinguished from the one which he wished to be eaten with the Levites in the place that the Lord had chosen, in his temple. In the interpretation made from the Hebrew, however, we find the distinction more clearly. It says:

“In the third year you shall set apart another tenth of everything that is produced for you at that time, and you shall store it within your gates. Then the Levite, who has no other portion or inheritance with you, and the foreigner, the orphan, and the widow who are within your gates shall come; and they shall eat and be satisfied, so that the Lord your God may bless you in all the works of your hands that you do.”

First, the wording “in the third year” is fuller and clearer. For one intervening year is understood. In the Septuagint, however, when it says “after three years,” it is uncertain whether it means that the intervening years are to be counted, so that this was to take place every third year. Further, when it says, “You shall set apart another tenth,” it clearly shows that this is distinct from the tenth which he wished the offerer himself to eat with his household and the Levites in the place which the Lord had chosen. This other tenth he commanded him to place within his gates, not to bring to the place where the Lord wished his name to be invoked. “And the Levite shall come,” he says, “who has no portion or inheritance with you, and the foreigner, the orphan, and the widow who are within your gates, and he shall eat.” Hence it is plainly true that the Lord did not wish this tenth to be held in common by the one who offered it and those for whom it was intended; rather, he commanded that it be distributed solely to those who had nothing else—among whom he placed the Levite first.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the remission of the seventh year, and on the servant whose ear is pierced with an awl

(CHAP. XV.) “In the seventh year you shall grant remission, and it shall be observed in this manner: whoever is owed something by his friend, neighbor, or brother shall not be able to demand it, because it is the Lord’s year of remission.”

In this chapter, piety and love are especially commended to us. Through the remission of the seventh year, we are commanded to show mercy and charity toward our poor neighbors, and therefore we ought to hope for a future recompense from the Lord. Hence the Apostle exhorts us, saying: “Let us not grow weary in doing good. For in due time we shall reap, if we do not grow weary. Therefore, while we have opportunity, let us do good to all, especially to those who belong to the household of faith” (Gal. VI). Writing to a disciple, he likewise says: “Exercise yourself in piety. For bodily exercise is useful for a little, but piety is useful for everything, holding the promise of the life that now is and of the life to come” (I Tim. IV). Hence Truth itself also says in the Gospel: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven; give, and it will be given to you. With the measure with which you measure, it will be measured back to you” (Luke VI).

“From the foreigner and the sojourner you shall demand it; from your kinsman you shall not have the power to reclaim it,” etc.

He calls “foreigner” and “sojourner” the one who is outside the Church and outside the Christian religion. A “kinsman” is the one who is our brother and who, established within the Church, worships with us the one Lord. Thus he makes a distinction between the foreigner and the citizen so that we may understand that the one who remains with us in the unity of faith is nearer to us than the one who is alien to Christ in worship and observance. And although we ought to observe justice toward all people, we should nevertheless have a gentler affection toward our neighbors, precisely because they are our members and stand with us in the unity of our body and of Christ. Therefore we ought to love them as ourselves.

For this reason it is added: “There shall be absolutely no needy or beggar among you, so that the Lord your God may bless you in the land which he will give you as a possession.” We ought therefore, as far as possible, to care for our neighbors in their needs as we would for ourselves, because the performance of a work is the proof of love. Hence John says: “If anyone has the world’s goods and sees his brother in need, but closes his heart against him, how does the love of God remain in him? My little children, let us not love in word or tongue, but in deed and truth” (I John III).

“Beware lest perhaps an impious thought steal upon you and you say in your heart: ‘The seventh year, the year of remission, is approaching’; and you turn your eyes away from your poor brother, unwilling to lend him what he asks, lest he cry out against you to the Lord and it become a sin for you. But you shall give to him, and you shall not act deceitfully in relieving his needs, etc.”

The Septuagint reads:

“Take heed to yourself, lest there be a hidden word of iniquity in your heart, saying: ‘The seventh year, the year of remission, is approaching,’ and your eye become evil toward your needy brother, and you do not give to him. Then he will cry out against you to the Lord, and there will be great sin in you.”

Magnificently he called this a “hidden word,” since no one who is capable of thinking dares to say that a loan should not be given to the needy because the year of remission is approaching. God, in his mercy, commanded both that a loan be given when someone is in need and that it be remitted in the year of remission. How, then, will anyone remit mercifully in the year when remission is required, if he cruelly thinks that nothing should be given at the time when it ought to be given?

“When your Hebrew brother or sister has been sold to you and has served you for six years, in the seventh year you shall let him or her go free.”

He did not wish these purchased servants to be released in the year which everyone was required to observe as the seventh year. Rather, they were to be released in the seventh year after their purchase, whenever that seventh year occurred for them.

“But if he says, ‘I do not wish to go out, because he loves you and your household and finds that he is well with you,’ you shall take an awl and pierce his ear at the door of your house, and he shall serve you forever, etc.”

With regard to the commands concerning the Hebrew servant—that he serve for six years and be released freely without payment—the apostolic authority commands Christian servants to remain subject to their masters, lest the name of God and the doctrine be blasphemed.

From this it is sufficiently clear what was commanded mystically. God commanded that the ear of the one who refused that freedom be pierced with an awl at the doorpost. A Hebrew boy, if he should happen to fall into servitude, is commanded to serve for six years, but in the seventh year he is to be released free. If he refuses to leave servitude because of his wife and children, his ear is pierced, and he becomes a servant forever.

This is not spoken of the present age but of the future. For after serving through the six ages of this world, we are freed on the seventh day, the eternal Sabbath—provided that we do not wish to be free while we are still in this world serving sin. But if we refuse, our ear will be pierced as a testimony to our disobedience, and with our wives and children, whom we have preferred to freedom—that is, with the flesh and its works—we shall remain forever servants of sin.

This may also be understood in another way.

*(From Gregory.)* It must be understood that although both the active and the contemplative life come from God’s grace, one is necessary for us, while the other depends upon our will. For who, having come to know the Lord, does not enter his kingdom unless he first practices good works? Without the active life, therefore, they cannot enter if they neglect to do the good works that they are able to do. The active life, then, is necessary; the contemplative life depends upon the will. Hence it is said to Moses:

“If you buy a Hebrew servant, he shall serve you for six years; in the seventh year he shall go out free, without payment,”

and the rest that follows.

“Hebrew” is interpreted as “one who passes over.” A Hebrew servant is bought when someone who has already passed over from this world in his mind is subjected to the service of almighty God. For the one who desires to serve the true God is the one who has learned to pass over from this world in his mind. Thus “Moses passed over so that he might see the vision” (Exod. III). Thus David, when he “saw the wicked exalted above the cedars of Lebanon, passed over, and he was no more” (Ps. XXXVI), because we may perhaps think that the power of the wicked is something great unless we pass over in our minds to the enduring world.

The Hebrew servant who has been purchased is commanded to serve for six years, so that in the seventh he may go out free without payment. What is signified by the number six except the perfection of the active life? What is signified by seven except the contemplative life? He serves for six years and goes out free in the seventh: one who has perfectly performed the active life passes into the freedom of the contemplative life.

It should also be noted that he goes out free without payment because, after they have done everything, such people call themselves unworthy servants. Just as the active life itself came to them as a gift, so undoubtedly the contemplative life will also come by grace.

“With whatever garment he entered, with such a garment he shall go out.”

For it is entirely necessary that each of us persevere in what he has begun and remain to the end of the work in the intention with which he began. The one who passes to the contemplative life is the one who has not changed the garment of his intention in the active life.

There are some who, even before they join the service of almighty God, already love to do good. Others learn good works after they have come into the service of almighty God. Thus the one who had diligently practiced good works even before coming into God’s service is a Hebrew servant purchased with a wife. Often such a person can pass into the contemplative life and yet not abandon the active life. Hence it is added there:

“If he has a wife, and the wife goes out with him.”

The wife goes out with him into freedom when the one who has attained contemplation does not abandon outwardly the activity of good works by which he can benefit others.

“But if the master gives him a wife, and she bears sons and daughters, the woman and her children shall belong to her master; he himself shall go out with his garment.”

The master gives the purchased servant a wife when a preacher, whom he has rightly dedicated to almighty God, joins him to a good work. For preachers are also called masters, as it is said to the prophet Elisha concerning his preacher: “Do you know that your master is being taken away from you?” [The text appears corrupt here.]

The wife of the purchased servant bears sons and daughters when a good work generates strong or tender fruits for him. But the woman given by the master remains with that same master, together with her children; the servant himself goes out with his garment because the good work, or the fruit of that good work, is reckoned to the preacher’s reward. He himself, persevering in the intention of his desire, goes out free into contemplation through heavenly grace.

“But if the servant says, ‘I love my master, my wife, and my children; I will not go out free,’ the master shall offer him to the gods, and he shall be brought to the door and the doorposts. His master shall pierce his ear with an awl, and he shall be his servant forever.”

The servant loves his master when he carefully preserves the preacher’s words in his mind. He loves his wife and children and refuses to go out free when, loving the active life and its fruits, he does not wish to pass into contemplation, because, recognizing that he possesses good works in the service entrusted to him, he refuses to pass into the repose of freedom.

The master who has arranged for him to remain in the active life offers him to the gods when he is instructed by his preacher in the sayings of the ancient Fathers, who were priests for us on the way of almighty God. He is led to the door of the tabernacle so that he may hear something about entrance into the eternal tabernacle and carefully recognize the day of the dreadful judgment. He must not seek to please human beings through the good works he performs.

Thus his ear is pierced with an awl when his mind is struck by the subtle fear of God. Pierced through by the sharpness of the word, he learns, in everything he does, always to await entrance into the kingdom, and to carry his ear as though it had been pierced at the door and doorpost of the tabernacle.

He will be a servant forever so that he may be free after this age. For he is a servant in this age who has resolved to serve human beings through the active life, so that after the present age he may attain true freedom. Of this Paul says: “For creation itself will be liberated from the slavery of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God” (Rom. VIII). Then true freedom will exist in us, when our adoption reaches the glory of the children of God. At present, therefore, not only is the active life in servitude, but even contemplation, by which we are lifted above ourselves, does not possess freedom of mind; it only imitates it, because that innermost rest is seen in an enigma.

## CHAPTER IX. On sacrificing the firstborn to the Lord, and on not working with the firstborn of an ox

(IBID.) “Whatever male firstborn is born among your herds and flocks, you shall consecrate to the Lord your God.”

We are commanded to consecrate the firstborn to the Lord when we are instructed to apply to God, the giver of all good things, the beginnings of our good will and good works, rather than to ourselves. Whatever good exists in us, he has bestowed upon us as his gift; it is not the achievement of our own effort. Hence James says: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (Jas. I). Paul likewise says: “For God is the one who works in us both to will and to accomplish, according to his good pleasure” (Phil. II).

But if something in our thought is slight, or bears a stain in our conduct or speech; if something was lame in the progress of our activity, blind through ignorance of mind, or deformed or weak in some respect, we must not sacrifice this to God—that is, we must not attribute it to him—but to our own weakness. For it belongs to corruptible and frail humanity to sin. Hence it is written: “There is no one on earth who does good and does not sin.”

[Note: [Col. 0893D] The passage is corrupt.]

“As for the house, the day …” [The wording is corrupt; the surviving text appears to concern our ability to restrain ourselves from sins.]

It must be asked whether what the Greeks call πρωτότοκα (*prōtotoka*), which can only be rendered in Latin as *primogenita* (“firstborn”), is to be understood only of those born from mothers. Such offspring are properly said to be brought forth rather than begotten. For “to bring forth” is τείκτειν (*teikteîn*), which belongs to the female; hence πρωτότοκον (*prōtotokon*) is used. “To beget,” however, is γεννᾷν (*gen­nân*), from which the Latin *primogenitus* (“firstbegotten”) is properly derived.

From females, the *primitiva*—that is, those brought forth first—were given. The first were begotten by males, if, for example, they were begotten from widows who had already given birth. Otherwise they could not be those who “open the womb,” which the law specifically wished to designate as the firstborn owed to the Lord.

If there is such a distinction in these expressions, it is not without reason that the Lord is not called by the Father *monotokos* (μονότοκος, “only-born”), but *monogenēs* (μονογενής), that is, “only-begotten,” meaning “the unique one.” Of the dead, he is called *primogenitus* (“firstborn”) in Latin, because the Latin word could not be formed according to ordinary usage in the same way. In Greek he is called πρωτότοκος (*prōtotokos*), not πρωτογενής (*prōtogenēs*), as though the Father had begotten one equal to himself, while creation had brought forth another.

When he is called “the firstborn of all creation,” the Greek reads πρωτότοκος (*prōtotokos*). This can be understood according to the new creation, of which the Apostle says: “Therefore, if there is any new creation in Christ”—from which he is the firstfruits—“because, as firstfruits, he rose in such a way that he would no longer die, and death would no longer rule over him” (II Cor. V). What is promised at the end is the future of the new creation which is in him. But this distinction must not be asserted rashly; it must be investigated more carefully in the Scriptures.

For it raises the question how it could be said in Proverbs: “Firstborn, I say to you, son”—that is, in whose person should this be understood? If it is said from the person of God the Father to Christ, it is scarcely possible to affirm that the same one is called both firstborn and only-begotten, since we too are sons of God. He is called only-begotten, however, because he alone is from the substance of the Father and is coequal and coeternal with the Father. It is remarkable whether sacred Scripture distinguishes “to bring forth” and “to beget” by the clearest evidence.

“You shall not work with the firstborn of an ox, and you shall not shear the firstborn of your sheep.”

What else, through the example set forth here, did Moses forbid than the life of those who are beginning well being occupied with human affairs? To plow with the firstborn of an ox is to display the beginnings of a good way of life in public activity. To shear the firstborn of sheep is to strip our nascent good works from the covering of their hiddenness before human eyes.

We are forbidden to work with the firstborn of an ox and restrained from shearing the firstborn of sheep, because, even if we have begun to practice something good and vigorous, we ought not immediately bring it into the open. When our life begins in a simple and innocent manner, it is fitting that it should leave behind the coverings of its secrecy, rather than display itself before human eyes as though its fleece had been removed.

Therefore the firstborn of oxen and sheep should be used only for divine sacrifices, so that whatever simple and innocent thing we happen to begin, we may sacrifice it on the altar of the heart for the honor of the inner Judge. It is unquestionably accepted by him with greater willingness when, hidden from human beings, it is not stained by any desire for praise.

Often the beginnings of a new way of life are still mixed with the carnal life. For this reason they should not be disclosed too quickly, lest, when the good things that are pleasing are praised, the mind—deceived by its praise—be unable to detect in them the evils that are displeasing.

We understand the firstborn of an ox as the good activity of the weakness of our earliest age. Yet one must not plow with it, because, while the first years of our adolescence or youth are still upon us, we ought not yet to preach, lest the plowshare of our tongue dare to cut the soil of another’s heart.

As long as we are weak, we must contain ourselves within ourselves, lest, by displaying our tender virtues too soon, we lose them. Planted saplings, if they have not first taken root in the earth, quickly wither when touched by the hand. But once they have firmly rooted, the hand may touch them without harming them. Winds push against them, but the force of the winds does not injure them. Walls that have been built, however, collapse when struck unless they have first been dried by their own moisture.

Thus, as long as the mind has not been thoroughly dried of the moisture of its depravity, it ought not to be touched by another’s tongue, lest, before it has fully received strength, it lose its stability; lest, when struck, it fall; lest, like a rootless sapling, it be shaken by gusts stronger than it can endure and wither.

Therefore only what is firm should be displayed as an example. The mind must first grow strong, and only afterward be shown for the benefit of its neighbors—when it can no longer fall after being lifted up by praise, nor wither after being struck by criticism.

For although it is said to Timothy, “Command and teach these things. Let no one despise your youth” (I Tim. IV), it must be understood that his youth was already advanced in years, though not in conduct. Nevertheless, in sacred language youth is sometimes called adolescence. Hence it is written: “Rejoice, young man, in your youth” (Eccl. XI).

## CHAPTER X. The command to celebrate the Passover for the Lord in the month of new crops

[Col. 0895D] (CHAP. XVI.) “Observe the month of new crops and the first month of spring, so that you may celebrate the Passover for the Lord your God, because in this month the Lord your God brought you out of Egypt by night. You shall sacrifice the Passover to the Lord your God from the sheep and cattle, in the place which the Lord your God will choose so that his name may dwell there.”

He calls the first month of the Hebrews the “month of new crops.” Among them it is called Nisan, among the Greeks ξαντικός (*xantikos*), and among the Latins April. It is called the month of new crops because in it bundles of ears of grain—that is, the firstfruits of the month—were offered to the Lord by the reaper through the priest. Thus we read in Leviticus that the Lord commanded the children of Israel:

“When,” he says, “you have entered the land which I will give you, and you have reaped its crop, you shall bring bundles of ears, the firstfruits of your harvest, to the priest. He shall lift up the sheaf before the Lord, so that it may be acceptable for you” (Lev. XXIII).

For this reason they are also commanded to celebrate the Passover—that is, the *pascha*—for the Lord, so that they may celebrate their redemption from Egypt with a fitting festival. Through this example we too are instructed: since by God’s grace we have been liberated from spiritual Egypt and have put on the new person, we must henceforth walk in newness of life, consecrating to God the firstfruits of good works and always presenting to him the acceptable offering of a religious life.

We should also always remember why that solemnity was called *pascha*, a name which we may translate as “passing over”: namely, so that, proceeding from worse things to better, we may abandon dark Egypt and strive to reach the promised land in happiness.

What is the meaning of the addition of “cattle,” when he commended the sacrifice of the Passover—or *pascha*—as being from a sheep alone, which he commanded to be taken from sheep, from young sheep or goats? This is understood mystically on account of Christ, whose bodily origin is from both the righteous and sinners. He did not say “from sheep or goats,” although strictly speaking sheep cannot be understood as coming from goats, but lest the Jews, if “or from goats” had been said, suppose that a goat was to be understood.

It was said, however, “from sheep and goats.” What, then, do the cattle signify here? Is it on account of the other sacrifices that were to be offered on those days of Unleavened Bread?

“No leaven shall appear within all your borders for seven days.”

We too must strive in every way, if possible, to leave the enticements of this world and not walk in the leaven of old malice and wickedness, but in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth. This is the new way of life of the human being, who has left behind the former person with his companions.

For them the feast is completed over seven days; for those days which continually revolve in their own order, the Lamb is slain for us every day, and the Passover is celebrated every day—provided that we have no leaven of malice and wickedness, and that, having been renewed, we take no delight in anything belonging to the corruption of the old life.

For what else is leaven except the corruption of nature? It too, having first departed from its natural sweetness, has been corrupted by an adulterous sourness.

“Nothing of its flesh, which was sacrificed in the evening, shall remain until morning on the first day.”

Because the words of divine majesty and the great mysteries must be examined with the utmost diligence, we must penetrate all his commandments by examining, understanding, and practicing them before the day of resurrection appears, during the calling of this present life.

But because it is very difficult for the whole discourse of the Lamb to be understood and for all its mystery to be penetrated, Exodus rightly says: “But if anything remains, you shall burn it with fire” (Exod. XII). We burn with fire what remains of the Lamb when, regarding the mystery of what we cannot understand and penetrate about his incarnation, we humbly reserve it by the power of the Holy Spirit, so that no one may presumptuously dare either to despise or to condemn what he does not understand. By committing these matters to the fire, he reserves them for the Holy Spirit.

“You shall not be able to sacrifice the Passover in any of your cities, but in the city which the Lord your God will choose so that his name may dwell there. You shall sacrifice the Passover in the evening, at sunset, when you came out of Egypt; and you shall cook and eat it in the place which the Lord your God will choose. In the morning you shall rise and go to your tents.”

The Passover lamb is commanded to be eaten in one house, and the Passover is likewise commanded to be sacrificed in one place—that is, in one catholic Church. Outside it, no one can rightly celebrate the Passover.

For this reason the legislator forbids celebrating the Passover in any city, because every assembly that exists outside the Church—that is, those of the Jews, heretics, and pagans—is to be detested in every way.

“In the evening,” therefore—that is, in the final age of the world, when the true Sun set in his passion and when Egyptian captivity was destroyed by our Redeemer—the legitimate and most pleasing Passover was accomplished for God. All the faithful ought faithfully to observe its ordinance during the time of the present life, “because Christ, as Paul testifies, our Passover, was sacrificed” (I Cor. V).

Therefore, during our mortal life, we ought to celebrate it worthily, not in the old leaven or in the leaven of malice and wickedness, but in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.

When it says, “In the morning you shall rise and go to your tents,” it shows that, after the divine service has been completed, in the labor of the present life and at the morning of the future resurrection, we must migrate to the eternal tents and there rest from every work. There alone we must rejoice in the reward we have received.

Hence it follows:

“For six days you shall eat unleavened bread, and on the seventh day, because it is the assembly of the Lord your God, you shall do no work.”

The number seven, therefore, on account of the Sabbath, signifies the future rest, where there is no longer any time, place, or reason for working, but where all who are worthy devote themselves perpetually to the praises and contemplation of the Creator.

## CHAPTER XI. On the celebration of Pentecost and its ceremonies
*(The same passage.)* “You shall count for yourself seven weeks from the day when you put the sickle to the standing grain, and you shall celebrate the festival of weeks to the Lord your God, a voluntary offering from your hand, which you shall present according to the blessing of the Lord your God, etc.”
