It must be asked how he commanded the observance of what he says: [Col. 0897D] “You shall count for yourself seven weeks, beginning from the putting of the sickle into the standing grain.” You shall begin counting seven weeks; and you shall keep a festival of weeks to the Lord your God, offering whatever your hand is able to offer, according to whatever the Lord your God grants you, and you shall feast in the sight of the Lord your God.

For if this Pentecost was to be observed by the whole people, are we to believe that everyone was commanded to put the sickles into the harvest on one and the same day? But if each person observes this fiftieth day for himself, counting from the day on which he puts in the sickle, it is not one day for the whole people. The one day, however, is that which is reckoned from the sacrifice of the Passover until the day when the Law was given on Sinai.

[Col. 0898A] But neither the time nor the number of this Pentecost is kept by the Jewish people; by us, however, it is observed both contemplatively and literally. For the Lawgiver, wishing to make his intention clearer, commanded that fifty days be counted from the second day of the Sabbath in Leviticus, plainly intending the Lord’s Day to be understood. For this is the second day of the Sabbath. On this day the Resurrection took place. Seven weeks are counted until the second day completing the week. On the Lord’s Day, again, we celebrate the festival of Pentecost, on which we were deemed worthy to receive the coming of the Holy Spirit.

It was not without reason that they observed the coming after seven weeks, but so that we might understand that the old Law commanded nothing worldly, nothing akin to the ancient corruption, for those who desire to receive God; rather, [Col. 0898B] it commanded that a new sacrifice be offered to the Lord. For when the Spirit came, he renewed our entire life, confirming the tradition of Christ and establishing the way of life which he perfected in them. For he says: “He will take from what is mine and declare it to you.”

For this reason he did not come on another day of the week, but on the day on which the Resurrection took place. And an intelligible sheaf was offered, so that this too might be demonstrated: the new way of life that reformed us by freeing us from the corruption of antiquity was corrected through Christ’s Resurrection and the coming of the Holy Spirit.

The offering itself also makes clear the kind of sacrifice he commanded to be made, as we find it plainly written:

“And thus,” he says, “you shall offer a new sacrifice to the Lord, from all your dwellings. Two loaves of firstfruits, from two-tenths [Col. 0898C] of fine flour fermented, which you shall bake as firstfruits for the Lord; and thus you shall offer with the loaves seven unblemished yearling lambs, and one young bull from the herd, and two rams.”

By calling it a “new sacrifice,” he excluded the sacrifices of the Law and the former sacrifices, and introduced the evangelical sacrifices in their place. Then, by adding “from your dwellings,” he signified the Church and desired that the things mentioned be offered to it. For he did not say “from all dwellings,” but “from all your dwellings,” so that he might indicate, in an absolute sense, one particular dwelling, concerning which David says: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house” (Ps. LXXXIII). And again: “One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I shall seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life” (Ps. XXVI).

[Col. 0898D] The two loaves of firstfruits, then, are the Law and the Gospel. For they are loaves containing food for the souls of the faithful. They are also firstfruits—or, as the Septuagint has it, “set apart”—because all wisdom belongs to the uncircumcision, yet they are separated from and joined to that which is external.

They are therefore made from two-tenths of fermented fine flour: from the teaching that transmits both the perfect divinity and the perfect humanity of God. They cannot otherwise be baked except through such teaching, yet they are firstfruits for the Lord. For the Lord first perfected the Law, and afterward taught the Gospel:

“Hear, for it was said to the ancients: ‘You shall not kill.’ But I say to you: Everyone who is angry with his brother without cause shall be liable to judgment” (Matt. V).

[Col. 0899A] Here he joined the Law to the Gospel; for this reason they are called his firstfruits. Luke also confirms this, showing us the true firstfruits, when he writes: “I composed the first account, O Theophilus, concerning all the things that Jesus began to do and teach” (Acts I).

He also commanded that seven yearling lambs, unblemished, be offered with them, signifying the gifts that belong to the Spirit. Concerning these Solomon said in Proverbs: “Wisdom built herself a house; she erected her pillars” (Prov. IX). Isaiah expressed it more clearly: “And the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him.” Nor did he conceal what the gifts were or what their number was. He added: “The Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and truth, and the Spirit of the Lord filled him.”

He calls these gifts “lambs” for the sake of showing [Col. 0899B] that the Holy Spirit is one with Christ, concerning whom it was said: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world. Therefore no one can say, ‘Jesus Christ,’ except in the Holy Spirit” (John I).

Therefore the present offering does not irrationally contain, together with the seven lambs, a bull from the herd. Rather, it clearly signifies him who was made from the herd—that is, from Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and David according to the flesh.

He joined to this two unblemished rams: the exalted commandments and virtues which, like other sheep, must provide protection and safety for those who, as it were, are driving away the intelligible enemy. What are these commandments?

“If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have, give to the poor, and come, follow me” (Matt. X).

The greatest commandment is to sell what one possesses and give it to the poor. [Col. 0899C] It is also the greatest commandment to follow Christ, so that, despising the possession of earthly things, we may strive to do everything according to the Lord’s will; for this is what it means to follow him.

These commandments are therefore called rams, both because of the unblemished life and because of the perfect conscience. Since rams are superior to the entire flock, their sacrifices and libation—that is, knowledge and correction—are a sweet-smelling offering to that Lord concerning whom Paul said:

“But thanks be to God, who always leads us in triumph in Christ Jesus and manifests through us the fragrance of knowledge, because we are the good fragrance of Christ” (II Cor. II).

## CHAPTER XII. On the observance of the seventh month and the solemnity of the tabernacles; and that every male must be presented three times a year in the sight of the Lord.

[Col. 0899D] *(The same passage.)* “You shall also celebrate the solemnity of the tabernacles for seven days, when you have gathered in the produce from your threshing floor and winepress; and you shall feast during your festival, you and your son and daughter, your male servant and female servant, and also the Levite and the resident alien, the orphan and the widow who are within your gates. For seven days you shall celebrate festivals to the Lord your God, in the place which the Lord will choose, etc.”

He therefore called it the festival of tabernacles because it lasts seven days. Whoever uses the present world as though it were a tabernacle can have a festival and rejoice in it because of his expectation of the future. And whoever knows that, if the earthly house of this dwelling is dissolved, a building not made by human hands receives him in heaven—[Col. 0900A] such a person will be able to overcome the wisdom of the world and recognize that it is passing and temporary.

It must also be understood that the Lawgiver signifies not only this, but also that one ought to direct one’s gaze toward the future age. This, without any doubt, you will find represented both by the number and by the tabernacles.

For, as it is written in Leviticus, the festival is commanded to begin on the fifteenth day. This number is composed of seven and eight: one signifies the present age, while the other represents the future. Therefore, after commanding that the festival be completed in seven days, he again mentioned other days as most celebrated and most holy. He did not place them together with the seven, but after them and apart from them, as the future age is separate. It follows the present age, but it is something else.

[Col. 0900B] After the harvest of every fruit had been completed, therefore, he commanded the solemnity of the tabernacles to be observed and ordered people to feast with sons and daughters, male and female servants, Levites and resident aliens, orphans and widows. By this he indicates that, after the work of good deeds has been completed and after the harvest of many virtues has been gathered, one will then rejoice and be glad with friends.

Then each person will truly exult over the reward received who here remembers that he was generous in his giving. Then the solemnity of the tabernacles is truly celebrated, when possession is granted not of things that change, but of eternal dwellings. Concerning these the Savior says in the Gospel: “In my Father’s house are many dwellings” (John XIV). And again: “Make friends for yourselves,” he says, “from the mammon of unrighteousness, so that, when you fail, they may receive you into the eternal tabernacles” (John XVI).

[Col. 0900C] “Three times a year every male of yours shall appear in the sight of the Lord your God, in the place which he will choose: at the solemnity of unleavened bread, at the solemnity of weeks, and at the solemnity of tabernacles.”

What does it mean that, while women are passed over in silence, the Law commands males to be presented in the sight of the Lord, except that our Creator, rejecting whatever is soft, fragile, and weak in our way of life, demands from us strong works of virtue?

For if, in faith in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, we devote ourselves during the present life to good works in order to obtain an eternal reward, then without doubt we worthily establish our male character before the sight of the Lord.

[Col. 0900D] “You shall not appear before the Lord empty-handed; but each person shall offer according to what he has, according to the blessing of the Lord his God which he has given him.”

The person who brings nothing with him from the fruit of his labor appears empty-handed in the sight of the Lord. One person sweats in pursuit of honors; another burns with the desire to increase his wealth; another pants after the acquisition of riches. But because everyone who dies leaves all these things behind, he appears empty-handed before the Lord, since he has brought nothing with him before the Judge.

Therefore he is salutarily admonished through the Law, which says: “You shall not appear in the sight of the Lord empty-handed.” Whoever has not provided for the reward of life by doing good appears empty-handed in the sight of the Lord.

Hence the Psalmist says to the righteous: “But they shall come, they shall come with rejoicing, carrying their sheaves” (Ps. CXXV). [Col. 0901A] For those who display in themselves the righteous works by which they may deserve life come carrying their sheaves to the examination of judgment.

## CHAPTER XIII. On appointing teachers and judges at the gates, on not accepting persons or gifts, and on rendering just judgments.

[Col. 0901A] *(The same passage.)* “You shall appoint judges and teachers in all your gates, which the Lord your God gives you throughout your tribes.”

Thus those arriving from every direction may immediately find judges and teachers ready at the entrance to the city, from whom they may receive just judgments.

Mystically, however, he admonishes the leaders of the Churches to stand at the gates—that is, in the words of the apostles and prophets—and to administer just judgments to each person according to the ordinances of the divine Law. [Col. 0901B] They must observe truth and beware of avarice, lest, if they themselves turn away from the truth through falsehood or greed, they become abominable before the eyes of God.

Hence it follows: “You shall not show partiality or accept gifts, because gifts blind the eyes of the wise and alter the words of the righteous.”

He does not mean that those who are truly wise and righteous are overturned by the desire for gifts, but that those who appear wise and righteous in their own eyes frequently fall. To them the prophet says: “Woe to you who are wise in your own eyes and prudent in your own sight” (Isa. V).

Hence Wisdom says: “There are ways that seem righteous to human beings, but their end leads down to the depths of hell” (Prov. IV).

[Col. 0901C] Hence the Savior speaks to such people in the Gospel, saying: “Woe to you who justify yourselves before human beings; but God knows your hearts” (Luke XVI).

For those who are truly wise and righteous never put perishable things before truth and justice, but at all times strive to remain in equity.

“You shall pursue justice, and justice alone, so that you may live and possess the land which the Lord your God will give you.”

He pursues justice unjustly who is stirred to defend justice not by zeal for virtue but by love of a temporal reward. He pursues justice unjustly who is not ashamed to sell the very justice he claims to uphold. To pursue justice justly, therefore, is, in defending justice, to seek justice itself.

## CHAPTER XIV. On not planting a sacred grove beside the altar of the Lord, on not setting up statues, and on not sacrificing blemished animals.

[Col. 0901D] *(The same passage.)* “You shall not plant a sacred grove or any tree beside the altar of the Lord your God; nor shall you make or set up for him a statue, which the Lord your God hates.”

Through these two Testaments he cuts off the occasion of idolatry, which the nations used to practice by setting up images for themselves in sacred groves and shrines and worshiping idols.

Mystically, beside the altar of faith he forbids the establishment of every fruitless thing, whether idle speech or wicked works, as well as the darkness of ignorance. He does not permit any fiction of falsehood or error to be joined to the truth of the catholic faith.

[Col. 0902A] It is forbidden that a grove be planted in the temple. Groves consist of leafy and fruitless trees, planted solely for the pleasure of sight. Such are also the pagans, who arrange their reasoning with verbal elegance, not so that they may turn people away from their ways, but so that they may delight them and persuade them through such seduction.

We, however, according to God’s command, do not plant a grove beside the altar; around the faith of the Lord we compose nothing with fruitless words and no allurements of secular eloquence. Rather, with the sole purity of truth, we hold to the knowledge of preaching.

The Apostle avoided planting this grove in the preaching of wisdom when he said: “We speak not in words taught by human wisdom, but in the teaching of the Spirit and in power.”

“You shall not sacrifice to the Lord your God a bull or a sheep in which there is a blemish or any defect, because it is an abomination to the Lord your God” (I Cor. I).

Understand every blemish as every sin, which, wherever it is found, produces deformity. Therefore the Lord’s offering—whether in one who works bravely, whom the bull signifies, or in one who walks in simplicity, whom the sheep represents—is good when it is made without the contagion of sin, because every sin is contrary to truth and its association will not please justice.

## CHAPTER XV. On apostates who, abandoning God, served foreign gods; and on the requirement that two or three witnesses always be produced in individual cases.

[Col. 0902B] *(The same passage.)* “When there are found among you, within one of your gates which the Lord your God gives you, a man or woman who does evil in the sight of the Lord your God [Col. 0902C] and transgresses his covenant, going and serving foreign gods and worshiping them, and the moon and all the host of heaven, which I have not commanded, etc.”

The entire Law of the Lord especially detests error and idolatry and overthrows it everywhere, because it is the greatest crime to render divine honor to a creature. This is what the pagans do, as do even wicked Catholics who, although they do not depart from the unity of the Church in their belief, are nevertheless found, because they are devoted to various vices, to serve the devil more through earthly desire than to serve God through an abundance of good works.

He commands that such people be stoned, because he foresaw that they would be condemned by a strict sentence: “At the mouth of two or three witnesses, the one who is to be killed shall perish.”

[Col. 0902D] What does it mean that the guilty person is said to perish “at the mouth of two or three witnesses,” except that he is convicted by the testimony of the Law, the Prophets, and the Gospels, since he is found to be not devoted to divine worship? Hence the Savior says in the Gospel: “The word that I have spoken to you will judge him on the last day.”

## CHAPTER XVI. That difficult judgments are to be referred to priests, and that the disobedient are to be punished by death.

*(CHAPTER XVII.)* “If you perceive that a judgment is difficult and ambiguous among you, between blood and blood, case and case, leprosy and non-leprosy, and you see the words of the judges within your gates differing, arise and go up to the place which [Col. 0903A] the Lord your God will choose. You shall come to the priests of the Levitical order and to the judge who is in office at that time; you shall inquire of them, and they shall declare to you the truth of the judgment. And you shall do whatever the one who presides in the place which the Lord has chosen tells you, and they shall teach you according to his law, etc.”

By this decree the Lawgiver teaches the order of ecclesiastical ministry, so that the priests and prelates of God’s Churches may reverently administer ecclesiastical judgments according to the authority given to them by God, and may justly distinguish the cases and actions of individuals.

[Col. 0903B] He especially commends that each person strive to administer these judgments not according to his own free choice, but according to the decrees of the Lord’s Law. Nor should anyone, out of favor or hostility toward another, accept a person and alter his judgment; rather, in all matters he must observe the justice of the Lord’s Law.

And because it is necessary that subjects also submit to the discipline of their rulers, he immediately demonstrates the punishment that follows the disobedient and proud, saying:

“But the person who acts proudly and refuses to obey the command of the priest who ministers to the Lord your God at that time shall die by the judgment of the judge. You shall remove the evil from your midst, and so forth.”

“The person who refuses to obey the command of the priest shall die,” he says—that is, the command of the priest who, having become a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek, appointed pastors, that is, his vicars, to govern the Church which he acquired with his blood, so that, acting as his ambassadors, they might preach the Gospel throughout the whole world.

He himself demonstrates how great their authority is when he says: “Whoever hears you hears me; and whoever despises you despises me. But whoever despises me despises the one who sent me” (Luke X).

It is therefore fitting that the person who is not afraid to despise the power of the Divinity receive the sentence of his own condemnation.

[Col. 0903C]

## CHAPTER XVII. On establishing a king over the Israelites from their own people and not from foreigners, and on the lawful right of a king.

*(The same passage.)* “When you have entered the land which the Lord your God will give you, possessed it, and lived in it, and you say, ‘I will set a king over me, as all the nations around me have,’ you shall set over you the one whom the Lord your God chooses from among your brothers. You may not make a man of another nation king over you who is not your brother.”

[Col. 0903D] It may be asked why the people displeased God when they desired a king, since here the request appears to be permitted. But it should rather be understood that this was not in accordance with God’s will: he did not command it to happen, but permitted it to those who desired it. Nevertheless, he commanded that the king should not be a foreigner but a brother—that is, a native of the same people, not an outsider.

The words “you may not” are to be understood as “you must not.”

“When he has been established, he shall not multiply horses for himself, nor bring the people back to Egypt by increasing his cavalry, especially since he commanded you never again to return by the same road. He shall not have many wives, who might entice his heart, nor immense quantities of silver and gold, etc.”

[Col. 0904A] When he spoke of the king, he said: “He shall not multiply wives for himself, lest his heart turn away; and he shall not greatly multiply silver and gold for himself.”

Hence it is asked whether David did not act against this command, since he did not have only one wife. For it is evident that Solomon transgressed this command, both in women and in gold and silver.

But from this it is rather understood that kings were permitted to have more than one wife. They were forbidden to multiply them; and this prohibition is not transgressed if they were few, as David’s were, but not many, as Solomon’s were. Yet when he added “lest his heart turn away,” he seems chiefly to have commanded that the king should not, by multiplying wives, come to foreign women, through whom Solomon’s heart was turned away from God.

[Col. 0904B] Nevertheless, multiplication in general was prohibited, so that even if he had multiplied wives only from among the Hebrews, he could rightly be accused of acting against this command.

But the fact that Deuteronomy commands him to have it written for himself and to read it all the days of his life shows that he must not proudly follow his own desires, but humbly preserve the divine commandments.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On priests and Levites, that they should not have possessions and inheritances among the other tribes, but should be sustained by the Lord’s distributions.

*(CHAPTER XVIII.)* “The priests and Levites—all who belong to the same tribe—shall have no portion or inheritance with the rest of Israel, because they shall eat the sacrifices of the Lord and his offerings, and they shall receive nothing else [Col. 0904C] from the possession of their brothers. For the Lord himself is their inheritance, as he said to them.”

In both the Old and the New Testament, the ministers of the altar and servants of the Lord’s temple are commanded to receive nourishment from the abundance of offerings and from the gift of tithes; they are not permitted in any way to desire the acquisition of earthly possessions.

Hence the Lord commanded the apostles and preachers of the Gospel in the Gospel, saying:

“Go and preach, saying, ‘The kingdom of heaven has drawn near.’ Heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse lepers, cast out demons. You have received freely; give freely. Do not possess gold or silver, or money in your belts; no bag for the journey, or two tunics, or sandals, or a staff. [Col. 0904D] For the worker is worthy of his wage,” or “of his food” (Matt. X).

Hence Paul, speaking to the Corinthians, says: “Do you not know that those who work in the sanctuary eat what comes from the sanctuary, and that those who serve the altar share with the altar? So also the Lord ordained that those who proclaim the Gospel should live from the Gospel.”

And writing to Timothy he says: “No one serving as a soldier for God involves himself in secular affairs, so that he may please the one to whom he has proved himself. For even the one who competes in the contest is not crowned unless he competes lawfully. The farmer who labors ought first to receive from the fruits” (II Tim. II).

For it is not fitting that the person who ought always to stand before the divine should be occupied in acquiring earthly profit. [Col. 0905A] The Lord himself is the inheritance of those who serve him devotedly and earnestly; and nothing can be lacking to the person who possesses him who possesses all things.

“This shall be the judgment of the priests from the people and from those who offer sacrifices: whether they sacrifice a bull or a sheep, they shall give the priest the shoulder and the stomach, the firstfruits of grain, wine, and oil, and a portion of wool from the shearing of the sheep.”

It is written in Leviticus, where the Lord says: “I have taken the breast of elevation and the shoulder of separation from the children of Israel, from the peace offerings, and I have given them to Aaron the priest and to his sons as an everlasting statute, from all the people of Israel.”

By the breast he signifies faith and the confidence which he desires to be offered to the Lord by the person who wishes to be saved, because without faith it is impossible to please God.

[Col. 0905B] The right shoulder also, from the peace offerings, falls among the priest’s firstfruits. The right shoulder signifies good actions. Therefore the person who wishes to be saved must offer both faith and actions.

But he assigned the breast to the sons of Aaron, who are exalted in life, and the right shoulder to the priest, who bears the image of Christ. For this reason the Lawgiver fittingly shows that only the priest can complete this sacrifice. To believe and purpose good things belongs to us through God’s gift; but to begin works, complete them, and bring what has been begun to its conclusion belongs to divine grace. Therefore the Apostle Paul said: “It depends not on the one who wills or the one who runs, but on God who shows mercy” (Rom. IX).

For it belongs to God alone to direct actions; for this reason the arm is also called God’s.

[Col. 0905C] We are commanded to give the firstfruits of grain, wine, and oil, and a portion of wool from the shearing of the sheep to the priests, because whether in bodily support or in the benefits of spiritual things, we must always humbly and devotedly share spiritual support with our teachers. The Apostle Paul himself exhorts us to this, saying: “Let the one who is instructed in the word share all good things with the one who instructs him” (Gal. VI).

“If a Levite goes out from one of your cities, from anywhere in Israel where he dwells, and desires to come to the place which the Lord chooses, he shall minister in the name of the Lord his God, like all his brothers. The Levites shall stand at that time before the Lord. He shall receive the same portion of food as the others, except for what is owed to him in his own city from his ancestral inheritance.

[Col. 0905D] “But if a Levite comes from one of your cities, from anywhere among the children of Israel where he dwells, according to the desire of his soul, to the place which the Lord chooses, etc.”

That is, if he desires to go to the place where the Lord is invoked and to minister in the name of the Lord his God, like all his brothers, the Levites who stand before the Lord, they shall eat their allotted portion, apart from the sale that is according to the family.

What sale he means is obscure, unless perhaps it is because he commanded that tithes and firstborn animals be sold by those who lived far away, lest they be forced to carry many things to the place where the Lord was invoked, or to drive the animals there, only to buy them again there for the same price. He had commanded that the Levite who remained in that city should have a share there, from which those tithes and firstborn animals were owed.

[Col. 0906A] Therefore he said that this was owed to the Levite according to the family, since, by the inheritance through which he succeeds his parents, what was provided for his parents ought to be maintained for him.

## CHAPTER XIX. On prohibiting all wicked practices, and on the prophet who was to be raised up among the Jewish people in the likeness of Moses.

*(The same passage.)* “When you have entered the land which the Lord your God will give you, beware lest you desire to imitate the abominations of those nations; and let there not be found among you anyone who purifies his son, or makes his daughter pass through fire, or consults diviners, or observes dreams and omens. Let there not be a sorcerer, enchanter, or one who consults a python-spirit or diviners, [Col. 0906B] to seek truth from the dead, etc.”

Since he forbids inspectors of portents to exist among God’s people, it must be asked how these portents, which are forbidden to be inspected, are distinguished from those which are given divinely so that what they signify ought to be declared—as with all the miracles found in Scripture that signify something pertaining to the rule of faith.

For example, we say what was signified by the fleece that was wet while the threshing floor was dry, or dry while the threshing floor was wet, as well as by Aaron’s staff, which flowered and produced almonds, and by other things of this kind.

Just as divinations, which he subsequently forbids, are distinguished from the preachings or announcements of the prophets, so inspections of prodigies must be distinguished from the meanings of divine miracles.

“But the Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet [Col. 0906C] from your people and from your brothers like me. You shall listen to him, as you requested from the Lord your God at Horeb, when the assembly was gathered and you said: ‘I will no longer hear the voice of the Lord my God, nor will I see this great fire anymore, lest I die.’ And the Lord said to me: ‘They have spoken well in all things. I will raise up for them a prophet from the midst of their brothers, like you, and I will put my words in his mouth. He shall speak to them everything that I command him. Whoever does not wish to hear his words, which he will speak in my name, I myself shall be his avenger, etc.’”

[Col. 0906D] Although some wish, in the historical sense, to understand this statement as referring to all the holy prophets who prophesied among the children of Israel, whom Moses said should be heard as he himself was, because, filled with the same Spirit with which he wrote the Law, they too uttered their prophecies with truthful mouths, nevertheless we can understand no one better than the Lord himself of the prophets—Jesus Christ—to be indicated here. The books of the Old Testament also call him the true prophet, and the Gospel names him by the title of prophet.

Hence the crowds, after being satisfied by him and seeing the sign he had performed, said among themselves: “This is truly the prophet who is to come into the world” (John VI).

And elsewhere, when the same Mediator between God and human beings raised the widow’s son, “fear seized all, and they glorified God, saying: ‘A great prophet has arisen among us,’ and, ‘God has visited his people’” (Luke VII).

[Col. 0907A] This prophet, then, the Lord raised up for the Israelites from the midst of their brothers—that is, from the seed of David—like Moses, because Jesus did not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it. And he put his words in his mouth; whoever does not wish to hear the words that he speaks in the Lord’s name, the Lord himself becomes his avenger, when he consigns that person to be tormented by everlasting punishment.

## CHAPTER XX. On appointing cities of refuge for those who commit homicide unintentionally.

## (CHAPTER XIX)

“After the Lord your God has destroyed the nations whose land he is going to give you, and you have taken possession of it and lived in their cities and houses, you shall set apart three cities for yourself in the midst of the land [Col. 0907B] that the Lord your God will give you to possess. Carefully prepare the road, and divide the whole territory of your land equally into three parts, so that the fugitive who has fled because of homicide may have a nearby place to which he can escape,” and so forth.

Moses established three cities of refuge beyond the Jordan for homicides—that is, for those who had committed homicide unintentionally—and he commanded Joshua to designate three others on this side of the Jordan, in the land of promise. Mystically, he indicates that before receiving baptism, everyone who wishes to be saved from sins and liberated from spiritual enemies must sincerely confess faith in the Holy Trinity; and after the washing of the sacred font, must usefully conduct himself in faith, hope, and charity. Thus, living religiously in this world—which was created and endowed with the number six—after the perfection of good works, he should await eternal rest in the blessed repose of holy souls.

When Scripture says that the road must be carefully prepared and the whole territory divided equally into three parts, so that the one to be saved may more easily escape his enemies, it shows that preachers of the peoples must, with every diligence, by word and example, care for the salvation of the sick, and must communicate the same faith equally throughout the whole earth of the holy Church, so that each person may recognize that the way of truth and the gate of faith are open to him. If they do not wish to enter, they should know in advance that they will rightly be condemned.

“This shall be the law concerning the homicide who flees, whose life must be preserved: whoever strikes his neighbor unknowingly, and who is shown not to have had any hatred against him the day before yesterday or yesterday, but simply to have gone with him into the forest to cut wood, and while cutting wood the axe slips from his hand, and the iron, falling from the handle, strikes and kills his companion, he shall flee to one of the cities mentioned above and live there. Otherwise, the nearest relative of the slain man, driven by grief, might pursue him, overtake him if the road were longer, and strike the soul of one who is not guilty of death; for it is shown that he had previously held no hatred against the slain man.”

We go into the forest with a friend whenever we turn with some neighbor to examine our sins; and we cut wood simply when, with pious intention, we cut away the vices of sinners. But the axe slips from the hand when a rebuke extends too far in harshness; and the iron leaps from the handle when speech in correction exceeds proper severity. It strikes and kills the friend because the insult that has been spoken kills its hearer by driving the spirit of love away.

For the mind of the person being corrected suddenly falls into hatred, but immoderate reproof subjects it to this hatred more than it ought. Yet the one who carelessly strikes the wood and extinguishes his neighbor must flee to three cities, so that, protected by their defense, he may live. If, turning to the laments of repentance, he hides himself within the unity of the sacrament under hope, faith, and charity, he is not held guilty of the homicide he committed. When the relative of the slain man finds him, he does not kill him, because when the strict Judge comes—the one who joined himself to us through participation in our nature—he will certainly not demand vengeance for the guilt from one whom his pardon, hope, faith, and charity have hidden.

Thus the guilt is forgiven because it was not committed with deliberate malice.

“But when the Lord your God enlarges your borders, as he swore to your fathers, and gives you all the land that he promised them—provided that you keep his commandments and do what I command you today, love the Lord your God, and walk in his ways at all times—you shall add three more cities for yourself and double the number of the three cities already mentioned, so that innocent blood may not be shed in the midst of the land that the Lord your God will give you to possess, and you may not be guilty of blood,” and so forth.

How this was done is shown by the book called *Joshua*, when it records that Joshua, at the Lord’s command, designated six cities of refuge for homicides who had committed homicide unintentionally: Kedesh in Galilee, in Mount Naphtali; Shechem in Mount Ephraim; and Kiriath-arba, that is, Hebron, in the hill country of Judah; and beyond the Jordan, east of Jericho, Bezer, situated in the plain, in the wilderness of the tribe of Reuben; Ramoth in Gilead, of the tribe of Gad; and Golan in Bashan, of the tribe of Manasseh.

These cities were established for all the children of Israel and for the resident foreigners living among them, so that anyone who unknowingly struck and killed a person might flee there and not die at the hand of the relative who wished to avenge the shed blood, until he stood before the people to present his case.

Mystically, if someone strikes another through envy or hatred with the sword of malice and leads him into the death of the soul, he himself will be liable to eternal death. Hence Truth himself says: “If anyone causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it would be better for him that a millstone be hung around his neck and that he be drowned in the depths” (Matthew 18). And John says: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer. And you know that no murderer has eternal life abiding in him” (1 John 3).

Such a person is commanded to be torn away from the Lord’s altar, because he is unworthy of the Lord’s sacraments and is rightly removed from participation in the sacred altar. He cannot in any way deserve to be restored to pardon except through worthy repentance.

But one who has injured someone not out of a deliberate intention of malice, but through carelessness or ignorance, has cities of refuge—namely, the Catholic Church. There, constraining himself through the distress of repentance, he should remain throughout the whole period of the present life, devoting himself to good works. If he places his hope in the death of the supreme Pontiff, that is, of his Redeemer, he will undoubtedly be saved forever.

## CHAPTER XXI. On false witnesses, who are not to be accepted, but, if discovered, are to be duly punished

(IBID.) “One witness shall not stand against anyone, whatever the sin or crime may be; but every word shall stand on the testimony of two or three witnesses.”

Although historically this divine judgment must be observed, nevertheless, when we contend against any impious persons or heretics, we must also call the holy Scriptures to testify. Our perceptions and testimony have no credibility without these witnesses. Therefore, for proof, it is more fitting that, when I affirm a word of my understanding, I bring forward two witnesses: the New and the Old Testament. I also bring forward three: the Gospel, the Prophet, and the Apostle. Thus every word will stand.

“And when, after examining the matter with the greatest diligence, they discover that the false witness has spoken a lie against his brother, they shall do to him what he intended to do to his brother. You shall remove the evil from your midst, so that the others, hearing of it, may have fear and never again dare to do such things. You shall not pity him, but shall exact life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot.”

Concerning this it is also written in Leviticus: “Whoever kills or strikes a man shall be put to death. Whoever strikes an animal shall pay its equivalent, that is, life for life. Whoever inflicts a blemish on any of his fellow citizens, as he has done, so shall it be done to him: fracture for fracture, eye for eye, tooth for tooth shall be restored. Whatever blemish he has inflicted, he shall be compelled to endure. Whoever strikes or kills a man, or, according to the Septuagint, whoever strikes a man’s soul, shall be put to death” (Leviticus 24).

And who strikes a man’s soul except one who entices him to impiety and draws him into blasphemous speech, in which he deserves to die the worst death of sin, which is the true death of the soul? For this reason he commands that such a person die the death he has caused.

Yet when he says “the soul of a man,” he chiefly means the animal man—that is, one who cannot understand the things of the Spirit. Concerning him the Apostle Paul says: “The animal man does not perceive the things that belong to the Spirit of God. For they are foolishness to him, and he cannot understand them, because they are spiritually discerned” (1 Corinthians 2). Whoever strikes such a man brings about death.

But if he strikes an animal—that is, one who lives merely as cattle do—what does David say concerning him? “Man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared with foolish beasts and became like them” (Psalm 48). He shall pay its equivalent, that is, life for life.

Nor, because he has led a sinner or an ordinary person who lacks subtle discernment concerning God into error, is he thereby entirely worthy of pardon. But if he struck him without leading him perfectly into impiety or causing him to depart from God altogether, yet said or did certain things and inflicted the blemish of sin, he will likewise suffer punishment for this.

For Scripture says: “Whoever inflicts a blemish on any of his fellow citizens, as he has done, so shall it be done to him. Fracture for fracture—or, according to the Septuagint, crushing for crushing—eye for eye, tooth for tooth.”

Either he crushed the virtue that the other possessed, when that person, by teaching or urging evil, causing scandal, slandering, or falsely accusing him, injured his neighbor; or he blinded his eye—that is, his knowledge—by doing any one of the things mentioned; or he injured his tooth, that is, the power of his words.

Scripture customarily understands teeth as words, as David shows when he says: “The sons of men: their teeth are weapons and arrows, and their tongue is a sharp sword” (Psalm 56)—or a sharp blade. Concerning Christ, the patriarch Jacob said in his blessings: “His eyes are more beautiful than wine, and his teeth whiter than milk” (Genesis 49). The clear and open sayings of Christ’s Gospel are brighter than the legal milk.

Therefore, whoever harms some part of what has been said will necessarily suffer a similar blemish himself in the future judgment. If he harmed or crushed another’s virtue, his own will be crushed. If he obscured knowledge, his own knowledge will be counted as nothing. If he harmed another through authoritative words, the Judge will render his own speeches fruitless and useless.

## CHAPTER XXII. On establishing the law of war, and on the fearful and other persons unfit for warfare who are to be dismissed

(CAP. XX.) “Hear, Israel: Today you are about to engage in battle against your enemies. Let not your heart be afraid; do not fear, do not retreat, and do not dread them, because the Lord your God is in your midst, and he will fight for you against your enemies to rescue you from danger.”

In the Septuagint this judgment is likewise read as follows: “For the Lord your God, who goes before you, will himself fight your enemies together with you and save you.”

See how, in spiritual conflicts also, one must hope for and ask the assistance of God—not so that we do nothing, but so that, aided by him, we may cooperate. For he says, “He will fight together with you,” thereby showing that they themselves must also do what was to be done.

“The commanders of the individual divisions shall proclaim aloud in the hearing of the army: ‘Who is the man who has built a new house and has not dedicated it? Let him go and return to his house, lest he die in battle and another man perform its duty. Who is the man who has betrothed a wife and has not taken her? Let him go and return to his house, lest he die in battle and another man take her,’” and so forth.

These words may seem troubling, as though those who have already dedicated their buildings, already eaten the produce of their new plantings, and married their betrothed wives would die in battle under better conditions than those who have not yet done so.

But since human affection is held by such things and people esteem them greatly, it must be understood that these instructions are given to those advancing into battle so that anyone whose heart is bound by such concerns may be revealed when he returns. Otherwise he might act less courageously because he fears that he will die before dedicating his house, drinking from his new vineyard, or marrying his betrothed.

Indeed, insofar as the woman is concerned, it is better for another man to marry her while she is untouched than as a widow. But, as I have said, these regulations were established to test the hearts of the men.

“Who is the fearful man, fainthearted? Let him go and return to his house, lest he make the hearts of his brothers fearful, as he himself has been terrified by fear.”

By these words he teaches that no one can undertake the army of the profession of contemplation or spiritual warfare if he is still afraid to strip himself of earthly works, lest he return again through weakness of mind and, by his example, call others back from evangelical perfection and weaken them through unbelieving fear.

Such men are therefore commanded to withdraw from the battle and return to their houses, because they cannot wage the Lord’s wars with a divided heart. “A double-minded man is unstable in all his ways” (James 1).

Such persons ought not even to undertake the beginning of renunciation. It is better for them to remain in the active life than, while tepidly pursuing contemplation, to involve themselves in greater danger. “For it is better not to vow than to vow and not fulfill” (Ecclesiastes 5).

Likewise, the man who has taken a wife is prohibited from such warfare, as is the one who has planted a vineyard, representing the propagation of children. A servant of a wife cannot serve in the divine army; nor can anyone attain the practice of contemplation who is still fixed in the pleasure of the flesh. “No one serving as a soldier for God,” says the Apostle, “entangles himself in worldly affairs, so that he may please the one to whom he has proved himself.”

## CHAPTER XXIII. On first offering peace to enemies, and, if they refuse to enter into a treaty, utterly destroying them; and on not cutting down fruit trees

(IBID.) “Whenever you approach a city to attack it, you shall first offer it peace. If it accepts and opens its gates to you, all the people who are in it shall be saved, and shall serve you under tribute. But if they refuse to enter into a treaty and begin war against you, you shall besiege it. When the Lord your God delivers it into your hand, you shall strike every male in it with the edge of the sword, except for the women, children, livestock, and everything else that is in the city. You shall divide all its spoil among the army, and you shall eat from the plunder of your enemies that the Lord your God has given you.”

The city that the Israelites approach in order to attack signifies, according to allegory, the assemblies of heretics—or, more generally, the world, which is devoted to idolatry and resists the Christian religion. According to tropology, it also signifies our outer man, which is corrupted according to the desires of error [Col. 0912A] and opposes the spirit.

When a Catholic—who is truly a Jerusalemite—undertakes such a battle, he is first commanded to offer peace, that is, to preach Christ for belief. “For he himself,” in Paul’s words, “is our peace, who made both one” (Ephesians 2).

Whoever receives the word of the Son of God and opens to him the doors of his inner heart, so that Christ may receive hospitality within him, will be saved together with all the faculties and affections of his soul. By rightly paying tribute through devotion to good works, he gains the perpetual salvation of his soul.

For this reason the Savior says to the apostles in the Gospel: “Into whatever city or village you enter, ask who in it is worthy, and remain there until you depart. When you enter a house, greet it, saying: ‘Peace to this house.’ And if the house is not worthy, let your peace return to you” (Matthew 10).

Whoever refuses to enter into a treaty of peace but begins instead to fight must be attacked, because no vice, no error, and no wickedness may be consented to. A treaty must not be made with them; rather, all their strength—which is signified by the male sex—should be punished by the edge of the spiritual sword, which is the word of God.

But if some yield to rebukes and repent of their wicked actions—for this is signified by the persons of the women, children, and livestock—they happily become the saving spoil of Christ’s soldiers and are beneficially brought into the possession of the holy Church.

What follows—“Of the cities that will be given to you, you shall permit no one at all to live, but shall kill them with the edge of the sword: namely, the Hittite, the Amorite, the Canaanite, the Perizzite, the Hivite, and the Jebusite, as the Lord your God has commanded you, lest they teach you to commit all the abominations that they themselves have practiced for their gods”—signifies that no vice in our conduct should be spared. Rather, we must resist it with divine zeal, lest, if we spare our spiritual enemies, we ourselves become corrupted in our pleasures before his eyes, become abominable, and appear worthless. As a result, abandoned by him, we may fall into the joy of our enemies, so that, rejoicing over our ruin, they say in their hearts: “Aha, aha, our soul has swallowed it up” (Psalm 35).

“When you besiege a city for a long time and surround it with fortifications in order to capture it, you shall not cut down the trees from which one may eat, nor shall you destroy the countryside around it with axes, because it is a tree and not a man, and cannot increase the number of warriors against you. But if there are trees that are not fruit-bearing but wild, and are suitable for other uses, cut them down and build siege works, until you capture the city that is fighting against you.”

Why does he forbid the cutting down of fruit trees from which one may eat, but permit wild trees to be cut down for the construction of siege works or for various uses? It is because those persons who are capable of producing the shoots of knowledge and the fruits of virtues must in some way be spared in the exercise of judgment, lest through careless judgment they be injured excessively, so that the usefulness of future growth is entirely cut off from them.

Hence the Apostle admonishes and instructs us, saying: “Brothers, if someone is overtaken in any transgression, you who are spiritual should restore such a person in a spirit of gentleness, considering yourself, lest you also be tempted. Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Galatians 6).

But those who have wild perceptions and disordered, undisciplined habits, so that they are suited to no virtuous use, must be torn away from this perverse intention and wicked practice and converted to better use.

For this reason the same Apostle commands that certain sinners be handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord. Nor should one eat with such persons or share in anything with them, so that, brought to shame, they may repent.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the corpse of a murdered man that has been found

(CAP. XXI.) “When the corpse of a murdered man is found in the land that the Lord your God is going to give you, and the perpetrator of the killing is unknown, your elders and judges shall go out and measure the distances from the place of the corpse to the surrounding cities. They shall determine which is nearest. Then the elders of that city shall take a heifer from the herd that has not been put under a yoke and has not plowed the soil with a plow, and they shall lead it to a rough and rocky valley that has never been plowed [Col. 0913C] and has received no seed. There they shall cut the neck of the heifer.

Then the priests, the sons of Levi, shall approach, whom the Lord your God has chosen to minister to him and to bless in his name, and according to whose word every matter, and everything unclean or clean, is to be judged. All the elders of that city shall come to the slain man, wash their hands over the heifer that was struck down in the valley, and say: ‘Our hands did not shed this blood, nor did our eyes see it. Be merciful to your people Israel, whom you have redeemed, O Lord, and do not in any way reckon innocent blood in the midst of your people Israel,’ and the guilt of blood will be removed from them,” and so forth.

If this chapter is considered according to the letter, it has a poor meaning; but according to spiritual understanding, it contains a great sacrament.

“When,” it says, “the corpse of a murdered man is found in the land that the Lord your God is going to give you, and the perpetrator of the killing is unknown.”

It should be noted that some have wished to understand this slain man as Adam, the first man. But it seems to me more appropriate to apply this figure to the second Adam, that is, to our Redeemer, who received the sentence of death from the Jewish people in the land of your possession and bore the saving cross for the whole world.

The perpetrator of his killing is unknown—namely, the devil, who was the author of his betrayal. He is not said to be unknown because he is not recognized, since the Gospel plainly says: “Jesus knew, before the day of the Passover feast, that his hour had come to pass from this world to the Father. Having loved his own who were in the world, he loved them to the end. And when supper had taken place, the devil had already put it into the heart of Judas Iscariot, the son of Simon, to betray him” (John 13), and so forth.

Rather, he is called unknown because, being invisible by nature, he does not appear to human eyes. The elders and judges are commanded to go out and measure the distances from the place of the corpse to the surrounding cities, so that they may investigate from which of them the killing of the corpse [something is missing] occurred. [Note: [Col. 0913D] Something is missing.]

The apostles and holy teachers, who are designated by the names “judges” and “elders,” learned through the testimony of the sacred Scriptures that no people, no nation, was ever so ready and inclined to accomplish the slaughter of the innocent as the Jewish people, who are known to have shed with stained hands not only the blood of the prophets but also the blood of the Lord himself.

Therefore, to complete the mystery, they are commanded to take a heifer from the herd that has not been put under a yoke and has not plowed the soil with a plow. This heifer signifies the flesh of our Redeemer, descended from the herd of the patriarchs and prophets. It never bore the yoke of sin, nor was it in any way produced through intercourse with a man; rather, it came forth into the world from a virgin womb, made fruitful by the Holy Spirit and free from every contagion of sin, as the life that brings salvation to the human race.

This flesh is also proclaimed to have been crucified by the elders of the city—that is, by the apostles and apostolic men—for the expiation of our sins.

“And they shall lead it,” he says, “into that rough and rocky valley which has never been plowed and has received no seed, and there they shall cut the neck of the heifer.”

What, then, is this rough and rocky valley except earthly Jerusalem, which the prophet Isaiah called the Valley of Vision? This valley is read to be rough and rocky because it was always hard and untamed, and exceedingly rough with the thorns of vices. It was “never plowed” because it never perfectly submitted to holy teachings, nor received the seed of the Gospel; instead of fruit it produced thorns, and instead of grapes it produced wild grapes.

Hence the Savior says to it in the Gospel: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those who are sent to you, how often I wanted to gather your children as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were unwilling!” and so forth (Luke 13).

There they cut the necks of the heifer, because there they crucified the flesh of the Savior.

It follows: “Then the priests, the sons of Levi, shall approach, whom the Lord your God has chosen to minister to him and to bless in his name; according to their word every matter, and everything clean or unclean, shall be judged. The elders of that city shall come to the slain man, wash their hands over the heifer that was struck down in the valley, and say: ‘Our hands did not shed this blood, nor did our eyes see it. Be merciful to your people Israel, whom you have redeemed, O Lord, and do not reckon innocent blood in the midst of your people Israel.’”

Who, then, are these priests and elders to whom such a matter and such a ministry are entrusted, except the holy apostles and preachers of the Gospel, to whom the Lord himself has entrusted the governance of the entire ecclesiastical order?

They wash their hands over the flesh of the heifer when they show their works to be clean in Christ’s Passion. Although they mystically imitate the sacraments of that Passion daily in the offering, nevertheless they keep their hearts and works entirely pure from every fraud and deceit of the Jews. According to their ministry, they continually desire and implore peace for the Christian people, so that, rather than vengeance for their crime, salvation may be granted to them as a gift because of their faith—those who are always ready to obey the Gospel of Christ.

## CHAPTER XXV. On a beautiful captive woman

(IBID.) “If you go out to battle against your enemies, and the Lord your God delivers them into your hand and you take captives, and among the captives you see a beautiful woman, love her, and wish to have her as your wife, you shall bring her into your house. She shall shave her hair, cut her nails, and remove the garment in which she was captured. Sitting in your house, she shall mourn her father and mother for one month. Afterward you shall go in to her, sleep with her, and she shall be your wife,” and so forth.

Let the Jews say how these things are observed among them. What is the reason, what is the purpose, for shaving the woman’s head and cutting her nails? Suppose, for the sake of argument, that the man said to have found her encountered her in such a condition that she had neither hair nor nails. What would she have that the law commands to be removed?

But for us, whose warfare is spiritual and whose weapons are not carnal but powerful through God, if we find a beautiful woman—that is, a soul created beautiful by God—in a pagan manner of life, and wish to unite her to the body of Christ, then, after laying aside the worship of idolatry, she is clothed in the mourning garments of repentance. She mourns her father and mother—that is, every memory of the world and its carnal allurements.

Then, by the razor of the word and teaching of God, all the sin of her unbelief, which is dead and empty, is cut away. This is what the hair of the woman’s head and her nails signify. Finally, cleansed and purified by the saving washing, she is joined to the holy people of God—when she has nothing dead on her head and nothing in her hands belonging to what is called the death of unbelief, so that she carries nothing unclean or dead either in her perceptions or in her actions.

That he commands her to be taken as a wife after thirty days signifies faith and work through the number three and the number ten. Through faith in the Trinity and through the work of the Law, therefore, every soul that truly becomes Israelite is rightly joined to the body of Christ, clinging to him in the spotless sincerity of faith and the purity of works.

Others have thought that this beautiful woman signifies some rational discipline, found expressed wisely among the Gentiles. When we discover such a discipline, we must first remove and cut away from it all the impurity of its superstition, and then adopt it for the pursuit of truth.

For the disciplines of the Gentiles possess nothing entirely pure, since among unbelievers there is no wisdom to which some impurity or superstition has not been added.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On two wives, one beloved and the other hated
«(Likewise.) If a man has two wives, one beloved and the other hated, and she bears him children, and the son of the hated wife is the firstborn, and he wishes to divide his property among his sons, he may not make the son of the beloved wife firstborn and set him before the son of the hated wife; rather, he shall acknowledge the son of the hated wife as firstborn and give him a double portion of all that he possesses, for he is the beginning of his children, and the birthright belongs to him.»

[Cols. 0916B–0917C] Sometimes, when Scripture speaks allegorically, it refers one matter to the Synagogue, another to the Church, another to the soul, another to the mystery of the Word, and another to the various forms and qualities of souls, which the spirit discerns and judges. Hence, in the chapter of the Law that follows, you should understand not two souls, but the different qualities of one soul.

There is a lovable form of the soul that desires pleasures, flees labor, avoids compunction, and neglects God’s judgment. It is lovable because it appears sweet and pleasant for a time: it does not move the mind but delights it. The other is more sorrowful, being consumed by zeal for God. Like a strict wife who does not want her companion to commit adultery, who neither tolerates nor permits it, it indulges the body in nothing, grants nothing to pleasure or delight, rejects hidden disgrace, and follows the harshness of labor and the burdens of danger.

If, then, both wives bear children by him, he says that he cannot place the firstborn son of the beloved wife before the firstborn son of the hated wife in the establishment of the inheritance, since he knows that the son of the hated wife is the firstborn. I do not think that this signifies merely a simple precedence, as though there were two firstborn sons, but only that the son of the hated wife alone has the privilege of the firstborn. For “firstborn” means the one born first. The saints, however, are firstborn, because “every male that opens the womb shall be called holy to the Lord” (Luke II). Yet not every holy person is firstborn.

Thus, in Numbers, you have: “Behold, I have taken the Levites in place of all the firstborn among the children of Israel who open the womb among the children of Israel. For on the day when I struck down every firstborn of Egypt, I sanctified every firstborn of Israel.” Therefore the Levites are taken in place of the firstborn, as though they were the holy ones. We know that the firstborn are holy from the Epistle written to the Hebrews, where we read: “But you have drawn near to Mount Zion, and to the city of Jerusalem, and to thousands of angels, to the Church of the firstborn” (Hebrews XII). Therefore, just as the firstborn of the Church are holy, so also are the Levites, since they too are firstborn—not holy by the order of birth, but by the gift of sanctification. Levi was the third son of Leah, certainly not the first. Yet the one who is sanctified is the one who opens the womb.

What womb? Hear him say: “Sinners have gone astray from the womb” (Psalm LVII). Once you have understood the firstborn who opens the womb, understand the womb of the good mother, from which the saints do not go astray, but sinners do. The Levites, moreover, are taken from the midst of Israel because they have nothing in common with the people, whose secular firstborn are scattered abroad. For the firstborn of this world belong to another mother, from whose womb Paul was set apart when he was called to the grace of God; and therefore, being separated from the midst of the people, he received the Word, which is in the midst of our heart. Hence it was said: “There stands among you one whom you do not know” (John I).

Our excursion from one Law to the other was therefore not pointless: it was so that we might show that the son of the beloved woman—that is, of the more lax and pleasure-loving one—is not the firstborn, although the words of the preceding chapter express this, Scripture saying: “You cannot place the son of the beloved woman firstborn, since you know that the son of the hated woman is firstborn.” He is truly firstborn who is the holy father of a holy mother; just as that is the true mother from whose womb there came not true children, but sinners.

Therefore, the son of the false mother is not truly a son, nor a true firstborn; but, as though he were firstborn, he is supported with provisions so that he will not lack, not honored so that he may be rich. The other, however, received a double portion of everything, so that he might abound. Likewise, in Genesis you find that the patriarchs were given two garments each as a gift by their brother Joseph when they were sent back to their father, to signify the discovery of Joseph, the brother whom their father had believed dead.

Thus the firstborn received the privilege of the inheritance, Scripture saying: “This is the beginning of his children, and the birthright belongs to him.” From God’s firstborn Son come the holy firstborn; and from that Beginning—because he himself is the beginning and the end—the holy one is called the Beginning. The Son is the Beginning, to whom the privilege of the firstfruits belongs, in accordance with what was said to Abraham: “Cast out the slave woman and her son; for the son of the slave woman shall not be heir with my son Isaac” (Genesis XXI).

We are taught by the divine oracle that this refers more to the inheritance of virtues than to money, the Lord saying: “Whatever Sarah says to you, listen to her voice, for in Isaac shall your seed be called” (ibid.). What other inheritance was there in Isaac except an inheritance of holiness, which ennobled the father? He made the slave woman’s son great among the nations, as though conferring the simpler elements of an inheritance. But to Sarah’s son he gave a double portion, since not only temporal things but also heavenly and everlasting things were bestowed upon him.

[Cols. 0917D–0918A] Again, according to the allegory, this man who is said to have two wives can represent the Lord Christ, who joined two peoples to himself in the bond of marriage, namely the Jews and the Gentiles. The Synagogue of the Jews may be called hated, since, according to the testimony of the Lawgiver, it always acted contentiously against the Lord. Stephen reproaches it in the Acts of the Apostles, saying: “Stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit; as your fathers did, so also do you” (Acts VII).

The beloved wife is the Church from the Gentiles. But this man cannot make the son of the beloved wife firstborn and set him before the son of the hated wife, because the Lord Christ does not wish to place the Church from the Gentiles before his first Church, which was in Jerusalem and from which our apostles and first teachers came. Rather, he will acknowledge the son of the hated wife as firstborn and give him a double portion of all that he possesses: for he first gave that people the Law and the Prophets and knowledge of his name; and the Savior himself was born from that people and, at the time of his incarnation, preached the Gospel there above all. “For he is the firstborn of his children, and the birthright belongs to him.” Whoever wishes to know these matters more fully should read the Epistle of blessed Paul the Apostle to the Romans; then he will recognize that everything said here is true.

## CHAPTER XXVII. [Cols. 0918B–0921D] On a rebellious and insolent son; and on a man sentenced to death and to be hanged on a gibbet, but buried on that same day

«(Likewise.) If a man has a rebellious and insolent son who does not obey the command of his father or mother, and, when disciplined, refuses to obey, they shall seize him and bring him to the elders of that city and to the gate of judgment. They shall say to them: “This son of ours is insolent and rebellious; he refuses to listen to our admonitions; he gives himself to revelry, luxury, and banquets.” Then the people of the city shall stone him, and he shall die. Thus you shall remove the evil from your midst, so that all Israel, hearing of it, may fear.»

That obedience has always pleased God, while rebellion and insolence have always displeased him, is attested by the books of the Old and New Testaments. Thus it is written: “Obedience is better than sacrifice” (Ecclesiastes IV), and to listen is better than to offer the fat of rams, because rebellion is like the sin of divination, and refusing to submit is like the crime of idolatry.

The old Law therefore commands that a disobedient and vicious son be buried under stones and die. The Gospel likewise does not spare those who remain uncorrected; rather, through teachers, it commands that offenders be rebuked with severe reprimands and corrections, which the stones signify. For it in no way spares vices but favors virtues:

“When a man has committed an offense punishable by death and, having been sentenced to death, is hanged on a gibbet, his corpse shall not remain on the wood; you shall by no means defile the land that the Lord your God has given you as a possession.”

This man may be understood as every baptized person who, when he has sinned, must be sentenced to death—that is, to guilt—for which he must be punished by the torment of death. He will be hung on a gibbet, since his crime is made manifest among the people through punishment. Hence the Apostle commands that those who sin be rebuked before everyone, so that the others may also have fear.

When it says, “His corpse shall not remain on the wood, but shall be buried on the same day,” it signifies that repentance for sins must not be postponed from one day to another, but must be undertaken immediately after the sin. Thus, before the end of the present life, a person should strive through confession, repentance, and good works to hide his sin from the eyes of God. For he is cursed by God who hangs on the wood—that is, in sin, if he perseveres in it.

Sin can be understood by the name of the wood, because our first ancestor sinned first upon the wood. “You shall by no means,” he says, “defile your land.” Since, therefore, the land of our flesh is polluted by the filth of sins, we must strive with all our strength to cleanse it through repentance and the shedding of tears, lest its foulness produce scandal for others and, in the end, torment for us.

Here, however, a very difficult question arises from the statement: “Cursed by God is everyone who hangs on the wood.” Certain heretics have wished to transfer this saying into a calumny against Christ’s Passion, failing to understand that human death results from the punishment of sin and is therefore itself called sin—not because a person sins while dying, but because what causes him to die came from sin.

In one sense, “tongue” properly means the flesh that moves inside the teeth beneath the palate; in another sense, “tongue” means what is done through the tongue. In this latter sense one speaks of the Greek tongue and the Latin tongue. Similarly, in one sense “hand” properly means the bodily member that is moved for work; in another sense, “hand” means the writing produced by the hand. We say, “His hand has been tested,” “I have your hand,” and “Take back your hand”: here “hand” properly means the human limb. Yet I do not suppose that the writing is a human being, although it is called a “hand” because it is manifest.

So too, sin means not only the evil deed itself, which deserves punishment, but also death itself, which came about through sin and has therefore been called sin. Christ did not commit that sin by which he would be guilty of death; but he took upon himself the other—that is, death, which was inflicted upon human nature because of sin—for our sake. He hung this upon the wood. This is what was cursed through Moses: death was condemned so that it might not reign, and cursed so that it might perish.

Therefore, through Christ, this sin was condemned—the sin that was ours—so that we might be freed and not remain condemned while sin reigned. Why, then, does Faustus marvel that sin is cursed, that death is cursed, and that the mortality of the flesh without Christ’s sin is cursed, although it came about in Christ from human sin?

For he took a body from Adam, since the virgin Mary who bore Christ came from Adam. God had said in paradise: “On the day when you touch it, you shall die the death” (Genesis II). This is the curse that hung on the wood.

He denies that Christ was cursed who also denies that he died. But whoever confesses that he died, and cannot deny that death comes from sin and is therefore also called sin, should hear the Apostle saying: “Our old man was crucified together with him” (Galatians III), and should understand whom Moses said was cursed.

Therefore the Apostle, following this, says of Christ: “He was made a curse for us” (ibid.), just as he was not afraid to say, “He died for all,” which is to say, he was cursed, because death itself comes from the curse. Every sin is a curse, whether it is the sin itself that is committed so that punishment may follow, or the punishment itself, which is otherwise called sin because it comes from sin.

Christ took upon himself our punishment without guilt, so that by it he might loose our guilt and bring our punishment to an end. I would be speaking from my own ingenuity if the Apostle did not repeat this so often that he both awakens those who sleep and silences those who bring accusations:

“God sent his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and on account of sin he condemned sin in the flesh” (Romans VIII).

That flesh, therefore, was not sinful flesh, since it did not come into Mary through a male transmission of mortality. Yet because death comes from sin, that flesh, although from a virgin, was nevertheless mortal; precisely because it was mortal, it had the likeness of sinful flesh. Accordingly, he calls this sin when he says: “That he might condemn sin in the flesh on account of sin.”

Again, elsewhere he says: “He made him who knew no sin to be sin for us, so that we might become the righteousness of God in him” (II Corinthians V).

Why, then, would Moses have been afraid to say “cursed,” when Paul was not afraid to say “sin”? Clearly, the prophet ought both to have foreseen and to have foretold this, prepared to be reproved by heretics together with the Apostle. Whoever reproves the prophet for saying “cursed” will be compelled to reprove the Apostle for saying “sin”; for a curse is certainly the companion of sin.

Nor is there any greater offense because he added “by God,” saying: “Cursed by God is everyone who hangs on the wood.” If God did not hate our sin and death, he would not have sent his Son to undergo and destroy them. Why, then, is it surprising that what God hates is cursed by God? For he gives us immortality—which will come when Christ appears—all the more willingly because he mercifully hates our death, which hung on the wood when Christ died.

As for the addition of “everyone,” so that it might appear that “everyone who hangs on the wood is cursed,” Moses did not fail to foresee that the righteous too would be on the cross. Rather, he rightly foresaw that heretics would deny the true death of the Lord and would therefore wish to separate Christ from this curse, in order to separate him also from the reality of death.

If that death was not real, then no curse hung upon Christ crucified on the wood, because he was not truly crucified. But against heretics who would arise in the distant future, Moses cries out from afar: “You evade without cause,” you who are displeased by the truth of Christ’s death. “Cursed is everyone who hangs on the wood.” Not this one or that one, but everyone without exception! Even the Son of God? Yes, absolutely. For this is what you do not want; this is what you strive to avoid and from which you lead others astray.

You are displeased that he was cursed for us because you are displeased that he died for us. He would then be outside the curse of that Adam if he were outside Adam’s death. But when he received death from man and for man, he did not disdain to receive from him and for him also the curse that accompanies death—not even he, indeed not even the Son of God, ever living in his own righteousness but dead because of our offenses in the flesh assumed from our punishment.

Thus he is always blessed in his righteousness, but cursed because of our offenses, in the death assumed from our punishment. For this reason “everyone” was added: so that Christ might not be said not to belong to the true death if, through foolish reverence, he were separated from the curse joined to death.

Whoever is faithful according to the truth of the Gospel should nevertheless understand that there is no insult to Christ in Moses’ calling him cursed—not according to the divinity of his majesty, but according to the condition of our punishment, because he was hung on the wood. Nor is Christ praised by the Manichaeans when they deny that he had mortal flesh in which he could suffer a true death. From the prophetic curse, the praise of humility is understood; from this heretical supposed honor, the charge of falsehood is brought.

Therefore, if you deny that he was cursed, you deny that he died. If you deny that he died, you are now fighting not against Moses but against the Apostle. But if you confess that he died, confess that he took upon himself the punishment of our sin without our sin.

Now, when you hear “the punishment of sin,” believe either that it comes from blessing or from a curse. If the punishment of sin comes from blessing, wish always to remain in the punishment of sin. But if you wish to be freed from it, believe that through the justice of the divine sentence it came from a curse.

Confess, then, that he received the curse for us whom you confess to have died for us. Understand that Moses intended nothing else when he said, “Cursed is everyone who hangs on the wood,” except: “Mortal is everyone, and dying is everyone, who hangs on the wood.”

He could have said, “Cursed is every mortal,” or “Cursed is everyone who is dying.” But this is what the prophet asserts: he knew that Christ’s death would hang upon the cross, and that heretics would arise who would say, “He did hang on the wood, but only in some appearance, not so that he would truly die.”

Therefore, by crying out, “Cursed,” he cried out nothing other than that he truly died. He knew that the death of sinful man, which he himself took upon himself without sin, came from the curse in which it was said: “If you touch it, you shall die the death” (Genesis III).

The serpent hung upon the wood pertains to this matter. It signifies that Christ did not feign a false death, but hung upon the wood of his Passion that true death in which the serpent, by its evil persuasion, had cast man down.
