These people refuse to recognize that true death, and therefore they are not healed from the serpent’s poison, just as all who looked upon it in the wilderness were healed.

Thus we admit that the unlearned say that being fastened to the wood is one thing and hanging on the wood another. For if some think that this question can be resolved by saying that Judas was the one cursed by Moses, since he hanged himself with a noose, they should first know whether he hanged himself from wood or from stone.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. [Cols. 0921D–0922C] On not passing by a wandering ox or sheep, but returning it to one’s brother; likewise concerning a donkey and a garment

**(Chapter XXII.)** «You shall not see your brother’s ox or a wandering sheep and pass it by, but you shall return it to your brother, even if your brother is not nearby and you do not know him. You shall bring it into your house, and it shall remain with you until your brother seeks it and receives it.»

According to the literal sense, this sentence teaches equity and kindness: each person should not refuse to extend to another the benefit that he ought to receive from another, in accordance with the Savior’s saying, in which he commanded: “Whatever you wish people to do to you, do the same to them” (Matthew VII).

According to the allegory, however, it reveals a venerable mystery. Our brother, according to the assumption of human nature, is Christ, who, after his resurrection, sent word through the women to his disciples, saying: “Go, tell my brothers to go to Galilee; there they will see me” (Matthew XXVIII).

This brother’s ox or sheep wanders when someone who has been called from the yoke of the Law to the faith, or any simple Catholic, is led into error by heretics. We are commanded to bring these animals into our house—that is, to receive them into our concern and care—and to keep them with us in the house of the Church through the unity of faith and peace, until our aforesaid brother, coming to judgment, reclaims it, which had previously wandered by departing from him.

Then follows: «Likewise concerning a donkey, every garment, and everything belonging to your brother that has been lost: if you find it, do not neglect it as though it were another’s. If you see your brother’s donkey or ox fallen on the road, do not despise it, but lift it up with him.»

The donkey signifies a Gentile, whose lowliness and uncleanness we must not despise; rather, insofar as we can, we should call him to the faith and to our common religion. The garment signifies outward works. If we see them deviating from the path of righteousness in someone, we must direct them into the way of justice.

Above all, we must take care not to despise any of our brothers who are wandering or sinning out of proud arrogance. Instead, with a compassionate mind, we should grieve over their fall and strive, as far as we are able, to restore them more successfully through the grace of God.

Finally, if you see any Jew or Gentile who is ignorant of the Law or dull in understanding suddenly fall into sin on the road of the present life, we ought to come to his aid with compassion and mercy, so that he may again deserve to obtain the grace of Christ through repentance and good effort.

For this reason the Apostle Paul instructs us, saying: “Brothers, if someone is overtaken in any offense, you who are spiritual should restore such a person in a spirit of gentleness, considering yourself, lest you also be tempted. Bear one another’s burdens, and thus you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Galatians VI).

## CHAPTER XXIX. [Cols. 0922D–0923B] That women ought not to wear men’s clothing, nor men women’s clothing

**(Likewise.)** «A woman shall not wear a man’s clothing, nor shall a man use a woman’s clothing; for whoever does these things is an abomination before the Lord.»

Another edition has the passage as follows: «A man’s weapons shall not be upon a woman.» It wishes “weapons” to be understood—that is, instruments of war. Some have interpreted it in this way as well.

Mystically, however, when it says, “Let a woman not wear a man’s clothing,” it reveals what the Apostle says: “I do not permit a woman to teach in the Church” (I Corinthians XIV). For neither priesthood nor teaching is granted to women in the Church.

Nor should a man be clothed in women’s clothing. Whoever is a man and exercises authority in the Church should not have anything feminine or soft in his teaching.

Morally, it teaches that nature clothes each sex with garments suited to different uses: each sex has a different color, movement, manner of walking, and strength. “I do not permit a woman,” he says, “to teach or to exercise authority over a man.” How unbecoming it is for a man to perform women’s work! Let them then give birth; let them labor in childbirth—those who curl their hair like women do. Yet women veil themselves, while these men wage war.

Those who follow ancestral customs had an excuse, although those customs were barbarous, as among the Persians, Goths, and Armenians. Nature, however, is greater than one’s homeland.

What shall we say of others who think this should be attributed to luxury, so that they keep men with curled hair and neck-rings in their service, while they themselves wear long beards and let their hair hang loose? Chastity is rightly not preserved where the distinction between the sexes is not maintained. Nature’s instruction is evident in the Apostle’s words:

“It is disgraceful for a woman without a veil to pray to God. Does not nature itself teach you that if a man has long hair, it is a dishonor to him, but if a woman has long hair, it is her glory, since her hair is given to her as a covering?” (I Corinthians II).

## CHAPTER XXX. [Cols. 0923C–0925A] On chicks and birds, and eggs, found in a nest

**(Likewise.)** «If, while walking along the road, you find a bird’s nest in a tree or on the ground, with the mother sitting above the chicks or eggs, you shall not take her with her young, but shall let her go, while taking the young for yourself, so that it may be well with you and you may live for a long time.»

We travel along the road when we pass through the present life. A bird’s nest is in a tree or on the ground when the words of the historical account belong either to the contemplative life or to the active life. The precepts of the active life are a bird’s nest on the ground; the precepts of the contemplative life are a nest in a tree.

The mother sits over the chicks or eggs when the historical account itself fosters spiritual understanding. Some passages, in plain speech, produce what are like chicks; others convey their meaning in such a way as to lead the reader’s mind from them to higher things, as though they still contained beneath them eggs from which chicks were to be brought forth. Eggs are laid for this reason: so that chicks may be drawn from them.

There are also certain matters belonging to the contemplative life that appear at first through images, so that afterward they may be seen as they are in their own power and nature. Paul says: “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face” (I Corinthians XIII).

When the blind man had begun to receive light through the laying on of the Redeemer’s hands, he was asked what he saw, and he said: “I see men as though they were trees walking” (Matthew XVIII). A human being is rational by nature, whereas a tree is neither sentient nor living. What does this blind man, once enlightened, signify except the human race? When the Lord opens the eyes of contemplation for it, it first sees certain things in an enigma, so that afterward it may be able to behold the true and rational heavenly hosts as they are.

Hence it is added there: “Then he again placed his hands upon his eyes, and he began to see; and he was restored, so that he saw everything clearly.” First, therefore, he saw through a mirror by means of resemblance; afterward he saw clearly through perfection.

In these words, then, the mother bird sits over the eggs for the contemplative life, because sacred history, beginning in an enigma, introduces something through which it may later reveal a stronger reality and produce living chicks.

The Apostle Paul also, when he learned that certain people were living incontinently, admonished them, saying: “Because of fornication, therefore, let each man have his own wife, and let each woman have her own husband” (I Corinthians VII). Since a wife should be taken only for the sake of producing children, lest anyone fall into the guilt of fornication, he granted married couples something from which they might still rise to better things. Thus he who granted what could lead the minds of married people toward lawful intercourse placed eggs in the active life, as a mother bird places them on the ground—that is, in history.

The holy preachers likewise prefer to love God rather than fear him. But if they do not introduce fear, they do not lead people to love. Therefore they customarily speak first of terrifying things and afterward of sweet things, as it is said through the Psalmist: “They shall speak of the might of your terrors, and they shall recount your greatness” (Psalm CXLIV). Then it follows: “They shall pour forth the memory of the abundance of your sweetness, and they shall rejoice in your righteousness” (ibid.).

When, therefore, they terrify in order to call people to love, they lay eggs. “Perfect love casts out fear” (I John IV). Then the chicks begin to live, when they no longer succumb to fear.

The Law itself also laid eggs when it said: “An eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth” (Leviticus XXIV). But afterward it produced chicks when it said: “You shall not seek vengeance, nor shall you remember the injury done by your fellow citizens.”

It should be noted, however, that the following is said about this mother of the chicks: “You shall not take her with her young, but shall let her go, while taking the young for yourself.” This means that in certain passages the historical sense must be passed over, so that only the chicks of this mother—that is, the meaning of the spiritual understanding—may become nourishment for us, and so that it is not the mother but the spiritual meaning that satisfies our senses.

When we read that the gold and silver of the Egyptians were secretly taken by the people of Jerusalem through a deceptive request, and again when we read that carnal sacrifices were offered to almighty God, what else is present in this nest of words except that the mother is to be released and the young retained?

When we draw intellectual vigilance from certain secular writers in defense of the truth and turn their eloquence to the use of righteousness, what else are we doing than taking gold and silver from the Egyptians, so that we may become rich from it and they may be shown to be poor? As it is written: “Bringing every understanding into captivity in obedience to Christ” (II Corinthians X).

And when we subdue our bodies through abstinence, what else are we doing than offering carnal sacrifices to almighty God? As Paul again says: “That you may present your bodies as a living sacrifice” (Romans XII).

We therefore release the mother and eat the chicks when we leave aside the examples of the historical account but retain in our minds the meanings of its allegories. For the one lives a long time who, through spiritual understanding, attains the years of eternity.

# BOOK THREE

[Col. 0925]

## CHAPTER I. [Cols. 0925A–0926A] On the building of a new house, so that a wall may be placed around the roof, lest blood be shed when someone slips and falls headlong

**(Likewise.)** «When you build your house, you shall make a wall around the roof, lest blood be shed in your house and you become liable for another person when he slips and falls headlong.»

Mention is made of such a construction in the building of the Temple, where it is written: “And he built a platform over the whole house, five cubits high” (I Kings VI). This refers to the low parapets that were built around the upper roof of the house, lest anyone who reached a higher place suddenly fall to the ground.

Mystically, it teaches us to raise ourselves at all times through the defense of right faith and divine protection, and, as far as depends on us, to maintain the guardianship of humility. Otherwise, if we appear to gather certain forms of virtue in the structure of our way of life or in the preaching of others, they may perish through our carelessness and laziness. As a certain wise man said, “He carries dust into the wind who gathers virtues without humility.”

Whoever neglects to place a defense of faith in his teaching or examples is guilty of the blood—that is, the life—of all who perish through it, because through his negligence he has lost those whom he could have preserved.

## CHAPTER II. On not sowing a vineyard with another kind of seed, and on not plowing with an ox and a donkey together

**(Likewise.)** «You shall not sow your vineyard with another kind of seed, lest both the seed that you have sown and what grows from the vineyard be sanctified together.»

Here we can understand the vineyard as doctrine, or as the people entrusted to teachers, where the wine of spiritual grace ought to be produced. But it prohibits sowing another seed there, since it absolutely does not permit heresy to be introduced.

The good seed is the Word of God. The wicked seed is the error that the enemy sowed in the Lord’s field, as is read in the Gospel (Matthew XI). Every possible care must therefore be taken that no error be found mixed into one’s teaching, lest what has been bestowed upon us as a divine gift be corrupted by our fault.

«You shall not plow with an ox and a donkey together.»

By the ox is understood the people of the circumcision, placed under the yoke of the Law; by the donkey, the people of the Gentiles belonging to the Gospel. He plows with an ox and donkey together who receives the Gospel in such a way that he does not abandon the ceremonies of Jewish superstitions, which had gone before in shadow and image.

At times, moreover, the life of those who work well is signified by the ox, and the foolish stupidity of fools by the donkey. What, then, does “You shall not plow with an ox and a donkey together” mean? It is as though he were saying: Do not join the fool to the wise in preaching, lest through the one who is unable to carry out the task you obstruct the one who is capable.

Anyone can, if necessary, yoke an ox and a donkey together without harming the work. But no one should join the wise and the foolish as companions so that they announce the Word of God with equal authority, rather than one commanding and the other obeying, without causing scandal.

## CHAPTER III. [Cols. 0926B–0926D] On not wearing a garment woven from wool and linen; and on making cords in the fringes at the four corners of the cloak

**(Likewise.)** «You shall not wear a garment woven from wool and linen.»

Wool signifies simplicity, while linen signifies subtlety. Certainly, a garment made of linen and wool conceals the linen within and displays the wool on the surface. Therefore, a person wears a garment woven from wool and linen when, under the language of innocence, he conceals the subtlety of malice within.

This is according to the moral sense. According to the allegory, however, to mix wool or purple with linen garments, and to wear a garment of linen and wool, is to live disorderly and to wish to mix professions of different kinds: for example, a holy nun may possess bridal ornaments, or a woman who, unable to remain continent, has married may assume the appearance of a virgin. This is sin in every respect.

The same applies if something unsuitable from a different kind or region is woven into anyone’s life. What was then represented in garments is now revealed in conduct.

«You shall make cords in the fringes at the four corners of the cloak with which you cover yourself.»

Moses had also commanded that they make hyacinth-colored fringes at the four corners of their cloaks, so that the people of Israel might be distinguished. Just as circumcision in the body gave the Jewish nation a sign, so the garment was to have some distinguishing feature.

In the Gospel, too, the superstitious teachers are reproved because, seeking popular approval and pursuing profits from women, they made large fringes and tied very sharp thorns into them, so that, when they walked or sat, they would sometimes be pricked and, as though by this reminder, be recalled to the duties of God and the ministries of his service.

## CHAPTER IV. On the man who disparages his wife by accusing her of an infamous sexual offense before the marriage began
“(IBID.) If a man takes a wife and afterward hates her, and seeks grounds on which to divorce her, bringing against her a very serious charge and saying, ‘I took this woman as my wife, and when I approached her I did not find her a virgin,’ then her father and mother shall take and bring the tokens of her virginity before the elders of the city who sit at the gate. The father shall say: ‘I gave my daughter to this man as his wife. Because he hates her, he has brought against her a very serious charge, saying, “I did not find your daughter a virgin”; but these are the tokens of my daughter’s virginity.’ They shall spread the garment before the elders of the city. The elders of that city shall seize the man and flog him; moreover, they shall condemn him to a fine of one hundred shekels of silver, which he shall give to the girl, because he has brought a very serious charge against a virgin of Israel. She shall remain his wife, and he shall not be permitted to divorce her for the whole of his life. But if what he alleges is true, and virginity is not found in the girl, they shall cast her out beyond the doors of her father’s house; and the men of her city shall overwhelm her with stones, and she shall die, because she has committed a disgraceful act in Israel by committing fornication in her father’s house. Thus you shall remove evil from your midst.”

From this it sufficiently appears how the law wished wives to be subject to men and almost their servants: for although it says that, if the husband’s testimony against his wife were shown to be true, she would be stoned, yet he himself is not in turn stoned if it is established that the charge was false. Instead, he is merely punished and fined, and is ordered to remain permanently attached to the woman from whom he had wished to be separated. In other cases, however, the law ordered that anyone who had injured another by false testimony, if convicted, should be put to death, and commanded that he suffer the same penalty which the other would have suffered had the charge been true.

Allegorically, we may understand this passage to mean that, if a teacher takes a people under his care and governance and afterward, because of greed and ambition for greater authority, or for any other unlawful reason, wishes to abandon the church entrusted to him and falsely imposes upon it a very serious charge—whether of heresy or disobedience—claiming that he did not find it in the virginity in which the Apostle said he had betrothed the church of the Corinthians, “to present a pure virgin to one man, to Christ” (II Cor. XI), then the girl’s father spreads the garment before the elders of the city as proof of his daughter’s virginity, when the people’s works and faith are judged among the teachers of the Church by comparison with the divine Testaments. For God is the Father of all, by whose judgment hidden things are revealed. And when, by the judgment of the divine books, he discovers that that teacher has been corrupted more by envy or greed than that he has spoken truthfully about the conduct and faith of those subject to him, he is to be corrected by the authority of the Church and reproved by all; and he is to be compelled to spend one hundred shekels of silver on the girl—that is, to devote the perfection of teaching and care to the people entrusted to him. Nor will he ever be able to dismiss her, because according to canonical ordinance he is not permitted to transfer himself from his own church to another without synodal authority.

But if that people is found to have been violated or corrupted by vices, and he afterward refuses to correct it through amendment, then, expelled beyond the doors of the house of the supreme Father—that is, beyond the thresholds of the holy Church—by the judgment of the bishops, it is to be overwhelmed with the stones of a severe anathema, because it did not fear to corrupt the Catholic faith, nor afterward wish to do penance for the wickedness it had conceived or to correct itself.

## CHAPTER V. Concerning the adulterer or adulteress, and concerning the man who abducts another’s betrothed.

“(IBID.) If a man sleeps with another man’s wife, both shall die, that is, the adulterer and the adulteress; and you shall remove evil from Israel.”

Insofar as this pertains to the historical sense, the legislator prosecutes adultery in Israel. Mystically, however, it signifies that it is not permissible for a Jew or a heretic to corrupt the Church of Christ, which is understood to be his bride and wife, because she has been joined to him by the right of faith and love. If such adultery has been committed, the corrupter and the corrupted together must either die to sin through repentance, or, if they remain impenitent, be consigned to eternal punishment through vengeance.

“If a man betroths a virgin girl, and someone finds her in the city and lies with her, you shall bring both of them out to the gate of that city, and they shall be overwhelmed with stones: the girl, because she did not cry out while she was in the city; the man, because he humbled his neighbor’s wife. Thus you shall remove evil from your midst. But if a man finds in the field a girl who is betrothed, and seizes her and lies with her, he alone shall die. The girl shall suffer nothing, and she is not guilty of death, because, just as a robber rises against his brother and kills him, so the girl has suffered violence. She was alone in the field; she cried out, and there was no one to rescue her.”

In this chapter and the two that follow, the law likewise condemns bodily fornication, just as it did in the two preceding chapters. According to the mystery, however, spiritual fornication can here be indicated. This girl therefore signifies either the ecclesiastical people or the Christian soul married to the divine Word. If a Jew, heretic, schismatic, or pagan finds her established in the city of the Catholic Church and there defiles her with error, while she herself gives him her consent in error and does not reveal him to others so that he may be corrected for his deviation, both are guilty of death.

But if that person has become Christian yet has not been received into the fellowship of the saints, being instructed in the true faith only outside the Church through catechesis, and there is corrupted and seduced by falsehood by some erring person, then that seducer ought to be punished by anathema, while she is to be recalled to the faith she had begun and liberated from her enemies through the grace of baptism.

## CHAPTER VI. Concerning the man who lies with a girl not yet betrothed.

“(IBID.) If a man finds a virgin girl who has no husband, and seizes her and lies with her, and the matter comes to judgment, the man who slept with her shall give the girl’s father fifty shekels of silver and shall have her as his wife, because he humbled her; he shall not be permitted to divorce her for all the days of his life.”

But if someone finds a virgin girl who is not betrothed and, using force against her, sleeps with her, he shall give her father fifty didrachmas of silver, and she shall be his wife, because he humbled her; he shall not be permitted to divorce her for any length of time.

It is rightly asked whether this punishment means that he cannot divorce her for all time, when he has violated her disorderly and unlawfully. For if we wish to understand that she cannot—that is, ought not—to be divorced for all time because she has become his wife, we are confronted by the provision in which Moses permitted a man to give a bill of divorce and dismiss her (Deut. XXIV). But in the case of women whom they violate unlawfully, he did not wish this to be permitted, lest it appear that he had acted in mockery, pretending that he had taken her as his wife rather than truly and deliberately marrying her. The same command was given concerning the woman against whom a man had brought an accusation because her virginity had not been found.

“No man shall take his father’s wife, nor uncover her covering.”

According to the condition in which he created us, Christ is our Father; his wife is the Church. No man is permitted to transfer the dignity of this bridegroom to himself or to violate his bride. He violates her if he turns to himself the love that he ought to preserve for the Bridegroom, seeking his own praise rather than God’s from the gift of virtue or preaching that he has received. Every teacher ought to strive to turn the whole love of the people entrusted to him toward God and to seek the glory and honor of the one whose gift enabled him to receive what he gives to others, saying to the Lord with the prophet: “Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory, for the sake of your mercy and your truth” (Ps. CXIII).

## CHAPTER VII. Concerning eunuchs and *mazerim*, and concerning the Ammonites and Moabites: the decree of the law.

“(CHAP. XXIII.) No eunuch whose testicles have been crushed or cut off and whose member has been amputated shall enter the assembly of the Lord.”

When it is said that a eunuch whose testicles have been crushed or cut off and whose member has been amputated shall not enter the assembly of the Lord, it shows that all who live softly and do not perform manly work cannot remain in the congregation of the saints and are not considered worthy to enter the kingdom of heaven—especially since Truth himself says in the Gospel: “The kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matt. XI).

“No *mazer*, that is, one born of a prostitute, shall enter the assembly of the Lord up to the tenth generation.”

Who is one born of a prostitute except one who is degenerate in understanding and conduct, or one whom the depravity of heretics has made degenerate in receiving the sacraments, or one stained by paganism or Jewish observance? Such a person is to be received within the Church only when, through the integrity of faith, he has spiritually observed the Decalogue of the law according to the teaching of the holy Gospel and has properly renounced carnal conduct through the Holy Spirit. Hence, when someone asked the Savior about his salvation, he replied: “If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments” (Matt. XIX). And again: “I am the door. If anyone enters through me, he will be saved, and he will find pasture” (John X).

“Ammonites and Moabites shall not enter the assembly of the Lord, even to the tenth generation, forever, because they were unwilling to meet you with bread and water on the way when you came out of Egypt, and because they hired Balaam son of Beor from Mesopotamia of Syria against you, to curse you. But the Lord your God would not listen to Balaam; instead, he turned his curse into your blessing, because he loved you. You shall not make peace with them, nor seek their good, all the days of your life, forever.”

Another edition reads: “An Ammonite and a Moabite shall not enter the assembly of the Lord forever.”

The question arises how Ruth entered, since she was a Moabite and from her the flesh of the Lord took or derived its origin, unless perhaps this passage mystically prophesied that she would enter when it said, “up to the tenth generation.” For generations are reckoned from Abraham and Lot, who fathered the Moabites by his daughters; and, counting Abraham himself, ten generations are found to be completed up to Salmon, who fathered Boaz, who was Ruth’s second husband. They are: Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Judah, Perez, Hezron, Aram, Amminadab, Nahshon, and Salmon. Salmon fathered Boaz, who took the widow Ruth as his wife; and thus it appears that after the tenth generation the line produced offspring in the Church of the Lord, namely Boaz, by fathering children.

But why “and forever” was added still deserves inquiry. Was it because thereafter no soul from the Ammonites and Moabites would enter that church of the Hebrew people, after this prophecy had been fulfilled in the tenth generation? Or was it rather said, “up to the tenth generation,” so that by the number ten he wished an entire multitude to be understood, and thus explained it in a sense by adding and saying, “and forever”? If that is so, Ruth appears to have been admitted contrary to the forbidden command.

Or did he prohibit Ammonite men from being admitted, but not Ammonite women—that is, men from that people, but not women—especially since, when the Israelites overthrew those nations, they were ordered to kill all the men, but not the women except those who had known intercourse with a man, since they themselves had seduced the people into fornication? They wished the virgins to remain alive, not charging them with the guilt for which that nation deserved to be overthrown. The law also recalled this here, as though someone might ask why it did not wish Moabites and Ammonites to be admitted into the Church of the Lord, and added: “Because they did not meet you with bread and water on the way when you came out of Egypt, and because they hired Balaam son of Beor from Mesopotamia against you to curse you.” These offenses were not charged against the women even when that nation was defeated, since they wished to preserve them alive.

But the fact that Ammonites and Moabites are not permitted to enter the Church forever signifies that heretics must always be excluded from the Church. For he says: “Avoid a heretical man after one or two admonitions” (Titus III).

## CHAPTER VIII. Concerning the Idumean and the Egyptian, who are not to be abhorred.

“(IBID.) You shall not abhor the Idumean, because he is your brother, nor the Egyptian, because you were an outsider in his land. Those who are born from them shall enter the Church of the Lord in the third generation.”

By the Egyptian and the Idumean the present life is signified. Although, by renouncing it, we turn away from the Egyptian land—that is, from our former way of life—and from the desire of the world, yet, while we remain subject to the necessities of this world, we do not entirely extinguish the Egyptian nation, so to speak, even though we separate ourselves from it through a certain discrimination. We do not think about superfluous things, but, according to the Apostle, are content with daily food and clothing (I Tim. VI).

When it is said, “Those who are born from them shall enter the Church of the Lord in the third generation,” it signifies that a person of the world can then be joined to God’s saints when he has perfectly believed in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, or when he has been adorned with hope and charity.

“When you go out against your enemies to battle, guard yourself from every evil thing.”

By this sentence the legislator chiefly instructs the spiritual soldiers of Christ to guard themselves from every sin and vice, against which they must always fight spiritual enemies. Hence the Apostle Paul also spoke such words to his hearers: “Everyone who contends in the arena abstains from everything. They do this to receive a perishable crown, but we an imperishable one, and so forth.”

## CHAPTER IX. Concerning one who has been polluted by a nocturnal dream, and concerning the digestion of food.

“(IBID.) If there is among you a man who has been polluted by a nocturnal dream, he shall go outside the camp and shall not return until he has washed himself with water in the evening; and after sunset he shall return to the camp.”

The law sets forth many things in the sacraments and shadows of future realities. Thus a certain material formlessness in semen, which is destined, once formed, to produce the human body, has been placed as a sign of a formless and uneducated life. Since a person must be cleansed from this formlessness by the form and instruction of teaching, that purification was commanded after the emission of semen as a sign of this matter.

For sin does not occur in dreams, yet purification is commanded even there. Or if someone thinks that this is sin, supposing that it occurs only because of some such desire—which is unquestionably false—are women’s customary monthly periods also sins? Yet the antiquity of the law commanded women to be purified from them as well, solely because of that material formlessness which, after conception, is added as though for the construction of the body. Thus, when it flows formlessly, the law wished it to signify an undisciplined mind, flowing and dissolving indecently without the form of discipline; and it signifies that the mind ought to be formed when the law commands such bodily flow to be purified.

Finally, is dying a sin? Or is burying the dead not also a good work of human compassion? Yet purification is commanded on that account as well, because the dead body, when life has departed, is not itself a sin but signifies a soul deserted by righteousness.

What is signified here by a nocturnal dream except hidden temptation? Through it, something shameful is conceived in the heart by a dark thought, though it is not completed in bodily action. But one polluted by a nocturnal dream is commanded to go out, because it is fitting that someone polluted by an unclean thought should consider himself unworthy of the fellowship of all the faithful, set the merit of his fault before his eyes, and despise himself in comparison with the estimation of the good.

To go out polluted beyond the camp therefore means that one struggling with a shameful assault should despise himself in comparison with the continent. When he has washed with water in the evening, he turns, in despising his failing, toward the laments of repentance, so that by his tears he may wipe away every sin which hidden pollution accuses in the mind.

But he should return to the camp after sunset, because, when the heat of temptation has cooled, it is necessary for him once again to take confidence toward the fellowship of the good. He returns to the camp after the sun has gone down when, after the laments of repentance, he is restored to presume upon the merits of the faithful, with the flame of unlawful thought cooled, so that he does not consider himself far removed from the others, since he rejoices that he has become clean through the death of his inward ardor.

“You shall have a place outside the camp to which you may go for the necessities of nature, carrying a stake on your belt. When you have sat down, you shall dig around, and, after relieving yourself, you shall cover what you have excreted with the excavated earth. For the Lord your God walks in the midst of the camp, to rescue you and deliver your enemies to you, so that your camp may be holy and no uncleanness may appear in it, lest he abandon you.”

From the womb of our mind, burdened by the weight of corruptible nature, certain superfluous thoughts burst forth like the burdens of the belly. But we must carry a stake beneath our belt, so that, always girded and ready to seize ourselves, we may have around us a sharp goad of compunction which continually pierces the earth of our mind with the pain of repentance and covers what foulness erupts from us.

The excretion of the belly is covered with earth by means of the stake when the superfluity of our mind, examined by subtle reproof, is hidden before the eyes of God through the goad of its compunction.

## CHAPTER X. Concerning not handing over a fugitive slave to his master.

“(IBID.) You shall not hand over to his master a slave who has fled to you. He shall dwell with you in the place that pleases him, and shall rest in one of your cities; you shall not afflict him.”

“You shall not hand over to your master a slave who has been placed with you by his master.” This does not mean that his master placed him with you, that is, entrusted him to you; for he would rather have said “deposited.” But he said “placed with you by his master,” that is, joined to you when he had departed from that master. Therefore he forbids not the receiving but rather the returning of fugitives. What this means may be doubtful, unless we understand these words to be addressed to a nation and people, not to one individual. Thus he forbade a man fleeing from another nation to this nation, to which he was speaking, to be returned to his master, that is, to his king. Achish, king of Gath, also observed this in the case of David, when David fled to him from the face of his master, that is, King Saul. He explains this most plainly when he says of the man himself: “The fugitive shall dwell among you, in every place that pleases him.”

Mystically, however, the preacher commands the assembly not ever to hand over to his former master—who wishes greedily to reclaim him—the person who has fled from diabolical slavery, that is, from unbelief or the burden of sins, to repentance and faith in Christ, by rejecting him and casting him into despair. Rather, it should place him under the protection of the Catholic faith and the guardianship of the holy Church, so that there he may truly rest and not return again to his former service.

## CHAPTER XI. That no harlot or fornicator among the children of Israel is to exist, and that neither a prostitute’s wages nor the price of a dog is to be offered in the house of the Lord.

“(IBID.) There shall not be a harlot among Israel, nor shall there be a fornicator among the children of Israel.”

Here he manifestly forbade fornication, showing that it is a sin for both men and women to mingle even with persons outside their marriages, when he forbids both being prostitutes and going to prostitutes, whose shame is publicly for sale. In the Decalogue he does not seem openly to have forbidden this under the name of adultery, since adultery is ordinarily understood only as violation of marriage. We discussed there what seemed to us to be the case.

Spiritually, however, he intimates that it is in no way permissible for a Christian soul to mingle itself with the errors of heretics; nor for one who is an adopted son of God the Father to give himself over to impurity and lust, or to enter into an abominable covenant with the devil. Hence the teacher of the Gentiles says: “Flee fornication; for God has not called us in uncleanness but in sanctification. Do not bear the yoke with unbelievers. For what participation has righteousness with iniquity? Or what agreement has the temple of God with idols? Or what fellowship has light with darkness? What concord, moreover, has Christ with Belial? Or what portion has the faithful with the unfaithful? What agreement, moreover, has the temple of God with idols? For you are the temple of the living God, as God says: ‘I will dwell with them and walk among them, and I will be their God and they shall be my people. Therefore go out from among them and be separated,’ says the Lord, ‘and do not touch what is unclean, and I will receive you; and I will be a father to you, and you shall be sons and daughters to me,’ says the Lord Almighty” (II Cor. VI).

“You shall not offer a prostitute’s wages, nor the price of a dog, in the house of the Lord your God, whatever it is that they have vowed; for both are an abomination before the Lord your God.”

“You shall not offer a harlot’s wages, nor the exchange of a dog, in the house of the Lord your God for any vow; for it is an abomination to the Lord your God—and not one of these things, but both.” For he forbids a dog to be used for the redemption of firstborn animals, which he commands to be done with other unclean animals, namely horses and asses, and whatever animals assist a human being; and in Latin such beasts of burden are called *jumenta* from *juvando*, “helping.” But concerning a dog, did he also refuse this concerning a pig? And why he refused it must be investigated; and, if he refused it concerning all such animals, why he made the dog alone an exception in this place.

As for the prostitute’s wages, the reason for mentioning them seems to be that above he prohibited there being a prostitute among the daughters of Israel, or any son of Israel using a prostitute; and lest the thought arise that this sin could be expiated if something from it were offered in the Temple, it had to be said that it is an abomination to the Lord.

Morally, however, it is shown that, just as a prostitute’s wages are an abomination to the Lord, so also is the gift of rapacity. For dogs signify rapacious persons. An offering made from plunder cannot please God; hence Wisdom says: “The Most High does not approve the gifts of the unrighteous, nor does he regard the offerings of the unrighteous, nor will he be propitiated for their sins by the multitude of their sacrifices. He who offers a sacrifice from the substance of the poor is like one who sacrifices a son before his father’s eyes” (Ecclus. XXXIV).

## CHAPTER XII. He forbids usury and carrying away grapes from a neighbor’s vineyard; likewise, he forbids reaping a neighbor’s grain with a sickle.

“(IBID.) You shall not lend to your brother at interest money, crops, or any other thing whatever, but to a stranger. But to your brother you shall lend without interest what he needs, so that the Lord your God may bless you at all times in the land which you are entering to possess.”

By this sentence the legislator teaches kindness and justice, because he forbade us to collect interest through fraud and avarice, and commands us to bestow charity upon the needy. Our brother is every Catholic person, to whom, in the spiritual sense, we ought freely to give the fruit of the word, so that he may partake with us of heavenly food. A stranger is any unbeliever and wicked person, to whom we lend money at interest when, in return for the word of preaching that we have bestowed, we demand repentance for sins and, in addition, faith with good works from him.

In Holy Scripture money is understood in two ways. One is metallic money, which is altogether forbidden to be lent at interest, since it is a vice of covetousness to wish to demand what you do not know that you lent. The Lord Jesus Christ indeed had this money, which he gave to Judas to distribute to the poor; he did not lend it at interest when, to instruct us, he granted it to the needy with pious generosity. The other kind is that which, according to the Gospel, we are urged to lend at interest, namely most holy preachings and divine ordinances. For he says: “You knew that I am a hard and austere man. Ought you not to have entrusted my money to the bankers, so that, when I came, I might indeed have demanded with interest what is mine?” Thus this equivocal word is understood according to the character of the passages.

“When you enter your neighbor’s vineyard, eat as many grapes as you please; but do not carry any out with you.” In this place we may understand the vineyard as either Holy Scripture, where spiritual grace is found, or the Catholic Church, which we read is represented in the Gospel parable under the name of a vineyard. Our neighbor, whose vineyard it is, is the Redeemer of humankind. Whoever enters this vineyard is permitted to eat its grapes, that is, to believe Christ’s incarnation and partake there in his sacraments. But this grace may by no means be carried outside, that is, outside the Church, because the flesh of the lamb is commanded to be eaten in one house.

“If you enter your friend’s grainfield, you shall pluck ears and rub them in your hand, but you shall not reap with a sickle.” For what is it to enter a friend’s grainfield except to meditate devoutly upon the law of Christ, who is our true friend? There we are permitted to pluck ears and rub them in our hand—that is, in fitting places to bring the letter of the law to a spiritual meaning. But to reap with a sickle—that is, to twist all the Scriptures into an evil meaning—is entirely forbidden. There are, therefore, certain passages in the divine Testaments which instruct faith historically; others which train us morally for holy conduct; and still others which show venerable mysteries, not according to history but according to allegory. Therefore the diligent reader needs the greatest discernment everywhere, so that in the aforesaid grainfield of the Lord he may cautiously seek wholesome food for himself, yet not through rashness incur judgment for having injured the harvest.

## CHAPTER XIII. Concerning dismissing a hated wife with a bill of divorce.

“(CHAP. XXIV.) If a man takes a wife and has her, and she does not find favor in his eyes because of some indecency, he shall write a bill of divorce, put it in her hand, and dismiss her from his house. And when she has gone out and taken another husband, and he too hates her and gives her a bill of divorce and dismisses her from his house, or certainly dies, her former husband shall not be able to receive her again as his wife, because she has been defiled and made abominable before the Lord, etc.”

The Savior explains this passage more fully: Moses commanded a bill of divorce to be given because of the hardness of hearts [Note: [Col. 0935D] The passage is corrupt.], not granting separation, but preventing murder (Matt. XIX). For it is much better that a sorrowful discord occur than that blood be shed through hatred. There were many causes for dismissing wives under the old law. But in the Gospel the Lord made an exception only for fornication; all other troubles, should any arise, he commands to be borne resolutely for the sake of marital fidelity and chastity. He also calls adulterous the man who marries a woman released from her husband. The Apostle Paul sets a limit to this matter, saying that this is to be observed as long as her husband lives, but that when he has died permission to marry is given (I Cor. VII). He himself also maintained this rule and showed that in it there is not merely counsel, as in some admonitions, but a command of the Lord, when he says: “To those who are married I command—not I, but the Lord—that a woman not depart from her husband” (ibid.).

“But if she departs, let her remain unmarried or be reconciled to her husband. And let not a husband dismiss his wife.” I believe this is in a similar form: if he dismisses her, let him not take another, or let him be reconciled to his wife. For it is possible that he dismissed his wife because of fornication, which the Lord wished to be an exception. But if he were not permitted, while the husband from whom she departed lives, to marry another woman, nor the husband to take another wife while the wife whom he dismissed lives, then much less is it lawful to commit illicit fornications with anyone whatever. More blessed, indeed, are marriages which have been able, whether for the begetting of children or even with this earthly offspring set aside, to preserve continence between themselves by mutual consent; for neither is the command violated by which the Lord forbids a spouse to be dismissed. One does not dismiss her when one lives with her not carnally but spiritually, and that is observed which is said through the Apostle: “It remains that those who have wives should be as though they had none” (ibid.).

Mystically, however, this man represents Christ, who took a wife when he wished to join the synagogue to himself. He had also long before betrothed her when he gave her the law in justice, judgment, and mercy, as is written in Moses. But she did not find favor in his eyes because of her unbelief and the indecency of idolatry. Therefore he wrote her a bill of divorce by establishing the Gospel, in which it is most plainly declared that she was unworthy of this spiritual union, since in persecuting Christ she delivered him to the cross and chose rather that Barabbas the robber be given to her than the Lord and Savior. The bill of divorce was given into her hands when authority was given to her to crucify the Redeemer; hence she deservedly merited to be cast off, and she was dismissed from her house when she was expelled from the holy Church. Hence also, in the Gospel, the Lord himself, preferring to them the faith of the centurion, says: “Many shall come from east and west and shall recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven; but the children of this kingdom shall be cast into outer darkness, where there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matt. VIII).

What follows—“And when she has gone out and taken another husband, and he has hated her because of her indecency and given her a bill of divorce because he has dismissed her from his house, the former husband shall not be able to receive her again because she has been defiled and made abominable”—signifies that, although after Christ’s passion and resurrection the apostles sought by their preaching to summon the synagogue to repentance and Catholic faith and wished to join her in spiritual marriage, she was nevertheless unworthy of fellowship with her former husband. For, defiled by error and made abominable in her pleasures, she remained in her former foulness. Hence we read that the apostles of Christ, Paul and Barnabas, at Antioch, shaking the dust from their feet against the Jews, said: “It was necessary that the word of God first be spoken to you; but since you reject it and judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts XIII).

Tropologically, a man takes a wife when he undertakes the care of an earthly occupation. When he has recognized its foulness, he gives a bill of divorce and dismisses her from his house, because an earthly occupation which was fiercely loved before it was possessed is often recognized, once possessed, to be foul, when it is seen to be defiled by sins. Therefore let the man dismiss her from his house, so that he may cast her love from his mind. Let her, having gone out, take another husband, because another desires the earthly occupation which you abandon. But perhaps it too will at some time become hateful to him, so that he may beneficially dismiss it. It is well said, moreover, “He has dismissed her, or certainly has died,” because each person either dismisses an earthly care or dies—that is, he either does not yield to it from his heart, or through it utterly dies in the life of his soul. Therefore, whether the husband who follows her dismisses her or has died, the former husband cannot receive her as his wife because she is defiled. That is, one who has once abandoned earthly care and concern for the present life must never return to it, because by his own judgment he has already defiled it: he first abandoned it because he recognized it to be defiled. Hence it is rightly added: “Do not cause the land which the Lord your God has given you to possess to sin.” For one defiles his land who pollutes his body with carnal desires and the lusts of this world. Therefore it is very necessary that he hasten vigorously to subdue ambition for the present life, lest it perhaps gain power to rule. And when an earthly occupation has once been rejected, it must not be sought again, lest one who seemed to have put his hand to the plow look back (Luke IX).

## CHAPTER XIV. Concerning one who has newly married: that no public obligation is to be imposed upon him.

*(Same place.)* “When a man has recently taken a wife, he shall not go forth to war, nor shall any public duty be imposed upon him; but he shall remain free from liability to his household, so that he may rejoice with his wife for one year.”

What else is suggested to us by this statement except that all who bind themselves to carnal desires should recognize that they are unfit for the governance of the Church and for spiritual understanding? Hence the Apostle Paul instructed his disciple, saying: “Lay hands hastily on no one” (1 Tim. 5). And again: “No one serving as a soldier for God involves himself in secular business, so that he may please the one to whom he has proved himself” (2 Tim. 2).

“You shall not take as a pledge the lower or upper millstone, because he has set his soul in pledge to you.”

For sometimes we use *to take* to mean *to carry away*. Hence those birds that are eager to seize prey are called *hawks* (*accipitres*); and the Apostle Paul says: “For you endure it if someone devours you, if someone takes from you” (2 Cor. 11), as though he were saying, “if someone robs you.”

A pledge is the sinner’s confession before his creditor. A pledge is taken from a debtor when a confession of sin is already obtained from the sinner. The upper and lower millstone are hope and fear. Hope lifts one upward, while fear presses the heart downward. Yet the lower and upper millstones are necessarily joined to one another, so that neither can usefully exist without the other. Therefore hope and dread must continually be joined in the sinner’s heart, because he hopes for mercy in vain if he does not also fear justice; and he fears justice in vain if he does not also trust in mercy.

The removal of the upper or lower millstone as a pledge is prohibited because the person who preaches to a sinner must so arrange his preaching with wise pastoral judgment that, without abandoning hope, he does not remove fear, nor, after removing hope, leave the sinner in fear alone. He removes the upper millstone if he says to someone weeping over his sin that there is no forgiveness for what he has committed. He removes the lower millstone if he flatteringly indulges the sinner and says: “Do evil as far as you can without fear, for God is merciful and ready to forgive.” But both millstones are rightly retained when hope is joined with fear that brings amendment, and fear is joined with hope.

## CHAPTER XV. On the man who has enticed and sold his brother, and on the precaution against leprosy

*(Same place.)* “If a man is found enticing one of his brothers, the children of Israel, and, after selling him, has received payment, he shall be put to death; and you shall remove the evil from your midst.”

Scripture says this repeatedly when it commands that the wicked be put to death. The Apostle also used this expression when he said: “For what have I to do with judging those outside? Are you not judging those who are within? Remove the evil person from among yourselves” (1 Cor. 5). For the Greek text has *τὸν πονηρόν*, which is also written here. This is usually interpreted as “the malicious one” rather than simply “evil.” Nor does it say *τὸ πονηρόν*, that is, “the malicious thing,” but *τὸν πονηρόν*, “the malicious person.” From this it is evident that he intended someone who had committed an act of such a kind that he deserved excommunication. For excommunication now accomplishes in the Church what execution accomplished then.

The apostolic statement may nevertheless be understood otherwise: each person may have been commanded to remove evil, or the malicious person, from himself. Which interpretation would be more acceptable if the Greek text contained “this evil” or “this malicious thing,” rather than “this malicious person”? As it stands, however, it is more credible that the statement concerns a person rather than a vice. Yet it may also elegantly be understood that a person should remove an evil person from himself, in accordance with the saying: “Put off the old man” (Eph. 4). Explaining this, he says: “The one who used to steal must steal no longer.”

“Take careful heed that you do not contract the plague of leprosy, but do whatever the priests of the Levitical race teach you, according to what I commanded them; diligently fulfill it.”

Here it appears that every priest was a Levite, although not every Levite was a priest. Figuratively, Scripture teaches us to be careful lest we be stained by the leprosy of error or be led astray by the cunning of heretics. “For their word, in Paul’s phrase, spreads like cancer” (2 Tim. 2); and if it is allowed to spread, it contaminates our entire way of life and plunges the soul into hell.

## CHAPTER XVI. On not reclaiming a pledge, and on not withholding the wages of the needy and the poor

*(Same place.)* “When you demand from your neighbor something that he owes you, you shall not enter his house to take away the pledge, but shall stand outside, and he shall bring out to you whatever he has. But if he is poor, the pledge shall not remain with you overnight; you shall return it to him immediately before sunset, so that, sleeping in his garment, he may bless you, and you may have justice before the Lord your God.”

It rightly appears to belong to the work of mercy that the creditor should not enter the debtor’s house, lest the debtor be disturbed; yet by this command the debtor himself is also admonished to bring the pledge outside to the creditor. But because it commands that the pledge of a needy person be returned on the same day, so that he may sleep in it who has nowhere else to sleep, it reasonably prompts the question why it did not instead command the creditor not to take a pledge that must be returned that very day. If this was intended to compel the debtor, how would it urge him to repay, when he knew that he would recover the pledge on the same day? Or perhaps this was intended as a reminder, so that he would not forget to repay and then fail to do so if he truly had the means. This is especially so because he is overcome by the mercy of his creditor, toward whom he ought not to be ungrateful if he has received back the pledge in which he may sleep. At the same time, when the debtor has not repaid, the creditor ought to believe that he lacks the means, since he requires this mercy: that the pledge be returned to him precisely because he has nothing else in which to sleep.

“You shall not withhold the wages of your needy and poor brother, whether he is a resident alien who dwells with you in the land and within your gates; but you shall pay him his wages on the same day, before sunset, because he is poor and sustains his life by them, lest he cry out against you to the Lord and it be counted as sin against you.”

According to the historical sense, the law commends to us an attitude of mercy and fairness in our dealings with the needy and poor. According to the allegorical sense, however, it instructs the people how they ought to care for their preachers. They are poor in spirit, to whom the Lord commanded in the Gospel “to carry neither purse, nor bag, nor sandals on the road, and not to have two tunics, nor even money in their belts” (Luke 10). And he added how they should hope to obtain what they needed, saying: “The laborer is worthy of his wages.” Hence Paul also says: “The farmer who labors ought to receive a share of the fruits” (2 Tim. 2). The Lord likewise ordained that “those who proclaim the Gospel should live by the Gospel.” And again: “If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it a great matter if we reap your material things?” (1 Cor. 9).

Therefore, before sunset, the payment for their labor must be given by those subject to them to the teachers themselves, because what they need ought to be provided for them in the present life, while the future reward remains secure—a reward they will receive in eternal life from the giver of all good things.

## CHAPTER XVII. On not putting fathers to death for their sons, nor sons for their fathers; and on not perverting the judgments of the resident alien and the orphan

*(Same place.)* “Fathers shall not be put to death for their sons, nor sons for their fathers, but each person shall die for his own sin.”

Behold, not only did the prophets say this; the law also says that each person must be put to death for his own fault, not for that of his father or son. What, then, is meant when God is said to repay the sins of fathers upon their children, to the third and fourth generation? Is this understood of children not yet born, on account of original sin, which the human race also drew from Adam? Here, however, the distinction concerns those already born, so that each person dies for his own sin. For someone who was already born when his father sinned does not derive anything from his father’s sin.

But when it says there, “to those who hate me,” it is clear that even that condition can be changed if the children do not imitate the deeds of their parents. The consequence derived from Adam is also repaid temporally, because all die on account of it; but it is not repaid eternally to those who have been spiritually regenerated by grace and have remained in that state to the end.

Nevertheless, it may reasonably be asked: if the sins of fathers are repaid upon the children who hate God, why “to the third and fourth generation,” with the first and second either omitted, or with the punishment not continuing into the remaining generations so long as impiety and imitation of evil parents persist? Or did he wish by this number—since the number seven is understood—to signify totality? And for that reason did he not use seven itself and say “to the seventh generation”? Thus everyone would be understood, because in this way he more clearly indicated the reason for the perfection of the number.

It is called perfect because it consists of these two numbers: three, the first complete odd number, and four, the first complete even number. Hence I also think that the prophetic saying is intended in this sense, which is repeatedly expressed: “For three transgressions and for four I will not turn away.” By this he wished all impieties to be understood rather than three or four.

“You shall not pervert the judgment of the resident alien or the orphan, nor shall you take the widow’s garment as a pledge.”

“You shall not bend the judgment of the resident alien, the orphan, and the widow, and you shall not take their garment as a pledge.” Why did he forbid the judgment of these three to be perverted, but forbid the garment of the widow alone—not theirs as well—to be taken as a pledge? It was because he commended the judgments of all three as matters requiring protection: the resident alien, because he is in a foreign land; the orphan, that is, the child without parents, because he lacks parents; and the widow, because she has no husband.

But when he forbids the garment of the widow to be taken as a pledge, I think he carefully warns that those women should truly be called widows who are also poor. The Apostle clearly shows this when he says: “If any widow has children or grandchildren, let her first learn to manage her own household piously and to repay her parents in kind, for this is acceptable before the Lord. But she who is truly a widow and desolate has set her hope on God and persists in prayers night and day” (1 Tim. 5).

He calls her a true widow who has no one by whom she may be supported, because she is deprived not only of her husband but also of descendants and every form of assistance. He would not call a rich woman desolate. Therefore the garment pledged by a poor woman must not be taken away.

But if the thought arises: what if she has many garments that are not necessary but superfluous—how can she be understood as a true widow? The text answers that she is not only not desolate but also lives in luxury, as it says: “She who lives in luxury is dead while she lives” (the same passage). This woman is set against the true widow, as though such a woman were not a widow at all. Those rich women who do not wish to enter another marriage are praised for their continence, not commended for desolation. They are widowed only of their husbands, not of all other resources.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On leaving a sheaf in the harvest, and on the remnants of olives and the trees

*(Same place.)* “When you reap your field and, forgetting a sheaf, leave it behind, you shall not return to take it, but shall allow the resident alien, the orphan, and the widow to take it, so that the Lord your God may bless you in all the work of your hands. If you gather the fruit of your olive trees, whatever remains on the trees you shall not return to gather, and so forth.”

When it admonishes that no one should gather the sheaf forgotten during the harvest, and that no one should return for the olive or grape left behind, but says that what has been neglected should be gathered by the needy and left for them, the thought may perhaps arise: what if these things, left by the owners of the fields, are gathered not by the needy but by dishonest people?

First, however, it must be considered that the person who leaves them does so with the intention that the needy may have what is left. Then, when these things are left for the people, those who do not need them are simultaneously admonished not to seek them. If they do seek them, what else should they be judged to be doing but invading the property of others—and, what is more serious, the property of the poor?

Thus both groups are addressed by these commandments: those who own the fields, so that they may mercifully leave these things behind; and those who are not needy, so that they may abstain from them. Both matters are stated: by whom they are to be left and for whom they are to be left.

## CHAPTER XIX. On correcting sinners with blows; and on not muzzling the ox that threshes grain on the threshing floor

[Col. 0941C] *(Chapter 25.)* “If there is a dispute between some people and they appeal to the judges, then the one whom they determine to be righteous they shall declare to have justice, while the one whom they determine to be wicked they shall condemn for his wickedness. But if they see that the one who sinned is deserving of blows, they shall throw him down and have him beaten in their presence. The number of blows shall correspond to the measure of the sin, but only to the extent that they do not exceed forty, lest your brother, being disgracefully lacerated, lie before your eyes.”

“If there is a quarrel between people, and they go up to judgment, and the judges judge and justify the righteous”—the judges must be understood as the ones judging, not those who are said to have the quarrel. Then it follows: “and they rebuke the wicked. And if the one who acted wickedly is judged deserving of blows, you shall set him in the presence of the judges, and they shall beat him before them according to his wickedness; they shall beat him forty times, and shall not add more. But if they add to beating him with these blows, your brother will be disfigured very severely before you.”

It should be noted that, although he commanded that those sins be corrected with blows which were not deserving of punishment by death—and this with so few blows—he nevertheless called the person who is beaten “wicked,” or one who acts wickedly. Thus we may know that Scripture did not speak as many people do, when we read it carelessly and suppose that adultery is not wickedness because those who commit it appear to have sinned against a human being, even though the law commands that this sin be punished by death. We have said that those impieties are more serious when there are certain sins punished by forty blows, although they appear to be less serious.

There is therefore a lighter wickedness, deserving of a beating, and a more serious wickedness, deserving of death. Likewise, among those sins that appear to be committed not against God but against a human being, some are deserving of death, while others are subject to correction, beating, or a lighter pardon [or punishment, *poena*]. The Septuagint translators are clearly known to have spoken in this way, since they also called the wickedness of the person deserving of blows “wickedness.”

As for the command that offenders be corrected with forty blows according to the measure of their sin, it has already been stated that the number forty symbolically signifies this present age, in which the Church, spread throughout the four parts of the world, lives under the law’s Decalogue. We are therefore struck with the number forty when, in this time of repentance, we are scourged by disciplinary blows.

Every sinner ought therefore to be worn down by temporal scourges, so that he may be found purified at the judgment. Blessed is the person who is corrected by the Lord. No eternal hostility could afflict those whom the discipline of repentance has struck here. For if we are beaten because of our sins, we will be found there without sin.

“You shall not muzzle the ox that threshes your grain.”

“You shall not bind the mouth of the ox that threshes,” it says, because under the name of the ox the life of every person who labors is signified. In one passage the Apostle Paul speaks reproachfully and sorrowfully because no one had shared with him in the matter of giving and receiving; elsewhere he explained this openly, saying: “If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it a great matter that we should reap your material things?” (1 Cor. 9). This is what is signified by “You shall not muzzle the ox that threshes.”

Hence the same Apostle says elsewhere: “The laborer is worthy of his wages” (1 Tim. 5). Scripture therefore wishes material support to be provided for teachers, from whom people receive spiritual things. Because preachers are occupied with teaching, they cannot provide what they need for themselves.

## CHAPTER XX. On the man who dies without children, so that the deceased man’s brother may take his wife and raise up offspring for his brother

*(Same place.)* “When brothers dwell together and one of them dies without children, the wife of the deceased shall not marry another, but his brother shall take her and raise up offspring for his brother; and he shall call the first son born from her by the name of the deceased, so that his name may not be erased from Israel. But if he is unwilling to take his brother’s wife, who is due to him by law, the woman shall go to the gate of the city and appeal to the elders, saying: ‘My husband’s brother refuses to raise up his brother’s offspring in Israel and refuses to take me as his wife.’ Immediately they shall summon him and question him. If he answers, ‘I do not wish to take her as my wife,’ the woman shall approach him before the elders, remove his sandal from his foot, spit in his face, and say: ‘Thus shall it be done to the man who does not build up his brother’s house’; and his name shall be called in Israel, ‘The House of the Unshod.’”

“But if brothers dwell together and one of them dies, and he has no offspring, the wife of the deceased shall not go outside to another; her husband’s brother shall enter to her, take her as his wife, and live with her. And whatever child is born shall be established under the name of the deceased, and his name shall not be erased from Israel, and the name of the deceased shall remain.”

The law appears to have commanded that a brother take his brother’s wife for no other reason than to raise up offspring for the brother who died without children. When it says, “He shall be established under the name of the deceased, and his name shall not be erased from Israel,” the phrase “the name of the deceased” seems to mean that the child who is born is to be called by the name by which the deceased was called, so that the deceased is in some way propagated through him.

For this reason we thought it better to resolve, according to the custom of adoption, the Gospel question concerning Joseph’s two fathers: Matthew mentions one, namely the one who begot Joseph, while Luke mentions the other, whose son Joseph was, since neither of them gave Joseph the name of the deceased.

Unless perhaps the statement “He shall be established under the name of the deceased” does not mean that he takes the deceased’s name, but that, from the deceased’s name—that is, as his son, not as the son of the one whose seed generated him—he is established as heir to the deceased, for whom offspring has been raised up. The added phrase, “And his name shall not be erased from Israel,” may be understood not to mean that the child subsequently receives his name, but that the deceased would otherwise appear to have died without descendants, and therefore his name remains—that is, his memory.

For even if he himself had begotten a son, he would not necessarily have given the child his own name so that his name would not be erased from Israel. Rather, his name would not be erased because he would not have departed this life without children; and his brother is commanded to accomplish through the deceased’s wife what the deceased himself could not accomplish.

Even if there had been no brother, a kinsman would take the wife of a man who died without sons in order to raise up offspring for his brother, as Boaz did by taking Ruth, so as to raise up offspring for her kinsman, whose wife she had been and by whom she had borne no child. Yet the child born from her was established under the deceased’s name, because he was called his son; and thus the name of the deceased was not erased from Israel. Nevertheless, he was not called by the deceased’s name.

Since this is so, the Gospel question may be resolved even more fully in two ways: one of those whom Matthew and Luke mention as different may have been related closely enough to the other to take his wife, while each could have had different ancestors and forebears farther back. For if they had been sons of brothers, they would have had one grandfather; but that is not the case. According to Matthew, Matthan is Joseph’s grandfather; according to Luke, however, it is not Matthan but Matthat.

If someone supposes that the names are so similar that the scribes made an error in a single letter, producing such a small and almost nonexistent difference, what will he say about their fathers? According to Luke, Matthat was the son of Levi; according to Matthew, Matthan is found to have been born from Eleazar. Thus, going upward from that point, their fathers and grandfathers are different, and then their ancestors continue to differ up to Zerubbabel. In Luke, Zerubbabel is approximately the twentieth ancestor upward from Joseph; in Matthew, approximately the eleventh.

Zerubbabel is believed to be the same person in both genealogies because in both evangelists his father is found to be Shealtiel, although it could have happened that there was another man of the same name, with a father bearing that same name as the father of the other Zerubbabel. For from that point upward their ancestors again differ. Luke gives Zerubbabel a different grandfather, Neri, while Matthew gives Jeconiah. From there upward there is no agreement until David is reached—through Solomon in Matthew and through Nathan in Luke.

It seems extremely difficult that there was no closer relative to take his brother’s wife than one who was related to David at so distant a degree and not joined to him by some nearer relationship, since in Luke he is almost the fortieth ancestor from Joseph, while in Matthew he is approximately the twenty-seventh.

Or, if relatives were also sought among those related through the female line in order to take the wives of deceased men, it could have happened that there was someone related in this way who begot Joseph from the wife of his relative who died without children. Thus one man could be his natural father and another his father according to the law. Their relationship would not appear among their fathers, grandfathers, and later ancestors because they were related not through male but through female lines.

Nevertheless, if this were so, David would not eventually appear as one common father. Or if someone argues that this could have happened, where do we place the fact that Scripture’s custom is not to insert women in genealogies in place of men, just as no evangelist inserted women there at all? When mothers are mentioned, they are mentioned only together with the fathers.

Accordingly, either no closer relative was available to take the deceased man’s wife, so that the origin of the relationship had to be traced back to David, or adoption made one of them Joseph’s father.

*(From Gregory.)* Figuratively, the deceased brother is the one who, appearing after the glory of the resurrection, said: “Go, announce it to my brothers” (Matt. 28). He departed as though without children because he had not yet completed the number of his elect.

The surviving brother is commanded to take this man’s wife, because it is surely fitting that responsibility for the holy Church be entrusted to the one who is able to govern her well. When he refuses, the woman spits in his face, because whoever does not care to benefit others from the gifts he receives is reproached by the holy Church for possessing those gifts; she spits or casts saliva in his face, as it were.

His sandal is removed from one foot so that he may be called “The House of the Unshod.” For it is written: “Your feet shod with the preparation of the Gospel of peace” (Eph. 6). Therefore, if we care for our neighbor as we care for ourselves, we fortify both feet with sandals. But whoever considers his own advantage and neglects the interests of his neighbors loses, as a disgrace, the sandal of one foot.

## CHAPTER XXI. On two men who quarrel and a shameless wife; and that one ought not to have different weights in one’s bag

*(Same place.)* “If men have a quarrel among themselves and one begins to fight against the other, and the wife of one of them, wishing to rescue her husband from the hand of the stronger man, puts out her hand and seizes his private parts, you shall cut off her hand, and your eye shall not spare her.”

What else is signified by these two men who are fighting except dissension between a Catholic and a heretic? Contention is necessary where the two have differing aims. One is a persistent follower of error; the other is a diligent defender of truth. Truth must not in any way yield, but must resist error courageously, according to the saying in Wisdom: “Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he appear wise to himself” (Prov. 26). Hence Paul also boasts that he did not yield to such people even for an hour.

The wife who, in her shameless attempt to defend her husband, seizes the private parts of the stronger man can, unless I am mistaken, be more fittingly understood as representing those subjects who have been subjugated to heretics. If, through some false disgrace or shameful action, she wishes to stain the conduct of a Catholic or defame his teaching, such a plot must be cut off in every way, and no pity should be shown to one who has so abominably rejected justice.

“You shall not have in your bag different weights, a greater and a lesser; nor shall there be in your house a larger and a smaller measure. You shall have a just and true weight, and your measure shall be equal and true, so that you may live long upon the land which the Lord your God gives you. For the Lord will abominate the person who does these things and opposes all justice.”

The same legislator also forbids this in Leviticus. Solomon likewise pronounces a corresponding judgment: “A large weight and a small one, and double measures, both are unclean before the Lord. Whoever does this will be caught in his own schemes” (Prov. 20).
