Therefore we must strive not only in the bodily but also in the spiritual sense neither to have different weights in our hearts nor double measures in the house of our conscience. That is, we must not ourselves presume upon the indulgence that weakens the rule of distinction, while burdening those to whom we preach the word of the Lord with stricter commands and heavier weights than we are able to bear.

When we do this, what else are we doing but weighing or measuring the Lord’s reward and harvest with different weights and measures? If we distribute these things one way to ourselves and another way to our brothers, we are rightly reproved by the Lord because we have different scales or double measures, according to Solomon’s saying: “A double weight is an abomination to the Lord, and a deceitful scale is not good in his sight” (Prov. 21).

## CHAPTER XXII. On erasing Amalek from under heaven

*(Same place.)* “Remember what Amalek did to you on the way, when you were going out from Egypt: how he met you and struck down the rear of your army, those who were weary and had sat down, when you were exhausted from hunger and labor, and he did not fear God. Therefore, when the Lord your God gives you rest and subjects all the surrounding nations in the land that he promised you, you shall erase his name from under heaven; take care not to forget.”

In the name Amalek, which is interpreted as “one who licks blood,” the figure of spiritual wickedness is expressed. These spiritual powers oppose us as we depart through baptism from spiritual Egypt, and whenever they see people grow weary on the road of virtue through sin, they strive especially to overthrow them.

Therefore, whenever the Lord gives us the opportunity, we must overthrow these peoples in every way and, as far as possible, drive their suggestions from the seat of our soul and erase them. Otherwise, if, following the example of Saul, we preserve some remnant of them in our mind, we may be overthrown together with them as a consequence of disobedience.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On offering the firstfruits of crops, and on giving tithes to the Levites

*(Chapter 26.)* “When you enter the land that the Lord your God is going to give you to possess, and you have taken possession of it and dwell in it, you shall take some of all your crops as firstfruits and place them in a basket. You shall go to the place that the Lord your God chooses, so that his name may be invoked there. You shall approach the priest who is serving in those days and say to him: ‘Today I declare before the Lord your God that I have entered the land concerning which he swore to our fathers that he would give it to us.’ The priest shall take the basket from your hand and set it before the altar of the Lord your God.

“And you shall speak in the presence of the Lord your God: ‘A Syrian was persecuting my father, who went down into Egypt and sojourned there with very few people. He grew into a great and strong nation, of infinite number. The Egyptians afflicted us and persecuted us, imposing very heavy burdens. We cried out to the Lord, the God of our fathers; he heard us, looked upon us, our humiliation, our labor, and our distress, and brought us out of Egypt with a strong hand and an outstretched arm, with great terror, signs, and wonders. He brought us into this place and gave us a land flowing with milk and honey. And therefore now I offer the firstfruits of the crops of the land that the Lord has given me.’ You shall set them down in the presence of the Lord your God and worship the Lord your God. You shall feast on all the good things that the Lord your God has given you and your household—you, the Levite, and the resident alien who is among you.”

Through these words, by which the Israelites were instructed how, in the land of their possession, they should offer the firstfruits in a basket to the Lord in thanksgiving for having been rescued from Egypt, we too are instructed that, when we enter through the spiritual Jordan—that is, through baptism and faith in the Holy Trinity—into the land of the Church, we should place in the basket of our conduct the firstfruits of every good thing and bring them to God upon the altar of the catholic faith.

Thus our priest may receive them there, namely the one whom God has made our high priest according to the order of Melchizedek. There we should confess to the Lord and say to him that the spiritual Syrian, whose name is interpreted as “exalted” or “moistening,” persecuted our father—namely, our original ancestor—so that he deceived him through pride and gluttony, made him a transgressor, and deprived him of possession of paradise.

Thus he became a resident alien in the Egypt of this world, where he sojourned with very few people, because, while many followed idolatry, few remained faithful. But after more people had arisen through the institution of the law, who received knowledge and belief in the one God, spiritual Egyptians—namely, evil spirits—afflicted them. By placing upon them the heaviest burdens of sins, they oppressed the human race.

But almighty God, our maker and creator, looked upon our humiliation, our labor, and our distress. He sent his only-begotten Son, who is called the hand and arm of God, to rescue us from the power of darkness and transfer us to a place of peace, so that we might become children of light. He gave us a land flowing with milk and honey, namely the present Church, where there is the milk of innocence and simple teaching by which the young in understanding may be nourished, and sweet honey of varied knowledge by which the mature in understanding may be satisfied.

Whoever offers such gifts to God can celebrate a spiritual banquet in the house of God with the true Levites and resident aliens. With God’s ministers and his brothers, and with all who rightly understand that they are resident aliens and pilgrims in this world, he will be happily refreshed and filled with the food of virtue and spiritual knowledge.

[Col. 0947C] “When you have completed the tithe of all your crops, in the third year, the year of tithes, you shall give it to the Levite, the resident alien, the orphan, and the widow, so that they may eat within your gates and be filled. You shall say in the presence of the Lord your God: ‘I have brought what was sanctified from my house, and I have given it to the Levite, the resident alien, the orphan, and the widow, as you commanded me. I have not transgressed your commandments, nor have I forgotten your order. I have not eaten any of it in my mourning, nor separated any of it for an unclean use, nor spent anything from it in a funeral rite.’”

What does it mean that, among the things he is commanded to say, the person who has completed all the commandments in giving tithes and in everything he was commanded to give or spend is also commanded to say, with praise and commendation of himself, “I have not given any of it to the dead”? Does this prohibit the funeral rites that the nations customarily observe?

## CHAPTER XXIV. On erecting stones on Mount Ebal and smoothing them with plaster; on building an altar from unhewn and polished stones; and on offering a burnt offering upon it
### Chapter 27

“Moses and the elders of Israel commanded the people, saying: Keep every commandment that I command you. When you have crossed the Jordan into the land that the Lord your God will give you, you shall set up great stones and smooth them with plaster, so that you may write upon them all the words of this law after crossing the Jordan, when you enter the land that the Lord your God will give you, [Col. 0948A] a land flowing with milk and honey, as he swore to your fathers. Therefore, when you have crossed the Jordan, set up the stones that I command you today on Mount Ebal, and smooth them with plaster; and build there an altar to the Lord your God, from stones untouched by iron, from unhewn and unpolished stones. You shall offer upon it a burnt offering to the Lord your God, and sacrifice peace offerings; you shall eat there and feast before the Lord your God. You shall write upon the stones all the words of this law clearly and distinctly, etc.”

How this was done is recounted more fully in the Book of Joshua. After defeating the enemies, Joshua built an altar to the Most High God from whole stones into which iron had not been introduced, as Moses had commanded; and he offered sacrifice, [Col. 0948B] and wrote the Deuteronomy of the law of Moses upon the stones.

Let us therefore see what these stones are from which the altar is built. All who believe in Christ Jesus are called living stones. Concerning them the Apostle says: “You are living stones built into a spiritual house” (1 Peter 2). Iron was not introduced into them, because they are incorrupt and undefiled in flesh and spirit, and they have not received the flaming darts of the Evil One. These make one altar through the unity of faith and the harmony of charity. In them also Jesus our Lord rewrote Deuteronomy—that is, the second law of the Gospel. Let us therefore hear him say: “It was said to the ancients: You shall not commit adultery. But I say to you, if anyone looks at a woman in order to desire her, he has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matthew [Col. 0948C] 5). Jesus inscribes this law in the hearts of believers; he writes it in the minds of those who are worthy of the construction of the altar.

### Chapter 25

Concerning those who will stand to pronounce blessings on Mount Gerizim, and likewise those who will stand on Mount Ebal to pronounce curses, and concerning the curses or blessings recited there.

“On that day Moses also commanded the people, saying: These shall stand to bless the Lord on Mount Gerizim after crossing the Jordan: Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Joseph, and Benjamin. Opposite them, these shall stand for the cursing on Mount Ebal: Reuben, Gad, and Asher, Zebulun and Dan, and Naphtali. And the Levites shall proclaim to all the men of Israel in a loud voice, etc.” [Col. 0948D]

This was indeed done in the time of Joshua. They stood, as Moses had commanded in Deuteronomy: six tribes on Mount Gerizim to bless the people. These were the more noble tribes, namely Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Joseph, and Benjamin. The six less noble sons stood opposite them on Mount Ebal to pronounce curses. Among them were Reuben, who had defiled his father’s bed; Zebulun, Leah’s last son; and the sons of the maidservants.

This is what the history of the Old Testament relates. But we must examine what is conveyed in the account through mystical interpretation. Who, then, are those who proceed beside Mount Gerizim, and who are those who proceed beside Mount Ebal? Those who proceed in this [Col. 0949A] place beside Mount Gerizim to pronounce blessings figuratively represent those who come to salvation, inflamed not by fear of punishment but by love of the heavenly promise. The others, however, the half who proceed beside Mount Ebal, where the curses were pronounced, represent those who fulfill what is written in the law not out of love for blessings or promises, but from fear of future punishments, so that they may attain salvation.

All proceed around the ark, namely those who do not withdraw from the bosom of the Church. Yet we know that those are nobler who, from desire for goodness itself and love of eternal blessing, do what is good than those who pursue good because of evils. Jesus alone, therefore, can gather minds and hearts of this kind from all peoples and establish some on Mount [Col. 0949B] Gerizim for blessing, and others on Mount Ebal for cursing—not so that they may receive curses, but so that, fearing the prescribed curses and the punishments appointed for sinners, they may take care not to incur them and may correct themselves through the punishment of fear.

“And the Levites,” he says, “shall proclaim, saying to all the men of Israel in a loud voice.” Why did he command the Levites to speak to the men of Israel in a loud voice, unless he wished to show Christ’s priests that they must preach the word of God to the peoples not sluggishly but earnestly? Thus they may know what dangers threaten them if they transgress God’s commandments, and what benefits will follow them if they obey God’s precepts, since consolation is promised in the present life and an eternal reward in the future.

The curses, [Col. 0949C] therefore, or blessings contained in the Book of Deuteronomy may also be understood historically as applying to those who loved earthly prosperity or feared that earthly losses would befall them. But Christians must be much more careful lest, through disobedience concerning spiritual things and virtues, they suffer poverty of the former rather than lack of earthly possessions. For we often read that perfect men suffered want of present goods yet were filled with an abundance of virtues, as the Apostle Paul frequently testifies happened to himself and his fellow workers, saying: “Until this present hour we hunger and thirst, and are naked and beaten, and are unstable, and we labor, working with our own hands. We are cursed, and we bless; we suffer persecution, and we endure; [Col. 0949D] we are blasphemed, and we entreat. We have become as the refuse of this world, the filth of all” (1 Corinthians 4). And again: “I will gladly boast,” he says, “in my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may dwell in me. Therefore I am pleased with weaknesses, insults, necessities, and afflictions for Christ. For when I am weak, then I am strong” (2 Corinthians 2).

Such curses, however, were pronounced against sinners:

“Cursed is the man who makes a carved or molten image, an abomination to the Lord, the work of the hands of craftsmen, and sets it up in secret. And all the people shall answer: Amen.”

This chapter not only condemns the idolatry committed through images, but also rejects every error [Col. 0950A] of heretics. They are the craftsmen of vanity and superstitious doctrines, who practice incantations and spells. Whoever follows error instead of truth, whether secretly or openly, is clearly designated a worshiper of idols, whether among those in authority or among subjects. For all alike ought to praise what is good and detest what is evil.

“Cursed is he who does not honor his father,” and so forth.

It is fitting, therefore, for everyone to honor his earthly father and mother. But much more ought all people to worship and honor with every reverence and devotion the Father of all, God, and the mother, the Church. This also includes reverence for spiritual teachers, since the Lord says to his disciples: “Whoever honors you honors me, [Col. 0950B] and whoever despises you despises me.”

“Cursed is he who moves his neighbor’s boundary marker.”

By this testimony he forbids avarice and condemns heresy. The person who moves his neighbor’s boundary marker is one who, not content with the faith and teaching of the orthodox, introduces new superstitions and sects through pride. Whoever does this will undoubtedly be liable to eternal cursing.

Hence it follows:

“Cursed is he who causes the blind to wander from the road.”

He causes the blind person to wander on the road who makes the simple and inexperienced deviate from the path of truth by false teaching along the way of the Scriptures. The Apostle shows how destructive this is when he says: “If anyone does not love the Lord Jesus Christ, let him be accursed. Maranatha” (1 Corinthians 5). And elsewhere: “Whoever,” he says, “follows this [Col. 0950C] rule, peace and mercy be upon them, and upon the Israel of God” (Galatians 6).

“Cursed is he who perverts the judgment of the resident alien, the orphan, and the widow.”

Historically, no one may render an unjust judgment against anyone. But allegorically also, it is not right to oppress unjustly the spiritual resident alien, orphan, or widow: the orphan, of whom it is written in the psalm, “To you, Lord, the poor person is entrusted; you will be the helper of the orphan” (Psalm 9); and the widow, concerning whom the same Prophet says in the person of the Lord, “Blessing her, I will surely bless her” (Psalm 131).

“Cursed is he who lies with his father’s wife and uncovers her covering.”

It is clear that every incestuous act is an abomination before God. Nevertheless, through this sentence the lawgiver, according to allegory, [Col. 0950D] strikes at heretics and schismatics who, through error, in some manner corrupt the bride of Christ, who is the Father of all because he is the Creator of all.

According to tropology, this prohibits anyone from defaming his father’s wicked conduct by wickedly imitating it, or from spreading disgrace upon his father’s name by repeating in deed what had rightly been condemned in him.

“Cursed is he who lies with any animal.”

Historically, it is the height of folly to commit adultery with brute animals; indeed, it is disgraceful to follow the folly of the Gentiles. When a man or woman gives themselves so completely to foreign pleasures that they are not merely captured by them through indolence but cling closely to them and unite with them, maintaining prolonged and lasting intercourse with them, that person is guilty of death. [Col. 0951A]

“Cursed is he who lies with his sister, the daughter of his father or the daughter of his mother.”

A person spiritually defiles his sister when, through erroneous teaching or evil example, he stains another person’s soul. For our one Father is God, and the holy Church is our mother. We are brothers and sisters.

“Cursed is he who lies with his mother-in-law.”

Typically, the mother-in-law signifies the evil desire of our corrupt action, because desire is the mother of every sin. This must be carefully observed: whenever sinful desire arises in us, we must resist it and not join ourselves to it in action. For, as it is decreed in Leviticus concerning this crime, the one who commits it ought to be burned alive with fire, [Col. 0951B] because that person is guilty of the fire of Gehenna unless, through the fire of repentance, he washes himself clean of this stain.

“Cursed is he who secretly strikes his neighbor. And all the people shall say: Amen.”

To kill a person openly or secretly is a sin. It is therefore surprising that he wrote only that the one who secretly strikes his neighbor is cursed, unless perhaps we say that a person secretly strikes his neighbor when he hates him in his heart. The Apostle John says: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer. And you know that no murderer has eternal life abiding in him” (1 John 3). Hence it is also written in Leviticus: “You shall not hate your brother in your heart, but openly rebuke him, lest you bear sin because of him” (Leviticus 19).

“Cursed is he who accepts gifts in order to strike down an innocent [Col. 0951C] person.”

Whoever recalls Judas’s deed, when he betrayed his master for money, can understand how destructive the evil of avarice is.

“Cursed is he who does not remain in the words of this law and does not fulfill them in deed.”

This sentence appears more serious than the others because it comprehends generally both what has been stated above and what has not yet been stated. For who can remain without transgression in all the words of the law, since Paul says: “All who rely on works of the law are under a curse, because no one will be justified before God by the law” (Galatians 3)? No one could escape the harm of this curse—not even the lawgiver himself—unless he were freed from it through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ. Hence the aforementioned [Col. 0951D] Apostle says: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us, because it is written: ‘Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree,’ so that the blessing of Abraham might come upon the Gentiles in Christ Jesus.” Here Peter says: “Christ died once for our sins, the righteous for the unrighteous, so that he might bring us to God, put to death in the flesh but made alive in the spirit” (1 Peter 3).

### Chapter 28

“But if you hear the voice of the Lord your God, so as to do and keep all his commandments that I command you today, the Lord will make you higher than all the nations that dwell upon the earth. And all these blessings will come upon you and overtake you, if only you listen to his commandments.” [Col. 0952A]

Just as he previously foretold future curses and punishments for the disobedient, so now he promises blessings and rewards to the obedient.

“Blessed are you in the city, and blessed in the field.”

Historically, the meaning is easy to understand: he foretells prosperity to the Jews, within and outside the city, as a reward for obedience, and promises an abundance of fruits and animals. Allegorically, however, he promises the Christian people, through their own devotion, not merely eternal happiness but perpetual blessedness.

Blessed is the person in the city who devotes himself in the holy Church to divine contemplation. Blessed is the person in the field who labors in the practice of good works. Through these two forms of conduct, every believer will be pleasing to God.

“Blessed is the fruit of your womb, and the fruit of your land.”

By the fruit [Col. 0952B] of the womb he indicates the inward thoughts and counsels of the mind; by the fruit of the land, the outwardly useful actions of the body. Through these two forms of life—namely, the contemplative and the active—the holy Church nobly conducts herself in this world, and hopes that in the future she will possess the heavenly kingdoms with Christ.

“Blessed is the fruit of your animals, the herds of your cattle, and the folds of your sheep.”

Through the kinds of animals he signifies the orders of those subject to others. In the Church there are some who, instructed by teachers, offer them assistance from their own goods, receiving spiritual nourishment from them while supplying them with bodily sustenance. Others are able to labor according to what has been commanded them. Still others, content with their simplicity alone, strive through the innocence of their lives to please God. For each person has his own gift from God: one in this way, another in that.

[Col. 0952C] Whoever strives to multiply the gift received according to his ability and in accordance with God’s commandments will please God and will be approved by human beings.

“Blessed are your storehouses, and blessed are your reserves.”

The storehouses signify the keeping of virtues; the reserves signify the intention of a good will. For according to the extent to which each person labors within his ability, his reward and good will will be preserved for him. Even if his good will sometimes does not achieve its effect, he will nevertheless not lose his just reward, because for those who love God all things work together for good, and on earth there will be peace for people of good will.

“Blessed shall you be when you enter and when you go out.”

This is what the Savior says in the Gospel: “I am the door. If anyone enters through me, [Col. 0952D] he will be saved, and he will find pasture” (John 10). The person who enters here into faith will receive the food of wisdom and the pasture of virtues; and, going out from the present life, will receive a sure recompense for good deeds.

He also enters through that door who inwardly meditates upon and considers something according to the Catholic faith and in conformity with God’s will. He goes out when, according to that same faith, he also works some good deeds outwardly before people for the praise of God, preparing himself as an example.

“The Lord will cause your enemies who rise up against you to fall before you. They will come against you by one road and flee from you by seven.”

Whoever keeps God’s commandments scatters the ranks of evil spirits and dissipates their power. Those who had come together to do harm, terrified, try to flee in different directions. [Col. 0953A]

“The Lord will send a blessing upon your storehouses and upon all the works of your hands, and he will bless you in the land that you receive.”

He will bless the storehouses when he pours the grace of his Spirit into the secrets of the heart. He will bless the works of the hands when he grants the capacity for virtues to good endeavors. He will bless in the land and the Lord will raise up a people for himself when he makes his saints abound in the land of the Church through the grace of heavenly gifts.

Hence it also follows:

“If you keep the commandments of the Lord your God and walk in his ways, all the peoples of the earth will see that the name of the Lord has been invoked over you, and they will fear you; and the Lord will cause you to abound in all good things.”

The enemies fear the people of the [Col. 0953B] Church when evil spirits, seeing the name of Christ shining within God’s elect through faith and outwardly through works, flee in fear; their wickedness will not be able to resist them. Hence it is written: “Resist the devil, and he will flee from you” (James 4). And Peter says in his Epistle: “Be sober and watchful, because your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, prowls around seeking someone to devour. Resist him, firm in faith, knowing that the same sufferings are being endured by your brotherhood throughout the world” (1 Peter 5).

The Lord will cause his saints to abound in all good things when, in this life, he increases their merits through good works and, in the future, rewards them with heavenly prizes.

“The Lord will open his excellent treasury, heaven, [Col. 0953C] to give rain to your land in its season.”

Here we may understand heaven to mean the prophets, or the apostles, or preachers of the word of God, concerning whom it is written: “The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the work of his hands.” The Lord opens them to give rain when, through the gift of the Holy Spirit, he grants them the ability to proclaim divine teaching, so that the hearts of carnal people, watered by this rain, may bring forth the growth of good works.

“You will lend to many nations, and you yourself will receive no loan.”

The Church will lend to many nations when she dispenses charisms of divination to individuals. She receives no loan from any of them because she seeks not a present but a future recompense. For she surpasses all through the gift of God and is the head of the whole world, not the tail; she is always above and never below. [Col. 0953D] Although she suffers the pressures and persecutions of the wicked in this world, she is stronger than her adversaries and excels all through faith and virtue.

It follows:

“The Lord will set you as the head and not as the tail; you will always be above and not below, if you listen to the commandments of the Lord your God that I command you today, [Col. 0954A] and keep and do them, and do not turn aside from them either to the right or to the left; and if you do not follow foreign gods or worship them. You shall not depart from any of [Col. 0954D] the words that I command you today, to the right or to the left, to go after foreign gods and serve them. But if you do not wish to hear the voice of the Lord your God, to keep and do all his commandments and ordinances that I command you today, all these curses will come upon you,” etc.

Since the right hand is used in praise, the things that are on the right are not being condemned there, but the person who turns aside into them—that is, the person who claims for himself what belongs to God. Therefore it is said in Proverbs: “Do not turn aside to the right or to the left. For he knows the ways that are on the right, but those on the left are perverse” (Proverbs 4). Thus the things on the right that the Lord knows are good.

“Therefore the Lord knows the ways of the righteous, and the path of the wicked will perish,” as it is read in the psalm (Psalm 1). Why, then, is it said, “Do not turn aside to the right”? The passage immediately explains by adding: “For he himself will make your paths straight.” Let us not suppose that the things on the right known by the Lord are not straight. Rather, as I have said, to turn aside into them means to wish to attribute to oneself, and not to his [Col. 0954B] grace, what is upright. Finally, as I have said, he adds: “For he himself will make your paths straight, and he will lead all your ways in peace.”

Therefore, when it is said in this passage of Deuteronomy, “You shall not depart from all the words that I command you today, to the right or to the left, to go after foreign gods and serve them,” this is not said because gods could also be understood as being on the right. Rather, either earthly places are meant, because on their right or left the nations had other gods whom they worshiped, or the statement concerning other gods must be pronounced separately, so that there are two meanings.

One meaning is: You shall not depart from all the words that I command you, to the right or to the left, according to the interpretation I explained above. The other meaning is: to go after other [Col. 0954C] gods and serve them; here too the words “You shall not depart from all the words that I command you today” are to be understood.

If we wish to state the entire meaning, we shall have to repeat the preceding words, which are common to both senses, so that just as it says there, “You shall not depart from all that I command you today, to the right or to the left,” so here it may be repeated: “You shall not depart from all that I command you today, to go after foreign gods and serve them.” For by departing from the words that were commanded, one also goes after other gods; this is not the only commandment. Or perhaps God does not wish us to depart only from what he commanded concerning not going after foreign gods, but from everything he commanded. Yet he wished to commend this especially, so that after the general command, by which he warned that one must not depart from any of the words of his commandments, he might also commend this separately.

The words “to the right or to the left” can also be understood in this way: They did not command us to go after foreign gods either because of those things that are sought for the sake of happiness or because of those things that are avoided for the sake of unhappiness. That is, neither for the sake of what people love nor in opposition to what they hate should help be sought from other gods; nor should they be worshiped in order to win their favor so that they may benefit us, or to placate them so that they may not harm us.

For it is also written in the psalm concerning certain people: “Their mouth has spoken vanity, and their right hand is a right hand of iniquity” (Psalm 143). This is because they suppose that a person becomes blessed through possessions that both the good and the wicked can have. Thus their right hand is [Col. 0955A] a right hand of iniquity, because those who consider it a right hand are wicked. It is not a true right hand, but the right hand of those whose mouth has spoken vanity.

“They called the people blessed to whom these things belong.” Rather, as the psalm immediately adds, blessed is the people whose Lord is their God. This is the true right hand of righteousness, not of iniquity.

Therefore one must not go after foreign gods—neither to the right, so that a person may suppose that he becomes blessed through them, nor to the left, so that, supposing himself to become miserable through their opposition, he may worship them in order to turn that misery away.

Or, if we understand the right hand as eternal things and the left as temporal goods, let holy Scripture be understood to warn in this passage that they must be worshiped neither for the sake of the former nor for the sake of the latter.

“If you will not listen to the voice of the Lord your God, to keep and perform all his commandments and statutes that I command you today, all these curses will come upon you and overtake you. Cursed shall you be in the city, and cursed shall you be in the field,” etc. Just as he promised blessings and perpetual happiness to those who kept God’s commandments, so conversely, by the same categories that he previously enumerated among the blessings, he foretells curses and everlasting fire for those who refused to observe the divine precepts: for just as the reception of the good makes those who receive it blessed, so its deprivation condemns sinners.

“The Lord will send upon you hunger and thirst and rebuke in all the works that you undertake, until he crushes and swiftly destroys you because of your most evil devices, in which you have forsaken me.” He speaks of hunger not for bread, nor of thirst for water, but of hearing the word of the Lord, and of the barrenness of virtues that the impious suffer deservedly because of their perversity, since they are not worthy to receive divine grace. Hence it is written, the Lord saying: “I will command my clouds not to rain upon them” (Isa. V). Yet deservedly, because of their perversity, they endure pestilence—that is, the disturbance of virtues—and the tempest of wicked spirits, until at the end they are torn from the soil of the Church through the ministry of angels and handed over to be punished in the prisons of hell. For until then the Lord’s net draws both good and bad fish, until it reaches the shore; and then the good are gathered into vessels, while the bad are cast outside.

“The Lord will strike you with poverty, fever and chill, burning heat and feverish heat, [Col. 0955D] corrupted air and mildew; and he will pursue you until you perish.” The Lord will strike sinners with fever when, by a just judgment, he abandons them to suffer the chill of unbelief and the burning heat of carnal desires. He will give them corrupted air when he permits the reprobate to lead a polluted life. For bodily life is aptly signified by air, since the human body is given life by the breathing of air. As for what follows—“and it will pursue you until you perish”—this must not be understood as though God caused someone to perish by pursuing him. He tempts no one, for he himself is not the tempter of evil; rather, he wills that all people be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth. It should instead be understood that he sometimes permits this to happen, because nothing occurs in created things except at the Lord’s command or with his permission, and nothing on earth is without cause. Who, moreover, could be so impiously foolish as to say that God cannot turn into good whatever human evil wills he chooses? When he does so, he acts through mercy; when he does not, he acts through judgment. For “he has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills.”

“The heaven above you shall be bronze, and the earth that you tread shall be iron.” He compares the elements by which all the fruits of the universe are nourished with the hardest metals, because human sins cause the order of things to be changed, so that what was created for the consolation of the human race is turned toward its correction. Hence it is written: “The world fights for him against the senseless” (Wis. V). Allegorically, however, the heaven will be bronze for those who transgress God’s law, when they deserve no clemency from holy teachers but experience the harshest discipline, because they themselves have chosen to possess not a heart of flesh and a gentle disposition, but a heart of stone and an iron mind. Hence the old law was written on stone and given to the hard-hearted Jewish people, so that the nature of its recipients might be revealed by the gift bestowed upon them.

“The Lord will give the rain of your land as dust, and ashes shall descend upon you from heaven until you are crushed.” Thus, just as dust and ashes are not fruitful, so the teaching imparted to you will not cause shoots of virtue to spring up in you, but will foretell everlasting destruction for the one who remains uncorrected. By dust we can understand the barrenness of good works, and by ashes the burning of eternal fire, because the chaff of sins is consumed [Col. 0956C] by the unquenchable fire of hell.

“The Lord will hand you over, falling before your enemies. You will go out against them by one road, and flee by seven; and you will be scattered through all the kingdoms of the earth.” Just as the Jews, because of the blindness of their hearts, did not deserve to be defended by the Lord against their enemies but were scattered by their enemies throughout the entire breadth of the world, so it is certain that all enemies who refuse to return to the Lord through repentance do not deserve to be rescued from the power of wicked spirits, but are plunged together with them into various punishments. Hence it is written: “Behold, your enemies, O Lord, shall perish, and all who practice iniquity shall be scattered” (Ps. XCI).

“Your corpse shall be food for the birds of the air and the beasts of the earth, and there shall be no one to drive them away.” In the corpse, future punishment after death is signified. Then the beasts of the earth and the birds of the air—which we understand as none other than the powers of the air—tear apart with various punishments those who have despised God’s commandments. And there is no one to drive them away, because there is no one to rescue them from that place when the Lord rejects them. Hence the Psalmist says to the Lord: “There is no one who remembers you in death; and in hell, who will confess to you?” (Ps. VI.)

“The Lord will strike you with the ulcer of Egypt, with the part of the body through which excrement is discharged, and also with scabies and itching, so that you cannot be cured,” etc. The ulcers of Egypt were wounds and swollen blisters. The Philistines, however, suffered pain in their hindquarters, when their souls were rotting. Such afflictions are appropriately inflicted upon unbelievers and despisers when due retribution is paid out according to their merits. In another sense, the ulcers represent the deceitful and purulent malice of this age; the blisters, swelling and inflated pride; and the scabies and itching, the heat of anger and the madness of rage. These things, therefore, are deservedly inflicted upon sinners in the present life through the agency of the enemy. After the end of life, however, they will endure in eternal torments the foulness of the crimes signified by the hindquarters.

“May the Lord strike you with madness and blindness, so that you grope at midday as a blind man is accustomed to grope in darkness, and do not direct your ways.” The Jews were struck with madness when they slanderously claimed that the Son of God, who performed signs and miracles by the power of the Holy Spirit, cast out demons by Beelzebub, the prince of demons. They groped at midday [Col. 0957B] like a blind man in darkness when, at the sixth hour of the day, they cried out that the Savior of the world was guilty and demanded that he be crucified. Hence the darkness that they possessed inwardly in their minds was shown outwardly through the darkening of the heavenly lights at the very hour of the Lord’s passion. But, blind in heart, they did not direct their ways, because they were unwilling either to repent of their sins or to believe the truth. Therefore they will suffer accusation for all time, and, oppressed by acts of violence, will have no deliverer.

Likewise, all heretics and schismatics are struck with madness, and grope at midday like blind men when, while the Gospel shines throughout the whole world, they themselves are enveloped in the darkness of error and demonstrate this in their own souls by refusing to agree with the Catholic faith in their doctrines. Therefore they will suffer accusation for all time, because they labor in vain. For the Church of Christ disregards wicked suggestions, and “the gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Matt. XVI).

“You shall take a wife, and another man shall sleep with her. You shall build a house, and not dwell in it. You shall plant a vineyard, and not gather its grapes. Your ox shall be slaughtered before your eyes, and you shall not eat of it,” etc. Because of the transgression by which the Israelites transgressed God’s commandments, they abandoned the land of their possession and suffered the loss of their animals. So also all the greedy and those entangled in crimes, although they labor greatly in the present, lose the fruit of their labor, because at the end their works will be destroyed together with them.

In the wife, the people associated with the faithlessness of heretics may be understood; the devil corrupts this people by spiritual fornication when he leads it astray into error. Likewise, in the name of animals a subject person may be signified, and these are now torn away by heretics when the heretics themselves are deprived of both life and teaching. These things can also be applied to the Jewish people, because everything that that people had prepared for itself figuratively by writing and teaching is now converted spiritually to the use of the Church.

“Your sons and your daughters shall be given to another people while your eyes look on, and they shall fail from your sight all day long; and there shall be no strength in your hand.” Under the name of sons and daughters he designates disciples whom either Jews or heretics had brought up. They shall be given to another people when they are entrusted to the Christian people, so that there they may learn the truth, which previously they could in no way learn from their former teachers. When Jews and heretics see this, their eyes will fail, because they are entirely unable to bring to completion the purpose they exercise in commending their doctrines.

“Let a people whom you do not know eat the fruit of your land and all your labors,” etc. Whatever the former people labored over in the books or observances of the law has all been bestowed upon the Church’s people for spiritual instruction. The Church itself will enjoy abundance, while they will fail in vanity. Thus will be fulfilled what the Lord says through the prophet Isaiah: “Behold, my servants shall eat, and you shall hunger; behold, my servants shall drink, and you shall thirst; behold, my servants shall rejoice, and you shall be confounded; behold, my servants shall praise because of the joy of their heart, and you shall cry because of the sorrow of your heart, and howl because of the anguish of your spirit. And you shall leave your name as a curse for my chosen ones, and the Lord shall slay you; and he shall call his servants by another name, in which the one who is blessed upon the earth shall be blessed in the Lord.”

“May the Lord strike you with a very evil ulcer upon your knees and calves, so that you cannot be healed from the sole of your foot to the crown of your head.” In the knees and calves he signifies either the removal of strength or the stability of one’s position. Therefore, because Jews or heretics exercised their malice from the beginning of their will to the completion of their deeds, it is deservedly said of them that they are struck from the sole of the foot to the crown.

Hence Isaiah also threatens such people, saying: “Woe to the sinful nation, to the people laden with iniquity, to the wicked seed, to the criminal children. They have forsaken the Lord, they have blasphemed the Holy One of Israel, they have turned backward. Why should I strike you again, adding transgression? Every head is sick, and every heart is sorrowful. From the sole of the foot to the crown, there is no health in it,” etc. (Isa. I.) By metaphor he teaches that from the rulers to the lowest people, from the teachers to the ignorant multitude, there is health in no one, but that all agree with equal fervor in impiety.

Therefore, when he says, “There is no health in it,” he refers this to the final captivity, when, after Titus and Vespasian and the ultimate destruction of Jerusalem under Aelius Hadrian, there has been no remedy up to the present day. Thus is fulfilled what is written: “All have turned aside; together they have become worthless; there is none who does good, not even one” (Ps. XIII). What follows—“there is no health in it”—may be understood either of the people, or of the body, or of the head.

“The Lord will lead you, and the king whom you set over yourself, to a nation that you and your fathers do not know. There you shall serve other gods, of wood and stone, and you shall become a ruin, a proverb, and a byword among all the peoples to whom the Lord will lead you.” Because of its sins, the Lord led the ancient nation of the Israelites into captivity together with its king, as happened in the case of Hoshea, king of Samaria, whom Shalmaneser, king of the Assyrians, led into captivity with the ten tribes. Likewise, Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, led the Jewish people into Chaldea with Jehoiakim and [Col. 0959A] Zedekiah, the kings of Judah.

But now also, in the time of the New Testament, all who stray from the faith—heretics, or wicked Catholics who despise God’s commandments and refuse to obey the Gospel of Christ—are taken captive by wicked spirits through various vices; and finally, if they do not correct themselves, they will be plunged into the abyss of hell. There is no distinction between master and servant, soldier and king, teacher and disciple; rather, God’s just judgment will repay each person according to his own merits. Hence it is written: “The Lord will destroy from Israel the man who does this, both teacher and his disciple” (Mal. II).

“But I wish to remind you, though you know everything once for all, that Jesus, having saved the people from the land of Egypt, afterward destroyed those who did not believe. And the angels who did not preserve their own rank, but abandoned their dwelling, I have kept in everlasting bonds under darkness for the judgment of the great God” (Jude V).

“You shall sow much seed in the land but gather little, because locusts will devour everything. You shall plant and cultivate a vineyard, but you shall not drink wine or gather anything from it, because it will be devastated by worms. You shall have olive trees throughout all your territories, but you shall not anoint yourself with oil, because they will shed their fruit and perish,” etc.

Note, reader, that locusts devour the seed, worms devastate the vineyard, and olives fall and perish. Be watchful, therefore, lest perhaps spiritual locusts and worms consume, devastate, and take away from you the grace that you received as a divine gift, and lest what was bestowed upon you for the increase of your salvation, through your negligence, come instead to your ruin. For the Psalmist says: “You have given joy in my heart: from the time of grain, wine, and oil” (Ps. IV). “Bread strengthens the heart of man; wine gladdens the heart of man, and oil makes his face shine” (Ps. CIII). And blessed is the one who watches and guards his garments, lest he walk naked.

“The stranger who dwells with you shall rise above you, and shall be higher than you. You shall descend, and shall be lower. He shall lend to you, and you shall not lend to him. He shall be the head, and you shall be the tail. All these curses shall come upon you, and, pursuing you, shall overtake you until you perish, because you did not listen to the voice of the Lord your God, nor keep his commandments and statutes that the Lord commanded you.”

This chapter clearly describes the rejection of the Israelites and the election of the nations, because, in accordance with the voice of the Truth, which said to the Jews themselves, “The kingdom of God shall be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits; thus the first shall be last, and the last first” (Matt. XXI), and in accordance with the prophecy of Anna: “The barren woman has borne many, and she who had many children has grown weak, because she did not listen to the voice of the Lord her God and did not keep his commandments” (Matt. XX).

Foreseeing the ruin of that people, the Lord wished to convert them through compassion and repeated warnings: first through the law, second through the prophets, third through the priests and teachers, and finally through his only-begotten Son and his apostles. Hence we read that “when Jesus drew near to Jerusalem, seeing the city, he wept over it and said: ‘If you too had known, and indeed on this your day, the things that make for peace—but now they are hidden from your eyes. For days will come upon you, and they will surround you on every side, and cast you down to the ground, and your children who are within you; and they will not leave in you one stone upon another, because you did not recognize the time of your visitation’” (Luke XIX).

The Creator of all deigned to visit this city through the mystery of his incarnation, but it did not remember that fear of him and love for him. Hence also, through the prophet, birds of the air are brought forward as witnesses in the rebuke of the human heart: “‘The kite,’ he says, ‘in the sky knows its time; the turtledove, the swallow, and the stork have kept the time of their coming. But my people have not known the judgment of the Lord’” (Jer. VIII).

For this reason they were frequently handed over to the nations for plunder, and finally to the Roman rulers for perpetual destruction; and all the kinds of curses written in the book of the law came upon them. Likewise, certain condemnation awaits those who receive God’s grace ungratefully. For, according to Paul’s word, if someone who violates the law of Moses dies without mercy on the testimony of two or three witnesses, how much worse punishment do you think will be deserved by one who has trampled underfoot the Son of God, regarded as profane the blood of the covenant by which he was sanctified, and insulted spiritual grace? For we know who said: “Vengeance is mine; I will repay” (Ps. CXXXIV). And again: “For the Lord will judge his people. It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.”

Therefore it is good to take precautions, lest eternal destruction overtake the sinner who remains unrepentant.

“For the Lord will give you a fearful heart, failing eyes, and a soul consumed with sorrow.” Because of their faithlessness, the Jews were given a fearful heart. Hence it is written: “There they trembled with fear where there was no fear” (Ps. LII). Their priests said to them: “You see that we accomplish nothing. Behold, the whole world has gone after him. If we let him go on like this, everyone will believe in him. And the Romans will come and take away our place and our nation” (John XI).

What they feared happened to them, but from the source they had not expected. They thought that loss would come to them from the faith in Christ, whereas it came upon them more truly because of their faithlessness and their persecution of Christ and his apostles.

“And your life shall be hanging before you; you shall fear night and day, and shall not trust in your life.” What could be worse, among the curses that came upon the Jews as a deserved consequence of their pride and impiety, than to see their life—that is, the Son of God—hanging, and not believe in their life?

For when curses are spoken prophetically, they do not arise from the evil wish of one who invokes harm, but from the prophetic Spirit that foretells. Those that arise from an evil wish are forbidden when it is said: “Bless, and do not curse.” Yet such expressions are often found in the speech of the saints, as the apostle Paul says: “Alexander the coppersmith showed me many evils; may the Lord repay him according to his works” (II Tim. IV). In that other passage, however, the Apostle seems, as one angered and indignant, even to have wished evil: “Would that those who trouble you would cut themselves off!” (Gal. V).

If you consider the person of the writer, you will understand that, through a very elegant ambiguity, he wished them well. For there are eunuchs who cut themselves off for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. Faustus too would have seized upon this meaning if he had brought a devout palate to the Lord’s food.

Thus, perhaps, the words “You shall see your life hanging, and shall not believe in your life” sounded to the Jews as though, amid the threats or stratagems of their enemies, they would see their life hanging in uncertainty and would not believe themselves to be victorious. But when the Son of the Gospel hears, “For he wrote of me,” in this very ambiguity of meaning he sees what the prophecies project upon the threshold and what they imply to human beings. Immediately Christ, the life of humanity, hanging upon the cross, comes before him, and the Jews who do not believe in him for the very reason that they see him hanging there.

Someone else might quickly say, among the other curses that do not pertain to understanding anything about Christ through the reading, that only this one passage there concerns Christ: “You shall see your life hanging, and shall not believe in your life.” For it could not be that, among various curses attributed by prophecy to an impious people, this too should be included. But I, and those who think with me somewhat more attentively about that evangelical and dominical saying, understand that the Lord did not say, “For he also wrote about me,” as though he were believed to have written other things that do not concern Christ; rather, he said, “For he wrote about me,” so that we might search through the whole intention of Scripture with no other purpose than to understand the grace of Christ. Accordingly, we recognize that the other curses in this reading too were foretold because of Christ.

## CHAPTER XXVI. A commemoration of how the Lord led the children of Israel through the desert for forty years, and their garments were not worn out nor their footwear consumed by age

### (CHAP. XXIX.)

“These are the words of the covenant that the Lord commanded Moses to establish with the children of Israel in the land of Moab, besides the covenant that he made with them at Horeb.”

The Septuagint: “These are the words of the covenant that the Lord commanded Moses to establish for the children of Israel in the land of Moab, besides the covenant that he made with them at Horeb.”

He shows from what source the book of Deuteronomy received its name, as though it were a second law; for there is more repetition of the former law in it than anything else. There are few things in it that were not already contained in what was first given. Yet these are not called two Testaments, although these words may seem to sound that way. Both are one Testament, which in the Church is called the Old Testament. For if they were to be called two Testaments because of these words, there would already be not two but several, apart from the New Testament. Scripture speaks of a Testament in many places, such as the one made with Abraham concerning circumcision, or the earlier one made with Noah.

“You saw all that the Lord did before your eyes in the land of Egypt to Pharaoh and all his servants, and all the trials of that land, the great signs and portents that your eyes saw.”

The Septuagint: “And you saw everything that the Lord your God did in the land of Egypt before you—to Pharaoh and all his servants and all his land—the great trials that your eyes saw, those great signs and wonders and the strong hand. Yet the Lord did not give you a heart to know, eyes to see, or ears to hear until this day.”

How, then, did he say above, “You saw the great trials that your eyes saw,” if the Lord did not give them eyes to see and ears to hear? They saw with the body but did not see with the heart, since the eyes of the heart are also spoken of. Therefore he began with the words, “The Lord God did not give you a heart to know.” The two things that follow belong to this: “eyes to see and ears to hear,” that is, to understand and obey.

But when he says, “The Lord God did not give you,” he would not say this by way of mere rebuke and accusation unless he also intended it to be understood as belonging to their guilt, so that no one might consider himself excusable on this account. At the same time he shows both that, without the help of the Lord God, they cannot understand or obey with the eyes and ears of the heart, and that, if the Lord’s help is absent, human fault is not thereby excusable, because God’s judgments, though hidden, are nevertheless just.

“I led you for forty years through the desert. Your garments were not worn out, nor were the shoes of your feet consumed by age. You did not eat bread, and you did not drink wine or strong drink, so that you might know that I am the Lord your God,” etc.

From this it appears that the Israelites were able to carry so much wine among their supplies when they went out from Egypt that they could consume it quickly. For if they had brought absolutely nothing with them, where would it have come from when it is said: “The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play”? This could not be said of water, since Moses’ own very explicit words show that the cry was not the beginning of war but the beginning of wine (Exod. XXXII).

### (IBID.)

“For you know how we dwelt in the land of Egypt and how we passed through the midst of the nations. As you passed through them, you saw the abominations and filth of their idols—wood and stone, silver and gold—which they worshiped. Take care lest there be among you a man or woman, a family or tribe, whose heart is turned away today from the Lord your God, so that he may go and serve the gods of those nations, and lest there be among you a root producing gall and bitterness. When he hears the words of this oath, let him bless himself in his heart, saying: ‘I shall have peace, and I shall walk in the perversity of my heart.’ Let him take the drunkard together with the thirsty, and the Lord will not forgive him.”

The Septuagint: “Is there anyone among you, man or woman, family or tribe, whose mind has turned away from the Lord your God, to go and serve the gods of those nations? Is there in him no root growing upward in gall and bitterness? And it shall be, when he hears the words of this curse, that he will suppose in his heart, saying: ‘May holy things be granted to me, because I walk in the error of my heart,’ so that the sinner may not at the same time destroy the one who is without sin. God will not be willing to be merciful to him; rather, then the anger of the Lord and his jealousy will burn against that man, and all the curses of this covenant that are written in this book of the law shall cling to him.”

It is said, “Is there anyone among you?” so that we may understand it as an inquiry, lest perhaps there should be such a person. If there were one, however, he is greatly terrified, lest anyone, hearing those curses, should say in his heart, “May holy things be mine”—that is, “May the curses be holy to me”—“because I walk in the error of my heart,” meaning: “May these things not happen to me; may these evils not be mine, but holy things,” that is, favorable and harmless things, “because I walk in the error of my heart,” namely, by following after the gods of the nations and serving them as though with impunity.

“No,” he says, “it shall not be so. The sinner must not at the same time destroy the one who is without sin.” It is as though he were saying: “Beware lest someone who thinks such things persuade any one of you of them.” “God will not be willing to be merciful to him,” whether to the one thinking such things or to the one to whom such things have been persuaded, just as he himself supposed when he said, “May holy things be mine,” as though in this way turning away from himself the force of the curse. “But then the anger of the Lord and his jealousy will burn against that man,” when he thinks to turn it away from himself by saying in his heart, “And all the curses of this covenant that are written in this book of the law shall cling to him.”

Certainly, all these things cannot happen to one person, for he could not die as many times as there are kinds of death mentioned here. But he said “all” in the sense of any and every kind, so that the one to whom some of the things by which he perishes happen may not be exempt from all of them.

When he says, “So that the sinner may not at the same time destroy the one who is without sin,” the Greek has ἀναμάρτητον (*anamártēton*). This must not be understood as though he were calling someone entirely cleansed and free from every sin ἀναμάρτητον, that is, “without sin.” Rather, he means the one who is without the particular sin under discussion, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin” (John XV)—not every sin, but the sin by which they did not believe in him.

God also says to Abimelech concerning Sarah, Abraham’s wife: “I know that you did this with a pure heart” (Gen. XX). He did not mean that Abimelech’s heart was so pure that he was like those of whom it is said, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. V). Rather, he had a heart pure from the sin under discussion, because, insofar as it concerned him, he had not desired another man’s wife.

When he says, “Let him take the drunkard together with the thirsty, and the Lord will not forgive him,” this is the same as what another edition has: “Let not the sinner destroy the one who is without sin.” It is as though he were saying: One must beware lest the person who is drunk with malice and idolatry seduce into error the one who has a desire to learn and know the truth, because this kind of offense does not easily obtain forgiveness. In this saying heretics are especially struck, since, full of deceit and falsehood, they both seduce and are seduced; their end also certainly brings destruction.

### (CHAP. XXX.)

“The Lord your God will restore your captivity and have mercy on you; and he will again gather you from all the peoples among whom the Lord previously scattered you. If you have been dispersed to the ends of heaven, from there the Lord your God will gather you back, and he will take you and bring you into the land that your fathers possessed, and you shall possess it. And, blessing you, he will make you more numerous than your fathers were. The Lord your God will circumcise your heart and the heart of your offspring, so that you may love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul, so that you may live.”

The Septuagint: “The Lord will cleanse your heart completely, and the heart of your offspring, so that you may love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul, so that you may live.”

This is an evident promise of grace. For the Lord promises that he will do what he customarily helps [Al.: commands] to be done.

## CHAPTER XXVII. That the Lord’s commandment is not placed far away, but is near

### (IBID.)

“The commandment that I give you today is not above you, nor is it placed far away, nor is it situated in heaven, so that you can say: ‘Who among us can ascend to heaven, to bring it to us so that we may hear it and fulfill it in action?’ Nor is it placed across the sea, so that you may make excuses and say: ‘Who among us can cross the sea and bring it to us, so that we may hear and do what has been commanded?’ Rather, the word is very near you, in your mouth and in your heart, so that you may do it,” and the rest.

The Septuagint: “Because this commandment that I give you today is not beyond measure, nor is it far from you. It is not in heaven, saying—that is, so that you may say—‘Who will ascend for us into heaven and take it for us, so that, hearing it, we may do it?’ Nor is it across the sea, saying—that is, so that you may say—‘Who will cross the sea for us and take it for us, so that, hearing it, we may do it?’ This word is very near you, in your mouth and in your hands, to do it.”

“This is the word of faith,” says the Apostle, “which belongs to the New Testament.” But one may ask why he earlier called those things commandments that are written in this book of the law, unless it is because all these things signify spiritual realities belonging to the New Testament, if they are properly understood.

One may likewise ask why, where this passage says, “Nor is it across the sea, so that you may say: ‘Who will cross the sea for us and take it for us?’” the Apostle said, “Or who will descend into the abyss?” and, explaining this, added, “that is, to bring Christ back from the dead.” The reason is that he called the sea the whole of this present life, which is crossed by death, so that in a certain sense the sea comes to an end and death itself is called “across the sea,” as though it lay beyond this life, which is signified by the name of the sea.

Moreover, where this passage adds, “and in your hands,” the Apostle says only, “in your mouth and in your heart.” He pursued this even to the end, saying: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. X). With good reason, the version translated from the Hebrew, as far as we have been able to examine it, does not contain “in your hands.”

Nevertheless, I do not think that this was added by the translators of the Septuagint without reason, unless they wished it to be understood that the hands themselves, by which works are signified, must also be understood in relation to the heart, where faith exists—the faith that works through love. For if the things God commands are done outwardly with the hands but are not done in the heart, no one is so foolish as to suppose that the commandments are fulfilled. But if love, which is the fullness of the law, dwells in the heart, then even if someone cannot act with the bodily hands, he has peace—certainly together with people of good will.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. That Moses foretold Joshua’s leadership of Israel, and that Moses himself wrote the law and handed it over to the priests, the sons of Levi, to guard

### (CHAP. XXXI.)

“Moses summoned Joshua and said to him before all Israel: ‘Be strong and courageous. For you shall bring this people into the land that the Lord swore to their fathers that he would give them, and you shall divide it among them by lot. And the Lord, who is your leader, himself will be with you; he will not abandon you or forsake you,’” etc.

Thus Moses’ words to Joshua express the testimony of the law concerning our Lord Jesus Christ, because the law and the prophets clearly testify that our Redeemer will distribute the land of the future homeland to each person according to his own merits, and that he himself will fulfill all God’s promises. Hence the Psalmist testifies concerning that land, saying: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living. Wait for the Lord; act courageously, and let your heart be strengthened, and endure for the Lord” (Ps. XXVI).

He himself will bring God’s people into the land that the Lord swore to their fathers that he would give them, because without doubt all who will reach the joys of the heavenly kingdom will arrive there under his leadership. For the Truth itself says: “No one comes to the Father except through me” (John XIV). “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man, who is in heaven” (John III).

Whoever is united to Christ through faith—namely, the faith that works through love—will rejoice together with the head that he will reign forever. As for what is said, “He himself will be with you, and he will not abandon you or forsake you,” this clearly signifies the unity of the Father and the Son.

Hence the Lord himself also says in the Gospel: “The one who sent me is with me; and he has not left me alone, because I always do what pleases him” (John VIII). And again: “The Father, who dwells in me, himself does the works” (John XIV). The Father never abandons the Son, because he was never separated from the Son, with whom and with the Holy Spirit he is always the one and only God.

“Thus Moses wrote this law and handed it over to the priests, the sons of Levi, who carried the ark of the covenant of the Lord, and to all the elders of Israel. And he commanded them, saying: ‘After seven years, in the year of remission, at the Feast of Tabernacles, when all Israel has assembled to appear before the Lord their God, in the place which the Lord will choose, you shall read the words of this law before all Israel, with them listening and the whole people gathered together,’” and so forth.

Moses gave the law to the priests in order to show that the sanction of the divine law was especially entrusted to Christ’s priests, so that they might impress upon the people that, in their rank, they received not an earthly dignity but the rights of a heavenly militia. “‘After seven years,’ he says, ‘in the year of remission, at the Feast of Tabernacles, you shall read the words of this law before all Israel.’” What is signified by seven years, if not the present life, which runs according to the number seven, that of the days? Or by seven years the time of the old law is expressed because of the Sabbath. After seven years, therefore, in the year of remission, the law is commanded to be read in the assembly of the people, because, once the mode of the old observance had been completed, the spiritual rite of the New Testament had already succeeded it.

“For when the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons of God” (Gal. IV). And what is signified by the year of remission if not the year of grace, which the Savior himself, reading in the synagogue from the prophecy of Isaiah, declared to be the acceptable year of the Lord and the day of retribution? In the same way, the Feast of Tabernacles is nothing other than the state of the present Church, where, in the tabernacles of our sojourn, beneath the shade of fruitful trees—that is, of holy men—we have chosen to dwell amid their teachings and examples, and where we especially need the help of divine protection.

For it is then that the law must be read in the place which the Lord has chosen, because it is then above all that one must devote oneself to teaching in the Church of Christ. That place too is the one which the Lord has chosen, so that his name might dwell there. But when we have reached the land of our possession, we shall remain no longer in tabernacles [Col. 0966D] but in the city of the heavenly King, that is, in the heavenly Jerusalem, rejoicing always and forever, and saying with the Psalmist: “As we have heard, so also have we seen, in the city of our God; God founded it forever.”

# BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0965]

## CHAPTER ONE. That Moses wrote the words of the law in a scroll and completed it, and commanded the Levites to place it in the ark of the covenant of the Lord, so that it might be there as a testimony against them.

(IBID.) “After Moses had therefore written the words of this law in a scroll and completed it, he commanded the Levites who carried the ark of the covenant of the Lord, saying: ‘Take this book and place it beside the ark of the covenant of the Lord your God, so that it may be there as a testimony against you,’” and so forth.

When Moses was writing Deuteronomy, he entrusted it to the Levites so that they might place it beside the ark of the Lord, so that it might serve there as a testimony. Spiritually, this shows that the Gospel of Christ, whose type is Deuteronomy, must be stored in the memory of the Church through the ministry of faithful priests—that is, true Levites—for the Church is truly the ark of the Lord, since heavenly treasures are stored there.

There, therefore, are preserved the two tablets of the covenant, that is, the books of the law and of the Gospel. There is the urn containing the manna, because there the incarnation of Christ, which contains the food of eternal life, is guarded. There is Aaron’s rod which had blossomed, because there Christ’s priesthood, remaining perpetually, is established.

“‘So that it may be there,’ he says, ‘as a testimony against you.’” To those who preserve the words of God’s law, they become a means of salvation and healing for their souls; but to those who despise them and do not believe, they will be a testimony to their obstinacy and a reproach for their disobedience.

Hence the Savior says in the Gospel: “Blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it” (Matt. VII). And again:

“Everyone, therefore, who hears these words of mine and does them will be like a wise man who built his house upon rock. And the rain fell, and the rivers came, and the winds blew, and they rushed upon that house, and it did not fall, for it had been founded upon rock. And everyone who hears these words of mine and does not do them will be like a foolish man who built his house upon sand. And the rain fell, and the rivers came, and the winds blew, and they rushed upon that house, and it fell; and its ruin was great.”

And again:

“Amen, amen, I say to you: whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life and will not come into judgment, but has passed from death to life.”

But to the unbelieving and contemptuous he says:

“Do not suppose that I shall accuse you before the Father. There is one who accuses you: Moses, in whom you hope. For if you believed Moses, you would perhaps believe me also, for he wrote about me. But if you do not believe his writings, how will you believe my words?”

And elsewhere:

“‘I,’ he says, ‘judge no one, but there is one who judges. The word that I have spoken to you will judge him on the last day” (John XII).

“Moses therefore spoke the words of this song in the hearing of the entire assembly of Israel and completed it to the end.”

This song, which Moses sang as a testimony to Israel, does not convey merely a simple history but is filled with spiritual understanding. In part, according to the historical sense, it reproaches the Israelites for their faithlessness despite the exceedingly abundant benefits bestowed upon them by the Lord. In part, through allegory, it instructs the holy Church concerning heavenly mysteries. In part, through tropology, it urges each of the faithful toward uprightness of conduct.

Therefore, a sober reader ought to preserve the truth of Scripture in the historical sense; in allegory, to consider the meaning of the heavenly mysteries; and in tropology, to learn the usefulness of good disciplines. Thus, instructed by this threefold distinction, he may be raised to that heavenly theory—that is, to the contemplation of hidden things—and to the sublimity of divine contemplation.

One must also carefully consider the statement that Moses speaks the words of the song and completes them to the end, if perhaps this admonishes us that whoever strives to praise God with his mouth should not contradict him by his deeds. For a gift is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner. Therefore the Lord himself says in the Gospel:

“Whoever loosens one of these least of my commandments and teaches will be called least in the kingdom of heaven. But whoever does them and teaches them will be called great in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V).

The beginning of this song is as follows.

## CHAPTER II. The Song of Moses, a foretelling of future things and filled with the mysteries of Christ.

[Col. 0968B] (CHAP. XXXII.) “Hear, O heavens, what I shall speak; let the earth hear the words of my mouth.”

In accordance with the opening of the prophet Isaiah, it is written:

“Hear, O heaven, and listen with your ears, O earth, because the Lord has spoken” (Isaiah I).

Above, in the same book, it was indicated in the title which prophet it was, whose son he was, what he saw against Judah and Jerusalem—or through Judah and Jerusalem—and at what time he saw it. Now he summons heaven and earth to listen, signifying by heaven the heavenly and angelic powers, and by earth the race of mortals. He does this by *metonymy* (μετωνυμικῶς), indicating the things contained by means of those that contain them.

For since, through Moses, the Lord had called heaven and earth as witnesses when he gave his law to the people of Israel and had said, “Attend, O heaven, and I shall speak; let the earth hear the words of my mouth,” after the people’s transgression he again calls the same witnesses, so that all the elements may know that God has justly been provoked to anger in order to avenge the violation of his commandments.

Instead of “heaven,” the Hebrew has “heavens” in the plural, especially since he has said “hear,” that is, a form expressed in the plural rather than the singular. But some wish *coelos* to be said in the plural while being understood in the singular, according to the way in which we call individual cities Thebes and Athens. It is also an idiom of the Hebrew language that all words ending in the syllable *-im* are masculine and plural, such as *cherubim* and *seraphim*, while those ending in *-oth* are feminine and plural, such as *sabaoth*.

And it should be noted that Isaiah says to the heavens, “Hear,” and to the earth, “Listen with your ears.” For things that are lofty possess greater understanding, while things that are lower are enveloped in earthly senses. Hence the Savior says in the Gospel: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear” (Matt. XI).

Therefore, if anyone is a heaven and possesses citizenship in heavenly things, let him hear spiritually what is being said. If anyone is earthly, let him follow the simple historical sense. Some think that he summons heaven and earth to hear as though they were living beings, in accordance with what is said elsewhere about the earth: “He looks upon the earth and makes it tremble; he touches the mountains, and they smoke” (Ps. CIII), although this belongs to God’s power, not to earthly understanding.

“Let my teaching gather into rain; let my speech flow like dew, like a shower upon grass and like drops upon the meadow, for I shall invoke the name of the Lord.”

He compares the speech of God’s law to beaten rain and dew, because it seeks the sprouts of spiritual fruits from the hearts of the faithful. For these are the field and vineyard of the Lord, from which he seeks a pleasing fruit, namely, good works.

We find a similar comparison in the prophet Isaiah:

“As the rain and snow descend from heaven and do not return there again, but water the earth, soak it, make it germinate, and give seed to the sower and bread to the eater, so shall my word be which goes forth from my mouth. It shall not return to me empty, but shall accomplish whatever I have willed, and shall prosper in the things for which I sent it” (Isa. LV).

But because Moses said that his teaching would gather into rain, in order to show clearly what this rain was, he added, saying:

“For I shall invoke the name of the Lord.”

To invoke the name of the Lord, therefore, is to preach the Gospel of Christ. Whoever hears it and produces the fruit of good works will undoubtedly possess the heavens.

“Give greatness to our God, for God’s works are perfect, and all his ways are judgments.”

To magnify the Lord is to proclaim the majesty of the Savior with a believing heart, a devout mouth, and good deeds together. Hence Mary, the mother of the Lord, says in her song:

“My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit rejoiced in God my Savior” (Luke I).

“God’s works,” he says, “are perfect.” What works, then, are those? Hear Moses speaking in the book of Genesis:
