“Thus the heavens and the earth were completed, and all their adornment. And God completed on the seventh day his work which he had made; and he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had accomplished” (Gen. II).

The work of God, therefore, is the redemption of the human race. When he completed it, he showed us the spiritual Sabbath by resting in the tomb.

“All his ways are judgments,” because all his commandments are true. Hence the Psalmist says:

“The law of the Lord is blameless, converting souls; the testimony of the Lord is faithful, giving wisdom to the little ones” (Ps. XVIII).

And again:

“The judgments of God,” he says, “are true, justified in themselves. More desirable than gold and an abundance of precious stones, and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb. Moreover, your servant keeps them; in keeping them there is great reward.”

And elsewhere:

“With my lips,” he says, “I have proclaimed all the judgments of your mouth. God is faithful and without any iniquity, just and upright.”

Faithful, because he undoubtedly fulfilled what he promised. Without any iniquity, because supreme equity in no way admits fellowship with iniquity. Just, because he will repay unrepentant sinners with punishment for their evils. Upright, because, to those who act worthily and repent well, everlasting life.”

“They sinned against him, not his children in their defilements.”

How are they not children of God, except because they are not of faith?

“But to all who received him he gave power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name” (John I).

Hence the Lord said to the Jews who were unwilling to receive faith in him and who despised his teaching:

“You are of your father the devil, and you wish to do the desires of your father. He was a murderer from the beginning and a thief” (John VIII).

And Stephen said to those same Jews:

“Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute? And they killed those who foretold the coming of this righteous one, whose betrayers and murderers you have now become—you who received the law through the disposition of angels and did not keep it” (Acts VII).

Therefore, whoever sins incorrigibly proves that he is not a son of God.

But the edition produced by the Seventy Translators reads as follows:

“They sinned, not his children, the blameworthy ones,” which in Greek is τέκνα μωμήτα, “blameworthy children.” Some have translated this as “blameworthy children,” some as “defiled children,” and some as “vicious children.” Hence there is no great question here—indeed, no question at all.

But what rightly moves us to inquire is this: if “they sinned not against him” is stated generally, since whoever sins does not sin against God—that is, does not harm God, but himself—how should we understand what is read in the Psalm: “Against you alone I have sinned” (Ps. L); and in Jeremiah: “We have sinned against you, O patience of Israel, Lord”; and again in the Psalm: “Heal my soul, for I have sinned against you” (Ps. XL)? And whether “to sin against God” is the same as “to sin into God,” [Col. 0970B] or whether there is some distinction between them.

Hence Eli the priest said: “If he sins against God, who will pray for him?” (1 Sam. II).

I shall say for the moment what presently seems to me to be the case. Those who understand these matters better may perhaps perceive something better—or perhaps we ourselves may do so at another time, when the Lord gives assistance.

To sin against God means to sin in matters belonging to the worship of God. For what I have mentioned indicates nothing else. Thus the sons of Eli were sinning, to whom their father said these things. In the same way, one must think that people also sin against human beings who belong to God.

For Scripture records that God said to Abimelech concerning Sarah:

“For this reason I spared you, so that you would not sin against me” (Gen. XX).

But to sin against the Lord—or rather, to have sinned against the Lord—unless perhaps some passage is found somewhere that resists this interpretation, seems to me appropriately said of those who do not perform a devout repentance for their sin, so that the Lord who forgives may be glorified.

For when David gives the reason for saying, “Against you alone I have sinned, and I have done evil before you,” he adds:

“So that you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged” (Ps. L).

Or when God says:

“Judge between me and my vineyard” (Isa. V).

Or it may be understood of the Lord Jesus Christ, who alone could most truly say:

“For the ruler of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me” (John XIV),

that is, nothing of sin deserving death.

“But so that the world may know that I love the Father, and as the Father commanded me, so I do. Rise, let us go from here.”

It is as though he were saying: Even if the ruler of this world pursues the lightest sins with the punishment of death, he has nothing in me. But “Rise, let us go from here,” that is, so that I may suffer. For in what I suffer, I fulfill the will of my Father; I do not pay the penalty for my own sin.

And when Jeremiah says, “We have sinned against you, O patience of Israel, Lord” (Jer. XIV), this is certainly said supplicatively in repentance, with hope of salvation through pardon. And when it is said, “Heal my soul, for I have sinned against you” (Ps. XL), the same thing is being done: God is glorified by forgiving.

For great is his mercy, so that they may return to him who says that he does not desire the death of a sinner, provided only that the sinner turns back and lives.

Hence David himself, not only in the Psalm but also when the Lord rebuked him through the prophet, replied—not without hope of the Lord’s mercy:

“I have sinned against the Lord” (2 Sam. XII).

A wounded person appears, in a sense, to be entrusted to a physician when, in order to be healed, he submits himself to the physician’s hands, so that the work of medicine may be accomplished in him.

In this song, however, the prophet was foreseeing certain future people who would sin against the Lord in such a way, offending him by their great iniquities, that they would neither wish to repent nor return to the Lord to be healed. Concerning them it is also said:

“For they are flesh, and a spirit that goes and does not return” (Ps. LXXVII).

It can also be understood in this way: “They sinned, not against him,” according to the sense that they did not harm him by their sin, but themselves.

“A crooked and perverse generation—do you repay the Lord in this way?”

The Savior also marked their faithlessness with a similar denunciation in the Gospel. When they tested him and sought a sign from him, he replied:

“A crooked and perverse generation seeks a sign, and no sign will be given it except the sign of the prophet Jonah” (Matt. XII).

Likewise John the Baptist said to the crowds of Jews coming to him:

“Brood of vipers, who showed you how to flee from the coming wrath? Therefore produce fruits worthy of repentance, and do not wish to say, ‘We have Abraham as our father.’ For God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham” (Matt. III).

The Jewish generation was always a crooked and perverse one, ungrateful for God’s benefits; in return, it continually repaid him with various transgressions, the filth of idols, and provocations.

“Foolish and senseless people, is he not himself your father, who possessed you, made you, and created you?”

According to the power of nature, there is one God, the Father and Creator of all, “because from him and through him and in him are all things.”

God created man when he established the matter from which man could be formed. He made him when he fashioned him according to his own image and likeness. He possessed him when, having expelled errors, he claimed him for himself through his faith and grace.

The foolish and senseless people, therefore, were the Jewish nation, which neither venerated its Creator and Maker—with whom the law had most clearly acquainted it—with fitting worship, nor, mindful of the benefit by which he had specially claimed it in Egypt, rescuing it through miracles and wonders from the hand of its enemies, ceased to fashion idols and bestow divine honor upon them.

He had given it manna from heaven, guidance through the Red Sea and the wilderness by the ministry of angels; yet it made idols for itself, conferred divine honor upon them, and foolishly offered sacrifices, saying:

“These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you out of the land of Egypt.”

“Remember the days of old; consider the generations, each one. Ask your father, and he will tell you; your elders, and they will say to you” (Exod. XXXII).

He recalls ancient deeds to their memory, commanding them to question their fathers and learn from them how they had been delivered by divine aid and repeatedly protected from their enemies, so that in this way, at least, they might be summoned to repentance for their sins and, stripping themselves of every error, might hasten to draw near to the truth.

Here “fathers” should be understood not as just any dull and foolish men, but as teachers of the law and preachers of the Gospel, through whose teachings and examples a person can advance toward divine understanding.

Hence the Apostle writes to the Corinthians:

“For though you have ten thousand tutors in Christ, you do not have many fathers. For in Christ Jesus, through the Gospel, I begot you” (1 Cor. IV).

And to the Hebrews:

“We had fathers of our flesh as educators, and we respected them. Shall we not much more obey the Father of spirits and live? And they indeed instructed us for a few days according to their own will; but he does so for what is beneficial, so that we may receive his sanctification” (Heb. XII).

“When the Most High was dividing the nations, when he was separating the sons of Adam, he established the boundaries of the peoples according to the number of the sons of Israel. But the Lord’s portion is his people; Jacob is the cord of his inheritance.”

He gives the historical arrangement of the distribution of the human race: since the multitude of human beings is so great that their number cannot be encompassed by human reckoning, the Lord chose the sons of Israel alone from so vast a multitude as his inheritance, so that he might make known his name and power and reveal the secrets of his will through the judgments of the Law and the writings of the prophets. Thus, earlier in the present book, he declared:

“The Lord your God chose you, so that you might be his special people, from all the peoples who are upon the earth” (Deut. VII).

Not because you surpassed all the nations in number was the Lord joined to you and chose you, since you are fewer than all the peoples, but because the Lord loved you, kept the oath that he swore to your fathers, brought you out with a strong hand, and redeemed you from the hand of Pharaoh, king of Egypt. And you shall know that the Lord your God—he himself is your God—is the strong and faithful one, keeping his covenant and mercy with those who love him and those who observe his commandment, for a thousand generations; and repaying those who hate him, immediately destroying them and not delaying further, promptly rendering to them what they deserve. Therefore keep the commandments, statutes, and judgments that I command you today to perform.

According to another edition, however, the text reads: “He established for him the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels of God.” And in Daniel’s vision, where the angel recounted that the prince of Persia resisted him, something else seems to be suggested to us (Dan. VIII). For the ministries of angels are believed to have been appointed over individual nations and individual human beings, so that human nature may be subjected to their governance and protection according to the disposition of almighty God and may be guarded from its enemies. Hence, when the Lord was teaching in the Gospel that the little ones should not be scandalized, he immediately added:

“Their angels in heaven always see the face of my Father, who is in heaven” (Matt. XVIII).

Since that heavenly city consists of angels and human beings, and we believe that so many human beings will ascend to it as there remained elect angels, as it is written: “He established the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels of God,” we too ought to draw something from those distinctions among the heavenly citizens for the practice of our way of life, and kindle ourselves through good pursuits toward an increase of virtue.

For since it is believed that so great a multitude of human beings will ascend there as the multitude of angels who remained, it follows that the human beings who return to their heavenly homeland should themselves imitate something of those ranks as they go back there. The distinct ways of life of individual human beings correspond to the orders of the various ranks, and they are assigned to their lot through similarity of conduct.

But the Lord’s portion is spiritual Jacob, “and the cord of his inheritance.” The true Israel, namely the catholic Church, is spoken of by the Psalmist:

“The cords fell to me in pleasant places; indeed, my inheritance is pleasant to me” (Ps. XV).

In Scripture, cords customarily signify at one time the allotments of measurements, at another sins, and at another faith. Because of the allotments of hereditary possessions, it is said: “The cords fell to me in pleasant places; indeed, my inheritance is pleasant to me.” Cords fall in pleasant places when, through humility of life, lots of a better homeland receive us.

Again, because sin is signified by a cord, the prophet says:

“Woe to those who draw vanities with cords of iniquity” (Isa. V).

Iniquity is drawn with cords of vanity when guilt is extended through its increase. Hence the Psalmist says:

“The cords of sinners have encompassed me.”

Since a cord is twisted by adding to it so that it grows, sin is rightly represented by a cord, for when it is defended by a perverse heart it is often multiplied.

Again, faith is expressed by a cord, as Solomon bears witness, saying:

“A threefold cord is not easily broken” (Eccl. IV).

For faith, woven from knowledge of the Trinity by the mouths of preachers, remains strong in the elect but is dissolved in the heart of the reprobate alone.

“He found him in a desert land, in a place of horror and vast solitude. He surrounded him, taught him, and guarded him like the pupil of his eye.”

The Lord found Israel in a place of horror and vast solitude; and on Mount Sinai, when he gave the Law, he entered into a covenant with him, bestowed manna from heaven, brought water from the rock, gave quail meat, and, leading them about in that same wilderness for forty years, taught them his commandments.

But it is reasonably asked how he says that he protected them like the pupil of his eye, when very many of them fell in the wilderness. Unless perhaps we say that they were protected and guarded only so long as they kept God’s commandments. But when they transgressed them, he immediately struck them with plagues, and they were devastated by their enemies.

Mystically, however, the Lord found Israel in a desert land when he brought the Church out of the error of the world, where there was the horror of idolatry and no remembrance of God. The Lord therefore leads the Church around when, extending it throughout all the regions of the world, he directs it along the path of his commandments; and, making his will known to it through the Holy Spirit, he preserves it everywhere with complete guardianship—signified by the pupil of the eye—against heretics and persecutors.

Another comparison follows:

“As an eagle provoking its young to fly, and hovering over them, spread its wings, took them up, and carried them on its shoulders.”

Naturalists relate that the eagle—so called from the sharpness of its eyes—has such keen sight that, while it is carried over the seas on motionless wings and is invisible to human eyes, it can see from such a height little fish swimming in the water; then, descending like a missile, it seizes its prey and drags it to the shore with its wings. It is also said to turn its gaze toward the rays of the sun.

Thus it exposes its young, hanging from its talons, to the sun’s rays; and those whose gaze it sees holding steady it preserves as worthy of their lineage. But if it sees any turn their gaze away, it casts them off as degenerate.

Eagles are also said, when they see their young growing feathers in the nests, to strike them with their wings and provoke them to fly from the nest. They build their nests in rocks and trees, and in their nests the stone called aetites is found, which some have called gagates; it is useful for many remedies and loses nothing in fire.

Investigators of nature further report that eagles do not so much die of old age as of hunger, because their upper beak grows so much that its hooked shape can no longer be opened. But when it sees danger threatening from this, it bluntens its beak against a very hard rock until it returns again to its former use. Hence the prophet says to the faithful soul in a mystical expression in the Psalm:

“Your youth will be renewed like the eagle’s” (Ps. CII).

According to the literal sense, the likeness of the eagle shows that the Lord helped his people by provoking them to possess the land of Canaan through warfare, and, by helping them, protected them from their enemies.

According to the mystical sense, however, this eagle signifies the Lord the Savior. He possesses the likeness of an eagle because by his death he snatched the prey from the hostile enemy and, after his resurrection, carried to the heights of heaven the flesh that he had assumed for the redemption of the human race. By his words and examples he exhorts us to follow him there and strive toward it in devotion, where he himself ascended in the body. Hence he says in the Gospel:

“Where the body is, there the eagles will be gathered” (Luke XVII).

The other examples that we have given concerning the eagle can likewise be transferred figuratively to him and to his children. For just as the eagle has keen sight, so that, lifted above the seas on motionless wings and invisible to human eyes, it sees from such a height little fish swimming in the deep, seizes them as prey, and drags them to the shore, so our Redeemer, exalted above all the heavens and bodily removed from human sight, nevertheless sees in the sea of this world, through the gaze of his majesty, those whom he may rescue as a saving prey and draw by the cord of his love to the shore of eternal blessedness.

Hence he himself says in the Gospel:

“And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw everything to myself” (John XII).

He exposes his young—that is, his sons, reborn to him through the grace of baptism—to the rays of the eternal sun through contemplation. Those whom he sees possessing a steadfast gaze in contemplation he preserves perpetually as worthy of his lineage. But if he sees any turn the gaze of their mind downward toward lowly and carnal desires, he casts them off as degenerate.

This eagle nests in rocks and trees because among those whom it sees to be firm in faith and fruitful in virtue it brings forth the fruitfulness of spiritual offspring. There the gem and that most precious pearl are born, which the sacred Gospel text says the spiritual merchant acquired for himself after selling all his possessions (Matt. XV).

As for the eagle striking its excessive beak against a rock and thus restoring it to its former condition, this signifies that holy men, whenever they perceive anything excessive and harmful to themselves in their way of life, break it by striking it against the rock, Christ; and, renewing themselves through the grace of God and good discipline, they are made fit again for their former service.

The Lord alone was his leader, and there was no foreign god with him.

It is clear that the one and only God liberated Israel from Egypt, not the false idols that the Egyptians worshiped. So too, in our rescue from spiritual Egypt, there is no other than the same God who once rescued the Israelites—namely, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, one God and threefold, great and almighty, who through the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ brought about the mystery of our salvation.

Let heretics therefore recognize how miserably they depart from the true faith when, through schism, they separate themselves from the catholic Church: they are subject to as many idols as they have errors.

“He established him upon a lofty land, so that he might eat the fruits of the fields.”

He calls Palestine a lofty land because, compared with the land of Egypt, which is flat and watered, it appears mountainous and rugged.

In another sense, the lofty land is the holy Church, which is very exalted in virtues and knowledge. There, once established, the faithful eat the fruits of spiritual fields, because there the good seed, the word of God, germinates—yielding in one case thirtyfold, in another sixtyfold, and in another a hundredfold—so that each person finds sufficient nourishment according to his capacity.

“That he might suck honey from the rock, and oil from the hardest stone.”

Another edition reads:

“They sucked honey from the rock, and oil from the firm rock.”

Yet nowhere is anything of this sort read according to the historical sense, if the entire sequence of the Old Testament is reviewed. Nowhere did that people suck honey from a rock, nor oil. But according to Paul’s saying, the rock was Christ; those who saw the deeds and miracles of the same Redeemer of ours sucked honey from the rock.

They sucked oil from the firm rock who, after his resurrection, were worthy to be anointed through the outpouring of the Holy Spirit. Thus he gave honey from the firm rock when, while the Lord was still mortal, he showed his disciples the sweetness of his miracles. But the firm rock poured forth oil because, after his resurrection, when he had become incapable of suffering, he caused the gift of holy anointing to flow through the breathing forth of the Spirit.

Of this oil the prophet says:

“The yoke will rot before the face of the oil” (Isa. X).

We were held under the yoke of demonic domination, but we have been anointed with the oil of the Holy Spirit; and because the grace of freedom has anointed us, the yoke of domination has rotted away.

“Butter from cattle, and milk from sheep, with the fat of lambs and rams, the sons of Bashan, and goats with the marrow of wheat, and the blood of the grape.”

Although these words, according to the historical sense, indicate the fertility of the land of Canaan, in a higher sense they demonstrate the abundance of grace that the holy Church received through the gift of its benefactor.

They received butter from cattle who learned the fullness of faith from the examples of the patriarchs. They took milk from sheep who received, for their own edification, simplicity of mind or the capacity for teaching from the innocent life of the fathers. They received these things together with the fat of lambs and rams—that is, with the richness of the apostles’ charity and of those whom the apostles had instructed in the faith—for the nourishment of their minds.

By the name of rams the apostles and men of apostolic dignity are signified, because they are the leaders of God’s flock. Hence it is said in the Psalm:

“Bring to the Lord, sons of God; bring to the Lord the sons of rams” (Ps. XXVIII).

What is added, “the sons of Bashan,” belongs to the same meaning, because Bashan is interpreted as “fatness.” The sons of fatness are those who have been instructed in the disciplines of the New Testament, in which a multitude of knowledge and greatness of virtues reside.

Yet these gifts were not sufficient unless goats were added as well. Goats represent penitents, because they were offered for sin under the Law. For it is not enough for the faithful to possess the gifts of virtues unless they also have penitence for their transgressions.

Hence the one who was both king and prophet, and to whom it was promised concerning the incarnation of Christ that he would be born from his seed, prayed to the Lord for his sins, saying:

“Wash me more fully, Lord, from my iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin. For I know my iniquity, and my sin is always before me” (Ps. L).

And so that all the benefits mentioned above might be increased by a more excellent gift, he added: “the marrow of wheat and the blood of the grape.”

For what is signified by the marrow of wheat except the body of Christ? And what is signified by the blood of the grape except the cup of the New Testament in the blood of Christ? Among the many gifts granted to the ecclesiastical people through God’s goodness, this surpasses them all: that he supplied them for eternal salvation with the sacraments of his body and blood in the preparation of bread and wine.

It follows:

“They would drink the purest wine.”

For all God’s gifts are bestowed upon believers who think rightly and worthily about them, without any sediment of wickedness or reproach. But just as the carnal Israelites once abused God’s gifts and, made worse by his most generous benefits, fell into idolatry, so, alas, not a few ungrateful people relapse into vices after receiving God’s benefits; and what was granted to them for salvation they turn to their own destruction.

Hence it follows:

“The beloved grew fat and kicked. He grew fat, became stout, and grew broad. He abandoned God who made him and departed from God his Savior. They provoked him with strange gods and aroused him to anger with their abominations. They sacrificed to demons and not to God, to gods whom they did not know. New and recent gods came, whom their fathers had not worshiped.”

The ancient Israelites did this historically, as is sufficiently expressed in their books. But now also spiritual Israelites, when they turn the gifts of God granted to them in knowledge and virtues for divine service toward heresy or hypocrisy, are shown to serve idols and not God, offering worship to demons and not to God. Our fathers—that is, the patriarchs, prophets, apostles, and evangelists—certainly did not do this.

For this reason these idolaters incur the consequence that, provoking the most merciful Lord by their evil deeds, they will find him severe and stern, although they might have possessed him as propitious:

“You abandoned the God who begot you and forgot the Lord, your creator.”

The Lord begot the Israelites in a certain sense through the Law and circumcision. He also begot the Israelite people through the grace of baptism and the sanctification of the Holy Spirit. But whoever is not afraid to forget him will justly experience the Lord’s anger against him through punishment.

Hence it follows:

“The Lord saw and was stirred to anger, because his sons and daughters provoked him. And he said: I will hide my face from them, and I will consider their end.”

Nothing is more grievous among punishments than to be deprived of the presence and vision of God. Hence the Psalmist beseeches the Lord, saying:

“Do not cast me away from your face” (Ps. L).

And again he says:

“Do not turn your face away from me.”

Job likewise speaks to the Lord:

“Do not hide me from your face” (Job XIII).

Since, therefore, the sons and daughters—that is, human beings of both sexes—provoked him through the evil deeds they committed, they do not deserve his mercy. Abandoned by him, they will be proved at their end to have an angry God, that is, “he will consider their end”: their torments will be made manifest.

“For it is a perverse generation and unfaithful children. They provoked me with what is not a people, and I will stir them to anger with a foolish nation.”

Since the Israelites abandoned God and worshiped idols, forsaking the true and only God and serving vanity, they were handed over for plunder to nations that at that time had not yet deserved to be called the people of God.

Similarly, ecclesiastical people who have abandoned the truth and turned toward error, unless they repent of their evil deeds, will be handed over for punishment in the prisons of hell to wicked spirits who, through their pride, lost their angelic dignity.

Demons can rightly be called a foolish nation, because they hate justice and love iniquity.

“A fire has been kindled in my anger, and it will burn to the depths of hell.”

Of those whom scourges condemn and do not free, it is written:

“You struck them, and they did not grieve; you consumed them, and they refused to accept discipline” (Jer. V).

For such people the scourges begin in this life and continue in eternal punishment. Hence Moses says:

“A fire has blazed up from my anger, and it will burn to the depths of hell.”

So far as present punishment is concerned, it is rightly said: “A fire has blazed up from my anger.” But with regard to eternal condemnation, the following is appropriately added: “And it will burn to the depths of hell.”

Although some customarily say what is written—“God will not avenge the same thing twice” (Nahum I)—they nevertheless fail to attend to what is said by the prophet concerning the wicked: “Crush them with a twofold destruction”; and to what is written elsewhere:

“Jesus, having saved the people from the land of Egypt, destroyed a second time those who did not believe.”

If we accept these statements, it must nevertheless be understood that those struck by this sin and dying in their sin cannot be punished twice for any single fault, because their punishment begins here and ends there. Thus, for those who remain uncorrected, there is one scourge: it begins temporally but is consumed in eternal punishments. In this way, for those who utterly refuse correction, the striking of present scourges becomes the beginning of the torments that follow.

It follows:

“It consumed the earth and its produce.”

It consumes the earth and its produce when the flame of eternal vengeance burns sinful flesh on account of the works of lust. The produce of the flesh properly consists in the works of carnal desire:

“fornication, impurity, shamelessness, debauchery, the service of idols, sorcery, enmities, strife, jealousy, anger, quarrels, dissensions, factions, envy, murder, drunkenness, reveling, and things like these. Those who do such things, as Paul testifies, will not obtain the kingdom of God” (Gal. V).

“And it will burn the foundations of the mountains.”

This occurs when it consumes in eternal torments the wicked plans of the proud, by which they believed they could sin with impunity.

“I will gather evils upon them.”

This will happen when he recalls not only their evil deeds but also their thoughts and wicked words, for which they will be punished. He will fill his arrows against them when he reveals his anger and indignation through various torments.

“They will be consumed by hunger.”

That is, not by lack of food or drink, but by the perpetual barrenness of good works.

“And birds will devour them with a most bitter bite.”

Namely, wicked spirits will tear them with the most savage mouth, reproaching them for their past sins.

“I will send the teeth of beasts against them, together with the fury of those that drag themselves over the earth and of serpents.”

Beasts and serpents are wicked spirits. They are called beasts because of their ferocity and serpents because of their cunning. Beasts and serpents drag the reprobate over the earth with their teeth in fury when, after having previously persuaded carnal people through flattery in order to seduce them, they later demand from sinners what they had persuaded them to do, with a raging mind, in order to torment them.

“Outside, the sword will lay them waste, and inside, terror.”

The sword will lay the impious waste outside, and terror will be within, when at the final vengeance the burning of eternal fire tortures the body on every side, while inwardly the greatness of anguish oppresses the mind. Hence it is written:

“Their worm will not die, and the fire will not be extinguished. The young man together with the virgin, the nursing child together with the old man” (Isa. LXVI).

By enumerating every age, he shows that no age is to be spared in the evident vengeance inflicted upon those whom the same worship of idolatry had defiled.

Allegorically, however, in the young man he shows the wanton and lustful; in the virgin, one barren of good works; in the nursing child, the dull; and in the old man, the sluggish and useless. All these he will consume according to God’s vengeance at the final punishment, because admonition and correction do not now restrain them from sins.

“And he said: Where are they? I will cause their memory to cease among human beings.”

God’s question is not ignorance but correction. Anyone who sees the Jews expelled from the promised land and scattered throughout the whole world can readily recognize the fulfillment of this sentence.

In general, however, this fate threatens all sinners and impenitent people: they will be removed from the land of the saints, and their memory will not be counted among the assembly of the elect. Hence, in the fifty-first Psalm, the future punishment of the head of all the wicked, together with his whole body, is foretold by the Psalmist. After enumerating the individual kinds of vices, he adds:

“Therefore God will destroy you forever; he will tear you away and remove you from your tent, and your root from the land of the living.”

“But because of the anger of the enemies I delayed, lest perhaps their enemies should become proud and say: Our hand is exalted, and God did not do all these things.”

For this reason the Lord often endured the former people by patiently bearing with them: lest the nations neighboring them should blaspheme his name and power.

Hence Moses said to the Lord, who was angry because of Israel’s sin and wanted to destroy them:

“Do not, I beg you, Lord, let the Egyptians say: He brought them out deceitfully in order to kill them in the mountains and wipe them from the earth. Let your anger rest, and be appeased concerning the wickedness of your people. Remember Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, your servants, to whom you swore by yourself, saying: I will multiply your offspring like the stars of heaven; and I will give your offspring this whole land of which I have spoken, and you shall possess it forever. And the Lord was appeased, so that he did not do the evil that he had spoken of doing to his whole people” (Exod. XXXII).

Likewise, when we have sinned, he sustains us because of his great power and patience, unwilling that anyone should perish but desiring all to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. In accordance with the Apostle’s saying to the Romans:

“Do you suppose, O man, who judge those who do such things and yet do them yourself, that you will escape the judgment of God? Or do you despise the riches of his goodness, patience, and long-suffering, not knowing that the kindness of God leads you to repentance? But according to your hardness and unrepentant heart, you are storing up for yourself wrath on the day of wrath and the revelation of the righteous judgment of God,” and so forth (Rom. II).

And lest wicked spirits should perhaps glory in our destruction on account of their strength, as though they had obtained the victory by their own power—for they are always striving to overturn the sentence of the Most High, who decreed that human beings should possess in heaven the place of the fallen spirits—

“The Jewish nation is without counsel and without understanding; would that they were wise and provided for their end.”

The Jewish nation, and likewise the impious, is without saving counsel, because it does not know how to provide for its future, so as to escape the vengeance impending on account of its sins and avoid the eternal torment of infernal punishments.

“How could one pursue a thousand, and two put ten thousand to flight? Is it not because their God sold them, and the Lord shut them in?”

Whoever truly recognizes the greatness of God will clearly understand that his destruction does not arise from any weakness of God’s power but from the permission of his just judgment. For it could in no way happen that one should pursue a thousand and two put ten thousand to flight unless the Lord had handed them over and, casting them away as hated, had shut them into the hands of their enemies.

“For our God is not like their god, and our enemies are judges.”

The Lord our God is true and just, but the idols of the nations are false and useless. Not only our own people but even our adversaries confirm this. Hence we frequently read that, when the Jews were handed over to their enemies because of their unbelief and injustice, they were rightly reproved by those enemies, as Jeremiah says in his Lamentations:

“Enemies saw her and mocked her Sabbaths” (Lam. I).

We must therefore be exceedingly careful lest our enemies, provoked by our evil deeds, break out into blasphemy against God when they see us overcome and reduced to nothing because of our sins, and attribute to their own power what has happened not through their strength but through the judgment of the Lord.

“For their vine is from the vine of Sodom, and from the fields of Gomorrah. Their grapes are grapes of gall, and their cluster is most bitter.”

In the sacred Scriptures the Synagogue or Jerusalem is often compared with Sodom and Gomorrah, because just as those cities wickedly abused God’s gifts, so these have always proved ungrateful for his benefits.

Hence Isaiah says of them:

“Unless the Lord of hosts had left us a seed, we would have become like Sodom and would have been made like Gomorrah. Hear the word of the Lord, rulers of Sodom; listen with your ears to the law of our God, people of Gomorrah,” and so forth (Isa. I).

The Lord’s vineyard, as it is written in the same prophet, was the house of Israel. It was then turned into the bitterness of gall when it plotted the death of Christ. Hence, while he hung upon the cross, they offered him vinegar mixed with gall on a reed, so that this might show that they had corrupted with the gall of their malice the knowledge of the Law that they had received rightly. When the giver of the Law came to them, they refused to receive him; indeed, they provoked and afflicted him.

In another sense, this sentence also strikes at the wickedness of heretics. Although at first they received the pure doctrine of spiritual grace from the holy preachers, they nevertheless did not fear to stain it with their errors. Therefore their entire teaching has been turned into the bitterness of gall and wormwood.

“Their wine is the gall of dragons, and the incurable venom of asps.”

The faithlessness of the Jews and the cunning of heretics are plainly compared with the gall of dragons and the venom of asps. Just as serpents conceal bitterness and venom within themselves so that they may harm the unwary unexpectedly, so Jews and heretics conceal their malice beneath deceit and fraud, in order more easily to destroy the imprudent.

It is rightly called the incurable venom of asps, because the error of heretics, whatever it has invaded, unless one frees oneself from it, undoubtedly destroys one forever.

“Are not these things stored up with me and sealed in my treasuries?”

It is characteristic of the human race to forget the past quickly; things that once seemed great, as time passes, also fade from memory. But it is not so with God, where there is neither past nor future, but the present is always present. What passes away from us is preserved there and will not be handed over to oblivion.

It is therefore necessary that we strive to erase the sins we committed long ago through immediate repentance before the eyes of God, lest perhaps in the future, when the time of vengeance comes, he reckon our debts to us and say:

“You did these things, and I was silent. You wickedly thought that I was like you; I will rebuke you and set them before your face.”

“Vengeance is mine, and I will repay them in due time, so that their foot may slip.”

With the Lord, the time and manner of vengeance are certain. But because his mercies are many, “let us go before his face with confession, and let us exult to him in psalms. Let us humble our souls in fasting”; let us watch and pray, “for who knows whether God may turn and forgive, and leave a blessing behind him?”

The day of destruction is near, and the times hasten to arrive. The day of vengeance is near for each person because it is certain, and what eventually ends cannot be long-lasting. Whatever is temporal—whether a human life or the course of the world—becomes small when compared with eternity. Therefore it is said, “and the times hasten to arrive,” because temporal things quickly come to an end.

According to the historical sense, however, the vengeance of the Israelites drew near. From the time they began to rebel, they never entirely ceased until they lost both the place of the kingdom and the prosperity of life. For after they had killed the prophets and crucified the Savior, adding new offenses to their ancient seditions, they provoked the Romans against themselves by rebelling. The Romans destroyed the city, burned the temple, killed the people by famine and sword, and scattered the survivors throughout the whole world. There they wander in uncertain dwellings, remaining uncertain of the hope of future things.

“The Lord will judge his people, and he will have mercy on his servants.”

The Lord will judge his people when he separates his elect from the reprobate. For “to judge” is sometimes understood as “to distinguish,” and at other times as “to condemn.”

Hence the Prophet says to the Lord in the Psalm:

“Judge me, O God, and distinguish my cause from an unholy nation; deliver me from the unjust and deceitful man” (Ps. XLII).

Here “judge” is used in the sense of discernment. Elsewhere, however, the Prophet cries out to the Lord:

“Judge, O Lord, those who harm me; fight against those who fight against me” (Ps. XXXIV).

There “judgment” is used in the sense of condemnation.

The Lord will judge his saints when, separating them from sinners on the day of judgment, he places them at his right hand. But he will place their enemy and persecutors on the left, so that they may receive certain condemnation with the devil and his angels in hell:

“These will go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life.”

Then what follows in the preceding verse will be fulfilled:

“And he will have mercy on his servants.”

For in heavenly blessedness he will bestow eternal mercy upon his faithful.

This verse can also be referred to the final conversion of the Jews, when, through God’s mercy, after the full number of the nations has entered into the faith, all Israel will be converted to that same faith through divine grace and will be saved.

“He will see that the hand has become weak, and that even those who were shut in have failed; and the survivors have been consumed. And he will say: Where are their gods, in whom they trusted? From whose victims they ate the fat and drank the wine of their libations. Let them rise and help you, and protect you in your necessities.”

He will see that the hand has become weak when he makes it evident that the works of evil that they committed in idolatry and in other transgressions were powerless—when, reduced to nothing, they have benefited nothing those who performed them.

“And even those who were shut in have failed.” This means either that the Jews, led into captivity by their enemies, were consumed there, or that all the impious, handed over to the power of demons, will no longer prevail.

“And the survivors have been consumed,” because, departing from this life, they will no longer possess the power or ability to do anything. Hence it is written in Ecclesiastes:

“Whatever your hand can do, do it earnestly, because there is neither work, nor reason, nor wisdom, nor knowledge in the underworld, where you are hastening” (Eccl. IX).

What follows—“Where are their gods, in whom they trusted?”—and the rest signifies that idolaters will have no assistance on the day of necessity from the idols to which they previously offered worship.

Nor will lovers of the world, who through greed—for greed is the service of idols—stored up money in the world, and who devoted themselves to pleasures and debauchery, whose god was their belly and whose glory was in their shame, because they minded earthly things, take anything with them from all their labor when, on account of their sins, they are dragged by wicked spirits into Tartarus.

“See that I alone am, and there is no other God besides me.” This admonition applies generally to all human beings, so that, abandoning the falsehood of idols and the deception of heretics, as well as the filth of every iniquity, they may turn to worship the one and only God, the Father and the Holy Spirit, through the Catholic faith [Col. 0982D]; and may love him with all their heart, all their soul, and all their strength, carefully keeping his commandments and judgments, so that they may deserve to become heirs of the heavenly kingdom.

“I kill and I make alive; I strike, and I heal, and there is none who can rescue from my hand.” Almighty God wounds in two ways those whom he takes care to restore to salvation. Sometimes he strikes the flesh, and the hardness of the mind melts away in fear of him. By wounding, therefore, he recalls them to salvation, when he afflicts his elect outwardly and gives them life inwardly. Rightly does he speak through Moses: “I kill and I make alive; I strike, and I heal.” He kills in order to give life; he strikes in order to sanctify, because he warns outwardly for the very purpose of not inflicting wounds inwardly. He strikes the hardness of our mind with the desire for himself, but by striking he heals, because, pierced by the dart of his terror, he recalls us to a sense of righteousness.

Our hearts are diseased when they are satisfied by no love of God; when they do not feel the distress of their pilgrimage; when, toward the weakness of their neighbor, they do not languish with even the slightest feeling of compassion. But when God strikes insensible minds with the arrows of his love, he immediately makes them sensitive through the love of charity.

“I will raise my hand to heaven; I will say, I live forever.” Another edition reads as follows: “For I will lift my hand to heaven, and I will swear by my right hand, and I will say: I live forever.” To raise or lift one’s hand to heaven is to show that the power of his eternity is exalted above all things. To swear by the right hand is, through the Son—who is called the right hand of God—to confirm his promises in the sight of human beings and to reveal his eternity to those who believe in him through the Gospel, because his power is eternal power, and his kingdom shall not perish.

“If I sharpen my sword like lightning, and my hand takes hold of judgment, I will repay vengeance upon my enemies, and I will requite those who hate me.” To sharpen God’s sword like lightning is to exercise sudden vengeance upon his enemies. For the hand of God to take hold of judgment is, through just retribution, to repay each person according to his own merits, as it is written: “For the Son of Man is in the glory of his Father with his angels, and then he will repay each person according to his works” (Mark VIII). And the Apostle says: “We shall all stand before the tribunal of Christ, so that each one may receive according to what he has done in the body, whether good or evil” (Romans XIV).

“I will make my arrows drunk with blood, and my sword shall devour flesh.” An arrow strikes a person when he is unaware; and because it is not foreseen, it kills suddenly. The arrows of the Lord are swift acts of vengeance. Although they are now hidden from the eyes of the wicked, they will suddenly be revealed in the condemnation of the lost; and the sword of God eats flesh because, at the final judgment, his sentence kills those who think according to the flesh.

“From the blood of the slain and from the captivity of the stripped head of the enemy.” In the statement about the blood of the enemies, what was said earlier is understood: “I will make my arrows drunk with blood.” The Lord makes his arrows drunk with the blood of the slain when he exercises vengeance upon the multitude of his enemies. Then the plans of wicked minds, in which they trusted that they could sin with impunity, will be exposed.

The heads of the wicked may also be understood as the teachers of those who go astray, upon whom the final vengeance rebounds, because those who were the cause of sins will experience losses in the retribution of punishments. Hence it is written in the Apocalypse: “And blood came forth from the lake as far as the bridles of the horses” (Revelation XIV). That is, the vengeance of torments proceeded as far as the rulers of peoples. Indeed, as far as the devil and his angels, in the final conflict, will extend the vengeance for the blood poured out by the saints, as it is written: “You sinned in blood, and blood shall pursue you.”

“Praise his people, you nations, because he will avenge the blood of his servants, and he will repay vengeance upon their enemies.” All nations will praise the people of God when they see the Church of God appearing gloriously in the presence of its Creator, while its persecutors, for the blood of the martyrs shed by them and for all the evils they committed in this life, are confined through the ministry of wicked spirits in the fire of eternal Gehenna.

Then the good will also praise the good they see, because they are pleased with the reward they possess. And the wicked, established in punishments and repenting within themselves, will say: “These are the ones whom we once held in derision and as an object of reproach. We senseless people considered their life madness and their end without honor. How, then, are they counted among the children of God, and how is their lot among the saints?” And the Lord will be gracious to the land of his people (Wisdom V).

This will occur when he establishes the holy Church, which until then he had governed amid adversities, permanently amid prosperity—in the heavenly kingdom, namely, where it will rejoice without end and sing praises to the Lord forever together with the holy angels.

“And the Lord spoke to Moses on that same day, saying: Go up this mountain of Abarim—that is, ‘of passage’—to Mount Nebo, which is in the land of Moab opposite Jericho; and see the land of Canaan, which I will give to the children of Israel to possess, and die on the mountain. When you have ascended it, you shall be joined to your peoples, just as Aaron your brother died on Mount Hor and was gathered to his people, because you transgressed against me in the midst of the children of Israel, at the waters of contradiction, and so forth.”

Abarim is the mountain on which Moses died, and it is interpreted as “passage”; Nebo is interpreted as “enclosure.” Nebo is also said to be a mountain in the land of Moab opposite Jericho, above the Jordan, on the summit of Pisgah. It is shown to those ascending from Libya, from the city; and, situated near Mount Peor, it retains its ancient name, from which the surrounding region is still called Pisgah.

Moses therefore dies in Abarim and on Mount Nebo opposite Jericho, across from the Jordan, because the law and circumcision proceeded as far as the coming of Christ and the sacrament of baptism. There they were enclosed, because “Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes.” Moses saw the promised land but did not enter it, because he foresaw in the spirit and foretold in the law the future grace of Christ, but did not remain in the body until that grace was present so that he might see it. This was granted to Christ’s apostles; and therefore those blessed men testify, by the voice of that very truth, that what many righteous people and prophets desired to see and hear was most gloriously granted to them to behold in the present (Matthew XIII).

## CHAPTER III. On the blessings of Moses upon the individual tribes

(CAP. XXXIII.) “This is the blessing with which Moses, the man of God, blessed the children of Israel before his death, and he said.”

This order of arrangement rightly and reasonably suits the subject: Moses, bringing his Deuteronomy to an end, concluded its final portion with a blessing, prefiguring that Christ, after completing his Gospel and accomplishing his passion and resurrection, finally, when he was about to ascend into heaven, blessed his disciples with raised hands: “And it came to pass, while he blessed them, that he departed from them and was carried up into heaven” (Luke XXIV).

For this blessing, by which the children of Israel are blessed in Deuteronomy, which is the second law, clearly pertains to the grace of the New Testament. In it the mysteries of the ancient law are disclosed, and true Israelites receive through the man Jesus Christ the blessing that was prophesied through Moses, the man of God.

Hence the Apostle says: “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ” (II Corinthians I). And it is fitting that, as Moses’ death approached, the children of Israel were enriched with spiritual blessing, because, while the shadow of the law—which promised earthly things—is destroyed, the reality of heavenly gifts is revealed.

Moses therefore foresees in the prophetic spirit the coming of our Savior and the future grace of the New Testament. Recounting what was past, he joyfully continues from the voice of the primitive Church, saying: “The Lord will come from Sinai, and he has dawned for us from Seir.”

Through the names of the places he demonstrates the effects of events. Sinai is interpreted as “my jar,” or “my measure,” or “commandment.” Seir means “hairy” or “bristling.” Paran means “their ferocity,” or “fruitful.”

Sinai, therefore, represents the Old Testament. Holding a fixed measure of commandments according to the decree of the Decalogue, it knows how to command but does not know how to help. It liberates its followers through the spirit of love, but through fear of punishment it binds them, subject to servile bondage.

Hence the teacher of the nations, writing to the Galatians, expressed allegorically, through the two wives and the two sons of Abraham, the figure of the two testaments and the two peoples, saying: “It is written that Abraham had two sons: one by a slave woman and one by a free woman. But the one who was of the slave woman was born according to the flesh, while the one who was of the free woman was born through the promise. These things are spoken allegorically” (Galatians IV). “For these are the two covenants. One indeed is from Mount Sinai, generating bondage, which is Hagar. For Sinai is a mountain in Arabia, joined to the Jerusalem that now exists, and it is in bondage with its children,” and so forth.

The Lord Jesus Christ therefore came from Sinai because he became known to believers through the reading of the law and the prophets. From there he came, because whoever understands finds him there. For he himself, “beginning with Moses and all the prophets, interpreted to the disciples, to whose hearts he desired to come through faith, in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself” (Luke XXIV).

He also dawned from Seir, because, born according to the flesh from the harshest thorns of Jewish malice and unbelief, he illuminated the minds of believers through the rising of a new light, like the true sun of righteousness. Concerning him the Lord says through the prophet: “But for you who fear my name, the sun of righteousness shall rise, and healing shall be in his wings” (Malachi IV). And concerning him Balaam says: “A star shall rise from Jacob, and a man shall arise from Israel” (Numbers XXIV).

It is fitting that Seir—also called by other names, Edom or Esau—designates the Jewish people, because, pursuing the pleasures of the flesh, they lost the glory of their birthright through a dish of lentils; and, supplanted in faith by the younger people, they lost the grace of the blessing promised to them.

The Lord Christ appeared from Mount Paran because the more fiercely the ferocity of the unbelieving people raged against him, the more conspicuously and abundantly knowledge of his divinity increased. By handing him over to death and violently demanding his crucifixion, they sought to erase his name. But from the very place where he humbly lay hidden amid the insults of his passion, he shone forth more splendidly through the power of his resurrection. He subdued even his fiercest killers, overcoming the hardness of their unbelief and bringing them under the yoke of faith. Three thousand believed in him on one day, then five thousand, and afterward countless others. Those who had previously rejected him as though he were a Samaritan and had a demon afterward clung to him with an inseparable bond of faith and charity.

Concerning them it is said here: “And with him were thousands of holy ones.” It continues: “In his right hand was a fiery law.”

The elect are called the right hand of God. Therefore, in the right hand of God there is a fiery law, because the elect do not hear the heavenly commandments with a cold heart; rather, they burn toward them with the flames of inward love. The word is brought to the ear, and the mind, angry with itself, is consumed by the flame of inward sweetness.

Alternatively: The right hand of our Lord Jesus Christ is the preaching of the Gospel, through which eternal blessedness is promised—not temporal happiness, which is usually signified by the left, as in the law. Concerning this the bride speaks in the Song of Songs: “His right hand shall embrace me” (Song of Songs II). In this right hand there is a fiery law, namely love, poured into the hearts of the elect through the gift of the Holy Spirit. Concerning it the Apostle says: “Therefore the fullness of the law is love” (Romans XIII).

For this love is especially commended in the Gospel, when the Lord says: “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you. By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John XIII).

This love, poured out upon the apostles by the Holy Spirit appearing in fire on the tenth day after the Ascension, inscribed the whole fullness of the law in their minds as though by the finger of God, and makes all the elect shine through the fervor of the Spirit in their works.

But because this law was proclaimed through Christ not to one people, as the law of Moses was, but to all the nations, it immediately adds: “He loved the peoples.”

The first to fulfill the law of charity, which he commanded us to keep, was Christ himself, loving both peoples—the people of circumcision and the people of uncircumcision—and, coming to preach peace to us who were far away and peace to those who were near, because through him we both have access to the Father in one Spirit.

His most merciful passion commends this love, which he undertook for the salvation of the whole world. Concerning it he himself says: “No one has greater love than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John XV).

The Apostle kindles us to imitate this charity, namely, to observe the law perfectly, saying: “Be imitators of God, as beloved children, and walk in love, just as Christ loved us and gave himself for us as an offering and sacrifice to God for a fragrant aroma” (Ephesians V).

“All the saints are in his hand” (Ephesians V).

There is no partiality with God; rather, in every nation, whoever fears God and practices righteousness is acceptable to him. “All the saints are in his hand.” For all who have been justified in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and in the Spirit of our God, and who hear the Lord commanding, “Be holy, because I also am holy,” are protected from every evil by his power.

Concerning all of them he speaks figuratively in the Gospel: “And I give them eternal life, and they shall never perish, and no one shall snatch them out of my hand” (John X).

From the harmonious multitude of all the saints, therefore, the one most glorious kingdom of Christ is formed. Isaiah says to it: “And it shall be a crown of glory in the hand of the Lord, and a diadem of the kingdom in the hand of your God. And those who draw near to his feet shall receive his teaching” (Isaiah LXII).

The feet of the Lord Jesus Christ are the holy apostles and evangelists, whose teaching runs throughout the whole world. Concerning them it is written: “How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of those who proclaim peace, who proclaim good things” (Romans X).

Therefore, all who reverently draw near to these feet through devotion of faith, piety, and obedience should not be troubled that they did not see Christ himself teaching in the flesh; nor should they fear that they might be deceived by human beings as though they were merely human. For Christ speaks through their mouth, and through their feet the teaching of the Head is heard. Hence he himself says: “Whoever hears you hears me” (Luke X). And Paul cries out: “Do you seek proof of the one who speaks in me—Christ?” (II Corinthians XIII.)

All are therefore taught by him, even through the mouths of holy preachers, by whose hand the Church of all the elect is governed.

Or certainly, “those who draw near to his feet shall receive his teaching,” because the mysteries of the knowledge of Christ are revealed above all to those who, burning with spiritual desire, meditate day and night upon the evangelical and apostolic writings.

But because these things have been spoken about the evangelical law, those whose voice Moses represents next speak about the Mosaic law and say: “Moses commanded us a law, the inheritance of the multitude of Jacob.”

For this was the whole usefulness of the law: to command people to live justly, to avoid injustice, and faithfully to await the inheritance promised to the offspring of Abraham. But by commanding and not also assisting, it did not justify people from sins; rather, it even made sinners transgressors. Hence the Apostle says: “Where there is no law, neither is there transgression”; and again: “The law entered so that the trespass might abound” (Romans IV).

This was so that, when people recognized their weakness and therefore desired the help of the Mediator more ardently, grace might abound all the more when Christ came. Through that grace, the multitude of Jacob, concerning which it is written, “The multitude of believers was of one heart and one soul, in the seed of Abraham, which is Christ” (Acts IV), might receive the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom.

Since this multitude was redeemed from the curse of the law and received the blessing of grace, it is beautifully designated under the name of Jacob, to whom a promise concerning Christ is plainly made: “He shall be with the Most Upright, when the princes of the people are gathered together, together with the tribes of Israel.”

After Jacob had been blessed by the angel whom he overcame, he immediately received the name Israel, which, properly according to the Hebrews, means “upright of God.” A man who sees God does so not in the elements but in the sound of the voice.

Thus also the Jewish people, converted to faith in Christ and blessed by him after the resurrection—the one whom they had been commanded to overcome in his passion—received a new dignity of name, so that, on account of the perfection of righteousness, they might be called Israel, that is, “most upright.” To them God also speaks through Isaiah: “Hear, Jacob, my servant, and most upright one, whom I have chosen” (Isaiah XLIV).

Among this most upright people, therefore, Christ the King—who speaks in the Psalm, “But I have been appointed king by him over Zion, his holy mountain”—is promised to be present, dwelling by faith in their heart and making them his illustrious kingdom, just as he had previously promised through Moses: “You shall be for me a priestly kingdom and a holy nation” (Exodus XIX). And Micah had foretold: “And the first power, the kingdom of the daughter of Zion, shall come” (Micah IV).

The harmonious fullness of this kingdom is shown by the following words, when it says: “Namely, when the princes of the people are gathered into the unity of faith,” that is, the holy apostles, concerning whom it is written: “You shall appoint them princes over all the earth” (Psalm XVIII), together with the tribes of Israel, from all of whom an innumerable multitude believed in Christ the Lord.

Hence James also writes an Epistle to the twelve tribes that were in dispersion. The princes of the people are beautifully prophesied first, and the tribes to be gathered afterward, because the apostles were called to faith first, and afterward all the tribes were gathered through them.

As we said above, this was fulfilled in part at the first coming of the Savior. It will be fulfilled completely when, according to the Apostle, “the fullness of the nations has entered, and thus all Israel will be saved” (Romans XI).

But because Father Augustine, in his Book of Questions on Deuteronomy—from which we have set down much above—offered certain comments on this same blessing, we have judged that they should be placed here. Since he followed the edition of the Septuagint interpreters, he begins as follows:

“This is the blessing with which Moses, the man of God, blessed the children of Israel before he died. And he said: The Lord came from Sinai, and dawned from Seir for us; he hastened from Mount Paran with many thousands of Kadesh. At his right hand were angels with him, and he spared his people; and you sanctified all beneath your hands, and these are beneath you. And he received from his words the law that Moses commanded us, the inheritance of the assemblies of Jacob. And he shall be in the Beloved as prince, when the princes of the peoples are gathered together, together with the tribes of Israel.”

This prophecy must not be neglected. For it plainly appears that this blessing pertains to the new people whom the Lord Christ sanctified, and that these words are spoken by Moses from their person, not from Moses’ own person, as becomes evident in what follows.

For if it was said, “The Lord came from Sinai,” because the law was given on Mount Sinai, what does the following statement mean: “And he dawned from Seir for us,” since Seir is a mountain of Idumea, where Esau reigned? Moreover, when Moses blessed the children of Israel with these words, as Scripture had foretold, how does he himself say: “And he received from his words the law that Moses commanded us”?

It is plainly a prophecy, as we said, announcing beforehand the new people sanctified by the grace of Christ. They are called by the name of the children of Israel because they are the seed of Abraham—that is, they are children of the promise—and its interpretation is “seeing God.”

Since, therefore, the Lord came from Sinai, Christ must be understood, because Sinai is interpreted as “temptation.” He came from the temptation of passion, the cross, and death.

“And he dawned from Seir.” Seir is interpreted as “hairy,” which signifies the sinner. Thus Esau was born hated. But because light rose for those who were sitting in darkness and in the shadow of death, he dawned from Seir.

At the same time, it is not absurd to understand this as having been foretold concerning the nations, signified by the name Seir—for it is a mountain belonging to Esau—namely, that the grace of Christ would come to the people of Israel. Hence the Apostle says: “So they too have now disbelieved in your mercy, so that they also may obtain mercy.”

They therefore say: “He dawned from Seir for us, and he hastened from Mount Paran,” that is, from the fruitful mountain; for that is what Paran means, and it signifies the Church.

“With many thousands of Kadesh.” Kadesh is interpreted as “changed” and “holiness.” Many thousands were therefore changed and sanctified through grace, with whom Christ came for the Israelites who were to be gathered afterward.

It continues and says: “At his right hand were angels with him.” This requires no exposition.

“And he spared,” it says, “his people,” granting the remission of sins.

From there he turns his speech to him himself and says: “And all were sanctified beneath your hands, and these are beneath you.” They are not proud or seeking to establish their own righteousness; rather, they acknowledge grace and submit to the righteousness of God.

“And he received,” it says, “from his words.” He received the law that, it says, Moses commanded us—that is, his people. He received the law from his words because, from his teaching, they understood the law: the very law that Moses commanded us.

He himself also says in the Gospel: “If you believed Moses, you would believe me, for he wrote about me” (John V).

That people did not receive the law when they did not understand it; they received it only when they understood it—receiving it from his words and being freed from the old veil.

Turning to the Lord, he calls this the inheritance of the assembly of Jacob, which must be understood as heavenly rather than earthly, eternal rather than temporal.

“And he shall be,” he says, “in the Beloved as prince.” The Lord Jesus himself will be prince in the Beloved people, when the princes of the peoples—that is, of the nations—are gathered together with the tribes of Israel, so that what was said above may be fulfilled: “Rejoice, nations, together with his people.”

For blindness has occurred in part in Israel until the fullness of the nations enters, and thus all Israel is saved.

“Let Reuben live and not die, and let him be small in number.”

In the preceding discourse he had specifically prophesied the salvation of the primitive Church, which was chosen from the Jews. Now, bestowing individual blessings upon the individual tribes, he designates the true Israelites from both peoples. At one moment he prophesies about Christ, at another about the apostles, at another about the primitive Church from the Jews, and now generally about the whole Church together. That the people of the elect consists of twelve spiritual tribes, John, the beloved of the Lord, describes in the mystical Apocalypse.

“Let Reuben live,” he says, “and not die.”

Reuben is interpreted as “son of vision,” as his mother says: “God has seen my humiliation.” He is the firstborn of the patriarch Jacob.

He therefore signifies the elect people from the Jews, to whom divine mercy granted this: although, by denying and crucifying God, they had consigned themselves to eternal death, they were pierced with compunction at the preaching of the holy apostles, repented of their error, and, believing in Christ, lived by faith—though they had already been dead through unbelief.

Hence he is rightly called “son of vision,” because he is saved through the regard of divine mercy. Concerning this the Psalmist prays: “See my humiliation and my labor, and forgive all my sins” (Psalm XLII). And the Lord says to Hezekiah: “I have heard your prayer; I have seen your tears.”

This people, though small in number in comparison with the unbelieving nation of its own people, was nevertheless great and glorious in faith.

The Prophet therefore does not pronounce this as a wish of cursing, but, foreseeing the future blindness of that people, declares it together with the sentence of divine judgment:

“This is the blessing of Judah. Hear, Lord, the voice of Judah, and bring him to his people.”

Through Judah, whose name is interpreted as “confession,” the universal Church is signified, in which there is the confession of true faith and the praise of God. Here “confession” is understood as praise and thanksgiving, as his mother says: “Now I will confess to the Lord.”

She is therefore the true bride of Christ who, amid all the virtues with which she is adorned, does not exalt herself in anything, but gives praise and thanks to her bridegroom.

For her the Prophet prays that the voice of her faith and holy desire may be heard by the Lord. Concerning her he speaks elsewhere in the same way: “With my voice I cried to the Lord, and he heard me from his holy mountain” (Psalm III).

And he prays that she may be brought into the heavenly kingdom to her apostles—that is, to the patriarchs, prophets, and apostles through whom she was begotten in Christ—when what was foretold in the Gospel has been fulfilled: “For many will come from the east and from the west, and will recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew VIII).

Concerning this entrance it is said to the faithful servant: “Enter into the joy of your Lord.”

“His hands will fight for him, and his helper will be against his adversaries.”

Earlier he had poured out a prayer to the Lord; now he promises the Lord’s assistance to Judah himself. Let Judah therefore not presume upon his own strength, lest through that very arrogance he fall before his enemies, as it is written of the proud: “They were driven out and could not stand” (Ps. 35). Rather, let him always trust in the strength of him who says: “Have confidence; I have conquered the world” (John 16).

For his hands fought for him upon the wood of the cross against spiritual wickedness, so that through death he might destroy him who held the power of death. Against all his adversaries and persecutors he remains his helper, so that, having gained victory over his enemies, he may rejoice and say: “And upon my high places he will lead me, victorious, singing psalms” (Hab. 3). And again: “Lord, you have crowned us with the shield of your good will” (Ps. 5). For he himself conquered in us, and for his victory he crowns us with mercy and compassion.

“Levi also said: Your perfection and your doctrine are for your holy man.”

These words are spoken of the apostolic choir, of the army of all the martyrs, and of every order of the perfect—those who, dying for the Lord, fulfilled the perfection of charity and, renouncing everything, attained the summit of evangelical teaching. As true Levites, they had no portion in the earth, but said with the Prophet: “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance” (Ps. 15); and again: “I said, Lord, my portion is to keep your law” (Ps. 118).

Levi learned and received this admirable perfection from him who says in the Gospel: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Luke 9). And again: “Whoever loses his life for my sake will find it unto eternal life” (John 12).

For he is the holy man who did and taught all these things, as the Evangelist says of him: “What Jesus began to do and to teach.” Hence Levi’s holy man is said to be his, since he clung to that singular and divine holiness out of exceeding love, imitating him by fighting for the truth even unto bloodshed.

Therefore, concerning his passion, it is immediately added: “Whom you tested in temptation and judged at the waters of contradiction.” This is said by apostrophe to the Father. “For this holy man was tested,” as the Apostle says, “in every respect according to our likeness, except for sin” (Heb. 4).

But the devil inflicted the greatest temptation when he stirred up the souls of the Jews against his death with such obstinacy that they all cried out with one voice: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27).

When he had completed every temptation that he endured after the forty-day fast, as the Evangelist records, “the devil departed from him for a time” (Luke 4). But when the passion was at hand, the Lord Christ, explaining both the temptation that threatened him and his own thoroughly proven love and obedience, said: “For the prince of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me. But so that the world may know that I love the Father, and that I do as the Father commanded me: rise, let us go from here” (John 14).

And he rose for his passion, in which he endured the assault of the contradicting crowds of peoples like the force of overflowing waters. By the judgment of God the Father, who did not spare his own Son but delivered him up for us all, he was sentenced to death and accepted the passion of the cross.

Hence he himself said to his judge: “You would have no power against me unless it had been given to you from above” (John 19). And observe that the one who is tested and judged is called a man, because the Lord of majesty endured all these things in true humility, while remaining impassible in his divinity.

The exposition continues concerning the perfection of spiritual Levi:

“Those who said to their father and mother, ‘I do not know you’; and to their brothers, ‘I do not recognize them’; and who did not know their children: they kept your word and observed your covenant. Your judgments, O Jacob, and your law, O Israel.”

All this was fulfilled by the holy apostles, the martyrs, and all the perfect. Yielding to no affection, they looked upon fathers, mothers, brothers, and children—who wished to obstruct their purpose and from whom they were inwardly separated—as strangers and outsiders, and so, by the privilege of a special virtue above all the faithful, they are praised for having kept Christ’s word and covenant, and for having guarded the judgments and law of the true Jacob and Israel.

The chosen people are rightly called Jacob and Israel, because in this age they supplant vices, and in the age to come they will enjoy the vision of God. His judgments and law are specifically Christ’s commandments and the teaching of the Gospel.

The one who desires to know God more intimately is the one who, out of love for his goodness, desires not to know those whom he knew according to the flesh. For divine knowledge is diminished by a serious loss if it is divided with knowledge according to the flesh.

Everyone must therefore become, in some sense, a stranger to relatives and close associates if he wishes to be joined more truly to the Father of all. Thus he may love those whom, for God’s sake, he usefully neglects all the more firmly because in them he no longer recognizes the changeable affection produced by bodily kinship.

Certainly, even in temporal matters, we ought to benefit those to whom we are more closely joined more than others, because a flame extends a fire to the things brought near it, though it first burns the place where it arises. We ought to acknowledge the bond of earthly kinship, but nevertheless, when it obstructs the mind’s course, to disregard it, so that a faithful soul, kindled by devotion to God, may neither despise those joined to it here below nor, after rightly ordering them within itself, fail to rise above them with the greatest love.

We must therefore work with vigilant care lest affection for the flesh steal upon us and turn the steps of the heart away from the straight path, lest it hinder the gift of heavenly love and press the rising mind downward beneath an imposed weight.

Everyone ought to have compassion for the needs of relatives in such a way that, through compassion, he nevertheless does not allow the force of his purpose to be obstructed. Affection may indeed fill the heart’s inward parts, but it must not turn the person away from his spiritual purpose.
