For holy men do not fail to love their bodily relatives when necessary assistance is required; rather, through love of spiritual things they overcome that very affection within themselves, moderating it with such discernment that through it they do not deviate even slightly from the straight path.

The cows signify this well for us. Beneath the ark of the Lord, as they went toward the mountains, they advanced at once with affection and with resolute purpose. Having left their calves shut up at home, as it is written, they went onward lowing: they gave voice from the depths of their hearts, yet did not turn their steps aside from the path they had undertaken.

“They shall place incense in your anger, and a holocaust upon your altar.”

Historically, this is read as having been done by Aaron in the Book of Numbers when, because of the rebellion that arose among the people on account of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram, he ran into the midst of the assembly, which the fire was already destroying, and offered incense. Standing between the dead and the living, he prayed for the people, and the plague ceased.

In another sense, through the prayers of the saints—which are the sweetest incense before the Lord—the vengeance justly impending over a sinful people is softened. The purer the mind of such people has been cleansed of every touch of earthly desire, and the more it burns solely with heavenly longings, the more effectively their prayer appeases the anger of God. Like incense, it burns in God’s sight; and, like a most spotless holocaust, it rises from the altar of the devout heart into heaven on the flame of holy devotion.

This applies especially to the holy apostles and martyrs, through whose prayers God is often appeased toward the sins of his people, and who offered themselves wholly to the Lord as a holocaust upon God’s altar—that is, for the faith of Christ. Hence Scripture says of them: “As gold in the furnace he tested them, and as a holocaust offering he accepted them” (Wis. 17).

This is God’s altar beneath which John saw in the Apocalypse the souls of those slain for the word of God and for the testimony of Jesus crying out (Rev. 6). Concerning them it is added:

“Bless, Lord, his strength, and receive the works of his hands.”

The strength of the holy martyrs is blessed when their unconquered endurance is rewarded with heavenly glory. The same thought seems to be repeated in other words by the addition: “And receive the works of his hands.”

Now they are given individual white robes, as we read in the Apocalypse—namely, the blessed joy of their souls. At the future judgment, after receiving immortal and glorious bodies in the resurrection, they will shine, as Scripture says: “And they shall run to and fro like sparks among the reeds” (Wis. 3).

Thus they will consume their adversaries, empty in mind and fruitless in deed. Concerning the punishment of these adversaries it immediately follows:

“Strike the backs of his enemies, and let those who hate him not rise again.”

They seemed to themselves to be shedding the blood of so many holy martyrs with impunity. But a punishment was being prepared for them, as though upon their backs, a punishment they did not know how to foresee: namely, eternal condemnation, into which they would fall and from which they would no longer be able to rise.

They are struck by such a blow as Solomon describes: “And the rod is for the back of the senseless.” This will be displayed before the eyes of those who are struck when, placed in hell according to the Book of Wisdom and looking upon the glory of the holy martyrs whom they had hated here, they will say with late and fruitless repentance:

“These are they whom we once held in derision and made a reproachful example; we fools considered their life madness and their end without honor. How are they counted among the sons of God, and how is their lot among the saints?”—and so forth.

“And Benjamin said: The beloved of the Lord shall dwell in him securely.”

For in the Book of Genesis we read that Judah said to Joseph in Egypt concerning Benjamin: “His father loves him dearly. Therefore, if I enter before your servant, our father, and he is absent, while his life depends upon this boy’s life, when he sees that he is not with us, he will die.”

According to the historical sense, this appears to refer to Benjamin’s being loved both by the patriarch and prophet Jacob, his father, who was filled with the Spirit of God; and to the fact that, by God’s providential arrangement, the place where his worship was to be established most fully was assigned to his tribe—namely, Jerusalem, where God’s temple and altar were built.

Therefore it is added: “He shall dwell as in a bridal chamber all day long,” because at that time Jerusalem was the place that the Lord chose so that his name might be there.

Allegorically, however, our Lord Jesus Christ himself is the beloved of God the Father, concerning whom he said: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3). He dwells in the Father’s strength, because he sits at the right hand of power and reigns on high.

This may also be understood of his humanity, because in it the divinity dwells securely, having united it to himself in the unity of one person.

When it says, “He shall dwell in the bridal chamber, and between his shoulders he shall rest,” this signifies that, in the Virgin’s womb, the Church—joined to the heavenly Bridegroom—rests upon the strength of Christ’s power and finds the greatest confidence and repose of mind in his works.

In another sense, Benjamin, whose name was changed from “son of sorrow” into “son of the right hand,” signifies blessed Paul, who was suddenly changed from a persecutor into an apostle and became a chosen vessel for Christ.

He himself testifies that he was of this tribe, and here, through the prophetic Spirit, his future birth is foreseen. It was fitting that, just as the precursor—or rather the angelic dignity—of John the Baptist was foretold beforehand, so the teacher of the nations should be prophesied, amid the great mysteries of the Church, as destined to come in faith and truth for the grace of the whole world.

Loved by the Lord with exceptional affection, he was suddenly transformed from a persecutor into a preacher. He learned the Gospel through the revelation of Christ; he was caught up to the third heaven; in paradise he heard secret words that it is not permitted to human beings to speak.

Christ dwelt in his mind with such confidence of faith that, amid countless dangers, he boldly proclaimed him before nations, kings, and the children of Israel, crying out: “For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Phil. 1). And again: “In all confidence, as always, so now also, Christ will be magnified in my body, whether by life or by death” (ibid.).

Concerning this soul, adorned with every flower of virtue and most beautiful and beloved by Christ, it is further said: “He shall dwell as in a bridal chamber all day long.”

This may mean that he always enjoyed marvelous delight in Christ’s spiritual marriage, and that he made it fruitful with the offspring of divine understanding, never abandoning the secret recesses of his most peaceful heart to the disturbance of any vice.

Or certainly it may mean that Christ, dwelling in him as in a most beautiful bridal chamber, joined to himself through Paul’s preaching the virginal minds of believers—indeed, the Churches of diverse peoples—as a handsome bridegroom, more beautiful than the sons of men. Concerning them the Psalmist sings: “Virgins shall be brought to the king after her; her companions shall be brought to you” (Ps. 44). And to one of these he himself said: “For I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (2 Cor. 11).

How greatly his glorious labors, in which he toiled in evangelical teaching, were pleasing to Christ is shown by the words that follow, when it is further said of him: “And between his shoulders he shall rest.”

By the shoulders, with which we carry burdens, his most steadfast endurance is signified. Christ rested in him all the more willingly because Paul gloried in enduring everything for Christ even amid the harshest labors. He deserved to be embraced by Christ all the more closely because no labor and no tribulation separated him from Christ’s embrace.

When he enumerated his various dangers, he said: “But in all these things we overcome through him who loved us” (Rom. 8)—as though he were saying: “We conquer everything that opposes us for Christ because our mind does not withdraw from the arm of his love.”

“Joseph also said: His land is from the blessing of the Lord, from the fruits of heaven, and from the dew and the abyss lying beneath; from the fruits produced by the sun and the moon; from the summit of the ancient mountains; from the fruits of the everlasting hills; from the produce of the earth and from its fullness. May the blessing of him who appeared in the bush come upon Joseph’s head and upon the crown of the Nazirite among his brothers. His beauty is like that of the firstborn bull; his horns are the horns of the rhinoceros. With them he shall scatter the nations to the ends of the earth,” and so forth.

According to the historical sense, in the blessing of Joseph’s land, the fertility of the land is signified—the fertility possessed by the two tribes descended from Joseph, Ephraim and Manasseh—whether in the abundance of crops and fruits or in the feeding of livestock.

By comparing Joseph’s horns with the horns of a rhinoceros, it signifies that the tribe of Ephraim would one day hold the chief position among the ten tribes that separated from the house of David in the days of Rehoboam, son of Solomon, and reigned in Samaria.

Spiritually, however, the land of Joseph, whose name means “increased,” is the Church of the Lord Jesus Christ, concerning which the Psalmist sings: “You have blessed your land, O Lord” (Ps. 84).

Founded upon the firm stability of faith in him, it is filled with the riches of virtues not by its own power but by the blessing of the Lord of hosts, as Paul says: “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ.”

Having received the seed of the word of God in the Gospel, this land is shown to offer fruit—one hundredfold in virgins, sixtyfold in those practicing continence, and thirtyfold in the chastity of marriage.

Joseph signifies Christ, who, rejected by the Jews as though by his brothers, became ruler throughout the whole Egypt of this world and freed the entire human race from the eternal famine of want by distributing the grain of the Gospel.

He proved in himself that the name Joseph had received its true fulfillment, so that all might recognize that this one is truly the Savior of the world.

“From the fruits of heaven and from the dew and the abyss lying beneath.”

“Heaven” signifies the unity of faith and teaching, concerning which the Apostle says: “Whether I or they”—that is, the holy apostles and evangelists—“so we preach, and so you believed.” Elsewhere this is expressed in the plural: “The heavens declare the glory of God, and the firmament proclaims the works of his hands” (Ps. 18).

God dwells in these heavens, which shine with sublime life and contemplation as in his own heaven: there he thunders terrors, rains consolations, and flashes with miracles. Concerning this heaven it is written: “The heaven of heaven belongs to the Lord” (Ps. 113), because it is illumined not by human teaching but by the Spirit of God alone, with the brightness of heavenly wisdom.

Its fruits are fragrant and most pleasant fruits of virtue, by which the land of the holy Church is enriched most abundantly as it advances through their contemplation. Concerning these fruits the Lord said to them: “You did not choose me, but I chose you and appointed you to go and bear fruit, and that your fruit should remain” (John 15).

The dew descending from this heaven is the heavenly preaching of wonderful subtlety and grace. Through it the hearts of believers are watered inwardly, so that they do not wither in the heat of temptations but flourish with the unfading freshness of virtues.

Mystically, Jacob’s blessing speaks of this dew: “May God give you of the dew of heaven and of the fatness of the earth an abundance of grain, wine, and oil” (Gen. 27).

But the land of our Joseph flourishes in richer fertility when, from the inner grace given to us, it draws vital moisture as though from the abyss lying beneath, and when, from that place, the fountain of life rises, just as the Lord’s paradise is watered. Scripture says: “A spring rose from the earth, watering the whole surface of the earth” (Gen. 2).

Concerning this abyss, the Book of Ecclesiasticus says of the Savior: “For from the sea his understanding abounded, and his thought was from the great abyss” (Ecclus. 24).

For the word of a teacher waters someone outwardly in vain unless the inwardly watering grace of the Creator is present.

Hence it is further added: “From the fruits produced by the sun and the moon.”

The sun of justice is the Lord Jesus Christ, who says of himself in the Gospel: “Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Mark 12). Explaining this, John says: “We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3).

The fruits of this sun are the gifts of spiritual charisms. Enumerating them, the Apostle says: “The fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, gentleness, faith, modesty, self-control, chastity” (Gal. 5).

The moon of his sun is made manifest through the fruits when the holy Church is enriched with the endowment of spiritual gifts through the service of the Spirit of Jesus Christ. Hence the Apostle says: “To each one of us grace was given according to the measure of Christ’s gift” (Eph. 4)—that is, these are the fruits of the sun and the moon: the former gives, the latter receives.

Therefore, let the moon always look upon its sun with complete devotion, lest, if it turns away from him through pride, it fail to deserve illumination by his rays.

Concerning this moon it is said in the Song of Songs: “Who is this who comes forth like the rising dawn, beautiful as the moon,” and so forth (Song 6).

“From the summit of the ancient mountains, from the fruits of the everlasting hills.”

The ancient mountains are the patriarchs; they are also the prophets, lofty in life and sublimely raised to contemplate the mysteries of God. The everlasting hills are the other just men of the Old Testament, like pious and humble sons, founded with immovable firmness upon the faith of those mountains.

Contemplating the excellence of the Lord, Isaiah says of these mountains and hills: “It shall come to pass in the last days that the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be prepared on the summit of the mountains, and it shall be exalted above the hills” (Isa. 2).

The land of Joseph is blessed by the fruits of these mountains and hills when the Church of Christ, through the teaching of prophecy and their example of virtue, bears fruit in the faith of Christ with readier devotion.

It must be observed that above, in the fruits and dew of heaven, evangelical teaching is signified; here, in the virtue of the ancient mountains and the fruits of the everlasting hills, the teaching of the Law and prophecy is signified. The land of Joseph is enriched by both, because the holy Church is instructed by the pages of both Testaments and formed for the practices of holy conduct by the virtues of the fathers, both new and old.

Hence it is said to the same bridegroom in the Song of Songs: “All fruits, my beloved, new and old, I have kept for you” (Song 7). And he himself says in the Gospel: “Every scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven is like a householder who brings forth from his treasure new things and old” (Matt. 13).

Thus the Manichaeans and the Jews rightly could not receive an inheritance in this most prosperous land: the former do not accept the Old Testament, while the latter do not accept the New Testament. Concerning the abundance of this land it is further added:

“And from the produce of the earth and from its fullness.”

These words clearly show that this land, to which such an abundance of things is promised, must not be understood carnally as that portion of the inheritance which the sons of Joseph received in the land of Canaan, but spiritually as extending throughout the whole world.

It is therefore plainly the Church of Christ, fruitful throughout the world with the manifold produce of righteousness and filled with the abundance of spiritual gifts by her Joseph, of whom it is written in the Gospel that he was “full of grace and truth,” and “of his fullness we have all received” (John 1).

Hence it follows:

“May the blessing of him who appeared in the bush come upon Joseph’s head and upon the crown of the Nazirite among his brothers.”

The whole Joseph—that is, his head and his body—is filled with blessing. Hence the Apostle says: “He is the head of the body, the Church” (Col. 1); and again: “We, though many, are one body in Christ, and individually members one of another” (Rom. 12).

But the fullness of every blessing is assigned to the head, so that from it, according to the measure of his gift, it may descend into the whole body and into its individual members. Hence, under the figure of Aaron the priest, the Psalm sings of him: “Like ointment upon the head, which ran down upon the edge of his garment,” and so forth (Ps. 132).

By the privilege of incomparable grace, he surpasses all his brothers—that is, the faithful—and shines forth with the sevenfold grace of the Spirit, like a true Samson, a Nazirite from his mother’s womb, that is, consecrated to God, distinguished as though by seven untouched locks of hair.

The prediction that the blessing of him who appeared in the bush and said to Moses, “I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Jacob, and the God of Isaac” (Exod. 3), would come upon Joseph’s head plainly shows that the promise God made to those patriarchs would be fulfilled in Christ.

This means that all the nations of the earth would be blessed in their seed. Concerning his future passion and the glory of the resurrection that immediately followed, it is added:

“His beauty is like that of the firstborn bull.”

He is the bull and the fatted calf whom the most merciful father sacrificed for his repentant son, as though begotten according to the flesh from the stock of the patriarchs, like one from chosen cattle.

But on the third day he was raised from the dead and appeared gloriously to his disciples. John speaks of him in the Apocalypse: “The firstborn of the dead and the ruler of the kings of the earth” (Rev. 1). Paul says: “But now Christ has risen from the dead, the firstfruits of those who sleep” (1 Cor. 15; the supplied citation reads “XVIII”).

After prefacing the glory of the resurrection, he immediately adds a word concerning the power of the passion:

“His horns are the horns of the rhinoceros.”

The horns of the cross are signified. Concerning them Habakkuk says: “Horns are in his hands; there his strength is hidden” (Hab. 3). Explaining this, the Apostle says: “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2).

Although through the weakness of the flesh he clung to these horns like a ram crowned with the thorns and briars of those who mocked him, he nevertheless proved, through the incomparable strength of that very passion, to be a unicorn: victor over death, and through death destroying him who held the power of death.

Hence Paul says: “What is weak in God is stronger than human beings” (1 Cor. 1). And again: “He erased the record of debt that stood against us with its decrees, which was hostile to us; he removed it from our midst, fastening it to the cross. He stripped principalities and powers and exposed them publicly, triumphing over them in himself” (Col. 2).

The text continues concerning the horns of the most victorious cross:

“With them he shall scatter the nations to the ends of the earth.”

For through the preaching of the cross he subjected the whole world and all the ends of the earth to his faith by a hidden judgment, separating the chaff from the grain and unbelievers from believers. The proclamation of his passion is condemnation to some and salvation to others, as the Apostle says:

“We are the good fragrance of Christ before God, both among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing: to the one, an odor of life unto life; to the other, an odor of death unto death” (2 Cor. 2).

And again: “The word of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to those who are being saved—that is, to us—it is the power of God” (1 Cor. 1).

And elsewhere: “We preach Christ crucified: to the Jews, a stumbling block; to the Gentiles, foolishness; but to those who are called, Jews and Greeks alike, Christ the power of God and the wisdom of God” (ibid.).

## (Year 834.) Three Books of Blessed Rabanus Maurus, Abbot of Fulda and Archbishop of Mainz, on the Book of Joshua

(From Martène, *Amplissima Collectio*, vol. IX, p. 668, from a Cistercian manuscript.)

[Col. 999]

## Preliminary Observation

[Col. 999A] Rudolf the priest, his disciple, says in the Life of Rabanus, chapter 9, that Rabanus wrote four books on the Book of Jesus Nave. Trithemius, in Book III, chapter 3 of that same Life of Rabanus, mentions only two. Our old manuscript, of good quality, contains three, comprising a complete work.

Rabanus wrote these books while still abbot of Fulda, for Frideric, whom the same Rabanus testifies in the prefaces to his books on Judges and Ruth to have been bishop of Trajectum—namely Utrecht among the Frisians.

Meanwhile, Bishop Frideric suffered martyrdom for the faith of Christ and was later entered into the calendar of the saints on July 18. Several years after Frideric’s murder, Rabanus presented these same books on Joshua to the emperor Lothar, as that emperor himself testifies in a letter to Rabanus appended to Rabanus’s Commentary on Ezekiel.

Among the many distinguished matters scattered throughout this work, you will learn, reader, of some period of residence by Rabanus in the regions of the East, of which neither Rudolf nor Trithemius makes mention. For in commenting on the words of chapter 11, verse 8, he writes:

“Up to great Sidon. Although I myself have stayed in the regions of Sidon several times, I never discovered that there were two Sidons, one great and another small, insofar as the matter concerns the earthly location.”

This journey of Rabanus seems to belong to his youthful years, when he was not yet a teacher at Fulda, perhaps not even a monk, much less abbot of Fulda or archbishop of Mainz.

[Col. 999A]

## Dedicatory Letter to Frideric, Bishop of Trajectum

[Col. 999B] To the most blessed lord and greatly venerable Frideric, bishop, in the duty of true charity, Rabanus, the most worthless servant of the servants of God, sends greetings in Christ.

Many who know your holiness praise your zeal and diligence in meditating upon the sacred Scriptures—and rightly so, because you are constant in reading and frequent in teaching, as the order of your office requires. The Savior calls you, with the apostles, the light of the world and has placed you as a lamp, illumined by the true light, upon a lampstand, so that you may shine for all who are in the house of God.

Hence many of the brothers honor your veneration and, by honoring you, love you. You are also greatly beloved by us because you summon not only those who are present but also those who are absent to fraternal love, and by wholesome exhortation urge us to undertake with you the common work of studying God’s law.

What you do is not unreasonable, although we are unequal and unworthy for this task, since you seek confirmation of the sacred law where you received the beginning of your Christian religion. The most holy bishop and blessed martyr of Christ, Boniface, converted the people of the Frisians, over whom your beloved self presides, to the faith of Christ not only by his word but also by the shedding of his blood.

You therefore act reasonably in seeking the patronage of your ministry from him from whom you first received the function of your office and see. For this reason also, the aforementioned martyr, through his servant, graciously provides the consolation that you sought from him.

Since you have asked us for the comfort of divine reading, we have sent you a book that I compiled from the sayings of the holy Fathers, presented in the allegorical interpretation of the history of Jesus Nave. In this work, in a few places, because of the smallness of our understanding, wherever it was necessary, I inserted certain material by the grace of God.

I ask that you adapt it to the benefit of the brothers who are with you, so that from the type of the historical Jesus they may learn the mystery of the true Jesus, namely, the Lord and Savior, who redeemed us by his blood and saved us from the weakness with which, because of our sins, we were burdened.

Several years ago I lent you, for copying, a treatise on Matthew’s Gospel that I had composed at the request of Archbishop Haistulf, of blessed memory. But since I have not yet been able to receive it back, I have sent you the present work in place of a reward, so that, at least prompted by this favor, you may return the loan that you received.

Read carefully Jesus Nave, who prefigured Jesus Christ typologically not only in name but also in his deeds. He crossed the Jordan, overthrew the kingdoms of the enemies, divided the land among the victorious people, and through the individual cities, villages, mountains, and boundaries described the spiritual kingdoms of the Church and of the heavenly Jerusalem.

Thus you will recognize that the text of this book agrees with the evangelical reading, which displays the coming, preaching, passion, triumph, and victory of the Lord and Savior. By conquering death, he acquired for himself dominion over the heavenly, earthly, and infernal realms. Ascending into heaven and sitting at the right hand of the Father, he will come as judge of the living and the dead; and, according to the testimony of the apostle Jude, he will judge not only human beings but also angels.

In his Epistle he wrote as follows:

“I wish to remind you, though you know all things once for all, that Jesus, having saved the people from the land of Egypt, afterward destroyed those who did not believe. And the angels who did not preserve their own principality but abandoned their dwelling he has reserved in eternal chains under darkness for the judgment of the great day” (Jude 5).

Concerning the certainty of that day, the first of the apostles, Peter, instructs us in his Epistle, saying:

“Let this one thing not escape your notice, beloved: that one day with the Lord is as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day. The Lord is not slow concerning his promises, but deals patiently for your sake, not wishing anyone to perish but everyone to return to repentance.

“But the day of the Lord will come like a thief. On that day the heavens will pass away with great force, and the elements will be dissolved by heat. Since all these things are to be dissolved, what sort of people ought you to be in holy conduct and devotion, waiting for and hastening the coming of the day of the Lord, through which the burning heavens will be dissolved and the elements will melt in the heat of fire?

“But we await new heavens and a new earth according to his promises, in which righteousness dwells. Therefore, beloved, while you await these things, strive to be found by him spotless and blameless, in peace; and regard the patience of our Lord as salvation” (2 Pet. 3:8).

Therefore, holy Father, always keep before your eyes the day of this most sacred advent, and prepare yourself joyfully to meet the heavenly Judge with the lamps of good works shining. Thus, finding his grace, may you deserve to hear, together with those who will stand at his right hand:

“Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matt. 25:34).

May he himself grant that we joyfully hear this promise and receive that gift together—the Lord Jesus Christ, who has graciously rescued us from the power of darkness and summoned us into his kingdom.

We wish you good health, holy Father, and ask that you remember us in your sacred prayers. May the divinity of our Lord Jesus Christ preserve your life forever.

[Col. 1001B]

## The Commentaries on Jesus Nave Begin

## Book One

[Col. 1001]

## Chapter One

[Col. 1001C] The Lord’s address to Joshua concerning the duties of his leadership.

## (Chapter I)

“And it came to pass after the death of Moses, the servant of the Lord, that the Lord spoke to Joshua son of Nun, the minister of Moses, and said,” etc.

God bestowed upon our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ the name that is above every name. The name that is above every name is Jesus. And because this name, Jesus, is above every name, therefore “at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth.” And because this name is above every name, therefore throughout many generations no one was called by it as a surname.

Moses wrote the book of Genesis, in which we read about Abraham and those who were descended from him, among whom there are very many; yet none of them was deemed worthy to be called Jesus. Abel was not called Jesus, nor was the one who began to invoke the name of the Lord God, nor was the one who pleased God and was translated, whose death was never found—nor was Noah, who alone in his generation was found righteous before God. Nor was the one who had received the promises of the covenant, Abraham, nor the one born from him, Isaac; nor Jacob the Supplanter, nor any of his sons. Moses was faithful in all God’s house, yet he had not been called Jesus.

But I first find the name Jesus in Exodus, and I wish to observe when the name Jesus is first given as a surname. “Amalek came,” it says, “and fought against Israel; and Moses said to Jesus at Raphidim” (Exod. XVII). This is the first occurrence of the name Jesus: “Choose for yourself,” he says, “strong men from all the sons of Israel, and go out and fight against Amalek tomorrow” (ibid., v. 9).

Moses confesses that he cannot lead the army; he confesses that he cannot prevail, although he had brought the people out of the land of Egypt. Therefore, he says, he called Jesus and said, “Choose for yourself strong men,” he says, “and go out.” You see to whom he yielded the task of waging war against Amalek. Here, at the first occurrence of the name Jesus, we see him as commander of an army—not one to whom Moses assigned the leadership, but one who succeeded him in the primacy.

Moses cannot choose strong men. “You,” he says, “choose for yourself strong men from all the sons of Israel.” Here, therefore, where I first learn the name Jesus, I immediately also see the sacramental mystery: Jesus leads the army. “And it came to pass, when Moses raised his hands, Israel prevailed; but when he lowered his hands, Amalek prevailed” (Exod. XVIII).

Jesus therefore becomes stronger and conquers when Moses raises his hands. That people was defeated by Amalek when Moses did not raise his hands, but they hung down. For these are the people to whom it is said: “If you believed Moses, you would also believe me; and behold, you seek to kill me, you who do not keep the law” (John V).

This is the Jesus to whom Moses says: “The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet like me; you shall hear him. Every soul that does not hear that prophet shall be destroyed from among the people, etc. And behold, you seek to kill me, you who do not keep the law” (Deut. XVIII).

At this point the law has been dismissed, Moses’ hands have been lowered, the unbelief of the Jews has prevailed, and Amalek—that is, the devil—conquers. He conquered the Jews when they crucified Christ and did not believe when they saw the signs, because it had been said of them in the law: “You shall see your life hanging on a tree, and you shall not believe him” (Deut. XXVIII).

For when the law and the works of the law had ceased among them—since, while seeking to establish their own righteousness, they were not subject to the righteousness of God—Moses’ hands were lowered, unbelief prevailed, and the people were defeated.

But Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar were left in the camp to judge the people. Jethro, too, was left behind to judge the people with them. Jesus, however, was not left behind, but followed Moses up the mountain.

Here there is a remarkable addition of the word: “I have not come to abolish the law, but to fulfill it” (Matt. V). Jesus followed Moses, fulfilling the law in that it is said that he stood beside Moses. How did he stand beside him? Not as a second, not as an inferior, but as helper and protector.

And what of this: when Jesus is first named, the name of his father is not given, nor on the second or third occasion; but when his father is named Nave, he himself is called not Jesus but Auses (Num. XIII). Among those who were sent as spies, his name is written as Auses.

Perhaps it seems to me that, in accordance with the office of a spy, he was called not Jesus but Auses, and was named the son of Nave. But when he returned after completing his task, while all were terrified, he alone lifted up those who had fallen and alone raised the people from despair, then he is called Jesus by Moses; he is not called the son of Nave, but the one to whom Moses says: “Lead out the army and fight against Amalek.”

Let us consider his greatness in this respect. When the radiance of Moses’ face so dulled the sight of all the sons of Israel that no one could look upon the appearance of his face, Jesus not only gazed upon his face, but also remained within the inner part of the tabernacle, acquainted with its mysteries.

By what indication, then, do they perceive all these things? By this: that this book does not so much recount the deeds of the son of Nave as portray for us the mysteries of the Lord Jesus. For the one who assumed the command after the death of Moses is the one who will lead the army and fight against Amalek. And what was foreshadowed there on the mountain by outstretched hands, he fastens to his cross, triumphing in himself over principalities and powers.

Moses died, for the law ceased, since “the law and the prophets were until John” (Matt. XI, 13).

Do you want me to produce proofs from Scripture that Moses is called the law? Hear what he says in the Gospel: “They have Moses and the prophets; let them hear them” (Luke XVI)—where he is plainly calling the law “Moses.”

Moses, the servant of God, therefore died; for the law died, and the legal commandments have now ceased. If, then, you consider Jerusalem overthrown, the altar destroyed, sacrifices nowhere, neither victims nor libations anywhere, priests nowhere, high priests nowhere, and nowhere the ministries of the Levites—when you see all these things have ceased, say that Moses, the servant of God, has died.

If you see no one coming three times a year into the presence of the Lord, offering gifts in the temple, slaughtering victims, keeping the Passover or eating unleavened bread, offering firstfruits, or preserving the firstborn—when you do not see any of these things being celebrated, say that Moses, the servant of the Lord, has died.

But when you see the nations entering into the faith, churches being furnished, altars sprinkled not with the blood of animals but preserved by the precious blood of Christ; when you see priests and Levites ministering not the blood of bulls and goats but the word of God through the grace of the Holy Spirit, then say that Jesus, after Moses, has assumed and obtained the leadership—not that Jesus who is the son of Nave, but Jesus the Son of God.

When you see that “Christ our Passover has been sacrificed,” and that we eat the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth; when you see in the Church the fruits of righteousness in good soil—thirtieth, sixtieth, and hundredfold; righteous married women, widows, virgins, and martyrs; when you see the seed of Israel multiplied in those who were born not of blood, nor of the will of man, nor of the will of the flesh, but of God; and when you see the children of God who had been scattered gathered together into one according to their own will; when you see the people of God baptized, not withdrawing from common life, but keeping free from the working of sin—when you see all these things, say that Moses, the servant of God, has died, and that Jesus the Son of God holds the leadership.

But let us see what the Lord said to Jesus:

“Moses my servant is dead. Arise and cross this Jordan, you and all the people with you, into the land that I will give to the sons of Israel. Every place upon which the imprint of your feet shall tread, I will give to you, as I said to Moses, from the wilderness and Lebanon as far as the great river Euphrates.”

Perhaps you ask how our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, was also the minister of Moses. It was because, when “the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the law” (Gal. IV). By being made under the law, he became the minister of Moses.

God said that they should cross into the land—not the land Moses gave, but the land which, he says, “I give you.” You see, therefore, that after Moses’ death God gives the promised land to the people of Israel through Jesus.

What land? Without doubt that of which the Lord says: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall inherit the land” (Matt. V).

“Every place,” he says, “wherever you climb by the imprint of your feet, I will give it to you.” What are the places that we climb by the imprint of our feet, except the letter of the law, laid upon the ground and lying below? No one, therefore, who follows the letter of the law ever climbs.

But if you are able to ascend from the letter to the spirit, and to climb from the history to a higher understanding, then you have truly climbed to an elevated and lofty place, which you will receive from God as an inheritance.

If, then, in the things that you read in the figurative Scriptures, you understand the forms to be heavenly things, and seek with mind and understanding the things above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God, then you too will receive that place as an inheritance, since the Lord and Savior says: “Where I am, there will my servant be also” (John XII).

If, therefore, by faith, purity, life, virtue, and those footprints of your feet which Jesus washed, you reach Christ seated at the right hand of God and walk upon that place, God will give it to you. You will become not only an heir of God but also a joint-heir with Christ.

“Just as I was with Moses, so I will be with you; I will not abandon you, nor forsake you. Be strong and courageous, for you shall divide this land by lot among this people, the land concerning which I swore to your fathers that I would give it to them. Therefore be strong and very courageous, so that you may keep and do the whole law which Moses my servant commanded you. Do not turn away from it to the right or to the left, so that you may understand all that you do,” etc.

*(From Augustine.)* The Lord says to Jesus son of Nave: “And as I was with Moses, so I will be with you.”

Not only by this testimony, but also in Deuteronomy (chapter XXXIV), it is demonstrated by many proofs that Moses died in such a way as to be the servant of God and pleasing to God, although that punishment was fulfilled in him, namely, that he should not enter the promised land.

From this it may be understood that the Lord is angry in some respect even with his good servants, and punishes them temporarily, while nevertheless counting them among those vessels in his house that are for honor and useful to the Lord, to whom he will give the promises of the saints.

## Chapter II. Joshua’s command to the sons of Israel concerning the preparation of provisions for the journey, and the people’s reply to him

“And Joshua commanded the leaders of the people, saying: ‘Cross through the middle of the camp, command the people, and say: Prepare provisions for yourselves, because after three days you shall cross the Jordan and enter to possess the land which the Lord your God will give you.’”

*(From Augustine.)* The question arises how, after the Lord had spoken to Jesus son of Nave, exhorting and strengthening him and promising that he would be with him, that same Jesus commanded the people through the scribes to prepare provisions because they would cross the Jordan after three days, when they are found to have crossed the Jordan only after many more days.

After giving this command to the people, he sent spies into Jericho, since, once the Jordan had been crossed, that city was the first to be encountered. They, however, turned aside to Rahab, the prostitute, and were hidden by her. Although the king sought them, they were not found; and she let them down through the window and advised them to hide in the mountains for three days. Four days therefore seem to have been consumed.

Afterward, when they reported what had happened to them, Jesus moved out at dawn with the whole people from the place where he was. When he came to the Jordan, he turned aside and remained there. Then the people were again instructed to prepare themselves for crossing the Jordan during three days, with the ark of the Lord going before them.

From this it is understood that the arrangement he caused to be announced to the people—that they should prepare provisions as though they were going to cross the river after three days—was a human arrangement. For as a human being he could hope that this would be possible if the spies returned quickly. Since they were delayed, it is understood—although Scripture is silent about it—that the remaining events were fulfilled according to divine arrangement, so that Jesus might now begin to be glorified among the people and it might be shown that the Lord was with him as he had been with Moses.

This too is said to him as he is about to cross the river, as it is written. The Lord said to Jesus: “On this day I will begin to exalt you before all the sons of Israel, so that they may know that, as I was with Moses, so I will also be with you.”

Nor should it seem incredible that even those with whom God spoke wished to undertake something according to a human arrangement, while nevertheless seeing that God was their ruler, and that their plans were changed by the providence of the one by whom they were governed.

Moses himself, as a human being, had thought that he should hear the causes of the people in such a way that, by undertaking an intolerable burden, he would be unable to benefit either himself or them. His arrangement was changed by divine intervention, when his father-in-law also suggested and advised this very thing, and God approved the advice.

“And he said also to the Reubenites and Gadites and to half the tribe of Manasseh: ‘Remember the word which Moses, the servant of the Lord, commanded you, saying: The Lord your God has given you rest and all this land. Your wives, your children, and your livestock shall remain in the land which Moses gave you beyond the Jordan. But you shall cross over armed before your brothers, all you who are mighty in war, and fight for them until the Lord gives rest to your brothers, as he has given it to you; and they too shall possess the land which the Lord your God will give them. Then return to the land of your possession, and you shall dwell in it, in the land which Moses, the servant of the Lord, gave you beyond the Jordan, toward the rising of the sun,’” and the rest.

*(From Adamantius.)* Let us therefore consider what form is represented by these two and a half tribes, which receive the land of their inheritance through Moses, and what form is represented by the remaining nine and a half tribes, which receive the promise of the holy land through Jesus.

First of all, I think it impossible that it happened by chance that those who receive their portion through Moses were firstborn. Reuben is the firstborn of Leah; Gad is the firstborn of Zilpah; and Manasseh is the firstborn of Aseneth, daughter of the Egyptian Petepre, priest of Heliopolis, whom Joseph took as his wife.

I could never be persuaded, therefore, that it happened by chance that all those whose inheritance was apportioned through Moses were firstborn. Rather, I think that in them the form of peoples was already foreshadowed: one people appearing firstborn according to the order of nature, and another receiving the blessing of inheritance through the grace of faith.

Nor is rest first given to those who receive their inheritance through Moses—that is, to those who pleased God through the law—unless they help their brothers in battle. Only the women and infants receive rest through Moses; the others do not rest but go out to aid their brothers.

See how those who were justified in the law before the advent of Jesus Christ, my Lord, come to the aid of me, who labor today in the contest of this life and engage in battle against enemies—that is, opposing powers.

See how Isaiah offers assistance and enlightens me with the words of his reading. See Jeremiah girded and ready, helping us, and driving away the fiercest enemies—the darkness of my heart—with the arrows of his book.

Daniel too girds himself for assistance when he instructs and warns us concerning Christ’s presence and kingdom and the future deceit of Antichrist. Ezekiel is also present, marking out for us heavenly mysteries in the fourfold circles of the wheels and enclosing wheel within wheel.

Hosea leads twice six companies of the prophetic host. All go forth with their loins girded in the truth they proclaim, to aid their brothers, so that, instructed by their books, we may not be ignorant of the devil’s cunning.

These, then, who are strong men, armed and girded about their loins with truth, go out to help us. Their number is completed, and they fight together with us.

But the infants and women do not go out to our battle. Nor is this surprising, for one who does not speak is not called a man. How, then, could one who has said nothing help me—one in whose writings I find nothing to read, whose answer does not instruct me?

The apostle called woman a weak vessel (I Pet. III). Therefore, let the weak vessel not come to the conflict, lest it be broken and perish. Thus it is also said of Jesus the Lord in the Gospels: “He shall not break a bruised reed” (Matt. XII).

Since women are commanded to be taught at home by their husbands and are placed more in the role of disciples than of teachers, let no one who cannot teach me come to my aid.

What, then, do these who come from the land distributed by Moses say to Jesus? “As we obeyed Moses,” they say, “so we shall obey you.”

Nothing is truer than that everyone who hears Moses also hears Jesus our Lord, for Moses wrote about Jesus. Therefore the Lord, rebuking those who, because they do not believe him, do not believe Moses either, says: “If you believed Moses, you would also believe me, for he wrote about me” (John V).

Yet it does not seem pointless to me that these are not three whole tribes, nor are those who obtain their inheritance through Jesus nine whole tribes, but here there are two and a half and there nine and a half. Thus one tribe is divided into two parts, so that neither here is the number three completed, nor there are ten perfect and whole tribes brought to completion.

By this, I think, it is indicated that those earlier people who lived under the law did indeed possess knowledge of the Trinity, but not wholly and perfectly, only in part. For they lacked knowledge in the Trinity of the incarnation of the Only-Begotten.

Although they not only believed in his coming but also proclaimed it, they were nevertheless unable to see and attain what they believed, just as the Lord said to his disciples concerning them: “Many righteous men and prophets desired to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear and did not hear it” (Luke X).

Their faith was not complete because the dispensation of the flesh had not yet been fulfilled in Christ. What we now believe to have happened and been fulfilled, they believed only as something future.

Therefore those tribes are neither two nor outside the faith of the Trinity; nor are they three whole and perfect tribes, lest the mystery of the blessed Trinity appear already to have been fulfilled in them. Rather, they reach the number three.

And, as the Lord said, they desired to see what we have seen and to hear what we have heard, but they could not, because the Son of Man had not yet been exalted, nor had the fullness of time come.

Something else also troubles me. I think that perhaps even in the advent and incarnation of Jesus we do not yet have what we have called perfect and complete. Even if he is led to the cross and consummated in all things, and even if he rises from the dead, he does not disclose to us by himself everything that is perfect.

We still need another work to open and reveal everything to us. Hear the Lord himself saying: “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot hear them now. But the Spirit of truth will come, who proceeds from the Father; he will receive from what is mine, and he will declare all things to you” (John XVI).

You see that not only among those represented by Moses is this third number shown not to be completed, but Jesus also still says to his disciples: “You cannot yet hear unless that Paraclete, the Spirit of truth, comes,” because through him and in him the perfection of the Trinity is fulfilled.

Since, then, the nine and a half tribes are those governed under Jesus, and not the complete ten—the number said to be consummate and perfect in all things—the same reasoning is certainly found here: that which is said to be reserved by our Lord Jesus appears incomplete and partial with respect to the Holy Spirit.

For although repentance and conversion from evil to good are proclaimed through the Lord and Savior, forgiveness of sins is given to all who believe, and all things that seem to tend toward perfection in him are fulfilled, nevertheless the perfection and summit of all good consists in this: that after all these things a person should be found worthy to receive the grace of the Holy Spirit.

Otherwise nothing will be considered perfect in one who lacks the Holy Spirit, through whom the mystery of the blessed Trinity is fulfilled.

Do you want me to prove to you still more clearly that, among the earlier people whom Moses foreshadowed in the two and a half tribes, not everything was whole and perfect?

That history also makes this clear which is written in this book of Jesus son of Nave: the true altar was in the land administered by Jesus, but those who were beyond the Jordan—that is, Reuben, Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh—made an altar for themselves, not a true altar, but one that bore the type and likeness of the true altar that was with Jesus.

Do not therefore be surprised if those who had built neither a true nor a complete altar had not received complete knowledge of the Trinity.

For this reason, too, they are not said to have cast down many enemies or numerous kings of the opposing powers. “They defeated,” it says, “only Sihon, king of the Amorites, and Og, king of Bashan, and the Amalekites beyond the Jordan.”

But when Jesus leads the army, five kings fall at once, having fled into caves; and they do not merely fall, but are also hanged upon a tree. Now twenty-nine are slaughtered together, immense multitudes of the opposing army are struck down, and all who possess the holy land in uncleanness are destroyed—all who hold the land flowing with milk and honey in the bitterness of wickedness.

“As we obeyed Moses in all things, so we shall obey you; only may the Lord God be with you as he was with Moses. Whoever contradicts your mouth and does not obey all the words that you command him shall die,” etc.

The Reubenites and Gadites, together with half the tribe of Manasseh, therefore condemn the Jewish people for disobedience, saying: “As we obeyed Moses in all things, so we shall obey you,” while by their pledge they offer testimony corresponding to the command of the lawgiver.

For Moses says: “The Lord will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers. You shall hear him as you heard me; but whoever does not hear that prophet, his soul shall be destroyed from among his people” (Deut. XVIII).

But when the Lord and Savior came and preached the Gospel, they were always not devoted and obedient but ungrateful and hostile toward him, cursing the man born blind who had been enlightened by him and saying: “You are his disciple; but we are disciples of Moses” (John IX).

And when Pilate said, “Shall I crucify your king?” they answered: “We have no king except Caesar” (John XIX).

Therefore what their parents had called down upon them came upon them, so that they should die the death: they experienced not only eternal condemnation in soul but also the destruction of their bodies, being everywhere consumed by famine, struck by pestilence, killed by the sword, and scattered throughout the whole world in the most cruel captivity.

## Chapter III. Concerning the spies sent from Shittim to the city of Jericho and saved by a prostitute

“Joshua son of Nun therefore sent two men secretly as spies from Shittim, and said to them: ‘Go and inspect the land and the city of Jericho.’ They went and entered the house of a woman who was a prostitute, named Rahab, and rested with her,” and the rest.

This Jesus sends two spies to the city of Jericho, and they are received by Rahab the prostitute. That Jesus, the leader of the people, manifests the Lord Christ both by his name and by his deed.

Jericho, however, is the world, to which the Lord Jesus Christ sent the two Testaments to examine human conduct. For, in order to test more fully the faith of believers or the obstinacy of rebels, before the advent of his judgment he sent, as it were, two spies— the Law and the Gospel.

Rahab represents the Church, which has been gathered from foreign and alien nations and which, previously living in the desires of the flesh, committed fornication with idols. Concerning such people the Lord says “that they will go before you into the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. XXI).

She alone, therefore, receives these Testaments of the Lord and preserves them faithfully. She does not hand them over to her enemies at all; rather, she is willing to face danger, provided that she herself may be kept unharmed and safe.

She firmly believed that the world would fall, just as that woman believed the city would fall. For herself and for the salvation of all her people she made a covenant with the Lord’s Testaments. In her house she placed scarlet—the sign of blood. If anyone is found outside this house, he will in no way escape the ruin of the age and the conflagration of the world.

*(From Adamantius.)* Spies are sent by Jesus into Jericho and are received by Rahab the prostitute. These spies, who are sent before Jesus, may also be understood as the angels of God, as it is written: “Behold, I send my angel before your face, who prepares your ways before you” (Matt. XI). This is confirmed invisibly through others, but visibly in John, concerning whom this too is written.

Finally, concerning John’s baptism the Lord says that “the scribes and Pharisees did not believe him, but the prostitutes and tax collectors believed and were baptized” (Matt. XXI).

Thus what happened here is also fulfilled: the prostitute received Jesus’ spies, through whom it is reported that she was rescued from the destruction of the entire hostile nation.

But let us finally see who this prostitute is. She is called Rahab. Rahab is interpreted as “breadth.” What, then, is this breadth except the Church of Christ, which has been gathered from sinners as from a prostitute?

And she says: “The place is too narrow for me; make me a place where I may dwell. Who raised these children for me?” (Isa. XLIX). And again it is said to her: “Enlarge your stakes and extend your tents” (Isa. LIV).

This, then, is the breadth that received Jesus’ spies.

I remember once disputing in a certain church about the two prostitutes of whom it is written in the Third Book of Kings (III Kings III), who had come to Solomon’s judgment. One of them had a living infant. I examined the matter more carefully and said that this prostitute was the one to whom Solomon—not that Solomon, but the one who came to make peace between those in heaven and those on earth—commanded that the living infant be returned. The other, who had a dead infant, represented either the synagogue of the earlier people or those who had fallen into heresy.

There is also the other prostitute whom the prophet Hosea is commanded to take (Hos. I), unquestionably as a figure of this woman who has been consecrated from the nations.

This woman, then, who receives Jesus’ spies, is also called a prostitute. But she places those whom she has received above, establishing them in the lofty and elevated mysteries of faith. No one who is sent by Jesus is found below and lying upon the ground; rather, he remains in the higher and loftier places.

But this prostitute who receives them is made a prophet from being a prostitute, for she says: “I know that the Lord your God has given you this land.”

You see how she was once a prostitute, impious and unclean, but now she has been filled with the Holy Spirit. She confesses concerning the past, believes concerning the present, and prophesies and foretells concerning the future.

Thus Rahab, whose name is interpreted as “breadth,” is enlarged and advances, until her sound goes out through the whole earth. Japheth, too, is similarly interpreted as “enlargement.”

But let us see what this wise prostitute did with the spies. She gives them a mystical and heavenly counsel, having nothing earthly in it: “Go away,” she says, “through the mountainous country.”

Do not walk through the valleys; avoid low and depressed things. Proclaim what is lofty and sublime.

She herself received the scarlet sign, which bore the appearance of blood. For she knew that there was salvation for no one except in the blood of Christ.

This command is also given to the woman who had once been a prostitute: “All who are found in your house shall be saved; but whoever goes out of your house, we shall be free from this oath of yours.”

If anyone therefore wishes to be saved, let him come into this house of the woman who was once a prostitute. If anyone from that people wishes to be saved, let him come into this house in which Christ’s blood is present as the sign of redemption.

For among those who said, “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. XXVII), Christ’s blood is for condemnation. Jesus had been appointed for the fall and resurrection of many; therefore, for those who oppose his sign, his blood becomes punishment, but for those who believe, salvation.

Let no one persuade himself otherwise; let no one deceive himself. Outside this house—that is, outside the Church—no one will be saved. If anyone goes outside, let him be guilty of his own death. This is through the sign of blood, because this is the purification established through blood.

As for the fact that the sign hangs in the window, I think this indicates that the window illuminates the house and through it our sight is illuminated, but that we receive only as much light as is sufficient for our eyes and our use.

Since the incarnation of the Savior does not grant us a true and complete vision of the Godhead, but through his incarnation has enabled us to see the light of the Godhead as through a window, it therefore seems to me that the sign of salvation was given through the window. Through this sign all who are found in the house of the woman who was once a prostitute obtain salvation—in water and the Holy Spirit, in the blood of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.

## Chapter IV. Concerning the crossing of the sons of Israel through the channel of the Jordan and the division of the waters at the entry of the Lord’s ark

### (Chapter III)

“Joshua therefore rose during the night and moved the camp. They went out from Shittim and came to the Jordan, he and all the sons of Israel, and they remained there for three days.”

Every place therefore receives the righteous person, and every creature offers him the service that is his due. To sinners every creature is hostile: the earth attacked them, the air itself attacked them, and heaven attacked them.

But for the righteous, even things that seem inaccessible are made level and easy. The righteous person crosses the Red Sea as though on dry land, whereas the Egyptian, if he wishes to cross, is drowned, and the sea does not become a wall for him on the right and left.

And lest you perhaps be offended that the things which happened earlier do not now happen in you, who are listening to these things, everything is fulfilled in you according to the mystical meaning.

For you, who recently abandoned the darkness of idolatry and desire to approach the hearing of the divine law, now first leave Egypt when you have been enrolled among the catechumens and have begun to obey the ecclesiastical commandments.

Therefore, according to the custom of the Israelites, you must remain for three days before entering the Jordan, so that you may learn the faith of the Holy Trinity: how, having been baptized in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, you may receive forgiveness of all sins; and how thereafter you must live, so that, walking in newness of life, you may be found worthy to enter the heavenly kingdom.

*(Ibid.)* “When these things had been completed, the heralds passed through the middle of the camp and began to cry out: ‘When you see the ark of the covenant of the Lord your God and the priests of the Levitical lineage carrying it, you too shall rise and follow those who go before you.’”

Having departed from the Red Sea and been stationed in the desert encampments, you devote yourself each day to hearing the law of God and beholding the face of Moses revealed through the glory of God.

But if you also come to the mystical font of baptism, and, with the priestly and Levitical order standing there, are initiated into those venerable and magnificent mysteries—those know them whom it is permitted to know—then, together with the ministries of the priests, after the Jordan has been crossed, you will enter the promised land.

There Jesus receives you after Moses, and he himself becomes your guide on the new journey.

The text continues:

*(The same passage.)* “Let there be between you and the ark a distance of two thousand cubits, so that you may see it from afar and know by what way you are to enter, since you have not traveled by it before; and take care not to approach the ark,” and so forth. (From Augustine.) The ark was ordered to go far ahead so that it could be seen by the people. For such a great host, if it proceeded close behind it, would not see it going before them, nor know by what route to follow. From this action we are to understand that the pillar of cloud, which used to give the signal for breaking camp and to show the way, had already withdrawn and was no longer visible to them. Hence it happened that even that three-day period was announced as a matter of human arrangement. Now, therefore, with Jesus as their leader, they follow the ark of the Lord, the cloud having been withdrawn, as though the veil had been removed. Consider finally what is said about them: “The people,” he says, “were two thousand cubits from the ark of the covenant, while the priests and Levites were nearest, indeed very near, so that the ark of the Lord and the divine law were carried upon their shoulders.” Blessed are those who deserve to be near to God. But remember what is written: “Those who draw near to me draw near to fire” (Isa. LXV). If you are gold or silver and draw near to fire, you will shine back far more splendidly and brilliantly because of the fire. But if, having been placed upon the foundation of such great faith, you are conscious that you have built upon it wood, hay, and straw (I Cor. III), then, if you draw near to fire with such a building, you will be consumed. Blessed, therefore, are those who are near, so that the fire may illumine them and not burn them. Israel, too, will be saved, but will be saved while standing far away; and he journeys not by his own strength but with the assistance and guidance of the priests.

*(The same passage.)* “And the Lord said to Joshua: Today I will begin to exalt you before all the people of Israel, so that they may know that just as I was with Moses, so I am also with you,” and the rest. How many things had already been accomplished! The Red Sea had been crossed on foot, manna had been given from heaven, springs had burst forth in the wilderness, the law had been given through Moses, and many signs and wonders had been performed in the wilderness; yet nowhere is it said that Jesus had been exalted. But when the Jordan is crossed, it is said to Jesus: “On this day I begin to exalt you in the sight of the people.” For Jesus is not exalted before the mystery of baptism; rather, the beginning of his exaltation before the people is taken from that event. If all who are baptized into Christ Jesus are baptized into his death—and the death of Jesus is completed in the exaltation of the cross—then rightly Jesus is first exalted for each of the faithful when he reaches the mystery of baptism, because it is written “that God exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Phil. II).

*(The same passage.)* “And Joshua said to the children of Israel: Behold, the ark of the covenant of the Lord of all the earth will go before you through the Jordan. Prepare twelve men from the tribes of Israel, one from each tribe. And when the priests carrying the ark of the Lord of all the earth place the soles of their feet in the waters of the Jordan, the waters below will flow away and fail, while the waters coming from above will stand in one mass.” The people are led by the priests and journey toward the promised land. Such and so great is the people under the instruction of the priests that it deserves to be enrolled in that order. For if someone is of such a kind that the streams of the Jordan cease for him, even the elements themselves will show reverence: part of the river’s waters will spring backward and be checked behind them, while another part will rush down into the Salt Sea and fail there. Yet I do not think that even this was written without a mystical meaning: one part of the Jordan’s waters sinks into the sea and flows forth in bitterness, while another part remains in sweetness. If all who are baptized preserved the sweetness of heavenly grace that they had received, and no one were turned toward the bitterness of sins, it certainly would not have been written that part of the river had been submerged in the whirlpools of the Salt Sea. Therefore, I think that these words indicate the diversity among the baptized, which we ourselves—something I recall with grief—often see happening: those who receive holy baptism, when they again surrender themselves to worldly affairs and the allurements of lust, and when they drink the salty cup of greed, take their form in that portion of the waters which flows into the sea and perishes amid the salty waves. But that portion which remains steady and preserves its sweetness signifies those who hold unwaveringly to the gift of God that they have received. And rightly there is one portion belonging to those who are saved, because there is one bread that descended from heaven and gives life to this world; there is one faith, one baptism, and one Spirit by whom all are given to drink in baptism, and one God, the Father of all.

*(The same passage.)* “Then the people went out from their tents to cross the Jordan, and the priests who carried the ark of the covenant proceeded before them,” and so forth. Meanwhile, the priestly and Levitical order, which showed the way to the people of God who came out of the land of Egypt, is itself the order that teaches the people to leave Egypt—that is, to pass from the errors of the world through the vast wilderness, meaning to traverse the various kinds of temptations, and to avoid being harmed by serpents, which are the bites of demons and the poisons of evil suggestions. If someone should happen to be bitten by a serpent in the wilderness, the priestly order is the one that shows him the bronze serpent hanging upon the cross; whoever looks upon it—that is, whoever believes in the one whose figure that serpent represented—will thereby escape the demonic poisons. The priestly and Levitical order is the one that stands beside the ark of the covenant of the Lord, in which the law of the Lord is carried, undoubtedly so that they themselves may illumine the people with the commandments of God, as the Prophet says: “Your word is a lamp to my feet, O Lord, and a light to my paths” (Ps. CXVIII). This light is kindled through the priests and Levites. But if someone from this order places the kindled lamp under a bushel rather than on a lampstand, so that it may shine for everyone in the house, let him consider what he must do when the Lord of light begins to demand an account for those who, receiving no illumination from the priests, walk in darkness and are blinded by the obscurity of their sins.

*(The same passage.)* “Now the Jordan had filled the banks of its channel at the time of harvest.” (From Augustine.) “The Jordan was full along its entire bank, as in the days of the wheat harvest.” This seems incredible in our regions; but there, as those who know report, the wheat harvest occurs at the beginning of spring. At that time the river is fuller than during the winter.

**CHAPTER IV.**

“But the priests who carried the ark stood in the middle of the Jordan until everything had been completed that the Lord had commanded Joshua to tell the people, as Moses had instructed him. And the people hastened and crossed. When everyone had crossed, the ark of the Lord also crossed. The priests, too, proceeded before the people. (From Adamantius.)”

Concerning those who crossed the Red Sea, the Apostle said, “all were baptized into Moses, in the cloud and in the sea” (I Cor. X). But concerning those who crossed the Jordan, we too may speak in a similar manner: all were baptized into Jesus in the Jordan, so that the events reported as having taken place in the Jordan bear the form of the sacrament celebrated through baptism.

But the statement that is written—“The people hastened and crossed the Jordan, and the ark of the covenant of the Lord”—does not seem to me to have been added by the Holy Spirit without purpose, when it says that “the people hastened to cross.” Therefore I think that we too, when we come to saving baptism and receive the sacraments of the word of God, must not conduct the matter carelessly or sluggishly; rather, we must hasten and press forward until we have crossed everything. To cross everything means to fulfill everything that is commanded.

Let us therefore hasten to cross—that is, to fulfill first what is written: “Blessed are the poor in spirit” (Matt. V)—so that, laying aside all arrogance and embracing the humility of Christ, we may deserve to reach the promised blessedness. But when we have fulfilled this, we must not stop or cease; we must cross also what follows, so that we may hunger and thirst for righteousness. We must cross what follows as well, so that we may mourn in this world. The remaining things, too, must quickly be crossed, so that we may become meek, remain peacemakers, and thereby be able to be sons of God. We must also hasten so that by the virtue of patience we may cross the burden of persecutions.

When we seek each of these things pertaining to the glory of virtue—not sluggishly or half-heartedly, but with all urgency and speed—this, it seems to me, is what it means to cross the Jordan with haste. But once we have crossed and have been able to obtain what we ought to obtain, then concern for diligence and caution must again take its place, lest, proceeding too carelessly, our steps should be poured out through some unexpected fall. As the Prophet also says: “My steps had almost slipped” (Ps. LXXII).

**CHAPTER V. On the sons of Reuben and Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh, and on the twelve stones that Joshua carried from the channel of the Jordan and set up at Gilgal.**

*(The same passage.)* “The sons of Reuben and Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh, armed, went before the children of Israel, as Moses had commanded them. And forty thousand fighting men advanced in companies and formations across the plains and open country of the city of Jericho.”

Our concern to preserve virtues ought not to be less than our concern to acquire them. Or do you not think that this is signified for you when it is said that forty thousand armed and equipped men crossed over to battle before the Lord in order to conquer the city of Jericho? Let us ask who these are whom Scripture calls armed or equipped. I do not dare to presume anything and pronounce judgment on my own authority. Let us rather be taught in such matters by the writings of the Apostles.

Let us learn who these armed men are from Paul’s explanation. Hear what he himself says: “Therefore gird your loins with truth” (Eph. VI). You see, then, that Paul knows those who are girded with the belt of truth. Thus truth must also be our belt, provided that we preserve the sacramental meaning of this warfare and this belt. For if truth is our belt, by which we are girded for the service of Christ, then whenever we speak falsely and a lie proceeds from our mouth, we are ungirded from the service of Christ and released from the belt of charity. Let us therefore be girded with truth, lest we be ungirded in falsehood. Rather, let us imitate those forty thousand men who were girded and went before the Lord, and let us always be tightly girded with truth.

Do you wish to learn what battles and wars we must undertake after baptism? Learn it again, not from me, but from the Apostle himself. He teaches you, saying: “For our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against rulers and authorities, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly places” (Eph. VI).

These things that have been written are forms and figures. For the Apostle says: “All these things happened to them as a figure; but they were written for our correction, upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (I Cor. X). If, therefore, they were written for our sake, what are you waiting for? Let us go out to war, so that the first city of this world may be conquered by us, and the proud walls of wickedness and sin may be destroyed.

Perhaps you are looking around to see by what route you should proceed, and what field of combat you ought to seek—what I am about to say may perhaps seem new to you, but it is nevertheless true—and are looking for it somewhere outside yourself. The battle is within you; the conflict you are to wage is inward. That evil structure which must be overthrown proceeds from your own heart; your enemy comes from your own heart. These are not my words but Christ’s. We have heard him say: “For from the heart proceed evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false testimonies, blasphemies, greed, wickedness, deceit” (Matt. XV). Do you see how large and what kind of army of your enemies proceeds against you from your own heart? These are the ones whom we must first strike down; these are the ones whom we must first overthrow in the front line. If we have demolished their walls, we shall also be able to cut them down to destruction, leaving none of them to report or breathe again. If none of them has risen again at all in our thoughts, then through Jesus that rest will be granted to us, so that each may rest under his own vine and under his own fig tree, when there is no longer anyone to terrify the children of Israel.

Nevertheless, forty thousand armed men cross the Jordan, girded before the Lord for battle. Then Scripture says: “On that day the Lord magnified Joshua before all Israel, so that they feared him as they had feared Moses while he was still alive,” and the rest.

There had indeed been an exultation for the son of Nun, so that as leader of that people he might be magnificent in the eyes of those whom he governed. But let us see how our Jesus, my Lord, the leader and ruler of this people, is exalted in the sight of the whole race of the children of Israel. I think that he was always exalted and lofty before the Father, but what is necessary is that God the Father exalt him in our sight.

He is exalted in my sight when the sublimity and loftiness of his divinity are revealed to me. When, then, were the heights of his divinity revealed to me? Surely when I crossed the Jordan, holding in the various sacraments the future weapons for battle. “And they feared,” it says, “Jesus as they had feared Moses.” Everyone who is under the law fears Moses; but when he passes from the law to the Gospel, his observance changes and his fear changes as well, as the Apostle says: “Through the law I died to the law, so that I might live to God; and I have been crucified with Christ. It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. II).

*(The same passage.)* “The twelve stones also, which they had taken from the channel of the Jordan, Joshua set up at Gilgal,” and so forth.

Thus, when the children of Israel crossed the Jordan, they took twelve stones from the middle of the river and set them up as a testimony at the place of the second circumcision, signifying for us that when we rise from the washing we must carry with us the firmest examples of apostolic life, whose testimony we should always contemplate as a pattern for the imitation of virtue.

*(The same passage.)* “Joshua also set up twelve other stones in the middle of the channel of the Jordan, where the priests who carried the ark of the covenant of the Lord had stood, and they are there to the present day.”

These twelve stones that were set up in the middle of the channel of the Jordan likewise signify the apostolic order, just as do those that were carried out of the Jordan and established at Gilgal. For whoever desires to receive the grace of baptism must receive it according to apostolic tradition; and thus, stripped of the old person and clothed with the new, while remaining throughout his life in the camp of the Church, he must strive in faith and conduct to preserve the standard of apostolic teaching.

**CHAPTER VI. On the second circumcision of the children of Israel, which was performed with stone knives at Gilgal; and on their keeping the Passover on the fourteenth day of the month toward evening in the plains of Jericho, where they ate the produce of the land and, on the following day, unleavened bread, because the manna had ceased for them.**
