*(CHAPTER V.)* “At that time the Lord said to Joshua: Make stone knives for yourself and circumcise the children of Israel a second time. He did what the Lord had commanded and circumcised the children of Israel on the Hill of Foreskins. The reason for the second circumcision was this: all the people who had come out of Egypt, all the men of military age, had died in the wilderness through the long circuits of the journey; all of them had been circumcised. But the people who had been born in the wilderness during the forty years of travel through the vast desert were uncircumcised,” and the rest.

In this command it is asked why he said “again.” For one man was not to be circumcised twice. But because the one people consisted partly of circumcised persons and partly of uncircumcised persons, it was said “again,” so that the circumcised people might be circumcised again—not the individual person, but the people. The following statements also demonstrate this. It is therefore clear that not everyone was involved, but only some. Some of the sons of those who came out of Egypt were uncircumcised within that people, and Jesus could circumcise them—namely, the sons of those who had begotten children in the wilderness and had refused to circumcise them because they were disobedient to the law of God.

There is therefore no reason for those who think that people who possess the sacrament of Christian baptism must be rebaptized to suppose that this testimony of the law supports them. No single person was circumcised twice; rather, the people had been circumcised in some members but were still uncircumcised in others. And even if it could somehow happen that God commanded a person to be circumcised twice, could one say that this had been commanded because they had been circumcised by the Egyptians, or by certain heretics separated from the fellowship of the Israelites? Since it is also sufficiently clear why God gave this command, people cannot find here any defense for their error.

(From Isidore.) Let the Jews ask how anyone can be circumcised a second time with bodily circumcision. Once circumcised, he no longer has anything that can be removed a second time. But for us, for whom the law is spiritual, this is appropriately explained. We say that the first circumcision took place through the law in Egypt. But if someone passes from the law through the baptism of the Jordan to the Gospel, then he receives a second, spiritual circumcision through the rock, which is Christ. Thus purified by such circumcision, he is free from the reproach of Egypt—that is, from the allurements of bodily vices.

The name of the place, Gilgal, which is interpreted as “revelation,” shows that while one has walked through the wilderness of this life in the foreskin of unbelief, one’s eyes have been blinded. Yet let us consider what this statement itself means: that “today he has taken away the reproach from the children of Israel.” All human beings, even if they have been instructed through Moses, nevertheless bear the reproach of sins. Who can be found to have acted in accordance even with the observance of the law? Hear, finally, the one who says: “According to the righteousness that is in the law, living without blame” (Phil. III); yet he himself declares and says: “For we too were once foolish, unbelieving, wandering astray, serving various desires and pleasures, living in wickedness and envy, hateful and hating one another” (Tit. II). Do these things not seem to you to be the reproaches of Egypt?

But from the time Christ came and gave us a second circumcision through the baptism of regeneration and purified our souls, we cast all these things away and, in their place, take up the testimony of a good conscience toward God. Then, through the second circumcision, the reproaches of Egypt were removed from us and the vices of sins were purified.

Therefore, if someone has been wholly converted, if he has truly and faithfully departed from the Jordan’s waters from the depths of his heart, if he has been purified by the second circumcision through the Gospel, let him not fear the reproaches of past offenses. You hear that today the reproach of Egypt has been removed from you. In the Gospels the Lord signifies this when he says: “Your sins are forgiven you; but now do not sin anymore, lest something worse happen to you” (John V).

For if, after the remission of sins, you no longer sin, the reproach of Egypt has truly been removed from you. But if you sin again, the former things will again revolve upon you—all the more because it is a much greater crime to trample upon the Son of God and profane the blood of the covenant than to neglect the law of Moses. The one who fornicates after the Gospel bears a much greater reproach than the one who, placed under the law, fornicates, because the former takes the members of Christ and makes them members of a prostitute.

You see, therefore, how much heavier and more abundant reproaches will return upon you if you neglect these things. Finally, no one will now accuse you merely as guilty, but will condemn you for sacrilege, because it is said: “Do you not know that your bodies are the temple of God? If anyone violates the temple of God, God will destroy him” (I Cor. III).

*(The same passage.)* “After all had been circumcised, they remained in the same place in the camp until they were healed,” and the rest.

For it is not enough for us to be circumcised; we must also be healed after circumcision—that is, until the scar itself closes over the wound of circumcision. When is the scar of circumcision’s wound closed? I think that to be circumcised by Jesus means to be free from vices: to lay aside evil habits and the worst practices, foul and disorderly behavior, and whatever overflows beyond the rule of honesty and piety.

But when we do this at the beginning, we are in a certain sense constrained by the difficulty of novelty, and, as though with some labor and pain of soul, we exchange old habits and faults for a new way of life. Therefore, as I said, there is a certain difficulty at the beginning in stripping off what we are able to cut away and in taking up the first and second things. This, then, seems to me to be the period when we are said to remain, as it were, in the pain of our circumcision, until we are healed by the scar’s closing.

We close the scar when we already fulfill the new practices without difficulty, and what previously seemed unusual and difficult becomes habitual for us. Then we are truly brought in as healed when, free from vices, we turn virtue through new practice into our nature.

*(The same passage.)* “The children of Israel remained at Gilgal and kept the Passover on the fourteenth day of the month toward evening in the plains of Jericho. And on the following day they ate of the produce of the land, unleavened bread and parched grain of that same year. The manna ceased after they had eaten of the produce of the land; nor did the children of Israel use that food any longer, but they ate of the produce of the land of Canaan in that present year.”

“The children of Israel kept the Passover on the fourteenth day of the month.” For they ought not to eat the flesh of the lamb before circumcision—that is, before they are healed. But after they have been healed, it is said that the children of Israel kept the Passover on the fourteenth day of the month. You see, therefore, that no unclean person keeps the Passover, no uncircumcised person, but only one who is clean and circumcised, as the Apostle explains when he says: “For Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed. Therefore let us celebrate the festival, not with the old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” (I Cor. V).

But when the people left the land of Egypt, they carried dough with them; when they had no bread, manna rained down for them. But when they came to the holy land and began to receive the fruits of the region of palms, the manna ceased for them, and then they began to eat the produce of the land.

Thus three general kinds of food are described. The first is what we eat when we leave the land of Egypt, but this suffices only for a short time. After it, manna succeeds. Third, we take the fruits of the holy land itself. In these distinctions, as far as the understanding of my smallness can grasp, I think the following is indicated.

The first food is what we carried with us when we left Egypt—that is, a small amount of secular learning, or even, if someone has perhaps touched upon something of the liberal arts, something that can help us a little in the wilderness. Once placed in the wilderness—that is, in this life in which we now are—we also eat manna, insofar as we are instructed by the teachings of divine law.

But whoever has deserved to enter the promised land—that is, to attain what has been promised by the Savior—will eat fruits from the region of palms. Truly, the one who has conquered the enemy and reached the promises will find the fruit of the palm.

For it is certain that however great the things may be that we can now understand or perceive in the law of God and the divine Scriptures, those things will be much higher and loftier which, when the riddle has ceased, all the holy will deserve to behold face to face. For “what no eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man—these are the things God has prepared for those who love him” (I Cor. II).

**CHAPTER VII. Where the commander of the Lord’s army appeared to Joshua, whom he himself worshiped; and Joshua’s speech to the people concerning the conquest of the city of Jericho.**

*(The same passage.)* “When Joshua was in the field of the city of Jericho, he lifted up his eyes and saw a man standing opposite him, holding a drawn sword. He went toward him and said: Are you one of ours or one of our adversaries? He replied: Not at all; rather, I am the commander of the army of the Lord, and now I have come. Joshua fell prostrate upon the ground and, worshiping, said: What does my Lord say to his servant? ‘Take off your sandal from your foot,’ he said, ‘for the place on which you stand is holy.’ And Joshua did as he had been commanded.”

Looking with his eyes, he saw the commander of the Lord’s army, as though he had not looked before but only then looked in order to see the commander of the Lord’s army. Yet when Jesus saw him, he did not see him as an ordinary man; he understood that he was a power. He did not yet understand, however, whether the figure he saw was one of the divine powers or one of the opposing powers. Therefore he asked and inquired, saying: “Are you one of ours or one of our adversaries?” And he replied: “I am the commander of the army of the power of the Lord; now I have come.”

When Jesus heard this, he worshiped and said: “Lord, what do you command your servant?” What does Jesus teach us through this? It is undoubtedly what the Apostle says: “Do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God” (I John IV). Jesus therefore recognized not only that he was from God, but that he was God; for he would not have worshiped him unless he had recognized God.

Who else is the commander of the army of the power of the Lord except our Lord Jesus Christ? For the whole army of heaven—whether angels, archangels, powers, dominions, principalities, or authorities—all these things that were made through him serve under that commander who is the prince of princes, who grants principalities to princes. For he is the one who says in the Gospel: “Be in authority over ten cities” (Luke XIX). He is the one who, having received the kingdom, returned.

But meanwhile let us consider what the present reading offers. Jesus is in Jericho; the enemies still possess the city, and Jesus has not yet captured it. Yet it is already said to Jesus: “Take off your sandal from your foot, for the place on which you stand is holy.” How, then, is Jericho holy ground when it is held by enemies?

But lest this perhaps be the meaning indicated—that wherever the commander of the power of the Lord comes, that place will be holy—I venture to say something further: even where Moses stood, the place was not holy in itself, but the presence of the Lord with Moses had sanctified it. Therefore it was said to him: “Untie the strap of your sandal, for the place on which you stand is holy ground.”

Thus, if we draw near to the Lord in life and merits, and become worthy for God to stand beside us, it is also said to us that we should remove from the feet of our soul whatever bond of mortality may be attached to them. These are the feet that Jesus washed; unless he washes them, we will have no share with him.

Therefore, if we release our soul and senses from every bond of mortal concern, God will immediately and gladly be present and stand beside us. But let us see what follows.

## CHAPTER VI

“Now Jericho was closed and fortified because of fear of the children of Israel, and no one dared go out or enter. And the Lord said to Joshua: ‘Behold, I have given Jericho into your hand, together with its king and all its mighty men. Go around the city, all the warriors, once each day. Thus you shall do for six days; but on the seventh day let the priests take seven trumpets, the kind used at the jubilee, and let them go before the ark of the covenant of the Lord. And you shall go around the city seven times, and the priests shall sound the trumpets. And when the voice of the trumpet has sounded longer and more sharply, and has resounded in your ears, let the whole people raise a very great shout; and the walls of the city shall fall to their foundations, and each person shall enter by the place opposite which he has stood,’” and so forth.

*(From Isidore.)* Jericho is surrounded and attacked, yet against it no sword is brought, no battering ram is directed, and no missiles are hurled: only seven priestly trumpets are employed continuously for seven days, and thus, as the ark is carried around it, the walls of Jericho are thrown down.

Jericho, by interpretation, means “moon.” The moon, however, represents the form of this world, because just as the moon wanes through its monthly cycles, so this world, running toward the completion of the ages, falls through its daily diminutions. In the ark the Church is represented; in the bronze trumpets strong preachers are understood. Thus the Israelites carry the ark around this city of Jericho for seven days while the bronze trumpets sound, and its walls fall through the presence of the ark and the sound of the bronze trumpets. For in this present time, which revolves through the alternation of seven days, the ark is carried—that is, the Church moves as it circles the whole world.

When our Lord Jesus Christ came, whose advent that earlier Joshua, the son of Nun, prefigured, he sent the priestly apostles, carrying hammered trumpets—that is, the glorious and heavenly teaching of preaching. Matthew was the first to sound the priestly trumpet in the Gospel; Mark, Luke, and John likewise sang, each with his own priestly trumpet. Peter also resounds with the two trumpets of his Epistles, as do James and Jude. John further added the sounding of a trumpet through his churches, and Luke by recording the deeds of the apostles. Finally came that one who said, “For I think that God has displayed us apostles as the last” (I Cor. IV), and who, thundering through the trumpets of his fourteen Epistles, cast down to their foundations the walls of Jericho, all the engines of idolatry, and the teachings of the philosophers.

I am also deeply moved by what the narrative records: that not only did the priests sound their trumpets so that the walls of Jericho might fall, but that when the sound of the trumpet was heard, the whole people is said to have howled with a great howl—or, as other copies have it, to have shouted with a great jubilation. And although this expression appears to have been translated improperly—for the Greek has **ἀλαλαγμός** (*alalagmós*), which properly signifies neither “jubilation” nor “howling,” but rather indicates the cry by which, in time of war, an army raises a concerted shout and customarily encourages itself unanimously to battle—nevertheless, in the Scriptures this term is usually rendered “jubilation” rather than “howling,” as in: “Shout joyfully to God, all the earth” (Ps. LXV); and again: “Blessed is the people that knows jubilation” (Ps. LXXXVIII).

This statement also moves me: what is the magnitude of this deed that makes the people blessed? It did not say, “Blessed is the people that knows the mysteries,” or that knows the order of heaven, earth, and the stars; but it says, “Blessed is the people that knows jubilation.” Elsewhere the fear of God makes a person blessed, for it says: “Blessed is the man who fears the Lord” (Ps. CXI). Elsewhere, too, several kinds of people are called blessed, such as the poor in spirit, the meek, the peacemakers, and the pure in heart (Matt. V). Here, however, blessedness is poured out, and some such great cause of blessedness is indicated that it makes the whole people blessed, provided that it knows jubilation.

Therefore it seems to me that this jubilation indicates a certain disposition toward concord and unanimity. If such a disposition occurs among two or three disciples of Christ, the heavenly Father grants them whatever they ask in the Savior’s name. But if the blessedness is so great that the whole people remains harmonious and unanimous, so that all speak the same things and remain in the same understanding and the same judgment, then, when such a people raises its voice unanimously, what is written in the Acts of the Apostles (chap. V) will take place: an earthquake occurred where the apostles were then praying with one accord, together with the women and Mary, the mother of Jesus. When the earthquake has occurred, everything earthly will also be destroyed and fall, and the world will be overturned.

Finally, hear our Lord and Savior, still encouraging his own soldiers, and see how he says: “Take courage; I have conquered the world” (John XVI). With that leader, therefore, the world has already been conquered for us, and its walls have collapsed—those on which the people of the world relied.

But each one of us must also fulfill these things in himself. You have Jesus as your leader within you through faith. Make hammered trumpets for yourself if you are a priest; for you have become a royal race, and “a holy priesthood” has been spoken concerning you. Make hammered trumpets for yourself from the Scriptures; from them draw your meanings, from them your words. This is why they are called hammered trumpets. Sound upon them; and if you sound upon such trumpets—that is, upon psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs—and if you carry the ark of the covenant around seven times—that is, if you do not separate the precepts of the Mosaic Law from the evangelical trumpets, but also demand from yourself the agreement of jubilation, namely, if the people of your thoughts and senses, which is within you, always gives forth a concordant and harmonious voice, and you do not at one time speak the truth and at another stain yourself with the falsehood of flattery toward a powerful person; if leniency does not at one time make you indulgent and anger at another time savage; if you are not found arrogant toward the lowly and humble toward the proud; finally, if there is not a battle within you, while the flesh desires against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh—”

*(From Isidore.)* If these things are now harmonious and concordant within you, you quickly emit the voice of jubilation, because the world that formerly rebelled against you has been destroyed and cast down. At the voices of the preachers, as at the sound of trumpets, the walls of Jericho—that is, the world’s arrogance and the proud obstacles of unbelief—fall, until at the end of time the last enemy, death, is destroyed.

And from the destruction of the impious, the single house of Rahab, like the one Church, is delivered: cleansed from the storm of fornication through the window of confession and in the blood of remission. This prostitute dwells in Jericho, as in this mortal age. In order that she may be saved, she hangs scarlet from the window of her house, as from the mouth of her body; this is the sign of Christ’s blood, by which confession is made for the remission of sins unto salvation. Those who were found in her house were saved from the destruction of the city, and all who are found within the Church alone are saved; outside this house—that is, outside the Church—no one is saved.

### THE SAME PLACE

“And Joshua said to all Israel: ‘Shout, for the Lord will give you the city. Let this city be accursed, and everything in it belong to the Lord. Only Rahab the prostitute shall live, together with all who are with her in the house, because she hid the messengers whom we sent. But beware lest you touch anything of what has been commanded, and become guilty of transgression, and all the camp of Israel fall under sin and be troubled,’” and the rest.

What is indicated in these words is this: See that you have nothing worldly within you; do not bring worldly wickedness or any evasion from the world with you into the Church. Let every worldly way of life be accursed for you. Do not mingle worldly things with divine things; do not insert worldly business into the services of the Church.

This is what John sounds with the trumpet of his Epistle when he says: “Do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world” (I John II). And Paul likewise says: “Do not be conformed to this age” (Rom. XII). Those who do these things receive what belongs to the accursed thing.

Those also who, although they are Christians, celebrate the festivals of the pagans bring the accursed thing into the Church. Those who investigate human lives and events by the courses of the stars; those who inquire into the flight of birds and other such practices formerly observed in the world—these bring the accursed thing from Jericho into the Church, pollute the camp of the Lord, and cause the people of God to be defeated.

There are also many other sins through which the accursed thing is brought from Jericho into the Church, by which the people of God are defeated and overthrown by their enemies. Or does the Apostle not prescribe these same things when he says: “A little leaven corrupts the whole lump”? (I Cor. V.)

## CHAPTER VIII

### On the fact that Joshua caused Rahab the prostitute, her house, and her family to live and dwell among the children of Israel, and on the curse pronounced against the city of Jericho

### THE SAME PLACE

“But Joshua allowed Rahab the prostitute, her father’s household, and everything she had to live, and they dwelt in the midst of Israel to the present day, because she had hidden the messengers whom he had sent to spy out Jericho.”

I would like to ask the Jews, and those who are indeed called Christians but still preserve a Jewish understanding in the Scriptures, how they explain that Rahab the prostitute was added to the house of Israel even to the present day. How is Rahab said to have been added even to the present day? For this is the custom of Holy Scripture: to speak of things that remain until the end either of life or of the age. For example, it says: “He is the father of the Moabites to the present day” (Gen. XIX), which means until the consummation of the age. Again, in the Gospel it says: “This saying has been spread among the Jews to the present day” (Matt. XXVIII)—that is, for as long as the age endures.

But how is Rahab the woman said to have been added to the house of Israel to the present day? Is succession through posterity not attributed to the mother, so that she may be understood to be preserved in the renewal of her offspring? Or should it rather be understood that she truly has been joined and associated with Israel to the present day?

And if you wish to see more clearly how Rahab is joined to Israel, consider how a branch of the wild olive is grafted onto the root of the good olive. You will understand how those who have been grafted in by faith onto Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob are rightly said to have been placed and added to Israel to the present day. For, rooted in them, we are branches of the wild olive taken from the nations—we who once played the prostitute, worshiping wood and stone as God. We have been added to them to the present day and have become Christians through faith.

### THE SAME PLACE

“At that time Joshua pronounced a curse, saying: ‘Cursed before the Lord be the man who rises up and rebuilds this city, Jericho. Upon his firstborn let him lay its foundations, and upon his youngest let him set up its gates.’”

That this curse was fulfilled in the time of the kings is clear, since in the First Book of Kings, concerning the reign of Ahab, it is written: “In his days Hiel of Bethel built Jericho: in Abiram his firstborn he founded it, and in Segub his youngest he set up its gates” (III Kings XVI).

The meaning is evident. When the aforementioned builder of the city began to lay its foundations, his firstborn, whose name was Abiram, died; and when he attempted to complete the city and fortify its gates, he lost the youngest of his sons, named Segub. Joshua had foretold by his curse that this would happen when he destroyed the city and handed it over to the accursed thing, saying: “Cursed before the Lord be the man who rises up and rebuilds the city of Jericho. Upon his firstborn let him lay its foundations, and upon his youngest let him set up its gates.”

Since, however, Hiel means “living to God,” and Bethel is interpreted as “house of the Lord,” Hiel of Bethel restores the walls of Jericho, which Joshua had destroyed and accursed, whenever one of those who had assumed the religious habit in the Church returns to commit the crimes from which the Lord Jesus had freed him on the day of baptism. He luxuriously resumes the pomps of the devil that he himself had accursed, and, bringing forth from Bethel, as it were, the teachings of errors or the tales of the pagans against the ecclesiastical truth with which he had been instructed, he revives the ruins of Jericho.

Such a person is rightly accursed before the Lord. He loses his firstborn in the foundation of the impious city and his youngest in the setting up of its gates, because he loses both the foundations of faith, from which good buildings ought to begin, and the barriers of good action, by which they ought to be brought to completion.

## CHAPTER IX

### On the fact that Achan, son of Carmi, appropriated for himself something from the accursed thing of the city of Jericho, and on the punishment inflicted upon him

### CHAPTER VII

“Thus the Lord was with Joshua, and his name became known throughout all the land. But the children of Israel transgressed the commandment and appropriated something from the accursed thing. For Achan, son of Carmi, son of Zabdi, son of Zerah, of the tribe of Judah, took something from the accursed thing. And the Lord was angry against the children of Israel,” and so forth.

*(From Augustine.)* In what happened when Achan of the tribe of Judah stole something from the accursed thing of the city of Jericho contrary to the Lord’s command, and because of his sin the three thousand who had been sent against Ai turned their backs to the enemy, with thirty-six of them killed, and the people were greatly terrified, Joshua prostrated himself before the Lord with the elders. He received the answer that this had happened because the people had sinned. God also threatened that he would not be with them unless they removed the accursed thing from among themselves. When the guilty man was revealed, he was not killed alone but together with all that belonged to him.

The question is commonly raised how it is just for punishment to be inflicted upon some for another person’s sins, especially since in the Law the Lord said (Ezek. XVIII) that neither fathers are to be punished for the sins of their children nor children for the sins of their fathers. Is that command meant for human judges, so that they should punish no one for another person’s offense, while God’s judgments are not of this kind? For by his deep and invisible counsel he knows how far even a temporal punishment and salutary terror among human beings should extend.

Nothing terrible, insofar as the administration of the whole world is concerned, happens to mortals when they die, since they are destined to die at some time. Yet among those who fear such things, discipline is established, so that each person may not care only for himself in the people, but that they may show concern for one another, and, as members of one body and one person, some limbs may be solicitous for others.

Nevertheless, one must not believe that even in punishments inflicted after death one person can be condemned in place of another. Punishment of this kind is inflicted only in matters that were destined to have an end, even if they did not reach their end in that particular way. At the same time, it is shown how closely the whole community is joined together in the people, so that individuals are not judged as isolated persons but, like parts, as belonging to the whole.

Thus, through the death of a few on account of one person’s sin, the whole people was admonished to seek out what had been committed, as though in an entire body. It was also signified how great an evil it would be if the whole congregation had sinned, since not even one person could be judged in such a way that the others might be secure from him.

But if Achan had been discovered and apprehended by someone, and, charged with that crime, had been brought before Joshua for judgment, one should by no means think that a human judge would have punished either someone else in his place or with him who had no share in his deed. For Joshua was not permitted to exceed the commandment of the Law given to human beings: that no one, by the judgment assigned or permitted to a human being over another human being, should consider one person punishable for another’s sin.

God, however, judges with a far more hidden justice. He is able, even after death—which a human being cannot do—either to free or to destroy. Therefore, as for visible afflictions or deaths among human beings, since these can harm or benefit those upon whom they are inflicted, the Lord knows in the secret of his providence how to distribute them justly to each person, even when he appears to avenge the sins of some upon others.

Invisible punishments, however, which can do nothing but harm and cannot benefit, no one suffers from another’s sins under God as judge, just as under a human judge no one ought to suffer these visible punishments except for his own fault. For in matters requiring punishment within human jurisdiction, God commanded the human judge to do what he himself does in his own judgment, to which human power does not aspire.

### THE SAME PLACE

“Then Joshua took Achan, son of Zerah, and the silver, the cloak, and the golden rod, together with his sons and daughters, oxen and asses, sheep, the tent itself, and all his possessions; and all Israel with him brought them to the valley of Achor. There Joshua said: ‘Because you have troubled us, may the Lord trouble you on this day.’ And all Israel stoned him, and everything that belonged to him was consumed by fire. They also piled over him a great heap of stones, which remains to the present day. And the fury of the Lord was turned away from them; therefore the name of that place was called the valley of Achor to this day.”

*(From Augustine.)* It is rightly asked: since the Lord commanded that the man who had stolen from the accursed thing should be burned when he was identified, why did Joshua cause the identified man to be stoned by the people instead? Was he required to die in the manner that Joshua, who followed the Lord more closely, was able to understand from the words of the one giving the command?

We should therefore ask rather why the Lord called stoning “fire” than believe that Joshua did anything other than what the Lord commanded. For no one could have been wiser in understanding the Lord’s words, nor more obedient in carrying them out.

That punishment could be signified by the name “fire” is attested by Scripture in Deuteronomy, where it says to the children of Israel: “And I brought you out of the iron furnace, out of Egypt” (Deut. IV). Here he clearly wished a harsh tribulation to be understood.

Two explanations occur to me—not so that both should apply, but so that one of them may apply—as to why he was not burned with all that belonged to him by an evident fire.

If the Lord judged his sin to be such that, once expiated by that punishment, he would not punish him eternally, then, because of that expiation and purification, the punishment appropriately received the name “fire.” No one would be led toward this interpretation if visible fire had literally consumed him; rather, everyone would remain with what he plainly saw fulfilled and would seek nothing further.

But now, since, on account of the words of God and the deed by which those words could not be transgressed, it is most correctly said that stoning too was fire, we may elegantly recognize that the man was purified by that punishment so that he would not perish thereafter in that sin. The vessels in the Book of Numbers signify the same thing, for they are commanded to be purified by fire (Num. XXXI).

But if that sin was such that even after this life Gehenna would receive him, Joshua wanted him to be stoned so that the statement of the Lord—“He shall be burned with fire”—might be understood as referring to what the Lord himself would do, not to what was to be done by the people. If the Lord had said, “You shall burn him and everything that belongs to him with fire,” there would be no room for this interpretation. But since the wording is such that God appears rather to have foretold what would happen to him than to have commanded what should be done to him by human beings, Joshua, who understood the divine words as so great a prophet, could not have acted better than by killing him with stones rather than flames. Otherwise, the words of the Lord might have appeared to be fulfilled in those fires, although he wished them to be understood as having been spoken for another reason.

Nor should it trouble us that God foretold not only that he himself but also everything belonging to him would be burned by fire. For he says: “He shall be burned with fire, and everything that belongs to him.” Everything that belongs to him can be understood as his works, which he said would be burned together with him, just as the Apostle says concerning certain works consumed by fire: “But he himself will be saved” (I Cor. III).

If Achan’s sin is to be understood in such a way that he would also be punished with eternal fire, then, when Joshua punished him, the people stoned his sons and daughters together with the animals and everything he possessed. Yet Joshua did this not by human judgment but by the prophetic Spirit—either understanding “everything that belongs to him” in such a way that he did not regard his children as excluded, and imposing the punishment of stoning in place of fire, or signifying through the other things belonging to him, and also through his children, the works that God would burn in him after death.

Nevertheless, it should not for that reason be believed that they were burned with the punishment of hellfire for their father’s sin, from which they were innocent even after death. This death, which awaits all, although it comes from the first sin, is nevertheless useful when accelerated for certain people, since we have been born in such a way that we must necessarily die. Hence it is written of a certain person: “He was taken away lest wickedness should change his understanding” (Wis. IV, 11).

By what judgment or mercy of God this was inflicted, whether upon his sons or upon the thirty-six men, since all were strangers to his sin, remains hidden with the one in whom there is no iniquity. Yet this is clear: the people ought to have sought what had been committed with terror, and the others feared imitating his deed all the more intensely because human weakness is especially horrified by the prospect of being subjected to so great and so just a hatred from the people, and of dying through one’s own sin together with the descendants whom one had thought would be left for the propagation of the race.

Nor should we pass over without purpose the fact that, when one person sinned, anger came upon the whole people.

*(From Adamantius.)* How did this happen? When the priests who preside over the people wish to appear kind toward offenders, and, fearing the tongues of sinners lest they speak ill of them, forgetful of priestly severity, refuse to fulfill what is written—“Rebuke the sinner before all, so that the others may also have fear” (I Tim. V)—and again, “Remove the evil from among yourselves” (I Cor. V)—and, not inflamed with zeal for God, fail to imitate the Apostle who says, “I delivered such a man to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved” (ibid.), nor strive to fulfill the Gospel command that, if they see someone who, even after correction by two or three witnesses and then after correction by the Church, has not been reformed, they should expel him from the Church and regard him as a pagan and a tax collector (Matt. XVIII)—then, while they spare one person, they plot the destruction of the whole Church.

But let us see whether perhaps this great and so severe bitterness of the sin has an interior meaning.

*(From Isidore.)* There is much beauty in words, and much in the speeches of philosophers and rhetoricians, all of whom belong to the city of Jericho—that is, are people of this world. Jericho, as has been said, represents the world.

Therefore, the person who defrauds Jericho of its accursed thing and hides it in his tent is the one who inserts worldly customs into the secrets of the Church; who, while remaining under the worship of God, loves the festivals or spectacles of the world; who consults diviners, haruspices, and augurs; or who recommends other rites that were formerly practiced in Jericho, that is, in this world.

Because he introduces the culture of worldly conduct after putting on the garment of faith, he takes, as it were, a cloak from the accursed thing. The person who defrauds Jericho of its accursed thing is also the one who brings the doctrines of heretics and the superstitious studies of secular literature into the Church.

This is the golden rod, fashioned in lucid speech. Arius, Marcion, and Basilides defrauded it. They stole golden rods from Jericho and attempted to introduce an unsound philosophical sect into the Church and to pollute the whole Church of the Lord, so that many others were destroyed through them. Therefore, rejected as accursed, they were overwhelmed and extinguished, as though beneath a heap of stones, by the multitude of their sins.

Their author and destroyer came from Ai—that is, the devil. Having conquered certain believers through their impiety, he is in turn separated and conquered, and, hung upon the wood by the people of God, is put to death by the power of the cross.

## CHAPTER X

### On the conquest of the city of Ai and the killing of its king
(CAP. VIII.) “The Lord said to Joshua: ‘Do not fear or be afraid; take with you the whole multitude of fighting men, and arise and go up against the town of Ai. Behold, I have delivered its king, its people, its city, and its land into your hand. You shall do to Ai and its king as you did to Jericho and its king; but you shall seize its spoil and all its animals for yourselves. Set an ambush for the city behind it.’ And Joshua arose, and the whole army of warriors with him, to go up against Ai; and he chose thirty thousand strong men and sent them by night, commanding them and saying: ‘Set an ambush behind the city; do not go far away, and all of you shall be ready. But I and the rest of the multitude that is with me shall approach the city from the front,’” and so forth. (From Augustine.)

That God commands Jesus, speaking to him, to set ambushes behind him—that is, warriors lying in wait to ambush the enemy—teaches us that those who wage a just war do not act unjustly by using such means. A just man ought to consider above all in these matters only that he undertake a just war, for it is not lawful for everyone to wage war. Once he has undertaken a just war, whether he conquers by open battle or by ambush makes no difference with respect to justice.

Just wars are ordinarily defined as those that avenge injuries: when a people or city against which war is to be waged has either neglected to punish what its own people have wickedly done, or to restore what was taken away through injustice. But that war which God commands is also unquestionably just, since there is no iniquity with him, and he knows what ought to be done to each person. In such a war, the commander of the army, or the people themselves, must be judged not so much the author of the war as its minister.

Jesus, sending thirty thousand warriors to subdue Ai, said to them: “You shall lie in ambush behind the city, and you shall not be far from the city, and all of you shall be ready; and I and all the people who are with me shall approach the city. And when those who dwell in Ai come out against us, as before, we shall flee from their face. And when they come out after us, we shall draw them away from the city, and they will say: ‘These men are fleeing from our face as before.’ But you shall rise from the ambush and enter the city. According to this word you shall act; behold, I command you.”

It must be asked whether every intention to deceive is to be counted as a lie; and, if so, whether a lie by which someone who deserves to be deceived is deceived can be just. If not even this can be found to be a just lie, it remains that what was done by means of the ambush must be referred to the truth according to some meaning.

God commands Jesus, the leader of the people, to divide the people into two parts: one part is to pretend to flee, while the other remains in ambush, by which Ai is to be deceived. When these arrangements have been made, the king of Ai sees Jesus and the children of Israel from a distance and is stirred to battle against them. But when they pretend to flee, the others pursue them more fiercely and, as though about to carry away spoils from the enemy, all go out together, so that, as Scripture says, they leave the city empty.

But after they have advanced to the appointed place, Jesus turns and gives a signal for those who were in ambush to rise and strike the backs of the enemy. Thus the last and the first enclose the enemy between them and kill them all. In this way, after those who inhabited Ai had been defeated, they hanged their king on a tree.

When these things are heard, it is plausible that listeners would say: “What is this to me? What benefit is it to me if I learn that those who inhabited Ai were defeated?” For if similar or even greater wars have been fought or are being fought, why did the Holy Spirit take care that, leaving aside the destruction of so many great and noble cities, the battle of the city of Ai should be written down and entrusted to the sacred books?

First, we were defeated on account of our sins, and those who inhabited Ai killed very many of us. Ai is interpreted as “chaos”; and we know chaos to be the place or dwelling of hostile powers, whose king and ruler is the devil. Coming against him, Jesus divides the people into two parts: some he places in front, and others behind, so that they may unexpectedly come against the enemy from the rear.

Do you see whether the first part of the people is that of which he says, “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matt. XV), and of which the Apostle says, “Grace and peace to every person who does good, to the Jew first and to the Greek” (Rom. II), that is, to the Gentile? Thus the first people, placed in front and apparently fleeing with Jesus, are followed by the later people gathered from the Gentiles. These, coming unexpectedly from behind—“five” [as printed; the sense is uncertain]—strike the adversaries more fiercely. In this way the people overthrow and conquer the middle host of demons.

But perhaps you will say to me: “How, then, is the earlier people placed as though fleeing, and as though they were fleeing from those who followed?” For those who follow Jesus have turned away from the legal burdens and commandments, from observance of the Sabbath, from circumcision of the flesh, and from the slaughter of sacrifices. Yet they do not flee, because they have followed Jesus, the perfection and fullness of the law.

After all this, the king of Ai is also said to have been hanged on a double tree. A mystery is concealed in this passage, hidden from very many. But as we pray, we shall attempt to disclose all these things, not by our own opinions, but by the testimonies of divine Scripture.

Above we said that the king of Ai may be compared with the devil. Here it is worthwhile to understand how he was crucified on a double tree. The cross of our Lord Jesus Christ was double. The saying may seem strange and new to you. When I say that the cross was double, I mean that it consists of a double aspect and a twofold reality: visibly, the Son of God was crucified in the flesh; invisibly, on this cross the devil, together with the principalities and powers, was fastened to the cross.

Does this not seem true to you if I produce the Apostle Paul as a witness to these matters? Hear, then, what he himself declares: “And he took what was contrary to us, removed it from our midst, fastening it to his cross; he stripped the principalities and powers and led them openly in triumph, triumphing over them on the tree of the cross” (Col. II). Other copies read, “triumphing over them in himself.” But among the Greeks it reads, “on the tree.”

Thus there is a double meaning in the tree of the Lord’s cross. One is the meaning spoken of by the Apostle Peter, namely, that Christ, having been crucified, left us an example. The second cross was the trophy over the devil, on which he was crucified and defeated. Therefore the Apostle Paul said: “But far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. VI).

You see that here too the Apostle disclosed a twofold meaning of the cross. For he says that two contrary things have been crucified: the holy and the sinful, the world and that form which, as we said above, is undoubtedly that of Christ and the devil. We are crucified to the world when the prince of this world comes and finds nothing in us; and the world is crucified to us when we do not receive the desire of sin.

But if there is perhaps a more attentive listener, he may say: “The pattern of these matters seems appropriate, but something still troubles me: the devil and his army, so far as the figure of the history shows, have been destroyed. How, then, do we still see the devil and the hostile powers possessing such strength against the servants of God that even the Apostle Peter warns us with great care and says that we must be watchful, ‘because our adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking whom he may devour’ (I Pet. V)?”

Let us see, then, whether we can find here something worthy in the utterances of the Holy Spirit. Christ’s coming is understood in one way as having occurred in humility, and in another as hoped for in glory. This first coming in the flesh is called, in a mystical expression, his shadow in the holy Scriptures, as the prophet Jeremiah also says: “The breath of our nostrils, Christ the Lord, of whom we said, ‘In his shadow we shall live among the nations’” (Lam. IV).

Gabriel too, when he announced his birth to Mary, said: “The power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke I). From this we understand that in his first coming these things are shadowed forth, while their fulfillment and perfection will be completed in his second coming.

Therefore the Apostle says, “He raised us up with him and made us sit together in the heavenly places” (Eph. II). Yet we certainly do not see believers already raised up or sitting in the heavenly places. These things are now shadowed forth through faith, because in mind and hope we are lifted up from earthly and dead works and raise our heart from earth toward heavenly things. This, however, will be fulfilled in his second coming, so that what we now anticipate by faith and hope we shall then also possess bodily in the actual realization of things.

So it must be understood concerning the devil that he was indeed defeated and crucified, but only for those who have been crucified with Christ. For all believers and all peoples he will then be crucified. Then what the Apostle says will be fulfilled: “As in Adam all die, so also in Christ all shall be made alive” (I Cor. XV).

Here too there is a hidden mystery of the figure. The people will be divided into two parts: some will be first, and others last. When they have united in one purpose with Jesus, then the devil will no longer exist at all, because death will no longer exist.

Do you wish us to establish these things also by divine testimonies? Hear the Apostle saying: “For this we say to you by the word of the Lord: we who are alive, who remain until the coming of the Lord, shall not precede those who have fallen asleep. For the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the trumpet of God; and the dead who are in Christ will rise first. Then we who are alive, who remain, shall be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet Christ in the air; and so we shall always be with the Lord” (I Thess. IV).

Concerning the devil he says: “The last enemy to be destroyed is death” (I Cor. XV). He is then truly conquered when this mortal nature is swallowed up by life.

(CAP. VIII.) “When all who had pursued Israel as it went toward the desert had been killed, and had fallen by the sword in that same place, the children of Israel returned and struck the city,” and so forth.

What do you think Jesus signified by fleeing? Let us see whether perhaps there is something that we conquer by fleeing, and whether flight is a perfect virtue. The Apostle Paul teaches us, saying: “Flee fornication” (I Cor. VI). You see, therefore, a certain spirit of fornication that we must flee if we wish to remain chaste, devout, and pure in Christ. This flight brings blessedness.

Not only must the spirit of fornication be fled, but likewise, just as it is said, “Flee fornication,” let us hear what he says to us: Flee anger, flee greed, flee envy and jealousy, flee slander and evil conversations (Col. III; I Pet. II; Eph. V)—though I do not know who escapes them.

Such was the army of Ai, from which Jesus taught his soldiers to flee. Perhaps it was concerning these that he instructed his disciples, saying: “If they persecute you in one city, flee to another” (Matt. X). And if they persecute us into another, let us flee into a third. He therefore wants us to flee from such enemies; he wants us to be far removed from such evils.

(IBID.) “Joshua did not withdraw the hand which he had extended upward while holding the shield, until they had killed all the inhabitants of Ai,” and so forth.

When the Jews read these things, they become cruel and thirst for human blood, thinking that the saints likewise struck down those who inhabited Ai, so that none was left among them who could be saved or flee. They do not understand that mysteries are shadowed forth in these words. Rather, what is indicated to us is that from those whose dwelling is chaos, and who have ruled in the abyss as demons, we must leave absolutely none, but kill them all.

We kill demons not by destroying their substance itself, but because their work and purpose is to make human beings sin—and their life consists in our sinning—without doubt their destruction occurs when we do not sin.

Thus the inhabitants of Ai are killed: the saints destroy them and leave none of them behind. These are undoubtedly those who guard their heart with every diligence, lest evil thoughts proceed from it. They also guard their mouth, so that no evil word comes out of it. This means leaving none behind who might escape with them, nor allowing any evil word to escape.

Act, then, you also. Let us prepare ourselves for such battles; let us strike Ai with the edge of the sword and extinguish all the inhabitants of chaos, all the hostile powers. Would that even now, while I am speaking the word of God to you, I could strike the heart of the breast! If I do this, it is certain that with the sword of my mouth I shall strike fornication, strike wickedness, restrain fury, and extinguish whatever other evils there may be with the edge of the sword—that is, by the word of my mouth—and leave none of them who may be saved or flee.

For if we extinguish all our enemies, then we shall truly celebrate a feast to God and, after our adversaries have been defeated, rejoice with joyful solemnity. Something of this kind also seems to me to be signified by the holy prophet in the Psalms, where he says of himself: “In the mornings I killed all the sinners of the earth, to destroy from the city of the Lord all who work iniquity” (Ps. C).

If the city of the Lord is understood as the Church of the living God, teachers cast out of the Church and kill those who work iniquity—namely, the opposing and hostile powers of demons, which compel human beings to sin by teaching and instructing them. They also disclose the mysteries hidden in the divine writings from passages such as those in which we are now engaged.

Or let us understand the city of the Lord as the soul of each one of us, which is built by the Lord from living stones—that is, from various and diverse virtues. From this city too every holy and diligent person will cast out sinners, that is, will kill the worst thoughts and perverse desires at the morning of his rising.

For the righteous man says: “In the mornings I will meditate on you, because you have been my helper” (Ps. LXII). What is this morning except our Lord Jesus Christ, who is the true light rising in our hearts and illuminating the darkness of our ignorance, making us see light in his light?

Therefore, whenever you read in Scripture of the battles, killings, and slaughter of the righteous, and that the saints spare none of their enemies—in fact, that if they spared them, it would be counted against them as a sin, as it was counted against Saul when he kept alive Agag, king of Amalek—understand the battles of the righteous in the manner explained above, because these are battles waged by them against sin.

How will the righteous remain righteous if they preserve even a small amount of sin within themselves? Therefore it is said of them that they left behind neither one who could be saved nor one who could escape.

(IBID.) “He commanded them, and they took his corpse down from the cross, threw it at the entrance of the city, and heaped a great pile of stones over it, which remains to the present day,” and so forth.

What does it signify that the corpse of the king of Ai, by Joshua’s command, was taken down from the cross and thrown at the entrance of the city, except that, after the devil has been condemned through Christ’s passion, every believer, immediately upon entering faith and receiving baptism, renounces him according to the command of our Savior and utterly rejects his worship?

“Having heaped a great pile of stones over him”—that is, a multitude of harsh judgments by which his faithlessness or wickedness is rejected and condemned. This heap remains to the present day because the disgrace of his condemnation continues forever for the devil himself and his angels. For just as their correction will never come, so the punishment of their condemnation will never cease.

(IBID.) “Then Joshua built an altar to the Lord God of Israel on Mount Ebal, as Moses the servant of the Lord had commanded the children of Israel,” and so forth.

Let us see what all these things signify and what edification the present reading provides for us. All who believe in Jesus Christ are said to be living stones, as Scripture foretells, saying: “You are living stones, built into a spiritual house, offering acceptable sacrifices to God through Jesus Christ” (I Pet. II).

As we know to be observed among earthly stones, the stones that are stronger and more powerful are first cast into the foundations, so that the whole house of the building can be entrusted to them and placed upon them. Others that follow—that is, those somewhat inferior to them—are arranged next to those in the foundation. Those that are still lower are placed somewhat higher above the foundation. Then, within the body of the stones, those that are weaker are placed higher up, close to the very peaks of the roof.

So understand also now concerning living stones that some are in the foundations of this spiritual building. Who are those placed in the foundations? The apostles and prophets. For Paul himself teaches this when he says: “Built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus our Lord himself as the cornerstone” (Eph. II).

And so that you, hearer of these things, may prepare yourself more eagerly for the construction of this building, so that you may be found as a stone nearer to the foundation, learn that Christ himself is also the foundation of the building we have now described. For the Apostle says: “No one can lay any foundation other than the one that has been laid, which is Jesus Christ” (I Cor. III).

Blessed, therefore, are those who build upon this noble foundation and construct religious and holy works. But in this building of the Church there must be an altar. Hence I think that all among you who are suitable as living stones, and ready for this purpose, so that they may devote themselves to prayers, offer supplications to God day and night, and sacrifice the victims of their petitions, are those from whom Jesus builds the altar.

But consider what praise is attributed to these altar-stones. “As Moses the lawgiver said,” it says, “build an altar from whole stones into which no iron has been driven.” What do you think these whole stones are? Each person’s conscience knows who is whole and who is incorrupt, undefiled in flesh and spirit. He does not receive the flaming darts of the wicked one—that is, the darts of desire—but restrains and repels them with the shield of faith.

Or who is the person who has never received the iron of combat, the iron of war, or the iron of disputes, but has always been peaceful, always quiet and gentle, grounded in the humility of Christ?

These, then, are the living stones from which our Lord built an altar of whole stones into which no iron had been driven, so that he might offer burnt offerings and a sacrifice of salvation upon them.

I think that such whole and undefiled stones could be the holy apostles, all together forming one altar because of their unanimity and harmony. For they are reported to have prayed together in one accord and, opening their mouth, to have said: “You, Lord, who know the hearts of all” (Acts I).

Those, therefore, who can pray in unanimity with one voice and one spirit may perhaps be worthy—all of them together—of building one altar upon which Jesus may offer sacrifice to the Father.

Nevertheless, let us also strive to say the same things together, in unanimity and of one mind, doing nothing through contention or empty glory, but remaining in one understanding and one judgment. Perhaps we too may become suitable stones for the altar. For the Lord our God does not abandon us.

## BOOK TWO

[Col. 1035]

## CHAPTER ONE

On Joshua’s writing the Deuteronomy of the law of Moses upon stones before the children of Israel, and on his reciting the law of blessing and cursing before all the people.

(IBID.) “And Joshua wrote upon the stones the Deuteronomy of the law of Moses, which Moses had arranged before the children of Israel.”

“He wrote,” it says, “Jesus wrote upon the stones of the altar the Deuteronomy of the law of Moses, and he wrote it in the sight of the children of Israel.” How did he write it, and how could the son of Nun at that time inscribe the whole law upon the stones of the altar? Therefore he foreshadowed the type as he wished.

For the moment, let us see how our Jesus wrote upon living and whole stones the Deuteronomy, which is called the giving of the second law. If you wish to see how Jesus writes a second law after the first law has been weakened, hear him saying in the churches: “It was said to the ancients, ‘You shall not kill’; but I say to you that everyone who is angry with his brother is a murderer” (Matt. V).

And again: “It was said to the ancients, ‘You shall not commit adultery’; but I say to you that whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (ibid., v. XXVII). “It was said to the ancients, ‘You shall not swear falsely’; but I say to you, ‘Do not swear at all’” (ibid., v. XXXIII).

You see the Deuteronomy that Jesus wrote upon living and whole stones, upon tablets that are human hearts—not with ink, but with the Spirit of the living God.

But if you wish to know more clearly in whose hearts Jesus wrote the law and in whose he did not write it, I shall also make this clear to you from the authority of Scripture, so that you may receive consolation, you who have been called from the Gentiles, and need not fear the boastfulness of those who glory that they received the law of Moses inscribed on tablets and sheets.

Concerning those whose hearts the Lord Jesus has inscribed with the law, Paul says: “For when Gentiles who do not have the law by nature do what belongs to the law, these, though they do not have the law, are a law for themselves. They show the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience bearing witness to them” (Rom. II).

Therefore, if you see Gentiles coming to Jesus, believing in him, and fulfilling the work of the law—which those who received the law are unable to fulfill—do not hesitate to say of them that Jesus has written the Deuteronomy upon these whole stones.

I am indeed troubled by what Scripture adds afterward: “And Jesus wrote,” it says, “the Deuteronomy upon the stones before the children of Israel.” How could he write so large a book, with the children of Israel standing by and remaining there, without their departing until the writing of so many verses had been completed? Or how could the altar-stones contain the contents of so large a book?

Let the Jewish defenders of the letter, who do not understand the spirit of the law, tell me how this is shown in the history of the Old Testament. But among them, even to this day, when Moses is read, a veil lies over their heart. For us, however, when we turn to the Lord Jesus, the veil is removed, because “where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” for our understanding.

Therefore the Lord Jesus does not need much time to write the Deuteronomy, to engrave the law a second time in the hearts of believers, and to mark it with the spirit of understanding in the minds of those who are worthy of building the altar. As soon as someone has believed in Jesus Christ, the law of the Gospel is written in his heart and inscribed in the sight of the children of Israel.

For heavenly powers, the ministries of angels, and the Church of the firstborn were present when the sacrament of faith was entrusted to you. If we rightly understand Israel as meaning “a mind that sees God,” this is most rightly said of the ministering angels, according to the Lord’s saying concerning infants—and you too were an infant in baptism: “Their angels always see the face of my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. CXVIII).

Before these children of Israel, therefore, who were present at the time when the sacraments of faith were entrusted to you, seeing the face of God, Jesus wrote the Deuteronomy in your heart.

(IBID.) “All the people, and the elders, commanders, and judges stood on both sides before the priests who carried the ark of the covenant of the Lord, the stranger as well as the native. Half of them stood beside Mount Gerizim, and half beside Mount Ebal, as Moses the servant of the Lord had commanded. And first he blessed the people of Israel,” and so forth.

Around this ark of the covenant everyone who is truly Israel walks; he is not far from it. The Levites and priests also carry it upon their shoulders. Indeed, all who live in priestly religion and holiness—not merely those who seem to sit in the priestly assembly, but especially those who act as priests, whose portion is the Lord and who have no share on earth—are truly the priests and Levites of the Lord. They carry the law of God upon their shoulders by doing and fulfilling the works written in the law.

“And the proselyte,” it says, “and the native were present together, half beside Mount Gerizim and half beside Mount Ebal.” How shall we explain these things also? We need God’s help if we are to discuss and explain divine words in our own words.

Who are the halves that walked beside Mount Gerizim, and who are the halves that, although they too are saved, nevertheless could not walk beside Mount Gerizim but walk beside Mount Ebal? Mount Gerizim has blessings, while Mount Ebal has the curses that threaten sinners.

For, as it is written in Deuteronomy (CHAP. XXVII), they appointed six tribes to bless on Mount Gerizim. These six tribes are the more noble and excellent ones: Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Joseph, and Benjamin. The other six, the less noble, were appointed for cursing; among them was Reuben, who went up upon his father’s bed and defiled his father’s couch, and Zebulun, who was Leah’s youngest son.

This is what the histories of the ancients relate as having happened. But how shall we refer this historical narrative to mystical understanding, so that we may show who those are who walk beside Mount Gerizim and who those are who walk beside Mount Ebal?

I see two classes among those who, inflamed with desire for the heavenly promises, strive with the utmost zeal and diligence lest even the smallest blessedness pass them by. They desire not only to receive blessing and to be made partakers in the lot of the saints, but also to stand in the presence of God and always be with the Lord.

Others likewise strive toward salvation, but are not so inflamed by love of blessings and desire for the promises. Rather, they keep this before their eyes and say: “It is enough for me not to go into eternal fire; it is enough for me not to be cast into the outer darkness.”

Since such variety of purpose exists among individual believers, it seems to me that this passage signifies that the half who walk beside Mount Gerizim, the mountain chosen for blessing, represent figuratively those who come to salvation not through fear of punishment but through desire for blessings and promises.

The other half who walk beside Mount Ebal, where the curses were pronounced, represent those who, through fear of evils and dread of punishments, fulfill the things written in the law and attain salvation.

Only God knows, among all the children of Israel, who is inflamed by desire for goodness itself and does what is good, and who moves toward goodness through fear of Gehenna and the terror of eternal fire, striving and hastening to fulfill what has been written.

For it is certain that those who do what is good out of desire for goodness itself and love of blessings are more noble than those who pursue goodness out of fear of evil. Therefore only Jesus, who can discern such minds and dispositions among the whole people, appoints some on Mount Gerizim for blessings and others on Mount Ebal—not so that they may receive curses, but so that, looking upon the prescribed curses and the punishments established for sinners, they may take care not to incur them.

(IBID.) “After this he read all the words of the blessing and the curse, and everything that was written in the book of the law. He left untouched none of the things that Moses had commanded, but repeated them all before the entire multitude of Israel, women and children and the strangers who dwelt among them.”

The historical explanation is easy: how the son of Nun read all the words of the law that Moses wrote before the whole assembly of the children of Israel. But it does not seem unprofitable to show how our Lord Jesus does this for his people.

I think that whenever Moses is read to us, and through the grace of the Lord the veil of the letter is removed, we begin to understand that the law is spiritual. For example, when the law says, “You shall not muzzle an ox while it is threshing” (Deut. XXV; I Cor. IX), it is not about oxen that it speaks, but about the apostles.

Again, when the law says that “Abraham had two sons, one by a slave woman and one by a free woman” (Gal. IX), I understand in this the two Testaments and the two peoples.

This law, understood in this way, which Paul calls spiritual, is read by Jesus the Lord. He is the one who recites these things in the ears of the whole people, commanding us not to follow the letter that kills but to hold fast to the Spirit that gives life.

Jesus therefore reads the law to us when he reveals to us the mysteries of the law. For we who belong to the Catholic Church do not despise the law of Moses, but receive it—provided that Jesus reads it to us. Thus we shall be able to understand the law rightly, if Jesus reads it to us, so that as he reads we may grasp its meaning through understanding.

Yet we must also say what Scripture teaches: that this word condemns us, because not all who hear the law are immediately the Church of the children of Israel [the wording is uncertain]. If there is a distinction between hearers of the law and the Church of the children of Israel, the hearer is excluded from salvation.

Attend, therefore, more carefully to the words of Scripture: “There was not a single word among all that Moses commanded which Jesus did not read in the ears of the whole Church of the children of Israel.” And pay attention to the women, the infants, and the proselytes.

The Lord Jesus knows that there are other ears besides these bodily ears that he requires for hearing the law. Hence, in the Gospel, after he had taught the various things that had to be taught, he adds and says: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear” (Matt. XI). If he had said this of bodily ears, it would plainly have been superfluous. No one who lacked ears had gathered to hear his words.

But because he knew that what had been said must be received in the ears of the inner person—that is, in the understanding of the heart—for it is useless to hear a word if it is not retained and kept in the heart, he therefore demanded ears from his hearers.

We say that strong food is given to strong men, namely, to those of whom the Apostle says: “Solid food belongs to the perfect, from whom he prepares for himself a Church without stain or wrinkle or anything of that kind” (Hebr. V).

Those whom he distinguishes under the names of women, infants, and proselytes we should understand as some who still need milk, or who, being weak like women, eat vegetables.

But if the whole Church is taken together, the men are understood to be those who know perfection in all things and go armed against the wiles of the devil. The women are those who do not yet perform by themselves what is useful, but imitate the better and follow their examples, from whom they are also said to have a head. Infants are those who, having recently received the faith, are nourished on the milk of the Gospel. Proselytes appear to be catechumens and those who are already striving to join themselves to the faithful.

John too, sharing a similar understanding of these distinctions, wrote about them in his Epistle (I Epistle, chap. II), distinguishing the proper actions of each age.

Nevertheless, hear Jesus reciting the law to you and revealing spiritual understanding in your hearts. Do not remain proselytes, that is, catechumens, for too long; but hasten to receive the grace of God, so that you too may be counted in the Church of the children of Israel.

And you infants, “do not become children in your understanding, but be infants in wickedness.” In understanding, he says, be mature.

But let us see what is written after this.

## CHAPTER II

On the gathering of the nations against Joshua to fight him, and on the deceit of the Gibeonites by which they deceived Joshua and the princes of Israel.

### (Chapter IX)

“When they heard this, all the kings across the Jordan who were in the hill country and in the lowlands, along the coast and on the shore of the Great Sea; and those also who lived near Lebanon—the Hittite, the Amorite, the Canaanite, the Perizzite, and the Jebusite—assembled together with one accord and one purpose, to fight against Joshua and Israel.”

The history of the events themselves needs no explanation, since what happened is evident. [Col. 1040A] Nevertheless, from these visible events that took place, let us contemplate the battles and triumphs of our Lord Jesus the Savior, although we also see these things visibly fulfilled in him himself.

For the kings of the earth, the senate, the people, and the Roman rulers assembled in order to attack the name of Jesus and Israel together. Indeed, they decreed by their laws that there should be no Christians. Every city, every order, attacks the Christian name. But just as all those kings who then assembled against Jesus could accomplish nothing, so now neither kings, rulers, nor those opposing powers can prevent the Christian race from spreading more widely and abundantly. For it is written: “The more they humbled them, the more they multiplied and grew exceedingly strong” (Exod. I).

We are confident, moreover, that our invisible enemies will not only [Col. 1040B] be unable to overcome us, but that, with Jesus Christ our Lord conquering, Satan will swiftly be crushed under the feet of his servants. For with him as our leader, we, his soldiers, conquer, so that we may say—as it is written in Ezra—“Victory is from you, Lord, and I am yours; blessed are you, God of truth” (3 Esdras IV).

“(The same passage.) But those who lived in Gibeon, hearing all that Joshua had done to Jericho and Ai, and devising a cunning plan, took provisions for themselves, old sacks which they loaded upon donkeys, and torn and mended wine-skins, and very old shoes, which had been sewn with patches as evidence of their age; and they put on old garments. The bread which they carried for their journey was hard and crumbled into pieces. [Col. 1040C] They went to Joshua, who was then staying in the camp at Gilgal, and said to him and to all Israel together: ‘We have come from a distant land, wishing to make peace with you,’” and so forth.

(From Augustine.) The Gibeonites came to Jesus with old bread and sacks, so that they might be thought—as they had pretended—to have come from a distant land, and thus be spared. For the Lord had commanded that they should spare no one who inhabited those lands into which they were entering.

Some Greek and Latin manuscripts read: “And taking old sacks upon their shoulders.” Others, which seem more reliable, do not have “upon their shoulders,” but “upon their donkeys.” The similarity of the words in Greek easily caused the error, and for this reason the Latin copies also vary: for **ὤμων** and **ὄνων** [Col. 1040D] differ little from one another. The former is the word for “shoulders,” the latter for “donkeys.” The reading concerning donkeys is therefore more credible, since they said that they had been sent from a distant people. It is consequently evident that they were envoys, and that they could more plausibly have carried their necessities on donkeys than on their shoulders, since they could not have been numerous; and Scripture records that they carried not only sacks but also wine-skins.

(From Adamantius.) Many different classes among those who come to salvation are therefore signified. Accordingly, I think that these Gibeonites, whose history has been recounted, represent a certain small portion of those who are to be saved—yet saved in such a way that they do not escape being branded with a mark of some kind.

You see how they are condemned to become woodcutters and [Col. 1041A] water-carriers, in service to the people and in ministry at God’s altar, because they approached the children of Israel with deceit and cunning, wearing old rags and old shoes and carrying food consisting of old bread.

These people therefore come to Jesus with all their old things and ask only this from him: that they may be saved. In their figure, something of this kind seems to me to be shown. There are some in the Church who believe and have faith in God, who submit to all the divine commandments, who are even devout toward the servants of God and desire to serve them, but who are not sufficiently ready or suitable for the adornment or ministry of the Church. In their actions and personal conduct they are quite unclean and inwardly entangled, and they do not entirely put off the old person with his deeds. [Col. 1041B]

Just as these people were covered with old rags and old shoes, so, apart from believing in God and appearing devoted to the servants of God or to the worship of the Church, they introduce no correction or renewal into their conduct. Our Lord Jesus does grant such people salvation; but, in a certain sense, their salvation does not escape the mark of disgrace.

A similar figure is also described in the little book called *The Shepherd*. It says:

“What is the tree called the elm, which bears no fruit, yet supports the vine that bears very much fruit? Because it serves as a support for the vine, which, relying upon its strength, is able either to bear or to preserve much fruit, the elm also, although fruitless, appears necessary and useful precisely because it serves the fruitful vine.”

Understand something similar [Col. 1041C] in the Gibeonites. They did not put off the old person with his deeds, yet they minister to the saints, serve them, and provide some benefit. In this sort of order they receive salvation from Jesus, with an oath interposed.

I would not wish to obtain salvation in the order of the Gibeonites, nor to be numbered among the woodcutters or water-carriers. I would desire to receive an inheritance in the promised land among the Israelites.

It must certainly be observed that heretics commonly bring an accusation when they read this passage—those who do not accept the Old Testament—and say: “See how little humility Joshua son of Nun possessed, that, while granting salvation to people who had come to him as suppliants, he imposed upon them a mark of disgrace and a yoke of slavery.”

If a soul insufficiently instructed in the divine Scriptures hears this, [Col. 1041D] it can immediately become weakened and endangered, so that it may flee from the Catholic faith. They do not understand the tricks by which they are being deceived. Jesus rendered toward them a judgment appropriate to the measure of their faith.
