Rahab the prostitute, however, who in perfect faith received the Israelite spies with complete devotion, together with her entire household, was fully received into fellowship and membership among the people. It is written concerning her that “she has been joined to the children of Israel to this present day.”

But these people, because they did not love fellowship with the Israelite nation so much as they approached Jesus through fear for their own destruction, with cunning and deceit, how could they merit by servile fraud the freedom of life and participation in the kingdom?

[Col. 1042A] Finally, do you wish to know what condition Jesus justly assigned them because of the baseness of their mind? They themselves say in what follows:

“Because we heard how greatly the Lord did for you by the Red Sea and in the wilderness.”

Although, in saying this, they acknowledged that they knew and had heard of the divine wonders, they nevertheless did nothing worthy of faith or of admiration for such great acts. Therefore, seeing that their purpose in faith was narrow and small, he preserves toward them the most just moderation: they deserved salvation because they had offered at least a little faith, but they did not receive the fullness of the kingdom or freedom, because their faith was not ennobled by any accompanying works.

For James declares that faith without works is considered dead (James II).

Nevertheless, we must recognize how many figures [Col. 1042B] we are taught through such shadows. If there are among us people whose faith has only this quality—that they come to church, bow themselves, perform services, honor the servants of God, and contribute something to the adornment of the altar or church, but do not take pains to cultivate their conduct, correct their actions, lay aside their vices, practice chastity, restrain anger, suppress greed, curb rapacity, or remove from their mouths evil speech, foolish talk, buffoonery, and the poisons of slander—let them know that, if they are such people and refuse to correct themselves, and if they persist in these things until extreme old age, they will receive from Jesus the Lord a share and lot together with the Gibeonites.

(From Isidore.) Such people therefore carry within the Church, [Col. 1042C] for a time only, something like a sign of salvation; but among the Israelites—that is, among the saints of God—they do not attain the eternal kingdom and freedom.

“(The same passage.) And they did not strike them, because the leaders of the multitude had sworn to them by the name of the Lord, the God of Israel. Then all the common people murmured against the leaders, who answered them: ‘We swore to them by the name of the Lord, the God of Israel, and therefore we cannot touch them,’” and so forth.

(From Augustine.) It may be asked how the Hebrews believed that the oath made to the Gibeonites had to be kept, since they had sworn to them as though they had come from a distant land, just as the Gibeonites had lied. For they knew that, if the Hebrews discovered that they lived in the land which had been promised to them and which they were to retain after its inhabitants had been killed, they would have to be destroyed.

[Col. 1042D] Thus, when the Gibeonites lied that they had come from a distant land, the Israelites swore to them. Afterward, when they discovered that the Gibeonites lived there, where all whom they found were to be destroyed according to God’s command, they nevertheless did not wish to break their oath. Although they had learned that the Gibeonites had lied, they preferred to spare them because of the oath. They could, of course, have said that they had sworn to those whom they had believed the Gibeonites to be—that is, people coming from a distant land—but once they had discovered the truth, the Lord’s command concerning them ought to have been fulfilled, so that they too, like the others, might be destroyed.

God, however, approved this and was not angry with those who spared them, although they had not consulted him concerning who these people were and had therefore allowed themselves to be deceived by them. Hence [Col. 1043A] they should not improperly be thought to have feared God deceitfully, even if they wished to deceive human beings for the sake of their own salvation. For this reason the Lord was not angry with those who swore the oath or with those who spared them—so much so that afterward he avenged the Gibeonites themselves, as members of his people, against the house of Saul, as the history of the Books of Kings shows.

And because the oath was thus kept, although it was made concerning people who had lied, so that the judgment might be bent toward mercy, this did not displease God. For if, on the contrary, they had sworn to kill people whom they believed to be Gibeonites in the promised land, and had afterward learned that those people were foreigners from that land and had come from a distant place, there is no reason to suppose that they would have destroyed them in order to fulfill their oath. For, moved by the very mercy of sparing others, holy David also, after [Col. 1043B] the words in which he had sworn to kill Nabal—though he certainly knew whom he had sworn to kill—preferred to spare him and not fulfill his oath in a more difficult matter. He judged that it was more pleasing to God not to do what he had sworn in anger to do harm, than to carry it out.

### Chapter III

Concerning the five kings of the Amorites who assembled to fight against Gibeon, and concerning Joshua’s battles against them.

### (Chapter X)

“Adonizedek, king of Jerusalem, therefore sent to Oham, king of Hebron, and to Pharam, king of Jarmuth, and also to Japhia, king of Lachish, and to Dabir, king of Eglon, saying: ‘Come up to me and bring assistance, so that we may attack Gibeon, because [Col. 1043C] it has defected to Joshua and to the children of Israel.’ Accordingly, the five kings of the Amorites assembled and went up: the king of Jerusalem, the king of Hebron, the king of Jarmuth, the king of Lachish, and the king of Eglon, together with their armies. They encamped around Gibeon and attacked it,” and so forth.

All those who had previously been friends became enemies of the Gibeonites after the latter had entered into friendship and fellowship with the children of Israel and had received from them a covenant of peace. The Jebusite king of Jerusalem, having invited four other kings to join him, attacked the Gibeonites in order to destroy them.

But when the Gibeonites saw that five kings had conspired to fight against them, they did not trust in their own strength and resources. Instead, they sent to Jesus asking for assistance. He, by divine permission, came to the Gibeonites to bring them help.

Then wondrous things were [Col. 1043D] shown from heaven. The Lord rained down hailstones from above and destroyed the army of the five who were fighting against Jesus. Seeing that the divine right hand was fighting alongside him and that everything was proceeding successfully, Jesus raised a new and marvelous prayer toward heaven, saying:

“Let the sun stand over Gibeon, and the moon over the valley of Elon, until I have defeated this people.”

And the sun and moon stood in their place until the Lord had overcome their enemies. The sun stood in the midst of heaven and did not hasten toward setting for the space of one day. There was no day like it either before or afterward, when God obeyed the voice of a human being, because the Lord fought for Israel.

Those five kings fled and hid themselves in the cave of Makkedah.

These events, as recorded in the history, [Col. 1044A] proclaim the miracles of divine power to all ages and need no interpretation from outside, since the light of the events themselves shines forth in them. Let us nevertheless inquire what spiritual meaning is contained in them.

When the human soul has joined itself to the Word of God, it must not doubt that it will immediately have enemies, or that those whom it previously had as friends will be turned into adversaries. It should expect to suffer this not only from human beings, but should know with certainty that the same thing threatens it from opposing powers and spiritual wickedness.

Thus, whoever seeks friendship with Jesus should know that he must endure the hostility of many. Let the apostle Paul be heard confirming the same thing when he says: “All who desire to live piously in Christ suffer persecution” (2 Tim. III). Solomon also says something similar: [Col. 1044B] “My son,” he says, “when you approach the service of God, prepare your soul for temptation” (Ecclus. II).

The Gibeonites, therefore, whatever their condition may be, are now also attacked because of their friendship with Jesus. Although they are woodcutters and water-carriers—that is, although they are of the lowest standing in the Church—they are nevertheless said to be attacked for this very reason: that they belong to Jesus.

Yet the Gibeonites are not abandoned or despised by Jesus, or by the leaders and rulers of the Israelites; rather, they bring assistance to their weakness. Does it not seem to you that this is what the apostolic command does and prescribes among us: “Encourage the fainthearted, support the weak, be patient toward all” (1 Thess. V); and again: “You who are stronger, bear the weaknesses of the weak” (ibid.)?

[Col. 1044C] “(The same passage.) Joshua went up from Gilgal, and with him all the army of warriors, men of great valor. And the Lord said to Joshua: ‘Do not fear them, for I have delivered them into your hands; none of them will be able to withstand you,’” and so forth.

(From Augustine.) When the Gibeonites, besieged by the kings of the Amorites, had sent to Jesus so that he might come to their aid, Scripture continues as follows:

“Jesus himself went up from Gilgal, and all the fighting people with him, every man strong in valor. And the Lord said to Jesus: ‘Do not fear them, for I have delivered them into your hands; none of them will stand before you.’”

The Lord was not consulted as to whether he should go to them; instead, he foretold victory to those who wished voluntarily and rightly to assist their own people.

Thus, even though he had not been consulted, [Col. 1044D] he could have warned them concerning the Gibeonites—who they were, since they had falsely claimed to be from a distant land—unless he had approved the oath that compelled them to spare those who had submitted. For they had believed in God, whom they had heard promise his people that he would overthrow those nations and possess their land; and in a certain sense he rewarded their faith by not exposing them.

“(The same passage.) When they were fleeing from the children of Israel and were on the descent of Beth-horon, the Lord hurled great stones upon them from heaven as far as Azekah; and many more died from the hailstones than those whom the children of Israel had struck with the sword.”

The stones are hailstones of harsh vengeance sent from heaven against the enemies of God’s people; or they are divine threats [Col. 1045A] proclaimed in the sacred Scriptures against the wicked, where the fire of Gehenna and eternal punishment are foretold to them.

(From Adamantius.) In this way, then, Jesus, together with his leaders and powers, is present with those who are attacked because of his name by opposing powers. He not only grants assistance in battle, but also lengthened the duration of the day, extending the periods of light and dispersing the coming of night. Hence it follows:

“(The same passage.) Then Joshua spoke to the Lord on the day when he delivered the Amorite into the sight of the children of Israel; and he said before them: ‘Sun, do not move against Gibeon, and moon, against the valley of Ajalon.’ And the sun and moon stood still. Is this not written in the Book of the Just? The sun stood in the midst of heaven and did not hasten to set for the space of one day. There was no day before [Col. 1045B] or afterward so long, when the Lord obeyed the voice of a human being and fought for Israel. And Joshua returned with all Israel to the camp at Gilgal.”

(From the same author.) Let us therefore try, if we can, to show how our Lord Jesus extended the light and made the day longer, either for the salvation of human beings or for the destruction of opposing powers.

From the time when the Savior came, the end of the world was at hand. Indeed, he himself was already saying: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matt. III). Yet he held back and restrained the day of consummation and prevented it from arriving.

For God the Father, seeing that the salvation of the nations could be accomplished through him alone, says to him: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession to the ends of the earth” (Ps. II).

Until the Father’s promise [Col. 1045C] to the Church is fulfilled, until it grows among diverse nations and the whole multitude of the Gentiles enters, and then all Israel is saved, the day is lengthened and the setting is delayed. The sun has never set, but is always rising, while the sun of righteousness pours the light of truth into the hearts of believers.

But when the measure of believers has been filled and the increasingly degraded and darkened age of the final generation has arrived; when, as iniquity increases, the love of many grows cold, and very few remain in whom faith can be found—then the days will be shortened.

The same Lord, therefore, knows how both to extend the day when it is the time of salvation and to shorten the day. The span of light is prolonged for us, so that we may walk honorably as in the day and perform works of light.

But let us also consider what it means that the five kings [Col. 1045D] fled and took refuge in a cave. We have often said that Christians have a twofold battle. For the perfect, such as the apostle Paul, who says, “Their struggle was not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, and against spiritual wickedness in the heavenly places” (Eph. VI), the battle is of one kind.

For those who are lower and not yet perfect, however, the battle is still against flesh and blood—against those who are still attacked by carnal vices and weaknesses. I think this too is indicated in the present passage.

We said that the Gibeonites were attacked by five kings, and that their figure is represented by those who are imperfect. These people, then, are attacked by five kings.

The five [Col. 1046A] kings signify the five bodily senses: sight, hearing, taste, touch, and smell. Through one or another of these, each person must necessarily fall into sin. The five senses are compared with those five kings who attack the Gibeonites—that is, carnal people.

“(The same passage.) For the five kings fled and hid themselves in the cave of the city of Makkedah. And it was reported to Joshua that five kings had been found hiding in the cave of Makkedah. He commanded his companions, saying: ‘Roll great stones to the mouth of the cave and appoint industrious men to guard those who have been shut in,’” and so forth.

That they are said to have fled into a cave may perhaps indicate this: a cave is a place excavated deep within the earth. Thus [Col. 1046B] these senses, which we have explained above, when they have sunk into earthly actions while situated in the body, and have done nothing for the work of God but everything for the service of the body, are said to have fled into caves.

It must nevertheless be understood that these very kingdoms, whose kings are now defeated by Jesus and flee into caves, afterward come into the lot of the saints and are called the Lord’s portion, as in the case of the kingdom of Jerusalem, or of Achis, or of Hebron.

I think this indicates that these five senses, which we have explained above, when situated in the body, are conquered by Jesus so that unbelief and lack of faith are driven from them and they die to sin. Once they cease serving sins, the soul afterward uses those same senses as servants to accomplish the righteousness of God.

Thus it happens [Col. 1046C] that in Jerusalem, where a wicked and most evil king had previously reigned, David, mighty in hand, and peaceful Solomon afterward reign. For evil powers also sit beside those bodily senses which we mentioned above, inciting them to evil desires and shameful services by offering them to the soul.

If faith in Christ overcomes these evil powers, and they are hung upon the wood of his cross, so that he triumphs over them upon the wood; and if, having slain them upon the wood of his cross and driven them from their kingdom, the soul becomes God’s portion—then Jerusalem becomes the kingdom of God, and a temple is built in it for the Lord.

Did not the man who said, “For we too were once foolish, unbelieving, wandering, and serving various desires and pleasures? [Col. 1046D]” (Titus III), understand this concerning himself?

For what else is meant by the statement that Jerusalem was once under the rule of Adonibezek, or that other cities were under other rulers? In the meantime, Jesus kills the enemies—not teaching cruelty by this, as the heretics suppose, but signifying the mysteries that are to come through the things they do.

When Jesus kills those kings who hold the kingdom of sin within us, we are able to fulfill what the Apostle said: “Just as we presented our members as servants to iniquity for iniquity, so now let us present our members as servants to righteousness unto justification” (Rom. VI).

What, then, is it that is blamed in this passage as though it were cruelty? “It is written,” he says: “Place your feet upon their necks and kill them.” Yet this is not [Col. 1047A] cruelty, but humanity and kindness.

Would that you were such a person as could place your feet upon serpents and scorpions, and upon every power of the enemy; that you could trample upon the lion and the dragon, and upon the basilisk—the little king that once reigned in you and nourished within you the kingdom of sin. Then, when all those who reigned in you through the work of sin had been killed, Jesus our Lord alone would reign in you.

### Chapter IV

Concerning Joshua’s battle against the city of Makkedah, and against Libnah, and against Lachish, which he struck with the edge of the sword.

(IBID.) “On the same day Joshua also captured Macedan and struck it with the edge of the sword, killing its king and all its inhabitants. He left in it not even the smallest remnant,” etc.

The battles waged through Jesus, and the slaughter of kings and enemies, must be understood as shadows and types of heavenly realities—specifically, of those battles in which our Lord Jesus, with his army and commanders, that is, with the peoples of believers and their leaders, fights against the devil and his angels. For he is the one who fought in Paul and in the Ephesians against the principalities and powers, against the rulers of this darkness, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places (Eph. VI).

And observe, ungrateful heretic, how the new things agree completely with the old. The ancients were promised the kingdom of the holy land, a land flowing with milk and honey; at that time this land was held by sinners, wicked inhabitants, and kings. Jesus came into this land with the army of the Lord and with Israelite commanders; he conquers all, kills them, and takes possession of it, and as the reward of victory he receives the kingdoms of those whom he defeated.

The kingdoms of heaven are not promised to you through the Gospels. Yet these kingdoms are neither empty nor desolate: they have their inhabitants, sinners and wicked spirits, apostate angels. There dwell those against whom Paul, sounding forth with the apostolic trumpet, urges you to battle. And just as Jesus said there that your warfare would be against the Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites, so Paul also declares this to you, saying: “Your struggle will not be against flesh and blood”—that is, we shall not fight in the manner in which the ancients fought, nor shall our battles on earth be against human beings—“but against principalities, against powers, [Col. 1047D] against the rulers of the darkness of this world” (Eph. VI).

You now surely understand in what places such battles must be undertaken by you. Or, if your understanding is insufficient unless the places themselves are identified for you in explicit words, listen to what follows: “against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places.” You have heard who must be driven from the heavenly places by war, so that you may be able to receive those places and the kingdoms of heaven as your inheritance.

And does not the Lord also clearly indicate this in the Gospel when he says: “From the days of John the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and those who use force seize it” (IBID.)?

“Then he crossed with all Israel from Macedan to Lebna and fought against it. The Lord delivered it, together with its king, into the hand of Israel. They struck the city with the edge of the sword, along with all its inhabitants, and left no remnant in it; and they did to the king of Lebna as they had done to the king of Jericho. From Lebna he crossed with all Israel to Lachis, and, having arranged the army around it, besieged it,” etc.

Would that we were worthy for the Lord Jesus to open his hall to us through his wisdom, introduce us into the treasures of his wisdom and knowledge, and deign to disclose to us more fully and open more perfectly the figures which we now attempt little by little to behold and inspect in part, as though through a mirror and in an enigma. You would see how it would become clear to us which spiritual enemy, above all, is represented by the prince of Macedan, who now attacks Israel; and likewise by the prince of Lachis and the prince of Lebna. Or you would see what form of vice or error, by which the soul is entangled, is represented within oneself by each of those whom the people of God, with Jesus as their leader, kill—namely, those who hear his commandments and keep his precept. To them he grants the power to tread upon serpents and scorpions and upon all the power of the enemy.

Let us therefore pray that our feet also may be such—so beautiful and so strong that they can tread upon the necks of enemies, and tread upon the serpent’s head in such a way that it cannot bite our heel. For whoever fights under Jesus as leader against hostile powers ought also to obtain what is written concerning the former warriors: “All the people,” it says, “returned unharmed to Jesus, and no one among the children of Israel uttered a sound with his tongue” [Col. 1048C].

You see, then, that those who serve as soldiers under Jesus must return unharmed from battle. They must never receive a wound from the flaming darts of the evil one; they must not be defiled in heart, stained in thought, or give place to demonic wounds through anger, desire, or any other occasion.

As for the added statement that no one uttered a sound with his tongue, it seems to me to show that no one boasted of the victory or attributed it to his own strength because he had prevailed. Rather, knowing that Jesus is the one who grants victory, they did not make a sound with their tongues. The apostle Paul understood this well when he said: “Yet not I, but the grace of God which is with me” (I Cor. XV).

Consider also whether this may refer to the Lord’s command in which he says (Luke XVII): “When you have done all these things, say: We are unprofitable servants; we have done what we were obliged to do.” For by this too he seems similarly to prohibit boasting over successful deeds.

But Marcion, Valentinus, Basilides, and the others with them, because they do not wish to understand these things as befits the Holy Spirit, have departed from the faith and involved themselves in many impieties. They put forward one Lord of the Law and another creator and judge of the world, as though the written passages were cruel because they command the enemies’ necks to be trodden upon and the kings of that land, which they violently invade, to be hanged upon wood.

Would that my Lord Jesus, the Son of God, grant this and command me to trample under my feet the spirit of fornication; to tread upon the necks of the spirit of anger and fury; to trample upon the demon of greed; to trample upon boasting; and to crush beneath my feet the spirit of pride. And when I have done these things, may I hang the sum of the accomplished work not upon myself but upon his cross, following Paul, who says that “through him the world has been crucified to me” (Gal. VI), and remembering what we mentioned above: “Yet not I, but the grace of God which is with me” (I Cor. XV). If I should deserve to act in this way, I shall be blessed.

And it is also said to me what Jesus said to the ancients (Deut. XXXI): “Act manfully and be strengthened before them, because the Lord God has delivered all your enemies into your hands.”

(IBID.) “Thus Joshua struck the whole hill-country, the southern region, the lowland, and Asedoth, together with their kings. He left no remnant in them, but killed everything that breathed, just as the Lord God of Israel had commanded him,” and the rest.

My Lord Jesus Christ is a warrior against hostile powers. He cast them out of the cities they possessed—that is, from our souls—and killed the kings who reigned in our souls, so that sin might no longer reign in us. After he has killed the king of sin in the city of our soul, our soul becomes the city of God; God reigns in it, and it is said to us: “The kingdom of God is within you” (Luke XVII).

This, then, which the heretics accuse of cruelty, is a work of the highest mercy: what the Lord Jesus first prefigured through the son of Nun, city by city, he now fulfills in truth, soul by soul, among believers. He deigns to make those souls which were possessed by evil and most wicked kings, in accordance with the prince of the power of the air, the spirit now at work in the children of unbelief, after these have been expelled and killed, the dwelling of God and the temple of the Holy Spirit, so that the members that had served under an unjust king—serving iniquity for impurity—may now serve righteousness for sanctification.

Understand, then, that he killed the king of Jericho, the king of Ai, the king of Lebna, the king of Lachis, and the king of Hebron so that all those who previously, under the worst kings, served the law of sin might now live under the laws of God.

But if we examine more carefully and diligently the interpretations of the names themselves, we shall find that the significance of the names can be applied sometimes to the understanding of an evil kingdom and sometimes to that of a good one. For example, Lebna is interpreted as “whiteness.” Whiteness, however, has different meanings: there is the whiteness of leprosy, and there is the whiteness of light. It is therefore possible that the interpretation of this name indicates the difference between two conditions: Lebna may have possessed the whiteness of leprosy under wicked kings; but after it was destroyed and overthrown, Lebna came under the Israelite kingdom and received the whiteness of light. In Scripture this whiteness is presented both commendably and blameworthily.

Likewise, Lachis is interpreted as “way.” A way is regarded in Scripture both commendably and blameworthily, as is not difficult to prove. Thus it says in the Psalm: “The way of the ungodly shall perish” (Ps. II). And elsewhere, conversely: “Make straight paths for your feet” (Isa. LVII, 14). It can therefore be understood that at first Lachis was the way of the ungodly; but after it was destroyed and overthrown, when the Israelites later ruled, it was brought onto a straight way.

Similarly, Hebron is said to mean “union” or “marriage.” At first the union of our soul was with an evil man, with the worst husband, the devil. After he was destroyed and extinguished, the soul was freed from the law of its former and worst husband and joined to a good and legitimate husband, the one of whom the apostle Paul says: “I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a pure virgin to Christ” (II Cor. I).

Thus the meaning of the names themselves agrees with the true condition of each city. I think that this is the better way to understand the Israelite wars: Jesus is thought to fight in this way, destroying cities and overthrowing kingdoms. For in this way the statement that he overturned and devastated each city, leaving nothing in it that breathed, neither one who might be saved nor one who might escape, will appear more reverent and more merciful.

Would that the Lord might cast out and extinguish from the souls of believers who belong to him and whom he claims for his kingdom—and from my own soul as well—all former evils in such a way that no perception of wickedness might breathe in me any longer; that no inclination toward any evil desire might be preserved in me; and that no evil word might remain to escape from my mouth.

Then, purified from all former evils under Jesus as leader, I shall be able to become one of the cities of the children of Israel, concerning which it is written: “The cities of Judah shall be built, and they shall dwell in them” (Ps. LXVIII). For even now Jesus destroys and builds each one of our souls.

And just as we said when we were expounding Jeremiah, who had received words in his mouth with which he might overthrow, build, uproot, and plant, so now also, in the matters before us, I think we must understand—not according to the heretics or according to the Jews, but as it was said there to Jeremiah: “Behold, I have appointed you today over nations and kingdoms, to uproot, overthrow, and destroy, and afterward to build and plant” (Jer. I). So also we must believe concerning the deeds written as accomplished through Jesus—or rather, concerning the things that even now are accomplished in us through our Lord Jesus.

For the first work of the word of God is to uproot preceding evils, the thorns and thistles of vices. While these evil roots hold the ground occupied, it cannot receive good and holy seeds. Therefore the necessary and primary work of the word of God is to uproot the plants of sin and to pull up and consume by fire every plant that the heavenly Father did not plant.

The second work is to plant. What does God plant? Moses says: “God planted a paradise” (Gen. II). But God also plants now, and every day he plants in the souls of believers. In the soul from which he has cut out anger, he plants gentleness; from the soul from which he has cut out pride, he plants humility; from the soul from which he has uprooted lust, he plants chastity; from the soul from which he has eradicated ignorance, he implants knowledge.

Does it not seem to you that this is the kind of planting God performs, rather than the planting of lifeless earthly trees?

There is also, above all, this work of the word of God: to destroy the buildings of the devil that he has constructed in the human soul. For he has built towers of pride and walls of arrogance in each one of us. The word of God overturns and demolishes these, so that, according to the Apostle, we may deservedly become God’s cultivated field and God’s building, established upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Jesus Christ himself as the chief cornerstone. From him the structure grows together into a temple of God in the Holy Spirit. Thus at last we may deserve to become heirs of the holy land in the portion of Israel, after all our enemies have been extinguished and killed, so that none of them remains breathing within us, but only the Spirit of Christ breathes within us through works, words, and spiritual knowledge, according to the teaching of Jesus Christ our Lord.

## CHAPTER V. On Jabin, king of Hazor, and the other kings who gathered together to fight against Israel, whom Joshua struck with the edge of the sword, hamstrung their horses, and burned their chariots with fire.

(CAP. XI.) “When Jabin, king of Hazor, heard this, he sent to Jobab, king of Madon, and to the king of Shimron, and to the king of Asaph, and also to the kings of the north who lived in the hill-country and in the plain south of Cinneroth; in the lowlands and in the regions of Dor beside the sea; and to the Canaanite in the east and west, and to the Amorite, the Hittite, the Perizzite, and the Jebusite in the hill-country; and to the Hivite who lived at the foot of Hermon in the land of Mizpah.

“And they went out, all of them with their troops, a very numerous people, like the sand that is on the seashore; and horses and chariots, an immense multitude. All these kings gathered together at the waters of Merom to fight against Israel.

“And the Lord said to Joshua: Do not fear them, for tomorrow at this same hour I shall deliver all these men wounded before Israel. You shall hamstring their horses and burn their chariots with fire,” etc.

“Another edition has the passage as follows: ‘When Jabin, king of Assur, heard this,’ it says, ‘he sent to Jobac, king of the Amorites, and to the king of Simeron, and to the king of Baza, and to the kings who were around great Sidon and throughout the hill-country; and in Arabia, which is opposite Cenereth; and to the plains and to Fanendor; and to the Canaanites who were on the coast, in the east; [Col. 1051D] and to the Amorites who were on the coast, and to the Cethaeans, the Perizzites, and the Jebusites who were on the coast and in the hill-country; and to the Hivites who were beneath the desert of Mosoma.

“And they went out, they and their kings with them, like the sand of the sea in multitude, and horses and very many chariots. All these kings gathered and joined together at the water of Mara to fight against Israel.

“Then the Lord said to Jesus: Do not fear their appearance, because tomorrow at this hour I shall deliver them wounded before Israel. You shall hamstring their horses and burn their chariots with fire.

“And Jesus came, with all the people of warriors who were with him, against them at the water of Mara, and suddenly fell upon them in the hill-country. The Lord delivered them into the hands of Israel, and they pursued them as far as great Sidon, and as far as Massesoth at the water of Mara, and as far as the plains of Masse toward the east. They slaughtered them until none of them remained who could escape.

“And Jesus did to them as the Lord had commanded him. He hamstrung their horses and burned their chariots with fire. At that time Jesus turned back and seized Assur, and killed its king with the sword.’”

You see how many wars are stirred up against Jesus and the Israelite people by hostile powers and wicked demons. Before the coming of our Lord and Savior, all these demons possessed human souls in peace and security; they reigned in their members and minds.

But when the grace and mercy of our Savior God appeared on earth, teaching us to live piously and holily in this world, separated from every contagion of sin, and enabling each soul to receive again its freedom and the image of God in which it was created from the beginning, for this reason battles and wars arise against those unjust former possessors.

And if the first are crushed, many more will rise afterward, gathering and conspiring together for evil—those who are always at odds with the good. And if they are defeated a second time, still other and more wicked powers will rise a third time. And perhaps, the more the people of God increase and grow and multiply, the more of them will conspire to attack it.

Let us attempt, as God grants us the ability, to examine each of the kings of the hostile armies and, according to the meaning of each name, to contemplate also the work performed by its wickedness.

The first of all, who is named as the author of this war and who gathers the others and invites them to a criminal conspiracy, is called Jabin; he was king of Assur. For he is the one who is also said to have summoned the others.

Jabin is interpreted as “sense” or “prudence.” What, then, is this sense or prudence except the one whom the prophet Isaiah called “great sense”? For he says: “I shall bring upon you great sense, the prince of the Assyrians, who said: By my strength I shall act, and by the wisdom of my sense I shall remove the boundaries of nations and plunder their strength” (Isa. X).

This, then, is the one who is there called “great sense,” the king of the Assyrians. Here he is Jabin, sense and prudence. For it is written that the serpent in paradise was more prudent than all the beasts that were upon the earth. And the steward of iniquity is also said to have acted prudently in the things he did (Luke XVI).

Thus Jabin is king of Assur. Assur is interpreted as “hall.” The whole earth, then, is the hall of this king, who holds dominion over the whole earth as though over a single hall: he is the devil.

Would you like to see that the earth is his hall? It is written in the Gospels (Luke XI) that the strong man sleeps securely in his hall until the stronger one comes, binds him, and takes away what he possessed. The king of the hall, therefore, is the prince of this world.

He sends to Jobac, for he is the one who sends to all the nations and invites them to battle. He sends to the king of Marom. Jobac is interpreted as “hostilities,” while Marom means “bitternesses.” The devil therefore sends to another hostile power, undoubtedly one of the fallen angels, who is king of bitternesses. Through his authority and activity all the bitternesses and hardships inflicted upon miserable mortals come about in this world.

There are various kinds of sin. Nothing can be more bitter than sin, even if certain sins initially appear sweet, as Solomon writes: “In the end it is more bitter than gall, and sharper than the edge of a sword, though it seemed sweet at the beginning” (Prov. V).

The nature of righteousness is the opposite. At the beginning it appears more bitter than gall, but at the end it is found sweeter than honey, when it has produced the fruit of virtue.

The devil therefore sent to Jobac, the king of bitterness and hostility. He also sends to King Simeron, whose name is interpreted as “hearing.” But hearing appears to have a double meaning. Sometimes it is understood positively, when God hears a person, as Simeon, one of the patriarchs, received his name because God had heard his mother’s prayer. Conversely, “hearing” is used when someone listens to the devil’s command.

For the devil is accustomed to say: “If you fall down and worship me, I shall give you all these things” (Matt. IV). But if you follow Jesus, you say to him: “I shall worship the Lord my God, and him alone shall I serve” (IBID., X).

Those who belong to his side hear him, just as this Simeron did: hearing him, he came to battle against Jesus.

He also sends to King Zife. Zife is interpreted as “How does it flow?”—as though spoken by someone expressing wonder, since it is truly astonishing how all the carnal things of this world flow away, and how those things that unbelieving people regard as lasting and eternal are fleeting and perishable.

But the person who considers the nature of things and observes how the goods of this life, as they are thought to be, are always changing and passing away, says: “How does it flow?”

The devil also summons against the children of Israel those who are around great Sidon [Note: [Col. 1053D] This mention of a journey is noteworthy, since nothing similar is found elsewhere.].

Although I have stayed in the regions of Sidon several times, I have never discovered, so far as the earthly location is concerned, that there are two Sidons, one great and the other small. But if we return to the interpretation of the name, which signifies “huntress” or “hunters,” I see that among the hostile powers, in which there are many differences, some are hunters in small things and others hunters in great things—that is, some deceive souls through small sins, others through great ones.

For example, when the soul is deceived by the pleasures of the world and the delights of the flesh, it must be said to have been captured in a small thing. But when it denies providence or worships demons as though they were the Lord, it must be considered to have been deceived in a great thing.

Therefore he now sends to great Sidon, so that they may gather as though for a hunt against the children of Israel.

He also sends to the hill-country. The hill-country is to be understood as every understanding that exalts and raises itself against the knowledge of God.

He also sends into Arabia. Arabia is interpreted as “ambushes.” He therefore invites the ambushing powers, which attack human souls not by force or through open assaults, but by unexpected ambushes and cunning deceptions—perhaps like those of whom the prophet says: “He lies in ambush in secret, like a lion in his den; he lies in ambush to seize the poor” (Ps. X).

But if someone is such as Paul, he says confidently: “For we are not ignorant of his devices” (I Cor. II).

He also sends to Cenereth. Cenereth is said to mean “like lamps”—not lamps, but “like lamps.” A lamp is one thing; something like a lamp is another.

John was a burning lamp, because he was an angel of light. But that person is like a lamp who transforms himself into an angel of light.

And if you wish to know still more clearly the difference between the lamps and the things like lamps that are in Cenereth, listen to the Savior saying to his disciples: “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning” (Luke XII).

The burning lamps are those who teach the catholic faith in the Church and illuminate the people of God with the word of truth. But those who teach heretical doctrines through false assertions drawn from testimonies of Holy Scripture seem, because they read the Scriptures, to light lamps; yet because they use false assertions, they are not lamps but things like lamps.

He also sends to the plains. For it was necessary that he summon into his alliance those who are in the plains and have lowly and earthly thoughts.

He also sends to Fenendor, which is interpreted as “conversion.” Conversion is understood in two ways. There is the conversion by which a person turns to the Lord, or by which a person is turned by God toward good. But there is also another conversion, by which King Jabin—that is, the devil—turns souls toward himself.

We have explained this also above concerning Simeron. Such must be considered the conversion that happened to the Galatians, about which the Apostle said: “You were running well; who hindered you?” (Gal. V)—that is, who turned you away from the good course and the straight way?

He also sends to those who were in the coastal regions, to the Canaanites near the waves. They are interpreted as “as though shaken,” that is, those who are always agitating everything with their movements and waves.

And he sends to the coastal Amorites. The Amorites are interpreted as “those who grow bitter,” like those whom we discussed above.

Such, then, is the catalogue of the entire army of invisible enemies who are gathered by King Jabin to attack us who follow Jesus, our leader and Savior.

But what does the Lord say? “Do not fear their appearance,” he says, “because tomorrow at this hour I shall deliver them into your hands.”

I see that today we cannot crush all of them or kill them all; but tomorrow they will be destroyed—that is, after the consummation of this age. Then every hostile power will be destroyed, and then it will be completely conquered, when you hear those who are on the left being told: “Go into the eternal fire which God prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. XXV).

Then we also, if we have conquered and have been able to obtain the kingdom by following Jesus as leader, shall receive the kingdom that the Father prepared for his saints and for those who have fulfilled his commandments and righteous ordinances.

[Col. 1055A] (IBID.) “Thus Joshua struck them all, leaving no remnant of them. He did as the Lord had commanded him: he hamstrung their horses and burned their chariots with fire. Then he immediately returned, captured Hazor, and struck its king with the sword.”

It is said that God gave Jesus the command that, after he had conquered all the enemies mentioned above, he should spare none of them but should hamstring their horses. Thus, as though fulfilling the Lord’s command, Jesus did what the Lord had instructed him.

First of all, we say to those who want these things understood only according to the letter that, if any enemy had survived, it would indeed seem reasonable for the horses to be hamstrung, so that the enemy who turned to flee could not use them. But since it is said that none of the enemies who breathed was left, why are the horses also commanded to be hamstrung, when they could plainly have been useful to the victors for service and transportation?

Would you like to know that the Israelites normally took care to preserve animals for this purpose and utility, reserving beasts for their own use after defeating their enemies? In Numbers we read that, when they went out at God’s command to fight against the Midianites, after defeating the enemy they reserved several thousand donkeys from the enemy’s spoil for their own use (Num. XXXI). There is no report there that they killed the donkeys after overcoming the enemy.

Let us therefore compare Scripture with itself and compare spiritual things with spiritual things, and let us ask why it is not written of the donkeys that they were hamstrung, nor are the spoil and animals of the Midianites said to have been killed, but rather to have benefited Israelite use.

Of these others, however, who had no donkeys but horses, the Lord himself gives the command and says: “Hamstring their horses”—and Jesus fulfilled this just as the Lord commanded.

Do we think that this happened by chance, so that the enemy horses were killed while the donkeys were preserved? Do we suppose that anything accidental occurs in God’s commands? Or does it appear more fitting to think that Scripture indicates something mystical in these matters?

In fact, the children of Israel are never reported to have used horses; and the Law gives no command concerning horses, but does give commands concerning donkeys, since they appear to exist for aiding human labor and carrying burdens. Horses, however, are more associated with the destruction of human beings; for what is done through them in battles is understood as the movement of a lustful animal and a proud neck.

Thus donkeys are frequently placed in Scripture as a type of the nations, just as the Savior showed when he sat upon a donkey; he is never reported to have sat upon a horse.

And when he sends the disciples to untie the donkey and its colt, he says to them: “If anyone asks you, say: The Lord has need of them” (Matt. XXI). Sitting upon it, he enters Jerusalem, and he is never said to have entered while sitting on a horse.

The prophet had also foretold this concerning him, that he would come to Jerusalem sitting upon a donkey, saying: “Behold, your king comes to you, gentle, sitting upon a beast of burden” (Zech. IX); “and upon a young colt, the foal of a donkey. And he shall destroy the chariot from Ephraim and the horse from Jerusalem.”

You see, therefore, that according to the prophet’s judgment, the one who sits upon a donkey destroyed the chariot of Ephraim and the horse from Jerusalem. For this reason it seems to me that the donkeys, as we said, preserve the figure of those from the nations who believe, upon whom the Lord is written to have sat.

The horses that are destroyed, and the chariots, preserve the figure of those who, having been placed in the heavenly regions, fell through lust and pride, when they offered themselves as inciters to desire the daughters of human beings and followed the one who said: “I shall set my throne above the cloud, and I shall be like the Most High” (Isa. XIV).

Perhaps this is why the prophet also says: “The horse is false for salvation” (Ps. XXXII). And again he says concerning those who trusted in demons: “Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we shall call upon the name of the Lord our God” (Ps. XIX).

For he would not have compared a chariot and a horse with God, insofar as he expects invocation; rather, he plainly showed that just as we invoke the true God, so they invoke chariots and horses—that is, demons—which those nations invoked who waged war against Israel.

(IBID.) “For Hazor had formerly held the chief position among all these kingdoms. He struck all the souls that lived there. He left no remnant in them, but devastated everything to destruction; he burned the city itself with fire, and captured all the surrounding cities and their kings,” and the rest.

Jabin, however, was king of Assur, and Assur is interpreted as “hall,” as has already been shown above. This is the Assur that is said to hold the chief position among all these kingdoms. It is understood as the prince of this world, reigning in the hall—that is, over the earth—or, more accurately, in the vices of the flesh. It is also the prince of all those kings whose power we previously explained according to the interpretation of their names, and who are said to have been killed by Jesus.

We, if we are truly serving as soldiers under Jesus as leader, must cut away their vices from within ourselves. Having received the spiritual sword, we must hamstring all this cavalry of the worst vices. We must also burn the chariots—that is, cut away from ourselves every spirit of arrogance and exaltation—and no longer invoke horses or weapons, but the name of the Lord our God.

But how will this also be fulfilled within us: “Let none be left who breathes”? We must see who it is that, according to the Lord’s command, is not even permitted to breathe.

For example, if anger rises in my heart, it may happen that I do not carry out the works of anger, whether deterred by fear or restrained by dread of future judgment. But this, he says, is not enough. You must act so that not even the agitation of anger itself has a place within you. For if the mind boils and is disturbed, even if it does not complete the deed, that very disturbance is unbecoming to one who serves under Jesus as leader.

The same must be understood concerning the vice of desire, sadness, and all the rest. The disciple of Jesus must act concerning all these things so that none of them breathes at all in his heart. Otherwise, if the habit or thought of even some small vice is left in the heart, it may grow strong with the passage of time, gradually acquire strength while remaining hidden, and finally bring us back to our vomit, so that the last state of the person to whom this happens becomes worse than the first.

(IBID.) “The children of Israel divided among themselves all the spoil of these cities and the livestock, after killing all the people.”

(From Augustine.) This must in no way be regarded as cruelty: Jesus left no living person in the cities delivered to him because the Lord had commanded this. Those who thought that God himself was thereby cruel, and for this reason refuse to believe that the true God was the author of the Old Testament, judge the works of God as perversely as they judge human sins. They do not know what each person deserves to suffer, and they consider it a great evil when those destined to fall are cast down and mortals die.

(From Adamantius.) “Blessed is the one who shall seize and dash your little ones against the rock” (Ps. CXXXVI). These are the little ones of Babylon, who are understood as nothing other than evil thoughts, which confuse and disturb our heart—for this is what Babylon means. When these thoughts are small and only beginning, they must be seized and dashed against the rock, which is Christ, and they must be killed at his command, so that nothing remains in us that breathes.

(IBID.) “As the Lord had commanded Moses his servant, so Moses commanded Joshua, and he fulfilled everything. He did not pass over a single word of all the commandments that the Lord had given Moses,” and the rest.

Here Moses is called the word of the Law itself, just as the Gospel also says: “They have Moses and the prophets; let them hear them” (Luke XVI).

The Law, then, commands us to kill all the kings of sin who provoke us to sin, just as Jesus did, and he did not transgress anything of all that Moses established for him. We have said, according to the order of our earlier exposition, that whatever the Law of God—now called Moses—establishes, Jesus fulfills in us. He is the one who kills vices within us and overthrows the most wicked kingdoms of sin.

It can also be said of our Lord and Savior himself that Jesus did everything Moses commanded in the Law and transgressed nothing. For the Apostle says: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the Law” (Gal. IV).

If, then, he was made under the Law, he fulfilled, together with the Law, everything that the Law commanded, in order to redeem us from the curse of the Law. He also says concerning himself: “I have not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it” (Matt. V).

## CHAPTER VI. On the fact that Joshua captured all the kings of Canaan and their cities by fighting, except the Hivite who lived in Gibeon.

(The same.) “Joshua fought for a long time against these kings. There was no city that surrendered itself to the Israelites, except the Hivite who dwelt in Gibeon; he captured them all by warfare.” The Septuagint reads: “And there was no city that was not handed over to the Israelites” [Col. 1058A].

(From Augustine.) It is asked how this can be true, since afterward, neither in the times of the judges nor in the times of the kings, were the Hebrews able to capture all the cities of those seven nations. It must either be understood in this way: that Joshua approached no city in battle which he did not capture; or certainly that none remained uncaptured among those cities that were in the regions mentioned above. For all the regions in which the cities concerned were located have been enumerated, and the conclusion was made: “He captured them all in battle.”

(From Adamantius.) He did not say that Joshua captured some in battle and did not capture others; rather, he captured them all—that is, he seized them all and destroyed them all. For the Lord Jesus cleansed every kind of sin and destroyed them all. We were all once foolish, unbelieving, astray, enslaved to various desires, living in wickedness and envy, hateful and hating one another—and this includes every kind of sin found in human beings before they believe. He therefore rightly says that Jesus killed all who went out to battle, for no kind of sin is so great that Jesus, who is the Word and Wisdom of God, is not superior to it. He surpasses and conquers everything.

Do we not believe that every kind of sin is removed when we come to the saving washing? The Apostle also indicates this when, after listing every kind of sin, he adds at the end: “And such were some of you; but you were washed, but you were sanctified in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Cor. 6) [Col. 1058B–C]. In this way, therefore, he is said to have captured them all in battle and to have killed them all.

(The same.) “For it had been the Lord’s decision that their hearts should be hardened, and that they should fight against Israel, fall, receive no mercy, and perish, just as the Lord had commanded Moses.”

(From Augustine.) According to the Septuagint, it is read as follows: “Because through the Lord their hearts were strengthened, so that they might go out to battle against Israel and be exterminated, so that no mercy might be shown them, but they might be exterminated, as the Lord said to Moses.” Thus it is said that through the Lord their hearts were strengthened—that is, hardened—as in the case of Pharaoh. There is no doubt that this happened justly by a profound divine judgment, when God abandons a person and the enemy takes possession [Col. 1058D]. This must be understood in the same way as there.

But another question arises here: how is it said that their hearts were strengthened for this purpose—that they should rise up for battle against Israel—and that for this reason the Israelites should not show them mercy, as though mercy ought to have been shown if they had not fought, when God had commanded that none of them be spared? The Israelites spared the Gibeonites because, pretending that they had come from a distant land, they had obtained an oath from them and the Israelites kept it.

But since the Israelites did, in some cases, voluntarily show mercy, contrary to God’s command, it should be understood that this was said so that these enemies fought in such a way that they would not be spared, and so that the Israelites themselves would not, by neglecting God’s command, be moved by them to mercy. Under Joshua’s leadership—who carefully observed all the divine commands—it cannot be believed that this could have happened.

Nevertheless, Joshua himself would not have destroyed these people so quickly unless they had risen up against him in complete agreement. In that case it could have happened that, if they had not been defeated by him, who was concerned to fulfill God’s commands, they would have remained until the time when they could be spared after Joshua’s death, when those who followed him no longer observed God’s commands with such care. Indeed, while he was still alive, the Israelites spared some of them, merely subjecting them to their authority, and they were unable to conquer others.

Yet these things did not happen under his leadership. They occurred when he had grown old and withdrawn from warfare, merely dividing the land among them. Since he was no longer fighting, they retained some portions of the land already free of enemies, while they captured other portions by fighting. That they were unable to conquer some of them was also part of divine providence, as will become clear at the appropriate places in the Scriptures [Col. 1059A–B].

(From Adamantius.) Mystically, it was brought about by the Lord that their hearts should grow strong and that they should come out to battle against Israel, so that they might be destroyed. For when the hostile powers that produce sins in us do not come, do not provoke us to sin, and do not challenge us to battle, they cannot be killed or exterminated. Therefore God is said to permit—or rather, almost to incite—the opposing powers to come out against us for battle, so that we may win the victory and they may suffer destruction.

For this reason it seems to me that there is an innumerable multitude of opposing powers, since almost every human being has certain spirits working to produce different kinds of sin in them. For example, there is a spirit of fornication, a spirit of anger, another of greed, and another of pride. If there is someone who is disturbed by all these evils, he must be thought to have all these spirits—or even more—as enemies within him. Thus, too, there are believed to be several spirits assigned to each person, because human beings do not each have only one vice or commit only one sin; rather, each person appears to commit many.

Nor should it be thought that there is one spirit of fornication who leads astray the person who, for example, fornicates in Britain and the person who does so in India or elsewhere, or that there is one spirit of anger who disturbs different people in different places. I think rather that there is one prince of fornication, but innumerable spirits who serve him in this task, and that in each individual person different spirits, serving under that prince, urge them toward such sins [Col. 1059C].

Similarly, I believe that there is one prince of the spirit of anger, but innumerable spirits acting under him, who kindle sins of this sort in each individual. In the same way, there is one prince of greed, as also of pride and of the other evils.

For this reason the Apostle does not speak of one principality among the opposing powers, but of several, against whom he writes that we all must wage war (Eph. 6). Yet there is also a prince of all these, as it were a superior being, higher in wickedness and crime, who agitates the whole world. Each of these individual powers urges people toward sin only in part through particular kinds of sin; but he, like the commander of all the princes and the master of the entire abominable army, stirs up the whole world.

When we were discussing Jabin, we disclosed his figure above, insofar as our understanding was able to grasp it.

Blessed, therefore, is the one who, continually holding the spiritual sword, does not remove it from the necks of these enemies whom we have mentioned above. As the prophet Jeremiah also says: “Cursed is the one who does the work of God negligently” (Jer. 48), and removes his sword from the blood of his enemies [Col. 1059D–1060A].

If we understand this literally, we would necessarily have to shed blood without ceasing. The Jews, who are entirely flesh and blood, think this way and therefore become cruel and merciless, saying that a curse has been placed upon those who cease from shedding blood; hence their feet are swift to shed blood.

Let such an interpretation belong to them, since they are flesh and blood. But may God grant me never to do the work of the Lord negligently, never to remove the spiritual sword of the Word of God from the blood of the opposing powers, and to put them to death in each of those who hear.

The very kinds of demons are also killed within us if, after hearing these things, we do not perform their works.

It is said in what follows that Joshua took all the land, as the Lord commanded Moses.

## CHAPTER VII. That Joshua took all the land, as the Lord spoke to Moses, and gave it as a possession to the Israelites according to their portions and tribes, and the land rested from the battles [Col. 1060C].

(The same.) “So Joshua took all the land, just as the Lord had spoken to Moses, and gave it as a possession to the Israelites according to their portions and tribes; and the land rested from its battles.”

I do not see that Joshua son of Nun took the land. For how much land did he take, when he possessed only Judea? But our Lord Jesus truly took all the land, in that a multitude of believers from every land and from all nations gathered to him.

It is also added afterward, once Jesus had taken all the land: “And the land rested,” it says, “from its battles.” How can this truly be said of the son of Nun, since the land never really ceased from wars during his lifetime? But this is fulfilled in my Lord alone.

If you consider yourself, who came to Jesus and through the grace of baptism received remission of sins, then even in you the flesh does not fight against the spirit, nor the spirit against the flesh: your land has ceased from its battles. If you carry Christ Jesus in your body, then, when all battles within you have ceased, you will become peaceful and will be called a son of God.

But this will happen after you have passed through the wars and conquered your adversaries. Then rest will be given to you, so that you may rest beneath your vine, which is Christ, and beneath the Holy Spirit, and thus give thanks to God the almighty Father in Christ Jesus our Lord.

## CHAPTER VIII. The number of cities that Joshua conquered and gave to the Israelites as a possession [Col. 1061A].

(Chapter 12.) “These are the kings of the land whom Joshua and the Israelites struck beyond the Jordan, toward the western region, from Baalgad in the plain of Lebanon to the mountain whose portion rises toward Seir. Joshua gave it as a possession to the tribes of Israel, assigning to each its portion, both in the hill country and in the plains and lowlands. In Asedoth, the wilderness, and the south, there were the Hittite, the Amorite, the Canaanite, the Perizzite, the Hivite, and the Jebusite,” and so forth.

Joshua’s battle and victory among foreign peoples signifies the battle and victory of our Lord Jesus Christ, which he, the head of the Church, daily wages and completes through his members [Col. 1061B].

The seven nations whom the Israelites defeated in battle signify spiritual wickedness, against which the people of God ceaselessly struggle. This can be understood from the meanings of their names: Hittite is interpreted as “one who fears” or “one who is stupefied”; Girgashite as “one who expels the settler”; Amorite as “bitter”; Canaanite as “merchant,” or “one who moves” or “one who is ashamed”; Perizzite as “one who separates” or “one who scatters”; Hivite as “wild,” “most evil,” or “one who gathers stones”; and Jebusite as “trampled.”

What is represented by the Hittite except the fear and stupor of the devil, who is signified by his constant effort to terrify the servants of Christ? The evil one acts so that the losses of present things and the troubles of persecutions become a terror to Christ’s soldiers, in order that he may more easily provoke and seduce them toward the pleasures of the world and the desire for present things [Col. 1061C].

And who is shown in the Girgashite except the one who fraudulently expelled the settler from paradise? Who is designated in the Amorite except the one who is altogether bitter and full of indignation? What is suggested by the Canaanite except the most wicked merchant, who through greed stirs up lawsuits and quarrels?

And who is indicated by the Perizzite except the one who, through evil jealousy, separates a person from God and leads him to hell, and scatters discord among those who are united in spirit?

In the Hivite, no one is more aptly represented than the one who is everywhere wild, hard, and most evil. The Jebusite, too, by its name signifies the devil’s insolence: through his own pride he exalts himself, but through the humility of Christ’s servants he is despised, trampled, and crushed [Col. 1061D].

As long as the holy Church journeys in this world, it always has such wicked powers as adversaries; nevertheless, in hope of victory, it never ceases to fight against them. Thus Israel is described as fighting under Joshua beyond the Jordan, toward the western region, from Baalgad in the plain of Lebanon to the mountain whose portion rises toward Seir, and as striking them. For when the people of the faithful recognize the troops of enemies gathered against them, they always strive to reach the palm of victory, both on level ground and in difficult places, in prosperity and in adversity. Baalgad is interpreted as “their assembly.”

The tribes of Israel possess their individual portions, both in the hill country and on the plains and lowlands, and in Asheroth and the wilderness. So holy men strive to possess their souls through patience, and through the weapons of righteousness, on the right and on the left, through glory and disgrace, through ill repute and good repute, they rejoice to remain in the same state of equity [Col. 1062A].

But having touched on these matters briefly, let us see what the number of cities that the Israelites captured in battle under Joshua signifies figuratively. The kings of thirty-two cities fell while fighting together with him.

What does the number thirty signify except faith in the Holy Trinity together with observance of the Ten Commandments? And what does the number two signify except the two Testaments and the two commandments of charity, upon which the whole Law and the Prophets depend?

The soldiers of Christ therefore know no other way to wage war under the true King than through the power of faith and observance of God’s commandments; and in this way they faithfully desire to receive the reward of their labor [Col. 1062B]. This may also be understood as signified by the same number. For thirty-two is four times eight, while true possession consists in the eight beatitudes, because through them the kingdom of heaven is attained. But no one will reach it unless he hastens to ascend there, according to the teaching of the four Gospels, by the chariot of the virtues.

The cities whose kings are recorded as having been defeated there numbered thirty-two:

- Jericho, interpreted as “moon”;
- Ai, “eye” or “fountain”;
- Jerusalem, “vision of peace”;
- Hebron, “participation in sadness” or “strength”;
- Jerimoth, “fearing death” or “the height of death”;
- Lachish, “way” or “a man for himself”;
- Eglon, “calf of their mourning” or “of their festivity”;
- Gezer, “cutting off” or “division”;
- Debir, “speaking” or again “fearing”;
- Geder, “wall” and “hedge”;
- Hormah, “his anathema”;
- Areth, “rising up from descent”;
- Lempna, “brightness” or “bricks”;
- Adullam, “their testimony”;
- Makkedah, “burning” or “eastern”;
- Bethel, “house of God”;
- Daphua, “fruit from a tree,” not “from wickedness”;
- Apher, “he digs” or “earth”;
- Aphec, “contained” or “continence”;
- Sharon, “prince of sadness”;
- Madon, “contradiction” or “dwelling”;
- Hazor, “arrow of light”;
- Semeron, “its guardian” or “he saw the name”;
- Achshaph, “medicine”;
- Taanach, “answering” or “humility”;
- Megiddo, “its fruits” or “its upper room”;
- Ledes, “sanctity”;
- Jachanae, “he possessed the people”;
- Ermeli, “condemnation” or “one who contends”;
- Dor, “generation”;
- Gilgal, “vows” or “revelation”;
- Thersa, “pleasing.”

But if we turn these names according to their interpretations toward spiritual understanding, we shall undoubtedly find there the destruction of vices and the advancement of virtues [Col. 1062C–D].

The soldier of Christ must first recognize his own frailty and mutability, which is signified by Jericho, interpreted as “moon.” Then he must lift up the eyes of his mind to contemplate heavenly things and, attending to the future, reach the fountain of eternal life. Whoever drinks from it will never thirst; thus he reaches the vision of peace, which is signified by Jerusalem.

Next he must consider the evils he has committed, experience salutary sorrow for them, and practice works of virtue, as is expressed in the name Hebron. Then, fearing future death and the height of everlasting death, which is expressed by the name Jerimoth, he must take up virtue through Lachish [Col. 1063A] and travel the way of righteousness, which leads to eternal life.

During all this he must devote himself to compunction of heart, recognizing that he has been placed in the pilgrimage of this life, and must strive with all his strength to attain, through God’s grace, the festivity of the future homeland, which is signified by the name Eglon.

Through the meaning of Gezer, let him cut off the pleasure of the flesh and scatter the enemy’s wicked suggestion. Let him speak what is right, which the name Abi signifies, and let him fear the future judgment of the heavenly Judge, because people will give an account on the day of judgment for every idle word they have spoken on earth.

Let him fortify himself with the wall of faith, as Gezer teaches, and renounce the devil and his works through perpetual anathema, as Hormah reminds us.

Thus, after the descent into vices, let him rise into the citadel of virtues; this is what Areth urges by its name. Through the names Lempna and Adullam, instructed by the testimonies of Scripture, let him direct his brightness toward the eternal light.

Through Makkedah, let him also put on the rising of the true light and burn up the enemy’s schemes and counsels, so that he may remain perpetually in our Bethel, which is the holy Church of God. There, according to the interpretation of Apher, let him labor in his flesh so that, according to the meaning of Daphua, he may receive the fruits of eternal life.

Let him possess continence and confound the prince of sadness, that is, the devil. Enlightened by divine light, let him contradict the devil’s persuasions. These four names of cities—Aphec, Sharon, Madon, and Hazor—teach all these things through their interpretations [Col. 1064A].

Let him guard his heart with all diligence, as Semeron suggests, and through the name Achshaph learn to seek the medicine of the sacred Scriptures. Warned by Taanach, let him preserve humility everywhere. By the name Megiddo, let him recognize the fruit of virtues and learn to desire the sublimity of contemplation.

Thus he will truly reach holiness, which Tedes signifies, and will be able to be present and useful in many ways, as Lakanae demonstrates by its name. He despises death because he has condemned vices, as Ermeli figuratively shows. Existing as a participant in divine generation through the name Dor, he will be called a peaceful son of God.

Passing by heavenly revelation over the wheel of the present life through Gilgal [Col. 1064B], he finally recognizes, in the name Thersa, that he pleases the Most High, when he is transferred from the dwelling-place of this world to the heavenly kingdom and to the perpetual vision of God, in accordance with what the Psalmist says: “I shall be pleasing before the Lord in the light of the living” (Ps. 55). And again: “I shall please the Lord in the land of the living” (Ps. 114).

I have therefore briefly noted these things; I have not expounded them. I have done so so that the reader may know what sublimity of divine wisdom is found in the sacred Scriptures, and that everything discovered there can rightly be transferred to his own edification by anyone who does not neglect to look upon it with the eye of sound faith and meditate upon it diligently.

# BOOK THREE

[Col. 1063]

## CHAPTER I. On Joshua’s old age and the Lord’s word to him [Col. 1063C].

“Joshua was old and advanced in age.”

Presbyters, or elders, are not called by this name because they have lived a long life; rather, they are honored by this title because of the maturity of their understanding and the dignity of their venerable life—especially when the phrase that follows is added to “presbyter”: “full of days.”

For if someone who appears to be a presbyter or elder is to be called so because of the length of his life, whom else ought this title to fit more than Adam the first, or certainly Methuselah or Noah, who are clearly said to have lived in this world for more years than the others? Yet we see that none of them is reported by Scripture to be called a presbyter or elder. Rather, Abraham, who lived for a much shorter time, is the first in the Holy Scriptures to be called a presbyter or elder (Gen. 24).

The Lord also said to Moses: “Choose for yourself from the whole people elders whom you yourself know to be worthy” (Exod. 3).

But you too, listener, observe throughout all Scripture whether you can find this designation—“elder and full of days”—placed upon any sinner.

Here, then, it is the voice of the Holy Spirit pronouncing Jesus a presbyter or elder, advanced in days. For it says: “Jesus was a presbyter or elder, advanced in days.” This could certainly not be said of a sinner, because a sinner is not advanced in days [Col. 1063D–1064C]. He does not stretch forward toward what lies ahead, forgetting what is behind; rather, he is always turned backward and returns to his vomit, and therefore is not fit for the kingdom of heaven. But the one who is always stretching forward toward what lies ahead is advanced in his days.

“And the Lord said to him: You have grown old and are advanced in age, and a very extensive land remains, which has not yet been divided by lot,” and so forth.

I do not know whether this can be understood in this passage as being said by the Lord to Joshua on account of his physical old age. Everyone saw it; everyone knew it. What could be so great in these divine responses that people should explain them by saying to an old man, “You are old,” when everyone saw and knew this?

But it seems to me that through these words the Lord gives Joshua son of Nun a great testimony when he says to him: “You are advanced in days.”

Insofar as it is lawful for us to speak or disclose divine mysteries, I think that just as this sun makes day for the world, so the Sun of righteousness makes certain days spiritual, which are illumined by the radiance of truth and the lamp of wisdom.

If someone spends this present life under God’s commandments—this life which, as Jacob said, is “of few and evil days” (Gen. 47)—and keeps himself undefiled by the world, and subdues all his adversaries and enemies, he is spiritually advanced beyond these few and evil days and is promoted to those eternal and good days marked by the light of the eternal Sun.

Jesus, therefore, is to be understood as being pronounced advanced in days in this same manner, according to the divine responses.

But since we have undertaken to refer what is said about Joshua also to our Lord and Savior, who is so rightly understood as a presbyter and elder, advanced in days, as he who is the beginning, the firstborn of all creation? Perhaps for this reason he alone is truly and perfectly called the presbyter, before whom there is no one.

Thus, although there are people called presbyters, elders, or high priests in the Scriptures, the Lord Jesus is the prince among high priests. Just as he is the chief among shepherds, so he must be regarded as the chief among presbyters or elders [Col. 1065A–B], and as the chief among bishops.

Whatever honorable title there may be, he is believed to be the first and chief in it, and the Savior of those who believe, because he is the head of all.

Hear also the divine response that says: “You are advanced in days, and a very great amount of land remains.”

Earlier, as we observed, it was said that the land had ceased from them and that Jesus had taken all the land. Yet now it is written that a very great amount of land remains. Do you think these statements contradict one another? Is this to be suspected lightly?

Let us return to spiritual understanding, and in it you will find nothing contradictory.

Consider first the coming of our Lord and Savior, when he came to sow his seed throughout the world. See how he took possession of the whole land by the mere sowing of the seed, how he drove from it the opposing powers and the fallen angels who had occupied the minds of the nations, and how he meanwhile sowed the Word and spread the Churches. This was his first possession of the whole land.

But follow, listener, the subtle lines of the Word, and I will show you how he also took possession a second time of this land, which is now said by Joshua to be a very great amount of land left over.

Hear Paul speaking about it: “He must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet” (Heb. 10).

This, then, is the land that is now said to be left in great abundance, until all are placed beneath his feet, and through this inheritance he takes possession of all.

“And this,” he says, “is the land that remains: all the territory of the Philistines,” and many other things that follow.

Much still remains, insofar as our times are concerned, which we see has not yet been subjected to the feet of Jesus; all of it must necessarily be taken possession of. For there can be no end to things unless everything has first been subjected.

Thus the prophet also says (Zech. 9) that all the nations, serving him, extend from the ends of the rivers to the ends of the earth before him. Ethiopians will come from beyond the banks of the rivers; Ethiopians will offer sacrifices. From this it is clear that at his second coming Jesus will take possession of this great land that remains.
