Blessed, however, are those who were taken possession of at his first coming. They will truly be in grace, for while many adversaries resist and many enemies attack, they receive the inheritance of the land of promise through warfare and arms [Col. 1065C–1066A].

But when someone is subjected by necessity—when even the last enemy, death, must be destroyed—then those who are subjected will no longer be in grace.

(Chapter 13.) “To the south are the Hivites, all the land of Canaan, and Maara of the Sidonians, as far as Apheca and the borders of the Amorite and its boundaries. The region of Lebanon also extends toward the east, from Baalgad beneath Mount Hermon until one enters Hamath. All those who dwell in the mountain country, from Lebanon to the waters of Misrephoth, and all the Sidonians. I am the one who will destroy them from before the Israelites. Let it therefore come as Israel’s inheritance, as I commanded you” [Col. 1066B].

Although he had listed many nations, he said of the Sidonians alone: “I myself will exterminate all the Sidonians from before the Israelites.”

The Canaanites were named; those from the borders of Ekron and from the regions to the left of the rivers were named; and many other nations were named. Yet of the Sidonians alone the Lord said that he would overthrow them.

As we have already said, the Sidonians are interpreted as “hunters.” Who are these evil hunters whom the Lord exterminates, except those opposing powers of which the prophet says: “They prepared snares beneath my feet” (Ps. 56), with which they hunt and deceive the souls of sinners?

The Lord therefore exterminates these hunters. When such hunters have perished, when no one remains to set snares and nets in order to deceive souls into sin, then each person will rest beneath his vine and beneath his fig tree.

## CHAPTER II. On the division of the land among the individual tribes of Israel, and on the fact that he gave the tribe of Levi no possession, but that the sacrifices and offerings of the Lord, the God of Israel, are their inheritance.

(The same.) “And now divide the land as a possession among the nine tribes and the half-tribe of Manasseh, because Reuben and Gad have taken possession of the land that Moses, the servant of the Lord, gave them beyond the Jordan toward the east,” and so forth [Col. 1066C].

It has been read that Moses gave an inheritance to certain people; afterward it is read that Joshua also, according to the Lord’s command, distributed the inheritance. Moses therefore distributed the inheritance first, and Joshua second.

Now understand Moses as the Law. Those who lived according to the Law received the inheritance first, but they received it from the land of promise. Then, after they received the land of their inheritance—for they do not possess or divide it, but wait until it is distributed to them by Joshua as their allotted share—is it not clearly what the Apostle says when, writing to the Hebrews about the earlier fathers, he says that they pleased God through faith, and adds: “Although all these received approval through faith, they did not obtain the promise, since God had provided something better for us, so that apart from us they might not be made perfect” (Heb. 11)?

They therefore have their promise, and they have rested, and they were judged worthy through Moses to receive the inheritance. Nevertheless, they too still fight and are engaged in battle on behalf of those who serve under Joshua.

But you may ask who those fighters are and what battle they wage. I think it is this: all those fathers who fell asleep before us fight together with us and help us by their prayers.

I also heard an elder teacher say something of this kind concerning the passage in Numbers (chap. 4) where it is written that “that synagogue will lick up this synagogue as a calf licks up the green grass of the field.” He said: Why was such a comparison chosen except because this is what the passage ought to be understood to mean: the synagogue of the Lord that preceded us prays for us among the saints, and in its tongue consumes the opposing synagogues—that is, it consumes our adversaries through prayers and supplications [Col. 1067A–B]?

We therefore must not fight our invisible enemies with weapons, but with prayers and the words of the Lord, with meditation, works, and right thoughts. The fathers were armed in this way also, conquering through faith and works.

Those who receive the Law serve as shadows and copies of the heavenly things, since the Law is the shadow of the true Law. In the same way, those who divide the inheritance of the land in Judea are correspondingly the copy and shadow of the heavenly division.

The reality was therefore in heaven, while the shadow and copy of the reality were on earth. As long as this shadow stood on earth, there was an earthly Jerusalem, there was a temple, there was an altar, and there was visible worship. There were high priests and priests; the cities and villages of Judea also remained, together with all the things now recorded in this book [Col. 1067C].

But when, at the coming of our God and Savior descending from heaven, truth sprang up from the earth and righteousness looked down from heaven, the shadows and copies fell. Jerusalem fell; the temple fell; the altar was removed, so that there would be no place where one ought to worship, whether on Mount Gerizim or in Jerusalem. Rather, true worshipers who worship the Father worship in spirit and truth.

Thus, when the reality was present, the type and shadow ceased. When the temple that was fashioned by the Spirit of God and the power of the Most High in the Virgin’s womb was present, the temple fashioned from stones was destroyed.

The high priest of the good things to come was present; the high priests of bulls and goats ceased. The Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world came; the lamb taken from the flock ceased, slaughtered for so many ages to no purpose and in vain.

The division of the inheritance is therefore reported as having occurred first and second: the first through Moses, and the second—and the more powerful—through Joshua. Moses assigned possession beyond the Jordan to the tribe of Reuben, the tribe of Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh; all the others received their inheritance through Joshua [Col. 1067D].

We have already explained how those who lived according to the Law pleased God, preceding in time those who reach the promises through faith in Jesus, yet do not receive what is perfect. They await those who come later and please God at a different time but with one faith, as the Apostle said: “Would that they might attain perfection without us” (1 Cor. 4).

[Col. 1068A] (Likewise.) “But to the tribe of Levi he gave no possession; rather, the sacrifices and offerings of the Lord, the God of Israel, are themselves his inheritance, as he spoke to him,” and so forth.

Neither Moses gave the Levites an inheritance, nor did Jesus. What else, then, should we understand except that there are certain people in the Lord’s Church who surpass the rest of humanity by strength of character and the grace of their merits, and to whom the Lord himself is said to be their inheritance? And if it is permissible to hear such things and to disclose something of the hidden mystery, let us see whether this may perhaps be what secretly reveals the figure of the priests and Levites: that among the whole people—I mean those who are being saved—the greater and far more numerous part consists undoubtedly of those who believe simply and please the Lord, in the fear of God, through good works, honorable conduct, and approved actions. [Col. 1068B] But there are few, very few, who devote themselves to wisdom, keep their mind pure and undefiled, and cultivate their souls in every distinguished virtue; by the grace of their teaching they illuminate for the other, simpler people the path on which they walk and by which they come to salvation. These perhaps are designated under the name of Levites and priests, whose inheritance is the Lord himself, who is Wisdom, and whom they are said to have loved more than all others.

Yet I find a certain difference between what Moses distributed and what Jesus distributed. When Moses distributed the land beyond the Jordan to the two and a half tribes, he did not give the Levites the portion of dwelling that belonged to them. Jesus, however, gave dwelling places not only to the tribes whom he himself distributes, but also to those who had been settled beyond the Jordan by Moses. For dwelling places are assigned to the Levites in each of the tribes, so that we might recognize the mystery as all the more magnificent. This Levitical and priestly order, which devotes itself to the wisdom and knowledge of God, could not receive from Moses a lot of habitation, because Moses was not the minister of truth but of the exemplary shadow. Jesus, however, our Lord, who was the Wisdom of God, himself provides dwellings for the wise.

Moses could not say, “Go, sell everything that you have, give it to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come, follow me” (Matt. XIX). For this is to give a portion to the Levites. Nor could Moses say, “Whoever does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple” (Luke XIV). [Col. 1068D] Moses could not say: “For everyone who does not hate his father or mother, brothers and sisters and children, and even his own life, cannot be my disciple” (ibid., v. 26). Moses could not do this; therefore he could not distribute the dwellings of the priests or Levites.

Blessed, then, is the one who presents himself as such and is found to be perfect in all those things that Jesus commands, so that he may receive from Jesus a lot in the heavenly dwelling in the future. Concerning him the Lord himself says: “Father, I desire that where I am, these also may be with me” (John XVII). And: “Just as I and you are one, so may these also be one in us” (ibid., v. 21).

But if, hearing that the Lord is called the inheritance of the perfect and the eminent, you do not know or are uncertain what is signified under this name, listen: the Lord is Wisdom. Whoever, then, has the Lord as his inheritance receives the inheritance of wisdom. The Lord is called righteousness. Whoever has the Lord as his inheritance receives the inheritance of righteousness. The Lord is peace; the Lord is redemption; the Lord is salvation; and in the Lord are hidden the treasures of wisdom and knowledge. All these things will be received as an inheritance by the one whose inheritance is the Lord.

Nevertheless, even these people, for whom the wisdom of God, the word of God, truth, and righteousness are said to be an inheritance, meanwhile receive dwelling together with those whose inheritance is held on earth. Through their association, those who are not yet able by themselves to become participants may become sharers in the wisdom and knowledge of God, and in his truth and word. [Col. 1069B] Thus the divine dispensation extends even to the least, so that those who cannot principally become capable of divine grace may deserve to be enlightened through association with the saints. In this way what the Apostle says to the Corinthians concerning the saints of Jerusalem is fulfilled: “that our abundance may become for their want” (2 Cor. VIII), so that their abundance also may become for your want.

Thus even now the Levites and priests, who do not possess land, are commanded to dwell together with the Israelites, so that the priest and Levite may receive from the Israelite the earthly things that they do not possess, and in turn the Israelite may receive from the priest and Levite the heavenly and divine things that he does not possess. For the law of God has been entrusted to the priests and Levites, so that they may devote themselves to this alone and attend to the word of God without any anxiety. But, again, in order that they may be free for this work, they must make use of the services of the laypeople. For if the layperson does not provide the things necessary for the priests and Levites, they will be occupied with such matters—that is, with bodily concerns—and will be less free for the law of God. If they are not free and do not devote themselves to the law of God, you will be in danger; for the light of knowledge that is in them will be darkened because you have not supplied oil for the lamp, and through your fault what the Lord said will occur: “When the blind leads the blind, both will fall into the pit” (Matt. XV). [Col. 1069C]

And what the Lord said will also be fulfilled: “If the light that is in you is darkness, how great is the darkness!” (Matt. VI.) Therefore, so that the light of knowledge may shine in the priests, let their lamp always be burning. You must fulfill your duty; you must complete God’s command concerning service to the priests. But if, after receiving from you the things that are necessary, they nevertheless do not pursue greed but have earned a blessing, while they themselves neglect to devote themselves to learning, to attend to the word of God, and to meditate on God’s law day and night, they will see how they are to render an account to the Lord for your souls.

## CHAPTER III. That the nine and a half tribes received their lots through Eleazar the priest and Joshua son of Nun, while the two and a half tribes received their portions through Moses beyond the Jordan

(CAP. XIV.) “This is what the children of Israel possessed in the land of Canaan, which Eleazar the priest, Joshua son of Nun, and the heads of families gave them, dividing everything by lot among the tribes of Israel, as the Lord had commanded through Moses, for the nine tribes and the half-tribe. For Moses had given possession beyond the Jordan to the two and a half tribes, except for the Levites, who received nothing among their brothers but had succeeded to their place,” and so forth.

Let us learn from the Law how necessarily the division of the land was written down—a division made first through Moses and second through Jesus—not so that we should preserve both arrangements, but so that, explaining the meaning of each, we should hold fast only to the one delivered to us by Jesus our Lord.

Accordingly, the land that Moses distributed beyond the Jordan, Jesus, the prince of the tribes of Israel, distributed to those in the holy land and the good land. You see, then, that when the true inheritance of the holy land begins to be distributed by him—that is, by the Savior—the true and spiritual princes of Israel will also be appointed. Who should we think the princes of our tribes, or the princes of the Church, are, except the holy apostles, to whom the Savior says: “You also shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. XIX)?

The priest is also included in the division, namely, the mysterious and mystical word of God. For it says that “Jesus and Eleazar will come together to divide the land.” Let us see who was the first to receive an inheritance from Jesus. “Caleb,” it says, “son of Jephunneh.” He asked for and received it first, before the others, for certain reasons and with certain words that have been written down—words that can also instruct us toward salvation.

[Col. 1070C] Caleb is said to be interpreted first of all as “heart.” Who, then, is “as a heart” except the one who devotes himself to understanding in everything? For no other member of the body is said to be in the Church except that which is more excellent for us, the heart—that is, the person who conducts everything with reason and foresight and orders all things as though he were nothing other than the heart.

His father Jephunneh is also interpreted as “conversion.” Caleb, therefore, is the son of conversion. Who except the person converted to the Lord will bring forth such a fruit from himself and beget a son who is a heart? Everyone, then, who occupies himself with divine meanings and acts prudently and rationally in all things is Caleb.

At first he was instructed by Moses, but afterward by Jesus, whom he attended, saying: “You know the word that the Lord spoke to Moses, the man of God.” You know the word that he spoke. For who else can know the word that the Lord spoke to Moses except Jesus alone? No one understood the Law as Jesus taught it. He taught and opened everything; he revealed to Paul “that the law is spiritual” (Rom. VII).

## CHAPTER IV. Caleb’s address to Joshua concerning the land of Hebron, which he requested to be given to him

(Likewise.) “Caleb son of Jephunneh, the Kenizzite, spoke to him: You know what the Lord spoke to Moses, the man of God, concerning me and you at Kadesh-barnea. I was forty years old when Moses, the servant of the Lord, sent me from Kadesh-barnea to examine the land, and I reported to him what seemed true to me. But my brothers who had gone up with me discouraged the heart of the people; nevertheless I followed the Lord my God. And Moses swore on that day, saying: The land on which your foot has trodden shall be your possession and that of your sons forever,” and the rest.

“Moses spoke,” he says, “concerning me and concerning you.” Concerning you, this is what the Lord said: “If you believed Moses, you would certainly also believe me, for he wrote about me” (John V). But what did he say concerning me—that is, concerning Caleb, who is the heart? It is certain that Moses wrote concerning the heart, since he wrote everything prudently and wisely.

He says, then: “Today I am as strong as I was then.” For the holy person is equally strong in present things and in past things, in the last things and in the former things, in the Gospels and in the Law. Thus he says that he is strong today under Jesus as he was then under Moses, because the watchful heart is strong in the mysteries of both Testaments.

Let us also examine his request, what Caleb son of Jephunneh asks from Jesus: “I ask you,” he says, “for this mountain,” as the Lord says, “on that day.” The holy person seeks nothing lowly or abject, nothing lying in sunken valleys, but asks for a lofty mountain—a mountain on which there are great and fortified cities. He asked for these things because he knew how to wage war, as it is written: “The wise man will seize fortified cities and destroy the stronghold in which the impious trusted” (Prov. XXI).

When Solomon said this, do you suppose that he meant to teach us that the wise man would capture cities and destroy fortifications built of stones? Or does it rather indicate that the cities and walls are the impious doctrines and the syllogisms of philosophers by which they establish various impieties and things contrary to the divine law, observed among pagans and barbarians? These should be assigned to such people, as should the fortified cities set upon mountains—those which heretics place, as it were, upon lofty mountains through their assertions.

The wise person, then, preaching the word of truth, destroys these cities and overthrows the deceitful towns with the battering ram of truth, just as Paul said: “destroying arguments and every height that exalts itself against the knowledge of God” (2 Cor. X). Thus even now this most wise Caleb stands before Jesus, promises that he is strong for war, and is ready for battle. [Col. 1071D] He therefore asks that permission or authority be granted to him to engage the dialecticians of the age, those who confirm falsehoods as truths, so that he may refute and overcome them and overthrow everything they have built through false assertions.

Therefore, when Jesus saw his eagerness, he blessed him, it says—that is, because he asked for and heard such things. You too, if you wish to devote yourself to study, meditate prudently on the Law, and become a heart in the law of God, can overthrow those magnificent and fortified cities—that is, the assertions of falsehood—so that you too may deserve to be blessed by Jesus and receive Hebron.

Hebron is interpreted as “union” or “marriage.” Through this it may perhaps be shown that the double cave purchased by the patriarch Abraham is the place in which the marriages and remains of the patriarchs lie: Abraham with Sarah, Isaac with Rebekah, and Jacob with Leah.

Caleb therefore deserved to receive the remains of the patriarchs as an inheritance, undoubtedly because, through the wisdom that was vigorous in him, and because he had understood under both Moses and Jesus the meaning of that union, he had perceived the reason why Abraham lay there with Sarah alone, where neither Hagar nor Keturah had deserved to be joined to him; and why Jacob appeared to lie there with Leah alone, while neither Rachel, who had been more greatly loved, nor any of his concubines had been joined to him in the tomb.

Thus the prudent and wise Caleb receives an inheritance in the memorials of the patriarchs. Jesus assigns to him Hebron, the metropolis of the nations of the Anakim, and his lot remains there to this day.

The name Hebron was formerly Cariath-arba. Adam the great is buried there in the land of the Anakim, and the land ceased from warfare. Cariath-arba is therefore interpreted as “the city of four.” Although it is corruptly written Arboe in the Greek manuscripts, in the Hebrew manuscripts it is read Arbe, that is, “four,” because three patriarchs—Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—were buried there, together with the great Adam, as is written in this book, that is, in Joshua son of Nun, although some suppose that he was buried at the place of Calvary.

This same Hebron was formerly the metropolis of the Philistines and the dwelling place of giants; afterward it became David’s kingdom and, in the tribe of Judah, a priestly and refuge city. It lies approximately twenty-two miles south of Aelia. Abraham’s oak, also called Mamre, was still being shown until the reign of King Constantius, and his mausoleum may be seen at the present time. Although a church has now been built there by our people and surrounds the place, all the nations superstitiously worship the terebinth, because Abraham once received angels as guests beneath it.

It was therefore first called Arbe, and afterward received the name Hebron from one of Caleb’s sons. Read the Book of Chronicles.

## CHAPTER V. Concerning the lot of the children of Judah, and how Caleb destroyed from Hebron the three sons of Anak: Sesai, Ahiman, and Talmai

(CAP. XV.) “Thus the lot of the children of Judah according to their clans was this: from the border of Edom, the wilderness of Zin toward the south, and as far as the extreme end of the southern region,” and so forth.

(From Augustine.) It is customary for Scripture to call the four regions of the world “fields” and “regions.” In the distribution of the boundaries of the tribe of Judah, however, only two are mentioned, while two are omitted. For it is written: “The boundaries of the tribe of the children of Judah according to their clans were from the borders of Idumea, from the wilderness of Zin toward the west”; and when the boundaries toward the west had been described, then afterward those toward the east: “the whole Salt Sea,” it says. It omitted the other two regions, namely, the north and the south.

See, then, whether these things are not filled with mysteries, even if we cannot individually perceive or explain them all. Nevertheless, as the Lord deigns to grant and as we are able to receive, we shall attempt to examine each one.

“The boundaries of Judah,” it says, “were according to their clans, from the borders of Idumea, from the wilderness of Zin, toward the west.” The boundaries of Judah, therefore, are near the borders of Idumea. Idumea, as we have often already said, is interpreted as “earthly.” After earthly things, then, the boundaries of Judah immediately follow, but “from the wilderness,” it says, “of Zin.” Zin is interpreted as “temptations.” After temptations, therefore, the boundaries of Judah’s inheritance follow.

The west and the east are named, as are the neighboring places that we mentioned above, indeed the bordering places. The Valley of Egypt is also designated near the western regions, the region that is from the wilderness toward the west; toward the east, however, the boundaries are enclosed by the Salt Sea.

After this, it says, “from the hills that extend toward the west”; and from there one ascends from the west as far as Barnea, and thus continues westward to Kadesh. “These are their boundaries from the southwest; and from there it proceeded as far as the Valley of Egypt.”

You see how it names the western regions, the southwest, Egypt, and the setting of the sun—without doubt so that everyone may know that all these things must be escaped and traversed, in order finally to reach the royal tribe, concerning which the Apostle says: “It is certain that our Lord Jesus Christ arose from Judah” (Heb. VII).

The wilderness of Zin is from the borders of Idumea. A little earlier we said that the wilderness of Zin signifies temptations. Therefore, we must cross the desert of temptations so that we may reach the inheritance of the children of Judah. But we must ascend the ascent of the hills of Akrabbim, which is interpreted as “of the scorpion.”

We must pass over and trample those scorpions, undoubtedly those of whom the Savior says: “Behold, I have given you power to tread upon serpents and scorpions” (Luke X). Whoever wishes and desires to enter the inheritance of the tribe of Judah must ascend these ascents, trample and escape the scorpions that obstruct the way. Hence I think that this journey must be made, because the Lord said to the prophet Ezekiel: “Son of man, you walk in the midst of scorpions” (Ezek. II).

“And the boundaries,” it says, “extend as far as Kadesh.” Kadesh is interpreted as “holy” or “sanctification.” The boundaries of Judah therefore reach as far as sanctification.

Let us also see what the boundaries are on the eastern side—not because we now wish to make a catalogue of places, but so that we may contemplate the images of the mysteries signified through them. It is said, then, that the boundaries of Judah toward the east are the Salt Sea. After this, in its region, the Fountain of the Sun and a city are named; and in this same tribe there is also the City of Letters.

Everyone who wishes to enter the portion of the children of Judah must first cross the Salt Sea, overcome the storms of this life and of this world, and escape all the things in this world that, because of their uncertain use and slippery nature, are compared with the waves of the sea. Then he can reach the land of Judah and approach the Fountain of the Sun.

What, then, is the Fountain of the Sun, or the City of the Sun? Surely it is of the one concerning whom it is written: “For you who fear my name the sun of righteousness shall rise” (Mal. IV). If you first escape the Salt Sea, you will find the fountain of this sun in the land of Judah. What fountain? Certainly the one of which Jesus said: “Whoever drinks of the water that I shall give him will have in him a fountain of water springing up into eternal life” (John IV).

When you have found the fountain of this sun such as we have described, you will also find its city. “For there is,” it says, “also a city of the sun.” A city of the sun is said to exist in Egypt. But that city of the sun which is in Egypt received the name of this sun, which the heavenly Father commands to rise upon the good and the wicked. The city that is in Judea, however, belongs only to the saints, because it is the city of God; and the fountain mentioned above, having become a river, makes glad the city of God.

You too, if you are fortified on every side and surrounded by the wall of self-control, if you are enclosed by towers of patience and greatness of soul, become a city of God. But if you add to all these things the light of knowledge, as Isaiah says, “Illuminate for yourselves the light of knowledge,” and if the sun of righteousness shines within you, you also become a city of the sun, or you will receive the city of the sun as the lot of your inheritance.

Moreover, if you devote yourself to the law of God, so that you meditate on it day and night, and the book of the law does not depart from your hand, as was said to Jesus; and if you remember the Savior’s command in which he says, “Search the Scriptures” (John V)—if you devote yourself to such studies and obtain instruction in the divine law either by reading or by listening, the City of Letters becomes your portion.

We have examined these matters according to the capacity of our understanding and, indeed, according to the capacity of your hearing. But true knowledge and a deeper understanding of these things will belong to those who deserve to attain the true inheritance of the true and only-begotten Son of God, which was promised to those who have loved him perfectly.

(Likewise.) “But to Caleb son of Jephunneh he gave a portion among the children of Judah, as the Lord had commanded him: Cariath-arba of the father of Anak; this is Hebron. Caleb destroyed from it the three sons of Anak, Sesai, Eman, and Talmai, of the stock of Anak. From there he went up against the inhabitants of Dabir, which was formerly called Cariath-sepher, that is, the City of Letters.”

Let us first examine why Caleb received the metropolis, and that metropolis which is named first among all the other metropolises in the land of promise. [Col. 1074D] “Anak” is interpreted as “empty humility” or “empty response.” Caleb therefore received the metropolis of empty humility.

It is certain that there are two kinds of humility. One is praiseworthy, concerning which the Savior says: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matt. XI). Of this humility it was said: “Everyone who humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke XIV); and again: “Humble yourselves under the most powerful hand of the Lord” (1 Pet. V).

There is also another humility, blameworthy humility belonging to sinners, such as that which Scripture describes in the unlawful intercourse of Amnon, of whom it is written that “he humbled Tamar his sister” (2 Sam. XIII). This, then, is empty humility.

Caleb took, or destroyed, the metropolis and killed the three sons of Anak, who were sons of empty humility. After they had been killed, he possessed the city and did what is written in what follows.

Who, then, are the sons of empty humility whom Caleb exterminated? The first is Susi, which is interpreted as “outside me,” that is, “outside the holy one”—the son of empty humility whom Caleb exterminated. Indeed, he is outside the Lord.

The other is Ahiman, which is interpreted as “my brother outside counsel,” or “a brother without counsel.” For all brothers born from empty humility are certainly without counsel.

The third is Talmai, which is interpreted as “precipice” or “suspension,” signifying that there is nothing stable in him, but that everything is wandering and falling headlong.

Caleb therefore exterminated and killed these three sons of Anak, and after them he also went up against Dabir. Dabir was formerly called the City of Letters.

Dabir is interpreted as “speech,” but Dabir was formerly called the City of Letters. Thus I understand the entire Old Testament to be the City of Letters; and let us understand this Scripture, which we are now attempting to expound, to be the City of Letters. Later it becomes Dabir, which means “speech.” For this is what formerly existed in letters and was understood according to the letter; now, with the Lord revealing it, it has become speech in the churches, as the apostles first speak and expound it and draw out from it spiritual speech.

Individual teachers of the churches likewise have made the letter of the Law into their evangelical speech and exposition.

Who, then, are the three sons of Anak whom Caleb—in whose person we had described the virtue of the Law—kills? Empty humility must be understood as that which all the poets and philosophers of the world have regarded as divinity, because the things they conceived were both lowly and unworthy of God.

What is as emptily lowly as either asserting or believing that pieces of wood and stones are gods? The first son of this empty humility is the one called “outside me.” That is, their first understanding is both outside the truth and outside the Lord.

The second is Ahiman, “a brother without counsel.” Certainly this too is a brother of that error which is pursued without counsel. For what is more without counsel than to abandon the Lord, who brought us into being, and follow gods whom we ourselves have made?

The third understanding of error is Talmai, “precipice” or “suspension.” For the final outcome of this error is shown in a precipice and the depth of hell.

The Law therefore cut off these pagan notions, as sons of Anak and of ancient error; even according to the letter it proclaims the true Lord and Creator of all things.

## CHAPTER VI. Concerning Caleb’s saying, “Whoever strikes Cariath-sepher and captures it, I will give him my daughter Achsah as a wife”; and how Othniel son of Kenaz, Caleb’s younger brother, captured it; and concerning Achsah’s request to her father Caleb that he give her watered land

(Likewise.) “Caleb said: Whoever strikes Cariath-sepher and captures it, I will give him my daughter Achsah as a wife. Othniel son of Kenaz, Caleb’s younger brother, captured it; and he gave him his daughter Achsah as a wife. As they were traveling together, her husband urged her to ask her father for a field. And she sighed as she sat upon the donkey. Caleb said to her, ‘What is the matter?’ She answered him: ‘Give me a blessing. You have given me southern and dry land; add watered land to it.’ And Caleb gave her upper and lower watered land,” and so forth.

Othniel is interpreted as “the response of God.” The response of God may be called the person to whom the Lord responds—that is, the person to whom he reveals secrets and discloses mysteries.

This, then, is the one who can receive the City of Letters of the Old Testament and destroy the letter that brings death: Caleb’s younger brother. I, however, am Caleb’s brother from the younger Church. Having cut down and demolished the letter of the Law, I seek in it the spiritual meaning.

I cut down the letter when I no longer eat unleavened bread according to the letter, observe Passover with the Jews, or care for the Sabbath according to the letter. For it has been promised to me that if I destroy the City of Letters, I shall receive the daughter of my elder brother.

Formerly I was the son of Kenaz, which is interpreted as “rejection.” For who was as rejected as we Gentiles, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel, without hope, and without God in this world?

My earlier brother, whose daughter I now receive because I destroyed the City of Letters, was the son of Jephunneh, which is interpreted as “conversion.” He therefore gives me his daughter: the Law gives knowledge or understanding to me, the younger brother, according to what is written: “The kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits” (Matt. XXI).

It must nevertheless be understood that the Law to which we have now assigned the person of Caleb is one thing, and the letter of the Old Testament, which we have figuratively called the City of Letters, is another.

Having received his daughter, the letter, I, her younger brother, lead her away from her father’s house. As she came with me, sitting upon the donkey—the very one, undoubtedly, that the Savior’s disciples had untied—she says to her father: “Give me a blessing, father.” And she received Gonethlam the lower and Gonethlam the upper. The Apostle now states this more clearly: “Having the promise of life, both of the present life and of the future” (1 Tim. IV).

The Savior also promises that those who follow the perfection of his word will receive a hundredfold in this age and eternal life in the future. Thus to receive Gonethlam the lower and Gonethlam the upper in blessing is what has been described. May we too deserve to attain this blessing.

(From Gregory.) In the tropological sense, Achsah sits upon the donkey when the soul presides over the irrational movements of its flesh. She sighs and asks her father for watered land because the grace of tears must be sought from our Creator with great groaning.

There are some who have already received as a gift the freedom to speak on behalf of righteousness, to protect the oppressed, to give what they possess to the needy, and to possess the ardor of faith; but they still do not have the grace of tears. These certainly possess southern and dry land, but they still need watered land. For although they are established in good works, through which they are great and fervent, they must nevertheless mourn the evils they formerly committed, either through fear of punishment or through love of the heavenly kingdom.

Although contrition is divided into many forms, since penitents mourn their individual sins one by one—for this reason Jeremiah also says in the voice of penitents, “My eye has brought down divisions of waters” (Lam. III)—there are principally two kinds of contrition, because the soul that thirsts for God is first pierced by fear and afterward by love.

At first it afflicts itself with tears because, when it recalls its evils, it fears that it may suffer eternal punishments for them. But when fear has been consumed by a long anguish of grief, a certain security born of the hope of pardon arises, and the spirit is inflamed by love of heavenly joys.

The one who first wept lest he be led to punishment afterward begins to weep most bitterly because he is kept from the kingdom. For the mind contemplates the choirs of angels, the fellowship of the holy spirits, and the majesty of the inner vision of God. It grieves more because it lacks eternal goods than it previously grieved when it feared eternal evils.

Thus perfect contrition born of fear hands over to the soul the contrition of love. This is well described in the figurative narrative of this sacred and truthful history.

Therefore, as I said, since there are two kinds of contrition, her father gave her upper watered land and lower watered land. The soul receives upper watered land when it afflicts itself with tears because of its desire for the heavenly kingdom; it receives lower watered land when it fears the punishments of hell and weeps.

The lower is indeed given first, and afterward the upper watered land. But because the contrition of love surpasses the other in dignity, it was necessary to mention the upper watered land first and the lower afterward.

## CHAPTER VII. That the children of Judah could not destroy the Jebusite inhabitant of Jerusalem, who dwelt with them; and that the children of Ephraim did not kill the Canaanite who dwelt in Gezer
*(SAME PLACE.)* “But the sons of Judah were unable to defeat the Jebusite, inhabitant of Jerusalem. And the Jebusite dwelt with the sons of Judah in Jerusalem to the present day,” and so forth.

*(From Adamantius.)* The sons of Judah wished to destroy or kill the Jebusites from Jerusalem, but they were unable to do so; consequently, the Jebusites dwelt with the sons of Judah in Jerusalem [Col. 1077D] to the present day. Beginning with the letter, let us ask those who think that these things can stand according to the literal sense: what does the phrase “to the present day” mean? Scripture uses this expression to signify the perpetuity of the age, as when it says: “Do not withdraw from the Lord to the present day” (Josh. 22); that is, as long as the age endures. Let them therefore show me how the Jebusites can dwell with the sons of Judah in Jerusalem as long as the age endures, since not even the sons of Judah themselves dwell in Jerusalem. Therefore, this too cannot be true: that the Jebusites dwell there with the Jews.

But let us understand these things spiritually, taking up the Gospel parable that speaks of the weeds: “Let both grow together; lest, while wishing to uproot the weeds, you uproot the wheat along with them also” (Matt. 13). Just as, then, in the Gospel the weeds are permitted to grow together with the wheat, so likewise the Jebusites who are here in Jerusalem—that is, in the Church—are those who lead a dishonorable and degenerate life, who are perverse in faith, actions, and their entire manner of conduct. Nor is it possible for the Church to appear to contain neither an impious person nor any sinner, as though all in it were holy and blessed, with no stain of sin detected at all. But just as it is said of the weeds, “lest, while uprooting the weeds, you uproot the wheat along with them,” so this may also be said concerning those in whom sins are either doubtful or hidden. We are not speaking of those who are openly and manifestly criminal and yet are not expelled from the Church.

Hear, then, Scripture saying that the sons of Judah could not destroy the Jebusites, but dwelt with them to the present day. Therefore, I beg you who are faithful to order your life and conduct in such a way that you neither suffer scandal yourselves in anything nor cause scandal to others. Let it be your greatest concern and utmost caution that no polluted person enter into this holy way of life of yours, and that no Jebusite dwell with you. For you see that Scripture says that the sons of Judah could not drive the Jebusites out of Jerusalem. “Jebusites” is interpreted as “a trampling-down.” Since, therefore, we cannot drive out all those who trample us, let us immediately expel those whom we can—those whose sins are manifest; for where sin is not evident, we can expel no one from the Church—“lest, while uprooting the weeds, we uproot the wheat along with them also.”

Yet what he said troubles me: that they could not drive out the Jebusites, that is, those whose name is interpreted as “a trampling-down.” Let us therefore see who the tramplers in the Church are. Without doubt they are those of whom the Lord said in the Gospel: “Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor throw your pearls before swine, lest they trample them with their feet and, turning, tear you apart” (Matt. 7). These, then, are the Jebusites who hear the word of God unworthily. When they hear it, they neither depart as unbelievers nor remain faithful; but, having received knowledge of the mysteries and investigated the more hidden matters of our faith, they turn and tear us apart, rending our hearts by their contradictions, trampling the pearls of the Lord’s word and defiling the ornaments of faith. Of these, therefore, it is said that the sons of Judah could not drive the Jebusite out of Jerusalem to the present day.

*(CHAP. XVI.)* “And the sons of Ephraim did not kill the Canaanite who dwelt in Gezer; and the Canaanite dwelt in Ephraim to the present day.”

“Ephraim” is interpreted as “fruitfulness.” Whoever, therefore, bears fruit and grows in faith cannot exterminate the Canaanite, the worst seed, the accursed seed, the seed always in motion and always uncertain—for this is what “Canaanite” is interpreted to mean. It is certain that, together with the one who bears fruit and grows, the Canaanite always dwells; for temptation and disturbance never cease from him. But if you truly bear fruit in God and see someone restless, turbulent, and unstable, know that he is a Canaanite. You cannot drive him out of the Church, because the sons of Ephraim could not destroy the Canaanite.

Observe what the Apostle advises when he says: “Withdraw from every brother who walks disorderly” (2 Thess. 3). But since Solomon (Prov. 22) urges that what we read be written three times in the heart, I shall bring to your ears something else, beyond what we have said, that has occurred to my heart: “You also do what is written, so that when one speaks, the others may judge” (1 Cor. 14). As I say what I think, you must discern and examine whether it is right or less than right.

We have often said that “Jerusalem” is interpreted as “vision of peace.” If, then, Jerusalem has been built in our heart—that is, if the vision of peace has been established in our heart—and we constantly behold and preserve in our heart the Spirit who is our peace, provided that we are so fixed and stable in this vision of peace that no evil thought or plan of any sin ever rises in our heart, then we could say that we are in Jerusalem and that no one dwells with us except those who are holy.

But even if we attain great progress and cultivate ourselves with the greatest diligence, I do not think that anyone can possess such purity of heart that he is never stained by the contagion of an opposing thought. It is certain that Jebusites dwell with the sons of Judah in Jerusalem. We have not said this, however, so that we may neglect to drive them out as far as possible; rather, we must act and strive daily to drive them out of Jerusalem. But, as it is written, we cannot drive them all out at once.

The same must be understood concerning those who bear fruit, because they are called sons of Ephraim, and they too must always drive Canaanites—wandering and slippery thoughts—from their souls. God, however, can cast out the Jebusites and Canaanites from the sons of Ephraim. Let us therefore entreat the Lord himself that, casting evil thoughts away from us, he may implant in us good thoughts worthy of the heavenly city Jerusalem, in which nothing polluted or filthy may be found that could accuse us on the day of judgment on account of the thoughts of our conscience; rather, may purity of heart be found in us.

[Col. 1079D] *(SAME PLACE.)* “And the Canaanite dwelt in the midst of Ephraim to this day as a tributary,” and so forth.

According to another edition, it is read as follows: “And Ephraim did not destroy the Canaanite who dwelt in Gezer; and the Canaanite dwelt in Ephraim to this day, until Pharaoh king of Egypt went up, seized the city, and burned it with fire; and he slaughtered the Canaanites and Perizzites who dwelt in Gezer, and Pharaoh gave it as a dowry to his daughter.”

*(From Augustine.)* Concerning what is said about Pharaoh, I wonder whether we ought to understand it as spoken prophetically, since this history is thought to have been written at the time when those events were still recent. What significant thing could have been selected to be spoken prophetically when past events are being narrated, while greater and especially necessary future events are passed over in silence? Therefore, it should rather be thought that the Seventy Translators—who are said to have interpreted with prophetic authority through their marvelous agreement—added these words, not as announcing future events, but because they themselves lived at the time when they remembered that these things had happened and had read in the Book of Kings that this event had taken place in the days of the kings (3 Kings 9).

This seemed more credible to us because we examined the translation made from the Hebrew and did not find this there, just as we did not find what was said about Jericho: that whoever rebuilt it would incur the curse pronounced by Jesus. For it is written: “And Jesus adjured them on that day: Cursed be the man who shall raise up and build that city. On his firstborn shall he lay its foundation, and on his youngest shall he set up its gates.” Up to this point it is found in the translation from the Hebrew. But what follows—“And so Oza did, who founded it from Bethel in Abiron, his firstborn, and set up its gates in Segub, his youngest” (3 Kings 16)—is not read there. Hence it appears to have been inserted by the Seventy, who knew that the event had occurred.

*(From Adamantius.)* The Canaanites are said to have been among the sons of Ephraim on three occasions. If we carefully observe how the Canaanites are said to have been with the sons of Ephraim three times, and if the Lord grants us the ability to investigate the sequence of the statements—what is reported as having happened first, second, and third—we shall perhaps not be unbelieving, because these things were truly written not merely so that a narrative of events might be handed down to us, but because they are filled with divine and God-worthy mysteries.

First, then, it was said that Ephraim did not destroy the Canaanite who dwelt in Gezer, but the Canaanite dwelt in Ephraim to the present day and became a servant under tribute. Pharaoh, king of Egypt, also went up, seized the city, burned it with fire, slaughtered the Perizzites who dwelt in Gezer, and gave it as a dowry to his daughter.

Second: “And it happened,” he says, “when the sons of Israel became strong, that they made the Canaanites subject; but they did not utterly exterminate them.”

Third, when the men of the tribe of Ephraim opposed Jesus, wishing, because they were more numerous and stronger, to receive a larger portion according to their numbers, they were ordered to go up into the forest and make a larger place for themselves. So that they might occupy wider spaces, they were ordered to exterminate the Canaanite.

Let us therefore see what the three-part account concerning the Canaanites signifies. First, the Canaanite is indeed with us and is under tribute, but is not obedient to us or our servant. Second, he also becomes a servant and obedient.

Here let us understand the Canaanite as our flesh, or the things belonging to the flesh. At first it is with us—that is, joined to the soul—but it is not obedient to it, except insofar as it pays tribute; it does perform a service in acting or moving, yet it lusts against the spirit and is not obedient to the soul, but yields to its own desires. If, however, we have already made some progress, the flesh becomes our servant, obedient and subject to the progress of our soul, once the soul has made the flesh both obey and serve it.

The third stage is perfection. If we have already reached perfection, the Canaanite is said to be exterminated by us and handed over to death. Hear how this is fulfilled in our flesh, when the Apostle says: “Put to death, therefore, your members that are upon the earth: fornication and uncleanness” (Col. 3), and the other things that follow. Again he says: “Those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires” (Gal. 5). Thus, thirdly—that is, when we come to perfection, put our members to death, and carry the death of Christ in our body—we exterminate the Canaanites from ourselves.

Nor should we pass over without notice what is said: that Pharaoh sent for and seized the city of Gezer, in which the Canaanite dwelt with Ephraim, and gave it as a dowry to his daughter. “Gezer” is interpreted as “construction.” If, then, body and soul dwell in one and the same construction—that is, joined and associated with one another—so that the soul lives carnally and does not hasten to make the flesh obedient and subject to itself, there is danger that Pharaoh may come from Egypt and lead the unhappy soul away captive, so that he may hand it over as a dowry to his daughter.

For if you consider what the Apostle Paul said (Rom. 7:23)—that another law rises up in our members and takes us captive into the law of sin—you will understand how that Pharaoh, who is the author and king of sin, registered as a dowry the soul that lives carnally.

## CHAPTER VIII. The speech of the sons of Joseph to Joshua and his reply to them

*(CHAP. XVII.)* “And the sons of Joseph spoke to Joshua and said: Why have you given me the possession of one lot and one cord, when I am such a great multitude and the Lord has blessed me? Joshua said to them: If you are a great people, go up into the forest and cut out spaces for yourself in the land of the Perizzite and the Rephaim, because the possession of Mount Ephraim is too narrow for you,” and so forth.

The sons of Joseph raise the question of a larger inheritance. They ask for a lot, saying to Jesus: Why have you given us as an inheritance one lot and one measured portion? “But I am a great people, and the Lord has blessed me.” If, then, we too are a great people and the Lord has blessed us, let us hear from Jesus: “A great people—go up into the forest, clear it for yourself, prepare a place for yourself in the land, and purge the Perizzites and the Rephaim.”

It is necessary for us to drive out the Perizzites. We find that “Perizzites” is interpreted as “fruitfulness.” But, as we have often said concerning all the other names, this too has a twofold interpretation. There is a good fruitfulness and a bad fruitfulness, as is indicated in the Gospels: “A good tree bears good fruits” (Matt. 7). We must therefore expel whatever does not bear good fruit, cut off the fruits of sin, and cleanse the fruits of righteousness.

But he also says: “Expel,” or rather “conquer,” the Rephaim from yourself. We find that “Rephaim” is interpreted as “relaxed mothers.” There is in our soul a certain power that gives birth to understanding and is, as it were, the mother of those sensations or understandings that proceed from us, according to what is said sacramentally of the soul as of a woman: “She will be saved through the bearing of children, if she remains in faith and truth” (1 Tim. 2).

This, then, is the mother—that is, this power—in the soul in which a strong, vigorous, and robust generation gives birth to strong and powerful understandings, which cannot be overcome by the one who contradicts within you. In others, however, this power is relaxed and slackened, as is shown by their perceptions, when certain sluggish and foolish thoughts are reported, containing no strength in themselves.

This, therefore, is signified under the name “Rephaim”: that there are relaxed mothers in us who give birth to undisciplined and useless understandings. And he rightly preserved the character of the spiritual interpretation, and did not say that the warlike Canaanite was to be exterminated.

But what did Jesus answer him? “If you are a great people and possess strength, you shall not have one lot, because you have a forest, and you shall cleanse it.” You see that this is said for our spiritual understanding: we must cleanse the forest that is useless and, by cutting down the useless and fruitless trees within us, make new fields there, which we may continually renew and from which we may obtain fruit—thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and a hundredfold.

Does not the Gospel passage also announce the same to us, saying: “Behold, the axe is laid at the roots of the trees. Therefore every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire”? (Matt. 3.) Jesus, son of Nave, gave these commands to our predecessors concerning the cutting down of fruitless trees; the Lord Jesus sets forth these commands for us in the Gospels. And how is it not true that the shadow went before and the truth followed?

But when he added: “If you cleanse the forest, it will be yours when you have exterminated the Canaanites”—we have already explained above how the Canaanite, when placed with us, first pays tribute; second, becomes obedient and subject; and third, is said to be exterminated in the mortification of our members.

If we understand these things correctly, and if the Lord grants us, by his grace, to understand them in this way, it will have been worthwhile to bring into public view something from these secrets and hidden things, to bring into our knowledge what had been kept concealed, and, in accordance with what we have said, to strive to subdue more quickly and make obedient the Canaanite who is with us. For if we leave and neglect him, Pharaoh, king of Egypt, will come and begin to give our place as a dowry to his daughter and hand us over as captives to the law of sin.

But may this be far from Israelite nobility: that an Israelite should serve Pharaoh’s daughter, and that the one whom God has already brought out of the land of Egypt should again serve Pharaoh, who was drowned in the Red Sea. Let us therefore observe, as Jesus says here, that we may prevail against the Canaanites. Otherwise, if they should perhaps prevail over us and take possession of us, they will make us Canaanites instead of Israelites, just as the one overcome by the lust of the flesh became such a person, to whom the prophet Daniel says: “You are the seed of Canaan and not of Judah; beauty has deceived you” (Dan. 16).

Let it not happen to us to hear, “seed of Canaan,” since cursed Canaan, the boy, is a servant to his brothers.

## CHAPTER IX. How Joshua sent messengers to measure the land of Canaan and describe it according to the number of each people; how he divided it into seven parts and gave it to the sons of Israel as a possession, to each according to his lots

*(CHAP. XVIII.)* “And all the sons of Israel assembled at Shiloh, and there they fixed the tabernacle of testimony, and the land was subject to them. Seven tribes of the sons of Israel remained, which had not yet received their possessions. Joshua said to them: How long will you languish in idleness and not enter to possess the land that the Lord God of your fathers has given you? Choose three men from each tribe, so that I may send them; let them go, travel through the land, and describe it according to the number of each multitude, and let them report to me what they have described. Divide the land for yourselves into seven parts. Let Judah remain within its boundaries on the southern side, and the house of Joseph on the north. Describe the land between them in seven parts. You shall come here to me, so that before the Lord your God I may cast lots for you, because there is no portion of the Levites among you; rather, the priesthood of the Lord is their inheritance. Gad, Reuben, and half the tribe of Manasseh have already received their possessions beyond the Jordan, on the eastern side, which Moses, the servant of the Lord, gave them,” and so forth.

In ordinary human practice, when something is divided by lot, the lot seems to fall fortuitously to one person and another lot to another. In sacred Scripture, however, this is not so. I often asked myself whether the holy fathers had entrusted such a great and important matter to lots. If this had happened among the saints, then there would be nothing remarkable concerning other people or nations if there were nothing extraordinary in the things said to have been divided by lot.

Let us see, therefore, whether we may perhaps find something set forth in Scripture that reveals to us what power is contained in lots. Let us begin with Leviticus, where it is written: “And they shall take,” he says, “two lots: one lot for the Lord, and one lot for the scapegoat”—that is, for the one sent away. “And upon whichever the lot of the scapegoat falls, they shall take that goat, lead it alive into a desert place, and release it for its dismissal; but they shall sacrifice the other goat to the Lord” (Lev. 16), along with the other things recorded there, which those who read them certainly know.

Again, there Moses divided by lot the land for the tribe of Reuben, the tribe of Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh, who had requested beyond the Jordan the land that the sons of Israel had requested. Jesus himself, in accordance with the Lord’s command, gave a lot to Caleb son of Jephunneh and to the tribe of Judah. He gave Ephraim and the part of the tribe of Manasseh that remained; after this he assembled the sons of Israel in the assembly and said: “I shall cast lots and bring them forth before the Lord, if you first describe the land and bring me its description.”

After this, then, when lots had been cast, the inheritance was distributed to the people of God. This lot was cast not by chance, but according to what had been predestined by God. In fact, the tribe of Benjamin first received its lot where Jerusalem was; afterward the tribe of Simeon received the second, then Issachar, then Zebulun, then Asher, afterward Naphtali, and then Dan. The three tribes descended from Jacob’s concubines came last among these.

I was seeking within myself the rationale of lots, so that from the many testimonies of Scripture I might recognize what was hidden. I found in Scripture that even Gentiles used lots. When Jonah was sailing and a storm pressed hard upon them, those who were sailing with him said to him: “Let us cast lots and learn on whose account this great evil has come upon us” (Jonah 1), as though the lot possessed enough power to reveal on whose account danger threatened those at sea. Although they were Gentiles and strangers to knowledge of God, they were not deceived in this belief; rather, the lot revealed to them the truth concerning Jonah.

Investigating these matters, I also find Solomon saying in Proverbs: “The lot restrains disputes and decides between the mighty” (Prov. 18), showing, as it were, that disputes cease where the lot is cast.

But when I found that the Old Testament contains not a few references to lots, I turned also to the New Testament, to see whether lots are perhaps despised there, or whether their use is mentioned somewhere. I find that at one time, when one apostle was lacking in number and it was necessary to appoint another in place of Judas, the apostles assembled—men who were certainly much wiser than those who now ordain bishops, presbyters, or deacons—and chose two and set them in the midst. Yet they did not allow themselves to decide which one they would make whomever they wished. “But after praying,” he says, “they cast lots,” so that one of the two whom they had set before God might be chosen: Joseph, who was called Barnabas and surnamed Justus, and Matthias. “And the lot,” he says, “fell upon Matthias, and he was numbered with Christ’s apostles” (Acts 1).

Since reason had preceded, the lot no longer conveyed chance but, through prudence, a divine judgment.

Still I asked whether the lot is mentioned in the New Testament in relation to Christ or the Church, or in mystical matters that appear to concern the soul. I find Paul writing to the Ephesians and saying concerning Christ: “In whom,” he says, “we have been called by lot, having been predestined according to the purpose of him who works all things according to the counsel of his will, so that we might be for the praise of his glory, in whom we first hoped, in Christ” (Eph. 1). To the Colossians he writes: “Giving thanks to God the Father, who has made us fit to share in the portion of the lot of the saints in light” (Col. 1).

Having gathered so many testimonies from the holy Scriptures concerning the mention of lots, so that from consideration of many passages we might grasp more carefully the power of the matter, I have not yet been able, from all these things, either to see a clear meaning fully revealed or to free my mind from fear of declaring and setting forth something so important.

For the present, insofar as the matter permits, it will suffice that what was indicated to us by the lot cast by the apostles has occurred: wherever a lot is mentioned after sound faith and preceding prayer, the lot declares openly to human beings what the will of God holds hidden.

According to the interior understanding, as Paul seems to indicate when he says, “in the portion of the lot of the saints in light,” and “called by lot in Christ,” we must consider whether a lot is cast not only for human beings but also among the heavenly powers. Perhaps some power presides over this office—one that, for example, now provides Joshua son of Nave with guidance in distributing an inheritance by lot, not according to some arbitrary favor, but according to what it knows to please God. It guides the lot so that the one whom it knows to hold the first place before the Lord receives what is first, so that what is held secretly with God may also be shown to human beings through the governance of the lot; another is made to occupy the second place and another the third.

I think this applies not only on earth but also in heaven. Such a lot, distinguished according to the contemplation of merits before the Lord, was also in effect at that time when the Most High divided the nations and scattered the sons of Adam (Deut. 32), and established the sons of the nations according to the number of the angels of God. “And the Lord’s portion became Jacob, Israel the cord of his inheritance.”

You see that here too he says that Israel is the Lord’s portion and cord—that is, his lot. Are we therefore to think that it happened by chance that one angel received responsibility for that nation, for example, the Egyptians; another for the Idumeans or Moabites; and another for India or for any one of the nations that are upon the earth?

Even if these nations are said to have been divided by lot according to the number of the angels of God, nevertheless that lot—as we said concerning human beings—because it makes public the judgment of God that is hidden, must also be believed to have existed there, so that each angel received that nation for his division according to his merit and virtue.

And why should I speak of great and general matters, when it must be said that even what happens to each one of us occurs not without such a lot, which is administered according to God’s judgment? For example, one of us may by lot receive at birth one kind of life and another another kind.

Or consider what we have often shown from the holy Scriptures concerning what occurs among human beings: that good angels are present with human beings, as are hostile ones. Surely it is not by chance or without judgment that this angel is assigned to that soul—for example, that one should be Peter’s guardian and another Paul’s, or another the guardian of one of the children in the Church. Concerning their angels the Lord says that “they always see the face of my Father who is in heaven” (Acts 12). We must certainly not doubt that, by the judgment of God—who perceives either the dignity of those angels or something concerning our soul, as well as the quality of each one of us—each receives a guardian through a certain mystical lot directed by Christ’s dispensation.

For my part, insofar as this concerns my opinion, I think it may be said boldly even of those powers that have received the ministries of this world that it is not by chance or accident that one power benefits the labors and germinations of the earth, another more forcefully supplies the streams of rivers, another governs the rains, another the winds, another marine creatures, and another terrestrial animals and the various things produced from the earth. In each of these there are ineffable mysteries of divine dispensation, so that all things may be assigned to their proper and fitting service through each individual power.

For the Apostle says: “Are they not all ministering spirits, sent out for service on behalf of those who are to inherit salvation?” (Heb. 1.)

Following these examples, we must also believe that the lots mentioned with the authority of Scripture are drawn through Jesus, that inheritance is determined, and that each tribe receives its portion through divine dispensation. Through the ineffable providence of God, the portion of the future inheritance is foreshadowed in these present lots. For the Law is said to contain a shadow of future goods, and, as the Apostle says concerning those who have come to the Lord Jesus Christ: “You have approached Mount Zion and the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem” (Heb. 12).

There is a city in heaven called Jerusalem, and there is Mount Zion. It is certainly not without cause that Benjamin received Jerusalem and Mount Zion in his lot. The structure of that heavenly Jerusalem undoubtedly required that some earthly Jerusalem should already be given to Benjamin, preserving the figure and form of the heavenly one.

Likewise, concerning Benjamin it must be said that for a definite reason Hebron, or other individual cities, were assigned to the lot of Judah and that individual cities were recorded for each tribe, unless it is because those heavenly places in which Jerusalem and Zion are said to exist—and without doubt the other places near or joined to them—contained in heaven the cause and rationale that was represented on earth through distribution by lot.

Hence divine wisdom arranged that certain place-names should be written in Scripture, containing a kind of mystical interpretation, through which it is indicated to you who perceive these things by what principles they are ordered, and that they are administered neither by chance nor fortuitously.

For if it were thought to have happened by chance, for example, that one angel was called Michael and another Raphael; or, descending to human matters, that one patriarch was called Abraham, another Isaac, and another Israel; and not even among women did this happen by chance, but certainly according to divine reason, that one was called Sarah from Sarai, and that one was called Israel from Jacob, or Abraham.

And just as it is certain that each angel or human being receives names from the offices and actions assigned to him, so it follows that there are also certain heavenly places and cities, just as the heavenly Jerusalem and Zion are spoken of. There are also other places whose type and image are contained by those that exist on earth and that are now mystically designated for us in this Scripture through Jesus son of Nave.

I think it was concerning these cities that it was said: “The cities of Judah shall be built, and they shall dwell there and inherit it” (Ps. 68). Concerning these also the Lord and Savior says: “There are many dwelling places with my Father” (John 14). And concerning these cities we must believe that the Lord says to the servant who has traded well: “Have authority over ten cities” (Luke 19), and to another, authority over five.

We have dared to bring these things concerning the division of the land of Judah’s lots before you, insofar as was permitted, prompted by the Scripture that speaks of the heavenly Jerusalem and Mount Zion, and likewise says that the other things written are in heaven—things that have given us an occasion to understand all these matters as mysteries described in heaven.

[Col. 1087B] *(SAME PLACE.)* “And the Amorite remained to dwell in Elon and in Salumin; and the hand of Ephraim became heavy upon them, and they became tributaries to them.”

*(From Augustine.)* This was already happening contrary to the Lord’s command. Jesus was still alive, but as their leader he was no longer present in those battles because of old age. Therefore it is said that the Lord caused their hearts to be strengthened, since they had conspired together to go to war against Jesus, so that this mercy might not be extended to them contrary to God’s command: if they remained unconquered and, while Jesus grew old or died, were left for the sons of Israel to conquer, the Israelites might spare them contrary to the Lord’s command, whereas Jesus would not have done so.

*(From Adamantius.)* “Amorite” is interpreted as “bitter” or “bitterness.” Those who dwell in Elon, which is interpreted as “peace,” therefore remain peaceful, while bitternesses dwell among those who are militant and among the peaceful. The militants are those who, placed in the contest, strive to conquer demonic dwellings and destroy them; the peaceful are those who, overcome by carnal desires, have sought the peace of the soul. Yet in both the opposing power of bitterness strives to persevere and remain. From this we may understand something of the kind in the statement that the Amorite remained among them.

For example, if a hostile demonic power, a troop arising from bitterness, besieges someone’s body, it disturbs and dulls those who fall. Many prayers may be offered, many fasts, and many beneficial exorcists’ impositions of hands. Yet, when torments are inflicted upon it through invocation of God’s name, it prefers to endure them rather than depart from the person whom it shamelessly and wickedly besieges.

The same must be understood here concerning those called Amorites, who remain and persist in dwelling in Elon and Salumin. To show truly that they persist while enduring punishments and scourges, Scripture says: “And the hand of Ephraim became heavy upon the Amorites.”

Upon whom does the hand of Ephraim become heavy? Whether through the imposition of the hands of exorcists, as we have said, or through good actions and good works, the hand of Ephraim is said to become heavy upon unclean spirits. Good deeds that impose a weight afflict the race of demons and the opposing powers. For the better we act and the more we conduct ourselves in what is good, the more burdensome and troublesome these things become to them.

But what is agreeable and acceptable to them, and in a certain way fulfills their will, is the person who lives within dullness and wicked acts. Whoever, however, makes his hand heavy upon them through his good actions, even if he cannot drive them out completely, certainly makes them tributaries and subject.

## CHAPTER X. How the sons of Israel gave Joshua son of Nave a possession in their midst, according to the Lord’s command
### CHAPTER XIX. On the fact that the children of Israel gave Joshua, son of Nun, an inheritance in their midst, according to the Lord’s command

“They gave the children of Israel an inheritance to Joshua, son of Nun, in their midst, according to the Lord’s command: the city which he requested, Timnath-serah, in the hill country of Ephraim; and he built the city and lived in it,” and so forth. (From Adamantius.)

What meekness and humility the blessed Jesus displayed—he who was worthy to bear the name of Jesus our Lord and Savior—is made clear. For he says: “The children of Israel gave, he says, a lot to Jesus, son of Nave, among themselves, by the Lord’s command. They gave him the city which he requested, Timnath-serah, which is in the hill country of Ephraim; and he built the city and lived in it.”

He is the one who gave an inheritance to all the children of Judah; he who gave Ephraim and half the tribe of Manasseh; he who gave an inheritance to that illustrious Caleb, son of Jephunneh; he who sent three men from each tribe to traverse and survey the whole land and show it to him; he who cast lots for everyone and reserved himself for last. Why do you think he wished to be last of all? Without doubt, so that he might be first of all.

He did not even presume to take an inheritance by lot for himself, but received it from the people; and the people give him an inheritance from whom he himself had received it. For thus it is written: “And the children of Israel gave a lot to Jesus, son of Nave.”

But these things happened to them figuratively as a pattern for us, so that we too might keep the commandment which this man fulfilled in deed, namely: “The greater you are, humble yourself all the more before the Lord, and you will find favor” (Ecclus. III). Again it is written: “If they appoint you leader, do not exalt yourself, but be among them as one of themselves” (Ecclus. XXXII).

Consider, therefore, how he led the people—he who had brought them into the holy land, into the land of promise. He was the successor of Moses, yet he did not permit himself to take the lot of the land; instead, he waited to receive a small portion.

Jesus, worthy of this name, builds the very place which he received and constructs it, so that he may truly make it worthy of God’s gift and divine inheritance. But since we are accustomed to refer to our Lord and Savior the things written about Jesus, perhaps this whole people of ours also gives some portion to my Lord Jesus and grants him, as it were, a place for his dwelling.

But lest what is said seem insulting, let us inquire how we servants give him a place of dwelling. If I can become good, I shall give the Son of God a place in myself. And the Lord Jesus builds the place he has received from me in my soul, making in it impregnable walls and lofty towers, so that, if I should prove worthy, he may build in me a dwelling worthy of himself and the Father. Thus he adorns my soul and makes it capable of his wisdom [Col. 1089A] and of all holiness—so much so that he may even cause the Father to enter with him, make his dwelling in it, and dine at such a soul on the food which this person has given him.

Let us therefore see what sort of place this is in which Jesus desires to dwell. “On the mountain,” he says, “of Ephraim,” that is, on a fruitful mountain. Who, do you think, are the fruitful mountains in us in which Jesus may dwell? Surely those in whom are the fruits of the Holy Spirit: “joy, peace, patience, charity” (Gal. V), and the others—in whom are fruitful mountains that bear the fruits of the Spirit and are lofty in mind and hope.

And although such people may be few, nevertheless, if there are even a few of them, the Lord Jesus dwelling in them—he who is the true light of all—will send out the rays of his light even upon all the rest, whom he has not yet brought principally beneath his dwelling.

Now, then, let us see what the stone swords are with which Jesus circumcises the children of Israel. But pray for us, so that our discourse may be living and effective, sharper than every sword. Jesus the Lord will grant us that the word of God which we speak to you may circumcise all uncleanness, cut away impurity, remove vices from those who act, and amputate everything by which the power of the mind and natural effectiveness are concealed. Thus, through the word of God—which is now called the stone sword—you will be circumcised by Jesus; and you will hear that today he has taken away from you the reproach of Egypt.

What benefit is it to have come out of Egypt if we carry with us the reproaches of Egypt? What benefit is it to walk through the wilderness? That is, what help is it that in baptism we renounced the world while retaining the former filth of our conduct and the uncleanness of carnal vices? Therefore, after crossing the Red Sea—that is, after the grace of baptism—the carnal vices of our former way of life must also be taken away from us through Jesus Christ our Lord, so that only then may we be able to be free from the reproaches of Egypt.

Those very swords and stone knives, then, with which we are circumcised a second time by Jesus, are placed in the same place which Jesus requests and receives: in the place which he possesses in the soul of the righteous. In that place he also stores the swords.

We have often shown that the sword signifies the word of God, by which sins are cut away and cleansed from the soul of those who hear. This power of the divine word is therefore stored in the one who has been given the word of knowledge and the word of wisdom, so that, at the proper time, that soul—filled through the gift of the Holy Spirit with the word of wisdom and the word of knowledge—may bring forth swords in the Church and circumcise a second time those who require a second circumcision.

But when he says “stone swords,” that is, knives made from rock and not fashioned by an artisan’s work in iron, he immediately shows that the word of God, which can circumcise uncleanness from the hearts of its hearers, does not come from the art of grammar or rhetoric; nor has it been subdued by the hammers of teachers or polished by the cultivation of study. Rather, it descends from that rock which was cut without hands from the mountain, filled the whole world, and bestowed spiritual gifts upon believers.

### CHAPTER XI. On the cities of refuge established for the protection of those who have struck a person’s life unintentionally and without deliberation

### (CHAPTER XX)
