“And the Lord spoke to Joshua, saying: Speak to the children of Israel and say to them: Set apart the cities of refuge about which I spoke to you through Moses, so that anyone who strikes a person unintentionally may flee there and escape the anger of his kinsman who is the avenger of blood, when he has fled to one of these cities. He shall stand before the gate of the city and explain to the elders of that city the things that prove his innocence; and they shall receive him and give him a place to dwell,” and so forth.

I can designate nothing more appropriately by the cities of refuge than the holy Church, where the sinner receives the hope of pardon through repentance and where the innocent finds secure protection for his salvation.

But because the law distinguishes between one who deliberately kills a person and one who commits homicide unintentionally, it mystically demonstrates that if someone, through envy or hatred, strikes another with the sword of malice and leads him into the death of the soul, he himself will be liable to eternal death.

Hence the Truth himself says: “If anyone causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble, it would be better for him that a millstone be fastened around his neck and that he be plunged into the depths” (Matt. XVIII). And John says: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer; and you know that every murderer does not have eternal life abiding in him” (1 John III).

Such a person is commanded to be torn away from the Lord’s altar, because, unworthy of the Lord’s sacraments, he is rightly removed from participation in the sacred altar; nor does he deserve in any way to be restored to pardon except through worthy repentance.

But one who has harmed another not through a deliberate intention of malice, but through negligence or ignorance, has the Church as a refuge—namely, the Catholic Church. There he must restrain himself through the distress of repentance and remain, throughout the whole time of his present life, devoting himself to good works. And if he places his hope in the death of the supreme Pontiff, that is, his Redeemer, he will assuredly be saved eternally through him.

### (IBID.)

“And they appointed Kedesh in Galilee, in the hill country of Naphtali; and Shechem in the hill country of Ephraim; and Kiriath-arba, that is Hebron, in the hill country of Judah. And beyond the Jordan, opposite the eastern side of Jericho, they established Bezer, situated in the plain wilderness, from the tribe of Reuben; and Ramoth in Gilead, from the tribe of Gad; and Golan in Bashan, from the tribe of Manasseh. These cities were established for all the children of Israel and for the resident foreigners who lived among them, so that anyone who had struck a person unintentionally might flee there and not die at the hand of his kinsman, who desired to avenge the shed blood, until he stood before the people to present his case.” (From Bachiarius.)

Behold, you have six cities of refuge; enter them, if you please. And if, perhaps, because of your knowledge of sins, you do not dare to enter those which are in the land of promise—that is, in the Church—there is Bezer near the Jordan, in the wilderness. Its name is interpreted as “narrowness,” that is, a small or modest monastic cell. It will suit you especially well that it belongs to the lot of Reuben, the one who illicitly defiled his father’s bed.

There is also Ramoth, from the lot of Gad, which is interpreted as “lofty death” or “vision of death.” Truly, repentance should be called a lofty death, since, when his members have been mortified, a person is led to the heights of heaven, from which he had previously fallen. Or, in comparison with that humble death which generally threatens all flesh, it is reasonably called lofty, because it is far nobler to die through repentance than to be dissolved by this common death.

But if we wish to understand it as “vision of death,” it can be interpreted in this way: when we are engaged in repentance and set the torments of hell before our eyes, we see the very appearance of death, from which we are freed by the benefit of repentance.

Remain mindful that you are practicing repentance in the city of the son of a slave-woman, because everyone who sins is a slave of sin; and, taking the form of a slave, humble yourself even unto death.

There is Golan in the territory of Manasseh, which is interpreted as “rolling.” Let it remind you that you must roll about in sackcloth and ashes. And this occurs in the territory of Manasseh, whose name is interpreted as “forgetfulness,” so that you may forget the things you did before and stretch yourself toward what lies ahead.

Dwell here, then, so that through the narrowness of death and rolling you may escape the persecutor’s anger and find the hope of salvation.

Then, if you accomplish something useful in these places, you will also be able to reach Kedesh in the land of promise, which is in Galilee. Its name is interpreted as “holy,” so that, when in tribulation you have cast away the work of corruption, access to the holy Church may also be granted to you. Thus, in the lot of Naphtali—which is called “the vine released”—you may be found worthy to participate in the sacrament of the Lord’s blood.

Nor is access to Hebron closed to you. Its name is interpreted as “union” or “marriage.” For your soul will return to its husband, that is, to the Spirit of God, from whom it had been widowed for the time of its sins.

Thus you will also be able to enter the sixth city, Shechem, which our Joseph receives as an inheritance—for this reason he was buried there. Its name is interpreted as “shoulder” or “labor,” so that you may show that through the labor of repentance you have been carried back from your error on Christ’s shoulders and joined to the ninety-nine sheep, becoming the hundredth; for Shechem itself is recorded as having been purchased from foreigners for one hundred lambs.

These cities were therefore given to the Levites, because the Church was entrusted to holy teachers. They are comprehended in the number six because perfection of doctrine and conduct is well suited to those who hold the position of teachers, so that their subjects may always have something in the conduct and teaching of their superiors from which they can progress.

Hence the Lord himself says to the apostles in the Gospel: “You are the light of the world, and you are the salt of the earth. Be perfect, just as your heavenly Father is perfect. Let your light shine before people, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. V). (From Isidore.)

But the Levites did not receive an inheritance of land because Jesus our Lord himself is their inheritance, as it is written: “I am their inheritance, and no possession shall be given to them in Israel” (Num. XVIII). “For I am their possession.”

God wished to be called the inheritance and possession of the clergy because they have become ministers of his altar and are themselves a lot; hence *clerus* is interpreted as “lot.”

Therefore, the one who strives to be poor in spirit so that he may serve God without any impediment rightly possesses God as an inheritance, so that he may fittingly say with the Psalmist: “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance and my cup” (Ps. XV).

But the fact that the dwellings of the Levites are assigned by Jesus throughout all the tribes signifies that those who devote themselves to knowledge in the Church of God and administer the grace of teaching receive again from all those to whom they distribute divine things the earthly support which they do not possess, so that what the Apostle commanded may be fulfilled: “If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it a great thing if we reap your carnal things?” (1 Cor. IX).

And rightly are these men said to be divided among all the tribes, because they live through the provision of everyone.

### CHAPTER XII. On the sons of Levi who requested from Eleazar the priest and from Joshua, son of Nun, cities in which to dwell and their suburbs for feeding their livestock

### (CHAPTER XXI)

“And the heads of the families of Levi approached Eleazar the priest, and Joshua, son of Nun, and the leaders of the clans of each tribe of the children of Israel. They spoke to them at Shiloh, in the land of Canaan, and said: The Lord commanded through Moses that cities be given to us for dwelling, [Col. 1092C] and their suburbs for feeding our livestock. And the children of Israel gave from their possessions, according to the Lord’s command, cities and their suburbs,” and so forth.

(From Augustine.)

All the children of Israel received their lots in the land, but for the Levites God alone is sufficient as an inheritance. Yet because, by God’s command, the Levites receive the first fruits and tithes of the produce from the children of Israel, it was fitting that they should also receive tithes from the land, so to speak, and from the dwellings—for these belong to everyone.

Therefore, the leading men who were among the children of Levi approached Eleazar the priest, Jesus son of Nave, and the leaders of the tribes of the children of Israel at Shiloh, in the land of Canaan, and said: “The Lord commanded through Moses that cities be given to us for dwelling, and their suburbs for our animals.”

It was therefore necessary that a lot also be cast concerning the suburbs and the cities, lest the division carried out among the Levites appear to have been indiscriminate and accidental.

Just as the distribution by lot which took place among the children of Israel had a rationale by which one person was considered worthy of the first lot and another of the second—we have discussed this earlier as best we could—and just as those who received territory beyond the Jordan through Moses, and those who received it in the land of promise through Jesus, were assigned their portions, with the first lot falling to Benjamin and afterward to the others, among whom Dan was last, so there must necessarily be some rationale also in the order of the priestly and Levitical lot, so that one receives the first lot, another the second, and another the third, through which this or that place is assigned to each.

The sons of Levi are said to be Gershon, Kohath, and Merari, and it is shown that Kohath held primacy in honor—that is, those who were sons of Kohath through Amram. For from him came Moses, Aaron, and Miriam.

Thus, from Kohath one part became the priestly people, namely Aaron and his sons. Moses, however, must be regarded either as belonging to the priestly order or, if there is anything higher than the priesthood, as belonging to that higher order.

There is another arrangement concerning his sons. But among the sons of Kohath, those descended from Issachar, Hebron, and Odiel held the second place in the tribe of Levi. Then, after this, the descendants of Gershon receive their portion in relation to Kohath, in third place; and Merari is last of all.

This is the distinction between the first, second, third, and fourth orders, which we first observed in the Book of Numbers. After the twelve tribes had been arranged around the ark of the Lord’s testimony, to keep watch over the four regions of the world, three tribes were stationed in the east, three in the south, three toward the sea in the west, and three in the north, which is the region of the north wind.

Here too these groups are assigned according to the same order in the four regions of the world. In the east, where the tribe of Judah was situated—the tribe which was first among the others—Aaron and his sons are placed. Kohath and the rest who were appointed to carry the ark of the Lord’s testimony on their shoulders and to blow the trumpets are stationed there.

When the first trumpet sounded, those who were in the east moved the camp; when the second sounded, those who were in the south rose; the third was for the west, and the fourth for the north.

You see what order and what distinction are described in Scripture and in the sequence of events, and how nothing is done except with moderation and order. Look more carefully, and you will find these things arranged in this way throughout all Scripture.

But if it is difficult for you to lead the watchful eye of the heart through all the books, at least in this passage observe more attentively the things that are recounted.

“The lot of Kohath comes out first,” he says, “and it was assigned to the priestly sons of Aaron who were among the Levites.” To whom should the first lot have fallen, and to whom should primacy have been given, except to Aaron, the first high priest, first in the merits of life, first in honors and virtue?

It is clear to us, at least now, that the lot is not so accidental, but that a heavenly power is present, directing it according to the judgment of divine providence.

Where, then, does this just lot assign the first dwellings to the sons of Aaron? “In the tribe of Judah,” he says, “and the tribe of Simeon, and the tribe of Benjamin,” twelve cities by lot.

You see how dwellings are distributed among chosen men and chosen tribes.

Who, then, ought to receive the second lot? “The sons of Kohath,” he says, “who remained after the sons of Aaron.” And which tribes do they receive? “In the tribe of Ephraim, and in the tribe of Dan, and in half the tribe of Manasseh,” ten cities by lot.

Who are the third? “The sons of Gershon,” he says. And in which tribes do they receive their lots? “In Issachar, Asher, and Naphtali, and in half the tribe of Manasseh,” which is in the territory of Panitis, twelve cities.

Who are the last among the Levites? “The sons of Merari,” he says, “these last.” And let us see in which tribes they receive their portions. “From the tribe of Reuben beyond the Jordan, and from the tribe of Zebulun,” which is itself the last among the sons of Leah, “they receive twelve cities as their lot.”

But as we touch upon matters that deserve closer attention in these passages, we shall not be reluctant to indicate at least their principal points, even if we cannot disclose their deeper meanings. In this way, each hearer may receive from them an opportunity to seek a higher and mystical understanding.

Since the world has four regions, Kohath receives the first lot among the sons of Levi in the eastern region, with those tribes which themselves also hold primacy over all the others. See, therefore, how everything corresponds.

It is certain that among the four regions of the world the eastern quarter is regarded as the nobler. And which of all the remaining tribes is considered more noble than Judah? The priests, the sons of Aaron, are said to receive the first lot among the first three regions of the world, together with Gershon and Merari, who were first among the sons of Levi.

If, then, the three sons of Levi receive the east, while the west—where Reuben, Simeon, and Gad were situated—is assigned by the second lot to Gad and the tribe of Simeon, Merari first receives Reuben; and again, in the Book of Numbers, Merari receives Zebulun third from the east, so that justice may be preserved in the lot which is assigned according to God and may direct the minds of believers toward contemplating the mystery of the age to come.

After this come those who were toward the sea, that is, Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasseh. When Gad had received the tribe of Benjamin by the second lot, the others of his family received Ephraim by lot.

After this come those who were from half the tribe of Manasseh, who was in the territory of Gershon; and again Gershon himself receives the other half of the tribe of Manasseh.

But because it was necessary that those who were in the north should receive something of priestly grace, lest they appear to have been wholly stripped of heavenly gifts, among those whose order was last in the north—namely Dan, Naphtali, and Asher—Gad again, not among the priests but among the others, receives the first lot in Dan; Gershon receives the second in Asher; and the third, that is, Gershon, receives it in Naphtali.

Who can rise to the level of all these things and comprehend them? Who can even remember and observe the order of the mysteries? Considered according to the literal sense alone, the narrative is difficult to explain, and the intermingling of places and persons contained in the history is difficult to unravel.

What shall we say about the sacraments represented through these events, in which the future distributions of the inheritance are foreshadowed, and through which the division of the holy land—the land which the meek will receive as an inheritance—will be carried out?

Who could explain the different positions of the camps? How will this distribution be made in the resurrection among each of the saints according to the priestly or Levitical order, so that, as the Apostle says, everything may not take place in confusion in the resurrection, but each may come in his own order?

“Christ the beginning; then those who are Christ’s, at his coming, when he hands over the kingdom to God and the Father, and when he has subjected every principality and power to him.” Without doubt, there will be such distributions and orders and the meanings of the trumpets.

But the fact that, besides the six cities of refuge, the Levites receive forty-two other cities unmistakably signifies the preaching of the saints. They possess the teaching which consists of the Decalogue of the Law and the fourfold number of the Gospel, as though they possessed forty-two cities. Two are added to these because everything they preach is announced in both a moral and a mystical sense.

### CHAPTER XIII. On the fact that all the land of Canaan was given by the Lord to Israel as a possession, and that they possessed it in peace

### (IBID.)

“And the Lord gave Israel all the land which he had sworn to give their fathers, and they possessed it and lived in it. And he gave them peace on every side with all the surrounding nations; none of their enemies dared resist them, but all were brought under their power. Not one word of all the good things which he had promised to them failed, but everything was fulfilled in fact.”

(From Augustine.)

It is rightly asked how this should be understood, since Israel did not eradicate the nations occupying the land of promise—not only until the day of Joshua’s death, but even afterward—although, after defeating some of them, they remained in the same promised inheritance.

How should we understand the statement: “And the Lord gave Israel all the land which he had sworn to give their fathers, and they inherited it and lived in it; and the Lord gave them rest on every side, as he had sworn to their fathers; no one stood before them from among all their enemies; the Lord delivered all their enemies into their hands; not one of all the good words which the Lord had spoken to the children of Israel failed; everything came to pass”?

Everything must be considered carefully. First, it must be seen that the land of the nations was promised to the Israelites.

Seven nations are repeatedly mentioned, as it is written in Exodus: “And the Lord said to Moses: Go, ascend from here, you and your people whom you led out of the land of Egypt, into the land which I swore to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, saying: I will give it to your offspring; and at the same time I will send my angel before you. And he will drive out the Amorite, the Hittite, the Perizzite, the Girgashite, the Hivite, the Jebusite, and the Canaanite” (Exod. XXXIII).

It therefore appears that God promised the land of these seven nations to the patriarchs.

It is also written much more explicitly in Deuteronomy: “But if you approach a city to attack it and summon it with an offer of peace, if they answer you peacefully and open their gates to you, all the people found in the city shall be tributary to you and subject to your obedience. But if they do not obey you and make war against you, you shall besiege it, and the Lord your God will deliver it into your hands. You shall kill every male in it with the edge of the sword, except the women. You shall take as spoil the furnishings, all the cattle, and everything that is in the city, and all its equipment; and you shall consume all the plunder of your enemies which the Lord your God will give you.

“Thus you shall do to all the cities that are very far from you, which are not among the cities of these nations. But from the cities which the Lord your God gives you to inherit their land, you shall not preserve any living creature; rather, you shall devote them to destruction: the Hittite, the Amorite, the Canaanite, the Perizzite, the Jebusite, the Hivite, and the Girgashite, as the Lord your God commanded you” (Deut. XX).

Here too it is clear that the land of these seven nations was promised as an inheritance, so that the Israelites, after defeating those nations and destroying them utterly, might possess it.

As for the others who were found farther away, beyond these nations, he wished them to become tributary to the Israelites if they did not resist. But if they resisted, he wished them also to be killed and destroyed, except for the livestock and whatever could be taken as spoil.

Again, in another passage of Deuteronomy, we read: “And it shall be, when the Lord your God brings you into the land which you are about to enter in order to inherit it, and removes great and numerous nations from your presence—the Hittite, the Girgashite, the Amorite, the Perizzite, the Canaanite, the Hivite, and the Jebusite, seven nations great and numerous and stronger than you—and the Lord your God delivers them into your hands, you shall strike them and utterly destroy them. You shall not make a covenant with them, nor shall you show them mercy, nor shall you enter into marriage with them. You shall not give your daughter to his son, and you shall not take his daughter for your son,” and so forth (Deut. VII).

Accordingly, these and other passages of Scripture often show that the children of Israel received the lands of these seven nations as an inheritance in such a way that they were to dwell there in place of those who had previously occupied them.

Nevertheless, in Genesis not only these seven nations but eleven are promised to the offspring of Abraham. For we read: “On that day the Lord God made a covenant with Abraham, saying: To your offspring I will give this land, from the river of Egypt to the great river Euphrates: the Kenites, the Kenizzites, the Kadmonites, the Hittites, the Perizzites, the Rephaim, the Amorites, the Canaanites, the Hivites, the Girgashites, and the Jebusites” (Gen. XV).

This question is resolved if we understand that this prophecy preceded the event in which Solomon was to extend and enlarge the boundaries of his kingdom. Of him it is written: “And all Solomon’s plans which he had determined to build in Jerusalem, in Lebanon, and throughout all the land of his possession; all the people who remained from the Hittite, the Amorite, the Perizzite, the Hivite, and the Jebusite, who were not of Israel—that is, from the descendants of those who remained with them in the land, whom the children of Israel had not destroyed—Solomon subjected to tribute to this day” (1 Kings IX).

Behold, Solomon subjected the remaining peoples who were to be defeated and destroyed entirely by God’s command to tribute, although according to God’s command he ought to have destroyed them. Nevertheless, once subjected, they were possessed as tributaries.

A little later we read: “And he was ruling over all the regions, from the River to the land of the Philistines and to the borders of Egypt” (1 Kings IV).

Here is where what God had foretold in Genesis, chapter XV, when he spoke to Abraham and made the promise, was fulfilled. By “the River” the Euphrates is understood; for in those regions the great river can be understood even when its proper name is not added.

This cannot be understood of the Jordan, since the Israelites had already obtained lands both on this side of the Jordan and beyond the Jordan before Solomon’s reign.

Therefore, from the Euphrates River in the eastern regions to the borders of Egypt, which was their western boundary, the Book of Kings says that Solomon’s kingdom extended.

At that time, therefore, more territory was subjected than the seven nations had occupied. Consequently, at that time not seven but eleven nations were reduced to servitude.

For what is written in the Book of Kings, “to the borders of Egypt” and “from the River,” when Scripture wished to show how far the kingdom extended from east to west, is expressed in Genesis, when the boundaries were defined from west to east, in these words: “From the river of Egypt to the great river Euphrates” (Gen. XV).

The river of Egypt, which forms the boundary separating the kingdom of Israel from Egypt, is not the Nile. It is another, smaller river which flows through the city of Rhinocorura, and from there the land of promise begins as one proceeds eastward.

Thus it had been determined for the children of Israel that they themselves should inhabit the lands of the seven nations after those nations had been exterminated and destroyed; but that they should rule over the others as subjects and tributaries as far as the Euphrates River.

And although in this they had not obeyed God, because they had spared some of those whom they ought to have exterminated and made them obedient, God nevertheless fulfilled the faithfulness of his promise in the time of Solomon.

Now, therefore, in the Book of Joshua son of Nave, which we have undertaken to examine, how can the statement be true: “And God gave Israel all the land which he had sworn to give their fathers, and they inherited it”?

How did he give them the whole land while Joshua was still alive, when they had not yet overcome even the remnants of those seven nations?

For what follows—“And they inherited it”—is true, because they were there and settled there.

Then what it adds—“And the Lord gave them rest on every side, as the Lord had sworn to their fathers”—is true because, while Joshua was still alive, the remnants of those nations did not yield to them, but none of them dared to harass them in war in the lands where they had settled.

For this reason the statement that follows is also made: “No one stood before them from among all their enemies.”

But when it says, “The Lord delivered all their enemies into their hands,” it intended us to understand those enemies who had dared to come out against them in battle.

Then, when it says, “Not one of all the good words which the Lord had spoken to the children of Israel failed; everything came to pass,” it wishes this to be understood as follows: although they had already acted against the Lord’s command by sparing some of the seven nations and making them obedient, those people were nevertheless still alive among them.

Therefore, after saying “of all the words,” it adds “good,” because the curses appointed for those who despised and transgressed had not yet come upon them.

It remains, then, that the statement “The Lord gave Israel all the land which he had sworn to give their fathers” should be understood in this way: although remnants of those nations still remained to be crushed and destroyed—or, in the case of other nations as far as the Euphrates, to be subjected if they did not resist or destroyed if they did resist—they were nevertheless left for their use as objects of training.

This was so that, being weak through carnal feelings and desires, they might not be unable to bear with moderation and in a salutary manner the sudden prosperity of temporal possessions, but might instead be lifted up and quickly perish. This will be demonstrated appropriately elsewhere.

The whole land was therefore given to them because even that part which had not yet been given into their possession had already been given for a certain use as an exercise.

When it says, “No one stood before them from among all their enemies,” one may ask how this is true, since it was written earlier concerning the tribe of Dan that its enemies did not permit it to descend into the valley and prevailed against it in the mountains.

But what we said earlier, when Scripture mentioned the twelve sons of Jacob born in Mesopotamia, where Benjamin had not been born, must also be understood here: the eleven tribes were counted for the whole people, according to a rule that is sufficiently familiar to us from other passages of Scripture.

If one asks why this tribe did not obtain sufficient territory in the lot that fell to it and was afflicted by those who held the land, we must believe that this lies within God’s secret counsel.

Nevertheless, when Jacob blessed his sons, he said such things concerning this Dan that it is thought that the Antichrist would arise from that very tribe (Gen. XLIX).

For this reason we do not undertake to say more about it now, since the question can also be resolved in this way: no one stood before them from among all their enemies while they were waging war together under the command of one leader, before the territories to be defended had been divided among the individual tribes.

### CHAPTER XIV. On the fact that Joshua dismissed the Reubenites, the Gadites, and half the tribe of Manasseh to their possessions in peace
## Chapter XXII

“Then Joshua summoned the Reubenites, the Gadites, and half the tribe of Manasseh, and said to them: ‘You have done everything that Moses, the servant of the Lord, commanded you; you have also obeyed me in everything, and have not abandoned your brothers for this long time until the present day, keeping the commandment of the Lord your God. Since, therefore, the Lord your God has given your brothers rest and peace, as he promised, return and go to your tents and to the land of your possession which Moses, the servant of the Lord, gave you beyond the Jordan, etc.’” (From Adamantius.)

After this, Jesus summons the sons of Reuben, the sons of Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh, who had fought alongside him to overcome Israel’s enemies, and dismisses them to go to their inheritance, giving them certain gifts as well, as it is written. In this he appears to indicate the mystery that, when the fullness of the Gentiles had entered and those who had been educated and instructed through Moses received from the Lord Jesus what had been promised to them—and those who had brought assistance to us, placed as we are in combat, through prayers and supplications—then, because they had not yet obtained the promises while awaiting the completion of our calling also, as the Apostle says, they finally attain the perfection that had been deferred for them, together with the gifts they receive from Jesus, so that each may dwell in peace, with every war and every attack brought to an end.

After this we read that the sons of Reuben, the sons of Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh, who were beyond the Jordan, built a very large altar. The remaining sons of Israel, not knowing why this altar had been built, sent Phinehas, son of Eleazar, son of Aaron the priest, together with ten men chosen from each tribe, so that, if they had perhaps done this as though they were abandoning God, having become apostates and acting against God’s command, they might be attacked by the rest of the sons of Israel; but if not, they might learn the reason.

They, however, give an explanation concerning the altar and say: “We know that the true altar is with you, and that Jesus dwells among you. We have made this altar in imitation of the altar constructed among you, so that among us there may be a representation and image of the true altar, lest perhaps tomorrow you should wish to say: ‘The Jordan is the boundary between us and you; it itself makes the division, and therefore you have no share in our altar.’” They sent them this reply.

But let us see what sacramental meaning this deed contains. The former circumcised people are designated in Reuben, who was the firstborn, and also in Gad, who likewise was the firstborn of Zilpah; Manasseh too was a firstborn. When I say “firstborn,” I am speaking according to chronological precedence. These things, then, are said lest any division or separation should appear between us and those who were righteous before Christ’s coming, but so that it might be shown that, although they lived before Christ’s coming, they were nevertheless our brothers.

Although they had an altar then, before the Savior’s coming, they nevertheless knew and understood that it was not the true altar, but the form and image of that future true altar. They knew this because true sacrifices, those capable of taking away sins, were not offered on the altar belonging to the firstborn people, but on this one, where Jesus was. Here the heavenly sacrifices are completed; here the true offerings are completed. Thus there comes to be one flock and one shepherd: those former righteous people and those who are now Christians.

I also wish, as proof of this, to recall a certain story, if the Lord should grant that we can discover its spiritual explanation. Once the people fell in the wilderness and were dying (Num. XVI). Aaron the high priest came and stood between those who were dying and those who were alive, so that the destruction of death might not spread any further among the rest.

My true high priest and Lord came and stood in the middle between the dead and the living—that is, between those among the Jews who received his presence and those who not only did not receive him but killed themselves rather than him, saying: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. XXVII). Hence “all the righteous blood that has been shed upon the earth, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah, whom they killed between the temple and the altar” (Matt. XXIII), would be required of that generation which said: “His blood be upon us and upon our children.”

These, then, are a portion of the people who celebrate neither the unleavened bread nor the feast days properly, but whose feast days have been turned into mourning and whose songs into lamentation. They were unable to celebrate the feast in the place that the Lord God chose.

We did not, indeed, say to them, “You shall have no share in this altar or in the inheritance of the Lord”; rather, they themselves voluntarily rejected the true altar and the heavenly high priest. Their misfortune has gone so far that they have both lost the image and failed to receive the truth. Therefore it is said to them: “Behold, your house shall be left to you desolate” (Matt. XXIII).

For the grace of the Holy Spirit has been transferred to the Gentiles; the solemnities have been transferred to the Gentiles; and a high priest—not imaginary but true—has been chosen according to the order of Melchizedek. He must offer true sacrifices, that is, spiritual sacrifices, among us, where the Church and temple of God are built from living stones, which is the Church of the living God, and where the true Israel is.

## Chapter XV

Joshua’s speeches to the people, and the remembrance of the Lord’s commandments and benefits, which were bestowed upon them most abundantly by him.

### Chapter XXIII

“Behold, today I am entering upon the way of all the earth, and with all your heart and all your soul you shall know that, of all the words which the Lord promised he would fulfill for us, not one has failed without effect,” and so forth. (From Augustine.)

When Jesus speaks of his approaching death—“I am returning along the way”—we find in the interpretation that is from the Hebrew, “I am entering upon the way.” Thus what the Septuagint said, “I am returning, as it was said to man, ‘until you return to the earth from which you were taken’” (Gen. III), must be understood according to the body.

According to the soul, however, if we wish to understand it as it is stated in Ecclesiastes, “And the spirit will return to God who gave it” (Eccli. XII), I do not think this can be said of everyone, but of those who have lived in such a way that they deserve to return to the Lord as to the author by whom they were created. For this cannot rightly be understood even of those concerning whom it is said: “A spirit that goes and does not return” (Ps. LXXVII).

Now, if this holy man Jesus son of Nave had not added, “as do all who are upon the earth,” there would be no question; for we would believe nothing else about him than what we read—that he was worthy of this. But since “as do all who are upon the earth” has been added, it is surprising if what the Latin translator rendered “I am returning” should not rather be rendered “I am running through” or “I am running forth,” if this can express what the Greek has, ἀποτρέκω (*apotrékō*), for everyone runs through or runs forth along the way of this life when they reach its end.

But because this verb occurs where Rebecca’s parents say to Abraham’s servant, “Behold Rebecca; take her, run back, and let her be the wife of your master,” this verb has likewise been translated in this passage.

### Chapter XXIV

“Thus says the Lord God of Israel: ‘Beyond the river your fathers dwelt from the beginning: Terah, the father of Abraham, and Nahor; and they served foreign gods. Therefore I took your father Abraham from the borders of Mesopotamia and brought him into the land of Canaan,’ etc.”

What the Septuagint translators have is: “And I took your father Abraham from beyond the river and led him through the whole land.” “The interpretation that is from the Hebrew has: ‘And I brought him into the land of Canaan.’” It is therefore surprising that the Septuagint wished to put “the whole land” in place of “the land of Canaan,” unless, looking toward the prophecy, they wished what was most certainly to be fulfilled in Christ and in the Church to be understood as already accomplished by virtue of God’s promise. The true seed of Abraham is not in the children of the flesh but in the children of the promise.

### The same passage

“You crossed the Jordan and came to Jericho, and the men of that city fought against you,” and so forth.

“And those who dwelt in Jericho fought against you.” One may ask how this is true, since they protected themselves merely by keeping their gates closed and by the circuit of their walls. Yet it is correctly said, because closing one’s gates against an enemy belongs to warfare; they did not send ambassadors to seek peace. If it had been said, “They fought against you,” it would have been false; for war does not consist in continuous fighting, but sometimes in frequent battles, sometimes in rare ones, and sometimes in none. It is nevertheless war when there is, in a certain sense, armed hostility.

### The same passage

“And I sent hornets before you, and drove them out from their places, the two kings of the Amorites, not by your sword or bow; and I gave you a land on which you had not labored, and cities which you had not built, that you might dwell in them, vineyards and olive groves which you had not planted,” and so forth.

What does it mean that, among the other things Jesus son of Nave recalls the Lord having done for the Israelites, he says: “He sent wasps before you and drove them from your presence”? This is also read in the Book of Wisdom (chap. XII), yet nowhere among the events that took place is it found that this happened.

Or perhaps, by transferring the word, he intended “wasps” to be understood as the sharp stings of fear, by which they were, as it were, pierced through rumors flying about, so that they fled; or as hidden aerial spirits, of which the Psalm says, “through evil angels” (Ps. LXXVII). Unless someone should say that not everything that happened was written down, and that this too happened visibly, so that real wasps are intended.

### The same passage

“Choose today what seems good to you, whom you ought especially to serve: whether the gods whom your fathers served in Mesopotamia, or the gods of the Amorites in whose land you dwell. But I and my house shall serve the Lord.”

And the people answered Joshua and said: “Far be it from us to abandon the Lord and serve foreign gods. The Lord our God himself brought us and our fathers out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery; he performed great signs before our eyes; he guarded us along the whole way by which we traveled and among all the peoples through whom we passed; and he drove out all the nations, including the Amorite who inhabited the land into which we entered. Therefore we shall serve the Lord, for he is our God.”

And Joshua said to the people: “You will not be able to serve the Lord, for he is a holy and mighty God, a jealous one; he will not forgive your crimes and sins. If you abandon the Lord and serve foreign gods, he will turn against you, afflict you, and overthrow you, etc.”

What does Jesus mean when he says to the people, “You will not be able to serve the Lord, because God is holy”? Is it because it is in some way impossible for human frailty to conform to his holiness through perfect service?

When they heard this, they ought not merely to have chosen his service but also to have relied upon his help and mercy—something understood by the one who said in the Psalm: “Do not enter into judgment with your servant, for no living person will be justified in your sight” (Ps. CXLII).

But they chose instead to rely upon themselves, believing that they could serve God without any offense, so that even then they might begin what the Apostle expressed concerning them: “For, being ignorant of God’s righteousness and seeking to establish their own, they have not submitted to God’s righteousness” (Rom. X).

Thus the law was already entering among them, so that transgression might increase, and afterward grace might abound all the more through the Lord Christ, who is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes.

### The same passage

“‘You are witnesses,’ he said, ‘that you yourselves have chosen the Lord to serve him.’ And they answered, ‘We are witnesses.’ ‘Now therefore,’ he said, ‘remove the foreign gods from your midst and incline your hearts to the Lord God of Israel,’” and so forth.

What does this same Jesus mean when he says to the people, “And now remove the foreign gods that are among you, and direct your hearts to the Lord God of Israel”? We should not believe that they still had among them any images of the nations, since above he praised their obedience. Or, if they had them, how could prosperity have followed them after so many threats of the law, when such vengeance had been taken against them because one of them had stolen something devoted to destruction?

Finally, Jacob said this to those who had gone out with him from Mesopotamia, where idols were worshiped so thoroughly that Rachel even stole her father’s (Gen. XXXI). After Jacob’s admonition they gave up what they had; from this it became clear that he had spoken thus because he knew that they possessed such things.

But now, after this admonition by Jesus son of Nave, no one brought forward anything of the kind. Nevertheless, we must not think that he commanded this pointlessly. For he did not say, “Now remove the foreign gods, if there are any among you,” but spoke altogether as one who knew they were present: “which,” he says, “are among you.”

Accordingly, the holy prophet perceived that in their hearts there were thoughts about God alien to God, and he admonished them to remove those thoughts. For whoever conceives of God as being such as God is not carries an alien and false god in his thought.

Who, however, thinks of God as he truly is? Therefore, as long as the faithful are pilgrims away from the Lord, they must remove from their hearts the vain phantoms that rush upon them and impose themselves upon those who think, as though God were such and such a being as he certainly is not. They must direct their hearts faithfully toward him, so that he may reveal himself through his Spirit in the manner and measure he knows to be beneficial for us, until every falsehood is taken away. Hence it is said: “Every human being is a liar” (Ps. CXV).

When not only impious falsehood but also the mirror and riddle have passed away, we shall know face to face, just as we have been known. As the Apostle says: “Now we see through a mirror in a riddle, but then face to face; now I know in part, but then I shall know just as I have been known” (1 Cor. XIII).

## Chapter XVI

How Joshua struck a covenant before the Lord at Shechem, wrote all the words of the covenant in the book of the law of God, and placed it upon a great stone beneath the oak that was in the sanctuary of the Lord.

### The same passage

“Therefore Joshua made a covenant on that day; he set before the people commandments and judgments at Shechem. He wrote all these words in the book of the law of God. He took a very great stone and placed it beneath the oak that was in the sanctuary of God, and he said to all the people: ‘Behold, this stone shall be a witness for you, because it has heard all the words of the Lord that he spoke to you, lest perhaps afterward you should wish to deny and lie to the Lord your God.’”

“And Jesus established a testament for the people on that day, and gave them law and judgment at Shiloh, before the tabernacle of the Lord God of Israel. He wrote these words in the book of the law of God. He took a great stone and set it beneath the terebinth before the Lord. And Jesus said to the people: ‘Behold, this stone shall be a witness for you, because it has heard all that was spoken by the Lord, whatever he said to you today. And it shall be a witness for you in the last days, when you have lied to the Lord your God.’”

Those who do not hear these words merely on the surface but examine them somewhat more deeply must not suppose that so great a man was so foolish as to believe that the words of God which he spoke to the people had been heard by an inanimate stone. Even if it had been fashioned by an artisan in human likeness, it would certainly have been counted among those of whom the Psalm sings: “They have ears, but they will not hear” (Ps. CXIII).

For it is not only the idols of the nations made of gold and silver that do not hear; nor, if they are of stone, do they hear. Through this stone he plainly signified the one who was a stone of stumbling to unbelieving Jews and a rock of offense; who, although rejected by the builders, became the cornerstone. He was prefigured also by that rock which, struck with a piece of wood, poured forth drink for the thirsty people. Concerning it the Apostle says: “They were drinking from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ” (1 Cor. X).

Therefore this outstanding leader circumcised the people with stone knives. Those stone knives were buried with him also, so that they might disclose to posterity a profound mystery that would be beneficial.

Thus we must understand this stone also, although visibly set up, spiritually as a future witness against unbelieving Jews—that is, against liars—of whom the Psalm says: “The enemies of the Lord have lied to him” (Ps. LXXX).

For it was not without reason that, although Moses, the servant of God—or rather God through him—had already established for the people the testament that was in the ark called the Ark of the Covenant, and although so great a multiplicity of sacraments and commandments had been written in the books of the law, it was nevertheless also said here: “Jesus established a testament for the people on that day.”

The repetition of the testament signifies the New Testament. The same is signified by Deuteronomy, which is interpreted as “second law,” and by the renewed tablets after the earlier ones had been broken. What was to be fulfilled in one way had to be signified in many ways.

Now, the fact that the stone was set beneath the terebinth signifies what happened when the rod was applied to the rock so that water might flow, because here too the stone was not set up without wood. It was placed beneath because it would not have been raised upon the cross unless it had been subjected in humility; or because, at the time when Jesus son of Nave did this, the mystery still had to be veiled.

The wood of the terebinth exudes a medicinal tear. This is the tree placed here by the Septuagint translators, although according to other translators “oak” is read.

### The same passage

“And he dismissed the people, each to his own possession.”

It is truly surprising that, at least in the last words with which Joshua, the man of God, addressed the people, he reproached them for nothing—not even for sparing those nations whom the Lord had commanded them to destroy utterly under the ban.

For it is written: “And it happened that, when the sons of Israel had grown strong, they made the Canaanites tributary, but they did not destroy them utterly” (Josh. XVII).

At first Scripture testified that they had not been able to do this. But now, after they had prevailed sufficiently to make them obedient, their failure to destroy them utterly was certainly contrary to the Lord’s command—something that had never occurred while Jesus was leading the army.

Why, then, did he not reproach them in his final address for having neglected the Lord’s command in this matter?

Or perhaps, when Scripture previously said that they had not been able to do it—obviously before they prevailed—we must also believe that, after they had prevailed, they were afraid. Perhaps, if the nations were prepared to obey but the Israelites refused to spare them, the nations would have been driven by desperation to fight against them more fiercely, and the Israelites would not have been able to overcome them.

The Lord therefore did not wish to count this human fear against them, although it reveals a certain weakness of faith. If their faith had been strong, they would have followed what happened when Jesus himself fought. Because they did not possess such great faith, even after they had prevailed over their adversaries they did not dare, out of fear, to fight them until their destruction.

As I have said, the Lord did not count this fear against them as arising from malice, pride, or contempt of his command, but as coming from weakness of spirit, when he spoke to them for the last time through Jesus.

Hence the Apostle also says: “Alexander the coppersmith showed me many evils; the Lord will repay him according to his works” (2 Tim. IV). But concerning those who abandoned him when he was in danger, not from malice but from fear, he said: “At my first defense no one stood by me; everyone abandoned me. May it not be counted against them” (ibid.).

## Chapter XVII

The death of Joshua and his burial, and the death of Eleazar and his burial; also concerning Joseph’s bones, brought out of Egypt and buried at Shechem, in the portion of the field that Jacob had bought from the sons of Hamor, the father of Shechem, for one hundred young sheep.

### The same passage

“After this Joshua son of Nun, the servant of the Lord, died, being one hundred and ten years old. They buried him within the borders of his possession, at Thamnath-sare, which is situated on Mount Ephraim, on the northern side of Mount Gaash.”

In some people Jesus lives, while in others he has died. Jesus lives in Paul, in Peter, and in all those who can rightly say: “I live, yet it is no longer I; Christ lives in me” (Gal. II); and, “For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Phil. I). In such people, then, Jesus is rightly said to live.

In whom has Jesus died? Without doubt, in those who, by repeatedly repenting and then sinning again, are said, as it were, to insult Jesus’ death. Concerning them the Apostle writes to the Hebrews: “Crucifying again for themselves the Son of God and holding him up to contempt” (Heb. VI).

The Lord himself also gave a most beautiful distinction concerning this in the Gospels when he says: “Whoever confesses me before human beings, I too will confess him before my Father who is in heaven. But whoever denies me before human beings, I too will deny him before my Father” (Matt. X).

You see that, concerning those who confess, he said that they confess “in him,” as though he himself lived in them and performed the works of life. But concerning those who deny, he did not preserve the same verbal likeness by saying, “Whoever denies in me, I will also deny in him.” Rather he said, “Whoever denies me before human beings, I too will deny him before my Father,” to show that the one who denies is outside him, whereas the one who confesses is in him.

The fact that Jesus’ death is mentioned as occurring after one hundred and ten years shows that, through Christ’s death, all who rightly observe the commandments of the law will come to everlasting blessedness after the end of the present life.

His burial is described as being within the borders of his possession, at Thamnath-sare, on Mount Ephraim and in a part of Mount Gaash. This signifies that in the Catholic Church, which is Christ’s possession and where the fruit of virtues is produced, the remembrance of Christ’s passion is celebrated daily with solemnity and honor.

Thamnath is a city of Jesus in the tribe of Ephraim, situated on Mount Gaash. Jesus son of Nave was buried on its northern side, and even to this day his distinguished tomb is shown near the village of Thannan.

Thamnath-sare is interpreted as “the number of the new covering.” And daily in the Church, among the other words of divine ordinance, from the multitude of the sons who serve Christ, in the sacrament of the Mass, we hear: “This is the cup of the New Testament in my blood, which will be poured out for you and for many for the forgiveness of sins. Whenever you do this, you shall do it in remembrance of me.”

### The same passage

“Israel served the Lord throughout all the days of Joshua and of the elders who lived for a long time after Joshua, and who knew all the works that the Lord had done in Israel.” (From Adamantius.)

Blessed is the one who serves the Lord in the days of Jesus, who is illumined by his word and wisdom, who is enlightened by his commandments, and who receives the light of knowledge from his teaching.

In a secondary place, however, blessed is the one who comes after him and serves the Lord in the days of the elders who were after Jesus. Who are these elders who were either with Jesus or after Jesus, if not the apostles? They too illumine our hearts through their writings and commandments, and they themselves cause certain days to arise within us from that light which they received as participants in the true light.

Whoever, therefore, is illumined and instructed by the apostles’ commandments, and is instructed for the service of the Lord by apostolic rules, is the one who is said to serve the Lord in the days of the elders who were after Jesus.

### The same passage

“They also buried the bones of Joseph, which the sons of Israel had brought out of Egypt, at Shechem, in the portion of the field that Jacob had bought from the sons of Hamor, the father of Shechem, for one hundred young sheep; and it became the possession of the sons of Joseph.”

It should be noted that Josephus, the Jewish historian, recalls Joseph and his brothers in the second book of the *Antiquities* as follows:

“He too died after having lived one hundred and ten years, remarkable in virtue, arranging everything rationally, and exercising his authority humbly. This was certainly the cause of such good fortune for him among the Egyptians and among those who came from elsewhere, although he had suffered the sort of false accusation we mentioned earlier. His brothers also died happily in Egypt, having been reunited there; their descendants later brought back their bodies and buried them in Hebron. Joseph’s bones, however, were finally brought into Canaan when the Hebrews departed from Egypt. For Joseph had bound them by oath to do this.”

Mystically, Joseph’s bones signify the death of our Redeemer. True Israelites take him from the Egypt of this world, where he was crucified according to the flesh, and transfer him to Shechem, to the portion of the field that Jacob bought for one hundred young sheep, when they bury the remembrance of his passion in the field of their hearts. Thus, following his example, they learn to bear labors, to have patience, and to persist in good works.

This is signified by Shechem, which is interpreted as “shoulder.” Our Jacob therefore bought this field as a possession for one hundred young sheep, because by the price of his blood he acquired the Church, where he has young sheep that have come up from the laver, so that he may be the shepherd of a hundred sheep while he holds the angelic and human sheepfolds under his authority.

### The same passage

“Eleazar son of Aaron also died, and they buried him at Gibeah of Phinehas his son, which had been given to him on Mount Ephraim.”

The fact that Eleazar’s death is mentioned immediately after Joshua’s death signifies that, after the passion and resurrection of our Redeemer, the old priesthood came to an end and the legal sacrifices were completed. The priesthood of the New Testament necessarily followed, in which the flesh and blood of the immaculate Lamb are offered daily upon the sacred altars and are beneficially received by the mouths of the faithful as nourishment for their souls. Thus, as the shadow of the law withdraws, the truth of the Gospel is revealed through our Lord Jesus Christ himself.

## (A.D. 834)

Commentaries of Blessed Rabanus Maurus, Abbot of Fulda and Archbishop of Mainz, on the Book of Judges and Ruth.

## Letter of Bishop Hunbert to Rabanus

To the illustrious, deservedly distinguished, and most excellent father, Rabanus Maurus: Hunbert, although unworthy but endowed with the episcopal mitre, sends unfading salvation in Christ Jesus.

I have read your letters, dearest brother, which you wrote to the holy man of blessed memory, Archbishop Haistulf, at the beginning of the book that you composed through your own labor and most prudent intellect for the preaching of the Christian people throughout the yearly cycle. In it you discuss delightfully the observance of the Lord’s Day and the feasts of the saints, as well as faith, hope, and charity, together with the other forms of virtue.

I have also read the other three books that you made for the same venerable man, which you chose to call *On the Instruction of Clerics*. The first of these relates the ecclesiastical orders and the four divine charisms. The second contains an account of the office of the canonical hours, various feasts, fasts, and prayers. The third gives a not undistinguished instruction concerning how divine Scripture should be learned and expounded, and what benefit human philosophy confers upon ecclesiastical teachers.

Having read these works, insofar as the capacity of my little intellect permitted, I understood that you had embraced, with praiseworthy breadth and brevity, everything necessary for the holy Church of God.

I say to you truthfully that it cannot be expressed with what joy of heart I rejoiced and gave thanks to God, who wished to have so useful a vessel in his holy Church in these times, from which both the one seeking a large drink and the one seeking a small drink may draw and drink.

From that day, I confess, I greatly desired to become a participant in your friendship, so that at least at some time I might be deemed worthy to receive writings of yours that had long since been scattered far and wide. For this reason I sent you a short letter, admonishing you in brotherly charity not to allow the keenness of your mind to grow dull or fall asleep through idle leisure, but to remain diligent, vigilant, tireless, and always useful in the house of the Lord, searching the sacred Scriptures daily and relying upon the authority of the Fathers who came before.

For we read: “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden.” Likewise, in another place: “No one lights a lamp and places it under a measuring basket, but rather upon a lampstand, so that it may give light to all who are in the house.”

I have heard that you have composed a discourse on the Eptateuch, as well as commentaries on the Gospel of Matthew and on the Books of Kings, writing and dictating many useful things with the assistance of heavenly grace and likewise relying upon the authority of the ancients.

Therefore, because of our friendship, I beg your fraternity to make an effort to write to me and send me your little works. Chosen from the judgments of the ancient ecclesiastical writers like flowers gathered from different meadows, they adorn the house of the Lord and beautify anyone who loves them.

Finally, because I believe you will grant what I have requested, I am sending parchment on which I hope first to receive those books that your intellect composed on your Eptateuch.

I do not ask for these, however, as though writers of this work were lacking among us. For we have Origen, Victorinus, Ambrose, Jerome, Cassian, Isidore, Augustine, Fulgentius, and the distinguished and most eloquent pontiff Gregory, together with the other Fathers, whose names I do not think it necessary for me to enumerate to you.

They are so well known to your diligence that I can truthfully say that their tongue has become your discourse. What they expressed with remarkable beauty and excessive length of speech, you, wisely and skillfully following in their footsteps, comprehend in a concise, honey-sweet, and flowing style. For, as the distinguished teacher Isidore says, a brief and succinct exposition does not create weariness through prolixity; a lengthy and obscure speech is tiresome, while a brief and clear one is pleasing.

I therefore ask your diligence, after reading through these little lines of this letter, if your will should judge it appropriate, to order that it be placed at the beginning of the little book that I have asked you to copy for me, so that the affection and the result of our mutual love and fellowship may alike appear.

May God the Son of God, the author of all good things, preserve your blessedness, which intercedes for us, safe forever.

The relics that you requested, dearest brother, I have sent through the bearer of these letters. For the rest, know that from the innermost affection of my heart I am always willing and ready for everything that your will may decide to command.

I always desire that your fraternity may be well, dear friend, and mindful of us.

> Hail, holy Father, deservedly blessed throughout the world;
>
> You are our honor, holy Father, deservedly so.
>
> May Christ Jesus, God, be your sure helmet;
>
> May he preserve you always and everywhere. Farewell.

## Preface dictated to Bishop Hunbert

To the most beloved Lord, greatly deserving of obedience in the worship of the sincerest charity, and venerable father, Hunbert the bishop: Rabanus, the least of the servants of God, servant in Christ, sends greetings.

Having received the letter of Your Holiness, which you wished to address to my lowliness, I rejoiced greatly, because in it I recognized your diligent industry and your flourishing talent in the study of divine letters. For this I humbly gave thanks to the Lord, because he has granted you both a devoted exercise in meditation on his law and, through it, a wholesome instruction for his people.

Therefore, since your fatherhood has deigned to seek some consolation from our lowliness, out of love for God and also for your affection in him, I profess in this work that I wish to be your servant [Col. 1109C] and, insofar as divine grace grants its approval, a willing helper in your good endeavor. May God’s will alone be done in bringing the work to completion, for he is the one who has given both the will and the accomplishment.

Furthermore, since you deigned to write to me requesting that I send you our little work on the Heptateuch, I have done what I could. I have now sent, consecrated to your name, the final part of it—that is, the work on Judges and Ruth—which I presently had at hand. The commentaries on the earlier books, namely, on the Pentateuch of Moses, which I composed with no little labor at the request of the holy man Freculf, I have already sent to him to be copied again. When I receive them back, I shall send you a written copy of them.

As for the exposition of Joshua son of Nun, I recently sent it to Friduric of blessed memory, bishop of the Church of Utrecht. Likewise, when it has been returned to me, if it is God’s will, I shall take care to entrust it to you. And I intend most willingly to devote to you not only those works but everything that can come from us for your benefit. Only refresh our weakness with sacred prayers and pious exhortations, for I am weighed down not merely by the distress of my own illness but also by anxiety over the common danger that now hangs heavily over us. Therefore I especially need your prayer and the mercy of almighty God, lest I fail amid tribulations, necessities, dangers, and various temptations.

Know, then, that the work I am sending you has been composed not only from the sayings of our predecessors, which I found written in their books, but also from our own labor, insofar as divine grace has allowed us to accomplish it [Col. 1110B]. Thus it presents partly the opinions of the Fathers and partly, wherever I judged it necessary, the small measure of our own understanding. Your prudence knows how both to praise their wisdom and eloquence and to tolerate our sluggishness and rusticity; and you know how to fulfill that saying of the Apostle: “Bearing with one another in charity” (Ephesians 4); and again: “Bear one another’s burdens,” he says, “and so you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Galatians 6).

In the first two books of the commentaries, the history of Judges is expounded in a mystical sense; and in the third, Ruth—whom some authors associate with the Book of Judges, while others place her separately—is explained to a considerable extent.

As you read these things again, if you find anything suitably expounded in them, attribute it to him from whom all good comes [Col. 1110C]. Whatever you find otherwise, attribute rather to our weakness and ignorance than to malice, and for this strive to intercede with pious prayers before almighty God, so that through his aid it may be forgiven and corrected. Before him nothing imperfect in our weakness is hidden, as the Psalmist testifies, saying: “My imperfection your eyes have seen” (Psalm 138).

It is therefore especially fitting for you, most reverend Father, who in the Church of God have been entrusted with the office of judging on God’s behalf, to read the Book of Judges diligently, vigorously to imitate their good deeds and just judgments, and to defend God’s people against the slaughter of their enemies with spiritual weapons. In accordance with the teaching of the teacher of the nations, by which he instructed his disciple, keep watch diligently, labor piously, do the work of an evangelist, and fulfill your ministry [Col. 1110D]. Thus, when the prince of shepherds, the King of kings, and the judge of the living and the dead appears, you may receive together with the other holy bishops of God’s Church the unfading crown of glory, and may hear from Truth itself that evangelical testimony by which he praises the servant who has labored well and faithfully distributed his master’s money, saying: “Well done, good and faithful servant! Because you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matthew 25).

May almighty God—the Trinity and undivided Unity—grant that you perpetually share this joy with the holy angels and chosen souls in the heavenly kingdom. We always wish Your Blessedness well in Christ, holy Father; remember us.

[Col. 1111]

# COMMENTARIES ON THE BOOK OF JUDGES BEGIN

## BOOK ONE

### CHAPTER ONE

On the fact that after Joshua’s death the children of Israel consulted the Lord about which of them should become their leader against the Canaanites; and on the killing of Adonibezek the king, and the assault upon the Canaanites and the city of Jerusalem.

(CAP. 1.) After the death of Joshua, the children of Israel consulted the Lord, saying: “Who will go up before us against the Canaanite and be the leader of the war?” And the Lord said: “Judah shall go up; behold, I have handed the land over to him.” And Judah said to his brother Simeon: “Go up with me into my allotted territory and fight against the Canaanite, so that I too may go with you into your allotted territory.” And Simeon went with him; Judah went up, and the Lord handed the Canaanite and the Perizzite over to them, and so forth.

At the end of the Book of Joshua, the narrator briefly carried the history forward to the point at which the children of Israel turned aside to worship foreign gods. In this book, however, he returns to the sequence of events, showing what happened after the death of Joshua son of Nun. The book therefore does not begin at the time when the people turned to worship idols, but with the earlier intervening events that took place before they reached that point.

“And it came to pass, after Jesus had died, that the children of Israel asked the Lord, saying: ‘Who shall go up with us against the Canaanite as leader, to fight against him?’ And the Lord said: ‘Judah shall go up; behold, I have given the land into his hand.’”

Here it is asked whether a man named Judah was meant, or whether—as is customary—he called the tribe itself by that name. But those who questioned the Lord after the death of Joshua son of Nun were seeking a leader; hence it is thought that the name of an individual man is expressed [Col. 1111C]. Yet since Scripture does not ordinarily name leaders when they are appointed without also mentioning the origin of their parents, and since it is established that Israel had leaders after Joshua, the first being Othniel son of Kenaz, it is more correctly understood that the name Judah signifies the tribe of Judah. For the Lord wished to begin crushing the Canaanites through that tribe.

And when the people had asked about a leader, the Lord’s answer served to make them understand that God did not wish the whole people to wage war against the Canaanites. Thus he said: “Judah shall go up.” Scripture then continues: “And Judah said to Simeon his brother”—that is, tribe to tribe. For the sons of Jacob called Judah and Simeon by those proper names, together with their other brothers, were certainly no longer alive [Col. 1111D]. Rather, the tribe of Judah said to the tribe of Simeon: “Go up with me into my allotted territory, and let us fight against the Canaanite; and I too will go with you into your allotted territory.” It is clear that the tribe of Judah asked the other tribe for assistance, intending to repay it when they too began to possess what was necessary in their own territory [Col. 1112A].

“They found Adonibezek at Bezek, and they fought against him, and they struck down the Canaanite and the Perizzite. But Adonibezek fled; they pursued and captured him, cutting off the ends of his hands and feet, and so forth.”

Who, then, can this Adonibezek better signify than the devil, the ancient enemy and adversary of all righteousness, who reigns in Bezek—that is, in splendor or in empty contempt? Adonibezek is interpreted as “lord of lightning.” The Apostle says of this same ancient enemy: “For Satan himself transforms himself into an angel of light” (2 Corinthians 11).

All his power and authority, however, are vanity. The sons of Judah—that is, the sons of confession—and the sons of Simeon—that is, the sons of being heard—fight against him when all the faithful battle against him with the shield of faith and the weapons of the virtues. They capture and strike him, cutting off the ends of his hands and feet, when they strive manfully to sever the beginnings of evil action and the traces of wicked example, so that the deceit of the Evil One may not find an opportunity for sudden deception, once his power to inflict harm has been taken away through spiritual combat.

“Therefore, the sons of Judah attacked Jerusalem, captured it, struck it with the edge of the sword, and handed the entire city over to the fire. Afterwards they went down and fought against the Canaanite who lived in the hill country, in the south, and in the plains. Judah proceeded against the Canaanite who lived in Hebron, whose ancient name was Kiriath-arba; he struck Sheshai, Ahiman, and Talmai. From there he went against the inhabitants of Debir, whose former name was Kiriath-sepher, that is, ‘city of letters.’”

Josephus mentions this place in the fifth book of his *Antiquities*, saying:

> “Meanwhile they besieged Jerusalem. Although they captured it only after a long time, they killed all who lived there. For the fortification of its walls above them and the nature of the place offered very strong resistance. Therefore they encamped at Hebron, and after capturing it they killed everyone.”

There still remained a race of giants, who were exceedingly remarkable because of their height and forms, unlike those of any other human beings. Their bones are shown to this day, unequal in size to any of those whose existence was believed. He had assigned this race especially as a task to the Levites, and they had also given land as a gift together with two thousand cubits, by Moses’ command [the printed wording is corrupt]; for he was one of the scouts whom Moses sent into Canaan.

### CHAPTER TWO

That Caleb promised his daughter in marriage to the man who would strike down Kiriath-sepher; and that Achsah, Caleb’s daughter, asked her father to give her irrigated land.

(IBID.) “And Caleb said: ‘Whoever strikes Kiriath-sepher and devastates it, to him I will give my daughter Achsah as a wife.’”

This too was mentioned in the Book of Joshua. But it is reasonably asked whether it happened while Joshua was alive and has now been repeated by recapitulation, or whether it happened after his death, once it had been said, “Judah shall go up,” and Judah began to fight against the Canaanites, in which war all these events are reported.

It is more credible that it happened after Joshua’s death, but that it was then mentioned beforehand by prolepsis, that is, by anticipation, as were other events. For now, when the deeds carried out against the Canaanites by the tribe of Judah are being explained, the order of the narrative proceeds through the various military actions of Judah, concerning whom the Lord had said after Joshua’s death: “Judah shall go up.”

“And afterwards the sons of Judah went down to fight against the Canaanite who lived in the hill country, the south, and the plain. Judah went to the Canaanite who dwelt in Hebron, and Hebron came out to face him. Its name was formerly Kiriath-arba, and he struck Sheshai, Ahiman, and Talmai, the sons of Anak. From there they went up against the inhabitants of Debir, whose former name was the city of letters. And Caleb said: ‘Whoever strikes the city of letters and captures it, to him I will give my daughter in marriage.’”

It is therefore evident from this sequence of events that this happened after Joshua’s death. At the time when the cities given to Caleb were being mentioned, the narrator took the opportunity to anticipate what happened later. Yet I do not think that Scripture wished without reason to mention here that Caleb’s daughter was given as the victor’s reward.

Another question arises concerning Caleb’s daughter. In the Book of Joshua she is described as follows: “And it came to pass, as she entered, that she conferred with him, saying: ‘I shall ask my father for a field.’ And she cried out from the donkey,” and so forth. There she asks her father for a field, and it is granted to her.

Here, however, it says: “And it came to pass, as he entered, Othniel urged her to ask her father for a field.” But there is no contradiction between what is said there—“as she entered”—and what is said here—“as he entered.” They were entering the road together. And where it is said there that “she conferred with him,” that is, with her husband, saying, “I shall ask my father for a field,” and she cried out from the donkey and asked: by the fact that she conferred with him, she was urged to ask. One of these details is stated there and the other here. Both could therefore be expressed in this way: “She conferred with him, saying, ‘I shall ask my father for a field’; but he urged her, and she cried out from the donkey.”

Moreover, there she is reported to have asked for a field, and the name of the field itself is not omitted. Here, however, although she was urged by her husband to ask for a field, she is not said to have asked for a field when she cried out from the riding animal—what is called there a donkey—but for a supply of water, because she had been given land in the southern region [Col. 1114A].

Hence it is added: “When she sighed while sitting on the donkey, Caleb said to her: ‘What do you have?’ And she replied: ‘Give me a blessing. You have given me dry land; give me also land irrigated with water.’ So Caleb gave her the upper irrigated land and the lower irrigated land.”

Spiritually, the soul sits upon a female donkey when the soul presides over the irrational movements of its flesh. Sighing, it asks its father for irrigated land, because the grace of tears must be sought from our Creator with great groaning.

There are some who have already received as a gift the freedom to speak for justice, protect the oppressed, give their possessions to the needy, and possess the fervor of faith; but they still do not have the grace of tears. These indeed possess southern and dry land, but they still need irrigation. For having been placed in good works, in which they are great and fervent, they ought to mourn the evils they previously committed, either through fear of punishment or through love of the heavenly kingdom.

Although contrition is divided into many forms, since penitents mourn their individual sins one by one, Jeremiah also says from the voice of penitents: “My eye has brought down divisions of waters” (Lamentations 3). Nevertheless, there are principally two kinds of contrition, because the soul thirsting for God is first pierced by fear and afterward by love.

First it afflicts itself with tears, because, while recalling its evils, it fears that it will suffer eternal punishments for them. But when fear has been consumed by the long anxiety of grief, a certain security born of confidence in forgiveness arises, and the mind is kindled by love of heavenly joys [Col. 1114C].

The mind contemplates the choirs of angels, the fellowship of the holy spirits, and the majesty of the inner vision of God. It mourns more intensely because it is absent from everlasting goods than it mourned earlier when it feared eternal evils. Thus perfect contrition brings the sting of love to the soul after the sting of fear. This is well represented in this sacred and truthful historical narrative.

Since, as I have said, there are two kinds of contrition, her father gave her upper irrigated land and lower irrigated land. The soul receives upper irrigation when it afflicts itself with tears out of desire for the heavenly kingdom [Col. 1114D]; it receives lower irrigation when it fears the punishments of hell and dreads them with tears. The lower irrigation is indeed given first and the upper afterward, but because the contrition of love surpasses the other in dignity, it was necessary for the upper irrigation to be mentioned first and the lower afterward.

### CHAPTER THREE
