That the sons of the Kenite, relatives of Moses, went down from the City of Palms with the sons of Judah and lived with them; and that Judah possessed the hill country but could not destroy the inhabitants of the valley.

(IBID.) “The sons of the Kenite, relatives of Moses, went down from the City of Palms with the sons of Judah into the wilderness of his allotted territory, which is south of Arad, and they lived with him.”

Here is Josephus:

> “They also gave land for possession to the sons of Jethro the Midianite, who was Moses’ father-in-law. For they left their homeland, followed them, and were with them in the wilderness.”

Judah captured Gaza with its borders, Ashkelon, and Ekron with its boundaries. The Lord was with Judah, and Judah possessed the hill country. He could not destroy the inhabitants of the valley, because they had many chariots equipped with scythes.

They gave Hebron to Caleb, as Moses had said; and he destroyed from it the three sons of Anak.

When I treated this passage in the Book of Joshua, where it is written, “The Lord gave Israel all the land,” although they did not yet possess many parts of it, I said that “all the land was given” could be understood in this way: what was not given for possession was given for a certain purpose of training. This appears much more clearly here [Col. 1115B], since the cities that Judah did not inherit are mentioned, and it is said: “The Lord was with Judah, and Judah inherited the hill country, because they could not inherit the inhabitants of the valley.”

Who would not understand that this too belonged to the fact that the Lord was with Judah, so that he would not be exalted by suddenly possessing everything? For when it adds how Rechab opposed him and that they had iron chariots, it says that Judah himself was afraid—not the Lord who was with Judah.

If it is asked why he feared, since the Lord was with him, the prudent understanding is that God, in his favor, restrains even in the hearts of his own people the excesses of excessive prosperity, so that he turns enemies to their advantage: one purpose when enemies are defeated, another when they are feared [Col. 1115C]. For the angel of Satan is certainly the enemy of the saints; yet the Apostle says that he was given to him as a tormentor, lest he be exalted by the greatness of his revelations (2 Corinthians 12).

“And they gave Hebron,” it says, “to Caleb, as Moses had spoken, and he inherited from it three cities of the sons of Anak, and removed from it the three sons of Anak.”

This too was stated in the Book of Joshua, since it happened while Joshua was alive; but here it is mentioned by recapitulation, while Scripture is speaking about Judah, from whom Caleb came.

### CHAPTER FOUR

That the sons of Benjamin could not destroy the Jebusite in Jerusalem; nor did Manasseh destroy the Canaanite in the cities of its allotted territory, but lived with them. After Israel had grown strong, it made them tributaries and did not wish to destroy them.

(IBID.) “The sons of Benjamin did not destroy the Jebusite, the inhabitant of Jerusalem; and the Jebusite lived with the sons of Benjamin in Jerusalem to the present day.”

It is asked how it can have been said, “They did not destroy the Jebusite who lived in Jerusalem,” or, “The sons of Benjamin did not inherit it; and the Jebusite lived with the sons of Benjamin in Jerusalem to the present day,” when it was stated above that the same city had been captured and burned by Judah, after the Jebusites found there had been killed.

We must recognize that this city was shared by two tribes, Judah and Benjamin, as the division of the land itself shows, the division made by Joshua son of Nun [Col. 1116A]. This is Jebus, which is Jerusalem. For this reason these two tribes remained with the Temple of the Lord when the others—apart from Levi, which was the priestly tribe and received no territory in the division—separated themselves from the kingdom of Judah with Jeroboam.

It must therefore be understood that Judah did indeed capture and burn the city, killing those who were found there, but that not all the Jebusites were destroyed—either because some were outside the city or because they were able to flee. The surviving Jebusites were admitted by the sons of Benjamin, with whom Judah shared that city, and they lived there together.

Accordingly, where it is said, “The sons of Benjamin did not inherit the Jebusite,” this may be understood to mean that they were able—or wished—to make them tributaries. Or, alternatively, “The Jebusite lived there” was said because Benjamin did not hold the land without him, since it possessed the land that had belonged to him [Col. 1116B].

Manasseh likewise did not destroy Beth-shean, Taanach with its villages, the inhabitants of Dor and Jibleam, or Megiddo with its villages; and the Canaanite began to live with them. Manasseh did not inherit Beth-shean, which is the city of Scythians; today, it is said to be called Scythopolis.

It may seem surprising how a city of Scythians could have existed in those regions, so far removed from Scythia. But it may similarly seem surprising how Alexander of Macedon could have founded the city of Alexandria so far from Macedonia. Therefore, just as he did this by waging war far and wide, so the Scythians, when at some time they advanced far away while waging war, could have founded this city.

For it is read in the history of the nations that the Scythians once held almost all of Asia, when they went to meet the king of the Egyptians who had rashly declared war against them. Terrified by their arrival, he withdrew into his own kingdom [Col. 1116C].

“After Israel had grown strong, it made them tributaries and did not wish to destroy them.”

Something similar was already stated in almost the same words in the Book of Joshua. Therefore, either it is said here by an anacephalaeosis, or it was said there by prolepsis—that is, either it is recapitulated here, or anticipated there.

For what does the Canaanite, plainly a pagan people, signify if not vice? We enter the promised land through great virtues, because we are strengthened by an inner hope of eternity. But while we are engaged in lofty deeds, when we retain certain lesser vices, we allow the Canaanite to dwell in our land. Yet he becomes tributary, because we humbly turn that very vice, which we cannot subdue, to the use of our advantage. Thus the mind recognizes its own lowliness even amid the highest achievements, insofar as it cannot conquer by its own strength even the small things it desires.

Hence it is rightly written again: “These are the nations whom the Lord left, in order to train Israel through them.” Certain small vices are retained for this purpose: so that our vigilant intention may continually exercise itself in the struggle, and so that we may not become proud of victory when we see enemies living within us, enemies whom we still fear to overcome.

Israel is therefore instructed through the nations that have been left, when the pride of our virtue is restrained by certain small vices, and when, through the small things that resist it, it learns that it cannot overcome greater things by its own power.

[Col. 1117A] “The Amorite constrained the sons of Dan in the hill country and did not give them room to descend to the plains.”

“And the Amorite oppressed the sons of Dan in the hill country, because he did not permit them to descend into the valley.”

This too was either mentioned beforehand in the Book of Joshua, or recapitulated here.

### CHAPTER FIVE

That the angel of the Lord went up from Gilgal to the place of weeping and rebuked Israel for its sins and negligence.

(CAP. 2.) “The angel of the Lord went up from Gilgal to the place of weeping and said: ‘I brought you up from Egypt and brought you into the land concerning which I swore to your fathers and promised that I would never break my covenant with you; provided only that you would not make a covenant with the inhabitants of this land and that you would overthrow their altars. But you did not wish to listen to my voice. Why have you done this? Therefore I did not wish to destroy them from before you, so that you might have enemies and their gods might become a ruin for you.’”

Another edition reads: “And the angel of the Lord went up upon Mount Clauthmos.” The writer of the book called the place by this name because he wrote afterward; for when the angel of the Lord went up upon it, it was not yet called by that name.

It received its name from weeping, because in Greek *Clauthmos* means “weeping.” For there the people wept when they heard from this angel the words of the Lord rebuking them because they had been disobedient: they had not exterminated the nations according to his command, although they had prevailed over them. Instead, they chose to make them tributaries rather than kill and destroy them, as the Lord had commanded [Col. 1117C].

Whether they did this by despising God’s command or through fear—lest their enemies should fight more fiercely against them for the sake of preserving their lives than for the sake of refusing tribute—they undoubtedly sinned both by disregarding what had been divinely commanded and by failing to trust that the one who had commanded them could help them.

The reason he did not say this to them through Joshua—if, indeed, he had already commanded it to be done while Joshua was alive, rather than its having been mentioned beforehand as something that began after his death—is that he wished to reproach them all through the angel. While Joshua was alive, not all had yet done this, although some may perhaps already have begun.

It is more credible, however, that nothing of this kind began while Joshua son of Nun was alive. Rather, the children of Israel held as much land under him as was sufficient for their settlement, although in their allotted territories they had room to grow, gain strength, and continue exterminating their adversaries.

Therefore, after Joshua’s death, once they had become strong enough to do this, they preferred to keep the Canaanites as tributaries according to their own will rather than kill and destroy them according to God’s will. For this reason the angel was sent to rebuke them.

As for the fact that this was mentioned in the Book of Joshua, I think it was more likely mentioned beforehand: Joshua himself, if he wrote the book called Joshua, knew prophetically that it would happen after his death; or, if the book was written by someone else, that author knew that after Joshua’s death the event had already happened, and therefore mentioned it beforehand in that book [Col. 1118A].

What does the angel of the Lord mean, among the other words of the divine threat, when he says, “Therefore I did not wish to destroy them from before you, so that you might have enemies and their gods might become a ruin for you,” except that we should understand that some sins also arise from God’s anger?

God was indignant and threatened them because the gods of the nations among whom the Israelites had chosen to live, rather than exterminate them, would become a stumbling block to them—that is, they would cause them to stumble against the Lord their God and live under his displeasure. It is plainly evident that this is a great sin.

### CHAPTER SIX

That Joshua dismissed the people to go to their possessions, and that they served the Lord throughout his days and throughout the days of the elders who lived long after him.

[Col. 1118B] (IBID.) “Joshua therefore dismissed the people, and the children of Israel went, each to his own possession, to take possession of it.”

There is no doubt that this is repeated by recapitulation. For the death of Joshua son of Nun is also mentioned in this book, so that, as though from the beginning, everything might be briefly introduced: how the Lord gave them the land, how they lived under the judges, and what they had already endured. Then the narrative returns again to the sequence of the judges, beginning with the first who was appointed.

“And they served the Lord throughout all his days and throughout the days of the elders who lived long after him, and who knew all the works of the Lord that he had done with Israel.”

The people therefore served the Lord throughout all the days of Joshua and throughout all the days of the elders who came after Joshua.

Blessed is the one who serves the Lord in the days of Joshua, who is illumined by his word and wisdom, who is enlightened by his commandments, and who receives the light of knowledge from his teaching.

In a secondary sense, however, the one who comes after this person is also blessed: the one who serves the Lord in the days of the elders who lived after Joshua. Who are these elders, whether those who were with Joshua or those who came after him, except the apostles? They too illumine our hearts through their writings and commandments, and they themselves bring about in us certain “days” from that light which they received as participants in the true light.

Therefore, whoever is illumined and instructed by the apostles’ commandments, and is trained or established for the service of the Lord by apostolic rules, is the one who is said to serve the Lord in the days of the elders who came after Joshua [Col. 1118D].

Would you like to see that, just as the Savior was the true light that enlightens every person coming into this world (John 1), so the apostles also were the light of the world? In the Gospel it is written that the Lord said to them: “You are the light of the world” (Matthew 5).

If the apostles too are the light of the world, then undoubtedly through their precepts and commandments they illumine the days in which we serve the Lord.

Nor do I think that what he said—“throughout all the days of the elders who lived long after Joshua”—was said without purpose. The elders who came after Joshua are called long-lived, or “of long days,” and it belongs to God alone to know which of the elders came after Joshua and made the longer day—that is, which one sent forth the greater light from himself: whether Paul or Peter, Bartholomew or John.

Nevertheless, the saints are called “of long days.” By contrast, when the world is filled with scandals, when love grows cold because iniquity increases (Matthew 24), and when the Son of Man comes and scarcely finds faith on the earth (Luke 18), then the days are not said to be long but are said rather to be shortened, as the Lord said: “Unless those days had been shortened, no flesh would be saved” (Matthew 24).

Evil days, then, are said to be shortened; but good days, in which we serve the Lord, are long-lived, lasting a long time and possessing, in a sense, great extent.

Observe, however, that the Gospel also indicates this when it says that those days will be shortened for the sake of the elect (Matthew 24). Therefore the evil days—the days of iniquity and scandal—are shortened for the elect. But the days of the holy elders are long-lived and extended.

Nor should we pass over the further point that has occurred to us as we speak—and would that, with the Lord’s prompting, it might occur to us more fully! He said that the people served the Lord throughout all the days of Joshua. He did not say that Joshua had only one day; rather, there are many days of Joshua.

What, then, are the many days that we place within this framework of interpretation? I think that one of his days is justice, another sanctification, another prudence, another mercy; and so, one by one, perhaps every good of the virtues counts as a day of Joshua, in which the Lord is served, because through these virtues the Lord is pleased in the soul.

Count patience also as his day, and gentleness, piety, goodness, and everything that belongs to virtue; call each of these his day. Thus you will serve the Lord throughout all the days of Joshua—that is, in all these virtues.

For the teaching of holy Scripture does not wish you to possess some of these virtues while neglecting others, but to serve God adorned with all these virtues and established in their works.

In the same way, a person has within himself the days of the elders and serves God in their days, fulfilling what the Apostle Paul says: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (1 Corinthians 11).

It says, “in the days of the elders who knew all the works of the Lord.” Who is the one who knows all the works of the Lord except the one who does them?

The same understanding should be applied here to the statement, “who knew every work of the Lord.” It does not merely say, “who knew the work of the Lord,” but adds, “who knew every work of the Lord”—that is, those who knew the Lord’s work of justice, the work of sanctification, patience, gentleness, piety, and everything that proceeds from God’s commandments and is called the Lord’s work.

But just as there is the work of the Lord, so undoubtedly there is a work opposed to it, the work of the devil. For it is certain that just as justice is the work of God, injustice is the work of the devil; and just as gentleness is the work of God, anger or fury is the work of the devil.

Those who do his work, therefore, are said to know the Lord. Nor should we pass over how he adds: “who knew the great works of the Lord that he did in Israel.”

For what are some of the Lord’s works that could be called “great” in distinction from others? I think that every work of God is indeed great, but according to the capacity of those for whom he works, when the works are compared with one another, some are called great works of the Lord and others small.

For example, he led the children of Israel out of Egypt with a strong hand and an outstretched arm; he struck Egypt with heavenly prodigies; he made a way through the sea; he gave manna to the people in the wilderness; he spoke from heaven to Moses; and he gave the written law on tablets of stone. Are these not great works of God?

But if you compare with them the fact that God so loved this world that he gave his only Son for the salvation of the world (John 3), you will find all those things small beside the greatness of this work. We too must know and believe this work, and perform the works of the Lord not carelessly but faithfully and attentively, so that we may be found in the days of Jesus Christ and in the days of his holy elders and apostles, with whom we may deserve to receive a share in the heavenly inheritance, through our Lord Jesus Christ.

### CHAPTER SEVEN

Joshua son of Nun, the servant of the Lord, died at the age of one hundred and ten; that whole generation was gathered to its fathers; and the children of Israel did evil in the sight of the Lord, served the Baals, and abandoned the Lord, the God of their fathers.

*(The same passage.)* Joshua son of Nun, servant of the Lord, died at the age of one hundred and ten, and they buried him within the boundaries of his inheritance, at Thamnath-sare, in the mountain of Ephraim, north of Mount Gaash. And that whole generation was gathered to its ancestors. Then another generation arose, who did not know the Lord or the works that he had done for Israel.

But, just as we had undertaken to refer what was being read concerning the son of Nun to our Lord Jesus Christ, so we must see how it is also fitting to say of him himself that Jesus died. I think, speaking according to the authority of Holy Scripture, that in some people Jesus lives, while in others he is dead. In Paul Jesus lives, and in Peter and in all those who can rightly say, “For I live, yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2). And again he said, “For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Phil. 1). In such people, therefore, Jesus is rightly said to live.

But in whom is Jesus dead? Without doubt, in those who, repeatedly repenting and then sinning again, are said, as it were, to insult the death of Jesus. Concerning them the Apostle writes to the Hebrews: “Crucifying again for themselves the Son of God and exposing him to public disgrace” (Heb. 6). You see, then, that among sinners Jesus is said not only to be dead, but also to be crucified and mocked by them.

But consider yourself as well. Whenever you think about greed and desire to seize what belongs to others, can you say that Christ lives in you? Or if you plot adultery, if you are driven by rage, inflamed by resentment, goaded by envy, rave in drunkenness, are lifted up by pride, or act violently with cruelty, can you say in all these things that Christ lives in you?

If, then, Christ is dead in sinners because nothing of justice, nothing of patience, nothing of truth, and none of all that Christ is, operates in them, whereas among the saints whatever is done is Christ who is said to perform it—as the Apostle also says, “I can do all things through Christ who strengthens me” (Phil. 4)—the other generation, which does not know the Lord Jesus (Matt. 15), is the generation of evil thoughts and most wicked desires that proceed from the heart. This is the generation that does not know the Lord Jesus, nor the great work that he did in Israel.

You see that sinners go so far as to forget even that great and glorious work which the Lord performed: that he was crucified for our sins and rose for our justification (Rom. 4). Therefore I believe that, fearing this forgetfulness, the Apostle Paul said to his foremost disciple Timothy: “Remember that Jesus Christ has risen from the dead” (2 Tim. 2). For he knew that forgetfulness of so great a work—that he rose from the dead—could arise if a sinful generation emerged in the heart.

And the children of Israel did evil in the sight of the Lord, served the Baals, and abandoned the Lord, the God of their ancestors, who had brought them out of the land of Egypt. They followed foreign gods, the gods of the peoples who lived around them; they worshiped them and provoked the Lord to anger, abandoning him and serving Baal and Astaroth.

This shows that those who were unbelieving and impious in the time of the Savior bowed their knees to the Baals and worshiped images. But those who believe and fulfill the works of faith did not bow their knees to the Baals. Nowhere, in fact, do the histories, or the Gospels, or any other writings report that anyone in the Savior’s time bowed the knee to images. Rather, this is said of those who were bound and, as it were, shackled by their sins.

Hence it is clear that whenever we sin and are said to be captives under the law of sin, we bow our knees to the Baals. But we were not called for this, nor did we believe for this purpose: to serve sin again and bow our knees again to the devil. Rather, we were called to bow our knees in the name of Jesus, because “in the name of Jesus every knee bows, in heaven and on earth and under the earth” (Phil. 2), and to bow our knees to the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, from whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named (Eph. 3).

But what benefit is it to me if, coming to prayer, I bend the knees of my body to God while bending the knees of my heart to the devil? If I do not stand firm against the devil’s schemes, I have bent my knees to the devil. If I do not stand steadfastly against anger, I have bent my knees to anger. Likewise, if I do not resist lust with constancy, I have bent the knees of my heart to lust. And in each thing that is opposed to God I will be seen to do the same, unless I stand firm and courageously, as did those who worshiped the Baals and abandoned the God of their ancestors, who brought them out of the land of Egypt.

Let us not suppose, therefore, that because we do not appear to worship images, these things do not also concern some among us. Whatever each person worships above all else, whatever he admires and loves beyond everything, is his god. This, finally, is what God demands of a human being before and above all things through his commandment: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your strength” (Deut. 6). He desires, as it were, to anticipate and claim for himself all the affections of the human mind, knowing that whatever someone loves with his whole heart, soul, and strength is his god.

It should be noted that another edition has this passage as follows: “And they served Baal and the Astartes.” It is commonly said that among the peoples of those regions Baal was the name for Jupiter, while Astarte was the name for Juno; the Punic language is also thought to confirm this. For the Punic people seem to call “lord” *Baal*, so that *Baal-samem* is understood to mean “lord of heaven”; among them *samem* means “heavens.” Juno, without question, is called *Astaroth* by them.

Since these languages do not differ greatly from one another, Scripture is rightly believed here to say of the children of Israel that they served Baal and the Astartes—that is, Jupiter and Junos. It should not be troubling that it does not say *Astarte*, that is, “Juno,” but uses the name in the plural, as though there were many Junos. It wished the meaning to refer to the multitude of images: each individual image of Juno was called Juno, and thus it wished as many Junos to be understood as there were images.

I think that the reason for the variation is that it wished to mention Jupiter in the singular and Juno in the plural. For the same reason, the many images could also have led to *Jupiters* being used in the plural. This—that is, the plural form *Junos*—we find in the Greek text according to the Septuagint, whereas in the Latin text it was singular. In the text that did not have the Septuagint translation but was taken from the Hebrew, we read *Astaroth*, not *Baal* but *Baalim*. If, however, these names signify something else in Hebrew and Syriac, it nevertheless remains clear that they were other gods, and false ones, whom Israel ought not to have served.

“And they worshiped,” it says, “foreign gods, the gods of the nations who were around them, and provoked the Lord to anger.” See what sins accomplish: we are said to provoke to anger the one in whom there is not only no movement of anger, but no other passible movement at all. He remains immutable in his nature and is never disturbed by the emotions of anger. I, however, through the things in which I sin, bring anger upon myself, as the Apostle says: “You yourself teach these things; according to your hardness and impenitent heart, you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of God’s righteous judgment, who will repay each according to his works” (Rom. 2).

So they provoked the Lord to anger, abandoned God, and worshiped Baal and Astarte; and the Lord’s fury was kindled against Israel, and he delivered them into the hands of plunderers. As long as someone serves God, he is not delivered into the hands of plunderers. But when he abandons God and begins to serve his own passions, it is said of him that God delivers him over to dishonorable passions. And again: “He delivered them over to a reprobate mind, to do what is unfitting.” Why? “Because,” it says, “they were filled with every kind of injustice, wickedness, fornication, greed, and all the rest” (Rom. 1).

So also here: those who served and worshiped the Baals and Astartes were delivered by God into the hands of plunderers, and they came under the power of their enemies. This is how we should understand God’s delivering those whom he delivers: not that he himself hands anyone over, but that he abandons as unworthy those who do not cultivate him in such a way as to cleanse themselves from vices and allow God willingly to dwell within them.

When he withdraws and turns away from a soul situated in uncleanness and vices, that soul is said to have been delivered over because it is found empty of God and is invaded by an evil spirit. Let us therefore watch with the utmost care and hasten to cleanse ourselves from vices and evil desires, so that we may be able to retain God within us and so that he may deign to dwell in us, finding delight in our actions, words, and thoughts.

## CHAPTER VIII  
### How the angry Lord delivered Israel into the hands of plunderers, but, when they repented, raised up judges again to free them from the hands of their destroyers

*(The same passage.)* The Lord was angry with Israel and delivered them into the hands of plunderers, who captured them and sold them to the enemies living round about. They could not resist their adversaries; wherever they wished to go, the hand of the Lord was against them, as he had spoken and sworn to them, and they were greatly afflicted.

The Lord raised up judges who would free them from the hands of their destroyers, but they would not even listen to them. They fornicated with foreign gods and worshiped them; they quickly abandoned the way on which their ancestors had walked, and, though they heard the Lord’s commandments, they did everything contrary to them, and so forth.

Another edition has it thus: “And he sold them into the hand of their enemies round about.” It is commonly asked why it says “he sold,” as though some price had been given. Yet the Psalm also says: “You sold your people without a price” (Ps. 43). And the prophet says: “You were sold for nothing, and you shall not be redeemed with silver” (Isa. 52).

Why, then, were they sold if it was for nothing and without a price, rather than given away? Perhaps it is a usage of Scripture that someone who is given away may also be called “sold.” The best sense here is found in the statements, “You were sold for nothing” and “You sold your people without a price”: those to whom you handed over the people were impious. They did not deserve to have that people handed over to them by worshiping God, so that their worship might appear as the price.

As for the statement, “You shall not be redeemed with silver,” it does not say “with a price,” but “with silver,” so that the price of redemption may be understood. Thus the Apostle Peter says: “You were not redeemed with silver and gold, but with the precious blood of an unblemished lamb” (1 Pet. 1). By “silver” the prophet signified every kind of money when he said, “You shall not be redeemed with silver,” because they were indeed to be redeemed at a price—the blood of Christ—but not at a monetary price.

When the Lord says, “I will no longer drive out from before them any of the nations that the son of Nun left and abandoned to test Israel, whether they would keep the way of the Lord and walk in it, as their ancestors kept it or not,” and when the Lord left these nations so that he would not remove them at that time and did not deliver them into the hands of Jesus, the reason is sufficiently shown why Jesus did not destroy all those nations in battle: if this had happened, there would have been no peoples among whom they could be tested.

They could have been left for their benefit if, when tested among them, they were not found reprobate. If they had been found to be what the Lord had commanded them to be, those nations would then have been removed from before them, provided they lived accordingly, and there would have been no need for them to be exercised by wars.

The Lord’s words should be understood as extending this far: “Because this nation has so greatly abandoned my covenant, which I commanded their ancestors, and they did not obey my voice, I will no longer remove from before them any man”—that is, any adversary. The remaining words belong to the writer, who explains why the Lord said that he would not remove the man from the nations that Jesus son of Nun had left.

Then, adding the reason why he had left them, he says: “And he left them to test Israel, whether they would keep the way of the Lord and walk in it, as their ancestors kept it or not.” He wishes us to understand that the ancestors who had been with Jesus kept the way of the Lord—that is, they kept it during the time when he was alive.

Earlier he had reported that another generation arose after those who had lived with Jesus, and that the transgressions which offended the Lord began with them. The nations had been left for the testing—that is, the proving—of this later generation and had not been exterminated by Jesus.

Then, lest anyone suppose that Jesus had arranged this by his own human judgment, so that those nations would be left, Scripture adds: “And the Lord left these nations, so that he would not remove them quickly, and he did not deliver them into the hands of Jesus.”

Then it continues: “These are the nations that Jesus left in order to test Israel by them—all those who had not known all the wars of Canaan—for the sake of the generations of the children of Israel, to teach them war.” The purpose, then, was their testing: they were to learn to wage war with as much devotion and obedience to God’s law as their ancestors, who had pleased the Lord God even in warfare. This does not mean that war itself is desirable, but that devotion is praiseworthy even in war.

As for what follows—“But those who were before them did not know them”—what else should be understood but the nations whom those who came before them did not know in battle, and who were left for the testing, that is, the proving, of this generation?

Then, listing them, he says: “Five satrapies of the foreigners,” which he describes more clearly in the Books of Kings. Satrapies are, as it were, small kingdoms ruled by satraps; this name was, or remains, a title of some distinction in those regions.

“And all the Canaanite,” he says, “and the Sidonian, and the Hivite dwelling in Lebanon, before Mount Hermon as far as Lebo-hamath”—for which Aquila translated “the entrance of Hamath”—“and it happened that Israel was tested among them.”

It is as though he said: “This happened so that Israel might be tested among them, to see whether they would obey the Lord’s commandments.” This was not so that God, who knows all things, including the future, might come to know it, but so that they themselves might know, and might either glory in or be convicted by their own conscience, whether they would obey the Lord’s commandments that he had given their ancestors through Moses.

Since they were thus shown to themselves not to have obeyed God among those nations that had been left for their testing—that is, their exercise and proving—God therefore said either this passage, in which the angel was openly sent and explicitly spoke, or the earlier statement: “Because this nation has so greatly abandoned my covenant, which I commanded their ancestors, and they did not obey my voice, I will no longer remove from before them any man.”

In Deuteronomy, speaking in God’s person concerning these hostile nations, it is said: “I will not drive them out in one year, lest the land become desolate and the wild beasts multiply against you. Little by little I will remove them, until you multiply, grow, and inherit the land” (Deut. 7).

The Lord could have kept this promise toward the obedient, so that the extermination of those nations would occur as the Israelite population increased, when their numbers ensured that the lands from which the adversaries were expelled would not remain desolate.

As for the statement, “Lest the wild beasts multiply there,” it is remarkable if he did not wish bestial desires and lusts to be understood metaphorically—desires that commonly arise from the sudden acquisition of earthly prosperity. For God could not have been able to exterminate human beings while being unable to deal with wild beasts, either by destroying them or, rather, by preventing them from being fed.

## CHAPTER IX  
### How, because of the evil deeds of the Israelites, the angry Lord delivered them into the hands of Chusan-Rishathaim, king of Mesopotamia, and they served him for eight years; but when they cried out again to the Lord, he raised up a savior for them and freed them through Othniel, son of Kenaz, the younger brother of Caleb

*(Chapter 3.)* The children of Israel lived among the Canaanite, Hittite, Amorite, Perizzite, Hivite, and Jebusite peoples. They took their daughters as wives, gave their own daughters to their sons, and served their gods. They did evil in the sight of the Lord and forgot their God, serving the Baals and the Astartes.

The Lord was angry with Israel and delivered them into the hand of Chusan-Rishathaim, king of Mesopotamia, and they served him for eight years.

When the children of Israel did evil in the sight of God, forgot the Lord their God, abandoned him, and served the Baals and the groves of the nations, then, storing up wrath for themselves, they were delivered by God’s just judgment into the hands of their enemies, in accordance with what the present reading has declared.

“Into the hand,” it says, “of Chusan-Rishathaim, king of Mesopotamia.” Chusan-Rishathaim is interpreted as “their humiliation.” They were therefore delivered into the hand of one who would humble them. Because they had acted impiously against the Most High in the heights of the mountains, they were consequently delivered by him into humiliation.

But do not suppose that this divine providence applied only to the ancients: that those who were impiously exalted would be handed over to be humbled, and that contrary things would be cured by a salutary medicine of opposites. Even now, for the omnipotent God’s Church, there is a similar salutary providence. Even now there is a Chusan-Rishathaim, king of Mesopotamia, to whom souls are delivered for humiliation and affliction when, rejecting Christian humility, they surrender themselves to pride and arrogance.

The vice of pride is exceedingly hateful in God’s sight, because, as Scripture says, “Pride is the beginning of departure from God” (Eccl. 10). And elsewhere Scripture says: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (1 Pet. 5).

If someone, despising the humility of Christ—who, although he was God, became human for our sake and humbled himself even to death—is lifted up and carried away toward powers and worldly dignities, and rushes toward them, not shrinking from or recoiling at the methods by which he seeks to attain them, even if those methods are contrary to faith and religion, provided only that he obtains what he desires, the result is that he does evil in the sight of the Lord.

After he has acquired the highest insignia of power and climbed to the very summits of pride, he is cast down from there and delivered to this Chusan-Rishathaim, one of the rulers of the air, just as another is delivered to Pharaoh and another to Chiram, in order to humble the one who had been excessively exalted, afflict him, and crush him until he comes to his senses and seeks the Lord. While he was established in pride and arrogance, he did not know the Lord.

Now let us see what those who are delivered over on account of sin and placed in tribulation do. Certainly they do what is written: “They cried to the Lord when they were in trouble, and he delivered them from their distresses; he brought them out of darkness and the shadow of death and broke their bonds” (Ps. 106).

But let that most dreadful odor be removed, I ask, from all this holy Church, and especially from those who minister in holy things, so that we may become, as Paul said, “the good odor of Christ” (2 Cor. 2). Otherwise the Lord may become angry, and we may provoke the Holy One of Israel to anger, and he may deliver us into the hands of Chusan-Rishathaim, so that we may learn in the tribulation of our correction the humility that we ought to have taught in the knowledge of Christ.

But observe the kindly Lord, who mingles mercy with severity and measures the punishment itself with a just and compassionate deliverance. He did not deliver the offenders over forever. Rather, he says: As long as they served the Baals, so long would they also serve Chusan-Rishathaim—that is, eight years.

Learn this also, listener, whoever you are who are conscious of some error: for as long as you know that you have gone astray, and for as long as you have sinned, humble yourself before God for that same length of time and make satisfaction to him in penitential confession.

Do not wait for Chusan-Rishathaim to humble you, with necessity unwillingly forcing repentance upon you. Instead, forestall the hands of this torturer yourself. If you correct yourself and reform yourself, God is gracious and merciful, and he restrains vengeance from the one who forestalls it by repentance (1 Cor. 2).

Let us also consider that while those who had been delivered over for their offenses continued to serve Chusan-Rishathaim and did not cry out to the Lord, no one was raised up who could save them. But when they cried to the Lord, then the Lord raised up a savior for Israel and saved them. He calls Othniel their savior; Othniel is interpreted as “the time of God for me.”

And they cried to the Lord, who raised up a savior for them and freed them—namely, Othniel, son of Kenaz, the younger brother of Caleb. The spirit of the Lord was upon him, and he judged Israel. He went out to battle, and the Lord delivered Chusan-Rishathaim, king of Syria, into his hand, and he defeated him. Then the land rested for forty years.

Through this Othniel, that earlier people was rescued from the servitude of humiliation, and peace was restored to the people, whom pride and the various crimes of the populace had formerly driven away.

But since we said that Chusan-Rishathaim the king might be understood spiritually as one of the adversaries and a prince among the powers of the air, it seems to me to follow that this Othniel, who was raised up to free the people, is likewise one of the heavenly host and archangelic ranks, sent to assist those who are heirs of salvation (Heb. 1). These are the saving angels represented in the figures of Othniel and Aoth. For, as we have often shown, we are attacked not only by hostile powers, but divine and good powers are also sent by the Lord to our aid.

Let us nevertheless see who this Othniel was, and of what family and nobility. “The son,” it says, “of Kenaz, brother of Caleb”—that praiseworthy and admirable man Caleb, who was the companion and associate of Jesus son of Nun, concerning whom we have discussed, as far as we could, what seemed appropriate in its places.

What, then, does Scripture say about this Othniel? After saying that the children of Israel cried to the Lord, it says: “The spirit of the Lord came upon Othniel, and he judged Israel.” Do you suppose there is someone among us who sends up such a strong and righteous cry to God that he is worthy to be heard, and that the people deserve to receive a judge—a judge whom the spirit of God fills, so that he can exercise right judgment?

For this reason the book itself is called *Judges*, and the judges who judged the people are described in it. Just as the other books are called *Kings* or *Kingdoms*, in which each king is described according to how he ruled and what he did, so in this little book the deeds of the judges are related. It records not only whether something was rightly and usefully done by them, but also whether something blameworthy was committed.

If you ask why both kinds of deeds were recorded, the answer is this: the present leaders or judges of the Church, observing what was praiseworthy in those men, should follow the examples of their predecessors; and if anything in them is condemned, the present leaders should take care to avoid and shun it.

Great, therefore, is the praise reported of this first judge, Othniel: that the spirit of God came upon him, and that through the spirit of God he judged Israel. I do not well remember another concerning whom this was said.

There are, then, even today very many judges of all the churches under heaven, to whom judgment has been entrusted not only over deeds but also over souls. Yet I do not know whether there is any such judge of the Church whom God considers worthy to fill with his spirit, so that, just as this Othniel was adorned by the testimony of Scripture, those whom we desire to be like him may likewise deserve God’s testimony.

He says, then: “The spirit of the Lord came upon him, and he judged Israel; he went out to war, and the Lord delivered Chusan-Rishathaim the king into his hand.” Why? Because the spirit of the Lord was in him, and his hand was strengthened against Chusan-Rishathaim.

After this he says that the land rested under that judge for forty years. Do you see how abundant divine mercy is? The children of Israel served for eight years because of the sins of many; because of the righteousness of one, they continued in peace for forty years.

Scripture testifies that the Promised Land rested from wars for forty years under Othniel the judge—roughly as long as the beginnings of the Roman Empire were able to remain at peace under King Numa Pompilius alone.

But what is said afterward? “And Othniel son of Kenaz died.” I see a dangerous matter here. Othniel died. Why? Because the people were no longer worthy to have such a judge.

Finally, in what follows it says of his death: “And the children of Israel again added to their evil deeds in the sight of the Lord.”

## CHAPTER X  
### How the Lord delivered sinful Israel into the hand of Eglon, king of Moab, but again mercifully freed them through Aod, son of Hierte, who was ambidextrous and killed Eglon

*(The same passage.)* The Lord strengthened Eglon, king of Moab, against Israel.

Consider that, because they were no longer worthy to have such a leader, the good judge was taken away from them. And because they did evil in the sight of the Lord, a most wicked enemy, Eglon king of Moab, was raised up against them.

You see that our sins provide strength to our enemies. When we do evil in the sight of the Lord and sin, our adversaries are turned against us by the Lord, and strength is given to hostile powers.

Whether you examine this according to the literal sense, you will find it so: they would not prevail otherwise. Or if you consider it in relation to spiritual beings, hostile powers likewise would not prevail against us, nor would the devil himself be able to prevail in anything against us, unless we supplied him with strength from our vices. He would be very weak against us unless we made him strong through sinning and unless, through our sins, he found a place to enter and rule within us.

Therefore the Apostle also warns us beforehand, saying: “Do not give place to the devil” (Eph. 4). So here too we read that, after the children of Israel did evil in the sight of the Lord, they gave place to the devil.

For the Lord strengthened Eglon king of Moab and joined to him all the children of Ammon and Amalek. Not only was he himself strengthened by the sins of the children of Israel, it says, but wicked allies from the children of Ammon and Amalek were also joined to him, so that together with him they might attack Israel.

“And the children of Israel served Eglon king of Moab for fifteen years.” Observe that divine Scripture also indicates the measures of punishment: there it says eight years, and here fifteen. It is certain that the periods of correction are determined according to the measure of sin and the duration of our way of life.

These fifteen years of servitude passed, and it is not reported that they cried to the Lord or turned away from their wickedness. But after fifteen years it is again said that the children of Israel cried to the Lord, and the Lord God raised up for them a savior, Aod son of Gera, son of Jemini, a man ambidextrous.

See what kind of man this is who is raised up to save Israel. He has nothing left-handed in himself, but has two right hands; this is what “ambidextrous” means. He is truly a worthy leader of the people and judge of the Church: he does nothing left-handed, and his left hand does not know what his right hand does. He is right-handed in both respects—right-handed in faith and right-handed in actions. He has nothing of those who are placed on the left, to whom it is said: “Depart from me, workers of iniquity; I do not know you” (Matt. 7), and, “Go into the eternal fire that God prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25).

I think we may confidently understand that, in the spiritual sense, all the saints are also called ambidextrous. Conversely, the devil and his rulers may, if the expression is permitted, be called “left-handed on both sides.” Everything they do is left-handed, everything is perverse, and everything is assigned to the eternal fire together with those who are on the left.

But let us see what this ambidextrous judge does. They sent gifts through him to Eglon king of Moab. He had made for himself a double-edged sword, with a handle in the middle, a handspan long; and he girded himself with it beneath his cloak on his right thigh, and so forth.

You see that everything Aod carries is right-handed. He is right-handed in his hands and right-handed in his feet. He carries the sword on his right thigh so that he may approach the king of Moab and kill him.

We said earlier that those whom God is said to raise up as saviors or judges for the salvation of the people and the liberation of the children of Israel bear the image of certain rulers from the heavenly army and of the powers above, which God sends to assist those who cry to him with their whole heart and, through conversion and repentance, incline divine mercy toward themselves.

But lest this seem presumptuous to our hearers, we ought to confirm it from the authority of Scripture. It is written in Exodus that our ancestors, the children of Israel, after serving for a long time under the Egyptians and the most savage king Pharaoh in making clay and bricks, cried to the Lord. The Lord himself said: “The cry of the children of Israel has come up to me” (Exod. 12). He visibly led them out by sending Moses.

Scripture also reports that a destroying angel was sent to devastate all the firstborn of Egypt, while touching none of the Israelites. Thus it is made clear that a heavenly power was at work: after devastating and overthrowing the Egyptians, it brought the children of Israel out from the yoke of servitude.

Similarly, the histories report that under Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians, an angel of the Lord was sent. In a single night he struck down and killed one hundred and eighty-five thousand enemies, and freed both the city from the siege and the people from the imminent destruction (2 Kings 19).

So now also we must recognize the same sequence. Whenever we are handed over into captivity because of our sins, let us cry to the Lord—not with the mouth, but with the mind—so that the sorrow of the heart may draw a fountain of tears from the eyes, like the one who said: “Every night I wash my bed; I water my couch with my tears” (Ps. 6).

If we turn away from evil in such a way that we do not again touch evil; if we cease from pride in such a way that we think nothing proud or arrogant; then the Lord also sends us his heavenly power, through which we are freed from the yoke of demonic servitude.

That power does everything on our behalf with a right hand and for our prosperity. It makes us abandon the left-hand path that leads to destruction and recalls us to the true way—the one who says, “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14), Christ Jesus our Lord.

It may be asked whether Aod the judge lied when he killed Eglon king of Moab. When he was alone and lying in wait for him in order to strike him, he said to him: “I have a secret word for you, O king,” so that Eglon would send away all those who were with him. When this had been done, Aod again said: “I have a word of God for you, O king.”

But this need not be a lie, since Scripture commonly calls even an event a “word,” and in truth that is what it was. When he said “a word of God,” this should be understood to mean that God had commanded him to do it, since God had raised him up as a savior for his people, and such things rightly had to be done by divine direction in those times.

It is also reasonably asked how, according to the Septuagint, King Eglon could have been extremely thin and how fat could have enclosed the wound when he was struck. We should understand this as an expression in which the opposite is meant, just as a grove is called a *lucus* although it has no light, and “to abound” is said where there is none, and “he blessed the king” is used instead of “he cursed,” as is written in the Book of Kings concerning Naboth.

For in the translation that is not according to the Septuagint but is from the Hebrew, we find: “Now Eglon was exceedingly fat.”

But Aoth, having carefully closed the doors of the upper room and secured them with a bolt, went out through the rear door. The king’s servants entered and saw the doors of the upper room closed, and so forth. It may be puzzling how Eglon’s servants opened the doors with a key, since Aoth had not locked them with a key; or, if he had locked them with a key, how he did not take it away with him, so that they could not open them with a key. Therefore either another key was brought, or the kind of fastening was such that it could be closed without a key but could not be opened without one (3 Kings 13). For there are certain things of this sort, such as those called *veruclata* (barred fastenings).

But let us see how Aoth, whose name means “praise,” brought his own principality to an end. History has taught us, from what is written about King Eglon, how this very wise Aoth, employing a certain artifice—or, so to speak, a crafty but praiseworthy deception—killed the tyrant Eglon, whose name means “rolled” or “a wheel.” Therefore the judges of our people ought to be such as this Aoth, whose name means “praise,” so that they may cut off and destroy all the rolling movements and wheelings of an evil path, and kill the king of the Midianites. The Midianites, moreover, are interpreted as “flows” or “outpouring.”

Who, then, is the prince or leader of this flowing and dissolute nation—who can he be understood to be other than the discourse of that philosophy which judges pleasure to be the highest good? Let the evangelical word, which is compared with a sword, kill and destroy him; and let the prophetic word itself be enclosed by the discussions of the two-edged teacher in their belly and deepest inward parts, so that, enclosing them with the assertion of truth, it may extinguish every sense of perverse doctrine and gross understanding that exalts and raises itself against the spiritual knowledge of Christ. In this way, fighting in the word of God, let every judge of the Church become an Aoth who is himself praiseworthy, of whom the Lord says: “Well done, good and faithful servant; because you have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things” (Matt. 25).

## CHAPTER XI. On Samgar son of Anath, who struck down six hundred men of the Philistines with a plowshare and defended Israel

(IBID.) “And Moab was humbled on that day under the hand of Israel, and the land rested for eighty years.” Under the judge Aoth, Israel had peace in the promised land for eighty years—twice the period that was memorable among the Romans under King Pompilius.

After him came Samgar son of Anath, who struck down six hundred men of the Philistines with a plowshare, and he too defended Israel.

The Septuagint has: “And after him Samgar son of Anath arose, and struck down the foreigners, six hundred men, apart from the calves of cattle, and he saved Israel.”

How this Samgar fought for Israel after Aoth and is said to have saved Israel may be questioned. For they had not again been taken captive or bound beneath the yoke of slavery. But “he saved” should be understood as meaning not that an enemy had inflicted harm, but that he was not permitted to inflict it; for we must believe that the enemy began the attack and was driven back by this man’s victory.

But what the addition “apart from the calves of cattle” means is obscure. Perhaps he also inflicted slaughter upon cattle while fighting, and thus it was said that he killed six hundred men, apart from what he did among the cattle that were killed. But why did he mention calves? Is it perhaps a customary Greek expression to call even fully grown animals “calves”? For people in Egypt are reportedly accustomed to speak in this way, just as among us chickens are called “young ones” regardless of the age of the hens.

The translation from the Hebrew does not have “apart from the calves of cattle,” as does the version according to the Septuagint; but the Hebrew version does have “six hundred men killed with a plowshare,” which this version does not have.

Let us now consider what the beginning of *Samegach* is like. *Samegach* is interpreted as “a sojourner there.” It is true that all who are people of God are sojourners in this world and inhabitants of the earth, as was also the one who said: “For I am a sojourner with you on the earth, and a pilgrim, like all my fathers” (Ps. 38; Ps. 118).

Therefore the Holy Spirit calls this Samegach a resident there—that is, here—for what is “there” to the Holy Spirit who is in heaven is “here” to us.

What, then, is said of Samegach? “He struck down,” it says, “six hundred Philistines with the plow-handle and plowshare.” I see another kind of praise in Samegach. This man fights with a plow, whereas Aoth fought with a sword. He conquers with a plow; nevertheless, he too overcomes and casts down the Philistines.

It may therefore happen that a judge of the Church does not always draw the sword—that is, does not always employ the authority of the word and the sharpness of correction—but sometimes also imitates a farmer. As though plowing the soil of the soul and repeatedly cutting into it with gentle admonition, he prepares it to receive seeds.

Thus the Philistines too will be killed when we do not use arguments and sharpness against our opponents, but drive vices and sins from the souls of our hearers by rustic and simple admonition.

And you yourself, O hearer, be a farmer of your own soul. Use the plow that Samegach uses. But when you have put your hand to the plow, do not look back—that is, after you have taken up your cross and followed Christ; after you have renounced the world and the things that are in the world, do not look back; do not seek again what, for Christ’s sake, you had counted as dung.

For if you always keep your hand upon this plow, so that you can confidently say: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Gal. 6), then, when you say this to yourself, “Ten thousand shall fall at your right hand, and a thousand at your left, but they shall not come near you” (Ps. 90).

Nor does it seem to me an idle statement that Samegach is said to have struck down six hundred Philistines. Why was it necessary to specify the number, unless perhaps by that very number he more clearly indicated what we discussed above? For the number six, multiplied until it reaches six hundred, represents this world, which is said to have been completed in six days. Thus the one to whom the world has been crucified through Christ’s cross is said to have struck down six hundred men with a plow.

And the children of Israel again did evil in the sight of the Lord after the death of Aoth, and the Lord delivered them into the hand of Jabin, king of Canaan, who reigned in Asor. He had as commander of his army a man named Sisara. He himself lived in Aroseth of the nations. And the children of Israel cried to the Lord; for he had nine hundred iron chariots, and for twenty years he had severely oppressed them.

“And the children of Israel,” he says, “continued to do evil in the sight of the Lord, and Aoth died.” In these words that principle is preserved which we pointed out above: the good leader of the people dies because of the people’s sins. For when they have become unworthy and have done evil in the sight of the Lord, the man of God is taken away from them.

But perhaps our people will say: “When the Church of God is without a judge, even if the former has died, another is appointed.” We may perhaps say something boldly, yet we are saying what is written. The ruler of the people and judge of the Church is not always given by God’s decision; rather, he is given according to what our merits demand. If our actions are evil and we do evil in the sight of God, rulers are given to us according to our own heart. I will prove this to you from the Scriptures.

Listen, then, to what the Lord says: “They made themselves a king, but not by me; and a prince, but not according to my counsel.” This appears to have been said about that Saul whom the Lord himself had chosen and commanded to become king. But because he had been chosen not according to God’s will but according to the merit of the sinful people, the Lord denies that he had established him with his own will or counsel.

Let us therefore understand that something similar happens in the Churches: according to the merits of the people, either a ruler powerful in word and deed is granted by God to the Church, or, if the people do evil in the sight of the Lord, such a judge of the Church is given that the people suffer hunger and thirst under him—not hunger for bread or thirst for water, but hunger for hearing the word of the Lord (Rom. 8).

Let us therefore act and pray in such a way that divine indignation may never condemn us to hunger and thirst for the word; that one who instructs us by word and deed, who offers himself to the people as a perfect example in conduct and integrity, in patience and gentleness, may never be taken away from us.

For if we do evil in the sight of the Lord—that is, if we act wickedly, if we do our own will rather than God’s—then Aoth dies, Samegach is taken away, our praise is darkened, and we are delivered into the hands of Jabin, king of Canaan.

Jabin is interpreted as “sense” or “prudence.” Therefore, if we do not approve of having God in our knowledge, the Lord gives us over to a debased mind, “filled,” he says, “with all unrighteousness, wickedness, fornication, greed; full of envy, murder, strife, deceit, whispering, slander, hateful to God, insolent, arrogant, boastful, disobedient to parents, foolish, faithless, heartless, merciless” (Rom. 1).

You see who they are and what kind of people are handed over to a debased mind—those who are handed over to Jabin, the prince of the Canaanites.

“And the prince,” he says, “of Jabin’s army was Sisara, and he lived in Aroseth of the nations, and he had nine hundred iron chariots. And the children of Israel cried to the Lord.”

Here too the same principle that we identified above is observed: the children of Israel do not know how to cry to the Lord until they have been delivered into the hands of Jabin, or until they have been afflicted by Sisara, the commander of his army, who, it says, had nine hundred iron chariots with which the stiff-necked people would be afflicted.

Sisara is interpreted as “vision of a horse.” He is an animal rather than a spiritual being: he sees only what belongs to the animal nature, and that is his vision and his constant perspective. Therefore the animal person, the one who is according to the flesh, always persecutes the one who is according to the spirit (Gal. 4), until the spiritual person understands and examines all things and recognizes from whom help must be sought.

Then, when the soul has cried to the Lord, prophecy is raised up for it, represented by Debbora, and according to the grace and understanding of prophecy the people of the Church are governed—or the understanding of each person’s mind and soul is now directed.

## CHAPTER XII. On Debbora and Barach, who struck down Jabin, king of the Canaanites, and his commander Sisara

(CHAPTER 4.) “Now Debbora, a prophetess, the wife of Laphidoth, judged the people at that time. She sat beneath the palm tree that was called by her name, between Rama and Bethel, on Mount Ephraim. And the children of Israel went up to her for every judgment.

“She sent and summoned Barach son of Abinoem from Cades of Nepthali and said to him: ‘The Lord God of Israel has commanded you: Go, descend, and lead an army to Mount Tabor. Take with you ten thousand fighting men from the children of Nepthali and from the children of Zabulon. I will bring Sisara, commander of Jabin’s army, his chariots, and all his multitude to you at the brook Kishon, and I will deliver them into your hand.’

“And Barach said to her: ‘If you come with me, I will go; if you do not wish to come, I will not proceed.’ She said to him: ‘I will certainly go with you, but in this undertaking victory will not be credited to you, because Sisara will be delivered into the hand of a woman.’”

The apostle Paul’s statement is certainly true: “Every Scripture inspired by God is profitable for teaching, for reproof, for instruction, and for discipline in righteousness” (2 Tim. 3). What, then, does this Scripture contain—which we unquestionably confess to be divinely inspired—that benefits us for teaching, reproof, discipline, and righteousness?

What benefit is gained if we read only what has been recited: “Debbora,” it says, “a woman, a prophetess, the wife of Laphidoth, judged Israel at that time”? And again: “Debbora sat beneath the palm tree between Rama and Bethel, on Mount Ephraim, and the children of Israel went up to her to be judged.”

What instruction, teaching, or righteousness do the things that follow provide us—whether concerning Barach, Jael, or even Sisara, Jabin’s military commander? Let us therefore see whether through these events we may perhaps be taught something worthy, as also from the other Scriptures, about deeper and more hidden mysteries.

First, although very many male judges are reported to have existed in Israel, of none of them is it said that he was a prophet, except of Debbora, a woman. Even the opening words of this passage provide no small consolation to the female sex and encourage women not to despair because of the weakness of their sex, but to understand and believe that purity of mind, not difference of sex, merits this grace.

But let us see what hidden mystery of inner understanding breathes through the passage. Debbora is interpreted as “bee” or “speech.” We also said above that Debbora should be understood as a figure of prophecy, which is represented by the bee. For it is certain that all prophecy produces honeycombs of sweet heavenly teaching and the sweet honeys of divine speech. Hence David also sang: “How sweet are your words to my palate, more than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth” (Ps. 118). And elsewhere he says that the judgments of God are more precious than gold and very costly stones, and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb (Ps. 18).

Let us also consider where the prophetess is said to sit and where her place is described as being: “Beneath the palm tree,” it says, “between Rama and Bethel.” Prophecy has its seat beneath the palm tree, because David says: “The righteous shall flourish like the palm tree” (Ps. 91). Through its instructions, prophecy leads the one whom it has educated to the palm of the heavenly calling of God in Christ Jesus our Lord.

She is said to sit between Rama and Bethel. Rama is interpreted as “exalted,” while Bethel means “house of God.” See in what places prophecy is said to sit: between the exalted place and the house of God. Nothing lowly, nothing cast down, nothing vile can be found in the seat of prophecy.

Solomon likewise, when describing the seat of wisdom, says that she either stands at the gates of cities, dwells in the fortifications of the walls, or acts freely in the high towers (Prov. 8–9). In this way, then, the prophecy now represented by Debbora is said to dwell between the house of God and the exalted places. For it does not teach us to seek the things that are on earth, but those that are in heaven and on high, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God (Col. 3). Prophecy urges us to ascend there; there it strives to set its disciples.

“First of all,” it says, “she sent and summoned Barach to herself.” Barach is interpreted as “flashing” or “lightning.” A flash has light, but not a lasting light: it shines briefly and then ceases.

This Barach therefore seems to me to represent the former people, who were first called through prophecy and invited to hear the words of God and receive the gifts of the divine law. They did shine, and for a short time flashed in the splendor of the law, but they did not remain long and could not retain a continuous radiance of light.

When Debbora—that is, prophecy—said to Barach: “The Lord God of Israel has commanded you, and you are to ascend Mount Tabor and take ten thousand men,” and the other things that are written, let us see what Barach replied in the person of the people to prophecy.

“‘I will not ascend,’ he says, ‘unless you also ascend with me, because I do not know the day on which the Lord will send his angel with me.’”

You see how prophecy brought the words of God to those former people and told them that they had been commanded to ascend the mountain. But they make excuses and say: “I will not ascend unless you ascend with me.” Their excuse is true, but their promise is false. It is certain that they did not ascend the mountain of God; but their promise that they would ascend with prophecy is false. For they did not follow prophecy in believing in the one of whom all prophecy was written beforehand: Christ.

Therefore Debbora says to him: “I will go with you; nevertheless, know that you will not have the primacy on the path that you are taking, but the Lord will deliver Sisara into the hand of a woman.”

She clearly shows that primacy will not remain with that people, nor will the palm of victory remain with them; rather, Sisara is delivered into the hands of a woman named Jael.

It is described that, when Barach pursued Sisara, commander of the Philistines, according to the instruction of Debbora—that is, of prophecy—he himself could not capture him. But a foreign woman named Jael encountered Sisara as he fled. This woman had previously made a covenant of friendship with him. When he turned aside to her in order to hide, he asked her for water to drink, but she gave him milk.

After she had placed him at her sides and covered him with skins, she drove a stake through his cheekbones or jaws with a hammer. Then, meeting Barach as he pursued him, she showed him Sisara already dead and prostrate.

What mystery, then, does this entire narrative reveal to us? Jael, this foreign woman of whom prophecy said that victory would be in the hand of a woman, represents the Church, which has been gathered from the foreign nations.

Jael is interpreted as “ascent,” because in truth there is no other ascent by which one ascends to heaven except through the Church, by means of the manifold wisdom of God. She, therefore, while ascending from bodily things to spiritual things and from earthly things to heavenly things, kills Sisara.

We have already said above that Sisara represents carnal vices and the animal or earthly person. *Choikos* (Greek: χοϊκός) means “earthly” or “made of dust.” For Sisara is interpreted as “vision of a horse,” concerning whom Scripture says: “Do not become like a horse or a mule, which have no understanding” (Ps. 31).

She kills him with a tent peg—that is, she casts him down by the sharpness and power of the wood of the cross. And it is not without cause that she is described as having pierced his cheeks with the peg. That mouth which spoke from carnal considerations, and that teaching which preferred the glory of the flesh and persuaded the wise men of the world that one ought to live in pleasures and indulgence, that mouth, I say, is fastened and pierced with the wood of the cross.

For the way of pleasure that philosophy had proclaimed broad and spacious, Christ has shown us to be the narrow and constricted way of salvation.

Thus Jael, the Church, handed over the leader of vices, Sisara, covered with skins—that is, lulled to sleep through the mortification of the members—to eternal sleep.

Yet afterward Jael, the Church, also encounters Barach, the former people, as he pursues Sisara. Israel pursued the law of righteousness, but did not attain to the law. The Church therefore meets even him and shows him her work; she shows him the victory brought to completion and invites him into fellowship with the prostrate enemy.

For the apostle’s statement is true: “When the fullness of the nations has entered, then all Israel will be saved” (Rom. 11).

Therefore primacy is indeed in the hand of the foreign woman, but Barach is not excluded from a share in glory. He began first, but he reached the goal last. Indeed, while he arrives, the foreign Jael in a certain sense seizes the passing victory.

The same pattern appeared earlier in Esau and Jacob, the brothers (Gen. 27). While Esau pursued the things of the wilderness and lingered in the forests, Jacob, coming before him and likewise presenting to his father the food prepared by his mother’s counsel, received the primacy of the blessing.

So also in the Gospel, when the Lord was going to raise the ruler’s daughter, the woman who suffered from a flow of blood came before him and, through her faithful touch, obtained healing first.

If diligent hearers also seem to seek some meaning in the fact that Jael is said to have given him milk to drink when he had asked for water, let us see whether something of a mystical or allegorical character may perhaps be shown from this as well.

In the holy Scriptures, milk is said to be the food of the first moral instruction, which is delivered to beginners as to little children. For one must not immediately give beginners the deep and more secret mysteries; rather, correction of conduct, amendment of discipline, religious behavior, and the first elements of simple faith are given to them.

This is the milk of the Church; these are the first lessons of her little beginners. To those who possess a good intention of making progress, this food gives life and salvation. But to those who prefer contrary things, whose hearts are set on luxury, lust, greed, and every form of impiety, such teaching brings death and destruction.

Thus it happens that the same foods by which the good are nourished suffocate the wicked, and where there is life for the godly, there is death for the ungodly.

Finally, to make what we are saying clearer by an example: wine benefits healthy people who are in sound condition and, as Scripture says, gladdens the heart of a healthy person; but if feverish people drink it, it immediately brings them harm and destruction. Thus the same thing, taken in different ways, gives life to one person and death to another.

So too we should understand that Sisara, this animal person and leader of vices, was destroyed through the teaching of the Church, which he did not receive in faith.

Let every soul also strive to lull and extinguish within itself this Sisara through evangelical and apostolic milk. For if someone, having been instructed by these teachings, puts to death his members that are upon the earth—greed, fornication, and the other things that the holy Apostle lists (Col. 3)—he will be seen to have killed Sisara within himself. Thus what is fulfilled in the person of the Church is also shown to be fulfilled by each person in his own soul.

Therefore, since, as we have said, Sisara was indeed pursued by the former people but was killed by this woman, the Church of the nations, and the palm of victory was given into her hand, at the consummation of all things—that is, at the end of the world—a song will also be sung to the Lord through Debbora.

In that song primacy will indeed be given to Jael, the Church of the nations, yet praise of Barach will not be silenced. Rather, one reward of victory will be given both to the first and to the last.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the mystical song that Debbora and Barach son of Abinoem sang to the Lord after the victory

(CHAPTER 5.) “And Debbora and Barach son of Abinoem sang on that day, saying: ‘You who freely offered your lives from Israel to danger, bless the Lord.’”

Sisara, with his army and iron chariots by which he attacked the people of God, has been overcome. Prophecy foretold through Debbora that this would happen; and after victory had been given into the hand of a woman, Debbora is recorded as having sung this song as though it were praise of her victory.

But if we remember what was said above according to the mystical form—what Debbora represents, what Barach represents, what image is held by Jael, the woman who alone cast down the adversary of God’s people, and what image is represented by Sisara himself, who was overthrown by a foreign woman through the power of wood—we understand that all these things are mysteries to be fulfilled in the last times and at the end of the world through the Church.

This song is described as her victory hymn, that is, her praise after victory: the song of that time when the last enemy, death, will be destroyed. Then Debbora will rejoice—that is, the glory of prophecy will be illuminated—because what she foretold has been fulfilled.

Then Jael, that is, the Church, will overcome the common enemy of all. After the fullness of the nations has entered, then Barach, that is, the remnant of Israel, will be saved and received into fellowship with the victory (Rom. 11).

Then, if we are worthy, we too shall sing this song, filled with mystical and prophetic mysteries. But let us see what Debbora and Barach say at the beginning of this spiritual song.

“‘You who freely offered your lives from Israel to danger,’ they say, ‘bless the Lord.’”

Who are these who freely offered their lives to danger, except the apostles, prophets, and martyrs, as well as the other righteous, who prepared their lives for trial on account of the service of God and patiently endured the adversities of this world?

All the saints and elect freely offer their lives to danger when they devotedly accept confession of Christ’s name and resolve to persevere courageously in the true religion. They surrender their lives to danger because, despising their persecutor, they do not fear being united through faith with the one whom they understand the world to persecute with the greatest hatred.

Hence Truth itself says to the disciples in the Gospel: “If the world hates you, know that it hated me before you” (John 15). And again: “You will be hated by all because of my name” (Luke 21). Hence Paul says: “All who wish to live piously in Christ suffer persecution” (2 Tim. 3).

They are therefore urged to bless the Lord because, when they overcome their enemies after the final death has been destroyed, they will receive an eternal reward and sing everlasting praises to the Lord in heaven with the holy angels forever.

“Hear, kings; receive it with your ears, princes.”

He calls those who are summoned to hear the word of God “kings.” Rejoice, O people of God, as you hear the insignia of your nobility. You are called to hear the word of God, and you are called as a king, not as common people.

For it has been said to you: “A royal and priestly race, a people for acquisition” (1 Pet. 2). Since you are kings, it is rightly said that our king, Christ the Lord, is “King of kings and Lord of lords.”

But just as you exalt yourselves in the title of your nobility, so you must learn what each of you must do in order to become a king. I will define it for you briefly.

Christ’s reign in you makes you king over all; for “king” is derived from ruling.
