Therefore, if the mind rules in you and the body obeys; if you bring the desires of the flesh beneath the yoke of your authority; if you restrain the nations of vices with the tighter reins of sobriety, then you are rightly called a king, since you have learned to rule yourself rightly.

When you have become such a person, you will rightly be summoned as a king to hear the divine words.

But what follows indicates something more bodily: “Receive it with your ears, all you satraps.” Just as a satrap is inferior to a king, so “receiving with the ears” seems inferior to “hearing.” Hearing belongs to the inner person, as the Lord also said: “Let the one who has ears for hearing hear” (Matt. 15). But receiving with the ears belongs to outward and bodily hearing.

Therefore those who ought to hear are called kings, while those who receive with their ears are called satraps.

“I am, I am she who will sing to the Lord; I will sing praises to the Lord, the God of Israel.”

Blessed are those who can sing a song to the Lord. The voice of the righteous therefore says here: “I will sing to the Lord, and I will sing praises to the God of Israel.”

Who, do you think, has such a musical voice and such a pure spirit and sincere mind that his song can delight the divine hearing? Surely the one who has no hoarse sound of sin within him, who carries no offense on his tongue and no heaviness in his spirit. He can rightly say: “I will sing to the Lord; I will sing praises to the God of Israel.”

He sings to the Lord who praises him worthily through the devotion of his heart and the service of his mouth. He sings praises who honors him by good works.

Let us therefore see how the song itself begins.

“Lord, when you went out from Seir and passed through the regions of Edom, the earth was shaken; the heavens and the clouds poured down water; the mountains flowed before the Lord, and Sinai before the Lord God of Israel.”

The Lord went out from Seir because he was born according to the flesh from the Jewish people, a people exceedingly harsh with the thorns of wickedness and unbelief.

He passed through the regions of Edom when he grew there through the stages of youth and spread the light of faith everywhere by preaching the Gospel. Finally, coming to the cross, he wonderfully fulfilled the mystery of our redemption through his passion and resurrection.

The name Edom, or Esau, as also Seir, designates the same Jewish people. For Seir is interpreted as “hairy” or “rough”; Esau as “empty” or “vain”; and Edom as “red” or “ruddy.”

Because that people followed the delights of carnal desires and the vanity of the world, it lost the glory of its primacy as though over a dish of lentils, and, supplanted by the faith of the younger people, it lost the grace of blessing that had been promised to it.

Therefore the Lord migrated through his preachers from the harsh and ungrateful Jewish people to the salvation of the nations.

But let us hear what happened then.

“The earth,” it says, “was shaken”—that is, the hearts of carnal people were shaken with fear.

“The heavens and the clouds poured down water,” when the apostles and prophets interpreted the will of God in sacred words.

“The mountains flowed before the Lord,” when the pride of persecutors and of the powerful of this world was destroyed.

“And Sinai before the Lord God of Israel.” Through Sinai, where Moses received the law from the Lord, the Jewish people, to whom that law was given, is designated.

But just as the mountains flowed before the Lord, so also Sinai flowed before the Lord God of Israel, because neither the arrogance of the Jews nor that of the nations could in any way resist the Lord’s presence. Their pride and arrogance were overcome and cast down by the power of the highest virtue, so that many of them, converted to repentance for their sins and washed by the grace of baptism, were changed from persecutors into evangelists.

Thus Saul, the fiercest persecutor among the Jews, became the apostle Paul. Many from the nations were likewise transformed into preachers of the Gospel, such as Dionysius the Areopagite, Trophimus of Ephesus, Gaius, and Aristarchus, Paul’s Macedonian companions, along with the others who adhered to the apostles’ discipleship (Acts 9).

“In the days of Samgar son of Anath, in the days of Jael, the paths rested; and those who entered upon them walked by winding byways.”

We said above that Samgar, whose name is interpreted as “sojourner” or “settler,” signifies the preacher of the divine word, who, relying on the Lord’s plow, cultivates the hearts of his hearers through the Gospel.

Jael, the foreign woman, whose name is interpreted as “ascent” or “rest of God,” signifies the Church, in which one truly ascends to the kingdom of heaven. For there the way to eternal life is opened to all who rightly believe; and there is God’s rest, where his will is fulfilled daily.

Hence the divine voice says through the prophet: “Upon whom will my spirit rest, except upon the humble and quiet person who trembles at my words?” (Isa. 66).

In the days of these two, therefore, the paths rested, because through divine grace the gifts of peace were granted to the faithful.

And those who entered upon them walked by winding byways, when persecutors of Christians and heretics—who attempted to enter the Church not with devotion to the faith but by the craft of wickedness—were scattered by divine judgment. Because they neglected to walk in the path of peace, they wandered through the twists and turns of error.

This did not mean that the most just mercy of the Godhead caused them to err, but that by a just judgment, because of their sins, he permitted them to fall into error.

Hence Solomon says: “Whoever walks uprightly will be safe, but whoever walks in crooked ways will fall at once” (Prov. 10). And again: “The man who wanders from the way of instruction will dwell in the assembly of giants” (Prov. 21).

For this reason the Psalmist also says: “The Lord gave them over to the desires of their heart, and they went according to their own wills” (Ps. 80). And elsewhere it is written: “Woe to the sinner who enters the earth by two paths” (Sir. 2).

“The strong men in Israel ceased, and they rested until Debbora, a mother in Israel, arose.”

Who are these strong men who ceased in Israel except the prophets and righteous men who, in their time, held primacy among God’s people, guiding them by their counsels and assisting them with their consolations?

But they rested—that is, they received the sleep of death—and therefore ceased, because, with death intervening, they could not remain. Thus, as the practice of the old law gradually declined, the one whom Debbora the mother—that is, true prophecy—foretold as future might already come: the one who himself would give the blessing, who gave the law, who was the seal of the law and of all the prophets.

Hence Truth itself says in the Gospel: “The law and the prophets were until John” (Matt. 11). Paul likewise says: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law” (Gal. 4). And again: “Christ,” he says, “is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. 10).

New battles the Lord chose. What are these new battles, if not the struggles of virtues against sins and vices? These, indeed, the Lord chose, because he approves them. Hence Paul says: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, against the world-rulers of these darknesses, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Eph. VI). And again: “I,” he says, “run not as though toward an uncertainty; I fight not as one striking the air. Rather, I chastise my body and bring it into subjection, lest perhaps, after preaching to others, I myself should be rejected” (I Cor. IX).

Thus they are new battles in which evil is not repaid with evil, but evil is overcome through good; in which the soldier of Christ fights patiently against his enemies with the shield of faith, the breastplate of righteousness, the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit (Rom. XII; Eph. VI). The king of this warfare is Christ, who says to his disciples: “By your patience you will possess your souls” (Luke XXI); and he grants his servants triumph and victory. Hence it follows: “He himself overturned the gates of the enemies.” What, then, are the gates of the enemies, if not the gates of death—the gates of hell—namely, wicked men and heretics, through whom evil spirits wage war against Christ’s servants? But he will overturn these gates when he exposes, crushes, and scatters their schemes, threats, and deceits, and when through his humble servants he despises and reduces to nothing the things that seemed great and strong to the proud.

“The shield and spear did not appear among the forty thousand of Israel.” He places the shield and spear for earthly weapons, in which carnal people and the people of this age trust. But these are unnecessary for the spiritual. Earthly armor has no place in spiritual camps; therefore it does not appear there, because it is not found there, where forty thousand Israelites fight against spiritual enemies. The number forty, consisting of ten multiplied four times, appropriately suits Christ’s soldiers—that is, true Israelites, in whom there is no deceit—who, observing the precepts of the Decalogue according to evangelical teaching, defend and guard the camp of the Church. Striving in this way throughout the whole period of the present life, until the consummation of the age, they desire to obtain the inheritance of the heavenly homeland by a blessed triumph.

Here it should be noted that the prophet Isaiah once described the times of this struggle, saying: “From Zion the law will go forth, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem; and he will judge the nations and rebuke many peoples. They will beat their swords into plowshares and their spears into pruning hooks. Nation will not lift up sword against nation, nor will they train any longer for battle, O house of Jacob. Come, let us walk in the light of the Lord” (Isa. II). This occurs when, as truth shines forth, every hardness of our heart is broken by the plowshare of Christ in the New Testament, and the thorns of vices are uprooted, so that the seed of God’s word may grow into crops. Thereafter we shall eat the fruit of the labor of our hands, when they come rejoicing, carrying their sheaves.

[Col. 1141B]

“My heart loves the leaders of Israel. You who willingly offered yourselves to danger, bless the Lord.” The leaders of Israel are the holy teachers. The soul of the righteous says that it loves them because they willingly offered themselves to danger: agreeing with the will of their teacher and Lord, they do not fear going amid the scandals of persecutors. Hence the Lord says to his disciples: “Behold, I send you as sheep among wolves” (Matt. X). And again: “They will hand you over,” he says, “to councils, and in their synagogues they will scourge you; and you will be led before kings and governors on my account, as a testimony to them and to the nations” (ibid.).

One of them answered those who, thinking in worldly terms, wished to advise him for the moment and through such advice prevented him from going among his enemies, saying: “For I am ready not only to be bound, but also to die in Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus” (Acts II). And in the Acts of the Apostles we read that the apostles went rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they had been considered worthy to suffer dishonor for the name of the Lord Jesus (Acts V).

[Col. 1142B]

“Bless the Lord, you who have mounted shining asses, who sit in judgment and walk on the road—speak.” Another edition reads: “Bless the Lord, you who have mounted beasts, sitting upon chariots and upon shining asses.”

What does it mean to mount a beast? In the end, this body of mine is a beast; for it has been given to serve the soul and to minister to it. I, however, am the same inner person who has mounted this beast, and to whom it is said that he should bless the Lord. If, therefore, you have truly mounted above the body, have become superior to bodily desires, and the movements of your body are governed by the bridle of the mind and the guidance of the inner person, it is said of you: “You have mounted a beast,” so that you may bless the Lord.

But what does the following mean: “Sitting upon chariots,” he says, “and shining above asses”? What are these shining asses understood to be? Scripture says that those who sit upon chariots and shine above asses ought to bless the Lord. To me, as in passages of great difficulty, it seems to mean something like this: When my beast—that is, my body—has come under the yoke of God’s word, then the chariot of my body begins to shine. This ass, that is, my flesh, is said to shine when it has been adorned with the splendor of chastity and purity. Thus it is rightly said that the soul, sitting upon a shining ass, blesses the Lord and praises him among those who rejoice.

“You who sit,” he says, “in judgment and walk on the road, speak.” What is sitting in judgment, if not preserving justice in judging? And what is walking on the road, if not doing good in the present life according to God’s commandments? Such people are urged to speak—that is, to praise—because those who chastise their bodies and restrain them from sins, who judge their neighbors justly, and who burn brightly on the road of truth by believing rightly and acting well, praise the Lord of all properly and rationally.

Those who serve sins cannot worthily praise the Lord. Hence it is said through the Psalmist: “Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord. Blessed are those who search his testimonies and seek him with their whole heart” (Ps. CXVIII). “For those who practice iniquity have not walked in his ways.” And elsewhere it is written: “Praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner” (Eccli. II).

[Col. 1143A]

“Where the chariots were dashed together and the army of the enemies was strangled, there the justice of the Lord and his mercy toward the strong men of Israel are recounted.” “Where,” he says, “the chariots were dashed together”—that is, where the power of demons was shattered—and “the army of the enemies was strangled,” namely, where the tumult of evil spirits was suppressed, “there the justice of the Lord is recounted,” because there the justice of the Lord was revealed, where victory was granted to Christ’s servants. There also mercy toward the strong men of Israel is recounted, where the faithful are shown to have been aided by God’s mercy.

Therefore the destruction of the enemies is rightly proclaimed when carnal pleasure is crushed, justice is preserved in judgment, and the rectitude of faith is guarded together with good works. Hence it follows: “Then the people of the Lord descended to the gates and obtained the chief power.” Through justice, therefore, the people of the Lord will seize the gates of the enemies and obtain the chief power, because the sacrifice acceptable to the Lord is that which is offered in justice and equity. Therefore he says: “The righteous were strengthened in Israel.”

Among other nations, those who are stronger in bodily power are called powerful in battle; but in Israel those who are more righteous are called more powerful in wars. For justice, even when weak in strength, conquers; whereas injustice, even when it has many strong defenders, is overcome. Thus, among this people of ours—that is, among the people of God—we either overcome through justice or are defeated through injustice.

[Col. 1143D]

“Arise, arise, Deborah; arise and take up the song.” When does prophecy arise? Certainly at the coming of Christ, when all that was written about his coming is fulfilled. It not only rises itself, but also raises peoples to faith. For this is what it means to speak the song: that the Gospel be proclaimed to all the nations of Christ.

“Arise, Barak, and seize your captives, son of Abinoam.” It was said above that Barak, which is interpreted as “lightning” or “flashing,” signifies the former people, who flashed for a short time in the splendor of the law, but did not remain long and could not retain a continuous radiance of light. Now he himself is urged to arise and seize his captives, and he is likewise remembered as the son of Abinoam. Abinoam is interpreted as “the father’s answer” or “the beauty of my father.”

What, then, does it mean that Barak is urged to capture captives, if not that the Jewish people are admonished through the books of the law and the prophets to turn to faith in Christ? This is what it means to capture captives: that those who are now captive to error and vices may be rescued from them and become captives of truth and righteousness. Thus the one will rightly take captivity from the enemies who preserves the answer of the heavenly Father and the beauty of right faith and virtues.

Note that Deborah is first urged to arise and speak the song, and then Barak to arise and seize captives. For first, by God’s just judgment, it happened—according to Paul’s word—that the fullness of the nations, believing through the prophecy of the prophets, should enter into the faith of Christ, and thus all Israel should be saved (Rom. XI). So also in this time the remnant has been saved according to the election of grace. Hence it follows: “The remnant of the people was saved; the Lord fought among the strong.”

While the apostles and preachers of the Gospel remained steadfast in the faith of Christ and overcame the threats and punishments of persecutors through patience, the Lord’s power became known, and consequently not a few from the Jewish people came to the faith of Christ. Some of them are also converted each day, but the completion of their conversion will be reserved for the end, after the fullness of the nations has entered.

[Col. 1144B]

“From Ephraim he wiped them out in Amalek.” Through Ephraim, therefore, the younger son, to whom the dignity of the firstborn was granted when the patriarch Jacob blessed him, the faithful people from the nations is signified. Younger in time within the grace of Christ, but greater in faith, it is the people to whom the whole privilege of the Israelite people has passed.

This people wiped out the enemies in Amalek because, through zeal for God and strength of faith, they strive to wipe from their hearts the wicked suggestion of evil spirits, who always desire the destruction of humanity.

“And after him, from Benjamin, among your peoples, O Amalek.” Through Benjamin, who was changed from “son of sorrow” into “son of the right hand,” the apostle Paul is signified. He was suddenly changed by God’s calling from a persecutor into an apostle and became a chosen vessel for Christ (Acts IX). He himself testifies that he was from this tribe. But he was appointed by divine command to destroy the peoples of Amalek, because through him, especially among the nations, both idolatry and the deception of diabolical error were destroyed.

[Col. 1144D]

“From Machir leaders descended, and from Zebulun those who would lead the army to battle.” Machir, which is interpreted as “he will restore” or “he sold,” is the firstborn of Manasseh, the firstborn of Joseph. It signifies the former people, from whom leaders—that is, the apostles and teachers of the primitive Church—descended. Being the Lord’s most faithful money-changers, they restored and renewed through evangelical preaching the natural law and moral integrity that had nearly been blotted out among human beings through forgetfulness and abuse. Having become leaders of spiritual warfare, they fought the enemies bravely.

Likewise Zebulun, which is interpreted as “dwelling of strength,” signifies the Church from the nations, exceedingly strong for every endurance of suffering. It gave from itself leaders in the Lord’s battle, because it sent forth from itself preachers of the Gospel and watchmen of God’s people, who would bravely crush the camps of the enemies and guard Christ’s soldiers unharmed.

[Col. 1145A]

“The leaders of Issachar were with Deborah, and they followed the footsteps of Barak.” Issachar, whom the patriarch Jacob called a strong ass (Gen. XLIX), and whose name is interpreted as “reward,” refers to the people of the nations, whom the Lord purchased at the price of his blood.

This Issachar is written to be a strong ass because formerly the gentile people were like a brute and lustful animal, existing without any rational understanding. Now, however, it is strong, submitting its neck to the dominion of the Redeemer and humbly bearing the yoke of evangelical discipline.

It sent forth its leaders with Deborah and Barak because, instructed by the words of the prophets and the examples of the patriarchs, it produced from itself noble leaders, fit to battle against the enemies and defend the camps of the Church. In all things they preserved the footsteps of their earlier fathers, never turning aside into the byways of error, but despising death and struggling for the truth to the end of life.

Hence it follows: “He gave himself to danger, as though into a precipice and abyss.” They could in no way fear death who desired to pour out their blood for Christ.

[Col. 1145B]

“Ruben, divided against himself, displayed the contention of the great-hearted.” Ruben, who was the firstborn of Israel, signifies the former people, of whom the Lord says through the prophet: “From Egypt I called my firstborn, Israel” (Hos. XI). But when this Ruben was divided, “the contention of the great-hearted was displayed,” since the Jews, divided from the fellowship of the good on account of their faithlessness, always desired to wage wars, disputes, and contentions against Christ’s spiritual soldiers.

Hence it is that the chief priests and leaders of the Jews plotted deceitfully against the apostles—indeed, against the Lord himself—how they might destroy them. Thus we read in the Gospel that the chief priests and the whole council sought false testimony against Jesus in order to put him to death (Matt. XXVI). And in the Acts of the Apostles it is written that the leaders, elders, and scribes of the Jews assembled against the apostles in Jerusalem, together with Annas the chief priest, Caiaphas, John, Alexander, and all who were of priestly descent (Acts IV).

Thus the contention of the great-hearted was found there, where those who seemed to be the greatest among the Jewish people contended in their pride against the truth of the Gospel and the teaching of the apostles, together with the rest of the crowd.

It follows:

[Col. 1145D]

“Why do you dwell between the two boundaries, to hear the whistling of the flocks?” By this sentence he reproves those who, devoted to various superstitions, wished to agree neither with the law nor with the Gospel. Here we should understand these “boundaries” in the sense in which it is written elsewhere: “Do not move the boundaries of your fathers” (Prov. XXII).

The old law was to be observed in its own time. But not only had the scribes and Pharisees defiled it with their traditions; the rest of the common people had also polluted it with very many transgressions. Yet when our Redeemer came and the Gospel shone throughout the whole world, they did not wish to turn from error to repentance or flee for refuge to the grace of Christ. Rather, they chose to hear the whistling of the flocks—that is, to follow the harmful sects of heretics—rather than the truth of God’s covenants.

The bride in the Song of Songs, abhorring these flocks, says to the bridegroom: “Tell me, you whom my soul loves, where you pasture, where you lie at midday, lest I begin to wander among the flocks of your companions” (Song I). The flocks of the companions, therefore, are gatherings of heretics. They give an empty whistle when they strive to commend falsehood instead of truth to their hearers. Whoever follows them after being divided from the unity of the faithful is soon found, through pride, to love contentions and to rise up in hatred against the good.

Hence the preceding sentence is repeated: “Ruben, divided against himself, displayed the contention of the great-hearted.” For not only the Jews, but also all heretics and schismatics who, in their pride, aspire to hold primacy, divided from the Church, always persist in contention and discord. They are found to be harmful everywhere not only to the good but also to one another. Hence Solomon says: “Among the proud there are always quarrels, but those who do everything with counsel are governed by wisdom” (Prov. XIII).

[Col. 1146B]

“Gilead rested beyond the Jordan, and Dan was free for the ships.” Some manuscripts read Gad instead of Gilead. What is signified by Gilead, which is interpreted as “heap of witness,” or by Gad, which is said to mean “girded,” if not the Israelite people? It can rightly be called either “heap of witness” or “girded,” because, possessing the Old Testament written in the law and the prophets, it trusted that it would thereby be safe and fortified on every side.

But it rested beyond the Jordan because, loving the goods of the present life and an abundance of possessions, it believed these sufficient for salvation. Therefore it did not wish to advance beyond the Jordan, because it rejected the grace of baptism and in no way sought the goods of the future life.

“Dan, therefore, was free for the ships.” Since Dan is interpreted as “judgment” or “judging,” it can here more appropriately be understood as the people of the Church. It is rightly called “judgment” or “judging,” because judicial authority appears to have been conferred upon it by the Lord.

Hence the Truth himself says to the apostles in the Gospel: “Amen, I say to you, that you who have followed me, in the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, will also sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. XIX). And in the Apocalypse twenty-four elders are described as sitting upon their thrones (Apoc. IV), so that through this sitting the dignity of the holy Church, which has sprung from the patriarchs and apostles, might be expressed in the heavenly kingdom.

This people, therefore, is free for the ships because, established amid the danger of the present life and relying upon the mystery of the Lord’s cross, it strives through God’s mercy to overcome the storm of persecutions. It is also free from earthly affairs, and through holy preachers casts the net of the Gospel into the sea of this world, so that, rescuing human beings from the turbulent waves of the age, it may lead them to the harbor of rest and to the liberty of the future homeland.

[Col. 1146D]

“Asher dwelt on the seashore and remained in the harbors.” Asher, which is interpreted as “blessedness,” can signify no one better than our Redeemer, in whom we have hope of eternal blessedness, without whom no one will attain true blessedness. For he says: “No one comes to the Father except through me” (John XIV). And again: “I am the door; if anyone enters through me, he will be saved, and he will enter and go out and find pasture” (John X). And again: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV).

This Asher, therefore, dwelt on the seashore and remained in the harbors because, having conquered the prince of death and destroyed death itself, he rose again in glory as a victorious triumphant one. Ascending into heaven, he sits at the right hand of God the almighty Father. He no longer dies; death will no longer rule over him. Remaining in the rest of eternal blessedness, he awaits the day of judgment, until all his enemies are placed beneath his feet, when he will render to each person a definite recompense according to his own merits.

The souls of the saints may also appropriately be understood in the figure of Asher. Having crossed the waves of the age and overcome the storm of persecutions, they already stand in the harbor of eternal rest. They will not return again to the labors of the present life, but, victorious with their King, they assist our warfare by their prayers—not by laboring, but by reigning—as much as is fitting. They greatly desire that we too should one day triumph, so that we may enjoy eternal joy with them forever.

[Col. 1147B]

“But Zebulun and Naphtali offered their souls to death in the region of Rome.” In Zebulun and Naphtali the apostles and apostolic men who faithfully exercise leadership in the Church are signified. The first apostles, who were leaders of the Churches, came from those tribes that received their inheritance in Galilee, where our Lord Jesus Christ taught especially. Of them it is said: “The leaders of Zebulun and the leaders of Naphtali.”

These men offered their souls to death, fighting in the region of Rome—which is interpreted as “seeing something” or “the heights”—when, for the salvation of the faithful and the enlargement of the Church, which Naphtali signifies, or for the heavenly glory toward which they directed their minds, they struggled even unto death. No troubles of persecutions could turn them away from this intention and zeal. Persevering in the Christian contest, they obtained in the heavenly kingdom the crown of glory for their struggles (Eph. VI).

[Col. 1147D]

“Kings came and fought. The kings of Canaan fought in Taanach, beside the waters of Megiddo, yet they took no spoils.” The kings of Canaan are evil spirits, namely the principalities and powers of these darknesses, who stir up persecutions and wars in the world against Christ’s soldiers. Canaan, interpreted as “their movement,” signifies this.

These kings therefore fought in Taanach—that is, in humility—beside the waters of Megiddo, whose name means “his fruits,” when they strive through the pretense of false humility to deceive and to draw Christ’s servants away from abstinence toward the allurements of pleasures.

Hence the ancient serpent, flattering our first parents in paradise, made his suggestion and drew them by enticement toward what he desired, saying to the woman: “Why has God commanded you not to eat from every tree of paradise?” The woman answered him: “We eat of the fruit of the trees that are in paradise; but concerning the fruit of the tree that is in the middle of paradise, God commanded us not to eat of it and not to touch it, lest perhaps we die” (Gen. III). The serpent said to the woman: “You will certainly not die. For God knows that on whatever day you eat from it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like gods, knowing good and evil.”

But these kings, overcome by the power of the true King and our Savior Jesus Christ, took no spoils as plunderers. For although they flattered the Church while fighting against it, and although they threatened death, they achieved nothing and captured nothing, because the gates of hell will not prevail against it (Matt. XVI). The serpent indeed lies in wait for its heel, but it will crush his head; and power has been given to it by its King to tread upon serpents, scorpions, and every power of the enemy (Gen. VI; Luke X).

[Col. 1148B]

“From heaven the battle was fought against them. The stars, remaining in their order and course, fought against Sisera.” “From heaven,” he says, “the battle was fought against them,” because this war was arranged by divine command, and all the enemies were overthrown by heavenly power.

For the stars—that is, the saints, concerning whom it is written through the Prophet: “He numbers the multitude of the stars and calls them all by name” (Ps. CXLVI), and the Apostle says: “Star differs from star in glory” (I Cor. XV)—remain in their order and course. Each remains in the calling to which God called it and labors usefully against the spiritual Sisera, according to what divine grace grants it to be able to do.

This spiritual Sisera is the prince of the world, who can rightly be called “exclusion from joy,” because he is always a stranger to and deprived of true joy. The saints fight against him continually, since throughout the whole period of the present life they do not cease to wage war against him inwardly and outwardly.

[Col. 1148C]

“The torrent of Kishon dragged away their corpses, the torrent of Cadumin, the torrent of Kishon.” What is demonstrated by a torrent, if not sudden overthrow? Kishon is interpreted as “they struck against” or “their hardness.” What, under this name, is signified if not the wickedness of the evil?

Striking against it, all the impious and enemies of God’s people have brought upon themselves the ruin of everlasting death. Hence it is said in Proverbs: “The wicked will be caught in their own snares” (Prov. XI). And again: “Their wickedness blinded them” (Wis. II).

The present life is rightly called a torrent because of the passing course of its waters, and also because of the winter it possesses in its various temptations and tribulations. It dragged away the corpses of the impious because, on account of their many crimes, it delivers the dead bodies of sinners to everlasting destruction, namely to the pool of hell, where they will feel the torment of punishments.

Hence Cadumin, which is interpreted as “useless resurrection,” is also mentioned there, because on the last day the impious will not rise for rest, but so that they may be thrust into eternal fire with the devil and his angels.

[Col. 1148D]

“Trample down, my soul, the strong men; the hooves of the horses fell upon those fleeing with violence and upon the strongest of the enemies rushing headlong.” The company of the saints exhorts itself to despise the ferocity of persecutors. Although they can kill the body—that is, a corruptible thing—they cannot kill the soul, which remains forever (Matt. X).

“The hooves of the horses,” he says, “fell upon those fleeing with violence.” What is signified by the hoof of a horse if not the end of the proud? The horse’s hoof falls beneath the assault of those fleeing when all the arrogance of the proud, which pursues fleeting and perishable things, is crushed at the end of the present life. The strongest of the enemies will rush headlong when, after judgment has been carried out, all who practice iniquity will perish from the city of the Lord, and all the nations that forget the Lord will plunge into hell.

[Col. 1149A]

“Curse the land of Meroz,” said the angel of the Lord; “curse its inhabitants, because they did not come to the help of the Lord, to the aid of his strongest men.” What can we understand by the land of Meroz if not the vanity of this world or the flux of carnal desires, which all sacred prophecy condemns and detests?

Meroz is interpreted as “water of execrations.” And worldly desires are rightly called “water of execrations,” because they execrate the divine covenants by prohibiting them as useless—or rather, harmful—to God’s servants. The angel of the Lord—that is, the apostolic company and the whole order of holy teachers—commands that this land be cursed, because it proves harmful to all who follow it. It includes all its inhabitants in the same curse, because it leads those who love and follow it into everlasting woe.

They did not come to the help of the Lord, to the aid of his strongest men, when they refused to believe the Gospel as the apostles preached it throughout the whole world and did not consent to receive the word of God. Therefore, corrupted by their pleasures, they became abominable, because, despising the author of life, they devised iniquity in their hearts.

The Jewish people may also appropriately be understood under the name of the land of Meroz. It bound itself by an oath when, upon receiving the law, it said: “Cursed is everyone who does not remain in the words of this law and carry them out in deed” (Deut. XXVII). All those whom the grace of Christ did not free from the curse of the law were bound by this curse.

The angel of the Lord therefore rightly curses the inhabitants of this land, because they did not come to the help of the Lord, to the aid of his strongest men. In dealing with the preachers of the holy Gospel, they were found everywhere not merely to be non-assistants but adversaries.

Hence the mediator of God and human beings himself, who because of the mystery of the Incarnation is called the angel of the great counsel, is read in the Gospel to have reproached the cities in which many of his mighty works had been performed for not having repented. He said to them: “Woe to you, Chorazin; woe to you, Bethsaida. For if the mighty works that were performed in you had been performed in Tyre and Sidon, they would long ago have repented in sackcloth and ashes. Nevertheless, I say to you, it will be more bearable for Tyre and Sidon on the day of judgment than for you” (Matt. XI).

Again he says to the lawyers: “Woe to you lawyers, because you have taken away the key of knowledge. You yourselves did not enter, and those who were entering you hindered” (Luke XI). Hence Paul, testifying in the Acts of the Apostles to the Jews that Jesus is the Christ, says: “But when they contradicted and blasphemed, he shook out his garments and said to them: ‘Your blood be upon your own heads; I am clean. From now on I will go to the nations’” (Acts XVIII).

[Col. 1150A]

“Blessed among women is Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite; let her be blessed in her tent.” We said above that Jael, which is interpreted as “ascent” or “rest of God,” signified the Church gathered from the nations. Through the ascent of virtues it is lifted on high, and in its gentleness and devotion the Spirit of God is recognized to rest.

She is blessed among women because she is appropriately praised by all holy souls. She was also the wife of Heber the Kenite, since she is proclaimed to be the most noble bride of Christ the King and our Lord, the triumphant conqueror of death. For Heber is interpreted as “entering into combat,” and Kenite as “possession” or “my treasurer.”

Who can more fittingly be called “entering into combat” than our Redeemer, who contended with the prince of the world and, overcoming him by his death, became possessor of heaven and earth? Concerning him the Apostle said: “Christ became obedient to the Father for us unto death, even death on a cross. Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth—and every tongue should confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (Phil. II).

“Let Jael be blessed,” he says, “in her tent”—that is, in the Catholic Church, which is spread throughout the whole world. There also the faith of the nations is praised, proclaimed, and everywhere made known.

[Col. 1150B]

“To him who asked for water she gave milk,” when she opposed the simplicity of mortality to the devil, who was burning in his members with luxury, lust, and avarice. “And in a bowl she offered choice butter,” when in the teaching of the apostles she displayed the gift of supreme love.

“She put her left hand to the tent-peg and her right hand to the hammers of the craftsmen.” What is expressed by the left hand if not the activity of the outer person, and by the right if not the devotion of the inner person?

Our Jael therefore put her left hand to the tent-peg when, in the likeness of Christ’s cross, she mortified carnal desires in herself through abstinence. She put her right hand to the hammers of the craftsmen when she prepared the intention of her mind to meditate upon the books of the holy apostles and prophets. These are the true craftsmen, who fashion heavenly armor in the house of the holy Church and hand it over to Christ’s soldiers for fighting against spiritual enemies.

It was therefore rightly said that Jael, occupied with both hands at the tent-peg and the hammers, struck down the enemy of her people, because by preaching God’s law and displaying good examples of the virtues, she killed the most savage enemy.

[Col. 1150D]

“She struck Sisera, seeking the place of the wound in his head, and forcefully pierced his temple.” With a tent-peg—or stake—and a hammer she killed him, piercing the temple of his head, because she destroyed pride, which is the head of every sin—“for the beginning of every sin is pride” (Eccli. X)—in human hearts through the humility of Christ’s Passion.

“Between her feet he fell; he failed and died. Before her feet he rolled and lay lifeless and wretched.” The wicked plunderer is described as falling and lying dead between the feet of a woman because the ancient enemy is recognized to have been overcome, prostrated, and crushed beneath the feet of the Church. Through the power granted to it by Christ, the Church conquers, condemns, and tramples down every dominion of death.

Hence in Genesis the Lord says to the serpent concerning the woman: “She will crush your head, and you will lie in wait for her heel” (Gen. III). And hence the Savior says to his disciples in the Gospel: “Behold, I give you power to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and upon every power of the enemy” (Luke X).

The most wicked destroyer therefore lies lifeless and wretched before the feet of the woman when each day he is put to death through the faith, hope, and patience of the faithful, and at the end is swallowed up in victory. “There will no longer be death, nor mourning, nor crying, because the former things have passed away” (Apoc. XXI).

[Col. 1151B]

“His mother looked out through the window and howled, and spoke from the upper room.” For who is the mother of this spiritual Sisera—that is, of all the wicked—if not impiety, which is the mother and inventor of every iniquity?

Hence it is written in the book of Jesus son of Sirach: “The beginning of human pride is to apostatize from God, because the heart of the human being departs from the one who made him” (Eccli. X).

This mother grieves and, in a certain sense, howls in the hearts of the impious when she sees idolatry failing through the preaching of the Gospel throughout the whole world. Looking through the window and the upper room of worldly arrogance, she speaks in this way: “Why is his chariot delayed in returning? Why have the feet of his chariots been slow?”

What are the chariots and carriage of the devil if not human beings devoted to various errors and vices? The prince of the world, who reigns over all the sons of pride, drives the chariots like one holding power in wickedness and possessing the kingdom of evil. It is not enough for him to mount a single horse; he drives many at once, compelling many at once with twisted whips and blows.

Whoever you see more shameful in luxury, fiercer in unbelief, more terrible in avarice, and more criminal in impiety—know that he belongs to Pharaoh’s chariots. The devil sits upon such people, yokes them to his carriage, rides and flies along upon them, and drives them with loosened reins across the open fields of crimes.

[Col. 1151D] One of his wives, wiser than the rest, answered these words of his mother-in-law: “Perhaps he is now dividing the spoil, and the most beautiful of the women is being chosen for him.”

Above we said that impiety, which first invented idolatry, is the mother of this spiritual Sisera, because it nourishes and fosters his members—that is, the impious and sinners—in various crimes. But now, because his wife is mentioned here as wiser than the others, we may appropriately understand her as worldly wisdom. For just as it is written concerning divine wisdom, when Solomon says, “I loved her and sought her from my youth, and I sought to take her as my bride, and I became a lover of her beauty” (Wis. 8), so also the cleverness of the pagans preferred worldly philosophy to earthly riches and to all other things.

[Col. 1152A] In her own times she favored impiety, praising the worship of demons; and therefore she spoke to this most wicked mother in a flattering manner, testifying with her profane mouth that the power of false gods ruled the world, attributing all the battles and victories of kings to their might, and saying that the enjoyment of present things, as something most beautiful, was fitting for their honor. Hence what follows says: “Garments of various colors are handed over to Sisera as spoil, and he gathers diverse furnishings for adorning the necks.”

By garments of various colors we may understand the ornaments of idols, or the poems of poets, which the pagans composed in various meters in honor of their gods; and by diverse furnishings, the various services of false priests, which they most zealously devoted to their idols. But just as all these things were frivolous in estimation, so also they appeared shameful in practice. Therefore spiritual Deborah, bringing her song to an end, concluded in this way: “Thus may all your enemies perish, O Lord; but may those who love you shine like the sun at its rising.”

“Sinners will perish from the face of God, and the righteous will rejoice in the presence of God, delighting in gladness.” But when he says, “Those who love you, as the sun shines at its rising, so may they shine,” he either shows figuratively, by comparison with that most splendid element, the greatest glory of the saints in heaven; or, according to the mystery, he promises the saints in the life to come a likeness to the incorruption of Christ’s humanity, since he is called the sun of righteousness (Matt. 4). Hence the apostle John, writing in his Epistle to believers, says: “Beloved, we are now children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3).

## CHAPTER XIV. How the children of Israel, because of their sins, were handed over into the hands of Midian for seven years and were grievously oppressed

### (CHAP. VI.)

After that prophetic song of Deborah and Barak had been completed, the writer of the history returns to the order of his narrative and wishes to display the truth of what happened, saying:

“And the land rested for forty years. But the children of Israel did evil in the sight of the Lord, who handed them over into the hand of Midian for seven years, and they were greatly oppressed by them.”

The land rests as long as sin rests. But the land is said to be moved—that is, those who inhabit the land—when sins begin to move and disturb human souls. Therefore what the present reading now contains was written: “And the land rested,” it says, “for forty years. And the children of Israel did evil in the sight of the Lord, and the Lord handed them over into the hand of Midian for seven years. And the hand of Midian prevailed over Israel.”

While righteousness was in the land—that is, in those who inhabit the land—the land is said to have rested. But when iniquity increased and they did evil in the sight of the Lord, then, it says, “the Lord handed them over into the hands of Midian for seven years.” The Midianites are not said to have prevailed over the Lord’s people so long as the people guarded the Lord’s commandments. But when they began to neglect the divine commands, the hand of the enemy became stronger and more powerful against them.

Against that former people, therefore, bodily enemies rose up when they sinned; but against us, who are called Israel according to the Spirit, a spiritual enemy undoubtedly rises when we neglect God’s commandments. When we despise Christ’s precepts, the hand of the demons becomes stronger against us, and we too are handed over to our enemies when we depart from grace. But let us see what happened to those who were handed over because of their sins.

“They made for themselves caves and caverns in the mountains and very strongly fortified places for resistance. And whenever Israel had sown, Midian, Amalek, and the rest of the eastern nations would ascend, pitching their tents among them, and, as if they were in pastures, they would lay everything waste as far as the entrance of Gaza,” and so forth.

This is what happened to Israel according to the flesh. He sowed the land; but because he had been handed over on account of his sins to enemies who rose against him, he reaped corruption instead of crops. But let us consider what can happen to us, who are called Israel according to the Spirit.

There are times when we sow, and the enemies cannot corrupt the seeds we sow; they cannot lie in wait for our cultivation. But there are also times when we sow, and what we sow is corrupted. The apostle Paul teaches us about this difference in sowing. Hear what he himself says: “He who sows in the flesh will reap corruption from the flesh; and he who sows in the Spirit will reap eternal life from the Spirit.”

These, then, are those whose seeds the Midianites corrupt: those who sow in the flesh. These are the ones whose fruits are destroyed and perish. But those seeds that are sown in the spirit the Midianites cannot corrupt. For hostile powers cannot ascend to the spiritual fields and violate the newly plowed lands of those who do not sow upon thorns, but renew their newly plowed fields for themselves.

But something else must also be added—for I wish to admonish myself together with you concerning the guarding of seeds and the diligence required for spiritual fruits. It frequently happens that someone, laboring greatly in spiritual work, produces many fruits, fills his granaries with the harvest of righteousness, and stores many good works in the chamber of his conscience. But afterward, if he grows negligent and, after his labor, inclines toward pleasures and excesses, all those good seeds and the fruits of holy work are corrupted when lust gains dominion.

For when sin has entered stealthily and taken the human mind captive, so that it no longer looks to the commandments of God or willingly ascends the difficult path of virtue, everything that had previously been gathered into the granaries of the conscience perishes. Therefore we must heed the admonition of Holy Scripture, which says: “Guard your heart with all vigilance” (Prov. 4). The heart must therefore be guarded from every sin, especially in a time of persecution.

If it happens to someone that for a certain period he gathers the fruits of righteousness, acquires works of virtue, and cultivates himself with every highly approved discipline, but in a time of persecution denies the faith, that man has emptied all that he had stored up and has suddenly become naked and destitute of all his resources. For the labor sought for a long time and gathered with great difficulty has suddenly all been poured out. As the prophet says: “None of all his righteous deeds that he has done will be remembered” (Ezek. 18).

“For all their flocks would come with their tents, and an innumerable multitude of people and camels covered everything like locusts, laying waste whatever they touched.”

Suppose that the Midianites, who are interpreted as “outside judgment,” gathered against Israel. Suppose that these who are outside God’s judgment, who sinned outside the law and will perish outside the law (Rom. 2), gathered against Israel. Suppose also that Amalek came, which is itself interpreted as “the people who lick.” [Col. 1154B] Suppose that this earthly nation, devoted to the belly and to gluttony, came to attack Israel—the carnal attacking the spiritual Israel.

What does it mean that the children of the East are also mixed in with these and are said to have come with them to attack Israel? You might say to me, my listener, that if it had been written that the children of the West gathered with them, I would have no question. You might say to me, according to allegorical principles, that the children of the West are the children of darkness, and that they are joined to those nations—those outside the judgment of God and devoted to the belly—which attack those who strive to see the Lord with their mind.

But now, when it is said that the children of the East came with Midian and Amalek, how can this appropriately be explained? Let us therefore see whether in such difficult passages of Scripture we can find in these divine pages some worthy meaning.

Everyone who takes upon himself the name of Christ becomes a child of the East. For thus it is written concerning Christ: “Behold, the man whose name is East” (Zech. 6). Whoever, therefore, takes upon himself the name of Christ is said to be a child of the East.

But not all who receive the name of Christ also remain in Christ’s Church. If, then, you see heretics reckoned indeed by the name of Christ, but attacking the Church of God, taking up arms against the faith of Christ, attacking the Lord’s people, and stirring up wars against the catholic faith, do not hesitate to say that these are indeed children of the East, but that they have come with the Midianites and the Amalekites to fight against God’s people. For heretics, together with pagans and Jews, persecute the Church of God. I think these are the ones designated by the children of the East.

“Thus,” he says, “all Midian, Amalek, and the children of the East gathered together, went up, came upon them, and encamped in the valley of Jezreel.”

Those who wish to attack God’s people place their camp in valleys—in depressed and low-lying places? “In the valley,” he says, “of Jezreel.” We find that Jezreel is interpreted as “seed of God.”

Do you see where the adversaries place their camp? They did not dare to go where the fruits of the Spirit already appeared to have been born, but where the seed of God still lies, where the fruit has not yet risen. For the one who went out to sow the word sows in every place.

But hear the Lord himself saying what the seed of God usually suffers: “Another,” he says, “fell beside the road, and the birds of heaven came and snatched it away.” Explaining this later, he said: “Those who were sown beside the road are those who hear the word of God and receive it with joy. But the devil comes and takes away from their heart what was sown” (Luke 8).

Thus these too now come to the seed of God and wish to take it from the hearts of those in whom it has been sown, because they find them lying in valleys and pursuing whatever is lowest. For they belong to those who receive the word of God humbly and unworthily and, so to speak, with a Jewish understanding; therefore the demons can snatch it from their hearts.

But whoever ascends from the humility of the letter to the heights of the Spirit, and, fleeing carnal understanding, pursues in higher things what belongs to the Spirit of God—from such a person neither the Midianites nor the Amalekites can steal anything. Nor will the children of the East themselves be able to plunder one who has been established on the lofty summit of spiritual understanding. They therefore place their camp in the valleys.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 1155]

## CHAPTER I. How, after Israel had been humbled and cried out to him, the Lord sent a prophet to remind them of God’s past benefits

### (CHAP. VI.)

Israel was greatly humbled in the sight of Midian and cried out to the Lord, asking for help against the Midianites. He sent them a prophetic man, who spoke:

“Thus says the Lord God of Israel: I made you come up from Egypt, brought you out of the house of slavery, and delivered you from the hand of the Egyptians and of all the enemies who afflicted you. I drove them out before you, gave you their land, and said: I am the Lord your God. Do not fear the gods of the Amorites, in whose land you dwell. But you did not wish to listen to my voice,” and so forth.

Why the name of this prophet is not given—a thing very unusual in Scripture—the reason is hidden, although I do not think there is no reason. But because, after the words in which he reproached the people for their disobedience, Scripture continues by saying, “And the angel of the Lord came and sat beneath the oak that was in Ophrah,” it is not unreasonable to understand that this angel was indicated under the name of “man,” so that after speaking these words he came to the oak mentioned and sat there.

It is well known that angels are accustomed to be called by the name of men, although it does not readily or clearly occur that one who was an angel should be called a prophet. We do, however, read of one who was a prophet being called an angel. But if prophetic sayings of angels are known—that is, sayings by which they foretold future events—why could an angel not now be designated by the name “prophet”? Nevertheless, as I said, no explicit and manifest testimony on this matter is found.

In the Septuagint, however, it is read as follows: “The Lord is with you, powerful in strength.” When the angel of the Lord says, “The Lord is with you, powerful in strength,” “powerful” is nominative, not vocative; that is, “The Lord who is with you is powerful,” not “You are powerful.”

## CHAPTER II. How the angel of the Lord came to Gideon while he was threshing wheat with a staff on the threshing floor and commanded him to free Israel from the hands of its enemies; and concerning the burnt offering that Gideon himself presented to God through the ministry of the angel sent to him

Gideon said to him: “I beg you, my lord, if the Lord is with us, why have all these things overtaken us? Where are his wonders, which our fathers recounted to us, saying, ‘The Lord brought us out of Egypt’? But now he has abandoned us and handed us over into the hands of Midian.”

The Lord looked at him and said: “Go in this strength of yours, and you will deliver Israel from the hand of Midian. Know that I have sent you.”

He answered: “I beg you, my lord, with what shall I deliver Israel? Behold, my family is the least in Manasseh, and I am the youngest in my father’s house.”

According to the Septuagint, Gideon answered the angel: “In me, Lord”—that is, “Look upon me: with what shall I save Israel? Behold, my thousand is the weakest in Manasseh.” This is understood to mean that he was appointed over a thousand men, whom Scripture calls *chiliarchs* in Greek—or perhaps it means something else.

The Lord said to him: “I will be with you, and you will strike Midian as one man.”

He said: “If I have found favor before you, give me a sign that it is you who are speaking with me. Do not depart from here until I return to you, bringing an offering and presenting it to you.”

He answered: “I will await your arrival.”

Gideon entered, cooked a young goat, and made unleavened loaves from a measure of flour. He placed the meat in a basket, poured the broth into a pot, carried everything beneath the oak, and presented it to him.

The angel of the Lord said to him: “Take the meat and the unleavened loaves, place them on that rock, and pour the broth over them.”

When he had done this, the angel of the Lord extended the tip of the staff he held in his hand and touched the meat and the unleavened loaves. Fire rose from the rock and consumed the meat and the unleavened loaves, and so forth.

It must be observed that, according to the Septuagint, Gideon did not say to the angel, “I will offer a sacrifice to you,” but rather, “I will offer my sacrifice and place it in your presence.” Hence it must be understood that he wished to offer the sacrifice not to the angel, but through the angel.

The angel himself clearly demonstrates this. He did not take the sacrifice from him as though it belonged to himself, but said to him: “Take the meat and the unleavened loaves, place them beside that rock, and pour out the broth.” When Gideon had done this, the angel of the Lord extended the tip of the staff that was in his hand and touched the meat and the unleavened loaves, and fire was kindled from the rock and consumed the meat and the unleavened loaves.

Thus, in the sacrifice Gideon offered, the angel fulfilled the office of a minister. A human minister, as a human being, would have supplied fire without a miracle; but this angel supplied it miraculously. Finally, Gideon then recognized that he was the angel of the Lord. For Scripture immediately adds: “And Gideon saw that he was the angel of the Lord.”

Previously, therefore, he had spoken as though with a man, although he believed him to be a man of God. He wished to offer the sacrifice in his presence, as though he might be helped by the presence of his holiness.

It may be asked why Gideon dared to offer a sacrifice to God outside the place where God had commanded it. God had forbidden sacrifice to be offered to him outside his tabernacle; the temple later succeeded that tabernacle. In Gideon’s time, however, the tabernacle of God was at Shiloh, and therefore sacrifice could lawfully be offered only there.

But it must be understood that at first he had thought the angel a prophet and had consulted God through him about offering the sacrifice. If the angel had forbidden it, it certainly would not have been done. But because he approved it and consented that it be done, Gideon followed God’s authority in carrying it out.

For God established those lawful regulations in such a way that he gave laws not to himself but to human beings. Therefore whatever he himself commanded beyond those regulations must be understood as fulfilled not by transgressors but rather by the pious and obedient, as in Abraham’s case when he was commanded to sacrifice his son (Gen. 22).

Thus Elijah too offered sacrifice outside the tabernacle of the Lord in order to convict the priests of the idols (1 Kings 18). It must be understood that he did this by the Lord’s command: God ordered him, as a prophet, through revelation and inspiration to do so.

Moreover, the practice of sacrificing outside the tabernacle had become so widespread that Solomon too is found to have offered sacrifice on the high places, and his sacrifice was not condemned (1 Kings 3). Yet kings are censured when, among their praiseworthy deeds, they did not destroy the high places where the people were accustomed to sacrifice contrary to God’s law; and the king who destroyed them is praised with greater commendation.

Thus God tolerated rather than forbade the custom of his people, who, although sacrificing outside his tabernacle, did not offer to foreign gods but to the Lord their God. In this way too he listened to those who offered.

But who would not understand that what Gideon did was arranged through the angel so that it might occur prophetically, in which prophecy that rock was commended? The sacrifice was not offered to the rock; rather, fire is said to have come forth from it to consume the sacrifice.

Whether, therefore, the water poured forth when the rock was struck in the wilderness, or the fire, signifies the gift of the Holy Spirit, which the Lord Christ poured out upon us in richest measure. This gift was signified by water in the Gospel, where he himself says: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, as Scripture says, rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (John 7). The evangelist then adds: “He said this about the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive.”

It was also signified by fire, where, when he came upon those gathered together, we read: “Tongues divided like fire appeared to them, and one rested upon each of them” (Acts 2). The Lord himself also says: “I came to cast fire upon the earth” (Luke 12).

When Gideon was threshing a harvest of wheat beneath an oak tree with a staff and separating the grain from the chaff, he saw an angel and received from him an oracle that he should lead God’s people from the power of their enemies into freedom.

This Gideon plainly bore the figure of Christ. Under the shadow of the sacred cross, established in the mystery of the incarnation, which had been predestined to come, he separated the elect of the saints from the chaff of vices by the uprightness of judgment, as though by means of a staff.

When this Gideon heard from the angel that, although the thousands of the nations would fail, the Lord would free his people from their enemies through one man, he immediately cooked a young goat. At the angel’s command he placed its flesh together with unleavened bread upon the rock and poured the broth over it. When the angel touched them with the tip of his staff, fire immediately burst forth from the rock; thus the sacrifice that was being offered was consumed.

By this judgment it appears that the rock was a type of Christ’s body, as Paul testifies: “The rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10).

Already then, therefore, it was declared in mystery that the Lord Jesus, crucified in his flesh, would abolish the sins of the whole world, and would cleanse not only the sins of actions but also the desires of souls. For the flesh of the young goat refers to guilt, and the broth to the enticements of desire, as it is written: “The people desired a most evil desire and said, ‘Who will feed us meat?’” (Num. 11).

The angel’s extending of the staff and touching of the rock from which fire came forth showed that the Lord’s flesh, filled with the divine Spirit, would burn away all the sins of human condition. Hence the Lord also says: “I came to cast fire upon the earth” (Luke 12).

The man, learned and prescient of future events, perceived the heavenly mysteries. Therefore, in accordance with the oracles, he slaughtered the bullock assigned by his father to the idols, and he himself sacrificed another seven-year-old bullock to God. By this act he most clearly revealed that, through the Lord’s coming, all the sacrifices of paganism were to be abolished, and that only the sacrifice of the Lord’s passion was to be brought to God in the worship of the people for our redemption.

For that bullock was a type of Christ, in whom dwelt the sevenfold fullness of spiritual virtues, as Isaiah said (Isa. 11).

What is meant by threshing wheat with a staff except separating, by upright judgment, the graces of virtues from the chaff of vices? But the angel appears to those who do these things, because the more diligently people cleanse themselves from outward things, the more fully the Lord announces inward realities to them.

He commands the young goat to be sacrificed—that is, every desire of our flesh—and the flesh to be placed upon the rock, with the broth poured over it. Whom else does the rock signify except him of whom Paul says: “The rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10)?

We place flesh upon the rock when, in imitation of Christ, we afflict our body. He also pours the broth of the flesh over it who, in Christlike conduct, has emptied himself even of carnal thoughts. For something liquid from flesh is, as it were, poured upon the rock when the mind is emptied of the flow of carnal thoughts. Yet the angel immediately touches it with his staff, because the power of divine help never abandons our intention.

Fire comes out of the rock and consumes the broth and the flesh, because the Spirit from the Redeemer burns our heart with such a flame of compunction that it consumes everything unlawful in it, both in deed and in thought. He watches perfectly and carefully so that he not only refuses to perform wicked deeds but also wipes away whatever melts shamefully within him through his thoughts.

## CHAPTER III. How the Spirit of the Lord clothed Gideon, who sounded the trumpet and summoned the house of Abiezer to follow him; and concerning the sign of the fleece that Gideon requested from the Lord

### (IBID.)

“The Spirit of the Lord clothed Gideon. He sounded the trumpet and summoned the house of Abiezer to follow him. He sent messengers throughout Manasseh, and it too followed him; and he sent other messengers to Asher, Zebulun, and Naphtali, and they came out to meet him.”

“He summoned,” it says, “Abiezer after him,” although Abiezer was nowhere present. Abiezer is interpreted as “my father’s help.” Therefore he appears to have invoked not some human being but the help of the supreme Father.

Meanwhile he also sends for auxiliary forces to be summoned. The peoples assemble, and the whole army gathers to Gideon.

Gideon said to the Lord: “If you will save Israel by my hand, as you have spoken, behold, I will place this fleece of wool on the threshing floor. If there is dew on the fleece alone and dryness over all the land, I shall know that by my hand, as you have spoken, you will deliver Israel.”

And it happened so. When he rose early in the night and squeezed the fleece, he filled a bowl with dew.

He said again to the Lord: “Let not your anger burn against me if I test you once more, seeking a sign through the fleece. I ask that the fleece alone be dry and that all the land be wet with dew.”

And God did that night as he had asked: there was dryness on the fleece alone, and dew over all the land, and so forth.

Gideon therefore foresaw the mystery of victory, yet, although strong and faithful, he still sought fuller evidence from the Lord concerning the future victory. For one night he placed a fleece of wool on the threshing floor, so that dew would be found only upon it and dryness over the entire land; then again he placed the fleece, so that dew would fall over the whole land and the fleece would be dry.

Someone might perhaps ask whether he seems to have been like an unbeliever, since he had already been instructed by frequent signs. Far from it. He was not uncertain; rather, he foresaw future mysteries, which, being prudent, he carefully examined so that he might believe the mystery more fully once he had understood the oracle.

What, then, is the fleece drenched with dew and the threshing floor dry, and afterward the threshing floor drenched and the fleece dry, except that at first one nation, the Hebrews, possessed the mystery of grace while the whole world was empty; but now, in the manifestation of Christ, the whole world possesses it, while that nation is empty?

That threshing floor signifies the whole world. When the whole world was dry, producing no fruit because of pagan superstition, that heavenly dew of visitation was then upon the fleece. But afterward, when the sheep of the house of Israel, represented under the figure of the fleece, had perished, and those sheep had denied the fountain of living water, the dew of faith dried up in the breasts of the Jews, and that divine rain diverted its grace into the hearts of the nations.

Therefore now the whole world is moistened by the dew of faith, while the Jews lack prophecy and all the gifts of grace. It is no wonder that those who have been deprived by the Lord of the abundance of prophetic rain suffer the dryness of unbelief, since he says: “I will command the clouds above not to rain rain upon it” (Isa. 5).

He signified that nation by the name of “fleece” either because it was to be stripped of the authority of its teaching, as sheep are stripped of their wool, or because it knew that the same rain which it did not wish to have preached to it through its leaders would be revealed to others—that is, to the uncircumcised nations.

## CHAPTER IV. The Lord’s command to Gideon that he dismiss the multitude of the people; how twenty-two thousand men departed from him and only ten thousand remained with him

### (CAP. VII.)

The Lord said to Gideon: “The people with you are too numerous, and Midian will not be handed over into their hands, lest Israel boast against me and say, ‘I was delivered by my own strength.’ Speak to the people and proclaim in the hearing of all: Whoever is fearful and timid, let him return.”

They departed from Mount Gilead, and twenty-two thousand men returned from the people; only ten thousand remained.

What does it mean that the fearful and timid, after it had been proclaimed to them that the fearful should withdraw from the camp, were found to have departed in the number of twenty-two thousand, except that all who do not remain in the unity of faith and the fellowship of love are rightly rejected from Christ’s army, where spiritual enemies are slaughtered as the reprobate?

For the number two, which is the first number divided from unity, does not always have a good meaning in Holy Scripture, but sometimes has the opposite meaning. Observe, reader, that in twenty-two the number eleven, which signifies transgression of the law, is contained twice; and you will understand that whoever does not preserve the bonds of unity and love is a transgressor of the law.

But, by contrast, those who were found steadfast in spirit in the battle were marked by the number one thousand multiplied by ten. For the number ten is one and first in that progression which proceeds from ten to one hundred; therefore it can signify the unity of faith and the fellowship of holy love.

The ten commandments, therefore, belong to the law. Hence it is clear that whoever is a faithful executor of the law is a most genuine guardian of faith and charity.

Nor does it seem without mystery that twenty-two thousand are said to have withdrawn from Gideon’s camp on Mount Gilead, while ten thousand remained there. Gilead is interpreted as “heap of testimony,” where the fearfulness of the Jews and the steadfastness of the nations were tested.

For while the Jews, possessing the letter of the law, feared losing the goods of the present life and therefore refused to come to the faith of Christ, they were rejected as degenerate and reprobate. But the nations, understanding the law and the prophets spiritually and therefore hoping for future goods, sought Christ’s grace with steadfast hearts, believing that they could thereby be saved eternally.

## CHAPTER V. The testing of the people at the waters, where, out of the ten thousand, only three hundred remained for battle; and how he armed them with trumpets, lamps, and jars
*(Same place.)* The Lord said to Gideon: “The people are still numerous. Bring them down to the water, and there I shall test them. Whoever I tell you is to go with you, let him go; but whoever I forbid to go, let him return.” When the people had gone down to the water, the Lord said to Gideon: “Those who lap the water with their tongue, as dogs are accustomed to lap, you shall set apart by themselves; but those who drink while bending their knees shall be on the other side.” The number of those who had lapped the water, putting it from their hand to their mouth, was three hundred men. But all the rest of the multitude had drunk on bended knee, etc.

Most Latin codices do not have *with his hand*, but only *with his tongue*, because they understood the preceding words, “as dogs.” The Greek, however, has both: *with his hand, with his tongue*, so that it may be understood that they scooped up the water with their hand and put it into their mouth. This was like the way dogs drink: they do not draw in the water they drink by placing their mouth to it, as oxen do, but seize it with the tongue into the mouth [Col. 1161B], just as these men are understood to have done when they put water into their mouths with their hand and received it with their tongue.

The translation from the Hebrew expresses this more clearly in these words: “The number of those who had lapped the water, with the hand putting it into the mouth, was three hundred men.” For people do not ordinarily drink in such a way that, without the work of their hand, their tongue draws up water like a dog’s. Or perhaps these men had been commanded to do this; but when they had gone down to the water to drink, many drank on bended knee, since that could be done more easily and with less effort. A few, however, did not bend the knee but stooped and drank like dogs, using water thrown into the mouth by hand.

Their number, since they were three hundred, suggests the sign of the cross because of the Greek letter Τ (tau), in which this number is signified. Here also it was prefigured that the nations would believe more fully in the Crucified One, since this is a Greek letter. Hence the Apostle signifies all the nations by the name “Greeks” when he says, “To the Jew first, and to the Greek,” and “to Jews and Greeks” (Rom. I), often in this way mentioning circumcision and uncircumcision, because the Greek language so excels among the languages of the nations that through it all of them may suitably be signified.

This number must also be noticed in Abraham’s household servants, through whom he rescued his brother from his enemies, when Melchizedek blessed him in a great mystery (Gen. XIV). The fact that eighteen is added there—for they are reported to have been three hundred and eighteen—seems to me to signify also the time at which this would occur, namely, the third age, which was to be under grace. The first age is before the Law, the second under the Law, and the third under grace. Each of these ages is signified by the number six, because of perfection; for three times six makes eighteen.

Thus also that woman had been ill for eighteen years whom the Savior found bent over and raised upright, freeing her, as the Gospel indicates, from the bondage of the devil (Luke XIII). The fact that these men were tested in such a way that they were said to be like dogs in drinking signifies that the Lord chooses what is contemptible and ignoble (I Cor. I), for a dog is regarded as contemptible. Hence he says, “It is not right to take the children’s bread and throw it to dogs” (Matt. XV). David too, wishing to cast himself away as contemptible, called himself a dog when speaking to Saul (I Sam. XXIV).

In nearly all the deeds of the ancients great mysteries are signified [Col. 1162A], as we see happening also in this passage. Those who go down to the water—that is, those who come to the grace of baptism—must not fall prostrate on the ground, bend their knees, and yield to the temptations of the belly; rather, they must stand bravely and steadfastly, just as the Apostle also said: “Raise up the hands that hang down and the weakened knees, and make straight paths for your feet” (Heb. XII).

You have come to the water of baptism. This is the beginning of spiritual struggle and warfare. Here the beginning of your battle against the devil arises. If you are more relaxed, if you can easily be bent, how will you fight? How will you stand against the devil’s wiles? Therefore the Apostle also cries out: “Stand firm, then, and do not submit again to the yoke of slavery” (Gal. V). And again he says: “Stand firm in the Lord” (Phil. IV). And a third time he says: “For now we live, if you stand firm in the Lord” (I Thess. III).

The one, therefore, who is approved and chosen is he who, once he has come to the waters of baptism, does not know how to bend toward earthly and bodily necessities; who does not indulge his vices, nor lie prostrate because of the thirst for sin. Moreover, when Scripture says that they lapped the water with hand or tongue, I do not think that this is without a certain sacramental significance. It indicates, namely, that Christ’s soldiers must labor with both hand and tongue—that is, by deed and by word—because “whoever teaches and does them shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven.”

The fact that Scripture also introduced the likeness of a lapping dog seems to me to mean that this animal is named here because it is said to preserve, above all other animals, love for its own master, and is reputed not to erase its affection for him either with time or through mistreatment [Col. 1162C].

The three hundred alone, who prefigured the image of this sacrament, were chosen, approved, and consecrated for victory; by the sacrament of the number itself they could also overcome their adversaries. For there are three hundred, multiplying one hundred by three, and they bear the number of the perfect Trinity.
