Under this number Christ’s entire army is reckoned, in which we obtain the privilege of deserving to be enrolled.

With the three hundred Gideon went forth to battle, and he armed them not with weapons but with trumpets, lamps, and jars. For, as it is written there, they placed burning lamps inside jars; they held trumpets in their right hands and jars in their left. Coming close to their enemies, they blew the trumpets and smashed the jars; the lamps appeared [Col. 1162D], and the enemies, terrified on one side by the sound of the trumpets and on the other by the flashing of the lamps, were put to flight.

Of this battle the prophet says: “For you have broken the yoke of his burden and the rod of his oppressor, as on the day of Midian.” In rescuing the Gentiles, the Lord overcame the yoke of their burden when, by his coming, he freed them from the slavery of demonic tyranny. He also overcame the rod of their exactor when he destroyed in the hearts of the faithful the kingdom of that devil who, because of the deadly commission of vices, had been accustomed to exact the due tribute of punishments.

Why does the prophet bring such a battle into the middle of his prophecy and compare the victory of this struggle with the coming of our Redeemer? Did the prophet perhaps intend to show us that the victory of the battle fought under Gideon signified the coming of our Redeemer against the devil? Certainly such things were done there that, the more they surpass ordinary methods of warfare, the more they do not depart from the mystery of prophecy.

Who has ever come to battle with jars and lamps? Who, coming against weapons, has abandoned weapons? These things would surely have seemed ridiculous to us if they had not been terrifying to the enemies. But the victory itself bears witness that we must not regard lightly what was done.

Gideon, then, coming to battle, signifies the coming of our Redeemer, of whom it is written: “Lift up your gates, O princes, and be lifted up, eternal gates, and the King of glory shall enter. Who is this King of glory? The Lord strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle” (Ps. XXIII).

He prophesied this Redeemer of ours not only by deed but also by name. For *Gedeon* is interpreted as “going around in the womb.” Our Lord, through the power of his majesty, fills all things, and yet through the grace of his dispensation came within the Virgin’s womb.

What is “going around in the womb” except that almighty God, redeeming us by his dispensation, embraces all things in his divinity and assumes humanity within the womb—within which womb he was both incarnate and not confined? For he was within the womb according to the substance of weakness, and outside the world according to the power of his majesty.

*Madian* is interpreted as “from judgment.” The fact that his enemies were to be driven back and destroyed resulted not from any fault in the one who drove them back, but from the judgment of the one who judged justly. They are therefore called “from judgment” because, through the grace of the Redeemer, they draw even the merit of just condemnation into the meaning of their name.

Gideon goes to war against the enemies with three hundred men. The number one hundred is customarily understood to signify the fullness of perfection. What, then, is signified by the number one hundred multiplied by three except perfect knowledge of the Trinity? With these our Lord destroys the adversaries of the faith; with these he descends into the battles of preaching—those who can know divine things and understand perfectly what God is in the Trinity.

It must also be noted that this number three hundred is contained in the letter T, which bears the form of the cross. If what projects above the transverse line were added to it, it would no longer be merely the form of a cross but the cross itself. Since, then, the number three hundred is contained in the letter T, and through the letter T, as we have said, the form of the cross is displayed [Col. 1163D], it is not without reason that in these three hundred who followed Gideon those are signified to whom it was said: “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Matt. XVI).

Those who follow God take up the cross all the more truly the more vigorously they subdue themselves and are afflicted with compassion of charity toward their neighbors. Hence Ezekiel also certainly expresses through these three hundred, who are contained in the letter T as stated above, that the iron of the enemies is overcome by the wood of the cross (Ezek. IX).

They were brought to the river to drink water. Those who drew up the water on bended knees were removed from the intention of warfare. For water signifies the doctrine of wisdom, while the upright knee signifies right action. Those, therefore, who are said to have bent the knee while drinking water withdrew, being excluded from the struggle of the others, because Christ goes to battle against the enemies of the faith with those who, while drawing in the streams of doctrine, do not bend away from upright conduct.

All are said to have drunk water then, but not all are said to have done so with an upright knee. Those who bent their knees while drinking were rejected because, as the Apostle testifies, “it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law who will be justified” (Rom. II). Since, as we have said, looseness of conduct is signified by the bending of the knees, Paul rightly says again: “Raise up the hands that hang down and the weakened knees, and make straight paths for your feet” (Heb. XII).

Those, therefore, advance to battle under Christ’s leadership who show by their deeds what they announce with their mouths; who spiritually drink in the streams of doctrine and yet are not carnally bent toward wicked works, because, as it is written: “Praise is not fitting in the mouth of a sinner” (Ecclus. XV).

They went to battle with trumpets, lamps, and jars. And this, as we said, was the order of battle: they blew the trumpets; the lamps had been placed inside the jars; when the jars were broken, the lamps were displayed, and the enemies, terrified by their flashing light, were put to flight.

The trumpets therefore signify the cry of preachers, the lamps the brightness of miracles, and the jars the frailty of bodies. Our leader brought such men with him to the battle of preaching: men who, scorning the preservation of the body, would overthrow their enemies by dying and overcome their swords not with weapons and swords but with patience.

Our martyrs came armed to battle under their leader, but they resounded with trumpets, jars, and lamps. They blew the trumpets when they preached; they broke the jars when they exposed their bodies, destined to be dissolved in suffering, to the enemy’s swords; they shone as lamps when, after the dissolution of their bodies, they were seen to flash with miracles. By the law of truth, they believed that they had come into the battle.

They blew the trumpets so that the jars might be broken; the jars were broken so that the lamps might appear; the lamps appeared so that the enemies might be put to flight. That is: the martyrs preached until their bodies were dissolved in death; their bodies were dissolved in death so that they might shine through miracles; they shone through miracles so that by the divine light they might overthrow their enemies, so that the enemies would in no way resist God with uplifted heads but, subjected to him, would fear him.

It must also be noted that the enemies stood before the jars but fled before the lamps. Through the persecutors of the holy faith they resisted the preachers while the latter were still in the body; but after the dissolution of their bodies, when miracles appeared, they were put to flight, because, struck with fear, they ceased persecuting the faithful. They feared the preaching of the trumpets when the jars of the bodies had been broken and the lamps of the miracles had been seen.

We must also consider what is written there: they held the trumpets in their right hands but the jars in their left. We call whatever we value greatly “right”; what we regard as worthless we call “left” [Col. 1165A]. It is therefore rightly written there that they held the trumpets in their right hands and the jars in their left, because Christ’s martyrs regarded the grace of preaching as highly valuable but the usefulness of their bodies as of little worth.

Whoever values the usefulness of the body more than the grace of preaching holds the trumpet in his left hand and the jar in his right. If the grace of preaching is kindled in the first place and the usefulness of the body in the second, it is certain that the trumpets are held on the right and the jars on the left.

## CHAPTER VI. The Lord’s command to Gideon to descend into the camp of the Midianites, where, hearing someone recount a dream, he was strengthened and routed the camp of Midian with three hundred men.

[Col. 1165B] *(Same place.)* That same night the Lord said to him: “Rise, go down into the camp, for I have delivered them into your hand. But if you are afraid to go alone, let Phurah your servant go down with you. When you hear what they are saying, then your hands will be strengthened, and you will descend more confidently to the camp of the enemy.”

So he went down, and Phurah his servant with him, to the section of the camp where the armed guards were stationed. The Septuagint has: “Gideon himself and Phurah his servant went down to the section of the fifty who were in the camp.” Some Latin codices have: “To the part where there were fifty guards in the camp”; others: “To the fiftieth part of the camp.” This obscure statement has produced several interpretations: either it was that part of the camp guarded by fifty sentries, or fifty men are to be understood as having guarded the surrounding area in one section, and Gideon descended to where the fifty were [Col. 1165C].

Now Midian and Amalek and all the eastern peoples lay spread out in the valley like a multitude of locusts; their camels too were innumerable, like the sand that lies on the seashore.

Whoever speaks of heavenly things, whoever discusses spiritual matters, whoever reveals the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven—that person sounds the trumpet. He speaks with the trumpet who speaks of great and exceedingly great things, who unfolds the knowledge of Christ to human ears.

But why is the trumpet also called *horned*? Because it is said of the holy man: “His horn shall be exalted in glory” (Ps. III). Thus each trumpet is called horned insofar as it expounds the manifold knowledge of Christ and the mysteries of his cross, which is signified by the horn.

With this trumpet, therefore, while serving and fighting, we conquer foreign peoples, put enemies to flight, and do so even when their multitude is like locusts. For the multitude of demons is compared to locusts, since they have a dwelling neither in heaven nor on earth. Let the light of knowledge, the strength of divine speech, and preaching therefore precede us in this battle of works. Let us also fight while singing hymns, psalms, and spiritual songs, crying out to God, so that we may deserve to obtain victory from him.

*(Same place.)* When Gideon had come, someone was recounting a dream to his companion and described what he had seen in this way: “I saw a dream, and it seemed to me that a barley loaf, like a cake baked under ashes, rolled into the camp of Midian. When it reached the tent, it struck and overturned it, and leveled it completely to the ground,” etc.

The man who recounted this dream to his companion—and Gideon heard him—said that he had seen a barley loaf rolling through the camp, striking and overturning the tent of Midian. This, I think, is to be understood as meaning that, through bread—that is, through the contemptible things of the world, signified by the barley loaf—the Savior was to confound the proud.

They held lamps in their left hands and sounding trumpets in their right, and they cried out: “The sword of the Lord and of Gideon,” each standing in his place around the enemy camp, and the rest. The cry that Gideon ordered his three hundred men to utter—“The sword of the Lord and of Gideon,” or, according to the Septuagint, “The sword for the Lord and for Gideon,” that is, for this Gideon—signifies that the sword would accomplish what was pleasing to the Lord and to Gideon.

## CHAPTER VII. How Gideon sent messengers throughout all Mount Ephraim, ordering them to descend to meet Midian and seize the waters.

*(Same place.)* Gideon sent messengers throughout all Mount Ephraim, saying: “Descend to meet Midian, and seize the waters as far as Beth-barah and the Jordan.” All Ephraim cried out and seized the waters as far as Beth-barah and the Jordan. They captured two men of Midian, Oreb and Zeeb; they killed Oreb at the rock of Oreb and Zeeb at the winepress of Zeeb, and they pursued Midian, etc.

Gideon sends messengers to Mount Ephraim when our Redeemer directs his teachers to the catholic people, to a fruitful or increasing place where virtues bear fruit and the height of contemplation excels. He orders them to go to meet Midian and join him in battle against the enemies of the Church, those who turn aside from the judgment of truth—for that is what *Madian* signifies. They seize the waters as far as Beth-barah and the Jordan, namely, the waters of baptism, because there the army of the enemies is drowned and can advance no farther, where the kingdom of Christ succeeds.

The names of the places themselves aptly signify this. Beth-barah is interpreted as “house of humility” or “house of evening,” and Jordan as “their descent.” Humility is therefore displayed in the Church where vices are killed and sins laid aside [Col. 1166D]. There Ephraim’s enemies are driven back when believers renounce the devil and all his works and pomps.

Oreb and Zeeb, the princes of Midian, are captured and killed when the principalities and powers of this darkness are there triumphed over and the devil’s kingdom is scattered. *Oreb* is interpreted as “raven” or “dryness,” and *Zeeb* as “wolf.” These two names fittingly express the devil’s greed and ferocity; for, as the Apostle Peter testifies, he prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour (I Pet. V).

Oreb is killed at the rock of Oreb when the devil perishes in his own wickedness and hardness. Zeeb is killed at the winepress of Zeeb when, in the very pressure with which he afflicts and crushes the elect, he is overcome and confounded and shown to be worthy of eternal condemnation.

## CHAPTER VIII. How Gideon captured Zebah and Zalmunna, the leaders of the Midianites, and, taking thorns and briers, crushed and ground down the men of Succoth who mocked him, together with them.

*(Chapter VIII.)* Zebah and Zalmunna fled, but Gideon pursued and captured them, while their entire army was thrown into confusion. Returning from battle before sunrise, he seized a young man from the men of Succoth, questioned him about the names of the princes and elders of Succoth, and had him write down seventy-seven men. He came to Succoth and said to them: “Here are Zebah and Zalmunna, concerning whom you taunted me, saying: ‘Perhaps the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna are already in your hands, and for that reason you ask us to give bread to your men who are weary and exhausted.’” He therefore took the elders of the city, together with thorns of the desert and briers, and crushed and ground down the men of Succoth with them. He also overturned the tower of Penuel, killing the inhabitants of the city, etc.

What else are Zebah and Zalmunna, the leaders of the Midianites whom Gideon pursued and captured, meant to signify except philosophers and heretics, members of the devil? *Zebah*, which is interpreted as “victim,” can appropriately represent the philosophers and Gentile theologians who, through their books and cults, supplied food to demons. *Zalmunna*, interpreted as “shadow of disturbance,” signifies heretics, who always dwell in the darkness of error and do not deserve to be illuminated by the light of truth.

Our Gideon, pursuing and capturing such men, throws their entire army into confusion when, through the preaching of the Gospel, crowds of nations are converted from the error of idolatry and the schism of heretics to faith in Christ, while only those who are shown to have been the cause of error and unbelief for the others are marked as captives in the snare of error. Gideon later killed them with his sword, because at the final judgment the Judge of the living and the dead, with the devil and his angels, will deliver them to the Tartarus of hell by the sword of righteous vengeance.

The fact that this same Gideon, after his victory, crushed the men of Succoth and Penuel, who had spoken words of mockery and derision against him while he pursued his enemies, using thorns and briers, and overturned the tower of Penuel, killing the inhabitants of the city, signifies that our Redeemer, after his resurrection and ascension into heaven, crushed and ground down the Jews who mocked the evangelical preaching and the Christian religion, burdened as they were with unfruitful deeds and the thorns of sins, by the sword of righteous vengeance.

He overturned the tower of Penuel—that is, the city of Jerusalem itself—when, through Vespasian and Titus, the Roman commanders, the city was destroyed and the temple burned; some of its inhabitants died from famine, some were killed by the sword, and others were led into captivity.

This same event was prefigured in the forty-two boys at Bethel who mocked the prophet Elisha, saying, “Go up, baldhead! Go up, baldhead!” (II Kings II). For just as two bears came out of the forest and devoured the mocking boys, so those Roman commanders—that is, the two emperors mentioned above—came out of the forest of the nations and, in the forty-second year after Christ’s ascension into heaven, killed and destroyed those who insulted the Lord’s passion in Jerusalem, hemmed in and tightly enclosed on every side at the place of Calvary.

## CHAPTER IX. How the Israelites, asking Gideon to rule over them and his sons, gave him golden earrings taken from the spoil of the Midianites; from these Gideon made an ephod and placed it in his city, Ophrah, and it became a ruin to his household.

*(Same place.)* All the men of Israel said to Gideon: “Rule over us—you, your son, and your son’s son—for you have delivered us from the hand of Midian.” He replied: “I shall not rule over you, nor shall my son rule over you; the Lord shall rule over you.”

He said to them: “I ask one request of you: Give me the earrings from your spoil” (for the Ishmaelites were accustomed to wear golden earrings). They answered: “We shall gladly give them.” They spread out a cloak on the ground and threw the earrings from the spoil onto it. The weight of the earrings requested was one thousand seven hundred shekels, apart from the ornaments, necklaces, and purple garments that the kings of Midian were accustomed to wear, and apart from the golden collars on the camels.

Gideon made an ephod from it and placed it in his city, Ophrah. All Israel prostituted itself after it, and it became a ruin to Gideon and his entire household.

It is customary to ask what an *efud* or *ephod* is. If it is a priestly garment, as many say—or rather an overgarment, which is called *ependyma* in Greek, or *epomis*, which can more accurately be interpreted in Latin as “shoulder garment”—it is reasonably puzzling how Gideon could have made it from so much gold.

For this is how it is written: “The weight of the golden earrings that he had requested was one thousand seven hundred shekels of gold, besides the bracelets, necklaces, and purple coverings that were upon the kings of Midian, besides the collars that were on their camels’ necks. Gideon made it into an ephod and set it up in his city, Ophrah, and all Israel prostituted itself after it there; and it became a stumbling block to Gideon and his household.”

How, then, could this garment have been made from so much gold? The mother of Samuel also made an *efudbar* for her son, as we read (I Kings II), when she gave him to be raised in the temple. There it is clearer that this is a kind of garment.

Was it therefore said, “He set it up in his city,” so that it might be understood from this that it was made of gold? For it does not say “he placed it,” but “he set it up,” since it was so solid and strong that it could be made to stand—that is, once placed, it could remain standing.

When Gideon had made this unlawful object, all Israel prostituted itself after it by following it contrary to the law of God. Here it is not without reason that one asks: since it was not an idol—that is, an image of some false and foreign god—but an ephod, one of the sacred objects of the tabernacle belonging to the priestly vestment, how does Scripture call the people’s pursuit and veneration of it prostitution?

The reason is that, apart from the tabernacle of God, where were the things that God had commanded to be made, it was not lawful for anything similar to be made elsewhere. Therefore Scripture continues: “And it became a ruin to Gideon and his household,” that is, so that they might depart from the God who had been offended. For this too was, in a certain way, a kind of idol: something made by human hands outside God’s tabernacle was worshiped as God, whereas the very things commanded to be made in the tabernacle were directed toward the worship of God rather than being worshiped as God or as an image of God.

Nevertheless, through *efud* or *ephod*, by the figure of speech in which the whole is signified by a part, everything Gideon established in his city may be understood—something resembling God’s tabernacle, as though for the worship of God. Hence this may be the sin of Gideon: that outside God’s tabernacle he made something similar in which God was worshiped. It was not that he set up the ephod, made of solid gold, as an object to be adored; rather, from the gold taken as spoil he made things belonging to the ornaments or furnishings of the sanctuary. All these are signified by the word *ephod* because of the prominence, as I said, of the priestly garment.

The ephod itself was not commanded to be made from gold alone, if it is the shoulder garment of the priestly vestment. Nevertheless, it does contain some gold, for it was divinely commanded to be made of gold, violet, purple, scarlet, and fine linen.

But because the Septuagint translators arranged the passage in such a way that, after mentioning everything Gideon had received from the spoils [Col. 1169C], they added, “Gideon made it into an ephod,” it seems to have been said as though this had been made from all the things mentioned. Yet the expression may also be understood as signifying a part from the whole: “He made it into an ephod” may mean “he made an ephod from it,” or “he made the ephod from part of it,” not consuming all of it for the ephod but expending from it as much as was sufficient.

For in the translation from the Hebrew it is read as follows: “Gideon made an ephod from it.” What is written as *efud* among the Septuagint is reported to be called *ephod* in Hebrew.

Not all priests, however, used such a shoulder garment made of gold, violet, purple, scarlet, and fine linen; only the high priest did. Therefore the garment we mentioned as having been made for Samuel by his mother was certainly not of this kind, since when he was given to be raised, he was not the high priest but merely a boy.

Hence, as has been said, it is called *efudbar*, or rather *efodbach*, as those who know the Hebrew language assert; it is interpreted as “linen ephod.”

Gideon, however, made the garment that was the chief vestment and ornament of the high priest. Through it the other works of the sanctuary were also signified. He established this outside God’s tabernacle in his own city, and because of this sin it became a stumbling block to him and his household, so that the great number of his sons perished—as Scripture narrates afterward.

## CHAPTER X. How the land rested for forty years, during which Gideon ruled, and how Gideon himself had seventy sons by his wives but only Abimelech by his concubine.

*(Same place.)* Midian was humbled before the Israelites, and they could no longer lift up their heads; but the land rested for forty years, during which Gideon ruled.

A question arises that must not be passed over: how did the land rest for forty years in the days of Gideon, when, after the victory by which he delivered the Hebrews, he made an abomination from the gold of the spoils, and all Israel prostituted itself after it, and it became a stumbling block to him and his household? How, then, after such a great crime committed by both Gideon and the people, did the land rest for forty years, when Scripture usually shows that whenever the people prostituted themselves away from the Lord God, they lost peace rather than obtained it and were subjected to enemies rather than protected from their attacks?

It must be understood that Scripture has spoken by prolepsis, that is, by anticipation. Gideon made the ephod against the law of God from the gold taken after the enemies had been defeated and overthrown, because Scripture wished to state in one place both where the gold came from and what was done with it. But this sin occurred at the end of Gideon’s days, when the evils that Scripture subsequently relates also followed, after it had mentioned how many years the land rested during Gideon’s days. In a recapitulation, it mentioned those years—that is, it returned to the order that it had previously interrupted by mentioning first the scandal that occurred last.

Jerobaal, son of Joash, departed and lived in his own house. He had seventy sons, who came forth from his loins, because he had many wives. His concubine, whom he had in Shechem, bore him a son named Abimelech. Gideon, son of Joash, died in a good old age and was buried in the tomb of his father Joash at Ophrah, of the family of Ezri, etc.

Gideon died and left seventy sons, and one named Abimelech, born of a concubine. Abimelech hired worthless and wandering men for himself, and they followed him. He entered his father’s house and killed his brothers, seventy men, upon one stone. Only Jotham the youngest remained, because he had been hidden, etc.

If this event signified nothing prophetic, why would it have been written at such length that Gideon had seventy sons and many wives, as well as a concubine from whom he had one evil son? Since the deed was shameful, it would have been still more shameful if these things appeared in the divine books as an example for posterity—unless the events, through types and figures, displayed the image of some great reality.

Gideon, therefore, as stated above, extended forward a type of the Lord. His many wives are the many nations that have joined themselves to Christ through faith. His seventy sons are the seventy languages spread throughout the world, in which the Lord had generated sons for himself through faith.

Here he calls the concubine the Synagogue, which in the last times will believe in the Antichrist. Concerning it the Apostle John says in the Apocalypse: “They say that they are Jews, and are not, but are the synagogue of Satan” (Apoc. II). From this concubine, in the last times, the most wicked son—that is, the Antichrist—will be born. He will be the son of a slave woman, that is, of the sinful Synagogue, because “whoever commits sin is a slave of sin” (John VIII).

This man, after gathering wicked people to himself, as Abimelech did, will wickedly usurp the kingdom. Having killed the noble sons—that is, those who, believing in Christ from different nations and languages, have been generated by God—he will introduce persecution in order to kill all the saints.

## CHAPTER XI. How Abimelech killed all his brothers except Jotham alone, the youngest son of Jerobaal, who, having been hidden, alone escaped death, and concerning the parable of that same Jotham addressed to the men of Shechem.

### Chapter IX

And Joatham, the youngest son of Jerobaal, remained, and he hid himself. All the men of Shechem and every family of the city of Mello assembled; they went and made Abimelech king beside the oak that stood at Shechem. When this was reported to Joatham, he went and stood on the summit of Mount Gerizim, raised his voice, and cried out:

“Listen to me, men of Shechem; so may God listen to you. The trees went to anoint a king over themselves, and they said to the olive tree, ‘Rule over us,’ etc.”

“But, he says, the younger son alone remained of the seventy, born of a noble marriage, who had hidden himself. He ascended, he says, to the summit of Mount Gerizim and cried out in a loud voice to the people, presenting them with a parable from the sycamore.”

This younger son, then, who fled in order to escape the sword of the enemy, is a figure of the remnant of the people of Israel, who, when Elijah preaches in the last times, will believe and escape the sword of Antichrist. “He ascended,” he says, “to the summit of Mount Gerizim.” But why did he ascend the mountain? Because no one can either prophesy or escape the persecution of Antichrist unless he has first ascended the mountain of blessing—that is, to the height of faith and virtues. For this is Mount Gerizim, which Moses assigns to blessing.

And so, when he had ascended, he raised his voice and cried out: “Listen to me, men of Shechem.” The trees went to anoint a king over themselves and said to the olive tree, “Rule over us.” It answered them: “Can I abandon my richness, by which gods and human beings make use, and go to be promoted among the trees?” The trees then said to the fig tree: “Come and reign over us.” It answered them: “Can I abandon my sweetness and my exceedingly pleasant fruits, and go to be promoted among the other trees?” The trees also spoke to the vine: “Come and rule over us.” It answered them: “Can I abandon my wine, which gladdens God and human beings, and be promoted among the other trees?”

When the trees of the forest had been rejected by the olive, the fig tree, and the vine, they came to the thornbush to make it their king. But first let us see why the olive, the fig tree, and the vine did not wish to reign over the trees.

I think that the trees of the forest are vain and wandering human beings, prepared for eternal fire. Therefore the olive, the fig tree, and the vine rightly refused to reign: they were not worthy. The olive signifies the grace of the Holy Spirit and the anointing of peace. The fig tree bears the image of the sacred Law, as it is written in the Gospel: “A certain householder planted a vineyard, and in his vineyard he planted a fig tree” (Luke XIV). Who is the householder except God, who is the father of his household—that is, of all believers?

He planted a vineyard, that is, the people, because “he brought a vine out of Egypt.” Certainly, it was the people, not a vineyard, that he had brought out of Egypt. In this vineyard he planted a fig tree: that is, he placed the Law among his people. This Law cast the primitive people down to the ground like a fig tree producing large, dry, useless fruits; afterward it produced other fruits, namely, the Christian people, whom it brought to the proper maturity of evangelical discipline and to the exceedingly sweet richness of Christ, with glory and honor.

“But the vine,” he says, “did not wish to reign over them.” It is clear that the vine bears the type of our Savior, as he says in the Gospel: “I am the true vine” (John XV). Therefore, since that people who will serve Antichrist is already destined for a reprobate mind, as the Apostle said, and since it is necessary that the one who refused to believe the truth, Christ, should believe a lie—that is, Antichrist (2 Thess. II)—it was rejected both from the rule of the vine, that is, of Christ, and from the olive, that is, from the grace of the Holy Spirit, and from the fig tree, that is, from the sweetness of the divine Law; and it came to the thornbush.

The thornbush (*rhamnus*) is a kind of bramble commonly called the “bear-thorn,” exceedingly rough and thorny. Through it the type of Antichrist is rightly signified, for he will ravage the human race with every kind of harshness and savagery. “But fire,” he says, “will come out of the thornbush”—that is, iniquity from Antichrist—and will devour together with him all who trust in him.

Gideon, then, appears to have borne the image of Christ; his seventy sons signify the seventy languages or nations that, by believing, merited to become sons of God through a second regeneration. Abimelech, truly a son of a slave woman, bore the type of Antichrist: having gathered the lost nations, he will wickedly usurp the kingdom for himself and slaughter all the saints by force, persecution, and every kind of cruelty.

Joatham, however, was a figure of the saints. For just as Joatham withdrew by flight while the rest of the brothers were killed, so no one will be able to escape the persecution of Antichrist except the one who withdraws by flight and ascends the mountain of blessing. This is the mountain that the saints will surround, which holy Moses also placed in the blessings, as was said above, in Deuteronomy (Deut. XI).

According to the Septuagint, what is introduced here is the thornbush—that is, a certain kind of thorn—speaking as follows to all the trees that were inviting it to reign over them:

“If in truth you anoint me to reign over you, come and trust in my protection. But if not, let fire come out of the thornbush and devour the cedars of Lebanon.”

The meaning is obscure, but the punctuation that has been discovered makes it clear. It should not be read, “And if not, let fire come out of the thornbush,” but the sense should be divided as follows: “And if not,” and then continued: “Let fire come out of the thornbush”—that is, “If you do not trust in my protection,” or, “If you do not truly anoint me to reign over you, let fire come out of the thornbush and devour the cedars of Lebanon.”

These are the words of one threatening what he may do if they refuse to have it reign over them. Yet because it does not say, “Fire will come out of the thornbush and will devour the cedars of Lebanon,” but says, “Let it come out and devour,” the passage is more obscure than it would be if only the punctuation were in question. The threat is more forceful and, in a certain sense, more immediately effective if someone says, “If you do not do what I wish, let my anger rage against you”—that is, “Let it rage now”—than if he says, “It will rage,” threatening punishment in the future by a prospective form.

### Chapter XII

That after the death of Gideon the Israelites turned away and committed fornication with the Baals; and the Lord sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the inhabitants of Shechem, who began to hate him and to attribute to Abimelech and to the other leaders of Shechem who had helped him the crime of murdering the seventy sons of Jerobaal.

After Gideon had died, the Israelites turned away and committed fornication with the Baals. They made a covenant with Baal, so that he might be their god. They did not remember the Lord their God, who had delivered them from the hands of all their enemies round about, and so forth.

The Septuagint has: “And it came to pass, when Gideon was dead, that the Israelites turned away and fornicated after the Baals; and they made Baalberith a covenant for themselves, so that he himself might be their god.”

The Baals and Baalberith are to be understood as idols. Thus the transgression and fornication committed by the people after Gideon’s death was greater than that committed while he was alive on account of the *ephod*. For although that act had been illicit, it nevertheless concerned the sacred things of the tabernacle; this later fornication after idols, however, does not even have the false defense of ancestral religion.

Therefore, even if that *ephod* was made not at the end of Gideon’s life but earlier, God bore it patiently, so that peace continued in the land, because although what he had forbidden had been done, the people had not withdrawn far from the one who had commanded that something of this kind be made in his tabernacle and in his honor. But now he did not wish the graver offenses and the people’s most open fornication after idols to remain unpunished.

The Lord sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the inhabitants of Shechem, who began to hate him and to attribute to Abimelech his brother, and to the other leaders of the Shechemites who had helped him, the crime of murdering the seventy sons of Jerobaal and shedding their blood, and so forth.

“God sent forth an evil spirit between Abimelech and the men of Shechem.” Whether this expression signifies that God commanded or permitted the act cannot easily be determined. The Greek has *exapesteilen*—“sent forth”—for the word used here, and the same word occurs in the Psalms where we read: “Send forth your light” (Ps. XLII). Although in certain passages our translators have rendered the Greek *exapesteilen* as “sent” rather than “sent forth,” it can therefore be understood in this way: God sent forth the evil spirit as one wishing to go among them—that is, he gave the evil spirit power to disturb their peace.

Indeed, it did not seem absurd that an evil spirit should also be sent by the Lord for the sake of just retribution; consequently, some have translated *exapesteilen* as “let in” or “introduced.”

### Chapter XIII

That Gaal, the son of Obed, while seeking to turn the Shechemites away from Abimelech, was killed by him; and that he killed the men of the tower of Shechem by cutting branches from trees and using smoke and fire. Also concerning the death of Abimelech himself.

“Behold, Gaal the son of Obed has come to Shechem with his brothers, and is attacking the city against you. Therefore rise by night with the people who are with you, and lie in ambush in the field; and at first light, when the sun rises, rush upon the city. When he goes out against you with his people, do to him whatever you can,” and so forth.

The words that Zebul, the ruler of the city of the Shechemites, sent by messengers to Abimelech are also given by the Septuagint as follows:

“Now rise by night, you and the people with you, and lie in ambush in the field. And in the morning, as soon as the sun rises, you shall hasten and advance against the city.”

Some Latins have *maturabis* (“you will hasten”), while others have *manicabis*; the Greek has a phrase that could be expressed in English by “you shall rise at dawn.” Perhaps *maturabis* was said from *matutinum* (“morning time”), although the word can also be used at other times for hastening toward a task. I do not recall *manicabis* as a Latin word.

What troubles me is that, after saying “as soon as the sun rises,” the text adds “you shall rise at dawn,” although dawn itself—called *orthros* in Greek—signifies the time before the sun, which is now commonly understood as the time when the sky begins to grow light. It should therefore be understood that the word “morning” refers precisely to dawn. The addition “as soon as the sun rises” expresses that the action is not to be carried out after the sun has already risen, but as soon as the radiance of the rising sun appears.

For dawn becomes light from no other cause than that the sun’s light begins to reach the part of the sky that we see in the east, as the sun returns toward it. This is why, in the Gospel, one evangelist says that the same event took place at dawn, while it was still dark, and another says that it took place at sunrise: for even the faint light of dawn was produced by the sun rising—that is, coming toward its rising and casting its radiance through the nearness of its presence.

Some uneducated people have thought that this light does not belong to the sun but is the light that was created at the beginning, before God created the sun on the fourth day.

But those who lived in the tower of the Shechemites entered the temple of their god Berith, where they had made a covenant with him; from this the place had received its name, and it was very strongly fortified. Berith, therefore, is interpreted as “covenant.” Hence he says that the place was called by the name “covenant,” because the Shechemites had entered into a covenant with the idol in which they trusted to be protected.

When Abimelech heard that the men of the tower of Shechem had gathered together there, he went up Mount Zalmon with all his people. He seized an axe, cut off a branch from a tree, carried it on his shoulder, and said to his companions: “What you see me doing, do quickly.” Thus, cutting branches from the trees in competition with one another, they followed their leader. They surrounded the tower as a defense and set it on fire. And so it happened that, through smoke and fire, about a thousand men and women among the inhabitants of the tower of Shechem were killed, and so forth.

The historical account of how Abimelech overcame and destroyed the Shechemites after dissension and rebellion is well known. But the reader will benefit more if he attentively considers the allegory of the event with a sound eye of faith.

Whom can we better understand this Abimelech, the king of the rebellious, to be than Antichrist, the head and prince of all the wicked? He extinguished the men of the tower of Shechem by cutting branches from Mount Zalmon and using smoke and fire, just as Antichrist blinds the proud through the darkness of the mind and kills them with the fire of desire.

Abimelech is therefore interpreted as “my brother is king”; Shechemites as “shoulders”; and Zalmon as “consenting.”

Thus Abimelech, a degenerate and reprobate king, killed the Shechemites who stood in the tower by means of the burning foliage of their trees. Antichrist will similarly kill those who climb the tower of pride, having obtained the freedom of their own will, by cutting off with the axe of his wickedness and deceit the branches of their trees—that is, the deeds of reprobate human beings who wickedly consent to him. He will blind the eyes of their minds with the smoke of unbelief and suffocate them with the fire of rage and desire.

But just as Abimelech, after completing the slaughter, received a fitting retribution through the compensation of death, so Antichrist himself, after completing his wickedness in the slaughter of the saints, will at the end receive the reward of eternal condemnation from the just Judge.

The historian expresses this in what follows when he relates that Abimelech attacked the tower of the city of Thebez and perished after a woman threw a fragment of a millstone down upon his head and crushed his brain.

For what does this woman signify except the holy Church? Through the fragment of a millstone—that is, through the judgments of sacred Scripture—she crushes the head of Antichrist, which is the devil. She crushes his brain when she overturns the reasoning of his wickedness, preventing him from pouring the poison of his evil into human beings by preaching to them and displaying examples of good works. Finally, united to her Head and conquering death, she condemns forever the author of death, whom the Lord Jesus will indeed kill “with the spirit of his mouth” and destroy “by the brightness of his coming” (1 Thess. II).

### Chapter XIV

That after Abimelech there arose in Israel Thola, son of Phua, Abimelech’s uncle; after twenty-three years Jair the Gileadite succeeded him, and judged Israel for twenty-two years.

### Chapter X

After Abimelech, Thola, son of Phua, Abimelech’s uncle, arose as leader in Israel. He was a man of Issachar and lived in Sanir of Mount Ephraim; he judged Israel for twenty-three years and died and was buried in Sanir.

The Septuagint has: “And after Abimelech there arose to save Israel Thola, the son of his father’s brother, a man of Issachar.”

It calls him “the son of his father’s brother,” whereas it would be more orderly, customary, and clearer to say “the son of his uncle.” For he was the son of his uncle, as is found more clearly in the translation made from the Hebrew.

The expression “of the father’s brother” is therefore not declined from the nominative *pater fratris*, “father of a brother,” but from *patris frater*, “father’s brother”; that is, “uncle.” Whether one puts it in the nominative, *hic pater fratris* (“this father of a brother”), or *hic patris frater* (“this father’s brother”), it forms the genitive *huius patris fratris*, “of this father’s brother.”

But another question arises: how could this man of Issachar have been Abimelech’s uncle—that is, a man from the tribe of Issachar—when Abimelech’s father was Gideon, and Gideon belonged to the tribe of Manasseh?

How, then, were Phua and Gideon brothers, so that Phua could be Abimelech’s uncle and Thola, the son of that uncle, could succeed Abimelech according to this account?

Gideon and Phua could have had the same mother but different fathers, and thus could have been brothers on their mother’s side, not on their father’s. Women used to marry into tribes other than their own. Thus Saul, although he was from the tribe of Benjamin, gave his daughter to David, a man from the tribe of Judah; and the priest of Judah—plainly a man from the tribe of Levi—married the daughter of Joram the king, a man from the tribe of Judah.

This is why we read in the Gospel that Elizabeth and Mary were relatives (Luke I), although Elizabeth was descended from the daughters of Aaron. From this it is understood that a woman from the tribe of Levi and from the daughters of Aaron married into the tribe of Judah, so that a relationship arose between the two women and the flesh of the Lord was propagated not only from royal stock but also from priestly stock.

Jair the Gileadite succeeded Thola. He judged Israel for twenty-two years. He had thirty sons who rode upon thirty young asses, and they were rulers of thirty cities, which were called from his name Havvoth-jair—that is, “the villages of Jair”—in the land of Gilead to the present day. Jair died and was buried in a place called Camon.

Whom does this Jair the Gileadite better designate than our Redeemer, who is leader and king of the Christian people? The names themselves aptly demonstrate this. Jair is interpreted as “illuminating,” and Gilead as “heap of testimony.”

Our Lord is rightly called “illuminating,” of whom it is written in the Gospel: “He was the true light, which enlightens every person coming into this world” (John I); and to whom the Prophet says in the Psalms: “You illuminate wondrously from the everlasting mountains” (Ps. LXXV).

He is therefore from Gilead, because his knowledge is received from the sacred Scriptures; whoever seeks him there with a believing heart undoubtedly finds him.

He judged Israel for twenty-two years because all the faithful who lived under the Old Testament and the New lived under the judgment of his commandments. The number twenty, containing twice ten, signifies the perfection of the Law and the Gospel, in which the supreme and strongest emblem is the two commandments: love of God and love of neighbor. “On these two commandments,” as the Truth itself attests, “hang all the Law and the Prophets” (Matt. XXII).

Therefore the same Savior says to his disciples in the Gospel: “This is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you” (John XV).

This Jair has thirty sons sitting upon thirty young asses because those who are rightly called and are his sons keep the commandments of God in faith in the holy Trinity, and strive to tame the wantonness of their flesh properly and to rule themselves. Therefore they also deserve to be rulers of thirty cities, which were called by his name. Whoever, according to faith in the holy Trinity, fully receives knowledge of God’s Law through keeping his commandments is fit to be set over others.

They are called sons of light from the Light, just as Christians are named from Christ. Hence the Lord says to his apostles: “You are the light of the world. Let your light shine before human beings, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. V).

Jair is read as having died and been buried in a place called Camon. Camon is interpreted as “useless resurrection.” And what resurrection can more fittingly be called useless than the earthly Jerusalem? By refusing to believe, it made the Lord’s resurrection—which is useful and saving for believers—useless and destructive for itself. Therefore its people deserved to be called sons of darkness rather than sons of light, and sons of destruction rather than sons of resurrection.

Heretics or bad Catholics can also appropriately be understood under the name Camon. They are rightly called “useless resurrection,” because it benefited them nothing to be reborn through the grace of baptism when they chose again to become entangled in their former error and in the deeds of the old person. In them our Jair has, in a certain sense, died and been buried, because they have killed within themselves and buried under wicked behavior the grace of faith and the light of knowledge that they received as God’s gift.

### Chapter XV

That the Lord handed sinful Israel over to the hands of the Philistines and the Ammonites, but afterward, when they turned again to repentance, sent them a defender. Jephthah made a vow to the Lord and obtained victory over his enemies.

The Israelites, adding new sins to their former sins, did evil in the sight of the Lord. They served the idols Baalim and Astaroth, and the gods of Syria, Sidon, Moab, the Ammonites, and the Philistines; they abandoned the Lord and did not worship him. Therefore, angered against them, he handed them over to the hands of the Philistines and the Ammonites, and so forth.

The Israelites added to their service of the Baals and foreign gods, and they were handed over to the Ammonites. Then Jephthah the Gileadite, fleeing from the presence of his brothers, was appointed leader against the battle with the Ammonites. After returning in triumph, he sacrificed his daughter, who had been the first to meet him as he returned; for he had vowed that whatever first met him when he came back would be sacrificed to the Lord.

What, then, was being foretold in Jephthah except the Lord Jesus Christ our Savior? He withdrew from the presence of his brothers—that is, the Jews—and received rule among the nations. He fulfilled all the mysteries of human salvation as though bound by an oath, and, like a daughter, offered his own flesh to the Lord for Israel’s salvation.

We read that he swore to the Father and suffered death as the Only-begotten, as the Psalm says: “As he swore to the Lord, he vowed a vow to the God of Jacob” (Ps. CXXXI)—namely, that he would fulfill the mystery of religion in the passion of his flesh for the salvation of the human race.

These events, according to the history of what was done, were thus accomplished through Christ, so that they appear to have been completed through the religion by which he had sworn.

Among the other things that Jephthah commanded to be conveyed by messengers to the king of the Ammonites, he also said: “Will you not inherit whatever Chemosh your god shall inherit for you? And whatever the Lord our God shall inherit from before you, shall we not inherit?”

Some Latins thought this should be interpreted as follows: “Do you not possess whatever Chemosh your god has given you as an inheritance?” This can seem to imply that Jephthah affirmed that the god called Chemosh could give something as an inheritance to his worshipers.

Others have: “Do you not possess whatever Chemosh your god will possess?” This sounds as though Chemosh could possess something. Or perhaps this was said because, according to the song of Moses, the nations were placed under angels, the servants of God. Was the angel under whom the Ammonites stood therefore called Chemosh? Who would dare affirm this, when the statement may instead be understood according to the opinion of those people: he said that their god possessed this, or had given it to them as a possession.

The meaning is clearer in the Greek wording: “Will you not inherit whatever Chemosh your god shall inherit for you?” In the expression “for you,” the sense is understood as though it said, “as it seems to you.” He shall inherit it for you who think this—not because he himself could inherit anything.

Finally, in what follows—“And whatever the Lord our God shall inherit”—it does not say “shall inherit for us,” as though it meant “as it seems to us,” but says that he shall truly inherit from before you, because he took it from them and gave it to these people: “This,” he says, “we shall inherit.”

Concerning Jephthah’s daughter, the fact that her father offered her as a burnt offering to God because he had vowed in battle that, if he conquered, he would offer as a burnt offering whoever came out from the doors of his house to meet him—when he had made this vow, he conquered, and when his daughter met him, he fulfilled what he had vowed—is commonly considered a major and exceedingly difficult question.

Some wish to know its meaning and inquire piously; others, who oppose these holy Scriptures through ignorant impiety, especially bring this accusation against them: that the God of the Law and the Prophets took pleasure even in human sacrifices.

We first answer their calumnies by saying that the Lord of the Law and the Prophets—or, to speak more explicitly, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob—did not take pleasure even in those sacrifices in which the burnt offerings of animals were presented. Rather, because these sacrifices were symbolic and shadows of future things, he wished to commend to us the realities signified by them.

There was also a useful reason why those sacrifices were changed and were not only no longer commanded but actually forbidden to be offered: namely, so that we would not think that God truly took pleasure in such things according to carnal affection.

But whether future things ought also to have been signified through human sacrifices is rightly questioned—not because, in this matter, we ought to shrink from or fear the deaths of human beings who would one day die, if those who willingly accepted such things being done to them were commended to God in eternal reward. If this were true, this kind of sacrifice would not displease God. Yet that it does displease God is clearly attested by the same Scripture.

For although he wished and commanded that all the firstborn should be dedicated to him and belong to him, he nevertheless wished human firstborn to be redeemed by payment, so that people would not think that they ought to sacrifice to God the sons whom they had first brought forth (Exod. XIII).

Then Scripture speaks still more plainly. God disapproves of human burnt offerings so strongly that he forbids them, detesting such practices among other nations and commanding his people not to imitate them:

“When the Lord your God has exterminated the nations into whose land you are entering to inherit it from before you, and you have inherited them and dwell in their land, watch yourself, lest you seek to follow them after they have been exterminated from before you, and lest you seek their gods, saying, ‘As the nations do for their gods, so will I do also.’ You shall not do this to the Lord your God. For they have done for their gods the abominations that the Lord hates, since they also burn their sons and daughters in fire to their gods” (Deut. XII).

What could be shown more clearly by these testimonies of holy Scripture—to omit other passages of this kind—than that God, by whom this Scripture was given to the human race, not only does not love such sacrifices in which human beings are sacrificed but hates them?

He plainly loves and crowns the person who, as a righteous person suffering injustice, contends for the truth unto death, or is killed by enemies whom he has offended on account of righteousness, repaying good for evil—that is, love for hatred.

The Lord speaks of such righteous blood, from the blood of Abel to the blood of Zechariah (Matt. XXIII). Above all, he himself shed blood for us and offered himself as a sacrifice to God. He offered himself in such a way that he was killed by enemies for the sake of righteousness.

Thousands of martyrs imitated him, contending for the truth unto death and being sacrificed by pursuing enemies. Scripture says of them: “As gold in a furnace he tested them, and as a burnt offering he accepted them” (Wis. III). Hence the Apostle also says: “For I am already being poured out as a sacrifice.”

But Jephthah did not make a burnt offering of his daughter to the Lord in this way; rather, animals had been commanded to be offered, and human beings had been forbidden to be sacrificed.

What he did seems rather comparable to what Abraham did, which the Lord expressly commanded (Gen. XXII), although he did not command by a general law that such sacrifices should ever be offered to him; indeed, he entirely prohibited them.

Jephthah’s deed therefore differs from Abraham’s deed because Abraham offered his son when commanded, whereas Jephthah did what both the Law forbade and no special command ordered.

Moreover, not only later in his own Law but already at that time, God showed through Abraham’s own son how little he delighted in such sacrifices. After testing the father’s faith by commanding him, he nevertheless prevented him from killing his son and supplied a ram, by which the sacrifice could lawfully be completed according to the appropriate ancient custom of that time.

If anyone is troubled by how Abraham could have piously believed that God took pleasure in such sacrifices, if they are unlawfully offered to God, and therefore thinks that Jephthah also rightly believed that such a sacrifice could be acceptable to God, let him first consider that it is one thing to undertake something voluntarily and another to obey one who commands.

If a master commands a servant to do something outside the ordinary custom established in the household, and the servant does it in praiseworthy obedience, he is not therefore free from punishment if he presumes to do the same thing voluntarily.

Furthermore, Abraham had reason to believe that, because of the divine command, he should not spare his son—not because he believed that God lawfully accepted such victims, but because he believed that God had commanded this precisely in order to raise the slain man from the dead and thereby demonstrate something as a wise God.

This is also read of him in the Epistle entitled “To the Hebrews,” where his faith is praised because he believed that God could raise his son from the dead (Heb. XI).

Jephthah, however, without God’s command or request and contrary to his lawful precept, voluntarily vowed a human sacrifice. For it is written:

“Jephthah made a vow to the Lord and said: ‘If you truly deliver the Ammonites into my hand, then whoever comes out from the doors of my house to meet me when I return in peace from the Ammonites shall belong to the Lord, and I shall offer him as a burnt offering.’”

He plainly did not vow an animal that he could offer as a burnt offering according to the Law. It was neither customary nor possible that animals should come out to meet commanders returning victorious from battle.

As for mute animals, dogs usually run out to meet their masters, playing with them in affectionate service. Jephthah could not have been thinking of these, lest he appear to have vowed to God something not only unlawful but contemptible and, according to the Law, unclean.

He does not say, “Whatever goes out from the doors of my house to meet me, I shall offer it as a burnt offering,” but says, “Whoever comes out, I shall offer him.” Here he clearly thought of nothing other than a human being.

Yet perhaps he was not thinking of his only daughter, although who could precede her in such paternal glory—unless perhaps a wife? For he does not say *quaecumque* (“whatever female”), but *quicunque* (“whoever”) comes out from the doors of my house. Scripture commonly uses the masculine gender for either sex, as when it says of Abraham, “Rising from the dead” (Gen. XXIII), although it was his wife who had died.

Since, then, Scripture appears to have made no judgment concerning this vow and deed, as it made an entirely clear judgment concerning Abraham when he offered his son at God’s command, but merely left the matter in writing for readers to judge—just as it did with the deed of Judah, the son of Jacob, when he unknowingly went in to his daughter-in-law and, insofar as it depended on him, committed fornication because he thought she was a prostitute (Gen. XXXVIII)—and since Scripture neither approved nor condemned that act but left it to be evaluated and weighed in light of justice and God’s Law, we could now say that such a vow displeased God and that the punishment was brought upon it so that the father’s only daughter would meet him in particular.

If he had hoped for and desired that outcome, he would not have torn his garments as soon as he saw her and said: “Alas, my daughter! You have hindered me; you have become an obstacle before my eyes.”

Furthermore, after such a long delay of sixty days had been granted to his daughter, the Lord did not prevent him from sacrificing his only beloved child, as he had prevented Abraham. He allowed him to inflict upon himself the gravest bereavement by carrying out what he had vowed, without in any way propitiating God through the sacrifice of a human being.

We could therefore say that such a punishment had been repaid to that father so that the example of such a vow would not remain unpunished: otherwise people might think that they were vowing something great to God when they vowed human victims, and, more horrifyingly, their children; or else such vows might be considered not genuine but rather pretended, if those who made them hoped, following Abraham’s example, that God would prevent their fulfillment.

We could say these things, I repeat, unless two testimonies of the divine Scriptures in particular held us back from this judgment, compelling us to examine more carefully and cautiously, insofar as the Lord helps us, an event recorded in books of such authority, lest we pronounce a rash judgment in either direction.

The first testimony is that in the Epistle to the Hebrews this Jephthah is counted among such men that we hesitate to condemn him. It is written there:

“And what more shall I say? For time will fail me if I tell of Gideon, Barak, Samson, and Jephthah, and David and Samuel and the prophets, who through faith conquered kingdoms, worked righteousness, and obtained promises” (Heb. XI).

The second is that when Scripture narrates concerning him that he made such a vow and fulfilled it, it first says:

“And the spirit of the Lord came upon Jephthah, and he passed through Gilead and Manasseh, and passed through the watchtower of Gilead, and from the watchtower of Gilead crossed over against the sons of Ammon; and Jephthah made a vow to the Lord,” and so forth.

These words pertain to the very vow in question, so that everything done afterward appears to be understood as the work of the spirit of the Lord, which had come upon him.

These testimonies compel us to ask rather why the deed happened than to condemn too readily what was done.

But first, the point I mentioned from the Epistle to the Hebrews: among those praiseworthy men who are recalled there, it is not only Jephthah but also Gideon, of whom Scripture likewise says: “The spirit of the Lord strengthened Gideon” (Judg. 6). Yet not only can we not praise his deed—namely, that he made from the gold of the spoil an ephod, and “all Israel fornicated after it, and it became a scandal to the house of Gideon” (Judg. 8)—but, because Scripture here judges the matter most explicitly, we do not hesitate to condemn it. [Col. 1182A] Nevertheless, this does not constitute any injury to the spirit of the Lord, which strengthened him so that he might defeat the enemies of his people with such ease. Why, then, is he mentioned among those “who through faith conquered kingdoms, practiced righteousness, and obtained promises,” unless it is because Holy Scripture, while truthfully praising the faith and righteousness of such men, is not thereby prevented from also truthfully noting whatever sins it knows and judges ought to be noted? Indeed, in the matter of Gideon’s requesting a sign and, as he himself said, testing God with the fleece (Judg. 6), I do not know whether he did not transgress the commandment that says: “You shall not test the Lord your God” (Deut. 6). Nevertheless, even in his testing, the Lord displayed what he wished to foretell: in the fleece soaked with dew while the entire threshing floor around it was dry, he prefigured the first people, Israel, among whom the saints possessed heavenly grace like spiritual rain. [Col. 1182B] Then, in the threshing floor soaked with dew while the fleece was dry, he prefigured the Church spread throughout the whole world, possessing heavenly grace not in the fleece as in a covering, but openly, while that earlier people had become estranged from and dried up by the dew of the same grace. Yet it was not without reason that, because of the good and faithful life in which he should be believed to have died, he deserved such testimony in the Epistle to the Hebrews, among the faithful and those who practiced righteousness.

Whether, however, because after it was said, “The spirit of the Lord came upon Jephthah,” the events that followed—his making that vow, conquering his enemies, and fulfilling what he had vowed—should all be attributed to the spirit of the Lord, so that this sacrifice too should be regarded as one which the Lord commanded to be performed, as he did in Abraham’s case, I would not readily say. For a distinction can certainly be made in Gideon’s case: after the sin he committed when he made the ephod, after which the whole people fornicated, no prosperity of his is recorded; whereas after Jephthah made his vow, his famous victory followed—the very victory for the sake of obtaining which he had made the vow—and once he had obtained it, he fulfilled what he had vowed. [Col. 1182C]

Again, however, we must consider that although Gideon did not receive his victory after making the ephod, he did receive it after testing the Lord—which was certainly a sin—when, after slaughtering and defeating his enemies in a great massacre, he obtained deliverance for the people. For it is written: “And Gideon said to the Lord: Let not your indignation be kindled against me, and I shall speak once more; I shall test once more with the fleece” (Judg. 6). He feared God’s anger because he knew that by testing him he was sinning, something God most clearly forbids in his law. Yet this sin of his was followed both by the evidence of a wondrous sign and by the great success of victory and the people’s deliverance. God had already determined to help the afflicted people, and he made use of the mind of this leader, whom he had chosen for that task—not only of his faithful and devout mind, but also of one that was failing and sinning—to foretell what he wished and to accomplish what he had declared.

For God brought many benefits to his people not only through these men who, although they sinned, are nevertheless recounted among the righteous, but also through Saul himself, who was entirely rejected. The spirit of God came upon him too, and he prophesied—not while he was acting justly, but while he was raging against the holy and innocent man David (1 Sam. 10). The spirit of the Lord acts through both the good and the wicked, through those who know and those who do not know, accomplishing what it knows and has determined must be accomplished. Through Caiaphas too, the fiercest persecutor of the Lord, who did not know what he was saying, it uttered the remarkable prophecy that Christ ought to die for the nation (John 11).

Who acted, then, unless it was the spirit of the Lord, which cared to foretell future events, so that Gideon—wishing to test the Lord and not believing what had already been spoken to him through his hands concerning the people’s deliverance—should have this particular thought arise in his mind: first, the fleece soaked with dew and afterward dry, and the threshing floor first dry and afterward watered? His failure of faith should be attributed to his weakness and sin; but the fact that God used even such a mind for what had to be signified to the human race should be understood as belonging to God’s mercy and wondrous providence.

If someone says that Gideon did and said everything knowingly through prophetic revelation, so that such signs might be displayed through him; that he did not fail in faith, but believed what the Lord had already promised him; and that in prophetic action he wished to test the Lord with the fleece, so that his testing was without blame, just as Jacob’s deception (Gen. 27) was; and that when he said to the Lord, “Let not your indignation be kindled against me,” he did not say this because he feared the Lord’s anger, but because he recognized that the Lord was not angry when he did what, as a prophet, he understood—under the direction of the Lord’s spirit—to be necessary: let him say so as he sees fit, provided that he does not dare to excuse from sin whatever the Scripture itself condemned in the matter of the ephod. [Col. 1183C]

For even the deed by which the three hundred men—belonging by that very number to the sign of the cross—took earthen jars and enclosed burning torches within them, and when the jars were broken the suddenly flashing lights terrified so great a multitude of enemies: Gideon appears to have done this on his own initiative. Scripture does not say that the Lord instructed him to do it. Yet, since this was so great a sign, who but the Lord inspired Gideon’s mind and counsel to do it? He prefigured that his saints would possess the treasure of evangelical light in earthen vessels, as the Apostle says: “But we have this treasure in earthen vessels” (2 Cor. 4). When these vessels were broken in the passion of martyrdom, a greater brilliance of their glory flashed forth, overcoming the ungodly enemies of evangelical preaching with the unexpected brightness of Christ. [Col. 1183D]

Thus, whether through those who knew or those who did not know, the spirit of the Lord worked in prophetic times to prefigure and proclaim future events. Yet their sins should not for that reason be said not to have been sins, because God, who knows how to make good use even of our evils, also used their very sins to signify what he wished.

Therefore, if it was not a sin—whether to vow or to fulfill a sacrifice involving the death of any human being, even a parricidal sacrifice—because it signified something great and spiritual, then God forbade such things and testified that he hated them for no reason. For those things that he commanded to be done are likewise referred to some signification of great spiritual realities. Why, then, would he forbid those acts, since, on account of the same signification of those realities, they could have been performed licitly just as the others were? It is because human sacrifices did not please God, even when they signified something such as it is fitting to believe they signified: not when someone is killed by enemies because he wished to live rightly or refused to sin, but when one human being is slaughtered by another as a chosen victim, like an animal.

“But what if,” someone might say, “because animal victims, through having become customary, although they too are referred by those who understand correctly to the signification of spiritual realities, nevertheless made people less attentive to seeking the great mystery of Christ and the Church, God—wishing by a remarkable and unexpected event to rouse human minds as though from sleep, all the more because he had forbidden such sacrifices to be offered to him—arranged for something of this kind to be offered, so that the very astonishment would generate a great question, and the great question would raise the zeal of a devout mind to investigate the great mystery; and so the mind of a human being, searching devoutly, might draw up the Lord Christ, like a fish on a hook, from the depths of the Scriptures to the height of prophecy?”

We do not resist this explanation and consideration. But one question concerns the mind of the person making the vow, and another concerns the providence of God, who makes the best use of that person’s mind, whatever it may be. Accordingly, if the spirit of the Lord that came upon Jephthah absolutely commanded him to make this vow—a matter that Scripture has not disclosed—nevertheless, if the one who commanded it was he whose commands may not be disregarded, then not only is ignorance not to be blamed, but obedience is even to be praised. For even if a person were to kill himself—which, when done by human will and deliberation, is certainly a wicked act—it must plainly be understood as obedience rather than crime if it was commanded by God. We discussed this question sufficiently in the first book of *The City of God*.

But if Jephthah, following human error, thought that a human sacrifice ought to be vowed, then his sin was justly punished through his only daughter. He himself also seems to make this sufficiently clear in his words, when he says: “Alas, my daughter! You have hindered me; you have become an obstacle in my eyes,” while also tearing his garments. Yet even here his error possesses a certain praise of faith: he feared God, so that he might fulfill what he had vowed, and he did not evade the sentence of divine judgment against himself—whether he hoped that God would forbid it, as he had done for Abraham, or whether he resolved to carry out God’s will, understanding that God did not forbid it, rather than disregard it.

Nevertheless, it may rightly be asked here too whether those who understand the matter more truly do not understand that the Lord did not wish this to be done, and that God would rather have been obeyed if it had not been done, since he had shown both in the case of Abraham’s son and in his lawful prohibition that he did not wish it. Yet if Jephthah refrained from doing it for that reason, he would seem rather to have spared his only daughter than to have followed God’s will. Did he therefore understand more correctly that, in the fact that his daughter came out to meet him, God was acting as an avenger, and did he faithfully submit himself to a just punishment, fearing a harsher vengeance as though for evasion? [Col. 1185A]

For he believed that the soul of his good and virgin daughter would also be well received: she had not vowed herself to be sacrificed, but had not resisted her father’s vow and will, and had followed God’s judgment. For just as death may neither be voluntarily inflicted on oneself nor voluntarily inflicted on another, so, when God commands it, it must not be refused. By God’s appointment it must be undergone at whatever time he determines; and no one who refuses to endure it is striving to avoid it altogether, but only to postpone it.

Now let us inquire, as far as God helps us, and briefly explain what the spirit of the Lord prefigured in this event—whether through Jephthah’s ignorance or knowledge, through his imprudence or obedience, through his offense or faith. For this passage of Holy Scripture admonishes and urges us, in a certain way, to consider a powerful man of virtue. Jephthah is described as such; his name is interpreted as “opening.” The Lord Christ, as the Gospel indicates, “opened the understanding” of his disciples so that they might understand the Scriptures (Luke 24).

Jephthah’s brothers rejected him and expelled him from his father’s house, charging him with being the son of a prostitute, as though they themselves had been born of a legitimate wife (Judg. 11). The chief priests, scribes, and Pharisees did the same against the Lord. They appeared to boast of observing the law, as though he were abolishing the law and therefore were not a legitimate son. Although he had assumed a body from the holy Virgin, and that body was born for the faithful, nevertheless, insofar as his nation is concerned, his mother may also be called that Jewish synagogue. Let whoever wishes turn over the prophetic books and observe how often, and with how much severity and indignation of speech, that people are accused of their fornications like an immodest woman.

This is also the meaning of the very frequent references in this book: either when, after Gideon made the ephod, all Israel is read to have fornicated (Judg. 8), or when they went after the gods of the nations by whom they were surrounded. For this reason divine anger was aroused against them, so that they were crushed by the Ammonites for eighteen years.

But were not the priests, scribes, and Pharisees whom we said were prefigured in those people—who persecuted and expelled Jephthah as they did the Lord Christ, as though he were an illegitimate son—also born from that same Israelite people? Yet the resemblance is shadowed forth in this respect: those men, as I said, seemed to themselves, as observers of the law, rightly to expel as illegitimate one whom they thought acted contrary to the law’s commandments. In this sense that people is said to fornicate: by not observing the commandments of the law, it did not show fidelity to the law as to a husband.

Thus it is written of Jephthah: “And the sons of the wife grew up, and they expelled Jephthah.” The word translated “grew up” signifies figuratively “prevailed.” This was fulfilled in the Jews, who prevailed over Christ’s weakness, because he wished to endure from them what he ought to endure in his passion. The same thing was signified when Jacob prevailed over the angel with whom he wrestled (Gen. 32), for he wrestled with him in order to portend this very event.

They therefore said to Jephthah: “You shall not inherit in our father’s house, because you are the son of a prostitute.” It was as though they were saying what the Gospel says: “This man is not from God, because he keeps not the sabbath” (John 9). Presenting themselves as legitimate sons, they said to the Lord: “We were not born of fornication; we have one Father, God” (John 8).

## Chapter 11

“And Jephthah fled from the face of his brothers and dwelt in the land of Tob.” He fled because he concealed how great he was; he fled because he remained hidden from them while they raged. For “if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2). He fled because they saw the weakness of the dying man but did not see the power of the one rising again.

He dwelt in a good land—or, to speak more precisely, an excellent one. What is called *agathon* in Greek is called *optimum*—“excellent”—in Latin; it is interpreted as “Tob.” Here [the text is defective; apparently] his resurrection from the dead is to be understood. For what land is more excellent than an earthly body clothed with the excellence of immortality and incorruption?
