As for what is said of Jephthah—that after fleeing from the face of his brothers and dwelling in the land of Tob, men who were bandits gathered to him and went about with him—although even before the passion it was charged against the Lord that he ate with tax collectors and sinners, when he replied that the healthy have no need of a physician but the sick (Matt. 9), and although he was counted among the wicked (Isa. 53), when he was crucified among thieves and transferred one of them from the cross to paradise, nevertheless, after he rose again and began to exist according to what we explained above, in the land of Tob, wicked people gathered to him for the remission of sins and walked with him because they lived according to his commandments. This continues even now and will continue henceforth, until the wicked flee to him so that he may justify the ungodly who turn to him, and the unrighteous may learn his ways.

Now the fact that those who had rejected Jephthah—who was a Gileadite—turned to him, sought him out, and asked him to be the one through whom they might be delivered from their enemies, clearly prefigures that those who rejected Christ will turn back to him and find salvation in him. This may refer either to those whom the apostle Peter accused of that very crime, as is read in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 2), and whom he urged to turn to the one they had persecuted: they were cut to the heart and desired salvation from the one from whom they had alienated themselves. For what is being delivered from enemies except being delivered from sins? Thus he said to them: “Repent, and let each one of you be baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, and your sins will be forgiven you” (ibid.).

Or it may rather signify that calling of the people of Israel which is hoped for at the end. This seems more clearly indicated by the words: “And it came to pass after the days”—which certainly signifies after a period of time and thereby suggests that we should not understand the event as referring to the time immediately following the Lord’s passion, but to what will happen afterward. The same interpretation also seems to be suggested by the fact that the elders of Gilead came to Jephthah, so that by their old age we may understand later and final times. Gilead is interpreted as “rejecting” or “revelation.” Both meanings suit this event very well, because at first they rejected the Lord Christ, and afterward he will be revealed to them.

That Jephthah was sought as leader against the Ammonites, after whose defeat those who wished to fight against them under his leadership would be delivered, also has its meaning. Ammon is interpreted as “son of my people” or “people of sorrow.” This surely signifies either those enemies who, persisting in unbelief, are foretold as arising from that very people, or all those predestined for Gehenna, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth, like a people of sorrow (Matt. 8 and 22). Yet “people of sorrow” may also appropriately be understood as the devil and his angels, either because they acquire eternal misery for those whom they deceive, or because they themselves have been assigned to eternal misery.

Jephthah’s reply to the elders of Gilead elegantly expresses the prophecy still more clearly: “Did you not hate me, expel me from my father’s house, and dismiss me from among you? Why have you now come to me, when you are in distress?” Something similar was prefigured in Joseph, whom his brothers rejected by selling him (Gen. 37), but when they were afflicted by famine, turned to his aid and mercy (Gen. 42). Here, however, the foreshadowing of future events shines much more brightly: it was not precisely the brothers who had expelled Jephthah who came to him, but the elders of Gilead, [Col. 1187C] supplicating him on behalf of the entire people.

The same nation is called Israel, whether in those who existed at that time and rejected Christ, or in those who afterward returned to seek his help. To the people that is said—whether in its ancestors or in its descendants, which had drawn out and preserved its long hatred, but would at last turn back in those who will then be converted: “Did you not hate me and expel me from my father’s house?” For this was what those who persecuted him thought: that they had cast Christ down from the house of David, in which his kingdom will have no end (Luke 1).

And the elders of Gilead said to Jephthah: “We have now come to you otherwise.” It was as though the Jews converted to Christ were saying: “Then we came to persecute; now we come to follow.” They also acknowledge him as the one who would be their head against their enemies. He replies that if he defeats their enemies, he will be their ruler—something Gideon refused when the Israelites wished him to accept it. For he replied to them: “The Lord will rule over you.” A king is signified by the term “ruler,” although that people did not yet have one in the time of the Judges. They began to have kings with Saul, and afterward his other successors, who are recorded in the books of Kings. For in Deuteronomy, when they are instructed what sort of king they should have, if this should please them, he is not called a king there but a ruler (Deut. 17).

But because this Jephthah prefigured the one who is the true king—as was also written in the title affixed to his cross, which Pilate did not dare to erase or amend—we should understand the words, “I will be your ruler,” in this sense. They had said, “You will be our head,” because “Christ is the head of a man” (1 Cor. 11), and he himself is “the head of the body, the Church” (Eph. 5).

Finally, after Jephthah had delivered them from all their enemies, he did not become their king. We should therefore understand that what was said referred more to the prophecy concerning Christ than specifically to Jephthah, concerning whom Scripture concludes its account as follows: “And Jephthah judged Israel for six years; and Jephthah the Gileadite died and was buried in his city, in Gilead.” He judged Israel, therefore, as the other judges did; he did not reign as the rulers did who are recorded in the books of Kings.

After Jephthah had been appointed their leader, he sent messengers to the enemy first bearing words of peace. This shows the meaning of the Apostle’s words, in whom Christ was speaking: “If it is possible, insofar as it depends on you, live at peace with all people” (Rom. 12). It would take too long for us, in our haste, to examine all the words Jephthah sent to them. Nevertheless, insofar as they concern the signification of future events, they seem to me to be understood in such a way that Christ’s teaching may be discerned in them. They admonish us how we ought to walk—that is, how we ought to live—among those who have not been called according to the purpose, for “the Lord knows those who are his” (2 Tim. 2).

The fact that, when he was about to defeat his enemies, the spirit of the Lord came upon Jephthah signifies the Holy Spirit imparted to the members of Christ. The fact that he passed through Gilead and Manasseh, crossed the lookout of Gilead, and from the lookout of Gilead crossed over to the Ammonites signifies the progress of Christ’s members toward victory over their enemies.

Gilead is interpreted as “rejecting,” and Manasseh as “the necessity of passing through.” Those who are making progress must therefore pass beyond the rejecters—that is, the despisers. They must also pass through necessity, lest, when one who is progressing has passed beyond those who despise him, he yield to those who terrify him. They must also pass beyond the lookout of Gilead, since Gilead is also interpreted as “revelation.”

A lookout is a height from which one sees or looks down—that is, looks from above. The lookout of Gilead therefore seems to me appropriately to signify the pride of revelation, concerning which the Apostle says: “And because of the greatness of the revelations, I might not be exalted” (2 Cor. 12). This too must be passed beyond; one must not remain there, because of the danger of falling. Once these things have been passed through, the enemies are easily overcome. This is signified by the words: “And from the lookout of Gilead he passed over to the children of Ammon,” concerning whom we have already spoken as enemies.

“And Jephthah made a vow and said: If you will indeed deliver the children of Ammon into my hand, then whoever comes out of the doors of my house to meet me when I return in peace from the children of Ammon shall be the Lord’s, and I will offer him as a burnt offering.”

Whatever Jephthah may have had in mind at this point, judging by ordinary human reasoning he does not seem to have had his only daughter in mind. Otherwise, when he saw her coming out to meet him, he would not have said: “Alas, my daughter! You have hindered me; you have become an obstacle in my eyes.” For “you have hindered me” was said as though he judged himself to have been hindered from fulfilling what he had contemplated.

But whom could he have expected to come out first, since he had no other children? Did he have his wife in mind, and did God refuse to allow this to happen, while ensuring that it would not go unpunished, so that no one afterward would dare to do such a thing, and so that, through the great providence evident even in what occurred, the mystery of the Church might be prefigured? The prophecy, then, is composed from both elements: from what the one making the vow had in mind and from what happened against his will.

If he had his wife in mind, the wife is the Church of Christ: “Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh” (Gen. 2). “This is a great mystery,” says the Apostle; “but I am speaking of Christ and the Church” (Eph. 5).

But because this Jephthah’s wife could not be a virgin, the fact that his daughter came out instead and did not remain unavenged signifies both the forbidden sacrifice undertaken by the rashness of the one who made the vow and the virginity of the Church. Nor is it contrary to the truth that the same Church is signified by the name “daughter.” For whom else did that woman also represent when, after touching the fringe of the Lord’s garment and being healed, he said to her: “Daughter, your faith has saved you; go in peace” (Matt. 9)?

And certainly, as no one doubts, he himself openly indicated that he was the bridegroom when he called his disciples the sons of the bridegroom: “Can the sons of the bridegroom fast while the bridegroom is with them? But the days will come when the bridegroom will be taken away from them, and then they will fast” (ibid.).

The burnt offering, therefore, will be the Church, whom the blessed Apostle calls a virgin (2 Cor. 11), when, at the resurrection of the dead, what is written will be accomplished in all: “Death has been swallowed up in victory”; then “he will hand over the kingdom to God and the Father” (1 Cor. 15). That kingdom is the Church herself, and the king is the one whose figure the man who made the vow bore.

But because this will happen when the sixth age has been completed, a postponement of sixty days from her virginity was requested. For the Church is gathered from all the ages. The first of these extends from Adam to the Flood; the second from the Flood—that is, from Noah—to Abraham; the third from Abraham to David; the fourth from David to the deportation to Babylon; the fifth from that deportation to the birth of the Virgin’s son; and the sixth from that time to the end of this world.

Throughout these six ages, as though through sixty days, the holy virgin Church mourned her virginal state, because although it was virginal, it nevertheless contained sins to be mourned. On account of these, the one virgin spread throughout the whole world says every day: “Forgive us our debts.”

He preferred to call these same sixty days two months, as I think, because of the two men: one through whom death came, and the other through whom the resurrection of the dead came; and because of them the two Testaments are also spoken of.

As for the command given in Israel that, from day to day, they should come together for four days each year to lament Jephthah’s daughter, the Gileadite: I do not think that this signifies anything after the completed burnt offering, which will be eternal life, but rather the Church’s past times, in which those who mourned were blessed. Her universality was represented by the four days, on account of the four regions of the world through which she has been spread far and wide.

As a matter of historical fact, however, I do not think that the Israelites established this practice unless they understood that in this event God’s judgment had been directed more toward striking the father, so that no one afterward would dare to vow such a sacrifice. For why would mourning and lamentation have been decreed if that vow had brought joy?

If the later defeat of the people of Ephraim by this same Jephthah also refers to God’s judgment that will occur at the end, as the Lord himself says, “Bring here those who did not wish me to reign over them and kill them before me” (Luke 19), then the forty-two thousand who fell were not mentioned as an accidental number. For just as the two months, because of their sixty days, signify the number six and the six ages, so there too the product of six times seven signifies the same thing insofar as it pertains to the six ages of the world. Six times seven is forty-two; nor is it without reason that Jephthah himself judged the people for six years.

## Chapter 16

Concerning Manue and his barren wife, to whom the angel of the Lord promised a son, Samson, a Nazirite of the Lord; and concerning the burnt offering that the same Manue, instructed by the angel, offered to God.

## Chapter 13

There was a certain man from Saraa, from the tribe of Dan, named Manue, who had a barren wife. The angel of the Lord appeared to her and said: “You are barren and without children, but you shall conceive and bear a son. Therefore beware that you drink neither wine nor strong drink, and eat nothing unclean, because you shall conceive and bear a son whose head no razor shall touch. For he shall be a Nazirite of God from his infancy and from his mother’s womb, and he shall begin to deliver Israel from the hand of the Philistines.”

It may be asked how the angel, when announcing to Samson’s mother that she would have a son, could say that she was barren: “And now observe, and drink neither wine nor strong drink; eat no unclean thing.” For what is unclean except perhaps the dissolution of discipline, which had begun in Israel and had already weakened them so that they were ready to eat what God had prohibited among the various kinds of animals? Why should we not believe that those who were transgressing even into the worship of idols could have been much more inclined to do this as well?

When she came to her husband, she said to him: “A man of God came to me, with the appearance of an angel, exceedingly terrifying. When I asked him who he was, where he had come from, and by what name he was called, he would not tell me.”

In reporting to her husband how the angel had announced the future birth of her son, Samson’s mother said: “I asked him where he was from, and he did not announce his name to me.” It may be asked whether she spoke truthfully, since it is not recorded that she asked this while the angel was speaking to her. But we should understand that Scripture was silent about this there and recalled here what it had omitted there.

There is also an apparent inconsistency in the fact that she did not say, “I asked him what he was called, and he did not announce his name to me,” but said, “I asked him where he was from,” and then added, “He did not announce his name to me.” For she had not asked his name when she asked where he was from, but had asked about his place or city, since she thought he was a human being. She even called him a man of God, although he resembled an angel in appearance or form—that is, because she saw him to be so remarkable, as she herself reported.

But if the sentence is divided as follows—“I asked him where he was from and his name,” with “I asked him” understood with both expressions, followed by “he did not announce it to me”—there is no problem. The statement “he did not announce it to me” can refer to both: neither where he was from nor his name.

But he replied: “Behold, you shall conceive and bear a son. Beware that you drink neither wine nor strong drink, and do not eat anything unclean. For the child shall be a Nazirite of God from his infancy, and from his mother’s womb until the day of his death,” and so forth.

Likewise, although the woman said that the angel had told her that the child would be a Nazirite of God from the womb until the day of his death, this is not recorded as having been said by the angel. And what is recorded as having been said—“He shall begin to save Israel from the hand of the Philistines”—was not mentioned by the woman. Thus she omitted something she had heard, yet we must not believe that she said anything she had not heard. Rather, Scripture did not include all the angel’s words when it inserted into its narrative the angel’s speech to the woman.

It was said, however, “From the womb until the day of his death,” because in the law those were called Nazirites who had vows for a limited period, according to what Scripture commanded through Moses (Num. 6). Hence the commands given to this child—that no iron should come upon his head and that he should not drink wine or strong drink—were things Samson observed throughout his life, whereas those who were called Nazirites observed them for fixed days when they made and fulfilled their vows.

And Manue said to the angel of the Lord: “I beg you to comply with my request, and let us prepare a kid from the goats for you.” The angel of the Lord replied: “If you compel me, I will not eat your food. But if you wish to make a burnt offering, offer it to the Lord.” And Manue did not know that he was the angel of God, and so forth.

When Scripture says that Manue did not know that he was the angel of God, it is clear that his wife too believed him to be a human being. Thus, when he said to him, “Would you like us now to prepare a kid from the goats for you, in your presence?” he invited him as a human being, but in such a way that he might feast with him on what he had prepared as a sacrifice. For one does not ordinarily say “prepare a kid from the goats” unless a sacrifice is being made.

Thus the angel replied: “If you compel me, I will not eat your food,” thereby showing that he had been invited to a feast. Then he added: “And if you make a burnt offering, you shall offer it to the Lord.” He said, “If you make a burnt offering,” precisely because Manue had said, “Let us prepare a kid in your presence.”

Not every sacrifice was a burnt offering. A burnt offering was not eaten, because it was entirely consumed by fire; for this reason it was called a *holocaust*. Although the angel was not going to eat, he instructed him to make a burnt offering—not so much for himself as for the Lord, especially because at that time the people of Israel had become accustomed to sacrificing to any false gods. For this reason they had then offended God, so that he handed them over to their enemies for forty years.

[Col. 1192A] And when the flame of the altar rose into heaven, the angel of the Lord likewise ascended in the flame. When Manoah and his wife saw this, they fell facedown upon the ground, and the angel of the Lord no longer appeared to them. Immediately Manoah understood that he was the angel of the Lord and said to his wife: “We shall surely die, because we have seen the Lord,” and so forth.

What does it mean that, after the angel who had spoken with Manoah and his wife had revealed himself, Manoah said to his wife: “We shall surely die, because we have seen God”? It derives, namely, from that declaration of the Law where it is written: “No one can see my face and live” (Exod. XXXIII). They therefore thought, as human beings, that they had seen God, because such a great miracle had been performed: he who had previously spoken with them almost as a man had stood in the fire of the sacrifice. But [Col. 1192B] were they calling God the one who was in the angel, or were they calling the angel himself God? For this is what is written:

“And Manoah took a kid of the goats and offered the sacrifice upon the rock to the Lord, who works wonders; and Manoah and his wife were watching. And it came to pass, while the flame rose from the altar toward heaven, that the angel of the Lord ascended in the flame. When Manoah and his wife saw this, they fell upon their faces to the ground, and the angel of the Lord did not appear again to Manoah and his wife. Then Manoah knew that he was the angel of the Lord, and Manoah said to his wife: ‘We shall surely die, because we have seen God.’”

In these words, then, because he did not say, “We shall surely die, because we have seen the angel of the Lord,” but rather, “We have seen God,” the question arises whether they understood the Lord to be in the angel, or whether they called that same angel God. [Col. 1192C] The third possibility—that they thought the one who was an angel was God—cannot be maintained, since Scripture most explicitly says: “Then Manoah knew that he was the angel of the Lord.”

But why were they afraid of death? For Scripture in Exodus had not said, “No one shall see the face of an angel and live,” but had said, “my face,” when God was speaking. Or was Manoah so shaken by the very fact that he had recognized God in the angel’s presence that he feared death?

But when his wife answered him: “If the Lord had wished to kill us, he would not have accepted holocausts and a sacrifice from our hand, nor would he have shown us all these things, nor would he have caused us to hear such things,” did they believe that the angel himself had accepted the sacrifice, because they saw him standing in the flame of the altar? [Col. 1192D] Or did they understand that the Lord had accepted it, because the angel did this in order to show that he was an angel?

Whichever of these may be the case, the angel had nevertheless already said: “But if you make a holocaust, offer it to the Lord”—that is, not to me, but to the Lord. Therefore, the fact that the angel stood in the flame of the altar should rather be understood as signifying that the Angel of the Great Counsel, in the form of a servant—that is, in the man whom he was to assume—would not receive a sacrifice but would himself become the sacrifice.

What does it mean that the man is fearful at the vision of the angel, while the woman is bold, except that whenever heavenly things are revealed to us, the spirit indeed trembles with fear, yet hope takes courage? For hope rises to dare greater things precisely from the place where the spirit is shaken—when the mind, having first seen the things above, is lifted toward them. When the raised mind beholds the higher mysteries of heaven, every human strength trembles. [Col. 1193A]

## CHAPTER XVII. On the vengeance that Samson took upon the Philistines because his bride had been taken from him

**(CHAPTER XV.)** “The Philistines went up and burned both the woman and her father. Samson said to them: ‘Although you have done this, I will nevertheless exact vengeance from you, and only then will I rest.’ And he struck them with a great slaughter, so that, stunned, they placed the leg upon the thigh. Then he went down and dwelt in the cleft of the rock of Etam.”

In the edition of the Seventy interpreters this is read: “Samson struck the foreigners, shin upon thigh.”

[Col. 1193B] What does it mean that it is said that Samson struck the foreigners “shin upon thigh”? For who has a shin upon a thigh, since the shin is downward, extending from the knee to the ankle? Moreover, if the passage indicated the bodily place where he wounded them, would he have wounded all those whom he struck in one and the same part of the body? If this were credible, we might perhaps suppose that he fought with the shinbone of some animal as with a club, and struck them with it upon the thigh, just as it is written of him that he killed a thousand with the jawbone of an ass.

But even that, as I have said, is not credible: that while fighting he should have watched for only one place in which to strike them. Scripture does not say, “He struck them with a shin upon the thigh,” but, “the shin upon the thigh.” Clearly, then, an unusual expression creates the obscurity. For it is as though it said: “He struck them most astonishingly”—that is, so that, stunned with amazement, they placed a shin upon a thigh: specifically, one foot upon the thigh of the other leg, as people customarily sit when they are struck with astonishment.

It would be like saying: “He struck them hand to jaw,” that is, with such slaughter that they placed their hand to their jaw in sorrowful amazement. The translation made from the Hebrew sufficiently shows that this is the meaning. For it reads: “He struck them with a great slaughter, so that, stunned, they placed the shin upon the thigh.” This is equivalent to saying that they placed the shin upon the thigh, since the lower leg is certainly situated behind the thigh.

## CHAPTER XVIII. How three thousand men of Judah wished to deliver Samson into the hands of the Philistines, and how, after being handed over, he struck a thousand Philistine men with an ass’s jawbone

**(IBID.)** “Three thousand men of Judah therefore went down to the cleft of the rock of Etam and said to Samson: ‘Do you not know that the Philistines rule over us? Why did you wish to do this?’ He answered them: ‘As they did to me, so I have done to them.’ They said: ‘We have come to bind you and deliver you into the hands of the Philistines.’ He replied: ‘Swear to me that you will not kill me,’” and so forth.

The Seventy: “And Samson said to the men of Judah: ‘Swear to me that you will not kill me yourselves, but deliver me to them, lest you yourselves come against me.’”

What does Samson’s statement to the men of Judah mean: “Swear to me that you will not kill me yourselves, but deliver me to them, lest you yourselves come against me”? Some have interpreted the expression as meaning, “lest you come against me yourselves.” But that he said this so that he would not be killed by them is indicated by what is written in the Book of Kings: when Solomon ordered a man to be killed, he said, “Go, meet him” (III Kings II). This is not understood among us because it is not customary for us to speak in that way.

Thus, when military authorities say, “Go, lift him up,” meaning “Kill him,” who would understand it except someone familiar with the custom of that expression? It is also commonly said among us, “He will shorten him,” meaning “He will kill him”; and no one understands this except one accustomed to hearing it.

For this is the force of all expressions generally: just as languages themselves are not understood unless they are learned by hearing or reading, so also are their idioms.

And finding the jawbone—that is, the mandible—of an ass, which was lying there, he seized it and killed [Col. 1194B] a thousand men with it. And he said: “With the jawbone of an ass, with the mandible of a young ass, I destroyed them; I struck a thousand men,” and so forth.

Whom, then, are signified here by the jawbone of the ass, except the persons of the preachers of the Church? For our Redeemer, holding the simplicity and patience of preachers in the hand of his power, put them to death by means of their carnal vices. And when the jawbone had been cast upon the ground, he afterward poured forth water, because the bodies of preachers, given over to death, displayed great miracles to the peoples.

## CHAPTER XIX. How Samson carried away the doors of the gate of the city of Gaza with their posts by night and carried them to the mountain; and how he desired a prostitute in Gaza, by whom he was deceived through treachery

**(CHAPTER XVI.)** “He went also to Gaza, and there he saw [Col. 1194C] a prostitute, and he entered in to her. When the Philistines heard this, and it became known among them that Samson had entered the city, they surrounded him, placing guards at the city gate. There they waited in silence throughout the night, intending to kill him when he came out at dawn. But Samson slept until midnight. Then, rising, he seized both doors of the gate with their posts and bolt, placed them upon his shoulders, and carried them to the top of the mountain that faces Hebron,” and so forth.

Whom does that Samson signify in this deed, except our Redeemer? What does the city of Gaza signify except hell? And what is demonstrated by the Philistines except the faithlessness of the Jews? When they saw the Lord dead and his body already placed in the tomb, they immediately appointed guards and boasted that they had captured him—who had been revealed as the author of life—as though Samson had been captured in Gaza and held within the prison of hell.

But Samson at midnight not only went out; he also carried away the gates of the city. For our Redeemer, rising before dawn, not only came forth free from hell but also destroyed the very prison of hell, carried away its gates, and went up to the summit of the mountain: by rising, he removed the barriers of hell, and by ascending, he entered the kingdoms of heaven.

Samson was born by divine promise, and he had the accompanying Spirit. For we read that the Lord blessed him, and that the Spirit of the Lord began to accompany him into the camp. Therefore, foreseeing the future mystery, he sought a wife from among foreigners—a matter of which his father and mother, as it is written, were unaware—because it was from the Lord.

He was rightly considered stronger than the others, because, when the Spirit of the Lord directed him, under whose leadership he alone now put foreign peoples to flight, now, invincible in strength, tore a lion apart with his hands.

Would that he had been as cautious in preserving grace as he was strong in overcoming the beast! Perhaps this was not only a miracle of power, but also a mystery of wisdom and an oracle of prophecy. For it does not appear meaningless that, when he was advancing toward the mystery of marriage, a roaring lion met him, which he tore apart with his hands. In its body, as he was about to obtain the marriage he desired, he found a swarm of bees and took honey from its mouth, which he gave to his father and mother to eat.

The people of the nations possessed honey because it believed; it, which had formerly been a body of ferocity, is now Christ’s. Nor is the question he posed to his companions devoid of sacramental meaning, when he said: “From the eater came forth food, and from the strong came forth sweetness.”

Finally, it was so deeply mysterious that its revelation was sought for three days and could be revealed only through the faith of the Church on the seventh day, after the time of the Law had been completed and after the Lord’s Passion. For you have it written that the apostles did not understand for this reason: Jesus had not yet been glorified.

“What,” he said, “is sweeter than honey, and what is stronger than a lion?” They answered him: “If you had not subdued my heifer, you would not have discovered my riddle.”

O divine mystery! O evident sacrament! We have escaped the destroyer; we have conquered the mighty one. There is now the food of life where previously there was the wretched hunger of death; dangers are turned into salvation, bitterness into sweetness, grace has proceeded from offense, power from weakness, and life from death.

Nevertheless, some think that the marriage could not have been established except after the lion from the tribe of Judah had been killed. Therefore bees were found in his body—that is, in the Church—which store up the honey of wisdom, because after the Lord’s Passion the apostles believed more fully.

Thus Samson, as a Jew, killed that lion, but found honey in him as a figure of the redemption of the inheritance, so that “the remnant might be saved according to the election of grace” (Rom. XI).

“And the spirit of the Lord,” he says, “fell upon him, and he went down to Ashkelon and struck thirty men there.” For he who saw the mysteries could not fail to possess victory.

Thus, in their schools, those who resolve and explain the riddle first receive the distinction of a wise manner of life. Yet here they overwhelm him with another mystery: his wife is taken away. Therefore he sets fire to the foreigners’ sheaves with foxes, for he is accustomed by his cunning to deceive those who contend against the divine mysteries.

Hence he says again in the Song of Songs: “Catch for us the foxes, the little foxes that destroy the vineyards, so that our vineyards may flower” (Cant. II). He rightly called them “little foxes,” because they could not destroy larger vineyards, even though they were strong—and the devil is little.

Therefore Samson—that we may summarize the history, for the exposition of the whole reading must be reserved for its proper time—was unconquered as long as he possessed spiritual grace, like that people of God, chosen by the Lord: that Nazirite in the Law.

Samson was unconquered, indeed so invincible that with an ass’s jawbone he struck a thousand men. He was so full of heavenly grace that, when he thirsted, he even found water in the ass’s jawbone. Whether you apply this to the miracle or turn it toward the mystery, it signifies that among the humility of the Gentile people there would be both rest and triumph, in accordance with what is written: “Whoever strikes you on the right cheek, offer him the other also” (Matt. V).

Through this endurance of injury, which the mysteries of baptism teach, we triumph over certain goads of anger, so that, having undergone death, we may attain the rest of the resurrection.

That Samson, then, who dissolved cords woven with sinews, and new ropes as though they were soft threads; that Samson who, when the bonds of his hair had been fastened to a peg, felt nothing—so long as he possessed spiritual grace—that Samson, I say, after the Spirit of God departed from him, was greatly changed from the former Samson. He returned clothed in the spoils of the foreigners, degenerately bound and captured upon the knees of a woman, and was shorn of the hair in which his strength lay.

Did the hairs of his head have so much importance that, while they remained, his unconquered strength endured, but when his head was shorn, the man’s entire strength suddenly dissolved? It is not so, as though I thought such force belonged to bodily hair.

There are certain hairs of religion and faith: the hairs of the Nazirite perfected in the Law, consecrated in frugality and abstinence. By these hairs, the woman figuratively representing the Church—she who had poured oil upon the Lord’s feet—wiped away the traces of the heavenly Word. At that time she knew him also according to the flesh, in relation, that is, to the hairs of which it is said: “Your hair is like flocks of goats” (Cant. IV)—hairs growing from that head of which it is said: “The head of the man is Christ” (I Cor. XI).

And elsewhere: “The head is gold of Cephaz; his hair is black and beautiful.” The fir trees of the ship of Tarshish, floating above the waves, may provide the world with the safe rowing of salvation.

Thus, in the Gospel, our Lord, indicating that there are certain visible hairs of the head and intelligible hairs, says: “Even the hairs of your head have all been numbered by God” (Matt. X), signifying, of course, the deeds of spiritual virtues. For God does not concern himself with our hairs—although it is not unreasonable to think that nothing can be hidden from the majesty of God.

But what does it profit me if almighty God knows my hairs? It benefits and advances me if, as the ever-watchful witness of good works, he grants the reward of eternal glory.

Finally, Samson himself, declaring that these are not bodily but intelligible hairs, says: “If I am shorn, my strength will depart from me.” This concerns the mystery.

Now let us consider the sequence of the reading. Above you have: “The Lord blessed him, and the Spirit began to accompany him.” Below he says: “The Spirit of the Lord fell upon him.” Again he says: “If I am shorn, my strength will depart from me.” After he was shorn, see what Scripture says: “The Lord,” he says, “has departed from me.”

You see, therefore, that the one who accompanied him was himself the one who departed. The Lord, then, is the same as the Spirit of the Lord; that is, he called the Spirit of God “Lord,” just as the Apostle also says: “The Lord is the Spirit; and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (II Cor. III). You have, therefore, the Lord.

He also speaks of the Holy Spirit; for the Holy Spirit and the Son are not one person, but they are one. In this passage also he said “strength,” and signified the Spirit. For just as the Father is strength, so also the Son is strength, and the Holy Spirit is strength.

You have read of the Son that Christ is “the power and wisdom of God” (I Cor. I). We also read that the Father is strength, as it is written: “You will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power” (Matt. XXVI). Here he certainly called the Father “Power,” at whose right hand the Son sits, as it says: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand” (Ps. CIX).

The Lord himself also called the Holy Spirit “Power,” saying: “You will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you; for the Spirit himself is power” (Acts I). [Col. 1197B]

But when the Philistines had seized Samson, they immediately tore out his eyes, led him bound with chains to Gaza, shut him in prison, and made him grind.

The second point is that sometimes the eye is blinded first, and afterward the captured mind wanders through external desires, so that the blind mind does not know where it is being led and willingly submits itself to the allurements of the flesh. At other times, however, the desires of the flesh first boil over and, after long indulgence in unlawful action, close the eye of the heart.

For often the mind sees what is right but nevertheless does not boldly rise against what is perverse; it is defeated while resisting, when, though judging what it is doing, it is overcome by the pleasure of its flesh.

Because the eye of contemplation is usually lost first, and afterward the mind is subdued through the desires of the flesh by the labors of this world, Samson bears witness to this when he was captured by the foreigners. After he had lost his eyes, he was assigned to the mill, because evil spirits, once they have dug out the inward sharpness of contemplation with the goads of temptations, are sent outward into a circuit of labors. [Col. 1197C]

## CHAPTER XX. How blind Samson, brought to the banquet of the Philistines for their mockery, shook the two pillars of the house and, when the whole structure collapsed, killed many of his enemies along with himself

**(IBID.)** “And he took hold of the two pillars upon which the house rested, holding one with his right hand and the other with his left, and said: ‘Let my soul die with the Philistines.’ And when he had strongly shaken the pillars, the house fell upon all the rulers and the rest of the multitude who were there. He killed many more at his death than he had killed during his life,” and so forth.

Whose person is signified here by Samson, except that of our Redeemer? While Samson lived, he killed a few; but when the temple was overturned, he himself, dying, struck down a very great multitude of his adversaries.

Likewise, while our Lord was preaching, few of the Israelite people believed; but countless peoples of the nations followed the way of life when he died. While he was still living a passible life, he endured the proud; but, dead from that passible life, he struck them down.

This Samson had previously expressed the same thing figuratively in himself: while living, he killed a few; but when the temple was destroyed, he killed countless enemies as he died. For the Lord extinguished a few who were lifted up in pride while he lived, but many more when the temple of his body was dissolved; and, by dying, he struck down all at once the elect from among the nations whom he had endured while living.

And, to gather briefly together all that has been said about Samson: allegorically, Samson, once the Lord’s Nazirite, contains a certain figure of Christ. First, his birth is announced by an angel. Next, he is called a Nazirite, and he himself delivers Israel from its enemies. Finally, he overturns their temple, and many thousands of men who mocked him perish.

This birth of Samson, which is announced by an angel, first resembles the prophets who announced the Lord’s birth according to the flesh. It also resembles the angel who spoke to Mary, saying: “Mary, you have found grace before the Lord; you will conceive in your womb and bear a son, and his name will be called Emmanuel. For he will save his people from their sins” (Luke I).

Samson, however, is interpreted as “sun.” But since our Redeemer is also called the sun, hear the Lord Jesus himself called by that name through the prophet: “The sun of righteousness will rise for you, and healing is in his wings” (Matt. IV). Truly he is the sun of righteousness, who illumines the minds of all believers with heavenly light. Truly he is the Nazirite and Holy One of God, in whose likeness that Nazirite was so named.

When this Samson was advancing toward the mystery of marriage, a roaring lion met him. But who was represented in Samson, when he killed the lion that came against him as he went to seek a wife among foreigners, except Christ, who, intending to call the Church from the nations, says: “Rejoice, because I have conquered the world” (John XVI)?

What does the honeycomb extracted from the mouth of the slain lion signify except that, as we observe, the very nations of the earthly kingdom—which had previously roared against Christ—now, their ferocity destroyed, offer memorials of the sweetness of evangelical preaching?

Likewise, he expressed in himself the fact that while living he killed a few, but when the temple was destroyed he killed countless enemies as he died. For the Lord extinguished a few lifted up by unbelief while living, but many more when the temple of his body was dissolved; and, by dying, he struck down all at once those lifted up among the nations whom he had endured while living.

But the rest concerning him—how the treacherous woman shaved his head and delivered it to the foreigners for mockery, how he was captured, blinded, and assigned to the mill—does not figure Christ, but those who boast only in the name of Christ within the Church and are continually entangled in evil deeds.

The man signifies the rational sense within us, while the flesh is accepted figuratively as the woman. If, then, we yield to the woman—that is, to our flesh—when she flatters us with lust or other evil works, we are stripped bare and deprived of the grace of the Spirit signified by the Nazirite’s hair, and are deceived. Thus the devil mocks the proud and sinful when Christ’s grace has been violated, just as Samson was mocked after his hair had been cut.

But what does it mean that Samson, captured by the foreigners, after he had lost his eyes, was assigned to the mill, except that evil spirits, after they have dug out the sharpness of contemplation within by the goads of temptations, send a person outside to circle through labors? As has already been said above.

If that same person should at some time return by practicing repentance, the hair is restored, as it were: that is, when grace flourishes again, he is restored to virtue. Then, after the pillars of desire and lust have been overturned, he casts down the victorious enemies and, with the battle renewed, will triumph most courageously over all in the end.

## CHAPTER XXI. On the vengeance exacted by Israel against the Benjaminites for the outrage

**(CHAPTER XX.)** “All the children of Israel went out and were gathered together as one man, from Dan to Beersheba [Col. 1199B] and from the land of Gilead, to the Lord at Mizpah. All the corners of the peoples and all the tribes of Israel came together into the assembly of the people of God: forty thousand armed foot soldiers,” and so forth.

When all Israel had gathered and wished to avenge the tribe of Benjamin, which had been cast down into a carnal crime, Israel itself was first struck down, and only then did it utterly destroy the sinful tribe. This signifies that one who does not first judge himself does not know how to judge what is right in another.

Even if such a person perhaps knows by hearsay what he ought to judge as right, he is nevertheless unable to judge another’s merits rightly when his own conscience provides no standard of judgment through the testimony of innocence.

Thus, when the tribe of Benjamin had been overwhelmed by a carnal crime, all Israel gathered and wished to avenge the iniquity, but nevertheless Israel itself was struck down once and again in battle. After consulting the Lord about whether they should go to exact vengeance, they were commanded to proceed according to the divine voice; they went, lost once and a second time, and only then, striking the sinful tribe severely, almost completely destroyed it.

What does it mean that one is inflamed to avenge a crime and yet is first struck down himself, except that those who are to be cleansed are first struck twice because of the fault of others, and that those who hasten to correct the vices of others must come to exact vengeance only after they themselves have been made clean?

Hence, when certain men were lying in wait and bringing an adulterous woman forward to be punished, it was said to them: “Let him among you who is without sin cast the first stone at her” (John I). They were going to punish the sins of others while leaving their own behind. Let them therefore be called back inward to their conscience, so that they may first correct their own faults and then criticize those of others.

Therefore, whenever the vengeance of divine judgment ceases against us, it is necessary that our conscience itself rebuke us and that it raise itself against itself to the lamentations of repentance. It must not be lifted up against the good while being humble toward itself; rather, it must be severe against itself and submissive to all who are good.

[Col. 1199B]

# THE COMMENTARY ON THE BOOK OF RUTH BEGINS

## CHAPTER ONE

The journey of Elimelech and his wife Naomi, with their two sons, from Bethlehem of Judah into the land of Moab, in order to dwell there as foreigners

When examining the history of Ruth, we think that we must entreat the one who willed to be born from her stock and to live among human beings as a man—who is also God—to deign to enlighten us by his grace, so that he may grant us permission to bring forth, at an appropriate time, something from this history in a mystical sense, for his praise and for the benefit of the holy Church.

Thus everything may be understood as his gift: both that a foreign woman was graciously joined to the people of God, and that a woman without a tongue was permitted to proclaim the goodness and mercy of God.

Let us therefore first consider what is signified by what is written at the beginning of this history:

**(CHAPTER I.)** “In the days of one of the judges, when the judges ruled, there was a famine in the land.”

What does this famine in the land in the days of one judge signify except that, because of the scarcity of spiritual teachers and masters of the people of God—those to whom the authority of judging had been entrusted—a famine arose in the land of the synagogue, not of bread or food, but of hearing the word of God? This occurred when the Law itself was corrupted by Jewish traditions (Amos VIII), and the psalms, prophets, and also the divine histories were not understood truthfully according to their proper meaning, but were confused by foolish interpretation according to the carnal sense. [Col. 1200C]

“Therefore a man went away from Bethlehem of Judah to dwell as a foreigner in the region of Moab with his wife and two sons.”

Some have wished this man to be understood as the Decalogue of the Law, his wife as the Synagogue, and his two sons as the two honors or orders of dignity that appeared to rule in the place of government during the times of the Old Testament: namely, royal and priestly honor.

These orders excelled not only among the Jewish people but also among the other nations by right of authority. Therefore they in some manner acquired for themselves the union of two peoples, namely, Israelites and proselytes, as happened in the times of David, Solomon, and the other kings.

Others refer the man himself to the Lord Jesus Christ, who, born through a virgin in Bethlehem of Judah, wished to visit the pilgrimage of this world with his wife—that is, the holy Church, which he presented to himself beautiful, “not having spot or wrinkle” (Eph. V)—and with two sons, whom we may understand as the two orders of prophets and apostles.

They are rightly called sons because they are known to have been freed from the yoke of sin and ancient servitude by the blood of our Redeemer.

His name was Elimelech, his wife’s name Naomi, and his two sons were Maalon and Chelion, Ephratites from Bethlehem of Judah.

Elimelech is interpreted as “My God.” And who could more fittingly be called by this name than our Savior, to whom the Psalmist says: “Attend to the voice of my prayer, my King and my God” (Ps. V)? And the Apostle says: “Theirs are the fathers, and from them is Christ according to the flesh, who is over all, God blessed forever” (Rom. IX).

His wife was called Naomi, that is, “beautiful,” to whom the bridegroom says in the Song of Songs: “You are beautiful, my friend, sweet and lovely as Jerusalem, terrible as an army set in battle array.”

The two sons of Elimelech were Maalon and Chelion. The former is interpreted as “from a window,” or “from the beginning”; the latter as “completion.”

The first can properly represent the prophets in type, because through them, as through a window, the first light of faith spread throughout the world, and they were the first preachers of the true Light, who is Christ.

The one who follows, whose name is interpreted as “completion,” signifies the apostles, who explained in clear speech what the prophets had indicated enigmatically and brought it to the completion of full understanding. To them Truth itself says in the Gospel:

“Blessed are the eyes that see what you see, and the ears that hear what you hear. For I tell you that many prophets and righteous people desired to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear and did not hear it” (Luke X).

They are therefore rightly remembered as Ephratites and as having arisen from Bethlehem of Judah, because, nourished by heavenly bread, they gathered the fruit of believing peoples through the preaching of the Gospel.

“Ephratite” is interpreted as “fruitful,” Bethlehem as “house of bread,” and Judah as “confession.” [Col. 1201C]

Therefore the Lord commanded his disciples in the Gospel to feed the crowds themselves, saying to them: “You give them something to eat” (Luke IX). And again: “Go,” he says, “preach the Gospel of the kingdom” (Mark XVI). And again: “I chose you from the world, so that you should go and bear fruit, and that your fruit should remain” (John XV).

“When they had entered the region of Moab, they dwelt there; and Elimelech, the husband of Naomi, died.”

After teachers had been appointed by the Lord himself and sent for the salvation of human beings—teachers who first strove, according to the Lord’s command, to seek the sheep that had perished from the house of Israel—suddenly the Passion of the Redeemer intervened. After he had risen from the dead, he ascended into heaven with the flesh that he had assumed from humanity for the sake of humanity, and sat at the right hand of God.

His bride, that is, the holy Church, remained in the pilgrimage of this world with her sons, namely, the holy teachers. These had taken Moabite wives, one of whom was called Orpah and the other Ruth.

Thus the apostles and holy preachers associated themselves with the company of two peoples, because some of them were sent to preach to the circumcision, while others were sent to call the nations into the fellowship of faith.

Hence the Apostle Paul, writing to the Galatians, says: “For he who worked through Peter for the apostleship to the circumcision worked through me also among the nations. And when they recognized the grace that had been given to me, Peter and James and John, who seemed to be pillars, gave the right hand of fellowship to me and Barnabas, so that we should go to the nations, and they to the circumcision,” and so forth (Gal. II).

The names of the women express this well. For Orpah is interpreted as “her neck,” while Ruth means “seeing,” or “hastening,” or “defining.”

What is signified by Orpah except believers from the Jews? They are rightly named after the neck, because after the Lord’s resurrection they were the first to receive the strength of faith and the power of good works. Hence it is written concerning the primitive Church in Jerusalem:

“The multitude of believers was of one heart and one soul; nor did any of them say that anything he possessed was his own, but all things were common to them” (Acts IV).

What is signified by Ruth, who is adorned with the name meaning “seeing,” “hastening,” or “defining,” except the obedience and swiftness of the nations? Concerning them the Lord says through the Psalmist: “The people whom I did not know served me; at the hearing of the ear they obeyed me” (Ps. XVII). And again: “Ethiopia,” he says, “hastened to stretch out her hands to God” (Ps. LXVII).

These two peoples were therefore called by holy teachers into the fellowship of faith and joined through the Gospel to the society of the elect, so that from different flocks, according to the Lord’s declaration, there might be “one fold and one shepherd” (John X).

## CHAPTER II. How, after they had dwelt there for ten years, both of their sons died—namely, Maalon and Chelion—and the woman was left deprived of her two sons and her husband
*(The same.)* They remained there for ten years, and both died, namely Mahlon and Chilion. The woman was left bereaved of her two sons and her husband. And she arose to return to her homeland with both her daughters-in-law from the region of Moab. For she had heard that the Lord had looked favorably upon his people and had given them food.

Thus the two sons of Elimelech remained in the land of their sojourn for ten years and died, just as the apostles and prophets, after completing the pious labor they had undertaken in teaching the peoples and practicing the virtues, migrated from their dwelling in this world to the heavenly kingdom, so that, in return for fulfilling the Decalogue of the commandments, they might receive the denarius of eternal blessedness.

The woman was left bereaved of her two sons and her husband, just as holy Church, continuing her pilgrimage in this world after the Lord’s ascension into heaven, lacked the Savior’s bodily presence, although he is always with her in the majesty of his divinity. Nor could the apostles and prophets themselves, after the death of their present life, be with her in bodily fellowship, although she is daily aided by their prayers and writings.

The woman did indeed arise to return to her homeland with both her daughters-in-law, because she had heard that the Lord had looked favorably upon his people. In this way Mother Church applies herself with the greatest zeal to lead the peoples whom the apostles and prophets instructed in their time to the unity of faith and the fellowship of the Christian religion. For, as Scripture truthfully reports, she learned that “the righteous is never forsaken” (Psalm XXXVI), nor has his offspring lacked bread—namely, that bread which descended from heaven, the bread of life; whoever truly eats it will not die forever (John VI).

## CHAPTER III. How Naomi, having departed from the place of her sojourn, decided to return with both daughters-in-law to the land of Judah, and urged her daughters-in-law to return to the land of their birth

*(The same.)* And so she departed from the place of her sojourn with both daughters-in-law, and, already on the road returning to the land of Judah, she said to them: “Go to the house of your mother. May the Lord show you mercy, as you have shown it to the dead and to me. May he grant you to find rest in the houses of the husbands whom you are to receive.” And she kissed them, and so forth.

What does it mean that this woman appears to resist her daughters-in-law, lest they go with her to the land of Israel? It means that holy Church does not act indiscriminately but reasonably in the matters that must be undertaken, and accepts what ought to be accepted. Thus the apostle John also admonishes in his letter, saying: “Do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God” (1 John IV). She tests them in order to show that the gifts of God, which consist in divine charisms, are offered not to the unwilling but to the willing. For the grace of Christ, which is freely offered to human beings, seeks voluntary recipients, and a work or gift expended with an evil disposition will not please God.

Hence, when the Lord himself sought the firstfruits from Israel in the Law, he spoke to Moses, saying: “Speak to the children of Israel, that they take firstfruits for me: from every person who offers freely, you shall receive them” (Exodus XXV). Likewise, in the Gospel, the Savior answered the lawyer who was testing him: “If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments.” And again: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything you possess and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come, follow me” (Matthew XIX). For wherever a person’s will is required, compulsion is no longer imposed; rather, the choice of what is better is left to one’s own judgment.

If, however, you apply the words quoted above to the synagogue, they can aptly refer to it, because it draws back those who desire to come to the faith of Christ, especially where, overcome by truth, it acknowledges itself weak and exhausted, saying:

“Return, my daughters; why are you coming with me? Do I still have sons in my womb, so that you may hope for husbands from me? Return, daughters of Moab. For I am already worn out with old age and unfit for the bond of marriage. Even if I could conceive and bear sons this very night, if you were willing to wait for them until they grew and reached the years of puberty, you would become old women before you married. No, I beg you, my daughters, for your distress presses upon me more heavily, and the hand of the Lord has gone out against me.”

Observe the synagogue confessing the truth and not concealing the faults that have come upon it: abandoned by its husband and sons—that is, deserted by God—and deprived of its kings and priests, now sterile and too weak to conceive and bear sons fit for the service of God, because this alone was reserved for holy Church after the coming of Christ.

Then, raising their voices, they began to weep again. Orpah kissed her mother-in-law, but Ruth clung to her. Naomi said to her: “Look, your kinswoman has returned to her people and to her gods; go with her.” She answered: “Do not oppose me, so as to make me leave you and depart. Wherever you go, I will go; wherever you stay, I too will stay. Your people shall be my people, and your God my God. The land that receives you when you die shall receive me also; in that land I shall die, and there I shall receive a place of burial. May God do these things to me, and add more, if anything but death alone separates me from you.”

These two women signify the division among believers. One displayed the pain of separation in mourning yet withdrew from her mother-in-law; the other persevered with her by deliberate resolve. For some, after receiving the grace of baptism and the fellowship of faith, fall back into their former errors. Orpah represented their type, since she returned to her gods and her people. Others, however, follow with determined purpose and persistent zeal the grace they have received; Ruth represented their figure.

Accordingly, when her mother-in-law urged her to return with her companion to her homeland, Ruth said: “Do not oppose me. Wherever you go, wherever you stay, I too will stay,” and so forth. This statement plainly reveals a type of the faith of the nations. For in this way the Church from the nations, summoned to the Lord, leaves behind her homeland, which is idolatry, and abandons carnal conduct and desires. She professes that the Lord in whom the saints believed is her own Lord; that she will go to the place where Christ’s flesh ascended after his Passion; that for his name she will suffer in this world even unto death; and that she will be joined to the people of the saints, namely, the patriarchs and prophets.

Moses showed in his song that those coming from the offspring of Abraham would be joined to this fellowship, saying: “Rejoice, nations, with his people” (Deuteronomy XXXII)—that is, you who are from the nations, who will believe together with those who were chosen first, rejoice in eternal gladness.

## CHAPTER IV. How, after Orpah returned, Ruth remained with Naomi and reached the land of Judah

When Naomi saw that Ruth had firmly resolved to go with her, she did not oppose her or any longer persuade her to return to her own people. They therefore set out together and came to Bethlehem. When they entered the city, a swift report spread among everyone. The women were saying: “Is this that Naomi?” She said to them: “Do not call me Naomi”—that is, “beautiful”—“but call me Mara”—that is, “bitter”—“because the Almighty has filled me with great bitterness.”

Thus the people of the nations, with determined purpose, followed the holy preachers into the holy land and into the city of God, Bethlehem, so that there they might be instructed and prepared to receive the bridegroom who was born from the stock of Abraham—namely, that seed in whom all the nations of the earth would be blessed (Genesis XXII).

When Naomi replied to the women who said, “Do not call me Naomi,” that is, “beautiful,” “but call me Mara,” that is, “bitter,” and so forth, this signifies that holy Church, oppressed by the tribulation of persecutions, does not love the joys of the present world but seeks future glory in heaven. Hence the bride says in the Song of Songs:

“I am black but beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem, like the tents of Kedar, like the skin of Solomon. Do not look at me because I am dark, because the sun has discolored me. The sons of my mother fought against me” (Song of Songs I).

If you wish to refer Naomi’s foregoing words to the synagogue, it is found to have acknowledged its calamity, which after the coming of Christ it deservedly suffered because of its perversity. For this reason it refuses to be called most beautiful, since it sees the times of its prosperity coming to an end.

## CHAPTER V. How this was the season of the barley harvest when Naomi returned to Bethlehem with Ruth, her daughter-in-law

*(The same.)* Naomi therefore came with Ruth the Moabite, her daughter-in-law, from the land of her sojourn and returned to Bethlehem when the barley was first being harvested.

Naomi returned from her sojourn to her people and the city of Bethlehem when the Law turned the order of its account of the teaching of the peoples toward the mystery of Christ’s incarnation, so that it might explain and commend it to its hearers—and this at the time of the barley harvest.

For what does the barley harvest express if not the time of the Lord’s Passion, which was completed in the month of new grain, that is, the first month? It is therefore rightly said that Naomi came to Bethlehem with her daughter-in-law at the barley harvest, when the Law, which teaches that the Savior was born in Bethlehem, proclaims that he was killed at Passover, that is, in the month of new grain.

Similarly, holy Church applies all her effort to imbue the peoples whom she summons to the faith with the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation, Passion, and resurrection.

The barley harvest may also appropriately express the faith of the Jewish people, which, after the sacrament of Christ’s Passion had been completed, first came to the faith when the apostles preached. Elsewhere this people is also read to have been fed by the Lord himself with five barley loaves (John VI). Hence, in the Acts of the Apostles, when the Holy Spirit came upon the apostles on the day of Pentecost (Acts II), Peter preached and confirmed by the testimony of the Law and the prophets that the grace of the Holy Spirit had been poured out upon the one hundred and twenty believers; three thousand Jews were converted to the faith and baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus.

## CHAPTER VI. How Boaz, the kinsman of Elimelech, saw Ruth gathering the ears left behind by his reapers and asked who the woman was

*(CHAPTER II.)* Now Elimelech had a kinsman, a powerful man and a man of great wealth, named Boaz. “There was,” he says, “a man who was the kinsman of Elimelech.”

Who is this man who was Elimelech’s kinsman, if not our Redeemer, who was related to the Law and to the lawgiver? For he was promised through the Law, was born from the stock of the patriarchs, and according to the flesh had his origin among the Jewish people. Moses himself, speaking to the Israelites about him, says: “The Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brothers; you shall hear him as you hear me” (Deuteronomy XVIII).

This man is described as powerful and possessing great wealth. He is powerful because he defeated the ruler of the world and subjected the whole world to his dominion. He is also a man of great wealth because he is the possessor of heaven and earth, in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden. The abundance of every good virtue also belongs to his riches, because, according to the Apostle, he is the power of God and the wisdom of God.

“Named Boaz.” Boaz is called “the strength of God.” Hence Isaiah, recalling that a little child had been born, added concerning his greatness: “The government shall be upon his shoulder, and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counselor, God, Mighty, Father of the future age, Prince of Peace,” and so forth (Isaiah IX).

Ruth the Moabite said to her mother-in-law: “If you command me, I will go to the field and gather the ears that have escaped the hands of the reapers, wherever I find favor in the eyes of the kindly master of the field.” She answered her: “Go, my daughter.” So she went and gathered ears behind the reapers.

Here we may understand the field as the Church of the faithful; the harvest as holy people, who are worthy to be gathered into the Lord’s barns; the reapers as good angels; and the ears left behind as certain believers who, after certain saints have been transferred to the heavenly kingdom, have been left behind after the chosen angels as examples for those living in the present life.

Again, the field may signify the discipline of heavenly study; the harvest, spiritual understanding; the reapers, holy preachers; and the ears left behind, the sayings of the holy Scriptures which, because many things are hidden in mystery, appear to remain more plainly accessible for the exercise of those who meditate upon them.

Thus the people of the nations eagerly desire ecclesiastical discipline, so that they may be admitted to meditation on the divine Law and to the fellowship of the saints, and so that they may be refreshed either by spiritual teachings or by the examples of the saints. Otherwise the soul, empty of virtues, might feel perpetual hunger; instead, it acquires spiritual nourishment suited to its salvation, so that it has the means truly to live.

It happened that the field had a master named Boaz, who was of the family of Elimelech. “Behold,” it says, “he was coming from Bethlehem,” and he said to the reapers: “The Lord be with you.” They answered him: “May the Lord bless you.”

That field is described as belonging to Boaz, who was the kinsman of Elimelech, because holy Church belongs to no one else but the Lord Jesus alone, whose bride and body alone she is. Of him the Psalmist says: “The Lord is my strength and my praise” (Psalm CXVII). And again: “The Lord is strong; the Lord is mighty in battle” (Psalm XXIII). Jeremiah also says of him: “The Lord is with me like a mighty warrior” (Jeremiah XX).

He was Elimelech’s kinsman because he was born at Bethlehem and from the stock of David, and had testimonies from the Law and the prophets. He brought the words of salvation to his own household, because at his birth the multitude of the heavenly host sang, saying: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will.” Before his Passion, when he descended to Jerusalem, the crowd that had gathered for the feast came out to meet him with praises and palm branches, saying: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Matthew XXI).

Boaz said to the young man who was in charge of the reapers: “Whose girl is this?” He answered: “She is the Moabite who came with Naomi from the region of Moab. She asked permission to gather the ears left behind, following the footsteps of the reapers. From early morning until now she has been standing in the field, and she has not returned home even for a moment.”

What does it mean that Boaz asks the overseer of the reapers where Ruth was from, if not that our Redeemer, as though unaware, asks one of the apostles or one of the chief teachers who presides over a lesser order of priests about the faith of the nations, when he urges him to announce testimony concerning the faith and works of the Church among the nations?

Thus holy Church perseveres earnestly after the reapers—that is, after the preachers who gather the mysteries of Scripture—in the field of divine reading, so that she may gather into the bosom of her mind testimonies and examples of virtues sufficient for her salvation. She does this from the dawn of her shining faith until the perfection of her good work, and never returns to the house of her former superstition from which she departed. For, forgetting what lies behind, she reaches forward to what lies ahead, striving in every way to attain the prize of the heavenly calling.

## CHAPTER VII. How Boaz ordered Ruth to gather ears in his field without being troubled by anyone, and invited her to the meal

*(The same.)* Boaz therefore said to Ruth: “Listen, daughter. Do not go to gather in another field, and do not leave this place. Join yourself to my girls, and follow wherever they reap. For I have commanded my young men that no one molest you. And if you are thirsty, go to the bundles and drink from the water that the young men also drink.”

These words apply to no one better than to our Redeemer, who instructs and urges the people from the nations coming to him not to deviate even for a moment from the state of right faith into the errors of heretics and schismatics. Rather, he commands them to join themselves to holy souls, signified by the girls of Boaz, and to reap where they have reaped—that is, by meditating on the sacred Scriptures and fulfilling them through good works. In this way they may themselves drink beneficially from the draught of divine wisdom found in the books of the two Testaments, from which his young men—namely, the holy teachers—drink.

She fell on her face, bowed to the ground, and said to him: “Why have I found favor before your eyes, that you should take notice of me, a foreign woman?” He answered her: “Everything that you have done for your mother-in-law after the death of your husband has been reported to me: how you left your parents and the land in which you were born and came to a people whom previously you did not know. May the Lord repay you for your work, and may you receive a full reward from the Lord God of Israel, to whom you have come and under whose wings you have taken refuge.”

The Church from the nations gives thanks to the Savior because he has graciously deigned to regard her with the gaze of his mercy. He indicated to her that he was pleased that, after the death of her former husband—that is, error and the devil—she had left behind her idolatrous parents and the land of her birth, namely, carnal desires, and had desired to join herself to the people of the saints, who had previously been unknown to her while she followed the desire and deeds of the old person.

“May the Lord,” he says, “repay you for your work, and may you receive a full reward from the Lord God of Israel.” The work of the Church is the faith of Christ. Hence Truth itself says in the Gospel: “This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he sent” (John VI). She will receive a full reward from the Lord, because after the labor of the present life has ended, she will deserve to enjoy the eternal vision of God in heavenly glory. Hence the Lord says to his apostles: “Ask, and you shall receive, so that your joy may be full” (John XVI).

This reward will be given to the Church by the God of Israel, under whose wings she has taken refuge. The two Testaments are the wings of God; under them Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, protects all who take refuge in him. To him the Psalmist earnestly says: “In the shadow of your wings I hope, until iniquity passes away” (Psalm XVI).

She said: “I have found favor before your eyes, my lord, because you have comforted me and spoken to the heart of your servant, although I am not like one of your girls.”

These words reveal the humility of the Church from the nations. She declares herself unequal to so great a grace and in no way dares to compare herself with the primitive Church from the Jews. Hence, in the Gospel, when the Lord said under the figure of the Canaanite woman, “It is not right to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs,” she answered: “Yes, Lord, for even the little dogs eat from the crumbs that fall from the table of their masters” (Matthew XV).

Likewise, the centurion reverently kept the Lord, who wished to come to him, from entering, saying: “Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof; but only say the word, and my servant will be healed” (Matthew VIII).

Boaz said to her: “When the hour for eating comes, come here, eat bread, and dip your morsel in vinegar.”

The hour for eating had come when, after his resurrection, the Lord commanded his disciples: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to keep everything that I have commanded you” (Matthew XXVIII). Previously they had been told: “Do not go on the road of the nations, and do not enter the cities of the Samaritans” (Matthew X).

“Dip your morsel,” he says, “in vinegar.” What, then, is expressed by vinegar if not the Old Law, which, having long remained among the former people and having been corrupted by the traditions of the Pharisees, could no longer preserve its natural flavor? The Church is therefore commanded to dip her morsel in vinegar—that is, to learn that the mystery of Christ’s incarnation was foretold in the Old Testament, and to hold that mystery in faith all the more firmly because she recognizes that it was prefigured so long beforehand.

She sat beside the reapers, gathered roasted grain for herself, ate and was satisfied, and took the leftovers and arose to gather ears according to her custom.

Ruth sat beside the reapers when the gentile people joined themselves through faith to the holy preachers. She gathered roasted grain for herself when she examined with subtle discernment each word she heard. She ate and was satisfied when, receiving knowledge of the divine Law with devoted mind, she was beneficially refreshed. She took the leftovers and arose from there to gather ears according to her custom, because, retaining in her heart the words she had heard, she labored through persistent meditation in order to receive greater things.

Boaz commanded his young men, saying: “Even if she wishes to reap with you, do not hinder her. Also deliberately pull out some ears from your bundles and leave them behind, so that she may gather them without shame, and do not rebuke her while she gathers.”

The piety of the master of the field is recognized. When the mystical Ruth came to him, he not only permitted her to gather the ears of testimony that had been left behind, but, out of his generosity, voluntarily and additionally expended upon her unexpected bundles of knowledge. Notice also that he ordered her to gather without shame and that no one should despise her as she gathered. For he does not look down upon the weakness of an inexperienced people, nor permit anyone to reproach the convert for the errors of its former life; rather, he grants that the diligence of its study may have efficacy.

## CHAPTER VIII. How Ruth remained in his field until evening, threshed what she had gathered with a rod, found three measures, and returned carrying them to her mother-in-law

*(The same.)* She gathered in the field until evening, and, beating and threshing what she had gathered with a rod, found about an ephah of barley, that is, three measures. Carrying them, she returned to the city and showed them to her mother-in-law. She also brought out and gave her some of the leftovers of the food with which she had been satisfied.

Ruth threshes the grains from the bundles when holy Church draws the spiritual sense from the letter of the Law by the rod of discernment. She finds about an ephah of barley when, in the reading itself, she learns the Catholic faith through confession of the Holy Trinity. I therefore think that nothing else is signified by the measure of an ephah, which contains three measures, except a threefold confession within one faith, because within the one substance of the Godhead there is the distinct property of three persons.

Carrying this into the city, she shows it to her mother-in-law when the gentile people display their complete belief to holy Mother Church. Or, according to another sense, the Church presents to the mother synagogue the grace she received as a gift from her bridegroom, so that she may provoke her to faith and rejoice with her in the gift granted.

Christ alone, therefore, is the bridegroom. The woman who came from the nations had previously been a bride without resources and fasting; now, still unwedded (innuba) to Christ, though rich in harvest, she binds in the inner bosom of her mind the bundles of fruitful grain and the leftovers of the word. Thus she feeds with new nourishment that widow exhausted by the death of her son, the impoverished mother of a dead people, not leaving the widow destitute and seeking new ones.

Christ alone is the bridegroom, who does not begrudge even the synagogue the bundles of his harvest—if only it would not itself exclude itself. It had the opportunity to gather them for itself, but because its people are dead, as though deprived of a dead son, it gathered through the Church the bundles by which it might live.
