Those who come will carry them with rejoicing, as it is written: “Coming, they shall come with rejoicing, carrying their sheaves” (Psalm CXXV).

Her mother-in-law said to her: “Where did you gather today, and where did you work? Blessed be the one who showed you mercy.” She told her with whom she had worked and said the man’s name, that he was called Boaz.

Naomi answered her: “Blessed be he by the Lord, because he has preserved for the dead the same grace that he had shown to the living.” And again she said: “The man is our kinsman.” Ruth replied: “He also commanded me to remain with his reapers until all the harvest was finished.”

Mother Church recognizes the kinsman through the gratuitous benefits that the piety of the supreme master of the field bestowed upon the people of the nations, and by recalling his name she remembers the former benefits which she often enjoyed. Hence she says to the Lord with the Psalmist: “I remembered the days of old, and I meditated on all your works, and I will meditate on the works of your hands” (Psalm CXLII).

The synagogue also recognizes, when the Church from the nations has been proclaimed, the goodness and power of the Lord, the strength and kindness of its protector. At last, compelled by truth, it blesses the Lord’s name because he preserved for the dead the grace he had shown to the living. By extending the abundance of his generosity to the dead among the nations, who had long been buried in sins and idolatry—the grace he had once shown to the Jewish people when they made lavish use of his benefits—it confesses that he is its kinsman, because it remembers that the Savior had been promised to it from its own stock.

Christ is therefore the synagogue’s kinsman according to kinship of the flesh, and the Church’s kinsman according to spiritual union, because he is the head of the Church and the Church is his body.

When Ruth recalls that Boaz commanded her to join his reapers until all the harvest had been cut, it is a very familiar voice of Truth itself, persuading all who come to him to join themselves to his people for the reaping of the spiritual harvest rather than to strangers. Her mother-in-law herself agrees with this persuasion, saying: “It is better, my daughter, that you go with his girls to reap, and that no one resist you in another field.”

What the Church praises, the synagogue cannot contradict: those who love the truth make greater progress in fellowship with the preachers of the Gospel than in association with heretics and schismatics. For the alien field is the wicked teaching of the heretics, where there are always quarrels and disputes and never the tranquility of true peace.

Ruth therefore joined herself to the girls of Boaz and reaped with them until the barley and wheat were stored in the barns.

What is expressed by barley, which is food for brute animals, if not the letter of the Old Law, which was given as food to the Jews as to brute and senseless beasts? And what is designated by wheat if not the grace of the New Testament, which was bestowed for refreshment upon rational living beings?

There the flesh of bulls, rams, and goats is no longer offered upon the altar; rather, the flesh and blood of the immaculate Lamb are daily sacrificed by the faithful on the mystical altar under the appearance of bread and wine.

Spiritual Ruth therefore joined herself to the girls of Boaz in the mystical work of reaping until the barley and wheat were stored in the barns—that is, she adhered to the teachers in meditation on the sacred Scriptures until she had fully stored knowledge of the Old and New Testaments in the storehouses of her heart. Thus she would have sufficient nourishment for her soul and would no longer need, lacking provisions, to beg at the gates of strangers.

## CHAPTER IX. Naomi’s counsel to Ruth concerning how, through her own ingenuity, she might secure the future marriage with Boaz

*(CHAPTER III.)* After she had returned to her mother-in-law, she heard from her: “My daughter, I will seek rest for you and provide that it may be well with you. This Boaz, whose girls you joined in the field, is our kinsman, and tonight he is winnowing the barley floor. Wash therefore, anoint yourself, put on finer garments, and go down to the threshing floor.”

The primitive Church gives the people from the nations counsel about how they may reach fellowship with the true bridegroom and union with the Son of God.

“Tonight,” she says, “Boaz is winnowing the barley floor.” What other barley floor is this than the synagogue of the Jews, where the barley of the Law was stored? Our Boaz winnowed it when, preaching the Gospel in Judea, he examined the dispositions and intentions of individuals toward himself. Hence it is written of him in the Gospel: “Jesus did not entrust himself to them, because he knew everyone and had no need for anyone to testify about a person; for he himself knew what was in a person” (John II).

“Wash therefore, anoint yourself, put on finer garments, and go down to the threshing floor.” “Wash,” he says—that is, cleanse yourself with the water of baptism or with the tears of repentance; “anoint yourself” with the oil of chrism or with the spiritual anointing of the Holy Spirit. “Put on finer garments”—that is, prepare yourself with the adornment of every virtue. “And go down to the threshing floor”—hasten there, where you recognize the Son of God dwelling on earth and summoning the human race to his faith and grace.

It follows: “Let no one see you until the man has finished eating and drinking.” Why does she forbid her to be seen until the man has finished eating and drinking, if not because the faith of the Church from the nations did not appear openly until the Savior had fulfilled the mystery of his incarnation? He then lived bodily among human beings, used food and drink, and finally, before his Passion, dined with his disciples and entrusted to them the sacraments of his body and blood. After the mystery of Christ’s dispensation had been fulfilled, the Church from the nations approached the Catholic faith with confidence.

“When he goes to sleep, note the place where he sleeps. Then come, uncover the cloak with which he is covered at the feet, throw yourself down, and lie there. He himself will tell you what you must do.”

I think that the sleep of slumber signifies nothing other than the sleep of death that Christ accepted in his Passion for our salvation, through which he acquired possession of all things. He says: “And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all things to myself” (John XII).

The Church from the nations is therefore commanded to note the place of Christ’s Passion and death, to come and uncover the cloak with which he is covered at the feet, and to throw herself down and lie there. It is as though she said:

“Acknowledge Christ who suffered for you. Come with a devoted mind and examine the covering of the letter of the Old Testament, in which the mystery of Christ’s incarnation is hidden beneath the veil of figures. When you have learned that salvation has been promised to you through it, flee with exceptional humility to his aid and remain there always without any alteration caused by error.”

“He himself will tell you what you must do,” because you must learn from him the order of your salvation.

But if you apply these words of Naomi to the synagogue, you will find them echoed in the voices of the Law and all the prophets: after Christ’s Passion, the Church from the nations would come to the faith. Hence there is the passage of the prophet Isaiah:

“Because of the crime of my people I struck him, and he will give the wicked for his burial and the rich for his death, because he committed no iniquity, nor was deceit found in his mouth. And the Lord willed to crush him in weakness. If he gives his life for sin, he will see long-lived offspring, and the will of the Lord will be directed in his hand. Because his soul labored, he will see and be satisfied. By his knowledge my righteous servant himself will justify many, and he will bear their iniquities. Therefore I will distribute many to him, and he will divide the spoils of the strong, because he handed over his soul to death, was reckoned among criminals, himself bore the sin of many, and prayed for transgressors” (Isaiah LIV).

“Praise, barren woman who do not bear; sing praise and neigh, you who did not give birth, because the children of the deserted woman are many, more than those of the woman who had a husband, says the Lord” (Isaiah LIV).

## CHAPTER X. How Ruth, obeying the counsel of her mother-in-law, noted where Boaz was sleeping and, coming to his feet, threw herself down

*(The same.)* She answered: “Whatever you command, I will do.” She went down to the threshing floor and did everything her mother-in-law had commanded her.

The obedience of the Church obtained the fulfillment of her desire. She consented in word and immediately fulfilled it in deed, and therefore the most just Judge granted her request. Hence the Lord himself, praising the faith of the Church in the Canaanite woman, immediately granted what she asked, saying to her: “O woman, great is your faith; let it be done for you as you wish” (Matthew V).

When Boaz had eaten and drunk and had become more cheerful, and had gone to sleep, she came secretly beside the heap of sheaves and, uncovering him at the feet, threw herself down.

Our Lord ate and drank when, at the mystical supper, he gave his apostles the sacraments of his body and blood. Thus, as it is written, his servants shared in his body and blood, and he himself likewise partook of the same.

He became more cheerful because he was certain of his resurrection and our redemption. He went to sleep beside the heap of sheaves when he completed his Passion according to the testimonies of the sacred Scriptures. Hence, on the same night on which he was betrayed, he said to his disciples: “The Son of Man goes as it is written of him” (Matthew XXVI). And elsewhere: “It is necessary,” he said, “that everything written about me in the Law, the prophets, and the Psalms be fulfilled” (Luke XXIV).

Or certainly, his sleeping beside the heap of sheaves means that through his death he released companies of faithful souls from the prisons of hell. For after he gave up his spirit on the cross, he descended to hell, shattered the gates of death, and, triumphing, rose from there in glory.

To this bed of our Redeemer the Church hastened. When she uncovered him at the feet—that is, when the mystery of his incarnation was revealed—she humbly prostrated herself there, seeking pardon and salvation.

And behold, in the middle of the night the man was startled and troubled. He saw a woman lying at his feet and said to her, “Who are you?” She replied, “I am Ruth, your maidservant. Spread your cloak over your servant, because you are a near kinsman.”

What does it mean that this man, seeing a woman in the middle of the night, was startled, except that, when the world was enveloped in the darkness of error, Christ showed us, after the coming of faith, something sudden and wondrous concerning the Church? Thus we read that he himself marveled at the faith of the centurion, who prefigured the unbelief of the Gentile people (Matt. 8)—not because, as though ignorant, he was astonished at something new [Col. 1213C], but so that, knowing all things, he might show us the wondrous character of the Gentiles’ faith, which had always been certain in his sight. He saw the woman lying at his feet because he beheld the Church humbly venerating the mystery of his incarnation. He asked who she was because he sought her profession of faith. But she asked that his cloak be spread over her because above all she desired the grace of his faith and protection.

And he said: “Blessed are you, daughter, because you have surpassed your former mercy by your later mercy, since you did not follow young men, whether poor or rich. Therefore do not fear; whatever you say to me, I will do for you.” She who asked that the cloak be spread over her deserved to receive a blessing, because whoever fully receives the grace of faith will likewise possess the blessing of spiritual virtues. [Col. 1213D] “You have surpassed,” he says, “your former mercy by your later mercy, since you did not follow young men, whether poor or rich.” The former mercy was that, seeking her own welfare, she abandoned the errors of idolatry. The later mercy is that, after she came to Christ, she steadfastly persevered in his faith. “You did not,” he says, “follow young men, whether poor or rich.” He calls heretics and schismatics “young men,” because they do not possess the maturity of sound judgment but, always unstable, follow various errors. The Church therefore did not follow them in any way, because she abhorred all the faithlessness of heretics and the wantonness of sinners.

“Whatever,” he says, “you say to me, I will do for you.” In the same way the Lord spoke to his disciples in the Gospel, saying: “Ask, [Col. 1214A] and you will receive” (John 16). And again: “Ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you” (Matt. 17). And again: “If you ask the Father for anything in my name, he will give it to you” (John 16). Whatever, therefore, full faith asks in a salutary manner, the kindness of the supreme giver grants.

For all the people who dwell within the gates of my city know that you are a woman of virtue, and I do not deny that I am your near kinsman. But there is another nearer than I. Remain here tonight, and in the morning, if he wishes to retain you by right of kinship, the matter is well settled. But if he does not wish to do so, I will receive you without any hesitation.

The gates of Christ’s city are the prophets and apostles, concerning whom the Psalmist, speaking in the person of the Church, says: “But it is good for me to cling to God, to place my hope in the Lord God, [Col. 1214B] that I may proclaim all your praises at the gates of the daughter of Zion” (Ps. 72). Alternatively, the gates are the divine books of the city itself, by whose instruction we entered the Catholic faith. All who dwell beside these gates therefore know that this woman is a woman of virtue, because it is firmly persuaded in the hearts of all the faithful that the Church of the Gentiles is exceedingly rich in the aid of the virtues. Concerning this woman it is written in Proverbs: “Who will find a strong woman? Her price is from afar and from the ends of the earth,” and so forth. Hence the clarity of her teaching, the greatness of her knowledge, the truth of her faith, the abundance of her good works, the steadfastness of her patience, and the perfection of her charity are everywhere proclaimed.

But what does it mean that Boaz here does not deny that he is Ruth’s near kinsman, but asserts that another is nearer to him? [Col. 1214C] How, then, is anyone nearer to the Church than Christ, who is her head? This kinship, however, according to the mystery, refers not to relationship of descent but to precedence in time. The near kinsman is understood to be John the Baptist, whom the Jews supposed to be the Christ (John 1), but he in no way appropriated the name of bridegroom for himself; rather, he reverently reserved it for the true bridegroom, saying: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears his voice…” (John 3). John was nearer because he was born earlier in the world; but when he declined the partnership of marriage, the true bridegroom received his bride.

There are those who wish this near kinsman to be understood as the Decalogue of the Law itself. It seemed nearer to the Synagogue [Col. 1214D] than the Gospel, since it was specially given to that people through Moses and preceded grace in time.

Thus Ruth slept at his feet until the night had passed. He arose before people recognized one another. Ruth, in the spiritual sense, slept at the feet of Christ when, in hope of his incarnation—from which she believed certain salvation would come to her—she patiently awaited him as though resting. This continued until the night had passed, that is, until the darkness of unbelief had been removed. She arose before people recognized one another because, before the carnal Jews, instructed by the teaching of the Law, properly understood the rights of their nature, the Church summoned from the Gentiles shook off the sleep of inactivity, arose at the dawn of the emerging faith, [Col. 1215A] and hastened to come to the grace of Christ.

And Boaz said: “Take care that no one knows that you came here.” How, then, could the conversion of the Gentiles to the faith have remained hidden, when throughout the whole world it is proclaimed, praised, and celebrated? But he commanded her to take care that no one know this—that is, to beware of seeking human praise for her way of life, but divine glory.

So also in the Gospel the Lord himself gave instructions concerning the giving of alms and the practice of prayer, saying: “When you give alms, do not sound a trumpet before you, as the hypocrites do in the synagogues and in the streets, so that they may be honored by men. Truly I tell you, they have received their reward. But when you give alms, do not let your left hand know what your right hand is doing, so that your alms may be in secret, [Col. 1215B] and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you openly. And when you pray, you shall not be like the hypocrites, who love to pray standing in the synagogues and at the street corners, so that they may be seen by men. Truly I tell you, they have received their reward. But when you pray, enter your room, and after shutting the door, pray to your Father in secret; and your Father, who sees in secret, will repay you openly” (Matt. 6).

## CHAPTER XI. Ruth’s return to her mother-in-law, carrying six measures of barley and telling her mother-in-law everything that had happened.

**(The same passage.)** And again: “Spread,” he says, “the little cloak with which you cover yourself, and hold it with both hands.” When she had spread it and held it, he measured six measures of barley and [Col. 1215C] placed them upon her.

He commands her to spread the cloak—that is, to expand her faith—and to hold it with both hands, namely, by putting into practice what she had received in her believing heart. He measured six measures of barley and placed them upon her when, according to the capacity of her understanding, he granted her the measure of perfect action, so that inwardly and outwardly she might be enriched with the gift of faith and virtues and appear everywhere glorious through divine generosity. Moreover, the number six may signify here that, in the sixth age, the Lord himself granted the barley of the Law to the Church of the Gentiles as food through the mystery, so that she, previously needy of spiritual nourishment, might thereafter be enriched by his grace.

Carrying this, she entered the city, came to her mother-in-law, and told her everything that the man had done [Col. 1215D] for her, and so forth. The Church of the Gentiles, enriched by Christ’s gift and laden with the fruits of virtues, returns to her mother-in-law—that is, to the primitive Church or to the Synagogue of the Jews—telling her all the great things the Lord had done for her, so as to stir up the ancient Church to rejoice with her, or to summon the Synagogue to conversion. For it is characteristic of piety that one should be neither sparing nor envious in what has been given, but generous and benevolent in the good things one possesses.

And Naomi said: “Wait, daughter, until we see how the matter turns out; for the man will not rest until he has completed what he has said.” The Church faithfully and confidently proclaims this to all the nations: that the Truth fulfills its words and never ceases in any way [Col. 1216A] to fulfill its promises, saying the Gospel saying: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matt. 4). And again: “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved; but whoever does not believe will be condemned” (Mark 16). And again: “For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, so that everyone who believes in him should not perish but have eternal life” (John 3).

## CHAPTER XII. Boaz’s ascent to the city gate and his conversation with his kinsman about taking Ruth in order to raise up the offspring of his deceased kinsman.

**(Chapter 4.)** Boaz therefore went up to the gate and sat there. What does it mean for our Boaz to go up to the gate except that Christ brings to fulfillment the prophecy [Col. 1216B] written concerning his incarnation? He sat there because he assumed flesh in the womb of the Virgin, from which he could appear to human beings. Concerning this gate Ezekiel had formerly written as follows: “And he turned me toward the way of the gate of the outer sanctuary, which faced east; and it was closed. And the Lord said to me: This gate shall be closed; it shall not be opened, and no man shall pass through it, because the Lord God of Israel has entered through it, and it shall remain closed. The prince himself shall sit in it, to eat bread before the Lord. He shall enter by way of the vestibule of the gate, and he shall go out by way of it” (Ezek. 44).

When he saw the kinsman mentioned earlier passing by, he said to him: “Turn aside for a little while and sit here,” calling him by his name. [Col. 1216C] He turned aside and sat down.

Boaz saw the kinsman passing by when Christ willed the Law, established temporarily for the Jewish people, to exist. He ordered it to turn aside toward him because he inclined it to testify to the mystery of his dispensation. Alternatively, he saw the kinsman passing by when, observing the coming of his forerunner hastening along in the manner of human life, he mercifully directed him toward the office of herald, calling him by his name when, through the message of the archangel Gabriel, he foreordained for him the name by which he would be called, John.

Boaz then took ten men from the elders of the city and said to them: “Sit here.” When they had sat down, he spoke to the kinsman: “Naomi, who has returned from the region [Col. 1216D] of Moab, is selling the portion of the field belonging to our brother Elimelech. I wished you to hear this and to tell you, in the presence of all those sitting here and the elders of my people: If you wish to possess it by right of kinship, buy and possess it. But if it displeases you, tell me so that I may know what I ought to do. For there is no other kinsman besides you, who are first, and me, who am second.”

These ten elders signify the Fathers of the Old Testament, who fully observed the Decalogue of the Law and recognized that Christ’s incarnation was prefigured there. Our Boaz summoned them to himself when he wished to have them as witnesses to his coming. He convened the teachers of the Law and offered them Naomi’s portion of the field for purchase when he displayed to the teachers of the Synagogue the portion of the people that remained in the times of the already appearing grace, so that they might recognize their weakness and entrust to the true physician for completion [Col. 1217A] what they themselves could not accomplish. Hence it is also read in the Gospel that the Lord himself first commanded lepers whom he was to cleanse to go to the priests and offer the gift that Moses had commanded as a testimony to them; and as they went, they were immediately cleansed (Luke 17).

## CHAPTER XIII. How the man, unwilling, in the presence of his witnesses, removed his sandal from his foot and handed it to Boaz.

**(The same passage.)** But he replied: “I will buy the field.” Boaz said to him: “When you buy the field from the hand of the woman, you must also take Ruth the Moabite, who was the wife of the deceased, in order to raise up the name of your kinsman in his inheritance [Col. 1217B].” He replied: “I yield my right of kinship, for I must not destroy the posterity of my family. Use my privilege, which I willingly declare myself ready to surrender.”

When, by mentioning the purchase of the field together with the taking of the wife, he foretold that the purchaser would acquire both, he signified that the possession of the people is nothing other than the Church’s union in spiritual marriage with Christ. Christ raised up the ancient name of the sons of God, which the saints had possessed from the beginning, as we read in Genesis: “The sons of God saw the daughters of men, that they were beautiful” (Gen. 6); and Luke wrote that Adam was the son of God (Luke 6). Christ raised this up in the Church of the Gentiles through his grace.

Hence we read in the Gospel of John: “As many as received him, he gave power to become sons of God, to those who believe in his name, who were born not from bloods, [Col. 1217C] nor from the will of the flesh, nor from the will of man, but from God” (John 1). The Decalogue of the Law, although it had many proselytes under it, could in no way raise up this name among the nations. But after the fullness of time came, when the ordinance of almighty God had decreed that the Law should die—that is, come to an end—so that he might come who had given the blessing before the Law, he truly brought about the fulfillment of what had previously been said: “In the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ there they shall be called sons of the living God” (Hos. 1).

If, however, you refer these words to John, the Lord’s forerunner, you will find him yielding to Christ by right of kinship, since he is proved to have spoken similar words in the Gospel. For the historical kinsman said to Boaz: “I yield my right of kinship; for I must not destroy the posterity of my family. Use my privilege, which I willingly declare myself ready to surrender.” [Col. 1217D] And John, when the crowds questioned him about his baptism, replied: “I baptize with water; but one stands among you whom you do not know. He is the one who is to come after me, who was made before me, whose sandal strap I am not worthy to loosen” (John 1).

And elsewhere, when John’s disciples disputed with the Jews about purification, he said: “A man cannot receive anything unless it has been given to him from heaven. You yourselves bear me witness that I said, ‘I am not the Christ, but I have been sent before him.’ He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices with joy because of the bridegroom’s voice. Therefore this joy of mine is fulfilled. [Col. 1218A] He must increase, but I must decrease. He who comes from above is above all. He who is from the earth is earthly and speaks of the earth” (John 3).

John therefore yielded to Christ because he in no way claimed for himself the privilege of his dignity. The Old Law likewise yields to the Gospel because by its own effort it could in no way bring about the salvation of the Gentiles. For, as Paul testifies, “the Law entered so that transgression might abound; but where transgression abounded, grace abounded even more” (Rom. 5). There is indeed a rejection of the preceding commandment because of its weakness and uselessness: “For the Law brought nothing to perfection” (Heb. 7). But the introduction of a better hope, through which we draw near to God, has been bestowed on us through the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ.

[Col. 1218B] For this was formerly the custom in Israel among kinsmen: whenever one yielded his right to another, so that the transfer might be firm, the man removed his sandal and gave it to his kinsman. This was the testimony of surrender in Israel. The kinsman therefore said to Boaz: “Take off your sandal,” and he immediately removed it from his foot.

What can we understand by the sandal here except the covering of mysteries? The Law therefore removed the sandal from its foot and gave it to Christ, because it could not, through its teachers, bring the covering of the sacraments to the people’s understanding by advancing through the letter. But it bestowed this honor upon our Redeemer, because this grace was to be hoped for and attained by all the nations from him and no other.

John therefore did not claim the sandal for himself but for Christ [Col. 1218C], because he understood that the most noble bride belonged not to him but to Christ. Hence he declared himself unworthy to loosen Christ’s sandal. Finally, because people supposed John to be the Christ—a supposition that John himself denied—he rightly declared himself unworthy to loosen the strap of Christ’s sandal, as though he openly said: “I cannot uncover the Redeemer’s footprints, because I, undeserving, do not appropriate the name of bridegroom.”

This may nevertheless be understood in another way. For who does not know that sandals are made from dead animals? When the Lord came in the flesh, he appeared, as it were, shod: in his divinity he assumed the dead matter of our corruption. Hence through the Prophet he also says: “Upon Edom I will stretch out my sandal [Col. 1218D]” (Ps. 69). Edom signifies the Gentiles, while the sandal signifies the mortality that was assumed. The Lord therefore declares that he will extend his sandal over Edom because, when he made himself known to the Gentiles through the flesh, his divinity came to us as though shod.

But the human eye is not sufficient to penetrate the mystery of this incarnation. It cannot in any way investigate how the Word became embodied, how the supreme and life-giving Spirit was animated within the mother’s womb, or how he who has no beginning exists and is conceived. The sandal strap, therefore, is the binding of the mystery. John cannot loosen the strap of his sandal because even he, who recognized the incarnation through the spirit of prophecy, is not sufficient to investigate its mystery.

What, then, does it mean to say, [Col. 1219A] “I am not worthy to loosen the strap of his sandal,” except openly and humbly to confess his ignorance? It is as though he plainly said: “What wonder if the one has been brought forth before me whom I consider to have been born after me, yet whose birth’s mystery I do not comprehend?”

## CHAPTER XIV. How Boaz confirmed Ruth’s marriage before the witnesses, and how all of them prayed for their prosperity.

**(The same passage.)** But he said to the elders and to all the people: “You are witnesses today that I have acquired everything that belonged to Elimelech and Cheleon and Mahalon from Naomi, and that I have taken Ruth the Moabite, the wife of Naalon, in marriage, in order to raise up the name of the deceased in his inheritance, so that his name may not be erased from his family, his brothers, and [Col. 1219B] his people. You, I say, are witnesses of this matter.”

All the people who were at the gate and the elders replied: “We are witnesses.”

Boaz calls witnesses to the wife of the deceased, lawfully acquired by him, and to the property of Chelion and Mahalon, handed over by Naomi. This signifies that Christ has sufficient testimony from both Testaments: the people of the Gentiles, whom the completed Decalogue could not lead to the production of spiritual offspring, he himself made fertile by the seed of the Word and made the mother of spiritual progeny. He possesses everything that the earlier and later saints have had in the possession of virtues, because whatever true dignity and honor has existed anywhere or at any time belongs to his glory and generosity.

The blessing of the ten elders shows [Col. 1219C] that all nations are to be saved and blessed in the name of Jesus. For among the Greeks, *iota* signifies ten; as the first letter of the Lord Jesus’ name, it indicates the number ten. This fact, as we have said, demonstrates that all nations are to be saved and blessed through him.

Therefore let no one hesitate to believe these things as they have been stated, since he sees that everything was anticipated from the beginning by preceding figures, manifested and fulfilled through the Lord’s coming, and that what remains is likewise to be accomplished in this way. All the voices and figures of the Holy Scriptures harmonize in truth, and those things have been fulfilled that he promised through his Son Jesus Christ, our Lord, King, and Savior.

May the Lord make this woman who enters [Col. 1219D] your house like Rachel and Leah, who built up the house of Israel, so that she may be an example of virtue in Ephratha and have a celebrated name in Bethlehem.

All the people of the saints pray for the prosperity of the Church of the Gentiles, so that she may fully receive the same grace of fruitfulness that the first parents of the Israelite race possessed. Since this birth is spiritual, let us explain what these women mentioned above signify mystically.

Although Jacob’s two free wives are thought to pertain to the New Testament, because we have been called in freedom, they are not two without reason. It is because two lives are proclaimed to us in the body of Christ: one temporal, in which we labor, and the other eternal, in which we shall contemplate the love of [Col. 1220A] God.

Leah is interpreted as “laboring”; Rachel as “vision,” “beginning,” or “word.” The activity of this life, in which we live by faith, is laborious in its works and uncertain as to the outcome by which it will reach the benefit of those whom we wish to help. This is Leah, Jacob’s first wife; and for this reason she is also said to have had weak eyes, for “the thoughts of mortals are timid, and our plans are uncertain” (Wis. 9).

The hope of the eternal contemplation of God, possessing certain understanding of the truth, is Rachel. Hence she is also said to have had a beautiful face and attractive appearance (Gen. 29). Every devout and diligent person loves her, and for her sake serves the grace of God, by which our sins, even if they were like scarlet, will be made white as snow (Isa. 1).

[Col. 1220B] “May your house also be like the house of Perez, whom Tamar bore to Judah from the offspring that the Lord will give you through this young woman.”

It is appropriate that, in the blessing of Boaz and Ruth, the birth of Perez from Tamar should be recalled, because he represented the people of the Gentiles in that he emerged before his brother Zerah at birth (Gen. 38). Zerah first put out his hand, on which the midwife tied a scarlet thread; but when he drew his hand back inside, the one born afterward, who is called Perez, extended his hand and came forth by being born.

Figuratively this showed that Israel first put out its hand toward the works of the Law, and contracted it stained with the blood of the prophets and of the Savior himself. Afterwards the people of the Gentiles burst forth, so that “the last shall be first, and the first shall be [Col. 1220C] last” (Matt. 20).

The very name Tamar also suits the same mystery, for Tamar is interpreted as “changing” or “bitterness.” Thus, changing her dress, she also changes her name: she who had previously been ugly and bitter in idolatry now becomes sweet in repentance. But if the name of bitterness remains in her in every respect, it is not the bitterness in which she offered gall to the Lord, but that in which Peter wept bitterly. Judah in Latin means “confession”; therefore bitterness must be mingled with confession, so that true repentance may be signified.

By this repentance the Church, established among all the nations, is made fruitful. “For it was necessary for Christ to suffer and to rise on the third day, and for repentance and forgiveness of sins to be preached in his name throughout all the nations, beginning from [Col. 1220D] Jerusalem” (Luke 24).

The very dress of a prostitute is also a confession of sins. Tamar bears the type of the Church called from the Gentiles (Gen. 38), sitting in this dress at the gate of Evam, or Enahin, which is interpreted as “fountains.” For, like a deer running to springs of water, she ran to reach the seed of Abraham.

Our Tamar conceives without the mystical Judah knowing it, because concerning her it was foretold: “The people whom I did not know shall serve me” (Ps. 18). She received secretly a ring, a necklace, and a staff, because she is signified by calling, adorned by justification, and exalted by glorification. “Those whom he predestined, he also called; those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified” (Rom. 8). [Col. 1221A] But these things, as I have said, are still hidden, where the holy conception of fruitfulness also takes place.

## CHAPTER XV. How Ruth bore Boaz a son named Obed, and how Naomi placed him in her lap and served as his nurse and bearer.

**(The same passage.)** Boaz therefore took Ruth, received her as his wife, and went in to her; and the Lord granted her conception, and she bore a son.

After the Church had been joined to Christ through the faith of the Gentiles, the Holy Spirit bestowed grace upon her and made her the mother of spiritual offspring, so that she who had previously been barren and despised might afterward become the mother of many children. Concerning her the prophetess Hannah says: “The barren woman has borne many, and she who had many children has [Col. 1221B] grown weak” (1 Sam. 2).

Accordingly it follows: “The women said to Naomi: Blessed be the Lord, who has not allowed a successor to fail from your family, so that his name might be called in Israel; and may you have one who comforts your soul and nourishes your old age.”

For the mother Church, whom Christ has made fruitful by the gift of his Spirit, is always abundant and rich in spiritual offspring. When some depart from this age and migrate to perpetual light, others immediately succeed them in their place, so that the Christian name may remain perpetually throughout the world and that this most holy mother may receive consolation in her old age from a new offspring, when she sees her race expand and grow day by day and in no way wither (Ps. 70). [Col. 1221C]

This judgment may also be transferred to the fathers of the Old Testament who were under the Synagogue. As the patriarchs and prophets departed, apostles and evangelists succeeded them. Thus it came about that the city of God, Jerusalem, was never deprived of divine favor, but was always full, praising and rejoicing.

Hence the Psalmist, speaking to the king and to the king’s son, says: “Instead of your fathers, sons have been born to you; you will appoint them rulers over all the earth. They will remember your name, Lord, throughout every generation and progeny” (Ps. 44).

It follows:

“For the son of your daughter-in-law, who loves you, has been born to you; he is much better for you than if you had seven sons.”

The daughter-in-law of the Synagogue is the Church gathered from the Gentiles, who married Christ, the Son of God born from the Jewish people. [Col. 1221D] The women—that is, the individual souls of the saints—say to the spiritual Naomi, who is the Synagogue, that the son born from her daughter-in-law, namely the Christian people born from the mother Church, is better for her than seven sons. These seven sons signify the multitude of people who were instructed and born through the teaching of the Law in the times of the Old Testament. Concerning them it is written that they were always turned away in their hearts toward Egypt; that they provoked God when they went up to the Red Sea; that they considered the desirable land worthless; that they did not believe his words; that they murmured in their tents; that they did not heed the voice of the Lord; and that they sacrificed their sons and daughters to demons and poured out innocent blood—the blood of their sons and daughters, [Col. 1222A] whom they sacrificed to the carved images of Canaan.

Finally, after carrying out the slaughter of the servants, they killed the heir himself, casting him outside the city, and killed his orphans (Matt. 21)—namely, the apostles—saying: “The Lord will not see, nor will the God of Jacob understand” (Ps. 94).

Naomi received the child, placed him in her lap, and served as his nurse and bearer. The intelligible Naomi, therefore, carried the child whom she had not been worthy to beget through the Law, having received him through the mystery of prophecy and bearing him hidden beneath the veil of the letter and in the figure of signs. In a certain sense she served as nurse and bearer, though she was not worthy to be honored with the privilege of a mother.

The neighboring women congratulated her and said: “A son has been born to Naomi,” and they called his name Obed.

[Col. 1222B] Here we may understand the neighboring women as those who congratulated the woman in the Gospel when she found the drachma she had lost (Luke 15)—namely, the heavenly powers, who are as near to supreme Wisdom as they approach it through the grace of continuous vision.

The angelic virtues and powers therefore rejoice at the spiritual birth of the Church and call his name Obed, which is interpreted as “serving,” since they desire that he should fight and serve with them in the camp of the heavenly King. Hence in the Apocalypse the angel, fearing to receive from a human being the worship owed to God, prevented John, who wished to worship him, saying: “See that you do not do this. I am your fellow servant and the fellow servant of your brothers the prophets [Col. 1222C] and of those who keep the words of this book. Worship God” (Rev. 19 and 22).

What does it mean that before the Redeemer’s coming angels were worshiped by human beings and remained silent, but afterward refused to be worshiped, except that, after they saw our nature—which they had previously despised—assumed above them, they feared to see it subjected to them? They no longer dared to despise as weak beneath them the nature which they venerate above them, namely in the King of heaven; nor do they disdain to have as their companion the human being whom they worship as God above them.

What is added concerning Obed, that he was the father of Jesse, the father of David, demonstrates the lineage of spiritual generation. Obed, as we have said, is interpreted as “serving”; Jesse as “sacrifice of the island” or “incense”; and David as “strong of hand” [Col. 1222D] or “desirable.”

Whoever serves God vigorously offers him an acceptable sacrifice and incense of the sweetest fragrance through works of virtue and devotion to prayer. Thus strengthened by faith and devotion, he will be desirable and exceedingly pleasing to God.

Hence the angel who appeared in a vision to the centurion Cornelius declared that his continual prayers and frequent almsgiving were acceptable to God (Acts 10). For this reason Wisdom also says: “Enclose almsgiving in the heart of the poor, and it will intercede for you against every evil; it will fight on your behalf against your enemy, as though upon the shield of the mighty and the spear” (Ecclus. 29). “No evils will meet the one who fears the Lord, but in temptation God will preserve him and deliver him from every evil” (Ecclus. 33).

## CHAPTER XVI.

[Col. 1223A]

Recapitulation of Boaz’s genealogy, from Perez, the son of Judah, to David, the son of Jesse.

**(The same passage.)** These are the generations of Perez: Perez begot Hezron; Hezron begot Aram; Aram begot Amminadab; Amminadab begot Nahshon; Nahshon begot Salmon; Salmon begot Boaz; Boaz begot Obed; Obed begot Jesse; Jesse begot David.

Prudent reader, note that there are ten generations from Perez, the son of Judah, the son of Jacob, to David. You will recognize that the entire intention of the Law points toward our Redeemer, who was born from the seed of David, so that it might proclaim his saving coming to the world and reveal that the fullness and perfection of the whole Law reside in [Col. 1224A] him: “For Christ is the end of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. 10).

Before the Law was given, therefore, the patriarch Jacob testified in Judah’s blessing concerning the incarnation of the Mediator between God and human beings, saying: “The scepter shall not be taken from Judah, nor the ruler from his thighs, until he comes who is to be sent; and he shall be the expectation of the nations” (Gen. 49).

Concerning David, who was the tenth born from the seed of Judah, Scripture likewise says: “The Lord swore truth to David, and he will not frustrate him: ‘From the fruit of your womb I will place one upon my throne’” (Ps. 131).

Thus it will be evident to you that the oracles of all the patriarchs and prophets pertain to the dispensation of the Lord, our Savior and Redeemer Jesus Christ.

**1057 CHAP. VI.**—Concerning how Joshua captured all the kings of Canaan and their cities in battle, except the Hivite who dwelt in Gibeon.

**1060 CHAP. VII.**—Concerning how Joshua took all the land, as the Lord had spoken to Moses, and gave it as a possession to the children of Israel according to their portions and tribes; and the land rested from the wars.

**1061 CHAP. VIII.**—The number of cities that Joshua captured and gave to the children of Israel as a possession.

**1063 BOOK THREE**

**1063 CHAPTER ONE.**—Concerning Joshua’s old age and the Lord’s speech to him.

**1066 CHAP. II.**—Concerning the division of the land among each of the tribes of Israel, and that he gave no possession to the tribe of Levi; rather, the sacrifices and offerings of the Lord God of Israel were their inheritance.

**1069 CHAP. III.**—Concerning how the nine and a half tribes received their lots through Eleazar the priest and Joshua son of Nun, while the two and a half tribes received their portions through Moses beyond the Jordan.

**1070 CHAP. IV.**—Caleb’s address to Joshua concerning the land of Hebron, which he requested to be given to him.

**1072 CHAP. V.**—Concerning the lot of the children of Judah; and that Caleb destroyed from Hebron the three sons of Anak: Sesai, Ahiman, and Tholmai.

**1075 CHAP. VI.**—Concerning Caleb’s declaration: “Whoever strikes Kiriath-sepher and captures it, I will give him my daughter Achsah as a wife.” Othniel son of Kenaz, Caleb’s younger brother, captured it. And concerning how Achsah, Caleb’s daughter, asked her father to give her watered land.

**1077 CHAP. VII.**—That the children of Judah could not destroy the Jebusite who inhabited Jerusalem, and he dwelt with them; and that the children of Ephraim did not kill the Canaanite who lived in Gezer.

**1081 CHAP. VIII.**—The speeches of the children of Joseph to Joshua, and his response to them.

**1083 CHAP. IX.**—Concerning how Joshua sent messengers to measure the land of Canaan and describe it according to the number of each population; he divided it into seven parts and gave it to the children of Israel as a possession, to each according to his lot.

**1088 CHAP. X.**—Concerning how the children of Israel gave Joshua son of Nun a possession in their midst, according to the Lord’s command.

**1090 CHAP. XI.**—Concerning the cities of refuge, which were established for the protection of those who had struck and killed a person unknowingly and unintentionally.

**1092 CHAP. XII.**—Concerning the children of Levi, who asked Eleazar the priest and Joshua son of Nun for cities in which to dwell, and their suburbs for the support of their animals.

**1095 CHAP. XIII.**—Concerning how all the land of Canaan was given by the Lord to Israel as a possession, and they possessed it in peace.

**1098 CHAP. XIV.**—Concerning how Joshua dismissed the Reubenites, the Gadites, and half the tribe of Manasseh in peace to their possessions.

**1100 CHAP. XV.**—Joshua’s speeches to the people, and a commemoration of the Lord’s commands and his benefits, which he bestowed upon them in great abundance.

**1103 CHAP. XVI.**—Concerning how Joshua made a covenant before the Lord at Shechem, wrote all the words of the covenant in the scroll of the law of God, and placed it upon a great stone beneath the oak that was in the Lord’s sanctuary.

**1105 CHAP. XVII.**—Concerning Joshua’s death and burial, and the death and burial of Eleazar; and also concerning Joseph’s bones, which were brought out of Egypt and buried at Shechem, in the portion of the field that Jacob had bought from the sons of Emor, the father of Shechem, for one hundred young sheep.

[Col. 1234]

**1107 COMMENTARIES ON THE BOOK OF JUDGES AND RUTH**

**1107 Letter of Bishop Humbert to Rabanus**

**1109 Preface dictated for Bishop Humbert**

**1111 Here begin the Commentaries on the Book of Judges**

**1111 BOOK ONE**

**1111 CHAPTER ONE.**—Concerning how, after Joshua’s death, the children of Israel consulted the Lord about which of them should become their leader against the Canaanites. And concerning the killing of Adoni-bezek, and the attack on the Canaanites and the city of Jerusalem.

**1113 CHAP. II.**—Concerning how Caleb promised his daughter in marriage to the man who would strike Kiriath-sepher. And that Achsah, Caleb’s daughter, asked her father to give her watered land.

**1114 CHAP. III.**—That the descendants of the Kenite, Moses’ relative, went down from the City of Palms with the children of Judah and dwelt with them; and that Judah occupied the hill country but could not destroy the inhabitants of the valley.

**1115 CHAP. IV.**—That the children of Benjamin could not destroy the Jebusite in Jerusalem, nor did Manasseh destroy the Canaanite in the cities of its allotted territory; rather, they dwelt with them. But after Israel grew strong, it made them tributaries and did not wish to destroy them.

**1117 CHAP. V.**—That the angel of the Lord went up from Gilgal to the place of weeping and rebuked Israel for its sins and negligence.

**1118 CHAP. VI.**—That Joshua dismissed the people to go to their possessions, and they served the Lord throughout all his days and those of the elders who lived long after him.

**1120 CHAP. VII.**—Joshua son of Nun, the servant of the Lord, died at the age of one hundred, and that entire generation was gathered to its ancestors. The children of Israel did evil in the sight of the Lord, served the Baals, and abandoned the Lord, the God of their ancestors.

**1123 CHAP. VIII.**—That, angered against Israel, the Lord delivered them into the hands of plunderers; but when they repented, he raised up judges again to free them from the hands of their devastators.

**1125 CHAP. IX.**—Concerning how, angered by the evil deeds of the Israelites, the Lord delivered them into the hand of Chushan-rishathaim, king of Mesopotamia, and they served him for eight years. But when they again cried out to the Lord, he raised up a savior for them and delivered them through Othniel, son of Kenaz, Caleb’s younger brother.

**1128 CHAP. X.**—Concerning how the Lord delivered sinful Israel into the hand of Eglon, king of Moab, but again mercifully freed them through Ehud son of Gera, who was ambidextrous and killed Eglon.

**1131 CHAP. XI.**—Concerning Shamgar son of Anath, who struck six hundred men of the Philistines with a plowshare and defended Israel.

**1134 CHAP. XII.**—Concerning Deborah and Barak, who struck down Jabin, king of the Canaanites, and Sisera, his commander.

**1137 CHAP. XIII.**—Concerning the mystical song that Deborah and Barak son of Abinoam sang to the Lord after the victory.

**1152 CHAP. XIV.**—That, because of their sins, the children of Israel were delivered into the hands of Midian for seven years and were severely oppressed.

**1155 BOOK TWO**

**1155 CHAPTER ONE.**—That, when Israel was humbled and cried out to him, the Lord sent a prophet to remind them of God’s past benefits.

**1155 CHAP. II.**—Concerning how the angel of the Lord came to Gideon as he was beating grain with a rod on the threshing floor, commanding him to free Israel from the hands of its enemies; and concerning the burnt offering that Gideon offered to God through the ministry of the angel sent to him.

**1159 CHAP. III.**—That the spirit of the Lord clothed Gideon; blowing a trumpet, he summoned the house of Abiezer to follow him; and concerning the sign of the fleece that Gideon likewise requested from the Lord.

**1160 CHAP. IV.**—The Lord’s speech to Gideon, commanding him to send away the multitude of the people. There he dismissed twenty-two thousand men, and only ten thousand remained with him.

**1160 CHAP. V.**—Concerning the testing of the people at the waters, where only three hundred of the ten thousand remained for battle; he armed them with trumpets, lamps, and jars.

**1165 CHAP. VI.**—The Lord’s command to Gideon to go down to the camp of the Midianites. There, hearing someone recount a dream, he was encouraged, and through three hundred men he routed the camp of Midian.

**1166 CHAP. VII.**—That Gideon sent messengers throughout all the hill country of Ephraim, commanding them to go down to meet Midian and seize the waters.

**1167 CHAP. VIII.**—Concerning how Gideon captured Zebah and Zalmunna, the leaders of Midian, and, together with them, crushed and ground to pieces the men of Succoth who had insulted him, using thorns and thistles.

[Col. 1235]

**1168 CHAP. IX.**—Where the Israelites, asking Gideon and his sons to rule over them, gave him the golden earrings that they had taken as spoil from the Midianites. From these Gideon made an ephod and placed it in his city, Ophrah; and it became a ruin to his household.

**1170 CHAP. X.**—That the land rested for forty years, during which Gideon ruled, and that Gideon had seventy sons from his wives, but from his concubine he had only Abimelech.

**1171 CHAP. XI.**—That Abimelech killed all his brothers except Jotham alone, the youngest son of Jerubbaal, who, having hidden, alone escaped death; and concerning the parable of that same Jotham, delivered to the men of Shechem.

**1173 CHAP. XII.**—That after Gideon’s death the children of Israel turned away and committed fornication with the Baals. The Lord sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the inhabitants of Shechem, who began to detest him and the crime of the killing of the seventy sons of Jerubbaal.

**1174 CHAP. XIII.**—That Gaal son of Obed, seeking to turn the Shechemites away from Abimelech, was killed by him; and that Abimelech killed the men of the tower of Shechem with smoke and fire, after cutting down branches and boughs from the trees. And concerning Abimelech’s death.

**1175 CHAP. XIV.**—That after Abimelech, Tola son of Puah, Abimelech’s paternal uncle, arose in Israel; after twenty-three years he was succeeded by Jair the Gileadite, who judged Israel for twenty-two years.

**1177 CHAP. XV.**—That the Lord delivered sinful Israel into the hands of the Philistines and the Ammonites; but when they again turned to repentance, he sent them a defender. Jephthah, making a vow to the Lord, gained victory over the enemies.

**1190 CHAP. XVI.**—Concerning Manoah and his barren wife, to whom the angel of the Lord promised a son, Samson, a Nazirite of the Lord; and concerning the burnt offering that Manoah, instructed by the angel, offered to God.

**1193 CHAP. XVII.**—Concerning the vengeance that Samson took upon the Philistines because his bride had been taken from him.

**1193 CHAP. XVIII.**—That three thousand men of Judah wished to hand Samson over to the Philistines; when he had been handed over to them, he struck a thousand Philistine men with the jawbone of a donkey. And that at night he carried away the doors of the gate of the city of Gaza, with their posts, and carried them to the mountain.

**1194 CHAP. XIX.**—That Samson desired a prostitute in Gaza, by whom he himself was deceived through treachery.

**1197 CHAP. XX.**—That Samson, blind, was brought to a feast of the Philistines for their mockery; he shook two pillars of the building, and when the entire structure collapsed, he killed many of the enemies along with himself.

[Col. 1236]

**1199 CHAP. XXI.**—Concerning the vengeance carried out by Israel against the Benjaminites for the outrage.

**1199 HERE BEGINS THE COMMENTARY ON THE BOOK OF RUTH**

**1199 CHAPTER ONE.**—Elimelech and his wife Naomi’s journey with their two sons from Bethlehem of Judah to the land of Moab, to reside there as foreigners.

**1202 CHAP. II.**—That while they remained there for ten years, both their sons died, namely Mahlon and Chilion; and the woman was left bereaved of her two sons and her husband.

**1203 CHAP. III.**—That Naomi, departing from the place of her sojourn, decided to return with both daughters-in-law to the land of Judah, and urged her daughters-in-law to return to their native land.

**1204 CHAP. IV.**—That when Orpah turned back, Ruth remained with Naomi and reached the land of Judah.

**1205 CHAP. V.**—That it was the time of the barley harvest when Naomi returned to Bethlehem with Ruth, her daughter-in-law.

**1205 CHAP. VI.**—Concerning how Boaz, Elimelech’s kinsman, seeing Ruth gathering the ears of grain left behind by his reapers, asked who this woman was.

**1207 CHAP. VII.**—That Boaz ordered Ruth to gather ears of grain in his field without anyone troubling her, and invited her to the midday meal.

**1209 CHAP. VIII.**—Concerning how Ruth remained in his field until evening and, beating out with a rod what she had gathered, found three measures, which she carried back to her mother-in-law.

**1211 CHAP. IX.**—Naomi’s counsel to Ruth about how, by her ingenuity, she might secure a future marriage with Boaz.

**1212 CHAP. X.**—That Ruth, obeying her mother-in-law’s counsel, marked the place where Boaz was sleeping, and, coming up, threw herself down beside his feet.

**1215 CHAP. XI.**—Ruth’s return to her mother-in-law. She brought six measures of barley and related to her mother-in-law everything that had happened.

**1216 CHAP. XII.**—Concerning Boaz’s going up to the city gate and his conversation with his kinsman about taking Ruth, in order to raise up the offspring of his deceased kinsman.

**1217 CHAP. XIII.**—That, unwilling to do so, the man removed his sandal from his foot before his witnesses and handed it over to Boaz.

**1219 CHAP. XIV.**—That Boaz confirmed his marriage to Ruth before the witnesses, and that they all prayed for their prosperity.

**1221 CHAP. XV.**—Concerning how Ruth bore Boaz a son named Obed; Naomi took him into her lap and acted as his nurse and caregiver.

**1223 CHAP. XVI.**—A recapitulation of Boaz’s genealogy, from Perez son of Judah to David son of Jesse.

**END OF THE ONE HUNDRED EIGHTH VOLUME.**
